# Anatomy — A Narrated Question and Answer Bank

This is a bank of eleven thousand six hundred anatomy questions, written to be answered out loud. It is not a textbook read aloud. Every item follows the same three steps: the question, spoken with its options inside the sentence when it has options; then the words "The answer is" and the correct answer; then two to four sentences saying why that answer is right and, where it helps, why the tempting wrong answer is wrong. The answer always follows its question immediately, so nothing has to be held in mind and no answer key has to be waited for.

It is made for revision by ear: walking, driving, or between patients. Nothing can be re-read, no option can be scanned, and no diagram can be consulted, so the bank contains no figures and no image references. The one hundred and sixteen chapters follow twenty categories in order, beginning with anatomical terminology and the body cavities, then the skeleton, the joints and the muscles, then the heart and the vessels, the lymphatic system, and the nervous system, then the respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive and endocrine systems and the special senses. Regional and surface anatomy follow, then cross-sectional and imaging anatomy, embryology, anatomical relationships, and the clinical anatomy that connects a structure to the examination that finds it. The last category integrates everything: structure to function, structure to injury, structure to symptoms, and structure to the clinical examination.

The questions are of nine kinds. Three thousand four hundred and eighty are multiple choice, two thousand three hundred and twenty ask for a structure by name, one thousand seven hundred and forty describe what a radiograph or a section would show, one thousand one hundred and sixty turn on the relations between structures, one thousand one hundred and sixty are clinical anatomy, five hundred and eighty are true or false, five hundred and eighty are matching, three hundred and forty-eight are short answer, and two hundred and thirty-two test three-dimensional reasoning. They range from first-year recall to expert questions whose wrong answers are all defensible until the final step.

The image-based questions of the source blueprint have been rewritten as descriptions, because a voice cannot show a radiograph. Each one describes what the film, the section or the specimen would show and asks which structure or which interpretation fits. A note on the count: the blueprint this bank was built from is titled as a ten-thousand-question bank, but its category table asks for eleven thousand six hundred questions and its subsections were followed as written. Where one category's subsections added up to more than its own heading allowed, they were scaled back proportionally to that heading, so the total stands exactly as the category table gives it.

Every item is anatomically correct, including the wrong options, which are wrong for the stated reason rather than merely unlikely. Where a structure has a common variant, the variant is named as a variant and not taught as the rule. Clinical items are constructed illustrations, never real patients, and they are described as illustrations. The bank gives no drug, no dose, no route and no treatment: where a clinical correlation touches management, it names the structure involved and leaves the management to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

This is educational material. It does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher, and it is no substitute for examining a real body or a real patient. Used as a companion to proper teaching, it is a way to keep anatomy alive in the ear, one question at a time.

# Chapter 1 — Anatomical Terminology

Every conversation about the body depends on a shared set of words for where things are, and this chapter builds that vocabulary from the ground up. It covers the anatomical position, the directional terms that describe one structure relative to another, the planes in which the body can be cut, the axes about which its parts move, and the named regions of its surface. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The terms defined here belong to the body as a whole, and later chapters use them to describe particular bones, muscles, vessels, and nerves. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1. In a body standing in the anatomical position, which bone of the leg lies on the lateral side? The answer is the fibula. The tibia lies medially and carries the weight of the body. The fibula lies on the outer side and bears almost none of it, serving mainly as a place for muscles to attach.

Question 2. In the anatomical position, which way do the palms face: forward, backward, downward, or toward each other? The answer is forward. With the palms forward the thumb points away from the midline. A hand with the palm turned backward is not in the anatomical position.

Question 3. A prepared specimen shows a body standing upright with both palms rotated to face the back. Which way does the radius lie in that specimen? The answer is that the radius crosses over the ulna. That rotation is pronation, and it carries the lower end of the radius across the ulna. In the anatomical position the two bones lie parallel instead.

Question 4. In a body standing in the anatomical position, which forearm bone lies medial to the other? The answer is the ulna. The ulna lies on the little finger side of the forearm and the radius on the thumb side. When the palm turns to face the back, the two bones change places.

Question 5. Which statement about the feet in the anatomical position is correct: the soles are flat and the feet are together, the right foot is in front, the toes point outward, or the heels are raised? The answer is that the soles are flat and the feet are together. Turning the toes outward is a natural stance but not the reference position.

Question 6. What is the name of the position in which a person lies face upward with the limbs extended? The answer is the supine position. The belly and the front of the body face the ceiling, and the back rests against the surface. A person lying face downward is described as prone.

Question 7. A constructed illustration: a patient is brought in lying face upward, and the team must describe a wound on the front of the right thigh. Which posture supplies the words for that description? The answer is the anatomical position. The wound is described as anterior and on the right side, whatever the position of the bed.

Question 8. True or false: in the anatomical position the thumbs point toward the midline of the body. The answer is false. The palms face forward, so each thumb points away from the midline and each little finger points toward it. When the palm faces the body instead, the thumb turns inward.

Question 9. Which of these words means toward the head: superior, inferior, anterior, or posterior? The answer is superior. Superior means nearer the head end of the body and inferior means nearer the feet. Anterior means toward the front and posterior means toward the back.

Question 10. A described radiograph shows one hip in profile, with the outer surface of the joint nearest the film. Which directional word names that surface? The answer is lateral. Lateral means farther from the midline, and the inner surface nearer the midline is the medial surface.

Question 11. In a head viewed from the side, does the tip of the nose lie anterior or posterior to the external ear? The answer is anterior. The nose lies in the midline of the face, while the ear lies further back on the side of the head. The word anterior places the nose toward the front.

Question 12. Which gland lies immediately anterior to the upper part of the trachea in the neck? The answer is the thyroid gland. It wraps around the front and the sides of the airway just below the larynx. The trachea therefore lies posterior to it.

Question 13. In the head, which of these terms means toward the forehead: caudal, rostral, dorsal, or ventral? The answer is rostral. It is used in the head and the neck, where the long axis of the body bends forward. Caudal and dorsal mean toward the tail and the back, and ventral means toward the belly.

Question 14. A described dissection shows a broad muscle rising from the lower spine, crossing the inferior angle of the scapula, and twisting into a flat tendon at the front of the arm. Which muscle is it? The answer is the latissimus dorsi. It pulls the arm downward and backward and forms the posterior fold of the armpit.

Question 15. A constructed illustration: a wound on the side of the neck lies lateral to the midline and superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which large vein lies in that described zone? The answer is the external jugular vein. It runs down the surface of the neck over that muscle. The internal jugular vein lies deeper, so the muscle separates the two.

Question 16. Which statement about the words cranial and cephalic is correct: both point toward the head, both point toward the feet, both mean toward the back, or both mean toward the midline? The answer is that both point toward the head. Cranial is usually reserved for structures inside the skull, while superior stays the general term.

Question 17. Which of these pairs belongs together: superior with toward the feet, inferior with toward the head, anterior with toward the back, or lateral with away from the midline? The answer is lateral with away from the midline. A structure farther from the median plane is lateral, and one nearer it is medial.

Question 18. True or false: the word superior always means higher from the floor, whatever the body is doing. The answer is false. Superior means nearer the head end of the body, which is a fact about the body rather than the room. In a person lying face upward, the nose is superior to the umbilicus.

Question 19. Which organ lies immediately inferior to the diaphragm on the right side of the abdomen? The answer is the liver. The right dome of the diaphragm arches over the upper surface of the liver. On the left side the organs below the diaphragm are the stomach and the spleen.

Question 20. Which of these structures lies highest in the abdomen: the urinary bladder, the stomach, the rectum, or the sigmoid colon? The answer is the stomach. It lies in the upper part of the abdomen, just below the diaphragm. The bladder and the rectum lie in the pelvis, the lowest part of the trunk.

Question 21. A constructed illustration: pain that began around the navel later moves lower and to the right. Where has the pain moved, in the language of direction? The answer is inferior and lateral to the umbilical region. Such a shift is described with the words superior and inferior and with medial and lateral.

Question 22. Which two small glands sit immediately superior to the kidneys, one on each side, capping their upper poles? The answer is the adrenal glands. They lie in the fatty tissue around the kidney and are held there by the same layer of fascia. They move with the kidney when it descends.

Question 23. A described specimen shows the lower spine, with separate vertebrae above a fused triangular mass of bone. Which vertebra is the lowest separate one, and where does it lie? The answer is the fifth lumbar vertebra, immediately superior to the sacrum. Their junction is the lumbosacral joint, where the spine changes direction.

Question 24. Which of these is inferior in the normal standing body: the kidneys, the diaphragm, the lungs, or the bladder? The answer is the bladder. It lies in the pelvis, below the level of the other three. The kidneys and the diaphragm lie in the upper abdomen and the lungs fill the chest.

Question 25. Which structure sits immediately above the upper pole of the right kidney, and which organ rests against that same pole? The answer is the right adrenal gland, with the liver against the pole. The right kidney lies lower than the left because the liver occupies the space above it.

Question 26. Which statement holds for a person lying on the back: the nose is superior to the umbilicus, the sternum is inferior to it, the chin is inferior to the navel, or the knee is superior to the hip? The answer is that the nose is superior to the umbilicus. Superior and inferior follow the long axis of the body, not gravity.

Question 27. A described frontal radiograph of the chest shows the heart as a shadow in the middle, with the ribs crossing it and the spine faintly behind. Which surface of the heart lies closest to the film? The answer is the anterior surface. In that view the beam passes from the back to the front, so the film lies against the anterior chest.

Question 28. Which bony structures form the posterior wall of the thoracic cavity and lie behind the heart and the esophagus? The answer is the thoracic vertebrae. Twelve of them lie one above another in the midline of the back, each carrying a pair of ribs. Their bodies and the discs between them protect the spinal cord.

Question 29. Which of these structures lies directly anterior to the trachea in the upper chest: the esophagus, the arch of the aorta, the vertebral column, or the thyroid gland? The answer is the arch of the aorta. It crosses in front of the windpipe before turning backward. The esophagus lies behind the trachea.

Question 30. Immediately posterior to the body of the sternum lies which structure, and which gland occupies the same space in a child? The answer is the heart, with the thymus in front of it in the child. The heart sits behind the sternum and the costal cartilages. The thymus regresses with age.

Question 31. Which large vein lies immediately posterior to the neck of the pancreas, formed where the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein? The answer is the portal vein. It is created behind the neck of the pancreas and runs upward to the liver. The pancreas therefore lies in front of it.

Question 32. A constructed illustration: a blow lands on the back over the lower ribs. Which organ lies in that described zone and is exposed to injury from behind? The answer is the kidneys, which lie against the posterior wall of the abdomen. They sit behind the peritoneum, partly protected by the eleventh and twelfth ribs.

Question 33. Which of these structures lies posterior to the kidney: the twelfth rib, the peritoneum, the pancreas, or the ascending colon? The answer is the twelfth rib. It crosses the upper part of the kidney from behind on both sides. The peritoneum and the colon lie in front of the kidney.

Question 34. True or false: in a standing person the word dorsal points to the same side of the trunk as the word posterior. The answer is true. In the embryo the dorsal surface is the back, and in the trunk of an adult the words keep that meaning. For the hand, dorsal names the back of the hand.

Question 35. Which of these statements about the word medial is correct: it means nearer the midline, nearer the side, nearer the front, or nearer the head? The answer is nearer the midline. The median plane runs down the middle of the body. A structure closer to it than another is medial to it.

Question 36. A constructed illustration: a wound on the medial side of the upper thigh bleeds heavily just below the groin. Which structure lies in that described position within the femoral triangle? The answer is the femoral vein. In the triangle the vein lies medial to the artery, which lies medial to the nerve.

Question 37. Which bone forms the medial wall of the orbit, a thin plate that separates the eye from the nasal cavity and the ethmoid air cells? The answer is the ethmoid bone. Its paper-thin orbital plate is easily broken by a blow to the eye. The maxilla and the lacrimal bone also contribute to that wall.

Question 38. At the wrist, which structure lies medial to the radial artery: the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis, the tendon of the palmaris longus, the ulnar nerve, or the median nerve? The answer is the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis. It lies just medial to the artery, where both can be felt at the pulse point.

Question 39. A described cross section of the forearm shows two bones side by side with a membrane between them. On which side does the bone with the broad lower end lie? The answer is the lateral side. That bone is the radius, whose lower end is broad, the reverse of the ulna. The interosseous membrane joins their shafts.

Question 40. In the hand held in the anatomical position, which digit lies medial to the others and which lies lateral? The answer is the little finger medially and the thumb laterally. With the palm facing forward, the thumb points away from the body and the little finger points toward it.

Question 41. Which of these structures lies immediately lateral to the sternum in the upper chest: the internal thoracic artery, the trachea, the esophagus, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the internal thoracic artery. It descends just lateral to the sternum behind the costal cartilages. The other three lie nearer the midline.

Question 42. A described dissection of the neck shows a long thin muscle running from the upper chest to the mastoid process. Which muscle is shown, and which large vein lies medial to it? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with the internal jugular vein medial to it. The vein runs in the carotid sheath.

Question 43. A constructed illustration: a deep cut crosses the front of the wrist just distal to the skin crease, and the thumb cannot be opposed. Which nerve has most likely been divided? The answer is the median nerve. It lies superficially in the middle of the wrist and supplies the muscles that oppose the thumb.

Question 44. Which single bone forms the skeleton of the arm between the shoulder joint and the elbow, and is therefore the proximal bone of the upper limb? The answer is the humerus. Its head fits into the socket of the scapula above, and its lower end joins the radius and the ulna.

Question 45. Along the large intestine, which of these parts lies proximal to the others: the descending colon, the transverse colon, the sigmoid colon, or the rectum? The answer is the transverse colon. The colon runs up as the ascending, across as the transverse, and down as the descending and sigmoid parts. Proximal means nearer the beginning of that path.

Question 46. Which part of the small intestine lies immediately distal to the duodenum, and how is that part recognized at operation? The answer is the jejunum. It begins at the duodenojejunal flexure, which is fixed high in the abdomen. The jejunum is thicker walled and more vascular than the ileum that follows it.

Question 47. Which bone forms the proximal part of the lower limb skeleton and fits into the socket of the pelvis? The answer is the femur. Its head sits in the acetabulum, and its shaft runs down to the knee. The bones distal to it are the tibia and the fibula.

Question 48. Which of these pairs belongs together: the elbow with distal, the shoulder with distal, the wrist with proximal, or the knee with proximal? The answer is the elbow with distal, because the elbow is farther from the trunk than the shoulder. The knee is distal to the hip and the wrist is distal to the elbow.

Question 49. For an internal organ, which statement is correct: proximal and distal describe distance from the mouth along the gut, they describe distance from the skin, or they mean superior and inferior? The answer is that they describe distance from the mouth along a tube such as the gut. In the limbs they measure distance from the trunk.

Question 50. Name two structures that lie distal to the knee in the lower limb, spoken as a list. The answer is the tibia and the fibula. Both begin at the knee and run down to the ankle, where they form the bony frame of the leg. The bones of the foot lie distal to them in turn.

Question 51. True or false: a structure described as superficial lies nearer the surface of the body than one described as deep. The answer is true. In the forearm the skin is superficial and the bone is deep. In the brain the gray matter is superficial to the white matter.

Question 52. Which bone lies immediately deep to the skin along the front of the shin, with almost no muscle covering it? The answer is the tibia. Its sharp anterior border is the ridge felt down the front of the leg. The muscles lie on its lateral and posterior surfaces.

Question 53. Which structure lies immediately deep to the inguinal ligament at the midpoint between the front of the hip bone and the pubic symphysis? The answer is the femoral artery. It enters the thigh there, where its pulse can be felt, and the femoral vein lies just medial to it.

Question 54. Which of these layers lies most superficial on the front of the abdomen: the skin, the deep fascia, the muscle, or the peritoneum? The answer is the skin. Deep to it lie the fatty layer, the membranous layer, and the muscles of the abdominal wall. The peritoneum is the deepest of the four.

Question 55. A described dissection shows the flat muscles of the abdominal wall separated layer by layer. Which layer lies deepest of the three, and what does it become near the midline? The answer is the transversus abdominis, whose fibers run across the abdomen, and it becomes an aponeurosis that joins the rectus sheath.

Question 56. A constructed illustration: a small puncture below the middle of the clavicle lets air collect under the skin of the chest. Which layer has the air entered? The answer is the superficial fascia, the fatty layer just beneath the skin. Air tracks along that loose layer because it offers little resistance.

Question 57. Which vein is the most superficial at the front of the elbow: the basilic, the brachial, the cephalic, or the median cubital? The answer is the median cubital vein, which crosses the front of the elbow just under the skin. The brachial vein lies deep beside the artery.

Question 58. A described dissection identifies a vein crossing the surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and a plexus of nerves emerging from beneath it. Which structures are described? The answer is the external jugular vein and the cervical plexus. The plexus emerges from beneath the posterior border of the muscle.

Question 59. Which of these pairs belongs together: ipsilateral with the opposite side, contralateral with the same side, bilateral with both sides, or unilateral with neither side? The answer is bilateral with both sides. Ipsilateral means on the same side of the body and contralateral means on the opposite side.

Question 60. What word describes two structures that lie on the same side of the body, such as the right eye and the right ear? The answer is ipsilateral. The opposite word, contralateral, describes a pair such as the left eye and the right ear.

Question 61. A lesion of one cranial nerve weakens the muscles of the face on the same side as the lesion. Which word describes the relationship between the nerve lesion and the weak muscles? The answer is ipsilateral. The nerve and the muscles it supplies lie on the same side of the face.

Question 62. A described photograph shows a person with a scar on the left cheek and a drooping left eyelid, while the right side of the face moves normally. Which word describes the relation between the scar and the weakness? The answer is ipsilateral, because both lie on the left side.

Question 63. Fibers of the corticospinal tract that begin in the left cerebral hemisphere end where in the spinal cord, and what word describes that relation? The answer is the right side, which is the contralateral side. Most fibers cross in the medulla oblongata, and a small number descend ipsilaterally.

Question 64. Light from the left half of the visual field of each eye is carried to which side of the brain: the left occipital lobe, the right occipital lobe, or neither side? The answer is the right occipital lobe. Fibers from that half of each retina end in the opposite hemisphere.

Question 65. A described illustration: a person cannot lift the right corner of the mouth. Which word describes the side of the weakness relative to the brain lesion that commonly causes it? The answer is contralateral. A lesion of the left motor cortex weakens the right side, because the fibers cross.

Question 66. A constructed illustration: glass enters the upper neck behind the angle of the jaw, and the bleeding is deep. Which vessel lies in that described position, and which word names its course through the skull? The answer is the internal carotid artery, which enters the skull through the carotid canal.

Question 67. A described section through the skull names the outer and inner surfaces of the vault as two tables. Which table lies external and which lies internal? The answer is that the outer table is external and the inner table is internal. A blow may break the thin inner table without breaking the outer one.

Question 68. Which fibrous coat forms the external covering of the kidney and can be peeled away from it? The answer is the renal capsule. It is a smooth fibrous sheath wrapped directly around the organ. Around it lie a layer of fat and the renal fascia.

Question 69. Which word describes a structure lying nearer the center of an organ or a cavity, as opposed to one lying nearer its outer boundary: internal, external, superficial, or distal? The answer is internal. Its opposite is external, which describes the outer boundary. Superficial answers a different question, that of depth from the surface.

Question 70. A described coronal section through the head shows a thick plate of bone on each side of the cranial cavity, separated by a layer of spongy bone. Which plate lies internal? The answer is the inner table, with the outer table on the outside. The spongy layer between them is the diploe.

Question 71. True or false: the external oblique muscle lies superficial to the internal oblique muscle in the abdominal wall. The answer is true. The external oblique is the outermost of the three flat muscles, and the internal oblique lies immediately deep to it. Their fibers cross at a right angle.

Question 72. Which statement about the iliac arteries is correct: the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery, the external iliac artery supplies the pelvic organs, the internal iliac artery becomes the femoral artery, or both arise from the aorta? The answer is that the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery. It leaves the pelvis under the inguinal ligament.

Question 73. Which pair belongs together: the median plane with upper and lower parts, the coronal plane with right and left parts, the transverse plane with front and back parts, or the sagittal plane with right and left parts? The answer is the sagittal plane with right and left parts. The median plane is the sagittal plane through the middle.

Question 74. What is the name of the plane that passes through the midline of the body and divides it into equal right and left halves? The answer is the median plane. Every sagittal plane runs from front to back, but only the median one divides the body into two equal halves.

Question 75. Which plane divides the body into an upper part and a lower part: the sagittal plane, the coronal plane, the transverse plane, or the median plane? The answer is the transverse plane. It runs horizontally across the body at right angles to the long axis.

Question 76. A described section of the trunk shows both kidneys at one level, with the aorta and the inferior vena cava in front of the vertebral column. In which plane was this section cut? The answer is a transverse plane. The section lies across the body, so it shows structures from both sides.

Question 77. What name is given to a plane that runs parallel to the median plane but lies to one side of it, cutting the body into unequal right and left parts? The answer is a parasagittal plane. It runs from front to back but does not pass through the middle of the body.

Question 78. The sternum, the vertebral column, and the mediastinum all lie in which plane, and what does a section in that plane divide? The answer is the median plane, which divides the body into right and left halves. All three structures lie in the midline.

Question 79. Which statement about an oblique plane is correct: it cuts the body at an angle to all three reference planes, it parallels the median plane, it divides the body into equal halves, or it is another name for a transverse plane? The answer is that it cuts all three reference planes at an angle. The pelvic inlet is a familiar example.

Question 80. A described sagittal section through the head shows the corpus callosum as a curved band of white matter above the thalamus. Which plane was used, and does the section pass through both halves of the brain? The answer is a sagittal plane lying to one side of the midline, so it shows only one hemisphere.

Question 81. A described fracture line runs diagonally across the shaft of a long bone, from the upper part of one side to the lower part of the other. In which plane does the break lie? The answer is an oblique plane. The fragments can slide past one another along the slope of the break.

Question 82. The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by the first thoracic vertebra, the first ribs, and the top of the sternum. In which kind of plane does it lie, and how is that plane directed? The answer is an oblique plane, tilted downward and forward. The first ribs slope down from the spine to the sternum.

Question 83. Which axis passes through the body from front to back, at right angles to the coronal plane: the longitudinal axis, the transverse axis, the anteroposterior axis, or the vertical axis? The answer is the anteroposterior axis. The transverse axis runs from side to side, and the longitudinal axis runs from head to foot.

Question 84. A constructed illustration: a fall forces the ankle into a twist, and the foot turns outward. About which axis does the movement occur? The answer is a longitudinal axis. Turning the toes outward is rotation of the leg and the foot around a vertical axis.

Question 85. What axis runs from side to side through a joint, and about what movements does rotation around that axis occur? The answer is the transverse axis, which carries the movements of flexion and extension. A hinge joint such as the elbow moves about a single transverse axis.

Question 86. A described series of drawings shows a forearm bending at the elbow and then straightening again, with the hand moving forward and back in a plane that splits the body into right and left halves. About which axis does the movement take place, and in which plane? The answer is a transverse axis, in the sagittal plane.

Question 87. Which movement takes place about a longitudinal axis: flexion of the elbow, rotation of the head, abduction of the shoulder, or extension of the knee? The answer is rotation of the head. Turning the face to one side swings the head around a vertical axis through the neck.

Question 88. What is the fixed relation between an axis of movement and the plane in which the movement occurs? The answer is that the axis is at right angles to the plane. A joint that flexes in the sagittal plane therefore rotates about a transverse axis.

Question 89. Which statement about the long axis of a bone is correct: it runs along the shaft from end to end, it lies parallel to the midline, it crosses the joint at right angles, or it equals the axis of movement? The answer is that it runs along the shaft from end to end. The long axis of the femur runs from hip to knee.

Question 90. Name the plane and the axis for the movement of turning the palm to face the floor while the elbow stays at the side. The answer is the transverse plane and a longitudinal axis. The forearm rotates around its own long axis. The same words describe turning the head to look over one shoulder.

Question 91. Which body region lies between the neck above and the diaphragm below, and is bounded by the ribs and the sternum? The answer is the thorax, or chest. It contains the heart, the lungs, and the great vessels, and the diaphragm forms its floor. The region below it is the abdomen.

Question 92. Which of these regions lies in the middle of the abdomen around the navel: the epigastric region, the umbilical region, the hypogastric region, or the right iliac region? The answer is the umbilical region. It is the central of the nine regions into which the abdomen is divided.

Question 93. A described photograph marks the umbilicus, a vertical line down the middle, and two horizontal lines, one at the lowest ribs and one at the hip bones. Which regions do those lines mark? The answer is the nine regions of the abdomen, three across by three down. The upper middle region is the epigastric.

Question 94. Which pair belongs together: the axilla with the armpit, the popliteal fossa with the front of the elbow, the cubital fossa with the back of the knee, or the groin with the side of the chest? The answer is the axilla with the armpit. The popliteal fossa lies behind the knee.

Question 95. Which abdominal region lies between the umbilicus above and the pubic symphysis below, in the midline? The answer is the hypogastric region, also called the pubic region. It lies between the two iliac regions. In it lie the bladder when full and, in the female, the uterus.

Question 96. Which of these regions of the upper limb lies between the shoulder and the elbow: the forearm, the arm, the cubital fossa, or the axilla? The answer is the arm. In anatomical language the arm is the segment between the shoulder and the elbow, while the forearm lies between the elbow and the wrist.

Question 97. A constructed illustration: pain in the upper middle of the abdomen radiates to the right shoulder. Which region is described, and which structure beneath it can irritate the diaphragm? The answer is the epigastric region, with the gallbladder beneath it. Irritation of the diaphragm can refer pain to the shoulder.

Question 98. Which body region lies between the elbow above and the wrist below? The answer is the forearm. Its two bones are the radius and the ulna, and the muscles that move the wrist and fingers lie in it. The region above the elbow is the arm.

Question 99. A described photograph of the back shows a midline furrow, a rounded prominence at the base of the neck, and two flat triangular bones. Which surface regions are shown, and which vertebra forms the prominence? The answer is the back, with the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra forming it.

Question 100. The perineum is described as a diamond-shaped region divided into two triangles by a line between the two ischial tuberosities. Which triangle contains the anus and which the external urinary opening? The answer is that the anal triangle lies behind the line and the urogenital triangle in front. The perineum lies below the pelvic diaphragm.

To summarize, the anatomical position is the standing reference posture with the palms facing forward and the feet together and flat, and every directional term is defined from it. Superior and inferior follow the long axis of the body rather than gravity, while anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, proximal, distal, superficial, deep, internal, external, ipsilateral and contralateral each name a position relative to another structure. The three reference planes are the sagittal plane, which divides the body into right and left parts, the coronal plane, which divides it into front and back parts, and the transverse plane, which divides it into upper and lower parts, and every movement occurs about an axis at right angles to the plane in which it is seen. The named regions of the body, from the thorax and the abdomen to the axilla, the cubital fossa, the popliteal fossa and the perineum, give a shared vocabulary for the surface. Saying a structure's position aloud, relative to a named neighbor, is what fixes these terms in memory, and later chapters rely on them. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 2 — Body Cavities and Membranes

This chapter walks through the spaces inside the body and the membranes that line them. It takes the cavities in order, from the cranial cavity inside the skull through the vertebral, thoracic, abdominal and pelvic cavities, and then treats the smaller serous spaces of the pleura, the pericardium and the peritoneum together with the two layers that form each one. The last part turns to epithelial tissue, the sheet of cells that lines every one of those spaces and covers the surfaces of the body. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 101. Which cavity is enclosed by the bones of the skull, and what does it hold? The answer is the cranial cavity, which holds the brain with its membranes and the cerebrospinal fluid around it. The vault and the base of the skull form a rigid box that protects its contents.

Question 102. The floor of the cranial cavity is divided into three fossae. Which of them lies most anteriorly: the anterior cranial fossa, the middle cranial fossa, the posterior cranial fossa, or the infratemporal fossa? The answer is the anterior cranial fossa. It lies above the orbits and the nasal cavity and holds the frontal lobes of the brain.

Question 103. A described section through the base of the skull shows a shallow shelf above the orbits, a deeper hollow behind it, and a broad basin at the back. Which fossa does the shelf represent? The answer is the anterior cranial fossa. It is the highest of the three fossae and holds the frontal lobes.

Question 104. Which fold of dura mater forms a tent over the cerebellum and separates it from the occipital lobes of the cerebrum? The answer is the tentorium cerebelli. Its free inner edge bounds the tentorial notch, through which the midbrain passes. The falx cerebri, in contrast, stands upright between the two cerebral hemispheres.

Question 105. Which sickle-shaped fold of dura mater lies in the midline between the two cerebral hemispheres? The answer is the falx cerebri. It runs in the longitudinal fissure from the roof of the skull down to the corpus callosum. Its upper edge holds the superior sagittal sinus and its lower edge the inferior sagittal sinus.

Question 106. Which of these venous channels runs in the free lower edge of the falx cerebri: the superior sagittal sinus, the inferior sagittal sinus, the straight sinus, or the transverse sinus? The answer is the inferior sagittal sinus. It joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus.

Question 107. A constructed illustration: a blow to the temple is followed by a quickly enlarging collection of arterial blood between the skull and the dura mater. Which vessel has most likely been torn? The answer is the middle meningeal artery. It runs in a groove on the inner surface of the temporal and parietal bones. Its branches lie close to the bone, so a fracture there can tear them.

Question 108. True or false: the cranial cavity communicates with the vertebral cavity through the foramen magnum. The answer is true. The foramen magnum lies in the occipital bone at the base of the skull. The medulla oblongata, its membranes and the vertebral arteries pass through it.

Question 109. Which cavity is formed by the vertebral arches behind the bodies of the vertebrae, and what runs inside it? The answer is the vertebral cavity, which holds the spinal cord, its membranes and the cerebrospinal fluid around it. It begins at the foramen magnum and runs down to the lower part of the sacrum.

Question 110. Which of these lies outside the dura mater in the vertebral canal: the spinal cord, the cerebrospinal fluid, the epidural fat and venous plexus, or the arachnoid mater? The answer is the epidural fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus. That space lies between the dura mater and the periosteum lining the canal.

Question 111. The spinal cord tapers to a cone at its lower end. What is that cone called, and at what level does it lie? The answer is the conus medullaris, which ends at about the level of the first or second lumbar vertebra. Below it the canal holds a leash of nerve roots instead of cord.

Question 112. Which band of fibrous tissue lies immediately behind the bodies of the vertebrae, separating them from the dura mater of the spinal cord? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It runs inside the vertebral canal along the back of the vertebral bodies and the discs. In front of the bodies lies the anterior longitudinal ligament.

Question 113. In the adult the spinal cord ends well above the lower end of the canal. Which statement explains that: the cord outgrows the column, the column outgrows the cord, the filum terminale pulls the cord up, or the sacrum fuses early? The answer is that the column outgrows the cord. In the embryo they begin at the same level. The lower nerve roots must then travel down to reach their openings.

Question 114. A described magnetic resonance image of the lower back shows the vertebral canal below the end of the spinal cord filled with fine strands that fan downward. What is that bundle called? The answer is the cauda equina. It consists of the lumbar and sacral nerve roots running down inside the canal to their openings.

Question 115. A constructed illustration: a needle is placed in the midline of the lower back to sample cerebrospinal fluid below the second lumbar vertebra. Which space does the needle enter, and why is that level chosen? The answer is the subarachnoid space, which holds the fluid. The level is chosen because the cord has already ended above it, so only the moving roots of the cauda equina lie in the way.

Question 116. Which sheet of muscle forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and separates it from the abdominal cavity? The answer is the diaphragm. It is a dome-shaped muscle attached to the lower ribs, the sternum and the lumbar vertebrae. The esophagus, the aorta and the inferior vena cava pass through openings in it.

Question 117. Which of these divides the thoracic cavity into two lateral spaces and a central compartment: the diaphragm, the mediastinum, the pericardium, or the sternum? The answer is the mediastinum. It is the central partition between the two pleural cavities and holds the heart, the great vessels and the esophagus.

Question 118. Which of these pairs belongs together: the mediastinum with the space between the two lungs, the pleural cavity with the space around the heart, the pericardial cavity with the space around a lung, or the thoracic cavity with the space below the diaphragm? The answer is the mediastinum with the space between the two lungs. The pleural cavity surrounds a lung, and the pericardial cavity surrounds the heart.

Question 119. The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by the first thoracic vertebra, the first ribs, and which part of the sternum: the manubrium, the body, the xiphoid process, or the clavicle? The answer is the manubrium. That opening admits the trachea, the esophagus and the great vessels into the chest.

Question 120. A described coronal section through the chest shows two cone-shaped spaces, one on each side of a central mass, each lined by a smooth shiny membrane. What are those two spaces? The answer is the right and left pleural cavities. Each is lined by pleura and contains a lung. The central mass between them is the mediastinum.

Question 121. Which of these structures passes through the diaphragm at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra, together with the vagus nerves: the aorta, the inferior vena cava, the esophagus, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the esophagus. The aorta passes behind the diaphragm at the twelfth thoracic vertebra and the inferior vena cava at the eighth.

Question 122. The heart lies in the middle mediastinum. Which structures lie immediately in front of it and immediately behind it? The answer is the body of the sternum and the costal cartilages in front, and the esophagus and the descending aorta behind. The vertebral column forms the posterior wall behind those.

Question 123. A constructed illustration: a wound enters the chest just below the left fifth rib near the sternum. Which cavity is entered, and which structure lies immediately deep to that point? The answer is the pleural cavity, and the pericardium with the heart lies deep to it there. The left lung is notched over the heart, so the pericardium comes close to the chest wall at that spot.

Question 124. Which cavity lies below the diaphragm and above the pelvic inlet, and holds the stomach, the intestines, the liver and the kidneys? The answer is the abdominal cavity. It is bounded behind by the lumbar vertebrae and the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall. Above it the diaphragm separates it from the chest.

Question 125. Which of these forms the greater part of the muscular posterior wall of the abdominal cavity: the rectus abdominis, the psoas major and quadratus lumborum, the external oblique, or the transversus abdominis? The answer is the psoas major and the quadratus lumborum. They lie behind the peritoneum beside the lumbar vertebrae.

Question 126. Name in a sentence the muscle that forms the roof of the abdominal cavity and the bony ring that marks its lower limit. The answer is the diaphragm above and the pelvic inlet below. The diaphragm arches over the liver, the stomach and the spleen. The pelvic inlet is the brim of the pelvis, formed by the sacral promontory and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

Question 127. Which of these organs lies behind the peritoneum against the posterior abdominal wall: the stomach, the spleen, the kidney, or the transverse colon? The answer is the kidney. It lies retroperitoneally with its fat, its fascia and the adrenal gland above it. The stomach, the spleen and the transverse colon are all suspended within the peritoneal cavity.

Question 128. A described transverse section of the upper abdomen shows a large solid organ on the right, a muscular bag to the left of the midline, and a bony column behind them with two great vessels in front of it. Which structures are shown? The answer is the liver, the stomach and the vertebral column with the aorta and the inferior vena cava.

Question 129. Which vein crosses in front of the abdominal aorta just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, running from left to right? The answer is the left renal vein. It drains the left kidney into the inferior vena cava and is longer than the right renal vein.

Question 130. Which double layer of peritoneum suspends the coils of the small intestine from the posterior abdominal wall and carries their blood vessels and nerves? The answer is the mesentery. It is fan-shaped, with its root running down from the duodenojejunal flexure to the right iliac fossa. The vessels run between its two layers to reach the gut.

Question 131. The lesser sac lies behind the stomach. Which statement about it is correct: it communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen, it is completely closed in the adult, it opens into the pleural cavity, or it surrounds the spleen on every side? The answer is that it communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. That opening lies behind the free edge of the lesser omentum.

Question 132. Which cavity lies below the pelvic inlet, is bounded by the bones of the pelvis and the pelvic floor, and holds the bladder and the rectum? The answer is the pelvic cavity. It is the lowest part of the abdominopelvic cavity and is continuous with the abdominal cavity above.

Question 133. Which of these forms the floor of the pelvic cavity: the pelvic inlet, the pelvic diaphragm, the perineal membrane, or the inguinal ligament? The answer is the pelvic diaphragm, formed by the levator ani and the coccygeus muscles. It slopes downward and forward from the pelvic wall to the midline.

Question 134. A described median section of the female pelvis shows the rectum behind and the uterus with the vagina in front, with a narrow pouch dipping down between them. Which pouch is shown? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, which lies between the rectum and the uterus. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when a person lies on the back, so fluid settling in the abdomen gathers there.

Question 135. Which structure lies immediately in front of the rectum in the male pelvis and which in the female pelvis? The answer is the urinary bladder with the seminal vesicles in the male, and the vagina with the uterus in the female. The rectum lies behind both. The prostate lies below the bladder in the male.

Question 136. Which of these openings lies in the pelvic floor and transmits the urethra and, in the female, the vagina: the obturator foramen, the urogenital hiatus, the greater sciatic foramen, or the pelvic inlet? The answer is the urogenital hiatus. It lies in the front part of the pelvic diaphragm between the two levator ani muscles.

Question 137. The pelvis is divided into a greater part above and a lesser part below. In which plane does the boundary lie, and which two bony points mark it behind and in front? The answer is the oblique plane of the pelvic inlet, marked by the sacral promontory behind and the upper border of the pubic symphysis in front. The plane tilts downward and forward.

Question 138. A constructed illustration: a fracture of the pubic bones on both sides is followed by blood in the pelvis and difficulty in passing urine. Which structure lying behind the pubic symphysis is most likely injured? The answer is the urinary bladder, with the urethra below it. The bladder lies in the front of the pelvic cavity directly behind the pubic bones. A broken pubic ramus can therefore tear it.

Question 139. What is the narrow space between the two layers of pleura on each side of the chest called, and what does it hold? The answer is the pleural cavity, which holds only a thin film of fluid. It is a potential space rather than an air-filled one, because the two layers lie in contact.

Question 140. Which layer of pleura covers the surface of the lung itself and dips into the fissures between its lobes? The answer is the visceral pleura. It is firmly stuck to the lung and cannot be peeled from it. The parietal pleura, by contrast, lines the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum.

Question 141. Which part of the parietal pleura lines the inner surface of the ribs: the costal pleura, the diaphragmatic pleura, the mediastinal pleura, or the cervical pleura? The answer is the costal pleura. It covers the inner surface of the ribs and the intercostal muscles and the sides of the vertebral bodies.

Question 142. Air enters the pleural cavity and separates the lung from the chest wall. What is that condition called: a pneumothorax, a hemothorax, a pleural effusion, or an empyema? The answer is a pneumothorax, which means air in the pleural cavity. A hemothorax is blood in the cavity and an empyema is pus.

Question 143. A described radiograph of the chest taken at the end of a deep breath shows the lower edge of each lung sitting well above the level of the diaphragm at the side of the chest. What is the narrow space between the lung and the diaphragm at that point called? The answer is the costodiaphragmatic recess. It is the lowest part of the pleural cavity and the place where fluid first collects.

Question 144. Which of these structures lies immediately above the first rib, under a dome of pleura: the apex of the lung, the arch of the aorta, the trachea, or the first rib? The answer is the apex of the lung. It rises above the first rib into the root of the neck, covered by the cervical pleura. The subclavian artery and vein arch over that dome in front of it.

Question 145. Two nerves descend through the chest close to the root of each lung, one passing in front of the root and one behind it. Which lies in front, and which lies behind? The answer is the phrenic nerve in front and the vagus nerve behind. The phrenic nerve runs down on the mediastinal pleura to reach the diaphragm.

Question 146. A constructed illustration: a blunt injury to the left side of the chest breaks a rib, and both air and blood gather in the left pleural cavity. Which layer of pleura has been torn, and where does the fluid collect? The answer is the parietal pleura, which lines the chest wall, and the fluid settles in the costodiaphragmatic recess.

Question 147. Which sac encloses the heart, and what is the narrow space between its two inner layers called? The answer is the pericardium, and the space is the pericardial cavity. The sac has a tough fibrous outer layer and a serous inner layer folded into two sheets. The cavity itself holds only a film of fluid.

Question 148. Which of these is a function of the tough fibrous pericardium: it secretes the pericardial fluid, it prevents the heart from overfilling suddenly, it lines the inside of the lungs, or it carries the coronary arteries? The answer is that it prevents sudden overfilling. It is a strong, unyielding bag fused to the central tendon of the diaphragm below.

Question 149. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fibrous pericardium with the tough outer sac, the visceral pericardium with the lining of the chest wall, the parietal pericardium with the surface of the heart, or the pericardial cavity with the space around a lung? The answer is the fibrous pericardium with the tough outer sac. The visceral layer, also called the epicardium, is the one on the surface of the heart.

Question 150. Which of these describes the transverse sinus of the pericardium: a passage behind the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk, a passage behind the left atrium, the space between the two pleural cavities, or a fold of the visceral pleura? The answer is the passage behind the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk. A finger can be passed through it from one side to the other.

Question 151. A described section through the wall of the heart shows a smooth shiny layer lying directly on the muscle and continuous with the lining of the great vessels at the top. Which layer of the serous pericardium is shown? The answer is the visceral layer, which is also called the epicardium.

Question 152. Which structure lies immediately behind the left atrium and is related to it through the pericardium? The answer is the esophagus, with the descending aorta behind it. The esophagus descends in the posterior mediastinum against the vertebral column. Because of that relation, the left atrium lies directly in front of the esophagus.

Question 153. Which statement about the serous pericardium is correct: its parietal layer lines the fibrous sac, its visceral layer lines the chest wall, its two layers are continuous at the roots of the great vessels, or the cavity normally holds a large volume of fluid? The answer is that the two layers are continuous at the roots of the great vessels. The visceral layer covers the heart and the parietal layer lines the fibrous sac.

Question 154. A constructed illustration: fluid gathers quickly inside the pericardial sac, the heart cannot fill, and the pulse weakens. Which space is involved, and why does the tough outer layer matter? The answer is the pericardial cavity, and the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch quickly. Because it is unyielding, even a small volume of fluid raises the pressure inside and presses on the heart.

Question 155. Which membrane lines the wall of the abdominal cavity and covers the organs within it, and what is the space between its layers called? The answer is the peritoneum, and the space is the peritoneal cavity. It is a closed sac in the male, holding only a thin film of fluid. The parietal layer lines the wall and the visceral layer covers the organs.

Question 156. What is a double layer of peritoneum that attaches an organ to the abdominal wall or to another organ called? The answer is a fold of peritoneum, such as a mesentery, an omentum or a ligament. A mesentery attaches the gut to the posterior wall and carries its vessels and nerves.

Question 157. Which of these organs is completely surrounded by peritoneum and suspended within the abdominal cavity: the pancreas, the kidney, the spleen, or the abdominal aorta? The answer is the spleen. It lies in the left upper part of the abdomen and is covered by peritoneum except where the vessels enter at its hilum.

Question 158. Which of these parts of the gut lies behind the peritoneum and is fixed against the posterior abdominal wall: the stomach, the descending part of the duodenum, the transverse colon, or the spleen? The answer is the descending part of the duodenum, which is retroperitoneal. Most of the duodenum and the ascending and descending parts of the colon share that position.

Question 159. A described sagittal section of the abdomen shows a double fold of peritoneum hanging down from the greater curvature of the stomach like an apron over the coils of intestine. What is that fold? The answer is the greater omentum. It hangs down from the stomach and then turns back up to the transverse colon.

Question 160. Which structure lies immediately behind the epiploic foramen, so that it forms the posterior wall of that opening? The answer is the inferior vena cava. The foramen is bounded in front by the free edge of the lesser omentum and behind by the vena cava covered with peritoneum. The portal vein lies in that free edge in front.

Question 161. Which statement about the peritoneal cavity is correct: in the female it opens through the uterine tubes, it communicates with the pleural cavities, it is divided into two halves by the diaphragm, or it holds the kidneys? The answer is that in the female it opens through the uterine tubes, the uterus and the vagina. In the male it is a completely closed sac.

Question 162. A constructed illustration: after a blunt abdominal injury, a described radiograph shows a crescent of air under the right dome of the diaphragm. Which cavity holds the air, and which recess is its lowest part when the person lies on the back? The answer is the peritoneal cavity, and the hepatorenal recess is the lowest part in that position.

Question 163. What name is given to a smooth, moist, two-layered membrane that lines a closed body cavity and covers the organs inside it? The answer is a serous membrane. The pleura, the pericardium and the peritoneum are its three examples in the trunk. Each consists of a parietal layer on the wall and a visceral layer on the organ.

Question 164. Name the three serous membranes found in the trunk of the body. The answer is the pleura, the pericardium and the peritoneum. The pleura surrounds each lung and the pericardium encloses the heart. The peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity and covers the organs within it.

Question 165. Serous membranes have two layers. Which of these describes the parietal layer: it covers the surface of the organ, it lines the wall of the cavity, it forms the outer skin of the body, or it lines the inside of the gut? The answer is that it lines the wall of the cavity. The visceral layer is the one that covers the organ.

Question 166. Which of these best describes the fluid in a serous cavity: it nourishes the organ, it lets the two layers slide over each other with almost no friction, it carries oxygen, or it seals the cavity shut? The answer is that it lets the layers slide with almost no friction. The film of fluid is thin, and the two smooth surfaces slide over one another.

Question 167. A described section shows a smooth membrane whose two layers become continuous where a tube enters the organ it covers. What does that arrangement allow the organ to do? The answer is that it allows the organ to move inside the cavity. The visceral layer follows the organ while the parietal layer stays with the wall.

Question 168. True or false: the two layers of a serous membrane are normally separated by a cavity filled with a large pool of fluid. The answer is false. The two layers lie against each other, separated only by a thin film of fluid that lubricates them.

Question 169. Which of these pairs belongs together: the parietal layer with pain that is sharp and localized, the visceral layer with pain that is sharp and localized, the parietal layer with pain felt only in the midline, or the visceral layer with pain felt at the ribs? The answer is the parietal layer with sharp, localized pain. It carries the same somatic nerves as the body wall over it.

Question 170. Which layer of a serous membrane lies against the wall of the cavity, and which lies against the organ? The answer is the parietal layer against the wall and the visceral layer against the organ. The two are continuous where the vessels and ducts of the organ enter it.

Question 171. Sharp pain felt over the ribs when the pleura is irritated comes from which layer: the visceral pleura, the parietal pleura, the lung tissue, or the pleural cavity? The answer is the parietal pleura. It is supplied by the intercostal and phrenic nerves and is sensitive to pain, touch and temperature.

Question 172. A described dissection shows a membrane that lifts easily from the inner surface of the chest wall but cannot be peeled from the surface of the lung. Which two layers are being shown? The answer is the parietal pleura on the wall and the visceral pleura on the lung. The visceral layer is fused to the lung and follows it into the fissures.

Question 173. In the abdomen, which layer of peritoneum is supplied by the same somatic nerves as the body wall that lies over it? The answer is the parietal peritoneum. Pain from it is sharp and well localized over the affected area. The visceral peritoneum is supplied by the autonomic nerves of the gut and its pain is dull and poorly placed.

Question 174. Name in a sentence the two layers of the serous pericardium and say which of them is firmly attached to the heart muscle. The answer is the parietal layer, which lines the fibrous sac, and the visceral layer, which lies on the heart. The visceral layer is the one firmly attached to the muscle, where it is called the epicardium.

Question 175. True or false: pain from the visceral peritoneum is usually dull and felt in the midline, while pain from the parietal peritoneum is sharp and well localized. The answer is true. The visceral peritoneum follows the gut and receives autonomic nerves, so its pain is felt centrally and vaguely. The parietal peritoneum receives somatic nerves and places pain precisely over the inflamed area.

Question 176. What name is given to the tissue that covers the surfaces of the body, lines its cavities and tubes, and forms the glands? The answer is epithelial tissue. Its cells lie close together with very little material between them. It rests on a basement membrane and has no blood vessels of its own.

Question 177. Which of these is a characteristic of epithelial tissue: a large amount of material between the cells, a rich network of blood vessels within it, cells packed closely together, or a loose arrangement of cells? The answer is cells packed closely together. Epithelium is described as avascular, because its nourishment comes by diffusion from the tissue beneath it.

Question 178. A described section shows a single row of cells that are taller than they are wide, standing side by side on a thin basement membrane. Which type of epithelium is shown? The answer is simple columnar epithelium. It lines the stomach, the intestines and parts of the respiratory and reproductive tracts. Its height suits cells that secrete or absorb.

Question 179. On which thin layer do all epithelial cells rest, and what separates it from the tissue below? The answer is the basement membrane. It is a thin sheet of material between the epithelium and the connective tissue beneath. It gives the sheet a surface to stand on and a boundary to hold it.

Question 180. Which type of epithelium lines the air sacs of the lung, where gases must pass quickly between air and blood: simple squamous, simple cuboidal, stratified squamous, or transitional? The answer is simple squamous epithelium. It is only one cell thick, so the distance for diffusion is short. A thicker lining would slow that exchange.

Question 181. Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder and the ureter and can stretch as the bladder fills? The answer is transitional epithelium. Its surface cells are large and rounded, and they flatten as the organ stretches. It is also called urothelium. It lines the renal pelvis, the ureters, the bladder and the first part of the urethra.

Question 182. Which epithelium lines the trachea and sweeps mucus upward toward the throat: simple squamous, pseudostratified ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, or simple cuboidal? The answer is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. It looks layered because the nuclei lie at different heights, but every cell reaches the basement membrane. The cilia move the mucus and the particles trapped in it.

Question 183. A described section through thick skin shows many layers of cells, flattened and filled with a tough protein at the surface, over a deeper layer of dividing cells. Which epithelium is shown? The answer is stratified squamous keratinized epithelium. The surface cells are dead and packed with keratin, which makes the layer resistant to wear. The dividing cells lie deepest.

Question 184. True or false: epithelial tissue has no blood vessels of its own and is nourished by diffusion from the connective tissue beneath it. The answer is true. Because epithelium is avascular, oxygen and nutrients must travel from the vessels in the tissue below. An epithelium cannot survive once it is lifted from its bed.

Question 185. Which of these is not one of the shapes used to classify epithelial cells: squamous, cuboidal, columnar, or fibroblastic? The answer is fibroblastic. Squamous cells are flat and cuboidal cells are about as tall as they are wide. Fibroblasts are cells of connective tissue, not of epithelium.

Question 186. A described section of the small intestine shows a lining thrown into folds, and the free surface of every cell bears a dense fringe of fine projections. What are those projections called? The answer is microvilli, sometimes called the brush border. They are tiny folds of the cell membrane that increase the surface for absorption. They cannot move, unlike the cilia of the airway.

Question 187. What is the name of the motile, hair-like structure on the free surface of the cells lining the respiratory tract, built from microtubules? The answer is a cilium, and each cell carries many of them. They beat in a coordinated wave that moves mucus and trapped particles along the surface. Microvilli look similar but are not motile.

Question 188. A described section shows a tube lined by epithelium that leads to the surface, and deeper down a cluster of secretory cells around a small central lumen. What kind of gland is shown? The answer is an exocrine gland, whose secretion leaves through a duct. The cluster of cells is an acinus.

Question 189. Which of these is a single mucus-secreting cell scattered among the cells of the airway and the intestine: the goblet cell, the acinar cell, the basal cell, or the squamous cell? The answer is the goblet cell. It is a unicellular exocrine gland shaped like a wine glass. The other named cells take no part in that secretion.

Question 190. Which of these pairs belongs together: a tight junction with sealing the space between neighboring cells, a desmosome with the free passage of ions between cells, a gap junction with anchoring filaments, or a hemidesmosome with joining two cell tops? The answer is a tight junction with sealing the space between cells. A desmosome anchors neighboring cells to one another and a gap junction lets small molecules pass between them.

Question 191. Which epithelium lines the esophagus: simple squamous, stratified squamous non-keratinized, simple columnar, or transitional? The answer is stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium. Several layers protect the lining from the passage of food and the surface stays moist. A single layer would be worn through by the same traffic.

Question 192. A described section of a lining shows nuclei lying at several different levels, so that the epithelium looks like several layers, yet every cell reaches the basement membrane. Which epithelium is shown? The answer is pseudostratified columnar epithelium. All the cells are attached to the basement membrane but only some reach the free surface.

Question 193. Which structure lies immediately deep to an epithelium and carries the blood vessels that nourish it? The answer is the connective tissue beneath the basement membrane, often called the lamina propria in a mucous membrane. The epithelium itself has no vessels. Nutrition passes from those vessels across the basement membrane.

Question 194. A constructed illustration: a burn destroys the whole thickness of the epidermis over part of an arm. Which epithelium has been lost, and what allows the surface to be covered again? The answer is stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, and the dividing cells deep in the surviving follicles allow new cells to replace it.

Question 195. A constructed illustration: long-standing irritation of the lower esophagus changes its lining from the epithelium that resists abrasion to one that secretes mucus. Which two epithelia are involved? The answer is stratified squamous epithelium, which normally lines the esophagus, replaced by simple columnar epithelium. The two epithelia meet at the junction with the stomach.

Question 196. A constructed illustration: the ciliated lining of the airways is damaged and loses its cilia. Which function of that epithelium is lost? The answer is the movement of mucus with the particles trapped in it toward the throat. Without the cilia that layer must be coughed up or it collects. The mucus is still produced by the goblet cells.

Question 197. True or false: epithelial cells are joined to one another by junctions such as tight junctions and desmosomes, and the sheet rests on a basement membrane. The answer is true. The junctions hold the cells together and seal the space between them. The basement membrane anchors the whole sheet to the connective tissue beneath.

Question 198. Which of these pairs belongs together: simple squamous epithelium with rapid diffusion, stratified squamous epithelium with secretion of mucus, transitional epithelium with gas exchange, or simple cuboidal epithelium with protection against abrasion? The answer is simple squamous epithelium with rapid diffusion. Its single flat layer is the thinnest possible barrier. Stratified squamous epithelium is built for protection and transitional epithelium for stretching.

Question 199. Name in a sentence the two opposite surfaces of an epithelial cell and say what each one faces. The answer is the apical surface, which faces the lumen or the outside of the body, and the basal surface, which rests on the basement membrane. The two differ in structure because they do different work.

Question 200. In a section through a gland, the secretory cells stand around a central lumen. Which way do the cells face the lumen, and which way do they rest on the basement membrane? The answer is that the apical surfaces face the lumen at the center and the bases rest on the basement membrane outside. Secretion leaves by the apical end.

To summarize, the body is built around cavities that are named for the walls that enclose them. The cranial cavity holds the brain and the vertebral cavity holds the spinal cord, while the thoracic cavity is divided by the mediastinum into two pleural cavities and the pericardial cavity of the heart. Below the diaphragm the abdominal and pelvic cavities are lined by the peritoneum, a closed sac in the male that opens through the uterine tubes in the female. Every one of these spaces is lined by a serous membrane with a parietal layer on the wall and a visceral layer on the organ, and the thin film of fluid between them lets the two surfaces slide without friction. Epithelial tissue covers the surfaces of the body, lines every cavity and tube and forms the glands, resting on a basement membrane, holding its cells close together and taking its nourishment by diffusion. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 3 — Tissues

This chapter examines the four basic tissues of the body and the way each one is built, beginning with connective tissue and its cells, fibers and ground substance, then cartilage, bone, muscle tissue and nervous tissue, and closing with the features that let one tissue be told from another. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried forward in the mind. The tissues described here are the materials from which every organ is assembled. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 201. Which of the four basic tissue types consists of cells scattered through an abundant extracellular matrix that the cells themselves secrete? The answer is connective tissue. Its cells are widely separated by the material between them, and that material carries the fibers and the ground substance. Epithelium, muscle tissue and nervous tissue are far more crowded with cells and hold much less matrix.

Question 202. Which cell is the most numerous in ordinary loose connective tissue and is responsible for producing its collagen and its ground substance? The answer is the fibroblast. It lies between the collagen bundles and keeps them renewed throughout life. Macrophages, mast cells and fat cells are present in the same tissue but in much smaller numbers.

Question 203. Which of these gives loose connective tissue its resistance to pulling: collagen fibers, elastic fibers, reticular fibers, or ground substance? The answer is collagen fibers. Collagen is the commonest protein in the body, and its bundles resist tension. Elastic fibers stretch and recoil, and reticular fibers form fine supporting nets.

Question 204. Which fiber type forms the fine branching framework that supports the cells of a lymph node, the spleen and the bone marrow? The answer is the reticular fiber. It is a delicate collagen fiber that forms a net rather than a thick bundle. That net is the stroma on which the cells of those organs rest.

Question 205. Which statement about adipose tissue is correct: it stores energy in lipid droplets, it conducts electrical impulses, it lines the inner surface of blood vessels, or it forms the framework of the liver? The answer is that it stores energy in lipid droplets. The droplet fills the cell and pushes the nucleus to one edge. The tissue also cushions the body and insulates it.

Question 206. A described microscope field shows loose wavy bundles running in several directions, scattered flattened nuclei lying against the bundles, and clear spaces between them. Which tissue is shown? The answer is loose connective tissue, also called areolar tissue. The wavy bundles are collagen, and the clear spaces held ground substance and tissue fluid before the preparation was made.

Question 207. Which layer of connective tissue lies immediately deep to the skin and carries the fat that pads the body? The answer is the superficial fascia, also called the subcutaneous layer. It lies between the skin and the deep fascia that wraps the muscles. It is loose enough for fluid to spread along it.

Question 208. A constructed illustration: a clean laceration is repaired, and the wound is described as filling with a new tissue rich in small vessels, fibroblasts and loose matrix. Which tissue is filling the wound? The answer is granulation tissue. It is a temporary connective tissue built during repair. As it matures the vessels withdraw, collagen is laid down, and a scar forms.

Question 209. Which cell of connective tissue carries granules of histamine and heparin and lies close to small blood vessels? The answer is the mast cell. Its granules are released in allergic reactions and in local inflammation. Macrophages engulf material and plasma cells make antibody, so neither of those cells fits this description.

Question 210. True or false: in connective tissue the cells occupy more of the volume than the extracellular matrix does. The answer is false. Connective tissue is defined by an abundance of matrix, and its cells are widely scattered through it. Epithelium is the tissue in which cells are packed tightly together with almost nothing between them.

Question 211. Which of these pairs belongs together: fibroblasts with collagen, mast cells with myelin, plasma cells with lipid storage, or macrophages with ground substance? The answer is fibroblasts with collagen. Fibroblasts produce both the collagen fibers and the ground substance. Mast cells release histamine, plasma cells make antibody, and macrophages engulf debris.

Question 212. A described electron micrograph shows a bundle of long parallel fibrils with a repeating banded pattern across them. Which protein are those fibrils made of, and what does the banding represent? The answer is collagen, and the banding shows how the molecules overlap in regular steps. That regular overlap is what gives collagen its great tensile strength.

Question 213. Which statement about a tendon and a ligament is correct: a tendon joins muscle to bone and a ligament joins bone to bone, both join muscle to muscle, both lie inside a joint, or both are elastic cartilage? The answer is that a tendon joins muscle to bone and a ligament joins bone to bone. Both are dense regular connective tissue. A ligament holds two bones together.

Question 214. Which type of connective tissue forms the dermis of the skin and the fibrous capsule of an organ, with collagen bundles running in many directions? The answer is dense irregular connective tissue. Its bundles are tightly packed but not parallel, so the tissue resists pulling from any direction. Dense regular tissue has all its bundles in line instead.

Question 215. Which of these features separates connective tissue from epithelium: it is usually rich in blood vessels, it always sits on a basement membrane, it is avascular, or its cells form tight sheets? The answer is that it is usually rich in blood vessels. Epithelium is the avascular tissue, and it rests on a basement membrane. Cartilage is the connective tissue that lacks vessels.

Question 216. A constructed illustration: a person whose diet has long lacked fresh fruit and vegetables is described as having bleeding gums and wounds that will not heal.
