Which protein of connective tissue is deficient? The answer is collagen. Collagen synthesis needs vitamin C, so weak fibers form and the tissues that depend on them give way. This illustration is described to show the role of collagen.

Question 217. Which of these explains why loose connective tissue lies beneath most epithelia: it lets fluid and cells pass from the vessels to the epithelium, it bears the weight of the epithelium, it forms a waterproof barrier, or it gives rigid support? The answer is that it lets fluid and cells pass. That layer carries the capillaries that feed the avascular epithelium above it. White cells also travel through it.

Question 218. A described preparation of a tendon shows long wavy bundles running the length of the field, with rows of flattened nuclei between them and little ground substance. Which tissue is shown, and how does its structure serve its function? The answer is dense regular connective tissue. Its parallel bundles resist pull along one line, which is what a tendon needs. Few vessels run within it, so it heals slowly.

Question 219. Which tissue consists of a firm rubbery matrix with cells enclosed in small spaces, and has no blood vessels of its own? The answer is cartilage. Its cells, the chondrocytes, lie in lacunae within the matrix they secreted. Because it has no vessels, it is fed by diffusion from its surface.

Question 220. What is the name of the cell that produces and maintains the matrix of cartilage? The answer is the chondrocyte. It lies in a small cavity called a lacuna. While it is still laying down new matrix in growing cartilage, the same cell is called a chondroblast, and once the matrix closes around it, it becomes a chondrocyte.

Question 221. Which of these cartilages is the most widespread in the body and covers the ends of the long bones: hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, fibrocartilage, or bone? The answer is hyaline cartilage. It gives the smooth articular surface of joints and forms the costal cartilages and the rings of the windpipe. Elastic cartilage is found in the ear and the epiglottis.

Question 222. Which type of cartilage contains a dense network of elastic fibers and is found in the external ear and the epiglottis? The answer is elastic cartilage. Its fibers let it bend and then spring back into shape. Hyaline cartilage is far commoner, and fibrocartilage carries thick collagen bundles instead.

Question 223. A described section shows a smooth glassy matrix with rounded cells sitting in clear spaces, alone or in small groups, and no visible fibers. Which tissue is shown? The answer is hyaline cartilage. Its matrix looks glassy because the collagen fibers within it are too fine to be seen in an ordinary preparation. The cells of each group are the descendants of one parent cell.

Question 224. Which type of cartilage forms the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis: hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, fibrocartilage, or dense fibrous tissue alone? The answer is fibrocartilage. It carries thick bundles of collagen and resists both compression and pulling. It is the cartilage that comes closest to dense connective tissue.

Question 225. In the trachea, which tissue forms the rings that hold the airway open, and where are those rings incomplete? The answer is hyaline cartilage, and the rings are open at the back. The open side faces the esophagus, which lies behind the trachea. That gap is why a swallowed mouthful can bulge into the airway.

Question 226. A described cartilage has no blood vessels and is fed by diffusion from its covering. Which of these follows: it heals slowly after injury, it heals faster than bone, it cannot grow after birth, or it is replaced by muscle? The answer is that it heals slowly. Diffusion must carry every nutrient from the surface. Cartilage has no vessels of its own to bring them in.

Question 227. A constructed illustration: a joint is described as stiff and painful, and the smooth lining of its surfaces has been worn away. Which tissue has been lost in that description? The answer is hyaline cartilage, the articular cartilage of the joint. It has no blood vessels and almost no capacity to regrow. The bone beneath it is left exposed.

Question 228. Which statement about the growth of cartilage is correct: it grows both from within and from its surface, it grows only from within, it grows only at its surface, or it cannot grow after birth? The answer is that it grows both from within and from its surface. Interstitial growth divides the cells inside the matrix. Appositional growth adds new layers at the edge.

Question 229. A described specimen of an intervertebral disc shows an outer ring of parallel collagen bundles and an inner core of softer matrix with scattered cells. Which tissues form the ring and the core? The answer is fibrocartilage in the ring, called the annulus fibrosus, and a gel-like core, the nucleus pulposus. The core is a remnant of the notochord of the embryo.

Question 230. True or false: the surface of a moving joint is covered by hyaline cartilage, and that cartilage has no perichondrium over the articular surface. The answer is true. Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage that has no fibrous covering where it faces the joint cavity. It is nourished instead by the synovial fluid that bathes it.

Question 231. Which of these pairs belongs together: elastic cartilage with the external ear, hyaline cartilage with the intervertebral disc, fibrocartilage with the tracheal rings, or bone with the epiglottis? The answer is elastic cartilage with the external ear. Hyaline cartilage forms the tracheal rings, fibrocartilage forms the intervertebral discs, and the epiglottis is made of elastic cartilage as well.

Question 232. Name the three types of cartilage and give one site for each, spoken as a sentence. The answer is hyaline cartilage at the ends of the long bones, elastic cartilage in the external ear, and fibrocartilage in the intervertebral discs. All three have cells in lacunae and a matrix they secrete, and none of the three has vessels of its own.

Question 233. Which tissue is described as a hard matrix of mineral salts deposited around collagen fibers, with cells enclosed in small spaces that communicate with one another? The answer is bone tissue. The mineral gives it hardness and the collagen lets it bend rather than shatter. The small spaces are the lacunae, joined by narrow canaliculi.

Question 234. What is the name of the mature bone cell that lies in a lacuna and maintains the matrix around it? The answer is the osteocyte. Its long processes run through the narrow canaliculi to reach its neighbors. Osteoblasts build new matrix, and osteoclasts break the old matrix down.

Question 235. Which of these cells is responsible for resorbing bone: the osteoblast, the osteocyte, the osteoclast, or the chondrocyte? The answer is the osteoclast. It is a large cell with several nuclei that dissolves both the mineral and the collagen. The osteoblast lays down new matrix instead, and the chondrocyte belongs to cartilage.

Question 236. Which cell of bone lays down the soft unmineralized matrix called osteoid before it hardens? The answer is the osteoblast. It sits on the surface of the bone it is building and secretes collagen and ground substance around itself. Once the matrix closes around it, it becomes an osteocyte.

Question 237. Which statement about the periosteum is correct: it covers the outer surface of a bone except at the joints and where tendons attach, it lines the marrow cavity, it covers the articular cartilage, or it has no vessels? The answer is that it covers the outer surface except at the joints. The endosteum lines the marrow cavity. It also brings vessels and bone-forming cells to the surface.

Question 238. What is the name of the thin membrane that lines the inside of the marrow cavity and covers the inner surfaces of the bone? The answer is the endosteum. It is a single layer of cells that includes both osteoblasts and osteoclasts. Like the periosteum, it can lay down bone or remove it.

Question 239. A described ground section of bone shows concentric rings of matrix around a central channel, with dark spaces between the rings. What is the unit shown, and what is the central channel called? The answer is an osteon, also called a Haversian system, with the Haversian canal at its center. It carries a small artery, a vein and a nerve. The dark spaces hold the osteocytes.

Question 240. Which of these describes compact bone rather than spongy bone: it is organized into osteons, it is a mesh of trabeculae, it has large spaces filled with marrow, or it forms the interior of the vertebral bodies? The answer is that it is organized into osteons. Spongy bone is a mesh of trabeculae with marrow between them. It fills the ends of the long bones.

Question 241. In a long bone, which part lies between the two ends and contains the marrow cavity? The answer is the diaphysis, which is the shaft. It is a cylinder of compact bone around the marrow. The two ends are the epiphyses, each covered by articular cartilage and separated from the shaft in the growing bone by the epiphyseal plate.

Question 242. Which statement about the blood supply of a long bone is correct: the periosteal vessels and the nutrient artery both supply it, only the nutrient artery supplies it, the marrow has no vessels, or the articular cartilage carries the main artery? The answer is that both the periosteal vessels and the nutrient artery supply it. The nutrient artery enters through a foramen in the shaft. The periosteal vessels enter the outer surface.

Question 243. A constructed illustration: a child's long bone is injured at its growing end, and growth in length stops. Which structure has been damaged in the description? The answer is the epiphyseal plate, the layer of cartilage that lengthens the bone. Growth in length happens there. Growth in width continues from the periosteum.

Question 244. A described radiograph of a growing child's knee shows a dark band across the end of the thigh bone and another across the end of the shin bone, with a small separate bone in front. Which structure do the dark bands represent, and what is that separate bone? The answer is the epiphyseal plates, and the separate bone is the patella. The plates look dark because cartilage is not mineralized.

Question 245. Which of these pairs a bone cell with its action: the osteoclast breaks down bone, the osteoblast breaks down bone, the osteocyte builds new matrix, or the osteoclast becomes an osteocyte? The answer is that the osteoclast breaks down bone. The osteoblast builds matrix and the osteocyte maintains it. An enclosed osteoblast becomes an osteocyte and not an osteoclast.

Question 246. Which structure lies immediately deep to the periosteum on the outer surface of the shaft of a long bone: compact bone, spongy bone, the marrow cavity, or the endosteum? The answer is compact bone. The periosteum covers it, and the compact layer surrounds the marrow cavity. Spongy bone lies inside the ends of the bone.

Question 247. A constructed illustration: a described fracture heals through a soft stage and then a hard stage, and the hard swelling is later reshaped. Which tissue forms the hard stage? The answer is bone, laid down first as a callus of woven bone and later replaced by mature bone. Woven bone has irregular collagen and is weak. It is rebuilt along the lines of force.

Question 248. Which statement about the mineral of bone is correct: it is a calcium phosphate salt laid along and between the collagen fibers, it is pure calcium carbonate, it lies only on the surface, or it fills the marrow cavity? The answer is that it is a calcium phosphate salt laid along and between the collagen fibers. The mineral gives hardness and the collagen gives resilience. Together they let it bend rather than crack.

Question 249. True or false: spongy bone is weaker than compact bone simply because it contains fewer cells. The answer is false. Spongy bone is arranged as a mesh of trabeculae that follow the lines of force, and that arrangement gives it great strength for its weight. Its cells are as numerous as those of compact bone.

Question 250. A described section of the shaft of a long bone shows, from the outside inward, a fibrous layer, parallel rings around central channels, and a cavity crossed by fine strands. Name the three layers in order. The answer is the periosteum, compact bone and the endosteum. The rings around the central channels are the osteons. The strands crossing the cavity are trabeculae of spongy bone.

Question 251. Which of these explains why a bone that is not used loses mass: the balance between the osteoblasts and the osteoclasts shifts toward removal, the bone cells stop making collagen, the matrix dissolves, or the marrow fills with cartilage? The answer is that the balance shifts toward removal. Mechanical load stimulates new bone. A limb that is not used is rebuilt less and loses mass.

Question 252. A growing long bone has a plate of cartilage across each end. Which of these lies immediately on the shaft side of that plate: the metaphysis, the epiphysis, the articular cartilage, or the marrow of the epiphysis? The answer is the metaphysis, the flared part of the shaft next to the plate. The epiphysis lies on the other side. The articular cartilage covers its free surface.

Question 253. Which of these pairs belongs together: the osteoblast with bone formation, the osteocyte with bone resorption, the osteoclast with cartilage growth, or the chondrocyte with mineral deposition? The answer is the osteoblast with bone formation. The osteocyte maintains the matrix, the osteoclast resorbs it, and the chondrocyte makes cartilage rather than bone.

Question 254. Name the three kinds of cell found in bone tissue and say what each one does, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the osteoblast, which builds new matrix, the osteocyte, which maintains the matrix around it, and the osteoclast, which resorbs bone. All three are active throughout life, so bone is rebuilt continuously.

Question 255. Which of the three muscle types is described as having cross striations, many nuclei in each fiber, and voluntary control? The answer is skeletal muscle. Its fibers are long cylinders with many nuclei at the edge, and its striations are easy to see under the microscope. Cardiac muscle is also striated, but it is not under voluntary control.

Question 256. Which muscle type is found only in the wall of the heart and is described as striated and involuntary? The answer is cardiac muscle. Its cells are joined end to end at intercalated discs and branch to form a network. It contracts rhythmically throughout life without any conscious control, and it cannot be rested.

Question 257. Which of these muscle types has no cross striations: skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or all three? The answer is smooth muscle. It is found in the walls of the gut, the bladder and the blood vessels. Its cells are spindle shaped and each one has a single central nucleus.

Question 258. What is the name of the long multinucleated cell of skeletal muscle that runs the length of the muscle? The answer is the muscle fiber, also called a myofiber. It is formed during development by the fusion of many separate cells, which is why it carries several nuclei. Its nuclei lie just beneath the cell membrane.

Question 259. Which of these stores oxygen inside a muscle fiber and gives the tissue its red color: myoglobin, collagen, glycogen, or the sarcolemma? The answer is myoglobin. It holds oxygen within the fiber so that the muscle can work briefly before new blood arrives. Glycogen is the stored fuel, and the sarcolemma is the membrane of the fiber.

Question 260. A described microscope field from the wall of the small intestine shows elongated cells with a single central nucleus each, packed side by side, with no cross striations and no branching. Which muscle type is shown? The answer is smooth muscle. Its cells are spindle shaped and thickest in the middle. It contracts slowly and can hold the contraction.

Question 261. What is the name of the fine connective tissue sheath that wraps an individual muscle fiber in skeletal muscle? The answer is the endomysium. It is the finest of the three sheaths of a muscle, and it carries the capillaries that feed each fiber. The perimysium wraps bundles of fibers, and the epimysium wraps the whole muscle.

Question 262. Which of these describes a motor unit: one motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies, one fiber and all the neurons reaching it, one bundle of fibers, or one tendon with its muscle? The answer is one motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies. The fibers of a single unit are scattered through the muscle. Its size sets how fine the muscle control can be.

Question 263. Within a skeletal muscle, which sheath lies immediately around a bundle of fibers: the endomysium, the perimysium, the epimysium, or the sarcolemma? The answer is the perimysium. It wraps each bundle, which is called a fascicle, and carries the vessels and the nerves into the muscle. The epimysium is the outer covering of the whole muscle.

Question 264. A described section of the heart wall shows short branching cells joined end to end by dark bands, with one nucleus in each cell and faint cross striations. Which tissue is shown, and what are the dark bands called? The answer is cardiac muscle, and the bands are the intercalated discs. They hold the cells together. They also pass the impulse quickly from cell to cell.

Question 265. Which statement about the nuclei of the three muscle types is correct: skeletal fibers have several nuclei near the edge, cardiac cells have several in the middle, smooth cells have several each, or all three have one nucleus? The answer is that skeletal fibers have several near the edge. Cardiac and smooth muscle cells each have one nucleus. That nucleus lies in the middle of the cell.

Question 266. A constructed illustration: a described patch of the stomach wall loses its muscle, and that part of the wall becomes permanently weak and bulges. Which muscle type has been lost in the description? The answer is smooth muscle. The stomach wall has three layers of it, and a gap in that coat lets the wall give way. The other two muscle types do not occur there.

Question 267. In a skeletal muscle, which connective tissue layer lies between two neighboring bundles of fibers: the endomysium, the perimysium, the epimysium, or the deep fascia? The answer is the perimysium. Bundles of fibers are called fascicles, and the perimysium wraps each bundle. The deep fascia lies outside the epimysium and wraps the whole muscle.

Question 268. Which of these explains why cardiac muscle contracts as a single unit: its cells are joined by intercalated discs that pass the impulse quickly, its fibers are multinucleated, its cells have no striations, or it is supplied by many separate motor units? The answer is that the intercalated discs pass the impulse quickly. The heart therefore behaves as one unit. It needs no separate nerve ending for every cell.

Question 269. True or false: smooth muscle contraction is under conscious control and is therefore described as voluntary. The answer is false. Smooth muscle is involuntary, and it is found in the walls of the hollow organs and of the blood vessels. Skeletal muscle is the voluntary type, and cardiac muscle is involuntary as well.

Question 270. A described electron micrograph of skeletal muscle shows a repeating pattern of thick and thin filaments arranged in regular bands along the fiber. What is the functional unit of that repeating pattern called? The answer is the sarcomere, the segment between one Z line and the next. The thick and the thin filaments slide past one another when the fiber shortens.

Question 271. A constructed illustration: a cut divides the fibers of a skeletal muscle, but the fine sheath around each fiber survives. Which sheath is described, and does skeletal muscle regenerate well? The answer is the endomysium, and skeletal muscle regenerates only poorly. The surviving sheath can guide a few fibers across the gap, but scar tissue usually fills it instead.

Question 272. Which of these pairs belongs together: cardiac muscle with intercalated discs, skeletal muscle with a single central nucleus, smooth muscle with many nuclei in each fiber, or smooth muscle with cross striations? The answer is cardiac muscle with intercalated discs. Skeletal fibers carry several nuclei, smooth muscle cells have one, and smooth muscle has no striations.

Question 273. Which cell of nervous tissue is described as the conducting cell, with a cell body, dendrites and a long axon? The answer is the neuron. It receives signals on its dendrites and its cell body and sends them away along its axon. The supporting cells of nervous tissue are the glial cells.

Question 274. In the peripheral nervous system, which supporting cell wraps a single axon and forms the myelin sheath around it? The answer is the Schwann cell. Each one wraps a short segment of one axon. In the central nervous system the same work is done by the oligodendrocyte, which can myelinate several axons at once.

Question 275. Which type of cell forms the myelin sheath around axons in the central nervous system: the oligodendrocyte, the Schwann cell, the astrocyte, or the ependymal cell? The answer is the oligodendrocyte. One of them can myelinate several axons at the same time. The Schwann cell does the same work for the nerves outside the brain and the spinal cord.

Question 276. Which large star-shaped glial cell has processes that end on blood vessels and on neurons and helps to form the barrier between blood and nervous tissue? The answer is the astrocyte. Its processes cover the vessels of the brain and take part in the blood-brain barrier. It also helps to repair nervous tissue after injury.

Question 277. Which feature of a neuron fixes the direction in which its signal travels: the axon conducts away from the cell body and the dendrites toward it, the dendrites conduct away from the cell body, the cell body has no processes, or the myelin conducts toward it? The answer is that the axon conducts away from the cell body and the dendrites conduct toward it. The dendrites and the cell body receive the signal. The axon alone carries it away.

Question 278. A described section of the spinal cord shows a central mass of gray material shaped like a butterfly, ringed by white material, with a narrow channel at its center. Which substance is the gray material, and what is the channel? The answer is gray matter, which holds the cell bodies, and the channel is the central canal. The white matter outside carries the long tracts and owes its color to myelin.

Question 279. Which of these pairs a part of nervous tissue with what it contains: gray matter with cell bodies, white matter with cell bodies, gray matter with long myelinated tracts, or white matter with the central canal? The answer is gray matter with cell bodies. The cell bodies of neurons lie in the gray matter. White matter is white because of the myelin on the axons within it.

Question 280. In a peripheral nerve, which connective tissue sheath lies immediately around a single axon and its Schwann cell? The answer is the endoneurium. Around it, groups of axons form a fascicle wrapped in the perineurium. The whole nerve is wrapped in the epineurium, which is the thickest of the three.

Question 281. A constructed illustration: a nerve in the hand is divided completely, and sensation returns slowly from the cut toward the fingers over many months. What is happening along the nerve? The answer is that the axons are regrowing along the surviving sheaths. The endoneurial tubes guide them. This regrowth happens in the peripheral nerves only.

Question 282. Which statement about the myelin sheath is correct: supporting cells wrap the axon and speed the impulse, the neuron makes it itself, it slows the impulse, or it lies inside the axon? The answer is that supporting cells wrap it and it speeds the impulse. The gaps between the wrapped segments are the nodes of Ranvier. The sheath also insulates the axon from its neighbors.

Question 283. A described preparation of a peripheral nerve shows a bundle of axons, each wrapped in a spiral of many layers of membrane, with dark nuclei lying between the axons. What is the wrapping, and which cell made it? The answer is the myelin sheath, and it was made by the Schwann cell. Each Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon.

Question 284. In the brain, which cells line the cavities of the ventricles and help to move the cerebrospinal fluid? The answer is the ependymal cells. They form a single layer that lines the ventricles and the central canal of the spinal cord. The cerebrospinal fluid itself is made by the capillaries of the choroid plexus.

Question 285. True or false: neurons in the central nervous system divide readily to replace those lost after injury. The answer is false. Mature neurons do not divide, and the central nervous system has very little capacity to replace them. That is why the loss of nerve cells in the brain and the spinal cord is usually permanent.

Question 286. Which of these explains why a nerve fiber with a thick myelin sheath carries a signal faster than one with a thin sheath: the impulse jumps between the gaps, the sheath makes the axon wider, the sheath carries the impulse itself, or it stops the axon using energy? The answer is that the impulse jumps between the gaps. That jumping is called saltatory conduction. Each jump renews the impulse.

Question 287. A constructed illustration: an injury divides a nerve in the arm cleanly, and sensation returns over many months, while the same injury in the spinal cord leaves a permanent loss. Which property of the two tissues explains the difference? The answer is the ability of peripheral axons to regrow along the surviving sheaths. The endoneurial tubes guide them. The central nervous system forms scar tissue instead.

Question 288. Which of these pairs belongs together: the Schwann cell with the myelin of a peripheral axon, the oligodendrocyte with a peripheral axon, the astrocyte with the myelin of the brain, or the ependymal cell with the myelin of a nerve? The answer is the Schwann cell with the myelin of a peripheral axon. The oligodendrocyte myelinates axons in the central nervous system. The astrocyte supports and the ependymal cell lines the cavities.

Question 289. Which of the four basic tissues is described as cells packed closely together, resting on a basement membrane, with almost no material between them? The answer is epithelium. It covers surfaces, lines cavities and forms glands. Its cells are joined to one another at their sides, which is why it forms a continuous sheet.

Question 290. Which of these forms the outer layer of the skin and the lining of the mouth: epithelium, connective tissue, muscle tissue, or nervous tissue? The answer is epithelium. It covers the surface of the body and lines every cavity that opens onto it. The tissue immediately beneath it is connective tissue.

Question 291. A described microscope field shows a single layer of flat cells with flattened nuclei resting on a thin basement membrane, with loose connective tissue below. Which tissue is shown? The answer is simple squamous epithelium. Its thinness allows gases and fluids to pass across it quickly. It lines the air sacs of the lung and the inner surface of the blood vessels.

Question 292. Which type of epithelium is described as having several layers, with flat cells at the surface and taller cells beneath them? The answer is stratified squamous epithelium. Its many layers protect the surface where wear is heavy. The skin and the lining of the mouth and the esophagus are made of it.

Question 293. Which of these epithelia is best suited to moving a film of mucus along a tube: ciliated columnar epithelium, simple squamous epithelium, stratified squamous epithelium, or transitional epithelium? The answer is ciliated columnar epithelium. Its cilia beat in one direction and carry the film along. It lines the air passages and the uterine tube.

Question 294. A constructed illustration: a surface that must stretch as a hollow organ fills is lined by an epithelium whose cells change shape as the organ empties and fills again. Which epithelium is described, and where is it found? The answer is transitional epithelium, and it lines the urinary bladder and the ureters. When the organ fills, the cells flatten. When it empties, they become rounded again.

Question 295. Which statement about glands is correct: an exocrine gland keeps a duct to the surface and an endocrine gland does not, both keep a duct, neither keeps a duct, or an endocrine gland secretes onto the skin? The answer is that an exocrine gland keeps a duct and an endocrine gland does not. The endocrine gland passes its product into the blood. The exocrine gland pours it onto a surface.

Question 296. A described section shows a tube lined by a single layer of tall cells, some of which reach the basement membrane and some of which do not, with nuclei at several levels. Which epithelium is shown? The answer is pseudostratified columnar epithelium. It looks layered, but every cell rests on the basement membrane. The air passages are lined by it.

Question 297. Spatial reasoning: a described section is cut across a tube, so the tube appears as a circle with its lining all round. What is that section called, and what would a cut along the length show? The answer is a transverse section, and a cut along the length is a longitudinal section. The transverse view shows the wall as a closed ring. The longitudinal view opens it out.

Question 298. Which of these best separates a section of dense regular connective tissue from one of smooth muscle: wavy bundles with few nuclei against spindle cells with a central nucleus each, both showing cross striations, the muscle having no nuclei, or the connective tissue having many nuclei? The answer is wavy bundles with few nuclei against spindle cells with a central nucleus each. One of the two shows cross striations and the other does not. One is mostly matrix and the other is mostly cell.

Question 299. Name the four basic tissue types of the body and say in one sentence what each one does. The answer is epithelium, which covers and lines, connective tissue, which supports and binds, muscle tissue, which contracts, and nervous tissue, which conducts. Every organ of the body is built from these four in different proportions.

Question 300. Spatial reasoning: in a described section of the gut wall, which layer lies between the epithelium that lines the lumen and the muscle that moves the wall? The answer is the connective tissue layer of the wall, with its vessels and nerves. It lies outside the epithelium and inside the muscle. Contraction of the muscle narrows the lumen.

To summarize, the body is built from four basic tissues: epithelium, which covers and lines, connective tissue, which supports and binds, muscle tissue, which contracts, and nervous tissue, which conducts. Connective tissue is mostly extracellular matrix, made by fibroblasts, with collagen for strength, elastic fibers for recoil and reticular fibers for delicate nets, and its looser and denser forms differ in the way their fibers are arranged. Cartilage has cells in lacunae, no vessels of its own, and three varieties, hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage, while bone adds a mineralized matrix and the osteoblast, the osteocyte and the osteoclast. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary with many nuclei in each fiber, cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary and joined by intercalated discs, and smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary. Nervous tissue conducts through neurons and is supported by glial cells, of which the Schwann cell myelinates peripheral axons and the oligodendrocyte myelinates central ones. This chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 4 — Anatomical Variation

No two bodies are built to exactly the same plan, and this chapter is about the differences that count as normal rather than as disease. It covers the variations in number, position, shape and course that a student meets in the dissection room, and then turns to surface anatomy, the landmarks that can be seen and felt through the skin before anything is cut. It holds one hundred questions, and every one gives its answer straight after the question and then explains why that answer is right. Recognizing a variant for what it is, and knowing where a normal structure lies, are two halves of the same skill. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 301. What name is given to the arrangement in which the heart, the liver and the spleen are all mirrored from their usual sides? The answer is situs inversus totalis. Every thoracic and abdominal organ lies as a mirror image of the ordinary layout, with the heart pointing to the right.

Question 302. Which of these is a small separate mass of normal tissue found in about one person in ten: an accessory spleen, an accessory liver, an accessory kidney, or an accessory adrenal gland? The answer is an accessory spleen. It is a rounded nodule of splenic tissue, usually near the upper pole of the spleen.

Question 303. Which of these names a kidney anomaly in which the two lower poles are joined across the midline: a horseshoe kidney, a pelvic kidney, a duplex kidney, or a crossed kidney? The answer is a horseshoe kidney. The joining band crosses in front of the great vessels, and the organ rests lower than usual.

Question 304. A described radiograph of the abdomen shows the two renal outlines joined below by a band of tissue that crosses the midline in front of the aorta. Which anomaly is shown, and why does it sit lower than usual? The answer is a horseshoe kidney, held down because its isthmus catches beneath the inferior mesenteric artery.

Question 305. In a horseshoe kidney the two ureters leave the hila of the fused lower poles. Which part of the fused organ do they cross? The answer is the isthmus, which both ureters cross in front of. That relation explains why the band can obstruct the flow of urine.

Question 306. What is the name of the extra rib that arises from the seventh cervical vertebra and lies in the root of the neck, above the first rib? The answer is a cervical rib. It is present in well under one person in a hundred and is often found only when it presses on the nerves or the vessels of the arm.

Question 307. A constructed illustration: a young adult has wasting of the small muscles of one hand and numbness along the inner border of the forearm, with no injury to the arm. Which variant in the root of the neck explains the picture? The answer is a cervical rib, which stretches the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

Question 308. Which structures pass over a cervical rib and may be stretched by it: the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, the lower trunk of the brachial plexus with the subclavian artery, the phrenic nerve, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the lower trunk of the brachial plexus with the subclavian artery. Both cross the cervical rib behind the clavicle.

Question 309. A described radiograph of the lower neck shows a slender rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra and ending free in the soft tissues. Which of these is shown: a cervical rib, a lumbar rib, a bifid rib, or a sternal foramen? The answer is a cervical rib. It may join the first rib, and it is the commonest extra rib.

Question 310. What name is given to a kidney that fails to rise and comes to rest in the pelvis, usually in front of the sacrum and below the brim? The answer is a pelvic kidney. Its artery comes from the nearby iliac vessels instead of the aorta, and the condition is usually discovered by chance.

Question 311. Which vessel may cross in front of the ureter and obstruct it: the inferior mesenteric artery, an accessory renal artery, the gonadal artery, or the middle suprarenal artery? The answer is an accessory renal artery. Extra renal arteries are common and often arise from the aorta below the main one, passing in front of the ureter.

Question 312. A constructed illustration: an examiner asks a person to press the thumb against the little finger and then bend the wrist, and a thin tendon stands out in the middle of the front of the wrist. Which tendon is being tested? The answer is the palmaris longus. That movement tightens it, and its tendon can be felt just above the wrist crease.

Question 313. Which of these muscles is the one most often missing as a normal variant: the palmaris longus, the plantaris, the psoas minor, or the sternocleidomastoid? The answer is the palmaris longus. It is absent in about one person in seven, more often on the left and more often in women, while the others are missing far less commonly.

Question 314. Which small muscle of the calf has a thin belly and a long slender tendon, is absent in about one person in ten, and is therefore used by surgeons as a graft? The answer is the plantaris. It arises above the lateral head of the gastrocnemius and its tendon runs down beside the calcaneal tendon to reach the heel.

Question 315. A described dissection of the axilla shows a muscular slip that crosses from the latissimus dorsi to the pectoralis major, arching over the axillary vessels and the cords of the brachial plexus. What is this variant called? The answer is the axillary arch. It is a normal variant of the latissimus dorsi and it narrows the space of the axilla.

Question 316. In an axilla that contains an axillary arch, which structures lie immediately deep to the arch: the axillary artery and vein with the cords of the brachial plexus, the serratus anterior, the subscapularis, or the clavicle? The answer is the axillary artery and vein with the cords of the brachial plexus. The arch may press on them when the arm is raised.

Question 317. What is the name of the flat vertical muscle that lies on the front of the chest, superficial to the pectoralis major and parallel to the sternum, and is present in only a small minority of people? The answer is the sternalis. Its nerve supply comes from the intercostal nerves, which suggests that it belongs with the muscles of the abdominal wall.

Question 318. Which of these is an accessory head of the flexor pollicis longus, arising from the coronoid process of the ulna: the Gantzer muscle, the anconeus epitrochlearis, an accessory slip of the pronator teres, or an accessory palmaris longus? The answer is the Gantzer muscle. It lies in the deep flexor compartment of the forearm and may press on the anterior interosseous nerve.

Question 319. What is the name of the bony spur that projects from the anteromedial surface of the humerus about 5 centimeters above the medial epicondyle and is present in about one person in a hundred? The answer is the supracondylar process. A fibrous band runs from the spur down to the medial epicondyle and completes a tunnel over the median nerve.

Question 320. A constructed illustration: a person has weakness of the muscles of the thenar eminence and numbness of the palm, and a radiograph shows a small bony spur above the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Which nerve is compressed, and by what? The answer is the median nerve, trapped between the spur and the fibrous band that joins it to the medial epicondyle.

Question 321. A described radiograph of the lower end of the humerus, taken from behind, shows a small oval opening in the thin plate of bone between the olecranon fossa and the coronoid fossa. What is this opening called? The answer is the supratrochlear foramen, also called the septal aperture. It is a normal variant, commoner in women, and it is not a fracture.

Question 322. True or false: the patella may be formed from two separate bony pieces that never unite, so that a radiograph seems to show a broken bone. The answer is true. The condition is a bipartite patella, and the separate piece usually lies at the upper and lateral corner of the bone. Its margins are smooth and dense, unlike the sharp edges of a fracture.

Question 323. What is the name of the small sesamoid bone that lies in the tendon of the lateral head of the gastrocnemius behind the knee and is present in a minority of people? The answer is the fabella. It is a normal sesamoid bone and must not be mistaken for a loose body inside the knee joint.

Question 324. Which of these is an extra ossicle on the medial side of the foot, beside the tuberosity of the navicular bone: the accessory navicular, the os trigonum, the os peroneum, or the os vesalianum? The answer is the accessory navicular. It may be quite separate from the bone or joined to it by cartilage.

Question 325. An accessory navicular bone lies within a tendon on the medial side of the foot. Which tendon is it, and why does that matter? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior, which inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular. The extra bone lies inside the tendon, so the pull of the muscle can irritate the junction.

Question 326. What name is given to the separate ossicle that lies behind the talus, next to its lateral tubercle, and is present in a minority of people? The answer is the os trigonum. It begins as a separate center of bone that never joins the talus, and it can be pinched between the tibia and the calcaneus when the foot is pointed.

Question 327. Which artery is most often missing from the ring of vessels at the base of the brain: the anterior communicating artery, one posterior communicating artery, the basilar artery, or the anterior cerebral artery? The answer is one posterior communicating artery. A complete ring is found in only about one person in five.

Question 328. In a described dissection of the base of the brain the posterior cerebral artery arises from the internal carotid artery rather than from the basilar artery. What is that arrangement called? The answer is a fetal origin of the posterior cerebral artery. Most of its blood comes from the internal carotid, and the first part of the artery behind it is small.

Question 329. Which of these may arise as the last branch of the arch of the aorta and pass behind the esophagus to reach the right arm: the right common carotid artery, an aberrant right subclavian artery, the right vertebral artery, or the thyrocervical trunk? The answer is an aberrant right subclavian artery. It is the commonest anomaly of the arch.

Question 330. A constructed illustration: before an operation on the thyroid gland, imaging shows an artery passing behind the esophagus toward the right arm. Why does that finding matter to the surgeon? The answer is that the right recurrent laryngeal nerve does not recur. With no subclavian artery on that side to loop around, it runs straight from the vagus nerve to the larynx.

Question 331. What is the name of the narrow upward extension of thyroid tissue that runs from the isthmus toward the hyoid bone in many people? The answer is the pyramidal lobe. It is a remnant of the thyroglossal duct, along which the gland descended from the tongue, and it may be left behind when part of the gland is removed.

Question 332. A described magnetic resonance image of the neck shows thyroid tissue in the midline above the isthmus, reaching up toward the hyoid bone in front of the thyroid cartilage. Which structure is shown, and from what does it develop? The answer is the pyramidal lobe, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct, which marks the path the gland took as it descended.

Question 333. Which of these names an artery that ascends in the midline in front of the trachea to reach the thyroid gland: the inferior thyroid artery, the thyroidea ima artery, the superior thyroid artery, or the transverse cervical artery? The answer is the thyroidea ima artery. It usually arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, and a midline incision may meet it.

Question 334. Which of these sutures may persist into adult life as a midline seam running down the middle of the forehead: the sagittal suture, the metopic suture, the coronal suture, or the lambdoid suture? The answer is the metopic suture. It separates the two halves of the frontal bone in the child and usually closes by the end of the second year.

Question 335. A described radiograph of the skull shows a thin straight line running down the middle of the forehead. What is this line, and how is it told from a fracture? The answer is a persistent metopic suture. A suture has smooth, dense margins and lies in the midline, while a fracture has sharp and irregular edges.

Question 336. A described specimen of a skull shows a separate triangular piece of bone at the back of the vault, between the two parietal bones and above the occipital bone. What is this bone? The answer is the Inca bone, or interparietal bone. It is a separate center of ossification of the occipital bone that has not united.

Question 337. True or false: small extra bones may lie within the sutures of the skull vault, so that a suture looks broken on a radiograph. The answer is true. They are called sutural or wormian bones, and they are common along the lambdoid suture. Their rounded and dense margins separate them from the fragments of a fracture.

Question 338. True or false: the body of the sternum may contain a small opening in the midline where the two sternal bars did not fuse completely. The answer is true. It is called a sternal foramen, and it usually lies in the lower part of the body of the sternum, close to the heart and the great vessels.

Question 339. In a described specimen the transverse process of the lowest lumbar vertebra is fused to the sacrum, and the vertebra above carries the lowest free transverse process. What is this arrangement called? The answer is sacralization of the fifth lumbar vertebra, which leaves only four free lumbar vertebrae and moves the landmarks above it.

Question 340. A described radiograph of the abdomen shows a tongue of liver tissue extending below the costal margin on the right. What is this variant called? The answer is the Riedel lobe. It is a downward extension of the right lobe of the liver and is a normal variant rather than a tumor.

Question 341. Which of these describes a normal variant of the gallbladder in which the fundus is folded back on itself: a Phrygian cap, a Hartmann pouch, a double gallbladder, or an intrahepatic gallbladder? The answer is a Phrygian cap. The fold gives the fundus a rounded cap, and it does not by itself cause any symptoms.

Question 342. The appendix may lie in several positions. Which position is the commonest, with the appendix lying behind the cecum and running upward against the back wall of the abdomen? The answer is the retrocecal position. It explains why an inflamed appendix there can cause pain in the flank.

Question 343. A constructed illustration: a person has pain in the right flank and the right hip, made worse by extending the hip, and tenderness is felt deep behind the cecum. Which position of the appendix best explains the picture? The answer is a retrocecal appendix lying against the psoas muscle. Its position against that muscle is what makes stretching the hip painful.

Question 344. What is the name of the variant in which the ventral and dorsal parts of the pancreas keep separate ducts? The answer is pancreatic divisum. The two buds normally fuse and their ducts join, and when they do not, the dorsal duct drains most of the gland.

Question 345. A described magnetic resonance image of the upper abdomen shows two pancreatic ducts that do not join, the larger one opening separately into the duodenum. Which variant is shown, and which duct drains most of the gland? The answer is pancreatic divisum, in which the dorsal duct drains most of the gland through the minor papilla.

Question 346. Which of these is a remnant of the vitelline duct that hangs from the border of the ileum opposite its mesentery: a Meckel diverticulum, the Meckel cartilage, a pharyngeal pouch, or a urachal cyst? The answer is a Meckel diverticulum. It lies on the antimesenteric border of the ileum and it may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue.

Question 347. Which of these describes a left renal vein that divides and passes both in front of and behind the aorta: a retroaortic left renal vein, a circumaortic left renal vein, a double inferior vena cava, or a left-sided inferior vena cava? The answer is a circumaortic left renal vein. The ring it forms around the aorta matters when the renal vessels are clamped.

Question 348. Which of these pairs belongs together: a horseshoe kidney with fusion of the two lower poles, an accessory spleen with fusion of the two kidneys, a cervical rib with fusion of two ribs, or the Inca bone with fusion of two vertebrae? The answer is a horseshoe kidney with fusion of the two lower poles.

Question 349. Which of these pairs belongs together: an aberrant right subclavian artery with a course behind the esophagus, a thyroidea ima artery with a course beside the trachea, a pyramidal lobe with a course behind the aorta, or a cervical rib with a course behind the clavicle? The answer is an aberrant right subclavian artery with a course behind the esophagus.

Question 350. Name two muscles that may be absent in a healthy person as a normal variant. The answer is the palmaris longus and the plantaris. Neither is needed for the ordinary use of the hand or the foot, so their absence causes no weakness that a person would notice.

Question 351. Which surface landmark is formed by the ridge where the manubrium of the sternum meets its body, felt as a horizontal bar across the front of the chest? The answer is the sternal angle, also called the angle of Louis. It can be felt in everyone, and it is the starting point for counting the ribs and the intercostal spaces.

Question 352. The sternal angle lies at the level of which thoracic vertebra: the second, the fourth, the sixth, or the eighth? The answer is the fourth thoracic vertebra. The plane through the sternal angle also passes through the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, so it marks both that disc and the vertebra.

Question 353. At the sternal angle the second costal cartilage joins the sternum. Which rib therefore lies immediately below that cartilage, and which space lies below that rib? The answer is the second rib, so the space between the second and third ribs is the first one below the angle. Counting from there is how the other ribs are found.

Question 354. Which bony point forms the rounded prominence at the base of the back of the neck, felt best when the head is bent forward? The answer is the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra, called the vertebra prominens. It is the longest and most easily felt of the cervical spines.

Question 355. The highest point of the iliac crest lies at the level of which vertebra: the second lumbar, the fourth lumbar, the first sacral, or the twelfth thoracic? The answer is the fourth lumbar vertebra. The crests of the two hip bones lie on that level, and it is the level at which the lumbar spine is counted on the surface.

Question 356. The inferior angle of the scapula lies against the chest wall. At which vertebral spine does it lie when the arms hang by the sides, and which rib is at the same level? The answer is the spine of the seventh thoracic vertebra, with the seventh rib. The root of the spine of the scapula lies higher, at the third thoracic spine.

Question 357. A described photograph of a back shows a furrow down the midline, two dimples low in the back, and a rounded bony point at the base of the neck. Which structures make these marks? The answer is the spines of the vertebrae, the posterior superior iliac spines, and the seventh cervical spine. The dimples overlie the sacroiliac joints.

Question 358. Which bone can be felt in the front of the neck between the chin and the thyroid cartilage, moves when a person swallows, and lies at the level of the third cervical vertebra? The answer is the hyoid bone. It is the only bone of the body that does not articulate with another bone, being held in place by muscles and ligaments.

Question 359. The cricoid cartilage marks the start of which structure, and at which cervical vertebra does it lie: the pharynx at the fourth, the trachea at the sixth, the larynx at the third, or the esophagus at the seventh? The answer is the trachea at the sixth cervical vertebra. The cricoid is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.

Question 360. The carotid pulse is felt in the neck beside the larynx. At which level is it most easily felt, and which bony point of the sixth cervical vertebra lies just behind the artery? The answer is the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, with the carotid tubercle behind. The artery can be pressed against that tubercle.

Question 361. A constructed illustration: a midline swelling of the neck lies below the larynx and moves when the person swallows. Which membrane lies immediately beneath the skin at that point, and between which two cartilages? The answer is the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. It is the most superficial part of the airway in the neck.

Question 362. A described chest radiograph carries marks at the sternal angle, at the nipple and at the tip of the eleventh rib. Which structures lie at those three marks? The answer is the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, the fourth thoracic dermatome at the nipple, and the lowest part of the pleural cavity at the eleventh rib.

Question 363. In which intercostal space and which vertical line is the apex beat of the heart normally felt, at the point furthest down and out on the chest wall? The answer is the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. That point marks the apex of the heart, where the wall of the left ventricle comes closest to the surface.

Question 364. Where is the sound of the mitral valve best heard, and why not over the valve itself: at the apex, at the right edge of the sternum, at the left edge of the sternum, or in the second intercostal space? The answer is at the apex. The valve faces up and to the left, so its sound travels toward the apex of the heart.

Question 365. How far above the medial third of the clavicle do the apex of the lung and the cupola of the pleura reach in a healthy adult: about 1 centimeter, about 3 centimeters, about 6 centimeters, or about 10 centimeters? The answer is about 3 centimeters. Both rise above the clavicle, and the pleura reaches a little higher than the lung itself.

Question 366. What is the name of the triangular hollow on the back of the hand, bounded by the tendons of two muscles of the thumb, that appears when the thumb is fully extended? The answer is the anatomical snuffbox. The radial artery crosses its floor and can be felt there as a pulse.

Question 367. Which tendons form the boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox: the extensor pollicis longus and the abductor pollicis longus with the extensor pollicis brevis, the flexor carpi radialis and the palmaris longus, the extensor digitorum and the extensor indicis, or the flexor pollicis longus and the pronator quadratus? The answer is the extensor pollicis longus and the abductor pollicis longus with the extensor pollicis brevis.

Question 368. Which bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox: the scaphoid and the trapezium, the lunate and the triquetrum, the capitate and the hamate, or the pisiform and the triquetrum? The answer is the scaphoid and the trapezium. The radial artery crosses that floor between the tendons, and that is where its pulse is felt.

Question 369. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the outstretched hand, a person has tenderness deep in the hollow at the base of the thumb, though the radiograph looks normal. Which bone is injured, and why does it matter? The answer is the scaphoid. A branch of the radial artery enters it near its far end, so a break through the waist can starve the piece nearest the forearm.

Question 370. A described photograph of a hand shows the wrist bent, with a thin tendon in the middle of the front of the wrist and another running to the base of the thumb. Which tendons are these? The answer is the palmaris longus and the flexor carpi radialis. The palmaris longus is the one that may be absent.

Question 371. Which two bony points are joined by the inguinal ligament, felt as a ridge running across the groin? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. The ligament is the folded lower border of the tendon of the external oblique muscle.

Question 372. Which point marks the femoral pulse in the groin: the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, the mid-inguinal point halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, the pubic tubercle, or the umbilicus? The answer is the mid-inguinal point. The midpoint of the inguinal ligament lies a little medial to it and marks the deep inguinal ring.

Question 373. Which of these lies outside the femoral sheath within the femoral triangle: the femoral artery, the femoral vein, the femoral canal, or the femoral nerve? The answer is the femoral nerve. The sheath encloses the artery, the vein and the canal, while the nerve lies lateral to the artery and outside the sheath.

Question 374. A constructed illustration: a swelling appears in the groin below the inguinal ligament and just lateral to the pubic tubercle, and it enlarges when the person coughs. Which opening has it come through? The answer is the femoral canal. The femoral ring lies just medial to the femoral vein, so a swelling here lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

Question 375. A described photograph shows the back of a knee with a diamond-shaped hollow bounded by two tendons above and two muscle bellies below. Which muscles bound it, and which structure lies deepest within it? The answer is the biceps femoris and the semitendinosus above with the two heads of the gastrocnemius below. The popliteal artery lies deepest, against the bone.

Question 376. A described photograph of the back of the lower leg shows a thick cord running from the calf to the heel, standing out when the person rises on tiptoe. Which structure is shown? The answer is the calcaneal tendon, also called the Achilles tendon, which inserts into the back of the calcaneus.

Question 377. Which artery can be felt as a pulse in the groove between the back of the medial malleolus and the heel: the dorsalis pedis artery, the posterior tibial artery, the anterior tibial artery, or the fibular artery? The answer is the posterior tibial artery. It lies behind the medial malleolus, covered only by skin and a little fascia.

Question 378. Several structures pass behind the medial malleolus, between it and the calcaneus. Which lies nearest the bone, and which lies farthest from it? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior nearest the malleolus and the flexor hallucis longus farthest away. Between them lie the flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery and the tibial nerve.

Question 379. Which long vein begins at the medial end of the arch of the foot, runs up in front of the medial malleolus, and ends in the femoral vein? The answer is the great saphenous vein. It is the longest vein in the body, it lies just under the skin along its whole course, and it is often used as a graft.

Question 380. Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse felt: immediately lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus, immediately medial to that tendon, behind the lateral malleolus, or in the sole of the foot? The answer is immediately lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. Its course varies, so a missing pulse there does not prove that the artery is blocked.

Question 381. What is the name of the point on the abdominal wall, one third of the way along the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, where the appendix is usually tender? The answer is McBurney point. It overlies the base of the appendix in the usual position, though the appendix itself may lie elsewhere.

Question 382. The fundus of the gallbladder is marked on the surface at which point: the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, the tip of the twelfth rib, the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, or the level of the third lumbar spine? The answer is the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of the rectus abdominis meets the costal margin.

Question 383. Name the ribs between which the spleen lies when it is normal in size, and say which rib its long axis follows. The answer is the ninth, the tenth and the eleventh ribs, with the long axis along the tenth rib. The spleen lies behind them on the left, with its upper end close to the diaphragm.

Question 384. A constructed illustration: a person has pain under the right costal margin that worsens on deep breathing, and the pain is also felt over the right shoulder. Which organ lies beneath that point, and which nerve carries the second pain? The answer is the gallbladder, with the shoulder pain carried by the right phrenic nerve from the diaphragm.

Question 385. A described photograph of the abdomen has two vertical lines through the middle of the clavicle and two horizontal lines at the lowest ribs and the hip bones. Which scheme do those lines mark? The answer is the nine regions of the abdomen. The upper middle region is the epigastric, the central one the umbilical, and the lowest the hypogastric.

Question 386. Which plane, halfway between the upper border of the sternum and the pubic symphysis, crosses the body at the level of the first lumbar vertebra? The answer is the transpyloric plane. It lies about a hand's breadth below the sternal angle and is a useful level for finding several organs.

Question 387. Which of these lies in the transpyloric plane: the pylorus of the stomach, the fundus of the stomach, the umbilicus, or the place where the aorta divides? The answer is the pylorus. The plane also passes through the neck of the pancreas and the hila of the kidneys.

Question 388. What is the name of the angle on the back where the lower border of the twelfth rib meets the outer border of the muscle that runs up beside the spine? The answer is the renal angle. It lies over the lower pole of the kidney, and tenderness there may come from the kidney or from the pleura above it.

Question 389. A constructed illustration: a person has pain in the renal angle on the right, worse on breathing, and also felt over the right shoulder. Which two structures may be responsible? The answer is the kidney and the diaphragm, because the pleural recess lies just above the kidney. The phrenic nerve supplies both the diaphragm and the shoulder skin.

Question 390. Which spinal segment supplies the skin around the umbilicus? The answer is the tenth thoracic segment. The umbilicus lies at the level of the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, but its skin is supplied by the tenth thoracic nerve, because the segments do not follow the skeleton.

Question 391. Which dermatome includes the skin of the nipple: the second thoracic, the fourth thoracic, the sixth thoracic, or the eighth thoracic? The answer is the fourth thoracic. The dermatomes run around the trunk in bands, and the nipple is the classic landmark for the fourth thoracic segment.

Question 392. Which dermatome supplies the skin over the great toe and the inner side of the sole: the third lumbar, the fourth lumbar, the fifth lumbar, or the first sacral? The answer is the fifth lumbar. The first sacral segment supplies the outer border of the foot and the little toe, and the fourth lumbar supplies the skin over the medial malleolus.

Question 393. A described map of the hand shades three sensory territories: the little finger and the inner border, the thumb and the outer border, and the middle of the palm. Which nerves supply them? The answer is the ulnar nerve for the inner border, the radial nerve for the outer border, and the median nerve for the middle of the palm.

Question 394. True or false: the skin of the nipple lies in the fourth thoracic dermatome. The answer is true. The fourth thoracic nerve supplies a band that runs around the chest at the level of the nipple, over the pericardium and the pleura within.

Question 395. True or false: the skin around the umbilicus is supplied by the twelfth thoracic dermatome. The answer is false. The umbilicus lies in the tenth thoracic dermatome, while the twelfth thoracic segment supplies the skin just above the pubic symphysis. The two levels are easily confused because both lie near the front of the abdomen.

Question 396. Which of these pairs belongs together: the seventh cervical spine with the vertebra prominens, the fourth lumbar spine with the sternal angle, the seventh thoracic spine with the angle of the jaw, or the second sacral segment with the iliac crest? The answer is the seventh cervical spine with the vertebra prominens. The sternal angle lies at the fourth thoracic vertebra and the iliac crest at the fourth lumbar.

Question 397. Which of these pairs belongs together: the posterior tibial pulse with the groove behind the medial malleolus, the dorsalis pedis pulse with the groove behind the lateral malleolus, the popliteal pulse with the front of the knee, or the radial pulse with the front of the elbow? The answer is the posterior tibial pulse with the groove behind the medial malleolus. The other three are paired with the wrong surface.

Question 398. Which of these pairs belongs together: the femoral triangle with the inguinal ligament above, the popliteal fossa with the inguinal ligament above, the cubital fossa with the calcaneal tendon below, or the anatomical snuffbox with the mastoid process above? The answer is the femoral triangle with the inguinal ligament above. The popliteal fossa lies behind the knee and the cubital fossa in front of the elbow.

Question 399. Name the two bony points that are joined by the inguinal ligament, the ridge felt across the groin. The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. The ligament forms the floor of the groin and the upper boundary of the femoral triangle.

Question 400. A described section of the trunk is taken across the chest at the level of the sternal angle, and it shows the heart, both lungs and the vertebral column in cross section. In which plane is the section taken, and which disc does that plane mark? The answer is a transverse plane, at the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae.

To summarize, variation is normal, and the commonest variants each carry a name worth knowing: the horseshoe kidney whose isthmus is caught below the inferior mesenteric artery, the accessory spleen, the cervical rib, the pelvic kidney, the missing palmaris longus or plantaris, the accessory navicular within the tendon of the tibialis posterior, the posterior communicating artery that fails to complete the ring at the base of the brain, the aberrant right subclavian artery behind the esophagus, the pyramidal lobe of the thyroid gland, and the pancreatic divisum that leaves most of the gland draining through the minor papilla. Accessory bones such as the fabella, the os trigonum and the bipartite patella have smooth, dense margins that separate them from fractures, and persistent sutures such as the metopic suture and the wormian bones look the same. On the surface, the sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage and the fourth thoracic vertebra, the iliac crest marks the fourth lumbar vertebra, the inferior angle of the scapula marks the seventh thoracic spine, and the cricoid cartilage marks the sixth cervical vertebra. The femoral pulse lies at the mid-inguinal point, the popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, the dorsalis pedis artery is felt lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus, and the structures behind the medial malleolus run outward from the tibialis posterior to the flexor hallucis longus. Dermatomes close the list: the fourth thoracic at the nipple, the tenth thoracic at the umbilicus, the fifth lumbar over the great toe, and the first sacral along the outer border of the foot. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 5 — Imaging and Anatomical Orientation

This chapter is about finding structures on the surface of the body and about reading the pictures that show them inside it. It begins with the surface markings that can be felt or seen, and then turns to X-ray films, computed tomography, known as CT, magnetic resonance imaging, known as MRI, and ultrasound. It explains what a sagittal, a coronal and an axial image each show, and it names the bony landmarks that fix the level of every picture. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 401. Which ridge felt on the front of the chest marks the junction of the manubrium with the body of the sternum? The answer is the sternal angle, at the level of the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. The second costal cartilage joins the sternum there, so rib counting begins at that ridge.

Question 402. The transpyloric plane is a horizontal plane used to describe the upper abdomen. At which vertebral level does it lie: the twelfth thoracic, the first lumbar, the third lumbar, or the fifth lumbar? The answer is the first lumbar vertebra. The plane passes through the pylorus of the stomach and the neck of the pancreas, near the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.

Question 403. Which plane is drawn across the back through the highest points of the two iliac crests? The answer is the supracristal plane, at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra. It is the surface guide for choosing a level to sample cerebrospinal fluid, low enough that the spinal cord has ended.

Question 404. The umbilicus is a familiar landmark in the middle of the abdominal wall. Which vertebral level does it mark in the adult? The answer is the disc between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae. The level shifts with body build, so it is only an approximate guide.

Question 405. Which structure can be felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis: the femoral vein, the femoral artery, the femoral nerve, or the femoral canal? The answer is the femoral artery. The vein lies at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, medial to the artery, and the nerve lies most lateral.

Question 406. The inguinal ligament is a surface landmark at the groin. Which two bony points do its ends join? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. It is the folded lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, and the femoral vessels pass beneath its midpoint.

Question 407. A described photograph taken from behind shows a bony point in the midline at the base of the neck, most obvious when the head is bent forward. Which structure is shown? The answer is the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra. Its spine is the longest of the cervical spines, with the first thoracic spine just below.

Question 408. A constructed illustration: after a heavy object falls on the top of the foot, the pulse on the instep can no longer be felt. Between which two tendons is that pulse normally found? The answer is the tendon of extensor hallucis longus and the tendon of extensor digitorum longus. The dorsalis pedis artery runs between them.

Question 409. Which artery can be felt in the hollow at the base of the thumb when the wrist is drawn back? The answer is the radial artery, in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The hollow is bounded by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis on one side and extensor pollicis longus on the other.

Question 410. The surface point used to mark the appendix lies on a line between the umbilicus and the right anterior superior iliac spine. Where on that line does it lie: one third from the umbilicus, one half, two thirds, or at the iliac spine? The answer is two thirds of the way from the umbilicus, one third of the way up from the iliac spine. That point is named after McBurney.

Question 411. Which surface region lies between the twelfth rib and the outer border of the erector spinae muscle, and overlies the lower part of the kidney? The answer is the renal angle. Tenderness there points to disease of the kidney behind the peritoneum, whose lower pole lies nearest the surface at that spot.

Question 412. The line along which the pleura turns from the chest wall onto the diaphragm can be traced on the surface. Which rib does it cross in the midclavicular line, and which at the side of the chest? The answer is the eighth rib in the midclavicular line and the tenth rib in the midaxillary line. Behind, it reaches the twelfth rib.

Question 413. A constructed illustration: a clinician must choose a level to sample cerebrospinal fluid while keeping clear of the spinal cord. Which spinous process is identified by the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests? The answer is the fourth lumbar spine. The cord usually ends above it, at the first or second lumbar vertebra.

Question 414. A duct crosses the cheek and opens inside the mouth. Which tooth does it lie opposite: the upper first incisor, the upper second molar, the lower first molar, or the lower second incisor? The answer is the upper second molar. That duct is the parotid duct, and it crosses the masseter muscle before turning inward.

Question 415. Which cartilage of the larynx forms a complete ring and can be felt in the midline below the laryngeal prominence? The answer is the cricoid cartilage, at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra. The soft membrane between it and the thyroid cartilage above is the cricothyroid membrane.

Question 416. True or false: in an adult man the nipple usually lies over the fourth intercostal space. The answer is true. The position varies with body build, and greatly in women, so the sternal angle remains the more dependable guide to the fourth rib.

Question 417. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sternal angle with the eighth thoracic vertebra, the xiphisternal joint with the ninth thoracic vertebra, the highest point of the iliac crest with the second lumbar vertebra, or the pubic symphysis with the fifth lumbar vertebra? The answer is the xiphisternal joint with the ninth thoracic vertebra. The sternal angle lies at the fourth thoracic vertebra and the iliac crest at the fourth lumbar.

Question 418. A constructed illustration: a person with a fever is examined for an enlarged spleen, and percussion in the lowest part of the left axilla, below the tenth rib, becomes dull where it was resonant. Which organ has enlarged into that space? The answer is the spleen. It lies behind the stomach and the left costal margin and descends toward the left iliac fossa.

Question 419. Which rib forms the lowest point of the costal margin at the front of the abdomen: the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, or the tenth? The answer is the tenth. The margin is formed by the cartilages of the seventh to the tenth ribs, and the eleventh and twelfth ribs float free.

Question 420. Which joint at the lower end of the sternum can be felt in the midline as a small depression, and at which vertebral level does it lie? The answer is the xiphisternal joint, at the level of the ninth thoracic vertebra. It is where the xiphoid process joins the body of the sternum.

Question 421. A described photograph of a wrist held slightly bent shows a prominent tendon running to the base of the second metacarpal, with a pulse just lateral to it. Which tendon and which artery are shown? The answer is the tendon of flexor carpi radialis and the radial artery. Both cross the front of the wrist, the artery lateral to the tendon.

Question 422. The beat of the heart is sought on the chest wall. In which space does it usually appear: the third intercostal space at the sternal edge, the fourth in the midclavicular line, the fifth in the midclavicular line, or the sixth in the anterior axillary line? The answer is the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, where the right ventricle comes closest to the chest wall.

Question 423. A described area on the back is bounded above by the trapezius, laterally by the medial border of the scapula, and below by the latissimus dorsi. Which triangle is described, and why is it useful? The answer is the triangle of auscultation. Over it the chest wall is thin and free of muscle, so breath sounds are heard there with least interference.

Question 424. The great saphenous vein can be traced on the surface from the foot upward. Which side of the medial malleolus does it pass, and where does it join the deep venous system? The answer is that it passes in front of the medial malleolus and opens into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening in the thigh.

Question 425. The oblique fissure of the lung can be marked on the surface. From which vertebral spine does it begin behind, and which costal cartilage does it reach in front? The answer is the spine of the third thoracic vertebra and the sixth costal cartilage. The horizontal fissure runs forward from it along the fourth costal cartilage.

Question 426. On a plain X-ray film, four substances are compared. Which appears whitest because it blocks the beam most completely: air, fat, muscle, or metal? The answer is metal. Bone is the whitest natural tissue and air casts almost no shadow, so air appears black.

Question 427. What name is given to a structure that appears white on a radiograph because it absorbs the beam, and what name to one that appears black? The answer is radiopaque for the white structure and radiolucent for the black one. Bone is radiopaque and air is radiolucent, with fat between them.

Question 428. A described chest radiograph shows a white area in the right lung that has erased the outline of the right border of the heart, while the right half of the diaphragm is still sharp. Which lobe is consolidated: the upper, the middle, the lower, or the whole lung? The answer is the right middle lobe, which lies against the right heart border. The lower lobe lies against the diaphragm.

Question 429. A described radiograph of the chest shows a dense white area in the right lower zone that hides the outline of the right half of the diaphragm but leaves the right heart border clear. Which lobe is affected? The answer is the right lower lobe. It rests on the diaphragm and lies behind the middle lobe.

Question 430. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows two curved domes and a dark bubble of gas below one of them. Which dome lies higher, and which organ lies immediately beneath it? The answer is the right dome, with the liver beneath it. The left dome lies lower, with the stomach and spleen beneath.
