Question 431. A constructed illustration: a person falls on the outstretched hand and is tender in the hollow at the base of the thumb. Which bone is most likely broken there, and which artery crosses the floor of that hollow? The answer is the scaphoid, with the radial artery crossing the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. A break through the waist threatens the blood supply to the proximal part.

Question 432. Which of these pairs belongs together: air with the density of water, fat with the density of bone, water with the middle of the density scale, or bone with the density of air? The answer is water with the middle of the density scale. Air, fat, water, bone and metal shade from black to white in that order, so the other pairs are reversed.

Question 433. True or false: the heart looks larger on a chest radiograph taken with the beam passing from the front to the back than on one taken from the back to the front. The answer is true. When the beam travels from front to back the heart lies far from the film, so its shadow is thrown larger.

Question 434. A described lateral radiograph of the neck shows a small peg of bone rising from the second cervical vertebra into the ring of the first. Which structure is the peg, and which vertebra carries it? The answer is the dens of the axis, carried by the second cervical vertebra. The first cervical vertebra turns around it when the head rotates.

Question 435. What name is given to the branching dark pattern of air-filled airways seen against a white area of consolidated lung on a radiograph? The answer is an air bronchogram. The bronchi still hold air while the tissue around them has taken on the density of water, as in pneumonia and pulmonary edema.

Question 436. A described chest radiograph shows a white area in the left lung that has erased the left border of the heart while leaving the left half of the diaphragm sharp. Which part of the left lung lies against that border: the apical segment, the lingula, or one of the basal segments? The answer is the lingula, a tongue-like part of the left upper lobe, while the basal segments lie against the diaphragm.

Question 437. On the scale of density used in CT, which substance is chosen as the zero point? The answer is water. Air lies far below it at the black end of the scale and dense bone far above at the white end, so the scale runs from very negative numbers to very positive ones.

Question 438. A CT scan of the body is displayed with different window settings. Which setting shows the cortex of a bone best: the soft tissue window, the lung window, the bone window, or the brain window? The answer is the bone window. It stretches the small differences between dense tissues, while the others render bone uniformly white.

Question 439. A CT scan of the head is taken soon after an injury. Fresh blood in the cranial cavity appears how: darker than brain tissue, the same shade, brighter than brain tissue, or completely black? The answer is brighter than brain tissue. Fresh clotted blood is denser than brain, so it is called hyperdense, and it darkens as the clot ages.

Question 440. A described axial CT image of the chest shows a collection of air with a straight inner edge lying against the chest wall, and the lung compressed behind it. What is the collection? The answer is air in the pleural cavity, a pneumothorax. It is black because it has the density of air, and the straight edge is the pleural surface of the lung.

Question 441. A described axial CT image of the upper abdomen shows two vessels lying immediately in front of a vertebral body, one on each side of the midline. Which vessel lies to the left, and which to the right? The answer is the aorta on the left and the inferior vena cava on the right. The vena cava lies more anteriorly, against the liver.

Question 442. A constructed illustration: an older person falls, and a CT scan shows a crescent-shaped collection hugging the curve of one cerebral hemisphere, crossing the sutures, with the midline pushed aside. Which vessels have torn, and where has the blood collected? The answer is the bridging veins, which have bled into the subdural space. A crescent crosses suture lines, while an extradural collection is lens-shaped and stops at them.

Question 443. Name the two natural substances of the body that lie at the opposite ends of the density scale used in CT, one black and one white. The answer is air and bone. Air absorbs almost none of the beam and bone absorbs a great deal, while fat and water lie between them.

Question 444. A described CT image shows bright and dark lines radiating from a small metallic object and spoiling the picture around it. What is this appearance called: a partial volume effect, a streak artifact, a window setting, or a contrast phase? The answer is a streak artifact. The dense object absorbs the beam so unevenly that the reconstruction invents lines.

Question 445. A described CT image of the upper abdomen shows a long lobulated organ lying across the midline behind the stomach, with its tail reaching toward the spleen. Which organ is described, and what lies behind its neck? The answer is the pancreas, with the formation of the portal vein behind its neck. Its head lies within the curve of the duodenum.

Question 446. A described CT image of the pelvis shows a rounded structure in the midline, a hip joint on each side, and a dark collection of gas and feces behind it. Which structure lies in the midline: the uterus, the filled urinary bladder, the rectum, or the prostate? The answer is the filled urinary bladder. Urine has the density of water and appears gray, while the gas behind it is almost black.

Question 447. What name is given to the first image of a CT examination, a single view of the whole region taken so that the technologist can choose the levels of the slices to follow? The answer is the scout image, also called the topogram. It is a plain projection rather than a cross-section, and it carries markers that give each slice its level.

Question 448. On a T1-weighted magnetic resonance image, which tissue appears bright and which fluid appears dark? The answer is that fat appears bright and water appears dark. A T1-weighted image is the one on which anatomical detail is clearest, and cerebrospinal fluid is black on it.

Question 449. Which of these appears brightest on a T2-weighted magnetic resonance image: fat, muscle, cerebrospinal fluid, or cortical bone? The answer is cerebrospinal fluid. A T2-weighted image is the one on which fluid stands out, so it shows the fluid-filled spaces, while bone stays black.

Question 450. Which of these findings matters most before a magnetic resonance examination: a healed fracture of the wrist, a cardiac pacemaker, a history of asthma, or a tattoo on the arm? The answer is a cardiac pacemaker. A strong magnetic field can move or heat metal inside the body, so metal implants and electronic devices must be identified beforehand.

Question 451. A described sagittal magnetic resonance image of the knee shows a dark band running obliquely through the joint from the front of the tibia to the back of the femur. Which structure is that band? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur and is dark on both weightings.

Question 452. Which tissue of the body yields almost no signal on any magnetic resonance sequence, so that it is black whatever settings are used? The answer is cortical bone. It has very few mobile protons for the machine to detect, and air behaves in the same way, while marrow is bright because it contains fat.

Question 453. A described magnetic resonance image of the shoulder shows a muscle running above the head of the humerus and passing beneath a bony arch. Which muscle is it, and through which space does its tendon pass? The answer is the supraspinatus, whose tendon passes beneath the acromion through the subacromial space. That tendon is the one most often torn.

Question 454. A magnetic resonance image is taken with a setting that removes the signal of fat, so that a structure containing water stands out against the marrow. What is that setting called: the T1 weighting, the T2 weighting, fat suppression, or the scout view? The answer is fat suppression. It shows inflammation and fluid in bone and soft tissue, where fat would otherwise hide them.

Question 455. On a described magnetic resonance image of the spine, which structure lies within the vertebral canal immediately in front of the spinal cord: the ligamentum flavum, the posterior longitudinal ligament, the interspinous ligament, or the anterior longitudinal ligament? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. The ligamentum flavum lies behind the cord, and the anterior longitudinal ligament on the front of the vertebral bodies.

Question 456. Name two tissues that appear dark on both a T1-weighted and a T2-weighted magnetic resonance image. The answer is cortical bone and air. Neither contains enough mobile protons to give a signal, and flowing blood can appear dark in the same way.

Question 457. A constructed illustration: a described magnetic resonance image shows a rounded mass enlarging the pituitary fossa, and the structure above it is stretched and pushed upward. Which structure lies immediately above the pituitary gland? The answer is the optic chiasm. The gland sits in the sella turcica, and the chiasm above it is pressed on as the gland enlarges.

Question 458. What term describes a structure on an ultrasound scan that returns no echoes at all and appears completely black, such as the fluid in the gallbladder? The answer is anechoic. Simple fluid is anechoic, while solid organs such as the liver return many small echoes and appear gray.

Question 459. On a described ultrasound scan of the upper abdomen, which of these appears completely black with no internal echoes: the liver, the spleen, the pancreas, or the gallbladder full of bile? The answer is the gallbladder full of bile. Fluid returns no echoes, while the solid organs return a texture of gray echoes.

Question 460. A described ultrasound scan shows a bright curved line within the gallbladder, and behind it the echoes disappear into a dark band. What is that band: acoustic enhancement behind fluid, acoustic shadowing behind a stone, a window setting, or a streak artifact? The answer is acoustic shadowing behind a stone, because the stone reflects the sound and stops it reaching the tissues beyond.

Question 461. A described ultrasound scan shows a round dark structure within the kidney, and the echoes behind it are brighter than those beside it. What is the structure, and why are the echoes behind it brighter? The answer is a simple cyst, and the brightness is posterior acoustic enhancement. Sound passes more easily through fluid than through the tissue around it.

Question 462. A described ultrasound scan uses the Doppler effect to examine a vessel. What does the shift in frequency of the returning echoes show: the density of the tissue, the direction and speed of blood flow, the depth of the organ, or its temperature? The answer is the direction and speed of blood flow. Blood moving toward the probe shifts the echoes up in frequency, and blood moving away shifts them down.

Question 463. A constructed illustration: a described ultrasound scan of the thigh shows a dark tubular structure that does not flatten when the probe presses on it, while the artery beside it does. What has happened within that vessel? The answer is a clot within a deep vein. A normal vein collapses under gentle pressure, so a vein that stays open is the sign of thrombosis.

Question 464. On a described ultrasound scan of the neck, the lobe of the thyroid gland lies against the side of the trachea. Which large vessel lies immediately lateral to that lobe, and what lies immediately medial to it? The answer is the common carotid artery laterally and the trachea medially. The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the artery.

Question 465. A described ultrasound scan of the heart is taken with the probe on the upper abdomen and shows four chambers. Which chamber lies nearest the probe: the left atrium, the right atrium, the left ventricle, or the right ventricle? The answer is the right ventricle, the most anterior chamber of the heart. The left atrium is the most posterior.

Question 466. Which plane produces a sagittal image: one that divides the body into upper and lower parts, one that divides it into right and left parts, one that divides it into front and back parts, or one that cuts across a limb? The answer is a plane that divides the body into right and left parts. It runs from front to back, and the one through the midline is the median plane.

Question 467. Which band of white matter is seen in the midline on a sagittal image of the brain, arching above the thalamus and joining the two hemispheres? The answer is the corpus callosum. Only a section close to the midline shows it in this way, and the third ventricle lies below it.

Question 468. A described sagittal image of the head shows a bony hollow in the base of the skull, with a rounded gland inside it and an air space beneath. Which gland is shown, and in which bone does it lie? The answer is the pituitary gland, in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone.

Question 469. On a described sagittal image of the male pelvis, which structure lies immediately in front of the rectum and immediately behind the pubic symphysis? The answer is the urinary bladder. The prostate gland lies below the bladder, and the sacrum and coccyx lie behind the rectum.

Question 470. On a described sagittal image of the ankle, which bone lies directly above the calcaneus and carries the weight of the body onto the foot: the navicular, the talus, the cuboid, or the first metatarsal? The answer is the talus. It sits between the leg bones above and the calcaneus below and forms the ankle joint with the tibia.

Question 471. A described midline sagittal image of the chest shows a long muscular tube running down behind the windpipe and in front of the vertebral column. Which structure is shown, and what lies in front of it below? The answer is the esophagus, with the trachea in front of it above and the left atrium in front of it below.

Question 472. True or false: a sagittal image taken through the middle of the head shows the two cerebral hemispheres side by side in the same picture. The answer is false. A midline section lies between the hemispheres and shows the medial surface of each, so the two are never displayed side by side.

Question 473. A described section of the trunk shows the heart and one lung, with the vertebral column behind and the front of the chest wall in front, and only one kidney is visible. Which plane produced it, and why is it not the median plane? The answer is a parasagittal plane, cut to one side of the midline. A median section would lie between the lungs and show neither of them in section.

Question 474. Which plane divides the body into an anterior part and a posterior part: the sagittal plane, the coronal plane, the transverse plane, or the oblique plane? The answer is the coronal plane. It runs from side to side and from top to bottom, so the section is viewed from the front or from behind.

Question 475. A described coronal image of the abdomen shows the two kidneys on either side of the midline and two long vessels running down in front of the vertebral column. Which vessels are they, and which lies on the right? The answer is the aorta and the inferior vena cava, with the vena cava on the right.

Question 476. A described coronal magnetic resonance image of the brain shows the two lateral ventricles above a narrow channel that joins the third ventricle to the fourth. Which structure is that channel? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct, which runs through the midbrain. It is the narrowest part of the ventricular system, so it blocks most easily.

Question 477. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the face, clear fluid drips from the nose, and a described coronal CT image shows a break in the thin roof of the nasal cavity with air inside the skull. Which bone is broken? The answer is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The fibers of smell pass through it, so a break there may cost the sense of smell.

Question 478. On a described coronal image of the chest, the trachea divides into two main bronchi below the arch of the aorta. Which main bronchus is wider and more nearly in line with the trachea, and what lies immediately above the left one? The answer is the right main bronchus, with the arch of the aorta above the left. A swallowed object therefore enters the right bronchus more often.

Question 479. A described coronal image of the knee shows the medial meniscus. What is its shape, and to what is its outer edge attached: circular and free, C-shaped and attached to the medial collateral ligament, O-shaped and attached to the tibia, or flat and attached to the patellar tendon? The answer is C-shaped and attached to the medial collateral ligament, so a tear of that ligament often tears the meniscus too.

Question 480. A described coronal image of the upper abdomen shows the stomach in the middle, with the liver on one side and the spleen on the other. Which space lies immediately behind the stomach and in front of the pancreas: the greater sac, the lesser sac, the pleural cavity, or the retroperitoneal space? The answer is the lesser sac, also called the omental bursa.

Question 481. What name is given to the plane that cuts across the body at right angles to its long axis and produces a cross-sectional image? The answer is the axial plane, also called the transverse plane. A series of such slices, one below another, builds the pictures of a CT or MRI examination.

Question 482. On a described axial CT image of the head at the level of the thalamus, which space lies in the midline between the two lateral ventricles: the fourth ventricle, the third ventricle, the subarachnoid space, or the cerebral aqueduct? The answer is the third ventricle, a narrow slit of fluid between the two halves of the thalamus. The aqueduct lies below it, in the midbrain.

Question 483. A described axial CT image of the chest shows a small rounded structure lying against the right side of a thoracic vertebral body. Which vein is it, and where does it end? The answer is the azygos vein, which arches forward over the right main bronchus to join the superior vena cava.

Question 484. A described axial magnetic resonance image of the thigh shows three groups of muscle separated by dark bands of fascia. Which group lies at the back, and which nerve runs among its muscles? The answer is the posterior compartment, with the sciatic nerve between its muscles. The anterior compartment holds the quadriceps and the medial one the adductors.

Question 485. On a described axial CT image of the neck, the lobe of the thyroid gland lies beside the trachea. Which structures lie within the sheath that runs immediately lateral to the gland? The answer is the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve. The artery lies medial to the vein.

Question 486. On a described axial image at the level of the first lumbar vertebra, two vessels lie in front of the vertebral body. Which two are they: the aorta on the right and the vena cava on the left, the aorta on the left and the vena cava on the right, the portal and splenic veins, or the common iliac arteries? The answer is the aorta on the left and the inferior vena cava on the right. The vena cava lies the more anterior of the two.

Question 487. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the temple, a person is briefly stunned and then deteriorates, and a described axial CT image shows a lens-shaped collection between the skull and the brain, with the midline pushed aside. Which vessel has torn, and where does the blood lie? The answer is the middle meningeal artery, with blood in the extradural space. A lens shape that stops at the sutures marks it.

Question 488. On a described axial image of the upper abdomen, the neck of the pancreas lies immediately in front of which vessel: the aorta, the inferior vena cava, the superior mesenteric vein, or the left renal artery? The answer is the superior mesenteric vein, where it joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. The superior mesenteric artery arises behind the neck of the gland.

Question 489. On a described axial image of the male pelvis, a fold of peritoneum dips down between the bladder in front and the rectum behind. What is that pouch called? The answer is the rectovesical pouch. In the female the same fold dips between the bladder and the uterus and is called the rectouterine pouch.

Question 490. Which bony point in the midline of the back of the head is easily felt, and which muscle attaches to it? The answer is the external occipital protuberance, to which the trapezius attaches. It lies at the upper end of the furrow between the two sides of the back of the neck.

Question 491. A described image of the hip shows the greater trochanter of the femur. At the level of which structure of the pelvis does its tip lie: the anterior superior iliac spine, the pubic tubercle, the sacral promontory, or the fifth lumbar vertebra? The answer is the pubic tubercle. The trochanter lies about a hand's breadth below the highest point of the iliac crest.

Question 492. Which of these landmarks fixes the level of the second thoracic vertebra on the front of the chest: the jugular notch of the sternum, the sternal angle, the xiphisternal joint, or the fifth costal cartilage? The answer is the jugular notch of the sternum. The sternal angle lies two vertebrae lower, at the fourth thoracic vertebra.

Question 493. True or false: the words cephalad and caudad describe a direction, cephalad toward the head and caudad toward the feet. The answer is true. They are used to speak of the direction in which one image follows another, so a series taken from the feet upward runs cephalad.

Question 494. True or false: on an axial image displayed in the standard radiological convention, the left side of the picture is the patient's left side. The answer is false. An axial image is viewed from below, as though the observer stood at the patient's feet, so the patient's left appears on the right of the picture.

Question 495. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sagittal plane with the front and back parts, the coronal plane with the right and left parts, the axial plane with the upper and lower parts, or the oblique plane with two equal halves? The answer is the axial plane with the upper and lower parts. A sagittal plane divides the body into right and left and a coronal plane into front and back.

Question 496. Which of these pairs belongs together: CT with detailed bone structure, magnetic resonance imaging with detailed bone structure, ultrasound with the lungs beyond the chest wall, or a plain X-ray film with the spinal cord? The answer is CT with detailed bone structure. Magnetic resonance imaging shows soft tissue better, and ultrasound cannot see through bone or air.

Question 497. Which of these pairs belongs together: the coronal plane with a view from above, the axial plane with a view from below, the sagittal plane with a view from the front, or the oblique plane with a view from one side? The answer is the axial plane with a view from below, the standard convention for axial images. A coronal image is viewed from the front and a sagittal image from one side.

Question 498. A constructed illustration: a person is tender over the middle of the front of the wrist, and a described image shows the bone lying at the center of the carpal arch, between the scaphoid and the hamate. Which bone is it? The answer is the capitate, the largest bone of the wrist. Its head carries the third metacarpal bone.

Question 499. Name the two substances that lie between air and bone on the scale of density used in radiology, spoken in order from black to white. The answer is fat and water. Fat is only slightly denser than air, and water with soft tissue lies between fat and bone.

Question 500. A described image is cut in a plane that passes through the body at an angle, so that the right side of the skull and the left side of the jaw appear in the same picture. Which kind of plane produced it? The answer is an oblique plane. It cuts across all three reference planes at once, so it cannot be called sagittal, coronal or axial.

To summarize, the surface of the body carries landmarks that fix the level of everything beneath it: the sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage at the fourth thoracic vertebra, the transpyloric plane lies at the first lumbar vertebra, and the highest points of the iliac crests mark the fourth lumbar vertebra. On a radiograph the tissues shade from black to white in the order air, fat, water, bone and metal, and the silhouette sign tells which lobe of a lung lies against a lost border, while CT measures density in numbers and shows bone better than any other method. Magnetic resonance imaging uses no ionizing radiation, shows water brightly on a T2-weighted image and fat brightly on a T1-weighted one, and ultrasound returns no echoes from fluid and casts a shadow behind a stone. A sagittal image divides the body into right and left parts, a coronal image into front and back parts and an axial image into upper and lower parts, and the standard convention shows the patient's left on the right of an axial picture.

# Chapter 6 — General Osteology

This chapter examines bone as a tissue and as an organ, from the cells that build and dissolve it to the regions of a long bone and the marks that its attachments leave on the surface. It covers the structure of bone, the difference between compact and spongy bone, the periosteum, the endosteum, the medullary cavity, and the epiphysis, the metaphysis and the diaphysis, and it closes with the bone markings that a listener can name from a description. It holds one hundred questions in that order, and each gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is right. Nothing needs to be held in mind, and nothing needs to be looked at, because each item describes what a section or a radiograph would show. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 501. Which living cell of bone lies within a small cavity in the matrix, maintains the matrix around it, and communicates with its neighbors through fine channels? The answer is the osteocyte. A cell that buries itself in the matrix it has made becomes an osteocyte and lies in a lacuna. Its processes run in canaliculi, so it is fed without leaving its cavity.

Question 502. Which of these cells dissolves bone matrix and releases the mineral stored in it: the osteoblast, the osteocyte, the osteoclast, or the osteoprogenitor cell? The answer is the osteoclast. It is a large multinucleated cell formed by the fusion of monocyte precursors, and it sits in a shallow pit that it has eaten into the bone.

Question 503. A described ground section of compact bone shows a central hole surrounded by a series of rings, with small dark spaces lying between the rings. Which unit of bone is being described? The answer is the osteon. Its central canal carries a small vessel and a nerve, and the rings are concentric lamellae. The small spaces are the lacunae that hold the osteocytes.

Question 504. What name is given to the lengthwise channel that runs through the middle of each osteon and carries its blood vessel? The answer is the central canal. Each canal is lined by endosteum and holds a small vessel and a nerve fiber. Neighboring canals are joined by perforating canals that cross the cortex.

Question 505. Which substance gives the matrix of bone most of its hardness and its resistance to compression: collagen fibers, calcium phosphate in the form of hydroxyapatite, water, or the fat of the marrow? The answer is calcium phosphate in the form of hydroxyapatite. The crystals lie along and between the collagen fibers and give bone its stiffness, and the collagen gives it tensile strength.

Question 506. Within the wall of a long bone, the vessel in the periosteum reaches the central canal of a deeper osteon by which route, and how do those canals run? The answer is by the perforating canals, which cross the cortex at right angles to the long axis. They join the canals of neighboring osteons and reach the deepest part of the wall.

Question 507. Which part of the matrix lets a bone bend without breaking and so resists pulling forces: the mineral crystals, the collagen fibers, the ground substance, or the fat of the marrow? The answer is the collagen fibers. They make up about one third of the dry weight of the matrix and lie in a felted pattern. A bone with defective collagen becomes brittle.

Question 508. Which fine channels connect one lacuna to the next and allow the processes of neighboring osteocytes to meet? The answer is the canaliculi. They are very small tunnels radiating from each lacuna in every direction. The processes inside them touch at gap junctions, so the osteocytes reach the vessels of the central canal.

Question 509. Which of these statements about the mineral of bone is correct: it is calcium carbonate, it is sodium chloride, it is calcium phosphate laid down as hydroxyapatite, or it is pure calcium? The answer is calcium phosphate laid down as hydroxyapatite. The crystals lie in and around the collagen fibers, and their presence is what makes a bone cast a dense white shadow on a radiograph.

Question 510. A described section of a shaft wall shows several systems of rings, each with its own canal, and between them irregular patches of lamellae that belong to no single canal. Lamellae also lie flat against the outer and inner surfaces. What are the irregular patches called? The answer is interstitial lamellae. They remain from older osteons that have been partly removed during remodeling.

Question 511. True or false: the osteocytes lie in lacunae and communicate with one another through canaliculi rather than by direct contact of their cell bodies. The answer is true. Each cell body occupies its own small cavity, and only the thin processes leave it. The arrangement feeds the cell inside a hard matrix.

Question 512. Which cell of bone produces the unmineralized organic matrix that is called osteoid? The answer is the osteoblast. Osteoblasts line the surfaces of growing or remodeling bone and secrete collagen and ground substance. Mineral is laid down in the osteoid soon afterwards, and a cell buried in it becomes an osteocyte.

Question 513. Around which structure do the concentric lamellae of an osteon lie, and how is that structure supplied? The answer is the central canal, which holds a small blood vessel and a nerve. The lamellae are laid down around it, so the innermost lies nearest the vessel. Perforating canals join it to the vessels of the periosteum and the marrow.

Question 514. Which of these is the origin of the osteoclast: the osteoblast, the osteocyte, the periosteal fibroblast, or the fusion of monocyte precursors? The answer is the fusion of monocyte precursors. The osteoclast is a large cell with several nuclei and a ruffled border, and it belongs to the same family as the macrophage.

Question 515. True or false: about two thirds of the dry weight of bone matrix is mineral and about one third is organic material. The answer is true. The mineral is calcium phosphate in the form of hydroxyapatite, and the organic part is mainly collagen with ground substance. The proportion changes a little with age and with the bone examined.

Question 516. A described specimen taken from a healing fracture shows a disorganized meshwork of collagen with many irregular cells and no orderly rings. Which kind of bone is shown, and what is its fate? The answer is woven bone, also called immature bone. It is laid down quickly and is weak, so it is later replaced by lamellar bone.

Question 517. In which part of a long bone is the compact bone thickest: the epiphysis, the diaphysis, the metaphysis, or the medullary cavity? The answer is the diaphysis. Its wall is a tube of compact bone, thickest at the middle of the shaft, where bending forces are greatest.

Question 518. What name is given to the thin plates of bone that form the lattice of spongy bone? The answer is the trabeculae. They run in many directions and cross one another, leaving spaces that hold marrow. Each is only a few cell layers thick, so its cells are fed by diffusion.

Question 519. A described radiograph of the upper end of the femur shows a fine crisscross pattern of lines running through the neck. What does that pattern represent? The answer is the trabeculae of spongy bone arranged along the lines of stress. One group carries compression from the head toward the shaft, and another resists tension along the upper surface.

Question 520. Which statement about spongy bone is correct: it is built of trabeculae with marrow spaces, it is built of closely packed osteons, it lies only on the outer surface of a long bone, or it contains no cells? The answer is trabeculae with marrow spaces between them. Spongy bone fills the ends of long bones and the interior of flat and short bones.

Question 521. In the upper end of a long bone, which kind of bone lies immediately deep to the articular cartilage, and where does the compact bone lie? The answer is spongy bone, with a thin shell of compact bone at the surface. The trabeculae carry the load inward to the cortex, and the shell is thin because the force is spread widely.

Question 522. Which of these contains the greatest amount of compact bone: the body of a vertebra, the shaft of the tibia, the sternum, or the calcaneus? The answer is the shaft of the tibia. A shaft carries bending and twisting forces and needs a thick cortical wall, while the vertebral body and the calcaneus are mainly spongy bone and the sternum is spongy bone between thin tables.

Question 523. What name is given to the layer of spongy bone that lies between the two compact tables of a flat bone of the skull? The answer is the diploe. The outer table is thicker and curves smoothly, and the inner table is thin and brittle. A blow can crack the inner table without breaking the outer one.

Question 524. Which statement about the trabeculae of spongy bone is correct: they contain no lamellae, they are lamellar but do not form osteons, they remain woven bone throughout life, or they contain no living cells? The answer is that they are lamellar but do not form osteons. Their lamellae lie in flat or slightly curved plates, and the cells are fed by diffusion from the marrow.

Question 525. A described section of a shaft wall shows tightly packed rings, while a section from the upper end shows a loose network of thin plates. Which tissue is shown in each place? The answer is compact bone in the shaft wall and spongy bone in the upper end. The two are the same tissue arranged differently, each following the forces it must carry.

Question 526. A constructed illustration: a limb kept in a cast for weeks afterwards shows a thinner cortex and a wider marrow cavity on a radiograph. Which surface has been resorbed, and which bone has lost the most material? The answer is the endosteal surface, with the greatest loss from spongy bone, because bone that is not loaded is removed by osteoclasts. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 527. Which name is given to the dense outer layer of bone, the layer that forms the thick wall of a shaft and is also called cortical bone? The answer is compact bone. It is built of osteons packed closely together, with lamellae filling the spaces between them. Its density makes it appear white on a radiograph.

Question 528. In the wall of a shaft, which vessels supply the outer part of the cortex and which vessel supplies the inner part? The answer is the periosteal vessels for the outer part and the nutrient artery for the inner part. The nutrient artery enters the marrow cavity and sends branches outward through the endosteum, and the two supplies meet within the cortex.

Question 529. Which statement about the direction of the trabeculae is correct: they run at random, they follow the lines of stress, they lie only vertically, or they parallel the periosteum? The answer is that they follow the lines of stress. In the neck of the femur one group carries compression and another resists tension, and their crossing pattern keeps the bone strong while light.

Question 530. A constructed illustration: a vertebral body in an older person loses height under a moderate load while the cortex of the long bones stays intact. Why does the vertebral body fail first? The answer is that it is built mainly of spongy bone, whose trabeculae have a large surface area and are lost early when bone mass falls.

Question 531. A described radiograph of the spine shows the vertebral bodies with prominent vertical lines and a loss of the fine horizontal lines between them. Which tissue has been lost, and why do the vertical lines stand out? The answer is spongy bone, in which the horizontal trabeculae are lost first. The remaining vertical trabeculae carry the load and so appear more prominent.

Question 532. Which membrane covers the outer surface of a bone everywhere except where the bone is covered by articular cartilage? The answer is the periosteum. It is a tough fibrous sheath firmly fixed to the bone surface. It is absent from the articular surfaces and from sesamoid bones such as the patella.

Question 533. Which of these describes the two layers of the periosteum: an outer fibrous layer and an inner osteogenic layer, two fibrous layers, an inner fibrous layer and an outer bony layer, or a single layer of cartilage? The answer is an outer fibrous layer and an inner osteogenic layer. The outer layer is fibrous tissue with vessels and nerves, and the inner layer, the cambium, holds the osteoprogenitor cells.

Question 534. A described radiograph of a growing bone shows a tumor near the surface, with the membrane lifted off the cortex and a small triangle of new bone at the edge of the lifted membrane. Which structure has been raised? The answer is the periosteum. Its inner layer lays down new bone as it is pushed from the cortex, and that calcified new bone forms the triangle.

Question 535. Which fibers pass from a tendon through the periosteum and into the outer lamellae of the cortex, and what do they achieve? The answer is the perforating fibers, also called Sharpey fibers. They anchor the tendon so that the pull is spread over a wide area. The periosteum itself is fixed to the cortex the same way.

Question 536. Which of these surfaces of a bone is not covered by periosteum: the shaft of the tibia, the articular surface of the head of the femur, the outer surface of the ilium, or the mastoid process? The answer is the articular surface of the head of the femur. That surface is covered by hyaline cartilage instead, and periosteum is also absent from sesamoid bones.

Question 537. What is the name of the inner layer of the periosteum, the layer that contains the cells able to form new bone? The answer is the osteogenic layer, also called the cambium layer. It lies against the bone, deep to the fibrous layer. Its osteoprogenitor cells give rise to the osteoblasts that widen a bone and heal a fracture.

Question 538. A constructed illustration: a person is struck on the front of the shin, where the bone lies just under the skin, and the pain is severe although a radiograph shows no break. Which structure is injured? The answer is the periosteum. It is richly supplied with pain fibers, unlike the bone beneath it. A small bleed raises the membrane and causes sharply localized tenderness.

Question 539. Which statement about the periosteum in a child is correct: it is thicker and more active than in an adult, it is thinner and inactive, it is absent from all bones, or it is replaced by cartilage? The answer is that it is thicker and more active. Its osteogenic layer is busy widening the shaft throughout growth.

Question 540. A described dissection shows a membrane being lifted from the shaft of a bone; it comes away easily in the middle but stays fixed at the two ends. What is the membrane, and what holds it at each end? The answer is the periosteum, held at the joint margin where the cartilage begins and by the fibers of the tendons and ligaments that blend into it.

Question 541. The outer layer of the periosteum is built of which tissue, and what does it contain? The answer is dense irregular connective tissue, carrying blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves. Its fibers run in several directions, so the layer resists a pull from any direction.

Question 542. Which statement about the cortical blood supply is correct: periosteal vessels feed the outer part and the nutrient artery the inner part, the nutrient artery feeds only the marrow, the marrow feeds all the cortex, or the cortex has none? The answer is that periosteal vessels supply the outer part and the nutrient artery the inner part. The two sets meet within the cortex, so the wall survives when one route fails.

Question 543. In a growing bone, with which covering of the cartilaginous end is the periosteum continuous, and where does that covering stop? The answer is the perichondrium, the fibrous layer over the cartilage, with which the periosteum is continuous. The covering stops at the joint margin, where the articular cartilage is left bare.

Question 544. A constructed illustration: a direct blow lifts the periosteum from the shaft of the femur and blood collects beneath it in a long thin sheet. Which space has filled, and why does the blood not enter the marrow? The answer is the subperiosteal space between the membrane and the cortex. The cortex is intact, so the blood stays outside it.

Question 545. Which thin membrane lines the medullary cavity and covers the surfaces of the trabeculae inside a bone? The answer is the endosteum. It is one cell thick and has no fibrous layer. It also lines the central canals of the osteons and the perforating canals.

Question 546. Which of these best describes the endosteum: a single thin layer of cells with osteoprogenitor cells and osteoclasts, a tough sheet of dense connective tissue, a layer of hyaline cartilage, or a plate of compact bone? The answer is a single thin layer of cells. It contains flattened osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts, and osteoclasts lie against it where bone is removed.

Question 547. A described section shows the inner surface of the cortex and the surface of every trabecula lined by a thin sheet one cell thick, with marrow on one side and bone on the other. Which membrane is shown? The answer is the endosteum. It is seen on every internal surface, and that surface is very large.

Question 548. A constructed illustration: an older person who has been confined to bed loses bone, and the radiograph shows a thin cortex with a wide marrow cavity. Which surface is being resorbed to produce this change? The answer is the endosteal surface. Osteoclasts working there enlarge the cavity from within.

Question 549. Which statement about the endosteum is correct: it lines the canals inside compact bone as well as the marrow cavity, it covers only the outer surface, it is a layer of cartilage, or it is present only in children? The answer is that it lines the canals inside compact bone as well as the marrow cavity, reaching the deepest part of the cortex.

Question 550. Which cells lie against the endosteum where bone is being broken down, and what do they do to dissolve the mineral? The answer is the osteoclasts, which pump acid and enzymes into a sealed pocket against the matrix. The mineral dissolves in the acid and the collagen is digested. The cell then moves on, leaving a shallow pit.

Question 551. The periosteum covers the outer surface of the cortex and the endosteum its inner surface; where are the two layers continuous with each other? The answer is at the openings through which vessels pass and within the perforating canals. The lining follows the vessel as it crosses the cortex, so the internal and external surfaces share one cellular lining.

Question 552. True or false: the endosteum is a tough fibrous sheet that can be lifted from the bone in the same way as the periosteum. The answer is false. The endosteum is a thin layer of cells with no fibrous coat, so it cannot be peeled away.

Question 553. What name is given to the space that runs through the shaft of a long bone and contains the marrow? The answer is the medullary cavity, also called the marrow cavity. It is bounded by the cortex and lined by endosteum, and in an adult it holds mainly fat.

Question 554. Which of these is the main function of the red marrow in the medullary cavity: fat storage, blood cell formation, mineral storage, or the growth of cartilage? The answer is blood cell formation. Red marrow produces red cells, white cells and platelets, and yellow marrow stores fat.

Question 555. A described section along a shaft shows a hollow tube of dense bone around a central space filled with fatty tissue and a few darker islands. What is the space, and what fills it? The answer is the medullary cavity, filled mainly with yellow marrow and holding islands of red marrow, which can form blood cells when the need arises.

Question 556. A constructed illustration: after severe blood loss the fatty marrow of the long bones becomes active again and forms blood cells. Which cavity is involved? The answer is the medullary cavity. Yellow marrow can turn back into red marrow when the demand is high, giving the body extra surface for making new cells.

Question 557. In an adult, which of these sites holds red marrow: the shaft of the tibia, the sternum and the vertebral bodies, the middle of the femur, or the medullary cavity of the radius? The answer is the sternum and the vertebral bodies. Red marrow persists in the skull, ribs, sternum, vertebrae and pelvis, and in the upper ends of the femur and humerus.

Question 558. Which opening in the cortex of a long bone admits the artery that supplies the marrow? The answer is the nutrient foramen. The artery runs a slanting course through the cortex into the marrow cavity, and the canal points away from the growing end of the bone.

Question 559. Which of these pairs belongs together: red marrow with fat storage, yellow marrow with blood cell formation, red marrow with blood cell formation, or the medullary cavity with articular cartilage? The answer is red marrow with blood cell formation. Red marrow is the blood forming tissue of the adult skeleton, and yellow marrow stores fat.

Question 560. Which statement about the marrow of a young child is correct: the medullary cavities hold red marrow throughout, the cavities are filled with air, the cavities hold cartilage, or the cavities are empty? The answer is that they hold red marrow throughout. All the marrow of the skeleton is red at birth and forms blood cells, and yellow marrow appears later in the shafts.

Question 561. In the shaft of a long bone, which structures lie between the marrow cavity and the skin, in order from the cavity outward? The answer is the endosteum, then the compact bone of the cortex, then the periosteum. The endosteum lines the cavity, the cortex forms its wall, and the periosteum wraps the outer surface.

Question 562. A described radiograph of a long bone shows a dark band running down the middle of the shaft, wider in the middle than at the ends. What is the band, and why is it dark? The answer is the medullary cavity. Marrow contains much fat and little mineral, so it absorbs fewer x-rays than bone and appears dark on the film.

Question 563. In which of these bones does a true medullary cavity fail to develop: the humerus, the femur, the sternum, or the tibia? The answer is the sternum. Flat and short bones are built of spongy bone with marrow spaces between the trabeculae and have no central cavity.

Question 564. Which part of a long bone is the expanded end that lies beyond the growth plate and ossifies from its own center? The answer is the epiphysis. It carries the articular surface of the joint. Its own center of ossification appears after birth and fuses with the shaft when growth ends.

Question 565. Which kind of cartilage covers the articular surface of an epiphysis: hyaline cartilage, fibrocartilage, elastic cartilage, or calcified cartilage? The answer is hyaline cartilage. It is smooth and tough and has no blood vessels of its own, being nourished by the synovial fluid that bathes the joint.

Question 566. A described radiograph of a child's knee shows a dark band across the end of the femur, and beyond it a rounded mass of bone with its own outline. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the epiphyseal plate, which is the dark band, and the epiphysis beyond it. The plate is cartilage, so it absorbs fewer x-rays than bone.

Question 567. A constructed illustration: an adolescent feels sudden hip pain, and the radiograph shows the head of the femur still in its socket while the neck and shaft have shifted. Which structure gave way? The answer is the epiphyseal plate. The head is the epiphysis, and it has slipped on the plate while the metaphysis and shaft moved. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 568. Which statement about the blood supply of the growing epiphysis is correct: vessels cross the growth plate freely, the epiphysis has vessels of its own, the plate supplies it, or it has no blood supply? The answer is that the epiphysis has vessels of its own that do not cross the plate, which is why an infection of the shaft seldom reaches the joint.

Question 569. What name is given to an epiphysis that serves only as the attachment of a tendon and takes no part in a joint, such as the greater trochanter? The answer is a traction epiphysis, or apophysis. It grows in response to the pull of the muscle attached to it. The tibial tuberosity is another example.

Question 570. In a growing long bone the epiphyseal plate separates two regions; which lies on the joint side of the plate and which on the shaft side? The answer is the epiphysis on the joint side and the metaphysis on the shaft side. Growth in length occurs at the plate, so the epiphysis is pushed away from the shaft. When growth stops, the plate becomes a line.

Question 571. In the adult, what remains at the site of a closed epiphyseal plate: a band of hyaline cartilage, a thin line of bone called the epiphyseal line, a gap filled with marrow, or a layer of periosteum? The answer is a thin line of bone, the epiphyseal line. It marks where the plate lay and can often be seen on a radiograph.

Question 572. Name the two cartilages that lie in the region of the epiphysis of a growing long bone. The answer is the articular cartilage at the joint surface and the epiphyseal plate at its base. The cartilage covers the joint for life, and the plate is the site of growth in length.

Question 573. Which vessels supply the epiphysis of a growing bone, and which supply the metaphysis on the other side of the plate? The answer is the epiphyseal arteries for the epiphysis and the metaphyseal arteries for the metaphysis. The metaphyseal vessels are branches of the nutrient artery of the shaft.

Question 574. A constructed illustration: an infection begins in the shaft and spreads to the metaphysis but does not enter the joint. Which structure has held it back? The answer is the epiphyseal plate, which is avascular cartilage. In the older child it bars the way from the metaphysis to the epiphysis and the joint, while in a newborn the vessels cross it.

Question 575. What is the name of the region of a long bone that lies between the epiphyseal plate and the shaft? The answer is the metaphysis. It is the flared part of the shaft next to the plate. In the adult its site is marked by the epiphyseal line.

Question 576. Which of these is found in the metaphysis of a growing bone: the zone where calcified cartilage is replaced by bone, the smooth articular surface, the nutrient foramen, or the fibrous layer of the periosteum? The answer is the zone where calcified cartilage is replaced by bone. The metaphysis is the region of most active bone formation in the growing skeleton.

Question 577. A described longitudinal section of a growing bone shows a band of cartilage across the end, and below it a zone of bony spicules that widen into the shaft. Which two regions are shown below the joint? The answer is the epiphyseal plate and the metaphysis. The band is the plate, and the zone of new bone beneath it is the metaphysis.

Question 578. A constructed illustration: a tumor of bone arises in an adolescent at the lower end of the femur, just above the knee. Which region is the usual site, and why? The answer is the metaphysis. It is the region of fastest cell division in the growing skeleton, which is why a bone tumor is more common in a growing person than in an adult.

Question 579. Which statement about the metaphyseal arteries is correct: they are branches of the nutrient artery and end in loops at the plate, they supply the epiphysis, they cross the plate, or they supply the joint cartilage? The answer is that they are branches of the nutrient artery ending in loops at the plate, where the flow is slow and infection is favored.

Question 580. True or false: the metaphysis lies between the epiphyseal plate and the shaft, and it becomes the flared end of the shaft in the adult. The answer is true. In the child the metaphysis is the zone of newly formed bone next to the plate, and when growth ends the plate closes and the metaphysis merges with the epiphysis.

Question 581. Which of these pairs belongs together: the epiphysis with the growth plate, the metaphysis with the flare of bone next to the plate, the diaphysis with the joint surface, or the medullary cavity with the periosteum? The answer is the metaphysis with the flare of bone next to the plate. The epiphysis is the part beyond the plate and the diaphysis is the shaft.

Question 582. Which pair belongs together: the epiphyseal plate with the region between the epiphysis and the shaft, the epiphyseal line with the closed plate of the adult, the metaphysis with the smooth joint surface, or the endosteum with the outer surface of the bone? The answer is the epiphyseal line with the closed plate of the adult, which is the scar the plate leaves behind.

Question 583. Which statement about the diaphysis of a long bone is correct: it is the shaft, a tube of compact bone around the cavity, it is the end next to the joint, it is a plate of cartilage, or it is a thin shell of spongy bone? The answer is that it is the shaft, a tube of compact bone with a wall thickest in the middle.

Question 584. A described radiograph of a long bone shows a thick white tube, widest at its middle, with the ends expanding into a lacework of bone. Which region is the white tube, and what is its wall made of? The answer is the diaphysis, and its wall is compact bone. The cortex is thickest at the middle of the shaft, where bending forces are greatest.

Question 585. What name is given to the shaft of a long bone, the part that lies between the two ends? The answer is the diaphysis. It is built of compact bone around the medullary cavity, and it develops from the primary center of ossification. Its periosteum carries the vessels that supply the outer part of its wall.

Question 586. A cut is made straight across the middle of the diaphysis of a long bone. Which layers does the cut pass through, from the outside inward? The answer is the periosteum, the compact bone of the cortex, the endosteum, and then the medullary cavity with its marrow. The cut meets compact bone all around the cavity, and no spongy bone is present at that level.

Question 587. Name, in order from one end to the other, the three regions into which the length of a long bone is divided. The answer is the epiphysis, the metaphysis, the diaphysis, and then the metaphysis and the epiphysis of the other end. The epiphyses lie nearest the joints, the metaphyses flank the shaft, and the diaphysis is the shaft itself.

Question 588. In the development of a long bone, around which part of the cartilage model does the bony collar form, and which part of the adult bone does that collar become? The answer is that it forms around the middle of the model and becomes the diaphysis. Bone is laid down in the perichondrium there before the primary center appears. The ends stay cartilage and ossify later.

Question 589. What name is given to a large rounded projection on a bone that gives attachment to a muscle, such as the one on the humerus for the deltoid? The answer is a tuberosity. A smaller and sharper projection of the same kind is a tubercle. Both are marks left by the pull of a muscle or a ligament.

Question 590. Which of these is a depression in a bone that lodges another structure: a fossa, a process, a crest, or a tubercle? The answer is a fossa. A process, a crest and a tubercle are projections rather than depressions. The olecranon fossa of the humerus lodges the tip of the ulna when the elbow straightens.

Question 591. A described radiograph of the lower end of the femur shows two rounded masses separated by a deep notch, with a rough prominence above each. Which markings are described? The answer is the two condyles with the intercondylar fossa between them, and the epicondyles above. The condyles are smooth articular surfaces, while the epicondyles give attachment to ligaments.

Question 592. A constructed illustration: a blow to the outer side of the knee forces the joint inward, and the ligament attached to the inner side of the lower femur is torn. Which marking anchors that ligament? The answer is the medial epicondyle, a roughened projection just above the medial condyle. The ligament attached to it holds the joint against a force from the outer side.

Question 593. Which of these markings is a passage through bone for a vessel or a nerve: a foramen, a spine, a crest, or a tuberosity? The answer is a foramen. A nutrient foramen admits the artery of the marrow, and other foramina admit nerves and veins. A spine, a crest and a tuberosity are projections.

Question 594. Which of these pairs belongs together: a foramen with a passage for a vessel or a nerve, a fossa with a smooth surface, a crest with a hole, or a tubercle with a groove? The answer is a foramen with a passage for a vessel or a nerve. A fossa lodges a structure, a crest is a ridge, and a tubercle is a small projection.

Question 595. What name is given to a prominent ridge of bone that gives attachment to muscles and fascia, such as the ridge along the top of the hip bone? The answer is a crest. A smaller ridge is called a line. Both are raised marks produced where a muscle or a sheet of fascia pulls on the bone.

Question 596. Which of these is a small, smooth, flat or slightly concave surface where one bone meets another: a facet, a tubercle, a spine, or a foramen? The answer is a facet. A facet is covered by cartilage and takes part in a joint or in a sliding contact. A tubercle and a spine are projections, and a foramen is an opening.

Question 597. True or false: the size and the roughness of a bone marking usually reflect the size and the pull of the muscle attached there. The answer is true. A large muscle, or one that pulls at a poor mechanical advantage, leaves a larger mark. The mark grows through life as the bone responds to the load it carries.

Question 598. Which of these pairs belongs together: the greater trochanter with the attachment of hip muscles, the fovea with a nerve passage, the notch with a smooth joint surface, or the meatus with a pad of fat? The answer is the greater trochanter with the attachment of hip muscles. A fovea is a small pit and a notch is a depression at the edge of a bone.

Question 599. Name three kinds of opening or depression found on bones, with one example of each. The answer is a foramen, such as the nutrient foramen of a long bone, a fossa, such as the olecranon fossa of the humerus, and a groove, such as the groove on the back of the humerus for the radial nerve. Each lodges or transmits a named structure.

Question 600. Which statement about bone markings is correct: they are arbitrary, they record the attachments and passages of the bone, they appear only in old age, or they bear no relation to function? The answer is that they record the attachments, passages and articulations of the bone. A projection marks a pull, an opening marks a passage, and a smooth surface marks a joint.

To summarize, bone is a living tissue whose cells lie in lacunae and keep in touch through canaliculi, with osteoblasts forming the matrix, osteocytes maintaining it and osteoclasts dissolving it. Its matrix is about one third organic, mainly collagen, and two thirds mineral, the collagen giving toughness and the mineral hardness. Compact bone is built of osteons whose concentric lamellae surround central canals joined by perforating canals, while spongy bone is a lattice of trabeculae that follow the lines of stress. The periosteum covers the outside of a bone except at the articular surfaces, the endosteum lines every internal surface, and the medullary cavity holds the marrow. A long bone is divided into the epiphysis beyond the growth plate, the metaphysis next to it, and the diaphysis or shaft, and every bone is written over with the markings of its muscles, vessels and joints, from tuberosities and crests to foramina and fossae. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 7 — Cranial Bones

Bone has a small vocabulary of shapes, and this chapter tests that vocabulary before it turns to the bones of the skull. The first half covers general osteology: the processes that project from a bone, the tuberosities that give a tendon its grip, the condyles that carry a joint surface, the fossae that hold a neighbor, and the foramina that let vessels and nerves pass. The second half works through five cranial bones, the frontal, the parietal, the temporal, the occipital and the sphenoid. It holds one hundred questions, and every one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 601. Which term describes a projection that stands out from the surface of a bone, such as the spinous process of a vertebra? The answer is a process. A process grows out from the body or the shaft of a bone. Most processes give attachment to a muscle, a tendon or a ligament, and some also take part in a joint.

Question 602. Which of these is a process of the temporal bone: the mastoid process, the coronoid process, the olecranon process, or the xiphoid process? The answer is the mastoid process, the rounded projection felt behind the ear. The coronoid process belongs to the ulna and to the mandible, the olecranon process to the ulna, and the xiphoid process to the lower end of the sternum.

Question 603. In a vertebra, which process projects backward in the midline, and which two project to the sides? The answer is the spinous process behind and the transverse processes at the sides. The spinous process can be felt down the middle of the back. Each transverse process carries a facet for a rib in the thoracic region.

Question 604. The zygomatic arch is built from two processes. Which one forms its front part: the temporal process of the zygomatic bone, the zygomatic process of the temporal bone, the frontal process of the maxilla, or the mastoid process? The answer is the temporal process of the zygomatic bone, which meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone behind it.

Question 605. Which slender, pointed process hangs down from the under surface of the temporal bone, just in front of the mastoid process? The answer is the styloid process. Several small muscles of the tongue and the throat take origin from it, and the stylohyoid ligament runs from its tip to the hyoid bone. It is long in some people and short in others.

Question 606. The styloid process lies in which direction from the mastoid process, and which large vessel lies just medial to its tip? The answer is that it lies anterior and medial to the mastoid process, with the internal carotid artery just medial to its tip. The internal jugular vein lies lateral to that artery in the same sheath.

Question 607. A constructed illustration: an elongated styloid process is felt through the wall of the tonsillar fossa during an examination of the throat, and its tip lies beside the internal carotid artery. Which structure is being felt, and which vessel lies next to it? The answer is the styloid process, beside the internal carotid artery. This elongation is a variation and is usually without symptoms.

Question 608. A described radiograph of the elbow taken from the side shows a beak-shaped projection at the front of the upper end of the ulna, fitting into a hollow of the humerus when the arm is bent. Which structure is shown? The answer is the coronoid process of the ulna. It lies below the trochlear notch and is received by the coronoid fossa.

Question 609. Which process of the scapula forms the outer point of the shoulder and can be felt under the skin: the acromion, the coracoid process, the glenoid process, or the styloid process? The answer is the acromion, the flattened process that continues the spine of the scapula. The coracoid process lies in front of it and is covered by muscle.

Question 610. Name two processes of the temporal bone, spoken as a list. The answer is the mastoid process and the styloid process. The mastoid process is the rounded projection behind the ear canal, and the styloid process is the slender spike in front of it. The zygomatic process of the same bone forms the back of the cheek arch.

Question 611. A described dissection of the upper arm shows a rough elevation on the lateral surface of the middle of the humerus, where the deltoid muscle pulls on the bone. Which structure is shown? The answer is the deltoid tuberosity. It is a roughened area rather than a spike, which is what gives a muscle a firm grip on the shaft.

Question 612. On the upper end of the radius, which rounded roughened area receives the tendon of the biceps brachii? The answer is the radial tuberosity. It lies just below the neck of the radius, on the side that faces the ulna. The tendon of the biceps brachii turns around the bone to reach it.

Question 613. Which of these pairs belongs together: the radial tuberosity with the radius, the deltoid tuberosity with the ulna, the ischial tuberosity with the femur, or the tibial tuberosity with the fibula? The answer is the radial tuberosity with the radius. The deltoid tuberosity lies on the humerus, the ischial tuberosity on the hip bone, and the tibial tuberosity on the tibia.

Question 614. Which bony prominence of the hip bone bears the weight of the body in sitting and gives origin to the hamstring muscles behind the thigh? The answer is the ischial tuberosity, at the lower and back part of the hip bone. A bursa separates it from the skin, which is why it can be sat upon for long periods.

Question 615. A constructed illustration: a person reports soreness at the lowest point of the buttock after a long ride on a hard seat. Which bony structure is being pressed, and what lies between that bone and the skin? The answer is the ischial tuberosity, with a bursa between the bone and the skin. The bursa is a normal cushion.

Question 616. Which prominence stands out on the front of the upper end of the tibia, just below the knee, and receives the patellar ligament? The answer is the tibial tuberosity, the bony point felt below the kneecap. The tendon of the quadriceps muscle continues over the patella and attaches here.

Question 617. Which of these is a tubercle rather than a tuberosity: the greater tubercle of the humerus, the deltoid tuberosity, the radial tuberosity, or the ischial tuberosity? The answer is the greater tubercle of the humerus. A tubercle is a smaller rounded prominence, and a tuberosity is a larger one. Both tubercles of the humerus lie at its upper end.

Question 618. A described radiograph of the knee from the side shows a raised bony point on the front of the upper end of the tibia, separated from the shaft by a line that has not yet closed in a growing child. Which structure is shown? The answer is the tibial tuberosity, whose own center of bone joins the shaft in the late teens.

Question 619. The ischial tuberosity lies in which direction from the acetabulum, and which strong ligament is attached to its upper border? The answer is that it lies below and behind the acetabulum, and the sacrotuberous ligament is attached to its upper border. That ligament runs up to the sacrum and helps to close the lesser sciatic notch.

Question 620. Why does the deltoid tuberosity lie on the lateral surface of the humerus while the radial tuberosity faces medially? The answer is that each lies in the line of pull of its own muscle. The deltoid pulls on the shaft from the side, and the tendon of the biceps brachii crosses to the medial side of the radius.

Question 621. What is the name for the smooth, rounded articular surface at the end of a bone, such as the two at the lower end of the femur? The answer is a condyle. A condyle is covered with hyaline cartilage and takes part in a joint. It differs from a process, which is a projection for the attachment of soft tissue.

Question 622. Which two structures at the lower end of the femur are smooth, rounded and covered with cartilage for the knee joint? The answer is the medial condyle and the lateral condyle. They are separated behind by the intercondylar fossa and in front by a shallow groove for the patella.

Question 623. Which of these is a condyle: the occipital condyle, the mastoid process, the deltoid tuberosity, or the styloid process? The answer is the occipital condyle. The two occipital condyles lie on either side of the foramen magnum and articulate with the first cervical vertebra. The other three are processes or a tuberosity.

Question 624. Between the two condyles of the femur, which depression lies behind, and what crosses it? The answer is the intercondylar fossa, crossed by the cruciate ligaments. The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments pass through it in the middle of the knee. In front the two condyles are joined by a smooth surface for the patella.

Question 625. Which rounded projection forms the part of the mandible that fits into the joint with the temporal bone: the coronoid process, the condylar process, the angle of the mandible, or the mental protuberance? The answer is the condylar process, whose rounded head is the condyle of the mandible. The coronoid process lies in front of it.

Question 626. A described radiograph of the knee from the front shows two large rounded shadows at the lower end of the femur, separated in the middle by a notch. Which structures are shown? The answer is the medial and lateral condyles of the femur, with the intercondylar fossa between them. The shadow of the patella overlaps them in this view.

Question 627. A constructed illustration: a fall onto the point of the chin drives the lower jaw backward, and the force is carried along the bone. Which part of the mandible is most likely to break, and why? The answer is the neck of the mandible, below the condyle. It is the thinnest part of the bone on that path.

Question 628. Which statement about a condyle is correct: it is covered with hyaline cartilage, it is a rough area for tendon attachment, it is a hole for a vessel, or it is a depression that holds a nerve? The answer is that it is covered with hyaline cartilage, which lets the two surfaces of a joint glide on one another. A rough area for a tendon is a tuberosity.

Question 629. True or false: the occipital condyles lie on either side of the foramen magnum and articulate with the first cervical vertebra. The answer is true. Each condyle is a rounded surface that meets the corresponding facet of the atlas. This joint allows the head to nod, while turning the head happens lower down.

Question 630. In the knee seen from the front, which condyle of the femur lies nearer the midline, and which structure separates the two condyles at the back? The answer is the medial condyle, with the intercondylar fossa between them behind. The medial condyle reaches farther down than the lateral one, which is why the femur stands slightly oblique.

Question 631. Which hollow on the back of the lower end of the humerus receives the tip of the olecranon when the elbow is straightened? The answer is the olecranon fossa. It is a deep depression just above the trochlea, and the bone forming its floor is thin. The olecranon slides into it as the arm straightens.

Question 632. A described radiograph of the lower end of the humerus from the front shows two shallow hollows above the trochlea, one in the middle and one to the outer side. Which structures are shown? The answer is the coronoid fossa in the middle and the radial fossa to the outer side. The coronoid process and the head of the radius enter them when the elbow bends.

Question 633. Which of these is a depression on the scapula: the supraspinous fossa, the olecranon fossa, the iliac fossa, or the acetabular fossa? The answer is the supraspinous fossa, which lies above the spine of the scapula and holds the supraspinatus muscle. The olecranon fossa lies on the humerus, the iliac fossa on the hip bone.

Question 634. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraspinous fossa with the scapula, the olecranon fossa with the hip bone, the iliac fossa with the knee, or the acetabular fossa with the shoulder? The answer is the supraspinous fossa with the scapula. The infraspinous fossa lies below the spine of the same bone, and the subscapular fossa on its front.

Question 635. Which of these is a broad, smooth hollow on the inner surface of the hip bone that gives origin to a muscle of the same name: the iliac fossa, the olecranon fossa, the coronoid fossa, or the radial fossa? The answer is the iliac fossa, which gives origin to the iliacus muscle and forms part of the wall of the false pelvis.

Question 636. In a described radiograph of the straight elbow taken from behind, the tip of the ulna lies in a hollow in the lower end of the humerus. Which hollow is it, and what happens when the elbow bends? The answer is the olecranon fossa. When the elbow bends, the olecranon leaves it and the coronoid process enters the hollow in front.

Question 637. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the elbow the arm cannot be straightened fully, and a described radiograph shows a small piece of bone resting in the hollow behind the lower humerus. Which hollow is involved? The answer is the olecranon fossa, because the loose fragment blocks the tip of the olecranon from entering it.

Question 638. Which of these fossae lies inside the socket of the hip joint and does not bear weight: the acetabular fossa, the iliac fossa, the olecranon fossa, or the supraspinous fossa? The answer is the acetabular fossa, a depression at the bottom of the acetabulum. It holds fat and the ligament of the head of the femur, while the horseshoe-shaped surface around it takes the load.

Question 639. Which of these pairs belongs together: the olecranon fossa with the elbow, the iliac fossa with the ankle, the acetabular fossa with the shoulder, or the popliteal fossa with the wrist? The answer is the olecranon fossa with the elbow. The iliac fossa belongs to the hip bone, the acetabular fossa to the hip joint, and the popliteal fossa to the back of the knee.

Question 640. Name the three cranial fossae, from front to back, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior cranial fossa, the middle cranial fossa and the posterior cranial fossa. The front of the cranial base lies highest and the back lies lowest, so the floor steps down as it runs backward.

Question 641. What is the name for an opening or a passage through a bone, through which vessels and nerves travel? The answer is a foramen, and its plural is foramina. A foramen may be a short hole or a long canal. The skeleton is full of them, including one between each pair of vertebrae.

Question 642. Which opening in the occipital bone is the largest foramen in the body, and what passes through it? The answer is the foramen magnum. The medulla oblongata and its membranes pass through it, and so do the two vertebral arteries and the eleventh cranial nerve. The spinal cord becomes the medulla just above this opening.

Question 643. The vertebral arteries enter the skull through which opening: the foramen magnum, the jugular foramen, the foramen ovale, or the optic canal? The answer is the foramen magnum. The two arteries climb through the openings in the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae and then turn inward to reach it. The jugular foramen carries the internal jugular vein.

Question 644. The intervertebral foramina lie between which parts of neighboring vertebrae, and what passes through each one? The answer is that each lies between the lower part of one vertebral body and the upper part of the next, behind the disc, and a spinal nerve passes through it. The opening is bounded behind by the facet joint.

Question 645. A constructed illustration: a disc between two lumbar vertebrae bulges backward and to one side, narrowing the opening through which a spinal nerve leaves the canal. Which opening is narrowed, and which structure is compressed? The answer is the intervertebral foramen, and the spinal nerve within it is compressed.

Question 646. Which of these statements about the obturator foramen is correct: it lies below and in front of the acetabulum, it transmits the sciatic nerve, it lies above the hip socket, or it is a joint surface? The answer is that it lies below and in front of the acetabulum. It is bounded by the pubis and the ischium and carries the obturator nerve and vessels.

Question 647. A described radiograph of the pelvis shows a large oval opening on each side, below and in front of the rounded socket of the hip joint. Which structure is shown, and which nerve passes through it? The answer is the obturator foramen, with the obturator nerve passing through its upper part. The opening is closed by a fibrous membrane that the nerve pierces.

Question 648. The jugular foramen lies between which two cranial bones, and which large vein runs through it? The answer is that it lies between the occipital bone and the temporal bone, and the internal jugular vein runs through it. The ninth, tenth and eleventh cranial nerves also pass through it, just behind the carotid canal.

Question 649. True or false: a foramen and a fossa both describe an opening in bone. The answer is false. A foramen is an opening through which something passes, while a fossa is a shallow depression that holds a neighboring structure. The olecranon fossa holds the tip of the ulna, and the foramen magnum lets the spinal cord pass.

Question 650.
