The answer is the deep muscles of the back. Fat and vessels lie between them and the bone. The ligament is the deepest layer of the back wall.

Question 1085. Which ligament runs along the tips of the spinous processes from the seventh cervical vertebra down to the sacrum? The answer is the supraspinous ligament. It links the spines in the midline and is felt as a firm cord in the lower back. In the neck it is replaced by a broader sheet.

Question 1086. Which sheet of elastic tissue takes the place of the supraspinous ligament in the neck and gives attachment to muscles: the ligamentum nuchae, the ligamentum flavum, the interspinous ligament, or the posterior longitudinal ligament? The answer is the ligamentum nuchae. It runs from the skull down to the spines of the cervical vertebrae. It checks forward bending of the head.

Question 1087. A constructed illustration: a neck is forced suddenly into full backward bending. Which long ligament on the front of the bodies is stretched and may tear? The answer is the anterior longitudinal ligament. It lies against the front of the discs and bodies. Behind the torn ligament lie the disc and the body of the vertebra.

Question 1088. True or false: the ligamentum flavum is made largely of elastic fibers and helps the column to straighten after it has been bent forward. The answer is true. Its elastic recoil assists the return to the upright position. That same elasticity lets it stretch and fold instead of buckling.

Question 1089. Which membrane closes the space between the occipital bone above and the posterior arch of the atlas below? The answer is the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane. It is pierced by the vertebral artery. It takes the place of the ligamentum flavum at that level.

Question 1090. The tectorial membrane inside the skull is the upward continuation of which ligament: the posterior longitudinal ligament, the anterior longitudinal ligament, the ligamentum flavum, or the ligamentum nuchae? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It runs up over the dens and into the cranial cavity. It is broad above and narrow below.

Question 1091. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the neck shows a dark band lying along the back of the vertebral bodies inside the canal, with a clear space between it and the cord. Which structure is the band? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. The space in front of the cord is filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The ligament lies between the bone and that fluid.

Question 1092. Which ligament bridges the gap between the transverse processes of two neighboring vertebrae? The answer is the intertransverse ligament. It runs from one transverse process to the next on each side. It is best marked in the lumbar region and checks sideways bending.

Question 1093. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ligamentum flavum with the laminae, the ligamentum flavum with the bodies, the anterior longitudinal ligament with the spines, or the supraspinous ligament with the discs? The answer is the ligamentum flavum with the laminae. It bridges the gap between the flat plates of neighboring vertebrae. The anterior longitudinal ligament runs on the bodies, not on the spines.

Question 1094. Which of these ligaments checks backward bending of the vertebral column: the anterior longitudinal ligament, the posterior longitudinal ligament, the ligamentum flavum, or the interspinous ligament? The answer is the anterior longitudinal ligament. It lies on the front of the bodies, where backward bending stretches it. The other three lie behind the bodies and check forward bending.

Question 1095. A constructed illustration: a fall forces the trunk into strong forward bending and the spines of the lower back are pulled apart. Which ligaments are stretched in that movement? The answer is the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, together with the ligamentum flavum. All of them lie behind the bodies. The anterior longitudinal ligament is slack in that position.

Question 1096. Which band of the vertebral column is narrow in the lower back and leaves the outer part of the disc uncovered? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It is wide in the neck and narrow in the lumbar region. Because of this, a disc can bulge outward around its edge.

Question 1097. A described dissection of the back of the neck shows a broad elastic sheet in the midline between the skull above and the cervical spines below, with muscle attached to both of its surfaces. What is the sheet? The answer is the ligamentum nuchae. It is the thickened continuation of the supraspinous ligament above the seventh cervical vertebra.

Question 1098. Why does a lumbar disc bulge backward and outward rather than straight backward: the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow there, the anterior longitudinal ligament is weak there, the ligamentum flavum pushes the disc outward, or the disc has no outer ring? The answer is that the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow there. It covers only the middle of the disc. Its outer part is covered only thinly.

Question 1099. Name two ligaments that lie behind the vertebral bodies and check forward bending of the column. The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament and the ligamentum flavum. The supraspinous and interspinous ligaments help as well. All of them are stretched when the trunk bends forward.

Question 1100. Which statement about the cruciate ligament of the atlas is correct: it is the transverse ligament of the atlas with bands above and below it, it is the two alar ligaments, it is another name for the ligamentum flavum, or it lies outside the vertebral canal? The answer is the transverse ligament of the atlas with bands above and below it. It lies inside the canal, behind the dens.

To summarize, the atlas is a bony ring with no body and no spinous process, carrying the skull on its concave superior facets and receiving the dens of the axis in the front of its ring. The axis carries the dens upward and is the first vertebra whose spine can be felt in the midline below the skull, and the transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against the anterior arch while most rotation of the head takes place between these two vertebrae. The vertebral canal is formed by the vertebral foramina of successive vertebrae and holds the spinal cord, its coverings, cerebrospinal fluid, the roots of the spinal nerves, and, in the epidural space, fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus. Each intervertebral foramen lies between the notches of two neighboring pedicles and transmits the spinal nerve, the spinal artery, the intervertebral veins, and the recurrent meningeal nerve, with the intervertebral disc forming its front wall. The ligaments of the column, from the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments to the ligamentum flavum, the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, the ligamentum nuchae and the ligaments of the dens, bind the vertebrae together and check their movements. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 12 — Thoracic Cage

Every breath expands and settles the thoracic cage, and this chapter takes that cage apart piece by piece. It covers the twelve pairs of ribs and their parts, the sternum, the costal cartilages that join the two, the true ribs, the false ribs and the floating ribs, and the costal angles that mark the bend of each rib. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1101. How many pairs of ribs form the thoracic cage, and which of them are described as typical ribs? The answer is twelve pairs, with the third to the ninth called typical. A typical rib carries a head, a neck, a tubercle and a shaft with an angle and a costal groove. The first, second, tenth, eleventh and twelfth ribs depart from that pattern and are called atypical.

Question 1102. Which ribs are the typical ribs: the first to the sixth, the third to the ninth, the seventh to the tenth, or the eighth to the twelfth? The answer is the third to the ninth. Each of them shows the full set of features, with a head that carries two facets, a neck, a tubercle and a costal groove. The ribs above and below that range are atypical.

Question 1103. Name the parts of a typical rib in order from the vertebral column to the sternum. The answer is the head, the neck, the tubercle and the shaft. The head is the rounded end that meets the vertebral bodies, and the neck is the narrow part beyond it. The tubercle is the small bump past the neck, and the shaft is the long curved body of the bone.

Question 1104. A described radiograph of the chest shows a break in the sixth rib on the right, in the part of the bone that lies furthest back, just beside the shadow of the spine. Which part of the rib has broken? The answer is the angle of the rib. The angle is the bend where the shaft turns from its backward course into its forward course.

Question 1105. Which structures lie in the costal groove along the lower border of a rib: the intercostal artery alone, the intercostal nerve alone, the vein, the artery and the nerve together, or the pleura only? The answer is the vein, the artery and the nerve together. From above downward the order is vein, then artery, then nerve, so the nerve is the lowest of the three.

Question 1106. Within an intercostal space, does the neurovascular bundle lie nearer the rib above or the rib below? The answer is that it lies in the costal groove of the rib above. The groove runs along the lower border of that rib, so the bone shelters the bundle. The space itself is named after the rib above it.

Question 1107. Which small ridge on the upper surface of the first rib gives attachment to the scalenus anterior muscle? The answer is the scalene tubercle. It lies near the middle of that surface, between two shallow grooves. The first rib is the shortest, the broadest and the most sharply curved of the twelve.

Question 1108. On the first rib, which vessel lies in the groove in front of the scalene tubercle: the subclavian artery, the subclavian vein, the axillary artery, or the internal thoracic artery? The answer is the subclavian vein. The subclavian artery lies in the groove behind the tubercle instead. The vein therefore lies in front of the artery.

Question 1109. A described specimen shows the shortest and most sharply curved of the ribs, lying almost flat rather than sloping, with a fine ridge between two grooves on its upper surface. Which rib is it, and which muscle marks that ridge? The answer is the first rib, and the ridge is the scalene tubercle for the scalenus anterior.

Question 1110. A constructed illustration: a young adult reports aching in the arm and tingling along the little finger, and examination shows a weak hand grip and a reduced pulse at the wrist. A described radiograph shows an extra rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra. Which structures are compressed? The answer is the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery. A cervical rib is a recognized variation.

Question 1111. The head of the fourth rib articulates with which vertebrae: the fourth alone, the third and fourth, the fourth and fifth, or the third, fourth and fifth? The answer is the third and fourth. A typical rib head carries two facets, one for each of those bodies. A ridge between the facets meets the disc that lies between them.

Question 1112. The tubercle of a rib articulates with which part of a vertebra, and what kind of joint is formed? The answer is the transverse process of the vertebra of the same number, in a small synovial joint that lets the rib turn. The eleventh and twelfth ribs have no tubercle and therefore no such joint. The head forms the other joint between a rib and the vertebral column.

Question 1113. How many thoracic vertebrae carry ribs, and how does each rib reach the vertebra numerically corresponding to it? The answer is twelve, and each rib curves around to meet the vertebra of its own number. The first pair meets the first thoracic vertebra, the second pair the second, and so on. The twelfth rib is the last of the series.

Question 1114. True or false: the first rib is the longest and the least curved of the twelve. The answer is false. The first rib is the shortest, the broadest and the most sharply curved, and it lies almost flat. The seventh rib is the longest of the series, and the ribs below it grow shorter again.

Question 1115. Which ribs are described as atypical: the first, second, tenth, eleventh and twelfth, the third to the ninth, the fifth to the eleventh, or the seventh to the twelfth? The answer is the first, second, tenth, eleventh and twelfth. Each departs from the typical pattern in its own way. The tenth rib, for instance, usually carries a single facet on its head.

Question 1116. A described radiograph of the chest shows twelve pairs of ribs, with the lower ones sloping steeply down and forward and the upper ones running almost level. Which rib lies closest to the horizontal? The answer is the first rib. Its slope is the least, and each rib below it slopes more steeply. That is why the lowest ribs reach so much further down at the front.

Question 1117. A constructed illustration: a person falls against the edge of a step and breaks the seventh rib on the left in two places along its shaft. Which structure lying immediately deep to that rib is at risk? The answer is the lung and the pleural cavity around it. The inner surface of the rib faces the pleura, and a sharp fragment can tear it.

Question 1118. Which ribs are most often broken: the first and second, the fourth to the eighth, the ninth and tenth, or the eleventh and twelfth? The answer is the fourth to the eighth. They are the longest and the least sheltered by other structures. The first rib lies deep behind the shoulder girdle, and the floating ribs move freely.

Question 1119. An intercostal space is named after which rib, the one above it or the one below it? The answer is the rib above it. The space between the fifth and sixth ribs is therefore the fifth intercostal space. The neurovascular bundle of that space runs in the groove of the fifth rib.

Question 1120. Which muscle has its origin on the rough tuberosity on the outer surface of the second rib? The answer is the serratus anterior. Its other slips arise from the outer surfaces of the upper ribs behind it. Tracing the muscle backward leads to the medial border of the scapula.

Question 1121. Which muscle arises from the outer surfaces of the upper eight or nine ribs and passes backward to the medial border of the scapula: the pectoralis minor, the serratus anterior, the external oblique, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the serratus anterior. Its upper slips come from the first and second ribs, and the rest follow below.

Question 1122. A described specimen shows a rib whose head carries only one facet instead of two, whose neck is short, and whose shaft has a small angle but no groove on its lower border. Which rib is most likely shown? The answer is the eleventh rib. It meets the body of the eleventh thoracic vertebra alone. Its tip ends free among the muscles of the abdominal wall.

Question 1123. Which of these is not a feature of a typical rib: a head with two facets, a neck, a tubercle, or a spine? The answer is a spine. A spine belongs to a vertebra and not to a rib. The head, the neck, the tubercle and the shaft with its angle and groove make up the typical rib.

Question 1124. A described illustration shows five ribs on the left, each broken in two places, so that the piece of chest wall between the breaks moves inward when the person breathes in. Which statement explains that movement? The answer is that the free segment loses its bony continuity with the rest of the cage and follows the pressure around it.

Question 1125. Which muscle arises from the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs and runs down and forward to the front of the abdomen: the pectoralis major, the external oblique, the serratus anterior, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the external oblique. The muscle ends in a broad sheet that forms the front wall of the abdomen.

Question 1126. On which ribs is the costal groove absent or poorly formed? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth ribs, and the groove is also short in the first. The groove shelters the intercostal vessels and nerve on the inner surface of the shaft. A rib that carries no groove gives them no such shelter.

Question 1127. Which features are missing from the eleventh and twelfth ribs: the head and the shaft, the neck and the tubercle, the angle and the shaft, or the head alone? The answer is the neck and the tubercle. Without a tubercle they form no costotransverse joint. Their heads carry a single facet, which meets one vertebral body.

Question 1128. A described radiograph of the chest shows twelve curved bones on each side, running from the spine downward and forward, with the lowest ones crossing the shadow of the abdomen. What are these bones, and what do the lowest two do at their front ends? The answer is the ribs, and the eleventh and twelfth ribs end freely. They have no costal cartilage reaching the sternum.

Question 1129. The costal part of the diaphragm arises from which structures? The answer is the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and their costal cartilages. Those fibers arch upward to the central tendon of the diaphragm. Interdigitating with them are the fibers of the transversus abdominis below.

Question 1130. A constructed illustration: a described incision in the lower chest passes along the upper border of a rib, and the person later reports numbness in a band around the trunk at that level. Which structure was most likely divided? The answer is an intercostal nerve. The nerve lies in the costal groove of the rib above, lowest of the three structures there.

Question 1131. Which statement about the shape of the adult thoracic cage is correct: it is widest at the top, it is narrow above and wide below, or it is a cylinder of equal width throughout? The answer is that it is narrow above and wide below. The superior aperture is its smallest opening. The cage is widest at about the level of the eighth or ninth rib.

Question 1132. In which direction do the fibers of the external intercostal muscle run: downward and forward, downward and backward, straight up and down, or horizontally? The answer is downward and forward. The internal intercostal fibers run downward and backward, crossing them at right angles. The external muscle fills each space from the tubercle of the rib back to the costal cartilage in front.

Question 1133. Name the three parts of the sternum from above downward. The answer is the manubrium, the body and the xiphoid process. The manubrium is the broad upper part and the body is the longest. The manubrium and the body meet at the sternal angle, which can be felt through the skin.

Question 1134. The hollow felt at the top of the sternum between the two clavicles has which name: the jugular notch, the sternal angle, the xiphisternal joint, or the costal margin? The answer is the jugular notch, also called the suprasternal notch. It lies on the upper border of the manubrium. On each side of it is a notch for the medial end of the clavicle.

Question 1135. At which costal cartilage can the sternal angle be felt? The answer is the second costal cartilage. The sternal angle is the joint between the manubrium and the body of the sternum, and the second rib meets the sternum at that level. The first rib lies above it and is hidden by the clavicle.

Question 1136. The sternal angle lies at which level of the vertebral column: the junction of the second and third thoracic vertebrae, the junction of the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, the junction of the seventh and eighth thoracic vertebrae, or the level of the first lumbar vertebra? The answer is the junction of the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. The jugular notch lies at the level of the second thoracic vertebra.

Question 1137. Which large airway structure divides at the level of the sternal angle? The answer is the trachea, which splits into the two main bronchi there. The arch of the aorta also begins and ends at that level. The azygos vein joins the superior vena cava just below it.

Question 1138. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows the sternum as a straight band at the front, with a slight step where the upper part joins the lower. Which part of the sternum forms the upper band, and what is the step called? The answer is the manubrium above, meeting the body at the sternal angle. The angle marks the level of the second costal cartilage.

Question 1139. A constructed illustration: a driver is thrown forward against the steering wheel and afterward has pain over the middle of the chest, with a step felt in the bone there. Which bone is most likely broken, and which structure lies behind it? The answer is the body of the sternum, with the heart behind it. The illustration shows how a direct blow to the front of the chest is transmitted.

Question 1140. Which costal cartilages articulate with the body of the sternum: the first and second only, the second to the seventh, the third to the sixth, or the eighth to the tenth? The answer is the second to the seventh, with the second divided between the manubrium and the body. The first cartilage joins the manubrium alone.

Question 1141. At which vertebral level does the xiphisternal joint lie? The answer is the level of the ninth thoracic vertebra. The joint lies between the body of the sternum above and the xiphoid process below. It also lies at the apex of the angle formed by the two costal margins.

Question 1142. True or false: the jugular notch of the manubrium lies at the level of the second thoracic vertebra. The answer is true. The notch is the upper border of the manubrium, and the second thoracic vertebra lies behind it. That is why the notch is used as a starting point when counting down the chest.

Question 1143. Bone marrow samples are taken from which part of the sternum: the manubrium, the body, the xiphoid process, or the sternal angle? The answer is the body of the sternum. It lies just under the skin, and the marrow cavity within it is wide. The xiphoid is avoided because it is small and lies over the upper abdomen.

Question 1144. Which of these pairs belongs together: the manubrium with the jugular notch, the body with the clavicular notch, the xiphoid with the second costal cartilage, or the manubrium with the xiphisternal joint? The answer is the manubrium with the jugular notch. The second costal cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle.

Question 1145. A described specimen of a sternum shows a small round hole through the middle of the body, closed by a thin membrane. What is this feature, and why does it matter when a needle is passed into the bone? The answer is a sternal foramen, a variation in which the two plates of bone fail to fuse. The heart lies immediately behind it.

Question 1146. Which structure lies immediately behind the body of the sternum, and which gland occupies the same space in a child? The answer is the heart, with the thymus in front of it in the child. The heart rests behind the sternum and the costal cartilages. The thymus regresses with age.

Question 1147. A described examination finds a small ridge on the front of the chest at the level of the second rib, and the examiner counts downward from it. Why is that ridge chosen rather than the first rib? The answer is that the first rib lies behind the clavicle and cannot be felt. Counting down from it gives the number of each rib and space reliably.

Question 1148. What kind of joint is the sternal angle, between the manubrium and the body of the sternum? The answer is a secondary cartilaginous joint, the kind that has a disc of fibrocartilage between two surfaces covered by cartilage. It allows only a little movement. The joint between the body and the xiphoid is of the same kind.

Question 1149. A described illustration shows a young person in whom the lower part of the sternum is hollowed inward, so that the chest looks sunken in the middle. Which part of the sternum is displaced, and is the number of ribs changed? The answer is the body and the xiphoid, and the number of ribs is unchanged. Such a depression is a variation of the chest wall.

Question 1150. Which costal cartilage is the lowest that reaches the sternum: the fifth, the sixth, the seventh, or the eighth? The answer is the seventh. Its cartilage joins the lower end of the body of the sternum. The cartilages of the eighth, ninth and tenth turn upward and join the seventh instead.

Question 1151. Name two structures that lie at the level of the sternal angle. The answer is the second costal cartilage and the division of the trachea into the two main bronchi. The arch of the aorta also begins and ends at that plane. The disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae lies there as well.

Question 1152. A described radiograph taken from the front shows a flat vertical band of bone in the middle of the chest, overlying the shadows of the heart and the spine. Which bone is shown, and which of its parts can be made out? The answer is the sternum, with the manubrium above and the body below. The xiphoid often cannot be seen because it is cartilage.

Question 1153. What kind of tissue forms the costal cartilages? The answer is hyaline cartilage. Each cartilage continues its rib forward to the sternum or to the cartilage above it. The cartilage is flexible, so the chest wall can move with every breath. In later life it often becomes calcified and less yielding.

Question 1154. The costal cartilages of the eighth, ninth and tenth ribs join which structure in front: the sternum directly, the cartilage of the seventh rib, the xiphoid process, or the clavicle? The answer is the cartilage of the seventh rib. They join one another in turn to form a continuous sloping border. That border is the costal margin.

Question 1155. Which ribs contribute to the costal margin? The answer is the seventh to the tenth. Their cartilages join in a continuous arch on each side, sloping down and forward. The margin can be felt through the skin along the lower edge of the chest, and the eleventh and twelfth ribs take no part in it.

Question 1156. A described radiograph of an older adult shows thin lines of bone running from the front ends of the ribs to the sternum, where young cartilage would have cast no shadow. What are these lines? The answer is the calcified costal cartilages. Calcification of hyaline cartilage is a normal change with age. It does not mean that the ribs themselves have changed.

Question 1157. At the costochondral junction, which structure meets which? The answer is the bony shaft of the rib and its costal cartilage. The junction lies a short distance from the sternal end of the rib. The joint is immobile, because the bone and the cartilage are united directly.

Question 1158. A constructed illustration: a blow to the front of the chest leaves a person with sharp pain at one point on the costal margin, worse on deep breathing, and the tender spot is at the junction of bone and cartilage. Which junction is involved? The answer is a costochondral junction. The bone and the cartilage may separate there under a direct blow.

Question 1159. Which costal cartilages join one another in series rather than each reaching the sternum: those of the first and second, those of the eighth, ninth and tenth, those of the eleventh and twelfth, or those of the third and fourth? The answer is the eighth, ninth and tenth. Each turns upward and joins the cartilage above it. The eleventh and twelfth have no cartilage in front at all.

Question 1160. True or false: the costal cartilage is a piece of hyaline cartilage that continues the rib forward. The answer is true. It is the same tissue as the cartilage on the articular surfaces of joints. Its flexibility lets the chest wall bend during breathing.

Question 1161. Which of these pairs belongs together: the costochondral junction with the rib and its cartilage, the costovertebral joint with the rib and the sternum, or the costotransverse joint with the rib and the clavicle? The answer is the costochondral junction with the rib and its cartilage. The costovertebral joint lies between the head of the rib and a vertebral body. The costotransverse joint lies between the tubercle and a transverse process.

Question 1162. A described radiograph of the lower chest in an older adult shows the costal cartilages outlined by fine deposits of calcium, so that the front ends of the ribs appear capped by a faint shell. What does that appearance represent, and is the underlying rib diseased? The answer is calcification within the costal cartilages, a change of normal aging. The bony ribs themselves are unchanged.

Question 1163. In some people two adjacent costal cartilages are joined by a bridge of cartilage, so that the front of the chest is stiffer on that side. Which variation is that? The answer is fusion of two adjacent costal cartilages. It is seen most often among the lower cartilages. It is a normal variation rather than a sign of disease.

Question 1164. A constructed illustration: a person reports sharp pain along one costal margin, brought on by twisting, with a clicking sensation as one cartilage slips over the one above it. Which cartilages are most often involved? The answer is the eighth, ninth and tenth costal cartilages, where they join one another. Their junctions are the ones that give way.

Question 1165. In a transverse section across the chest at the level of the fifth rib, does the costal cartilage lie in front of or behind the bony shaft of the same rib? The answer is in front. The rib curves forward and downward, and its cartilage continues that course to the sternum. The cartilage therefore lies anterior to the part of the shaft behind it.

Question 1166. Name two joints that a typical rib forms with the vertebral column. The answer is the costovertebral joint and the costotransverse joint. The first lies between the head of the rib and the bodies of two vertebrae and the disc between them. The second lies between the tubercle and the transverse process.

Question 1167. Which ribs are the true ribs? The answer is the first seven pairs. Each has its own costal cartilage, and that cartilage reaches the sternum. They are also called the vertebrosternal ribs, because they join a vertebra behind and the sternum in front.

Question 1168. Why are the first seven ribs called true ribs: because they are longer than the others, because each reaches the sternum through its own cartilage, because they alone join the vertebral column, or because they are straighter? The answer is that each reaches the sternum through its own cartilage. The ribs below do not reach the sternum directly.

Question 1169. A described radiograph of the chest shows seven ribs on each side whose cartilages turn inward and meet the flat central bone at the front, while the ribs below stop short of it. Which ribs are the seven, and what name is given to them? The answer is the first seven, the true ribs. Their cartilages reach the sternum.

Question 1170. Which costal cartilage joins the manubrium directly rather than the body of the sternum? The answer is the first. It is short, thick and firmly united to the manubrium. The second cartilage is divided, part meeting the manubrium and part the body. The joint between the first cartilage and the manubrium allows almost no movement.

Question 1171. A constructed illustration concerns a person who has taken a severe blow to the top of the shoulder and is found to have a break of the first rib. Which large vessels running just above that rib may be injured with it? The answer is the subclavian artery and the subclavian vein. They cross the first rib on its upper surface.

Question 1172. Which costal cartilage reaches the sternum exactly at the sternal angle: the first, the second, the third, or the fourth? The answer is the second. It meets the sternum where the manubrium joins the body. The first lies above that level and the third below it. That is why the second rib is the one used to begin counting.

Question 1173. In the living body, does a true rib run downward from the spine to the sternum, or upward? The answer is downward and forward. The vertebral end of the rib lies higher than its sternal end. The lowest ribs slope the most steeply of all, which is why the costal margin lies so far below the upper chest.

Question 1174. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fourth rib with two facets on its head, the first rib with two facets on its head, or the twelfth rib with a costal groove along its lower border? The answer is the fourth rib with two facets on its head. The first and twelfth ribs each carry a single facet, and the twelfth has no costal groove.

Question 1175. Which ribs are the false ribs? The answer is the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh and twelfth. They are false because their cartilages do not reach the sternum directly. The upper three join the cartilage of the seventh rib, and the last two have no cartilage in front at all.

Question 1176. The eighth, ninth and tenth ribs are also known by which name: the vertebrosternal ribs, the vertebrochondral ribs, the vertebral ribs, or the sternal ribs? The answer is the vertebrochondral ribs. They join a vertebra behind and a cartilage in front. The eleventh and twelfth are the vertebral ribs, because they join only the vertebral column.

Question 1177. A described radiograph shows that on each side the shadows of the eighth, ninth and tenth ribs turn upward at their front ends and merge with one another, forming a continuous line that ends in the middle of the lower chest. What is that line? The answer is the costal margin. It is built from the costal cartilages of the seventh to the tenth ribs.

Question 1178. The costal cartilages of the eighth, ninth and tenth ribs all join which single structure? The answer is the costal cartilage of the seventh rib. Each joins the one above it, and the series ends on the seventh. The seventh cartilage then meets the lower end of the body of the sternum.

Question 1179. A constructed illustration concerns a person with a break of the ninth rib on the right, well forward along its shaft, and afterward bleeding into the abdomen. Which organ lies immediately deep to that rib on the right side? The answer is the liver. Its dome rises under the right costal margin. On the left at the same level lie the spleen and the stomach.

Question 1180. Which statement about the eighth, ninth and tenth ribs is correct: each reaches the sternum, each joins the cartilage of the rib above, each ends free in muscle, or each joins the thoracic vertebra below it? The answer is that each joins the cartilage of the rib above. The series ends on the seventh cartilage, which reaches the sternum.

Question 1181. True or false: the costal cartilage of the eighth rib joins the sternum directly. The answer is false. It joins the cartilage of the seventh rib, which in turn reaches the sternum. That is the reason the eighth rib is classed as a false rib.

Question 1182. Which of these pairs belongs together: the first to the seventh ribs with the true ribs, the eighth to the twelfth ribs with the true ribs, or the eleventh and twelfth ribs with the vertebrochondral ribs? The answer is the first to the seventh ribs with the true ribs. The eighth to the twelfth are the false ribs.

Question 1183. Name the false ribs and say where their cartilages end. The answer is the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh and twelfth. The cartilages of the eighth, ninth and tenth join the seventh cartilage and form the costal margin. The eleventh and twelfth have no cartilages reaching the front of the chest at all.

Question 1184. A described examination finds that the lowest intercostal space with a complete front wall lies between the seventh and eighth ribs. Which space is that, and in the groove of which rib does its bundle run? The answer is the seventh space, with its bundle in the groove of the seventh rib. The cartilage of the seventh rib reaches the sternum, so the space has a complete front wall.

Question 1185. Which ribs are the floating ribs? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth pairs. They are the last two and have no costal cartilage reaching the front of the chest. Each ends in a pointed tip among the muscles of the abdominal wall. They are also called the vertebral ribs.

Question 1186. Why are the eleventh and twelfth ribs called floating ribs: because they move with breathing, because their front ends are free, because they are not joined to the spine, or because they are the shortest? The answer is that their front ends are free. They have no costal cartilage joining the sternum or the costal margin. Every rib moves with breathing, so movement is not the distinguishing feature.

Question 1187. A described radiograph of the upper abdomen shows two short curved bones on each side, below the costal margin, tapering to points that end over the soft tissues of the flank. Which ribs are they, and what lies just behind them? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth ribs, with the kidneys behind them. They are the only ribs with no attachment in front.

Question 1188. The upper part of the kidney lies against the inner surface of which ribs? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth ribs, with the twelfth crossing the kidney from behind. The kidney therefore lies partly under the shelter of the floating ribs. The pleura may also reach down over the twelfth rib behind.

Question 1189. A constructed illustration concerns a blow to the flank that breaks the twelfth rib, after which blood appears in the urine. Which organ has most likely been injured? The answer is the kidney, which lies behind the lower ribs. The twelfth rib crosses its upper part from behind. The pleura may lie between the rib and the kidney as well.

Question 1190. The head of the twelfth rib articulates with which structures: the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae, the twelfth thoracic vertebra alone, the first lumbar vertebra alone, or the eleventh thoracic vertebra alone? The answer is the twelfth thoracic vertebra alone. The rib carries a single facet on its head. For the same reason it forms no costotransverse joint, because it has no tubercle.

Question 1191. A described specimen shows a short, sharply curved rib with a pointed front end, a single facet on its head, no neck, no tubercle and no costal groove. Which rib is it, and how does it differ from the eleventh? The answer is the twelfth rib, which is shorter and has no angle. The eleventh rib is longer and keeps a shallow costal groove.

Question 1192. True or false: the eleventh rib carries a shallow costal groove on its lower border, while the twelfth does not. The answer is true. The eleventh rib still has a small angle and a groove for the intercostal vessels and nerve. The twelfth is shorter and smoother, with neither a groove nor an angle.

Question 1193. Which of these pairs belongs together: the eleventh rib with a single facet on its head, the eighth rib with no cartilage in front, or the seventh rib with no attachment to the sternum? The answer is the eleventh rib with a single facet on its head. It meets only the eleventh thoracic vertebra. The eighth rib has a cartilage that reaches the costal margin, and the seventh reaches the sternum.

Question 1194. What name is given to the bend on the shaft of a rib where it turns from its backward course into its forward course? The answer is the angle of the rib, or the costal angle. It is the most sharply curved part of the bone. It lies only a short distance beyond the tubercle.

Question 1195. Which part of a rib is most often the site of a fracture: the head, the neck, the angle, or the costal cartilage? The answer is the angle. It is the point of greatest curvature and the weakest part of the bone. A break there usually follows a direct blow or a crush.

Question 1196. What is the name of the angle formed beneath the xiphoid process where the right and left costal margins meet? The answer is the subcostal angle, also called the infrasternal angle. It opens downward and lies at the apex of the two costal margins. Its size varies with the shape of the chest.

Question 1197. A described radiograph of the chest shows, on each rib, the point where the curve changes direction most abruptly, lying close to the shadow of the spine. Which part of the rib is shown, and is it nearer the vertebral or the sternal end? The answer is the angle, and it lies much nearer the vertebral end. It sits only a short distance beyond the tubercle.

Question 1198. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a person has pain at a point on the back of the chest beside the spine, and pressing there reproduces it exactly. Which part of which rib lies under the finger? The answer is the angle of a rib. The angle lies at the outer border of the long muscle that runs up the spine.

Question 1199. Which statement about the subcostal angle beneath the xiphoid process is correct: it is wider in the infant than in the adult, it is always a right angle, or it lies above the xiphoid? The answer is that it is wider in the infant than in the adult. The infant chest is rounder, and its costal margins flare outward more. With growth the cage lengthens and the angle narrows.

Question 1200. Which ribs provide the cartilages that form the costal margin, and where do the two margins meet? The answer is the seventh to the tenth ribs, and the margins meet at the xiphisternal joint. Each margin slopes down and forward from the seventh cartilage. The angle between the two margins is the subcostal angle.

To summarize, the thoracic cage is built from twelve pairs of ribs, the sternum, and the costal cartilages that join the two. The first seven ribs are the true ribs, because each reaches the sternum through its own cartilage, while the eighth to the twelfth are the false ribs, and among those the eleventh and twelfth end free as the floating ribs. The head of a typical rib meets two vertebral bodies and the disc between them, its tubercle meets the transverse process of the same number, and its costal groove carries the intercostal vein, artery and nerve in that order from above downward. The sternal angle, felt at the second costal cartilage and level with the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, is the landmark from which the ribs are counted. The costal margin is formed by the cartilages of the seventh to the tenth ribs, and the angle of a rib, just beyond its tubercle, is both the most sharply curved part of the bone and the one most often broken. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 13 — Pectoral Girdle

The pectoral girdle is the bony ring that carries the upper limb, and this chapter takes it apart piece by piece. It covers the clavicle, the scapula with its spine and fossae, the acromion, the coracoid process, and the glenoid cavity, in that order, with the relations and muscle attachments of each. It holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. The girdle has only two bones and two small joints, yet it is the most mobile part of the skeleton, which is why its anatomy is worth hearing said aloud. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1201. Which long bone lies across the root of the neck just beneath the skin and forms the only bony link between the upper limb and the trunk? The answer is the clavicle. Its medial end meets the manubrium of the sternum and its lateral end meets the acromion. Because it lies under the skin along its whole length, it is easily felt and easily broken.

Question 1202. Which part of the clavicle is enlarged and roughly quadrilateral: the medial end, the lateral end, the middle third, or the whole shaft? The answer is the medial end. It is the thicker end, and it articulates with the manubrium of the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint. The lateral end is flattened where it meets the acromion.

Question 1203. Which curve of the clavicle is convex forward, the medial part or the lateral part? The answer is the medial part. The bone is shaped like a flattened S, with the medial two thirds convex forward and the lateral one third concave forward. That reversed curve is one reason the bone breaks so often in its middle.

Question 1204. A described radiograph of the shoulder region shows a horizontal bone whose lateral third carries a small downward projection near its posterior border. Which bony point is shown? The answer is the conoid tubercle. It lies on the inferior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle at the back, and the conoid ligament attaches to it. The trapezoid line lies in front of it.

Question 1205. Which of these structures occupies the groove on the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle: the subclavius muscle, the pectoralis major, the deltoid, or the trapezius? The answer is the subclavius. It lies in the subclavian groove and pulls the clavicle downward and forward. The other three muscles attach nearer the ends of the bone.

Question 1206. Which muscle arises from the anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle, close to the sternum? The answer is the pectoralis major. Its clavicular head takes origin from the front of the medial half of the bone. The sternocleidomastoid attaches higher, on the superior surface of the medial third.

Question 1207. Which structures pass behind the clavicle in the narrow space between the bone and the first rib? The answer is the subclavian artery and vein together with the brachial plexus. They cross the first rib behind the middle of the clavicle. The vein lies in front of the artery, and the plexus lies behind the artery.

Question 1208. Which bone of the pectoral girdle lies most anteriorly and can be felt along its whole length: the clavicle, the scapula, the humerus, or the first rib? The answer is the clavicle. The scapula lies behind the ribs, so only its spine and its acromion can be felt. The humerus is covered by muscle.

Question 1209. A constructed illustration: a cyclist falls on the point of the shoulder, and afterward the shoulder on that side droops and the arm cannot be raised. Which bone of the girdle is most likely broken, and at which part? The answer is the clavicle, usually at its middle third. That part lies between the two curves and is the weakest point of the bone.

Question 1210. Which bone of the human body is the first to begin ossification, starting in the sixth week of development? The answer is the clavicle. It begins to form in membrane rather than in cartilage, which is unusual for a long bone. Its medial end adds a secondary center much later.

Question 1211. The clavicle acts as a strut. Which of these is the main consequence of losing it: the shoulder falls forward and toward the midline, the arm cannot bend at the elbow, the scapula fuses to the ribs, or the hand loses its grip? The answer is that the shoulder falls forward and toward the midline. Without the strut the limb moves inward, and the scapula is carried with it.

Question 1212. True or false: the clavicle articulates directly with the first rib. The answer is false. It articulates with the manubrium of the sternum at its medial end and with the acromion of the scapula at its lateral end. The first rib lies below it, joined to it only by the costoclavicular ligament.

Question 1213. A described CT scan of the shoulder shows the medial end of the clavicle sitting in a shallow socket on the upper corner of the sternum, with a disc between the two surfaces. Which joint is shown, and what kind of joint is it? The answer is the sternoclavicular joint, a synovial saddle joint with an articular disc. It is the only synovial joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.

Question 1214. In the sternoclavicular joint, which structure is the chief restraint against upward displacement of the medial end of the clavicle: the costoclavicular ligament, the interclavicular ligament, the articular disc, or the joint capsule? The answer is the costoclavicular ligament. It runs from the first rib and its cartilage to the impression on the inferior surface of the medial end. The disc and the capsule help, but this ligament is the strongest.

Question 1215. Which ligament attaches at the rough oval depression on the inferior surface of the medial end of the clavicle, and what is that depression called? The answer is the costoclavicular ligament, attaching at the impression for the costoclavicular ligament, also called the rhomboid fossa. It is the strongest bond between the clavicle and the first rib.

Question 1216. Which large nervous structure passes immediately behind the middle of the clavicle and lies at risk when that bone is fractured? The answer is the brachial plexus. It leaves the neck between the scalene muscles and runs behind the clavicle into the armpit. The subclavian artery and vein travel in the same narrow space.

Question 1217. Which muscle attaches to the posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle: the trapezium, the trapezius, the deltoid, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the trapezius. The deltoid takes origin from the anterior border of the same lateral third. The two muscles therefore pull the outer end of the clavicle in opposite directions.

Question 1218. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a patient holds the arm still, and the outer fragment of a broken clavicle lies lower and nearer the midline than the inner fragment. Which two forces explain that displacement? The answer is the pull of the sternocleidomastoid on the inner fragment and the weight of the arm on the outer one. The inner fragment is lifted, and the outer one sags.

Question 1219. Which joint does the lateral end of the clavicle form, and with which bone: the acromioclavicular joint with the scapula, the sternoclavicular joint with the sternum, the glenohumeral joint with the humerus, or the costoclavicular joint with the first rib? The answer is the acromioclavicular joint with the scapula. It is a small plane joint at the top of the shoulder.

Question 1220. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the shoulder shows a small fibrous band passing from the coracoid process upward and laterally to the underside of the clavicle. Which ligament is shown, and what does it prevent? The answer is the coracoclavicular ligament. Its two parts, the conoid and the trapezoid, hold the lateral end of the clavicle down. It stops the clavicle from riding up over the acromion.

Question 1221. Which muscle takes origin from the superior surface of the medial third of the clavicle and helps to turn the face to the opposite side? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid. Its clavicular head begins on that part of the bone and joins the sternal head. The two heads act on the head and the neck, not on the arm.

Question 1222. During raising the arm above the head, what movement does the clavicle perform about its own long axis: it rotates backward, it stays still, it rotates forward, or it dislocates? The answer is that it rotates backward. The clavicle turns at the sternoclavicular joint as the scapula rotates upward. That rotation adds range to the lift of the arm.

Question 1223. Which of these pairs belongs together: the conoid tubercle with the conoid ligament, the conoid tubercle with the trapezoid ligament, the subclavian groove with the trapezoid ligament, or the rhomboid fossa with the conoid ligament? The answer is the conoid tubercle with the conoid ligament. The trapezoid ligament attaches to the trapezoid line, and the rhomboid fossa holds the costoclavicular ligament.

Question 1224. Which muscle lies immediately above the medial end of the clavicle, and which joint lies immediately below its lateral end? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid above the medial end and the acromioclavicular joint below the lateral end. Both can be felt through the skin in a thin person. The clavicle separates them.

Question 1225. A constructed illustration: a large newborn cannot pass through the birth canal, and after delivery the baby does not move one arm and a crack is felt over the clavicle. Which bone is injured, and why is that bone the usual one? The answer is the clavicle, compressed against the maternal bone as the shoulders are delivered. It lies just under the skin, so it is the first bone to give way.

Question 1226. A described radiograph taken from above the shoulder shows the clavicle crossing the upper chest, and a second line of bone running from its middle toward the neck. Which two bones are shown, and what does the second line represent? The answer is the clavicle and the first rib. The first rib lies below and behind the clavicle, so it is seen through it. A break would interrupt its smooth upper border.

Question 1227. Which statement about the ossification of the clavicle is correct: it begins in membrane, it begins in cartilage, it has no secondary center, or it ossifies from the sternal end outward? The answer is that it begins in membrane. It is the first bone to ossify and the only long bone to form in this way. A secondary center appears at the sternal end much later.

Question 1228. Name the two ligaments that together form the coracoclavicular ligament, spoken as a list. The answer is the conoid ligament and the trapezoid ligament. They run from the coracoid process of the scapula to the inferior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle. Together they suspend the weight of the upper limb from the clavicle.

Question 1229. Which flat triangular bone lies on the back of the chest wall, covering the upper ribs, and moves with the arm? The answer is the scapula. It has three borders and three angles, and its lateral angle carries the socket for the head of the humerus. It is held in place by muscles rather than by a strong joint.

Question 1230. Over which ribs does the body of the scapula lie: the first to the fourth, the second to the seventh, the fifth to the tenth, or the eighth to the twelfth? The answer is the second to the seventh. The medial border runs down beside the vertebral column. The inferior angle rests at the level of the seventh rib.

Question 1231. Which bony ridge runs across the back of the scapula and separates two hollows? The answer is the spine of the scapula. It rises from the flat surface and turns forward at its outer end to form the acromion. The hollows above and below it hold the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus.

Question 1232. A described radiograph of the back of the shoulder shows a triangular plate of bone with a horizontal ridge dividing it into a smaller upper part and a larger lower part. Which bone is shown, and what is the ridge? The answer is the scapula, with its spine. The upper part is the supraspinous fossa and the lower part the infraspinous fossa.

Question 1233. At the upper border of the scapula, which structure passes below the superior transverse scapular ligament: the suprascapular nerve, the suprascapular artery, the axillary nerve, or the dorsal scapular nerve? The answer is the suprascapular nerve. The suprascapular artery passes above the ligament. The nerve then supplies the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus.

Question 1234. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the scapula and separates the bone from the ribs? The answer is the serratus anterior. It fills the plane between the costal surface of the scapula and the chest wall. Its slips arise from the upper ribs and reach the medial border.

Question 1235. Which hollow on the scapula faces the ribs and gives origin to the subscapularis? The answer is the subscapular fossa. It covers most of the costal surface of the bone. The subscapularis fills it and rotates the arm inward. Its ridges mark the attachment of the muscle.

Question 1236. Which rotator cuff muscle arises from the upper surface of the lateral border of the scapula: the supraspinatus, the teres minor, the subscapularis, or the teres major? The answer is the teres minor. It arises from the upper part of the dorsal surface of the lateral border and rotates the arm outward. The teres major arises lower down and is not part of the cuff.

Question 1237. True or false: the scapula is joined to the vertebral column by a synovial joint. The answer is false. The scapula has no joint with the axial skeleton at all. It is tethered by muscles, and its only bony path to the trunk runs through the clavicle and the sternoclavicular joint.

Question 1238. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the armpit, a patient cannot push the arm forward against a wall, and the medial border of the scapula stands away from the chest. Which muscle is paralyzed, and which nerve was injured? The answer is the serratus anterior, with the long thoracic nerve. That nerve runs down the chest wall on the surface of the muscle, where it is easily stretched.

Question 1239. Which muscle arises from the superior angle and the upper part of the medial border of the scapula and lifts the whole bone? The answer is the levator scapulae. It descends from the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae. It helps to raise the point of the shoulder.

Question 1240. The inferior angle of the scapula lies at the level of which rib and which vertebral spine: the fifth rib and the fourth thoracic spine, the seventh rib and the seventh thoracic spine, the ninth rib and the ninth thoracic spine, or the eleventh rib and the eleventh thoracic spine? The answer is the seventh rib and the seventh thoracic spine. That landmark is used to count ribs from behind.

Question 1241. A described cross section through the back of the chest shows a triangular bone lying against the ribs, with a muscle in the hollow on each side of a central ridge. Which hollow lies above the ridge and which below? The answer is the supraspinous fossa above and the infraspinous fossa below. The ridge between them is the spine of the scapula.

Question 1242. Which muscle takes origin from the ventral surface of the medial border of the scapula: the rhomboid major, the serratus anterior, the levator scapulae, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the serratus anterior. It arises by finger-like slips from the upper ribs and pulls the scapula around the chest wall. The rhomboids lie on the dorsal surface of the same border.

Question 1243. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraspinous fossa with the infraspinatus, the subscapular fossa with the supraspinatus, the infraspinous fossa with the subscapularis, or the supraspinous fossa with the supraspinatus? The answer is the supraspinous fossa with the supraspinatus. The infraspinous fossa holds the infraspinatus, and the subscapular fossa holds the subscapularis.

Question 1244. Which nerve supplies the rhomboid muscles and helps to hold the scapula against the chest wall? The answer is the dorsal scapular nerve. It arises from the fifth cervical spinal nerve root and runs down deep to the rhomboids. Injury weakens retraction of the scapula and lets the bone slide a little laterally.

Question 1245. Which part of the scapula lies immediately below the acromion, and which part lies immediately medial to the acromion? The answer is the glenoid cavity below it and the spine of the scapula medial to it. The acromion is the outer end of the spine. These three landmarks are felt as one continuous line on the top of the shoulder.

Question 1246. A described CT scan of the shoulder shows the scapula as a triangular plate on the back of the chest, with a ridge from its medial border to the shoulder socket and a notch near its upper border. Which notch is it, and what passes through it? The answer is the suprascapular notch, with the suprascapular nerve passing through it. The artery crosses above the ligament that roofs it.

Question 1247. A constructed illustration: a patient has a drooping shoulder and cannot shrug it, and the scapula on that side sits lower and rotated. Which muscle is paralyzed, and which nerve is damaged? The answer is the trapezius, with the eleventh cranial nerve. That nerve is superficial in the back of the neck, where it can be injured by a cut or by an operation there.

Question 1248. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows the coracoid process overlapping the upper part of the glenoid, with the spine of the scapula above and behind it. Which of these landmarks is the most anterior? The answer is the coracoid process. It hooks forward and laterally, so it lies in front of the socket. That is why it is felt in the groove between the deltoid and the chest.

Question 1249. During full elevation of the arm, what share of the movement takes place at the shoulder joint and what share at the scapula: about three to one, about two to one, about one to one, or about one to three? The answer is about two to one. For every 15 degrees of arm lift, roughly 10 occur at the shoulder joint and 5 at the scapula.

Question 1250. Which muscle arises from the subscapular fossa and forms the anterior wall of the rotator cuff? The answer is the subscapularis. It is the only one of the four cuff muscles that lies in front of the joint. It rotates the arm inward and is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

Question 1251. True or false: the scapula lies flat against the rib cage and cannot be moved independently of the humerus. The answer is false. The scapula glides on the chest wall and can be drawn forward, backward, up, and down. It must also turn upward before the arm can pass above the head.

Question 1252. Which muscle both protracts the scapula and turns it upward, and is therefore needed for lifting the arm above the head: the rhomboid major, the levator scapulae, the serratus anterior, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the serratus anterior. Working with the trapezius, it rotates the scapula so that the socket faces upward. Its paralysis prevents full elevation of the arm.

Question 1253. Which structure lies immediately deep to the medial border of the scapula and separates the bone from the ribs? The answer is the serratus anterior. It fills that plane, so the bone slides on muscle rather than on bone. Loose tissue between the muscle and the chest wall allows the scapula to glide.

Question 1254. A described specimen of the scapula is held with its smooth concave costal surface facing the viewer. Which hollow is seen, and what does it hold? The answer is the subscapular fossa, which holds the subscapularis. The ridges on its surface mark the attachment of the muscle fibers. The dorsal surface is the one divided by the spine.

Question 1255. From above downward, which two muscles attach to the dorsal surface of the lateral border of the scapula: the teres minor and the teres major, the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus, the subscapularis and the rhomboid major, or the deltoid and the trapezius? The answer is the teres minor above and the teres major below it. The long head of the triceps passes between them.

Question 1256. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the outstretched hand, a patient has deep shoulder pain, numbness over the outer upper arm, and a weak deltoid. Which nerve is injured, and which part of the girdle should be examined for a break? The answer is the axillary nerve, with the glenoid cavity and the surgical neck of the humerus. It winds close to the lower rim of the socket.

Question 1257. Name the two muscles that turn the scapula upward so that the arm can be raised above the head, spoken as a list. The answer is the trapezius and the serratus anterior. They work as a pair, one pulling at the spine and the other at the inferior angle. Without that rotation the arm cannot pass the vertical.

Question 1258. Which single feature explains why the scapula is so mobile: it joins the trunk through the clavicle and muscles only, it has a wide synovial joint with the ribs, it is fused to the first rib, or it hangs by ligaments from the vertebrae? The answer is that it joins the trunk through the clavicle and muscles only. There is no wide joint, so the bone can glide in many directions.

Question 1259. Which bony point forms the outer end of the spine of the scapula and is felt at the top of the shoulder? The answer is the acromion. It is flattened and turns forward and upward over the socket. It gives the shoulder its square outline and meets the clavicle.

Question 1260. With which bone does the acromion articulate: the humerus, the clavicle, the first rib, or the coracoid process? The answer is the clavicle. The two bones meet at the acromioclavicular joint at the top of the shoulder. The head of the humerus lies below the acromion and does not touch it.

Question 1261. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows a bony shelf lying over the top of the rounded head of the humerus, with a clear gap between the two. Which part of the scapula forms that shelf? The answer is the acromion. The clear gap beneath it holds the supraspinatus tendon and a bursa. Loss of that gap suggests that the head has moved upward.

Question 1262. What is the name of the angle at which the spine of the scapula turns forward to become the acromion? The answer is the acromial angle. It is felt as a bony corner at the back of the shoulder. The acromion then continues forward and slightly upward above the joint.

Question 1263. Which two muscles take origin from the borders of the acromion: the trapezius and the deltoid, the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus, the rhomboid major and the rhomboid minor, or the latissimus dorsi and the teres major? The answer is the trapezius and the deltoid. The trapezius attaches to the posterior border and the deltoid to the anterior and lateral borders. The two muscles therefore surround the point of the shoulder.

Question 1264. Which ligament stretches from the tip of the coracoid process to the acromion, and what does the arch it forms protect? The answer is the coracoacromial ligament, which forms the coracoacromial arch. The arch lies above the head of the humerus and the tendon of the supraspinatus. It helps to stop the head from moving upward.

Question 1265. True or false: the acromion always ossifies as part of the spine of the scapula and never has a separate center. The answer is false. It has its own center or centers, which may stay unfused as a separate piece. That normal variant is called an os acromiale and can be mistaken for a fracture.

Question 1266. A constructed illustration: a middle-aged patient has pain when the arm is lifted to the side, worst in the middle of the arc, and the pain eases when the arm is raised fully. Which tendon and which bursa lie in the narrow space most likely involved? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon with the subacromial bursa. Both lie just below the acromion, in the space roofed by that bone.

Question 1267. What kind of joint is the acromioclavicular joint: a plane synovial joint with a disc, a ball and socket joint, a cartilaginous joint, or a fibrous joint? The answer is a plane synovial joint with an articular disc. Its surfaces glide on each other during shrugging. Movement there adds to the range of the scapula.

Question 1268. Which of these pairs belongs together: the acromion with the clavicle, the acromion with the first rib, the coracoid process with the clavicle, or the glenoid cavity with the acromion? The answer is the acromion with the clavicle, which meet at the acromioclavicular joint. The coracoid process reaches the clavicle only by a ligament.

Question 1269. Which muscles attach to the posterior and anterior borders of the acromion, and what attaches to its medial border? The answer is the trapezius behind, the deltoid in front, and the coracoacromial ligament on the medial border near the tip. Those attachments fix the acromion on all sides.

Question 1270. A described MRI scan of the shoulder shows a bright collection of fluid in the space between the underside of the acromion and the tendon below it. Which space is shown, and which tendon lies in it? The answer is the subacromial bursa, with the tendon of the supraspinatus. The space is roofed by the acromion and the coracoacromial ligament.

Question 1271. Which of these structures prevents the head of the humerus from dislocating upward: the acromion with the coracoacromial arch, the glenoid labrum, the long head of the biceps, or the capsule of the joint? The answer is the acromion with the coracoacromial arch. It forms a bony and fibrous roof over the head. The labrum deepens the socket but does not stop upward movement.

Question 1272. Which structures lie immediately deep to the acromion, in order from the bone downward? The answer is the subacromial bursa, then the tendon of the supraspinatus, then the head of the humerus. The long head of the biceps also passes through the same space on its way to the socket.

Question 1273. Which bony process of the scapula projects forward and laterally below the outer end of the clavicle and is shaped like a bent finger? The answer is the coracoid process. It arises from the upper part of the lateral angle of the scapula. Three muscles and several ligaments attach to it.

Question 1274. Which two muscles arise from the tip of the coracoid process: the coracobrachialis and the short head of the biceps, the long head of the biceps and the brachialis, the pectoralis major and the deltoid, or the subscapularis and the teres major? The answer is the coracobrachialis and the short head of the biceps. Both pass into the arm and help to flex the shoulder.

Question 1275. Which notch lies on the superior border of the scapula, immediately medial to the base of the coracoid process? The answer is the suprascapular notch. The superior transverse scapular ligament closes it into a foramen. The suprascapular nerve passes through it, and the artery passes above the ligament.

Question 1276. Which muscle from the chest wall attaches to the coracoid process and pulls the point of the shoulder forward and downward? The answer is the pectoralis minor. It arises from the third, fourth, and fifth ribs. It inserts on the medial border and the upper surface of the process.

Question 1277. A described specimen of the scapula shows a strong hook of bone rising above the socket and pointing forward, with a notch just behind its base. Which process is shown, and which notch lies behind it? The answer is the coracoid process, with the suprascapular notch medial to its base. The hook gives attachment to three muscles.

Question 1278. Which two ligaments run from the coracoid process to the inferior surface of the clavicle: the conoid and the trapezoid, the acromioclavicular and the coracoacromial, the costoclavicular and the interclavicular, or the glenohumeral and the coracohumeral? The answer is the conoid and the trapezoid. Together they form the coracoclavicular ligament, which suspends the limb from the clavicle.

Question 1279. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the base of the coracoid process, and which lies immediately medial to it? The answer is the glenoid cavity laterally and the suprascapular notch medially. The coracoid therefore sits at the front of the upper end of the socket. Behind it runs the upper border of the scapula.

Question 1280. True or false: the coracoid process can be felt through the skin in the groove between the front of the shoulder and the chest. The answer is true. It lies deep in that groove, below the outer third of the clavicle. It can be rolled under the finger in a thin person.

Question 1281. Which ligament arises from the lateral border of the coracoid process and blends with the capsule of the shoulder joint: the coracohumeral ligament, the coracoacromial ligament, the conoid ligament, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the coracohumeral ligament. It passes to the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. It strengthens the upper part of the capsule.

Question 1282. A described radiograph of the shoulder taken from the side shows a strong hook of bone lying in front of the socket while another process lies above it. Which two processes of the scapula frame the joint in that view? The answer is the coracoid process in front and the acromion above. Between them runs the coracoacromial ligament.

Question 1283. Which statement about the coracoid process is correct: it is the point of the shoulder, it is felt in the groove between the deltoid and the chest, it articulates with the humerus, or it gives origin to the pectoralis major? The answer is that it is felt in the groove between the deltoid and the chest. It does not articulate with the humerus, and it gives origin to the pectoralis minor.

Question 1284. A constructed illustration: after a direct blow to the front of the shoulder, the tip of a hook-shaped process under the outer clavicle is tender, and the patient cannot pull the arm forward against resistance. Which process is injured? The answer is the coracoid process, from which the coracobrachialis and the short head of the biceps arise. The pectoralis minor also attaches there.

Question 1285. Which of these pairs belongs together: the coracoid tip with the short head of the biceps, the coracoid tip with the long head of the biceps, the coracoid base with the pectoralis major, or the coracoid process with the trapezius? The answer is the coracoid tip with the short head of the biceps. The long head of the biceps arises inside the joint from the supraglenoid tubercle.

Question 1286. Which shallow socket on the scapula receives the head of the humerus? The answer is the glenoid cavity, also called the glenoid fossa. It lies at the lateral angle of the scapula, facing outward. It is much smaller than the head that fits into it.

Question 1287. Which bone contributes the socket of the shoulder joint: the humerus, the clavicle, the scapula, or the first rib? The answer is the scapula. Its glenoid cavity forms the socket, and the head of the humerus forms the ball. The clavicle lies above the joint but takes no part in it.

Question 1288. Which ring of fibrocartilage is attached to the rim of the glenoid cavity and deepens it? The answer is the glenoid labrum. It rounds off the edge of the socket and grips the head of the humerus. It also blends with the capsule and with the origin of the long head of the biceps.

Question 1289. The glenoid cavity faces in which direction: straight up, laterally and slightly forward, straight back, or medially? The answer is laterally and slightly forward. The scapula lies on the back of the chest, so its socket must turn around the rib cage to face the arm. The upper end of the socket is narrower than the lower end.

Question 1290. Which tendon arises from the supraglenoid tubercle just above the glenoid cavity: the long head of the biceps, the short head of the biceps, the long head of the triceps, or the coracobrachialis? The answer is the long head of the biceps. It passes through the joint and then lies in a groove on the humerus. The short head arises from the coracoid process instead.

Question 1291. Which structure lies immediately below the glenoid cavity, and which muscle arises from it? The answer is the infraglenoid tubercle, from which the long head of the triceps arises. It lies at the upper end of the lateral border of the scapula. The tubercle above the socket is the supraglenoid one.

Question 1292. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows the rounded head of the humerus overlapping a shallow socket on a triangular bone, and the socket is narrower at the top than at the bottom. Which socket is shown, and what deepens its rim? The answer is the glenoid cavity, deepened by the glenoid labrum. The narrow upper end carries the supraglenoid tubercle.

Question 1293. Which feature of the glenoid cavity best explains why the shoulder dislocates more easily than any other joint: the socket is shallow and holds only about one third of the head, it is filled with fat, it faces backward, or it is lined by cartilage? The answer is the shallow socket, which holds only about one third of the head. The labrum and the cuff help, but the fit stays loose.

Question 1294. A constructed illustration: a patient falls with the arm forced up and back, and afterward the shoulder looks square and the deltoid cannot be felt to contract. Which nerve is usually injured in this kind of dislocation, and what is lost? The answer is the axillary nerve, with weakness of the deltoid and loss of feeling over the upper outer arm. The nerve winds close to the lower part of the socket.

Question 1295. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraglenoid tubercle with the long head of the biceps, the supraglenoid tubercle with the triceps, the infraglenoid tubercle with the biceps, or the infraglenoid tubercle with the coracobrachialis? The answer is the supraglenoid tubercle with the long head of the biceps. The infraglenoid tubercle belongs to the long head of the triceps.

Question 1296. Name the four muscles of the rotator cuff, spoken as a list. The answer is the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the subscapularis, and the teres minor. They arise from the scapula and blend with the capsule around the head of the humerus. They hold the head in the socket during movement.

Question 1297. The glenoid cavity is described as pear-shaped. Which of these statements is correct: it is wider below and narrower above, it is wider above and narrower below, it is perfectly round, or it is oval with its long axis across? The answer is that it is wider below and narrower above. The narrow upper part carries the supraglenoid tubercle. The lower front rim is the part torn in anterior dislocation.

Question 1298. A described cross section through the shoulder passes from front to back and shows the socket cut in half with the head of the humerus seated in it. In which plane was the section taken? The answer is a sagittal plane through the joint. It shows the socket and the head from the side, with the coracoid process in front and the acromion above.

Question 1299. A described MRI scan of the shoulder shows a dark triangular rim around the edge of the socket, continuous with the capsule above and torn below. Which structure is shown, and where is the tear? The answer is the glenoid labrum, torn at its lower front part. That tear follows the head of the humerus as it slips out of the socket.

Question 1300. A constructed illustration: a young athlete dislocates the shoulder several times, and each time the arm is forced outward and back. Which part of the glenoid rim is repeatedly injured, and which piece of bone may be chipped? The answer is the lower front part of the rim, with a chip of the bony edge. The damaged rim then fails to hold the head.
