To summarize, the clavicle is the only bony link between the upper limb and the trunk and the first bone to begin ossification, and it breaks most often at its middle third, where the sternocleidomastoid lifts the inner fragment and the weight of the arm drops the outer one. The scapula is a flat triangular bone lying over the second to the seventh ribs, with no joint to the axial skeleton, held by muscles alone, and carrying the spine, the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae behind and the subscapular fossa in front. The acromion and the coracoid process are the two hooks of the upper lateral scapula, the acromion roofing the shoulder and the coracoid giving origin to the coracobrachialis and the short head of the biceps, while the glenoid cavity is the shallow socket deepened by the labrum and steadied by the rotator cuff. The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch below the ligament, the axillary nerve winds close to the lower rim of the socket, and the long thoracic nerve runs on the serratus anterior, so each of these nerves marks a place where the girdle is vulnerable. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 14 — Upper Limb Bones

The bones of the upper limb carry the hand wherever the mind sends it, and this chapter works through the four groups that make that possible: the humerus of the arm, and the radius, the ulna and the carpal bones of the forearm and the wrist. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer at once and then explains why, so nothing has to be carried in mind. The items begin at the shoulder and move outward to the elbow and the wrist, testing the parts, the attachments and the relations of each bone in turn. The landmarks that can be felt through the skin are given particular attention, because a listener will meet them again at the bedside. This chapter is educational material and supports, rather than replaces, an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1301. Which bone of the upper limb is the single long bone of the arm, running from the shoulder joint above to the elbow below? The answer is the humerus. Its head fits the shallow socket of the scapula, and its widened lower end meets the radius and the ulna. Every muscle that moves the shoulder or the elbow pulls on this one bone.

Question 1302. Which rounded part at the upper end of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity of the scapula: the capitulum, the greater tubercle, the head, or the trochlea? The answer is the head. It is a smooth hemisphere directed upward and medially, and it forms one half of the shoulder joint. The capitulum and the trochlea belong to the lower end of the bone.

Question 1303. Which roughened elevation on the outer surface of the middle of the humeral shaft gives attachment to the deltoid muscle? The answer is the deltoid tuberosity. It lies about halfway down the shaft on the lateral side. A muscle that raises the arm therefore pulls on the middle of the bone rather than on either end.

Question 1304. At the upper end of the humerus, which of the two tubercles lies more laterally, and which three muscles of the shoulder attach to it? The answer is the greater tubercle, which receives the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor. The lesser tubercle lies in front of it and more medially and receives the subscapularis. The groove between the two is the intertubercular sulcus.

Question 1305. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows two rounded eminences at the upper end of the humerus, separated by a deep groove that runs down the front of the shaft. Which eminences are shown, and what runs between them? The answer is the greater and the lesser tubercles, with the tendon of the long head of the biceps in the intertubercular sulcus.

Question 1306. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the point of the shoulder, and afterward the shoulder looks flattened, the arm cannot be lifted away from the side, and the skin over the outer upper arm is numb. Which structure is injured? The answer is the axillary nerve, which winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies the deltoid.

Question 1307. The intertubercular sulcus of the humerus transmits the tendon of which muscle: the long head of the biceps brachii, the short head of the biceps brachii, the coracobrachialis, or the subscapularis? The answer is the long head of the biceps brachii. That tendon leaves the shoulder joint, runs down the groove, and is held there by a fibrous band. The short head lies medial to it.

Question 1308. True or false: the head of the humerus is larger than the glenoid cavity into which it fits. The answer is true. The head is about a third of a sphere, while the socket of the scapula is shallow and small. That mismatch is what gives the shoulder its wide range of movement and its tendency to dislocate.

Question 1309. Which set of three muscles attaches to the greater tubercle of the humerus: the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor; the subscapularis, the teres major and the latissimus dorsi; the deltoid, the coracobrachialis and the pectoralis major; or the biceps, the brachialis and the triceps? The answer is the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor. Those three with the subscapularis form the rotator cuff.

Question 1310. A described radiograph of the middle of the arm shows a groove running down the back of the humeral shaft, and the bone is broken across it. Which nerve and artery lie in that groove, and what does the nerve supply? The answer is the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery. The nerve supplies the triceps and the extensor muscles of the forearm.

Question 1311. A constructed illustration: after a fracture in the middle of the arm, the wrist hangs limp, the fingers cannot be straightened, and the back of the hand between the thumb and the index finger is numb. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the radial nerve, pressed against the bone in the radial groove.

Question 1312. Which smooth, rounded articular surface at the lower end of the humerus lies on the lateral side and receives the head of the radius? The answer is the capitulum. It is a rounded knob that meets the disc-shaped head of the radius. The pulley-shaped trochlea lies medial to it and articulates with the ulna.

Question 1313. Which prominent bony process can be felt at the inner side of the elbow, and which nerve passes behind it? The answer is the medial epicondyle, with the ulnar nerve running behind it. The nerve is superficial there, so a knock at the elbow gives the tingling of the funny bone.

Question 1314. Which hollow on the back of the lower humerus receives the olecranon when the elbow is straightened: the coronoid fossa, the radial fossa, the olecranon fossa, or the intercondylar groove? The answer is the olecranon fossa. It is a deep depression above the trochlea on the posterior surface. The coronoid and radial fossae lie on the front of the bone instead.

Question 1315. Which of these pairs belongs together: the capitulum with the ulna, the trochlea with the radius, the capitulum with the head of the radius, or the trochlea with the head of the radius? The answer is the capitulum with the head of the radius. The rounded capitulum meets the disc-shaped radial head, while the trochlea meets the trochlear notch of the ulna.

Question 1316. A constructed illustration: a child falls on the outstretched hand, and the described radiograph shows a break just above the condyles of the humerus with the lower fragment displaced backward. Which structures lying in front of the elbow are most at risk? The answer is the brachial artery and the median nerve, which pass in front of the joint. The deformity can also press on them.

Question 1317. A described radiograph of a straight elbow shows a beak of bone lying inside a hollow at the back of the lower humerus. Which process and which hollow are shown? The answer is the olecranon of the ulna, sitting in the olecranon fossa of the humerus. When the elbow bends, the process swings out of the fossa and the hollow is empty.

Question 1318. Which pulley-shaped articular surface at the lower end of the humerus articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna? The answer is the trochlea. It is shaped like a spool with a groove in the middle, and it lets the elbow bend and straighten like a hinge. It lies medial to the capitulum.

Question 1319. Which of these groups belongs together: the greater tubercle with the subscapularis, the lesser tubercle with the subscapularis, the deltoid tuberosity with the triceps, or the radial groove with the ulnar nerve? The answer is the lesser tubercle with the subscapularis. The other rotator cuff muscles attach to the greater tubercle, and the radial groove carries the radial nerve.

Question 1320. Which muscles take origin from the front of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, and which from the lateral epicondyle? The answer is the flexor muscles of the forearm from the medial epicondyle and the extensor muscles from the lateral epicondyle. The two epicondyles therefore give a simple rule at the bedside: the inner one bends the wrist and the fingers, the outer one straightens them.

Question 1321. Which statement about the anatomical neck of the humerus is correct: the capsule of the shoulder is attached along it, it is the commonest site of fracture, it lies below the two tubercles, or it closes the medullary cavity? The answer is that the capsule is attached along it. The surgical neck below the tubercles is the usual fracture site.

Question 1322. True or false: the deltoid is the only muscle that attaches to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. The answer is true. The tuberosity is a raised area on the lateral surface of the shaft, and it exists for that muscle alone. The other muscles of the region attach instead to the tubercles at the upper end or to the epicondyles below.

Question 1323. Which of these statements about the intertubercular sulcus is correct: it lies on the front of the upper humerus and carries the tendon of the long head of the biceps, it lies on the back of the shaft and carries the radial nerve, it lies below the deltoid tuberosity, or it separates the epicondyles? The answer is the first.

Question 1324. A described radiograph of the elbow shows two rounded prominences on either side of the joint at the lower end of the humerus. Which prominence is medial and which is lateral, and what lies behind the medial one? The answer is the medial epicondyle on the inner side and the lateral epicondyle on the outer side, with the ulnar nerve passing behind the medial one.

Question 1325. Which groove on the back of the humerus runs obliquely downward and laterally, carrying the radial nerve against the bone? The answer is the radial groove. It begins near the surgical neck and runs toward the lateral side of the shaft. Because the nerve lies directly on bone there, a fracture at that level is likely to injure it.

Question 1326. Which of these muscles does not attach to the humerus at all: the deltoid, the coracobrachialis, the subscapularis, or the serratus anterior? The answer is the serratus anterior. It arises from the outer surfaces of the upper ribs and inserts on the medial border of the scapula. The other three all have an attachment on the humerus.

Question 1327. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a person cannot grip with the ring and little fingers, the little finger is numb, and the described radiograph shows a fragment of bone at the inner side of the elbow. Which nerve is injured, and why not the median nerve? The answer is the ulnar nerve, behind the medial epicondyle.

Question 1328. Which part of the upper humerus lies inside the capsule of the shoulder joint and is covered by articular cartilage rather than by periosteum? The answer is the head of the humerus. The capsule is attached around the anatomical neck, so the head sits within the joint cavity. The tubercles lie outside the capsule and are covered by periosteum.

Question 1329. A supracondylar fracture in a child heals with the lower fragment tilted so that the forearm points inward when the arm is extended. What is this deformity called: cubitus varus, cubitus valgus, a dislocation of the radial head, or an olecranon spur? The answer is cubitus varus. Cubitus valgus is the opposite deviation, with the forearm carried outward.

Question 1330. Which structure winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, passing between the bone and the muscles that cover it? The answer is the axillary nerve, with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. It travels through a space bounded by the teres minor above, the teres major below and the long head of the triceps medially. A fracture at the surgical neck threatens it.

Question 1331. Which small prominence on the outer side of the elbow gives origin to the muscles that straighten the wrist and the fingers? The answer is the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. It lies at the lateral edge of the lower end, above the capitulum. Its counterpart on the inner side gives origin to the flexor muscles.

Question 1332. Which of these statements about the lower end of the humerus is correct: the capitulum lies lateral to the trochlea, the trochlea lies lateral to the capitulum, the epicondyles lie on the front of the bone, or the olecranon fossa lies on the front? The answer is that the capitulum lies lateral to the trochlea and meets the head of the radius.

Question 1333. A described radiograph of a child's elbow shows a small rounded ossification center at the medial side of the joint, separated from the shaft by cartilage. Which center is it, and why must it not be mistaken for a fragment? The answer is the center for the medial epicondyle, which appears later than the others and joins the shaft only toward the end of growth.

Question 1334. Name the two articular surfaces at the lower end of the humerus, spoken as a pair from lateral to medial. The answer is the capitulum and the trochlea. The capitulum receives the head of the radius, and the trochlea receives the trochlear notch of the ulna. Together they form the condyle of the humerus.

Question 1335. Why does the shoulder dislocate forward and downward more often than in any other direction: because the capsule is weak below and in front, because the glenoid cavity is deeper below than above, because the acromion blocks upward displacement, or because the biceps tendon holds the head back? The answer is the weak capsule below and in front.

Question 1336. Which bone of the forearm lies on the thumb side when the body is in the anatomical position? The answer is the radius. It is the lateral bone of the forearm and the broader of the two at the wrist. The ulna lies medial to it on the little finger side.

Question 1337. Which part of the radius takes part in the elbow joint: the head, the neck, the radial tuberosity, or the styloid process? The answer is the head. It is a disc-shaped upper end whose upper surface glides against the capitulum of the humerus. The neck below it is encircled by a ligament rather than by cartilage.

Question 1338. Which roughened prominence on the upper radius lies just below the neck, faces medially, and gives insertion to the biceps brachii? The answer is the radial tuberosity. Its position on the medial side of the bone is a useful reminder of how the tendon of the biceps twists as it reaches the forearm.

Question 1339. Which band of fibrous tissue encircles the head of the radius and holds it against the ulna, allowing it to spin but not to slide away? The answer is the annular ligament. It is attached to the front and the back of the radial notch of the ulna and forms about four fifths of a ring around the radial head.

Question 1340. A described radiograph of the wrist shows that the bony point reaching farthest down on the outer side is longer than the corresponding point on the inner side. Which bone carries the longer point, and what is that point called? The answer is the radius, and the point is its styloid process.

Question 1341. Which part of the lower radius is grooved to hold the tendon of the extensor pollicis longus: the dorsal tubercle, the ulnar notch, the styloid process, or the radial tuberosity? The answer is the dorsal tubercle, a small prominence on the back of the lower end around which the tendon runs. The ulnar notch receives the head of the ulna.

Question 1342. A constructed illustration: an older person falls onto the outstretched hand, and afterward there is a painful swelling at the wrist with the hand displaced backward, so that the wrist looks like a fork. Which bone is broken, and in which direction is the lower fragment displaced? The answer is the lower end of the radius, displaced backward and upward.

Question 1343. True or false: the shafts of the radius and the ulna are joined along their length by a fibrous membrane. The answer is true. The interosseous membrane stretches between the two interosseous borders. It gives attachment to muscles, keeps the bones apart, and carries part of the force that the hand receives up to the ulna.

Question 1344. Which of these pairs belongs together: the head of the radius with the radial notch, the head of the ulna with the radial notch, the head of the radius with the ulnar notch, or the head of the ulna with the trochlear notch? The answer is the head of the radius with the radial notch of the ulna, at the upper joint between the bones.

Question 1345. Which movement carries the lower end of the radius across the front of the ulna: supination, pronation, flexion, or abduction? The answer is pronation. The radius rotates around the ulna so that its lower end crosses to the medial side, and the palm turns to face the floor. Supination untwists the two bones and returns them to parallel.

Question 1346. A described radiograph of a forearm held with the palm facing forward shows two bones lying side by side, each with a narrow shaft and a wider end. Which bone lies lateral, and which bone lies medial? The answer is the radius laterally and the ulna medially. With the palm forward, the two bones are parallel and neither crosses the other.

Question 1347. Which pointed projection at the lower end of the radius forms the outer boundary of the wrist and can be felt as a bony knob just above the base of the thumb? The answer is the styloid process of the radius. It reaches farther down than the styloid process of the ulna on the other side of the wrist.

Question 1348. A constructed illustration: a fracture crosses the lower third of the radius, and the described radiograph shows that the head of the ulna no longer sits in its notch at the wrist. Which two injuries are present? The answer is a fracture of the distal radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint.

Question 1349. The radius rotates about the ulna during pronation and supination. Which structure forms the pivot at its upper end, and which at its lower end? The answer is the head of the radius turning within the ring of the radial notch and the annular ligament above, and the head of the ulna turning within the ulnar notch of the radius below.

Question 1350. Which two carpal bones articulate with the carpal surface of the radius: the scaphoid and the lunate, the lunate and the triquetrum, the scaphoid and the trapezium, or the pisiform and the lunate? The answer is the scaphoid and the lunate. The radius carries the hand at the wrist, and the ulna is separated from the carpus by a disc.

Question 1351. A described cross section through the lower end of the radius shows a broad bone with a concave surface below, divided into two facets, and a small notch on its medial edge. Which bone is this, and what does the notch receive? The answer is the radius, and the notch is the ulnar notch, which receives the head of the ulna.

Question 1352. Name the two bones of the forearm in the order in which they lie from lateral to medial in the anatomical position. The answer is the radius and then the ulna. The radius lies on the thumb side and the ulna on the little finger side. The order reverses when the forearm is fully pronated.

Question 1353. Which muscle inserts on the radial tuberosity: the biceps brachii, the triceps brachii, the brachialis, or the pronator teres? The answer is the biceps brachii. Its tendon crosses the front of the elbow and twists as it reaches the medial side of the bone. The brachialis inserts on the ulna instead.

Question 1354. Which muscle inserts into the lateral surface of the middle of the radial shaft and turns the forearm so that the palm faces downward? The answer is the pronator teres. It arises from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the coronoid process of the ulna and sweeps across to the radius. Its pull rotates the radius around the ulna.

Question 1355. When the forearm turns from the position with the palm forward to the position with the palm backward, the radius rotates about a longitudinal axis. In which direction does its lower end travel, and which bone stays still? The answer is that the lower end of the radius travels forward and medially across the front of the ulna, while the ulna stays in place.

Question 1356. A described radiograph shows a break through the lower end of the radius with the hand and the fragment displaced forward rather than backward. Which pattern is this: a backward displacement fracture, a forward displacement fracture, a fracture of the radial head, or a fracture of the ulnar styloid? The answer is a forward displacement fracture, the reverse of the commoner backward pattern.

Question 1357. A constructed illustration: a young child is lifted by the hand and afterward holds the arm still and will not use it, because the head of the radius has slipped partly out from under the ring that holds it. Which structure has given way, and at which end of the bone? The answer is the annular ligament at the upper end of the radius.

Question 1358. Which bone of the forearm forms the point of the elbow and carries the notch that grips the humerus? The answer is the ulna. Its upper end is thick and its lower end is small, the reverse of the radius. It lies on the little finger side of the forearm.

Question 1359. Which process of the ulna projects forward below the trochlear notch and forms the lower lip of that notch? The answer is the coronoid process. The olecranon forms the upper lip and the point of the elbow. The two are joined by the notch that receives the trochlea of the humerus.

Question 1360. The trochlear notch of the ulna articulates with which part of the humerus: the capitulum, the trochlea, the head, or the greater tubercle? The answer is the trochlea. It is a hinge joint, so the ulna can only bend and straighten on the humerus. The head of the radius meets the capitulum instead.

Question 1361. Which muscle inserts on the olecranon of the ulna, and what movement does its contraction produce? The answer is the triceps brachii, which straightens the elbow. It is the only muscle that inserts on that process, and the process gives it a lever arm behind the joint. Its long head also crosses the shoulder joint.

Question 1362. A described radiograph of the elbow taken from the side shows a broad notch on the upper ulna gripping the lower humerus, with a beak above it and a smaller projection below. Which three parts of the ulna are shown? The answer is the trochlear notch, with the olecranon above it and the coronoid process below it.

Question 1363. True or false: the ulna takes part in the wrist joint. The answer is false. The lower end of the ulna is separated from the carpal bones by a disc of fibrocartilage, so the ulna has no direct articular surface at the wrist. The radius alone carries the hand at that joint.

Question 1364. Which structure lies between the head of the ulna and the carpal bones and keeps the ulna from bearing weight at the wrist: the annular ligament, the articular disc, the interosseous membrane, or the flexor retinaculum? The answer is the articular disc. It is part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex and completes the socket for the carpus.

Question 1365. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the bent elbow, and the described radiograph shows a break through the beak of bone at the back of the joint with the fragment pulled upward; the elbow can no longer be straightened against resistance. Which structure is broken, and which muscle has pulled the fragment? The answer is the olecranon, pulled by the triceps brachii.

Question 1366. Which of these pairs belongs together: the olecranon with the biceps brachii, the coronoid process with the brachialis, the radial notch with the trochlea, or the ulnar styloid with the olecranon fossa? The answer is the coronoid process with the brachialis. The brachialis inserts on the front of the ulna just below the coronoid process, and the triceps inserts on the olecranon.

Question 1367. Which shallow depression on the lateral side of the coronoid process of the ulna receives the head of the radius? The answer is the radial notch. It forms the lateral wall of the upper radioulnar joint, and the annular ligament is attached to its edges. The radius spins against it during pronation and supination.

Question 1368. A described radiograph of the forearm after a fall shows a break through the upper part of the ulna together with displacement of the radial head at the elbow. Which two injuries are present, and which structure has given way? The answer is a fracture of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head, and the annular ligament no longer holds the head in place.

Question 1369. Which statement about the ulnar styloid process is correct: it receives the attachment of the articular disc but does not reach the carpal bones, it articulates directly with the triquetrum, it is longer than the radial styloid, or it lies at the upper end of the ulna? The answer is the first. It is a small projection at the lower end of the ulna.

Question 1370. A constructed illustration: a person who leans the inner side of the elbow on a desk for long periods develops tingling in the little finger and wasting of the small muscles of the hand. Which nerve is compressed, and where? The answer is the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, covered only by skin and fascia.

Question 1371. Which border of the ulna gives attachment to the interosseous membrane, and toward which bone does that border face? The answer is the interosseous border, which faces laterally toward the radius. It is the sharp lateral crest of the shaft, and the membrane that runs from it to the radius divides the forearm into front and back compartments.

Question 1372. Which statement about the head of the ulna is correct: it lies at the lower end of the bone, it lies at the upper end, it articulates with the humerus, or it gives insertion to the biceps? The answer is that it lies at the lower end, where it fits the ulnar notch of the radius.

Question 1373. Which ridge on the upper part of the ulna runs downward from the radial notch and gives origin to part of the supinator muscle? The answer is the supinator crest. It lies on the lateral surface of the upper shaft, blending with the radial notch above. The muscle wraps around the upper radius from it.

Question 1374. Which part of the ulna lies directly beneath the skin along the back of the forearm and is therefore the sharp edge that can be felt with a finger? The answer is the posterior border of the shaft. It is subcutaneous throughout its length, with no muscle covering it. That is why the ulna is so easily exposed to injury from behind.

Question 1375. A described cross section through the lower forearm shows two bones, one broad and one small, with a disc of fibrocartilage extending from the smaller bone to the carpus. Which bones and which structure are shown? The answer is the radius and the ulna at the wrist, with the articular disc separating the head of the ulna from the carpal bones.

Question 1376. Name two muscles that have an attachment on the ulna, spoken as a pair. The answer is the brachialis and the triceps brachii. The brachialis inserts on the coronoid process below the joint, and the triceps inserts on the olecranon above it. Many other muscles also arise from the shaft of the bone.

Question 1377. Which statement best explains why the elbow bends and straightens without the forearm rotating sideways: the ulna is a stable hinge on the trochlea while the radius rotates about it, the radius is fixed while the ulna rotates, the two rotate together, or the joint is a ball and socket? The answer is the first.

Question 1378. A transverse section is taken across the forearm just above the wrist. Which of the two bones lies lateral in that section, and which bone has a rounded head seen on the medial side? The answer is the radius laterally and the head of the ulna medially. At that level the radius is broad and the ulna is small.

Question 1379. The force of the hand passes through the radius at the wrist, yet a break in the ulnar shaft can still disturb that joint. Why: because the two bones are joined at both ends, because the ulna reaches the carpal bones, because the disc is ulnar, or because the ulnar styloid carries the load? The answer is that the two bones are joined at both ends.

Question 1380. How many carpal bones form one wrist, and how are they arranged? The answer is eight bones in two rows of four. The proximal row lies next to the radius and the distal row next to the metacarpal bones. The row of bones forms an arch whose concavity faces the palm.

Question 1381. Which carpal bone lies at the outer side of the proximal row, next to the radius and above the thumb: the lunate, the scaphoid, the triquetrum, or the pisiform? The answer is the scaphoid. It is the largest bone of the proximal row and takes the weight of the hand against the radius. The lunate lies medial to it.

Question 1382. Which carpal bone lies in the floor of the hollow at the base of the thumb, the hollow that is bounded by two tendons and is known as the anatomical snuffbox? The answer is the scaphoid. Its tubercle can be felt on the palm side of the wrist as a small rounded prominence.

Question 1383. A described radiograph of the wrist shows a crack running across the middle of one carpal bone in the proximal row, with no displacement. Which bone is most likely broken, and why is the break often missed? The answer is the scaphoid. The crack may be invisible at first, and the pain is felt in the hollow at the base of the thumb.

Question 1384. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the outstretched hand, and afterward there is tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb when the wrist is moved, though the described radiograph looks normal. Which bone is most likely broken? The answer is the scaphoid, the carpal bone that breaks most often.

Question 1385. Which carpal bone lies immediately distal to the scaphoid and the lunate and receives the two of them side by side? The answer is the capitate. It sits in the middle of the distal row and is the largest carpal bone. Its rounded head fits into the hollow formed by the scaphoid and the lunate.

Question 1386. With which carpal bone does the first metacarpal form the saddle joint that gives the thumb its wide movement: the trapezoid, the trapezium, the capitate, or the hamate? The answer is the trapezium. The joint between the two is a saddle, which allows the thumb to swing across the palm and to oppose the fingers.

Question 1387. Which carpal bone carries a curved hook-shaped process that can be felt on the front of the wrist near the base of the little finger? The answer is the hamate. The hook projects forward and gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum and to the small muscles of the little finger.

Question 1388. A described radiograph of the wrist shows the carpal bones in two rows; the largest bone lies at the center of the distal row, with the third metacarpal above it. Which bone is it, and which bone lies between it and the radius? The answer is the capitate, with the lunate between it and the radius.

Question 1389. Which of these pairs belongs together: the scaphoid with the first metacarpal, the trapezium with the first metacarpal, the hamate with the radius, or the pisiform with the radius? The answer is the trapezium with the first metacarpal. Those two form the saddle joint of the thumb, while the radius meets the scaphoid and the lunate.

Question 1390. A constructed illustration: a person has numbness of the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger, weakness of the muscles at the base of the thumb, and normal sensation over the little finger. Which nerve is compressed, and beneath which band? The answer is the median nerve, compressed beneath the flexor retinaculum in the carpal tunnel at the wrist.

Question 1391. The flexor retinaculum stretches across the front of the wrist and forms the roof of the carpal tunnel. To which two bones is it attached on the lateral side? The answer is the tubercle of the scaphoid and the ridge of the trapezium. On the medial side it attaches to the pisiform and the hook of the hamate.

Question 1392. True or false: the pisiform is a sesamoid bone that develops within the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris. The answer is true. It is the smallest carpal bone and lies in the proximal row on the medial side. It gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum and to a small muscle of the little finger.

Question 1393. Which carpal bone is the keystone between the radius above and the capitate below, and most often dislocates in a fall on the hand: the scaphoid, the lunate, the capitate, or the trapezium? The answer is the lunate. It sits in the middle of the proximal row and takes the capitate into its lower cup, and a fall on the hand can drive it out of the socket of the radius.

Question 1394. A described radiograph of the wrist shows the lunate still in its place against the radius while all the other carpal bones have shifted backward around it. Which injury is shown, and which bone has stayed behind? The answer is a dislocation of the carpus around the lunate, with the lunate still in the socket of the radius.

Question 1395. Which carpal bone lies in the distal row between the trapezium on one side and the capitate on the other? The answer is the trapezoid. It is smaller than both of its neighbors and articulates below with the second metacarpal bone. It has no movement of its own and moves only as the rest of the wrist moves.

Question 1396. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fifth metacarpal with the hamate, the fifth metacarpal with the trapezium, the second metacarpal with the pisiform, or the first metacarpal with the lunate? The answer is the fifth metacarpal with the hamate. The first metacarpal meets the trapezium, and the second meets the trapezoid.

Question 1397. A break across the waist of the scaphoid often heals badly because the blood supply enters at one end and runs backward along the bone. Which end receives the blood, and which end is left without it? The answer is that the vessels enter the distal part near the tubercle and the proximal pole is nourished in a backward direction, so that pole may die.

Question 1398. A described section across the wrist shows a tunnel bounded by an arch of carpal bones below and a tough band above, with tendons and a nerve packed inside. Which structure forms the floor, and which forms the roof? The answer is the carpal bones forming the floor and the flexor retinaculum forming the roof, with the median nerve between them.

Question 1399. Which of these structures does not pass through the carpal tunnel: the median nerve, the tendon of the flexor pollicis longus, the ulnar nerve, or the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It enters the hand through a separate channel between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate.

Question 1400. Why does compression within the carpal tunnel spare the sensation of the little finger: because the ulnar nerve supplies that finger and does not pass through the tunnel, because the little finger has no nerve supply, because the median nerve spares it, or because the radial nerve supplies it? The answer is that the ulnar nerve supplies the little finger and runs outside the tunnel.

To summarize, the humerus is the single bone of the arm, and each of its parts carries a name worth saying aloud. The greater tubercle takes the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor, the lesser tubercle takes the subscapularis, the radial groove carries the radial nerve against bone, the medial epicondyle shelters the ulnar nerve, and the lateral epicondyle gives origin to the extensor muscles. In the forearm the radius lies on the thumb side, with its head turning against the capitulum and its lower end carrying the hand, while the ulna forms the point of the elbow and is separated from the carpus by the articular disc. The eight carpal bones lie in two rows of four, with the scaphoid in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, the trapezium at the saddle joint of the thumb, the capitate at the center and the hook of the hamate beside the ulnar nerve. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 15 — Upper Limb Bones, Part Two

This chapter continues the survey of the upper limb bones and then turns to the ring of bone that carries the weight of the trunk into the lower limb. The first half examines the metacarpals of the palm and the phalanges of the fingers and the thumb; the second half examines the three bones that fuse to form each hip bone, the ilium, the ischium and the pubis. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. Everything is described in words, because the listener cannot see a bone, a radiograph or a specimen. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1401. Which five bones form the skeleton of the palm of the hand, lying between the wrist above and the fingers below? The answer is the metacarpals. Each is a long bone with a base that meets the carpus, a shaft, and a head that forms a knuckle. They are numbered from the first at the thumb side to the fifth at the little finger side.

Question 1402. What name is given to a bone of the hand that has a flattened base turned toward the wrist, a long shaft, and a rounded head that forms a knuckle at the back of the hand? The answer is a metacarpal. The base carries facets for the carpal bones and for its neighbors. The head carries the rounded surface of the knuckle joint.

Question 1403. How many metacarpal bones does one hand contain: four, five, six, or seven? The answer is five. They run side by side through the palm, so every finger and the thumb has a metacarpal of its own. The first belongs to the thumb and the fifth to the little finger.

Question 1404. Which bone of the palm lies between the trapezium above and the first phalanx of the thumb below? The answer is the first metacarpal. It is the only metacarpal that meets the trapezium, and its head carries the joint with the first phalanx of the thumb. Its shaft is set apart from the other four.

Question 1405. Which carpal bone receives the base of the third metacarpal: the trapezium, the trapezoid, the capitate, or the hamate? The answer is the capitate. It is the largest bone of the carpus. The trapezoid receives the second metacarpal, and the hamate receives the fourth and the fifth.

Question 1406. Which carpal bone lies immediately proximal to the base of the first metacarpal, and what kind of joint do the two form? The answer is the trapezium, and the two form the saddle joint of the thumb. That joint lies at the base of the thumb, separate from the wrist joint. Its shape is what lets the thumb swing across the palm.

Question 1407. Which metacarpal base carries a pointed process that rises between the bones of the wrist? The answer is the third metacarpal, which lies in the middle of the hand. The pointed process is its styloid process, and it can be felt at the back of the wrist.

Question 1408. A described radiograph of the hand shows one metacarpal set apart from the other four, with its shaft turned so that its palmar surface faces the fingers. Which bone is shown, and what does that position tell you? The answer is the first metacarpal, held in opposition. No other metacarpal lies at that angle.

Question 1409. A constructed illustration: after a punch against a hard wall, the back of the hand is swollen over the little finger and its knuckle has lost its outline. Which structure is injured? The answer is the neck of the fifth metacarpal. The head of the bone is tilted toward the palm by the pull of the muscles crossing the joint. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1410. The rounded bumps seen in a row across the back of a clenched fist are formed by which parts: the bases of the metacarpals, the heads of the metacarpals, the shafts of the metacarpals, or the first phalanges? The answer is the heads of the metacarpals. Each head is rounded and carries the joint with the first phalanx of its digit.

Question 1411. True or false: the first metacarpal is the only metacarpal whose growth plate lies at its base rather than at its head. The answer is true. In the first metacarpal the second center of ossification appears at the base, as it does in the phalanges. In the other four metacarpals it appears at the head.

Question 1412. Two small sesamoid bones lie in the tendons at the front of the thumb, one on each side of a joint. Which joint do they lie beside, and which tendons hold them? The answer is the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb, with the tendons of the short flexor of the thumb and the adductor of the thumb. They glide over the joint.

Question 1413. Which type of synovial joint is the metacarpophalangeal joint: a hinge joint, a saddle joint, a condyloid joint, or a plane joint? The answer is a condyloid joint. It allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and a small amount of rotation. The joint at the base of the thumb is the saddle joint of the hand.

Question 1414. A described cross section through the middle of the palm shows the five metacarpal shafts in an arch, with the middle raised and its two ends lower. Which two metacarpals lie lowest, and why does the arch matter? The answer is the first and the fifth. The arch lets the palm cup around an object, with the second and third metacarpals as its keystone.

Question 1415. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the outstretched thumb, and its base is painful and deformed just beyond the wrist. Which bone and which joint are involved? The answer is the first metacarpal and its carpometacarpal joint with the trapezium. A break there is unstable because the long abductor muscle of the thumb pulls the shaft away from the small basal fragment. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1416. In a hand held in the anatomical position, with the palm facing forward, which metacarpal lies immediately lateral to the fourth metacarpal? The answer is the third metacarpal. In that position the thumb and its metacarpal point laterally, and the bones are numbered from the thumb side inward. The third therefore lies between the second and the fourth.

Question 1417. Which muscles fill the spaces between the shafts of the metacarpals, and where do their tendons go? The answer is the interosseous muscles of the hand. They arise from the sides of the metacarpals. Their tendons cross the back of the hand to reach the bases of the first phalanges.

Question 1418. Which metacarpal is the shortest and thickest of the five, and which digit does it carry: the first, the second, the third, or the fifth? The answer is the first, which carries the thumb. Its greater thickness suits the powerful pinch of the thumb. The fifth metacarpal is the most slender of the five and the one most often broken.

Question 1419. A described radiograph of an adult hand shows five metacarpals in the palm. The outermost of them on one side carries a digit that has only two phalanges. Which metacarpal is that? The answer is the first metacarpal. It carries the thumb, the only digit with two phalanges instead of three.

Question 1420. Which of these pairs belongs together: the first metacarpal with the capitate, the second metacarpal with the trapezoid, the third metacarpal with the hamate, or the fifth metacarpal with the trapezium? The answer is the second metacarpal with the trapezoid. The third meets the capitate, the fourth and fifth meet the hamate, and the first meets the trapezium.

Question 1421. Name two bones with which the base of the fifth metacarpal articulates, spoken as a list. The answer is the hamate and the fourth metacarpal. Its base carries a facet above for the hamate and one beside it for the fourth metacarpal. That gives the little finger a little more movement.

Question 1422. Which statement about the metacarpals is correct: the fourth and fifth share the hamate, the first carries its growth plate at the head, the second is the longest of the five, or the heads of the metacarpals form the wrist joint? The answer is that the fourth and fifth share the hamate. The first has its growth plate at the base, and the third is the longest.

Question 1423. A constructed illustration: a fall forces the thumb sharply away from the index finger, and the side of the thumb joint that faces the index finger is tender and unstable. Which structure is torn? The answer is the collateral ligament on that side of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. Forced movement in that direction tears it. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1424. Which of these statements about the metacarpophalangeal joints is correct: they are hinge joints that allow only flexion and extension, they are condyloid joints that also allow abduction and adduction, their collateral ligaments are tight when the fingers are straight, or they lack a capsule? The answer is that they are condyloid joints that also allow abduction and adduction. Their collateral ligaments are tight in flexion, not in extension.

Question 1425. How many phalanges does one hand contain altogether, counting the thumb? The answer is fourteen. Each of the four fingers has three, and the thumb has two. That gives twelve for the fingers and two more for the thumb. They are the last bones of the upper limb.

Question 1426. How many phalanges does the thumb contain, and what are they called? The answer is two, the proximal phalanx and the distal phalanx. The thumb has no middle phalanx. The other four digits each have a proximal, a middle and a distal phalanx.

Question 1427. What are the three phalanges of a finger called, in order from the knuckle to the tip: proximal, middle and distal; upper, middle and lower; first, second and third; or basal, middle and terminal? The answer is proximal, middle and distal. The proximal phalanx meets the metacarpal, the middle lies between, and the distal carries the tip of the finger.

Question 1428. A described radiograph of the thumb shows the metacarpal, then a joint, and then only two phalanges. Which two phalanges are shown, and which one is missing? The answer is the proximal phalanx and the distal phalanx, with no middle phalanx. The joint between the two is the interphalangeal joint of the thumb.

Question 1429. Which type of joint are the interphalangeal joints of the fingers: hinge joints, saddle joints, condyloid joints, or pivot joints? The answer is hinge joints. Each allows flexion and extension in one plane and nothing else. A finger therefore has two hinge joints in series, one on each side of its middle phalanx.

Question 1430. Which phalanx of a finger ends not in a rounded head but in a broad, roughened tuberosity, and what rests upon that tuberosity? The answer is the distal phalanx. Its flattened end gives the fingertip its shape, and the nail and the pulp rest upon it.

Question 1431. The base of the middle phalanx carries two shallow facets that meet the rounded head of the bone above it. Which bone's head is that, and what kind of joint is formed? The answer is the head of the proximal phalanx, forming the proximal interphalangeal joint. The two facets sit astride the pulley, which keeps the joint a pure hinge.

Question 1432. True or false: the thumb has a middle phalanx like every other digit. The answer is false. The thumb has only a proximal phalanx and a distal phalanx, and therefore only one interphalangeal joint. The four fingers each have three phalanges and two interphalangeal joints.

Question 1433. The collateral ligaments of the metacarpophalangeal joints are tightest in which position: when the fingers are straight, when the fingers are fully bent, when the fingers are spread apart, or when the hand is turned palm upward? The answer is when the fingers are fully bent. Each runs from the back of the metacarpal head to the front of the phalangeal base, so bending winds it tight.

Question 1434. Which of these pairs belongs together: the distal phalanx with its broad tuberosity, the middle phalanx with the metacarpal head, the proximal phalanx of the thumb with two pulleys, or the distal phalanx of the thumb with the trapezium? The answer is the distal phalanx with its broad tuberosity. The proximal phalanx meets the metacarpal head, and the trapezium meets a metacarpal.

Question 1435. A described radiograph of the index finger shows a break across the broad tuft of the distal phalanx, with the fragments held in line. Which phalanx is broken, and why do such breaks usually stay in place? The answer is the distal phalanx. Fibrous septa run from the skin to the bone and splint the fragments, so the break rarely displaces.

Question 1436. Which structure lies immediately distal to the head of the first metacarpal? The answer is the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. The two meet at the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. On each side of that joint lies a collateral ligament, and the sesamoid bones lie in front of it.

Question 1437. On which sides of an interphalangeal joint do its collateral ligaments lie? The answer is one on each side, the medial and the lateral, joining the head of one phalanx to the base of the next. They are tight in every position and hold the hinge steady.

Question 1438. Which phalanx of a finger is the longest and which is the shortest? The answer is that the proximal phalanx is the longest and the distal phalanx the shortest. The middle phalanx lies between them in length. The thumb is the exception, since its proximal phalanx is short and stout.

Question 1439. A described dissection of a finger shows a fibrous sheet spreading over the back of the proximal phalanx and receiving the tendons of the forearm and of the hand. What is that sheet, and what does it do? The answer is the extensor expansion. It covers the back of the phalanges and lets one tendon bend the knuckle and straighten the joints beyond it.

Question 1440. A described radiograph shows one hand in full, with all its bones counted in a row. How many bones does an adult hand contain, and how are they divided? The answer is twenty-seven: eight carpals, five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges. The phalanges make up more than half of them. Only the thumb departs from the count of three phalanges.

Question 1441. Which phalanx receives the tendon of the deep flexor muscle of the fingers, and on which surface of that phalanx does it end? The answer is the distal phalanx, on the palmar surface at its base. The deep flexor muscle is the one that bends the tip of the finger.

Question 1442. A constructed illustration: a ball strikes the tip of an outstretched finger, and the tip is left drooping and cannot be straightened while the rest of the finger moves well. Which structure is injured? The answer is the extensor tendon where it attaches to the base of the distal phalanx. The pull of the tendon has avulsed it. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1443. A constructed illustration: a player grabs a jersey, the ring finger is pulled hard while already bent, and the tip can no longer be bent at all. Which structure has given way? The answer is the tendon of the deep flexor muscle of the fingers, torn from the base of the distal phalanx. It is the only tendon that bends the tip. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1444. True or false: the proximal interphalangeal joint of a finger permits a small amount of sideways movement, which is why a finger can be spread. The answer is false. The interphalangeal joints are hinges and allow movement in one plane only. Spreading the fingers happens at the metacarpophalangeal joints, where the fingers join the hand.

Question 1445. Which of these pairs belongs together: the metacarpophalangeal joint with the head of a metacarpal, the interphalangeal joint with the trapezium, the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb with a phalanx, or the wrist joint with the head of the fifth metacarpal? The answer is the metacarpophalangeal joint with the head of a metacarpal. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is formed with the trapezium.

Question 1446. A described specimen of the thumb shows a joint between two phalanges whose surfaces are shaped like a pulley and whose movement is confined to a single plane. Which joint is shown, and which movements does it allow? The answer is the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, which allows flexion and extension only. The wide arc of the thumb belongs to the joint at its base.

Question 1447. The rounded head of the proximal phalanx of a finger is received by the base of which bone, and what is that joint called? The answer is the middle phalanx, and the joint is the proximal interphalangeal joint. The head of the middle phalanx is received in turn by the base of the distal phalanx.

Question 1448. Which statement about a break of the tuft of the distal phalanx is correct: it usually stays in place because the skin and fibrous septa splint it, it always displaces, it is a break of the middle phalanx, or it separates the extensor tendon? The answer is that it usually stays in place because the skin and fibrous septa splint it. Such breaks are closed injuries.

Question 1449. Which movements does the metacarpophalangeal joint of a finger allow, and which movement does it lack? The answer is that it allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and a small amount of rotation. It cannot spin the finger on its own long axis the way the shoulder spins the arm. The interphalangeal joints beyond it are plain hinges.

Question 1450. Which feature of the head of a proximal phalanx keeps the interphalangeal joint in a single plane: a central ridge that fits a groove in the base beyond it, a flat surface with no ridge, a ball that sits in a socket, or a pair of sesamoid bones? The answer is a central ridge that fits a groove, called a pulley. It allows flexion and extension but no sideways swing.

Question 1451. Which of the three bones that fuse to form the hip bone is the largest, and where does it lie? The answer is the ilium, which forms the upper and widest part of the bone. Its broad upper part is the wing, and its lower part joins the other two bones in the socket of the hip.

Question 1452. Which border of the hip bone can be followed with the fingers from the front to the back, forming the rim of the pelvis? The answer is the iliac crest. It is the upper border of the wing of the ilium and runs in a gentle curve. It ends in front at the anterior superior iliac spine and behind at the posterior superior iliac spine.

Question 1453. The highest point of the iliac crest lies at the level of which vertebra: the twelfth thoracic, the second lumbar, the fourth lumbar, or the first sacral? The answer is the fourth lumbar vertebra. That level is used to find the space between the spines for a lumbar puncture.

Question 1454. A described radiograph of the back of the pelvis shows an ear-shaped patch of joint surface on each side of the sacrum, gripping it like a pair of hands. Which bone carries that surface, and which joint does it form? The answer is the ilium, and the surface forms the sacroiliac joint. Its ear shape interlocks the two bones.

Question 1455. Which smooth, concave surface on the inner side of the ilium lodges a muscle that runs down to the thigh: the iliac fossa, the iliac tuberosity, the arcuate line, or the gluteal surface? The answer is the iliac fossa, which lodges the iliacus muscle. That muscle fills the hollow and joins the psoas muscle to bend the hip.

Question 1456. The anterior superior iliac spine gives attachment to which two structures: the inguinal ligament and the sartorius muscle, the sacrotuberous ligament and the gluteus maximus, the rectus femoris and the inguinal ligament, or the iliacus and the psoas? The answer is the inguinal ligament and the sartorius muscle. The anterior inferior spine below it gives attachment to the straight head of the rectus femoris.

Question 1457. A constructed illustration: an adolescent kicks a football hard and feels a sudden pain at the front of the hip, and a small fragment of bone lies just above the hip joint. Which bony point has given way, and which muscle pulled it off? The answer is the anterior inferior iliac spine, pulled off by the straight head of the rectus femoris. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1458. Which bony point lies at the lower end of the front border of the ilium, just below the anterior superior iliac spine? The answer is the anterior inferior iliac spine. It gives attachment to the straight head of the rectus femoris muscle of the thigh.

Question 1459. The greater sciatic notch is converted into the greater sciatic foramen by which two ligaments: the inguinal ligament and the sacrospinous ligament, the sacrospinous ligament and the sacrotuberous ligament, the sacrotuberous ligament and the iliofemoral ligament, or the pubofemoral ligament and the ischiofemoral ligament? The answer is the sacrospinous ligament and the sacrotuberous ligament. The notch itself lies below the posterior inferior iliac spine.

Question 1460. A described radiograph of the hip bone of a young child shows three separate bones meeting in the socket of the hip, with a band of cartilage between them shaped like a letter Y. Which bones are shown, and where do they meet? The answer is the ilium, the ischium and the pubis, meeting in the acetabulum, where they fuse as growth ends.

Question 1461. The socket of the hip joint has a gap at its lower margin, bridged by a ligament so that a small opening remains. Which structure passes through that opening to reach the head of the femur? The answer is the round ligament of the head of the femur, carrying a small artery. The gap is the acetabular notch.

Question 1462. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior superior iliac spine with the inguinal ligament, the posterior superior iliac spine with the rectus femoris, the iliac fossa with the gluteus maximus, or the iliac crest with the sacrospinous ligament? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine with the inguinal ligament. The iliac fossa lodges the iliacus, and the crest gives attachment to the abdominal muscles.

Question 1463. True or false: the strong ligaments that bind the sacrum to the ilium are attached to the rough area just behind the ear-shaped joint surface of the ilium. The answer is true. That rough area is the iliac tuberosity. The ligaments that fill the space between it and the sacrum lock the two bones together, so that very little movement is possible.

Question 1464. Which part of the socket of the hip joint is formed by the ilium: the superior part, the anterior part, the posterior inferior part, or the floor of the notch? The answer is the superior part, rather more than two fifths of the socket. The ischium forms the posterior inferior part and the pubis the anterior part. The three meet in the floor of the socket.

Question 1465. Which ridge on the inner surface of the ilium runs downward and forward to join the pubis, marking the brim of the pelvis? The answer is the arcuate line. It divides the inner surface of the hip bone into a broad upper part and a narrow lower part. The pelvic cavity lies below it and the greater pelvis above.

Question 1466. A described specimen of the outer surface of the ilium shows three curved ridges running from the back of the bone toward the front. What are these ridges, and what do they separate? The answer is the gluteal lines, which mark the areas of origin of the gluteus minimus, the gluteus medius and the gluteus maximus.

Question 1467. A constructed illustration: a young sprinter feels a sudden tearing pain at the front of the hip while the leg is driven backward hard, and a small piece of bone lies just below the front spine of the ilium. Which muscle has pulled it off? The answer is the sartorius, from the anterior superior iliac spine. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1468. Which statement about the ilium is correct: its inner surface above the arcuate line forms part of the greater pelvis, its outer surface gives origin to the hamstring muscles, its lower part is excluded from the acetabulum, or its crest lies at the level of the second sacral segment? The answer is that its inner surface above the arcuate line forms part of the greater pelvis. The hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity.

Question 1469. Which part of the hip bone bears the weight of the body when a person sits: the iliac crest, the anterior superior iliac spine, the ischial tuberosity, or the pubic tubercle? The answer is the ischial tuberosity, the rough lower end of the ischium. The muscles of the back of the thigh arise from its upper part. The sacrotuberous ligament also attaches there.

Question 1470. Which small pointed projection of the hip bone separates the greater sciatic notch above from the lesser sciatic notch below? The answer is the ischial spine. It gives attachment to the sacrospinous ligament, which runs from it to the sacrum. The pudendal nerve hooks around it to reach the perineum.

Question 1471. The hamstring muscles arise from which part of the hip bone: the iliac crest, the anterior superior iliac spine, the ischial tuberosity, or the pubic tubercle? The answer is the ischial tuberosity. The semitendinosus, the semimembranosus and the long head of the biceps femoris all arise there. They cross the hip and the knee and bend both joints.

Question 1472. Which nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine, and returns through the lesser sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, the pudendal nerve, the obturator nerve, or the femoral nerve? The answer is the pudendal nerve. It curls around the sacrospinous ligament at the spine to reach the perineum. The sciatic nerve does not return.

Question 1473. A described radiograph of the pelvis taken from the front shows, on each side below the socket of the hip, a small pointed spur of bone. Which structure is that spur, and which two openings does it separate? The answer is the ischial spine, which separates the greater sciatic foramen above from the lesser sciatic foramen below.

Question 1474. The lesser sciatic notch lies between which two bony points? The answer is the ischial spine above and the ischial tuberosity below. The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments cross the notch and close it into the lesser sciatic foramen. Through that foramen pass the tendon of the obturator internus and the pudendal nerve.

Question 1475. Which of these statements about the ischium is correct: its spine gives attachment to the sacrospinous ligament, its tuberosity gives origin to the sartorius, its ramus forms the upper border of the obturator foramen, or its body forms the whole socket of the hip? The answer is that its spine gives attachment to the sacrospinous ligament. Its ramus forms the lower border of the obturator foramen.

Question 1476. True or false: the two bony points on which the body rests when sitting are the ischial tuberosities. The answer is true. They lie at the lower end of each hip bone and are covered by a bursa and a pad of fat. When the hip is flexed, they move relative to the skin and the gluteus maximus slides off them.

Question 1477. A constructed illustration: a young sprinter feels a sudden tearing pain deep in the buttock while stretching for a long stride, and a fragment of bone is seen beside the lower part of the ischium. Which structure has been pulled away, and by which muscles? The answer is the growing tip of the ischial tuberosity, pulled by the hamstrings. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1478. Which band of fibrous tissue runs from the back of the ilium and the sacrum down to the ischial tuberosity? The answer is the sacrotuberous ligament. It reaches the lower end of the ischium behind and below the ischial spine. With the sacrospinous ligament it closes the sciatic notches into foramina.

Question 1479. Which of these structures passes through the lesser sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, the tendon of the obturator internus, the femoral artery, or the superior gluteal nerve? The answer is the tendon of the obturator internus, which turns around the lesser sciatic notch to reach the buttock. The pudendal nerve and its vessels also pass through that foramen. The sciatic nerve uses the greater foramen.

Question 1480. Which process of the ischium runs forward and upward to meet the pubis and so close the lower part of the ring of bone around the obturator foramen? The answer is the ramus of the ischium. It joins the inferior ramus of the pubis below the obturator foramen.

Question 1481. Which statement about the ischial tuberosities is correct: they move relative to the skin when the hip is flexed, they lie in front of the hip joint, they form the front part of the socket of the hip, or they give origin to the sartorius? The answer is that they move relative to the skin when the hip is flexed. The gluteus maximus slides off them when the hip bends.

Question 1482. A described dissection of the buttock shows a small fluid-filled sac lying between a bony point of the ischium and the skin, where the weight of the body presses in sitting. Which structure is described? The answer is the bursa over the ischial tuberosity. It is a normal cushion there, and it can become inflamed by long pressure.

Question 1483. A described radiograph of the pelvis of a growing child shows a separate scale of bone at the lower end of the ischium, still divided from the rest by a line of cartilage. Why is that piece so easily torn away by a sudden pull? The answer is that it is a growing tip and its cartilage is weaker than the tendon that pulls on it.

Question 1484. Name two bony points of the ischium that the examining hand can reach, spoken as a list. The answer is the ischial tuberosity and the ischial spine. The tuberosity is easily felt beneath the buttock when the hip is flexed. The spine is reached only through the wall of the pelvis.

Question 1485. Which joint lies in the midline at the front of the pelvis, joining the two hip bones to each other? The answer is the pubic symphysis. It is a secondary cartilaginous joint between the bodies of the two pubic bones. A disc of fibrocartilage lies between them, and only a little movement is possible.

Question 1486. Which small bony point at the front of the pelvis gives attachment to the medial end of the inguinal ligament? The answer is the pubic tubercle. It lies at the outer end of the pubic crest, on the upper border of the body of the pubis.

Question 1487. The obturator canal, the small opening at the upper lateral angle of that foramen, transmits which structures: the femoral nerve and vessels, the obturator nerve and vessels, the sciatic nerve, or the tendon of the obturator internus? The answer is the obturator nerve and vessels. They pass from the pelvis into the medial part of the thigh. The obturator membrane closes the rest of the foramen.

Question 1488. Which part of the socket of the hip joint is formed by the pubis: the superior part, the anterior part, the posterior part, or the floor of the notch alone? The answer is the anterior part, about one fifth of the socket. The ilium forms the superior part and the ischium the posterior inferior part. The three meet in the floor of the socket.

Question 1489. A described radiograph of the front of the pelvis shows a large oval opening on each side below and in front of the socket of the hip. Which two bones bound that opening? The answer is the pubis and the ischium. The rami of the pubis bound it in front and above, and the ramus of the ischium behind and below.

Question 1490. Which joint lies immediately medial to the pubic tubercle and the pubic crest? The answer is the pubic symphysis, the joint between the two pubic bones in the midline. The crest is the ridge on the upper border of the body of the pubis, and the tubercle is its outer end.

Question 1491. The subpubic angle, the arch below the pubic symphysis, is wider in which pelvis and why: wider in the male pelvis because its bones are heavier, wider in the female pelvis because it must allow the birth of a child, equal in both, or absent in the female? The answer is that it is wider in the female pelvis. In the male pelvis the arch is narrow and pointed.

Question 1492. Which type of joint is the pubic symphysis: a synovial joint with a cavity, a secondary cartilaginous joint with a disc between the bones, a fibrous joint with no movement at all, or a saddle joint? The answer is a secondary cartilaginous joint with a disc between the bones. It allows only slight movement, which increases late in pregnancy.

Question 1493. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a person has pain in the front of the pelvis, and a break runs through the superior and inferior rami of the pubis. Why is the pelvic ring usually broken in two places? The answer is that it is a closed loop, so a break in one part must be accompanied by trouble elsewhere. The treating clinician decides the management.

Question 1494. A described radiograph of the pelvis shows the brim of the pelvis as a continuous line running from the sacrum forward and around to the pubic symphysis. Which ridges make up that line? The answer is the arcuate line of the ilium, the pecten pubis on the superior ramus, and the pubic crest. Together they form the line that divides the greater pelvis from the lesser.

Question 1495. Which of these pairs belongs together: the pubic tubercle with the medial end of the inguinal ligament, the pecten pubis with the tendon of the rectus femoris, the inferior ramus with the sacrotuberous ligament, or the body of the pubis with the gluteus medius? The answer is the pubic tubercle with the medial end of the inguinal ligament. The pecten pubis gives attachment to the pectineal ligament.

Question 1496. Name the three bones that meet in the socket of the hip joint, spoken as a list. The answer is the ilium, the ischium and the pubis. They meet in the floor of the acetabulum at a band of cartilage shaped like a letter Y, which closes when growth ends. The three together form one hip bone.

Question 1497. The brim of the pelvis is described as a plane that is neither horizontal nor vertical. How is it directed in the standing body, and what does it separate? The answer is that it is tilted forward and downward, and it separates the greater pelvis above from the lesser pelvis below. It runs from the sacral promontory behind to the top of the pubic symphysis in front.

Question 1498. Which statement about the pubis is correct: its superior ramus carries the obturator groove on its under surface, its inferior ramus meets the ilium, its crest lies at the level of the second sacral segment, or its body is the largest part of the hip bone? The answer is that its superior ramus carries the obturator groove. It transmits the obturator vessels and nerve.

Question 1499. Which two muscles arise from the two surfaces of the membrane that closes the obturator foramen, one inside the pelvis and one outside? The answer is the obturator internus within the pelvis and the obturator externus on the outer side. The internus turns around the lesser sciatic notch to reach the buttock. The externus lies on the outer surface of the membrane.

Question 1500. By what route does the weight of the trunk pass through the pelvis to the hip joint of the standing leg? The answer is from the sacrum through the sacroiliac joint into the ilium, and then down the bone above the socket into the femur. The pubis and the ischium act mainly as ties.

To summarize, the five metacarpals form the palm, each with a base at the wrist, a shaft, and a head that makes a knuckle, and the first is the shortest and thickest, carries its growth plate at its base, and joins the trapezium at a saddle joint that lets the thumb oppose the fingers. The others meet the trapezoid, the capitate and the hamate, and the third carries the styloid process. One hand holds fourteen phalanges, three in each finger and two in the thumb, and the interphalangeal joints are hinges while the metacarpophalangeal joints are condyloid and their collateral ligaments tighten as the fingers bend. Each hip bone is built from three bones that meet in the socket of the hip: the ilium, which forms the upper part and carries the iliac crest, the ear-shaped sacroiliac surface, the iliac fossa and the gluteal lines; the ischium, which carries the ischial spine, the lesser sciatic notch and the tuberosity that takes the weight in sitting; and the pubis, which carries the pubic crest and tubercle, the pecten pubis, the obturator foramen and the symphysis. The pelvic ring is a closed loop, so a break in one part is accompanied by trouble elsewhere in the ring, and the brim of the pelvis, tilted forward and downward, divides the greater pelvis from the lesser. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 16 — Pelvic Girdle

This chapter covers the pelvic girdle and the two bones of the lower limb that meet it, the femur and the patella. It begins with the acetabulum, the socket that receives the head of the femur, and then takes the obturator foramen below it and the sacroiliac region behind, where the spine joins the hip bone. From there it turns to the femur, from its head and neck to its condyles, and it ends at the patella, the sesamoid bone that rides in front of the knee. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. All measurements and relations are the ordinary textbook ones, and variation between healthy people is normal. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1501. Which three bones of the hip bone meet to form the acetabulum, the socket that receives the head of the femur? The answer is the ilium, the ischium and the pubis. In the child the three are separated by a Y-shaped cartilage that meets in the floor of the socket. In the adult they are fused into a single hip bone.

Question 1502. Of the three bones that meet in the acetabulum, which contributes the smallest part: the ilium, the ischium or the pubis? The answer is the pubis. The ilium forms the upper part of the socket and the ischium the lower and posterior part, each contributing about two fifths. The pubis adds only the front fifth, so its share is the smallest.

Question 1503. Which large opening lies immediately anteroinferior to the acetabulum in the hip bone? The answer is the obturator foramen. It lies below and in front of the socket and is closed by a membrane except at its upper margin. Because the two structures are neighbors, a break in the pubis or the ischium often reaches the rim of the socket.

Question 1504. A described dried hip bone shows a cup-shaped socket whose smooth articular surface is shaped like a horseshoe, open at its lower margin. Name the socket and the shape of that surface. The answer is the acetabulum, with its lunate surface. The horseshoe curves around a central depression that carries no cartilage, and its two ends are joined below by a ligament.

Question 1505. Which part of the acetabulum carries no articular cartilage: the lunate surface, the fossa, the rim or the transverse ligament? The answer is the fossa. It is the central depression of the socket, and it holds fat and the ligament of the head of the femur. The lunate surface around it is the part that bears the load.

Question 1506. What is the name of the fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the margin of the acetabulum, which deepens the socket? The answer is the acetabular labrum. It bridges the notch at the lower margin and grips the head of the femur around its equator. A tear of this rim can let the head shift within the socket.

Question 1507. A constructed illustration: a person is struck on the front of a bent knee, and the head of the femur is driven inward against the socket. Which part of the hip bone gives way? The answer is the quadrilateral plate, the flat sheet of bone that forms the medial wall of the acetabulum. A break that reaches it is described as a fracture of the anterior column.

Question 1508. The ligament of the head of the femur carries a small artery into the socket. From which artery does that vessel usually arise? The answer is the obturator artery. It sends a branch through the acetabular notch and along the ligament. In the adult it feeds only a small part of the head.

Question 1509. Which direction does the open face of the acetabulum point: straight laterally, anterolaterally and slightly inferiorly, posterosuperiorly or straight medially? The answer is anterolaterally and slightly inferiorly. The socket looks forward and outward as well as a little downward, which lets the femur swing forward and out to the side.

Question 1510. True or false: in the child the ilium, the ischium and the pubis are separated within the acetabulum by a Y-shaped cartilage. The answer is true. The three bones meet in the floor of the socket at the triradiate cartilage. It closes around puberty, after which the socket is a single piece of bone.

Question 1511. The sockets of the two hip bones face away from each other. Describe the direction of each opening and say how the two directions compare. The answer is that each opens laterally, forward and slightly downward, so the two openings point in opposite directions. The plane of one socket is the mirror image of the other.

Question 1512. A described computed tomography section through the pelvis shows a dense curved line of bone roofing the socket, and its slope is measured.
