Which part of the acetabulum is being assessed? The answer is the subchondral roof of the socket, often called the sourcil. Its slope shows how well the socket covers the head. A steep, short roof is the mark of a shallow socket.

Question 1513. Which smooth ridge runs forward along the inner surface of the ilium from the sacroiliac joint to the pubic tubercle? The answer is the arcuate line, which continues across the hip bone as the iliopectineal line. It marks the pelvic brim and divides the wide false pelvis above from the narrow true pelvis below. The pelvic organs lie beneath it.

Question 1514. A constructed illustration: a described socket fracture divides the bone into a front part running from the iliac crest to the pubis and a back part running from the greater sciatic notch to the ischial tuberosity. What are these two parts called? The answer is the anterior column and the posterior column. Each carries one wall of the socket, so a fracture of both leaves the socket free to displace.

Question 1515. In a child, which artery provides most of the blood reaching the growing head of the femur: the obturator artery, the medial circumflex femoral artery, the lateral circumflex femoral artery or the inferior gluteal artery? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery. Its branches climb the neck inside the capsule and enter the head at the growth plate.

Question 1516. Which spine of the ilium lies just above the acetabulum and gives origin to the straight head of the rectus femoris: the anterior superior iliac spine, the anterior inferior iliac spine, the posterior superior iliac spine or the ischial spine? The answer is the anterior inferior iliac spine. It sits on the front of the ilium immediately above the socket.

Question 1517. A described specimen of a hip bone shows a broad flat blade above and a deep cup below, with a large opening in front of the cup. Name the cup. The answer is the acetabulum. It is the socket that receives the head of the femur, and the opening in front of it is the obturator foramen.

Question 1518. What band bridges the gap at the lower margin of the acetabulum and completes the rim of the socket? The answer is the transverse acetabular ligament. It spans the notch and turns it into a small opening. Vessels and a small nerve branch pass through it into the socket.

Question 1519. A constructed illustration: a described radiograph of an infant hip shows a socket that is shallow and steeply roofed, with the head sitting high and to the outer side. Which structure has failed to deepen the socket? The answer is the acetabular labrum. When the socket does not grow around the head, the head drifts upward and the labrum may be folded into the joint.

Question 1520. Which statement about the artery of the ligament of the head of the femur is correct: it is the main supply, it comes from the obturator artery, it comes from the sciatic nerve or it comes from the femoral artery? The answer is that it comes from the obturator artery. It feeds only a small part of the head, because the vessels that climb the neck carry most of the blood.

Question 1521. Which opening in the skeleton is the largest of all, lying below and in front of the acetabulum? The answer is the obturator foramen. It is bounded by the pubis above and in front and by the ischium below and behind, and it is closed by a strong membrane. Only a small canal at its upper margin stays open.

Question 1522. Which two bones form the obturator foramen: the ilium and the ischium, the pubis and the ischium, the ilium and the pubis, or the sacrum and the ischium? The answer is the pubis and the ischium. The two rami of the pubis bound it in front and above, and the ramus of the ischium bounds it behind and below. The ilium takes no part in it.

Question 1523. True or false: the obturator canal lies at the upper margin of the obturator foramen and transmits the obturator nerve and vessels. The answer is true. The membrane closes the rest of the foramen, and only this small gap is left. Through it pass the nerve, the artery and the vein that share the name of the foramen.

Question 1524. Which muscle arises from the pelvic surface of the obturator membrane and the bone around it? The answer is the obturator internus. It covers the inner surface of the membrane and leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen. Its tendon turns a right angle around the ischial spine before it reaches the femur.

Question 1525. Which muscle arises from the outer surface of the obturator membrane: the obturator internus, the obturator externus, the piriformis or the quadratus femoris? The answer is the obturator externus. It covers the outer surface of the membrane and the bone around it. Its tendon runs up behind the neck of the femur and ends in the trochanteric fossa.

Question 1526. True or false: the obturator membrane closes the obturator foramen completely, leaving no gap. The answer is false. The membrane leaves a small opening at the upper margin, the obturator canal. The obturator nerve and vessels pass through that canal, and nothing passes through the membrane itself.

Question 1527. A constructed illustration: a slender and older person describes pain running down the inner side of the thigh, and a loop of bowel has slipped through a narrow gap at the front of the pelvis. Which gap is it? The answer is the obturator canal. The hernia presses on the obturator nerve, which explains the pain down the inner thigh.

Question 1528. A described dried pelvis shows an oval gap below and in front of each socket. In which sex is that gap smaller and more triangular in shape? The answer is the female. The female obturator foramen tends to be smaller and more triangular, while in the male it is larger and more oval. This is one of several differences used to tell a male skeleton from a female one.

Question 1529. The obturator nerve enters the thigh through the obturator canal. How do its two branches lie in relation to the adductor brevis? The answer is that one branch lies in front of the muscle and the other behind it. The anterior branch supplies the adductor longus and the gracilis, while the posterior branch supplies the adductor magnus.

Question 1530. The tendon of which muscle passes through the lesser sciatic foramen: the obturator internus, the obturator externus, the piriformis or the gluteus medius? The answer is the obturator internus. It leaves the pelvis through that foramen, bounded above by the sacrospinous ligament and below by the sacrotuberous ligament.

Question 1531. A constructed illustration: at a described operation at the groin, an artery is found crossing the lacunar ligament from above. Which artery is it? The answer is an abnormal obturator artery. It has arisen from the inferior epigastric artery instead of the internal iliac and runs where the lacunar ligament is divided.

Question 1532. Name, spoken as a sentence, two structures that pass through the obturator canal. The answer is the obturator nerve and the obturator artery. The obturator vein runs with them. All three leave the pelvis at the upper margin of the obturator foramen. That canal is the only part of the foramen that stays open.

Question 1533. Which groove runs obliquely across the inferior surface of the superior pubic ramus and forms the roof of the obturator canal? The answer is the obturator groove. The canal lies between this groove and the upper edge of the obturator membrane, and its floor is the membrane itself. The nerve and vessels run along it as they leave the pelvis.

Question 1534. Relative to the acetabulum, in which direction does the obturator foramen lie within the hip bone? The answer is anteroinferior to the socket, so it sits below and in front of it. The socket occupies the middle of the outer surface of the bone, and the foramen opens onto the lower part of the same surface.

Question 1535. Which structure does not pass through the obturator canal: the obturator nerve, the obturator artery, the obturator vein or the sciatic nerve? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen instead. The canal is too narrow and too far forward to carry a nerve of that size.

Question 1536. Which joint joins the ear-shaped auricular surface of the ilium to the ear-shaped surface of the sacrum? The answer is the sacroiliac joint. The two surfaces are covered with cartilage and interlock, and strong ligaments bind them together behind. Part of the joint is synovial and part is a fibrous union.

Question 1537. Which ligament is the strongest of those binding the sacroiliac joint: the anterior sacroiliac, the interosseous sacroiliac, the sacrospinous or the iliolumbar? The answer is the interosseous sacroiliac ligament. It fills the deep space between the iliac tuberosity and the sacrum and is the main restraint against movement. The anterior ligament is a thin sheet by comparison.

Question 1538. Which two ligaments convert the greater and lesser sciatic notches of the hip bone into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina? The answer is the sacrotuberous ligament and the sacrospinous ligament. The sacrospinous crosses the lesser notch and the sacrotuberous the greater. Together they close the open notches into two firm passages.

Question 1539. A described computed tomography scan of the pelvis shows both sacroiliac joints with irregular margins, erosions and bridges of new bone, and the two sides look alike. Which joints are shown, and what does the pattern suggest? The answer is the sacroiliac joints, in a pattern that suggests an inflammatory arthritis of the spine rather than simple wear. The changes begin at the lower end of the joint and spread upward.

Question 1540. Which structure leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle: the superior gluteal nerve, the sciatic nerve, the obturator nerve or the pudendal artery? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It is the largest nerve in the body and descends behind the hip joint into the thigh. The superior gluteal nerve leaves above the piriformis.

Question 1541. Which ligament runs from the transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra to the back of the iliac crest? The answer is the iliolumbar ligament. It anchors the lowest mobile vertebra to the hip bone and helps to steady the lumbosacral junction. A second band sometimes runs from the fourth lumbar vertebra, which is a normal variant.

Question 1542. When the sacrum tilts forward so that its promontory moves downward and forward, what is the movement called: nutation, counternutation, inversion or abduction? The answer is nutation. It narrows the pelvic inlet slightly and widens the outlet, and it is checked mainly by the sacrotuberous ligament. The opposite movement, counternutation, tilts the promontory backward.

Question 1543. The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and then returns through the lesser sciatic foramen. Around which structure does it hook as it turns back? The answer is the sacrospinous ligament. The nerve and the internal pudendal vessels pass between the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments. The turn carries them to the canal beside the ischial spine.

Question 1544. A described dried sacrum shows a gap at its lower end where the bony roof is missing, with two small horns on either side of the gap. What is the gap called, and what do the horns mark? The answer is the sacral hiatus, and the horns are the sacral cornua. The gap is where the laminae of the fifth sacral vertebra failed to fuse.

Question 1545. A constructed illustration: a young adult describes pain in the buttock and lower back that is worst in the early morning, and a described radiograph shows both sacroiliac joints narrowed and irregular. Which joints are affected? The answer is the sacroiliac joints, and the changes usually begin at the lower end and spread upward. The pattern belongs to an inflammatory arthritis, and its management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1546. True or false: the sacroiliac joint allows only a slight gliding movement, restrained by very strong posterior ligaments. The answer is true. The interlocking surfaces and the interosseous ligament limit movement to a few degrees. What movement there is helps the pelvis to absorb the weight of the trunk above it.

Question 1547. Which structures bound the greater sciatic foramen: the greater sciatic notch and the sacrotuberous ligament, the lesser sciatic notch and the sacrospinous ligament, the obturator membrane and the ischial spine, or the pubic ramus and the inguinal ligament? The answer is the greater sciatic notch and the sacrotuberous ligament. The sacrospinous ligament divides the space into the greater foramen above and the lesser below.

Question 1548. Which groove on the hip bone lies in front of the auricular surface and is deeper and more common in the female skeleton? The answer is the preauricular sulcus. It lies between the auricular surface and the greater sciatic notch. Because it is more marked in women, it is one of the features used when the sex of a skeleton is estimated.

Question 1549. When a person stands on one leg, which structures resist the tendency of the ilium to rotate and of the sacrum to tilt forward: the anterior sacroiliac ligament alone, the interosseous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, the inguinal ligament, or the obturator membrane? The answer is the interosseous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, helped by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments.

Question 1550. A described skeleton shows a triangular bone wedged between the two hip bones, with its broad base above and its tip below. Name the bone and say what joins its base. The answer is the sacrum, whose base sits above and joins the fifth lumbar vertebra. Its tip points downward to the coccyx, and its ear-shaped surfaces form the sacroiliac joints.

Question 1551. Which is the longest and strongest bone in the body, running from the hip to the knee? The answer is the femur. It carries the weight of the trunk and passes it on to the leg below. Its strength comes from its thick shaft and from the way its bony plates are arranged to resist the lines of force.

Question 1552. What is the small depression on the head of the femur called, and what occupies it: the fovea capitis, the trochanteric fossa, the intercondylar fossa or the linea aspera? The answer is the fovea capitis, which holds the ligament of the head of the femur. It lies just below and behind the center of the head, and the artery of the ligament runs through it.

Question 1553. Which statement about the angle between the neck and the shaft of the adult femur is correct: it measures about 125 degrees, about 90 degrees, about 60 degrees, or about 30 degrees? The answer is about 125 degrees. The angle is larger in the newborn and decreases as weight bearing begins. A value well below the usual one is called coxa vara.

Question 1554. A described specimen shows a long bone with a rounded head on a narrow neck, two prominences at its upper end, and a shaft that curves gently forward. Name the bone. The answer is the femur. The two prominences are the greater and the lesser trochanters. The head fits into the socket of the hip bone.

Question 1555. Which ridge runs across the front of the upper femur between the two trochanters? The answer is the intertrochanteric line. It marks the anterior boundary between the neck and the shaft and gives attachment to the iliofemoral ligament. Behind, the two trochanters are joined instead by the intertrochanteric crest.

Question 1556. Which structure lies on the posterior surface of the upper femur between the trochanters: the intertrochanteric line, the intertrochanteric crest, the spiral line or the gluteal tuberosity? The answer is the intertrochanteric crest. It carries a rounded bump called the quadrate tubercle, where the obturator externus inserts. The line lies on the front of the bone.

Question 1557. A constructed illustration: an older adult falls and breaks the neck of the femur within the capsule. Which artery must be torn for the head to lose its blood supply? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery. Its branches climb the neck inside the capsule, so a break within the capsule can divide them and starve the head.

Question 1558. On which surface of the upper femur does the lesser trochanter lie, and which muscle inserts into it? The answer is the posteromedial surface, and the muscle is the iliopsoas. Its tendon crosses the front of the hip joint and turns backward to reach the trochanter. The greater trochanter, by contrast, lies on the lateral side.

Question 1559. Which of these pairs belongs together: the greater trochanter with the gluteus medius, the lesser trochanter with the gluteus minimus, the linea aspera with the iliopsoas, or the adductor tubercle with the piriformis? The answer is the greater trochanter with the gluteus medius. The lesser trochanter receives the iliopsoas, the linea aspera the adductor group, and the adductor tubercle the adductor magnus.

Question 1560. Above the linea aspera, the posterior ridge of the femur splits into which lines: the spiral line and the gluteal tuberosity, the intertrochanteric line and crest, the arcuate line and the pectineal line, or the supracondylar lines? The answer is the spiral line and the gluteal tuberosity. Below, the ridge splits again into the two supracondylar lines.

Question 1561. Which vessel enters the shaft of the femur through a small canal on its posterior surface near the linea aspera? The answer is the nutrient artery of the femur. It usually arises from a perforating branch of the deep artery of the thigh. It travels within the medullary cavity toward the upper end of the bone.

Question 1562. A described radiograph of the hip shows that the smooth arc running along the lower border of the femoral neck no longer continues into the upper border of the obturator foramen. What is that arc called, and what does its break mean? The answer is the line of Shenton, and its break marks a displaced fracture of the neck or a dislocation of the hip. The upper end has moved upward.

Question 1563. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fovea capitis with the ligament of the head of the femur, the trochanteric fossa with the gluteus medius, the intertrochanteric line with the posterior capsule, or the adductor tubercle with the popliteus? The answer is the fovea capitis with the ligament of the head. The trochanteric fossa receives the obturator externus, and the adductor tubercle receives the adductor magnus.

Question 1564. At what level on the surface of the body does the tip of the greater trochanter lie? The answer is at the level of the pubic tubercle, about one hand's breadth below the iliac crest. It can be felt on the outer side of the hip when the thigh is rotated. In a displaced hip fracture the trochanter rises above its usual level.

Question 1565. Which muscle inserts into the trochanteric fossa on the medial side of the greater trochanter: the obturator internus, the obturator externus, the piriformis or the gluteus minimus? The answer is the obturator externus. Its tendon runs upward and backward behind the neck of the femur to reach the fossa. The other three end on the medial surface of the greater trochanter.

Question 1566. Which smooth triangular area lies on the back of the lower femur between the two supracondylar lines? The answer is the popliteal surface. The popliteal vessels rest against it as they cross the back of the knee. Its upper part is continuous with the linea aspera above.

Question 1567. Which of the two femoral condyles is longer and reaches farther downward: the lateral, the medial, neither, or are they equal? The answer is the medial condyle. It extends farther distally because the shaft of the femur slopes inward, and this keeps the joint line of the knee nearly horizontal when a person stands upright.

Question 1568. A described radiograph of an older adult shows a break across the neck of the femur, and the break lies within the capsule. Why is this break more likely to endanger the head than one farther out? The answer is that the vessels feeding the head run inside the capsule along the neck. A break within the capsule can tear them.

Question 1569. In a described adolescent hip, the growth plate of the femur has slipped so that the neck turns outward while the head stays in the socket. Which part has remained in place: the head, the neck, the greater trochanter or the shaft? The answer is the head, which stays in the acetabulum while the neck and shaft rotate outward. Weakness of the growth plate during rapid growth explains the slip.

Question 1570. A described coronal section of the upper femur shows a thick plate of bone running up the medial side of the neck toward the head. What is this plate called, and what does it do? The answer is the calcar femorale, a strong buttress that supports the medial part of the neck and helps to carry the weight of the body onto the head.

Question 1571. Which opening in the tendon of the adductor magnus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the thigh to the back of the knee? The answer is the adductor hiatus. Once the vessels have passed through it they are called the popliteal artery and vein. The tendon forms the opening just above the adductor tubercle.

Question 1572. Which prominence of the upper femur can be felt with the fingers on the outer side of the hip: the greater trochanter, the lesser trochanter, the adductor tubercle or the ischial tuberosity? The answer is the greater trochanter. It lies just under the skin on the lateral side of the hip. The lesser trochanter lies deep on the back of the bone and cannot be felt.

Question 1573. At birth the head and neck of the femur are turned forward more than they are in the adult. What is this twist called, and what happens to it with growth? The answer is torsion, and it decreases as the child walks and the limb bears weight. An excess of it left in the adult turns the toes inward.

Question 1574. A described radiograph of the shaft of the femur shows a thin dark line running obliquely through the cortex toward the upper end of the bone, with smooth edges on both sides. Is this a fracture? The answer is that it is a nutrient canal, not a break. The canal runs away from the knee and has smooth, dense margins. A fracture line has jagged edges instead.

Question 1575. Which of these pairs belongs together: the patellar surface of the femur with the patella, the intercondylar fossa with the patellar ligament, the medial epicondyle with the lateral collateral ligament, or the lateral condyle with the adductor tubercle? The answer is the patellar surface with the patella. The intercondylar fossa holds the cruciate ligaments, and the adductor tubercle sits on the medial epicondyle.

Question 1576. Which muscle tendon lies immediately in front of the hip joint and separates the joint from the femoral vessels? The answer is the iliopsoas tendon. It crosses the front of the capsule on its way to the lesser trochanter. A bursa lies between the tendon and the joint, and it is the largest bursa in the body.

Question 1577. Which surface of the lower femur articulates with the patella: the popliteal surface, the patellar surface, the intercondylar fossa or the linea aspera? The answer is the patellar surface. It lies on the front of the lower end between the two condyles. Its lateral part is broader and reaches higher than its medial part.

Question 1578. Which roughened ridge on the posterior surface of the femur, below and behind the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of the gluteus maximus? The answer is the gluteal tuberosity. It forms the upper end of the lateral lip of the linea aspera. When it is very prominent it makes a third trochanter, which is a normal variant.

Question 1579. Which statement about the intercondylar fossa of the femur is correct: it gives attachment to the cruciate ligaments, it receives the patella, it gives attachment to the adductor magnus, or it lodges the popliteal artery? The answer is that it gives attachment to the cruciate ligaments. The anterior cruciate ligament attaches to the medial surface of the lateral condyle.

Question 1580. What is the name of the small rounded prominence on the medial epicondyle of the femur, where the adductor magnus is inserted? The answer is the adductor tubercle. It caps the upper part of the medial epicondyle and can be felt just above the knee on the inner side. The medial collateral ligament attaches below it.

Question 1581. Which is the largest sesamoid bone in the body, lying in the tendon of the quadriceps femoris? The answer is the patella. It is a triangular bone that develops within the tendon in front of the knee. Because it lies inside the tendon, it has no periosteum of its own.

Question 1582. Within the tendon of which muscle does the patella develop: the quadriceps femoris, the biceps femoris, the gastrocnemius or the sartorius? The answer is the quadriceps femoris. The patella is a sesamoid bone formed inside that tendon. The tendon continues below the bone as the patellar ligament.

Question 1583. Which structure attaches to the apex of the patella, and which attaches to its base? The answer is that the patellar ligament attaches to the apex and the quadriceps tendon to the base. The ligament joins the apex to the tibial tuberosity, so the pull of the quadriceps passes through the bone to the shin. The base is the broader upper border.

Question 1584. Which bone is small and triangular, wider above than below, and carries the thickest articular cartilage in the body: the patella, the pisiform, the calcaneus or the talus? The answer is the patella. Its smooth back faces the femur and its rough front lies just under the skin, and the whole bone sits inside the quadriceps tendon.

Question 1585. Which facet of the patella lies along its medial border and touches the medial femoral condyle only when the knee is deeply bent? The answer is the odd facet. It is a narrow strip on the extreme medial edge of the articular surface. In full extension it does not touch the femur at all.

Question 1586. Which of the two main facets of the patella is the larger: the medial, the lateral, neither, or are they equal? The answer is the lateral facet. It is broader and more concave than the medial one and bears most of the load against the lateral femoral condyle. The medial facet is smaller and flatter.

Question 1587. A constructed illustration: a young person turns sharply on a bent knee, and the patella is described as having moved to the outer side of the joint. Which ligament is the main restraint that has been overcome? The answer is the medial patellofemoral ligament, which runs from the medial epicondyle of the femur to the medial border of the patella.

Question 1588. True or false: the articular cartilage of the patella is thicker than the cartilage anywhere else in the body. The answer is true. The cartilage on the back of the patella is the thickest in the body, which is why it withstands the great pressures of the kneecap against the femur. Its thickness also helps to spread that force.

Question 1589. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medial patellofemoral ligament with the medial epicondyle of the femur, the patellar ligament with the base of the patella, the quadriceps tendon with the apex of the patella, or the lateral retinaculum with the medial border? The answer is the medial patellofemoral ligament with the medial epicondyle.

Question 1590. Two constructed illustrations describe breaks of the patella. In the first, a direct blow leaves the bone broken into several pieces. In the second, a sudden contraction of the quadriceps tears the bone across. Which break is transverse, and why? The answer is the second, because the pull of the muscle separates the two halves. A direct blow crushes the bone instead.

Question 1591. Which ridge divides the back of the patella into its two main facets? The answer is the vertical ridge. It runs from the base to the apex and separates the larger lateral facet from the smaller medial one. In a living knee it fits into the groove between the femoral condyles.

Question 1592. When the knee is straight, how much of the patella rests against the femur: all of its back, only its lowest part, its upper part, or none of it? The answer is only its lowest part. In full extension the bone rides above the groove and rests against a pad of fat, so contact is limited to its lower margin.

Question 1593. A described radiograph of the knee shows a small separate piece of bone at the upper outer corner of the patella, with smooth dense edges, and there is no step in the rest of the bone. Is this a break? The answer is that it is a bipartite patella, a normal variant in which one ossification center has not fused. Its smooth, dense margins separate it from a fresh fracture.

Question 1594. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ligament of the head of the femur with the fovea capitis, the transverse acetabular ligament with the acetabular fossa, the interosseous sacroiliac ligament with the auricular surface, or the medial patellofemoral ligament with the lateral epicondyle? The answer is the ligament of the head with the fovea capitis.

Question 1595. Name, spoken as a sentence, one structure attached to the base of the patella and one attached to its apex. The answer is the quadriceps tendon at the base and the patellar ligament at the apex. The tendon pulls from above, and the ligament carries that pull down to the tibial tuberosity.

Question 1596. A described specimen of the knee region shows a small triangular bone whose pointed lower end is joined to a bony prominence below by a thick band. Name the bone, the prominence and the band. The answer is the patella, the tibial tuberosity and the patellar ligament. The band is the continuation of the quadriceps tendon.

Question 1597. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the front of the knee, and afterwards there is a gap between the broken pieces of the patella and the knee cannot be straightened. Why does the gap open? The answer is that the quadriceps tendon above and the patellar ligament below pull the pieces apart, and the retinacula at the sides are torn with them.

Question 1598. Which structures attach the sides of the patella to the femur and the tibia: the cruciate ligaments, the retinacula, the menisci or the coronary ligaments? The answer is the retinacula. The medial and lateral retinacula are expansions of the vasti that blend with the sides of the patella. They help to keep the bone centered in the groove.

Question 1599. Name, spoken as a sentence, the two bones that meet at the knee joint and carry the weight of the body through it. The answer is the femur and the tibia. The femur rests its condyles on the flat upper surface of the tibia. The patella lies in front of them within the quadriceps tendon.

Question 1600. A described lateral radiograph of the knee shows the patella lying well above the groove of the femur, so that only its lowest margin overlaps the front of the bone. What is this position called, and why does it matter? The answer is a high-riding patella. The bone enters the groove later than usual as the knee bends, so it is less firmly seated.

To summarize, the acetabulum is formed by the ilium, the ischium and the pubis, and its horseshoe-shaped lunate surface is the only part that bears the load of the head of the femur. The obturator foramen lies anteroinferior to the socket and is closed by a membrane except for the canal that carries the obturator nerve and vessels. Behind, the sacroiliac joint is bound by the interosseous ligament, the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments turn the sciatic notches into foramina, and nutation of the sacrum is checked by the ligaments behind the joint. The femur is the longest bone in the body, its head carries the fovea capitis, its neck meets the shaft at about 125 degrees, and the medial circumflex femoral artery supplies the head through vessels that climb the neck. The patella is the largest sesamoid bone, it lies in the quadriceps tendon, and its lateral facet is the larger of the two. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 17 — Lower Limb Bones

This chapter covers the bones of the lower limb below the knee: the tibia, the fibula, the tarsal bones, the metatarsal bones and the phalanges. It follows the weight-bearing line from the knee down to the tips of the toes, naming each bone, its parts, and the structures attached to it. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately in the same paragraph and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The bones of the foot are small and easily confused, and every description here is written to be heard rather than seen. All measurements and relations are the ordinary textbook ones, and variation between healthy people is normal. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1601. Which bone of the leg is the thick medial bone that carries the weight of the body down to the ankle? The answer is the tibia. It is the second largest bone in the body, exceeded only by the femur. The tibia lies medially and passes the weight from the knee to the foot, while the fibula beside it carries almost none.

Question 1602. Which of these four bones takes part in the knee joint: the tibia, the fibula, the talus, or the calcaneus? The answer is the tibia. Its two upper surfaces, the medial condyle and the lateral condyle, articulate with the femur. The fibula lies beside it but never enters the knee joint, and the talus and calcaneus lie far below.

Question 1603. A described radiograph of the knee shows the upper end of a leg bone broadened into two flat surfaces, with a raised central spike between them and a stout forward projection below. Which bone is shown? The answer is the tibia. The spike is the intercondylar eminence, and the forward projection is the tibial tuberosity, where the patellar ligament attaches.

Question 1604. What is the name of the bony prominence felt on the inner side of the ankle? The answer is the medial malleolus. It is the downward projection of the lower end of the tibia. The lateral malleolus, felt on the outer side, belongs to the fibula, and the two together grip the talus and form the bony frame of the ankle.

Question 1605. Which bone lies immediately lateral to the shaft of the tibia and is joined to it along most of its length by a tough membrane? The answer is the fibula. The interosseous membrane stretches between the two bones. It separates the muscles of the front of the leg from those of the back and gives them a surface to arise from.

Question 1606. Four structures lie around the knee: a band continuing the quadriceps tendon, a band from the outer thigh, the biceps femoris tendon, and the ligament on the inner side. Which attaches to the tibial tuberosity? The answer is the band continuing the quadriceps tendon, the patellar ligament. The iliotibial band reaches the tibia further out, and the biceps femoris tendon crosses to the fibular head.

Question 1607. A constructed illustration: a player takes a blow to the shin, the skin splits, and the broken bone lies exposed. Why is this injury so easily open? The answer is that the anteromedial surface of the tibia lies directly beneath the skin. Only skin and a thin layer of tissue cover the bone there, so a break presses through the surface.

Question 1608. What is the name of the sharp ridge that a finger can follow down the front of the leg? The answer is the anterior border of the tibia. It is the most prominent of the three borders of the shaft. It lies just beneath the skin with no muscle over it, so it is the part bruised in a kick to the shin.

Question 1609. A described cross section of the leg shows a triangular bone whose three borders are named anterior, medial and lateral, and whose sharpest border lies nearest the skin. Which bone is shown, and which border is nearest the front? The answer is the tibia, with its anterior border nearest the skin. Its lateral border gives attachment to the interosseous membrane.

Question 1610. Which of these features belongs to the tibia rather than to the fibula: the soleal line, the malleolar fossa, the styloid process, or the subcutaneous lateral surface? The answer is the soleal line. It is the oblique ridge on the posterior surface of the tibial shaft from which part of the soleus muscle arises. The other three features all belong to the fibula.

Question 1611. Which bone rests upon the upper articular surfaces of the tibia and completes the knee joint from above? The answer is the femur. Its two condyles roll and glide upon the condyles of the tibia. The patella lies in front of the joint within the quadriceps tendon, and it is the largest sesamoid bone in the body.

Question 1612. Which surface of the tibial shaft lies beneath the skin along its whole length and gives attachment to no muscle? The answer is the medial surface. It lies between the anterior border and the medial border and is covered only by skin and a thin layer of tissue. That is why a swelling or a fracture there shows so plainly.

Question 1613. A described specimen shows one small opening on the posterior surface of the tibial shaft, just below the soleal line. From which vessel does the artery that enters it come: the anterior tibial artery, the posterior tibial artery, the fibular artery, or the popliteal artery? The answer is the posterior tibial artery, whose nutrient branch enters the bone and divides within the shaft.

Question 1614. A described specimen shows the tibia broken across its middle while the fibula stays whole and the leg has not shortened. Which structure most limits the displacement: the patellar ligament, the interosseous membrane, the crural fascia, or the calcaneal tendon? The answer is the interosseous membrane, which with the unbroken fibula ties the two bones together along their shafts.

Question 1615. True or false: the tibia lies medial to the fibula and bears the weight of the body. The answer is true. The tibia is the thicker of the two bones, and its upper end takes the femur at the knee. The fibula lies on the lateral side of the leg and carries almost none of the body weight.

Question 1616. A described radiograph of the ankle shows a broad square projection on the inner side of the joint and a longer projection that reaches lower on the outer side. Which bones carry these two projections? The answer is the tibia on the inner side and the fibula on the outer side. The medial malleolus is shorter and sits higher than the lateral malleolus.

Question 1617. Which muscle arises from the oblique ridge that runs down and medially across the posterior surface of the upper tibia? The answer is the soleus. That ridge is the soleal line. The soleus joins the gastrocnemius above it, and the two muscles share the calcaneal tendon, which pulls upon the heel.

Question 1618. Which bone articulates with the lower articular surface of the tibia: the calcaneus, the talus, the navicular, or the cuboid? The answer is the talus. Its rounded upper surface, the trochlea, receives the tibia from above and the fibula from the side. The calcaneus lies below the talus, and the navicular lies in front of it.

Question 1619. Name the two bones whose lower ends form the bony socket that holds the ankle, spoken as a pair. The answer is the tibia and the fibula. Their malleoli grip the talus on either side to make the ankle mortise. The tibia carries the weight, and the fibula completes the ring and gives the socket its outer wall.

Question 1620. A described section through an adult lower leg shows the tibial shaft turning slightly outward as it descends, so that the foot lies a little lateral to the knee. Which term names that twist, and about which axis does it occur? The answer is lateral torsion of the tibia, about the long axis of the bone, a normal feature of the adult limb.

Question 1621. Which long thin bone lies on the outer side of the leg from the knee to the ankle? The answer is the fibula. It is slender, carries no weight from the knee, and serves chiefly to give attachment to muscles and to steady the ankle. Its head can be felt just below and behind the outer side of the knee.

Question 1622. The lower end of the fibula forms which prominence: the medial malleolus, the lateral malleolus, the tibial tuberosity, or the sustentaculum tali? The answer is the lateral malleolus. It projects downward on the outer side of the ankle and is easily felt through the skin. The medial malleolus belongs to the tibia and the sustentaculum tali to the calcaneus.

Question 1623. Which nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just below its head, where it lies against the bone? The answer is the common fibular nerve. It is the most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb because it is so exposed against the bone. Its branches supply the muscles that lift the foot.

Question 1624. A constructed illustration: a blow lands on the outer side of the upper leg, the neck of the fibula breaks, and the foot afterwards drags and cannot be lifted. Which structure was injured, and why? The answer is the common fibular nerve, pressed against the bone at the neck. The weakness of the muscles beyond that point produces the foot drop.

Question 1625. A described radiograph shows a slender bone whose upper end is a small rounded knob with a short spike beside it and whose lower end is a long pointed process. Which bone is shown, and what are its two ends? The answer is the fibula, with its head above and its lateral malleolus below. The spike on the head is the styloid process.

Question 1626. What is the name of the small joint between the head of the fibula and the outer side of the tibia, just below the knee? The answer is the proximal tibiofibular joint. It is a synovial joint that permits only slight movement. Its partner, the distal tibiofibular joint, lies at the ankle and is a fibrous joint instead.

Question 1627. Since the fibula carries no weight from the knee, what is its chief role: to bear weight at the ankle, to give attachment to muscles, to articulate with the femur, or to form the inner wall of the ankle socket? The answer is to give attachment to muscles and to steady the ankle. Several muscles of the leg arise from its shaft.

Question 1628. True or false: the fibula takes part in the knee joint and carries part of the weight of the body. The answer is false. The fibula does not reach the knee joint, and it carries no weight at all. It serves for the attachment of muscles and for the stability of the ankle.

Question 1629. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fibular head with the biceps femoris tendon, the fibular head with the patellar ligament, the lateral malleolus with the deltoid ligament, or the fibular neck with the tibial nerve? The answer is the fibular head with the biceps femoris tendon. The lateral malleolus anchors the lateral ankle ligaments, and the common fibular nerve lies at the neck.

Question 1630. Which structure attaches to the styloid process at the back of the head of the fibula: the lateral collateral ligament of the knee, the calcaneal tendon, the plantar fascia, or the tibialis posterior tendon? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament of the knee, also called the fibular collateral ligament. It runs from the fibular head to the outer condyle of the femur.

Question 1631. On the ankle, which malleolus reaches lower, the one on the inner side or the one on the outer side? The answer is the lateral malleolus of the fibula on the outer side. It reaches lower and further back than the medial malleolus of the tibia. That deeper grip helps to keep the ankle from rolling outward.

Question 1632. A constructed illustration: an ankle turns inward, and the bone felt on the outer side is tender and moves as a separate piece. Which joint has been disrupted: the ankle, the distal tibiofibular joint, the subtalar joint, or the midtarsal joint? The answer is the distal tibiofibular joint, with a break of the lateral malleolus, so the two bones no longer hold the talus in one ring.

Question 1633. A described cross section through the middle of the leg shows two bones joined by a membrane, one triangular and thick, the other slender with four borders. Which is which? The answer is that the tibia is the thick triangular bone, lying medially. The membrane between them separates the muscles of the front from those of the back.

Question 1634. What is the name of the border of the fibula that gives attachment to the interosseous membrane? The answer is the interosseous border, also called its medial border, which faces the tibia along the shaft. The other borders are named anterior, posterior and lateral. The lateral surface between them gives origin to the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis.

Question 1635. Which of these statements about the fibula is correct: it articulates with three bones at the ankle, it carries weight from the knee, it lies medial to the tibia, or its head receives the biceps femoris tendon? The answer is that its head receives the biceps femoris tendon. The fibula lies lateral and carries no weight, and its lower end joins only the ankle joint.

Question 1636. Name two muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg that arise from the shaft of the fibula, spoken as a pair. The answer is the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis. Both arise from the lateral surface of the shaft. Their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus and turn the sole of the foot outward.

Question 1637. Which of these structures binds the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula to each other at the ankle: the deltoid ligament, the interosseous tibiofibular ligament, the calcaneal tendon, or the plantar fascia? The answer is the interosseous tibiofibular ligament, the strongest part of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. That joint is fibrous, whereas the deltoid ligament binds the tibia to the talus.

Question 1638. A constructed illustration: a twisting injury breaks the fibula high near the knee, the ankle is badly displaced, and the inner side of the same ankle is tender. Which structures have failed? The answer is the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis together with the medial ligament of the ankle. The ring around the talus has given way, and the break lies far above it.

Question 1639. A described specimen shows a bone the length of the lower leg that ends below in a rounded knob with a shallow pit on its inner surface and never reaches the knee joint. Which bone is it, and what is the pit? The answer is the fibula, and the pit is the malleolar fossa. The posterior talofibular ligament attaches within that fossa.

Question 1640. Which of these features is found on the fibula rather than on the tibia: the fibular notch, the malleolar fossa, the tibial tuberosity, or the intercondylar eminence? The answer is the malleolar fossa. It lies on the medial and posterior surface of the lateral malleolus. The fibular notch is the shallow cut on the lower tibia that receives the fibula.

Question 1641. Which tarsal bone sits between the bones of the leg above and the calcaneus below and takes part in the ankle joint? The answer is the talus. Its rounded upper surface fits into the socket made by the tibia and the fibula. Almost no muscle attaches to the talus, which is why so much of its surface is covered with cartilage.

Question 1642. Which bone of the foot is the largest, forms the heel, and touches the ground behind? The answer is the calcaneus. The calcaneal tendon attaches to its back, and it carries the whole body weight as the heel strikes the ground. The talus rests upon it and forms the subtalar joint above.

Question 1643. Which tarsal bone lies between the head of the talus behind and the three cuneiform bones in front: the cuboid, the navicular, the calcaneus, or the lateral cuneiform? The answer is the navicular. Its name means little boat, because its hollowed back fits the rounded head of the talus. It is one of the keystones of the arch of the foot.

Question 1644. A described radiograph of the foot taken from above shows seven small bones in two rows, with one bone set between the ankle bones behind and the row in front. Which bone is that, and what does its position achieve? The answer is the navicular, which carries the weight of the arch forward into the front of the foot.

Question 1645. The cuboid lies immediately in front of one bone and immediately behind two others. Name those bones. The answer is the calcaneus behind it and the fourth and fifth metatarsals in front. The cuboid also touches the lateral cuneiform and the navicular along its inner side.

Question 1646. How many cuneiform bones take part in forming the foot, and which of them is the largest: two with the lateral the largest, three with the medial the largest, three with the intermediate the largest, or two with the medial the largest? The answer is three cuneiform bones, of which the medial is the largest. The medial cuneiform receives the first metatarsal.

Question 1647. A constructed illustration: a person lands from a height on both feet and breaks the bone between the ankle and the foot across its narrow neck. Which bone is injured, and why is its blood supply a concern? The answer is the talus. Its blood reaches it through a small channel in the neck, so a break there can starve the body of the bone.

Question 1648. True or false: the calcaneus receives the weight of the body from the talus and passes it to the ground at the heel. The answer is true. The talus rests upon the calcaneus at the subtalar joint, and the weight then travels backward to the calcaneal tuberosity and forward into the front of the foot.

Question 1649. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sustentaculum tali with the talus, the sustentaculum tali with the navicular, the cuboid with the talus, or the navicular with the calcaneal tendon? The answer is the sustentaculum tali with the talus. It is a shelf of bone on the calcaneus that carries the head of the talus, while the cuboid never touches the talus.

Question 1650. Which structure runs in the groove on the under surface of the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus: the flexor hallucis longus tendon, the tibialis anterior tendon, the plantar fascia, or the fibularis longus tendon? The answer is the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus, which passes forward beneath the shelf, whereas the fibularis longus tendon runs on the cuboid.

Question 1651. What is the name of the shelf of bone on the inner side of the calcaneus that projects beneath the head of the talus? The answer is the sustentaculum tali. It supports the talus and helps to hold up the arch of the foot. A groove on its under surface carries the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus.

Question 1652. A described section through the ankle shows a rounded bone held on both sides by bony walls, resting upon a broader bone below and touching a third bone in front. Name the bones described. The answer is the talus between the two malleoli, the calcaneus below it, and the navicular in front. The talus is the only foot bone that joins the leg.

Question 1653. Which tarsal bone lies directly beneath the talus and forms the joint through which the heel turns inward and outward? The answer is the calcaneus. That joint is the subtalar joint. It is not the ankle joint, which lies above the talus and moves the foot up and down.

Question 1654. A constructed illustration: a person falls from a ladder and lands upon the heel; the ankle is spared but the heel is broad and painful. Which bone is broken, and why is the ankle spared? The answer is the calcaneus. The force passes through the heel, so the talus is driven down into the calcaneus, and the ankle above receives little of it.

Question 1655. Which bone is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot: the cuboid, the navicular, the lateral cuneiform, or the calcaneus? The answer is the navicular. It lies at the summit of the arch between the talus behind and the cuneiforms in front. The cuboid belongs to the outer arch instead.

Question 1656. A described section through the foot is cut across the middle of the tarsus so that the talus and the calcaneus appear side by side, with the calcaneus below and lateral. Which plane was used, and which bone lies more lateral in the section? The answer is a coronal plane, and the calcaneus lies more laterally, as well as lower.

Question 1657. What is the name of the bony knob on the inner side of the foot, about halfway along the arch, where the tendon of the tibialis posterior attaches? The answer is the tuberosity of the navicular. The tendon of the tibialis posterior muscle inserts upon it. It is a useful landmark for the joint between the talus and the navicular.

Question 1658. A described oblique radiograph of the foot shows one line of bones running from the heel to the base of the first toe and another line crossing it at the middle of the foot. Which joints does the crossing line mark? The answer is the midtarsal joint, where the talus meets the navicular and the calcaneus meets the cuboid, also called the transverse tarsal joint.

Question 1659. Which tarsal bone articulates with the bases of the fourth and fifth metatarsals: the medial cuneiform, the intermediate cuneiform, the lateral cuneiform, or the cuboid? The answer is the cuboid. Its front surface carries two facets for those two bases. The lateral cuneiform receives the third metatarsal instead.

Question 1660. A constructed illustration: a foot turns inward sharply, the outer edge is painful, the bones of the midfoot stay whole, and the tenderness lies over the ligaments on the outer side of the ankle. Which structures have been stretched? The answer is the lateral ligaments of the ankle. Turning the sole inward stretches them, while the deltoid ligament is slackened.

Question 1661. Turning the sole of the foot inward and outward takes place at which joint: the ankle joint, the subtalar joint, the midtarsal joint, or the tarsometatarsal joint? The answer is the subtalar joint. The ankle moves only up and down, and the midtarsal joint adds only a slight twist.

Question 1662. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medial cuneiform with the first metatarsal, the intermediate cuneiform with the first metatarsal, the cuboid with the third metatarsal, or the navicular with the fifth metatarsal? The answer is the medial cuneiform with the first metatarsal. The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms receive the second and third metatarsals, and the cuboid takes the fourth and fifth.

Question 1663. How many metatarsal bones are there in one foot, and how are they numbered? The answer is five, numbered from the first on the inner side to the fifth on the outer side. Each one has a base near the ankle, a body or shaft, and a rounded head at the ball of the foot.

Question 1664. Which metatarsal bone is usually the longest, and which is the shortest and thickest? The answer is that the second is usually the longest and the first is the shortest and thickest. The first metatarsal carries the two sesamoid bones beneath its head and bears the weight of the great toe. The order of length varies a little between healthy people.

Question 1665. Which bone articulates with the base of the first metatarsal: the cuboid, the navicular, the medial cuneiform, or the calcaneus? The answer is the medial cuneiform. The first metatarsal rests upon the largest of the three cuneiform bones and carries the great toe. It usually has no facet toward the second metatarsal.

Question 1666. Which tendon inserts on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal: the tibialis anterior, the fibularis brevis, the fibularis longus, or the tibialis posterior? The answer is the fibularis brevis. It pulls upon that bony prominence, which projects from the outer border of the foot. The fibularis longus tendon runs beneath the foot to the medial cuneiform instead.

Question 1667. A described radiograph of the forefoot shows five long bones side by side, one of them short and stout and set a little apart. Which one is it, and what lies beneath its head? The answer is the first metatarsal, with two sesamoid bones beneath its head. Those small bones lie in the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis.

Question 1668. Which metatarsal lies immediately lateral to the medial cuneiform, with its base set into a recess between two bones? The answer is the second metatarsal. Its base is wedged between the medial and the lateral cuneiforms. That recess makes the base of the second metatarsal a keystone of the transverse arch at that level.

Question 1669. A constructed illustration: a recruit who has begun long marches develops pain over the shaft of a metatarsal, and a fine crack appears across it. Which bone is usually the one involved: the first, the second, the third, or the fifth? The answer is the second metatarsal, the longest of the five and so under the greatest bending strain. The crack comes from repeated stress, not one injury.

Question 1670. True or false: the first metatarsal lies on the outer border of the foot and is the longest of the five. The answer is false. The first metatarsal lies on the inner border beside the great toe, and it is the shortest and thickest of them. The fifth metatarsal forms the outer border of the foot.

Question 1671. The sesamoid bones beneath the head of the first metatarsal lie within which structure: the flexor hallucis longus tendon, the flexor hallucis brevis tendon, the tibialis posterior tendon, or the plantar fascia? The answer is the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis. Almost every foot has two of them, one medial and one lateral, gliding over a groove on the underside of the bone.

Question 1672. Which part of a metatarsal bone forms the rounded surface that presses on the ground at the ball of the foot? The answer is the head, the distal end of the bone. It is covered with cartilage and moves against the base of the first phalanx. The base lies at the other end of the bone and joins the tarsus.

Question 1673. Which metatarsal bases articulate with the cuboid rather than with a cuneiform bone? The answer is the fourth and the fifth. Their bases rest upon the cuboid on the outer side of the foot, while the first three metatarsals rest upon the three cuneiform bones. The joints between them are the tarsometatarsal joints.

Question 1674. A constructed illustration: a person stumbles off a step, the foot turns inward, and a small fragment is pulled from the base of the fifth metatarsal. Which tendon did the pulling, and what kind of injury is illustrated? The answer is the fibularis brevis, which inserts upon that tuberosity. The fragment is an avulsion at the tendon rather than a break across the shaft.

Question 1675. A described radiograph taken across the sole of the foot shows the bases of the metatarsals in a row with a gap between the first and the second. What occupies that gap in the living foot? The answer is a strong ligament running from the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal, which is recessed into the tarsus there.

Question 1676. What is the name of the joint line between the bases of the metatarsal bones and the tarsal bones: the midtarsal joint, the tarsometatarsal joint, the metatarsophalangeal joint, or the subtalar joint? The answer is the tarsometatarsal joint. It runs across the foot at the level of the cuneiforms and the cuboid. The midtarsal joint lies behind it.

Question 1677. Which of these pairs belongs together: the first metatarsal with the medial cuneiform, the first metatarsal with the cuboid, the fifth metatarsal with the navicular, or the third metatarsal with the cuboid? The answer is the first metatarsal with the medial cuneiform. The cuboid receives the fourth and the fifth metatarsals, and the lateral cuneiform receives the third.

Question 1678. What is the name of the bony prominence on the outer border of the foot, about halfway along, where the tendon of the fibularis brevis attaches? The answer is the tuberosity of the base of the fifth metatarsal. It can be felt easily and is often struck or bruised. It is also the site of an avulsion when the foot turns inward.

Question 1679. Which structures form the transverse arch of the foot at the level of the tarsometatarsal joints: the calcaneus and the talus, the cuneiform bones with the bases of the metatarsals, the heads of the metatarsals, or the phalanges? The answer is the cuneiform bones together with the bases of the metatarsals. The arch is held by ligaments and by the tendons crossing it.

Question 1680. A constructed illustration: a heavy object falls across the top of the foot and several metatarsals are broken at once. Why is the swelling between them so severe? The answer is that the metatarsals are bound together by ligaments and lie within tight compartments. Blood and fluid cannot spread freely, so the pressure between the bones rises.

Question 1681. Name the metatarsal whose base is set into a recess and acts as the keystone of the tarsometatarsal line, spoken as one name. The answer is the second metatarsal. Its base is wedged between the medial and the lateral cuneiforms. For that reason it moves less than any of the other four.

Question 1682. A described section across the middle of the metatarsals shows five bony rings joined by ligaments, the first and second bound closely together while the first metatarsal moves freely at its base. What does that arrangement permit? The answer is that the first metatarsal moves more freely than the others, since its base has no facet toward the second metatarsal.

Question 1683. How many phalanges, or toe bones, are there in one foot? The answer is fourteen. The great toe has two of them, and each of the other four toes has three. Every one of them has a base at the back, a body, and a head or a tuberosity in front.

Question 1684. Which toe has only two phalanges, and which ones are they? The answer is the great toe, which has a proximal and a distal phalanx but no middle one. Because it is short and stout it carries the greatest load in walking. The other four toes each have three phalanges.

Question 1685. How many phalanges does the second toe of a normal foot have: one, two, three, or four? The answer is three, a proximal, a middle and a distal phalanx. Only the great toe has two. A foot therefore holds fourteen phalanges in all, and the middle bone of the little toe is sometimes joined to the distal one as a normal variation.

Question 1686. Which bone of the foot forms the tip of a toe and carries a rough tuberosity on its under surface? The answer is the distal phalanx. The rough tuberosity gives the pulp of the toe something to rest against. The nail lies above the flattened upper surface of the same bone.

Question 1687. A described radiograph counts two bones beyond the metatarsal in the great toe and three in the second toe. How many joints does each toe show, and which joint is missing from the great toe? The answer is two joints in the great toe and three in the second toe, Each toe has one joint fewer than it has bones, and the great toe has no middle joint.

Question 1688. Which bone articulates with the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, and which two small bones lie beneath that joint? The answer is the first metatarsal, with the two sesamoid bones beneath its head. The joint between them is the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The sesamoid bones lie within the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis.

Question 1689. A constructed illustration: a bare foot stubs against a stone, the tip of the second toe is bent sharply upward, and the joint at the base of the toe is painful. Which joint is illustrated, and which structure holds it steady? The answer is the metatarsophalangeal joint. The plantar plate and the ligaments beneath it steady the joint, stretched here but not torn.

Question 1690. True or false: the great toe has three phalanges, just as the other toes do. The answer is false. The great toe has two phalanges, a proximal and a distal one. It is the only toe without a middle phalanx, although it is the thickest and strongest of them all.

Question 1691. What is the name of the bone at the very tip of each toe, the one that bears the nail? The answer is the distal phalanx. Its base joins the middle phalanx, or in the great toe the proximal phalanx. Its far end is flattened into a rough tuberosity for the pulp of the toe.

Question 1692. Which of these statements about the toe bones is correct: every toe has three phalanges, the fifth toe has none, the great toe has a proximal and a distal phalanx, or the phalanges lie behind the metatarsals? The answer is that the great toe has a proximal and a distal phalanx. The middle bone of the little toe is sometimes fused with the distal one.

Question 1693. Which of these pairs belongs together: the great toe with two phalanges, the great toe with three phalanges, the fifth toe with two phalanges in every foot, or the second toe with two phalanges? The answer is the great toe with two phalanges. The other four toes each have three, though the bones of the fifth toe are sometimes joined.

Question 1694. A constructed illustration: a dancer forces the great toe upward at its base, the joint becomes painful, and the small bones beneath it are bruised. Which structures lie in that position and are injured here? The answer is the two sesamoid bones within the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis, beneath the head of the first metatarsal.

Question 1695. A described dissection of a toe shows a short bone with a broad base, a slender body and a rounded head that lies within a fibrous sling. Which bone is it, and what is the sling? The answer is a proximal phalanx, and the sling is the fibrous sheath of the flexing tendons. The sheath holds the tendons close against the bone.

Question 1696. Which part of a phalanx forms the joint at its proximal end, and which part forms the joint at its distal end? The answer is the base proximally and the head distally. The base is broad and hollowed to receive the head of the bone behind it, and the head is rounded to fit the base of the bone in front.

Question 1697. Which joint lies between the head of a metatarsal and the base of a proximal phalanx: the tarsometatarsal joint, the metatarsophalangeal joint, the proximal interphalangeal joint, or the midtarsal joint? The answer is the metatarsophalangeal joint, which lies at the ball of the foot. The interphalangeal joints lie further forward, between the phalanges themselves.

Question 1698. Which structure lies immediately beneath the head of the first metatarsal and the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe? The answer is the pair of sesamoid bones within the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis. They are embedded in the tendon and glide over the underside of the metatarsal head, one medial and one lateral.

Question 1699. A described specimen shows the bone at the tip of a toe, flattened from above, with a rough tuberosity at its far end and a broad base behind. Which bone is it, and what lies over its flat upper surface? The answer is a distal phalanx, with the nail above it. The rough tuberosity gives the pulp something to attach to.

Question 1700. A described radiograph of a whole foot shows seven tarsal bones, five metatarsals and the toes, and the examiner asks how many bones the foot contains. Which count fits: twenty-four, twenty-six, twenty-eight, or thirty? The answer is twenty-six. Seven tarsal bones, five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges make that number, and the sesamoid bones beneath the first metatarsal are counted apart.

To summarize, the tibia is the thick medial bone of the leg and carries the weight of the body from the femur to the talus, while the fibula is slender, carries none of it, and serves for muscle attachment and the stability of the ankle. The medial malleolus belongs to the tibia and the lateral malleolus to the fibula, and the common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck. The tarsal bones are seven in number, with the talus taking the weight from the leg, the calcaneus forming the heel, the navicular as a keystone of the medial arch, and the cuboid articulating with the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges complete the foot, twenty-six bones in all, and the two sesamoid bones beneath the first metatarsal lie within the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis. Naming each bone aloud together with its neighbors is what fixes this map in memory, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 18 — General Classification

Joints hold the skeleton together and decide how much of it can move, and this chapter sorts them by the tissue that binds the bones. It works through the fibrous joints with their sutures, syndesmoses and gomphoses, the cartilaginous joints with their synchondroses and symphyses, and the synovial joints with their cavity, cartilage, capsule and fluid. It closes with the joints of the skull, where sutures and one freely movable joint share the same bony vault. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1701. Which class of joint unites two bones with dense fibrous tissue and allows almost no movement at all? The answer is a fibrous joint, also called a synarthrosis. Collagen fibers run from the substance of one bone into the substance of the other. The sutures of the skull are the clearest example, and the two bones there behave almost as one.

Question 1702. A joint between two bones has no cavity and holds its surfaces together with fibrous tissue. Which class does it belong to: a synovial joint, a cartilaginous joint, a fibrous joint, or a secondary cartilaginous joint? The answer is a fibrous joint. The absent cavity and the fibrous sheet between the bones place it in that class, while a synovial joint always has a cavity.

Question 1703. What kind of tissue forms the union in every fibrous joint, and how does the length of its fibers differ from one such joint to another? The answer is dense fibrous connective tissue, whose fibers vary in length. In a suture the fibers are very short, while in a syndesmosis a longer sheet separates the bones, and the longer the fibers, the more movement the joint allows.

Question 1704. The interosseous membrane of the forearm attaches to which border of the radius and which border of the ulna, and in which direction do its fibers run? The answer is the interosseous border of each bone, with the fibers running obliquely downward from the radius to the ulna. The membrane is a syndesmosis and not a suture.

Question 1705. Two flat bones of the skull vault meet edge to edge, united by a very thin layer of fibrous tissue. Which name fits that union: a gomphosis, a syndesmosis, a suture, or a symphysis? The answer is a suture. The bones meet edge to edge, with only an extremely thin fibrous layer between them. A symphysis is cartilaginous and a gomphosis holds a tooth.

Question 1706. A constructed illustration: a heavy fall drives the ankle bone upward between the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula, and the short fibrous bond joining those two bones tears. Which joint has been injured? The answer is the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis. When its fibers tear, the two bones separate and the ankle mortise widens, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1707. Are the fibrous joints of the skull permanent through life, and what becomes of many sutures in later years? The answer is that they are not permanent, because many sutures close and turn into solid bone. The process is called synostosis. The times differ from one suture to another and from one person to another.

Question 1708. True or false: a fibrous joint always allows free movement between the bones it joins. The answer is false. Fibrous tissue binds the bones closely together, so movement is very slight or entirely absent. Free movement belongs to the synovial joints, which have a cavity and synovial fluid between their surfaces.

Question 1709. One statement about a fibrous union is correct: the fibers of one bone continue into the other, the surfaces are lined by hyaline cartilage, a cavity separates the bones, or the union is replaced by scar tissue. The answer is that the fibers of one bone continue into the other. That continuity gives the union its great strength.

Question 1710. A described specimen shows two long bones lying side by side with a broad fibrous sheet between their facing borders, its fibers running obliquely from one bone to the other. What kind of union is shown? The answer is a syndesmosis of the fibrous class. The sheet is longer than the tissue in a suture, so it allows a small amount of movement.

Question 1711. What name is given to the thin layer of fibrous tissue that fills the gap between two skull bones at a suture? The answer is the sutural ligament. It is continuous with the periosteum outside the skull and with the dura mater inside. In the newborn it is wide enough to permit some movement of the vault during birth.

Question 1712. Which of these pairs belongs together: a suture with a tooth, a syndesmosis with a sheet of fibrous tissue, a gomphosis with the skull vault, or a synchondrosis with a joint cavity? The answer is a syndesmosis with a sheet of fibrous tissue. A suture belongs with the skull vault, and a gomphosis with a tooth in its socket.

Question 1713. Cartilage, either hyaline or fibrocartilage, unites the bones in which class of joint, and what is the other name for that class? The answer is the cartilaginous joint, also called an amphiarthrosis. No cavity lies between the bones, and the cartilage forms the whole union. The joints between the vertebral bodies and the pubic symphysis belong to this class.

Question 1714. A joint between two bones is filled by a pad of cartilage and has no cavity. Which two named kinds of joint belong to that class: suture and syndesmosis, synchondrosis and symphysis, hinge and pivot, or gomphosis and plane joint? The answer is the synchondrosis and the symphysis. The first is united by hyaline cartilage and the second by fibrocartilage.

Question 1715. One statement about the two kinds of cartilaginous joint is correct: a synchondrosis is usually temporary and a symphysis usually permanent, both are temporary, a symphysis is united by hyaline cartilage, or a synchondrosis has a cavity. The answer is that a synchondrosis is usually temporary and a symphysis usually permanent. The epiphyseal plate is replaced by bone, and the pubic symphysis persists for life.

Question 1716. What is the name of the cartilaginous joint in which hyaline cartilage unites the bones, such as the plate of cartilage near the end of a growing long bone? The answer is a synchondrosis. It is also called a primary cartilaginous joint. Because the cartilage is hyaline, the joint is usually a temporary one that disappears when the cartilage turns to bone.

Question 1717. Which cartilage unites the bones at a symphysis: hyaline cartilage alone, fibrocartilage, elastic cartilage, or a mixture of bone and fibrous tissue? The answer is fibrocartilage. A symphysis is also called a secondary cartilaginous joint. On each bony surface a thin layer of hyaline cartilage lies against the bone, with fibrocartilage between the two layers.

Question 1718. A described section through the growing end of a long bone shows a plate of smooth bluish cartilage between the shaft and the bony cap, with columns of cartilage cells in orderly rows and no cavity. What joint is shown? The answer is a synchondrosis, the epiphyseal plate. The columns of cells lengthen the bone, and when growth stops the plate is replaced by bone.

Question 1719. The first rib joins the sternum through which kind of cartilage, and what kind of joint is formed there? The answer is hyaline cartilage, forming a synchondrosis. The first costal cartilage fuses directly with the manubrium, so no cavity intervenes. The joints of the second to the seventh ribs with the sternum are synovial instead.

Question 1720. Which statement distinguishes a synchondrosis from a symphysis correctly: a synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage and a symphysis uses fibrocartilage, both use hyaline cartilage, a synchondrosis uses fibrocartilage and a symphysis uses hyaline cartilage, or neither contains cartilage? The answer is that a synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage and a symphysis uses fibrocartilage. That is why a synchondrosis is often temporary, since hyaline cartilage is readily replaced by bone.

Question 1721. A constructed illustration: a child has pain over the growing plate at the lower end of the femur after a twisting injury, and the imaging shows the plate widened. Which structure is injured? The answer is the epiphyseal plate, a synchondrosis of hyaline cartilage. An injury at the plate may disturb growth, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1722. Name the joint at the growing plate of a long bone and the joint between the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae, in that order. The answer is a synchondrosis first and a symphysis second. The first is a primary cartilaginous joint united by hyaline cartilage. The second is a secondary cartilaginous joint united by fibrocartilage.

Question 1723. Name the class of joint that has a cavity between the bones, a lining membrane that makes fluid, and free movement. The answer is a synovial joint. The other classes are the fibrous joints, which have no cavity, and the cartilaginous joints, which are filled by cartilage. Only the synovial class is freely movable.

Question 1724. Which class of joint is found at the shoulder, the elbow and the knee, and which single feature separates it from every other class? The answer is the synovial class, separated by its joint cavity. The cavity is lined by synovial membrane and holds a film of synovial fluid. Fibrous and cartilaginous joints have no such space.

Question 1725. A synovial joint moves in one plane only, like a door on its hinges. Which named type is it: a plane joint, a hinge joint, a saddle joint, or a ball and socket joint? The answer is a hinge joint. Its surfaces are shaped so that movement is confined to flexion and extension. The elbow is the standard example.

Question 1726. True or false: a synovial joint always has a cavity filled with fluid. The answer is true. The synovial membrane lines the capsule and secretes the fluid into the cavity. The fluid lubricates the surfaces and nourishes the articular cartilage, which has no blood vessels of its own.

Question 1727.
