One statement about classifying joints by structure and by function is correct: every fibrous joint is freely movable, every cartilaginous joint has a cavity, a synovial joint is always a diarthrosis, or a synarthrosis is always synovial. The answer is that a synovial joint is always a diarthrosis, because a cavity and fluid make free movement inevitable. Fibrous joints are called synarthroses and cartilaginous joints amphiarthroses.

Question 1728. At what line does the synovial membrane of a joint end, and what structure covers the joint surface inside that line? The answer is the margin of the articular cartilage, which covers the surface inside the line. The membrane does not cross the cartilage. That is why the cartilage itself has no synovial covering.

Question 1729. The rounded surface of one bone lies inside a ring formed by bone and ligament, and the joint turns about a single axis. Which type of synovial joint is that? The answer is a pivot joint. The joint between the first and the second cervical vertebrae is the standard example. The head turns around the upright peg inside the ring.

Question 1730. Which of these synovial joints is a saddle joint: the elbow, the joint at the base of the thumb, the shoulder, or the ankle? The answer is the joint at the base of the thumb. Its two surfaces are concave in one direction and convex in the other, which allows movement in two planes and lets the thumb cross the palm.

Question 1731. A described specimen shows two almost flat bony surfaces, one sliding over the other, with a capsule around them and no ridge on either surface. Which type of synovial joint is shown? The answer is a plane joint, also called a gliding joint. The surfaces are flat, so one glides on the other, as between the small bones of the foot.

Question 1732. Which statement about the shape of a synovial joint is correct: every joint moves about three axes, a hinge moves in two planes, the shape of the surfaces decides the number of axes, or a saddle moves in one plane? The answer is that the shape of the surfaces decides the number of axes. A hinge has one, a saddle has two, and a ball and socket joint three.

Question 1733. A constructed illustration: an older runner has pain and grating in the knee, and the smooth covering of the joint surfaces has worn away over the years. Which structure has failed? The answer is the articular cartilage of the synovial joint. It cannot renew itself well because it has no blood supply, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1734. A described specimen shows a rounded head sitting in a shallow socket whose rim deepens the cup only a little, and the joint moves freely in every direction. Which type of synovial joint is shown? The answer is a ball and socket joint at the shoulder. The shallow socket gives the widest range of movement but the least stability of the two examples of this type.

Question 1735. Which suture runs across the back of the skull, between the two parietal bones and the occipital bone? The answer is the lambdoid suture. It is named for its resemblance to the Greek letter lambda. Behind it lies the occipital bone, and in front of it lie the two parietal bones.

Question 1736. The joint between the two parietal bones in the midline of the vault is which kind of suture: a squamous suture, a serrate suture, a plane suture, or a schindylesis? The answer is a serrate suture. The two edges interlock like the teeth of a saw. The sagittal suture in the middle of the vault is the standard example.

Question 1737. Where the lower part of the temporal bone meets the parietal bone, the edges are bevelled and one bone overlaps the other. Which named suture is that: the coronal suture, the sagittal suture, the squamosal suture, or the lambdoid suture? The answer is the squamosal suture. Its bevelled edges overlap, which makes it a squamous suture.

Question 1738. Which suture separates the frontal bone from the two parietal bones? The answer is the coronal suture. It runs across the vault from side to side, roughly above the ears. It lies in a coronal plane, so it divides the front of the skull from the back.

Question 1739. A described skull viewed from above shows a joint between two bones whose edges interlock like the teeth of a saw, with no gap and no overlap. Which named kind of suture is shown? The answer is a serrate suture, at the sagittal suture in the midline of the vault. The interlocking edges resist separating forces.

Question 1740. The pterion is the meeting point of which four bones, and which two sutures cross there? The answer is the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones, with the coronal suture and the squamous suture meeting there. The thin bone at that point overlies the middle meningeal artery. A blow there can tear the artery.

Question 1741. Which statement about the fate of the skull sutures is correct: all of them remain fibrous for life, they close by synostosis at different ages in different people, they all turn into synovial joints, or they never close at all? The answer is that they close by synostosis at different ages in different people. A suture that closes early may change the shape of the skull.

Question 1742. Which of these pairs belongs together: the coronal suture with the two parietal bones, the sagittal suture with the frontal and occipital bones, the lambdoid suture with the occipital and parietal bones, or the squamosal suture with the two parietal bones? The answer is the lambdoid suture with the occipital and parietal bones. The sagittal suture lies between the two parietal bones.

Question 1743. The coronal suture runs across the vault from one side to the other. In which plane does that suture lie, and does it divide the skull into right and left parts or into front and back parts? The answer is a coronal plane, which divides the skull into front and back parts. A section along that suture would separate the frontal bone from the parietals.

Question 1744. A constructed illustration: a newborn has a soft gap at the meeting point of the sagittal and coronal sutures, and the gap bulges when the baby cries. What is that gap called? The answer is the anterior fontanelle. The sutures there are still membranous, so pressure inside the skull pushes the soft tissue outward, and the gap normally closes in the second year.

Question 1745. Which fibrous joint unites two bones by a sheet of fibrous tissue that is longer than the tissue in a suture, so that a little movement is possible? The answer is a syndesmosis. The greater length of the fibers allows the slight give. The interosseous membrane between the shafts of the forearm bones is an example.

Question 1746. The union between the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula is which kind of joint: a suture, a syndesmosis, a symphysis, or a synovial joint? The answer is a syndesmosis. Short fibrous bands join the two bones, and no cavity lies between them. The union holds the two bones together while the ankle moves.

Question 1747. A described dissection of the ankle shows a short thick band of fibrous tissue running from the lower end of the tibia to the lower end of the fibula, with no cavity between the bones. Which joint is shown? The answer is the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis, of the fibrous class. It allows only a trace of movement, enough to let the ankle mortise widen slightly.

Question 1748. What is the name of the fibrous joint between the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula, whose fibers are much shorter than those of the interosseous membrane above it? The answer is the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis. It lies just above the ankle joint. The ankle joint itself is a synovial joint and lies below it.

Question 1749. One statement about movement at a syndesmosis is correct: no movement is possible, a small amount occurs and is greatest where the fibrous sheet is longest, the joint has a cavity, or movement is as free as at a synovial joint. The answer is that a small amount occurs and is greatest where the sheet is longest. A syndesmosis has no cavity.

Question 1750. Which two groups of muscles take origin from the front and the back of the interosseous membrane of the leg, and which vessel passes between them? The answer is the extensor muscles in front and the flexor muscles behind, with the anterior tibial artery passing forward through the upper part of the membrane. The membrane therefore divides the leg into two compartments.

Question 1751. One statement about the interosseous membrane of the forearm is correct: it is a synovial joint, its fibers run between the radius and the ulna and carry force, it lies between the humerus and the ulna, or it prevents all movement. The answer is that its fibers run between the radius and the ulna and carry force between them. It still allows pronation and supination.

Question 1752. True or false: the inferior tibiofibular joint is a syndesmosis and not a synovial joint. The answer is true. The two bones are joined by fibrous bands and no cavity lies between them. Its movement is only a slight widening, which the ankle needs when the foot is lifted.

Question 1753. What is the name of the fibrous joint in which a peg of hard tissue fits into a socket and is held there by fibrous tissue, as a tooth is held in its bony socket? The answer is a gomphosis. The peg is the root of the tooth. The fibrous tissue is the periodontal ligament.

Question 1754. Which fibrous tissue holds a tooth in its socket: the sutural ligament, the periodontal ligament, the interosseous membrane, or the joint capsule? The answer is the periodontal ligament. It runs from the bone of the socket to the surface of the root. It also carries the small vessels and nerves that supply the tooth.

Question 1755. One statement about the gomphosis is correct: it joins two bones of the skeleton, it joins a tooth to bone and is not a union of two bones, it is a synovial joint, or it is a cartilaginous joint. The answer is that it joins a tooth to bone, not two bones. Some anatomists therefore exclude it from the joints of the skeleton.

Question 1756. In which two bones of the skull are gomphoses found? The answer is the maxilla of the upper jaw and the mandible of the lower jaw. Each tooth root sits in its own socket in one of those bones. The number of these joints equals the number of teeth present.

Question 1757. A described specimen of a jaw shows a row of pegs set into deep sockets, each peg held by a thin band of fibrous tissue running from the socket to the surface of the peg. Which joint is shown? The answer is a gomphosis, which allows only a slight springing movement. That small give cushions the tooth against the force of biting.

Question 1758. Name the fibrous joint that holds a tooth in its socket and the fibrous joint that unites the shafts of the tibia and the fibula, in that order. The answer is the gomphosis first and the syndesmosis second. The gomphosis binds a tooth to bone, while the syndesmosis binds two bones by a longer sheet of fibers.

Question 1759. Which cartilage unites the bones at a synchondrosis: hyaline cartilage, fibrocartilage, elastic cartilage, or fibrous tissue? The answer is hyaline cartilage. That is why a synchondrosis is called a primary cartilaginous joint. The epiphyseal plate and the joint between the first rib and the sternum are examples.

Question 1760. Which joint unites the first rib with the sternum, and to which functional class does it belong? The answer is a synchondrosis, which belongs to the amphiarthroses. Hyaline cartilage joins the first costal cartilage directly to the manubrium. The joint is therefore almost immovable, which helps to keep the first rib fixed when the arm moves.

Question 1761. Which of these is a synchondrosis: the pubic symphysis, the joint between the first rib and the sternum, the joint between two vertebral bodies, or the knee joint? The answer is the joint between the first rib and the sternum. It is united by hyaline cartilage. The pubic symphysis and the intervertebral joints are symphyses, and the knee is synovial.

Question 1762. A described section through a growing bone shows a plate of smooth bluish cartilage between the shaft and the bony end, with no cavity anywhere in it. What is that plate, and what kind of joint is it? The answer is the epiphyseal plate, and the joint is a synchondrosis. Growth in length takes place at that plate.

Question 1763. The spheno-occipital synchondrosis lies between which two bones of the skull base, and how is it directed? The answer is between the body of the sphenoid and the basilar part of the occipital bone, running across the base from side to side. It closes in early adult life, and until then it allows the base of the skull to grow.

Question 1764. One statement about the fate of a synchondrosis is correct: it remains cartilaginous for life, it is usually temporary and is replaced by bone, it turns into a synovial joint, or it becomes fibrocartilage. The answer is that it is usually temporary and is replaced by bone. The change is called synostosis, and the epiphyseal plate shows it best, since the plate disappears when growth stops.

Question 1765. Which cartilaginous joint unites the bony part of a rib with its costal cartilage, and which cartilage forms it? The answer is a synchondrosis, formed by hyaline cartilage. The joint lies between the end of the rib and the cartilage that continues forward to the sternum. Because the cartilage is hyaline, the joint allows only a trace of movement.

Question 1766. What name is given to the cartilaginous joint that unites two bones by a pad of fibrocartilage and remains permanent, such as the joint between the two pubic bones? The answer is a symphysis. It is also called a secondary cartilaginous joint. A thin layer of hyaline cartilage covers each bony surface, and fibrocartilage lies between them.

Question 1767. The joint between the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae is which kind of joint: a synchondrosis, a symphysis, a synovial joint, or a suture? The answer is a symphysis. A pad of fibrocartilage, the intervertebral disc, joins the two bodies. Small movements at each of these joints add up to the movement of the whole spine.

Question 1768. The pubic symphysis lies between which two bones, and which cartilage lies between their surfaces? The answer is the two pubic bones, with a disc of fibrocartilage between them. A thin layer of hyaline cartilage covers each bony surface. The disc is the pad that joins the bones.

Question 1769. True or false: the pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint. The answer is true. It is a secondary cartilaginous joint, united by fibrocartilage. No cavity lies between the two pubic bones. Its slight movement allows the pelvis a little give when weight is transferred from one leg to the other.

Question 1770. A described section through the middle of the pelvis shows a wedge of fibrocartilage between two bones, with a thin layer of hyaline cartilage on each bony surface and no cavity. Which joint is shown? The answer is the pubic symphysis, a secondary cartilaginous joint. The fibrocartilaginous disc is the feature that marks it as a symphysis rather than a synchondrosis.

Question 1771. One statement about the joint between the manubrium and the sternum is correct: it is synovial, it is a secondary cartilaginous joint in most people, it is a suture, or it never moves. The answer is that it is a secondary cartilaginous joint in most people. A disc of fibrocartilage lies between the two parts of the sternum, and in some people the joint later becomes bony.

Question 1772. A constructed illustration: late in pregnancy the pelvic joints soften, and the gap between the two pubic bones widens a little. Which structure widens, and what is the reason? The answer is the fibrocartilaginous disc of the pubic symphysis. Softening of the pelvic ligaments is a normal change in late pregnancy, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1773. Which of these is a symphysis: the epiphyseal plate, the pubic symphysis, the temporomandibular joint, or the sagittal suture? The answer is the pubic symphysis. It is united by fibrocartilage and is a secondary cartilaginous joint. The epiphyseal plate is a synchondrosis, the jaw joint is synovial, and the sagittal suture is fibrous.

Question 1774. Which of these pairs belongs together: a synchondrosis with fibrocartilage, a symphysis with hyaline cartilage, a synchondrosis with a temporary joint later replaced by bone, or a symphysis with a joint cavity? The answer is a synchondrosis with a temporary joint later replaced by bone. The epiphyseal plate is the clearest example. A symphysis is united by fibrocartilage and has no cavity.

Question 1775. Which smooth glassy cartilage covers the ends of the bones inside a synovial joint, and does it contain blood vessels? The answer is hyaline cartilage, and it contains no blood vessels and no nerves. It is nourished by the synovial fluid that bathes it. Because it has no blood supply, it heals poorly after injury.

Question 1776. Which structure secretes the fluid that fills the cavity of a synovial joint: the articular cartilage, the synovial membrane, the fibrous capsule, or the periosteum? The answer is the synovial membrane. It lines the inner surface of the capsule and stops at the margin of the articular cartilage. The fibrous capsule is the tough outer sleeve and secretes nothing.

Question 1777. A described section through a joint shows a tough sleeve of fibrous tissue attached to both bones, a smooth pink lining on its inner surface, and a thin film of fluid in the space between the bones. Which two layers are shown? The answer is the fibrous capsule outside and the synovial membrane inside. The membrane makes the fluid, and the capsule holds the joint together.

Question 1778. A constructed illustration: after a fall a knee swells with fluid, and the fluid lies inside the joint itself rather than in the skin. Which cavity holds it? The answer is the synovial cavity of the knee joint. The synovial membrane lines that cavity and secretes the fluid. The fluid is what fills the joint and makes it look swollen.

Question 1779. Which of these structures divides the cavity of a synovial joint into two separate compartments: the meniscus of the knee, the disc of the temporomandibular joint, the labrum of the hip, or a bursa beside the joint? The answer is the disc of the temporomandibular joint. It divides the cavity into an upper and a lower part, while a meniscus is only a partial crescent.

Question 1780. Which rule states that the nerve supplying a joint also supplies the muscles that move the joint and the skin over their attachments? The answer is Hilton's law. The same nerve therefore carries sensation from the joint and from the structures around it. That is why disease in a joint can be felt as pain over the muscles and skin the same nerve supplies.

Question 1781. A described specimen shows a socket with a raised rim of fibrocartilage around its edge, gripping the head of the bone inside it. What is that rim called? The answer is the labrum, here the acetabular labrum of the hip, with the glenoid labrum of the shoulder as the other example. It deepens the socket and helps to hold the head in place.

Question 1782. What is the name of the tough sleeve of fibrous tissue that surrounds a synovial joint and is attached to the bones on either side? The answer is the fibrous capsule. It is the outer layer of the joint wall. Thickenings in it form the capsular ligaments, and it resists the forces that would pull the joint apart.

Question 1783. A constructed illustration: a joint is kept still in a cast for several weeks, and afterward the joint is stiff and the smooth covering of its surfaces has thinned. Why does that covering suffer? The answer is that the articular cartilage has no blood vessels and depends on synovial fluid. Movement spreads the fluid over the cartilage, so without movement it is poorly fed.

Question 1784. One statement about the articular cartilage of a synovial joint is correct: it is rich in blood vessels, it has no blood vessels or nerves and repairs poorly, it is fibrocartilage like the meniscus, or the synovial membrane covers its free surface. The answer is that it has no blood vessels or nerves and repairs poorly, because it is nourished only by synovial fluid. Injury to it therefore heals slowly.

Question 1785. A described radiograph of a normal knee shows a clear dark gap between the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia. What fills that gap? The answer is the articular cartilage covering the two bone ends. Cartilage contains no calcium, so it casts no shadow, and the dark gap is the joint space.

Question 1786. A described dissection of a joint shows a band of white fibrous tissue running from one bone to the other across the joint, separate from the capsule. What is that band called? The answer is a ligament. It resists movement of the joint in one particular direction. Many ligaments are only thickenings of the capsule itself.

Question 1787. Which ligament of the knee lies outside the capsule and which lies inside it? The answer is that the fibular collateral ligament lies outside the capsule, while the anterior cruciate ligament lies inside it. Structures inside the capsule are bathed in synovial fluid, so injury there lets blood collect within the joint.

Question 1788. A constructed illustration: a twisting injury fills a knee joint with blood, and the joint cannot be straightened fully. Which structure inside the joint is most likely torn? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It lies inside the capsule, so its torn ends bleed into the cavity, and the joint then holds itself in the position that holds the most fluid.

Question 1789. A joint surface is described as convex in one direction and concave at right angles to that direction. What is that shape called? The answer is a saddle shape, which allows movement about two axes. The joint at the base of the thumb has this shape, and its two axes lie at right angles to each other.

Question 1790. A described section through a knee shows a crescent-shaped pad of fibrocartilage attached at both ends to the capsule but free along its inner edge. What is that pad, and what does it do? The answer is a meniscus. It deepens the surface, spreads the load, and helps the joint to glide, and its loose attachment leaves it open to tearing.

Question 1791. True or false: the synovial membrane covers the articular cartilage as well as the inner surface of the capsule. The answer is false. The membrane lines the capsule and stops at the margin of the cartilage. The cartilage is left bare so that it can meet the cartilage of the other bone.

Question 1792. A constructed illustration: an older person has a hip that has lost its smooth articular covering, the joint space has narrowed, and bone now rubs on bone. Which structure has failed? The answer is the articular cartilage of a synovial joint. It has no blood vessels and very few cells, so it does not regenerate.

Question 1793. Which of these pairs belongs together: articular cartilage with an abundant blood supply, the synovial membrane with the secretion of synovial fluid, the fibrous capsule with the lining of the cavity, or the meniscus with the joint at the base of the thumb? The answer is the synovial membrane with the secretion of synovial fluid. The membrane is the lining, and the capsule is the outer sleeve.

Question 1794. Which is the only freely movable joint of the skull, and which two bones does it join? The answer is the temporomandibular joint, which joins the mandible with the temporal bone. It lies just in front of the ear. All the other joints of the skull are fibrous or cartilaginous.

Question 1795. The articular surfaces of the temporomandibular joint are covered by which tissue: hyaline cartilage, fibrocartilage, bone, or synovial membrane? The answer is fibrocartilage. That covering is unusual for a synovial joint, where hyaline cartilage is the rule. Fibrocartilage resists the heavy wear of chewing.

Question 1796. A constructed illustration: a person yawns widely and feels a click and then pain in front of the ear, and the jaw shifts to one side. Which joint is involved, and which muscle pulls the disc forward? The answer is the temporomandibular joint, with the lateral pterygoid muscle. That muscle attaches to the disc and carries it forward with the bone.

Question 1797. A described specimen shows a joint between the mandible and the temporal bone, with a disc between the two surfaces and a capsule around them, and the surfaces are not covered by the usual glassy cartilage. Which joint is shown? The answer is the temporomandibular joint. It is the only synovial joint of the skull. Its covering is fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage.

Question 1798. In the temporomandibular joint, which compartment allows gliding and which allows hinge movement? The answer is that the upper compartment, between the disc and the temporal bone, allows gliding, and the lower compartment, between the disc and the mandible, allows hinge movement. Opening the mouth uses both. The disc moves forward with the condyle in the upper compartment.

Question 1799. Which of these pairs belongs together: the coronal suture with the occipital bone, the temporomandibular joint with a fibrous union, the spheno-occipital synchondrosis with the base of the skull, or the gomphosis with the vault of the skull? The answer is the spheno-occipital synchondrosis with the base of the skull. The coronal suture lies between the frontal bone and the parietals.

Question 1800. Name the kinds of joint that can be found in the skull, spoken as a list. The answer is the suture, the gomphosis at the teeth, the synchondrosis of the skull base, and the synovial temporomandibular joint. The sutures and the gomphoses are fibrous, the skull base joint is cartilaginous, and the jaw joint is synovial.

To summarize, the joints of the body are classified by the tissue that unites the bones. Fibrous joints, or synarthroses, include the sutures of the skull, the syndesmoses such as the interosseous membranes, and the gomphoses that hold the teeth in their sockets. Cartilaginous joints, or amphiarthroses, are either synchondroses, united by hyaline cartilage and usually temporary, as at the epiphyseal plate, or symphyses, united by fibrocartilage and permanent, as at the pubic symphysis and between the vertebral bodies. Synovial joints, or diarthroses, have a cavity, articular hyaline cartilage, a fibrous capsule, a synovial membrane and synovial fluid, and the shape of their surfaces decides how many axes they move about. Ligaments, discs, menisci and labra are the accessory structures that steady them, and the skull holds a suture, a gomphosis, a synchondrosis and one synovial joint at the jaw. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 19 — Vertebral Joints

This chapter takes the joints of the skull and the joints of the vertebral column together, because the two are built on different plans. It begins with the sutures of the vault and the fontanelles of the newborn, then the cartilaginous joints of the skull base and the one synovial joint of the head. It goes on to the joints between the vertebrae, from the discs and the facet joints to the ligaments that steady them. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately and then explains why, so nothing has to be held in mind. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1801. Which suture runs down the middle of the skull vault between the two parietal bones? The answer is the sagittal suture. It extends from the bregma in front to the lambda behind, and its interlocking edges make it a serrate suture. Its fibers are continuous with the pericranium outside and the dura mater within.

Question 1802. Which suture separates the frontal bone from the two parietal bones: the sagittal suture, the coronal suture, the lambdoid suture, or the squamous suture? The answer is the coronal suture. It crosses the vault from temple to temple, and behind it lies the pair of parietal bones. The sagittal suture lies farther back, in the midline.

Question 1803. Name the suture that separates the occipital bone from the two parietal bones at the back of the skull. The answer is the lambdoid suture. It slopes downward and forward on each side from the lambda, and its shape suggests the Greek letter lambda. The occipitomastoid suture continues the same line toward the base.

Question 1804. Which suture separates the parietal bone above from the squamous part of the temporal bone below? The answer is the squamous suture. Its edges are beveled, so the parietal bone overlaps the temporal bone rather like a roof tile. It lies above the ear on the side of the vault.

Question 1805. The metopic suture divides which bone into two halves in the newborn: the temporal bone, the frontal bone, the occipital bone, or the parietal bone? The answer is the frontal bone. The suture runs down the middle of the forehead and usually closes during the first few years of life. A trace of it in an adult is a normal variant.

Question 1806. Which of these pairs belongs together: the coronal suture with the frontal and the parietal bones, the sagittal suture with the occipital and the temporal bones, the lambdoid suture with the two temporal bones, or the squamous suture with the two parietal bones? The answer is the coronal suture with the frontal and the parietal bones. The sagittal suture joins the two parietal bones to each other.

Question 1807. What is the name of the point on top of the skull where the coronal suture meets the sagittal suture? The answer is the bregma. In the infant the same spot is felt as the anterior fontanelle, the soft diamond-shaped gap between the bones. It lies in the midline toward the front of the vault.

Question 1808. Which point marks the meeting of the sagittal suture with the lambdoid suture at the back of the vault? The answer is the lambda. It lies in the midline behind the bregma and is shaped like an inverted Y. In the newborn the same spot holds the small posterior fontanelle.

Question 1809. A described specimen of a newborn skull shows a diamond-shaped membrane-covered gap where the coronal and the sagittal sutures meet, with the frontal and the parietal bones around it. Which structure is described, and when does it usually close? The answer is the anterior fontanelle, which closes during the second year of life. It is the largest of the fontanelles.

Question 1810. Which fontanelle lies at the meeting of the sagittal and the lambdoid sutures: the anterior fontanelle, the posterior fontanelle, the sphenoidal fontanelle, or the mastoid fontanelle? The answer is the posterior fontanelle. It is triangular, much smaller than the anterior one, and it closes within the first few months after birth. The mastoid and sphenoidal fontanelles lie lower on the side of the skull.

Question 1811. True or false: the anterior fontanelle stays open longer than the posterior fontanelle. The answer is true. The posterior fontanelle closes within the first few months of life, while the anterior one is still open at the end of the first year. The anterior fontanelle is also the larger of the two.

Question 1812. What is the name of the H-shaped junction on the side of the skull where the frontal, the parietal, the temporal and the sphenoid bones come together? The answer is the pterion. It lies a little above and in front of the ear, in a thin part of the vault. It is the weakest point of the skull and an important surgical landmark.

Question 1813. Name the four bones that meet at the pterion, spoken as a list. The answer is the frontal bone, the parietal bone, the temporal bone, and the greater wing of the sphenoid. The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery grooves the inner surface deep to this point, so a blow here is dangerous. The junction varies in shape from one skull to another.

Question 1814. Which artery lies immediately deep to the pterion, grooving the inner surface of the skull? The answer is the middle meningeal artery. It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and divides into an anterior and a posterior branch. Its anterior branch runs upward and backward beneath the pterion.

Question 1815. A constructed illustration: a blow to the temple is followed by a brief recovery and then a deepening drowsiness, and imaging shows a lens-shaped collection between the skull and the dura mater. Which vessel has most likely been torn? The answer is the middle meningeal artery, torn where it crosses deep to the pterion. Blood then collects outside the dura mater, and the management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1816. A described dried skull shows a star-shaped point at the back of the side wall where the parietal, the occipital and the mastoid part of the temporal bone meet. Which landmark is described? The answer is the asterion. It lies behind and below the mastoid process and marks the site of the mastoid fontanelle in the newborn. The transverse and sigmoid venous sinuses meet deep to it.

Question 1817. Which venous channel lies immediately deep to the asterion, at the junction of the transverse and the sigmoid sinuses? The answer is the sigmoid sinus where it becomes the transverse sinus. The point is marked on the outside of the skull by the asterion. A surgeon placing a burr hole at this landmark must know the vein beneath it.

Question 1818. Which kind of suture has edges that interlock like the teeth of a saw: a squamous suture, a serrate suture, a plane suture, or a schindylesis? The answer is a serrate suture. The coronal, the sagittal and the lambdoid sutures are serrate, and their interlocking edges resist pulling forces. A squamous suture is beveled instead, and a plane suture has smooth edges.

Question 1819. What is the name of the joint in which a thin plate of one bone fits into a groove in another, as the rostrum of the sphenoid does with the vomer: a gomphosis, a syndesmosis, a schindylesis, or a synchondrosis? The answer is a schindylesis, a fibrous joint of the skull base. A gomphosis is the peg-in-socket joint of a tooth.

Question 1820. Which cartilaginous joint joins the body of the sphenoid bone to the basilar part of the occipital bone? The answer is the spheno-occipital synchondrosis. It lies in the midline of the skull base and is the chief growth center of the cranial base. It closes around the time of puberty, later than most growth plates of the body.

Question 1821. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of a child's skull base shows a band of cartilage in the midline between the sphenoid body and the basilar part of the occipital bone. Which joint is shown, and what happens to it? The answer is the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, which ossifies around puberty. Until then it allows growth in length of the skull base.

Question 1822. Which cartilage-filled fissure of the skull base lies between the petrous part of the temporal bone and the occipital bone, and which foramen lies at its posterior end? The answer is the petro-occipital fissure, with the jugular foramen at its posterior end. The fissure remains as a synchondrosis in the adult. The carotid canal opens in front of it.

Question 1823. The jugular foramen lies at the posterior end of which fissure of the skull base? The answer is the petro-occipital fissure. The fissure runs between the petrous temporal bone and the occipital bone and is filled with cartilage. The jugular foramen at its end carries the internal jugular vein and several cranial nerves.

Question 1824. True or false: the temporomandibular joint is the only synovial joint in the skull. The answer is true. Every other joint of the skull is fibrous or cartilaginous, and none of them has a joint cavity. The jaw joint alone has a cavity, a synovial membrane and synovial fluid.

Question 1825. The temporomandibular joint is best described as which kind of joint: a ball and socket joint, a saddle joint, a synovial joint of the modified hinge type, or a fibrous joint? The answer is a synovial joint of the modified hinge type. It is a hinge because the bones move on each other in one plane, and modified because it also glides forward.

Question 1826. Which two bones form the temporomandibular joint? The answer is the temporal bone and the mandible. The head of the mandible meets the mandibular fossa and the articular tubercle of the temporal bone. The joint lies just in front of the external acoustic meatus.

Question 1827. A described specimen shows a joint of the head opened from the side, with a fibrocartilaginous disc dividing its cavity into an upper and a lower compartment. Which joint is shown? The answer is the temporomandibular joint. The disc is the only fibrocartilaginous disc in the head, and it travels forward with the head of the mandible.

Question 1828. In which compartment of the temporomandibular joint does the gliding movement take place: the upper compartment, the lower compartment, both compartments equally, or neither compartment? The answer is the upper compartment, between the disc and the temporal bone. The lower compartment, between the disc and the head of the mandible, allows rotation. The two movements together open the mouth.

Question 1829. Which muscle attaches to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint and to the neck of the mandible? The answer is the lateral pterygoid muscle. It pulls the disc and the head of the mandible forward and is the chief muscle of protrusion. Because of it, the disc travels with the bone when the mouth opens.

Question 1830. A constructed illustration: after a wide yawn the jaw stays open and cannot be closed, and the chin is pushed forward. Where has the head of the mandible moved? The answer is anterior to the articular tubercle of the temporal bone. Both heads are pulled forward by the lateral pterygoid muscles and slip over the summit of the tubercle.

Question 1831. Besides the lateral ligament that thickens its capsule, which two ligaments are associated with the temporomandibular joint: the sphenomandibular and the stylomandibular, the alar and the apical, the anterior and the posterior longitudinal, or the transverse and the cruciform? The answer is the sphenomandibular and the stylomandibular ligaments. Neither strengthens the capsule, and the sphenomandibular ligament is the pivot about which the mandible swings.

Question 1832. A constructed illustration: a fracture crosses the neck of the mandible, and the fragment carrying the head is drawn forward and medially. Which muscle is responsible for that displacement? The answer is the lateral pterygoid muscle. It attaches to the neck of the mandible and to the disc and pulls both forward and medially. The rest of the mandible is pulled upward by the muscles of closure.

Question 1833. When the mandible is thrust forward in protrusion, in which plane does the head of the mandible move? The answer is the sagittal plane. Both heads glide forward and downward on the articular tubercles in that plane. Protrusion is therefore a movement in one plane, and it is checked by the posterior fibers of the temporalis muscle.

Question 1834. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sagittal suture with a fibrous joint, the spheno-occipital junction with a synovial joint, the temporomandibular joint with a cartilaginous joint, or a tooth in its socket with a synovial joint? The answer is the sagittal suture with a fibrous joint. The spheno-occipital junction is cartilaginous, the temporomandibular joint is synovial, and a tooth in its socket is fixed by a fibrous gomphosis.

Question 1835. Which statement about the sutures of the growing skull is correct: they are the main sites of growth in the vault, they fuse before birth, they prevent all movement, or they are synovial joints? The answer is that they are the main sites of growth in the vault, where bone is added at the sutural edges as the brain enlarges. A suture that fuses too early therefore stops growth in that direction.

Question 1836. A described radiograph of a young child's skull shows a raised ridge crossing the vault above one ear, with flattening of the forehead on that same side. Which suture has fused too early, and what has the fusion prevented? The answer is the coronal suture on that side, whose early fusion has stopped growth of the vault from front to back. The appearance is an illustration.

Question 1837. The atlanto-occipital joint is formed between the occipital condyles and which surfaces of the atlas: the superior articular facets, the inferior articular facets, the anterior arch, or the posterior arch? The answer is the superior articular facets. They are concave and receive the convex condyles of the occipital bone. The joint allows the head to nod.

Question 1838. Which statement about the atlanto-occipital joint is correct: it is a synovial ellipsoid joint and allows mainly nodding, it is a pivot joint and allows rotation, it is a fibrous joint, or it is a cartilaginous joint? The answer is that it is a synovial ellipsoid joint and allows mainly nodding. Flexion and extension of the head happen here, while most rotation happens at the joints below.

Question 1839. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the upper neck, in a constructed illustration, shows the dens of the axis displaced backward against the spinal cord, with a torn band that normally holds it against the anterior arch of the atlas. Which joint has been disrupted? The answer is the median atlantoaxial joint. The band is the transverse ligament of the atlas, whose rupture lets the dens move backward into the canal.

Question 1840. Which class of joint unites two vertebral bodies, with a pad of fibrocartilage between them? The answer is a secondary cartilaginous joint, or symphysis. The two bone surfaces are covered by thin plates of hyaline cartilage, and the disc between them is fibrocartilage. The joint allows slight movement in every direction.

Question 1841. What structure lies between the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae: a synovial cavity, an intervertebral disc, a bursa, or a layer of elastic cartilage? The answer is an intervertebral disc. It is built of an outer ring of fibrous tissue and a soft inner core. It cushions the bodies and allows the column to bend.

Question 1842. A described cross section through an intervertebral disc shows concentric rings of tough fibrous tissue around a soft, glistening center. What is the name of the outer ring? The answer is the annulus fibrosus. Its fibers cross from one lamella to the next and run obliquely between the vertebral bodies. The soft center within it is the nucleus pulposus.

Question 1843. What is the name of the soft, gel-like core of the intervertebral disc? The answer is the nucleus pulposus. It lies a little behind the center of the disc, nearer the back than the front. It is rich in water and in substances that hold water, and it acts as a cushion.

Question 1844. Which part of the annulus fibrosus is thinnest and therefore most likely to give way: the anterior part, the posterior and posterolateral part, the upper part, or the lower part? The answer is the posterior and posterolateral part. The ring is thickest in front and thinnest behind and behind to the side. That is why a disc usually herniates backward and to one side.

Question 1845. A constructed illustration: a person has pain shooting down one leg, and imaging shows disc material protruding backward and to the side into an intervertebral foramen. Which structure is being compressed? The answer is the spinal nerve as it leaves the canal through the foramen. A posterolateral protrusion meets the nerve where the foramen holds it.

Question 1846. A described sagittal magnetic resonance imaging scan of the lower back shows a disc bulging backward and indenting the sac of the meninges. Which structure has moved backward, and from where has it come? The answer is part of the disc, pushed out of its place between two vertebral bodies. The bulge is usually made of nucleus pulposus that has escaped through a tear in the annulus.

Question 1847. The posterior longitudinal ligament lies in which position relative to the intervertebral discs? The answer is immediately behind them, within the vertebral canal. It runs down the back of the vertebral bodies from the axis to the sacrum. Because of it, the discs lie between that ligament and the front of the canal.

Question 1848. Which ligament is narrow and weakest at its sides, so that it fails to check a disc that herniates backward and to one side: the anterior longitudinal ligament, the posterior longitudinal ligament, or the ligamentum flavum? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It is broad over the middle of each disc and narrow at its edges, so a posterolateral disc escapes beside it.

Question 1849. Which long ligament runs down the front of the vertebral bodies from the base of the skull to the sacrum? The answer is the anterior longitudinal ligament. It is broad and firmly attached to the front of each body and to each disc. It checks extension of the vertebral column.

Question 1850. Which ligament limits hyperextension of the vertebral column: the anterior longitudinal ligament, the posterior longitudinal ligament, the supraspinous ligament, or the ligamentum flavum? The answer is the anterior longitudinal ligament. It lies in front of the bodies, so throwing the head and trunk backward stretches it. The ligaments behind the canal check flexion instead.

Question 1851. The ligamentum flavum connects which parts of two adjacent vertebrae? The answer is their laminae. It runs from the lower edge of one lamina to the upper edge of the one below, on each side of the midline. It is yellow and elastic, and it forms part of the back wall of the vertebral canal.

Question 1852. Why is the elasticity of the ligamentum flavum important when the vertebral column bends forward: it pulls the vertebral bodies together, it helps the column straighten again, it prevents rotation, or it carries the spinal nerves? The answer is that it helps the column straighten again and keeps the elastic ligament from folding into the canal. It stores energy as it is stretched.

Question 1853. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior longitudinal ligament with limiting extension, the ligamentum flavum with connecting the spinous processes, the supraspinous ligament with connecting the vertebral bodies, or the posterior longitudinal ligament with limiting rotation? The answer is the anterior longitudinal ligament with limiting extension. The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae, and the supraspinous ligament joins the tips of the spinous processes.

Question 1854. Which structures form the boundaries of an intervertebral foramen? The answer is the bodies and the disc in front, the facet joints behind, and the pedicles of the two adjacent vertebrae above and below. The spinal nerve and its accompanying vessels pass through the opening. Narrowing of the foramen therefore traps the nerve.

Question 1855. Bending forward and backward at the waist happens in which plane and about which axis? The answer is the sagittal plane, about a transverse axis. Flexion carries the trunk forward and extension carries it back in that same plane. Lateral flexion, by contrast, happens in the coronal plane.

Question 1856. Turning the head to look over one shoulder happens about which axis: a transverse axis, an anteroposterior axis, a longitudinal axis, or an oblique axis? The answer is a longitudinal axis. The movement is rotation, and most of it happens between the atlas and the axis. It takes place in the transverse plane.

Question 1857. What kind of joint is a zygapophyseal joint, the joint between the superior and the inferior articular processes of two adjacent vertebrae? The answer is a synovial plane joint. It has a cavity, a synovial membrane and a capsule that is richly supplied with nerves. Its surfaces are flat or gently curved.

Question 1858. Which orientation do the articular facets of the cervical vertebrae have, and what does it allow: about 45 degrees to the horizontal, allowing free flexion, extension and rotation; vertical, allowing only rotation; sagittal, allowing only flexion; or horizontal, allowing no movement? The answer is about 45 degrees to the horizontal, allowing free flexion, extension and rotation. The thoracic facets lie vertically and favor rotation instead.

Question 1859. A described axial section through a lumbar vertebra shows the two facet joints with their surfaces turned almost directly forward and backward, in the sagittal plane. Which movement does this arrangement limit? The answer is rotation. It allows free flexion and extension, but turning the trunk about a vertical axis is checked by the bone.

Question 1860. A described axial section through a cervical vertebra shows a small joint at the side of the body, between a raised lip on the upper surface and the sloping lower surface of the vertebra above. Which joint is shown? The answer is an uncovertebral joint, also called a joint of Luschka. It is found only in the cervical region.

Question 1861. Between which structures do the uncovertebral joints lie, and in which vertebrae are they found? The answer is between the uncinate process of one cervical vertebra and the lower surface of the body above, from the third to the seventh cervical vertebra. They are small joints at the side of the disc. They appear during childhood and are prominent in adult life.

Question 1862. In which region of the vertebral column are uncovertebral joints found: the cervical region, the thoracic region, the lumbar region, or the sacrum? The answer is the cervical region. They lie at the sides of the bodies from the third to the seventh cervical vertebra. With age their edges grow into bony spurs that can narrow the intervertebral foramen.

Question 1863. A constructed illustration: an older person has neck pain and tingling in one arm, and imaging shows bony spurs at the side of the cervical bodies narrowing an intervertebral foramen. Which joints have produced the spurs, and what do the spurs compress? The answer is the uncovertebral joints, whose spurs press on the spinal nerve. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1864. Of the three joints that make up the atlantoaxial complex, which one is the pivot about which the head turns? The answer is the median atlantoaxial joint, between the dens of the axis and the ring formed by the anterior arch of the atlas and the transverse ligament. The two lateral joints between the articular facets glide at the same time.

Question 1865. Name the three joints that together make up the atlantoaxial complex, spoken as a list. The answer is the median atlantoaxial joint and the two lateral atlantoaxial joints. The median joint lies between the dens and the ring of the atlas, and the lateral joints lie between the articular facets on each side. Together they allow the head to turn from side to side.

Question 1866. What is the name of the joint between the occipital condyles and the first cervical vertebra? The answer is the atlanto-occipital joint. There is no intervertebral disc between the skull and the atlas. The joint is synovial and permits the nodding of the head.

Question 1867. The atlanto-occipital joint is which kind of joint: a fibrous joint, a secondary cartilaginous joint, a synovial joint, or a primary cartilaginous joint? The answer is a synovial joint. Each condyle has its own cavity and capsule, and the pair acts as one joint. The movements are flexion and extension of the head, with a little lateral bending.

Question 1868. True or false: there is no intervertebral disc between the atlas and the axis. The answer is true. The two vertebrae are joined instead by the median atlantoaxial joint and the two lateral joints, with their ligaments. A disc appears only below the axis, between the second and the third cervical vertebrae.

Question 1869. Which ligament holds the dens of the axis against the anterior arch of the atlas? The answer is the transverse ligament of the atlas. It stretches across the ring of the atlas behind the dens. If it ruptures, the dens can move backward and press on the spinal cord.

Question 1870. Which ligaments check rotation of the head at the atlantoaxial joints: the alar ligaments, from the dens to the occipital condyles; the anterior longitudinal ligament; the ligamentum flavum; or the supraspinous ligament? The answer is the alar ligaments, from the dens to the occipital condyles. They are taut when the head is turned and stop the movement.

Question 1871. The tectorial membrane is the upward continuation of which ligament? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It leaves the vertebral canal at the second cervical vertebra and runs up over the dens into the skull. It forms part of the back wall of the space that carries the spinal cord.

Question 1872. A described sagittal magnetic resonance imaging scan of the upper neck shows a broad band lying behind the dens and in front of the spinal cord, continuing upward from the back of the vertebral bodies. Which structure is shown? The answer is the tectorial membrane. It is the continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament and covers the alar and transverse ligaments.

Question 1873. A constructed illustration: a person whose transverse ligament of the atlas is lax bends the neck forward, and the dens moves backward against the spinal cord. Which joint is unstable, and which ligament has failed? The answer is the median atlantoaxial joint, with failure of the transverse ligament, so the dens is free to press on the cord. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 1874. A constructed illustration: disease has fused the joints of the upper two cervical vertebrae on both sides. Which movement of the head is most reduced? The answer is rotation, the turning of the head from side to side. Most of that movement happens at the atlantoaxial joints, and it is lost when they fuse. Nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint is preserved.

Question 1875. Which ligament connects the tips of the spinous processes from the seventh cervical vertebra down to the sacrum? The answer is the supraspinous ligament. It is a strong cord felt in the midline of the back. In the neck its place is taken by the nuchal ligament.

Question 1876. What is the name of the strong elastic band in the midline of the back of the neck, running from the external occipital protuberance to the seventh cervical vertebra? The answer is the nuchal ligament. It is the continuation of the supraspinous ligament in the neck. It gives attachment to muscles and checks excessive flexion of the head.

Question 1877. Above which vertebra is the supraspinous ligament absent: the first cervical, the seventh cervical, the first thoracic, or the twelfth thoracic? The answer is the seventh cervical. Above it the ligament is replaced by the nuchal ligament, which is thicker and elastic. The supraspinous ligament runs from the seventh cervical vertebra to the sacrum.

Question 1878. A described lateral radiograph of the neck, taken with the head bent forward, shows a fan-shaped widening of the gaps between the spinous processes. Which ligaments have been stretched? The answer is the interspinous and the supraspinous ligaments. They lie between and behind the spinous processes. The ligamentum flavum behind the canal is stretched as well.

Question 1879. Which of these pairs belongs together: the intervertebral joint with a secondary cartilaginous joint, the zygapophyseal joint with a fibrous joint, the costovertebral joint with a primary cartilaginous joint, or the sacroiliac joint with a fibrous joint? The answer is the intervertebral joint with a secondary cartilaginous joint. The zygapophyseal, the costovertebral and the sacroiliac joints are all synovial joints with capsules and synovial fluid.

Question 1880. The head of a typical rib articulates with which structures? The answer is the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae and the disc between them. The head carries two facets, one for each body, and a ridge between them that meets the disc. The joint is synovial and lies at the back of the chest.

Question 1881. Which ribs articulate with the body of only one vertebra: the first, the eleventh and the twelfth; the second, the third and the fourth; the fifth, the sixth and the seventh; or the eighth, the ninth and the tenth? The answer is the first, the eleventh and the twelfth. Each of these has a single facet on its head, while all the others meet two vertebrae and the disc between them.

Question 1882. What is the name of the joint between the tubercle of a rib and the transverse process of a vertebra? The answer is the costotransverse joint. It is a small synovial joint with a capsule. It is absent on the eleventh and the twelfth ribs, whose tubercles carry no articular surface.

Question 1883. The first costal cartilage joins the manubrium by which kind of joint: a synovial joint, a cartilaginous joint with no cavity, a fibrous joint, or a saddle joint? The answer is a cartilaginous joint with no cavity, a synchondrosis. The second to the seventh costal cartilages form synovial joints with the sternum instead. The first rib is fixed and needs no cavity.

Question 1884. A described section through a vertebral motion segment shows a small joint behind the vertebral body, between the superior articular process of one vertebra and the inferior process of the next, with a capsule and a smooth lining. Which joint is shown? The answer is a zygapophyseal joint, or facet joint. It is a synovial plane joint.

Question 1885. The lumbosacral joint lies between which two bones, and which ligament steadies it from the side? The answer is the fifth lumbar vertebra and the first piece of the sacrum, steadied by the iliolumbar ligament. The ligament runs from the transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra to the iliac crest. It resists forward slipping of that vertebra.

Question 1886. The iliolumbar ligament attaches to which two bony points? The answer is the transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra and the iliac crest, with a band to the ilium behind it. It anchors the lowest lumbar vertebra to the pelvis. It resists forward slipping of the fifth lumbar vertebra on the sacrum.

Question 1887. Which statement about the sacroiliac joint is correct: it is a synovial joint with fibrocartilage-covered surfaces and very slight movement, it is a fibrous joint with no cavity, it is a ball and socket joint, or it is a cartilaginous joint that fuses after birth? The answer is that it is a synovial joint with fibrocartilage-covered surfaces and very slight movement. Its irregular surfaces and strong ligaments allow only a small rocking.

Question 1888. True or false: the sacroiliac joint allows a wide range of movement between the hip bone and the sacrum. The answer is false. The joint is held by very strong ligaments, and its surfaces are irregular and interlocking. Only a few degrees of movement are possible, and that movement is called nutation and counternutation.

Question 1889. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cervical region with facets at about 45 degrees, the thoracic region with sagittal facets, the lumbar region with coronal facets, or the sacrum with horizontal facets? The answer is the cervical region with facets at about 45 degrees. The thoracic facets lie in the coronal plane and favor rotation, and the lumbar facets lie in the sagittal plane.

Question 1890. Name two structures that pass through an intervertebral foramen, spoken as a list. The answer is the spinal nerve, with its sheath, and the small arteries and veins that accompany it. The foramen also carries a small recurrent branch that returns to the canal. It lies between the pedicles of two adjacent vertebrae.

Question 1891. A constructed illustration: a young athlete has low back pain, and imaging shows a defect in the part of bone between the superior and the inferior articular processes of the fifth lumbar vertebra. Which joint has been affected? The answer is the zygapophyseal joint on that side, whose two processes are separated by the break in the pars interarticularis.

Question 1892. In a forward slip of the fifth lumbar vertebra on the sacrum, which structures give way first: the intervertebral disc and the facet joints, the sacroiliac ligaments, the hip joint, or the iliolumbar ligament? The answer is the intervertebral disc and the facet joints. The disc loses height and the facets open, so the body of the fifth lumbar vertebra slides forward on the first sacral vertebra.

Question 1893. A described lateral radiograph of the lower back shows a step in the posterior border of the vertebral bodies at the junction of the lowest lumbar vertebra and the sacrum. What has happened? The answer is a forward slip of the fifth lumbar vertebra on the sacrum. The posterior borders of the two bones no longer form a smooth line.

Question 1894. A constructed illustration: a person bends to the side, and the facet joints on the side toward which the trunk bends are pressed together while those on the other side are stretched. Which joints are involved, and in which plane does the movement occur? The answer is the zygapophyseal joints, in the coronal plane. Lateral flexion is usually accompanied by a little rotation.

Question 1895. How much of the turning of the head from side to side takes place at the atlantoaxial joints: about one half, about one quarter, almost none, or all of it? The answer is about one half. The rest is shared by the remaining cervical joints, which also contribute to rotation. Fusion of the atlantoaxial joints therefore removes half of the movement.

Question 1896. A constructed illustration: a person in a stationary car is struck from behind, and the head is thrown first backward and then forward. Which ligament is most stretched in the first phase? The answer is the anterior longitudinal ligament, which runs in front of the vertebral bodies and resists extension. The ligaments behind the canal are stretched in the second phase, when the head is thrown forward.

Question 1897. The articular facets of the thoracic vertebrae lie in which plane, and which movement do they favor: the coronal plane, favoring rotation; the sagittal plane, favoring flexion; the transverse plane, favoring extension; or an oblique plane, favoring side bending only? The answer is the coronal plane, favoring rotation, because the facets face backward and forward. The region therefore turns easily but bends forward with difficulty.

Question 1898. True or false: the nucleus pulposus has no blood vessels of its own and is nourished by fluid passing through the vertebral bodies. The answer is true. Only the outer layers of the annulus fibrosus receive small vessels. The central part of the disc depends on diffusion through the end plates, so it heals poorly after injury.

Question 1899. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan shows a small dome-shaped hollow pressed into the upper surface of a vertebral body and filled with disc material. What is this appearance called? The answer is a Schmorl node, in which part of the nucleus pulposus has pushed upward through the end plate into the body. It is common and is often found by chance.

Question 1900. Which change in the intervertebral disc is the ordinary result of aging: the water content of the nucleus pulposus falls, it gains water, the annulus fibrosus becomes elastic, or the disc is replaced by bone in every adult? The answer is that the water content of the nucleus pulposus falls and the disc loses height. The annulus then tears and bony spurs follow.

To summarize, the skull is held together almost entirely by fibrous joints: the serrate sutures of the vault, the squamous suture above the ear, and the plane joints of the face, with the bregma, the lambda, the pterion and the asterion marking where they meet. The fontanelles of the newborn close at different times, and the cartilaginous joints of the skull base, above all the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, let the base grow until puberty. The temporomandibular joint is the only synovial joint of the head, its fibrocartilaginous disc divides it into an upper compartment for gliding and a lower one for rotation, and the head of the mandible dislocates in front of the articular tubercle. The vertebral column is joined by the discs between the bodies, by the facet joints behind, and by ligaments whose names record their work: the anterior longitudinal ligament checks extension, the posterior longitudinal ligament is weakest at the sides, and the ligamentum flavum is elastic. The atlanto-occipital joint nods the head and the atlantoaxial joints turn it, while the cervical facets lie at about 45 degrees, the thoracic in the coronal plane and the lumbar in the sagittal plane. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 20 — Shoulder Complex

The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body and among the least stable, and this chapter works through the joints and the ligaments that trade one property for the other. It opens with eight questions on the vertebral joints, then follows the sternoclavicular joint, the acromioclavicular joint, the glenohumeral joint, the rotator cuff, the labrum and the ligaments of the shoulder. It holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer in the same paragraph as the question and then explains why that answer is right. Nothing has to be held in mind, and nothing depends on a figure or a diagram. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 1901. Which joints of the vertebral column are the plane synovial joints formed between the superior articular process of one vertebra and the inferior articular process of the one above? The answer is the facet joints, also called the zygapophyseal joints. Each has a loose capsule and receives branches of the dorsal ramus of a spinal nerve. Their sloping surfaces guide the direction in which the column is able to move.

Question 1902. Which statement about the facet joints of the cervical region is correct: their surfaces lie in a nearly horizontal plane, they lie in a vertical sagittal plane, they lie in a coronal plane, or they are absent above the second cervical vertebra? The answer is that their surfaces lie in a nearly horizontal plane. That slope allows free flexion, extension and rotation of the neck.

Question 1903. In the thoracic region, the facet joints of adjacent vertebrae face mainly in which plane, and which movement does that arrangement favor? The answer is the coronal plane, which favors rotation and side bending. The joint surfaces look backward and forward, so the chest part of the spine twists more readily than it bends.

Question 1904. Which statement about the lumbar facet joints is correct: they lie mainly in the sagittal plane and check rotation, they lie in the coronal plane and check flexion, they face horizontally and allow free twisting, or they are absent at the lowest level? The answer is that they lie mainly in the sagittal plane and check rotation. The lower back therefore bends forward and back freely but twists very little.

Question 1905. Which two parts make up an intervertebral disc, and which of them lies in the center? The answer is the annulus fibrosus on the outside and the nucleus pulposus in the center. The annulus is a ring of fibrocartilage whose fibers cross in layers, and the nucleus is a soft gel that spreads pressure sideways. No disc lies between the first and the second cervical vertebra.

Question 1906. Which ligament runs down the back of the vertebral bodies inside the vertebral canal, and which movement does it check? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament, which checks flexion. It lies within the canal and is narrower than the ligament that runs down the front of the bodies.

Question 1907. What are the small joints called that form between the raised lateral lip of a lower cervical vertebral body and the body above it, and why do they matter? The answer is the uncovertebral joints, also called the joints of Luschka. They lie at the sides of the bodies from the third to the seventh cervical vertebra.

Question 1908. Which joint provides most of the rotation of the head: the atlanto-occipital joint, a pivot joint between the first and second cervical vertebrae, the joint between the second and third cervical vertebrae, or a plane joint at the base of the skull? The answer is a pivot joint between the first and the second cervical vertebrae. The dens of the second turns inside a ring on the first.

Question 1909. Which joint is the only true bony connection between the upper limb and the axial skeleton? The answer is the sternoclavicular joint. It lies between the medial end of the clavicle and the manubrium of the sternum, with the first costal cartilage taking part. Every other link between the arm and the trunk is muscular or fascial.

Question 1910. Which kind of synovial joint is the sternoclavicular joint: a hinge joint, a saddle joint, a pivot joint, or a plane joint? The answer is a saddle joint, though it behaves like a ball and socket. Its two curved surfaces sit at right angles to each other, and a disc divides the cavity in two. That disc is what allows movement in so many directions.

Question 1911. A described specimen cut across the sternoclavicular joint shows two separate cavities with a fibrous plate between them, dividing the joint from side to side. Which structure is the plate, and what does it do? The answer is the articular disc, which divides the joint and checks inward movement of the clavicle. A blow on the outer shoulder drives the clavicle inward against it.

Question 1912. A described dissection at the base of the neck shows a short strong band running from the first rib and its cartilage upward and outward to the underside of the clavicle, with a small bursa splitting it into two parts. Which ligament is shown? The answer is the costoclavicular ligament, the strongest ligament of the sternoclavicular joint. It checks elevation of the shoulder.

Question 1913. Which statement about the movements of the sternoclavicular joint is correct: the clavicle can be raised, lowered, thrust forward, pulled back and rotated, it can only be raised and lowered, it becomes fixed after birth, or it allows no rotation at all? The answer is that the clavicle can be raised, lowered, thrust forward, pulled back and rotated. It turns about its own long axis as the arm goes overhead.

Question 1914. A constructed illustration: after a fall onto the point of the shoulder, a person has difficulty in swallowing and the arm feels heavy and swollen. Which injury explains the picture? The answer is a backward dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint, in which the medial end of the clavicle presses on the trachea, the esophagus and the great vessels. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1915. A described radiograph of the upper chest shows the medial end of the clavicle sitting above and in front of the manubrium, out of line with the other side. Which joint has moved, and in which direction? The answer is the sternoclavicular joint, with the clavicle displaced forward. Forward displacement is the common one. The medial end normally lies level with the manubrium.

Question 1916. Which ligament crosses the top of the manubrium between the two clavicles: the costoclavicular ligament, the interclavicular ligament, the coracoclavicular ligament, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the interclavicular ligament. It joins the two medial ends of the clavicles over the upper border of the manubrium and blends with both joint capsules. It helps to check downward movement of the shoulder.

Question 1917. Which structures lie immediately behind the sternoclavicular joint and are at risk when the clavicle is driven backward? The answer is the trachea, the esophagus, the great vessels of the neck and the brachial plexus. They lie directly behind the joint, with only a thin layer between them and the bone. That is why a backward dislocation here is treated as an emergency.

Question 1918. Which nerves supply the sternoclavicular joint: the suprascapular and axillary nerves, the medial supraclavicular nerve with the nerve to the subclavius, the long thoracic nerve alone, or the radial nerve? The answer is the medial supraclavicular nerve with the nerve to the subclavius. The first comes from the cervical plexus and the second from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. Every shoulder joint takes fibers from more than one source.

Question 1919. True or false: the medial end of the clavicle is the first part of the bone to ossify. The answer is false. The shaft ossifies first and the medial end last, and its growth plate does not close until the middle of the third decade of life.

Question 1920. Which of these pairs belongs together: the costoclavicular ligament with the first rib, the coracoclavicular ligament with the first rib, the transverse humeral ligament with the acromion, or the coracoacromial ligament with the clavicle? The answer is the costoclavicular ligament with the first rib. It passes from that rib and its cartilage to the underside of the clavicle. The coracoclavicular ligament runs down to the coracoid process instead.

Question 1921. Which joint lies between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial border of the acromion? The answer is the acromioclavicular joint. It is a small plane synovial joint at the top of the shoulder.

Question 1922. Which kind of joint is the acromioclavicular joint: a plane synovial joint, a hinge joint, a saddle joint, or a ball and socket joint? The answer is a plane synovial joint. Its flat surfaces glide on one another as the scapula turns.

Question 1923. Which ligament holds the lateral end of the clavicle down to the coracoid process, and which two parts does it have? The answer is the coracoclavicular ligament, made up of the conoid part and the trapezoid part. The conoid lies more medial and the trapezoid more lateral.

Question 1924. True or false: the superior part of the acromioclavicular ligament is weaker than the inferior part. The answer is false. The superior part is the stronger of the two and blends with the fibers of the trapezius muscle.

Question 1925. A constructed illustration: a person falls from a bicycle onto the point of the shoulder, and a tender step can be felt where the outer end of the clavicle meets the shoulder blade. Which joint is injured? The answer is the acromioclavicular joint. When the coracoclavicular ligament is torn as well, the clavicle rides higher than the acromion. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1926. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows the outer end of the clavicle projecting above the acromion, with the gap between the coracoid process and the clavicle wider than on the other side. Which structure has failed? The answer is the coracoclavicular ligament. Its conoid and trapezoid parts hold the clavicle down against the weight of the arm.

Question 1927. Which movements take place at the acromioclavicular joint: gliding with a little rotation, pure flexion and extension, abduction and adduction alone, or no movement at all? The answer is gliding with a little rotation. The scapula slides and turns on the outer end of the clavicle as the arm is raised. The movement is small, but without it the shoulder blade could not rotate.

Question 1928. Which ligament runs from the coracoid process to the acromion and forms an arch above the head of the humerus? The answer is the coracoacromial ligament. With the acromion and the coracoid process it completes the acromial arch.

Question 1929. A described section through the shoulder shows a flat fibrous band running above the head of the humerus from one bony point to another, with a bursa and a tendon lying beneath it. Which structures are described? The answer is the coracoacromial ligament above, with the subacromial bursa and the tendon of the supraspinatus below. The arch protects the tendon.

Question 1930. Which nerves supply the acromioclavicular joint? The answer is the suprascapular nerve, with a contribution from the lateral pectoral nerve. Fibers reach the joint from behind and from the front.

Question 1931. The clavicle is described as turning about its own long axis as the arm is raised overhead. In which plane does that movement take place, and about which axis? The answer is the transverse plane, about the long axis of the bone. The bone turns so that its curve follows the scapula as the shoulder blade rotates. The sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints share the movement between them.

Question 1932. Which statement about the two parts of the coracoclavicular ligament is correct: the conoid lies medial to the trapezoid, the trapezoid lies medial to the conoid, both lie in front of the clavicle, or both are attached to the acromion? The answer is that the conoid lies medial to the trapezoid. The conoid is the more vertical band and the trapezoid the flatter one. Both run from the coracoid process to the clavicle.

Question 1933. Which joint is the ball and socket joint of the shoulder, formed between the head of the humerus and the shallow cavity of the scapula? The answer is the glenohumeral joint. The head is about one third of a sphere and far larger than the socket that receives it. That mismatch is what gives the shoulder its great range of movement.

Question 1934. Which of these is the socket of the shoulder joint: the acromion, the glenoid cavity, the coracoid process, or the greater tubercle? The answer is the glenoid cavity, a shallow pear-shaped depression on the lateral border of the scapula. It is deepened only a little by a ring of fibrocartilage.

Question 1935. The shoulder joint is described as having more movement than any other joint in the body. Which feature of the glenoid cavity explains this? The answer is that the cavity is shallow and small compared with the head of the humerus, so the head can swing widely before bone checks it. The labrum, the capsule and the cuff make up the difference in soft tissue.

Question 1936. Which tendon lies within the cavity of the shoulder joint and passes over the top of the head of the humerus? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii. It begins at the supraglenoid tubercle and leaves through the groove between the tubercles. It lies inside the capsule but outside the synovial lining.

Question 1937.
