Which factors together keep the head of the humerus in its socket: the depth of the socket by itself, the rotator cuff with the labrum, the capsule and the pressure inside the joint, the ligaments by themselves, or the deltoid muscle by itself? The answer is the rotator cuff with the labrum, the capsule and the pressure inside the joint. No single one of them is enough on its own.

Question 1938. Which structure lies between the acromion and the tendon of the supraspinatus, and with which cavity does it often communicate: the subscapular bursa, the subacromial bursa, the subcoracoid bursa, or the axillary pouch? The answer is the subacromial bursa, which often communicates with the cavity of the shoulder joint. It also lies beneath the coracoacromial ligament.

Question 1939. A constructed illustration: after a fall the arm is held a little away from the side and turned outward, and the normal rounded contour of the shoulder has gone. Which injury is described? The answer is a forward dislocation of the shoulder joint, in which the head of the humerus lies in front of and below the glenoid. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1940. A constructed illustration: after a shoulder dislocation, the outer part of the shoulder cannot be lifted and the skin over it has lost sensation. Which nerve is involved, and where does it run? The answer is the axillary nerve, which winds around the surgical neck of the humerus through the quadrangular space. A fracture of that same neck can injure the nerve.

Question 1941. A described radiograph taken from the front shows the head of the humerus lying below and medial to the glenoid, with the shaft turned outward. Which joint is dislocated, and in which direction has the head moved? The answer is the glenohumeral joint, with the head displaced forward and downward, which is the common direction. The arm is usually held away from the side.

Question 1942. In which position is the shoulder joint most tightly packed: full abduction with lateral rotation, full adduction, the arm hanging at the side, or full medial rotation with the arm across the chest? The answer is full abduction with lateral rotation. There the capsule and the ligaments are wound tightly around the head. The arm hanging at the side is the loosest position of all.

Question 1943. Which muscles lie immediately behind the glenohumeral joint and form its posterior wall? The answer is the infraspinatus and the teres minor, with the long head of the triceps below them. They cover the back of the capsule.

Question 1944. Which arteries form the ring of supply around the surgical neck of the humerus and the tissues of the joint: the suprascapular artery alone, the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries with the suprascapular artery, the radial artery alone, or the deep artery of the arm? The answer is the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries with the suprascapular artery. They meet around the surgical neck and keep the head supplied.

Question 1945. Which movement of the shoulder joint carries the arm forward and upward in the sagittal plane? The answer is flexion. Extension carries the arm backward in that same plane.

Question 1946. Which muscle begins abduction of the arm during the first part of the movement: the deltoid, the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, or the teres major? The answer is the supraspinatus. It pulls the head of the humerus into the socket and sets the arm on its way. The deltoid then carries the greater part of the movement.

Question 1947. Which tubercle of the humerus lies immediately lateral to the groove that carries the long head of the biceps tendon, and which muscles are attached to it? The answer is the greater tubercle, to which the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor are attached. The lesser tubercle lies medial to the groove and receives the subscapularis.

Question 1948. A constructed illustration: a person cannot raise the arm above the head, and the shoulder blade begins to move early and travels much further than usual as the arm is lifted. Which mechanism is disturbed? The answer is the scapulohumeral rhythm, in which the scapula and the humerus normally move together in a fixed proportion. When the shoulder joint is stiff, the scapula does more of the work.

Question 1949. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the shoulder shows the head of the humerus riding high beneath the acromion, with the tendon above it thinned and drawn back. What does that appearance mean? The answer is a long-standing tear of the rotator cuff, which has allowed the head to rise. The space between the head and the acromion is narrowed.

Question 1950. Name two movements of the scapula that help the arm to reach above the head, spoken as a list. The answer is upward rotation and elevation. Upward rotation turns the glenoid upward so that the humerus can follow it, and elevation lifts the whole shoulder blade.

Question 1951. Which statement about the capsule of the shoulder joint is correct: it is lax and redundant below, it is tight in every position, it is attached to the surgical neck, or it has no synovial lining? The answer is that it is lax and redundant below. The lower part hangs in folds at the side as the axillary pouch. Above it is attached to the glenoid margin, below to the anatomical neck.

Question 1952. True or false: the shoulder joint is less stable than the hip joint because its socket is shallow. The answer is true. The glenoid cavity is far smaller than the head that sits in it, while the acetabulum wraps around most of the femoral head.

Question 1953. Which four muscles make up the rotator cuff, and what do their tendons have in common? The answer is the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor and the subscapularis. Their tendons blend with the capsule and merge into one sleeve. All four are inserted on the upper end of the humerus.

Question 1954. Which muscle of the rotator cuff lies in the fossa above the spine of the scapula and sends its tendon over the top of the shoulder joint: the infraspinatus, the supraspinatus, the teres minor, or the subscapularis? The answer is the supraspinatus. Its tendon passes beneath the acromion to the top of the greater tubercle. It begins abduction and steadies the head in the socket.

Question 1955. Which rotator cuff muscle lies in the fossa below the spine of the scapula and turns the arm outward: the subscapularis, the infraspinatus, the teres major, or the supraspinatus? The answer is the infraspinatus. It covers the back of the scapula below its spine.

Question 1956. Which rotator cuff muscle is the only one that lies on the front of the scapula, and on which tubercle does it insert? The answer is the subscapularis, which inserts on the lesser tubercle. It fills the hollow of the subscapular fossa and crosses the front of the shoulder joint. It is the most powerful medial rotator of the arm.

Question 1957. Which muscle lies immediately below the infraspinatus on the back of the scapula, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the teres minor, supplied by the axillary nerve. It runs from the lateral border of the scapula to the lowest facet of the greater tubercle. The infraspinatus above it is supplied by the suprascapular nerve instead.

Question 1958. Which nerve supplies both the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus: the axillary nerve, the suprascapular nerve, the upper subscapular nerve, or the radial nerve? The answer is the suprascapular nerve. It passes through the notch above the spine of the scapula and then through the notch beside the spine.

Question 1959. A described view of the shoulder from above shows a tendon running under a bony arch, frayed and thinned at the point where it meets the bone, with the joint surface below it still smooth. Which structure is damaged, and why there? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, damaged in the zone beneath the acromion, where its blood supply is poorest. That zone is also where the tendon rubs as the arm rises.

Question 1960. A constructed illustration: a person has pain when the arm is raised from about 60 to 120 degrees from the side, and the pain eases above that arc. Which structure is most likely involved? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus rubbing beneath the acromion. That painful arc is a described illustration and not a diagnosis. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1961. A described section through the shoulder shows a tendon passing beneath a bony arch, a fluid-filled sac between the two, and a small bony spur projecting from the arch above the tendon. Which structures are described? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, the subacromial bursa and a spur on the acromion. The spur narrows the passage through which the tendon must move.

Question 1962. A described cross section through the upper end of the humerus shows four flat tendons around the bone, merging above with the capsule, one in front and the others behind and above. Which structures form that sleeve? The answer is the tendons of the rotator cuff, the subscapularis on the front and the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor behind. Together they form a sleeve that holds the head in the socket.

Question 1963. Which statement about the rotator cuff is correct: its tendons fuse with the capsule of the shoulder joint, its tendons lie outside the capsule altogether, it has no muscle on the front of the scapula, or its tendons are inserted far down the shaft of the humerus? The answer is that its tendons fuse with the capsule. That blending is why a torn cuff and a painful joint often appear together.

Question 1964. Which of these pairs belongs together: the subscapularis with the lesser tubercle, the supraspinatus with the lesser tubercle, the infraspinatus with the coracoid process, or the teres minor with the spine of the scapula? The answer is the subscapularis with the lesser tubercle. The three muscles on the back of the scapula all reach the greater tubercle instead.

Question 1965. A constructed illustration: a heavy pack strap presses for hours into the hollow above the spine of the scapula, and afterward the arm cannot be turned outward and the muscle in that hollow feels wasted. Which nerve has been pressed upon? The answer is the suprascapular nerve, compressed at the notch above the spine of the scapula. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 1966. Which of these muscles turns the arm inward and lies on the back of the scapula: the teres major, the teres minor, the infraspinatus, or the deltoid? The answer is the teres major, which is not part of the rotator cuff. It runs from the lower angle of the scapula to the crest below the lesser tubercle. The teres minor beside it turns the arm the other way.

Question 1967. A tendon is described as lying inside the capsule of the shoulder joint but outside its synovial lining. What does that mean about where it lies? The answer is that it runs within the fibrous capsule while the synovial membrane wraps around it like a sleeve. It therefore glides in a tunnel of its own.

Question 1968. Which of these pairs belongs together: the teres minor with the lowest facet of the greater tubercle, the supraspinatus with the lowest facet, the subscapularis with the greater tubercle, or the infraspinatus with the lesser tubercle? The answer is the teres minor with the lowest facet of the greater tubercle. The supraspinatus takes the top facet and the infraspinatus the middle one.

Question 1969. Name the three muscles that are attached to the greater tubercle of the humerus, spoken as a list. The answer is the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor. They occupy the top, the middle and the lowest facets of the tubercle in that order.

Question 1970. True or false: when the rotator cuff is torn through, the head of the humerus tends to ride upward under the acromion. The answer is true. The cuff pulls the head into the socket, while the deltoid tends to lift it.

Question 1971. Which ring of fibrocartilage is attached around the rim of the glenoid cavity, and what is its shape in section? The answer is the glenoid labrum, which is triangular in section with its broad base on the bone. It follows the rim of the socket and blends with the capsule above.

Question 1972. Which structure blends with the glenoid labrum at the top of the socket and then runs away through the joint: the long head of the triceps, the long head of the biceps, the coracohumeral ligament, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the long head of the biceps. It arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and from the labrum beside it. The long head of the triceps arises below the socket.

Question 1973. A described view from inside the shoulder joint shows a triangular rim of tissue lifted away from the front and lower part of the glenoid, with the head of the humerus beside it. Which structure is detached? The answer is the glenoid labrum, torn at its front and lower part. That is the injury found after the head dislocates forward.

Question 1974. What name is given to the detachment of the front and lower part of the glenoid labrum that follows a forward dislocation of the shoulder? The answer is the Bankart lesion. The labrum is torn from the rim of the glenoid and the socket loses the depth it needs.

Question 1975. Which of these best describes the work of the glenoid labrum: it deepens the socket and gives the capsule and the ligaments a hold, it makes synovial fluid, it forms the head of the humerus, or it moves the scapula on the chest wall? The answer is that it deepens the socket and gives the capsule and the ligaments a hold. It increases the area over which the head and the socket touch.

Question 1976. Where does the glenoid labrum lie in relation to the capsule of the shoulder joint? The answer is between the joint cavity and the capsule, since the capsule and the synovial membrane both take hold at the rim. The fibrous capsule is attached along the outer edge of the labrum.

Question 1977. A described dissection of the shoulder from the front shows a tendon taking origin from a small bony point above the glenoid cavity, where its fibers blend with a ring of fibrocartilage. Which tendon is it, and which bony point gives it origin? The answer is the long head of the biceps, arising from the supraglenoid tubercle and from the labrum. That bony point lies just above the rim of the socket.

Question 1978. A constructed illustration: a person who has dislocated the shoulder several times feels the joint begin to slip whenever the arm is turned outward with the elbow at the side. Which structure has most likely failed? The answer is the front and lower part of the labrum together with the ligament beside it. Repeated dislocation stretches both until they no longer hold the head.

Question 1979. The glenoid labrum is described as having a poor blood supply, especially along its inner free edge. Which statement follows from that: a tear of it heals badly, a tear heals quickly, it makes the synovial fluid, or it carries the main supply to the head of the humerus? The answer is that a tear of it heals badly. Only the outer part, close to the bone, receives a useful supply.

Question 1980. Which part of the glenoid labrum lies nearest the origin of the long head of the biceps tendon, and which part is torn when the head of the humerus dislocates forward? The answer is that the upper part lies nearest the tendon's origin, while the front and lower part is torn in dislocation. Both are parts of the same ring.

Question 1981. A described MRI scan of the shoulder shows the upper part of the labrum separated from the rim of the glenoid, with fluid tracking into the gap, while the lower part of the rim looks intact. Which injury is described? The answer is a tear of the upper labrum at the point where the biceps tendon begins. The fluid outlines the split.

Question 1982. Name the ring of fibrocartilage that deepens the socket of the shoulder joint, and name the tendon that blends with its upper edge. The answer is the glenoid labrum, blending with the tendon of the long head of the biceps. The two are continuous where the tendon leaves the socket. A pull on one is felt by the other.

Question 1983. Which three thickenings of the fibrous capsule of the shoulder joint are named from their position? The answer is the upper, the middle and the lower glenohumeral ligaments. They are seen best from inside the joint, where no muscle covers the capsule. The lowest of the three is the strongest.

Question 1984. Which of the glenohumeral ligaments is the chief check against a forward dislocation when the arm is raised and turned outward: the upper one, the middle one, the lower one, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the lower glenohumeral ligament. In that position it lies in front of the head and stops it from sliding forward.

Question 1985. Which ligament runs from the coracoid process to the humerus and bridges the gap between the supraspinatus and the subscapularis? The answer is the coracohumeral ligament. It passes over the front and top of the capsule to reach the greater and the lesser tubercles.

Question 1986. Which ligament bridges the groove on the front of the humerus and holds the tendon that runs in that groove? The answer is the transverse humeral ligament. It spans the gap between the greater tubercle and the lesser tubercle. Beneath it runs the tendon of the long head of the biceps.

Question 1987. Which ligament of the shoulder region is not part of the capsule of the joint, yet forms an arch over the head of the humerus from the coracoid process to the acromion? The answer is the coracoacromial ligament. It protects the cuff beneath it and limits how far the head can rise. It takes no part in holding the acromioclavicular joint together.

Question 1988. Which ligament connects the coracoid process to the clavicle: the costoclavicular ligament, the coracoclavicular ligament, the coracoacromial ligament, or the acromioclavicular ligament? The answer is the coracoclavicular ligament. Its two parts, the conoid and the trapezoid, hold the outer end of the clavicle down. The coracoacromial ligament runs to the acromion instead.

Question 1989. A constructed illustration: with the arm hanging at the side and the elbow bent, the head of the humerus can be drawn downward much further than it should be, while the arm can still be raised. Which structures have failed? The answer is the coracohumeral ligament with the upper glenohumeral ligament. They hold the head up when the arm hangs at the side.

Question 1990. A described view from inside the shoulder joint shows three bands running down the front of the capsule, the lowest of them the thickest. Which structures are shown? The answer is the upper, the middle and the lower glenohumeral ligaments, of which the lowest is the strongest. They lie within the fibrous capsule itself.

Question 1991. Which ligament resists elevation of the shoulder and is the strongest ligament of the sternoclavicular joint: the interclavicular ligament, the costoclavicular ligament, the coracoclavicular ligament, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the costoclavicular ligament. It runs from the first rib and its cartilage up to the underside of the clavicle.

Question 1992. Which ligament lies immediately above the capsule of the shoulder joint, runs from the coracoid process to the two tubercles, and blends with the cuff? The answer is the coracohumeral ligament. It roofs the gap between the supraspinatus and the subscapularis.

Question 1993. Which ligament is the chief support of the outer end of the clavicle, and where does each of its parts lie relative to the other? The answer is the coracoclavicular ligament, whose conoid part lies medial to its trapezoid part. Both run from the coracoid process below to the clavicle above.

Question 1994. Which of these pairs belongs together: the transverse humeral ligament with the intertubercular groove, the coracoacromial ligament with the first rib, the costoclavicular ligament with the acromion, or the conoid ligament with the lesser tubercle? The answer is the transverse humeral ligament with the intertubercular groove. It roofs the groove and keeps the tendon of the long head of the biceps in place.

Question 1995. Which statement about the attachment of the capsule of the shoulder joint is correct: it is attached to the anatomical neck of the humerus, to the surgical neck, to the shaft, or to the glenoid rim only? The answer is that it is attached to the anatomical neck. The surgical neck lies outside the joint, so a fracture there does not open the cavity.

Question 1996. Which of these pairs belongs together: the costoclavicular ligament with the inner end of the clavicle, the coracoclavicular ligament with the first rib, the transverse humeral ligament with the glenoid rim, or the coracoacromial ligament with the lesser tubercle? The answer is the costoclavicular ligament with the inner end of the clavicle. It ties that end to the first rib, while the coracoclavicular ligament ties the outer end down.

Question 1997. A constructed illustration: a fall onto the outstretched hand drives the head of the humerus upward against the arch above it, and the person feels pain at the top of the shoulder. Which ligament receives the force, and which tendon beneath it is at risk? The answer is the coracoacromial ligament, with the tendon of the supraspinatus beneath it. The arch stops the head from rising further.

Question 1998. True or false: the glenohumeral ligaments are separate cords lying outside the fibrous capsule of the shoulder joint. The answer is false. They are thickenings of the capsule itself and are seen best from within the joint. Because muscle covers most of the capsule, these bands show only where no muscle lies.

Question 1999. A described dissection of the shoulder from the front, after the deltoid has been removed, shows a flat band running from the coracoid process across to the top of the humerus, lying over the gap between two cuff tendons. Which structure is described? The answer is the coracohumeral ligament, which roofs the front of the capsule and closes that gap. It also resists downward movement of the head when the arm hangs.

Question 2000. Which structure finally checks the head of the humerus when the arm is fully raised to the side: the coracohumeral ligament, the lower glenohumeral ligament, the acromion with the coracoacromial arch, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the acromion with the coracoacromial arch. The bony arch above the head is the last limit of pure elevation.

To summarize, the vertebral column moves differently at every level because its facet joints face in different planes, nearly horizontal in the neck, coronal in the chest and sagittal in the lower back, and the posterior longitudinal ligament inside the canal checks flexion. The sternoclavicular joint is the only bony link between the arm and the trunk, it holds an articular disc, and the costoclavicular ligament is its strongest check against elevation. The acromioclavicular joint is a plane joint held down chiefly by the coracoclavicular ligament, whose conoid part lies medial to its trapezoid part, and the coracoacromial ligament arches over the head of the humerus. The shoulder joint is a shallow ball and socket whose head is much larger than the glenoid, steadied by the labrum, by the capsule with its upper, middle and lower glenohumeral ligaments, and by the four tendons of the rotator cuff. The supraspinatus begins abduction and is the part most often torn beneath the acromion, the subscapularis medially rotates from the lesser tubercle, and the infraspinatus with the teres minor laterally rotates from the greater tubercle. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 21 — Elbow and Forearm

This chapter follows the upper limb from the shoulder to the fingertips, beginning with the ligaments that steady the shoulder. It works through the bony points of the elbow, its capsule and ligaments, the two bones of the forearm, the muscles that move it, and the nerves that cross the joint. It then turns to the wrist and the hand, whose small bones and long tendons do the fine work of the limb. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer straight after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2001. Which ligament passes from the coracoid process to the acromion and forms a bridge above the shoulder joint? The answer is the coracoacromial ligament. It arches over the head of the humerus. The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath it, and the arch keeps the head of the humerus from riding upward.

Question 2002. Which bone of the arm carries a spool-shaped surface that grips the ulna and a rounded head that meets the radius? The answer is the humerus. Its trochlea fits the trochlear notch of the ulna, and the capitulum takes the head of the radius. The olecranon fossa behind them takes the tip of the olecranon in extension.

Question 2003. Which of these bony points is the large bump felt on the inner side of the elbow: the capitulum, the medial epicondyle, the radial head, or the olecranon? The answer is the medial epicondyle. The common flexor tendon is attached to it, and the ulnar nerve lies in a groove behind it.

Question 2004. Which structure lies immediately posterior to the medial epicondyle and passes into the forearm beneath the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris? The answer is the ulnar nerve. A knock on it sends a tingling shock down the little finger. It lies close to the bone, covered only by skin and fascia.

Question 2005. A described radiograph of a young child's elbow shows a small bony center beside the lower humerus. Which center does it represent? The answer is the center for the capitulum, the first center of the lower humerus to appear. It fuses with the shaft years later, so the gap between them is normal and easily mistaken for a fracture.

Question 2006. Which bone lies on the little finger side of the forearm and ends above in the point of the elbow? The answer is the ulna. Its upper end carries the olecranon behind and the coronoid process in front, with the trochlear notch between them. The radius lies beside it on the thumb side.

Question 2007. Which of these structures forms the ring in which the head of the radius turns when the palm is turned up and down: the annular ligament, the olecranon, the coronoid process, or the radial tuberosity? The answer is the annular ligament. It encircles the head of the radius and holds it against the radial notch of the ulna.

Question 2008. True or false: the elbow is a simple hinge joint that permits movement in one plane only. The answer is false, though the statement is nearly right. The humerus and the ulna form a hinge, but the head of the radius turns in the annular ligament at the same level. That turn produces pronation and supination of the hand.

Question 2009. A constructed illustration: a small child is lifted by one hand and afterwards keeps the arm still and slightly bent. Which structure has slipped? The answer is the annular ligament, which has slipped over the head of the radius. The ligament is lax and the radial head is small in a young child. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2010. Name the two bones that meet the humerus at the elbow, spoken as a list. The answer is the radius and the ulna. The ulna lies on the little finger side and its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus. The radius lies on the thumb side and its head meets the rounded capitulum.

Question 2011. Which of these movements is produced by the muscles that cross the front of the elbow: supination, flexion, abduction, or rotation? The answer is flexion. They bend the forearm toward the arm, and the muscles behind the arm straighten it again. Supination belongs to the forearm and abduction to the shoulder.

Question 2012. Which disc-shaped structure sits at the top of the radius and turns against the capitulum above and the ulna beside it? The answer is the head of the radius. Its upper surface is hollowed to meet the rounded capitulum, and its rim is held in the ring formed by the annular ligament and the radial notch.

Question 2013. A described radiograph from the side shows the bent elbow, with a broad bony point in a hollow at the back of the lower humerus. Which structure is that point, and in which hollow does it lie? The answer is the olecranon, lying in the olecranon fossa. When the elbow straightens the point leaves the hollow, so the back of the elbow is flat.

Question 2014. Which nerve winds around the neck of the radius inside the supinator, where a fracture can injure it? The answer is the deep branch of the radial nerve, which becomes the posterior interosseous nerve. It supplies the extensor muscles of the fingers and the thumb, so their weakness is the sign of injury.

Question 2015. Which of these muscles is the strongest bender of the elbow, lying deep to the biceps: the brachialis, the brachioradialis, the triceps, or the anconeus? The answer is the brachialis. It reaches the ulna, so it bends the elbow in any position of the forearm. The brachioradialis bends the elbow best when the forearm is half turned.

Question 2016. Which muscle forms the rounded mass on the front of the arm and ends in a tendon that reaches the radial tuberosity? The answer is the biceps brachii. It arises by two heads, one from the scapula above the socket and one from the coracoid process. Its tendon also sends the bicipital aponeurosis into the deep fascia of the forearm.

Question 2017. A constructed illustration: a person who grips and twists with the forearm straight develops pain over the outer side of the elbow. Which tendon is strained? The answer is the common extensor tendon, attached to the lateral epicondyle. The illustration shows a pattern of overuse, not a real patient. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2018. Which of these statements about the carrying angle is correct: it is measured with the elbow straight, it is the same in men and women, it vanishes when the elbow bends, or it is produced by the triceps? The answer is that it is measured with the elbow straight, as the angle between the arm and the forearm. A slight angle is therefore normal.

Question 2019. A described cross section of the upper forearm shows two bones joined by a thin fibrous sheet. Which bone lies lateral, and which way do the fibers of the sheet run? The answer is that the radius lies lateral, and the fibers run downward and medially to the ulna. Force that travels up the radius from the hand crosses the sheet to the ulna.

Question 2020. Which of these pairs belongs together: the olecranon with the ulna, the capitulum with the ulna, the radial head with the humerus, or the coronoid process with the radius? The answer is the olecranon with the ulna, the point of the elbow that the triceps pulls on. The coronoid process is part of the ulna, the capitulum of the humerus, and the radial head of the radius.

Question 2021. Which projection of the ulna slides into the coronoid fossa of the humerus when the elbow bends? The answer is the coronoid process. It lies in front of the ulna, just below the trochlear notch. When the elbow bends fully, the process fills the small hollow above the trochlea.

Question 2022. Which of these structures forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa: the brachioradialis, the pronator teres, the biceps tendon, or the supinator? The answer is the pronator teres. The brachioradialis forms the lateral boundary and the line between the two epicondyles the upper boundary. The floor is the brachialis and the supinator.

Question 2023. Which structure lies immediately medial to the brachial artery in the middle of the cubital fossa? The answer is the median nerve. The biceps tendon lies lateral to the artery, so the three form a row from the thumb side outward. The bicipital aponeurosis covers the artery and the nerve as it crosses them.

Question 2024. A described section across the front of the elbow shows the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve in a row. In which plane was the section cut, and in what order do the three lie? The answer is a transverse plane, with the tendon first, the artery second and the nerve third. A section along the arm would show the joint in profile.

Question 2025. A described radiograph of a child's elbow shows a small bony fleck in front of the lower humerus. Which normal center does it represent, and why must it not be read as a fracture? The answer is the center for the capitulum, which appears in the first year. The gap between it and the shaft is normal until the two fuse.

Question 2026. Which muscle forms the mass at the back of the arm, arises by three heads and inserts into the olecranon? The answer is the triceps brachii. Its long head arises from the scapula below the socket and its other two heads from the back of the humerus. It is the chief extensor of the elbow and its tendon also steadies the joint.

Question 2027. Which of these muscles pulls the radius across the ulna so that the palm turns downward: the supinator, the pronator teres, the brachioradialis, or the anconeus? The answer is the pronator teres. It runs from the medial epicondyle and the coronoid process to the outer radius. The supinator turns the palm upward and the anconeus helps to extend the elbow.

Question 2028. A constructed illustration: a person who leans on the point of the elbow develops a soft swelling over the bone. Which structure is inflamed? The answer is the olecranon bursa, which lies between the skin and the olecranon. The illustration shows a common pattern, not a real patient. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2029. True or false: the biceps brachii is the strongest bender of the elbow. The answer is false. The biceps is a powerful bender and the strongest muscle that turns the palm upward, but the brachialis beneath it is the chief bender, and it works whatever the position of the forearm.

Question 2030. Name the three structures that lie in a row in the cubital fossa, spoken as a list from the thumb side to the little finger side. The answer is the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve. The tendon lies nearest the thumb and the nerve nearest the little finger, and the bicipital aponeurosis crosses over both.

Question 2031. Which of these structures passes between the two heads of the pronator teres: the ulnar nerve, the median nerve, the radial nerve, or the basilic vein? The answer is the median nerve. The ulnar nerve enters the forearm behind the medial epicondyle instead. The radial nerve divides above the elbow and its deep branch passes through the supinator.

Question 2032. A described dissection of the front of the elbow shows a flat fibrous band spreading from the biceps tendon into the deep fascia. Which structure is shown, and what does it cover? The answer is the bicipital aponeurosis, which forms part of the roof of the cubital fossa. It covers the brachial artery and the median nerve beneath it.

Question 2033. Which artery descends on the thumb side of the forearm and can be felt beating at the wrist? The answer is the radial artery. It begins at the elbow as the smaller of the two terminal branches of the brachial artery. It lies under the brachioradialis in the upper forearm and becomes superficial above the wrist.

Question 2034. Which structure lies between the brachialis on its medial side and the brachioradialis on its lateral side, and divides there into two branches? The answer is the radial nerve. Its superficial branch carries sensation from the back of the hand, and its deep branch supplies the extensor muscles through the supinator.

Question 2035. Which statement about the interosseous membrane is correct: its fibers run upward from the radius, it prevents movement between the bones, it carries force from the radius to the ulna, or it forms part of the elbow capsule? The answer is that it carries force from the radius to the ulna. Its fibers run downward and medially, so force on the hand crosses to the ulna.

Question 2036. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a child cannot bend the last joint of the thumb or index finger. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It supplies the long flexor of the thumb and the deep flexor fibers of the index and middle fingers. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2037. A described radiograph shows a break across the upper ulna with the head of the radius in front of the capitulum. Which pattern is described here? The answer is a break of the ulna with dislocation of the head of the radius. The annular ligament tears as the shaft bends and the head slips out. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2038. Which border of the ulna lies directly beneath the skin along the back of the forearm? The answer is the posterior border. It can be traced with a finger from the olecranon down to the wrist. The other borders lie hidden among the flexor and extensor muscles.

Question 2039. Which of these statements about the extensor muscles of the forearm is correct: all of them are supplied by the radial nerve, all by the median nerve, all by the musculocutaneous nerve, or all by the ulnar nerve? The answer is that all are supplied by the radial nerve. Most of them receive the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes through the supinator.

Question 2040. Which of these pairs belongs together: the brachialis with bending of the elbow, the triceps with turning the palm upward, the brachioradialis with straightening of the elbow, or the anconeus with turning the palm downward? The answer is the brachialis with bending of the elbow. The triceps and the anconeus straighten the elbow, and the brachioradialis bends it with the forearm half turned.

Question 2041. Which muscle runs along the outer side of the upper forearm and stands out when the elbow is bent against resistance? The answer is the brachioradialis. It arises from the lower part of the lateral ridge above the lateral epicondyle. It bends the elbow most strongly when the forearm is halfway between turning the palm up and down.

Question 2042. Which branch of the ulnar artery turns upward in front of the medial epicondyle to join the network of vessels around the elbow? The answer is the anterior ulnar recurrent artery. It climbs in front of the medial epicondyle to meet branches from above. That network keeps the lower arm supplied when the elbow is bent.

Question 2043. Which muscle arises from the common tendon on the medial epicondyle: the extensor carpi radialis brevis, the flexor carpi ulnaris, the supinator, or the brachioradialis? The answer is the flexor carpi ulnaris. The other three lie on the outer side of the elbow or the back of the forearm. The common flexor tendon gives rise to the muscles that bend the wrist and the fingers.

Question 2044. A described drawing of the back of the forearm shows muscles whose tendons pass under a fibrous band at the wrist. From which common attachment do they arise, and what do they do? The answer is the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle. They straighten the wrist and the fingers and pull the hand backward under the extensor retinaculum.

Question 2045. Which muscle wraps around the upper part of the radius and turns the palm upward? The answer is the supinator. It arises from the lateral epicondyle and from the ulna and wraps around the upper third of the radius. Its fibers run in the direction that unwinds the radius and so turns the palm to face forward.

Question 2046. Which of these structures forms the floor of the cubital fossa: the brachialis, the pronator teres, the biceps tendon, or the brachioradialis? The answer is the brachialis, helped below by the supinator. The brachioradialis and the pronator teres form the two sides of the triangle. The biceps tendon lies within the fossa and not in its floor.

Question 2047. Which of these descriptions of the radial nerve is correct: it runs in front of the humerus with the brachial artery, it runs against the back of the humerus, it passes behind the medial epicondyle, or it supplies the forearm flexors? The answer is that it runs against the back of the humerus, in the spiral groove, where a break can injure it.

Question 2048. True or false: the median nerve supplies every muscle on the front of the forearm except two. The answer is true, with one qualification. The flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of the deep flexor of the fingers are supplied by the ulnar nerve. Every other muscle there is supplied by the median nerve.

Question 2049. Which slender muscle of the front of the forearm has a long tendon that is absent in about one person in seven? The answer is the palmaris longus. Its tendon crosses the wrist in front of the flexor retinaculum and spreads into the palmar aponeurosis. Because it can be spared, surgeons use its tendon for grafts.

Question 2050. A described specimen shows a muscle arising from the medial epicondyle whose tendon splits into two slips before it reaches each finger. Which muscle is shown, and where does it attach? The answer is the flexor digitorum superficialis. Its slips straddle the deeper tendon and attach to the middle phalanx, so the deeper muscle can bend the last joint.

Question 2051. Which of these muscles arises from the common extensor tendon and helps to straighten and steady the wrist: the flexor carpi ulnaris, the extensor carpi radialis brevis, the pronator teres, or the flexor digitorum superficialis? The answer is the extensor carpi radialis brevis. The other three lie on the front of the forearm or arise from the medial epicondyle.

Question 2052. During turning of the palm, around which bone does the radius move, and through which two points does the axis pass? The answer is that the radius turns around the ulna, and the axis passes through the head of the radius above and the triangular disc below. So the upper end of the radius spins in its ring while the lower end swings around.

Question 2053. Which muscle arises from the lateral epicondyle and the back of the ulna and reaches the base of the fifth metacarpal bone? The answer is the extensor carpi ulnaris. It straightens the wrist and pulls the hand toward the little finger side, and with the flexor carpi ulnaris it is a chief mover in that direction.

Question 2054. A constructed illustration: after a deep cut on the inner elbow, a person cannot grip with the little and ring fingers or pinch the thumb and index finger together. Which nerve is divided? The answer is the ulnar nerve, which supplies the small muscles between the metacarpals and those of the little finger side. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2055. A described movement straightens the elbow against resistance and the tendon at the point of the elbow becomes taut. Which of these muscles is acting: the triceps brachii, the brachialis, the anconeus, or the biceps brachii? The answer is the triceps brachii, supplied by the radial nerve. It reaches the olecranon in the back of the arm and is the chief extensor of the elbow.

Question 2056. A described dissection of the inner side of the elbow shows a fan-shaped tendon attached to a bony point. Which bony point is shown, and which muscles arise there? The answer is the medial epicondyle and the flexor group that bends the wrist and fingers. The flexor carpi radialis, the palmaris longus, the flexor carpi ulnaris and the superficial flexor arise from it.

Question 2057. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supinator with the upper radius, the pronator quadratus with the elbow, the biceps brachii with the little finger, or the triceps with the radial tuberosity? The answer is the supinator with the upper radius, around which it wraps. The pronator quadratus lies at the lower ends of the bones, the biceps at the radial tuberosity, the triceps at the olecranon.

Question 2058. Which muscle forms the fleshy mass deep in the front of the forearm and bends the last joints of the fingers? The answer is the flexor digitorum profundus. It arises from the front of the ulna and the interosseous membrane and sends a tendon to the last phalanx of each finger. Its medial half is supplied by the ulnar nerve, the rest by the median nerve.

Question 2059. Which statement about the deep flexor of the fingers is correct: it is supplied entirely by the median nerve, entirely by the ulnar nerve, partly by each, or by the radial nerve? The answer is that it is supplied partly by each. The median nerve supplies the part for the index and middle fingers, the ulnar nerve the part for the ring and little fingers.

Question 2060. A constructed illustration: a break in the shaft of the humerus leaves the hand hanging and the fingers unable to straighten. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the radial nerve, in the spiral groove against the back of the humerus. The extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers lose their supply. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2061. Which structure crosses the front of the lower radius just above the wrist, between the tendons of the brachioradialis and the flexor carpi radialis? The answer is the radial artery. It becomes superficial there and its pulse can be felt against the bone, which is the usual place for taking a pulse at the wrist.

Question 2062. Which of these bones lies on the thumb side of the forearm: the radius, the ulna, the humerus, or the pisiform? The answer is the radius. It is the shorter and thicker of the two forearm bones. The ulna lies on the little finger side and the pisiform is a small bone of the wrist.

Question 2063. Which of these joints is the elbow: the joint between the two forearm bones, the joint between the humerus and the forearm bones, the joint between the forearm and the wrist, or the joint between the carpal rows? The answer is the joint between the humerus and the forearm bones. It is a hinge with the ulna and a pivot with the head of the radius.

Question 2064. Which fibrous arch lies just below the medial epicondyle, arching over the median nerve and the ulnar artery? The answer is the arch of the flexor digitorum superficialis. The median nerve and the ulnar artery pass beneath it as they enter the forearm. It is one of the places where the median nerve can be pressed upon.

Question 2065. A constructed illustration: a person cannot turn the palm upward against resistance and the biceps tendon cannot be felt at the elbow. Which structure is most likely torn? The answer is the tendon of the biceps brachii, torn from the radial tuberosity. With the elbow bent, the biceps is the strongest muscle that turns the palm upward. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2066. Which statement about the anconeus is correct: it lies on the front of the elbow, it helps to straighten the elbow, it turns the palm upward, or it arises from the medial epicondyle? The answer is that it helps to straighten the elbow and steady the joint. It is a small triangular muscle that continues the triceps down the forearm.

Question 2067. A described magnetic resonance image of the elbow shows a small pad of fat lifted forward from the lower humerus. What does that displacement indicate? The answer is fluid in the elbow joint, which has pushed the fat pad out of its usual place. The pad lies between the capsule and the bone and is normally hidden, so its appearance means swelling.

Question 2068. Which structure runs down the medial side of the forearm immediately medial to the ulnar artery? The answer is the ulnar nerve. The artery lies on its lateral side, nearer the thumb. Near the wrist the nerve passes lateral to the pisiform bone, and the artery passes with it. Both enter the hand outside the carpal tunnel.

Question 2069. Which flat muscle lies deepest in the front of the forearm near the wrist, running from the ulna across to the radius? The answer is the pronator quadratus. It pulls the radius across the ulna and so turns the palm downward, and it is the chief muscle of slow, unresisted turning.

Question 2070. Which statement about turning the palm is correct: the supinator acts best with the elbow bent, the biceps with the elbow straight, the pronator quadratus in slow turning, or the pronator teres only with the shoulder raised? The answer is that the pronator quadratus acts in slow turning. The biceps turns the palm upward best with the elbow bent, the supinator with the elbow straight.

Question 2071. Which bone lies in the floor of the hollow at the base of the thumb and is the one most often broken at the wrist? The answer is the scaphoid. The hollow is the anatomical snuffbox, bounded by tendons of the thumb. A break is easily missed because the bone lies hidden and the pain is often slight.

Question 2072. Which of these bones belongs to the row of carpal bones nearest the forearm: the capitate, the scaphoid, the trapezium, or the hamate? The answer is the scaphoid. The proximal row from the thumb side is the scaphoid, the lunate, the triquetrum and the pisiform. The other three bones named lie in the distal row.

Question 2073. A described radiograph shows a bone shaped like a boat beneath the thumb, with its lower part hidden behind the thumb bones. Which bone is described, and why is a break in it easily missed? The answer is the scaphoid. It lies at an angle across the wrist, so the part that breaks is often hidden and the bone is tender at the base of the thumb.

Question 2074. A constructed illustration: a person falls on the outstretched hand and feels pain in the hollow at the base of the thumb. Which bone is injured, and why? The answer is the scaphoid, whose blood vessels enter near its lower end and run backward. A break through the middle can cut off the supply to the proximal fragment. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2075. Which carpal bone is the largest, lies in the middle of the wrist and takes the base of the third metacarpal bone? The answer is the capitate. It sits at the center of the carpus, with the trapezoid on its thumb side and the hamate on its little finger side. It is the keystone of the wrist.

Question 2076. Which of these structures passes through the carpal tunnel: the ulnar nerve, the median nerve, the radial artery, or the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris? The answer is the median nerve. It lies just beneath the flexor retinaculum, with the finger flexor tendons around it. The ulnar nerve and the ulnar artery pass into the hand outside the tunnel.

Question 2077. Which structure lies just beneath the flexor retinaculum inside the carpal tunnel, more superficial than the tendons around it? The answer is the median nerve. It lies directly under the ligament at the wrist. Pressure there is one cause of tingling in the thumb, the index and the middle fingers.

Question 2078. True or false: the tendon of the palmaris longus passes through the carpal tunnel. The answer is false. It crosses in front of the flexor retinaculum and spreads into the palmar aponeurosis. The tendons beneath the retinaculum are those of the flexor muscles of the fingers and thumb, with the median nerve.

Question 2079. A described drawing of the palm shows a raised fleshy ridge at the base of the thumb and a smaller one at the base of the little finger. What are the two ridges called? The answer is the thenar and hypothenar eminences. The thenar eminence is formed by the muscles of the thumb, the hypothenar by those of the little finger.

Question 2080. Which pair belongs together: the flexor retinaculum with the carpal tunnel, the palmar aponeurosis with the extensor tendons, the extensor retinaculum with the flexor tendons, or the fibrous sheath with the wrist? The answer is the flexor retinaculum with the carpal tunnel, over which it arches. The palmar aponeurosis lies in the palm and the extensor retinaculum on the back of the wrist.

Question 2081. Which statement about the blood supply of the scaphoid is correct: the vessels enter near the thumb and flow backward, they enter near the forearm and flow toward the thumb, the bone has no supply of its own, or only the ulnar artery supplies it? The answer is that they enter near the thumb and flow backward, so a break through the middle starves the proximal fragment.

Question 2082. Which artery crosses the floor of the hollow at the base of the thumb, lying on the scaphoid and the trapezium? The answer is the radial artery. It passes between the tendons that bound the hollow and then turns into the palm. Its pulse can be felt there as well as at the front of the wrist.

Question 2083. A constructed illustration: an older person falls on the outstretched hand and the lower radius is bent backward with the hand. Which pattern is described? The answer is a break of the lower radius with the fragment displaced backward. It is an illustration, not a real patient. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2084. A described radiograph of a hand shows two small round bones lying beside the joint at the base of the thumb, in front of the first metacarpal bone. What are they? The answer is the sesamoid bones of the thumb. They lie within the tendons that cross the joint and are normal, not fragments of bone.

Question 2085. Which muscle forms the fleshy mound at the base of the thumb and draws the thumb away from the palm: the adductor pollicis, the abductor pollicis brevis, the first dorsal interosseous, or the flexor digitorum superficialis? The answer is the abductor pollicis brevis, supplied by the median nerve. The adductor pollicis pulls the thumb toward the palm and belongs to the ulnar nerve.

Question 2086. Name the four carpal bones of the row nearest the forearm, spoken as a list from the thumb side to the little finger side. The answer is the scaphoid, the lunate, the triquetrum and the pisiform. The pisiform is the small round bone on the front of the triquetrum. The other row holds the trapezium, the trapezoid, the capitate and the hamate.

Question 2087. Which of these bones is the metacarpal bone of the thumb: the first, the second, the third, or the fifth? The answer is the first. It lies at the outer edge of the hand and is shorter and thicker than the rest. Its base meets the trapezium in a saddle-shaped joint, which allows the thumb to reach across the palm.

Question 2088. Which of these movements of the hand at the wrist carries the hand toward the thumb side: bending the wrist forward, bending it backward, moving it toward the thumb, or moving it toward the little finger? The answer is moving it toward the thumb side. That movement is called radial deviation. Its opposite, toward the little finger, is ulnar deviation.

Question 2089. Which structure passes into the hand just lateral to the pisiform bone and lies outside the carpal tunnel? The answer is the ulnar nerve, with the ulnar artery beside it. It crosses the wrist in a small channel between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate. Because it lies outside the tunnel, pressure inside does not affect it.

Question 2090. A described dissection of the palm shows a tough fibrous sheet sending bands toward the fingers. What is the sheet, and what does it do? The answer is the palmar aponeurosis. It lies just under the skin and gives the palm a firm grip. It also protects the tendons and vessels beneath it.

Question 2091. True or false: the joint at the base of the thumb between the trapezium and the first metacarpal bone is a saddle joint. The answer is true. Its two curved surfaces sit at right angles to each other, so the thumb can move in two planes. The combination of those movements brings the thumb pad against the fingers.

Question 2092. Which of these tendons passes through the carpal tunnel: the flexor carpi radialis, the palmaris longus, the flexor pollicis longus, or the extensor carpi ulnaris? The answer is the tendon of the flexor pollicis longus. The other three lie outside the tunnel. Nine tendons and the median nerve pass through it.

Question 2093. A described section across the wrist shows the carpal bones in an arch with a fibrous band across the top. In which plane was the section cut, and what does the space beneath the band contain? The answer is a transverse plane, and the space is the carpal tunnel. It contains the tendons of the flexor muscles of the fingers and thumb, with the median nerve among them.

Question 2094. Which joint is the wrist joint proper: the joint between the radius and the ulna, the joint between the radius and the first carpal row, the joint between the carpal rows, or the joint at the base of the thumb? The answer is the joint between the radius and the first row of carpal bones. A disc of cartilage separates the ulna from that joint.

Question 2095. Which statement about the short muscles of the thumb is correct: the abductor pollicis brevis and the opponens pollicis are supplied by the median nerve, all of them by the ulnar nerve, the adductor by the median nerve, or all of them by the radial nerve? The answer is that the abductor pollicis brevis and the opponens pollicis are supplied by the median nerve.

Question 2096. A described photograph shows the fleshy mound at the base of the thumb flattened and the thumb in the plane of the palm. Which nerve is injured, and by what route does it reach the thumb muscles? The answer is the median nerve, whose small recurrent branch curls around the flexor retinaculum to the thumb muscles. Injury to it leaves the thumb unable to oppose.

Question 2097. Which of these pairs belongs together: the scaphoid with a boat, the lunate with a hook, the hamate with the moon, or the pisiform with a wedge? The answer is the scaphoid with a boat, since the word means a skiff. The lunate is named for the moon, the pisiform for a pea, and the hamate for its hook.

Question 2098. Which carpal bone lies at the base of the thumb, meets the first metacarpal bone and carries a ridge and a groove on its palmar surface? The answer is the trapezium. The ridge gives attachment to muscles of the thumb and the groove carries the flexor carpi radialis tendon.

Question 2099. A constructed illustration: a fall tears the ligament on the inner side of the thumb joint, and the thumb bends away from the index finger when stressed. Which structure is illustrated as torn? The answer is the ulnar collateral ligament of the joint between the first metacarpal and the first phalanx of the thumb. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2100. Which statement about the deep branch of the ulnar nerve is correct: it supplies the thenar muscles, it runs with the radial artery, it supplies the muscles between the metacarpals, or it lies in the carpal tunnel? The answer is that it supplies the muscles between the metacarpal bones. It also supplies two small muscles of the ring and little fingers and lies outside the carpal tunnel.

To summarize, the elbow is a hinge between the humerus and the ulna and a pivot between the humerus and the radial head, held by the collateral ligaments and by the annular ligament. The medial epicondyle carries the common flexor tendon with the ulnar nerve behind it, and the lateral epicondyle the common extensor tendon with the deep branch of the radial nerve through the supinator. The cubital fossa holds the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve in a row, and the interosseous membrane carries force from the radius to the ulna. At the wrist the scaphoid lies at the base of the thumb and is the bone most often broken, the median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel with the flexor tendons, and the ulnar nerve enters the hand outside it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 22 — Hip

This chapter takes up the joints that carry the body and the joint that places the hand, moving from the wrist and the hand to the hip in detail and closing with the cruciate ligaments of the knee. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer in the same paragraph as the question and then says why that answer is right, so no answer has to be carried in mind to the end. The hip is taken apart into its socket, the head of the femur, the capsule and the ligaments that steady them. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2101. At the wrist, the broad lower end of the radius joins which two bones of the carpus? The answer is the scaphoid and the lunate. The radius carries the hand, and its lower end meets those two bones of the proximal row. The head of the ulna is kept away from the carpus by a disc of fibrocartilage.

Question 2102. In the hollow at the base of the thumb, which carpal bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox? The answer is the scaphoid. Tenderness there after a fall points to that bone. The tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis form one border of the hollow.

Question 2103. Which bone of the wrist carries the saddle-shaped surface on which the first metacarpal sits? The answer is the trapezium. It lies at the radial side of the distal row of carpal bones. The joint it makes is the saddle joint, and it lets the thumb be carried across the palm.

Question 2104. Which carpal bone lies in the middle of the distal row, between the scaphoid and the hamate, and is the largest bone of the wrist? The answer is the capitate. It is the keystone of the carpus, and force passes through it from the middle of the hand to the radius. Its rounded head sits in a socket formed largely by the scaphoid and the lunate.

Question 2105. Which structure passes through the carpal tunnel with the flexor tendons: the median nerve, the ulnar nerve, the radial artery, or the ulnar artery? The answer is the median nerve. It lies just beneath the flexor retinaculum, the band that roofs the tunnel. The ulnar nerve and the ulnar artery reach the hand outside it.

Question 2106. Which structure crosses the front of the wrist superficial to the flexor retinaculum: the tendon of the flexor pollicis longus, the median nerve, the ulnar nerve, or the tendon of the flexor digitorum profundus? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It passes with the ulnar artery and then divides into a superficial and a deep branch. The other three lie inside the tunnel.

Question 2107. Which movement is the special gift of the saddle joint at the base of the thumb: simple flexion, rotation about the long axis of the arm, opposition, or pure gliding? The answer is opposition. That movement swings the thumb across the palm so that its pad meets the pads of the fingers. The joint also flexes, extends, abducts and adducts.

Question 2108. A constructed illustration: a fall drives the thumb away from the hand, and the ligament joining the first metacarpal to the proximal phalanx on the side toward the index finger gives way. Which ligament is injured? The answer is the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb. It resists exactly that force, and the injury is described as a skier's thumb.

Question 2109. Most of the flexion of the wrist is contributed by which joint: the radiocarpal joint, the midcarpal joint, the first carpometacarpal joint, or the distal radioulnar joint? The answer is the midcarpal joint. There the two rows of carpal bones fold on each other. The radiocarpal joint supplies most of the extension, and the other two joints serve the thumb and the forearm.

Question 2110. A described radiograph of the wrist shows a crack across the middle of the bone in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, and the fragment nearer the forearm looks denser. Which bone is broken, and why does that fragment often fail to unite? The answer is the scaphoid, whose blood enters at the far end and runs back toward the forearm. Such a break can starve the fragment near the forearm.

Question 2111. A described section through the wrist shows a triangular plate of fibrocartilage stretched between the lower end of the ulna and the carpus, keeping the ulna away from the carpal bones. What is that plate? The answer is the triangular fibrocartilage complex. It cushions the ulnar side of the wrist, so the ulna takes no direct part in the radiocarpal joint.

Question 2112. At the wrist, does the ulnar nerve lie medial or lateral to the ulnar artery? The answer is medial. Both structures cross the front of the wrist on the little finger side, with the nerve a little nearer the midline of the hand. The artery can be felt there, beside the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris.

Question 2113. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve leaves the palm by passing between which two bony landmarks, and how does it lie relative to the artery beside it? The answer is between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate, with the nerve medial to the artery. It then curves around the hook to supply the muscles of the little finger and the interossei.

Question 2114. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the outstretched hand, and a described radiograph shows the lower end of the radius broken, with the fragment nearer the hand displaced toward the back. Which bone is broken, and which nerve is most at risk? The answer is the radius, with the median nerve lying closest to it. Care of the fracture belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2115. A constructed illustration: an older person has a firm nodule in the palm with a cord that draws the fourth and fifth fingers into the palm, and the skin over the cord is tethered. Which structure is contracted? The answer is the palmar aponeurosis. The fibrous sheet thickens and shortens, pulling on the sheaths of those fingers. What is offered as treatment belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2116. True or false: the ulna articulates directly with the carpal bones at the wrist. The answer is false. A disc of fibrocartilage lies between the head of the ulna and the carpus. The radius alone takes the hand at the radiocarpal joint, and the ulna stays clear of it.

Question 2117. Which three bones of the pelvis meet to form the cup of the hip joint? The answer is the ilium, the ischium and the pubis. Their three parts join in the socket at a Y-shaped cartilage that closes in the second decade of life. The cup they make together is the acetabulum.

Question 2118. What is the name of the smooth horseshoe-shaped surface within the acetabulum that carries the weight of the body? The answer is the lunate surface. It is covered with hyaline cartilage and receives the head of the femur. Its two horns meet below at the notch in the rim.

Question 2119. What is the name of the rough, non-articular pit in the floor of the acetabulum? The answer is the acetabular fossa. It holds a pad of fat and gives attachment to the ligament of the head of the femur. Below, it is continuous with the notch in the rim.

Question 2120. Which ring of fibrocartilage is fixed to the margin of the acetabulum, deepens the socket and helps to seal the head of the femur within it? The answer is the acetabular labrum. It bridges the notch below and turns the socket into a deeper cup. A tear of it lets fluid cut into the rim and makes the hip catch and hurt.

Question 2121. True or false: the transverse acetabular ligament bridges the gap in the lower part of the rim of the socket. The answer is true. It spans the acetabular notch and so completes the ring of the socket. Beneath it a small gap remains, through which vessels and the ligament of the head pass.

Question 2122. Which part of the acetabulum bears the weight of the body in standing: the acetabular fossa, the lunate surface, the acetabular notch, or the transverse acetabular ligament? The answer is the lunate surface. Its broad upper part forms the roof of the socket and receives the load. The fossa and the notch bear no articular cartilage.

Question 2123. By about which year of life do the three parts of the acetabulum finish joining at the Y-shaped cartilage: the second year, the sixth year, the sixteenth year, or the thirtieth year? The answer is the sixteenth year. Until then the three bones are separated by the triradiate cartilage, which is seen clearly in the radiograph of a child.

Question 2124. Beneath the transverse acetabular ligament, the notch in the rim of the socket allows which structures to reach the inside of the joint: the sciatic nerve, the ligament of the head with its small vessels, the obturator artery alone, or the tendon of the iliopsoas? The answer is the ligament of the head with its small vessels. The sciatic nerve and the iliopsoas lie well outside the joint.

Question 2125. In the standing body, the opening of the acetabulum faces in which direction: straight laterally, directly forward, laterally with a tilt forward and downward, or straight upward? The answer is laterally, with a tilt forward and downward. The socket therefore covers the front and the top of the head. That tilt is one reason the hip dislocates backward more often than forward.

Question 2126. A described magnetic resonance image of the hip shows a thin cleft of fluid cutting into the front edge of the rim of the socket, with bruising of the bone beside it. Which structure is torn: the acetabular labrum, the ligament of the head of the femur, the transverse acetabular ligament, or the zona orbicularis? The answer is the acetabular labrum. The cleft enters the ring of fibrocartilage that deepens the socket.

Question 2127. Which statement about the acetabular labrum is correct: it is made of hyaline cartilage, it is fixed to the rim and increases the hold on the head, it lies within the acetabular fossa, or it is a fold of synovium? The answer is that it is fixed to the rim and increases the hold on the head. It is a ring of fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage.

Question 2128. A described radiograph of a child's pelvis shows a Y-shaped line of cartilage running through each socket and separating three bony parts. What is that line? The answer is the triradiate cartilage. It is the growth plate where the ilium, the ischium and the pubis meet. When the child stops growing, the three parts become one bone.

Question 2129. A described radiograph of an adult pelvis shows a socket whose roof slopes steeply, so that the head of the femur rides high and is only partly covered. What does this describe? The answer is a shallow socket, the kind seen when the hip has been undercovered since birth. The labrum is overloaded and the joint wears early. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2130. A described section through a hip shows a fat-filled pit in the floor of the socket, continuous below with the gap in the rim, and a band running from the pit to a depression on the head of the femur. What are those two structures? The answer is the acetabular fossa and the ligament of the head. The ligament crosses the joint and carries a small vessel in a child.

Question 2131. The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through a canal that lies in which position relative to the acetabulum, and which joint does that nerve also supply? The answer is below and in front of the socket, and the nerve supplies the hip joint. It gives off a branch to the joint as it passes through the canal on its way to the thigh.

Question 2132. Which muscle and its bursa lie immediately in front of the capsule of the hip, separating the joint from the femoral vessels? The answer is the iliopsoas. Its tendon glides over the front of the joint, and its bursa often joins the cavity of the joint. The femoral nerve lies on the surface of the muscle, with the artery just medial to it.

Question 2133. A constructed illustration: a newborn is examined and the head of the femur can be slipped out of the socket and back in again, and the fold of skin at the back of the thigh looks uneven. Which part of the joint is at fault? The answer is a shallow acetabulum with a steep roof. What is done about it belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2134. A constructed illustration: a young adult has pain at the front of the hip at the end of a deep squat, and a described radiograph shows an extra lip of bone over the front of the socket and a bump at the junction of the head and the neck of the femur. What is the mechanism? The answer is that the rim and the bump meet early. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2135. Which ligament runs from the pit on the head of the femur to the notch in the rim of the socket? The answer is the ligament of the head of the femur. It lies inside the capsule and is wrapped in synovium. It is slack in most positions and becomes taut when the hip is adducted.

Question 2136. What is the name of the small depression on the head of the femur where that ligament is attached? The answer is the fovea capitis. It lies a little below and behind the center of the head. It is the one part of the head not covered by articular cartilage.

Question 2137. Which artery provides most of the blood to the adult head of the femur? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery. Its branches run up along the neck beneath the capsule and enter the head near its edge. These are the vessels torn in a break across the neck.

Question 2138. The head of the femur forms what part of a sphere: one half, two thirds, the whole sphere, or one quarter? The answer is two thirds. Its surface is covered with hyaline cartilage except at the fovea, where the ligament of the head is attached. The shape lets it turn in the socket through a wide range.

Question 2139. In the adult, the angle between the neck and the shaft of the femur is about how many degrees: 90, 110, 125, or 160? The answer is about 125 degrees. In a young child the angle is larger, and it falls as the child begins to walk and to bear weight. A smaller angle is described as the neck bending inward.

Question 2140. Which vessel is the chief source of blood for the head of the femur in an adult: the obturator artery, the medial circumflex femoral artery, the lateral circumflex femoral artery, or the artery of the ligament of the head? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery. Its branches climb the neck under the capsule. The artery of the ligament is small in adults.

Question 2141. A described radiograph shows a break across the neck of the femur, with the line of the break lying inside the capsule. Which vessel is most likely to be damaged, and what is the danger? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery and its branches along the neck. If they are torn, the head loses its supply and part of it may die.

Question 2142. In a child, which artery adds a share of the blood supply to the head of the femur, entering through the pit where the ligament is attached: the inferior gluteal artery, the obturator artery through that ligament, the lateral circumflex femoral artery alone, or the first perforating artery? The answer is the obturator artery through the ligament of the head. Its share is larger in childhood.

Question 2143. A described radiograph of the hip of a child shows the head of the femur flattened and in part fragmented, with a widened joint space and thickened cartilage. What has happened? The answer is that the blood supply of the head has been interrupted, and the bone is being replaced. The head may later flatten and the neck may shorten.

Question 2144. A described magnetic resonance image of the hip shows a curved band of low signal running through the head of the femur, with a rim of swelling around it. What does this represent? The answer is bone that has lost its blood supply and is dying. The band separates living bone from dead bone. The same picture may follow a break across the neck.

Question 2145. Which tendon is attached to the lesser trochanter, the small prominence on the posteromedial side of the upper end of the femur? The answer is the tendon of the iliopsoas. The lesser trochanter lies behind and below the neck. Because it lies at the back, a break of the neck often leaves the lower fragment pulled upward.

Question 2146. Which muscle leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen just above the upper border of the greater trochanter, and which vessels leave just above that muscle? The answer is the piriformis, with the superior gluteal vessels above it. Below it pass the sciatic nerve and the inferior gluteal vessels. The muscle is the key to the gluteal region.

Question 2147. A constructed illustration: a person walks with a lurching gait and, when standing on one leg, the hip on the other side drops. Which muscle is weak, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the gluteus medius, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. That muscle holds the pelvis level when the opposite foot is off it.

Question 2148. A constructed illustration: a child limps and complains of pain at the knee, but the knee itself looks and moves normally. Why is the hip the likely source? The answer is that the hip and the knee share nerve supply from the same segments of the spinal cord. Fibers from the obturator and femoral nerves carry the pain to the knee.

Question 2149. True or false: the fovea capitis lies above the center of the head of the femur. The answer is false. It lies a little below and behind the center. That is why the ligament of the head is slack when the hip is extended and taut when the hip is adducted.

Question 2150. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fovea capitis with the attachment of the ligament of the head, the greater trochanter with the insertion of the iliopsoas, the lesser trochanter with the insertion of the gluteus medius, or the neck of the femur with the fovea? The answer is the fovea capitis with the attachment of the ligament of the head. The iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter.

Question 2151. Name two muscles that are attached to the greater trochanter of the femur, spoken as a list. The answer is the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus. The medius is attached to the lateral surface and the minimus to the front surface. The piriformis and the obturator internus with the gemelli reach its upper and medial borders.

Question 2152. Two angles describe the upper end of the femur: the angle between the neck and the shaft, and the angle by which the neck is twisted forward on the shaft. In which plane is each measured? The answer is that the first is measured in the frontal plane and the twist of the neck in the transverse plane. The twist points the knee and the foot forward.
