Question 2153. What is the name of the strong fibrous sleeve that encloses the hip joint and is attached above to the rim of the socket? The answer is the capsule of the hip joint. It is attached below to the front of the femur along the line between the two trochanters. Behind, it reaches only part way down the neck.

Question 2154. Along which line on the front of the femur is the capsule of the hip attached below? The answer is the intertrochanteric line. The line runs from the greater trochanter down and across to the lesser trochanter. In front, the whole of the neck therefore lies outside the joint.

Question 2155. What is the name of the ring of circular fibers deep within the capsule of the hip that forms a collar around the neck of the femur? The answer is the zona orbicularis. Its fibers run around the neck rather than along it, and they resist a pull that would separate the surfaces of the joint. The three named ligaments lie outside them.

Question 2156. Where is the capsule of the hip thickest: at the front, at the back, above the socket, or below it? The answer is at the front. It is reinforced there by the strongest ligament of the body. Behind, the capsule is thinner and reaches less far down the neck.

Question 2157. Which part of the neck of the femur lies outside the capsule of the hip: the whole of it, the front of it, the back of it, or none of it? The answer is the front. The capsule is attached in front along the intertrochanteric line. Behind, it reaches only part way down, so part of the back of the neck lies within the joint.

Question 2158. In which position is the capsule of the hip tightest: full flexion, full extension, abduction with flexion, or sitting? The answer is full extension. When a person stands, the capsule and its ligaments wind around the neck and steady the joint. That is one reason a standing person can rest without muscular effort.

Question 2159. In which position is the capsule of the hip slackest, so that the joint holds the greatest volume: full extension, flexion with abduction and lateral rotation, standing on one leg, or adduction with medial rotation? The answer is flexion with abduction and lateral rotation. That is the position a hip takes when it is filled with fluid and painful.

Question 2160. What does the synovial membrane of the hip cover: only the articular cartilage, the inner surface of the capsule together with the bone inside it and the ligament of the head, the outer surface of the capsule, or the labrum alone? The answer is the inner surface of the capsule with the bone inside it and the ligament of the head. Articular cartilage is not covered.

Question 2161. A described image of the hip after contrast has been placed in the joint shows the material running down the neck of the femur in front but stopping short behind, with a narrow collar of fibers around the middle of the neck. What structures are shown? The answer is the capsule of the hip and the zona orbicularis. The capsule reaches further down in front than behind.

Question 2162. A described magnetic resonance image of a painful hip shows fluid distending the joint and a second collection of fluid in front of the joint, beneath the muscle that flexes the hip. What is that second collection? The answer is the iliopsoas bursa, which communicates with the cavity of the hip in many people. When the joint is inflamed, the bursa fills with the same fluid.

Question 2163. Which bursa lies in front of the hip joint beneath the iliopsoas muscle and often communicates with the cavity of the joint? The answer is the iliopsoas bursa. It lies between the muscle and the front of the capsule. Because the two cavities may join, disease within the hip can spread into the bursa.

Question 2164. Which nerve lies immediately in front of the capsule of the hip, resting on the surface of the iliopsoas muscle? The answer is the femoral nerve. It lies in the groove between the iliopsoas and the psoas, within the fascia that covers them. The femoral artery lies just medial to the nerve.

Question 2165. A constructed illustration: a child with an inflamed hip lies with the hip flexed, abducted and turned outward, and cries when the hip is moved. Why is the limb held in that position? The answer is that the position gives the capsule the greatest volume. Fluid inside the joint stretches the capsule, and the hip is held where the stretch is least.

Question 2166. A constructed illustration: after a break across the neck of the femur, blood collects inside the capsule and the joint becomes tight. Which movement is lost first, and why? The answer is extension, because the capsule is tightest in extension and cannot stretch further when blood fills it. The joint is then held flexed. Care belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2167. Which of these pairs belongs together: the zona orbicularis with fibers that run around the neck, the iliofemoral ligament with the thinnest part of the capsule, the synovial membrane with the outer surface of the capsule, or the labrum with the acetabular fossa? The answer is the zona orbicularis with fibers that run around the neck. The synovial membrane lines the inside of the capsule.

Question 2168. A described transverse section through the hip shows that behind, the capsule stops well above the ridge on the back of the femur, while in front it reaches the line between the trochanters. Which part of the neck therefore lies within the joint? The answer is the back of the neck. A break there may lie inside the joint and endanger the vessels running along the neck.

Question 2169. Which ligament, shaped like an inverted Y across the front of the hip, is the strongest ligament in the body? The answer is the iliofemoral ligament. It runs from the front of the hip bone down to the line between the two trochanters. It checks extension of the hip when a person stands upright.

Question 2170. Which ligament runs from the ischium, below and behind the socket, upward and outward to the base of the greater trochanter? The answer is the ischiofemoral ligament. It is the weakest of the three ligaments that reinforce the hip. Its fibers spiral upward as they pass to the femur.

Question 2171. Which ligament arises from the pubis and blends with the front of the capsule of the hip, helping to limit abduction? The answer is the pubofemoral ligament. It runs downward and outward from the pubic part of the rim of the socket. It also helps to limit extension of the hip.

Question 2172. Which movement of the hip is chiefly checked by the iliofemoral ligament: flexion, extension, abduction, or medial rotation? The answer is extension. The ligament is taut when the hip is extended and slack when the hip is flexed. It is the chief reason a person can stand with little muscular effort.

Question 2173. Which ligament of the hip chiefly limits abduction: the iliofemoral, the pubofemoral, the ischiofemoral, or the ligament of the head? The answer is the pubofemoral ligament. It lies below the front of the joint, where a limb carried out to the side would stretch it. The iliofemoral ligament chiefly limits extension.

Question 2174. Which ligament chiefly resists medial rotation of the hip: the pubofemoral, the ligament of the head, the ischiofemoral, or the iliofemoral? The answer is the ischiofemoral ligament. It spirals from the ischium to the base of the greater trochanter and tightens as the thigh turns inward. The pubofemoral ligament resists abduction instead.

Question 2175. In which position is the ligament of the head of the femur taut: extension, abduction, adduction, or lateral rotation? The answer is adduction. The ligament runs from the pit on the head to the notch in the rim of the socket, and carrying the thigh across the midline stretches it. It carries a small artery to the head in a child.

Question 2176. Which ligament bridges the gap in the lower rim of the acetabulum and turns the notch into a foramen: the iliofemoral, the transverse acetabular, the pubofemoral, or the zona orbicularis? The answer is the transverse acetabular ligament. Vessels and the ligament of the head pass beneath it into the joint. It also completes the ring to which the labrum is fixed.

Question 2177. Which of these pairs belongs together: the iliofemoral ligament with the checking of extension, the pubofemoral ligament with the checking of medial rotation, the ischiofemoral ligament with the checking of abduction, or the ligament of the head with the carrying of a vessel into the socket? The answer is the iliofemoral ligament with the checking of extension. The pubofemoral ligament checks abduction, and the ischiofemoral checks medial rotation.

Question 2178. A described dissection of the front of the hip shows a thick band of fibers shaped like an inverted Y, running from the front of the hip bone to the ridge between the trochanters, with a thinner band below it passing toward the pubis. Which two ligaments are shown? The answer is the iliofemoral ligament and the pubofemoral ligament. The first is the strongest ligament in the body.

Question 2179. A described dissection of the back of the hip shows a band of fibers spiraling from the ischium upward and outward to the base of the greater trochanter, lying over the back of the capsule. Which ligament is shown, and how does it rank among the three? The answer is the ischiofemoral ligament, the weakest of the three. It resists medial rotation.

Question 2180. A described section through the socket shows a band of fibers crossing the gap in the lower rim and closing it into a hole, and a rounded cord passing through it to reach a pit in the floor of the socket. What are the band and the cord? The answer is the transverse acetabular ligament and the ligament of the head. They guide a small vessel into the joint.

Question 2181. The iliofemoral ligament is attached above to the front of the hip bone. Which bony point gives it part of that attachment and also gives origin to the straight head of the rectus femoris? The answer is the anterior inferior iliac spine. The ligament and the muscle therefore share the same landmark. Just above it lies the anterior superior iliac spine.

Question 2182. A constructed illustration: after a blow against the front of a bent knee, the hip is held flexed, adducted and turned inward, the limb looks short, and sensation is lost over the back of the thigh. Which injury does this describe? The answer is a backward dislocation of the hip with injury to the sciatic nerve. Care belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2183. True or false: the pubofemoral ligament helps to limit abduction of the hip. The answer is true. It lies below the front of the joint, where a thigh carried away from the midline stretches it. The iliofemoral ligament above it chiefly limits extension.

Question 2184. Which of these pairs belongs together: the iliofemoral ligament with the front of the joint, the pubofemoral ligament with the back of the joint, the ischiofemoral ligament with the front of the joint, or the ligament of the head with the outer surface of the capsule? The answer is the iliofemoral ligament with the front of the joint. The pubofemoral lies below and in front, and the ischiofemoral behind.

Question 2185. Name the three ligaments that reinforce the capsule of the hip, spoken as a list. The answer is the iliofemoral, the pubofemoral and the ischiofemoral ligaments. The iliofemoral lies in front, the pubofemoral below and in front, and the ischiofemoral behind. The strongest of the three is the iliofemoral.

Question 2186. Which ligament runs from the front of the tibia upward and backward to the inner side of the outer condyle of the femur? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It crosses the joint within the capsule. It stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur.

Question 2187. Which ligament of the knee runs from the back of the tibia upward and forward to the outer side of the inner condyle of the femur, and is the stronger of the two that cross? The answer is the posterior cruciate ligament. It is the strongest ligament of the knee. It stops the tibia from sliding backward on the femur.

Question 2188. Within the knee, the two ligaments that cross each other lie inside the capsule, yet a fold of synovium wraps around them. What are they called? The answer is the cruciate ligaments, the anterior and the posterior. Because they are wrapped in synovium, fluid from the joint does not bathe them directly. Their position helps to explain why they heal poorly.

Question 2189. Which movement of the knee does the anterior cruciate ligament chiefly resist: the tibia sliding forward on the femur, the tibia sliding backward, the knee bending, or the patella moving sideways? The answer is the tibia sliding forward on the femur. The ligament is taut when the knee is straight and when the tibia is turned inward.

Question 2190. Which movement of the knee does the posterior cruciate ligament chiefly resist: the tibia sliding forward, the tibia sliding backward, the knee straightening, or the patella being pulled upward? The answer is the tibia sliding backward on the femur. The ligament is taut when the knee is bent. It is the strongest ligament of the joint.

Question 2191. In which position is the anterior cruciate ligament most taut: the knee straight with the tibia turned inward, the knee bent with the tibia turned outward, the knee bent at a right angle, or the knee straight with the tibia turned outward? The answer is the knee straight with the tibia turned inward. In that position it checks both forward glide and hyperextension.

Question 2192. Which artery supplies the greater part of the blood reaching the cruciate ligaments: the femoral artery, the middle geniculate artery, the anterior tibial artery, or the obturator artery? The answer is the middle geniculate artery, a branch of the popliteal artery. Its branches enter through the fat pad and the synovial covering. That supply is meager, so a torn ligament heals poorly.

Question 2193. A described sagittal magnetic resonance image of the knee shows a dark band running from the front of the tibia upward and backward to the inner side of the outer condyle of the femur, crossing in front of another dark band. Which ligament is in front? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. The two bands cross like the limbs of the letter X.

Question 2194. A described dissection of the knee opened from behind shows a strong band rising from the back of the tibia and running upward and forward to the outer side of the inner condyle of the femur, with a small slip joining it from the outer meniscus. Which ligament is this, and what is the slip? The answer is the posterior cruciate ligament, with a meniscofemoral ligament beside it.

Question 2195. A described radiograph of the knee of a young person shows a flake of bone pulled from between the two spines on the top of the tibia, with the joint still in line. Which ligament has torn away its bony attachment? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament, which is attached to the front of that space. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2196. Within the notch between the condyles of the femur, which of the two cruciate ligaments lies in front of the other, and which condyle does each reach above? The answer is that the anterior cruciate ligament lies in front and reaches the outer condyle, while the posterior cruciate reaches the inner condyle. The two cross as they rise.

Question 2197. A constructed illustration: a person plants a foot and turns the body while the knee is slightly bent, feels a pop, and afterward the knee gives way on turning. Which ligament is torn, and which two structures are often injured with it? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament, often with the inner meniscus and the ligament on the inner side of the knee.

Question 2198. True or false: the posterior cruciate ligament is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments. The answer is true. It is the strongest ligament of the knee joint. It is taut when the knee is bent and stops the tibia from sliding backward on the femur.

Question 2199. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior cruciate ligament with the checking of forward glide of the tibia, the posterior cruciate ligament with the checking of forward glide, the medial meniscus with the lateral side of the knee, or the patella with the tibial spines? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament with the checking of forward glide. The posterior cruciate ligament checks backward glide.

Question 2200. Name the two ligaments that cross within the knee joint, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament and the posterior cruciate ligament. The anterior one is attached in front on the tibia and the posterior one behind. Both lie inside the capsule and are wrapped in synovium.

To summarize, the wrist is formed by the radius with the scaphoid and the lunate, the ulna being kept away by a disc of fibrocartilage, and the carpal tunnel carries the median nerve with the long flexor tendons while the ulnar nerve passes outside it. The socket of the hip is built from the ilium, the ischium and the pubis, deepened by the labrum and bridged below by the transverse acetabular ligament, and the head of the femur carries the fovea and depends for its blood on the medial circumflex femoral artery. The capsule of the hip is thick in front and thin behind, tightest in extension and lined by synovium, and the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments steady it, the iliofemoral being the strongest ligament in the body. At the knee the anterior cruciate ligament checks forward sliding of the tibia and the posterior cruciate ligament, the stronger of the two, checks backward sliding, and both lie inside the capsule but outside the synovial lining. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 23 — Knee

This chapter covers the knee and the ankle and the foot, the two regions where the lower limb meets the ground and takes the whole weight of the body. It begins with the ligaments of the knee, the medial collateral ligament and the lateral collateral ligament, then the menisci, the patella and the joint capsule, and it goes on to the bones, the ligaments and the arches of the ankle and the foot. It holds one hundred questions, and every question states its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. Every item can be answered by ear alone, without a picture or a list to consult. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2201. Which ligament of the knee runs from the medial epicondyle of the femur downward and forward to the medial surface of the tibia? The answer is the medial collateral ligament, also called the tibial collateral ligament. It is a broad flat band on the inner side of the joint. It checks a force that pushes the knee inward and opens the inner side of the joint.

Question 2202. Which of these four structures does the medial collateral ligament blend with: the lateral meniscus, the medial meniscus, the patellar tendon, or the iliotibial band? The answer is the medial meniscus. Its deep fibers attach to the outer margin of that plate of fibrocartilage. That attachment explains why the meniscus tears when the ligament is injured.

Question 2203. A surgeon passes a finger deep to the medial collateral ligament at the joint line. Which structure lies immediately deep to the ligament there? The answer is the medial meniscus, with the joint capsule between the two. The deep fibers of the ligament are fused to the capsule and the meniscus, so the medial meniscus is far less mobile than the lateral one.

Question 2204. A constructed illustration: a player takes a blow to the outer side of the knee, and the joint opens on the inner side. Which ligament is most likely torn, and what may it drag with it? The answer is the medial collateral ligament, often with the medial meniscus. The outside force drives the knee inward and stretches the inner side, and the bond between the two explains their injury together.

Question 2205. True or false: the medial collateral ligament lies outside the joint capsule and is not bathed in synovial fluid. The answer is true. It is an extracapsular ligament on the inner side of the knee. Its deep fibers do blend with the capsule, but the ligament itself lies outside the synovial cavity.

Question 2206. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the knee, cut from front to back, shows a dark band running from the inner side of the femur to the inner side of the tibia. Which structure is shown? The answer is the medial collateral ligament. Ligaments return little signal on magnetic resonance imaging and appear dark. Its tibial attachment lies well below the joint line.

Question 2207. Which movement does the medial collateral ligament mainly restrain: inward angulation of the knee, outward angulation, straightening of the knee, or rotation of the hip? The answer is inward angulation of the knee. The ligament tightens when the leg is pushed inward at the knee. Outward angulation is checked by the ligament on the outer side.

Question 2208. Within the medial collateral ligament, which part sends fibers that attach directly to the medial meniscus? The answer is the deep part, which blends with the joint capsule. It is these deep fibers, not the superficial band, that bind the meniscus. Their pull is what tears the meniscus along with the ligament.

Question 2209. Which statement distinguishes the medial collateral ligament from the lateral one: it is a rounded cord, it blends with the joint capsule, it lies outside the capsule, or it attaches to the head of the fibula? The answer is that it blends with the joint capsule. The ligament on the outer side is a rounded cord standing clear of the capsule.

Question 2210. Name the two bones to which the medial collateral ligament attaches, spoken as a list. The answer is the femur and the tibia. It begins on the medial epicondyle of the femur. It ends on the medial surface of the tibia, well below the joint line, so the whole inner side of the joint is braced.

Question 2211. Along the inner side of the knee, which three tendons spread out over the medial collateral ligament, and which structure lies deepest beneath them? The answer is the sartorius, the gracilis and the semitendinosus, with the ligament deepest. The three tendons fan out over the ligament as the pes anserinus. The ligament lies beneath that fan and takes its pull.

Question 2212. Which cord-like ligament runs from the lateral epicondyle of the femur down to the head of the fibula? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament, also called the fibular collateral ligament. It is a rounded cord on the outer side of the knee. It lies free of the joint capsule and is separated from the lateral meniscus.

Question 2213. Which of these bones does the lateral collateral ligament attach to below: the tibia, the fibula, the patella, or the first metatarsal? The answer is the fibula. Its lower end joins the head of the fibula, the slender bone on the outer side of the leg. The ligament sends no fibers to the tibia at all.

Question 2214. A constructed illustration: a blow lands on the inner side of the knee, and the outer side of the joint opens. Which ligament is torn, and which nerve may be stretched at the same time? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament, with the common fibular nerve. That nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just below the ligament, where it may be stretched.

Question 2215. Which structure lies immediately deep to the lateral collateral ligament and separates it from the lateral meniscus? The answer is the tendon of the popliteus muscle. It passes upward and inward through the gap between the ligament and the meniscus. That gap is one reason the outer meniscus is injured less often than the inner one.

Question 2216. A described dissection of the outer side of a knee shows a cord standing clear of the capsule, with a tendon slipping beneath it. Which ligament and which tendon are shown? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament and the tendon of the popliteus. The cord is separate from the capsule, unlike the ligament on the inner side.

Question 2217. True or false: the lateral collateral ligament attaches to the lateral meniscus. The answer is false. The lateral meniscus sends no fibers to that ligament. The tendon of the popliteus muscle lies between the two, and that separation keeps them apart. The medial meniscus, by contrast, is bound to the ligament on the inner side.

Question 2218. Which statement about the lateral collateral ligament is correct: the biceps femoris tendon splits around it, the medial meniscus blends with it, it fuses with the joint capsule, or it attaches to the tibia? The answer is that the biceps femoris tendon splits around it. The two parts of that tendon pass on either side of the cord, which stays free of the capsule.

Question 2219. Which ligament of the knee is the chief restraint against the knee bending outward, so that the joint opens on the outer side? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament. It tightens when the leg is pushed outward at the knee. The ligament on the inner side checks the opposite movement.

Question 2220. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral collateral ligament with the head of the fibula, the medial collateral ligament with the head of the fibula, the patellar tendon with the femur, or the iliotibial band with the medial tibia? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament with the head of the fibula. The medial ligament ends on the tibia instead.

Question 2221. A constructed illustration: after a knee is forced outward, the outer side of the joint is unstable and the foot cannot be lifted at the ankle. Which ligament and which nerve are involved? The answer is the lateral collateral ligament and the common fibular nerve. The nerve lies against the neck of the fibula just below the ligament, where it is easily stretched.

Question 2222. What name is given to the two C-shaped plates of fibrocartilage that sit on the upper end of the tibia within the knee? The answer is the menisci. Each lies on the articular surface of the tibia, one on either side. They deepen that surface and spread the load across it.

Question 2223. Which of these statements describes the shape of the medial meniscus: it is nearly a complete ring, it is a C-shaped plate, it is a flat disc, or it is a triangular bone? The answer is that it is a C-shaped plate. It is longer and more open than the lateral one. The lateral meniscus comes closer to a closed ring.

Question 2224. Why is the lateral meniscus more mobile: it is thinner, it is not tethered to the capsule as firmly, it has no blood supply, or it lies on the femur? The answer is that it is not tethered to the capsule as firmly. On the outer side the popliteus tendon separates it from the capsule, while the medial meniscus is bound along its whole rim.

Question 2225. Which structures hold the outer rim of each meniscus to the margin of the tibia? The answer is the coronary ligaments, short bands of the joint capsule. They run from the rim of the meniscus to the tibial margin. The medial meniscus is also bound to the deep fibers of the medial collateral ligament.

Question 2226. A constructed illustration: a person twists the knee while the foot stays fixed, and the joint locks so that it cannot be straightened. Which structure is most likely torn, and what is the mechanism? The answer is a meniscus, torn by rotation of the bent knee. The torn fragment slips between the surfaces and blocks extension. Locking of the joint is the sign described.

Question 2227. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the knee, cut across the joint, shows two dark triangular shapes with their points toward the middle of the joint. Which structures are shown? The answer is the menisci, seen in cross section. Their dark appearance follows from the dense fibrocartilage of which they are made.

Question 2228. A described section cut across the knee at the joint line shows a wedge of fibrocartilage on either side, fixed to the tibia below and free above. In which plane was the section cut, and why is the inner wedge less mobile? The answer is a transverse plane. The inner meniscus is bound to the capsule and to the deep fibers of the medial collateral ligament.

Question 2229. Which part of a meniscus heals after a tear: the outer rim, the inner edge, the whole plate, or none of it? The answer is the outer rim. That rim receives a blood supply from the capsule and is called the red zone. The inner part has no vessels of its own and is called the white zone.

Question 2230. True or false: a meniscus covers the whole of the articular surface of the tibia. The answer is false. Each meniscus covers only the outer part of that surface. The central area of the tibia is left uncovered by fibrocartilage. The plates deepen the surface rather than cover it.

Question 2231. Name the two horns of a meniscus, spoken as a list, and say where each is fixed. The answer is the anterior horn and the posterior horn. The anterior horn is fixed in front of the tibial surface and the posterior horn behind it. Short attachments anchor both ends to the bone.

Question 2232. A fragment of meniscus lies between the femur and the tibia and blocks extension, while its ends stay attached. Which injury is described: a bucket-handle tear, a radial tear, a horizontal tear, or a flap tear? The answer is a bucket-handle tear. A long strip splits from the inner edge, displaces into the joint, and keeps a bridge at each end.

Question 2233. Which bone is the largest sesamoid bone in the body, lying within the tendon of the quadriceps muscle in front of the knee? The answer is the patella. It is a triangular bone with its base above and its apex below. It is the only bone that develops inside a tendon.

Question 2234. Which of these structures continues below the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity: the quadriceps tendon, the patellar ligament, the iliotibial band, or the medial collateral ligament? The answer is the patellar ligament. It is the continuation of the quadriceps tendon beyond the bone. The quadriceps tendon itself attaches to the base above.

Question 2235. Which structure lies immediately behind the patella, between it and the femur, and what is its function? The answer is the articular cartilage of the patella, which faces the groove on the femur. It is the thickest layer of articular cartilage in the body. It spreads the pull of the quadriceps across the front of the knee.

Question 2236. A constructed illustration: a person kneels on a hard floor for a long time, and a fluid-filled swelling appears over the front of the knee. Which bursa is involved? The answer is the prepatellar bursa, which lies between the skin and the front of the patella. It is the bursa that takes the pressure of kneeling.

Question 2237. A described radiograph taken along the shaft of a bent knee shows the patella as a rounded shadow sitting between two ridges on the lower end of the femur. Which joint is shown, and which part of the patella takes the greater load? The answer is the joint between the patella and the femur. Its outer facet takes the greater load.

Question 2238. Which part of the patella meets the femur only when the knee is fully bent: the base, the medial facet, the odd facet, or the apex? The answer is the odd facet. It lies on the far inner edge of the articular surface. It comes into contact only in deep flexion, which is why it wears early in some people.

Question 2239. True or false: the patella increases the leverage of the quadriceps muscle. The answer is true. Standing away from the joint, it holds the tendon clear of the femur. That distance gives the muscle a longer lever arm, so the same pull has a greater turning effect.

Question 2240. Which of these pairs belongs together: the base of the patella with the quadriceps tendon, the apex of the patella with the quadriceps tendon, the base with the tibial tuberosity, or the apex with the femur? The answer is the base of the patella with the quadriceps tendon. The apex joins the patellar ligament below. The tendon above and the ligament below are one continuous band.

Question 2241. Which muscle of the thigh sends fibers into the inner border of the patella and pulls it inward during extension? The answer is the vastus medialis, whose lowest fibers are named the vastus medialis oblique. Those fibers slant down to the inner edge of the bone. They resist the outward drift of the patella.

Question 2242. When the angle between the line from the hip bone to the patella and the line from the patella to the tibial tuberosity is larger than usual, which is most likely: outward dislocation of the patella, inward dislocation, quadriceps paralysis, or a detached patellar ligament? The answer is outward dislocation of the patella. A larger angle directs the pull of the quadriceps more outward.

Question 2243. With the knee fully straight, the patella rests high against the front of the femur, and with the knee fully bent it lies lower within the groove. In which direction does the bone move as the knee bends, and why? The answer is downward, because the condyles of the femur roll backward over the tibia. The patella is carried with the quadriceps tendon.

Question 2244. What is the name of the fibrous sleeve that surrounds the knee joint, attached above to the femur and below to the tibia? The answer is the joint capsule. It is a strong fibrous layer lined on the inside by synovial membrane. It is incomplete in front, where the patella and its ligaments lie.

Question 2245. Which of these structures produces the synovial fluid of the knee: the joint capsule, the synovial membrane, the menisci, or the articular cartilage? The answer is the synovial membrane. It lines the inside of the capsule and covers the structures that lie within the joint. It secretes the fluid that lubricates the surfaces.

Question 2246. Which ligaments of the knee lie within the capsule but outside its synovial lining? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament and the posterior cruciate ligament. They are intracapsular but extrasynovial, wrapped in a fold of the synovial membrane. The synovial fluid therefore does not bathe them directly.

Question 2247. A constructed illustration: a knee that has been inflamed for weeks is swollen with clear fluid, and the fluid cannot be felt outside the capsule. Which structure produced the fluid? The answer is the synovial membrane, which lines the capsule. The fibrous capsule confines the fluid to the joint cavity. Its shape explains why the swelling appears where the capsule is thinnest.

Question 2248. A described view through an instrument inside the knee shows a smooth white lining over the inner wall of the cavity, with folds of tissue passing around two crossing ligaments in the middle. What is the white lining, and what are the folds? The answer is the synovial membrane, with the folds that wrap the cruciate ligaments. The membrane lines the cavity except at the articular surfaces.

Question 2249. Which opening in the capsule of the knee allows the tendon of a muscle to pass out of the joint: the opening for the popliteus tendon, the opening for the patellar ligament, the opening for the iliotibial band, or the opening for the medial collateral ligament? The answer is the opening for the popliteus tendon. No other muscle tendon leaves this joint.

Question 2250. True or false: the fibrous capsule of the knee is strengthened at the back by the oblique popliteal ligament. The answer is true. That ligament crosses the back of the joint and blends with the capsule. The back of the capsule is also reinforced by the tendon of the semimembranosus muscle.

Question 2251. Which bursa of the knee lies between the tendon of the semimembranosus muscle and the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle? The answer is the semimembranosus bursa. It lies in the inner part of the back of the knee. It often communicates with the joint cavity, which is why a swelling there can follow an effusion.

Question 2252. Which structure is a large pouch of the synovial cavity of the knee that extends upward beneath the quadriceps muscle: the prepatellar bursa, the suprapatellar bursa, the deep infrapatellar bursa, or the semimembranosus bursa? The answer is the suprapatellar bursa. Being part of the cavity, it fills when the joint fills.

Question 2253. Which of these pairs belongs together: the prepatellar bursa with the skin over the patella, the prepatellar bursa with the joint cavity, the suprapatellar bursa with the tibia, or the deep infrapatellar bursa with the femur? The answer is the prepatellar bursa with the skin over the patella. It lies in the loose tissue just beneath the skin. It does not normally open into the joint.

Question 2254. A constructed illustration: weeks after a knee injury the joint remains swollen, the pouch above the patella bulges, and the knee is held slightly bent. Why does the knee rest in that position? The answer is that the capsule is most relaxed in slight flexion, so the cavity holds the most fluid there. Bending the knee a little keeps the pressure lowest.

Question 2255. Which bone of the ankle carries the weight of the body from the leg to the foot, sitting between the two malleoli? The answer is the talus. It has no muscle attached to it. It passes the whole weight of the body to the heel and the forefoot.

Question 2256. Which three bones form the ankle joint: the tibia, the fibula and the talus; the tibia, the fibula and the calcaneus; the talus, the calcaneus and the navicular; or the tibia, the talus and the navicular? The answer is the tibia, the fibula and the talus. Those two bones form the socket that holds the talus.

Question 2257. A described radiograph taken from the front shows a square socket formed by two bones above and a rounded bone held inside it. Which joint is shown, and which bone lies within the socket? The answer is the ankle joint, with the talus within the socket. The socket is formed by the tibia and the fibula. The rounded upper surface of the talus fits it closely.

Question 2258. The deltoid ligament spreads from the medial malleolus in several bands. Which bone does its deepest and strongest band reach, and what does that band hold? The answer is the talus, which the band holds against the inner side of the socket. The other bands reach the calcaneus and the navicular. The deep band is the strongest part of the ligament.

Question 2259. A constructed illustration: a foot rolls inward under the body, the outer side of the ankle swells, and the joint is tender in front of the outer malleolus. Which ligament is most likely torn? The answer is the anterior talofibular ligament. It is the weakest and the most often injured of the ligaments on the outer side, and the strain falls on it first.

Question 2260. Which bone forms the heel and is the largest bone of the foot? The answer is the calcaneus. It lies below the talus and projects backward to form the heel. The tendon of the calf muscles attaches to its back. It is the first bone of the foot to meet the ground in standing and walking.

Question 2261. Which ligament of the ankle lies furthest back in the group on the outer side, so that it is torn last when the foot rolls inward: the anterior talofibular ligament, the calcaneofibular ligament, the posterior talofibular ligament, or the deltoid ligament? The answer is the posterior talofibular ligament. In the common sprain the front ligament tears first.

Question 2262. A described stress radiograph taken with the foot pushed inward shows a wide gap on the outer side of the ankle. Which ligaments have failed, and what else must be considered? The answer is the anterior talofibular ligament with the calcaneofibular ligament. A gap that wide means more than one ligament has torn, so injury to the ligaments joining the two leg bones must be excluded.

Question 2263. Which structures pass behind the medial malleolus, and in what order from front to back? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior, the tendon of the flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery with its veins, the tibial nerve, and the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus. All lie in a fibrous tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum.

Question 2264. Which bone of the foot lies between the talus behind it and the cuneiform bones in front, and receives the head of the talus in a socket? The answer is the navicular. It lies on the inner side of the midfoot. Its tuberosity can be felt on the inner border of the foot.

Question 2265. Which of these bones belongs to the midfoot rather than the hindfoot: the calcaneus, the talus, the cuboid, or the first metatarsal? The answer is the cuboid. The talus and the calcaneus form the hindfoot. The cuboid lies in front of the calcaneus and joins the fourth and fifth metatarsals.

Question 2266. Which of these pairs belongs together: the deltoid ligament with the medial malleolus, the deltoid ligament with the lateral malleolus, the anterior talofibular ligament with the medial malleolus, or the calcaneofibular ligament with the tibia? The answer is the deltoid ligament with the medial malleolus. The three ligaments of the outer side all arise from the lateral malleolus.

Question 2267. A constructed illustration: the foot is forced outward, the inner side of the ankle is injured, and the outer malleolus is broken. Which ligament and which bone are involved, and why do the two go together? The answer is the deltoid ligament and the lateral malleolus. The strong inner ligament resists the outward drive, and the outer bone gives way as the talus presses against it.

Question 2268. Which bony shelf of the calcaneus supports the talus from below and gives attachment to a strong ligament of the ankle? The answer is the sustentaculum tali. It projects inward from the inner side of the calcaneus. The spring ligament runs forward from it to the navicular bone.

Question 2269. Which statement about the joint below the ankle is correct: it is the main joint of turning the sole, it is a hinge that only bends the foot, it lies between the calcaneus and the navicular, or it is the same as the ankle joint? The answer is that it turns the sole inward and outward. It lies between the talus and the calcaneus.

Question 2270. A described radiograph of the foot taken from the side shows a large bone at the back forming the heel, a smaller bone above it, and a row of bones running forward. Which bones are shown, and which of them lies highest? The answer is the calcaneus, the talus and the metatarsals, with the talus highest. The arch descends from the talus forward to the toes.

Question 2271. The plantar fascia spreads from the heel to the front of the foot. Which structures lie immediately deep to it along the sole? The answer is the short muscles of the foot and the tendons that they cover. The fascia forms a tough band beneath the skin of the sole. It helps to hold up the arch of the foot.

Question 2272. What are the five long bones of the foot that run from the midfoot forward to the toes called? The answer is the metatarsals. Each has a base behind and a head in front. The first is the shortest and the thickest, and it carries the great toe.

Question 2273. Which of these numbers is the number of metatarsal bones in one foot: four, five, seven, or fourteen? The answer is five. The tarsal bones behind them number seven. The bones of the toes number fourteen, and the metatarsals themselves run from the midfoot forward.

Question 2274. A constructed illustration: a runner feels a sudden snap at the back of the heel, cannot rise on the toes, and a gap can be felt in the band above the heel. Which structure has ruptured? The answer is the calcaneal tendon, also called the Achilles tendon. It is formed by the calf muscles and attaches to the calcaneus, and the foot can no longer be pushed down.

Question 2275. Which tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and attaches mainly to the tuberosity of the navicular, holding up the arch of the foot? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior. It is the strongest support of the medial arch. When it fails, the arch drops and the foot flattens.

Question 2276. Which of these bones forms the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch: the calcaneus, the talus, the navicular, or the first metatarsal? The answer is the talus. It receives the weight from the leg and passes it to the arch behind and in front. The arch itself is completed by the calcaneus behind and by the navicular, the cuneiforms and the first three metatarsals in front.

Question 2277. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the ankle, cut across the joint just above the two malleoli, shows a dark band joining the tibia to the fibula. Which structure is shown, and what does it do? The answer is the tibiofibular ligament, which binds the two bones together. It holds the socket closed so that the talus cannot wedge the bones apart.

Question 2278. Which tendon turns under the cuboid bone on the outer side of the foot and crosses the sole to the inner border? The answer is the tendon of the fibularis longus muscle. It runs behind the lateral malleolus and grooves the underside of the cuboid. It ends on the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform and supports the arches.

Question 2279. How many phalanges does the great toe have, and what are they called? The answer is two, the proximal phalanx and the distal phalanx. Each of the other toes has three. The missing middle bone is what makes the great toe short and thick.

Question 2280. Which small bones lie within the tendons beneath the head of the first metatarsal: the cuneiform bones, the sesamoid bones, the accessory navicular, or the cuboid? The answer is the sesamoid bones. Two of them lie beneath the head of the first metatarsal, within the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis.

Question 2281. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medial longitudinal arch with the talus, the lateral longitudinal arch with the talus, the transverse arch with the calcaneus alone, or the medial arch with the cuboid alone? The answer is the medial longitudinal arch with the talus. The lateral arch is formed by the calcaneus, the cuboid and the fourth and fifth metatarsals.

Question 2282. Name three bones that take part in the medial longitudinal arch of the foot, spoken as a list. The answer is the calcaneus, the navicular and the first metatarsal. The talus rests upon the arch between them. The arch is held by the plantar fascia and by the tendons that run along the sole.

Question 2283. A described ultrasound scan of the sole of the foot shows a thick band running from the heel forward, swollen where it attaches to the heel. Which structure is shown, and why does it become painful? The answer is the plantar fascia, inflamed at its attachment to the calcaneus. It is stretched with every step as the arch flattens.

Question 2284. Which ligament runs from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular and is the chief support of the head of the talus? The answer is the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, also called the spring ligament. It lies beneath the head of the talus. If it stretches, the head of the talus drops and the arch of the foot gives way.

Question 2285. Why has the talus no muscle attached to it: because it is covered by cartilage, because the socket of the ankle holds it, because it is too small for a tendon, or because it fuses to the calcaneus? The answer is that the socket of the ankle holds it. Almost all of its surface is articular, so tendons pass over it.

Question 2286. A described computed tomography scan of the ankle shows a fragment of bone separated from the back of the tibia and a second fragment from the outer malleolus. Which injury is shown, and which structure between the two leg bones must be assessed? The answer is a fracture of both malleoli, with the tibiofibular ligament between the bones. If that ligament is torn, the socket is unstable.

Question 2287. Which of these structures occupies the channel between the talus and the calcaneus on the outer side of the foot: the tarsal tunnel, the sinus tarsi, the spring ligament, or the plantar fascia? The answer is the sinus tarsi. It is a funnel-shaped channel running inward between the two bones. It contains fat, vessels and ligaments and can be felt in front of the outer malleolus.

Question 2288. Which ligament, shaped like a triangle, spreads from the medial malleolus to the talus, the calcaneus and the navicular? The answer is the deltoid ligament. It is the great ligament of the inner side of the ankle. It is much stronger than the separate ligaments of the outer side.

Question 2289. Which movements take place at the ankle joint: bending and straightening of the foot, turning the sole inward and outward, both of these, or neither of these? The answer is bending and straightening of the foot. The ankle is a hinge between the leg and the talus. Turning the sole inward and outward takes place mainly at the joint below it.

Question 2290. A break of the fibula high near the knee, far from the ankle, with tenderness on the inner side of the ankle, is explained by which mechanism: the force traveled up from the ankle, a direct blow, a knee dislocation, or an ankle that escaped injury? The answer is that the force traveled up from the ankle. The inner ligament of the ankle tore first, and the strain passed up the bone.

Question 2291. A described radiograph of an ankle shows a clear space between the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula, wider than it should be. Which structure has failed, and what happens to the socket? The answer is the tibiofibular ligament, which has torn. The socket widens and the talus can shift within it.

Question 2292. Which muscle of the outer side of the leg ends on the base of the fifth metatarsal, and what movement does it produce? The answer is the fibularis brevis, which turns the sole outward. The fibularis longus lies beside it and crosses the sole. Both lie in the outer compartment of the leg.

Question 2293. Why can the foot turn inward and outward as well as bend up and down: because the ankle has two axes, because the joint below it has one sloping axis, because the midfoot joints are rigid, or because the ankle is a ball and socket? The answer is the joint below the ankle, with its sloping axis. Being oblique, that axis turns the sole and swings the front of the foot.

Question 2294. A described photograph of the inner side of an ankle shows a rounded bony knob with a fan-shaped band spreading downward from it in three directions. Which bone forms the knob, and which ligament is the fan? The answer is the medial malleolus of the tibia, with the deltoid ligament. The band reaches the talus, the calcaneus and the navicular.

Question 2295. Which statement about the bones of the foot is correct: the first metatarsal carries two sesamoid bones beneath its head, the fifth metatarsal has no tuberosity, the cuboid lies in front of the navicular, or the talus takes no part in the arches? The answer is that the first metatarsal carries two sesamoid bones beneath its head. The cuboid lies in front of the calcaneus, not the navicular.

Question 2296. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the foot shows a fibrous band running from the heel to the toes, and another band rising behind the ankle. Which structures are shown, and which one is inflamed in a painful heel? The answer is the plantar fascia below and the calcaneal tendon behind. The fascia is the one that becomes inflamed at the heel.

Question 2297. Why does a fracture of the neck of the talus threaten the bone: because the bone has no vessels of its own, because its vessels enter through the neck, because it lies outside the ankle joint, or because it is covered by the plantar fascia? The answer is that its vessels enter through the neck. A fracture there can cut them off, and the bone may die and collapse.

Question 2298. Which extra piece of bone, present in some people, lies at the inner border of the foot above the tuberosity of the navicular and may be mistaken for a fracture? The answer is the accessory navicular bone. It is a common variant within the tendon of the tibialis posterior and can become painful after a strain.

Question 2299. Which statement about the fibula at the ankle is correct: it bears almost none of the weight and still completes the socket, it bears half of the body weight, it forms the medial malleolus, or it takes no part in the joint? The answer is that it bears almost none of the weight and still completes the socket. The tibia carries the load through the talus.

Question 2300. A described cross section through the lower leg shows a triangular bone on the inner side and a slender bone on the outer side, joined by a strong membrane. What is the membrane, and what does it do at the ankle? The answer is the interosseous membrane, which joins the two bones along their shafts. It holds them together as the socket grips the talus.

To summarize, the knee is braced by the medial collateral ligament, which blends with the capsule and the medial meniscus, and by the lateral collateral ligament, a cord separated from the lateral meniscus by the popliteus tendon. The menisci are C-shaped plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the tibial surface, heal only at their outer rim, and tear with rotation of the bent knee. The patella is a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon that increases the leverage of that muscle and glides in the femoral groove, its odd facet meeting the femur only in deep flexion. The capsule is lined by synovial membrane, carries the cruciate ligaments outside that lining, and sends the suprapatellar pouch upward beneath the quadriceps. At the ankle the tibia and the fibula grip the talus in a socket, the deltoid ligament holds the inner side, and the three ligaments of the outer side are injured in the common sprain. The arches of the foot rest on the plantar fascia, the tibialis posterior tendon and the spring ligament, the joint below the ankle gives the foot its inward and outward roll, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 24 — General Muscle Anatomy

Every movement of the body comes from muscle, and this chapter sets out the general anatomy of that tissue rather than the details of particular named muscles. It follows the muscle fiber from its membrane and its filaments to the sheaths that bind the fibers into a belly, then the tendons and the broad aponeuroses by which a muscle takes hold of bone, then the origin and the insertion that fix the two ends of that pull, and finally the agonists, the antagonists and the helpers that carry a movement out. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2301. Which contractile cell is the basic unit of a skeletal muscle, and does it hold one nucleus or many? The answer is the muscle fiber, which holds many nuclei. A fiber forms in development by the fusion of many precursor cells, so its nuclei lie just beneath the surface membrane. A single fiber may run the whole length of a short muscle.

Question 2302. Which of these is the thin filament of a muscle fiber: myosin, actin, titin, or collagen? The answer is actin. Thin filaments are anchored at the Z line and are drawn toward the middle of the sarcomere by the thicker myosin filaments. Titin is an elastic protein that keeps the thick filaments centered, and collagen belongs to the connective tissue around the fiber.

Question 2303. A described microscopic section of a muscle fiber shows a dark band crossed at its middle by a thin darker line, and beside it a light band divided by another dark line. Which structure is the line in the light band? The answer is the Z line, which marks the boundary between one sarcomere and the next. The line in the middle of the dark band is the M line.

Question 2304. What name is given to the segment of a myofibril that lies between one Z line and the next? The answer is the sarcomere. It is the smallest unit that shortens when a muscle contracts. Within it, thin actin filaments slide past thick myosin filaments toward the middle of the segment.

Question 2305. During the contraction of a muscle fiber, which of these changes its length: the A band, the thick myosin filament, the sarcomere, or the thin actin filament? The answer is the sarcomere. The filaments themselves keep their length and slide past one another, so the A band stays the same while the sarcomere shortens.

Question 2306. Which structure lies within the fiber, wraps around each myofibril as a sleeve of flattened sacs, and stores the calcium that starts contraction? The answer is the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Its expanded ends, the terminal cisternae, lie close to a T tubule, and the three together form a triad.

Question 2307. What is the name of the narrow channel that is an inward fold of the sarcolemma and carries the signal for contraction deep into a muscle fiber? The answer is the T tubule. Because it is a fold of the surface membrane, its interior is continuous with the space outside the fiber. Two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum lie beside it.

Question 2308. Which ion must reach the cytoplasm of a muscle fiber before the myofilaments can slide: sodium, calcium, potassium, or chloride? The answer is calcium. It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the actin and lets the myosin heads attach. Sodium carries the signal along the membrane but does not switch the filaments on.

Question 2309. Name the two kinds of myofilament that make up a sarcomere, spoken as a list. The answer is actin and myosin. Actin forms the thin filament, which is anchored at the Z line, and myosin forms the thick filament, whose heads pull the thin filaments inward. The regular overlap of the two gives skeletal muscle its striated appearance.

Question 2310. Which pair belongs together: the Z line with the boundary of the sarcomere, the M line with the boundary of the sarcomere, the A band with thin filaments only, or the I band with thick filaments only? The answer is the Z line with the boundary of the sarcomere. The M line lies in the middle of the A band, which holds the thick filaments, while the I band holds only thin filaments.

Question 2311. True or false: the A band of a sarcomere is the dark band and it contains the thick myosin filaments. The answer is true. The dark appearance comes from the thick filaments together with the thin filaments that overlap them at each end of the band. The light I band beside it contains thin filaments alone.

Question 2312. A described cross section of a muscle shows a bundle of fibers wrapped in a sheath of connective tissue, and the whole muscle wrapped in a second sheath. What are those two sheaths called? The answer is the perimysium around the bundle and the epimysium around the whole muscle. The finest of the three sheaths lies inside the bundle.

Question 2313. What name is given to a bundle of muscle fibers wrapped together by perimysium? The answer is a fascicle. The fibers in a fascicle run in the same direction, so the bundle acts as one strand of the muscle. The pattern in which the fascicles are arranged gives a muscle its shape and its power.

Question 2314. A muscle whose fascicles run the whole length of the belly and pull on a tendon at each end is described by which of these words: pennate, parallel, circular, or convergent? The answer is parallel. A parallel muscle shortens over a long distance and can move a joint through a wide range. A pennate muscle packs in more fibers and pulls harder, but it shortens less.

Question 2315. A described specimen shows a muscle whose fibers run at a slant into a tendon that lies along one side of the belly only. How is that arrangement named? The answer is unipennate. In a bipennate muscle the tendon lies in the middle and fibers slant into it from both sides. A multipennate muscle has several such tendons and looks like a feather.

Question 2316. Which arrangement allows a muscle to produce the greatest force: a long parallel belly, many short fibers set at a slant, fibers forming a ring around an opening, or fibers converging on one tendon? The answer is many short fibers set at a slant, which is the pennate pattern. More fibers fit into the same volume, and each adds its pull. The price is a shorter range of movement.

Question 2317. A constructed illustration: after weeks in a cast, a limb is weak and the muscle feels smaller than the other side. Which part of the muscle has been lost? The answer is the myofilaments inside the fibers, which shrink when they are not used. The connective tissue sheaths remain, and the fibers can enlarge again when the muscle works.

Question 2318. In the thigh, which layer of connective tissue lies between the skin and the epimysium of the quadriceps, and sends a septum inward to the femur? The answer is the deep fascia, called the fascia lata in the thigh. It wraps the whole limb like a stocking and gives attachment to muscles. The epimysium lies deep to it.

Question 2319. Which protein lies along the actin filament and blocks the sites where the myosin heads would attach while the fiber is at rest? The answer is tropomyosin. It is held in that blocking position by troponin. When calcium binds troponin, tropomyosin shifts aside and the myosin heads can attach.

Question 2320. A described high magnification section shows a thick filament with fine elastic strands running from its middle to the Z line. Which protein forms those strands, and what is their task? The answer is titin. It springs back after the fiber has been stretched, and it keeps the thick filament centered in the sarcomere.

Question 2321. A constructed illustration: after the nerve to a limb muscle is cut, the muscle becomes weak and flat over several months. What has happened inside the fibers, and which sheaths remain? The answer is that the myofilaments are lost and the fibers shrink, while the endomysium, the perimysium and the epimysium stay. The muscle cannot recover unless the nerve grows back to it.

Question 2322. Which statement about a motor unit is correct: it is one muscle fiber with one nerve fiber, it is one motor neuron with all the fibers it supplies, it is all the fibers of one fascicle, or it is one muscle with its tendon? The answer is one motor neuron with all the fibers it supplies. Muscles that need fine control, such as those moving the eye, have small motor units.

Question 2323. In the arm, which nerve lies in the plane between the biceps brachii and the brachialis, after piercing the coracobrachialis? The answer is the musculocutaneous nerve. It supplies both of those muscles and then continues as a sensory nerve to the outer side of the forearm.

Question 2324. Which statement about the two kinds of skeletal muscle fiber is correct: type one fibers are fast and white, type one fibers are slow, red and resistant to fatigue, type two fibers resist fatigue best, or both kinds hold equal myoglobin? The answer is that type one fibers are slow, red and resistant to fatigue. Type two fibers contract faster and tire sooner. Postural muscles such as the soleus are rich in them.

Question 2325. During a maximal contraction, which statement about the bands of the sarcomere is correct: both the A band and the I band shorten, the A band shortens and the I band is unchanged, the A band is unchanged and the I band shortens, or neither band changes? The answer is that the A band is unchanged and the I band shortens. The thick filaments keep their length as the thin filaments slide inward.

Question 2326. What is the name of the tough cord of fibrous tissue that joins a muscle to a bone? The answer is a tendon. It is built of parallel bundles of collagen that resist being pulled apart. At its two ends the tendon blends with the muscle at one end and with the bone at the other.

Question 2327. Which of these tissues makes up the bulk of a tendon: loose fatty tissue, dense regular collagen, elastic cartilage, or smooth muscle? The answer is dense regular collagen. The bundles lie parallel to the line of pull, which is why a tendon is so strong in one direction and weak across it. A ligament is made of the same tissue.

Question 2328. Which tendon, the strongest in the body, is formed by the gastrocnemius and the soleus and ends on the heel bone? The answer is the calcaneal tendon, also called the Achilles tendon. The two calf muscles join above the heel, and the plantaris tendon lies beside them. The tendon reaches the calcaneus, where it can be felt as a taut cord.

Question 2329. A described section through the ankle shows a thick dark band passing behind the joint to reach the heel. Which structure is it, and what does it carry? The answer is the calcaneal tendon, which carries the pull of the calf muscles to the calcaneus. It lies just beneath the skin, and it stands out when the foot is pointed.

Question 2330. Which group of tendons forms a cuff around the shoulder joint and holds the head of the humerus against its socket: the tendons of the rotator cuff, the tendons of the forearm flexors, the tendons of the hamstrings, or the tendons of the calf? The answer is the tendons of the rotator cuff. Four short muscles blend with the capsule of the joint before they insert on the humerus.

Question 2331. Which tendon runs through the intertubercular groove of the humerus, held there by the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii. It arises from the supraglenoid tubercle above the shoulder joint and passes down the groove to join the muscle in the arm.

Question 2332. What is the name of the fibrous band that joins one bone to another, as opposed to the cord that joins a muscle to a bone? The answer is a ligament. It crosses a joint and holds the bones together while still allowing them to move. The band that joins muscle to bone is a tendon.

Question 2333. Which statement about a tendon and a ligament is correct: a tendon joins muscle to bone and a ligament joins bone to bone, both join muscle to bone, a tendon joins bone to bone, or neither contains collagen? The answer is that a tendon joins muscle to bone and a ligament joins bone to bone. Both are dense regular collagen, so only their two ends tell them apart.

Question 2334. A described ultrasound picture of the back of the ankle shows a band that is no longer continuous, with a dark gap between the two ends. Which structure has been torn, and what fills the gap? The answer is the calcaneal tendon, and the gap fills with blood and fluid. A normal tendon would appear as unbroken bright parallel lines.

Question 2335. True or false: a tendon has a poor blood supply, especially in its middle, and therefore heals slowly. The answer is true. Blood reaches a tendon mainly where it joins the muscle and where it joins the bone. The middle of a long tendon receives little, which is one reason a rupture there is slow to repair.

Question 2336. Which pair belongs together: the gastrocnemius with the calcaneus, the biceps brachii with the olecranon, the deltoid with the radial tuberosity, or the triceps brachii with the lesser tubercle? The answer is the gastrocnemius with the calcaneus. The triceps brachii ends on the olecranon, the biceps brachii on the radial tuberosity, and the deltoid on the deltoid tuberosity.

Question 2337. What name is given to the seam of fibrous tissue where the fibers of two muscles interlace, as in the floor of the mouth or the middle of the back of the neck? The answer is a raphe. It is not a tendon, because no bone lies at its ends. It is the meeting line of two muscles that share a task.

Question 2338. Which structure is a small fluid filled sac that lies between a tendon and a bone and lessens friction where the tendon changes direction? The answer is a bursa. It is lined by a synovial membrane and holds a thin film of fluid. A bursa differs from a tendon sheath, which wraps the tendon along its length.

Question 2339. A described microscopic section shows dense wavy bundles of collagen running in one direction, with flattened cells squeezed in rows between the bundles, and no blood vessels in the field. Which tissue is it? The answer is dense regular connective tissue, the tissue of a tendon. The flattened cells are the tendon cells that make and maintain the collagen.

Question 2340. A constructed illustration: while pushing off to run, a person feels a sudden snap at the back of the heel and can no longer point the foot. Which structure has given way? The answer is the calcaneal tendon. The illustration describes the usual story of a tendon that was already worn; what is done about it belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2341. Which structure wraps a tendon where it passes under a fibrous band at the wrist, and allows it to glide to and fro? The answer is a synovial tendon sheath. It has an outer fibrous layer and an inner layer that secretes fluid. Where a tendon rubs over a bone without such a sheath, a bursa takes its place.

Question 2342. Which receptor warns the muscle when the tension in its tendon becomes dangerous: the muscle spindle, the Golgi tendon organ, a free nerve ending, or a Pacinian corpuscle? The answer is the Golgi tendon organ. It lies in the tendon and fires as tension rises, which causes the muscle to relax. The muscle spindle measures length rather than tension.

Question 2343. A constructed illustration: repeated gripping and lifting brings pain to the outer side of the elbow, over the point where the forearm muscles take hold. Which tendon is involved? The answer is the common extensor tendon at the lateral epicondyle. The muscles that straighten the wrist and the fingers share that tendon, and its care belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2344. Which band of fibrous tissue holds the tendons of the wrist against the bones and forms the roof of the carpal tunnel? The answer is the flexor retinaculum. It stretches between the two rows of wrist bones and stops the tendons from bowing forward when the fingers bend. The median nerve passes beneath it with the tendons.

Question 2345. Which statement about the blood supply of a tendon is correct: it is rich throughout and heals quickly, it is richest in the middle and poorest at the ends, it is poor in the middle and comes mainly from the muscle end and the bone end, or a tendon holds no vessels at all? The answer is that it is poor in the middle and comes mainly from the ends.

Question 2346. A described section through the attachment of a tendon to bone shows fibers running obliquely into the bone and blending with its outer layer. Which fibers are they, and what do they achieve? The answer is Sharpey fibers. They fix the tendon into the bone and spread the pull of the muscle over a wide area instead of a single point.

Question 2347. Which statement about a small bone that develops inside a tendon is correct: it changes the direction of the muscle pull and reduces friction, it is made of elastic cartilage, it replaces the tendon, or it is found only in the hand? The answer is that it changes the direction of the pull and reduces friction. The patella is the largest example, lying in the tendon of the quadriceps.

Question 2348. What is the name of a broad flat sheet of fibrous tissue that takes the place of a tendon where a muscle is wide? The answer is an aponeurosis. It is built like a tendon, of parallel collagen bundles, but spread out as a sheet rather than gathered into a cord. It gives the muscle a wide grip on what it pulls.

Question 2349. Which of these is an aponeurosis: the calcaneal tendon, the fibrous sheet in the palm of the hand, the round cord behind the heel, or the anterior cruciate ligament of the knee? The answer is the fibrous sheet in the palm, which is the palmar aponeurosis. The others are a round tendon and a ligament.

Question 2350. Which aponeurosis turns its lower border inward to form the inguinal ligament along the groin? The answer is the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. Its lower edge thickens and rolls back on itself to make the ligament. It also leaves a gap, the superficial ring, above the pubic bone.

Question 2351. A described dissection of the palm shows a thick triangular sheet of fibrous tissue running from the wrist to the bases of the fingers, with long tendons lying deep to it. Which structure is it? The answer is the palmar aponeurosis. It protects the tendons, vessels and nerves beneath it and anchors the skin so that the grip does not slip.

Question 2352. Which broad aponeurosis covers the top of the skull and is tugged from front and back by the muscles of the scalp: the epicranial aponeurosis, the thoracolumbar fascia, the linea alba, or the plantar aponeurosis? The answer is the epicranial aponeurosis, also called the galea. The frontalis pulls it forward and the occipitalis pulls it back.

Question 2353. Which deep sheet of fibrous tissue in the lower back gives attachment to the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis, and lies behind the muscles that straighten the spine? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia. It stretches between the lower ribs, the spine and the pelvis, and it also wraps the deep muscles of the back.

Question 2354. True or false: an aponeurosis is a flattened tendon. The answer is true. It is made of the same parallel collagen bundles as a tendon but spread as a broad sheet. The aponeurosis of the external oblique and the plantar aponeurosis of the foot are two familiar examples.

Question 2355. Name two aponeuroses of the body, spoken as a list, one in the abdominal wall and one in the sole of the foot. The answer is the aponeurosis of the external oblique and the plantar aponeurosis. The first helps to hold the abdominal contents in place. The second runs from the heel to the toes and supports the arch.

Question 2356. A constructed illustration: a bulge appears in the groin above the pubic bone when a person coughs, and it passes through a gap in a flat fibrous sheet. Which sheet is it, and what is the gap called? The answer is the aponeurosis of the external oblique, and the gap is the superficial inguinal ring. The illustration is described rather than real.

Question 2357. Which midline band of fibrous tissue in the abdomen is formed by the interlocking aponeuroses of the two sides, and why is it a convenient line of approach? The answer is the linea alba. It runs from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis and carries few vessels, so it can be opened with little bleeding. It is the seam of the abdominal wall.

Question 2358. A described section through the sole of the foot shows a thick band of fibrous tissue running from the heel to the heads of the metatarsal bones, with short muscles deep to it. Which structure is it, and what does it do? The answer is the plantar aponeurosis, which supports the arch and holds the parts of the foot together.

Question 2359. Which structures lie deep to the bicipital aponeurosis where it passes from the tendon of the biceps to the deep fascia of the forearm? The answer is the brachial artery and the median nerve. The sheet therefore protects them, and the pulse of the artery can be felt just medial to the tendon.

Question 2360. A constructed illustration: a person has pain beneath the heel that is worst on the first steps of the morning and eases with walking. Which structure is the seat of the pain? The answer is the plantar aponeurosis where it takes hold of the heel bone. The illustration is constructed rather than drawn from a real patient, and its care belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2361. Which pair belongs together: the aponeurosis of the external oblique with the inguinal ligament, the palmar aponeurosis with the sole, the epicranial aponeurosis with the abdominal wall, or the plantar aponeurosis with the palm? The answer is the aponeurosis of the external oblique with the inguinal ligament, which is formed by its rolled lower border.

Question 2362. Above the umbilicus, which aponeuroses form the front of the sheath around the rectus abdominis? The answer is the aponeurosis of the external oblique together with the front layer of the internal oblique. The back of the sheath at that level is formed by the other layer of the internal oblique and by the aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis.

Question 2363. What name is given to the attachment of a muscle that is relatively fixed and usually lies nearer the trunk? The answer is the origin. When the muscle contracts it pulls the movable end toward this fixed end. If the far end is held still instead, the two ends exchange their parts.

Question 2364. From which two points does the biceps brachii arise: the olecranon and the radial tuberosity, the coracoid process and the supraglenoid tubercle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, or the lateral epicondyle and the ulna? The answer is the coracoid process, for the short head, and the supraglenoid tubercle, for the long head.

Question 2365. From which bone does the gastrocnemius arise, above the knee joint? The answer is the femur, from the back of its two condyles. Because it starts above the knee, the gastrocnemius crosses that joint and can help to bend it. The soleus arises below the knee from the tibia and the fibula.

Question 2366. A described dissection of the back shows a large flat muscle arising from the skull, the ligament of the neck and the spines of the thoracic vertebrae, and ending on the shoulder blade and the outer third of the clavicle. Which muscle is it? The answer is the trapezius. Its two sides together make a diamond across the upper back.

Question 2367. Which broad muscle arises from the spines of the lower thoracic vertebrae, the lumbar vertebrae and the iliac crest, and then turns forward to end on the humerus? The answer is the latissimus dorsi. Its fibers converge into a flat tendon that twists to reach the front of the upper arm. It forms the back wall of the armpit.

Question 2368. Which of these muscles arises from the sternum, the upper six costal cartilages and the medial half of the clavicle: the pectoralis major, the pectoralis minor, the serratus anterior, or the trapezius? The answer is the pectoralis major. Its fibers converge on the humerus and form the front wall of the armpit.

Question 2369. Which muscle arises from the xiphoid process, the lower six ribs and the upper lumbar vertebrae, and forms the floor of the thoracic cavity? The answer is the diaphragm. Its muscular fibers arch up from those origins and end in a central tendon. The two crura, its lowest parts, arise from the lumbar vertebrae.
