Question 2370. Which strap-like muscle arises from the pubic crest and the pubic symphysis and runs straight up the front of the abdomen? The answer is the rectus abdominis. It lies within a sheath formed by the aponeuroses of the flat muscles at each side, and its fibers are crossed by tendinous bands.

Question 2371. A constructed illustration: a person hangs from a bar and pulls the body upward until the chin reaches the hands. Which end of the elbow flexors is fixed in that action? The answer is the insertion, on the radius and the ulna, while the origin moves upward with the shoulders. The same muscle therefore reverses its two ends.

Question 2372. A muscle arises from the surface of the shoulder blade that lies against the ribs and passes around the joint to insert on the front of the upper end of the humerus. In which direction does it turn the arm? The answer is inward, toward the midline. Its line of pull lies in front of the joint, and the muscle described is the subscapularis.

Question 2373. Which pair belongs together: the trapezius with the spine of the shoulder blade, the latissimus dorsi with the coracoid process, the deltoid with the lesser trochanter, or the gastrocnemius with the radius? The answer is the trapezius with the spine of the shoulder blade. The other three are paired with bones they never touch.

Question 2374. Which statement about the reversal of origin and insertion is correct: it never happens, it happens only in the limbs, the same muscle can move either bone depending on which end is fixed, or it means the muscle has changed its nerve supply? The answer is that the same muscle can move either bone depending on which end is fixed. A chin-up lifts the body toward the bar by fixing the insertion.

Question 2375. Which of these decides whether an attachment is called the origin or the insertion: the size of the muscle, which end moves during the action, how deep the muscle lies, or the number of heads it has? The answer is which end moves during the action. The fixed end is the origin and the moving end is the insertion.

Question 2376. What name is given to the attachment of a muscle that moves when the muscle contracts and usually lies farther from the trunk? The answer is the insertion. It is pulled toward the fixed origin in the usual action. The two names describe a particular movement rather than a permanent label.

Question 2377. On which bony point does the biceps brachii insert: the radial tuberosity, the olecranon, the coronoid process of the ulna, or the styloid process of the radius? The answer is the radial tuberosity. Because it pulls on the radius, the muscle bends the elbow and also turns the palm upward.

Question 2378. Which muscle inserts on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus, roughly halfway down its shaft? The answer is the deltoid. It arises from the outer third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, and it lifts the arm sideways.

Question 2379. A described dissection of the front of the thigh shows a broad flat tendon that wraps the kneecap and continues below it to the shin. Which muscle group ends in that tendon? The answer is the quadriceps femoris. Its four parts share one tendon, which holds the kneecap and then continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.

Question 2380. A described dissection of the inner side of the knee shows three tendons inserting in a row on the upper part of the tibia, fanned out like the foot of a goose. Which muscles form that group? The answer is the sartorius, the gracilis and the semitendinosus. The group is named the pes anserinus, which means the goose foot.

Question 2381. True or false: when a muscle contracts in the usual way, its insertion is pulled toward its origin. The answer is true. The origin is the fixed point at that moment and the insertion moves toward it. When the far end is held instead, the pull turns the other way around.

Question 2382. Which muscle inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus, after arising from the sternum, the upper costal cartilages and the clavicle? The answer is the pectoralis major. Its fibers twist as they approach the bone, so the lower fibers insert above the upper ones.

Question 2383. Which of these muscles inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur: the iliopsoas, the gluteus medius, the adductor magnus, or the piriformis? The answer is the iliopsoas. It arises from the lumbar vertebrae and the inner surface of the ilium and bends the hip as it pulls on that small knob.

Question 2384. Name two muscles that insert on the coracoid process of the scapula, spoken as a list. The answer is the short head of the biceps brachii and the coracobrachialis. The pectoralis minor also ends there. All three pull on the same small bony hook.

Question 2385. Which ridge on the back of the femur receives the insertion of the gluteus maximus? The answer is the gluteal tuberosity. It lies below the greater trochanter and blends with the upper part of the linea aspera. The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle of the body and straightens the hip.

Question 2386. A constructed illustration: a person stumbles and cannot straighten the knee, and the band that should run from the kneecap to the shin is no longer felt. Which structure has torn? The answer is the patellar ligament, the continuation of the quadriceps tendon. It carries the pull of the thigh muscles from the kneecap to the tibial tuberosity.

Question 2387. Where does the trapezius insert: on the lateral border of the scapula, on the coracoid process, on the spine of the scapula with the acromion and the outer third of the clavicle, or on the lesser tubercle of the humerus? The answer is the spine of the scapula, the acromion and the outer third of the clavicle.

Question 2388. Which statement about the lower attachments of the diaphragm is correct: it is a purely tendinous sheet, it reaches the lumbar vertebrae through two muscular crura, it attaches only to the sternum, or it has no bony attachment at all? The answer is that it reaches the lumbar vertebrae through two crura. Its other origins are the xiphoid process and the lower six ribs.

Question 2389. What name is given to the muscle that is chiefly responsible for a movement, as opposed to the muscle that opposes it? The answer is the agonist, also called the prime mover. The muscle that opposes the movement is the antagonist, and it usually yields by lengthening under control.

Question 2390. With the palm facing up, which muscle is the prime mover in bending the elbow: the triceps brachii, the biceps brachii, the anconeus, or the extensor digitorum? The answer is the biceps brachii. It is at its strongest in that position because it also turns the palm upward. The brachialis beneath it bends the elbow in any position.

Question 2391. True or false: the antagonist of a movement stays completely relaxed while the agonist works. The answer is false. The antagonist usually lengthens under control and steadies the movement, and it may also shorten to brake it. A muscle that is paralyzed is different from one that is simply not the prime mover.

Question 2392. What name is given to a muscle that helps an agonist by preventing an unwanted movement, such as a muscle that stops the wrist from bending while the fingers close? The answer is a synergist. A fixator is different: it steadies the origin of the prime mover, as the shoulder blade is steadied when the arm is raised.

Question 2393. A described cross section through the middle of the arm shows two muscles in front and one large muscle behind, separated by a single bone. Which muscles are they? The answer is the biceps brachii with the brachialis in front and the triceps brachii behind. The humerus lies between them and gives the section its shape.

Question 2394. A constructed illustration: a person lifts a heavy box with a bent elbow and feels a tearing pain at the front of the arm. Which muscle is the prime mover that has been strained? The answer is the biceps brachii, with the brachialis lying beneath it. The illustration is described rather than real, and its care belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2395. Which pair belongs together: the supraspinatus with the first part of raising the arm, the teres major with raising the arm above the head, the subscapularis with turning the arm outward, or the infraspinatus with turning the arm inward? The answer is the supraspinatus with the first part of raising the arm.

Question 2396. Which muscles act as fixators of the shoulder blade while the arm is raised above the head? The answer is the trapezius and the serratus anterior, helped by the rhomboids. They turn the shoulder blade upward so that its socket faces the arm, which lets the arm pass the vertical.

Question 2397. A constructed illustration: a person cannot raise the arm sideways beyond the horizontal, and there is pain over the top of the shoulder. Which tendons are chiefly involved? The answer is the tendons of the rotator cuff, above all the supraspinatus as it passes under the acromion. The illustration is described, and its care belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2398. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the shoulder shows a gap in the dark band that passes beneath the bony arch of the acromion. Which tendon has torn? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, one of the four muscles of the rotator cuff. That tendon is the one most often injured as it passes through the narrow space.

Question 2399. A muscle arises from the front of the pelvis just above the hip socket and runs down in front of the hip joint to end on the shin. About which axis does its pull act, and which movement results? The answer is the transverse axis, producing flexion of the hip, because the line of pull lies in front of the joint.

Question 2400. Which statement about the levers of the body is correct: most joints act as third class levers, most act as first class levers, most act as second class levers, or the body uses no levers? The answer is that most joints act as third class levers. The muscle pull lies between the joint and the load, which favors speed and range of movement over force.

To summarize, a skeletal muscle fiber is a long multinucleated cell whose surface membrane carries the signal inward along the T tubules to a sarcoplasmic reticulum that releases the calcium for contraction. Within each sarcomere the thin actin filaments slide past the thick myosin filaments, so the light band and the central H zone narrow while the A band keeps its length, and the three sheaths named the endomysium, the perimysium and the epimysium bind the fibers into fascicles and the fascicles into a belly. A tendon is dense regular collagen that joins muscle to bone, and an aponeurosis is the same tissue spread as a flat sheet. The origin is the fixed attachment and the insertion the moving one, though the two exchange roles when the far end is held, and an agonist carries out a movement while its antagonist, its synergists and its fixators govern it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 25 — General Muscle Anatomy, Part Two

This chapter continues the general study of muscle by asking how muscles work against one another and how they are packed into groups inside the body. It deals first with antagonists, the muscles that oppose a movement, then with synergists and fixators, the muscles that help a movement or steady its base, and then with the fascial compartments that hold muscles into working sets. The second half turns to the face, where the muscles of facial expression lie in the superficial fascia and move the skin rather than a joint. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2401. Which muscle is the antagonist of the biceps brachii at the elbow? The answer is the triceps brachii. The biceps brachii lies on the front of the arm and flexes the elbow, and the triceps brachii lies on the back and extends it, so the two pull in opposite directions.

Question 2402. At the knee, which group of muscles opposes the quadriceps femoris: the adductor group, the hamstrings, the gluteal muscles, or the calf muscles? The answer is the hamstrings. The quadriceps femoris extends the knee and the hamstrings flex it, while the gluteal muscles act at the hip and the calf muscles at the ankle.

Question 2403. Which group opposes the flexor muscles that bend the wrist: the extensor muscles on the back of the forearm, the thenar muscles of the thumb, the interosseous muscles of the hand, or the muscles of the little finger? The answer is the extensors on the back of the forearm. They straighten the wrist against the flexors, while the interosseous muscles move the fingers.

Question 2404. When a muscle contracts and its antagonist at the same joint relaxes at the same moment, what is that arrangement called? The answer is reciprocal inhibition. Signals from the contracting muscle quiet the motor neurons that drive its opponent, which saves work at the joint and is built into walking and reaching.

Question 2405. A described dissection of the arm shows a two-headed muscle on the front of the humerus and a three-headed muscle on the back, with the elbow bent. Which of the two is the antagonist of that movement? The answer is the three-headed muscle, the triceps brachii. It extends the elbow and must lengthen for the joint to bend, while the two-headed muscle is the agonist.

Question 2406. Which muscle at the front of the hip opposes the gluteus maximus when the thigh is lifted forward? The answer is the iliopsoas. It runs from the lumbar vertebrae and the inner surface of the pelvis to the lesser trochanter of the femur, so it flexes the hip while the gluteus maximus extends it.

Question 2407. Which two muscles oppose the middle fibers of the deltoid, which lift the arm sideways: the pectoralis major and the latissimus dorsi, the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus, the rhomboid muscles and the trapezius, or the serratus anterior and the levator scapulae? The answer is the pectoralis major and the latissimus dorsi. Both draw the arm down and inward, while the supraspinatus assists the deltoid.

Question 2408. Which muscles oppose the serratus anterior, which draws the shoulder blade forward: the rhomboid major and rhomboid minor, the pectoralis minor, the subclavius, or the levator scapulae? The answer is the rhomboid major and rhomboid minor. They pull the shoulder blade back toward the vertebral column, while the pectoralis minor draws it forward and so assists the serratus anterior.

Question 2409. Which muscle crosses the front of the hip and opposes the hamstrings when the knee is straightened? The answer is the rectus femoris. It is the only part of the quadriceps femoris that crosses the hip as well as the knee, so it extends the knee and also lifts the thigh.

Question 2410. True or false: a muscle is called an antagonist only when it lies on the opposite side of a joint from the muscle it opposes. The answer is false. An antagonist is named by the movement it opposes, and its position about the joint is not the test.

Question 2411. Which muscle opposes the masseter when the lower jaw is opened: the temporalis, the medial pterygoid, the lateral pterygoid, or the buccinator? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. The masseter, the temporalis and the medial pterygoid all raise the jaw, while the lateral pterygoid pulls the head of the mandible forward and opens the mouth.

Question 2412. Which muscle on the front of the leg opposes the gastrocnemius and the soleus: the tibialis anterior, the fibularis longus, the flexor digitorum longus, or the plantaris? The answer is the tibialis anterior. It turns the sole inward as it lifts the foot, while the two calf muscles pull the heel up and point the foot down.

Question 2413. A constructed illustration: a person cannot lift the foot after an injury to the front of the leg. Which group has lost its pull, leaving the calf unopposed? The answer is the anterior compartment of the leg, whose muscles dorsiflex the ankle. With that group silent the foot droops. Examination and management belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2414. Which muscle inside the orbit opposes the orbicularis oculi and raises the upper eyelid? The answer is the levator palpebrae superioris. The orbicularis oculi closes the lids and the levator lifts the upper lid, and the two differ in nerve supply as well.

Question 2415. Which muscle opposes the genioglossus, which pulls the tongue forward: the styloglossus, the hyoglossus, the palatoglossus, or the geniohyoid? The answer is the styloglossus. It runs from the styloid process to the side of the tongue and draws it up and backward, so the two pull in opposite directions.

Question 2416. Which of these four pairs is a pair of antagonists: the biceps brachii with the brachialis, the quadriceps femoris with the hamstrings, the gastrocnemius with the soleus, or the deltoid with the supraspinatus? The answer is the quadriceps femoris with the hamstrings. The other three pairs work together, since both members of each bend, point or lift in the same direction.

Question 2417. Name the group of muscles that acts as the antagonist of the quadriceps femoris, spoken as a single group. The answer is the hamstrings. The group lies at the back of the thigh and holds the biceps femoris, the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, which cross both the hip and the knee.

Question 2418. A described dissection of the forearm shows a thick muscle mass on the front and another on the back, separated by deep fascia and by the two bones with their interosseous membrane. What relationship do the two masses have at the wrist? The answer is that they are antagonists. The front group flexes the wrist and fingers and the back group extends them.

Question 2419. What name is given to a muscle that works alongside the prime mover and helps it produce the same movement? The answer is a synergist. The prime mover is the muscle chiefly responsible for the movement, and its synergists add their pull in the same direction.

Question 2420. Which muscle lies on the front of the lower half of the humerus and joins the biceps brachii in bending the elbow? The answer is the brachialis. It arises from the front of the humerus and inserts on the ulna, and because it lies close to the joint it is the strongest of the elbow flexors.

Question 2421. Which four muscles make up the quadriceps femoris: the rectus femoris with the three vastus muscles, the biceps femoris with the semitendinosus, the sartorius with the gracilis, or the gluteus maximus with the gluteus medius? The answer is the rectus femoris with the vastus lateralis, the vastus medialis and the vastus intermedius. All four straighten the knee.

Question 2422. Which three muscles form the hamstrings at the back of the thigh: the biceps femoris, the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, the adductor magnus with the gracilis, the gluteus maximus with the piriformis, or the sartorius with the popliteus? The answer is the biceps femoris, the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus. All three arise from the ischial tuberosity and act at the knee and the hip.

Question 2423. Which small muscle lies above the spine of the scapula and begins the act of lifting the arm, working with the deltoid? The answer is the supraspinatus. It passes under the acromion to the greater tubercle of the humerus, and the deltoid continues the movement once it has begun.

Question 2424. What name is given to a muscle that steadies the origin of the prime mover so that the prime mover can act from a firm base? The answer is a fixator. It produces no movement at the joint it crosses, but it makes the movement elsewhere efficient.

Question 2425. A constructed illustration: a person reaches forward with both arms, and the shoulder blades are held firmly against the chest wall so that the deltoid pulls from a fixed base. Which muscles steady the shoulder blades there? The answer is the trapezius, the rhomboid muscles and the serratus anterior. They are the fixators of the movement.

Question 2426. A described dissection of the back of the chest shows a large triangular muscle running from the lower vertebrae to the arm, a smaller muscle beside it and a broad muscle above. Which of these shares the work of pulling the arm down and back? The answer is the latissimus dorsi, with the teres major beside it. The broad muscle above is the trapezius.

Question 2427. Which two muscles on the back of the leg point the foot down and raise the heel: the tibialis anterior and the extensor digitorum longus, the gastrocnemius and the soleus, the flexor hallucis longus and the tibialis posterior, or the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis? The answer is the gastrocnemius and the soleus. Both reach the calcaneus by the same tendon, and the soleus works hardest when a person stands still.

Question 2428. Which muscle lies in the deep part of the back of the forearm and joins the extensor digitorum in straightening the index finger? The answer is the extensor indicis. It reaches the index finger alone, while the extensor digitorum straightens all four fingers.

Question 2429. True or false: a synergist always produces the same movement as the prime mover it helps. The answer is false. Some synergists cancel a movement that the prime mover would otherwise produce, and so make the wanted movement cleaner. The muscles that steady the shoulder blade during a lift work in that way.

Question 2430. Which of these pairs belongs together: a fixator with a muscle that steadily holds a base, a synergist with a muscle that opposes a movement, an antagonist with a muscle that helps a movement, or a prime mover with a muscle that only steadies a joint? The answer is a fixator with a muscle that steadily holds a base. The other three pair the wrong term with the wrong description.

Question 2431. A described illustration shows a person lifting a heavy box, with the back straight and the shoulder blades drawn together before the elbows bend. Which muscles have acted before the elbows bend, and what is their role? The answer is the muscles that steady the shoulder blades, acting as fixators. They hold the scapulae so that the arm muscles pull from a firm base.

Question 2432. Name two muscles that act as synergists with the biceps brachii when the elbow is bent against resistance, spoken as a list. The answer is the brachialis and the brachioradialis. Both bend the elbow, and neither supinates the forearm as the biceps brachii does.

Question 2433. Which group of muscles steadies the head of the humerus in its socket while the deltoid lifts the arm: the rotator cuff, the thenar muscles, the adductor muscles of the thigh, or the muscles of the abdominal wall? The answer is the rotator cuff, formed by the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor and the subscapularis. They hold the head in place while the deltoid lifts the shaft.

Question 2434. A constructed illustration: the deltoid is healthy but the arm cannot be lifted, because the shoulder blade slides away from the chest wall whenever it is raised. Which structures have failed there? The answer is the fixators of the shoulder blade, chiefly the serratus anterior with the trapezius and the rhomboid muscles.

Question 2435. Which muscles lie in the anterior compartment of the arm, on the front of the humerus? The answer is the biceps brachii, the brachialis and the coracobrachialis. All three are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, and the triceps brachii lies behind them in the posterior compartment.

Question 2436. Which nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm: the radial nerve, the musculocutaneous nerve, the median nerve, or the ulnar nerve? The answer is the musculocutaneous nerve. It pierces the coracobrachialis and runs between the biceps brachii and the brachialis, while the radial nerve supplies the posterior compartment.

Question 2437. What structure divides the muscles of a limb into compartments and gives each compartment its own nerve and blood supply? The answer is the deep fascia with the intermuscular septa that run from it to the bone. The septa make closed spaces, and each space carries the vessels and nerves for the muscles within it.

Question 2438. Which muscles lie in the anterior compartment of the leg: the gastrocnemius and the soleus, the tibialis anterior with the long extensors of the toes, the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis, or the tibialis posterior with the long flexors of the toes? The answer is the tibialis anterior with the extensor digitorum longus and the extensor hallucis longus, which lift the foot and the toes.

Question 2439. Which muscles lie in the lateral compartment of the leg, and which nerve supplies them: the tibialis anterior with the deep fibular nerve, the fibularis longus and fibularis brevis with the superficial fibular nerve, the gastrocnemius with the tibial nerve, or the extensor digitorum longus with the medial plantar nerve? The answer is the fibularis longus and fibularis brevis with the superficial fibular nerve, which turn the sole outward.

Question 2440. A described cross section of the leg shows the tibia and the fibula with a membrane between them, and muscle masses in front of, behind and beside the bones, each wrapped in its own sheet of deep fascia. Which compartment lies between the two bones in front of the membrane? The answer is the anterior compartment. The posterior compartment lies behind both bones.

Question 2441. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the front of the leg, the tissue in one closed fascial space swells and the toes hurt when straightened. Which space is involved, and why does the pressure rise? The answer is the anterior compartment of the leg, a closed space bounded by deep fascia and bone. The fascia cannot stretch, so swelling raises the pressure. Assessment and management belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2442. Which muscles form the deep part of the posterior compartment of the leg, the part against the back of the two bones? The answer is the tibialis posterior, the flexor digitorum longus and the flexor hallucis longus, with the popliteus at the top. All are supplied by the tibial nerve.

Question 2443. In which part of the leg does the tibialis posterior lie: the anterior compartment, the lateral compartment, the deep part of the posterior compartment, or the superficial part of the posterior compartment? The answer is the deep part of the posterior compartment. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and turns the sole inward while supporting the arch.

Question 2444. Which structure separates the anterior compartment of the leg from the lateral compartment, and how is it attached? The answer is the anterior intermuscular septum, which runs from the deep fascia inward to the anterior border of the fibula. Its fibers are attached to the bone along the length of the compartment.

Question 2445. True or false: the compartments of the leg each receive their own nerve, so that weakness of one nerve weakens a recognizable group of muscles. The answer is true. The anterior compartment takes the deep fibular nerve, the lateral compartment the superficial fibular nerve, and the posterior compartments the tibial nerve.

Question 2446. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior compartment of the leg with the deep fibular nerve, the lateral compartment with the tibial nerve, the posterior compartment with the superficial fibular nerve, or the anterior compartment with the medial plantar nerve? The answer is the anterior compartment with the deep fibular nerve. The lateral compartment takes the superficial fibular nerve.

Question 2447. A described cross section of the thigh shows one large muscle mass in front, another behind and a third group along the inner side, separated by septa that run from a strong band of fascia around the limb to the femur. Which compartment holds the muscles that straighten the knee? The answer is the anterior compartment, which holds the quadriceps femoris. The posterior compartment holds the hamstrings.

Question 2448. A described transverse section through the middle of the leg is read with the fibula on the outer side and the tibia on the inner side. Which compartment lies against the outer surface of the fibula, and which lies behind both bones? The answer is that the lateral compartment lies against the fibula and the posterior compartment lies behind both bones.

Question 2449. Name the three compartments of the thigh and the action for which each is best known, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior compartment, which straightens the knee, the posterior compartment, which bends the knee and extends the hip, and the medial compartment, which draws the thigh inward.

Question 2450. A constructed illustration: a blow to the outer side of the knee leaves the foot unable to turn outward and the skin over the outer leg numb. Which nerve has been injured, and why is it exposed there? The answer is the common fibular nerve, as it winds around the neck of the fibula, where it lies against bone. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2451. Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, the muscles that move the skin of the face? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve, the facial nerve. Its branches spread through the face from the parotid region, and the muscles it supplies pull on the skin rather than on a joint.

Question 2452. Which muscle closes the eyelids: the levator palpebrae superioris, the orbicularis oculi, the corrugator supercilii, or the procerus? The answer is the orbicularis oculi. Its fibers form a ring about the eye, and the levator palpebrae superioris does the opposite and lifts the upper lid.

Question 2453. Which muscle closes and purses the lips: the buccinator, the orbicularis oris, the mentalis, or the risorius? The answer is the orbicularis oris. Its fibers form a ring about the mouth, while the buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth and the mentalis moves the chin.

Question 2454. Which muscle forms the wall of the cheek, presses it against the teeth and keeps food from collecting beside the gum? The answer is the buccinator. It runs from the back of the jaw forward to the angle of the mouth and is supplied by the seventh cranial nerve.

Question 2455. Which muscle runs from the cheekbone to the angle of the mouth and pulls that angle upward and outward in a smile? The answer is the zygomaticus major. The zygomaticus minor lies just above it and lifts the upper lip, and both are supplied by the seventh cranial nerve.

Question 2456. A described dissection of the face shows a ring of muscle about the mouth and, at the corner, a small knot where several flat muscles meet and interlace. What is that knot called, and which muscles meet there? The answer is the modiolus, where the orbicularis oris, the buccinator, the levator and depressor muscles of the angle and the zygomaticus major meet.

Question 2457. Which muscle lifts the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead: the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis, the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis, the corrugator supercilii, or the procerus? The answer is the frontal belly, which lies over the forehead. The occipital belly lies at the back of the head and pulls the scalp backward.

Question 2458. Which small muscle lies at the inner end of the eyebrow and draws it toward the midline and downward, making vertical folds above the nose? The answer is the corrugator supercilii. It lies deep to the frontal belly, and its pull produces the frown lines between the eyebrows.

Question 2459. Which muscle lies over the bridge of the nose and wrinkles the skin there: the procerus, the nasalis, the levator labii superioris, or the depressor septi? The answer is the procerus. It reaches the skin between the eyebrows, while the nasalis lies lower and compresses the nostril.

Question 2460. Which broad sheet of muscle lies in the superficial fascia of the neck, tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corner of the mouth downward? The answer is the platysma. It arises from the fascia over the chest and shoulder and is supplied by the cervical branch of the seventh cranial nerve.

Question 2461. Which muscle protrudes the lower lip, turns it outward and wrinkles the skin of the chin: the depressor labii inferioris, the mentalis, the depressor anguli oris, or the orbicularis oris? The answer is the mentalis. The depressor labii inferioris pulls the lower lip down rather than forward.

Question 2462. Which muscle lies over the back of the head and pulls the scalp backward, working across a broad fibrous sheet with the muscle over the forehead? The answer is the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis. The sheet between the two bellies is the epicranial aponeurosis.

Question 2463. Which muscle lies over the side of the nose and compresses the nostril: the procerus, the nasalis, the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, or the depressor septi? The answer is the nasalis, whose compressor part squeezes the nostril. The levator labii superioris alaeque nasi widens it instead.

Question 2464. Which of these pairs belongs together: the orbicularis oris with closing the lips, the orbicularis oculi with lifting the eyebrow, the mentalis with closing the eyelids, or the buccinator with turning the sole of the foot? The answer is the orbicularis oris with closing the lips. The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids and the buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth.

Question 2465. True or false: the muscles of facial expression lie in the superficial fascia and are attached to the skin at one or both ends. The answer is true. They arise from bone or fascia and insert into the skin, which is why their contraction moves the skin and produces an expression.

Question 2466. Which branch of the seventh cranial nerve supplies the frontal belly and the upper part of the orbicularis oculi: the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, or the cervical branch? The answer is the temporal branch. It crosses the zygomatic arch to the forehead, and the zygomatic branch supplies the lower part of the orbicularis oculi.

Question 2467. The duct of the parotid gland crosses the cheek and pierces which muscle, and opposite which tooth does it open into the mouth? The answer is the buccinator, opposite the second upper molar tooth. The duct crosses the masseter first and then turns inward through the cheek.

Question 2468. Which muscle lies below the eye and runs down to the upper lip, lifting it and deepening the fold from the side of the nose to the corner of the mouth? The answer is the levator labii superioris. It arises from the lower margin of the orbit.

Question 2469. Which muscle of the cheek lies deepest, against the lining of the mouth: the buccinator, the risorius, the zygomaticus major, or the levator anguli oris? The answer is the buccinator. It forms the deep wall of the cheek and is pierced by the duct of the parotid gland.

Question 2470. A described dissection of the cheek shows a small duct running forward across a muscle at the side of the jaw, then turning inward through the cheek wall opposite the upper molar teeth. Which muscle does the duct cross, and which does it pierce? The answer is that it crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator.

Question 2471. Immediately deep to the platysma in the neck lie the investing layer of deep cervical fascia and, beneath it, which large muscle running from the chest to the mastoid process? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid. The platysma pulls on the skin, while that muscle turns the head.

Question 2472. Which muscle draws the corner of the mouth straight outward and produces a flat, mirthless grin: the risorius, the zygomaticus major, the depressor anguli oris, or the levator anguli oris? The answer is the risorius, a slender band running across the cheek. The zygomaticus major lifts the corner instead of pulling it straight out.

Question 2473. Which muscle runs from the front of the lower jaw to the lower lip and pulls that lip downward and a little outward? The answer is the depressor labii inferioris. The depressor anguli oris lies beside it and pulls the whole corner of the mouth down.

Question 2474. Which muscle lies deep to the levator labii superioris and lifts the angle of the mouth: the levator anguli oris, the zygomaticus minor, the depressor anguli oris, or the buccinator? The answer is the levator anguli oris. It arises from the canine fossa of the upper jaw.

Question 2475. The seventh cranial nerve leaves the skull through which opening, and which gland does it enter immediately afterward? The answer is the stylomastoid foramen, and it enters the parotid gland. Inside the gland it splits into its five main branches for the face.

Question 2476. A described section through the scalp shows a broad sheet of fibrous tissue between a muscle at the back and a muscle at the front, with the skin above and the bone below. What is the sheet called? The answer is the epicranial aponeurosis, which the frontal belly pulls forward with the scalp and the occipital belly pulls backward.

Question 2477. Which muscle widens the nostril: the compressor part of the nasalis, the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, the depressor septi, or the procerus? The answer is the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, whose long name records its two actions. Its outer slip raises the upper lip and pulls the wing of the nose upward.

Question 2478. True or false: the buccinator is one of the muscles of mastication, because it lies beside the teeth and keeps food between them. The answer is false. The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression, supplied by the seventh cranial nerve, and it does not move the joint of the jaw.

Question 2479. Which muscle runs from the lower border of the jaw up to the corner of the mouth and pulls that corner downward: the depressor anguli oris, the depressor labii inferioris, the mentalis, or the platysma? The answer is the depressor anguli oris. The depressor labii inferioris moves only the lower lip.

Question 2480. Which of these pairs belongs together: the frontal belly with the occipital belly as antagonists across the scalp, the orbicularis oris with the buccinator as antagonists, the mentalis with the depressor labii inferioris as antagonists, or the procerus with the corrugator supercilii as antagonists? The answer is the frontal belly with the occipital belly. The other pairs lie side by side and help one another.

Question 2481. A described cross section through the cheek at the level of the upper molar teeth shows the skin outside, a layer of fat, muscles of the face, then the buccinator, and the lining of the mouth innermost. Which muscle forms the deepest part of the wall, and what passes through it? The answer is the buccinator, pierced by the duct of the parotid gland.

Question 2482. A described transverse section through the head is read with the nose in front and the ears behind. Which muscles of the face lie superficial to the buccinator, and where is the parotid gland? The answer is that the muscles of facial expression lie superficial to the buccinator, and the parotid gland lies at the side, in front of the ear.

Question 2483. Which muscle of facial expression is supplied by the cervical branch of the seventh cranial nerve? The answer is the platysma. It is the only muscle of facial expression that lies in the neck, and its pull tenses the skin of the neck and draws the corner of the mouth downward.

Question 2484. Which branch of the seventh cranial nerve supplies the depressor anguli oris, the depressor labii inferioris and the mentalis: the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the marginal mandibular branch, or the cervical branch? The answer is the marginal mandibular branch. It runs forward close to the lower border of the jaw, where it is easily injured.

Question 2485. A described dissection in front of the ear shows a gland wrapped around the back of the jaw, and emerging from its front edge a nerve that divides into branches running to the forehead, across the cheek and down to the neck. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve, which supplies the muscles of facial expression.

Question 2486. Which artery crosses the lower border of the jaw just in front of the masseter, and which branch of the seventh cranial nerve runs near it there? The answer is the facial artery, with the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve nearby. The nerve passes forward over the jaw to the muscles of the lower lip.

Question 2487. A described dissection shows two bellies of a thin flat muscle joined by a broad fibrous sheet that covers the top of the head, with the skin moving freely over the whole arrangement. What is this arrangement? The answer is the occipitofrontalis with its epicranial aponeurosis. The muscle inserts into the skin, so the scalp moves with either belly.

Question 2488. Which group of muscles is derived from the second pharyngeal arch and is therefore supplied by the seventh cranial nerve: the muscles of the tongue, the muscles of facial expression with the stapedius and the posterior belly of the digastric, the muscles of mastication, or the muscles of the pharynx? The answer is the muscles of facial expression with the stapedius and the posterior belly of the digastric.

Question 2489. Which muscle of facial expression arises not from bone but from the fascia over the chest and the shoulder? The answer is the platysma. Its fibers end in the skin of the neck, the lower jaw and the corner of the mouth, and no part of it is attached to bone.

Question 2490. Which of these muscles is not supplied by the seventh cranial nerve: the stapedius, the posterior belly of the digastric, the tensor tympani, or the stylohyoid? The answer is the tensor tympani, which is supplied by a branch of the fifth cranial nerve. The other three belong to the second pharyngeal arch.

Question 2491. A described dissection of the eyelid region shows a ring of muscle about the opening of the eye and, above it inside the orbit, a slender muscle running forward to the upper lid. Which closes the eye, and which lifts the lid? The answer is that the orbicularis oculi closes the eye and the levator palpebrae superioris lifts the lid.

Question 2492. The duct of the parotid gland leaves the front of the gland and runs forward across the face. Which muscle does it cross first at the side of the jaw, and where does it turn inward? The answer is that it crosses the masseter, then turns inward at the front edge of that muscle to pierce the buccinator.

Question 2493. A described dissection shows a nerve emerging from an opening behind the ear and entering a gland, inside which it divides into five branches that fan out over the face. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve, whose branches supply the muscles of facial expression.

Question 2494. Which muscle of the face is a slender band over the cheek that is absent in some people and very thin in others? The answer is the risorius, which draws the corner of the mouth straight outward when it is present. Such differences in the facial muscles are normal variations and not signs of disease.

Question 2495. A constructed illustration: the whole of one side of a person's face is weak, the forehead cannot be wrinkled and the eye cannot be closed, while the arm and the leg move normally. Which nerve is involved, and why does the forehead share in the weakness? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve of that side, which supplies the forehead as well as the lower face.

Question 2496. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the upper neck below the angle of the jaw, the lower lip on one side does not pull down and the corner of the mouth droops on smiling. Which branch has been injured? The answer is the marginal mandibular branch of the seventh cranial nerve, which crosses that region close to the jaw.

Question 2497. A constructed illustration: one cheek is weak, food collects between the cheek and the teeth on that side, and the person cannot blow out a candle. Which muscle is chiefly affected, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the buccinator, supplied by the buccal branch of the seventh cranial nerve.

Question 2498. A constructed illustration: the eye on one side cannot be shut, it waters, and its surface feels gritty because the lid does not sweep across it. Which part of which muscle has lost its nerve supply? The answer is the palpebral part of the orbicularis oculi, supplied by the seventh cranial nerve. Care of the eye belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 2499. A constructed illustration: a person cannot purse the lips, whistle or hold a thread between the lips, although the jaw and the tongue move normally. Which muscle is chiefly at fault? The answer is the orbicularis oris, the ring of muscle about the mouth, supplied by the buccal branches of the seventh cranial nerve.

Question 2500. A described dissection of the neck and the lower face shows a thin sheet of muscle running from the fascia over the chest up into the jaw and the corner of the mouth. What is this muscle, and what does it do to the skin? The answer is the platysma, which tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corner of the mouth downward.

To summarize, an antagonist is defined by the movement it opposes and not by its position, and reciprocal inhibition is the automatic quieting of an antagonist while its partner contracts. A synergist adds its pull to the prime mover or cancels an unwanted movement, and a fixator steadies the base from which the prime mover acts. Muscles are grouped into compartments by deep fascia and intermuscular septa, and each compartment holds a recognizable set of muscles with its own nerve and vessels, as the compartments of the leg and the thigh show. The muscles of facial expression lie in the superficial fascia, insert into the skin and are supplied by the seventh cranial nerve, and the frontal belly, the corrugator supercilii, the procerus, the orbicularis oculi, the nasalis, the orbicularis oris, the buccinator, the zygomaticus major, the levator and depressor muscles of the mouth, the mentalis and the platysma each move a particular area of skin. The buccinator lies deepest in the cheek, the duct of the parotid gland pierces it opposite the second upper molar tooth, and the branches of the seventh nerve cross the face from the parotid gland. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 26 — Head and Face

This chapter works through the muscles that move the lower jaw and the muscles that move the eye, two small groups whose actions are easy to confuse by ear. It begins with the four classic muscles of mastication, the masseter, the temporalis and the two pterygoid muscles, along with the smaller muscles that help to open the mouth, and it then turns to the six muscles that move the eyeball and to the levator of the upper eyelid. It holds one hundred questions, and every question is answered immediately after it is asked, with the reason given in the same paragraph, so that nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The order runs from the muscles of mastication to the muscles of the orbit. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2501. Which muscle of mastication forms the thick pad over the side of the jaw, arises from the zygomatic arch, and stands out when the teeth are clenched? The answer is the masseter. It inserts on the outer surface of the ramus and on the angle of the mandible. Its fibers run downward and slightly backward, so they lift the lower jaw against the upper one.

Question 2502. Which muscle of mastication is a broad fan in the temple whose tendon passes deep to the zygomatic arch and grips the coronoid process of the mandible? The answer is the temporalis. Its anterior fibers lift the jaw and its posterior fibers pull it backward. The deep temporal nerves enter it from the floor of the temporal fossa.

Question 2503. Which muscle of mastication arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and inserts on the inner surface of the ramus of the mandible? The answer is the medial pterygoid. It faces the masseter across the ramus, and the two together form a sling that lifts the lower jaw. It also helps to pull the jaw forward and to grind from side to side.

Question 2504. Which muscle of mastication has two heads that arise from the greater wing of the sphenoid and from the outer surface of the lateral pterygoid plate? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. Its fibers run backward and slightly upward to the neck of the mandible and to the disc of the temporomandibular joint. It is the only muscle of the group that pulls the jaw forward.

Question 2505. Which nerve supplies the muscles of mastication: the facial nerve, the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, or the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. The facial nerve moves the muscles of facial expression, the maxillary division is sensory, and the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue.

Question 2506. Which group of four muscles is taught as the muscles of mastication: the masseter, the temporalis and the two pterygoid muscles, the four suprahyoid muscles, the four muscles of the soft palate, or the muscles of facial expression? The answer is the masseter, the temporalis and the two pterygoid muscles. The suprahyoid muscles help to open the jaw, but they are not counted in that group.

Question 2507. Which duct crosses the outer surface of the masseter, turns inward through the cheek, and opens beside the upper second molar tooth? The answer is the parotid duct. It leaves the parotid gland in front of the ear and runs forward over the masseter. The facial artery also crosses the lower border of the mandible near the anterior edge of the same muscle.

Question 2508. When the two lateral pterygoid muscles contract together, which movement of the mandible do they produce: elevation, depression with protrusion, retraction, or tightening of the lips? The answer is depression with protrusion. They are the only muscles of the group that can pull the lower jaw forward. The digastric and the other suprahyoid muscles assist with the opening.

Question 2509. A constructed illustration: a fall onto the chin drives the head of the mandible backward, and the jaw deviates toward the injured side when the mouth opens. Which muscle of mastication is most likely to be involved? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. Its fibers insert on the neck of the mandible and on the joint disc, both of which are disturbed by the displaced condyle.

Question 2510. A described dissection of the cheek shows a flat muscle running from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the jaw, with a slender duct lying across it and a vessel crossing its lower border. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the masseter, crossed by the parotid duct. The vessel at its lower border is the facial artery.

Question 2511. Which muscle of mastication inserts on the coronoid process and the anterior border of the ramus of the mandible, and is reached only by passing deep to the zygomatic arch? The answer is the temporalis. Because its tendon lies behind the arch, the arch shelters it from a direct blow. Its posterior fibers are the main retractors of the lower jaw.

Question 2512. Which part of which muscle pulls the mandible backward after it has been pushed forward: the superficial fibers of the masseter, the posterior fibers of the temporalis, the medial pterygoid, or the lateral pterygoid? The answer is the posterior fibers of the temporalis. Their pull is almost horizontal, while the anterior fibers of the same muscle pull the jaw upward.

Question 2513. True or false: every muscle of mastication is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. The answer is true. The masseter, the temporalis and both pterygoid muscles receive branches of that division. The muscles that open the mouth, such as the digastric, are supplied by other nerves and are counted separately.

Question 2514. Which two nerves descend between the medial pterygoid muscle and the ramus of the mandible, and how do they lie relative to each other? The answer is the lingual nerve and the inferior alveolar nerve, with the lingual nerve in front. Both are branches of the mandibular division. The inferior alveolar nerve then enters the mandibular foramen.

Question 2515. Which statement about the origin of the two pterygoid muscles is correct: the lateral pterygoid from the medial surface of the plate, the medial pterygoid from its lateral surface, the lateral pterygoid from that lateral surface, or both from the medial surface? The answer is that the lateral pterygoid arises from the lateral surface. The medial pterygoid takes the medial surface of the same plate.

Question 2516. Name two muscles that lift the mandible, spoken as a short list. The answer is the masseter and the temporalis. The medial pterygoid is a third elevator and works with the masseter as a sling around the ramus. All three close the mouth, while opening is produced mainly by the suprahyoid muscles and by gravity.

Question 2517. A described radiograph of the jaw shows a slender process of bone rising in front of the neck of the mandible and a fan of muscle shadow above it filling the temple. Which process and which muscle are shown? The answer is the coronoid process, with the temporalis attached to it. The condylar process lies behind it.

Question 2518. A constructed illustration: after a deep cut in the cheek, a person cannot push the lower jaw forward, though the mouth still opens and closes. Which muscle is most likely to be weakened? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. It is the only muscle that protrudes the mandible. Elevation and depression depend on the other muscles of the group and on the suprahyoid muscles.

Question 2519. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the ramus of the mandible and runs almost vertically downward and forward from the base of the skull to the angle of the jaw? The answer is the medial pterygoid. The masseter lies on the outer side of the same bone. Together they form a sling that suspends the angle of the mandible.

Question 2520. Which muscle of mastication lies immediately deep to the zygomatic arch and fills the temporal fossa? The answer is the temporalis. The arch crosses over its tendon, and the deep temporal vessels and nerves lie between the muscle and the bone of the fossa. Its fan shape lets different parts of it pull the jaw in different directions.

Question 2521. Which muscle of mastication is the most powerful elevator of the lower jaw and is wrapped in a strong fascia that gives it a firm purchase? The answer is the masseter. Its fibers arise from the zygomatic arch and insert on the ramus and the angle of the mandible. In a person who grinds the teeth, it becomes visibly thickened.

Question 2522. Which structure passes between the two pterygoid muscles as it runs from the infratemporal fossa toward the pterygopalatine fossa: the maxillary artery, the facial artery, the inferior alveolar nerve, or the parotid duct? The answer is the maxillary artery. It crosses the region deep to the lateral pterygoid and then passes between the two pterygoid muscles.

Question 2523. Which pair belongs together: the masseter with elevation of the mandible, the lateral pterygoid with retraction, the medial pterygoid with depression, or the temporalis with protrusion? The answer is the masseter with elevation of the mandible. The temporalis also elevates the jaw, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes it and the medial pterygoid helps to grind.

Question 2524. The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication. Which further loss belongs to a lesion of that division: drooping of the corner of the mouth, numbness of the lower lip and chin, weakness of the tongue, or loss of smell? The answer is numbness of the lower lip and chin. The other three belong to other nerves.

Question 2525. The movements of the mandible take place at the temporomandibular joint, where a disc divides the joint into two parts. In which plane does the sliding movement of protrusion occur, and about which axis does the hinge movement of elevation occur? The answer is the transverse plane for sliding forward, and a transverse axis for the hinge.

Question 2526. Which muscle of mastication is the only one whose fibers run upward and backward from the base of the skull to the neck of the mandible? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. All the other elevators run downward from the skull to the jaw. That upward direction explains why its contraction pulls the mandible forward and downward.

Question 2527. A constructed illustration: a person cannot open the mouth more than a finger's width, and the jaw deviates to one side. The trouble lies in front of the ear, where a small muscle holds the disc of the joint forward. Which muscle is implicated? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. Its upper head attaches to the disc and to the capsule.

Question 2528. A described cross section through the head at the level of the upper molar teeth shows a vertical plate of bone, a muscle on each side of it, and a duct opening into the cheek. Which two muscles grip the plate? The answer is the masseter outside the ramus and the medial pterygoid inside it, with the parotid duct opening beside the tooth.

Question 2529. Which of these muscles does not belong to the group called the muscles of mastication: the masseter, the temporalis, the digastric, or the medial pterygoid? The answer is the digastric. It lies above the hyoid bone and helps to open the mouth. It is an accessory muscle of opening rather than one of the four muscles of mastication.

Question 2530. Which structure lies immediately medial to the temporomandibular joint and separates the joint from the middle ear, and which ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible? The answer is the tympanic plate of the temporal bone, and the sphenomandibular ligament. The ligament lies medial to the joint and behind the lateral pterygoid.

Question 2531. Which muscle of mastication arises partly from the greater wing of the sphenoid and partly from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. The upper head is the smaller of the two. Both heads converge on the neck of the mandible and on the disc of the temporomandibular joint.

Question 2532. Which statement about the blood supply of the muscles of mastication is correct: all are supplied by the facial artery, all are supplied by branches of the maxillary artery, the masseter alone is supplied by the lingual artery, or the pterygoid muscles are supplied by the ophthalmic artery? The answer is that all are supplied by branches of the maxillary artery.

Question 2533. True or false: the lateral pterygoid muscle takes part both in opening the mouth and in moving the jaw from side to side. The answer is true. Its fibers pull the head of the mandible forward and downward on the side that contracts. Alternate contraction of the two muscles produces the side to side movement used in grinding.

Question 2534. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the side of the head, the mouth cannot be opened and the jaw deviates toward the injured side. Which muscle is most likely trapped by the fractured arch above it? The answer is the temporalis. Its tendon passes deep to the zygomatic arch on its way into the temple. A depressed fracture of the arch can block that tendon.

Question 2535. When the muscles of mastication on one side are paralyzed, the jaw deviates toward the paralyzed side as the mouth opens. Which muscle acting on the sound side explains that deviation: the masseter, the temporalis, the lateral pterygoid, or the medial pterygoid? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. It pushes the sound condyle forward, so the chin swings away from it.

Question 2536. Which muscle of mastication arises from the medial surface of a plate of the sphenoid rather than from the base of the skull or from the zygomatic arch? The answer is the medial pterygoid. Its main head comes from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, with a small slip from the palatine bone. It inserts on the inner surface of the ramus.

Question 2537. Which pair belongs together: the masseter with the temporal fossa, the temporalis with the zygomatic arch, the medial pterygoid with the inner surface of the ramus, or the lateral pterygoid with the coronoid process? The answer is the medial pterygoid with the inner surface of the ramus. The masseter and the lateral pterygoid take origin from the arch and the sphenoid respectively.

Question 2538. Which nerve lies immediately deep to the lateral pterygoid muscle as both descend toward the mandibular foramen: the lingual nerve, the inferior alveolar nerve, the buccal nerve, or the chorda tympani? The answer is the inferior alveolar nerve. It passes down behind the lateral pterygoid and enters the mandibular foramen. The lingual nerve lies in front of it, nearer the tongue.

Question 2539. A described specimen shows the mandible removed, with a fan-shaped muscle above it attached to a coronoid process and a muscle strap below and behind attached to the angle. Which muscles are shown, and which of them lies inside the ramus? The answer is the temporalis above, and the medial pterygoid inside the ramus, with the masseter outside.

Question 2540. Which muscle of mastication lies immediately lateral to the lateral pterygoid plate and immediately deep to the tendon of the temporalis? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. Its fibers run backward from the plate to the neck of the mandible. The maxillary artery lies deep to it before it passes between the two pterygoid muscles.

Question 2541. Which muscle of mastication is responsible for the visible fullness in front of the ear in a person who clenches the teeth hard? The answer is the masseter. Its upper fibers arise from the lower border of the zygomatic arch. The parotid gland lies behind it and over its posterior part.

Question 2542. Which movement of the mandible is produced by the medial pterygoid when it contracts together with the lateral pterygoid of the opposite side: straight elevation, side to side grinding, wide opening, or retraction? The answer is side to side grinding. The two muscles pull the jaw in opposite directions, so the mandible swings across.

Question 2543. A described section through the infratemporal fossa shows a muscle running downward and forward to the angle of the jaw and a nerve descending just behind its lower border. Which muscle and which nerve are shown? The answer is the medial pterygoid, with the inferior alveolar nerve descending behind it toward the mandibular foramen.

Question 2544. Which of these statements about the temporalis is correct: it arises from the infratemporal crest, it inserts on the neck of the mandible, it is the widest elevator of the jaw, or it is supplied by the facial nerve? The answer is that it is the widest elevator of the jaw. Its fan covers the whole temporal fossa, and its anterior fibers lift the mandible.

Question 2545. True or false: the masseter and the medial pterygoid approach the mandible from opposite sides and together form a sling. The answer is true. The masseter lies on the outer surface of the ramus and the medial pterygoid on the inner surface. Both pull the angle upward and slightly forward, so together they close the mouth.

Question 2546. Which muscle of mastication arises partly from the pyramidal process of the palatine bone in addition to the lateral pterygoid plate? The answer is the medial pterygoid. That small slip broadens its origin at the back of the palate. It inserts on the rough surface on the inner side of the angle of the mandible, facing the masseter across the bone.

Question 2547. A described dissection shows the mandible divided at the midline and reflected, revealing four muscles attached to it, two on the outer surface and two on the inner. Which muscle lies nearest the front on the inner surface? The answer is the temporalis, inserting on the coronoid process, with the medial pterygoid behind it near the angle. The masseter and the lateral pterygoid lie outside.

Question 2548. A constructed illustration: after an injury in front of the ear, a person can still clench the teeth, but food collects between the cheek and the gums on that side. Which nerve is most likely damaged, and why is the bite preserved? The answer is the facial nerve, which supplies the buccinator. The muscles of mastication take the trigeminal nerve, so the bite is spared.

Question 2549. A described section through the head behind the cheek shows a thick muscle strap running from the base of the skull downward and forward to the angle of the mandible, with a nerve lying between it and the ramus. Which muscle and which nerve are shown? The answer is the medial pterygoid, and the inferior alveolar nerve, which descends between it and the bone.

Question 2550. Which pair belongs together: the masseter with depression of the mandible, the lateral pterygoid with protrusion, the medial pterygoid with retraction, or the temporalis with outward movement of the jaw? The answer is the lateral pterygoid with protrusion. No other muscle of the group pulls the lower jaw forward. Retraction is the work of the posterior fibers of the temporalis.

Question 2551. Which muscle arises from the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit and runs straight forward to the medial side of the eyeball? The answer is the medial rectus. It turns the eye inward toward the nose. It is the strongest adductor among the six muscles that move the eyeball.

Question 2552. Which extraocular muscle runs straight forward from the tendinous ring to the lateral side of the eyeball and turns the eye outward? The answer is the lateral rectus. It is supplied by the abducens nerve, the sixth cranial nerve, which enters its inner surface. Its action is pure abduction, with no twisting of the eye.

Question 2553. Which muscle of the orbit arises from the frontal bone above and medial to the opening of the orbit, passes through a fibrous loop, and inserts on the upper surface of the eyeball behind its equator? The answer is the superior oblique. The loop it passes through is the trochlea. It is supplied by the trochlear nerve.

Question 2554. How many extraocular muscles move each eyeball: four, five, six, or seven? The answer is six. Four of them are rectus muscles and two are oblique muscles. The levator of the upper eyelid is closely associated with them but is usually counted separately from the six.

Question 2555. Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle: the oculomotor nerve, the trochlear nerve, the abducens nerve, or the optic nerve? The answer is the abducens nerve, the sixth cranial nerve. The oculomotor nerve supplies four of the muscles that move the eye, and the trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique.

Question 2556. A described dissection of the orbit from above shows a flat muscle running straight forward from the apex and a second muscle whose tendon turns through a loop on the medial wall before running backward and outward. Which two muscles are shown? The answer is the superior rectus and the superior oblique, whose tendon passes through the trochlea.

Question 2557. Which extraocular muscle lies immediately below the levator of the upper eyelid and runs forward just above the eyeball? The answer is the superior rectus. The two travel together from the tendinous ring, and the same nerve branch supplies both of them. The superior rectus is the muscle that lifts the eye when the eye looks outward.

Question 2558. Which extraocular muscle arises from the floor of the orbit just lateral to the groove for the tear sac and runs upward and outward over the eyeball? The answer is the inferior oblique. It is the only extraocular muscle that arises from the front of the orbit. It turns the eye upward and outward when the eye looks up.

Question 2559. Which muscle turns the eye downward when the eye is turned inward toward the nose: the inferior rectus, the superior oblique, the inferior oblique, or the lateral rectus? The answer is the superior oblique. Its tendon passes through the trochlea, so its pull is directed backward and outward, and it depresses the adducted eye.

Question 2560. A constructed illustration: a person sees double when looking to the right, and the right eye cannot turn outward. The right eye rests turned inward. Which muscle is weak, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the right lateral rectus, supplied by the abducens nerve.

Question 2561. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the orbit in cross section shows a small muscle lying against the medial wall of the orbit and a larger one against its floor, with the optic nerve between them. Which muscles are shown? The answer is the medial rectus along the medial wall and the inferior rectus along the floor.

Question 2562. Which muscle of the orbit lifts the upper eyelid: the superior rectus, the levator of the upper eyelid, the superior oblique, or the orbicularis oculi? The answer is the levator of the upper eyelid. It arises above the tendinous ring and inserts into the skin of the lid and the upper tarsal plate. The orbicularis oculi closes the lid instead.

Question 2563. Name the two extraocular muscles that are not supplied by the oculomotor nerve, spoken as a list with their nerves. The answer is the lateral rectus, supplied by the abducens nerve, and the superior oblique, supplied by the trochlear nerve. All the other muscles of the orbit, including the levator of the upper eyelid, take the oculomotor nerve.

Question 2564. Which statement about the common tendinous ring is correct: it sits at the apex of the orbit, it surrounds the optic canal alone, it gives origin to all six extraocular muscles, or it lies at the front of the orbit? The answer is that it sits at the apex of the orbit. Four rectus muscles and the superior oblique arise from it, while the inferior oblique arises from the floor.

Question 2565. Which muscle lies immediately lateral to the optic nerve as it enters the back of the eye, and which muscle lies immediately above that nerve? The answer is the lateral rectus beside it and the superior rectus above it. The optic nerve enters the eye slightly medial to the center of the posterior pole.

Question 2566. Which muscle arises from the orbital floor beside the tear sac, passes outward and upward over the lower part of the eyeball, and runs almost at right angles to the other oblique muscle? The answer is the inferior oblique, which turns the eye upward and outward.

Question 2567. Why does the superior oblique muscle depress the eye when the eye is turned inward but not when the eye is turned outward? The answer is that its line of pull passes through the trochlea on the medial wall. The tendon then runs backward and outward, so the direction of its pull depends on where the eye is looking.

Question 2568. True or false: the four rectus muscles all arise from the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit. The answer is true. The superior oblique also arises there, close to the ring. The inferior oblique is the exception, because it arises from the floor of the orbit near its front.

Question 2569. A described cross section through the middle of the orbit, cut from side to side, shows four flat muscles arranged around the eyeball with the optic nerve in the middle and the levator of the lid above the topmost one. Which four muscles are these? The answer is the superior, medial, inferior and lateral rectus muscles.

Question 2570. Which extraocular muscle turns the eye straight inward: the medial rectus, the lateral rectus, the superior oblique, or the inferior oblique? The answer is the medial rectus. It runs straight from the tendinous ring to the inner side of the eyeball. The two oblique muscles twist the eye and lift or lower it rather than turning it inward.

Question 2571. Which nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure inside the common tendinous ring and then runs forward on the inner surface of the lateral rectus? The answer is the abducens nerve. It lies between the two heads of that muscle for part of its course. Its long path makes it the cranial nerve most often affected by raised pressure inside the skull.

Question 2572. A constructed illustration: a person has a drooping eyelid, the eye rests turned down and out, and the pupil is wide and does not narrow to light. Which nerve is affected, and which muscles explain the position of the eye? The answer is the oculomotor nerve, the third cranial nerve. The lateral rectus and the superior oblique are left unopposed.

Question 2573. Which statement about the origins of the oblique and rectus muscles is correct: the inferior oblique arises from the orbital floor and the medial rectus from the medial wall, the superior oblique arises from the orbital floor, both oblique muscles arise from the medial wall, or both rectus muscles arise from the orbital floor? The answer is that the inferior oblique arises from the floor and the medial rectus from the medial wall.

Question 2574. Which pair belongs together: the lateral rectus with the trochlear nerve, the superior oblique with the abducens nerve, the medial rectus with the oculomotor nerve, or the levator of the lid with the facial nerve? The answer is the medial rectus with the oculomotor nerve. The lateral rectus takes the abducens nerve and the superior oblique takes the trochlear nerve.

Question 2575. Which extraocular muscle runs from the tendinous ring straight forward to the top of the eyeball, below the levator of the upper eyelid? The answer is the superior rectus. It turns the eye upward, and because its line of pull is slightly oblique it also turns the eye inward and twists its upper pole toward the nose.

Question 2576. Which movement does the inferior rectus produce when the eye is turned outward: elevation, depression, inward twisting, or outward twisting? The answer is depression. When the eye is turned outward, the line of pull of the inferior rectus lies in the vertical plane, so its main action is to lower the eye. The superior oblique is the inward twister.

Question 2577. A described dissection of the orbit from the lateral side shows a muscle running forward above the eyeball and, below it, a tendon that turns through a loop on the medial wall before fanning out over the top and back of the globe. Which two muscles are shown? The answer is the superior rectus above and the superior oblique, whose tendon passes through the trochlea.

Question 2578. Which structures pass through the common tendinous ring in addition to the extraocular muscles that arise from it? The answer is the optic nerve, the ophthalmic artery, and the nasociliary nerve, with the abducens nerve entering through the ring as well. The frontal, lacrimal and trochlear nerves lie outside the ring.

Question 2579. Which statement about the insertion of the rectus muscles is correct: they insert into the sclera in front of the junction with the cornea, they insert into the sclera a short distance behind that junction, they insert into the cornea itself, or they insert into the sheath of the optic nerve? The answer is that they insert into the sclera a short distance behind the junction with the cornea.

Question 2580. Which extraocular muscle inserts on the upper surface of the eyeball behind the equator, after its tendon has passed through a pulley on the medial wall of the orbit? The answer is the superior oblique. Its tendon approaches the eye from the medial side and turns backward and outward to reach the sclera.

Question 2581. A constructed illustration: when a person looks to the right, the left eye moves inward poorly, while the right eye turns outward with a fine flickering movement. The fault lies not in the muscles but in the bundle that links the two nerve nuclei in the brainstem. Which muscle is weak, and on which side? The answer is the left medial rectus.

Question 2582. Which muscle is the only one of the six that arises from the front of the orbit rather than from the apex or from the upper medial wall: the superior oblique, the inferior oblique, the medial rectus, or the superior rectus? The answer is the inferior oblique. It springs from the orbital floor just lateral to the groove for the tear sac and passes upward and outward.

Question 2583. A described computed tomography scan through the orbit shows a thick band of muscle lying against the medial wall and a second band against the lateral wall, with the eyeball between them. Which muscles are shown? The answer is the medial rectus against the nasal wall and the lateral rectus against the outer wall.

Question 2584. Which pair of muscles shares the same nerve supply because they arise close together and act together: the superior rectus and the levator of the upper eyelid, the medial rectus and the lateral rectus, the two oblique muscles, or the inferior rectus and the superior oblique? The answer is the superior rectus and the levator of the upper eyelid.

Question 2585. Name the two muscles that lift the eyeball and the two that lower it, spoken as a short list. The answer is the superior rectus and the inferior oblique for lifting, and the inferior rectus and the superior oblique for lowering. The two oblique muscles work best when the eye is turned inward.

Question 2586. A thin sheet of smooth muscle lies just deep to the levator of the upper eyelid and helps to hold the lid raised. Is it supplied by the same nerve as the levator, and why does that matter? The answer is no. The levator takes the oculomotor nerve, while the smooth sheet receives sympathetic fibers, so the two can fail separately.

Question 2587. Which muscle of the orbit has a tendon that becomes broad and flat after it passes through a pulley, so that its pull is spread over the upper and lateral surfaces of the eyeball? The answer is the superior oblique. The broad tendon lets it twist and lower the eye.

Question 2588. Which statement about the action of the superior rectus is correct: it elevates the eye in every position of gaze, it elevates the eye best when the eye is turned outward, it depresses the eye when the eye is turned inward, or it turns the eye outward? The answer is that it elevates the eye best when the eye is turned outward.

Question 2589. True or false: the inferior oblique muscle turns the eye upward only when the eye is turned inward. The answer is true in practice.
