Its line of pull is oblique, so its lifting action is greatest when the eye is adducted toward the nose. It twists the upper pole away from the nose in every position of gaze.

Question 2590. A described MRI scan of the orbit taken from the front shows the optic nerve in the center, four muscles arranged around it like the spokes of a wheel, and a fifth muscle cut obliquely in the upper medial corner. Which muscle is the fifth one? The answer is the superior oblique, whose tendon turns through the trochlea in the upper medial part of the orbit.

Question 2591. A person cannot turn the eye downward and inward, though the eye moves well in every other direction. Which muscle is weak, and why is it the muscle that fails in that movement? The answer is the superior oblique. It is the main depressor of the adducted eye, because its tendon turns through the trochlea and pulls the eye backward and outward.

Question 2592. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the upper medial corner of the orbit, the eye cannot be turned downward when it looks toward the nose. Which muscle is injured, and through which structure does its tendon pass at that site? The answer is the superior oblique, whose tendon passes through the trochlea on the frontal bone.

Question 2593. Which pair belongs together: the inferior oblique with lifting the adducted eye, the superior oblique with lifting the adducted eye, the inferior rectus with lifting the abducted eye, or the medial rectus with twisting the eye? The answer is the inferior oblique with lifting the adducted eye. The superior oblique lowers the adducted eye, and the inferior rectus lowers the abducted eye.

Question 2594. Which muscle turns the upper pole of the eye away from the nose, that is, twists the eye outward: the superior oblique, the inferior oblique, the superior rectus, or the medial rectus? The answer is the inferior oblique. The inferior rectus also twists the eye outward, while the superior oblique and the superior rectus twist it the other way.

Question 2595. Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve, the fourth cranial nerve? The answer is the superior oblique. It is the only muscle in the body supplied by that nerve. The nerve enters the orbit above the tendinous ring and runs forward on the upper surface of the muscle.

Question 2596. Why does the superior rectus turn the eye inward as well as upward, while the medial rectus turns it inward alone? The answer is that the orbit runs forward and outward, so the line of pull of the superior rectus lies at an angle to the axis of the eye. The medial rectus lies in the horizontal plane.

Question 2597. A described dissection of the orbit from above shows the levator of the upper eyelid lifted away, revealing a muscle running forward to the top of the globe and a nerve entering its lower surface from the medial side. Which muscle and which nerve are shown? The answer is the superior rectus, supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.

Question 2598. Which single extraocular muscle both twists the eye and lifts it when the eye is turned inward: the superior rectus, the inferior rectus, the superior oblique, or the inferior oblique? The answer is the inferior oblique. Its oblique line of pull makes it a lifter and an outward twister of the adducted eye, while the superior oblique lowers the adducted eye.

Question 2599. A constructed illustration: a person with a weak superior oblique on one side tilts the head toward the opposite shoulder to avoid double vision. Which action of the weak muscle does that posture spare, and why does it relieve the double vision? The answer is the twisting action that keeps the upper pole of the eye turned toward the nose. Tilting the head the other way would call on the weak muscle.

Question 2600. A described MRI scan of the orbits taken from the front shows one eyeball resting turned slightly outward while the other looks straight ahead, and the muscle along the lateral wall of the affected orbit appears thin. Which muscle is at fault, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the lateral rectus, supplied by the abducens nerve.

To summarize, the muscles of mastication are the masseter, the temporalis and the two pterygoid muscles, all supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, and they lift, protrude and grind the lower jaw. The masseter lies outside the ramus of the mandible and the medial pterygoid inside it, so they form a sling, while the lateral pterygoid alone pulls the jaw forward and the posterior fibers of the temporalis pull it back. The six muscles that move the eyeball are the four rectus muscles and the two oblique muscles, all supplied by the oculomotor nerve except the lateral rectus, which takes the abducens nerve, and the superior oblique, which takes the trochlear nerve. The oblique muscles act most strongly when the eye is turned inward, and the rectus muscles act best when the eye looks along their line of pull. Naming the attachment, the nerve and the direction of pull together is what fixes each muscle in memory. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 27 — Neck

This chapter maps the neck, the narrow region between the base of the skull above and the thoracic inlet below that carries the airway, the food passage, the great vessels and the nerves between the head and the trunk. It works through the triangles of the neck and their boundaries, the muscles, the fascia and the spaces between the fascial layers, the arteries, the veins, the lymphatic channels and the cervical nerves, and it ends with the thyroid gland, the larynx and the root of the neck. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2601. Which muscle divides each side of the neck into an anterior triangle and a posterior triangle? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It runs from the upper part of the sternum and the medial part of the clavicle to the mastoid process behind the ear. Its diagonal course gives the neck its two great triangles.

Question 2602. Which broad muscle covers the back and the sides of the neck and takes its name from its shape? The answer is the trapezius. It arises from the base of the skull, the ligamentum nuchae and the spines of the thoracic vertebrae, and it inserts on the shoulder girdle. Its upper fibers elevate the shoulder.

Question 2603. Which of these structures forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck: the clavicle, the trapezius, the sternocleidomastoid, or the mandible? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid. The trapezius forms the posterior boundary and the clavicle the inferior boundary. The mandible lies far above, in the anterior triangle.

Question 2604. A described dissection shows the skin of the neck turned back, with a thin sheet of muscle lying immediately beneath it whose fibers run upward and medially across the whole front of the neck. Which muscle is described, and what does it do? The answer is the platysma. It tenses the skin of the neck and draws the lower lip and the corner of the mouth downward.

Question 2605. Which of these muscles lies below the hyoid bone and belongs to the infrahyoid group: the digastric, the stylohyoid, the mylohyoid, or the omohyoid? The answer is the omohyoid. Its inferior belly crosses the lower part of the posterior triangle and its superior belly lies in the anterior triangle. The other three lie above the hyoid bone.

Question 2606. Which muscle of the neck has two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon that is held to the hyoid bone by a loop of fascia? The answer is the digastric muscle. Its anterior belly lies in the submental triangle and its posterior belly in the submandibular triangle. The tendon pierces the stylohyoid muscle.

Question 2607. Which flat muscle forms the floor of the mouth and separates the sublingual space from the submandibular space? The answer is the mylohyoid. It runs from the mylohyoid line of the mandible to the body of the hyoid bone and meets its partner in a midline raphe. The anterior belly of the digastric lies below it.

Question 2608. Which nerve supplies the anterior belly of the digastric muscle: the facial nerve, the hypoglossal nerve, the nerve to the mylohyoid, or a branch of the cervical plexus? The answer is the nerve to the mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. The posterior belly of the same muscle is supplied by the facial nerve.

Question 2609. True or false: the posterior belly of the digastric muscle is supplied by the facial nerve. The answer is true. The facial nerve gives off its digastric branch as it leaves the stylomastoid foramen. The anterior belly has a different nerve supply, the nerve to the mylohyoid.

Question 2610. Which of these pairs belongs together: the mylohyoid muscle with the facial nerve, the mylohyoid muscle with the nerve to the mylohyoid, the stylohyoid muscle with the hypoglossal nerve, or the geniohyoid muscle with the facial nerve? The answer is the mylohyoid muscle with the nerve to the mylohyoid. The stylohyoid is supplied by the facial nerve.

Question 2611. A described cross section of the neck at the level of the thyroid gland shows a thick layer of deep fascia wrapping two long strap muscles on each side of the midline. Which fascia and which muscles are described? The answer is the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia around the sternohyoid and the sternothyroid. The same layer encloses the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius.

Question 2612. Which structure crosses the lower part of the posterior triangle of the neck and divides it into an occipital triangle above and a supraclavicular triangle below? The answer is the inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle. It runs from the superior border of the scapula toward the intermediate tendon near the clavicle. The transverse cervical vessels cross the same zone.

Question 2613. A sagittal section is cut exactly through the midline of the neck. Which of these structures does the section pass through: the internal jugular vein, the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the thyroid cartilage, or the brachial plexus? The answer is the thyroid cartilage. The midline plane carries the hyoid bone, the larynx, the trachea and the thyroid isthmus.

Question 2614. Which nerve supplies the sternohyoid, the sternothyroid and the omohyoid muscles: the ansa cervicalis, the hypoglossal nerve, the spinal accessory nerve, or the phrenic nerve? The answer is the ansa cervicalis. Its superior root carries fibers that travel briefly with the hypoglossal nerve, and its inferior root comes from the cervical plexus. The thyrohyoid is supplied separately.

Question 2615. A constructed illustration: during the removal of a lymph node in the posterior triangle of the neck, the shoulder droops afterward. Which nerve has been injured, and why was it at risk? The answer is the spinal accessory nerve, which runs superficially through the posterior triangle on its way to the trapezius. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2616. What is the name of the fascial tube that carries the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve through the neck? The answer is the carotid sheath. It begins at the base of the skull and continues into the thorax. The three structures keep the same relation to one another along it.

Question 2617. At which level does the common carotid artery divide into the internal and the external carotid arteries? The answer is the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of the fourth cervical vertebra. The cricoid cartilage below it marks the level of the sixth cervical vertebra, where the trachea begins.

Question 2618. True or false: the carotid sinus is a chemoreceptor that monitors the oxygen content of the arterial blood. The answer is false. The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor, a slight dilation at the origin of the internal carotid artery that responds to stretch and helps regulate blood pressure. The chemoreceptor at the bifurcation is the carotid body.

Question 2619. Which small chemoreceptor lies in the angle between the internal and the external carotid arteries and monitors the oxygen content of arterial blood? The answer is the carotid body. It is supplied by branches of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. The nearby structure that senses stretch and helps control blood pressure is the carotid sinus.

Question 2620. Which of these is a branch of the external carotid artery: the vertebral artery, the facial artery, the inferior thyroid artery, or the suprascapular artery? The answer is the facial artery. The vertebral artery and the inferior thyroid and suprascapular arteries belong to the subclavian system. The external carotid also gives the superior thyroid, the lingual and the occipital.

Question 2621. Within the carotid sheath, where does the internal jugular vein lie in relation to the common carotid artery? The answer is lateral to it. The vein runs down the outer side of the artery, and the vagus nerve lies behind and between the two. The sheath is attached behind to the prevertebral fascia.

Question 2622. Which of these is the first branch given off by the external carotid artery above its origin: the lingual artery, the superior thyroid artery, the facial artery, or the occipital artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery. It arises close to the bifurcation and runs down to the upper pole of the thyroid gland. The ascending pharyngeal artery may arise at the same level.

Question 2623. True or false: the internal carotid artery gives off no branches while it lies in the neck. The answer is true. It ascends from the bifurcation to the base of the skull without branching and enters the skull through the carotid canal. Its branches begin inside the cranial cavity.

Question 2624. A described dissection of the carotid triangle shows the common carotid artery dividing into two vessels, with a small body in the angle between them and a nerve running down behind the sheath. Which nerve is described? The answer is the vagus nerve. It lies in the carotid sheath behind and between the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery. The small body is the carotid body.

Question 2625. What is the name of the nerve that lies within the carotid sheath behind and between the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery? The answer is the vagus nerve. The vein lies lateral and the artery medial. The nerve keeps this relation from the base of the skull to the root of the neck.

Question 2626. Which artery of the neck ascends through the openings in the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae and enters the skull through the foramen magnum? The answer is the vertebral artery. It is usually the first branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery.

Question 2627. Which of these arteries arises from the first part of the subclavian artery and supplies the brain and the spinal cord: the costocervical trunk, the dorsal scapular artery, the vertebral artery, or the suprascapular artery? The answer is the vertebral artery. The costocervical trunk comes from the second part and the dorsal scapular artery usually from the third part.

Question 2628. At the root of the neck, which structure lies immediately anterior to the anterior scalene muscle: the subclavian artery, the subclavian vein, the brachial plexus, or the phrenic nerve? The answer is the subclavian vein. The subclavian artery and the brachial plexus pass behind the muscle, and the phrenic nerve lies on its anterior surface.

Question 2629. Which of these arteries arises from the second part of the subclavian artery behind the anterior scalene muscle: the vertebral artery, the costocervical trunk, the thyrocervical trunk, or the internal thoracic artery? The answer is the costocervical trunk, which gives the supreme intercostal and deep cervical arteries. The other three arise from the first part of the subclavian artery.

Question 2630. Which of these is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk: the deep cervical artery, the inferior thyroid artery, the internal thoracic artery, or the supreme intercostal artery? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery. The thyrocervical trunk also gives the suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries. The deep cervical and supreme intercostal arteries come from the costocervical trunk.

Question 2631. A constructed illustration: a deep cut in the lower part of the neck divides a superficial vein that crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and the bleeding is brisk. Which vein is involved, and which vein does it drain into? The answer is the external jugular vein, which drains into the subclavian vein. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2632. A described dissection of the front of the neck shows two small veins running close to the midline on either side of the infrahyoid muscles and joining across the midline above the sternum. Which veins are shown, and what is the arch they form called? The answer is the anterior jugular veins, which form the jugular venous arch.

Question 2633. Which of these pairs belongs together: the external jugular vein with the subclavian vein, the internal jugular vein with the subclavian artery, the anterior jugular vein with the internal carotid artery, or the retromandibular vein with the vertebral vein? The answer is the external jugular vein with the subclavian vein. The internal jugular vein joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

Question 2634. Which two veins unite to form the retromandibular vein: the superficial temporal and the maxillary veins, the facial and the posterior auricular veins, the internal jugular and the subclavian veins, or the superior and middle thyroid veins? The answer is the superficial temporal and the maxillary veins. The retromandibular vein lies in the parotid gland and divides into an anterior and a posterior division.

Question 2635. Which structure ends at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, and where does it lie in relation to the carotid sheath? The answer is the thoracic duct, which ends at that junction and lies behind the carotid sheath on the left. On the right the right lymphatic duct ends at the same junction.

Question 2636. Which of these statements about the thoracic duct is correct: it drains only the right side of the head, it ends at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, it lies in front of the carotid sheath, or it begins in the neck? The answer is that it ends at that junction on the left. It begins in the abdomen and drains most of the body.

Question 2637. Name the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus, spoken as a list. The answer is the lesser occipital nerve, the greater auricular nerve, the transverse cervical nerve and the supraclavicular nerves. All four emerge from behind the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and supply the skin of the neck and the ear.

Question 2638. The phrenic nerve is formed by fibers from which spinal nerves: the first and second cervical, the third, fourth and fifth cervical, the fifth and sixth cervical, or the first and second thoracic? The answer is the third, fourth and fifth cervical nerves. The nerve descends on the anterior scalene muscle into the chest. It supplies the diaphragm.

Question 2639. On which surface of the anterior scalene muscle does the phrenic nerve descend through the neck? The answer is the anterior surface. The nerve runs down the muscle from lateral to medial. At the root of the neck it passes in front of the subclavian artery and behind the subclavian vein.

Question 2640. A constructed illustration: a stab wound at the root of the neck is followed by a raised hemidiaphragm on the same side. Which nerve has been injured, and where do its fibers come from? The answer is the phrenic nerve, from the third, fourth and fifth cervical nerves. The illustration is anatomical only, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2641. Which branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle: the internal branch, the external branch, the recurrent branch, or the pharyngeal branch? The answer is the external branch. The internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and carries sensation from the larynx above the vocal folds. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all the other intrinsic muscles.

Question 2642. Which of these structures does the hypoglossal nerve cross in the upper part of the neck: the trachea, the internal and external carotid arteries, the phrenic nerve, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the internal and external carotid arteries. The nerve curves forward above the hyoid bone, deep to the posterior belly of the digastric. It supplies the muscles of the tongue.

Question 2643. A constructed illustration: a wound just below the angle of the jaw is followed by wasting of one side of the tongue and a tongue that deviates toward the injured side when put out. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the hypoglossal nerve, which supplies the muscles of the tongue. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2644. A constructed illustration: a tumor at the apex of the lung presses on the sympathetic trunk in the neck. Which signs appear on the same side of the face, and why? The answer is a drooping upper eyelid, a constricted pupil, a sunken appearance of the eye and loss of sweating. The sympathetic fibers concerned travel with the internal carotid artery.

Question 2645. What is the name of the chain of ganglia that lies behind the carotid sheath on the prevertebral muscles and sends branches to the cervical spinal nerves? The answer is the sympathetic trunk. Its uppermost swelling is the superior cervical ganglion. Its fibers travel with the internal carotid artery into the head.

Question 2646. The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves: the first to the fourth cervical, the fifth cervical to the first thoracic, the first to the fourth thoracic, or the fifth to the eighth cervical only? The answer is the fifth cervical to the first thoracic nerves. They form the roots and then the trunks of the plexus in the lower part of the posterior triangle.

Question 2647. A described dissection of the lower posterior triangle shows three muscles descending to the first two ribs, with a thick bundle of nerves emerging between two of them. Which muscles and which bundle are described? The answer is the three scalene muscles, with the brachial plexus emerging between the anterior and the middle scalene. The subclavian artery emerges with the plexus.

Question 2648. A constructed illustration: a person has an extra bone that springs from the seventh cervical vertebra and curves toward the first rib. Which structure is it, and which structures may it compress? The answer is a cervical rib, which may press on the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and on the subclavian vessels. Such a rib is a developmental variant.

Question 2649. A constructed illustration: a person reports aching in the arm and a heavy feeling in the hand whenever the arm is held overhead, because the lower trunk of the brachial plexus passes over a band at the thoracic outlet. Which space is narrowed? The answer is the space between the clavicle and the first rib. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2650. A described dissection of the neck shows a nerve curving around the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and running upward over the parotid gland toward the ear. Which nerve is described, and from which nerves does it come? The answer is the greater auricular nerve, from the second and third cervical nerves.

Question 2651. Which of these pairs belongs together: the greater auricular nerve with the skin over the parotid gland and the ear, the lesser occipital nerve with the skin of the front of the neck, the supraclavicular nerves with the skin of the back of the head, or the transverse cervical nerve with the skin over the shoulder? The answer is the greater auricular nerve with the skin over the parotid gland and the ear. The lesser occipital nerve supplies the scalp behind the ear.

Question 2652. Which of these pairs belongs together: the submandibular gland with the carotid triangle, the thyroid gland with the muscular triangle, the brachial plexus with the submental triangle, or the parotid gland with the carotid triangle? The answer is the thyroid gland with the muscular triangle. The submandibular gland lies in the submandibular triangle and the parotid gland lies around the angle of the jaw.

Question 2653. Which of these pairs belongs together: the superior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery, the inferior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery, the suprascapular artery with the internal carotid artery, or the facial artery with the thyrocervical trunk? The answer is the superior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery. The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

Question 2654. Name the three structures that lie within the carotid sheath, spoken as a list. The answer is the common carotid artery with its internal and external continuations, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve. The ansa cervicalis lies in the front of the sheath for part of its course, and the sheath is attached behind to the prevertebral fascia.

Question 2655. A described radiograph of the lower part of the neck shows an extra bony bar extending from the seventh cervical vertebra on one side and meeting the first rib. Which structure is shown, and which nervous structure lies immediately above it? The answer is a cervical rib, with the lower trunk of the brachial plexus lying above it. The subclavian artery also passes over the rib.

Question 2656. Where does the thyroid gland lie in relation to the larynx and the trachea, and in which layer of fascia is it wrapped? The answer is that it wraps around the front and the sides of the upper trachea below the larynx, inside the pretracheal layer of the deep cervical fascia. That wrapping is why it moves when the person swallows.

Question 2657. The isthmus of the thyroid gland lies in front of which structures: the first and second tracheal rings, the second to the fourth tracheal rings, the cricoid cartilage and the hyoid bone, or the bodies of the cervical vertebrae? The answer is the second to the fourth tracheal rings. The gland moves with the larynx when the patient swallows. Its lobes reach up to the thyroid cartilage.

Question 2658. Which structure lies immediately posterior to the isthmus of the thyroid gland? The answer is the trachea, with its second, third and fourth rings behind the gland. The gland is wrapped in the pretracheal fascia, which binds it to the airway. The esophagus lies behind the trachea.

Question 2659. Which artery supplies the upper pole of the thyroid gland: the inferior thyroid artery, the superior thyroid artery, the thyroidea ima, or the transverse cervical artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery, the first branch of the external carotid artery. It descends to the upper pole in company with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Question 2660. The inferior thyroid artery arises from which parent vessel: the external carotid artery, the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery, the costocervical trunk, or the internal thoracic artery? The answer is the thyrocervical trunk. It ascends to the lower pole of the gland after looping upward. Its relation to the recurrent laryngeal nerve is variable.

Question 2661. Where does the recurrent laryngeal nerve usually lie in relation to the branches of the inferior thyroid artery, and why does the relation matter? The answer is that the nerve passes between the branches of the artery, or deep to them, near the lower pole of the thyroid gland. The arrangement is variable and the nerve is at risk in operations on the gland.

Question 2662. Which small artery, present in only a minority of people, ascends in the midline in front of the trachea to supply the thyroid gland? The answer is the thyroidea ima, which arises from the brachiocephalic trunk or from the arch of the aorta. It runs upward in front of the trachea and must be remembered in operations on the midline of the neck.

Question 2663. Which statement about the parathyroid glands is correct: there are usually two of them, they lie on the anterior surface of the thyroid gland, they lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, or they lie inside the trachea? The answer is that they lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, usually four in number, two on each side. The inferior glands vary in position more than the superior ones.

Question 2664. A constructed illustration: after an operation on the thyroid gland, a person's voice becomes hoarse and weak. Which nerve has most likely been injured, and what is its course on the right side? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks around the right subclavian artery and ascends in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2665. A described specimen shows the thyroid gland in place, with a small separate nodule of the same tissue rising from the isthmus toward the hyoid bone. What is that upward extension called, and what does its presence explain? The answer is the pyramidal lobe, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct along which the gland descended during development. The trachea lies immediately deep to the isthmus.

Question 2666. Which cartilage of the larynx forms a complete ring shaped like a signet, narrow in front and broad behind? The answer is the cricoid cartilage. It lies at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra and is the only complete ring in the airway. The trachea begins below it.

Question 2667. Which of these cartilages of the larynx is unpaired: the arytenoid cartilage, the corniculate cartilage, the cricoid cartilage, or the cuneiform cartilage? The answer is the cricoid cartilage. The thyroid cartilage and the epiglottis are also unpaired. The arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages are paired.

Question 2668. Which bone of the neck lies between the mandible and the larynx, has greater and lesser horns, and does not articulate with any other bone? The answer is the hyoid bone. It is suspended by muscles and ligaments from the skull and the larynx. The thyroid cartilage lies below it.

Question 2669. A described radiograph of the front of the neck shows a small bone shaped like a horseshoe lying above a larger shield-shaped cartilage, with a leaf-like flap behind it. Which three structures are shown? The answer is the hyoid bone, the thyroid cartilage below it and the epiglottis behind. All three lie in the midline.

Question 2670. What is the name of the fold of mucous membrane in the larynx that contains the vocal ligament and vibrates to produce the voice? The answer is the vocal fold, also called the true vocal cord. The space between the two vocal folds is the rima glottidis. The vestibular fold lies above it and does not produce sound.

Question 2671. Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle: the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, or the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The cricothyroid is the only intrinsic muscle of the larynx not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Question 2672. Which movement takes place at the cricothyroid joint when the cricothyroid muscle contracts, and what does that do to the vocal folds? The answer is that the thyroid cartilage tilts forward and downward, which lengthens and tenses the vocal folds. The joint allows rotation and a little gliding. The result is a rise in the pitch of the voice.

Question 2673. Which structure forms the lid over the entrance of the larynx during swallowing: the epiglottis, the arytenoid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage, or the hyoid bone? The answer is the epiglottis. It is a leaf-shaped plate of elastic cartilage attached to the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone. It folds back over the opening of the larynx as the larynx rises during swallowing.

Question 2674. True or false: the thyroid gland lies deep to the pretracheal layer of the deep cervical fascia. The answer is true. That layer encloses the gland and binds it to the larynx and the trachea. This is why the gland moves up and down when the patient swallows.

Question 2675. A described section through the lower part of the neck in front of the trachea shows a layer of fascia that passes behind the strap muscles and encloses both the thyroid gland and the airway. Which layer is described? The answer is the pretracheal layer of the deep cervical fascia. It also encloses the esophagus behind the trachea and blends with the carotid sheath at each side.

Question 2676. Which tube of the neck begins below the cricoid cartilage, is held open by rings of hyaline cartilage, and lies in the midline in front of the esophagus? The answer is the trachea. Its rings are incomplete behind, where the esophagus lies against it. It continues into the chest and divides into the two main bronchi.

Question 2677. Which statement about the cartilaginous rings of the trachea is correct: they are complete rings, they are incomplete behind where the esophagus lies against the trachea, they are absent in the neck, or they lie only in the chest? The answer is that they are incomplete behind, where a sheet of smooth muscle closes the gap.

Question 2678. Which structure lies immediately posterior to the trachea in the neck, beginning at the level of the cricoid cartilage? The answer is the esophagus, which carries food from the pharynx to the stomach. It descends slightly to the left of the midline. Its upper end is closed by the cricopharyngeus muscle.

Question 2679. A described specimen of the larynx shows a membrane stretched between the arch of the cricoid cartilage below and the lower border of the thyroid cartilage above, with a small muscle lying over it. Which membrane and which muscle are shown? The answer is the cricothyroid membrane, with the cricothyroid muscle over it. The membrane lies in the midline just below the thyroid prominence.

Question 2680. Name two unpaired cartilages of the larynx, spoken as a list. The answer is the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage. The epiglottis is a third unpaired cartilage. The arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages are paired. The thyroid cartilage forms the prominence in front of the neck.

Question 2681. Which long muscle of the prevertebral group lies against the front of the cervical vertebral bodies and flexes the neck? The answer is the longus colli. It runs from the bodies of the upper thoracic and lower cervical vertebrae to the atlas. The longus capitis lies above it and reaches the base of the skull.

Question 2682. The anterior scalene muscle arises from which structures and inserts on which rib: the transverse processes of the third to the sixth cervical vertebrae and the first rib, the bodies of the cervical vertebrae and the second rib, the mastoid process and the clavicle, or the occipital bone and the first rib? The answer is the transverse processes of the third to the sixth cervical vertebrae and the first rib, at the scalene tubercle.

Question 2683. Which muscle of the neck separates the subclavian vein in front from the subclavian artery and the brachial plexus behind? The answer is the anterior scalene muscle. It runs from the cervical transverse processes down to the first rib. The phrenic nerve lies on its anterior surface.

Question 2684. Which two cervical vertebrae are unlike the others in shape: the first and the second, the third and the fourth, the fifth and the sixth, or the sixth and the seventh? The answer is the first and the second. The first has no body and no spine, and the second carries the dens. Together they allow most of the rotation of the head.

Question 2685. True or false: the first cervical vertebra has no body and no bony spine. The answer is true. It is a ring with an anterior arch, a posterior arch and two lateral masses. It articulates above with the occipital condyles and below with the second cervical vertebra.

Question 2686. What is the name of the upward peg of bone on the second cervical vertebra about which the first vertebra and the head rotate? The answer is the dens, also called the odontoid process. It lies inside the ring of the first cervical vertebra. It is held in place by the transverse ligament of the atlas.

Question 2687. A described radiograph taken through the open mouth shows the upper cervical spine, with a ring of bone around a central peg and two lateral masses on either side. Which two vertebrae are shown, and what holds the peg in place? The answer is the first and the second cervical vertebrae, and the transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens.

Question 2688. The uncovertebral joints of the cervical spine lie between which structures: the bodies of adjacent vertebrae, the uncinate processes of one vertebra and the body of the vertebra above, the articular processes of adjacent vertebrae, or the spinous processes? The answer is the uncinate processes and the body of the vertebra above. They lie from the third to the seventh cervical vertebrae, with the vertebral artery close by laterally.

Question 2689. Which layer of the deep cervical fascia encloses the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscles and forms the roof of the posterior triangle: the investing layer, the pretracheal layer, the prevertebral layer, or the carotid sheath? The answer is the investing layer. It also encloses the parotid gland and the submandibular gland. It is the outermost of the deep layers.

Question 2690. What is the name of the fascial layer that encloses the thyroid gland, the trachea and the esophagus and continues downward into the chest? The answer is the pretracheal layer of the deep cervical fascia. It lies behind the infrahyoid muscles. Behind the pharynx it is continued as the buccopharyngeal fascia.

Question 2691. The prevertebral layer of the deep cervical fascia extends laterally to form which covering: the sheath of the thyroid gland, the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus and the axillary vessels, the covering of the parotid gland, or the sheath of the carotid vessels? The answer is the axillary sheath. It follows the brachial plexus and the axillary vessels into the armpit.

Question 2692. Which layers of the deep cervical fascia contribute to the carotid sheath? The answer is the investing layer, the pretracheal layer and the prevertebral layer. The investing layer forms its anterior wall, the pretracheal layer its medial wall and the prevertebral layer its posterior wall. The sheath is attached to the prevertebral fascia behind.

Question 2693. A described cross section shows a narrow space between the back of the pharynx and the front of the prevertebral muscles, filled with loose tissue. Which space is described, and where does it extend? The answer is the retropharyngeal space, which reaches from the base of the skull down to the upper part of the posterior mediastinum. The buccopharyngeal fascia forms its front wall.

Question 2694. The retropharyngeal space is bounded in front by which structure: the prevertebral fascia, the buccopharyngeal fascia, the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia, or the carotid sheath? The answer is the buccopharyngeal fascia, which lies behind the pharynx. Infection in this space can reach the mediastinum.

Question 2695. A described sagittal section through the back of the pharynx shows a narrow space between two fascial layers that continues downward into the chest as far as the diaphragm. Which space is described, and what is its clinical importance? The answer is the danger space, which lies between the alar fascia in front and the prevertebral fascia behind. Infection can travel along it from the neck to the posterior mediastinum.

Question 2696. A constructed illustration: a spreading infection from the back of the throat passes down behind the esophagus into the chest. Along which space has it traveled, and what are the front and back boundaries of that space? The answer is the retropharyngeal space, bounded in front by the buccopharyngeal fascia and behind by the prevertebral fascia. The illustration is not a real patient.

Question 2697. A constructed illustration: an infection spreading from an infected lower molar tooth raises the floor of the mouth on both sides and pushes the tongue upward. Which spaces are involved, and which muscle forms the floor of the mouth? The answer is the submandibular and sublingual spaces on both sides, with the mylohyoid forming the floor. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2698. Which of these structures forms the upper boundary of the submandibular triangle: the hyoid bone, the lower border of the mandible, the posterior belly of the digastric, or the sternocleidomastoid muscle? The answer is the lower border of the mandible. The two bellies of the digastric form the other boundaries and the hyoid bone lies at their meeting point.

Question 2699. A described dissection of the submandibular region shows a large gland wrapping around the posterior border of the mylohyoid muscle, with an artery grooving its surface. Which gland is described, and where does its duct open? The answer is the submandibular gland, whose duct opens beside the frenulum of the tongue. The artery is the facial artery.

Question 2700. In a described transverse section of the neck at the level of the thyroid gland, where does the carotid sheath lie in relation to the trachea and the prevertebral muscles? The answer is lateral to the trachea and in front of the prevertebral muscles. The internal jugular vein forms its lateral part and the common carotid artery its medial part.

To summarize, the sternocleidomastoid muscle divides each side of the neck into an anterior triangle and a posterior triangle, and the investing, pretracheal and prevertebral layers of the deep cervical fascia define the carotid sheath, the retropharyngeal space and the danger space behind them. The common carotid artery divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, the internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck, and the internal jugular vein, the vagus nerve and the sympathetic trunk keep fixed relations to the artery within and behind the sheath. The cervical plexus gives the cutaneous nerves of the neck and the phrenic nerve, while the spinal accessory nerve runs superficially through the posterior triangle and is at risk there. The thyroid gland wraps the upper trachea inside the pretracheal fascia and receives the superior thyroid artery from the external carotid and the inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk, with the recurrent laryngeal nerve passing near the latter. The larynx is built from the thyroid, cricoid and epiglottic cartilages, and the cricothyroid muscle is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 28 — Back

The back carries the weight of the trunk and moves it, and this chapter examines the muscles that do that work. It begins with the superficial muscles, the broad sheets that tie the shoulder girdle and the arm to the spine, then turns to the deep muscles that span one vertebra to the next, and it closes with the erector spinae, the long mass that holds the trunk upright. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2701. A described dissection of the back shows a broad diamond-shaped sheet of muscle running from the base of the skull and the lower part of the neck to the middle of the back, with fibers that converge on the shoulder girdle. Which muscle is described? The answer is the trapezius. It takes its name from its shape, and it moves the shoulder blade rather than the arm itself.

Question 2702. Which of these movements does the trapezius produce: lifting the shoulder, drawing the arm down and back, bending the trunk to one side, or turning the head? The answer is lifting the shoulder. The upper fibers raise the shoulder girdle, while the middle and the lower fibers draw the shoulder blade toward the spine and steady it.

Question 2703. A described dissection of the upper back shows one flat muscle lying over another. The outer one reaches the outer end of the collarbone, and the inner one reaches the inner border of the shoulder blade. Which two muscles are shown? The answer is the trapezius over the rhomboid major. The rhomboid muscles lie against the chest wall, deep to the trapezius.

Question 2704. Which broad muscle of the back arises from the lower spine, the hip bone, and the lower ribs, and then twists into a narrow tendon that reaches the front of the upper arm? The answer is the latissimus dorsi. It forms the back wall of the armpit and gives that hollow its posterior fold.

Question 2705. Which nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi: the dorsal scapular nerve, the thoracodorsal nerve, the long thoracic nerve, or the spinal accessory nerve? The answer is the thoracodorsal nerve. It comes from the brachial plexus and runs down the back wall of the armpit to reach the deep surface of the muscle.

Question 2706. Which muscle lies immediately superficial to the rhomboid major: the trapezius, the latissimus dorsi, the serratus posterior superior, or the splenius capitis? The answer is the trapezius. The rhomboid muscles lie against the chest wall deep to the trapezius, and the serratus posterior superior lies deep to them again.

Question 2707. Which of these muscles arises from the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae and runs down to lift the top corner of the shoulder blade: the levator scapulae, the rhomboid major, the serratus posterior superior, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the levator scapulae. It raises the shoulder blade and tilts its lower angle toward the spine.

Question 2708. True or false: the trapezius is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve alone. The answer is false. The spinal accessory nerve carries the motor fibers, but small branches of the cervical plexus join the muscle to carry proprioceptive fibers, so it has two sources of nerve fibers.

Question 2709. A constructed illustration: during an operation in the back of the neck, a nerve that crosses the posterior triangle and lies on the surface of the trapezius is divided, and afterwards the shoulder droops. Which nerve was divided? The answer is the spinal accessory nerve. The trapezius loses its motor supply and can no longer hold the shoulder blade in place.

Question 2710. Which movement do the rhomboid major and the rhomboid minor produce: drawing the shoulder blade forward around the chest, drawing it back toward the spine, lifting the arm above the head, or turning the palm to face the floor? The answer is drawing the shoulder blade back toward the spine. They also hold that bone flat against the chest wall.

Question 2711. Which thin muscle lies deep to the rhomboid muscles, arises from the lower part of the neck and the upper thoracic spines, and runs down and out to the upper ribs? The answer is the serratus posterior superior. It takes its nerve supply from the intercostal nerves rather than from a posterior ramus.

Question 2712. Which of these forms the upper border of the triangle of auscultation: the trapezius, the latissimus dorsi, the spine of the shoulder blade, or the twelfth rib? The answer is the trapezius. The latissimus dorsi forms the lower border and the medial border of the shoulder blade the lateral border, and the floor of the gap is thin.

Question 2713. A described dissection of the lower back outlines a small gap whose sides are the latissimus dorsi, the external abdominal oblique, and the hip bone. What is this gap called, and what forms its floor? The answer is the lumbar triangle, with the internal abdominal oblique forming its floor. A loop of bowel can push through it and make a lumbar hernia.

Question 2714. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the thoracolumbar fascia in the lower back: the erector spinae, the latissimus dorsi, the serratus posterior inferior, or the trapezius? The answer is the erector spinae. The fascia wraps the long muscle mass of the back, and the latissimus dorsi attaches to the same sheet from the outside.

Question 2715. Which muscle attaches to the spine of the shoulder blade: the trapezius, the latissimus dorsi, the serratus posterior inferior, or the splenius capitis? The answer is the trapezius. Its middle fibers reach the acromion and the spine of the shoulder blade, and its upper fibers reach the outer third of the collarbone.

Question 2716. Which of these pairs belongs together: the latissimus dorsi with the front of the upper arm, the trapezius with the back of the upper arm, the rhomboid major with the front of the thigh, or the levator scapulae with the forearm? The answer is the latissimus dorsi with the front of the upper arm. Its tendon twists around the teres major and enters the groove in front of the shoulder joint.

Question 2717. Which deep muscle of the neck arises from the ligamentum nuchae and the upper thoracic spines and runs up and out to the mastoid process behind the ear? The answer is the splenius capitis. It lies in the first layer of the deep muscles and extends and turns the head.

Question 2718. A constructed illustration: after a long period of holding the neck in extension, a person has a burning pain that begins at the back of the head and spreads over the top of the skull. Which nerve is irritated, and where does it become superficial? The answer is the greater occipital nerve, which becomes superficial below the obliquus capitis inferior. It is the posterior ramus of the second cervical spinal nerve.

Question 2719. Which structures lie within the suboccipital triangle: the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve, the greater occipital nerve and the occipital artery, the spinal accessory nerve and the vertebral vein, or the second cervical nerve and the occipital artery? The answer is the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve, which is the posterior ramus of the first cervical spinal nerve.

Question 2720. Name two muscles of the back that attach to the mastoid process behind the ear. The answer is the splenius capitis and the longissimus capitis. The sternocleidomastoid from the front of the neck also reaches that same small bump.

Question 2721. Which group forms the long mass that runs up each side of the spine: the transversospinalis group, the erector spinae, the suboccipital group, or the levatores costarum? The answer is the erector spinae. It is the second layer of the deep muscles of the back and consists of the iliocostalis, the longissimus, and the spinalis.

Question 2722. A described dissection peels the superficial muscles from the back and shows a deep layer of short fibers that run upward and medially from one vertebra to the one above it. Which group is this? The answer is the transversospinalis group. It contains the semispinalis, the multifidus, and the rotatores.

Question 2723. Which part of the erector spinae lies most laterally and is named for the ribs and the hip bone it reaches? The answer is the iliocostalis. It runs from the hip bone and the lower ribs up to the angles of the upper ribs, and its highest part reaches the neck.

Question 2724. Which muscles lie immediately deep to the semispinalis capitis: the suboccipital muscles, the trapezius, the splenius capitis, or the levator scapulae? The answer is the suboccipital muscles. The semispinalis capitis is the largest of the deep muscles of the neck and covers the four short muscles at the base of the skull almost completely.

Question 2725. Which muscle is built of short bundles that spring from the transverse process of one vertebra and reach the spine of a vertebra two to four levels above it? The answer is the multifidus. Its bundles are thickest in the lower back, where they steady the joints between the vertebrae one at a time.

Question 2726. A constructed illustration: a person lifts a heavy box with the back bent forward and feels a sudden tearing pain beside the lower spine. Which muscle mass is most likely strained at that moment? The answer is the erector spinae. It must resist the forward bend of the trunk, and the strain is felt in the long mass beside the spine.

Question 2727. Which small muscles lie between the spines of neighboring vertebrae: the interspinales, the rotatores, the levatores costarum, or the intertransversarii? The answer is the interspinales. They are best developed in the neck and the lower back, and each one crosses only a single joint.

Question 2728. True or false: the deep muscles of the back are supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves. The answer is true. Those rami pass backward between the transverse processes and give branches to the deep muscles and to the skin of the back, while the superficial muscles of the back are supplied by anterior rami.

Question 2729. A described specimen shows a column of muscle on each side of the lumbar spine, wrapped in a thick fascial sheath and marked by faint grooves into separate strips. Which strips are these? The answer is the iliocostalis, the longissimus, and the spinalis, the three columns of the erector spinae.

Question 2730. Which part of the erector spinae lies closest to the spines of the vertebrae: the iliocostalis, the longissimus, the spinalis, or the levator costarum? The answer is the spinalis. It is the most medial column of the erector spinae and is best developed in the upper thoracic region, where it spans several levels.

Question 2731. Which thick muscle arises from the transverse processes of the upper thoracic and lower cervical vertebrae and reaches the occipital bone between the two nuchal lines? The answer is the semispinalis capitis. It is the largest muscle of the semispinalis group and extends and turns the head.

Question 2732. Which small deep muscles run from the transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae down and out to the rib below: the levatores costarum, the rotatores, the intertransversarii, or the serratus posterior inferior? The answer is the levatores costarum. They lie in the deepest layer beside the spine and can lift the ribs in inspiration.

Question 2733. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the trapezius but superficial to the serratus posterior superior: the rhomboid major, the latissimus dorsi, the splenius cervicis, or the semispinalis thoracis? The answer is the rhomboid major. From the surface inward at that point come the skin, the trapezius, the rhomboid muscles, and then the serratus posterior superior over the ribs.

Question 2734. A described computed tomography section of the lower back shows the spine in the middle and, behind it, two large oval masses of muscle separated by a fat-filled cleft. Which muscles are those masses? The answer is the erector spinae. One mass lies on each side in the fascial compartment behind the spine, and fat separates them at the midline.

Question 2735. From which of these does the erector spinae arise as a single mass: the sacrum and the hip bone, the ribs alone, the occipital bone, or the shoulder blade? The answer is the sacrum and the hip bone. It also takes fibers from the spines of the lower lumbar vertebrae and from the thoracolumbar fascia, and it splits above into its three columns.

Question 2736. A constructed illustration: a sharp instrument enters the back just below the tip of the shoulder blade, close to the spine, and the lung on that side later collapses. Through which gap did it most likely pass into the chest? The answer is the triangle of auscultation. Its floor is thin, and it is bounded by the trapezius, the latissimus dorsi, and the shoulder blade.

Question 2737. Which short muscle bounds the suboccipital triangle on its medial side and runs from the spine of the second cervical vertebra to the inferior nuchal line? The answer is the rectus capitis posterior major. It turns the head to the same side and is one of the four short muscles at the base of the skull.

Question 2738. How does the rhomboid minor differ from the rhomboid major: it lies below the major, it arises from the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra and the first thoracic vertebra, it inserts on the humerus, or it is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve? The answer is that it arises from the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra and the first thoracic vertebra. The major arises from the second to the fifth thoracic spines.

Question 2739. Which of these pairs belongs together: the trapezius with the spinal accessory nerve, the latissimus dorsi with the dorsal scapular nerve, the rhomboid major with the thoracodorsal nerve, or the levator scapulae with the long thoracic nerve? The answer is the trapezius with the spinal accessory nerve. The rhomboid muscles and the levator scapulae take the dorsal scapular nerve, and the latissimus dorsi takes the thoracodorsal nerve.

Question 2740. A described photograph of a standing person shows a rounded prominence at the base of the neck, a midline furrow down the back, and two flat triangles of muscle sloping out to the shoulder blades. Which muscles are shown? The answer is the trapezius muscles, with the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra forming the prominence at the base of the neck.

Question 2741. Which movement does the latissimus dorsi produce at the shoulder: raising the arm forward, drawing the arm downward and backward and turning it inward, lifting the shoulder blade, or straightening the elbow? The answer is drawing the arm downward and backward and turning it inward. When the arms are fixed, the same muscle pulls the trunk upward.

Question 2742. Which deep muscles are made of short bundles that run from the transverse process of one vertebra to the lamina of the vertebra above and are best developed in the thoracic region? The answer is the rotatores. Each bundle spans one or two levels, and they are the deepest members of the transversospinalis group.

Question 2743. A described dissection of the back of the neck reflects the trapezius and the semispinalis capitis and exposes a small triangle at the base of the skull. What lies inside that triangle, and what are its three borders? The answer is the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve, bordered by the rectus capitis posterior major, the obliquus capitis superior, and the obliquus capitis inferior.

Question 2744. Through which muscle does the greater occipital nerve pass on its way to the skin of the scalp: the obliquus capitis inferior, the semispinalis capitis, the splenius cervicis, or the rectus capitis posterior minor? The answer is the semispinalis capitis. That nerve is the posterior ramus of the second cervical spinal nerve, and it also pierces the trapezius before it reaches the skin.

Question 2745. Which of these muscles belongs to the superficial group of the back: the trapezius, the multifidus, the rotatores, or the interspinales? The answer is the trapezius. The superficial muscles connect the shoulder girdle and the arm to the trunk, while the multifidus, the rotatores, and the interspinales are deep muscles of the back.

Question 2746. A constructed illustration: a described procedure on the back of the neck passes close to the upper surface of the first cervical vertebra, and afterwards the patient is unsteady and the back of the brain loses part of its blood supply. Which vessel lies in that position? The answer is the vertebral artery, whose third part lies in the suboccipital triangle above the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra.

Question 2747. Which statement about the longissimus is correct: it lies between the iliocostalis and the spinalis, it lies medial to the spinalis, it lies superficial to the trapezius, or it belongs to the transversospinalis group? The answer is that it lies between the iliocostalis and the spinalis. It is the middle column of the erector spinae, and its capitis part reaches the mastoid process.

Question 2748. True or false: the upper fibers of the trapezius and its lower fibers pull the shoulder blade in opposite directions. The answer is true. The upper fibers lift the shoulder girdle while the lower fibers depress it, and when both act with the middle fibers they help to turn the shoulder blade upward for raising the arm.

Question 2749. Which slender muscle of the erector spinae runs from the upper thoracic transverse processes to the mastoid process and turns the head to the same side? The answer is the longissimus capitis. It lies deep to the splenius capitis in the neck and is often the smallest part of the longissimus.

Question 2750. Which thin muscle arises from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spines and runs upward and outward to the lower four ribs? The answer is the serratus posterior inferior. Its fibers point upward, the reverse of the serratus posterior superior above it, and it is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves.

Question 2751. Which muscle arises from the upper thoracic spines and reaches the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae: the splenius capitis, the splenius cervicis, the semispinalis cervicis, or the levator scapulae? The answer is the splenius cervicis. It lies below the splenius capitis and turns the neck to the same side.

Question 2752. Which small muscles lie between the transverse processes of neighboring vertebrae and are best developed in the cervical and lumbar regions? The answer is the intertransversarii. They bend the vertebral column to one side, and in the neck they are rich in proprioceptive fibers.

Question 2753. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the erector spinae in the lower chest and receives the lowest fibers of that muscle: the twelfth rib, the eleventh rib, the hip bone, or the peritoneum? The answer is the twelfth rib. The lowest fibers of the iliocostalis and the longissimus run to it, and it is short and easily felt in the back.

Question 2754. A described specimen shows four short muscles arranged around a triangle at the base of the skull, with one running from the spine of the second cervical vertebra to the transverse process of the first. Which muscle is that, and which border of the triangle does it form? The answer is the obliquus capitis inferior, forming the lower border.

Question 2755. Which action does the erector spinae perform when both sides contract together: bending the trunk forward, straightening the trunk and holding it upright, turning the head to one side only, or lifting the ribs? The answer is straightening the trunk and holding it upright. When only one side contracts, the trunk bends to that same side.

Question 2756. A constructed illustration: a described needle passes between the spines of the lower lumbar vertebrae and meets first a tough band, then a softer one, before the fluid is reached. Which two structures does it cross in that order? The answer is the supraspinous ligament and then the interspinous ligament. The strong yellow ligament lies deep to both.

Question 2757. Which muscle of the erector spinae runs from the spines of the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae up to the spines of the upper thoracic vertebrae? The answer is the spinalis thoracis. It is the medial column of the erector spinae and is best seen in the upper part of the back.

Question 2758. Which of these both lifts the shoulder blade and helps to turn it upward when the arm is raised: the levator scapulae alone, the upper fibers of the trapezius, the rhomboid minor, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the upper fibers of the trapezius. They work with the serratus anterior to turn the shoulder blade upward.

Question 2759. When a standing person bends the trunk to the left, in which plane does the movement take place, and what happens to the erector spinae on the right? The answer is the coronal plane, with the right erector spinae lengthening under control. The trunk moves from side to side in that plane while the spine turns about an axis running from front to back.

Question 2760. A described magnetic resonance imaging study of the lower back shows fat between the skin and the long muscles of the back, and a thin dark band wrapped around those muscles. Which structure is the dark band, and what does it enclose? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia, which encloses the erector spinae.

Question 2761. Which of these pairs belongs together: the obliquus capitis inferior with turning the head to the same side, the rectus capitis posterior minor with turning the head, the obliquus capitis superior with lifting the shoulder, or the rectus capitis posterior major with bending the neck the other way? The answer is the obliquus capitis inferior with turning the head to the same side. The two rectus muscles extend the head.

Question 2762. Which of these lies deepest: the semispinalis capitis, the splenius capitis, the trapezius, or the skin of the back of the neck? The answer is the semispinalis capitis. The layers from the surface inward are the skin, the trapezius, the splenius capitis, and then the semispinalis capitis over the suboccipital muscles.

Question 2763. Which muscle runs from the spine of the second cervical vertebra to the transverse process of the first and turns the head to the same side? The answer is the obliquus capitis inferior. It is the only suboccipital muscle that does not attach to the skull, and it forms the lower border of the suboccipital triangle.

Question 2764. Which vessel lies in a groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra: the vertebral artery, the internal carotid artery, the occipital artery, or the external jugular vein? The answer is the vertebral artery. It turns inward and upward there to enter the skull through the foramen magnum.

Question 2765. What does the multifidus do when only the bundles of one segment contract: it extends the whole trunk, it steadies that single joint between the vertebrae, it lifts the ribs, or it turns the head? The answer is that it steadies that single joint. The short bundles give the vertebral column local control, while the long erector spinae supplies the power.

Question 2766. A constructed illustration: a person holds the head turned and tilted back for a long time, and afterwards has a deep ache at the base of the skull with tenderness over one small muscle there. Which suboccipital muscle is tender, and which nerve lies beside it? The answer is the obliquus capitis inferior, with the greater occipital nerve beside it.

Question 2767. A described dissection shows a thick sheet of fascia attached to the spines of the vertebrae and splitting to enclose a long muscle mass, with the latissimus dorsi attached to its outer surface. Which sheet is described, and which muscle does it enclose? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia, enclosing the erector spinae.

Question 2768. Which of these small muscles lies between the transverse processes of two neighboring vertebrae rather than between their spines: the interspinales, the intertransversarii, the rotatores, or the multifidus? The answer is the intertransversarii. They are best developed in the neck and the lower back and bend the vertebral column to one side.

Question 2769. Which part of the erector spinae arises from the lower thoracic and lumbar region and inserts on the ribs and the transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae? The answer is the longissimus thoracis. It is the largest part of the longissimus and lies between the iliocostalis and the spinalis.

Question 2770. Which statement separates the iliocostalis from the longissimus: the iliocostalis attaches to the angles of the ribs, the longissimus lies lateral to the iliocostalis, the iliocostalis reaches the mastoid process, or the longissimus attaches to the hip bone only? The answer is that the iliocostalis attaches to the angles of the ribs. The longissimus lies medial to it, and its capitis part reaches the mastoid process.

Question 2771. A described cross section at the middle of the chest shows the rib cage as a ring of bone, the vertebral body behind, and three columns of muscle between the transverse processes and the skin. What are those columns, from lateral to medial? The answer is the iliocostalis, the longissimus, and the spinalis. The multifidus lies deep to the spinalis.

Question 2772. Which nerve supplies the four suboccipital muscles: the posterior ramus of the first cervical spinal nerve, the posterior ramus of the second cervical spinal nerve, the spinal accessory nerve, or the dorsal scapular nerve? The answer is the posterior ramus of the first cervical spinal nerve, also called the suboccipital nerve. It has no branch to the skin.

Question 2773. Which part of the trapezius arises from the spines of the lower thoracic vertebrae and inserts on the spine of the shoulder blade? The answer is the lower fibers. They pull the shoulder blade downward and, with the upper fibers, help to turn it upward when the arm is raised.

Question 2774. Which muscle forms the lower border of the triangle of auscultation and the posterior border of the lumbar triangle at the same time? The answer is the latissimus dorsi. It forms one border of both gaps because it crosses the back on its way from the spine to the arm.

Question 2775. Which of these muscles is supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves: the trapezius, the rhomboid major, the levator scapulae, or the multifidus? The answer is the multifidus. The first three are superficial muscles of the back and take anterior rami, while all the deep muscles of the back take posterior rami.

Question 2776. A constructed illustration: a person has pain in the lower back that worsens on standing and eases on lying down, and the tenderness lies over the thick fascial sheet beside the spine. Which structures are involved in this described picture? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia and the erector spinae that it encloses. That fascia anchors muscle to the spine and the hip bone.

Question 2777. Which muscle covers the widest area of the back and gives the armpit its posterior fold: the trapezius, the latissimus dorsi, the rhomboid major, or the serratus posterior inferior? The answer is the latissimus dorsi. It runs from the lower spine, the hip bone, and the lower ribs up to the front of the upper arm.

Question 2778. A described specimen of the lower back shows a thick sheet of fascia with a flat muscle attached to its outer surface and a small triangular gap just below that muscle at the edge of the back. What is the gap, and which muscle borders it above? The answer is the lumbar triangle, with the latissimus dorsi forming its upper and posterior border.

Question 2779. Which muscle of the erector spinae group is the longest, running from the sacrum and the hip bone as far up as the mastoid process? The answer is the longissimus. Its capitis part reaches the mastoid process, and its thoracis part is the largest of the three columns.

Question 2780. True or false: when the erector spinae on one side contracts alone, the trunk bends to the opposite side. The answer is false. The trunk bends to the same side as the contracting muscle, and when both columns work together they straighten the back and hold it upright against gravity.

Question 2781. Which of these pairs belongs together: the rectus capitis posterior minor with the posterior tubercle of the first cervical vertebra, the rectus capitis posterior major with the spine of the third cervical vertebra, the obliquus capitis superior with the spine of the second cervical vertebra, or the obliquus capitis inferior with the occipital bone? The answer is the rectus capitis posterior minor with the posterior tubercle of the first cervical vertebra. The major arises from the spine of the second.

Question 2782. Which statement about the deep muscles of the back is correct: the multifidus is supplied by the anterior rami, the rotatores span three or four levels each, the semispinalis capitis is supplied by the second cervical nerve, or the suboccipital muscles are supplied by the first cervical nerve? The answer is that the suboccipital muscles are supplied by the first cervical nerve. All the deep muscles of the back take posterior rami.

Question 2783. Which muscle of the transversospinalis group arises from the transverse processes of the lower thoracic vertebrae and reaches the spines of the upper thoracic and lower cervical vertebrae? The answer is the semispinalis thoracis. Its fibers cross four to six levels, more than the bundles of the multifidus below it.

Question 2784. A described section through the lower back shows the twelfth rib as a short bar of bone beside the spine, with muscle fibers running up to it from below and a large muscle mass on each side of the midline. Which muscle reaches that rib, and which mass lies beside the spine? The answer is the iliocostalis, beside the erector spinae.

Question 2785. A constructed illustration: a wound in the lower back, above the hip bone and behind the edge of the latissimus dorsi, allows a loop of bowel to appear beneath the skin. Which gap has it passed through, and what forms the floor of that gap? The answer is the lumbar triangle, whose floor is the internal abdominal oblique.

Question 2786. Which structure lies immediately below the vertebral artery within the suboccipital triangle: the suboccipital nerve, the greater occipital nerve, the spinal accessory nerve, or the occipital artery? The answer is the suboccipital nerve. It is the posterior ramus of the first cervical spinal nerve and runs between the artery and the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra.

Question 2787. Which muscle arises from the spines of the seventh cervical and the first thoracic vertebrae and inserts on the medial border of the shoulder blade at the level of its spine? The answer is the rhomboid minor. The rhomboid major lies below it and reaches further down the same border.

Question 2788. Which muscle arises from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spines and runs upward and outward to the lower ribs: the serratus posterior superior, the serratus posterior inferior, the levatores costarum, or the iliocostalis? The answer is the serratus posterior inferior. Its fibers point upward, and it takes its nerves from the lower intercostal nerves.

Question 2789. Name the three columns of the erector spinae, spoken as a list from lateral to medial. The answer is the iliocostalis, the longissimus, and the spinalis. Each column is named again for the region it occupies, as in iliocostalis lumborum or longissimus capitis.

Question 2790. Which of these lies in the deepest layer of the muscles of the back: the levatores costarum, the multifidus, the semispinalis thoracis, or the splenius capitis? The answer is the levatores costarum. The deepest layer also holds the interspinales and the intertransversarii, while the splenius lies in the first layer.

Question 2791. A described dissection of the side of the neck shows a thin muscle running from the upper thoracic spines up and out to the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae, lying deep to the larger muscle that reaches the mastoid process. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the splenius cervicis, deep to the splenius capitis.

Question 2792. Which muscle forms the lateral border of the suboccipital triangle and runs from the transverse process of the first cervical vertebra up to the occipital bone? The answer is the obliquus capitis superior. It extends the head and bends it to the same side.

Question 2793. The greater occipital nerve lies immediately below which muscle, and between which two bones does that muscle run? The answer is the obliquus capitis inferior, which runs between the spine of the second cervical vertebra and the transverse process of the first. The nerve turns around the lower border of that muscle on its way to the scalp.

Question 2794. A constructed illustration: a surgeon plans to move a broad muscle of the back to repair a defect on the chest wall and must keep its nerve intact. Which nerve must be preserved, and where does it run? The answer is the thoracodorsal nerve, which runs down the back wall of the armpit to the deep surface of the latissimus dorsi.

Question 2795. The bundles of the multifidus run upward and medially from one vertebra to another. Which way do they face in a transverse section, and do they cross the midline? The answer is that they lie in the groove beside the spine and never cross the midline. Each bundle spans two to four vertebrae in the lower back.

Question 2796. Which of these pairs belongs together: the trapezius with the eleventh cranial nerve, the latissimus dorsi with the dorsal scapular nerve, the multifidus with an anterior ramus, or the levator scapulae with the thoracodorsal nerve? The answer is the trapezius with the eleventh cranial nerve. The multifidus takes a posterior ramus, and the latissimus dorsi takes the thoracodorsal nerve.

Question 2797. Which muscle of the back is attached to the base of the skull, the ligamentum nuchae, and the spines of the lower cervical and all the thoracic vertebrae? The answer is the trapezius. Its fibers converge on the outer third of the collarbone, the acromion, and the spine of the shoulder blade.

Question 2798. A described image of the back of the neck, made with magnetic resonance imaging, shows a small nerve passing around the lower edge of a short muscle that runs from the spine of the second cervical vertebra to the first. Which muscle and which nerve are shown? The answer is the obliquus capitis inferior and the greater occipital nerve, which then pierces the semispinalis capitis.

Question 2799. Name two muscles of the deep group of the back that extend the head at the joint between the skull and the first cervical vertebra. The answer is the semispinalis capitis and the splenius capitis. The rectus capitis posterior major and minor and the longissimus capitis also extend the head.
