Question 2800. True or false: when the arms are fixed, the latissimus dorsi can raise the trunk. The answer is true. In climbing or on crutches, the muscle pulls the trunk up toward the fixed arm, and it is one of the strongest muscles of the back.

To summarize, the superficial muscles of the back connect the shoulder girdle and the arm to the trunk and are supplied by anterior rami: the trapezius by the eleventh cranial nerve, the latissimus dorsi by the thoracodorsal nerve, and the rhomboid muscles and the levator scapulae by the dorsal scapular nerve. The deep muscles of the back are supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves and are arranged in layers, the splenius muscles first, then the erector spinae, then the transversospinalis group of semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores, and last the deepest layer of levatores costarum, interspinales and intertransversarii. The erector spinae rises from the sacrum, the hip bone, and the thoracolumbar fascia as one mass and splits into the iliocostalis, the longissimus, and the spinalis, which straighten the trunk and bend it to the same side. At the base of the skull the four suboccipital muscles bound the suboccipital triangle, which holds the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve, while the greater occipital nerve winds below the obliquus capitis inferior. The triangle of auscultation and the lumbar triangle are the two named gaps of the back, and each is defined by muscles met in this chapter. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 29 — Back, Part Two

This chapter finishes the muscles of the back and then crosses the chest wall, and it deals with the two groups that move the trunk and the ribs. It begins with the transversospinalis group, the deep sheet of short oblique muscles that runs from a transverse process below to a spinous process above, and works through the semispinalis, the multifidus and the rotatores. It then turns to the pectoral muscles, the pectoralis major, the pectoralis minor, the subclavius and the serratus anterior, and it ends with the intercostal muscles, their three layers and the neurovascular bundle they enclose. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2801. Which group of deep muscles of the back takes its name from its two attachments, running from a transverse process below to a spinous process above, and lies in the gutter beside the vertebral spines? The answer is the transversospinalis group. Its fibers pass upward and medially, and it lies deep to the erector spinae, filling the groove between the transverse processes and the spines. It is arranged in three layers.

Question 2802. Which three muscles make up the transversospinalis group: the splenius, the erector spinae and the latissimus dorsi, the semispinalis, the multifidus and the rotatores, the trapezius, the rhomboid muscles and the levator scapulae, or the interspinales, the intertransversarii and the levatores costarum? The answer is the semispinalis, the multifidus and the rotatores. They form three layers from superficial to deep, and each deeper layer spans fewer vertebral levels than the one above it.

Question 2803. A described dissection of the neck shows the largest muscle of the semispinalis group, a thick rounded band running from the upper thoracic vertebrae to the base of the skull between the nuchal lines. Which muscle is it? The answer is the semispinalis capitis. It forms the rounded bulge felt below the external occipital protuberance, and the greater occipital nerve pierces it.

Question 2804. A described specimen shows a series of short muscles in the thoracic region, each running from the transverse process of one vertebra to the spinous process of the vertebra one or two levels above it. Which muscles are shown, and what is their action? The answer is the rotatores. They are best developed in the thoracic region and assist in turning the vertebral column to the opposite side.

Question 2805. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the erector spinae in the lumbar region, filling the gutter on each side of the spinous processes and taking origin from the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae? The answer is the multifidus. It lies between the erector spinae behind it and the vertebral laminae in front of it, and the rotatores lie deeper still.

Question 2806. From which bony points does the lumbar multifidus take origin: the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae alone, the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae together with the sacrum and the hip bone, the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae, or the costal cartilages of the lower ribs? The answer is the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae together with the sacrum and the hip bone. Its fibers then pass upward and medially.

Question 2807. A described illustration: after a long period of poor posture and repeated lifting, a person has wasting of the deep muscle beside the lumbar spines, and the lower back feels unstable on movement. Which muscle is described, and what is its normal action? The answer is the multifidus, which steadies and extends the vertebral column and is the chief stabilizer of the lumbar segments.

Question 2808. True or false: the rotatores are best developed in the thoracic region of the vertebral column. The answer is true. The thoracic part of the column carries the most rotatores, where each bundle spans one or two segments. In the lumbar region the multifidus takes their place as the dominant deep muscle of the back.

Question 2809. Which part of the semispinalis group arises from the transverse processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae and ends on the spinous processes of the second to the fifth cervical vertebrae? The answer is the semispinalis cervicis. It lies deep to the semispinalis capitis, and it extends the cervical part of the vertebral column and turns it to the opposite side.

Question 2810. Which of these pairs belongs together: the multifidus with the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae, the semispinalis capitis with the coracoid process, the rotatores with the mastoid process, or the semispinalis cervicis with the first rib? The answer is the multifidus with the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae. The other three attachments belong to muscles of the shoulder girdle and the neck.

Question 2811. When the semispinalis and the multifidus contract on one side only, toward which side do they turn the face and the trunk: the same side as the contraction, the opposite side, either side equally, or neither side, because they do not rotate the column at all? The answer is the opposite side. They run upward and medially, so they pull the spines toward the far side.

Question 2812. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the semispinalis capitis as that muscle passes from the upper thoracic vertebrae to the base of the skull? The answer is the semispinalis cervicis. It lies in front of and below the capitis part in the back of the neck, and the multifidus lies deeper still. All three belong to the same group.

Question 2813. A described section through the back of the neck shows a large muscle pierced in its lower part by a nerve that then runs upward over the scalp toward the top of the head. Which muscle and which nerve are described? The answer is the semispinalis capitis and the greater occipital nerve. That nerve is the medial branch of the posterior ramus of the second cervical spinal nerve.

Question 2814. Which part of the transversospinalis group is best developed in the lumbar region, where it forms the largest mass of the deep muscles of the lower back and covers the laminae on each side? The answer is the multifidus. Its lumbar fibers are the thickest in the group, and they take origin from the sacrum and the mammillary processes.

Question 2815. How many vertebral levels does a typical fascicle of the multifidus cross: one level, two to about four levels, six to eight levels, or the whole length of the vertebral column? The answer is two to about four levels. The rotatores cross only one or two levels, and the semispinalis crosses four to six, so the deeper the muscle the shorter its span.

Question 2816. Name two muscles of the transversospinalis group that extend the vertebral column when both of their sides act together. The answer is the multifidus and the semispinalis. Both of them also turn the column to the opposite side when one side acts, and they are supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves.

Question 2817. A described illustration: a person bends forward before lifting a heavy load and feels a sudden deep pain beside the lumbar spines, with spasm of the muscle there. Which muscle is most likely strained, and where does it attach below? The answer is the multifidus, which attaches to the sacrum and the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae.

Question 2818. In a transverse section through the lumbar region, the transversospinalis group occupies a defined zone. Between which two structures does the multifidus lie, and where does it sit relative to the spinous process? The answer is that it lies between the erector spinae behind and the vertebral laminae in front, in the gutter lateral to the spinous process.

Question 2819. Which statement about the nerve supply of the deep muscles of the back is correct: the transversospinalis group is supplied by the anterior rami of the spinal nerves, by the posterior rami, by the sympathetic trunk, or by the accessory nerve? The answer is the posterior rami. Each posterior ramus divides into branches and supplies the deep muscles of its own segment.

Question 2820. A described dissection shows the semispinalis thoracis as a thin sheet passing from the transverse processes of the lower thoracic vertebrae to the spinous processes of the upper thoracic and lower cervical vertebrae. How many segments do its fibers span, and what is its action? The answer is four to six segments, and it extends the thoracic part of the column.

Question 2821. Which muscle of the transversospinalis group lies deepest and is the shortest of the three, running from one transverse process to the spinous process of the vertebra one or two levels above, and is thickest in the thoracic region? The answer is the rotatores. They extend the column and are richly supplied with receptors for position sense.

Question 2822. Which muscle of the deep back takes origin from the transverse processes of the vertebrae from the sacrum upward and inserts on the spinous process of a vertebra two to four levels above, so that its bundles overlap like tiles? The answer is the multifidus. It is the middle layer of the transversospinalis group and the strongest of the three.

Question 2823. Which structure lies immediately superficial to the transversospinalis group in the back, forming the thick longitudinal ridge felt on either side of the midline? The answer is the erector spinae. The transversospinalis group lies in the gutter deep to it, and the rotatores form the deepest layer of the back muscles.

Question 2824. True or false: the greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the posterior ramus of the second cervical spinal nerve, and it pierces the semispinalis capitis on its way to the scalp. The answer is true. The nerve runs upward through the muscle and then supplies the skin of the back of the head. Its compression is a described cause of headache.

Question 2825. A described illustration: in a person with long-standing lumbar pain, the deep muscle beside the spines is found to be pale and wasted, with fatty tissue replacing its fibers on one side. Which muscle is described, and why does the finding matter? The answer is the multifidus, whose wasting leaves the lumbar segments less steady and is a described reason for pain to persist.

Question 2826. A described illustration: a needle placed beside the lumbar spines for a local block is said to lie where the posterior ramus of a spinal nerve runs. Which muscles does that ramus supply as it passes? The answer is the deep muscles of the back, including the multifidus and the rotatores. The block itself belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2827. Which part of the transversospinalis group forms the rounded bulge that can be felt at the back of the neck just below the occiput, and what is its main action? The answer is the semispinalis capitis, which extends the head and turns the face to the opposite side. The greater occipital nerve pierces it on its course to the scalp.

Question 2828. A described radiograph of the lumbar spine shows the spinous processes in a neat row down the midline, with a smooth gutter on each side of them. Which deep muscle fills those gutters, and does the radiograph show the muscle itself? The answer is the multifidus. The film shows the bone that the muscle lies against, not the muscle.

Question 2829. Which of these muscles does not belong to the transversospinalis group: the semispinalis capitis, the multifidus, the rotatores, or the spinalis thoracis? The answer is the spinalis thoracis, which belongs to the erector spinae. It lies closest to the spinous processes in the erector mass and runs between the lower thoracic and upper thoracic spines.

Question 2830. Name the three layers of the transversospinalis group in order from superficial to deep, and say how many vertebral levels each typically crosses. The answer is the semispinalis, the multifidus and the rotatores. The semispinalis crosses four to six levels, the multifidus two to four, and the rotatores only one or two.

Question 2831. Which of these pairs belongs together: the rotatores with the thoracic region, the multifidus with the cervical region only, the semispinalis capitis with the lumbar region, or the transversospinalis group with the anterior rami of the spinal nerves? The answer is the rotatores with the thoracic region, where they are best developed and most numerous.

Question 2832. Which arteries supply the deep muscles of the back: the anterior intercostal arteries, the dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries, the internal thoracic arteries, or the superior epigastric arteries? The answer is the dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries. They follow the posterior rami of the spinal nerves into the muscles they supply.

Question 2833. Which muscle lies immediately medial to the multifidus in the back, forming a slender band that runs between the spinous processes of adjacent vertebrae? The answer is the spinalis, the medial column of the erector spinae. It lies superficial to the multifidus and is best developed in the thoracic region, not in the lumbar region.

Question 2834. When the transversospinalis muscles of one side contract alone, to which side do they bend the trunk, and what rotation do they add? The answer is that they bend the trunk to the same side and turn it to the opposite side. Extension of the column is the effect when both sides act together, as in standing upright.

Question 2835. Which thick sheet of fibrous tissue encloses the erector spinae and the transversospinalis group in the lower back and also gives attachment to the latissimus dorsi and the gluteal muscles? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia. It forms a strong sleeve around the deep muscles and is a landmark in the surgery of the lumbar region.

Question 2836. A described magnetic resonance image of the lumbar region shows a band of muscle lying directly against the vertebral laminae on each side, much thinner on the left than on the right. Which muscle is shown, and why does its bulk matter? The answer is the multifidus, whose thickness is a described marker of segmental steadiness in the lower back.

Question 2837. A described illustration: during an operation on the lower back, a small nerve is cut as it crosses the lamina, and the muscle beside the spine on that side later wastes. Which nerve has been divided, and which muscle has lost its supply? The answer is a posterior ramus of a spinal nerve, and the multifidus of that segment.

Question 2838. Which of these muscles both extends the vertebral column and turns it to the opposite side: the iliocostalis, the longissimus, the multifidus, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the multifidus. The iliocostalis and the longissimus bend the column to the same side, and the latissimus dorsi moves the arm and not the column.

Question 2839. True or false: the transversospinalis group lies deep to the erector spinae and is therefore not visible until the erector spinae has been removed. The answer is true. The group occupies the gutter between the transverse processes and the spines, and the long mass of the erector spinae covers it from the sacrum to the skull.

Question 2840. Which layer of the transversospinalis group lies immediately deep to the semispinalis and immediately superficial to the rotatores, and is the thickest of the three in the lumbar region? The answer is the multifidus. It fills the gutter beside the spines and sends its bundles upward and medially across two to four segments before they end.

Question 2841. Which muscle of the deep back is described in the brief as the chief stabilizer of adjacent vertebrae, holding one segment steady against the next during movement? The answer is the multifidus, with the rotatores assisting it. These muscles are short, span few segments, and are among the most richly innervated muscles in the body.

Question 2842. A described dissection after removal of the erector spinae shows a fan of muscle arising from the sacrum, the hip bone and the lumbar mammillary processes and reaching upward to the thoracic and cervical spines, with the longest bundles in the middle of the fan. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the multifidus.

Question 2843. Which structure lies immediately anterior to the multifidus in the lumbar region, separating it from the vertebral canal and the spinal cord within it? The answer is the vertebral lamina, together with the ligamentum flavum that joins one lamina to the next. The thoracolumbar fascia and the latissimus dorsi lie behind the muscle instead.

Question 2844. Which of these is the main postural role of the transversospinalis group: to swing the arm, to hold adjacent vertebrae steady against one another, to raise the ribs in inspiration, or to bend the head forward? The answer is to hold adjacent vertebrae steady. That is why the group is rich in position-sensing receptors and is arranged in short segmental bundles.

Question 2845. Which muscle of the transversospinalis group is the most superficial of its three layers and the only one whose fibers reach as high as the skull? The answer is the semispinalis, whose capitis part ends on the occipital bone between the nuchal lines. The multifidus reaches only the cervical spines, and the rotatores stop within a segment or two.

Question 2846. A described illustration: after a deep injury to the back, a person reports an area of numbness in a narrow strip of skin beside the spine, with weakness of the deep muscles on the same side. Which nerve has been injured, and what is its normal territory? The answer is a posterior ramus of a spinal nerve, which supplies the deep back muscles and the overlying skin of that segment.

Question 2847. Which layer of the transversospinalis group is poorly developed or absent in the lumbar region, being best seen in the thoracic and cervical parts of the column: the semispinalis, the multifidus, the rotatores brevis, or the rotatores longi? The answer is the semispinalis, which is replaced in the lower back by the bulk of the multifidus.

Question 2848. A described dissection of the back of the neck shows three muscles of the semispinalis group lying one behind another, the largest reaching the skull and the smallest ending on the cervical spines. Which three muscles are shown, and what is the shared direction of their fibers? The answer is the semispinalis capitis, cervicis and thoracis, all running upward and medially.

Question 2849. Which statement about the deep muscles of the back is correct: they are supplied by the anterior rami of the spinal nerves, they are arranged in layers that span progressively fewer segments as they lie deeper, they lie superficial to the latissimus dorsi, or they all insert on the ribs? The answer is that they span fewer segments as they lie deeper, ending with the rotatores.

Question 2850. Which muscle of the transversospinalis group is the shortest and spans only the interval between one vertebra and the vertebra above it: the semispinalis, the multifidus, the rotatores brevis, or the erector spinae? The answer is the rotatores brevis. Its longer companion, the rotatores longi, spans two levels and is also confined mostly to the thoracic region.

Question 2851. The large fan-shaped muscle of the front of the chest has two heads and ends on the upper part of the humerus. On which part of the humerus does its tendon insert? The answer is the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus. The muscle forms the anterior fold of the armpit and gives the chest its broad outline.

Question 2852. Which two parts make up the pectoralis major: a clavicular head and a sternocostal head, a costal head and a vertebral head, a humeral head and a scapular head, or a superficial head and a deep head? The answer is a clavicular head and a sternocostal head. The sternocostal part also takes fibers from the sheath of the rectus abdominis below.

Question 2853. Which small triangular muscle of the chest lies deep to the pectoralis major, arises from the third, fourth and fifth ribs near their cartilages, and inserts on the coracoid process of the scapula? The answer is the pectoralis minor. It draws the scapula forward and downward, and it also tilts the lower angle of the scapula backward.

Question 2854. Which part of the axillary artery lies immediately behind the pectoralis minor, and what does that relation define for the surgeon? The answer is the second part of the artery. The muscle divides the artery into three parts, and the cords of the brachial plexus are named from their position around that second part.

Question 2855. A described dissection of the front of the chest shows a thick muscle with two heads, one from the clavicle and one from the sternum and the upper costal cartilages, ending in a flat tendon that twists onto the humerus. Which muscle is shown, and which groove receives the tendon? The answer is the pectoralis major, whose tendon enters the intertubercular sulcus.

Question 2856. Which nerves supply the pectoralis major: the long thoracic nerve alone, the lateral and medial pectoral nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, or the dorsal scapular nerve? The answer is the lateral and medial pectoral nerves. The lateral pectoral nerve supplies the clavicular part, and the medial pectoral nerve reaches the sternocostal part.

Question 2857. A described illustration: after an operation in the armpit, the medial border of the scapula stands away from the chest wall when the person pushes the hand against a wall. Which nerve has been injured, and which muscle has lost its supply? The answer is the long thoracic nerve and the serratus anterior, whose slips no longer hold the scapula flat.

Question 2858. True or false: when the scapula is held fixed, the pectoralis minor can help to raise the ribs during inspiration. The answer is true. With the shoulder girdle held steady, the muscle pulls upward on the third, fourth and fifth ribs, so it is counted among the accessory muscles of respiration.

Question 2859. Which small muscle lies in the groove on the under surface of the clavicle, running from the first rib and its cartilage to the bone above it, and what is its action? The answer is the subclavius. It steadies the clavicle and draws it downward, and it is supplied by the nerve to the subclavius from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.

Question 2860. Which of these pairs belongs together: the serratus anterior with the long thoracic nerve, the pectoralis major with the thoracodorsal nerve, the subclavius with the accessory nerve, or the pectoralis minor with the dorsal scapular nerve? The answer is the serratus anterior with the long thoracic nerve, which runs down on its outer surface and is at risk in operations on the armpit.

Question 2861. Which nerve passes through the pectoralis minor on its way to the pectoralis major: the lateral pectoral nerve, the medial pectoral nerve, the long thoracic nerve, or the intercostobrachial nerve? The answer is the medial pectoral nerve, which pierces the muscle before ending in the deep surface of the pectoralis major.

Question 2862. A described dissection shows a muscle with a series of finger-like slips from the outer surfaces of the upper ribs, passing backward around the chest wall to the deep surface of the scapula. Which muscle is described, and what is its main action? The answer is the serratus anterior, which pulls the scapula forward and rotates it so that the arm can be raised.

Question 2863. A described section through the chest wall below the armpit shows a muscle lying directly on the ribs, covered in front by the scapula and behind by the latissimus dorsi. Which muscle is shown, and which nerve runs on its surface? The answer is the serratus anterior, with the long thoracic nerve running down on it.

Question 2864. Which of these structures pierces the clavipectoral fascia: the cephalic vein, the median cubital vein, the axillary nerve, or the radial nerve? The answer is the cephalic vein. It pierces the fascia just below the clavicle to join the axillary vein, and it is accompanied through the same sheet by the thoracoacromial artery and its branches.

Question 2865. Name two muscles that pull the scapula forward on the chest wall, and say which of them is the more powerful. The answer is the serratus anterior and the pectoralis minor. The serratus anterior is the stronger of the two, and the pectoralis minor also tilts the scapula so that its lower angle swings backward.

Question 2866. Which statement about the clavicular head of the pectoralis major is correct: it extends the arm at the shoulder, it flexes the arm at the shoulder, it rotates the arm laterally, or it raises the scapula? The answer is that it flexes the arm at the shoulder. The sternocostal part instead brings the arm down and across the chest.

Question 2867. Which structure lies immediately anterior to the second part of the axillary artery and separates that part from the skin of the chest wall? The answer is the pectoralis minor. The first part of the artery lies above the muscle, and the third part lies below and lateral to it, where the arm begins.

Question 2868. In the chest wall, the pectoralis minor and the serratus anterior lie in different planes. How are the two muscles placed relative to each other, and what lies between them? The answer is that the pectoralis minor lies anterior and the serratus anterior lies posterior, with the ribs and the intercostal muscles between the two.

Question 2869. Which sheet of fascia stretches from the clavicle above to the floor of the armpit below, encloses the pectoralis minor, and is pierced by the cephalic vein? The answer is the clavipectoral fascia. Its lower part forms the suspensory ligament of the armpit, which holds the axillary contents against the chest wall.

Question 2870. Which nerve supplies the subclavius: the nerve to the subclavius from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, the long thoracic nerve, the medial pectoral nerve, or the suprascapular nerve? The answer is the nerve to the subclavius, a small branch of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus that reaches the muscle below the clavicle.

Question 2871. Which triangle of the chest wall is bounded above by the clavicle and below by the upper border of the pectoralis major, and carries the cephalic vein in its floor? The answer is the deltopectoral triangle. The vein runs upward there before it pierces the clavipectoral fascia to enter the axillary vein.

Question 2872. Which statement about the lateral pectoral nerve is correct: it passes above the pectoralis minor, it pierces the pectoralis minor, it runs down on the serratus anterior, or it supplies the latissimus dorsi? The answer is that it passes above the pectoralis minor. It then reaches the deep surface of the pectoralis major along with the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery.

Question 2873. Which two muscles bound the deltopectoral groove, and which vein runs in that groove: the deltoid and the pectoralis major with the cephalic vein, the pectoralis major and the pectoralis minor with the basilic vein, the deltoid and the trapezius with the external jugular vein, or the serratus anterior and the latissimus dorsi with the axillary vein? The answer is the deltoid and the pectoralis major, with the cephalic vein.

Question 2874. A described illustration: a newborn is found on one side to be missing the lower, sternocostal part of the pectoralis major, and the hand on the same side is small with short fingers. Which structure is deficient, and what is this described pattern called? The answer is the sternocostal head of the pectoralis major, in the described pattern known as Poland sequence.

Question 2875. Which layer of the intercostal muscles has fibers that run downward and forward, in the direction of the hands placed in the pockets, and reaches from the tubercle of the rib behind to the costal cartilage in front? The answer is the external intercostal. Its fibers lift the ribs when they contract, and it is the outermost of the three layers.

Question 2876. Within the costal groove of a rib, which structure lies lowest, nearest the inner edge of the bone: the intercostal vein, the intercostal artery, the intercostal nerve, or the collateral branch? The answer is the intercostal nerve. From above downward the groove holds the vein first, then the artery, and then the nerve.

Question 2877. A described cross section of an intercostal space shows three layers of muscle with a bundle of vessels and a nerve lying between the middle layer and the deepest one. Which layer is the deepest, and what is the bundle called? The answer is the innermost intercostal, and the bundle is the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

Question 2878. Between which two layers of the chest wall does the intercostal neurovascular bundle run, and why does that position matter? The answer is between the internal intercostal and the innermost intercostal muscles. That neurovascular plane carries the bundle around the chest wall, and it lies deep to the internal intercostal, so the vessels are shielded from the outer surface.

Question 2879. Where the external intercostal muscle stops short in front, what replaces it between the costal cartilages: the external intercostal membrane, the internal intercostal membrane, the clavipectoral fascia, or the supraspinous ligament? The answer is the external intercostal membrane. The internal intercostal layer is replaced behind by the internal intercostal membrane instead.

Question 2880. True or false: the fibers of the internal intercostal muscles run downward and backward, at right angles to those of the external intercostals. The answer is true. They run from the floor of the costal groove above to the upper border of the rib below, sloping back toward the vertebral column, and they depress the ribs in forced expiration.

Question 2881. Which is the deepest and most incomplete layer of the intercostal muscles, lying inside the internal intercostals and separated from them by the neurovascular bundle? The answer is the innermost intercostal. Its fibers run in the same downward and backward direction as the internal intercostals, and it is best developed in the middle of the chest wall.

Question 2882. Which of these pairs belongs together: the external intercostal with elevation of the ribs, the internal intercostal with elevation of the ribs, the transversus thoracis with elevation of the ribs, or the innermost intercostal with movement of the arm? The answer is the external intercostal with elevation of the ribs, which it lifts toward the one above it.

Question 2883. Which thin muscles lie on the inner surface of the lower posterior chest wall and run in the same direction as the internal intercostals but skip over one or more ribs: the levatores costarum, the subcostal muscles, the serratus anterior, or the transversus thoracis? The answer is the subcostal muscles, found near the lower ribs at the back.

Question 2884. A described illustration: a chest drain is passed through the chest wall into the pleural cavity. Which layers of the intercostal muscles must the operator pass through, in order from the outside inward? The answer is the external intercostal, then the internal intercostal, then the innermost intercostal. The procedure belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 2885. Which small muscles arise from the transverse processes of the lower cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae and run downward and laterally to the rib below, lifting it? The answer is the levatores costarum. They occupy the spaces behind the intercostal muscles and are supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves.

Question 2886. A described dissection of one intercostal space shows three muscle layers, the outermost running downward and forward, the next running downward and backward, and the deepest running in the same direction as the second but lying inside it. Which three muscles are shown? The answer is the external, the internal and the innermost intercostal muscles.

Question 2887. The intercostal nerves are the anterior rami of which spinal nerves: the cervical nerves, the first to the eleventh thoracic nerves, the lumbar nerves, or the sacral nerves? The answer is the first to the eleventh thoracic spinal nerves. The twelfth thoracic nerve is the subcostal nerve, which runs below the twelfth rib into the abdominal wall.

Question 2888. Which artery gives off the anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six intercostal spaces, and where does that artery itself descend? The answer is the internal thoracic artery. It runs down behind the costal cartilages just lateral to the sternum, and its branches pass sideways in the spaces to meet the posterior intercostal arteries.

Question 2889. Which arteries supply the posterior intercostal spaces of the first and second ribs: the descending thoracic aorta, the supreme intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk, the internal thoracic artery directly, or the musculophrenic artery? The answer is the supreme intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

Question 2890. A described illustration: after several ribs are broken in two places, the loose segment of the chest wall moves inward while the rest of the chest moves outward during inspiration. Which muscles can no longer hold that segment steady, and what is this described pattern called? The answer is the intercostal muscles, and the described pattern is a flail chest.

Question 2891. Which thin sheet of muscle lies on the inner surface of the front of the chest wall, running from the lower part of the sternum upward and outward to the costal cartilages? The answer is the transversus thoracis. Its fibers run in the same direction as the internal intercostals, and it draws the ribs and the cartilages downward.

Question 2892. The internal thoracic artery ends by dividing into which two branches: the superior epigastric and the musculophrenic arteries, the inferior epigastric and the external iliac arteries, the pericardiacophrenic and the bronchial arteries, or the thyrocervical and the costocervical trunks? The answer is the superior epigastric and the musculophrenic arteries.

Question 2893. A described cross section of the chest wall shows a needle passing between two ribs into the pleural cavity. Which part of the rib should the needle pass close to, and why? The answer is the upper border of the rib below, because the neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above and lies out of reach there.

Question 2894. Which of these pairs belongs together: the internal thoracic artery with the anterior intercostal arteries, the descending thoracic aorta with the anterior intercostal arteries, the subclavian artery with the intercostal nerves, or the azygos vein with the intercostal nerves? The answer is the internal thoracic artery with the anterior intercostal arteries.

Question 2895. A described illustration: a drain is to be placed in the fifth intercostal space. Which point of entry keeps clear of the intercostal vessels and nerve, and why? The answer is the middle of the space just above the rib below, because the bundle of that space runs in the costal groove of the rib above and turns upward behind.

Question 2896. Which intercostal nerve has no lateral cutaneous branch and sends a large branch to the brachial plexus: the first thoracic nerve, the second thoracic nerve, the sixth thoracic nerve, or the twelfth thoracic nerve? The answer is the first thoracic nerve. It runs in the first intercostal space, and its fibers reach the arm through the lower trunk of the plexus.

Question 2897. A described dissection of an intercostal space shows the main bundle running in the costal groove of the rib above and a smaller bundle running along the upper border of the rib below. What is the smaller bundle called, and what does it contain? The answer is the collateral bundle, holding a collateral branch of the intercostal nerve with its artery and vein.

Question 2898. Which structure runs in the costal groove of each rib below the intercostal artery, and from which spinal nerves does it come? The answer is the intercostal nerve, which comes from the anterior ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve. It is the lowest structure in the groove, so it is the one most often injured by a fracture.

Question 2899. A described illustration: after a fracture of a lower rib, a person has a band of numbness in the chest wall and weakness of the abdominal muscles on that side. Which nerves are involved, and where do they run? The answer is the lower intercostal nerves, which run in the costal grooves and then continue downward into the abdominal wall.

Question 2900. A described section of the chest wall in the midaxillary line shows, from the outside inward, the external intercostal, then the internal intercostal, then a bundle of vessels and a nerve, then the innermost intercostal, and finally the pleura. Which layer lies directly against the pleura? The answer is the innermost intercostal, with the bundle lying above it in the same space.

To summarize, the transversospinalis group is the deepest layer of the back muscles, running from a transverse process up to a spinous process in three layers, the semispinalis, the multifidus and the rotatores, all supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves, extending the trunk and turning it to the opposite side. The semispinalis is the longest and reaches the skull as the semispinalis capitis, which the greater occipital nerve pierces, while the multifidus is the thickest in the lumbar region and is the chief stabilizer of the lower back, and the rotatores are the shortest and are best developed in the thoracic region. The pectoral muscles move the shoulder girdle and the arm: the pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the arm, the pectoralis minor draws the scapula forward and downward and, with the scapula fixed, raises the ribs, the subclavius steadies the clavicle, and the serratus anterior, supplied by the long thoracic nerve, pulls the scapula forward. The intercostals form three layers, the external running downward and forward to lift the ribs and the internal and innermost running downward and backward to lower them, with the neurovascular bundle lying between the two deepest layers and the vein, the artery and the nerve arranged in that order from above downward in the costal groove. A needle enters just above the rib below, the first thoracic nerve has no lateral cutaneous branch and joins the brachial plexus, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 30 — Thorax

This chapter works through the muscular anatomy of the thorax and the abdomen, beginning with the diaphragm, the great dome of muscle that separates the two cavities, and then the muscles of the front abdominal wall, the rectus abdominis and the external oblique. It holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The chapter follows the diaphragm through its origins, its three great openings and the structures that pass through them, and then turns to the flat muscles that form the wall of the abdomen and the sheaths and ligaments they make. The questions are written to be answered out loud from the relations of each muscle rather than from a picture. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 2901. Which muscle forms the dome-shaped partition between the thoracic cavity above and the abdominal cavity below? The answer is the diaphragm. Its fibers arise from the sternum, the lower ribs and the lumbar vertebrae and converge upon a central tendon. When it contracts it flattens and enlarges the chest from above downward.

Question 2902. The central tendon of the diaphragm lies immediately below which structure, and which organ lies immediately below the tendon on the right side? The answer is the pericardium above and the bare area of the liver below. The heart rests upon the tendon, and the peritoneum does not cover the part of the liver that touches it.

Question 2903. A described radiograph of the chest taken at full inspiration shows one dome of the diaphragm standing higher than the other. Which dome is it, and why does it lie higher? The answer is the right dome, which is pushed upward by the liver beneath it. The left dome lies lower because the heart and the stomach occupy the space around it.

Question 2904. What is the name of the broad aponeurosis into which all the muscular fibers of the diaphragm insert? The answer is the central tendon. It lies high in the dome and is fused above with the pericardium. It is fibrous, so it does not shorten when the muscle contracts.

Question 2905. A described transverse section of the lower chest shows two curved domes of muscle meeting a fibrous sheet in the middle, with the heart above and the liver and the stomach below. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the diaphragm, which forms the floor of the chest and the roof of the abdomen at once. Its fibers rise from the body wall around it.

Question 2906. Which structures pass through the esophageal opening of the diaphragm, and which muscle fibers encircle that opening? The answer is the esophagus, the two vagal trunks and the esophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, encircled by a sling of fibers from the right crus. That sling contracts with the diaphragm and helps to close the opening.

Question 2907. A constructed illustration: irritation of the central part of the diaphragm causes pain felt at the tip of the shoulder. Which nerve carries that pain, and why is it felt so far from the diaphragm? The answer is the phrenic nerve, whose fibers enter the spinal cord at the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments, the same segments that serve the skin of the shoulder.

Question 2908. Which of these pairs belongs together: the caval opening with the eighth thoracic vertebra, the esophageal opening with the twelfth thoracic vertebra, the aortic opening with the tenth thoracic vertebra, or the caval opening with the tenth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the caval opening with the eighth thoracic vertebra. The esophagus passes at the tenth and the aorta at the twelfth.

Question 2909. Which nerve supplies the motor fibers of the diaphragm? The answer is the phrenic nerve, one for each half of the muscle. It arises in the neck from the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves and descends through the chest to reach the upper surface of the muscle. Division of one phrenic nerve paralyzes the same side.

Question 2910. True or false: the aorta pierces the muscular part of the diaphragm through an opening with a muscular margin. The answer is false. The aortic opening lies behind the diaphragm between the two crura, and the artery runs behind the muscle rather than through it. Because its margin is fibrous, contraction cannot pinch the aorta.

Question 2911. A described horizontal section across the chest at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra shows a muscular opening transmitting a tube with a plexus of nerves around it. Which opening is shown, and which of the three large openings lies highest? The answer is the esophageal opening, while the opening for the inferior vena cava lies highest, at the eighth thoracic vertebra.

Question 2912. Which of these structures passes through the opening in the central tendon of the diaphragm: the aorta, the esophagus, the inferior vena cava, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the inferior vena cava, which passes through the central tendon a little to the right of the midline and carries the right phrenic nerve with it. The aorta and the thoracic duct pass behind the muscle.

Question 2913. The right crus of the diaphragm is larger than the left and lies on which side of the esophageal opening, and from which bones does it arise? The answer is that it encircles the opening and arises from the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae. Its fibers form the sling around the esophagus. The left crus is shorter.

Question 2914. What name is given to the two muscular pillars of the diaphragm that arise from the lumbar vertebrae? The answer is the crura. The right crus arises from the upper three lumbar vertebral bodies and the left from the upper two. Between them pass the aorta and the thoracic duct.

Question 2915. Which of these structures passes behind the medial arcuate ligament of the diaphragm: the sympathetic trunk, the subcostal nerve, the twelfth rib, or the kidney? The answer is the sympathetic trunk. The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of fascia over the psoas major muscle. The subcostal nerve passes behind the lateral arcuate ligament instead.

Question 2916. A constructed illustration: a wound of the lower chest divides the phrenic nerve on one side, and on the next breath the injured dome of the diaphragm rises while the healthy dome descends. Which side moves upward, and why? The answer is the paralyzed side, which is pushed up by the pressure within the abdomen when the healthy half contracts.

Question 2917. Which muscle is the principal muscle of inspiration: the diaphragm, the rectus abdominis, the external oblique, or the internal intercostal muscles? The answer is the diaphragm. Its contraction lowers the domes and enlarges the chest from above downward. The flat abdominal muscles take part in forced expiration rather than quiet inspiration.

Question 2918. A described dissection of the diaphragm from below shows fibers running inward from the ribs, from the back of the xiphoid process and from the lumbar region, all meeting a trefoil-shaped sheet in the middle. Which parts of origin and which insertion are shown? The answer is the sternal, costal and lumbar parts, all inserting into the central tendon.

Question 2919. Which arched thickening of fascia passes over the psoas major muscle and gives origin to part of the diaphragm? The answer is the medial arcuate ligament. It is formed by the fascia over that muscle, and the sympathetic trunk passes behind it. The lateral arcuate ligament arches over the quadratus lumborum instead.

Question 2920. Which of these pairs belongs together: the central tendon with the inferior vena cava, the muscular part left of the midline with the aorta, the space between the crura with the esophagus, or the costal part with the thoracic duct? The answer is the central tendon with the inferior vena cava. The esophagus passes through the muscular part and the aorta between the crura.

Question 2921. What happens to the domes of the diaphragm during quiet inspiration: they flatten and descend, they rise, they stay still, or they move backward? The answer is that they flatten and descend. The muscle fibers shorten and draw the central tendon downward. This increases the vertical diameter of the chest.

Question 2922. Which structure lies immediately above the right dome of the diaphragm, and which organs lie immediately below the left dome? The answer is the right lung and pleura above, with the liver below it, and the stomach and the spleen below the left dome. The pleura dips into the recess around each dome.

Question 2923. A described radiograph shows a rounded shadow with a gas bubble and a fluid level beneath it on the left side, and the left dome of the diaphragm stands much higher than the right. Which organ lies below that dome, and what does the fluid level within it suggest? The answer is the stomach, and the level suggests that it is distended.

Question 2924. Which opening of the diaphragm transmits the thoracic duct together with the aorta? The answer is the aortic opening, which lies between the right and the left crus behind the muscle. The azygos vein also passes through it on the right side. Because it lies behind the muscle, it is never closed by contraction.

Question 2925. The diaphragm receives its motor supply from which nerve: the vagus nerve, the phrenic nerve, the intercostal nerves, or the sympathetic trunk? The answer is the phrenic nerve. It arises from the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves and runs down through the mediastinum. The lower intercostal nerves carry only sensation from the outer part of the muscle.

Question 2926. A constructed illustration: a newborn has difficulty in breathing, and a described radiograph shows loops of bowel in the left side of the chest. Through which gap in the diaphragm did the bowel most likely pass, and why is that side more often affected? The answer is the posterolateral gap, which closes last in development and lies on the left more often because the liver protects the right side.

Question 2927. Which statement about the costal part of the diaphragm is correct: its fibers interdigitate with those of the transversus abdominis, it arises from the outer surfaces of the lower six ribs, it arises from the first six ribs, or it inserts into the linea alba? The answer is that its fibers interdigitate with those of the transversus abdominis. The costal fibers arise from the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs.

Question 2928. Which arteries supply the upper surface of the diaphragm, and from which vessel do the inferior phrenic arteries arise? The answer is the pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic arteries above, and the inferior phrenic arteries from the abdominal aorta below. The musculophrenic artery runs along the costal margin and meets the other branches within the muscle.

Question 2929. True or false: the contraction of the diaphragm produces expiration. The answer is false, because its contraction produces inspiration. Expiration at rest follows the elastic recoil of the lungs and the chest wall as the muscle relaxes. A forced expiration uses the abdominal muscles, which push the relaxed diaphragm upward.

Question 2930. A described cross section of the lower chest at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra shows a muscular sheet with a fibrous center, and the inferior vena cava is seen passing through that fibrous part. Which opening is shown, and which nerve runs beside the vein? The answer is the caval opening, with the right phrenic nerve beside it.

Question 2931. Which of these openings of the diaphragm lies most posterior: the opening for the inferior vena cava, the opening for the esophagus, the opening between the crura, or the gap between the sternal and the costal parts? The answer is the opening between the crura, through which the aorta passes. It lies against the vertebral column, behind the muscle.

Question 2932. The left phrenic nerve pierces the diaphragm and then runs on which surface of the muscle, and beside which structure does it reach the esophageal opening? The answer is the abdominal surface, where it lies beside the esophagus and the vagal trunks. Both phrenic nerves descend upon the pericardium before piercing the muscle.

Question 2933. What is the name of the fibrous sheet at the center of the diaphragm into which its muscle fibers insert? The answer is the central tendon. It lies at the summit of the dome and is fused with the pericardium above it. Because it is fibrous it does not shorten, and the muscle pulls it downward.

Question 2934. Which statement about the sternal part of the diaphragm is correct: it arises by two slips from the back of the xiphoid process, it arises from the sternum, it arises from the first costal cartilage, or it has no bony origin? The answer is that it arises by two slips from the back of the xiphoid process. Between them and the costal part lies a gap for the internal thoracic artery.

Question 2935. A constructed illustration: a person has a bout of hiccups after a large meal, with sudden involuntary contractions of the diaphragm followed by sharp closure of the vocal folds. Which muscle is contracting, and through which nerve does the reflex run? The answer is the diaphragm, acting through the phrenic nerve. The reflex may begin with irritation of the stomach below the muscle.

Question 2936. A described section of the trunk shows both domes of the diaphragm, with the heart above them and the liver and the stomach below. In which plane was this section cut, and what would a section at right angles to it show instead? The answer is a coronal plane, which divides the body into front and back parts. A transverse section would show a single horizontal level.

Question 2937. The diaphragm is attached to which of the following: the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs, the outer surfaces of the upper six ribs, the first lumbar vertebra only, or the clavicle? The answer is the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and their costal cartilages. From there the fibers curve upward and inward to the central tendon. The outer surfaces give origin to other muscles.

Question 2938. A described radiograph taken at the end of a forced expiration shows both domes of the diaphragm much higher than on the earlier film. What has happened to the muscle, and which muscles helped to raise the domes? The answer is that the diaphragm has relaxed and been pushed upward by the abdominal muscles, chiefly the external oblique and the rectus abdominis.

Question 2939. Which opening of the diaphragm lies in the central tendon, and which large vein passes through it? The answer is the caval opening, transmitting the inferior vena cava. It lies a little to the right of the midline at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra. Because it lies in fibrous tissue, the vein is not compressed when the muscle contracts.

Question 2940. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medial arcuate ligament with the psoas major, the lateral arcuate ligament with the aorta, the median arcuate ligament with the quadratus lumborum, or the medial arcuate ligament with the kidney? The answer is the medial arcuate ligament with the psoas major. The lateral ligament arches over the quadratus lumborum and the median ligament over the aorta.

Question 2941. Which of these statements describes the position of the diaphragm: it separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity, it lies entirely within the abdomen, it forms the roof of the thoracic cavity, or it lies below the pelvis? The answer is that it separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. It is the floor of the chest and the roof of the abdomen at the same time.

Question 2942. Which structures lie immediately behind the lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm? The answer is the quadratus lumborum muscle with the subcostal nerve and vessels. The ligament is a thickening of the fascia over that muscle, and the twelfth rib lies behind it in turn. Its fibers run to the central tendon.

Question 2943. A constructed illustration: a person receives a blow to the left lower ribs, and a described radiograph later shows a raised left dome with bowel beneath it and a fracture of a lower rib. Which muscle has been torn, and through which gap can the abdominal contents now rise? The answer is the diaphragm, torn in its costal part near the posterolateral gap.

Question 2944. Which two arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and run upward onto the under surface of the diaphragm? The answer is the inferior phrenic arteries, one on each side. They lie below the muscle and supply its abdominal surface. Above, the muscle is supplied by branches of the internal thoracic artery.

Question 2945. Which of these structures passes through the esophageal opening of the diaphragm alongside the esophagus: the vagal trunks, the thoracic duct, the aorta, or the azygos vein? The answer is the vagal trunks, which lie upon the front and the back of the esophagus. The thoracic duct and the azygos vein pass through or behind the aortic opening.

Question 2946. A described specimen of the diaphragm viewed from below shows a fibrous trefoil in the center, and around it muscle fibers run in three directions from three different origins. Which origins are shown, and which one lies at the back? The answer is the sternal, costal and lumbar parts, with the lumbar part at the back upon the vertebral bodies.

Question 2947. Which statement about the levels of the three large openings of the diaphragm is correct: the caval opening lies highest, the aortic opening lies highest, the esophageal opening lies highest, or all three lie at the same level? The answer is that the caval opening lies highest. It lies at the eighth thoracic vertebra, the esophageal opening at the tenth and the aortic opening at the twelfth.

Question 2948. Name the three large openings of the diaphragm and one structure that passes through each, spoken as a list. The answer is the caval opening for the inferior vena cava, the esophageal opening for the esophagus and the vagal trunks, and the aortic opening for the aorta and the thoracic duct. Each opening is named for what it carries.

Question 2949. Which muscle forms the roof of the abdominal cavity and separates it from the chest? The answer is the diaphragm. Its dome rises on each side into the lower part of the chest. The liver and the stomach press against its under surface.

Question 2950. Which of these statements about the aortic opening is correct: it lies behind the diaphragm so that the muscle cannot compress the aorta, it lies in the central tendon, it is closed during inspiration, or it transmits the esophagus? The answer is that it lies behind the muscle, so contraction cannot compress the aorta. Flow through the aorta therefore continues throughout the breathing cycle.

Question 2951. Which muscles form the anterior wall of the abdomen, one on each side of the midline: the rectus abdominis and the pyramidalis, the diaphragm, the latissimus dorsi, or the serratus anterior? The answer is the rectus abdominis and the pyramidalis, with the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall behind them. The rectus runs vertically from the pubis to the chest.

Question 2952. Which muscle of the anterior abdominal wall is crossed by three fibrous bands, lies within a sheath whose posterior wall disappears below a certain line, and is the chief flexor of the trunk? The answer is the rectus abdominis. It runs from the pubic crest to the fifth, sixth and seventh costal cartilages. Its fibrous bands are the tendinous intersections.

Question 2953. A described dissection of the front of the abdomen shows a broad sheet of muscle whose fibers run downward and forward, with another sheet beneath it whose fibers run upward and forward. Which two muscles are shown? The answer is the external oblique upon the surface and the internal oblique deep to it. Their fibers cross at about a right angle.

Question 2954. Which of these structures marks the midline of the anterior abdominal wall: the linea alba, the inguinal ligament, the arcuate line, or the costal margin? The answer is the linea alba, the white fibrous band running from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis. The aponeuroses of the three flat muscles interlace within it, and it holds few blood vessels.

Question 2955. Which arteries lie posterior to the rectus abdominis and anastomose with each other within its sheath? The answer is the superior epigastric artery, descending behind the muscle from above, and the inferior epigastric artery, ascending behind it from below. They meet around the level of the umbilicus, so the muscle lies in front of both.

Question 2956. A constructed illustration: after a period of coughing, a person develops a painful swelling in the lower part of the rectus sheath, and a described scan shows a collection within the sheath below the umbilicus. Which vessel has most likely bled? The answer is the inferior epigastric artery, which runs behind the lower part of the rectus.

Question 2957. Which small triangular muscle lies in front of the lower end of the rectus abdominis and tenses the linea alba? The answer is the pyramidalis. It arises from the pubis and inserts into the linea alba. It is absent in a small proportion of people, which is a normal variation.

Question 2958. Which of these structures lies within the sheath of the rectus abdominis: the muscle with its arteries, nerves and lymph vessels, the peritoneal cavity, the kidney, or the small intestine? The answer is the muscle with its arteries, nerves and lymph vessels. The sheath is a fibrous compartment, and the peritoneum lies behind it, separated by the transversalis fascia.

Question 2959. True or false: the tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis are firmly attached to the front wall of its sheath but not to the back wall. The answer is true. That attachment holds the muscle in place and produces the grooves seen upon the surface. The back of the muscle slides freely within the sheath.

Question 2960. Which of these pairs belongs together: the rectus abdominis with the lower six thoracic spinal nerves, the rectus abdominis with the phrenic nerve, the external oblique with the femoral nerve, or the diaphragm with the ilioinguinal nerve? The answer is the rectus abdominis with the lower six thoracic spinal nerves. The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves supply only its lowest part.

Question 2961. What is the main action of the rectus abdominis: to flex the trunk forward, to extend the trunk, to rotate the trunk toward the same side, or to move the arm? The answer is to flex the trunk forward. Both muscles acting together bend the trunk, and one alone bends it toward its own side. They also compress the abdominal contents.

Question 2962. A described transverse section of the abdominal wall above the arcuate line shows a muscle enclosed between an anterior and a posterior layer of aponeurosis. Which muscle lies in that compartment, and which aponeuroses form the layer in front of it? The answer is the rectus abdominis, with the external oblique and the front lamina of the internal oblique in front of it.

Question 2963. Which fibrous line marks the lower limit of the posterior wall of the rectus sheath, below which the rectus lies directly upon the transversalis fascia? The answer is the arcuate line. It lies about midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis. Below it all three aponeuroses pass in front of the muscle.

Question 2964. Which layer lies immediately posterior to the rectus abdominis below the arcuate line, and which structures lie behind that layer? The answer is the transversalis fascia, behind which lie the extraperitoneal fat and the peritoneum. Above the arcuate line the posterior sheath of the rectus separates the muscle from the same fascia.

Question 2965. Which of these muscles bends the trunk forward and compresses the abdominal contents: the rectus abdominis, the diaphragm, the serratus anterior, or the levator scapulae? The answer is the rectus abdominis. It is assisted in flexion by the internal and the external oblique muscles. All three also raise the pressure inside the abdomen.

Question 2966. A constructed illustration: a person of small build lifts a heavy weight, and the abdominal wall gives way along the midline between the two rectus muscles. Which structure has stretched, and why does this happen more often after pregnancy or repeated straining? The answer is the linea alba, which is widest and thinnest near the umbilicus.

Question 2967. Which statement about the nerve supply of the rectus abdominis is correct: it comes from the lower six thoracic spinal nerves, it comes from the phrenic nerve, it comes from the femoral nerve, or it comes from the obturator nerve? The answer is that it comes from the lower six thoracic spinal nerves, which run forward between the internal oblique and the transversus.

Question 2968. Which structures form the posterior wall of the rectus sheath above the arcuate line? The answer is the aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis together with the posterior lamina of the internal oblique. Both pass behind the muscle there. Below the arcuate line that wall is missing.

Question 2969. A described surface view of the abdomen shows three or four horizontal grooves crossing a vertical muscle on each side of the midline, with a furrow between the two muscles. Which muscle and which grooves are shown? The answer is the rectus abdominis with its tendinous intersections, and the furrow is the linea alba.

Question 2970. Which of these statements about the tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis is correct: one lies at the level of the umbilicus, all of them lie below the umbilicus, there are always six of them, or they lie behind the muscle only? The answer is that one lies at the level of the umbilicus, with others at the xiphoid process and between the two. A fourth may lie below the umbilicus.

Question 2971. A described horizontal section of the abdominal wall below the arcuate line shows a vertical muscle lying upon a thin fibrous layer, with aponeuroses only in front of it. What lies behind the same muscle in a section taken above the arcuate line? The answer is a posterior sheath formed by the transversus abdominis and the internal oblique.

Question 2972. Which of these statements about the sheath of the rectus abdominis is correct: the external oblique aponeurosis always passes in front of the muscle, it always passes behind it, the transversus aponeurosis always passes behind it, or the internal oblique aponeurosis always passes behind it? The answer is that the external oblique aponeurosis always passes in front of the muscle.

Question 2973. Which muscle of the anterior abdominal wall has its fibers running vertically, and what is its lower attachment? The answer is the rectus abdominis, attached below to the pubic crest and the pubic symphysis. Above, it reaches the xiphoid process and the fifth to the seventh costal cartilages. It is the chief flexor of the trunk.

Question 2974. A constructed illustration: a person cannot rise from lying to sitting without using the arms, and the trunk cannot be bent against resistance. Which group of muscles is weak, and which nerves are likely to be affected? The answer is the muscles of the abdominal wall, chiefly the rectus abdominis, supplied by the lower six thoracic spinal nerves.

Question 2975. What effect does contraction of the rectus abdominis have upon the pelvis when the trunk is fixed: it tilts the pelvis backward, it tilts the pelvis forward, it rotates the pelvis about a vertical axis, or it has no effect? The answer is that it tilts the pelvis backward. The muscle pulls the front of the pelvis upward toward the chest.

Question 2976. From which surfaces of the ribs does the external oblique arise, and with which two muscles do its upper and lower fibers interdigitate? The answer is the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs, interdigitating above with the serratus anterior and below with the latissimus dorsi. Its fibers then run downward and forward.

Question 2977. True or false: the external oblique is the most superficial of the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall. The answer is true. Its fibers run downward and forward, those of the internal oblique run upward and forward, and those of the transversus abdominis run across the abdomen. The three lie in that order from the surface inward.

Question 2978. A described dissection of the abdominal wall shows the outermost sheet of muscle with its fibers running in the direction of a hand placed in a pocket, and its lower border thickened into a band running from the front of the hip bone to the pubis. Which structures are shown? The answer is the external oblique with its aponeurosis, and the band is the inguinal ligament.

Question 2979. Which band forms the floor of the inguinal canal, running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle? The answer is the inguinal ligament, the thickened lower border of the aponeurosis of the external oblique. The canal lies above it. Its medial end spreads into the lacunar ligament.

Question 2980. Which of these structures passes through the superficial inguinal ring: the spermatic cord in the male, the femoral artery, the inferior epigastric artery, or the obturator nerve? The answer is the spermatic cord in the male and the round ligament of the uterus in the female. The ring is a gap in the aponeurosis of the external oblique above and medial to the pubic tubercle.

Question 2981. Which of these pairs belongs together: the external oblique with the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs, the external oblique with the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, the internal oblique with the lower eight ribs only, or the transversus abdominis with the sternum? The answer is the external oblique with the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs.

Question 2982. In which direction do the fibers of the external oblique run: downward and forward, upward and forward, horizontally across, or vertically upward? The answer is downward and forward. Both hands placed upon the chest with the fingers pointing down and inward follow the same direction. Contraction of the right external oblique therefore turns the trunk to the left.

Question 2983. A constructed illustration: a person develops a bulge in the groin above and medial to the pubic tubercle after lifting, and the swelling passes through a gap in the aponeurosis of the external oblique. Which structure has given way, and into which canal does it open? The answer is the superficial inguinal ring, opening into the inguinal canal.

Question 2984. Which muscle of the abdominal wall rotates the trunk toward the opposite side when it contracts on one side? The answer is the external oblique. Because its fibers run downward and forward, it pulls the chest toward the opposite hip. The internal oblique on the same side rotates the trunk toward the same side.

Question 2985. A described specimen of the groin shows a triangular opening in a fibrous sheet, with a cord passing through it and a nerve lying upon the cord. Which opening is shown, and which nerve lies upon the cord? The answer is the superficial inguinal ring, with the ilioinguinal nerve. The cord is the spermatic cord.

Question 2986. Which of these statements about the inguinal canal is correct: its anterior wall is formed by the aponeurosis of the external oblique, its posterior wall is the inguinal ligament, its roof is the peritoneum, or its floor is the internal oblique? The answer is that its anterior wall is formed by the aponeurosis of the external oblique. Its floor is the inguinal ligament.

Question 2987. Which structure lies immediately deep to the aponeurosis of the external oblique in the lateral part of the anterior wall of the inguinal canal, and which structure forms the medial part of its posterior wall? The answer is the internal oblique laterally, and the conjoint tendon medially. The conjoint tendon is formed together with the transversus abdominis.

Question 2988. Which crescent-shaped expansion of the inguinal ligament turns downward and backward to reach the pecten of the pubis? The answer is the lacunar ligament. It forms the medial boundary of the femoral canal, and the femoral vein lies just lateral to it. It also takes part in the floor of the inguinal canal.

Question 2989. Which of these muscles forms the anterior wall of the abdomen together with the internal oblique: the external oblique, the diaphragm, the quadratus lumborum, or the erector spinae? The answer is the external oblique, the most superficial of the three flat muscles. Its aponeurosis passes in front of the rectus abdominis at every level.

Question 2990. A described computed tomography section of the abdominal wall shows the outermost muscle layer as a thin sheet running downward and forward, with the internal oblique deep to it running upward and forward. Which two muscles are shown, and why is the pattern easy to tell apart? The answer is the external and the internal oblique muscles, whose fibers cross at about a right angle.

Question 2991. Name two muscles of the anterior abdominal wall whose fibers run obliquely but in opposite directions, spoken as a list. The answer is the external oblique and the internal oblique. The external oblique runs downward and forward and the internal oblique upward and forward. Their crossing strengthens the wall.

Question 2992. A described dissection of the groin shows a fibrous band running from the front of the hip bone to the pubic tubercle, with a canal lying above it and a nerve running through the canal. Which band and which canal are shown, and what is the nerve? The answer is the inguinal ligament and the inguinal canal, with the ilioinguinal nerve.

Question 2993. Which flat muscle of the abdominal wall lies deepest: the external oblique, the internal oblique, the transversus abdominis, or the rectus abdominis? The answer is the transversus abdominis. Its fibers run across the abdomen at right angles to the midline. Its aponeurosis forms part of the posterior sheath of the rectus above the arcuate line.

Question 2994. A constructed illustration: a blow to the side of the abdomen below the ribs is followed by pain on twisting the trunk, and the outer muscle layer of that region is bruised. Which muscle is injured, and which movement will hurt most? The answer is the external oblique, and rotation of the trunk toward the opposite side will hurt most.

Question 2995. A described radiograph after a strain shows a small avulsion of bone at the front of the hip bone, at the point where a long fibrous band begins. Which band begins there, and which aponeurosis forms it? The answer is the inguinal ligament, formed by the lower border of the aponeurosis of the external oblique, running to the pubic tubercle.

Question 2996. Which of these actions does the external oblique perform when it contracts on one side alone: it rotates the trunk toward the opposite side, it rotates the trunk toward the same side, it extends the trunk, or it abducts the arm? The answer is that it rotates the trunk toward the opposite side. Both muscles acting together flex the trunk and compress the abdominal contents.

Question 2997. Which muscle forms the greater part of the anterior abdominal wall and gives off the aponeurosis that forms the inguinal ligament? The answer is the external oblique. It arises from the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs. Its fibers run downward and forward to the iliac crest, the linea alba and the pubis.

Question 2998. True or false: the aponeurosis of the external oblique passes behind the rectus abdominis below the arcuate line. The answer is false. It passes in front of the muscle at every level. Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses lie in front, so the rectus rests directly upon the transversalis fascia.

Question 2999. Which of these structures lies at the medial end of the inguinal ligament and forms the medial wall of the femoral canal: the lacunar ligament, the conjoint tendon, the pectineal ligament, or the arcuate line? The answer is the lacunar ligament. It turns backward from the medial end of the inguinal ligament to the pecten of the pubis.

Question 3000. Name the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall in order from the surface inward, and state one action they share, spoken as a list. The answer is the external oblique, the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis, and all three compress the abdominal contents. They also help to expel air and to steady the trunk.

To summarize, the diaphragm is the dome of muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen, arising from the xiphoid process, the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and the lumbar vertebrae, and inserting into the central tendon. Its three great openings are named for what they carry: the inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra, the esophagus with the vagal trunks passes through the muscular part at the tenth, and the aorta with the thoracic duct passes behind the muscle between the crura at the twelfth. The phrenic nerve from the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves is the only motor nerve of the diaphragm, and irritation of its central part is felt at the shoulder. The rectus abdominis runs vertically from the pubis to the fifth, sixth and seventh costal cartilages, is crossed by three tendinous intersections, and lies in a sheath whose posterior wall ends at the arcuate line. The external oblique is the most superficial of the flat muscles, arises from the lower eight ribs, runs downward and forward, and forms the inguinal ligament and the superficial inguinal ring. All the abdominal muscles compress the contents of the abdomen and raise the pressure within it, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 31 — Abdomen

The muscles of the abdominal wall and the muscles that move the shoulder are the subject of this chapter, and both groups repay close attention because they are tested again in the clinic. The first half follows the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis, the two deep flat muscles of the abdomen, through their layers, their nerve supply and their part in the groin. The second half turns to the shoulder muscles, above all the rotator cuff and the deltoid, and to the movements they produce.
