The chapter holds one hundred questions, and each one states its answer in the same paragraph as the question, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3001. Of the three flat muscles of the anterior abdominal wall, which one forms the middle layer? The answer is the internal oblique muscle. The external oblique lies superficial to it and the transversus abdominis lies deep to it. Its fibers run upward and medially, almost at right angles to those of the external oblique.

Question 3002. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the external oblique muscle: the internal oblique, the rectus abdominis, the transversus abdominis, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the internal oblique. It forms the middle of the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall. The transversus abdominis lies one layer deeper still, and the latissimus dorsi belongs to the back.

Question 3003. A described dissection shows one flat layer whose fibers run upward and medially and, immediately deep to it, a second layer whose fibers run across the abdomen. Which two muscles are shown? The answer is the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. The upward and medial direction belongs to the internal oblique, and the horizontal direction gives the transversus its name.

Question 3004. Between which two muscles of the abdominal wall do the lower thoracic nerves and the inferior epigastric vessels run? The answer is the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. That interval is the neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall. The segmental nerves pierce the muscles in turn on their way forward to the rectus sheath.

Question 3005. True or false: the transversus abdominis lies deep to the internal oblique muscle. The answer is true. The transversus abdominis is the innermost of the three flat muscles, and the transversalis fascia lies on its deep surface. Its fibers run across the abdomen rather than upward or downward.

Question 3006. Which muscle forms the innermost of the three flat layers of the abdominal wall? The answer is the transversus abdominis. It arises from the inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and the lateral part of the inguinal ligament. Its aponeurosis helps to form the rectus sheath.

Question 3007. In which direction do the fibers of the transversus abdominis run: downward and medially, upward and medially, horizontally across the abdomen, or vertically from the ribs to the pubis? The answer is horizontally across the abdomen. The name of the muscle describes that direction. The external oblique and the internal oblique lie superficial to it and cross it obliquely.

Question 3008. Which nerves supply the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis muscles? The answer is the lower thoracic spinal nerves and the first lumbar nerve. The nerves of the seventh to the twelfth thoracic segments and of the first lumbar segment reach the wall in the plane between the two muscles. The same nerves supply the external oblique and the rectus abdominis.

Question 3009. A constructed illustration: inflammation begins in the appendix, and the first pain is felt around the umbilicus. Which spinal segment carries that pain, and why is it felt in the middle of the abdomen? The answer is the tenth thoracic segment. The appendix carries visceral pain fibers that enter the spinal cord at that level, and the brain refers the pain to the skin around the navel.

Question 3010. Which of these pairs belongs together: the external oblique with fibers running downward and medially, the internal oblique with fibers running horizontally, the transversus abdominis with fibers running downward and forward, or the rectus abdominis with fibers running across the body? The answer is the external oblique with fibers running downward and medially. Those fibers point toward the groin, like the fingers of a hand placed in a trouser pocket.

Question 3011. Name the two muscles whose aponeuroses join to form the conjoint tendon above the pubis. The answer is the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. The common tendon inserts into the pubic crest and the pecten pubis. It lies behind the superficial inguinal ring and strengthens the medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

Question 3012. Above the arcuate line, which aponeuroses form the anterior wall of the rectus sheath and which form the posterior wall? The answer is the external oblique and one lamina of the internal oblique in front, with the other lamina of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis behind. The rectus abdominis therefore lies between two strong tendinous layers.

Question 3013. Below the arcuate line, what forms the posterior wall of the rectus sheath: the aponeurosis of the external oblique, the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis, only the transversalis fascia, or the parietal peritoneum? The answer is only the transversalis fascia. All three flat aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus abdominis below that line.

Question 3014. A described cross section through the anterior abdominal wall shows skin, two fatty layers, three flat muscles and a thin membrane on the inner surface. What is that membrane, and what lies immediately inside it? The answer is the transversalis fascia, with the parietal peritoneum inside it. A little extraperitoneal fat separates the two.

Question 3015. A described movement turns the trunk to the left about the long axis of the body. In which plane does the movement occur, and about which axis? The answer is the transverse plane and a longitudinal axis. The vertebral column acts as the pivot, and the abdominal muscles of one side produce the turn.

Question 3016. What is the name of the fibrous band in the midline of the anterior abdominal wall, formed where the aponeuroses of the flat muscles interlace? The answer is the linea alba. It runs from the xiphoid process down to the pubic symphysis. It is narrow below the umbilicus and wider above it.

Question 3017. Which muscle of the spermatic cord is derived from the lower fibers of the internal oblique: the cremaster, the dartos, the gubernaculum, or the pyramidalis? The answer is the cremaster. Its fibers accompany the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal and lift the testis in the cold. The dartos is smooth muscle in the skin of the scrotum.

Question 3018. A constructed illustration: a small hernia appears in the abdominal wall at the outer edge of the rectus sheath, below the umbilicus. Which named line has it crossed, and which muscles border that line? The answer is the linea semilunaris, where the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis meet the rectus sheath. A hernia that emerges there is called a Spigelian hernia.

Question 3019. Between which two muscles does the ilioinguinal nerve run before it enters the inguinal canal? The answer is the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. It is a branch of the first lumbar nerve. It crosses the inguinal canal in front of the spermatic cord or the round ligament.

Question 3020. True or false: a contraction of the internal oblique muscle on the right side rotates the trunk to the left. The answer is false. The internal oblique rotates the trunk to the same side as the muscle, so the right internal oblique turns the trunk to the right. The external oblique of the opposite side assists in that movement.

Question 3021. In which direction do the fibers of the external oblique muscle run? The answer is downward and medially, toward the midline and the groin. The fibers point like the fingers of a hand placed in a trouser pocket. They run at right angles to those of the internal oblique beneath them.

Question 3022. Which of these is the chief action of the transversus abdominis: flexion of the trunk, rotation of the trunk, compression of the abdominal contents, or extension of the trunk? The answer is compression of the abdominal contents. It also steadies the trunk and takes part in forced expiration and in coughing. It is not a rotator of the trunk.

Question 3023. A described photograph of a lean athlete shows a curved line at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath, with flat muscles lying beyond it. What is that line called, and which muscles lie beyond it? The answer is the linea semilunaris, with the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis beyond it. It runs from the ninth costal cartilage to the pubic tubercle.

Question 3024. Name the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall in order from superficial to deep. The answer is the external oblique, the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. Their aponeuroses cross the midline and interlace to form the linea alba. Two of them, the internal oblique and the transversus, form the conjoint tendon.

Question 3025. Which structure lies immediately behind the superficial inguinal ring and is formed by the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis? The answer is the conjoint tendon. It descends to the pubic crest and the pecten pubis. Behind it lies the medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, the part that gives way in a direct inguinal hernia.

Question 3026. A constructed illustration: a hernia pushes through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Which wall has given way, and which structure normally reinforces it? The answer is the posterior wall, reinforced by the conjoint tendon. A hernia that passes medial to those vessels is called direct.

Question 3027. Which small triangular muscle lies in front of the lower part of the rectus abdominis and is absent in some people? The answer is the pyramidalis. It arises from the pubis and ends in the linea alba, and it tenses that midline band. Its absence is a normal variation.

Question 3028. Which nerve is found in the plane between the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis: the ilioinguinal nerve, the femoral nerve, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, or the genitofemoral nerve? The answer is the ilioinguinal nerve. The femoral nerve and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh lie in the thigh, and the genitofemoral nerve lies on the surface of the psoas muscle.

Question 3029. Which of these pairs belongs together: the internal oblique with the pubic crest through the conjoint tendon, the transversus abdominis with the iliac crest, the external oblique with the lower three ribs, or the rectus abdominis with the thoracolumbar fascia? The answer is the internal oblique with the pubic crest through the conjoint tendon. The other three pair a muscle with one of its origins rather than with its insertion.

Question 3030. A described computed tomography image taken across the abdomen at the level of the third lumbar vertebra shows the flat muscles as thin bands at each side and the rectus muscles as two oval masses in front. Which muscle forms the deepest band at each side? The answer is the transversus abdominis. The internal oblique lies outside it and the external oblique outside that.

Question 3031. A described cross section of the lower abdominal wall shows the rectus abdominis backed only by a thin membrane, with no tendinous layer behind the muscle. At what level relative to the arcuate line was the section taken, and what is that membrane? The answer is below the arcuate line, with only the transversalis fascia behind the muscle. Above that line the section would have shown a tendinous layer behind the rectus.

Question 3032. The posterior fibers of the internal oblique muscle arise from the thoracolumbar fascia and end where? The answer is on the lower borders of the tenth, eleventh and twelfth ribs. Those fibers lie deep to the muscles of the back. They therefore take part in both the abdominal wall and the floor of the lower part of the thorax.

Question 3033. Which of these muscles flexes the trunk and rotates it to the same side: the internal oblique, the external oblique, the transversus abdominis, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the internal oblique. The external oblique of one side rotates the trunk to the opposite side, and the transversus abdominis does not rotate it at all.

Question 3034. What is the name of the line, about halfway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis, below which the posterior wall of the rectus sheath is formed only by the transversalis fascia? The answer is the arcuate line. Above it the posterior wall is tendinous and strong, and below it only a thin membrane separates the rectus abdominis from the peritoneum.

Question 3035. In a dissection of the lower abdominal wall, which finding shows that the level is below the arcuate line: all three aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus, the posterior wall is tendinous, the internal oblique lies superficial to the external oblique, or the rectus muscle is absent? The answer is that all three aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus. It lies about halfway between the umbilicus and the pubis.

Question 3036. True or false: the anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed throughout by the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. The answer is true. The internal oblique reinforces the lateral part of that wall. The posterior wall is formed by the transversalis fascia and, medially, by the conjoint tendon.

Question 3037. A described ultrasound image taken across the abdominal wall shows three thin muscular bands separated by bright lines, with the deepest band running across the screen from side to side. Which muscle is that deepest band, and what is the bright line deep to it? The answer is the transversus abdominis, with the transversalis fascia deep to it. Bright lines between the bands are the fascial sheets that separate them.

Question 3038. Which of these statements about the rectus abdominis is correct: it lies within the rectus sheath, it lies deep to the transversalis fascia, it lies between the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis, or it lies superficial to the external oblique? The answer is that it lies within the rectus sheath. The sheath is formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles and by the transversalis fascia.

Question 3039. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the lower right abdomen, a person reports burning pain and reduced sensation in the skin above the pubis and the upper part of the scrotum. Which nerve has been caught in the scar? The answer is the ilioinguinal nerve. It runs in the neurovascular plane and then through the inguinal canal, where it lies in front of the spermatic cord.

Question 3040. From which bony landmarks does the internal oblique muscle arise? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior two thirds of the iliac crest and the lateral half of the inguinal ligament. Its lowest fibers arch over the spermatic cord and give rise to the cremaster muscle. Its upper fibers end on the lower ribs.

Question 3041. Which strong fascia covers the deep muscles of the back and gives origin to the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia. It lies between the muscles of the back and those of the abdominal wall. It also gives attachment to the latissimus dorsi behind.

Question 3042. Which pairing of muscles rotates the trunk to the right, spoken as one answer: the right external oblique with the left internal oblique, the right external oblique with the right internal oblique, the right internal oblique with the right transversus abdominis, or the left external oblique with the left internal oblique? The answer is the right external oblique with the left internal oblique. Both of those muscles turn the trunk to the right.

Question 3043. Which muscles act in forced expiration, as in a cough: the flat muscles of the abdominal wall, the diaphragm alone, the erector spinae muscles, or the psoas major? The answer is the flat muscles of the abdominal wall. Their contraction raises the pressure inside the abdomen and pushes the diaphragm upward while the ribs are drawn down.

Question 3044. Which of these muscles lies in the posterior abdominal wall rather than in the anterior wall: the internal oblique, the transversus abdominis, the quadratus lumborum, or the rectus abdominis? The answer is the quadratus lumborum. It runs from the iliac crest to the twelfth rib and to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, and it bends the trunk to its own side.

Question 3045. A described image of the groin seen from behind shows a triangular area bounded below by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels and medially by the rectus sheath, with peritoneum bulging through it. Which region is shown, and which hernia passes through it? The answer is Hesselbach's triangle, through which a direct inguinal hernia passes. That triangle is a weak point of the posterior wall of the canal.

Question 3046. Which of these statements about the rectus abdominis is correct: it is crossed by three or four tendinous bands, it lies outside the rectus sheath, it has no attachment to the pubis, or it is supplied by the femoral nerve? The answer is that it is crossed by three or four tendinous bands. Those bands lie at the xiphoid process, at the umbilicus and between the two.

Question 3047. A constructed illustration: a person who has just lifted a heavy weight feels a sudden tearing pain low in one rectus abdominis, and a tender swelling appears within the muscle. Why does that swelling not cross the midline? The answer is that the rectus abdominis is enclosed in its own sheath on each side. The linea alba separates the two muscles and their sheaths down the middle of the wall.

Question 3048. Which of these pairs belongs together: the transversus abdominis with the lower thoracic and first lumbar nerves, the external oblique with the femoral nerve, the rectus abdominis with the obturator nerve, or the internal oblique with the ilioinguinal nerve alone? The answer is the transversus abdominis with the lower thoracic and first lumbar nerves. All three flat muscles share that same segmental supply.

Question 3049. Which of these structures passes through the deep inguinal ring: the ilioinguinal nerve, the spermatic cord, the inferior epigastric artery, or the femoral artery? The answer is the spermatic cord. The deep ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia. The inferior epigastric artery passes medial to the ring and marks its medial border.

Question 3050. A described dissection shows the posterior wall of the inguinal canal reinforced medially by a tendinous band. Which of these names that band and its wall: the conjoint tendon in the posterior wall, the conjoint tendon in the anterior wall, the inguinal ligament behind, or the transversalis fascia in front? The answer is the conjoint tendon in the posterior wall. It is formed by the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis.

Question 3051. Which muscle is the chief abductor of the arm at the shoulder joint? The answer is the deltoid. Its middle fibers lift the arm sideways, taking over from the supraspinatus after the first fifteen degrees. Its anterior fibers flex the arm and its posterior fibers extend it.

Question 3052. Which of these muscles belongs to the rotator cuff: the teres major, the teres minor, the deltoid, or the coracobrachialis? The answer is the teres minor. The cuff is made up of the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor and the subscapularis. The teres minor lies below the spine of the scapula, and its tendon joins the capsule of the joint.

Question 3053. Which muscle begins abduction of the arm during the first fifteen degrees of movement at the shoulder joint? The answer is the supraspinatus. It lies in the fossa above the spine of the scapula, and its tendon passes beneath the acromion to reach the greater tubercle. The deltoid then carries the movement on.

Question 3054. Which arch does the tendon of the supraspinatus pass beneath on its way to the greater tubercle of the humerus? The answer is the coracoacromial arch. The subacromial bursa lies between the tendon and the arch. That arch is formed by the acromion and the coracoid process with the ligament between them.

Question 3055. A constructed illustration: after a forward dislocation of the shoulder, the arm cannot be lifted sideways and the skin over the lateral part of the shoulder is numb. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the axillary nerve. It passes through the quadrangular space close to the surgical neck and supplies the deltoid and the teres minor.

Question 3056. True or false: the subscapularis muscle inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus. The answer is false. It inserts on the lesser tubercle. The three muscles of the cuff that lie behind the joint, the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor, insert on the greater tubercle.

Question 3057. Which nerve supplies the infraspinatus muscle: the axillary nerve, the suprascapular nerve, the lower subscapular nerve, or the thoracodorsal nerve? The answer is the suprascapular nerve. The same nerve supplies the supraspinatus, and it passes through the suprascapular notch. The axillary nerve supplies the teres minor instead.

Question 3058. Which nerve supplies the deltoid muscle? The answer is the axillary nerve. It winds through the quadrangular space together with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus may injure it, and the skin over the muscle then loses its sensation.

Question 3059. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows a shelf of bone above the head of the humerus, with the head lying below and medial to it. Which structure is that shelf, and which tendon lies just beneath it? The answer is the acromion, with the tendon of the supraspinatus beneath it. The subacromial bursa lies between the two.

Question 3060. Which of these pairs belongs together: the subscapularis with medial rotation, the infraspinatus with medial rotation, the teres minor with abduction, or the supraspinatus with adduction? The answer is the subscapularis with medial rotation. The infraspinatus and the teres minor rotate the arm laterally, and the supraspinatus begins abduction.

Question 3061. Which two structures pass through the quadrangular space, bounded above by the teres minor, below by the teres major, medially by the long head of the triceps and laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus? The answer is the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery. Both are at risk in a fracture of the surgical neck.

Question 3062. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the axilla, the medial border of the scapula stands away from the chest wall when the arm is pushed forward against resistance. Which nerve and which muscle are involved? The answer is the long thoracic nerve and the serratus anterior. That muscle normally holds the scapula against the ribs.

Question 3063. Which muscles rotate the arm medially at the shoulder joint: the infraspinatus and the teres minor, the subscapularis and the teres major, the deltoid and the supraspinatus, or the trapezius and the rhomboid muscles? The answer is the subscapularis and the teres major. The infraspinatus and the teres minor rotate the arm laterally instead.

Question 3064. Which nerves supply the subscapularis muscle? The answer is the upper and the lower subscapular nerves. Both arise from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. The lower subscapular nerve also supplies the teres major, and the muscle itself lies on the front of the scapula.

Question 3065. A described movement lifts the arm sideways away from the trunk. In which plane does the movement occur, and about which axis does the shoulder joint turn? The answer is the coronal plane and an anteroposterior axis. The humerus moves in that plane while the joint rotates about an axis running from front to back.

Question 3066. A described magnetic resonance image of the shoulder shows a gap in the tendon above the head of the humerus, with fluid collecting in the space between the tendon and the bone. Which tendon is torn, and which bursa lies in that space? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, with the subacromial bursa. Fluid collects in that bursa because it lies between the tendon and the bone.

Question 3067. Which muscles form the force couple that keeps the head of the humerus centered while the arm is abducted: the deltoid with the trapezius, the deltoid with the rotator cuff, the pectoralis major with the latissimus dorsi, or the biceps with the triceps? The answer is the deltoid with the rotator cuff. The cuff pulls the head downward and medially against the upward pull of the deltoid.

Question 3068. From which three bony points does the deltoid muscle arise? The answer is the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula. The muscle converges on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. Its anterior part takes origin from the clavicle and its posterior part from the spine of the scapula.

Question 3069. A constructed illustration: a person feels a sharp pain in the shoulder when the arm is raised above the head, worst between seventy and one hundred and twenty degrees of abduction. Which structures are being pinched, and under which arch? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon and the subacromial bursa beneath the coracoacromial arch. The tendon is pinched against the acromion as the arm rises under that arch.

Question 3070. Name two muscles that rotate the arm laterally at the shoulder joint, spoken as a list. The answer is the infraspinatus and the teres minor. Both run from the back of the scapula to the greater tubercle of the humerus. The infraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve and the teres minor by the axillary nerve.

Question 3071. Which tendon runs in the groove between the greater and the lesser tubercles of the humerus, and where does it go? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii. It leaves the groove and passes through the shoulder joint to attach to the rim of the glenoid socket, where it helps to steady the joint.

Question 3072. When the arm is lifted to the vertical, how much of the movement occurs at the shoulder joint and how much at the scapula: two thirds and one third, one third and two thirds, half and half, or all of it? The answer is two thirds at the shoulder joint and one third at the scapula. The scapula turns upward on the chest wall as the arm rises.

Question 3073. A described dissection of the axilla shows a nerve arising from the posterior cord and winding backward around the surgical neck of the humerus. Which nerve is shown, and what does it supply? The answer is the axillary nerve, which supplies the deltoid and the teres minor. It also carries sensation from the skin over the lower part of the deltoid.

Question 3074. True or false: the deltoid is the only muscle that can begin abduction of the arm from the side of the body. The answer is false. The supraspinatus begins the movement, and the deltoid takes over after the first fifteen degrees. When the supraspinatus is torn, the arm can often still be abducted once the movement has been started.

Question 3075. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraspinatus with the suprascapular nerve, the teres minor with the suprascapular nerve, the subscapularis with the axillary nerve, or the deltoid with the radial nerve? The answer is the supraspinatus with the suprascapular nerve. The teres minor belongs to the axillary nerve, the subscapularis to the subscapular nerves and the deltoid to the axillary nerve.

Question 3076. Which nerve supplies the trapezius muscle? The answer is the spinal accessory nerve, the eleventh cranial nerve. Small branches from the third and fourth cervical nerves carry sensation from the muscle but do not move it. The trapezius elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.

Question 3077. Which action does the serratus anterior perform on the scapula: it retracts the scapula toward the spine, it protracts the scapula around the chest wall and rotates it upward, it elevates the scapula toward the ear, or it depresses the scapula toward the hip? The answer is that it protracts the scapula and rotates it upward. Both actions are needed before the arm can be raised above the head.

Question 3078. A constructed illustration: over several months a shoulder becomes painful and then stiff, and movement is lost in every direction, while a radiograph shows no broken bone. Which structure is the site of the problem? The answer is the fibrous capsule of the shoulder joint, which becomes thickened and contracted. The joint surfaces themselves remain intact.

Question 3079. Which structure passes through the triangular space, bounded above by the teres minor, below by the teres major and laterally by the long head of the triceps? The answer is the circumflex scapular artery. It runs between those muscles to reach the back of the scapula. The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space instead.

Question 3080. In a complete tear of the tendon of the supraspinatus, which movement is lost first: abduction of the arm from the side, lateral rotation, medial rotation, or extension? The answer is abduction of the arm from the side. The person can still shrug the shoulder and swing the arm forward. The deltoid cannot start that movement on its own.

Question 3081. A described view of the inside of the shoulder joint shows a ring of fibrous tissue around the rim of the shallow socket, with a tendon arising just above it. What is that ring, and what does it do? The answer is the glenoid labrum, which deepens the socket and helps to hold the head in place. It is a fibrocartilaginous rim that may be torn when the joint dislocates.

Question 3082. Which nerve supplies the rhomboid major and the rhomboid minor? The answer is the dorsal scapular nerve, which carries fibers of the fifth cervical root. The same nerve also supplies the levator scapulae. Both rhomboids draw the scapula toward the spine and rotate it downward.

Question 3083. Which nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi: the thoracodorsal nerve, the long thoracic nerve, the dorsal scapular nerve, or the axillary nerve? The answer is the thoracodorsal nerve. It arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. The latissimus dorsi extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

Question 3084. Which three muscles attach to the coracoid process of the scapula? The answer is the coracobrachialis, the short head of the biceps brachii and the pectoralis minor. The first two arise from the tip of the process. The pectoralis minor inserts on its medial border.

Question 3085. On which part of the humerus does the deltoid muscle insert? The answer is the deltoid tuberosity, a rough area on the middle of the lateral surface of the shaft. The muscle pulls on that point to raise the arm. The radial nerve runs in the groove behind the same part of the bone.

Question 3086. A constructed illustration: a person has weakness of both the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus with deep pain in the shoulder but no loss of sensation in the skin. Where is the nerve most likely compressed: at the suprascapular notch, in the quadrangular space, behind the medial epicondyle, or in the carpal tunnel? The answer is at the suprascapular notch. That nerve carries no skin fibers, so sensation is spared.

Question 3087. Which movements does the pectoralis major produce at the shoulder joint: adduction, medial rotation and flexion, abduction and lateral rotation, extension and lateral rotation, or abduction alone? The answer is adduction, medial rotation and flexion. Its clavicular head helps to flex the arm, and its sternocostal head can extend the arm from the flexed position.

Question 3088. Which small muscle lies between the clavicle and the first rib, and what does it do? The answer is the subclavius, which steadies the clavicle and draws it downward. It is supplied by a small nerve from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. It lies in front of the vessels of the upper limb as they leave the neck.

Question 3089. A described photograph of the back shows a broad triangular muscle whose upper fibers run downward, whose middle fibers run across and whose lower fibers run upward, all converging on the shoulder. Which muscle is shown, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the trapezius, supplied by the spinal accessory nerve. Its upper fibers elevate the scapula, its middle fibers retract it and its lower fibers rotate it upward.

Question 3090. Which statement about the deltoid muscle is correct: its middle fibers abduct the arm, its anterior fibers extend the arm, its posterior fibers flex the arm, or all of its fibers adduct the arm? The answer is that its middle fibers abduct the arm. Its anterior fibers flex and medially rotate the arm, and its posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate it.

Question 3091. A described magnetic resonance image of the shoulder shows one tendon running to the greater tubercle just behind the joint, with a smaller muscle lying beneath it. Which two muscles are shown? The answer is the infraspinatus and the teres minor. Their tendons blend with the capsule of the joint and rotate the arm laterally.

Question 3092. Which structure lies immediately above the head of the humerus and separates the deltoid from the tendons of the rotator cuff? The answer is the subacromial bursa. It lets the cuff tendons glide beneath the acromion and the coracoacromial arch. It is the structure that becomes inflamed in painful abduction of the arm.

Question 3093. Which statement about the teres minor and the infraspinatus is correct: the teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve, the infraspinatus is supplied by the axillary nerve, both are supplied by the suprascapular nerve, or neither is supplied by the suprascapular nerve? The answer is that the teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve. The infraspinatus, which lies beside it, is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

Question 3094. Which rotator cuff muscle lies on the anterior surface of the scapula and therefore cannot be felt from behind: the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor, or the subscapularis? The answer is the subscapularis. It fills the fossa on the front of the scapula and inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus.

Question 3095. A described ultrasound image of the shoulder shows a tendon crossing above the head of the humerus, with a thin dark layer between the tendon and the bone and a bright line on the deep surface of the tendon. What are those two layers? The answer is the subacromial bursa above and the surface of the head of the humerus below. The bursa lets the tendon glide as the arm moves.

Question 3096. Which nerve pierces the coracobrachialis muscle on its way down the arm? The answer is the musculocutaneous nerve. It supplies the coracobrachialis, the biceps brachii and the brachialis. It then continues into the forearm as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. It is the nerve of the front of the arm.

Question 3097. Which muscle both flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder joint: the coracobrachialis, the deltoid, the teres minor, or the infraspinatus? The answer is the coracobrachialis. It runs from the coracoid process to the middle of the medial surface of the humerus. The other three muscles either abduct the arm or rotate it.

Question 3098. A constructed illustration: one person cannot raise the arm above the head and the shoulder droops, while another has a scapula whose medial border stands out when the arm is pushed forward. Which nerve is injured in the second person? The answer is the long thoracic nerve, which supplies the serratus anterior. The first person has a lesion of the spinal accessory nerve.

Question 3099. A described image across the shoulder shows a large muscle wrapping over the top of the joint, a group of muscles behind it and a tendon in a groove in front. Which muscle wraps over the top, and which tendon lies in the groove? The answer is the deltoid, with the tendon of the long head of the biceps in the groove. The muscles behind the joint are the rotator cuff.

Question 3100. A complete tear of the rotator cuff leaves the humeral head riding up under the acromion. Which of these explains it: the deltoid pulls up while the torn cuff no longer pulls down, the cuff pulls up while the deltoid pulls down, the biceps pulls up, or the triceps pulls up? The answer is the deltoid pulls up while the torn cuff no longer pulls down. Nothing then opposes the deltoid.

To summarize, the internal oblique is the middle of the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall, its fibers run upward and medially, and it rotates the trunk to the same side. The transversus abdominis lies deepest of the three, its fibers run across the abdomen, and its chief work is to compress the abdominal contents and to steady the trunk. Both are supplied by the lower thoracic spinal nerves and the first lumbar nerve, both take part in the conjoint tendon, and both lie in the neurovascular plane of the wall. Above the arcuate line the rectus sheath has a strong posterior wall, and below it only the transversalis fascia lies behind the muscle. At the shoulder, the supraspinatus begins abduction, the deltoid carries it on, and the four muscles of the rotator cuff hold the head of the humerus in the shallow glenoid socket. The infraspinatus and the teres minor rotate the arm laterally, the subscapularis rotates it medially, and the axillary nerve, the suprascapular nerve and the long thoracic nerve are the ones most often injured, so what this chapter offers is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 32 — Upper Limb

The muscles of the upper limb work in groups, and this chapter takes them in the order in which a listener meets them from the shoulder outward. It begins with the four muscles of the rotator cuff that steady the head of the humerus in its shallow socket, then moves to the arm, where the flexors and the extensor of the elbow lie in two compartments, and ends in the forearm, whose two bones and many muscles turn the palm and move the hand. It holds one hundred questions, and every one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3101. Which of the four rotator cuff muscles is torn most often: the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor, or the subscapularis? The answer is the supraspinatus. Its tendon passes beneath the acromion and the coracoacromial ligament, where it is squeezed against the head of the humerus with every overhead movement. The other three lie further from that arch.

Question 3102. Which muscle of the rotator cuff arises from the fossa on the front of the scapula and inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus? The answer is the subscapularis. It is the only cuff muscle that lies on the anterior surface of the scapula. It rotates the arm medially and helps to hold the head of the humerus against the glenoid.

Question 3103. Which nerve supplies both the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus? The answer is the suprascapular nerve. It arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and passes through the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse scapular ligament. It gives a branch to the supraspinatus and then continues into the infraspinous fossa.

Question 3104. Which muscle runs from the upper lateral border of the scapula to the lowest facet of the greater tubercle and rotates the arm laterally: the teres minor, the teres major, the infraspinatus, or the subscapularis? The answer is the teres minor. The teres major lies below it and rotates the arm medially, and the infraspinatus arises above it from the infraspinous fossa.

Question 3105. Which tendon of the rotator cuff lies immediately beneath the coracoacromial arch, and is therefore the one compressed when the arm is raised? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus. The arch is formed by the acromion and the coracoacromial ligament. Between the tendon and the arch lies the subacromial bursa, which is inflamed in the same movement.

Question 3106. A described magnetic resonance image of the shoulder, taken in the coronal plane, shows a gap filled with fluid in the tendon that crosses the top of the head of the humerus. Which tendon has torn? The answer is the supraspinatus, and fluid in the gap marks a full-thickness tear.

Question 3107. Which muscle arises from the whole of the infraspinous fossa and inserts on the middle facet of the greater tubercle? The answer is the infraspinatus. It is a lateral rotator of the arm and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve. It forms the rounded fullness below the spine of the scapula.

Question 3108. Which of these four rotator cuff muscles does not attach to the greater tubercle of the humerus: the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the subscapularis, or the teres minor? The answer is the subscapularis. Its tendon crosses the front of the joint to reach the lesser tubercle. The other three lie in a row on the greater tubercle, from above downward in that order.

Question 3109. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the shoulder, a person cannot begin to lift the arm away from the side, though a helper can raise it fully. Which structure is torn? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, which takes the first part of abduction before the deltoid can act.

Question 3110. True or false: the tendons of the rotator cuff blend with the fibrous capsule of the shoulder joint and become inseparable from it near their insertions. The answer is true. The cuff forms a sleeve around the front, the top and the back of the joint. This fusion lets the cuff both move the arm and steady the head of the humerus.

Question 3111. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraspinatus with the superior facet of the greater tubercle, the infraspinatus with the lesser tubercle, the subscapularis with the middle facet, or the teres minor with the highest facet? The answer is the supraspinatus with the superior facet, while the subscapularis takes the lesser tubercle.

Question 3112. Name the four muscles of the rotator cuff, spoken as a list. The answer is the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor, and the subscapularis. The first three arise from the back of the scapula and the last from its front. Together their tendons surround the shoulder joint and pull the head of the humerus into the glenoid.

Question 3113. Which nerve supplies the muscle that lies on the front of the scapula and rotates the arm medially: the suprascapular nerve, the axillary nerve, the upper and lower subscapular nerves, or the radial nerve? The answer is the upper and lower subscapular nerves. They arise from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

Question 3114. A described arthroscopic view of the shoulder shows a bare patch of bone on the greater tubercle where a tendon should be attached, with the tendon retracted toward the joint. Which structure has been lost? The answer is the insertion of the supraspinatus tendon. The bare patch is its footprint, left uncovered by the retracted end.

Question 3115. Which tendon passes through the gap between the supraspinatus and the subscapularis, a gap known as the rotator cuff interval? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps. It leaves the joint there and descends in the intertubercular sulcus. The coracohumeral ligament also crosses that interval and strengthens it.

Question 3116. Which muscle arises from the upper part of the lateral border of the scapula and inserts on the inferior facet of the greater tubercle? The answer is the teres minor. It is a lateral rotator of the arm and is supplied by the axillary nerve. It lies just below the infraspinatus and above the teres major.

Question 3117. A constructed illustration: a person reaches overhead and feels a sharp pain as the arm passes the middle of the arc. Which structures are being pinched, and in which space? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon and the subacromial bursa, in the subacromial space. The painful arc is the range in which the greater tubercle passes beneath the acromion.

Question 3118. Which muscle both forms part of the rotator cuff and starts the movement of raising the arm sideways: the infraspinatus, the supraspinatus, the subscapularis, or the teres major? The answer is the supraspinatus. It abducts the arm through the first part of the range, and the deltoid then carries the movement further. The teres major is not a cuff muscle and rotates the arm medially.

Question 3119. A described radiograph of the shoulder shows the head of the humerus sitting higher than its socket, almost touching the acromion. What does that position suggest? The answer is a tear of the rotator cuff. When the cuff no longer holds the head down against the pull of the deltoid, the head drifts upward. The normal space between the head and the acromion is lost.

Question 3120. True or false: the rotator cuff acts only as a passive tie that holds the head of the humerus in place and takes no active part in movement. The answer is false. The cuff is an active group of muscles that contracts during movement and steadies the head while the larger muscles move the arm. It is a dynamic stabilizer rather than a static ligament.

Question 3121. Which pair of rotator cuff muscles shares a single nerve supply, so that one lesion weakens both: the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus, the infraspinatus and the teres minor, the teres minor and the subscapularis, or the subscapularis and the supraspinatus? The answer is the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus, which share the suprascapular nerve.

Question 3122. Which structure lies immediately between the tendon of the supraspinatus and the arch of the acromion? The answer is the subacromial bursa. It is a flat sac that allows the tendon to glide beneath the bone. Because it communicates with the shoulder joint in many people, inflammation of one commonly affects the other.

Question 3123. Which artery runs with the suprascapular nerve through the suprascapular notch and supplies the muscles of the cuff on the back of the scapula? The answer is the suprascapular artery. It arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery. It reaches the back of the scapula above the transverse scapular ligament while the nerve passes below it.

Question 3124. How many muscles make up the rotator cuff: two, three, four, or five? The answer is four. They are the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor, and the subscapularis. Their tendons fuse with the capsule of the shoulder joint and form a cuff around the head of the humerus.

Question 3125. A constructed illustration: an older person has an old tear of the rotator cuff, and the head of the humerus now rides high. Which muscle is acting without its usual partner? The answer is the deltoid, whose upward pull is no longer balanced by the cuff.

Question 3126. A described transverse section through the shoulder shows a broad tendon wrapping the head of the humerus from the front, the top and the back. Which four muscles contribute to that wrapping? The answer is the subscapularis in front, the supraspinatus on top, and the infraspinatus with the teres minor behind. Their tendons merge with the capsule to form the cuff.

Question 3127. Which of these pairs belongs together: the subscapularis with lateral rotation, the infraspinatus with medial rotation, the supraspinatus with abduction, or the teres minor with extension of the elbow? The answer is the supraspinatus with abduction. The subscapularis rotates the arm medially, the infraspinatus and the teres minor rotate it laterally, and no cuff muscle acts on the elbow.

Question 3128. Which fossa of the scapula lies above the spine and gives origin to the muscle whose tendon passes under the acromion? The answer is the supraspinous fossa, and the muscle is the supraspinatus. The fossa is smaller than the infraspinous fossa below the spine. It is filled by the muscle, whose tendon then crosses the top of the joint.

Question 3129. Which movement is weakened first when the tendon of the supraspinatus is torn: rotation of the arm outward, the beginning of abduction of the arm, extension of the elbow, or pronation of the forearm? The answer is the beginning of abduction of the arm, which the deltoid can continue once it has started.

Question 3130. A described coronal section through the shoulder shows a bursa lying between a tendon and the underside of the acromion, and the bursa is thickened and filled with fluid. Which tendon lies deep to it? The answer is the supraspinatus. The bursa lies between the tendon and the arch formed by the acromion and the coracoacromial ligament. Thickening of the bursa narrows the space further.

Question 3131. Which rotator cuff muscle lies against the anterior surface of the scapula and is the only one to insert on the lesser tubercle: the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor, or the subscapularis? The answer is the subscapularis. It is a medial rotator of the arm, supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves. The other three all reach the greater tubercle behind it.

Question 3132. A described dissection of the shoulder has the deltoid reflected forward, exposing a tendinous sheet that covers the head of the humerus. Which sheet is exposed? The answer is the rotator cuff, with the subacromial bursa lying between the cuff and the acromion.

Question 3133. Which muscle lies immediately inferior to the infraspinatus on the back of the scapula, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the teres minor, supplied by the axillary nerve. It arises from the lateral border of the scapula below the infraspinatus. The two muscles work together as lateral rotators but have different nerve supplies.

Question 3134. Why does the tendon of the supraspinatus tear more often than the other cuff tendons: because it is the thinnest, because it passes beneath the acromion, because it has no nerve supply, or because it crosses two joints? The answer is that it passes beneath the acromion, and its blood supply is poor near the insertion, in the zone named for Codman.

Question 3135. The tendon of the supraspinatus crosses the top of the shoulder joint and ends on the superior facet of the greater tubercle. What does it lie against along the way? The answer is the fibrous capsule of the joint. Its fibers blend with the capsule before they reach the bone, and the subacromial bursa lies above it.

Question 3136. Which single bone forms the skeleton of the arm between the shoulder joint above and the elbow below? The answer is the humerus. Its rounded head fits into the glenoid cavity of the scapula, and its lower end joins the radius and the ulna. The arm is the segment above the elbow, while the forearm lies below it.

Question 3137. Which muscle of the arm both flexes the elbow and turns the palm to face upward: the brachialis, the triceps brachii, the biceps brachii, or the coracobrachialis? The answer is the biceps brachii. It is the strongest supinator when the elbow is flexed. The brachialis is a pure flexor, and the triceps brachii extends the elbow.

Question 3138. Which muscle arises from the coracoid process and inserts on the middle of the medial surface of the humerus? The answer is the coracobrachialis. It flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it on its way down the arm.

Question 3139. Which nerve pierces the coracobrachialis muscle on its way into the arm: the axillary nerve, the musculocutaneous nerve, the radial nerve, or the ulnar nerve? The answer is the musculocutaneous nerve. It enters the front of the arm through that muscle and then supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment. At the elbow it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

Question 3140. Which tendon lies in the intertubercular sulcus on the front of the upper humerus? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii. It leaves the shoulder joint and runs down the groove between the greater and the lesser tubercles. The transverse humeral ligament holds it in the groove.

Question 3141. Which muscle is the strongest flexor of the elbow, lying deep to the biceps brachii and inserting on the ulna? The answer is the brachialis. It arises from the front of the lower half of the humerus and inserts on the ulnar tuberosity. Because it attaches to the ulna rather than the radius, it flexes the elbow whatever the position of the forearm.

Question 3142. A constructed illustration: a person falls and breaks the shaft of the humerus at its middle, and afterwards the wrist cannot be straightened. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the radial nerve, in the groove on the back of the humerus. Its branches to the extensor muscles of the wrist lie beyond the fracture. The result is a wrist drop.

Question 3143. True or false: the median nerve gives off no branch to any muscle while it lies in the arm. The answer is true. In the arm it runs beside the brachial artery and gives no muscular branches at all. Its first muscular branches are given in the forearm, where it supplies most of the flexor group.

Question 3144. A described radiograph shows a fracture line through the upper humerus just below the rounded head, and the shaft is displaced. Which nerve is most at risk? The answer is the axillary nerve. It winds around the surgical neck, and the deltoid weakens when it is injured.

Question 3145. The triceps brachii has three heads. Which one arises from the back of the humerus below the groove that carries the radial nerve: the long head, the lateral head, the medial head, or the anconeus? The answer is the medial head. The lateral head arises above the groove, and the long head arises from the scapula.

Question 3146. Which of these pairs belongs together: the musculocutaneous nerve with the triceps brachii, the radial nerve with the coracobrachialis, the axillary nerve with the deltoid, or the median nerve with the biceps brachii? The answer is the axillary nerve with the deltoid. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the coracobrachialis, the biceps and the brachialis, and the radial nerve supplies the triceps.

Question 3147. Which small muscle lies at the back of the elbow, arises from the lateral epicondyle of the humerus, and is supplied by the radial nerve? The answer is the anconeus. It inserts on the lateral side of the olecranon and the upper part of the ulna. It helps to extend the elbow and steadies the joint during the movement.

Question 3148. Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa: the pronator teres, the brachioradialis, the biceps brachii, or the flexor carpi ulnaris? The answer is the brachioradialis. The pronator teres forms the medial boundary, and the line between the two epicondyles forms the base above. The biceps tendon and the brachial artery lie within the fossa.

Question 3149. A described radiograph of a child's elbow shows a fracture line just above the condyles of the humerus, with the lower fragment displaced backward. Which nerve and which artery lie most at risk? The answer is the median nerve and the brachial artery, both of which pass directly in front of the lower end of the humerus. The displaced fragment can stretch or tear them.

Question 3150. A described cross section through the middle of the arm shows two compartments separated by a band of deep fascia and a septum of bone. Which nerve lies in each? The answer is that the musculocutaneous nerve lies in the anterior compartment and the radial nerve behind, with the humerus between them.

Question 3151. The axillary nerve leaves the back of the axilla through a small space bounded by the teres minor above and the teres major below. What is that space called, and which vessel runs with the nerve? The answer is the quadrangular space, with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. Both pass around the surgical neck of the humerus.

Question 3152. At which point does the axillary artery become the brachial artery? The answer is at the lower border of the teres major muscle. Above that border the vessel is named the axillary artery. Below it, the brachial artery runs down the medial side of the arm beside the median nerve.

Question 3153. The musculocutaneous nerve ends in the forearm as which cutaneous nerve: the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm, or the palmar branch of the median nerve? The answer is the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which emerges on the outer side of the arm above the elbow.

Question 3154. Name the three muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm, spoken as a list. The answer is the coracobrachialis, the biceps brachii, and the brachialis. All three are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve. They flex the arm at the shoulder or the elbow, and the biceps also turns the palm upward.

Question 3155. From which point does the long head of the biceps brachii arise, and by what route does its tendon reach the arm: the coracoid process, the supraglenoid tubercle, the infraglenoid tubercle, or the greater tubercle? The answer is the supraglenoid tubercle. The tendon leaves the shoulder joint and runs down in the intertubercular sulcus. The short head arises from the coracoid process beside it.

Question 3156. True or false: the radial nerve supplies a small part of the brachialis muscle as well as the triceps. The answer is true. A branch of the radial nerve reaches the lateral part of the brachialis, while the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the rest. This double supply is one of the details that students most often miss.

Question 3157. A constructed illustration: a person who has used crutches under the arms for several weeks finds that the wrist hangs limp and the back of the hand feels numb. Which nerve has been compressed? The answer is the radial nerve in the axilla. The crutch presses it against the humerus, and the wrist drop follows.

Question 3158. A described specimen of the back of the arm shows a muscle with three heads, and when it is reflected the radial nerve and a deep artery come into view in a groove on the bone. Which muscle is it? The answer is the triceps brachii. The groove is the radial groove of the humerus, beside the deep artery of the arm.

Question 3159. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior compartment of the arm with the radial nerve, the posterior compartment of the arm with the musculocutaneous nerve, the anterior compartment of the arm with the musculocutaneous nerve, or the posterior compartment with the axillary nerve? The answer is the anterior compartment with the musculocutaneous nerve, and the posterior with the radial nerve.

Question 3160. Which bony prominence does the ulnar nerve lie behind as it passes from the arm into the forearm? The answer is the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The nerve crosses the back of the elbow in a groove behind that prominence. This is why a knock on the inner side of the elbow produces tingling in the little finger.

Question 3161. A fracture of the middle of the humeral shaft damages the radial nerve, yet the triceps still extends the elbow. Why is that: the triceps has another nerve, its branches leave the nerve above the groove, the triceps is not a true extensor, or the nerve recovers at once? The answer is that they leave the nerve above the groove, before its branches to the wrist extensors.

Question 3162. Which bony prominence can be felt on the inner side of the elbow, and which nerve lies behind it? The answer is the medial epicondyle of the humerus, with the ulnar nerve behind it. The epicondyle gives origin to the common flexor muscles of the forearm. The prominence is the reason the nerve is exposed to injury there.

Question 3163. The radial nerve leaves the back of the arm and reaches the front. Which structure does it pierce as it makes that crossing: the medial intermuscular septum, the lateral intermuscular septum, the bicipital aponeurosis, or the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the lateral intermuscular septum, between the brachialis and the brachioradialis.

Question 3164. A described angiogram of the arm shows a single large vessel running down the medial side of the limb beside the median nerve, giving branches to the muscles of the arm. Which vessel is shown, and where does it end? The answer is the brachial artery, which ends in the cubital fossa by dividing into the radial and the ulnar arteries.

Question 3165. A constructed illustration: a person lifting a heavy object feels a sudden snap at the front of the shoulder, and afterwards the belly of the biceps bunches into a low swelling. Which structure has ruptured? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps. It lay in the intertubercular sulcus, and the short head remains attached.

Question 3166. Which muscle forms the rounded contour of the shoulder, is supplied by the axillary nerve, and abducts the arm: the supraspinatus, the teres major, the deltoid, or the coracobrachialis? The answer is the deltoid. Its middle fibers abduct the arm after the supraspinatus has begun the movement. Its anterior fibers flex and rotate the arm medially, and its posterior fibers do the reverse.

Question 3167. Which large vein runs up the medial side of the arm and joins the brachial vein near the axilla? The answer is the basilic vein. The cephalic vein runs on the lateral side instead and reaches the shoulder. In the cubital fossa the median cubital vein joins the two.

Question 3168. Which muscle of the arm inserts on the olecranon process of the ulna: the biceps brachii, the brachialis, the triceps brachii, or the coracobrachialis? The answer is the triceps brachii. Its three heads join in a common tendon that ends on the olecranon. The anconeus lies beside it and shares the same nerve supply.

Question 3169. Which of the two bones of the forearm lies on the lateral or thumb side? The answer is the radius. The ulna lies medially, on the little finger side. In the anatomical position the two bones lie parallel, and the radius turns around the ulna during pronation.

Question 3170. Which muscle both pronates the forearm and helps to flex the elbow: the pronator quadratus, the supinator, the pronator teres, or the flexor carpi radialis? The answer is the pronator teres. It arises from the medial epicondyle and the coronoid process and inserts on the lateral surface of the radius. The pronator quadratus pronates without flexing the elbow.

Question 3171. Which flat muscle lies deep in the front of the distal forearm, directly on the two bones, and pronates the hand? The answer is the pronator quadratus. It runs from the front of the ulna to the front of the radius. It is the main pronator during slow, unresisted movement.

Question 3172. All the muscles of the front of the forearm are supplied by the median nerve except two. Which muscle is supplied by the ulnar nerve: the pronator teres, the flexor carpi radialis, the flexor carpi ulnaris, or the flexor digitorum superficialis? The answer is the flexor carpi ulnaris. The ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus is the other exception.

Question 3173. In which direction do the fibers of the interosseous membrane of the forearm run, and what force do they carry? The answer is that they run downward and medially from the radius to the ulna. The hand loads the radius, and the membrane passes that force to the ulna.

Question 3174. A described cross section through the middle of the forearm shows two bones with a membrane between them. Which bone lies on which side, and what lies between them? The answer is that the radius lies laterally and the ulna medially, with the interosseous membrane stretched between them. Muscle fills the space in front of both.

Question 3175. Which muscle of the forearm sends tendons to the middle phalanges of the fingers? The answer is the flexor digitorum superficialis. Each of its tendons splits into two slips to allow the deeper tendon to pass through. It flexes the middle joints of the fingers, and its tendons pass beneath the flexor retinaculum at the wrist.

Question 3176. The flexor digitorum profundus has a double nerve supply. Which part of it is supplied by the ulnar nerve: the lateral half, the medial half, the whole muscle, or none of it? The answer is the medial half, which moves the little finger and the ring finger. The lateral half is supplied by the median nerve.

Question 3177. A constructed illustration: an older person falls on the outstretched hand, and afterwards the lower end of the radius is displaced backward, giving the wrist a fork-shaped outline. Which bone is fractured? The answer is the distal radius, displaced backward and outward, and the ulnar styloid may be broken too.

Question 3178. True or false: every muscle of the front of the forearm is supplied by the median nerve. The answer is false. The flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus are supplied by the ulnar nerve. All the others are supplied by the median nerve or by its branches.

Question 3179. Which muscle wraps around the upper part of the radius, arises from the lateral epicondyle and the supinator crest of the ulna, and turns the palm upward? The answer is the supinator. It is supplied by the deep branch of the radial nerve. That nerve passes beneath the fibrous arch at the upper edge of the muscle.

Question 3180. Which of these pairs belongs together: the flexor carpi radialis with the ulnar nerve, the flexor digitorum superficialis with the radial nerve, the flexor carpi ulnaris with the ulnar nerve, or the pronator quadratus with the radial nerve? The answer is the flexor carpi ulnaris with the ulnar nerve, the one muscle of the superficial group supplied by that nerve.

Question 3181. At the wrist, the radial artery is felt for its pulse between which two tendons: the flexor carpi radialis and the brachioradialis, the palmaris longus and the flexor carpi ulnaris, the extensor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis, or the flexor digitorum superficialis and the flexor digitorum profundus? The answer is between the flexor carpi radialis and the brachioradialis.

Question 3182. A described radiograph of the wrist shows a break across the lower end of the radius, with the distal fragment tilted backward. Which normal relation has altered? The answer is that the normal forward tilt of the lower end of the radius is reversed, giving the fork-shaped outline.

Question 3183. A constructed illustration: after a forearm injury a person cannot bend the tip of the thumb or the tip of the index finger, yet sensation in the hand is normal. Which nerve is damaged? The answer is the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It supplies the deep flexors and carries no sensory fibers.

Question 3184. The median nerve enters the forearm between which two structures before it passes beneath the arch of the flexor digitorum superficialis? The answer is the two heads of the pronator teres, the humeral head and the ulnar head. It then runs down the middle of the forearm. The ulnar nerve enters between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris instead.

Question 3185. Which tendon forms the medial boundary of the small triangular hollow at the base of the thumb? The answer is the tendon of the extensor pollicis longus. The lateral boundary is formed by the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis. The radial artery crosses the floor of that hollow, over the scaphoid.

Question 3186. Which muscle of the forearm flexes the elbow most effectively when the forearm is midway between pronation and supination: the biceps brachii, the brachialis, the brachioradialis, or the pronator teres? The answer is the brachioradialis. The biceps works best with the palm upward, and the brachialis flexes in every position but has its best leverage in full supination.

Question 3187. Turning the palm to face the floor and then back to face the ceiling happens in which plane, and about which axis? The answer is the transverse plane, about a longitudinal axis that runs from the center of the head of the radius above to the head of the ulna below. The radius turns around the ulna. The elbow itself does not move.

Question 3188. Which structure must the deep branch of the radial nerve pass beneath as it enters the back of the forearm: the arcade of Frohse, the bicipital aponeurosis, the flexor retinaculum, or the interosseous membrane? The answer is the arcade of Frohse. It is the fibrous upper edge of the supinator, and the nerve beyond it is named the posterior interosseous nerve.

Question 3189. A constructed illustration: a fracture of the upper ulna is found together with a dislocation of the head of the radius at the elbow. Why do those two injuries belong together? The answer is that the broken ulna allows the head of the radius to leave the joint, and it will not return while the ulna remains bent.

Question 3190. A described transverse section is taken through the middle third of the forearm. Which structure lies directly between the two bones, and in which direction does it pass? The answer is the interosseous membrane, which passes downward and medially from the radius to the ulna. It divides the forearm into an anterior and a posterior compartment. Vessels pass through openings in it.

Question 3191. A described dissection of the back of the forearm has the superficial extensor muscles turned aside, revealing a deep group around the lower end of the radius. Which muscles are in that group? The answer is the supinator, the abductor pollicis longus, the extensor pollicis brevis, the extensor pollicis longus, and the extensor indicis.

Question 3192. Supination is strongest with the elbow bent to a right angle. Which fact explains that: the biceps brachii is a powerful supinator, the supinator muscle crosses only one joint, the pronator quadratus relaxes, or the radius is fixed by the wrist? The answer is that the biceps brachii is a powerful supinator and is at its best length when the elbow is flexed.

Question 3193. A constructed illustration: a person who repeatedly lifts a young child feels pain over the outer side of the wrist when the thumb is extended and the hand turns inward. Which tendons are inflamed? The answer is the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis, in the first compartment beneath the extensor retinaculum.

Question 3194. Which artery runs down the forearm in company with the ulnar nerve, and between which two heads do both pass at the elbow? The answer is the ulnar artery, which passes between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris with the nerve. Below the elbow it gives the common interosseous artery. It ends in the hand as the superficial palmar arch.

Question 3195. Which phalanx does the tendon of the flexor digitorum superficialis reach: the proximal, the middle, the distal, or none? The answer is the middle phalanx. Each tendon splits into two slips that attach to the sides of that bone. The deeper muscle, the flexor digitorum profundus, continues through the split to reach the distal phalanx.

Question 3196. Which nerve supplies the deep muscles on the back of the forearm, after it has passed beneath the supinator? The answer is the posterior interosseous nerve, the continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve. It carries no cutaneous sensation in the forearm. It ends as a small filament over the back of the wrist.

Question 3197. Name the three muscles whose tendons bound the small hollow at the base of the thumb, spoken as a list. The answer is the abductor pollicis longus, the extensor pollicis brevis, and the extensor pollicis longus. The first two form the lateral boundary, and the third forms the medial boundary. The radial artery crosses the floor.

Question 3198. Which muscle of the forearm is absent in some people, and is often used as a graft: the flexor carpi radialis, the palmaris longus, the pronator teres, or the flexor digitorum superficialis? The answer is the palmaris longus. It arises from the medial epicondyle and ends in the palmar aponeurosis of the hand.

Question 3199. A described dissection of the back of the wrist shows a broad band of fibrous tissue holding six sets of tendons against the bones, each set in its own sheath. What is that band called, and how many compartments does it form? The answer is the extensor retinaculum, which forms six compartments. The tendons pass beneath it in sheaths lined with synovial membrane.

Question 3200. A constructed illustration: a fracture of the lower radius comes with disruption of the joint between the two forearm bones at the wrist. Which pair is described: a broken radius with a disrupted distal radioulnar joint, a broken ulna with a dislocated radial head, a broken scaphoid alone, or a dislocated wrist with no fracture? The answer is the broken radius with the disrupted distal radioulnar joint.

To summarize, the rotator cuff is four muscles whose tendons fuse with the capsule of the shoulder joint: the supraspinatus, which begins abduction beneath the acromion, the infraspinatus and the teres minor, which rotate the arm laterally, and the subscapularis, which rotates it medially. In the arm, the anterior compartment is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve and the triceps by the radial nerve in the groove on the back of the humerus, while the brachial artery and the median nerve descend on the medial side. In the forearm, the median nerve supplies every flexor except the flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus, and the radial nerve supplies the extensors through its deep branch. The radius turns around the ulna in the transverse plane, and the interosseous membrane carries the load from the radius to the ulna. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 33 — Upper Limb, Part Two

This chapter takes the muscles of the hand and then the muscles of the pelvis and the hip. The first fifty questions belong to the hand, from the thenar and hypothenar groups through the lumbricals and the interossei to the tendons, the fibrous bands and the nerves that reach them. The second fifty belong to the pelvis and the hip, where the gluteal muscles, the short lateral rotators, the adductors and the muscles of the pelvic floor are set out in turn. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind until the end. The chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3201. Which muscle of the hand draws the thumb across the palm so that its pad meets the pads of the fingers: the abductor pollicis brevis, the opponens pollicis, the adductor pollicis, or the flexor pollicis brevis? The answer is the opponens pollicis. It lies deep to the short muscles of the thumb and rolls the first metacarpal toward the palm.

Question 3202. Which small muscle forms the rounded pad at the base of the little finger and pulls that finger away from the others? The answer is the abductor digiti minimi. It lies most superficially in the hypothenar eminence and abducts the fifth finger. The flexor digiti minimi brevis lies beside it, and the opponens digiti minimi lies deepest.

Question 3203. Which muscle lies in the skin of the palm and wrinkles it when the hand grips: the palmaris brevis, the palmaris longus, the first lumbrical, or the first dorsal interosseous? The answer is the palmaris brevis. It is a thin sheet just beneath the skin over the hypothenar eminence, the only muscle of the hand that moves the skin rather than a joint.

Question 3204. Which intrinsic muscles of the hand can flex the knuckles and straighten the joints between the knuckles and the fingertips at the same time? The answer is the lumbrical muscles. Four of them arise from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus and pass to the extensor expansions. The interossei share this action but also move the fingers sideways.

Question 3205. At the wrist, which structure passes through the carpal tunnel: the ulnar nerve, the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris, the median nerve, or the radial artery? The answer is the median nerve. It runs beneath the flexor retinaculum with the tendons of the deep and superficial flexors of the fingers.

Question 3206. Which muscle forms the fleshy mass at the base of the thumb and lies closest to the skin of the three short muscles there? The answer is the abductor pollicis brevis. It lies immediately deep to the skin and the palmar aponeurosis. The opponens pollicis and the flexor pollicis brevis lie deep to the abductor.

Question 3207. Which muscle lies in the first web space and is tested by pinching the thumb and the index finger together: the first dorsal interosseous, the adductor pollicis, the second palmar interosseous, or the first lumbrical? The answer is the first dorsal interosseous. It arises from the sides of the first two metacarpals that face each other and abducts the index finger. The adductor pollicis lies deeper in the same space.

Question 3208. A described dissection of the palm lifts the skin and the palmar aponeurosis and turns aside the tendons of the superficial flexor. A muscle with two bellies lies in the first web space. Which muscle is shown, and what does it do? The answer is the first dorsal interosseous, which abducts the index finger. The second dorsal interosseous lies in the second space and abducts the middle finger.

Question 3209. Into which structure do the tendons of the extensor digitorum, the lumbricals and the interossei all insert at the fingers: the palmar aponeurosis, the extensor expansion, the flexor retinaculum, or the deep transverse metacarpal ligament? The answer is the extensor expansion. It is a triangular sheet on the back of each finger, and its central slip reaches the base of the middle phalanx.

Question 3210. Which short muscle of the hand arises from the hook of the hamate and the flexor retinaculum and draws the fifth metacarpal forward? The answer is the opponens digiti minimi. It rotates the fifth metacarpal toward the palm, so the little finger can be cupped against the ring finger. The abductor digiti minimi arises partly from the pisiform instead.

Question 3211. Which muscle of the hand adducts the thumb toward the index finger and lies in the deepest plane of the first web space: the adductor pollicis, the abductor pollicis brevis, the opponens pollicis, or the first lumbrical? The answer is the adductor pollicis. It has an oblique head from the capitate and a transverse head from the third metacarpal, and it is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
