The expansion of the semimembranosus forms the oblique popliteal ligament over it.

Question 3421. A described dissection of the popliteal fossa shows a fat-filled diamond with a nerve lying nearest the skin, a vein and an artery beneath it, and a muscle forming the floor. Which muscle forms the floor? The answer is the popliteus. The nerve is the tibial nerve, and the vessels are the popliteal vein and the popliteal artery.

Question 3422. Which statement about the hamstrings is correct: the short head of the biceps femoris crosses the hip joint, the semitendinosus lies lateral to the biceps femoris, the semimembranosus lies deep to the semitendinosus, or the hamstrings are supplied by the obturator nerve? The answer is that the semimembranosus lies deep to the semitendinosus. The short head crosses only the knee, and the whole group is supplied by the sciatic nerve.

Question 3423. A constructed illustration: a deep cut across the back of the thigh in its lower third leaves a person unable to move the foot and without feeling over the sole. Which structure has most likely been divided? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It lies just deep to the long head of the biceps femoris at that level, where it is sheltered only by muscle.

Question 3424. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the biceps femoris with the head of the fibula, the semitendinosus with the greater trochanter, the semimembranosus with the tibial tuberosity, or the hamstrings with the femoral nerve? The answer is the biceps femoris with the head of the fibula. The semitendinosus ends on the medial tibia and the semimembranosus on the medial tibial condyle.

Question 3425. A constructed illustration: the examiner asks a person to bend the knee against resistance and palpates two cords at the medial side of the popliteal fossa. Which two structures are felt: the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, the biceps femoris and the iliotibial tract, the gracilis and the sartorius, or the two heads of the gastrocnemius? The answer is the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, the first lying superficial to the second.

Question 3426. Which muscle group forms the front of the thigh and is the great extensor of the knee? The answer is the quadriceps femoris. It has four parts, the rectus femoris and the three vastus muscles, and they share a common tendon that encloses the patella. All four parts are supplied by the femoral nerve.

Question 3427. Which nerve supplies the quadriceps femoris: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the sciatic nerve, or the common fibular nerve? The answer is the femoral nerve, which arises from the second, third and fourth lumbar spinal nerves. It also supplies the skin over the front of the thigh through its saphenous branch, which reaches the medial side of the leg.

Question 3428. Which part of the quadriceps is the only one that crosses the hip joint as well as the knee? The answer is the rectus femoris. It arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine and from a groove above the rim of the acetabulum. The other three parts arise from the femur, so they act at the knee alone.

Question 3429. In the front of the thigh, which part of the quadriceps lies immediately on each side of the rectus femoris? The answer is the vastus lateralis on the lateral side and the vastus medialis on the medial side. Both arise from the back of the femur and form the sides of the large muscle mass of the front of the thigh.

Question 3430. From which point does the rectus femoris arise: the anterior inferior iliac spine, the anterior superior iliac spine, the ischial tuberosity, or the pubic tubercle? The answer is the anterior inferior iliac spine, together with a reflection from the groove above the rim of the acetabulum. The anterior superior iliac spine gives origin to the sartorius instead.

Question 3431. A described dissection of the front of the thigh shows one muscle arising from the front of the hip bone and another lying directly upon the front of the femur. Which two parts of the quadriceps are shown? The answer is the rectus femoris and the vastus intermedius. The vastus lateralis and the vastus medialis lie beside them on either side.

Question 3432. Which part of the quadriceps lies deepest, directly upon the front and lateral surfaces of the femur? The answer is the vastus intermedius. It is hidden by the rectus femoris above it and by the other two vastus muscles beside it. Its fibers end in the deep surface of the quadriceps tendon.

Question 3433. A constructed illustration: the tendon below the kneecap is tapped and the knee jerks. Which muscle contracts, and which nerve carries that reflex? The answer is the quadriceps femoris and the femoral nerve. The response is lost when the third and fourth lumbar segments of the spinal cord or the nerve itself are damaged.

Question 3434. The quadriceps tendon attaches to which structures: the base of the patella and then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament, the head of the fibula, the pes anserinus, or the medial malleolus? The answer is the base of the patella and then the tibial tuberosity. The patella is a sesamoid bone that lies within the tendon.

Question 3435. True or false: the patella is a sesamoid bone that develops inside the tendon of the quadriceps femoris. The answer is true. It lies in front of the knee joint and increases the leverage of the quadriceps. Its posterior surface carries the thickest layer of articular cartilage in the body.

Question 3436. Which small muscle lies deep in the lower part of the front of the thigh, arising from the front of the femur below the vastus intermedius and ending in the synovial membrane of the knee joint? The answer is the articularis genus. It pulls the synovial membrane upward during extension so that the membrane is not trapped in the joint.

Question 3437. A described radiograph of the knee seen from the side shows a small sesamoid bone in front of the joint, with a band above it and another band below it. Which structures are shown? The answer is the patella, the quadriceps tendon above it and the patellar ligament below it. The shadow of the femur lies behind the bone.

Question 3438. Which part of the quadriceps is most often strained in a sprinting injury, because it acts at both the hip and the knee: the rectus femoris, the vastus lateralis, the vastus medialis, or the vastus intermedius? The answer is the rectus femoris. Working across two joints makes it act over a longer range than the vastus muscles. The injury usually occurs at the musculotendinous junction.

Question 3439. The femoral artery passes down the front of the thigh toward the opening in the adductor magnus. Which part of the quadriceps lies immediately behind it in the lower part of its course? The answer is the vastus medialis. The artery rests upon that muscle within the adductor canal, whose roof is a strong membrane blending with the muscle.

Question 3440. Name the four parts of the quadriceps femoris spoken as a list. The answer is the rectus femoris, the vastus lateralis, the vastus medialis and the vastus intermedius. The first of them crosses the hip joint, and the other three arise from the femur itself. All four straighten the knee.

Question 3441. The patellar ligament runs from the lower point of the patella to which structure: the tibial tuberosity, the head of the fibula, the adductor tubercle, or the medial malleolus? The answer is the tibial tuberosity. It is the continuation of the quadriceps tendon after that tendon has passed over the patella. The medial and lateral patellar retinacula pass down beside it.

Question 3442. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto a flexed knee, and afterward the knee cannot be straightened actively while a gap can be felt above the patella. Which structure is torn? The answer is the quadriceps tendon. The patella is pulled downward by the intact patellar ligament, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3443. Which part of the quadriceps arises from the intertrochanteric line and the medial lip of the linea aspera and sends an expansion to the medial side of the knee? The answer is the vastus medialis. Its lowest fibers run almost horizontally and are thought to resist lateral displacement of the patella. That expansion forms the medial patellar retinaculum.

Question 3444. Which statement about the medial and lateral patellar retinacula is correct: they are expansions of the vastus medialis and the vastus lateralis, they are parts of the joint capsule alone, they are formed by the sartorius and the iliotibial tract, or they are ligaments running from the patella to the femur? The answer is that they are expansions of the vastus medialis and the vastus lateralis.

Question 3445. A described transverse section of the lower thigh shows the femur surrounded by muscle on three sides, with one thin sheet lying directly upon the bone and two larger masses beside it. Which parts of the quadriceps are shown? The answer is the vastus intermedius upon the bone, with the vastus lateralis and the vastus medialis beside it.

Question 3446. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the rectus femoris with the anterior inferior iliac spine, the vastus lateralis with the ischial tuberosity, the vastus medialis with the greater trochanter, or the vastus intermedius with the ischial spine? The answer is the rectus femoris with the anterior inferior iliac spine. The vastus lateralis and the vastus medialis arise from the back of the femur instead.

Question 3447. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the knee a person cannot actively straighten the knee, yet the hip can still be flexed. Which structure is most likely torn: the patellar ligament, the fibular collateral ligament, the iliotibial tract, or the medial meniscus? The answer is the patellar ligament, because the rectus femoris remains attached above and can still flex the hip.

Question 3448. A constructed illustration: an active adolescent reports pain and a bony swelling at the tibial tuberosity that worsens with sport and eases with rest. Which structure is involved, and why is that age group affected? The answer is the tibial tuberosity at the insertion of the patellar ligament, where the growing apophysis is pulled upon. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 3449. A described dissection separates the quadriceps tendon into layers above the patella. A superficial band comes from a muscle that crosses the hip, and a deep sheet comes from a muscle lying on the femur. Which two parts of the quadriceps are shown? The answer is the rectus femoris and the vastus intermedius.

Question 3450. Which of these muscles does not belong to the quadriceps femoris: the rectus femoris, the vastus medialis, the sartorius, or the vastus intermedius? The answer is the sartorius. It is the longest muscle of the body, runs from the hip bone to the medial side of the tibia, and is supplied by the femoral nerve as well.

Question 3451. Which compartment of the leg lies in front of the interosseous membrane and holds the muscles that lift the foot? The answer is the anterior compartment. Its muscles dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes, and all of them are supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

Question 3452. Which nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg: the tibial nerve, the deep fibular nerve, the superficial fibular nerve, or the sural nerve? The answer is the deep fibular nerve. It reaches the compartment beside the anterior tibial artery after winding around the neck of the fibula.

Question 3453. Which muscle lies immediately lateral to the anterior border of the tibia and is the strongest dorsiflexor of the ankle? The answer is the tibialis anterior. It arises from the upper lateral surface of the tibia and inserts on the medial cuneiform bone and the base of the first metatarsal. It also inverts the foot.

Question 3454. Which of these muscles lies in the lateral compartment of the leg: the fibularis longus, the tibialis posterior, the flexor digitorum longus, or the extensor hallucis longus? The answer is the fibularis longus, together with the fibularis brevis. Both evert the foot and both are supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

Question 3455. In the lower part of the front of the leg, which structures lie between the tibialis anterior and the extensor hallucis longus? The answer is the anterior tibial artery and the deep fibular nerve. The vessels and the nerve run down that interval and cross the front of the ankle beneath the extensor retinaculum.

Question 3456. A described dissection of the calf shows a large muscle with two heads, a broad flat muscle deep to it, and a small muscle with a slender tendon between the two heads. Which three muscles are shown? The answer is the gastrocnemius, the soleus and the plantaris. All three of them are supplied by the tibial nerve.

Question 3457. Which muscle of the calf arises from the upper part of the fibula and from the soleal line of the tibia and does not cross the knee joint? The answer is the soleus. It lies deep to the gastrocnemius and joins it in the calcaneal tendon. Its many short fibers give it great power in standing.

Question 3458. A constructed illustration: after a long march a person has a tight and painful front of the leg, pain when the toes are passively curled, and numbness in the web space between the first two toes. Which compartment and which nerve are involved? The answer is the anterior compartment and the deep fibular nerve that supplies it.

Question 3459. Which structure passes forward through the interosseous membrane from the posterior compartment of the leg into the anterior compartment: the anterior tibial artery, the posterior tibial artery, the fibular artery, or the small saphenous vein? The answer is the anterior tibial artery. It passes through the upper part of the membrane and then descends upon it. The deep fibular nerve joins it lower down in the leg.

Question 3460. True or false: the calcaneal tendon is the common tendon of the gastrocnemius and the soleus. The answer is true. The two muscles are often called the triceps surae, and the plantaris tendon joins them on the medial side. The tendon inserts on the middle of the back of the calcaneus.

Question 3461. Which muscle forms the chief bulk of the calf and arises by two heads from the lower end of the femur? The answer is the gastrocnemius. It crosses the knee joint as well as the ankle, so it also helps to flex the knee. The small saphenous vein ascends between its two heads.

Question 3462. A described dissection behind the medial malleolus shows four tendons and a nerve passing into the sole. Which tendon lies closest to the bone? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior. Behind it in order lie the flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery, the tibial nerve and the flexor hallucis longus.

Question 3463. Which muscle of the deep posterior compartment is the chief invertor of the foot and inserts on the tuberosity of the navicular bone: the tibialis posterior, the flexor hallucis longus, the popliteus, or the flexor digitorum longus? The answer is the tibialis posterior. It arises from the back of the tibia, from the fibula and from the interosseous membrane. Its tendon also sends slips to the cuneiform bones and several metatarsals.

Question 3464. Which structure lies immediately behind the posterior tibial artery as both pass behind the medial malleolus? The answer is the tibial nerve. The order from the medial side is the tibialis posterior, the flexor digitorum longus, the artery, the nerve and the flexor hallucis longus. All of them pass beneath the flexor retinaculum.

Question 3465. Which muscle of the leg arises from the posterior surface of the fibula and the interosseous membrane and inserts on the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe? The answer is the flexor hallucis longus. Its tendon grooves the back of the talus and passes below the sustentaculum tali. It is a powerful flexor of the great toe.

Question 3466. Which statement about the nerves of the popliteal fossa is correct: the common fibular nerve lies medial to the tibial nerve, the tibial nerve supplies the short head of the biceps femoris, the common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, or the popliteal artery lies superficial to the tibial nerve? The answer is that the common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula.

Question 3467. A constructed illustration: a blow lands on the lateral side of the knee and the head of the fibula, and afterward the foot cannot be lifted and the toes drag on the ground. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the common fibular nerve, which winds around the fibular neck at that point. The illustration describes a pattern of injury, not a real patient.

Question 3468. A described dissection of the calf shows a muscle lying deep to the gastrocnemius whose fibers run downward and backward into a broad aponeurosis that joins the calcaneal tendon. Which muscle is described? The answer is the soleus. It arises from the soleal line of the tibia and from the upper part of the fibula.

Question 3469. Which movement of the foot is lost when the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg are paralyzed: eversion, inversion, dorsiflexion, or plantarflexion? The answer is eversion. The fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis turn the sole outward and are supplied by the superficial fibular nerve. The tibialis anterior and the tibialis posterior are the chief invertors of the foot.

Question 3470. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the tibialis anterior with the deep fibular nerve, the fibularis longus with the tibial nerve, the gastrocnemius with the superficial fibular nerve, or the tibialis posterior with the deep fibular nerve? The answer is the tibialis anterior with the deep fibular nerve. The other three muscles are supplied by the tibial nerve or the superficial fibular nerve.

Question 3471. What is the name of the strong fibrous band that runs down the back of the leg and attaches to the heel? The answer is the calcaneal tendon, also called the Achilles tendon. It is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. The gastrocnemius, the soleus and the plantaris all contribute to it.

Question 3472. Which statement about the deep fibular nerve is correct: it passes deep to the extensor retinaculum and ends in the web space between the first two toes, it supplies the skin of the lateral side of the foot, it passes behind the lateral malleolus, or it gives off the sural nerve? The answer is that it passes deep to the retinaculum to the first web space.

Question 3473. Which vessel runs down the back of the leg between the two heads of the gastrocnemius, accompanied by the sural nerve, and ends in the popliteal vein? The answer is the small saphenous vein. It begins behind the lateral malleolus and ascends in the subcutaneous tissue. The sural nerve lies beside it and supplies the skin of the lateral border of the foot.

Question 3474. A described dissection shows the popliteal artery dividing at the lower border of the popliteus, with one branch passing forward through the interosseous membrane and the other continuing down the back of the leg. Which two vessels are shown? The answer is the anterior tibial artery and the posterior tibial artery.

Question 3475. Which of these muscles inserts on the calcaneus by the calcaneal tendon: the tibialis anterior, the gastrocnemius, the tibialis posterior, or the fibularis longus? The answer is the gastrocnemius. It acts with the soleus to plantarflex the ankle. The tibialis posterior inserts on the navicular bone and the fibularis longus on the base of the first metatarsal.

Question 3476. A constructed illustration: a laceration behind the knee leaves a person unable to stand on tiptoe and without feeling over the sole, while the foot can still be lifted. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the tibial nerve. The ability to lift the foot remains because the anterior compartment is supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

Question 3477. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the flexor hallucis longus with the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe, the flexor digitorum longus with the calcaneus, the tibialis posterior with the head of the fibula, or the popliteus with the tibial tuberosity? The answer is the flexor hallucis longus with the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe.

Question 3478. True or false: the plantaris has a small fleshy belly and a long slender tendon that inserts on the calcaneus, and it is absent in some people. The answer is true. The muscle is a feeble flexor of the knee and a weak plantarflexor, and its absence causes no loss of function. Its slender tendon is sometimes used by surgeons as a graft.

Question 3479. Which muscle of the body has the longest tendon in proportion to its belly: the plantaris, the gastrocnemius, the tibialis posterior, or the flexor hallucis longus? The answer is the plantaris. Its small belly lies above the lateral head of the gastrocnemius, and its slender tendon runs down between the two heads to the calcaneus. It is supplied by the tibial nerve.

Question 3480. A described specimen of the front of the ankle shows a muscle whose tendon crosses the joint to reach the medial border of the foot. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the tibialis anterior. Its tendon is the most medial of the tendons on the front of the ankle, and it inserts on the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal.

Question 3481. Which statement about the deep fascia of the leg is correct: it forms septa that attach to the fibula and divide the leg into compartments, it covers only the back of the leg, it is continuous with the plantar aponeurosis alone, or it does not exist in the leg? The answer is that it forms septa attached to the fibula.

Question 3482. A transverse section of the leg at mid calf shows three compartments grouped around the fibula. Which compartment lies in front of the interosseous membrane, which lies on the outer side of the fibula, and which lies behind it? The answer is the anterior compartment in front, the lateral compartment on the outer side, and the posterior compartment behind.

Question 3483. What is the name of the thick fibrous band that stretches from the calcaneus to the bases of the toes and forms the tough sole of the foot? The answer is the plantar aponeurosis. It protects the vessels, the nerves and the muscles beneath it and helps to maintain the arches of the foot.

Question 3484. Which muscle of the first layer of the sole runs from the calcaneus to the medial side of the great toe: the abductor hallucis, the quadratus plantae, the adductor hallucis, or the flexor digiti minimi brevis? The answer is the abductor hallucis. It is supplied by the medial plantar nerve, a branch of the tibial nerve.

Question 3485. Which nerve enters the sole between the abductor hallucis and the flexor digitorum brevis and supplies the muscles of the medial side? The answer is the medial plantar nerve. It is a branch of the tibial nerve and also supplies the skin of the medial three and a half toes.

Question 3486. Which muscle of the sole lies in the second layer, arises by two heads from the calcaneus, and inserts into the tendon of the flexor digitorum longus, correcting its oblique pull: the quadratus plantae, the flexor digitorum brevis, the abductor hallucis, or the adductor hallucis? The answer is the quadratus plantae. It is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve and helps the long flexor to straighten its line of pull.

Question 3487. A described dissection of the sole shows the tendon of a long flexor dividing into four parts, and four small muscles arising from those tendons and passing to the extensor expansions of the toes. Which muscles are described? The answer is the lumbricals. The first is supplied by the medial plantar nerve and the other three by the lateral plantar nerve.

Question 3488. Which structures lie immediately deep to the plantar aponeurosis in the sole of the foot? The answer is the muscles of the first layer: the abductor hallucis, the flexor digitorum brevis and the abductor digiti minimi. The medial and lateral plantar nerves and vessels lie between the first layer and the second.

Question 3489. A constructed illustration: a person has pain under the heel that is worst on the first steps of the morning, with tenderness at the medial tubercle of the calcaneus. Which structure is involved? The answer is the plantar aponeurosis at its attachment. The condition is an overuse traction injury, and its management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 3490. Which statement about the interossei of the foot is correct: the dorsal interossei abduct the toes and the plantar interossei adduct them, both groups abduct the toes, both groups adduct the toes, or the dorsal group flexes the toes? The answer is that the dorsal interossei abduct and the plantar interossei adduct. Both groups are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.

Question 3491. Which muscle of the sole flexes the great toe and has two heads, with a sesamoid bone in each of its tendons? The answer is the flexor hallucis brevis. It lies in the third layer and is supplied by the medial plantar nerve. The sesamoid bones lie beneath the head of the first metatarsal bone.

Question 3492. Which statement about the nerve supply of the lumbrical muscles is correct: all four are supplied by the medial plantar nerve, all four are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve, the first is supplied by the medial plantar nerve and the remaining three by the lateral plantar nerve, or all four are supplied by the deep fibular nerve? The answer is that the first lumbrical is supplied by the medial plantar nerve.

Question 3493. A described specimen of the sole shows a swollen thickening of an interdigital nerve between the heads of the third and fourth metatarsals. Which structure is described? The answer is an enlargement of a plantar digital nerve, a common cause of pain in the forefoot. The specimen is described as an illustration of the normal course of the nerve.

Question 3494. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the abductor hallucis with the medial plantar nerve, the abductor digiti minimi with the medial plantar nerve, the first lumbrical with the lateral plantar nerve, or the dorsal interossei with the medial plantar nerve? The answer is the abductor hallucis with the medial plantar nerve. The others are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.

Question 3495. In which layer of the sole do the tendons of the fibularis longus and the tibialis posterior lie: the first, the second, the third, or the fourth? The answer is the fourth layer, the deepest one, which rests against the metatarsals and the interosseous muscles. The fibularis longus tendon crosses the sole to the first metatarsal.

Question 3496. Name two muscles of the sole that are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve, spoken as a list. The answer is the abductor digiti minimi and the quadratus plantae, and the interossei and the lateral three lumbricals may also be named. The medial plantar nerve supplies the muscles of the medial side instead.

Question 3497. Which tendon crosses the sole from the lateral side to insert on the base of the first metatarsal bone and the medial cuneiform, lying in the deepest layer of the sole? The answer is the tendon of the fibularis longus. It also helps to support the transverse arch of the foot, and its muscle lies in the lateral compartment of the leg.

Question 3498. True or false: the tendons of the flexor digitorum longus pass through openings in the tendons of the flexor digitorum brevis. The answer is true. The brevis tendon is split into two slips that let the long tendon pass through and then reunite behind it. The long tendon continues to the base of the distal phalanx.

Question 3499. In the sole the muscles are arranged in four layers. Which layer lies immediately deep to the plantar aponeurosis, and which lies against the metatarsal bones and the long tendons? The answer is the first layer in the first case and the fourth layer in the second, with the nerves and vessels running between the first and second layers.

Question 3500. Which small muscle lies on the dorsum of the foot, arises from the upper surface of the calcaneus, and divides into four tendons that join the long extensor tendons? The answer is the extensor digitorum brevis. It also has a part that goes to the great toe. It is supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

To summarize, the hamstrings are the biceps femoris, the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, they arise from the ischial tuberosity, they extend the hip and flex the knee, and all of them except the short head of the biceps femoris are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The quadriceps femoris is the rectus femoris with the three vastus muscles, it is supplied by the femoral nerve, it extends the knee, and the rectus femoris alone crosses the hip and also flexes it. The leg is divided by fascia and septa into an anterior compartment supplied by the deep fibular nerve, a lateral compartment supplied by the superficial fibular nerve, and a posterior compartment supplied by the tibial nerve, with the gastrocnemius and the soleus forming the calf and joining in the calcaneal tendon. The sole of the foot holds four layers of muscle, the first three supplied mainly by the medial and lateral plantar nerves, and the fourth layer carrying the interossei together with the tendons of the fibularis longus and the tibialis posterior. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 36 — Heart Anatomy

This chapter examines the heart itself: its four chambers, the valves that keep blood moving one way through them, the septa that divide it, and the great vessels that enter and leave its base. It holds one hundred questions, and every question is followed at once by its answer and by the reason that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. The same three-part shape is used throughout, and the reasons name the relations that make the answer true. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3501. Which chamber of the heart receives blood from the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava? The answer is the right atrium. Both of those large veins open into its smooth posterior wall, and the coronary sinus opens into it as well. From there the blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

Question 3502. Which chamber forms the right border of the heart as it is seen on a chest radiograph: the right ventricle, the right atrium, the left atrium, or the left ventricle? The answer is the right atrium. It lies at the right edge of the cardiac shadow, with the superior vena cava above it and the inferior vena cava below.

Question 3503. A described chest radiograph shows a rounded bulge along the upper right border of the cardiac shadow, where a vertical vein joins from above. Which chamber lies at that point? The answer is the right atrium. Its upper part receives the superior vena cava there, and that junction is what produces the slight bulge at the border.

Question 3504. Which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall? The answer is the left ventricle. It pumps blood into the aorta against the resistance of the whole body, so its wall is about three times as thick as that of the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs, where resistance is far lower.

Question 3505. Which chamber of the heart lies immediately in front of the esophagus and the descending thoracic aorta: the right atrium, the right ventricle, the left atrium, or the left ventricle? The answer is the left atrium. It forms most of the posterior surface of the heart, which is why an enlarged left atrium can press on the esophagus.

Question 3506. Which of these features belongs to the ventricles rather than the atria: pectinate muscles, a crista terminalis, trabeculae carneae, or a fossa ovalis? The answer is trabeculae carneae. These are the irregular muscular ridges of the ventricular wall. Pectinate muscles and the crista terminalis belong to the right atrium, and the fossa ovalis lies in the interatrial septum.

Question 3507. What is the name of the small ear-shaped pouch that projects from the upper part of each atrium and increases its capacity? The answer is the auricle. It is a thin-walled appendage with a narrow cavity. The auricle of the left atrium is a common place for a clot to form when the atrium does not empty properly.

Question 3508. A constructed illustration: a person with a long-standing irregular atrial rhythm is found to have a clot inside a small muscular pouch of the left atrium. Which part of the heart is described? The answer is the left auricle. Its narrow cavity and ridged wall allow blood to stagnate there when the atrium stops emptying in an orderly way.

Question 3509. True or false: the wall of the right ventricle is thicker than the wall of the left ventricle. The answer is false. The left ventricle has the thicker wall because it drives blood around the entire body. The right ventricle has a thinner wall because the lungs offer much less resistance to the flow of blood through them.

Question 3510. A muscular band crosses the cavity of the right ventricle from the interventricular septum to the anterior papillary muscle. Which structure is described: the moderator band, a chorda tendinea, the crista supraventricularis, or a pectinate muscle? The answer is the moderator band. It carries part of the right branch of the conducting system across the cavity so that both sides contract together.

Question 3511. A described transverse section through the heart shows one chamber with a nearly circular cavity and a thick muscular wall, and another chamber whose crescent-shaped cavity wraps around its front. Which chambers are shown? The answer is the left ventricle and the right ventricle. In this section the left ventricle is round and the right ventricle is a crescent against it.

Question 3512. Into which chamber of the heart does the coronary sinus empty? The answer is the right atrium. The coronary sinus is the main vein of the heart's own muscle, and it opens into the right atrium just above the opening of the inferior vena cava. A small fold of tissue guards its opening.

Question 3513. Which chamber of the heart lies most posteriorly, so that its enlargement is felt mainly from behind: the right ventricle, the right atrium, the left ventricle, or the left atrium? The answer is the left atrium. It forms most of the base of the heart and lies against the esophagus and the vertebral column.

Question 3514. Name the two chambers that receive blood and the two that pump it out, spoken as a list. The answer is the right atrium and the left atrium for the receiving chambers, and the right ventricle and the left ventricle for the pumping chambers. The atria are thin-walled and the ventricles thick-walled, which is what their names imply.

Question 3515. Which structure runs down the inner wall of the right atrium from the opening of the superior vena cava to the opening of the inferior vena cava? The answer is the crista terminalis. It is a vertical muscular ridge that separates the smooth posterior part of the atrium from the muscular part in front of it.

Question 3516. What name is given to the parallel muscular ridges that cover the inner surface of the right auricle? The answer is the pectinate muscles. They resemble the teeth of a comb, which is where the name comes from. Their arrangement lets the thin wall of the auricle contract without folding on itself.

Question 3517. A section of the heart is cut in a plane that runs across the body at right angles to its long axis, passing through the openings of the two atrioventricular valves. Which chambers does that section show? The answer is parts of all four chambers. The plane crosses the junction between the atria above and the ventricles below.

Question 3518. A constructed illustration: a penetrating wound enters the chest just to the left of the sternum at the level of the fifth rib and bleeds into the pericardial sac. Which chamber lies closest to that point? The answer is the right ventricle. It forms most of the anterior surface of the heart, directly behind the sternum.

Question 3519. Which chamber of the heart lies most anteriorly, immediately behind the sternum: the left atrium, the left ventricle, the right atrium, or the right ventricle? The answer is the right ventricle. It forms most of the front of the heart, while the right atrium forms the right border and the left ventricle forms the left border and the apex.

Question 3520. A described transverse section of the chest shows the heart with one thin-walled chamber lying immediately behind the sternum, a second chamber to its right, and a third with a much thicker wall behind and to the left. Which chamber is the thin-walled one in front? The answer is the right ventricle.

Question 3521. Which chamber of the heart lies directly behind the body of the sternum and the costal cartilages of the third, fourth and fifth ribs? The answer is the right ventricle. Most of the anterior surface of the heart belongs to it, with the right atrium at the right edge. A wound in this region reaches the right ventricle first.

Question 3522. Which part of the right ventricle is smooth-walled and leads upward to the pulmonary valve: the trabecular part, the conus arteriosus, the sinus of the venae cavae, or the auricle? The answer is the conus arteriosus, also called the infundibulum. It is the outflow tract, and its smooth wall contrasts with the ridged cavity below it.

Question 3523. What is the ordinary thickness of the muscular wall of the right ventricle in an adult heart? The answer is about 3 to 5 millimeters. The wall of the left ventricle in the same heart measures about 8 to 12 millimeters. That difference reflects the much lower resistance of the circulation through the lungs.

Question 3524. A constructed illustration: blood collects rapidly in the pericardial sac after a chest injury, and the thin-walled chambers cannot fill. Which chamber is compressed first, because it has the lowest internal pressure: the left ventricle, the right atrium, the left atrium, or the aortic root? The answer is the right atrium.

Question 3525. In which intercostal space, in the midclavicular line, is the apex beat of the heart normally felt: the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, or the second? The answer is the fifth intercostal space. The apex of the heart is formed by the left ventricle and lies at that point in most adults. It may be displaced in disease.

Question 3526. True or false: the apex of the heart is formed by the left ventricle. The answer is true. The apex is the pointed lower end of the heart, directed downward, forward and to the left. The right ventricle approaches it but does not form it.

Question 3527. What is the name of the small fold that guards the opening of the inferior vena cava into the right atrium? The answer is the valve of the inferior vena cava. It is a remnant of a larger fetal fold that once directed blood toward the interatrial opening. In the adult it is small and often has holes in it.

Question 3528. Which statement about the capacity of the four chambers is correct: the right ventricle holds much more than the left, the two ventricles hold about the same volume, the atria together hold more than the ventricles, or the left atrium is the largest chamber? The answer is that the two ventricles hold about the same volume as each other.

Question 3529. Which structure lies immediately behind the left atrium, separated from it by the pericardium alone, and what follows when the atrium enlarges? The answer is the esophagus. An enlarged left atrium can press on it and cause difficulty in swallowing. The same chamber also lies in front of the descending thoracic aorta and the vertebral column.

Question 3530. A described cross section of the heart shows a crescent-shaped chamber wrapped around a circular one, with a thick muscular septum between them and a valve leaflet hanging into the crescent. Which two chambers are shown? The answer is the right ventricle and the left ventricle. The crescent is the right ventricle, applied to the front of the round left ventricle.

Question 3531. Which valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle? The answer is the tricuspid valve. It has three cusps, named anterior, posterior and septal. The septal cusp lies against the interventricular septum, and the other two are attached to the wall of the ventricle.

Question 3532. Which valve of the heart has only two cusps: the tricuspid, the pulmonary, the mitral, or the aortic? The answer is the mitral valve. It lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle and is therefore also called the bicuspid valve. Its two cusps are named anterior and posterior.

Question 3533. A described radiograph of an older heart shows a dense curved line in the region of the left atrioventricular opening. Which valve has become calcified there? The answer is the mitral valve. Calcium in its ring shows as a curved density projecting to the left of the spine. The tricuspid valve would lie nearer the midline.

Question 3534. At which point on the chest wall is the sound of the mitral valve best heard? The answer is at the apex, in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. The valve itself lies behind the sternum, but its sound is carried to the apex by the direction of the jet of blood. Each valve is heard where its jet points.

Question 3535. Which structures keep the atrioventricular valves from being pushed back into the atria during contraction of the ventricles: the semilunar cusps, the papillary muscles with their chordae tendineae, the fibrous trigones, or the crista supraventricularis? The answer is the papillary muscles with their chordae tendineae.

Question 3536. Which valve lies between the left ventricle and the aorta? The answer is the aortic valve. It has three semilunar cusps, and two of them are named for the coronary arteries that arise from the sinuses behind them. Its cusps meet in the middle of the opening when the ventricle relaxes.

Question 3537. A constructed illustration: a person who becomes dizzy during heavy exertion is found to have a thickened, narrowed valve at the outlet of the left ventricle. Which valve is affected? The answer is the aortic valve. The left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to force blood through the narrow opening, and the supply to the brain suffers.

Question 3538. True or false: the pulmonary valve has three semilunar cusps and no chordae tendineae. The answer is true. The pulmonary valve and the aortic valve both have three cusps and no papillary muscles. The tricuspid and mitral valves have cusps that are held by chordae tendineae.

Question 3539. Which cusps of the aortic valve are named for the coronary arteries that arise behind them: the right and left cusps, the anterior and posterior cusps, the septal and mural cusps, or the superior and inferior cusps? The answer is the right and left cusps. The third cusp is the posterior one, and no coronary artery arises behind it.

Question 3540. Which pair belongs together: the mitral valve with the apex in the fifth intercostal space, the aortic valve with the apex, the pulmonary valve with the lower left sternal edge, or the tricuspid valve with the second right intercostal space? The answer is the mitral valve with the apex. The aortic valve is heard at the second right space.

Question 3541. What name is given to the two valves that guard the outflow tracts of the ventricles? The answer is the semilunar valves. The pulmonary valve guards the outflow of the right ventricle and the aortic valve guards that of the left ventricle. Their cusps are shaped like half moons, which is the source of the name.

Question 3542. A described dissection shows a dense plate of fibrous tissue at the base of the heart, with the four valves anchored to it and an insulating plane running through it. What is that structure? The answer is the fibrous skeleton of the heart. It also separates the muscle of the atria from the muscle of the ventricles.

Question 3543. Of the four valves of the heart, which one lies most anteriorly, closest to the chest wall? The answer is the pulmonary valve. It lies at the upper left of the heart and is the most superficial of the four. The aortic valve lies behind it and a little to the right.

Question 3544. A described preparation shows the anterior cusp of the mitral valve hanging directly below the opening of the aorta. What does that continuity mean for the surgeon who must work there: the two rings are separate, the aortic and mitral valves share a fibrous curtain, the tricuspid valve lies between them, or the septum divides them? The answer is that the two share a curtain.

Question 3545. A constructed illustration: a heart examined after a long illness shows the mitral opening narrowed by thick, fused cusps, with shortened chordae. Which valve is described, and which chamber behind it becomes enlarged? The answer is the mitral valve, with enlargement of the left atrium behind it, because that chamber must work harder to fill the ventricle.

Question 3546. How many cusps does the tricuspid valve have? The answer is three. They are named anterior, posterior and septal. Each cusp is tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles in the right ventricle, and the septal cusp lies against the interventricular septum.

Question 3547. Which valve guards the outflow tract of the right ventricle: the aortic valve, the mitral valve, the pulmonary valve, or the tricuspid valve? The answer is the pulmonary valve. It sits at the top of the conus arteriosus and opens into the pulmonary trunk. The aortic valve guards the outflow of the left ventricle.

Question 3548. A described specimen shows a valve with two cusps, each tethered by chordae to two papillary muscles, one in front and one behind. Which valve is it? The answer is the mitral valve. Its two papillary muscles are named anterior and posterior, and they lie in the left ventricle below the two cusps.

Question 3549. A described dissection follows the blood from the right atrium into the lungs. Which two valves does the blood cross on that path, and in which order? The answer is the tricuspid valve first and the pulmonary valve second. The same route is followed by anything that enters the right side of the heart and travels with the stream.

Question 3550. Which pair belongs together: the anterior cusp of the mitral valve with the aortic opening above it, the septal cusp of the tricuspid with the pulmonary opening, the posterior cusp of the aortic valve with the pulmonary trunk, or the anterior cusp of the tricuspid with the aortic opening? The answer is the anterior cusp of the mitral valve with the aortic opening above it.

Question 3551. Name the three structures that keep an atrioventricular valve closed during the contraction of a ventricle, spoken as a list. The answer is the cusps, the chordae tendineae and the papillary muscles. If any one of the three fails, the valve leaks, because the cusps can no longer meet squarely in the middle of the opening.

Question 3552. In an adult heart, roughly what is the diameter of the normal mitral opening when it is fully open: 1 to 2 centimeters, 3 to 4 centimeters, 6 to 7 centimeters, or 8 to 9 centimeters? The answer is 3 to 4 centimeters. The tricuspid opening is a little larger, and the two semilunar openings are smaller than either.

Question 3553. A constructed illustration: a person with a widened aortic root is found to have a valve whose cusps no longer meet in the middle, so blood leaks back into the left ventricle as it relaxes. Which valve is involved, and what is the result? The answer is the aortic valve, and the leak makes the left ventricle enlarge.

Question 3554. True or false: the mitral valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The answer is true. It is also called the bicuspid valve, because it has two cusps where the valve on the right side has three. The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle is the tricuspid valve.

Question 3555. What is the name of the fold that guards the opening of the coronary sinus into the right atrium? The answer is the valve of the coronary sinus. It is a thin crescent at the lower end of the opening, close to the opening of the inferior vena cava. It is a normal feature and varies greatly in size.

Question 3556. A described section through the base of the heart shows three pouch-like cusps above a fibrous ring, with a small opening behind one of them. Which valve is shown, and what is the small opening? The answer is the aortic valve, and the opening is the origin of a coronary artery.

Question 3557. Which structure separates the left ventricle from the right ventricle? The answer is the interventricular septum. Its greater part is thick muscle that bulges into the cavity of the right ventricle. Its upper part is a thin membrane, and the two parts meet along a curved line.

Question 3558. Which part of the interventricular septum is thin, lies just below the aortic valve, and is the usual site of a hole between the ventricles: the muscular part, the membranous part, the atrioventricular part, or the infundibular part? The answer is the membranous part. It is a small oval area, and a hole there is the commonest defect of the septum.

Question 3559. A described section through the heart shows a small defect in the upper part of the septum between the ventricles, immediately below the aortic valve and in front of the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve. Which part of the septum is defective? The answer is the membranous part of the interventricular septum.

Question 3560. Which chamber lies immediately to the right of the interatrial septum, and which lies to its left? The answer is the right atrium on the right and the left atrium on the left. The thin upper part of the septum carries the fossa ovalis, which is the remnant of the opening that joined the two atria before birth.

Question 3561. A constructed illustration: a newborn has a small hole in the membranous part of the interventricular septum and a loud murmur, but the skin is not blue. Why is the blood not blue? The answer is that the pressures on the two sides keep the shunt moving from the left ventricle into the right.

Question 3562. True or false: the fossa ovalis lies in the interventricular septum. The answer is false. It lies in the interatrial septum as the remnant of the foramen ovale, and it is seen from the right atrium. The interventricular septum carries no such depression.

Question 3563. What is the name of the muscular ridge that forms the upper border of the fossa ovalis: the crista terminalis, the limbus of the fossa ovalis, the moderator band, or the sinus of the venae cavae? The answer is the limbus of the fossa ovalis. It is the raised rim of the fetal opening, and the floor below it is thin.

Question 3564. What is the name of the oval depression on the right side of the interatrial septum? The answer is the fossa ovalis. It marks the site of the foramen ovale, through which blood passed from the right atrium to the left before birth. Its floor is thin and can be probed from the left side.

Question 3565. A section of the heart is cut in a plane that divides it into an anterior part and a posterior part, passing through the right atrium and the right ventricle. Which plane is it, and would it open the left ventricle as well? The answer is a coronal plane, and it would not open the left ventricle, which lies behind and to the left.

Question 3566. Which structure lies between the right atrium and the left ventricle, so that a hole there lets blood pass from the left ventricle into the right atrium: the membranous interventricular septum, the atrioventricular part of the septum, the muscular septum, or the fossa ovalis? The answer is the atrioventricular part of the septum.

Question 3567. A described four-chamber section shows two thin-walled chambers above and two thick-walled chambers below, divided by a septum that is complete except for a thin membrane near its middle. Which septum holds that thin membrane? The answer is the interventricular septum, whose membranous part lies at that point.

Question 3568. Which structure lies immediately behind the membranous part of the interventricular septum, so that a defect there may involve it: the tricuspid valve, the aortic valve, the mitral valve, or the pulmonary valve? The answer is the aortic valve. The membranous septum lies just below the aortic root, and the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve is close beside it.

Question 3569. Which pair belongs together: the foramen ovale with the fossa ovalis, the ductus arteriosus with the ligamentum teres, the ductus venosus with the ligamentum arteriosum, or the umbilical vein with the fossa ovalis? The answer is the foramen ovale with the fossa ovalis. The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, and the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver.

Question 3570. Which artery supplies the greater part of the interventricular septum? The answer is the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery. It runs down the front of the septum toward the apex. The posterior interventricular branch supplies the back of the septum, and the two branches meet near the apex.

Question 3571. A constructed illustration: a person has a hole in the muscular part of the interventricular septum, and the murmur is loud but the heart is not enlarged. Which part of the septum is affected? The answer is the muscular part. A hole surrounded by muscle is often small and tends to narrow as the muscle contracts.

Question 3572. The moderator band stretches from the interventricular septum to which structure: the anterior papillary muscle, the posterior papillary muscle, the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve, or the aortic valve? The answer is the anterior papillary muscle. The band therefore crosses the cavity of the right ventricle near its apex.

Question 3573. Name the two parts of the interventricular septum. The answer is the muscular part and the membranous part. The muscular part forms the greater part of the septum and is thick. The membranous part is a small thin area at the top, lying just below the aortic valve.

Question 3574. A described cross section of the heart shows the interventricular septum thick below and thin above, with muscle on both sides of the thick part and fibrous tissue around the thin part. Which part is which? The answer is that the thick lower part is muscular and the thin upper part is membranous.

Question 3575. Which is the largest artery in the body? The answer is the aorta. It begins at the aortic valve and ends by dividing into the two common iliac arteries in the abdomen. Its wall is thick and elastic, which lets it absorb the surge of each heartbeat and smooth the flow onward.

Question 3576. Which vessels arise from the aorta immediately above the aortic valve: the coronary arteries, the brachiocephalic trunk, the common carotid arteries, or the intercostal arteries? The answer is the coronary arteries. The right and left coronary arteries arise from the right and left aortic sinuses and supply the muscle of the heart itself.

Question 3577. A described chest radiograph shows a rounded bulge at the upper left border of the mediastinum, just below the point where the trachea divides. Which part of the aorta forms it? The answer is the aortic arch, and more exactly its knuckle. It lies to the left of the trachea and above the left pulmonary artery.

Question 3578. Which great vessel lies immediately in front of the aorta as the two leave the heart, and which lies behind? The answer is that the pulmonary trunk lies in front and to the left, while the aorta begins behind and to the right of it. The two vessels then spiral around one another as they rise.

Question 3579. A constructed illustration: a young person has a narrowed segment of the aorta just beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery, and the ribs show notches along their lower borders. Which segment is narrowed? The answer is the aortic isthmus, the short part of the arch between the left subclavian artery and the descending aorta.

Question 3580. Which statement about the pulmonary trunk is correct: it carries oxygenated blood away from the heart, it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, it carries blood from the lungs to the left atrium, or it is a branch of the aorta? The answer is that it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. It divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.

Question 3581. What does the ligamentum arteriosum connect: the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch, the aorta to the superior vena cava, the left pulmonary artery to the left atrium, or the aorta to the pulmonary veins? The answer is the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch. It is the fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus.

Question 3582. Which two veins unite to form the superior vena cava? The answer is the right and left brachiocephalic veins. They join behind the lower end of the right first costal cartilage. The superior vena cava then descends behind the right border of the sternum and opens into the right atrium.

Question 3583. Within the pericardium, how do the aorta and the pulmonary trunk relate to one another along their first few centimeters? The answer is that the pulmonary trunk begins in front of the aorta and to its left, and the two then spiral, so that the aorta comes to lie behind and to the right. Their cusps face in different directions.

Question 3584. Which pair belongs together: the superior vena cava with the right atrium, the pulmonary veins with the right atrium, the coronary sinus with the left atrium, or the inferior vena cava with the left atrium? The answer is the superior vena cava with the right atrium. The pulmonary veins enter the left atrium and the coronary sinus enters the right atrium.

Question 3585. A described angiogram of the ascending aorta shows two small branches leaving the sinuses just above the valve and running down in the grooves between the atria and the ventricles. Which vessels are shown? The answer is the right and left coronary arteries. They are the first branches of the aorta.

Question 3586. A constructed illustration: after a severe chest injury a described radiograph shows a widened upper mediastinum and a small collection of fluid on the left. Which structure is most likely torn at the point where it is fixed? The answer is the descending thoracic aorta at the isthmus, just beyond the left subclavian artery.

Question 3587. Which statement about the coronary arteries is correct: the right coronary artery usually supplies the sinoatrial node, the left coronary artery arises from the pulmonary trunk, the right coronary artery arises from the left sinus, or the coronary arteries arise from the left ventricle? The answer is that the right coronary artery usually supplies the sinoatrial node in most hearts.

Question 3588. Where does the coronary sinus open? The answer is into the right atrium, just above the opening of the inferior vena cava and in front of the interatrial septum. It is the main collecting vein of the muscle of the heart, and a small fold guards its opening.

Question 3589. A described dissection follows the right coronary artery from its origin. In which groove does it run, and where does it end in most hearts? The answer is the coronary sulcus, and it ends by turning down the back of the heart as the posterior interventricular branch. Along the way it supplies the right atrium and the right ventricle.

Question 3590. Which vessel drains most of the blood from the muscle of the heart itself: the coronary sinus, the superior vena cava, the pulmonary veins, or the azygos vein? The answer is the coronary sinus. It opens into the right atrium. The superior vena cava drains the head and the upper limbs, and the pulmonary veins drain the lungs.

Question 3591. A constructed illustration: a person has a blockage in the artery that runs down the front of the interventricular groove toward the apex. Which part of the heart is at risk? The answer is the front and the apex of the left ventricle, together with the front of the interventricular septum.

Question 3592. A described oblique view of the aortic arch shows three branches arising from its upper border, the first of them dividing almost at once. How many branches are shown, and which is the first? The answer is three, and the first is the brachiocephalic trunk. It divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

Question 3593. Which pair belongs together: the left common carotid artery with the left side of the head and neck, the brachiocephalic trunk with the right arm alone, the left subclavian artery with the right arm, or the right subclavian artery with the left side of the head? The answer is the left common carotid artery with the left side of the head and neck.

Question 3594. A described view of the back of the heart shows four veins entering the smooth posterior wall of one chamber, two on each side, and none of them has a valve. Which chamber is shown, and why is there no valve there? The answer is the left atrium, whose wall is smooth where the pulmonary veins enter.

Question 3595. A described dissection passes a finger behind the aorta and the pulmonary trunk and brings it out on the other side, all within the pericardium. Which space is the finger in: the oblique pericardial sinus, the transverse pericardial sinus, the coronary sulcus, or the aortic opening of the diaphragm? The answer is the transverse pericardial sinus.

Question 3596. Which small vein runs down the back of the left atrium and joins the coronary sinus? The answer is the oblique vein of the left atrium. It is a remnant of the left common cardinal vein of the embryo. It descends over the posterior wall of the left atrium on its way to the sinus.

Question 3597. A constructed illustration: a person has swelling of the face and the upper limbs with distended veins over the upper chest, while the legs are normal. Which large vein is obstructed? The answer is the superior vena cava. It drains the head, the neck, the upper limbs and the upper chest, so obstruction shows above the diaphragm.

Question 3598. Which structures lie immediately in front of the descending thoracic aorta as it passes down through the chest? The answer is the esophagus, which lies to its right and in front, and the root of the left lung. The aorta itself lies against the vertebral column, a little to the left of the midline.

Question 3599. In most people the aortic arch gives three branches. Which variation is common enough that a surgeon should expect it: a fourth branch, the left vertebral artery arising directly from the arch, an arch with only one branch, or a right-sided arch in most people? The answer is the left vertebral artery arising directly from the arch.

Question 3600. Name the three branches of the aortic arch, spoken in order from right to left. The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery. The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right common carotid and the right subclavian arteries.

To summarize, the right atrium receives the two venae cavae and the coronary sinus, and it forms the right border of the heart, while the left atrium lies most posteriorly, in front of the esophagus. The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber and lies behind the sternum, but the left ventricle has the thickest wall and forms the apex, which is felt in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Each atrioventricular valve is held shut by its cusps, chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, and the aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves with three cusps each, the pulmonary valve being the most anterior of the four. The interventricular septum is muscular below and membranous above, the membranous part lying just below the aortic valve, while the fossa ovalis with its limbus marks the site of the foramen ovale in the interatrial septum. The aorta leaves the left ventricle and gives off the coronary arteries from its sinuses before arching to the left, and the pulmonary trunk passes in front of it and to the left. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 37 — Heart Anatomy, Part Two

This chapter continues the study of the heart by following the vessels that supply and drain its own muscle and the sac that holds it. It covers the coronary arteries and the territories they serve, the coronary veins and the channels that return their blood, and the pericardium with its layers, its cavity, its sinuses and its attachments. It holds one hundred questions, and every question is followed at once by its answer and by the reason that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3601. From which aortic sinus does the left coronary artery arise: the right coronary sinus, the left posterior aortic sinus, the non-coronary sinus, or above the sinotubular junction? The answer is the left posterior aortic sinus, often called the left coronary sinus. It lies behind the left cusp of the aortic valve, while the right coronary artery arises from the right, or anterior, sinus.

Question 3602. Which artery runs down the front of the heart toward the apex, in the groove between the two ventricles? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery, also called the left anterior descending artery. It is one of the two terminal branches of the left coronary artery and supplies the front of both ventricles.

Question 3603. Which artery runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the back third of the interventricular septum? The answer is the posterior interventricular artery, also called the posterior descending artery. In most people it is a branch of the right coronary artery, which makes the heart right dominant, and it also supplies the back walls of both ventricles.

Question 3604. In most people, which artery gives the branch that supplies the sinoatrial node: the right coronary artery, the circumflex artery, the anterior interventricular artery, or the left coronary artery? The answer is the right coronary artery. Its nodal branch arises near the beginning of the artery and climbs to the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium.

Question 3605. A described coronary angiogram shows a wide vessel running down the front of the heart toward the apex and giving off small branches that dive into the muscle between the ventricles. Which vessel is shown, and which part of the septum do those branches supply? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery, whose septal branches supply the front two thirds of the septum.

Question 3606. In the anterior interventricular groove, which structure lies superficial to the anterior interventricular artery: the great cardiac vein, the middle cardiac vein, the coronary sinus, or the small cardiac vein? The answer is the great cardiac vein. It ascends from the apex beside the artery and crosses over it in the groove.

Question 3607. A constructed illustration: a person has sudden crushing central chest pain, and the tracing shows injury of the front wall of the left ventricle. Which artery is most likely blocked? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery, which supplies the front of the left ventricle, the apex and the front of the septum. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3608. True or false: each coronary artery opens into the aorta from within an aortic sinus, near the level of the sinotubular junction. The answer is true. The left artery opens in the left posterior sinus and the right artery in the right sinus, and the third sinus gives rise to no artery.

Question 3609. A small artery arises from the right aortic sinus through its own opening and runs down the front of the right ventricle toward the outflow tract. Which vessel is described: the conus artery, the right marginal artery, the sinoatrial nodal artery, or the circumflex artery? The answer is the conus artery. It has its own opening in some people and is then called the third coronary artery.

Question 3610. Which branch of the right coronary artery runs down the sharp lower border of the heart toward the apex? The answer is the right marginal artery. The sharp lower border is called the acute margin, and the artery supplies the front and the back of the right ventricle along it.

Question 3611. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior interventricular artery with the anterior interventricular groove, the circumflex artery with the posterior interventricular groove, the right coronary artery with the anterior interventricular groove, or the posterior interventricular artery with the coronary sulcus? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery with the anterior interventricular groove. The circumflex artery runs in the coronary sulcus instead.

Question 3612. A described coronary angiogram shows a long trunk dividing into two branches, one running down the front of the heart and the other turning around the left border. Which two branches are shown? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery, the two terminal branches of the left coronary artery, which divides near the left border of the pulmonary trunk.

Question 3613. Name the two arteries that supply the interventricular septum, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior interventricular artery and the posterior interventricular artery. The first supplies the front two thirds of the septum through its septal branches, and the second supplies the back third.

Question 3614. Which artery most often gives the branch that supplies the atrioventricular node: the circumflex artery, the anterior interventricular artery, the right coronary artery, or the left coronary artery? The answer is the right coronary artery. Its nodal branch arises near the point where the artery turns into the posterior interventricular groove. In a left dominant heart the circumflex artery supplies the node instead.

Question 3615. As the left coronary artery leaves the aorta, which structure lies immediately in front of it and which lies behind? The answer is the pulmonary trunk in front and the left auricle behind. The artery runs in the short space between them before it divides.

Question 3616. A constructed illustration: a young person has chest pain on exertion, and imaging shows part of the anterior interventricular artery dipping into the heart muscle instead of lying on its surface. What is that arrangement called, and why does it matter? The answer is a myocardial bridge. Each contraction compresses the tunneled segment. The arrangement is a common variant and usually causes no trouble.

Question 3617. How many openings do the coronary arteries normally make in the wall of the aorta: one, two, three, or four? The answer is two. One lies in the left posterior sinus for the left coronary artery and one in the right sinus for the right coronary artery, and an extra opening for the conus artery is present in some people.

Question 3618. The circumflex artery runs around the left border of the heart. In which groove does it lie, and does that groove separate the atria from the ventricles or the two ventricles from each other? The answer is the coronary sulcus, also called the atrioventricular groove, which separates the atria above from the ventricles below.

Question 3619. Which branch of the circumflex artery follows the rounded left border of the heart and supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle? The answer is the left marginal artery, also called the obtuse marginal artery. Its companion on the right side is the right marginal artery, which follows the sharp border.

Question 3620. A described cast of the coronary vessels shows two trunks leaving the aorta, one passing to the right and one dividing almost at once into two branches. How many main stems leave the aorta? The answer is two, the right coronary artery and the left coronary artery. The left one divides early into the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery.

Question 3621. Which part of the interventricular septum is supplied by the posterior interventricular artery: the front two thirds, the back third, the whole septum, or only the membranous part? The answer is the back third. The anterior interventricular artery supplies the front two thirds through its septal branches, and the membranous part at the top is supplied from both.

Question 3622. A constructed illustration: a person has an infarct of the right ventricle, and the blocked vessel runs in the groove between the right atrium and the right ventricle. Which artery is blocked? The answer is the right coronary artery, which supplies most of the right atrium and right ventricle. In a right dominant heart it also gives the posterior interventricular artery.

Question 3623. Where do the openings of the two coronary arteries lie in relation to the cusps of the aortic valve? The answer is within the aortic sinuses, above the attachments of the cusps and below the sinotubular junction. Because they open into the sinuses, the arteries fill mainly during diastole, when the cusps are closed.

Question 3624. Which of these is a branch of the right coronary artery: the circumflex artery, the anterior interventricular artery, the right marginal artery, or the left marginal artery? The answer is the right marginal artery. The circumflex and anterior interventricular arteries belong to the left coronary artery, and the left marginal artery is a branch of the circumflex.

Question 3625. Which branch of the anterior interventricular artery is the largest of the small vessels that run deep into the interventricular septum? The answer is the first septal artery, also called the first septal perforator. It supplies the front of the septum and part of the conducting tissue within it.

Question 3626. A described computed tomography angiogram of the heart shows a vessel passing between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle before it divides. Which vessel is shown? The answer is the left coronary artery. Its short trunk lies in that space and divides into the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery.

Question 3627. Why does a blockage of one coronary artery damage only its own territory, although the two arteries do meet: because the connections are too small, because the arteries never meet, because the veins carry blood backward, or because the muscle takes oxygen from the blood? The answer is that the connections are too small to carry blood, so the coronary arteries act as functional end arteries, with small channels at the apex and the crux.

Question 3628. Which of these pairs belongs together: the right coronary artery with the right atrioventricular groove, the circumflex artery with the anterior interventricular groove, the anterior interventricular artery with the posterior interventricular groove, or the posterior interventricular artery with the coronary sulcus? The answer is the right coronary artery with the right atrioventricular groove. The circumflex artery runs in the coronary sulcus on the left.

Question 3629. True or false: the left coronary artery carries more blood than the right coronary artery in the resting heart. The answer is true. The left ventricle does more work and receives the larger share of coronary flow, most of it during diastole, when the muscle is relaxed.

Question 3630. Which statement describes a right dominant heart: the right coronary artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery, the left coronary artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery, the right coronary artery gives off the anterior interventricular artery, or the circumflex artery gives off the right marginal artery? The answer is that the right coronary artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery, the arrangement found in most people.

Question 3631. A constructed illustration: a person has an infarct of the back of the left ventricle and of the back third of the interventricular septum. Which artery is most likely blocked? The answer is the right coronary artery, through its posterior interventricular branch. An infarct here often disturbs the atrioventricular node as well.

Question 3632. Which artery usually reaches the apex of the heart and supplies it? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery, which runs to the notch at the apex and turns around it. The posterior interventricular artery may share the supply of the apex from behind.

Question 3633. Which structure lies immediately deep to the epicardium in the atrioventricular groove on the right side of the heart? The answer is the right coronary artery. The grooves of the heart carry the coronary vessels in a layer of fat just under the epicardium.

Question 3634. A described specimen shows a heart in which the artery running in the posterior interventricular groove can be traced back around the right border to the right aortic sinus. What does this arrangement show? The answer is that the heart is right dominant. In a left dominant heart that same groove is supplied from the circumflex artery.

Question 3635. In about 40 per cent of people, which artery gives the branch that supplies the sinoatrial node: the circumflex artery, the anterior interventricular artery, the right coronary artery, or the posterior interventricular artery? The answer is the circumflex artery. In the remaining people that branch comes from the right coronary artery.

Question 3636. A constructed illustration: a tear in the wall of the aorta extends back along the root of the aorta, and blood collects around the heart. Which two vessels lie in greatest danger because of where they open? The answer is the two coronary arteries, whose openings lie in the aortic sinuses. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3637. Name two places on the surface of the heart where small connections between the two coronary arteries are most often found, spoken as a list. The answer is at the apex of the heart and at the crux, where the posterior interventricular groove meets the coronary sulcus. These channels are narrow and open only when flow falls.

Question 3638. Into which two branches does the left coronary artery usually divide: the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries, the right marginal and posterior interventricular arteries, the circumflex and right coronary arteries, or the anterior interventricular and right marginal arteries? The answer is the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries, both branches of the short left trunk.
