Question 3639. Which artery runs in the groove between the right atrium and the right ventricle and gives off the right marginal branch? The answer is the right coronary artery. It begins at the right aortic sinus, follows the groove around the right border, and then turns down between the ventricles at the back.

Question 3640. A described cast of the heart vessels shows a fine network lying over the surface of the heart and larger branches entering the wall between the ventricles. In which layer do these vessels lie? The answer is the epicardium, the outer layer of the wall. The coronary vessels lie in the fat beneath it, and only their smallest branches run within the muscle.

Question 3641. In a right dominant heart, which artery supplies both the atrioventricular node and the back third of the interventricular septum: the circumflex artery, the anterior interventricular artery, the right coronary artery, or the left coronary artery? The answer is the right coronary artery. Its posterior interventricular branch and its nodal branch both arise from it.

Question 3642. In the right atrioventricular groove, which chamber lies above the right coronary artery and which lies below it? The answer is the right atrium above and the right ventricle below. The groove separates the atrium from the ventricle, and the same groove carries the small cardiac vein.

Question 3643. What is the name of the point on the back of the heart where the posterior interventricular groove meets the coronary sulcus? The answer is the crux of the heart. The right coronary artery reaches this point in most people and turns down from it into the posterior interventricular groove.

Question 3644. Which statement about the blood supply of the conducting system is correct: the atrioventricular node is usually supplied by the right artery, the sinoatrial node always comes from the same artery, both nodes come from the left artery, or the nodes have no supply? The answer is that the atrioventricular node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery. The sinoatrial node comes from the right artery in most people and from the circumflex in the rest.

Question 3645. A described angiogram shows the branch running down the front of the heart stopping two thirds of the way to the apex, with no filling of the vessels beyond. Which artery is blocked, and which parts lose their supply? The answer is the anterior interventricular artery; the front wall of the left ventricle, the apex and the front two thirds of the septum lose supply.

Question 3646. Which vein begins at the apex of the heart, ascends in the anterior interventricular groove beside the anterior interventricular artery, and then turns into the coronary sulcus? The answer is the great cardiac vein. It is the longest vein of the heart and ends as the coronary sinus.

Question 3647. Into which chamber of the heart does the coronary sinus open? The answer is the right atrium. It opens between the opening of the inferior vena cava and the opening of the tricuspid valve, and a small fold, the valve of the coronary sinus, guards its mouth.

Question 3648. Which structure is the direct continuation of the great cardiac vein: the middle cardiac vein, the coronary sinus, the anterior cardiac vein, or the oblique vein of the left atrium? The answer is the coronary sinus. The great vein turns around the left border and widens into the sinus, which runs in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus.

Question 3649. Which vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove beside the posterior interventricular artery? The answer is the middle cardiac vein. It drains the back of both ventricles and opens into the coronary sinus near its end, and it is the companion of that artery.

Question 3650. Which vein runs in the atrioventricular groove on the right side of the heart beside the right coronary artery? The answer is the small cardiac vein. It follows the right margin and ends either in the coronary sinus or directly in the right atrium.

Question 3651. Which set of veins crosses the front of the right ventricle and opens directly into the right atrium rather than into the coronary sinus? The answer is the anterior cardiac veins. There are usually two or three of them, and they are therefore not seen in a cast of the coronary sinus.

Question 3652. Which channel carries the largest share of the blood that returns from the muscle of the heart: the anterior cardiac veins, the coronary sinus, the smallest cardiac veins, or the middle cardiac vein? The answer is the coronary sinus. Most of the venous blood from the wall of the heart drains through it into the right atrium.

Question 3653. A described cast of the veins of the heart shows a wide channel lying in the groove between the left atrium and the left ventricle at the back of the heart and opening into the right atrium. Which channel is shown? The answer is the coronary sinus, which lies in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus and is about 3 centimeters long.

Question 3654. Which of these pairs belongs together: the middle cardiac vein with the posterior interventricular groove, the great cardiac vein with the posterior interventricular groove, the small cardiac vein with the anterior interventricular groove, or the coronary sinus with the anterior interventricular groove? The answer is the middle cardiac vein with the posterior interventricular groove. The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior groove instead.

Question 3655. Which two structures open into the right atrium close together, one just above the other, with only one of them carrying blood from the muscle of the heart? The answer is the inferior vena cava and the coronary sinus. Both open into the smooth posterior part of the right atrium.

Question 3656. A constructed illustration: a catheter is passed into the main vein that drains the muscle of the heart, and it is briefly held up at the mouth of the vein by a thin fold of tissue. Which channel is being entered? The answer is the coronary sinus, and the fold is its valve. The fold is a normal structure and may be large in some people.

Question 3657. A described specimen shows a needle passed into a wide vein on the back of the heart and threaded until its tip lies in the right atrium. Which vein was entered? The answer is the coronary sinus, which receives the great cardiac vein and runs from left to right in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus.

Question 3658. True or false: the anterior cardiac veins empty into the coronary sinus. The answer is false. They open directly into the right atrium instead, while the coronary sinus receives the great, the middle and the small cardiac veins along with the posterior vein of the left ventricle.

Question 3659. Which of these veins drains directly into the right atrium without passing through the coronary sinus: the great cardiac vein, the middle cardiac vein, the anterior cardiac veins, or the oblique vein of the left atrium? The answer is the anterior cardiac veins, while the other three reach the right atrium through the coronary sinus.

Question 3660. Which small vein descends over the back of the left atrium and joins the great cardiac vein at the point where that vein becomes the coronary sinus? The answer is the oblique vein of the left atrium. It is the remains of the left superior vena cava of the fetus and may be absent in an adult.

Question 3661. The oblique vein of the left atrium joins the great cardiac vein at a particular point. What does that point mark? The answer is the beginning of the coronary sinus, at the left end of the posterior part of the coronary sulcus. The fold of tissue that accompanies the vein is the remnant of a fetal channel.

Question 3662. Which statement about the smallest cardiac veins is correct: they open directly into the chambers of the heart, they all open into the coronary sinus, they drain only the left ventricle, or they carry most of the venous blood of the heart? The answer is that they open directly into the chambers, mostly into the right atrium and the right ventricle.

Question 3663. A constructed illustration: in a person with a raised pressure on the right side of the heart, a little blood passes from the venous side to the arterial side through tiny channels in the wall of the heart. Which channels are described? The answer is the smallest cardiac veins, which open directly into the chambers. They have no valves, so blood can pass either way.

Question 3664. Which of these pairs belongs together: the small cardiac vein with the right atrioventricular groove, the great cardiac vein with the right atrioventricular groove, the middle cardiac vein with the anterior interventricular groove, or the anterior cardiac veins with the coronary sinus? The answer is the small cardiac vein with the right atrioventricular groove. It runs there with the right coronary artery.

Question 3665. Name two veins that empty into the coronary sinus beside the great cardiac vein, spoken as a list. The answer is the middle cardiac vein and the small cardiac vein. The coronary sinus also receives the posterior vein of the left ventricle and the oblique vein of the left atrium.

Question 3666. A described cast of the veins of the heart shows three channels converging on a single wide trunk that opens into the right atrium, one from the front, one from the back between the ventricles, and one from the lower right border. Which three veins are shown? The answer is the great, the middle and the small cardiac veins, all of which end in the coronary sinus.

Question 3667. Two small folds lie close together in the lower part of the right atrium. Which statement is correct: both guard the opening of the coronary sinus, one guards the coronary sinus and the other the inferior vena cava, one guards the superior vena cava and the other the coronary sinus, or both guard the tricuspid valve? The answer is that one guards the coronary sinus and the other guards the inferior vena cava.

Question 3668. As the coronary sinus runs along the back of the heart, which chamber lies above it and which lies below it? The answer is the left atrium above and the left ventricle below. The sinus lies in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus, and it ends by opening into the right atrium.

Question 3669. Which vein accompanies the right marginal artery along the sharp lower border of the heart: the right marginal vein, the middle cardiac vein, the oblique vein of the left atrium, or the great cardiac vein? The answer is the right marginal vein, which drains into the small cardiac vein or directly into the right atrium.

Question 3670. A described specimen shows a vein lying in the groove between the right atrium and the right ventricle, and another vein crossing the front of the right ventricle to reach the right atrium. Which veins are shown? The answer is the small cardiac vein and an anterior cardiac vein, and the anterior cardiac veins open straight into the right atrium.

Question 3671. Which vein is the longest in the heart: the great cardiac vein, the middle cardiac vein, the small cardiac vein, or the oblique vein of the left atrium? The answer is the great cardiac vein. It begins at the apex and runs the length of the front of the heart before becoming the coronary sinus.

Question 3672. Which statement about the venous drainage of the heart is correct: all of the venous blood passes through the coronary sinus, the anterior cardiac veins drain into the right atrium, the smallest cardiac veins carry most of the blood, or the coronary sinus opens into the left atrium? The answer is that the anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium. The coronary sinus carries the largest share but not all of it.

Question 3673. What is the name of the tough outer sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels? The answer is the fibrous pericardium. It is a strong layer of connective tissue that holds the heart in place within the chest, and inside it lies a thin serous layer.

Question 3674. What is the name of the thin serous layer that covers the surface of the heart itself? The answer is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium, also called the epicardium. It forms the outer layer of the heart wall, and the coronary vessels lie in the fat beneath it.

Question 3675. Which part of the pericardium is fused to the central tendon of the diaphragm: the visceral layer, the fibrous pericardium, the parietal serous layer, or the pericardial cavity? The answer is the fibrous pericardium. It is bound to the central tendon below and to the sternum in front by small ligaments.

Question 3676. What is the name of the space between the two layers of the serous pericardium, which in health holds only a thin film of fluid? The answer is the pericardial cavity. Its outer wall is the parietal layer and its inner wall is the visceral layer, and the film of fluid lets the two surfaces glide over one another.

Question 3677. Which nerve runs down the side of the fibrous pericardium between it and the parietal serous layer? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which is accompanied there by the pericardiacophrenic vessels. Because it lies on the pericardium, disease of the pericardium can cause pain felt at the shoulder.

Question 3678. Which artery supplies the fibrous and parietal layers of the pericardium: the pericardiacophrenic artery, a coronary artery, a bronchial artery, or a pulmonary artery? The answer is the pericardiacophrenic artery, a branch of the internal thoracic artery. The visceral layer is supplied instead by the coronary arteries.

Question 3679. A described transverse section of the chest shows a thick sac around the heart, a thin layer closely applied to the heart muscle, and a narrow space between the two. Which layers are shown? The answer is the fibrous pericardium outside, the parietal serous layer within it, and the visceral layer on the heart, with the pericardial cavity between.

Question 3680. The transverse pericardial sinus is a passage within the pericardial cavity. Which structures lie in front of it and which lie behind it? The answer is the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk in front, and the superior vena cava behind. A surgeon can pass a finger or a tube through the sinus behind the great arteries.

Question 3681. The oblique pericardial sinus lies behind which chamber of the heart, and which vessels bound it? The answer is the left atrium, bounded by the folds of serous pericardium around the four pulmonary veins and the inferior vena cava. It is a blind recess, and the transverse sinus lies above it.

Question 3682. A constructed illustration: fluid collects quickly in the pericardial cavity after a wound to the chest, and the heart cannot fill because the fibrous sac will not stretch. Which chambers suffer first? The answer is the right atrium and the right ventricle, because they are thin-walled and work at low pressure. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3683. Which statement about the innervation of the pericardium is correct: the visceral layer is sensitive to pain, the parietal layer is sensitive to pain, both layers are insensitive, or only the visceral layer has a nerve supply? The answer is that the parietal layer is sensitive to pain. It is supplied by the phrenic nerve and by the intercostal nerves.

Question 3684. True or false: the fibrous pericardium is continuous above with the outer coat of the great vessels. The answer is true. It blends with the outer coat of the aorta and the pulmonary trunk as they leave the heart, and below it is fused to the central tendon of the diaphragm.

Question 3685. A described chest radiograph shows the shadow of the heart lying inside a slightly wider shadow that follows the same outline, with a thin dark line of fat on each side. Which structure forms the outer shadow? The answer is the pericardium and the fat within it, and a widened shadow of this kind may mean that fluid has collected.

Question 3686. A constructed illustration: a person with a long-standing illness of the pericardium has the two serous layers stuck together by scar tissue, so that the heart is held in a rigid case. Which layer produces the fluid that normally prevents this? The answer is the serous pericardium. The parietal layer produces the fluid, and the visceral layer and the lymphatics remove it.

Question 3687. To which part of the diaphragm is the fibrous pericardium attached: the muscular part, the central tendon, the left crus, or the right crus? The answer is the central tendon. The attachment is firm, and the fibrous layer is also tied to the sternum by the sternopericardial ligaments.

Question 3688. A described transverse section through the chest shows the heart inside its sac, with a nerve running down each side of the sac just under its outer layer. Which nerve is shown, and what does it supply? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which supplies the diaphragm and lies between the fibrous pericardium and the parietal serous layer.

Question 3689. What is the name of the band of fibrous pericardium that ties the sac to the back of the sternum? The answer is the sternopericardial ligament. There are upper and lower bands, and they help to hold the heart forward in the chest.

Question 3690. Which chamber of the heart lies immediately in front of the esophagus and the descending aorta, with the pericardium between them? The answer is the left atrium. It forms the back of the heart, and that close relation is why an enlarged left atrium can press on the esophagus.

Question 3691. Which of these structures lies immediately outside the fibrous pericardium in the middle mediastinum: the parietal pleura and the lungs, the esophagus, the thoracic duct, or the trachea? The answer is the parietal pleura and the lungs, which lie on each side of the pericardium. Behind it lie the esophagus and the descending aorta.

Question 3692. True or false: because the fibrous pericardium is firmly fixed to the diaphragm and to the great vessels, it can stretch enough to hold a large amount of fluid without compressing the heart. The answer is false. The fibrous layer is strong but it is not elastic, so a rapid collection of fluid can obstruct the filling of the heart.

Question 3693. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fibrous pericardium with the central tendon of the diaphragm, the serous pericardium with the sternum, the pericardial cavity with the pleural cavity, or the epicardium with the fibrous pericardium? The answer is the fibrous pericardium with the central tendon of the diaphragm. The epicardium is the visceral serous layer on the heart.

Question 3694. A transverse plane is passed through the chest at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra, below the division of the trachea. Which structure lies in the midline in front of the vertebral column and behind the pericardium? The answer is the esophagus, with the descending aorta to its left.

Question 3695. A needle is passed from the left front of the chest toward the pericardial cavity. Which statement about the left lung and its pleura is correct: the lung covers the pericardium everywhere, the left lung has a notch where the pericardium meets the chest wall, the left lung lies behind the pericardium, or the pleura never comes near it? The answer is that the left lung has a notch there, and the pleura still lines its edges.

Question 3696. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows a dark strip of fat lying in front of the shadow of the heart, just behind the lower sternum. Within which structure does that fat lie? The answer is the pericardium, between its fibrous and serous layers, and the strip is a normal finding.

Question 3697. A constructed illustration: after a wound below the left fifth rib close to the sternum, blood collects in the pericardial cavity and the heart cannot fill. Which two structures lie closest to the wound? The answer is the right ventricle and the pericardium, since the right ventricle forms most of the front of the heart behind the sternum. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3698. When a person lies on the back, fluid in the pericardial cavity collects in the lowest part of the cavity. Which part is that: the transverse sinus, the oblique sinus, the part behind the sternum, or the part behind the left atrium? The answer is the part behind the left atrium, because the posterior part of the cavity is lowest in that position.

Question 3699. Which statement about the pericardial cavity is correct: it is continuous with the pleural cavity, it normally holds only a thin film of fluid, it lies outside the fibrous pericardium, or it contains the coronary arteries? The answer is that it normally holds only a thin film of fluid. The cavity is a potential space between the parietal and the visceral layers of the serous pericardium.

Question 3700. Which sequence correctly gives the layers crossed by a needle passed from the front of the chest into the pericardial cavity: skin, fibrous pericardium, parietal serous layer, then cavity; skin, parietal serous layer, fibrous pericardium, then cavity; skin, visceral layer, then cavity; or skin, pleural cavity, then cavity? The answer is skin, then fibrous pericardium, then the parietal serous layer, then the cavity.

To summarize, the left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus and divides into the anterior interventricular artery, which supplies the front of both ventricles and the front two thirds of the interventricular septum, and the circumflex artery, which runs in the coronary sulcus. The right coronary artery arises from the right sinus, runs in the right atrioventricular groove, and in most people gives the posterior interventricular artery, which supplies the back third of the septum; that arrangement is right dominance. The sinoatrial node is supplied by the right coronary artery in about 60 per cent of people and by the circumflex artery in the rest, while the atrioventricular node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery, so the coronary arteries behave as functional end arteries with small connections at the apex and at the crux of the heart. Most venous blood returns through the great, middle and small cardiac veins into the coronary sinus and so into the right atrium, while the anterior cardiac veins and the smallest cardiac veins open directly into the chambers. The pericardium has a fibrous layer fixed to the central tendon of the diaphragm, and a serous layer whose two parts enclose the pericardial cavity, with the transverse sinus behind the aorta and the pulmonary trunk and the oblique sinus behind the left atrium. The phrenic nerve and the pericardiacophrenic vessels run between the fibrous and parietal layers, which is why pericardial pain is felt at the shoulder, and because the fibrous layer cannot stretch quickly, a rapid collection of fluid can obstruct the filling of the heart. This chapter is educational material, and it does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 38 — Arteries

This chapter follows the aorta from the heart to its division in the abdomen and then traces the arteries that carry blood from the arch to the arm. It covers the ascending aorta, the aortic arch and its three branches, the carotid arteries, the subclavian arteries, the axillary artery through the armpit, and the brachial artery down to the elbow. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is right. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3701. Which great vessel begins at the aortic orifice of the left ventricle and curves backward after running upward and to the right? The answer is the ascending aorta. It lies inside the pericardium and is about 5 centimeters long. It gives off the two coronary arteries before it leaves the sac.

Question 3702. From which parts of the aortic root do the coronary arteries arise: the sinuses above the aortic valve, the pulmonary trunk, the left atrium, or the arch itself? The answer is the sinuses above the aortic valve. The right coronary artery arises from the right sinus and the left artery from the left sinus. The posterior sinus gives off no artery.

Question 3703. A described microscopic section shows an arterial wall whose middle coat is packed with elastic lamellae and holds almost no smooth muscle. Which vessel was sectioned? The answer is the aorta. It is an elastic artery, built to stretch with each heartbeat and recoil again. That elastic tissue smooths the pulse into a steadier flow.

Question 3704. In the posterior mediastinum, which structure lies immediately in front of and slightly to the right of the descending thoracic aorta? The answer is the esophagus. It descends in front of the aorta and crosses towards the left near the diaphragm. The thoracic duct lies behind it.

Question 3705. True or false: the abdominal aorta ends by dividing into the two common iliac arteries at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra. The answer is true. The division lies a little to the left of the midline. The small middle sacral artery continues downward from that point.

Question 3706. At which level does the aorta pass from the chest into the abdomen: the tenth, the eleventh or the twelfth thoracic vertebra, or the fourth lumbar vertebra? The answer is the twelfth thoracic vertebra. The aortic opening lies in the diaphragm, slightly to the left of the midline. The thoracic duct passes through the same opening.

Question 3707. Which single unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta arises below the aortic opening and supplies the upper part of the gut? The answer is the celiac trunk. It is short and wide and divides at once into the left gastric, the splenic and the common hepatic arteries. It arises at the twelfth thoracic vertebra.

Question 3708. Which of these branches of the abdominal aorta arises at about the second lumbar vertebra: the inferior mesenteric artery, the renal arteries, the celiac trunk, or the median sacral artery? The answer is the renal arteries. The right one lies a little lower than the left. The inferior mesenteric artery arises lower down, at the third lumbar vertebra.

Question 3709. A constructed illustration: a person has high blood pressure in both arms, and a described radiograph shows notches along the lower borders of several ribs. Which segment of the aorta is narrowed? The answer is the arch just distal to the left subclavian artery. The narrowing lies where the ductus arteriosus once joined, and enlarged intercostal arteries erode the ribs. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3710. Which of these pairs belongs together: the celiac trunk with the transverse colon, the superior mesenteric artery with the small intestine, the inferior mesenteric artery with the stomach, or the renal artery with the spleen? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery with the small intestine. The celiac trunk supplies the stomach, the spleen and the liver.

Question 3711. Which small unpaired artery leaves the back of the lower abdominal aorta and runs down over the front of the sacrum? The answer is the median sacral artery. It is the last small branch of the aorta. The paired lumbar arteries leave the sides of the aorta at the levels of the lumbar vertebrae.

Question 3712. A described angiogram of the abdomen shows a single wide trunk leaving the front of the aorta and dividing at once into three branches. Which trunk is shown? The answer is the celiac trunk. Its branches are the left gastric, the splenic and the common hepatic arteries.

Question 3713. Which vein ascends in the posterior mediastinum on the right of the vertebral column while the descending thoracic aorta descends on the left? The answer is the azygos vein. It lies against the right side of the vertebral bodies and arches over the root of the right lung.

Question 3714. Which of these is not a branch of the descending thoracic aorta: the bronchial artery, the esophageal artery, the posterior intercostal artery, or the superior thyroid artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery, which arises in the neck from the external carotid. The descending thoracic aorta gives bronchial, esophageal, pericardial and posterior intercostal branches.

Question 3715. Which small paired arteries arise from the lower part of the descending thoracic aorta and spread over the upper surface of the diaphragm? The answer is the superior phrenic arteries. They supply the part of the diaphragm nearest the aorta. The rest is supplied by the musculophrenic and pericardiophrenic arteries.

Question 3716. A constructed illustration: a person describes tearing chest pain that runs through between the shoulder blades, and one arm has a weaker pulse than the other. Which structure is the pain arising from? The answer is the wall of the aorta, where its layers have split. The split may extend along the arch. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3717. Which paired arteries arise from the abdominal aorta between the renal arteries and the inferior mesenteric artery and run down towards the pelvis? The answer is the gonadal arteries. In the male they are the testicular arteries and in the female the ovarian arteries. Each crosses in front of the ureter.

Question 3718. A described specimen shows the abdominal aorta opened from the front, with three unpaired openings in a row down its back wall. Which three trunks leave them, in order from above down? The answer is the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery. They arise at the twelfth thoracic, the first lumbar and the third lumbar vertebrae.

Question 3719. Which of the three branches of the aortic arch is the only one that arises to the right of the midline? The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk. The other two, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery, arise separately from the arch. The trunk then divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint.

Question 3720. Between which two landmarks does the aortic arch run, described in terms of the sternum and a vertebra? The answer is from the second sternocostal joint to the lower border of the fourth thoracic vertebra. The arch therefore lies in the superior mediastinum behind the manubrium. It begins and ends near the sternal angle.

Question 3721. Which of these vessels does not arise directly from the aortic arch: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, the left subclavian artery, or the right subclavian artery? The answer is the right subclavian artery, which arises from the brachiocephalic trunk. Only three vessels leave the arch itself.

Question 3722. Which nerve hooks beneath the aortic arch just behind the fibrous band that joins the arch to the left pulmonary artery? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The band is the ligamentum arteriosum, the remains of the ductus arteriosus of the fetus. The nerve loops under the arch and climbs back up the neck.

Question 3723. A described chest radiograph shows a rounded bulge on the left border of the mediastinum, just above the shadow of the left hilum. Which structure forms that bulge? The answer is the aortic arch, whose last part is often called the aortic knuckle. The arch passes backward and to the left over the left bronchus.

Question 3724. A constructed illustration: an infant is described as having noisy breathing and difficulty swallowing, and a described study shows a ring of vessels encircling both the windpipe and the food pipe. Which developmental error accounts for the ring? The answer is persistence of both the right and the left fourth aortic arches, forming a double aortic arch.

Question 3725. Which structure lies immediately in front of the aortic arch and divides behind it into the two main bronchi: the esophagus, the trachea, the thoracic duct, or the vertebral column? The answer is the trachea. The arch then crosses over the left bronchus. The esophagus and the thoracic duct lie behind the arch.

Question 3726. Which nerve crosses the front of the aortic arch from lateral to medial on its way down to the diaphragm? The answer is the left phrenic nerve. It passes in front of the arch and then continues down in front of the root of the left lung. The left vagus nerve crosses the arch behind it.

Question 3727. True or false: the whole of the aortic arch lies within the pericardial sac. The answer is false. Only the ascending aorta lies inside the pericardium, and the arch begins where the aorta leaves it. The arch lies in the superior mediastinum behind the manubrium.

Question 3728. Which of these pairs belongs together: the brachiocephalic trunk with the left arm, the left common carotid artery with the left side of the head and neck, the left subclavian artery with the right side of the head, or the arch with the lower limb? The answer is the left common carotid artery with the left side of the head and neck.

Question 3729. Which branch of the aortic arch lies in front of the trachea before it divides, and what are its two terminal branches? The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk, which ends in the right common carotid and the right subclavian arteries. It is the first and largest branch of the arch.

Question 3730. Which of these fetal channels connects the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch: the foramen ovale, the ductus venosus, the ductus arteriosus, or the umbilical vein? The answer is the ductus arteriosus. It joins the arch where the arch turns downward, just distal to the left subclavian artery. After birth it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

Question 3731. A described angiogram shows four separate vessels leaving the aortic arch, the last of them running to the right behind the esophagus. Which vessel is that last one? The answer is an aberrant right subclavian artery. It arises beyond the left subclavian artery and crosses behind the esophagus. Four branches from the arch are a common variant, not the rule.

Question 3732. A constructed illustration: during an operation near the arch in an adult with a persistent ductus arteriosus, a nerve that loops beneath the arch is said to be at risk. Which nerve is it, and why does it loop so low on the left? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks under the ligamentum arteriosum. On the right the same nerve hooks higher, under the right subclavian artery.

Question 3733. Which large vein lies in front of the three branches of the aortic arch in the superior mediastinum: the left brachiocephalic vein, the superior vena cava, the azygos vein, or the left internal jugular vein? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein. It crosses the midline in front of those branches. The thymus lies in front of it in a child.

Question 3734. Which of these statements about the aortic arch is correct: it lies in the posterior mediastinum, it lies in the superior mediastinum, it lies inside the pericardium, or it lies below the diaphragm? The answer is that it lies in the superior mediastinum. The arch sits behind the manubrium and above the heart. The descending aorta alone continues into the posterior mediastinum.

Question 3735. At which landmark does the common carotid artery divide into the internal and the external carotid arteries? The answer is the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The division lies at about the fourth cervical vertebra. The internal carotid then continues upward without branching in the neck.

Question 3736. Which of these structures lies within the carotid sheath: the external carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, the hypoglossal nerve, or the cervical sympathetic trunk? The answer is the internal jugular vein. The sheath also contains the common and internal carotid arteries and the vagus nerve. The sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath.

Question 3737. Which small structure lies at the fork of the common carotid artery and acts as a chemical sensor for the blood? The answer is the carotid body. It sits in the tissue at the crotch of the division and responds to a fall in the oxygen content of the blood. The carotid sinus holds the pressure sensors instead.

Question 3738. Which is the first branch of the external carotid artery above its origin: the lingual artery, the superior thyroid artery, the facial artery, or the occipital artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery. It turns forward and downward to the upper pole of the thyroid gland. The lingual and facial arteries arise higher up.

Question 3739. In the neck, which vessel lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery, and which nerve lies between the two behind them? The answer is the internal jugular vein, with the vagus nerve between and behind them. The vein overlaps the artery at the side and in front. All three lie within the carotid sheath.

Question 3740. True or false: the internal carotid artery gives off no branches during its course through the neck. The answer is true. It runs straight up from the fork to the base of the skull without a branch in the neck. Its first branch, the ophthalmic artery, is given off inside the skull.

Question 3741. A described dissection of the neck shows two arteries lying one behind the other above the fork of the common carotid, the deeper one giving off nothing in the neck. Which artery is the deeper one? The answer is the internal carotid artery. It begins on the outer side of the external carotid and passes backward and medially.

Question 3742. Which of these pairs belongs together: the carotid sinus with chemical sensing, the carotid body with pressure sensing, the carotid sinus with pressure sensing, or the carotid body with temperature sensing? The answer is the carotid sinus with pressure sensing. The sinus is the swollen first part of the internal carotid artery and holds stretch receptors. The carotid body is the chemical sensor.

Question 3743. Which cranial nerve crosses the internal and the external carotid arteries in the neck, running forward above the fork? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, the hypoglossal nerve. It crosses the front of both vessels just above the division. It then runs forward to the tongue, deep to the digastric muscle.

Question 3744. A constructed illustration: a person has brief attacks of weakness of the right hand and difficulty finding words, and a described study shows a rough plaque at the fork of the left common carotid artery. Which vessel does the plaque narrow? The answer is the left internal carotid artery. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3745. Which branch of the internal carotid artery passes through the optic canal with the optic nerve to supply the eye: the facial artery, the ophthalmic artery, the maxillary artery, or the superficial temporal artery? The answer is the ophthalmic artery. It arises inside the cranial cavity. The other three are branches of the external carotid artery.

Question 3746. Name the two terminal branches of the external carotid artery, spoken as a list. The answer is the maxillary artery and the superficial temporal artery. The external carotid ends inside the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible. The maxillary artery is the larger of the two.

Question 3747. A described radiograph of the base of the skull shows a vessel entering a canal in the petrous part of the temporal bone beside the jugular opening. Which vessel enters that canal? The answer is the internal carotid artery, which enters the carotid canal. It then turns forward and medially inside the skull. The external carotid stays outside.

Question 3748. Which of these arteries is not a branch of the external carotid artery: the ascending pharyngeal, the occipital, the posterior auricular, or the ophthalmic? The answer is the ophthalmic artery, which comes from the internal carotid. The external carotid gives eight branches, and the ascending pharyngeal is one of them.

Question 3749. A constructed illustration: a person has a firm swelling at the fork of the right common carotid artery, with a hoarse voice and a tongue that deviates to the right. Which two nerves near that fork account for those findings? The answer is the right vagus nerve and the right hypoglossal nerve. The vagus runs in the sheath beside the artery.

Question 3750. Which artery lies just in front of the ear and can be felt pulsing at the upper part of the temple: the facial artery, the occipital artery, the superficial temporal artery, or the maxillary artery? The answer is the superficial temporal artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid. The occipital artery runs behind the ear.

Question 3751. Which branch of the external carotid artery hooks over the lower border of the mandible just in front of the masseter muscle? The answer is the facial artery. It winds over the bone there and then runs up towards the angle of the mouth. Its pulse can be felt against the mandible.

Question 3752. A described cross section of the neck at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage shows one vessel dividing into two, with a large vein beside it and a nerve behind. Which three structures does the sheath hold there? The answer is the common carotid artery dividing, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve.

Question 3753. Which of these arteries is a true end artery, so that its blockage causes loss of the tissue it supplies with no help from neighbours: the facial artery, the central artery of the retina, the superficial temporal artery, or the maxillary artery? The answer is the central artery of the retina, a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It has no anastomosis elsewhere.

Question 3754. Which muscular band of the neck lies immediately in front of the lower part of the common carotid artery and partly covers it: the sternocleidomastoid, the omohyoid, the platysma, or the digastric? The answer is the omohyoid. Its inferior belly crosses the lower part of the carotid sheath. The sternocleidomastoid lies further lateral.

Question 3755. A constructed illustration: a person is described as having pain over the side of the head that is tender to touch, and the artery in front of the ear feels thickened. Which artery is described? The answer is the superficial temporal artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3756. Which of these explains why blocking one of the arteries that reach the base of the brain may not cause a stroke: those arteries are end arteries, they join in a ring at the base of the brain, they carry no blood to the cortex, or they join only over the scalp? The answer is that they join in a ring, the circle of Willis.

Question 3757. From which vessels do the right and the left subclavian arteries arise? The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk on the right and the aortic arch on the left. The right subclavian artery begins behind the right sternoclavicular joint. The left arises from the arch as its third branch.

Question 3758. By which muscle is the subclavian artery divided into three parts, and where does the artery end? The answer is the anterior scalene muscle, and the artery ends at the outer border of the first rib. The first part lies medial to the muscle and the second part behind it.

Question 3759. Which is the first branch of the subclavian artery: the internal thoracic artery, the vertebral artery, the thyrocervical trunk, or the costocervical trunk? The answer is the vertebral artery. It arises from the upper and back part of the first part of the artery and runs up through the cervical vertebrae openings.

Question 3760. Which of these arteries arise from the thyrocervical trunk: the vertebral artery, the inferior thyroid artery, the costocervical trunk, or the deep cervical artery? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery. The trunk also gives the suprascapular and the superficial cervical arteries. The vertebral artery arises separately.

Question 3761. In the root of the neck, which vessel lies in front of the subclavian artery, with the anterior scalene muscle between them? The answer is the subclavian vein. It crosses in front of both the artery and the muscle and then joins the internal jugular vein. The brachial plexus lies behind the artery.

Question 3762. A described dissection of the root of the neck shows an artery arching upward over the dome of the pleura, marking the first rib and passing behind a muscle that runs down to that rib. Which artery is shown? The answer is the subclavian artery. It rests on the cervical pleura and the first rib.

Question 3763. True or false: the third part of the subclavian artery, beyond the anterior scalene muscle, usually gives off no named branch. The answer is true. The named branches come from the first part and from the second part, where the costocervical trunk arises. A dorsal scapular artery sometimes arises from the third part.

Question 3764. Which two arteries arise from the costocervical trunk: the inferior thyroid and the suprascapular, the superior intercostal and the deep cervical, the vertebral and the internal thoracic, or the transverse cervical and the dorsal scapular? The answer is the superior intercostal artery and the deep cervical artery. The trunk arises behind the anterior scalene muscle.

Question 3765. A constructed illustration: a person is described as having numbness along the inner side of the forearm and a weak hand, and a described radiograph shows an extra rib from the seventh cervical vertebra. Which structures are compressed at the root of the neck? The answer is the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery, which pass over the first rib.

Question 3766. Which of these pairs belongs together: the internal thoracic artery with the abdominal wall above the navel, the vertebral artery with the scalp behind the ear, the costocervical trunk with the thyroid gland, or the thyrocervical trunk with the brain? The answer is the internal thoracic artery with the abdominal wall above the navel, through its superior epigastric branch.

Question 3767. Which artery runs down behind the costal cartilages about a finger's breadth from the edge of the sternum, and how does it end? The answer is the internal thoracic artery. It ends at the sixth intercostal space by dividing into the superior epigastric and the musculophrenic arteries. It lies in front of the transversus thoracis.

Question 3768. Which of these arteries ascends through the openings in the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae and then enters the skull through the foramen magnum: the internal carotid, the vertebral, the occipital, or the ascending pharyngeal? The answer is the vertebral artery, the first branch of the first part of the subclavian artery.

Question 3769. At the root of the neck, the thoracic duct arches upward and laterally to end at which junction, and which two veins meet there? The answer is the junction of the left internal jugular and the left subclavian veins. The duct empties into the left brachiocephalic vein. On the right the right lymphatic duct ends at the matching junction.

Question 3770. Which branch of the subclavian system passes above the upper border of the scapula, through the notch beneath the transverse ligament, to reach the back of the shoulder? The answer is the suprascapular artery, from the thyrocervical trunk. It takes part in the anastomosis around the scapula.

Question 3771. A described angiogram of the neck shows the vertebral artery filling from above and carrying blood downward towards the arm, with narrowing of the subclavian artery before the vertebral artery arises. Which part of which artery is narrowed? The answer is the first part of the left subclavian artery, so the flow in the vertebral artery is reversed.

Question 3772. Into which two arteries does the internal thoracic artery divide at its lower end: the superior epigastric and the musculophrenic, the inferior epigastric and the pericardiophrenic, the superficial epigastric and the deep circumflex iliac, or the subcostal and the lumbar? The answer is the superior epigastric and the musculophrenic arteries.

Question 3773. Which artery supplies the lower part of the thyroid gland and arises from the thyrocervical trunk: the superior thyroid, the inferior thyroid, the middle thyroid, or the thyroidea ima? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery, from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery. The superior thyroid artery comes from the external carotid.

Question 3774. A described dissection of the front of the chest shows an artery running down behind the costal cartilages with two veins beside it and sending small branches forward between the cartilages. Which artery is shown? The answer is the internal thoracic artery. Its perforating branches reach the skin of the chest and the breast.

Question 3775. Where does the axillary artery begin and where does it end? The answer is at the outer border of the first rib above and the lower border of the teres major muscle below. Between those two points it crosses the armpit and lies behind the pectoralis minor. Beyond it becomes the brachial artery.

Question 3776. Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts: the pectoralis major, the pectoralis minor, the teres major, or the subscapularis? The answer is the pectoralis minor. The first part lies above the muscle, the second part behind it, and the third part below it. The artery then continues as the brachial artery.

Question 3777. Which is the largest branch of the axillary artery, and into which two arteries does it divide? The answer is the subscapular artery, which divides into the circumflex scapular and the thoracodorsal arteries. It arises from the third part of the axillary artery. The thoracodorsal artery runs to the latissimus dorsi.

Question 3778. Which two branches arise from the second part of the axillary artery: the superior thoracic and the lateral thoracic, the thoracoacromial trunk and the lateral thoracic, the subscapular and the anterior circumflex humeral, or the posterior circumflex humeral and the superior thoracic? The answer is the thoracoacromial trunk and the lateral thoracic artery.

Question 3779. In the armpit, which vessel lies on the medial side of the axillary artery: the axillary vein, the cephalic vein, the basilic vein, or the subscapular vein? The answer is the axillary vein. It lies medial and in front of the artery in the armpit. The two are wrapped together with the cords of the brachial plexus in the axillary sheath.

Question 3780. True or false: the axillary artery and the cords of the brachial plexus share a fibrous sheath in the armpit. The answer is true. The sheath is a continuation of the prevertebral layer of the deep fascia of the neck. It lets the vessels and nerves slide together under the shoulder.

Question 3781. A described dissection of the armpit shows a trunk behind the pectoralis minor dividing into an artery that runs between the two pectoral muscles and one that follows the lower border of the pectoralis minor. Which trunk is shown? The answer is the thoracoacromial trunk, from the second part of the axillary artery.

Question 3782. Name two branches of the third part of the axillary artery, spoken as a list. The answer is the subscapular artery and the posterior circumflex humeral artery. The third part also gives the anterior circumflex humeral artery. The posterior circumflex humeral leaves through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve.

Question 3783. Which of these pairs belongs together: the posterior circumflex humeral artery with the triangular space, the circumflex scapular artery with the quadrangular space, the posterior circumflex humeral artery with the quadrangular space, or the circumflex scapular artery with the radial groove? The answer is the posterior circumflex humeral artery with the quadrangular space.

Question 3784. A constructed illustration: after a described fall the head of the humerus is said to lie in front of and below the socket of the shoulder, and the arm cannot be lifted. Which artery and which nerve are stretched over the displaced bone? The answer is the axillary artery and the axillary nerve, close to the surgical neck of the humerus.

Question 3785. A described fracture crosses the surgical neck of the humerus. Which artery that wraps around the bone at that level is most likely to be torn: the superior thoracic, the lateral thoracic, the anterior circumflex humeral, or the thoracodorsal? The answer is the anterior circumflex humeral artery. It runs forward around the surgical neck, where the break lies.

Question 3786. Which branch of the axillary artery runs down along the lateral border of the pectoralis minor towards the chest wall and supplies the breast? The answer is the lateral thoracic artery. It arises from the second part of the axillary artery. It continues down the side of the chest wall.

Question 3787. A described cross section through the armpit shows the artery with one cord of the brachial plexus on each side of it and a third behind it, and a large vein in front and to its medial side. In which part of the artery was the section taken? The answer is the second part, behind the pectoralis minor.

Question 3788. Which artery does the axillary artery become as it passes the lower border of the teres major: the radial artery, the brachial artery, the subscapular artery, or the profunda brachii? The answer is the brachial artery. It begins at the lower border of the teres major and runs down the medial side of the arm.

Question 3789. Where does the brachial artery begin and end? The answer is at the lower border of the teres major above and the neck of the radius below. It runs down the medial side of the arm in front of the triceps and then in front of the humerus. At the elbow it divides into the radial and the ulnar arteries.

Question 3790. Into which two arteries does the brachial artery divide in the cubital fossa: the radial and the interosseous, the radial and the ulnar, the ulnar and the interosseous, or the brachial and the profunda? The answer is the radial and the ulnar arteries. The division happens at about the neck of the radius.

Question 3791. In the upper part of the arm, on which side of the brachial artery does the median nerve lie, and what happens to that relation lower down? The answer is that the nerve begins lateral to the artery and crosses in front of it to lie medial. It crosses at about the middle of the arm. In the cubital fossa it lies medial to the artery.

Question 3792. Which is the largest branch of the brachial artery, and with which nerve does it run backward into the arm? The answer is the profunda brachii, also called the deep artery of the arm, which accompanies the radial nerve. Both pass back into the groove on the back of the humerus. It joins the network around the elbow.

Question 3793. Which branch of the brachial artery runs down with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle: the profunda brachii, the superior ulnar collateral artery, the inferior ulnar collateral artery, or the nutrient artery of the humerus? The answer is the superior ulnar collateral artery, which follows the ulnar nerve.

Question 3794. A described dissection of the front of the arm shows an artery running down the medial side of the biceps, crossed in front by a nerve at about the middle of the arm, with two veins beside it. Which artery is shown? The answer is the brachial artery. The nerve that crosses it is the median nerve.

Question 3795. A described transverse section of the arm at its middle shows a single bone with muscles around it and an artery lying in the front near the medial edge of the bone. In which compartment and at what depth does the artery lie? The answer is the front compartment, superficial to the brachialis muscle and deep to the deep fascia.

Question 3796. A described section of the limb is said to have been cut across just below the elbow. In what sideways relation do the radial and the ulnar arteries lie as they leave the cubital fossa? The answer is that the radial artery lies laterally and the ulnar artery medially. The radial artery runs down the outer side of the front of the forearm.

Question 3797. Where is the pulse of the brachial artery felt most easily: in the middle of the front of the arm, on the medial side of the arm beside the biceps, behind the medial epicondyle, or in the cubital fossa lateral to the biceps tendon? The answer is on the medial side of the arm beside the biceps, against the humerus.

Question 3798. A constructed illustration: after a described fall on the outstretched hand a child holds the elbow bent, and the hand is pale with no radial pulse felt. Which two structures cross in front of the lower end of the humerus and may be injured? The answer is the brachial artery and the median nerve, both lying close to the bone at the elbow.

Question 3799. Name two collateral branches of the brachial artery that help form the network around the elbow, spoken as a list. The answer is the superior ulnar collateral artery and the inferior ulnar collateral artery. The profunda brachii also sends a branch to that network. These vessels join the recurrent branches of the radial and ulnar arteries.

Question 3800. A described specimen of the front of the elbow shows an artery dividing into two branches at the neck of the radius, one passing deep to the pronator teres and one turning laterally under a muscle that runs to the wrist. Which artery divided? The answer is the brachial artery, dividing into the radial and the ulnar arteries.

To summarize, the aorta leaves the left ventricle as the ascending aorta, gives off the two coronary arteries from the sinuses above the valve, curves as the arch to end at the lower border of the fourth thoracic vertebra, and descends through the chest and the abdomen to divide into the two common iliac arteries at the fourth lumbar vertebra. The arch gives three branches, the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery, and the ligamentum arteriosum hangs from it with the left recurrent laryngeal nerve looping beneath. Each common carotid artery divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into an external carotid artery with eight branches and an internal carotid artery with none in the neck, and each subclavian artery runs in three parts about the anterior scalene muscle, giving the vertebral, internal thoracic and thyrocervical vessels from its first part. The axillary artery continues from the first rib to the teres major and is named in three parts by the pectoralis minor, and the brachial artery carries on from there to divide at the neck of the radius into the radial and the ulnar arteries. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 39 — Arteries, Part Two

This chapter continues the journey from the heart towards the tissues by following the arteries of the arm below the elbow and the arteries of the lower limb from the pelvis to the foot. It covers the radial artery and the ulnar artery with the arches they form in the hand, the common iliac, external iliac and internal iliac arteries, the femoral artery and its deep branch, the popliteal artery behind the knee, and the anterior tibial, posterior tibial and peroneal arteries of the leg. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. Several items describe what an arteriogram or a specimen would show, because a listener cannot look at a picture. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3801. Which artery is the smaller of the two terminal branches of the brachial artery, beginning at the level of the neck of the radius? The answer is the radial artery. It arises in the cubital fossa and runs down the lateral side of the forearm. The ulnar artery is the larger of the two terminal branches.

Question 3802. At the wrist, is the radial pulse felt just medial to the flexor carpi radialis tendon, just lateral to it, deep to the palmaris longus tendon, or behind the ulnar styloid process? The answer is just lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis. The artery rests there on the lower end of the radius, where its wall can be pressed against bone.

Question 3803. Which muscle tendon lies immediately medial to the radial artery in the lower part of the forearm? The answer is the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis. The artery lies between that tendon and the tendon of the brachioradialis. Both tendons can be felt at the wrist, with the artery between them.

Question 3804. Which artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, running over the scaphoid and the trapezium? The answer is the radial artery. It passes between the tendons that bound the snout-shaped hollow on either side. From there it turns into the palm to form the deep palmar arch.

Question 3805. A constructed illustration: a needle is placed in the radial artery at the wrist to sample arterial blood, and blood is obtained. Which structure lies immediately deep to the artery at that point and gives the needle a firm backing? The answer is the lower end of the radius. The artery lies on the bone there, which is why it can be compressed against it.

Question 3806. Which of these branches of the radial artery arises near the elbow and runs upward to join the network around the elbow joint: the radial recurrent artery, the princeps pollicis artery, the dorsal carpal branch, or the superficial palmar branch? The answer is the radial recurrent artery. It ascends between the brachioradialis and the brachialis and joins the profunda brachii artery. The other three lie far distal to the elbow.

Question 3807. A described arteriogram of the hand shows an arch in the palm formed mainly by a vessel that has turned around the lateral border of the wrist, with a smaller contribution from the medial side. Which arch is described? The answer is the deep palmar arch. The radial artery forms most of it, and the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery completes it.

Question 3808. Which artery of the hand arises from the radial artery and runs along the thumb to its tip: the princeps pollicis artery, the radialis indicis artery, the superficial palmar arch, or the anterior interosseous artery? The answer is the princeps pollicis artery. The radialis indicis artery runs to the index finger instead. The anterior interosseous artery lies in the forearm.

Question 3809. True or false: in the upper part of the forearm the radial artery lies deep to the brachioradialis muscle. The answer is true. It passes down under cover of that muscle before it reaches the lateral side of the wrist. In the lower forearm it becomes superficial and easy to feel.

Question 3810. Which nerve runs down the forearm lateral to the radial artery in its middle third and later emerges to supply the skin of the back of the hand? The answer is the superficial branch of the radial nerve. It lies lateral to the artery under cover of the brachioradialis. It becomes superficial near the wrist.

Question 3811. Which arch of the hand is formed mainly by the ulnar artery with a small contribution from the radial artery: the deep palmar arch, the superficial palmar arch, the dorsal carpal arch, or the plantar arch? The answer is the superficial palmar arch. The deep palmar arch is the one formed mainly by the radial artery. The plantar arch belongs to the foot.

Question 3812. A constructed illustration: before a procedure on the hand, a clinician presses on both arteries at the wrist and asks the person to clench and then open the fist. Which two vessels are being compressed in that described test? The answer is the radial artery and the ulnar artery. The test checks that each artery can supply the hand on its own.

Question 3813. Which artery of the forearm is the main vessel of the lateral side and ends in the palm by taking part in the deep palmar arch? The answer is the radial artery. It runs from the cubital fossa along the lateral border of the forearm. Its terminal part turns around the first metacarpal into the deep palm.

Question 3814. Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the anatomical snuffbox, with the radial artery passing deep to it: the extensor pollicis longus tendon, the extensor pollicis brevis tendon, the flexor carpi radialis tendon, or the extensor digitorum tendon? The answer is the extensor pollicis brevis tendon. It lies with the abductor pollicis longus tendon on the lateral side. The extensor pollicis longus tendon forms the medial boundary.

Question 3815. A described transverse section of the lower forearm shows one artery lying on the anterior surface of a bone, close to a tendon that runs to the wrist, with another artery deeper between the muscles. Which artery lies on the bone? The answer is the radial artery. It rests on the lower end of the radius, lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.

Question 3816. Name two branches of the radial artery that lie in the hand, spoken as a list. The answer is the princeps pollicis artery and the radialis indicis artery. The first dorsal metacarpal artery may also be named. All three arise as the radial artery turns into the deep palm.

Question 3817. Which artery, present in a small number of people, arises high in the arm from the axillary or the brachial artery and then follows the usual course of the radial artery in the forearm? The answer is a high origin of the radial artery. The variant matters when a pulse is sought near the elbow. The usual origin is at the neck of the radius.

Question 3818. In a described cross section of the distal forearm, the artery that can be pressed against the radius lies on the lateral side of the section. Which artery is it, and how does it lie relative to the artery on the medial side? The answer is the radial artery, which lies lateral to the ulnar artery. The ulnar artery runs on the medial side beside the ulnar nerve.

Question 3819. Which artery is the larger of the two terminal branches of the brachial artery, beginning at the neck of the radius and passing down the medial side of the forearm? The answer is the ulnar artery. It gives off the common interosseous artery in the upper forearm. It reaches the hand at the wrist beside the ulnar nerve.

Question 3820. In the upper part of its course, which muscle does the ulnar artery pass beneath: the pronator teres, the brachioradialis, the flexor carpi radialis, or the supinator? The answer is the pronator teres. It passes beneath that muscle and then between the two layers of the flexor muscles. The brachioradialis overlies the radial artery instead.

Question 3821. In the lower forearm, which nerve lies immediately medial to the ulnar artery? The answer is the ulnar nerve. The two run together towards the wrist, with the artery on the lateral side of the nerve. Both pass into the hand beside the pisiform bone.

Question 3822. The common interosseous artery divides into which two vessels: the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries, the radial and ulnar recurrent arteries, the princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arteries, or the medial and lateral plantar arteries? The answer is the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries. The anterior one runs down the front of the interosseous membrane. The posterior one passes through the membrane to the back of the forearm.

Question 3823. A constructed illustration: a wound at the medial side of the wrist divides a vessel that lies just lateral to the pisiform bone. Which artery is likely injured, and which nerve lies beside it? The answer is the ulnar artery, with the ulnar nerve beside it. Both pass through the short canal at the wrist on their way into the hand.

Question 3824. A described dissection of the front of the wrist shows a vessel and a nerve passing together superficial to the flexor retinaculum on the medial side. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve. They enter the hand beside the pisiform bone. The median nerve lies deeper, beneath the retinaculum.

Question 3825. Which artery forms the superficial palmar arch in the hand? The answer is the ulnar artery. The arch is completed on the lateral side by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. From the arch arise the common palmar digital arteries. The arch lies just beneath the palmar aponeurosis.

Question 3826. At the wrist, the ulnar artery passes through a short canal. Which structure forms the roof of that canal: the flexor retinaculum, the palmar aponeurosis, the extensor retinaculum, or the abductor pollicis brevis? The answer is the flexor retinaculum. The canal lies between that retinaculum and the pisiform bone. The extensor retinaculum lies on the back of the wrist.

Question 3827. True or false: in the lower forearm the ulnar nerve lies on the medial side of the ulnar artery. The answer is true. The two travel together towards the wrist in that order, nerve medially and artery laterally. They keep the same relation as they pass into the hand beside the pisiform bone.

Question 3828. Which branch of the ulnar artery turns deeply into the palm to complete the deep palmar arch: the deep palmar branch, the superficial palmar branch, the anterior interosseous artery, or the dorsal carpal branch? The answer is the deep palmar branch. It passes between the hypothenar muscles into the deep palm. The superficial palmar branch belongs to the radial artery.

Question 3829. Which of these pairs belongs together: the radial artery with the deep palmar arch, the radial artery with the superficial palmar arch, the ulnar artery with the arch on the top of the foot, or the ulnar artery with the anterior tibial artery? The answer is the radial artery with the deep palmar arch. The ulnar artery forms the superficial palmar arch.

Question 3830. A constructed illustration: a person who uses the heel of the hand as a hammer develops pain and pale fingers on the medial side of the hand. Which artery is compressed against the hook of the hamate bone? The answer is the ulnar artery. It passes through the canal at the wrist against that bone. The illustration is a teaching example, and management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 3831. A described specimen shows an artery in the upper forearm dividing into two vessels that run along the front and the back of the membrane between the two forearm bones. Which artery has divided? The answer is the common interosseous artery, dividing into the anterior and the posterior interosseous arteries. It is a branch of the ulnar artery.

Question 3832. In the lower forearm, which muscle lies immediately deep to the ulnar artery and separates it from the interosseous membrane? The answer is the pronator quadratus. The artery rests on that muscle as it approaches the wrist. The flexor digitorum profundus lies deep to the artery higher up.

Question 3833. Which artery runs down the back of the forearm between the superficial and the deep extensor muscles, accompanied by the posterior interosseous nerve? The answer is the posterior interosseous artery. It reaches the back of the forearm through the opening between the oblique cord and the interosseous membrane. It is a branch of the common interosseous artery.

Question 3834. Which artery runs down the front of the interosseous membrane between the flexor digitorum profundus and the flexor pollicis longus? The answer is the anterior interosseous artery. It is a branch of the common interosseous artery. It ends in the lower forearm by passing behind the pronator quadratus.

Question 3835. Name two arteries of the forearm that arise from the ulnar artery, spoken as a list. The answer is the common interosseous artery and the anterior ulnar recurrent artery. The posterior ulnar recurrent artery may also be named. All three arise in the upper part of the forearm.

Question 3836. At which level does the abdominal aorta divide into the two common iliac arteries? The answer is the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra. The division lies a little to the left of the midline. The small median sacral artery continues downward from that point.

Question 3837. Into which two vessels does each common iliac artery divide: the external and internal iliac arteries, the femoral and popliteal arteries, the renal and suprarenal arteries, or the obturator and gluteal arteries? The answer is the external and internal iliac arteries. The division lies in front of the sacroiliac joint. The obturator and gluteal arteries are branches of the internal iliac artery.

Question 3838. Which ligament does the external iliac artery pass beneath as it leaves the pelvis to enter the thigh? The answer is the inguinal ligament. The artery runs along the pelvic brim and then turns forward under the ligament. Beyond it, the vessel is named the femoral artery.

Question 3839. Into which two divisions does the internal iliac artery split after its short course into the pelvis? The answer is an anterior division and a posterior division. The posterior division supplies the buttock and the back of the pelvic wall. The anterior division supplies the pelvic viscera and the perineum.

Question 3840. Which of these arteries arises from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery: the superior gluteal artery, the obturator artery, the internal pudendal artery, or the inferior vesical artery? The answer is the superior gluteal artery. The iliolumbar and the lateral sacral arteries arise there too. The other three belong to the anterior division.

Question 3841. Which artery leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen and supplies the muscles on the medial side of the thigh: the internal pudendal artery, the obturator artery, the inferior gluteal artery, or the middle rectal artery? The answer is the obturator artery. It also sends a small branch to the head of the femur. The internal pudendal artery leaves through the greater sciatic foramen.

Question 3842. A described arteriogram of the pelvis shows a short trunk dividing into an anterior and a posterior group of branches, with one branch passing backward through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle. Which artery is that branch? The answer is the inferior gluteal artery. The superior gluteal artery leaves above the piriformis. Both come from the internal iliac artery.

Question 3843. A described arteriogram shows a vessel running upward and laterally towards the anterior abdominal wall above the inguinal ligament. Which artery is shown, and from which vessel does it arise? The answer is the inferior epigastric artery, arising from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament. It ascends behind the rectus abdominis muscle.

Question 3844. Besides the inferior epigastric artery, which other named branch does the external iliac artery give just above the inguinal ligament: the deep circumflex iliac artery, the superior gluteal artery, the middle sacral artery, or the superior vesical artery? The answer is the deep circumflex iliac artery. It runs laterally along the iliac crest. The other three arise from the aorta or from the internal iliac artery.

Question 3845. True or false: the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery after it passes beneath the inguinal ligament. The answer is true. The change of name happens as the vessel crosses the ligament. The femoral artery then enters the femoral triangle of the thigh.

Question 3846. Which tube crosses in front of the common iliac artery at the point where that artery divides? The answer is the ureter. It crosses the vessel at the pelvic brim as it descends towards the bladder. The ureter lies in front of the artery at that crossing.

Question 3847. Which of these pairs belongs together: the superior gluteal artery with the buttock, the obturator artery with the foot, the internal pudendal artery with the kidney, or the iliolumbar artery with the hand? The answer is the superior gluteal artery with the buttock. It leaves the pelvis above the piriformis and supplies the gluteal muscles. The obturator artery supplies the medial thigh instead.

Question 3848. Which artery passes out of the pelvis above the piriformis muscle through the greater sciatic foramen: the inferior gluteal artery, the superior gluteal artery, the internal pudendal artery, or the obturator artery? The answer is the superior gluteal artery. The inferior gluteal artery leaves below the piriformis. The internal pudendal artery leaves below it as well.

Question 3849. A constructed illustration: after a severe pelvic injury a person becomes pale and the pelvis feels unstable, and bleeding is thought to come from branches of the internal iliac artery. Which vessel supplies most of the injured structures in that described region? The answer is the internal iliac artery, whose branches supply the pelvic walls and the viscera. Control of such bleeding belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3850. Which small unpaired artery arises from the back of the abdominal aorta just above its division into the two common iliac arteries? The answer is the median sacral artery. It runs down the front of the sacrum. It is the continuation of the embryonic dorsal aorta.

Question 3851. A described cross section of the pelvis shows two large vessels lying against the medial wall of the iliac fossa, one on each side, with a tube crossing in front of each of them. Which vessels are shown? The answer is the two common iliac arteries and their divisions. The ureters cross them at the pelvic brim. The external iliac artery continues towards the thigh.

Question 3852. After the internal iliac artery is tied off in an emergency, blood still reaches the pelvic organs. Through which route does it arrive: through the median sacral and the superior rectal arteries, through the pulmonary artery, through the portal vein, or through the thoracic duct? The answer is through the median sacral and the superior rectal arteries, which anastomose with the internal iliac branches. The external iliac branches also contribute.

Question 3853. Which artery is the direct continuation of the external iliac artery after it passes beneath the inguinal ligament? The answer is the femoral artery. It begins at the mid-inguinal point and enters the femoral triangle. Its pulse can be felt there against the head of the femur.

Question 3854. In the femoral triangle, in what order do the femoral nerve, the femoral artery and the femoral vein lie from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein; artery, vein, nerve; vein, artery, nerve; or nerve, vein, artery? The answer is nerve, artery, vein. The nerve lies outside the femoral sheath. The artery and the vein lie inside it.

Question 3855. Which large vein lies immediately medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle? The answer is the femoral vein. It lies inside the same fibrous sheath as the artery.
