The femoral nerve lies lateral to the artery and outside the sheath. Above the inguinal ligament the same vein is named the external iliac vein.

Question 3856. Which large branch of the femoral artery arises about 4 centimeters below the inguinal ligament and supplies the deep muscles of the thigh: the profunda femoris artery, the inferior epigastric artery, the popliteal artery, or the obturator artery? The answer is the profunda femoris artery, also called the deep artery of the thigh. It gives the medial and the lateral circumflex femoral arteries.

Question 3857. A constructed illustration: a long catheter is passed into the femoral artery at the groin so that the heart can be examined from within. Which artery has been entered, and what is the name of the vessel at that point? The answer is the femoral artery, entered at the mid-inguinal point. It continues upward as the external iliac artery. The procedure itself belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 3858. A described arteriogram of the upper thigh shows a main trunk dividing into a vessel that continues downward and a large deep branch that turns backward among the muscles. Which two vessels are shown? The answer is the femoral artery and the profunda femoris artery. The deep branch is the main supply of the thigh muscles. It also gives the circumflex femoral arteries.

Question 3859. Which artery supplies the head and neck of the femur through small branches that run along the neck within the retinacula: the medial circumflex femoral artery, the lateral circumflex femoral artery, the obturator artery, or the inferior gluteal artery? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery. Interruption of them is a recognized cause of avascular change after a fracture.

Question 3860. True or false: the femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the pubic symphysis and the anterior superior iliac spine. The answer is true. The artery can be pressed against the head of the femur there. The mid-inguinal point lies a little medial to the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.

Question 3861. Through which opening in a muscle does the femoral artery leave the adductor canal to become the popliteal artery? The answer is the adductor hiatus, the opening in the adductor magnus muscle. The artery passes through it into the back of the knee. The femoral vein passes through the same opening.

Question 3862. A described cross section of the thigh shows a large vessel lying in a tunnel whose roof is formed by a long strap-like muscle and whose walls are formed by muscles on either side. Which artery lies in that tunnel? The answer is the femoral artery in the adductor canal. The saphenous nerve and the femoral vein lie with it.

Question 3863. Which artery of the lower thigh, a branch of the femoral artery or of the profunda femoris, accompanies the saphenous nerve and helps supply the knee joint: the descending genicular artery, the inferior epigastric artery, the middle genicular artery, or the anterior tibial artery? The answer is the descending genicular artery. It arises just above the adductor hiatus. The middle genicular artery comes from the popliteal artery instead.

Question 3864. Which nerve lies in the adductor canal beside the femoral artery and supplies the vastus medialis muscle? The answer is the nerve to vastus medialis. The saphenous nerve also lies in the canal. Both are branches of the femoral nerve. The artery, the vein and the two nerves run together towards the opening in the adductor magnus.

Question 3865. Which of these pairs belongs together: the profunda femoris artery with the deep muscles of the thigh, the inferior epigastric artery with the foot, the popliteal artery with the forearm, or the dorsalis pedis artery with the buttock? The answer is the profunda femoris artery with the deep muscles of the thigh. It is the main artery of that compartment.

Question 3866. Which branches of the profunda femoris artery pierce the adductor magnus muscle to reach the back of the thigh and supply its muscles? The answer is the perforating arteries, usually three in number. The third of them is the continuation of the profunda itself. They form an important collateral path when the femoral artery is blocked above them.

Question 3867. A described dissection of the front of the thigh shows three structures lying in a row from lateral to medial inside a fibrous sheath, with a fourth structure just outside the sheath on the lateral side. Which four structures are described? The answer is the femoral nerve outside the sheath, then the femoral artery, the femoral vein and the femoral canal inside it.

Question 3868. In a described cross section of the upper thigh, the femoral vein lies medial to the femoral artery and the femoral nerve lies lateral to the artery. Which of the three occupies the most lateral position? The answer is the femoral nerve. From lateral to medial the order is nerve, artery and vein. The femoral canal is the most medial space of the group.

Question 3869. Which artery does the femoral artery become after it passes through the adductor hiatus: the popliteal artery, the anterior tibial artery, the profunda femoris artery, or the obturator artery? The answer is the popliteal artery. The name changes as the vessel enters the back of the knee. The anterior tibial artery is one of the two branches into which the popliteal artery divides.

Question 3870. A constructed illustration: a deep cut in the femoral triangle bleeds heavily and the pulse beyond it is lost. Which artery is most likely divided, and why is the bleeding so brisk? The answer is the femoral artery. It is large and lies close to the skin at the mid-inguinal point. Control of such bleeding belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3871. Which artery begins at the adductor hiatus and ends at the lower border of the popliteus muscle? The answer is the popliteal artery. It runs down the back of the knee behind the joint. It divides into the anterior and the posterior tibial arteries.

Question 3872. Which structure lies immediately in front of the popliteal artery: the femur and the capsule of the knee joint, the popliteal vein, the tibial nerve, or the small saphenous vein? The answer is the femur and the capsule of the knee joint. The artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa. The vein and the nerve lie behind it.

Question 3873. Which vein lies immediately behind the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa? The answer is the popliteal vein. It lies superficial to the artery, that is, nearer the skin. The tibial nerve lies behind the vein. Artery, vein and nerve lie one behind another against the bone.

Question 3874. Which branch of the popliteal artery pierces the oblique popliteal ligament to reach the interior of the knee joint: the middle genicular artery, the superior medial genicular artery, the anterior tibial artery, or the sural artery? The answer is the middle genicular artery. It supplies the cruciate ligaments and the synovial membrane. The sural arteries supply the heads of the gastrocnemius.

Question 3875. A described radiograph of the lower thigh shows a fracture line just above the knee with the lower fragment displaced backward. Which vessel is at risk because it lies against the bone at that level? The answer is the popliteal artery. It lies directly against the lower end of the femur and the knee capsule. The displacement can stretch or tear it.

Question 3876. A described arteriogram of the knee region shows five small branches wrapping around the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia and joining one another in a network. What is that network called? The answer is the genicular anastomosis around the knee. It links the popliteal artery with branches of the femoral artery above.

Question 3877. At which level does the popliteal artery end by dividing: at the lower border of the popliteus muscle, at the middle of the thigh, at the ankle, or at the neck of the fibula? The answer is at the lower border of the popliteus muscle. There it divides into the anterior and the posterior tibial arteries. The level lies a little below the knee joint.

Question 3878. True or false: the popliteal artery is the most superficial structure in the popliteal fossa. The answer is false. It is the deepest structure there, lying against the bone and the joint capsule. The popliteal vein and then the tibial nerve lie behind it.

Question 3879. A constructed illustration: a knee is dislocated backward and the pulse at the ankle disappears. Why is the popliteal artery especially vulnerable in that described injury? The answer is that the artery is tethered above at the adductor hiatus and below at the lower border of the popliteus, so it cannot move with the joint. The injury is described only as an illustration. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 3880. Which of these pairs belongs together: the popliteal artery with the back of the knee, the popliteal artery with the front of the elbow, the popliteal artery with the palm of the hand, or the popliteal artery with the sole of the foot? The answer is the popliteal artery with the back of the knee. The brachial artery lies at the front of the elbow.

Question 3881. Which terminal branch of the popliteal artery passes forward through the opening in the upper part of the interosseous membrane? The answer is the anterior tibial artery. It reaches the front of the leg through that opening. The posterior tibial artery stays behind.

Question 3882. In some people the popliteal artery divides into its two terminal branches far above the knee. Which vessel then lies in an unusual place: the anterior tibial artery, the dorsalis pedis artery, the medial plantar artery, or the peroneal artery? The answer is the anterior tibial artery, which may then run in front of the popliteus muscle. This high division is a normal variant.

Question 3883. A described dissection of the back of the knee shows a diamond-shaped space bounded above by two muscles from the thigh and below by the two heads of a muscle of the calf, with vessels and nerves lying in fat within it. Which space is described? The answer is the popliteal fossa. Its floor is the femur, the knee capsule and the popliteus.

Question 3884. Which muscle forms the lower boundary of the course of the popliteal artery, the muscle at whose lower border the artery divides? The answer is the popliteus. It lies in the floor of the popliteal fossa. The artery ends at its lower border.

Question 3885. Name two branches of the popliteal artery that take part in the network around the knee, spoken as a list. The answer is the superior medial genicular artery and the inferior lateral genicular artery. The middle genicular artery and the other genicular arteries may also be named. All of them join the anastomosis around the joint.

Question 3886. Which artery begins at the lower border of the popliteus muscle, passes through the interosseous membrane and runs down the front of the leg? The answer is the anterior tibial artery. It is the smaller of the two terminal branches of the popliteal artery. It ends at the ankle as the dorsalis pedis artery.

Question 3887. Which artery continues the anterior tibial artery across the front of the ankle onto the top of the foot: the dorsalis pedis artery, the posterior tibial artery, the peroneal artery, or the medial plantar artery? The answer is the dorsalis pedis artery. Its pulse can be felt on the top of the foot. The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus instead.

Question 3888. In the lower part of the leg, between which two tendons does the anterior tibial artery lie as it approaches the ankle? The answer is between the tendons of the extensor hallucis longus and the extensor digitorum longus. Higher up it lies between the tibialis anterior and the extensor digitorum longus. The deep peroneal nerve runs beside it.

Question 3889. Where is the posterior tibial pulse normally felt: behind the medial malleolus, in front of the lateral malleolus, on the top of the foot, or in the popliteal fossa? The answer is behind the medial malleolus. The artery lies there between the malleolus and the tendo calcaneus. The pulse on the top of the foot belongs to the dorsalis pedis artery.

Question 3890. A constructed illustration: a fracture of the shaft of the tibia is complicated by a tense and painful anterior compartment of the leg. Which artery of that compartment is compressed? The answer is the anterior tibial artery. It runs in the anterior compartment with the deep peroneal nerve. Management of the compartment belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3891. A described arteriogram of the lower leg shows one vessel descending behind the medial malleolus and another passing forward above the ankle. Which two arteries are shown? The answer is the posterior tibial artery and the anterior tibial artery. The posterior one continues into the sole of the foot. The anterior one continues as the dorsalis pedis artery.

Question 3892. Which artery arises from the posterior tibial artery and runs down beside the fibula, giving a perforating branch above the ankle: the peroneal artery, the anterior tibial artery, the obturator artery, or the descending genicular artery? The answer is the peroneal artery, also called the fibular artery. It is the largest branch of the posterior tibial artery. Its perforating branch pierces the interosseous membrane above the ankle.

Question 3893. Which of these pairs belongs together: the posterior tibial artery with the sole of the foot, the posterior tibial artery with the back of the hand, the anterior tibial artery with the buttock, or the peroneal artery with the face? The answer is the posterior tibial artery with the sole of the foot. It divides into the medial and the lateral plantar arteries.

Question 3894. Which artery of the leg can be identified in a described dissection by its course beside the fibula and by a terminal branch that pierces the interosseous membrane above the ankle? The answer is the peroneal artery. Its perforating branch joins the network at the ankle and can replace the dorsalis pedis artery. That variant explains why a foot pulse may be felt when the anterior tibial artery is small.

Question 3895. A constructed illustration: after a crush injury of the leg the anterior compartment is tight, the deep peroneal nerve is failing, and yet the dorsalis pedis pulse is still felt. Why can that be? The answer is that the peroneal artery may keep the foot supplied through its perforating branch while the anterior tibial artery is compressed. A pulse therefore does not exclude raised pressure in the compartment.

Question 3896. In some people the dorsalis pedis pulse cannot be felt at all. Which explanation fits best: the artery may be replaced by the perforating branch of the peroneal artery, it is absent in everyone with heart disease, it appears only during exercise, or the anterior tibial artery never forms? The answer is replacement by the perforating branch of the peroneal artery. That replacement is a normal variant.

Question 3897. In the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus, which structure lies between the tendons of the flexor digitorum longus and the flexor hallucis longus? The answer is the posterior tibial artery, with the tibial nerve beside it. The tunnel is roofed by the flexor retinaculum. The artery divides within it into the medial and the lateral plantar arteries.

Question 3898. A described cross section of the calf shows a deep vessel lying behind the tibia on the posterior surface of a muscle that covers the interosseous membrane, with the soleus and the gastrocnemius behind it. Which artery is shown? The answer is the posterior tibial artery. It runs downward deep to the soleus on the tibialis posterior. The peroneal artery lies nearer the fibula.

Question 3899. Into which two arteries does the posterior tibial artery divide in the sole of the foot: the medial and lateral plantar arteries, the dorsalis pedis and arcuate arteries, the anterior and posterior tibial arteries, or the peroneal and sural arteries? The answer is the medial and lateral plantar arteries. The lateral plantar artery is the larger and helps form the plantar arch.

Question 3900. Which artery completes the plantar arch in the sole of the foot by joining the lateral plantar artery: the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery, the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery, the anterior tibial artery, or the medial plantar artery? The answer is the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery. It passes into the sole between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.

To summarize, the radial and the ulnar arteries continue the brachial artery below the elbow, the radial running on the lateral side of the forearm to form the deep palmar arch and the ulnar crossing to the medial side to form the superficial palmar arch. The abdominal aorta divides at the fourth lumbar vertebra into the common iliac arteries, each of which divides into an external iliac artery that becomes the femoral artery and an internal iliac artery whose branches supply the pelvic walls, the pelvic viscera and the buttock. The femoral artery passes through the femoral triangle and the adductor canal to become the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus, and the popliteal artery, the deepest structure behind the knee, ends at the lower border of the popliteus as the anterior and the posterior tibial arteries. The anterior tibial artery reaches the front of the leg through the interosseous membrane and continues as the dorsalis pedis artery, while the posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus to divide into the plantar arteries and gives the peroneal artery beside the fibula. At the groin the femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery and the femoral vein medial to it, and behind the knee the popliteal vein lies between the artery and the tibial nerve. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 40 — Veins

Veins return blood to the heart under low pressure, and the great veins that drain the body are mapped as carefully as the arteries beside them. This chapter follows that system in order: the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava with its abdominal tributaries, the portal circulation to the liver, and the jugular and subclavian veins in the neck. It holds one hundred questions, and every question states its answer at once and explains why it is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 3901. Which large vein is formed behind the first right costal cartilage and returns blood from the head, the neck, the upper limbs and the chest: the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, the portal vein, or the azygos vein? The answer is the superior vena cava. It is formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins and ends in the upper part of the right atrium. The azygos vein joins its back.

Question 3902. Name the chamber of the heart that the superior vena cava enters, and give the level of its opening. The answer is the right atrium, at the third right costal cartilage. The opening lies in the upper and posterior part of the chamber, and the blood then passes through the tricuspid valve.

Question 3903. A described radiograph of the chest, taken with the person lying flat, shows a vertical band forming the right border of the upper mediastinum, with the trachea to its left. Which structure forms that band, and why does it widen when the heart fails? The answer is the superior vena cava, which forms that border in the supine position and widens easily because its wall is thin and it has no valve.

Question 3904. The superior vena cava is about how long: 3 centimeters, 7 centimeters, 12 centimeters, or 17 centimeters? The answer is about 7 centimeters. Half of that length lies in the superior mediastinum and half in the middle mediastinum. The vein runs from the first right costal cartilage to the third.

Question 3905. Which vein arches forward over the root of the right lung and ends in the back of the superior vena cava? The answer is the azygos vein. It drains the posterior chest wall and the posterior intercostal spaces on both sides. It ends at the second right costal cartilage.

Question 3906. Which structure lies immediately behind the superior vena cava in the upper chest, and which nerve runs down its lateral side? The answer is the right main bronchus, with the right phrenic nerve beside it. The phrenic nerve passes in front of the root of the right lung, and the vagus nerve lies further back.

Question 3907. Which statement about the superior vena cava is correct: it lies to the left of the ascending aorta, it crosses in front of the trachea, it lies to the right of the ascending aorta, or it carries a valve? The answer is that it lies to the right of the ascending aorta. The trachea and the esophagus lie behind it, and the valve at the atrial opening belongs to the inferior vena cava.

Question 3908. A described venogram of the upper chest shows a wide channel on the right that receives a smaller vein arcing over the hilum of the lung. Which two veins are shown, and at what level do they meet? The answer is the superior vena cava and the azygos vein, meeting at the second right costal cartilage. The arch of the azygos vein passes over the root of the right lung.

Question 3909. In a described illustration, a person has swelling of the face and the neck with distended veins over the upper chest. Which vessel is obstructed: the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, the portal vein, or the splenic vein? The answer is the superior vena cava. Obstruction above the heart raises the pressure in the veins of the head, the neck and the arms, and blood returns by the azygos system.

Question 3910. Which two veins unite to form the superior vena cava, and where does that union take place? The answer is the right and left brachiocephalic veins, uniting behind the first right costal cartilage. Each is formed behind a sternoclavicular joint. The right one is nearly vertical, and the left one crosses the midline.

Question 3911. A constructed illustration: after a procedure in the upper chest, a described radiograph shows a widened mediastinum on the right, and the face is puffy. Which vein is compressed, and what does the widened shadow represent? The answer is the superior vena cava, and the shadow is the distended vein itself. The vein lies against the sternum, so its swelling shows on the film.

Question 3912. The left brachiocephalic vein crosses the midline in front of which structures: the trachea and the branches of the aortic arch, the esophagus and the descending aorta, the thoracic duct alone, or the root of the left lung? The answer is the trachea and the branches of the aortic arch. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise from the arch behind the vein.

Question 3913. A described cross section of the upper chest shows a vein lying in front of the trachea and behind the sternum, crossing the midline to join its fellow. Which vein is described, and what lies immediately in front of it? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein, with the thymus in front of it in the child. It is the longer of the two because it must cross the midline.

Question 3914. Which nerve descends in front of the root of the right lung and lies lateral to the superior vena cava? The answer is the right phrenic nerve, on its way to the diaphragm. The right vagus nerve lies behind the hilum instead, close to the trachea and the esophagus.

Question 3915. Which structure lies lateral to the superior vena cava in the middle mediastinum, and which lies medial to it? The answer is the right mediastinal pleura laterally and the ascending aorta medially. The right lung lies against the outer side of the vein, and the pericardium covers part of its lower portion.

Question 3916. The valve that guards the opening of a great vein into the right atrium is a remnant of which structure: the sinus venosus, the ductus venosus, the truncus arteriosus, or the septum primum? The answer is the sinus venosus. That valve belongs to the opening of the inferior vena cava. The superior vena cava has no valve at all.

Question 3917. True or false: the superior vena cava opens into the left atrium. The answer is false. It opens into the right atrium. The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins from the lungs, and the two atria are separated by the interatrial septum.

Question 3918. Blood in the superior vena cava has just come from which of these: the lungs, the liver, the head and the upper limbs, or the kidneys? The answer is the head and the upper limbs. The superior vena cava drains everything above the diaphragm, while the hepatic veins drain the liver and the pulmonary veins drain the lungs.

Question 3919. Which vein drains the second, third and fourth intercostal spaces of the left side into the left brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the left superior intercostal vein, which runs across the arch of the aorta. On the right side the same spaces drain into the azygos vein.

Question 3920. A described dissection of the upper mediastinum shows a long vein lying to the left of the trachea and crossing in front of the branches of the aortic arch. Which vein is it, and which two arteries does it cross? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein, crossing the left common carotid and the left subclavian arteries. It then joins the right brachiocephalic vein.

Question 3921. The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of which two veins, and at what level does that union lie: the two common iliac veins, the two renal veins, the two external iliac veins, or the two hepatic veins? The answer is the two common iliac veins. They unite in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra, to the right of the aortic bifurcation.

Question 3922. A constructed illustration: a described scan after an injury shows blood collecting behind the peritoneum on the right side of the lumbar spine. Which large vein lies in that position, and what is its relation to the aorta? The answer is the inferior vena cava, which lies to the right of the aorta and in front of the vertebral column. Its thin wall distends rather than contracts when torn.

Question 3923. Which vein returns blood from the lower half of the body to the right atrium, and on which side of the abdominal aorta does it ascend? The answer is the inferior vena cava, which ascends on the right of the aorta. It is the widest vein in the body, lying in front of the vertebral column behind the peritoneum.

Question 3924. The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at the level of which vertebra: the eighth thoracic, the tenth thoracic, the twelfth thoracic, or the second lumbar? The answer is the eighth thoracic vertebra. Its opening lies in the central tendon, next to the right phrenic nerve, while the aorta passes behind the diaphragm at the twelfth thoracic vertebra.

Question 3925. Which structure crosses in front of the inferior vena cava in the upper part of the abdomen, and what lies behind the vein? The answer is the third part of the duodenum, with the head of the pancreas beside it. Behind the vein lie the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae and the right psoas muscle.

Question 3926. A described transverse section of the abdomen at the second lumbar vertebra shows a wide thin-walled vein to the right of the midline, in front of a vertebral body. Which vein is shown, and what lies on its left? The answer is the inferior vena cava, with the abdominal aorta on its left. The right psoas muscle lies behind it and the peritoneum in front.

Question 3927. Which veins open into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm and carry blood away from the liver? The answer is the hepatic veins. They are the largest tributaries of the vein and they open into it against the bare area of the liver. Blood reaches the liver by the portal vein and leaves by these veins.

Question 3928. Which renal vein is longer and crosses in front of the aorta: the right, the left, both equally, or neither? The answer is the left renal vein, passing in front of the aorta below the superior mesenteric artery. The right renal vein is short and opens directly into the inferior vena cava.

Question 3929. True or false: the left suprarenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The answer is false. It drains into the left renal vein, and only the right suprarenal vein opens directly into the inferior vena cava. The left gonadal vein behaves in the same way.

Question 3930. A constructed illustration: a described scan shows a mass at the back of the upper abdomen pressing on the vein that ascends to the right of the aorta. Which vein is compressed, and which channels may enlarge around it? The answer is the inferior vena cava, with the azygos and lumbar veins enlarging as collaterals. Blood then reaches the heart by the veins of the back.

Question 3931. Which of these statements is correct: the right gonadal vein ends in the inferior vena cava, the left gonadal vein ends in the inferior vena cava, the right suprarenal vein ends in the right renal vein, or the inferior phrenic veins end in the portal vein? The answer is that the right gonadal vein ends in the inferior vena cava. On the left, those veins end in the left renal vein.

Question 3932. Which vein receives the left gonadal vein and the whole of the left suprarenal vein? The answer is the left renal vein, which crosses in front of the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava. On the right side those veins open directly into the inferior vena cava, so the left renal vein is longer.

Question 3933. A described radiograph taken after contrast has been injected into a vein of the leg shows a wide channel running up the right side of the lumbar spine and through the diaphragm. Which vein is shown, and where does it enter the chest? The answer is the inferior vena cava, which enters through the central tendon at the eighth thoracic vertebra.

Question 3934. The right renal artery has which relation to the inferior vena cava: it passes in front of it, behind it, above it, or through it? The answer is that it passes behind it. The right renal artery is longer than the left, and the right gonadal artery crosses in front of the vein instead.

Question 3935. Which structures lie immediately behind the inferior vena cava as it ascends through the abdomen, and which crosses in front of it? The answer is the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae and the right psoas muscle, with the third part of the duodenum crossing in front. The right sympathetic trunk also lies behind the vein.

Question 3936. Which vein connects the lumbar veins with the azygos system on the right side? The answer is the ascending lumbar vein, which runs up in front of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae. It joins the azygos vein above the diaphragm, linking the inferior vena cava with the chest.

Question 3937. Which of these pairs belongs together: the right gonadal vein with the left renal vein, the left suprarenal vein with the left renal vein, the right suprarenal vein with the right renal vein, or the left gonadal vein with the inferior vena cava? The answer is the left suprarenal vein with the left renal vein. On the right the corresponding veins open straight into the inferior vena cava.

Question 3938. How many veins unite to form the inferior vena cava, and where does that union lie: two, in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra; two, in front of the first lumbar vertebra; three, at the sacral promontory; or one, at the aortic bifurcation? The answer is two, in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra. That union lies behind the right common iliac artery.

Question 3939. A described cross section of the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus shows a wide vein on the right side of the vertebral column. Which vein is it, and what lies between it and the left side of the section? The answer is the inferior vena cava, with the aorta and the lumbar vertebrae between it and the left side.

Question 3940. A constructed illustration: a described scan of a thin person shows a vein compressed between the aorta behind and a branch of the aorta in front. Which vein is compressed, and which two vessels surround it? The answer is the left renal vein, caught between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. It is longer than the right vein and crosses in front of the aorta.

Question 3941. Which vein drains the under surface of the diaphragm on the right side into the inferior vena cava? The answer is the right inferior phrenic vein. The left one opens into the left renal vein or into the inferior vena cava. Both run beside the phrenic nerves.

Question 3942. In the upper abdomen the inferior vena cava lies behind which structure: the peritoneum, the right psoas muscle, the lumbar vertebrae, or the right crus of the diaphragm? The answer is the peritoneum, because the vein is retroperitoneal. The other three lie behind it, and the duodenum and pancreas lie in front of it.

Question 3943. Which veins drain the posterior abdominal wall into the inferior vena cava, and with which system do they connect above the diaphragm? The answer is the lumbar veins, which connect through the ascending lumbar veins with the azygos system. There are usually four pairs, running behind the aorta and the inferior vena cava.

Question 3944. A described radiograph of the abdomen in a person lying flat shows the right border of a wide vein over the right side of the lumbar spine, with a smaller vein ending in it from the right. Which veins are shown, and what does the smaller one carry? The answer is the inferior vena cava and a right lumbar vein, which carries blood from the muscles of the back.

Question 3945. The hepatic veins differ from the other tributaries of the inferior vena cava in which way: their blood has already passed through a second set of capillaries, they carry oxygenated blood, they open into the left atrium, or they have valves? The answer is that their blood has passed through a second set of capillaries, having come from the gut by way of the liver. The other tributaries return blood after one passage.

Question 3946. Which vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein? The answer is the portal vein, which carries blood from the gut, the spleen and the pancreas to the liver. It runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum and has no valves.

Question 3947. True or false: blood from the gut passes through two sets of capillaries before it reaches the heart. The answer is true. It passes first through the capillaries of the gut wall and then through the sinusoids of the liver. The hepatic veins then carry it to the inferior vena cava.

Question 3948. In the free edge of the lesser omentum the portal vein lies in which relation to the bile duct and the proper hepatic artery: behind both, in front of both, between the two, or below both? The answer is behind both, with the bile duct in front and to its right and the artery in front and to its left. The three form the portal triad.

Question 3949. A constructed illustration: a person vomits blood and a described examination shows enlarged veins at the lower end of the esophagus. Which vein has enlarged, and why? The answer is the left gastric vein, whose esophageal tributaries have enlarged because the pressure in the portal system has risen. Those tributaries drain into the azygos system and reach the superior vena cava.

Question 3950. A described venogram of the abdomen shows a wide vein running up from behind the pancreas toward the liver, with a smaller vein joining the system behind the pancreas. Which veins are shown, and where do they meet? The answer is the portal vein and the inferior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic vein behind the body of the pancreas.

Question 3951. Which vein carries blood from the spleen to the portal vein, and where does it run? The answer is the splenic vein, which runs behind the body and tail of the pancreas. It joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas and receives the short gastric veins.

Question 3952. Name the two veins whose union forms the portal vein, spoken as a list. The answer is the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein, which meet behind the neck of the pancreas. The inferior mesenteric vein often joins the splenic vein first, just before that meeting.

Question 3953. Which vein lies immediately to the right of the superior mesenteric artery in the root of the mesentery? The answer is the superior mesenteric vein, which ascends in front of the third part of the duodenum. The artery lies to its left, and the vein ends behind the neck of the pancreas.

Question 3954. Which of these pairs belongs together: the left gastric vein with the azygos system, the superior rectal vein with the internal jugular vein, the paraumbilical veins with the renal veins, or the splenic vein with the right atrium? The answer is the left gastric vein with the azygos system, by way of the veins of the esophagus. That connection opens when portal pressure rises.

Question 3955. Which of these veins carries blood toward the liver: the superior mesenteric vein, the inferior vena cava, the hepatic vein, or the renal vein? The answer is the superior mesenteric vein, which brings blood from the small intestine and the right half of the colon. The hepatic veins carry blood away from the liver.

Question 3956. Which vein drains the upper part of the anal canal into the portal system, and which veins drain the lower part into the systemic system? The answer is the superior rectal vein above and the middle and inferior rectal veins below. The two sets meet in the wall of the anal canal.

Question 3957. A described section through the lower end of the esophagus shows dilated veins in the wall beneath the mucosa, linking veins above with veins below. Which two venous systems meet there, and why do the veins dilate? The answer is the portal system, by way of the left gastric vein, and the systemic system, by way of the esophageal veins. They dilate when portal pressure rises.

Question 3958. The paraumbilical veins run in the round ligament of the liver and connect the portal vein with which veins of the abdominal wall: the superficial epigastric veins, the lumbar veins, the intercostal veins, or the internal thoracic veins? The answer is the superficial epigastric veins. When portal pressure rises they enlarge around the umbilicus, a pattern called a caput medusae.

Question 3959. True or false: the portal vein has valves that keep blood flowing toward the liver. The answer is false. The portal vein and its tributaries have no valves, so blood can flow either way when the pressure changes. That is why the connections with the systemic veins open.

Question 3960. A constructed illustration: a person with long-standing liver disease has dilated veins at the lower end of the esophagus, around the umbilicus and at the anal canal. How many places where portal and systemic veins meet are involved? The answer is three such places. At each one a portal tributary meets a systemic tributary, and a fourth route lies behind the peritoneum.

Question 3961. Which vein drains the upper part of the rectum into the portal system? The answer is the superior rectal vein, a tributary of the inferior mesenteric vein, which carries the blood to the splenic and portal veins. The lower rectum drains into the systemic veins instead.

Question 3962. A described specimen of the liver shows three structures entering the hilum, and the widest lies behind the other two. Which structure is the widest, and what are the other two? The answer is the portal vein, with the bile duct and the proper hepatic artery in front of it. All three run in the free edge of the lesser omentum.

Question 3963. Blood from the descending colon reaches the liver by which route: the superior mesenteric vein, the inferior mesenteric vein and then the splenic vein, the hepatic vein, or the lumbar veins? The answer is the inferior mesenteric vein and then the splenic vein. It drains the descending colon, the sigmoid colon and the upper rectum, and usually joins the splenic vein behind the pancreas.

Question 3964. Which vein runs immediately behind the body of the pancreas, and which vein joins it there? The answer is the splenic vein, which receives the inferior mesenteric vein and then joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas. It drains the spleen, the stomach and the pancreas.

Question 3965. Which statement about the portal triad is correct: the portal vein lies between the duct and the artery, the bile duct lies behind the portal vein, the portal vein lies behind the bile duct, or the hepatic artery lies behind the portal vein? The answer is that the portal vein lies behind the bile duct. The duct lies in front and to its right, the artery in front and to its left.

Question 3966. Which vein carries blood from the small intestine to the portal vein? The answer is the superior mesenteric vein, which receives the jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic and middle colic veins. It lies to the right of the artery of the same name.

Question 3967. Which of these pairs belongs together: the superior rectal vein with the inferior mesenteric vein, the middle rectal vein with the portal vein, the inferior rectal vein with the splenic vein, or the paraumbilical veins with the azygos vein? The answer is the superior rectal vein with the inferior mesenteric vein. The middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac veins.

Question 3968. Blood leaves the liver by which veins, and into which vessel do they open: the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava, the portal vein into the inferior vena cava, the hepatic veins into the portal vein, or the splenic vein into the aorta? The answer is the hepatic veins, opening into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. They carry blood that has already passed through the liver.

Question 3969. A described cast of the portal system shows a trunk running from the hilum of the liver down behind the pancreas, where two large veins join it, one from the left and one from below. Which vein is the trunk, and which two veins join it? The answer is the portal vein, joined by the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein.

Question 3970. A constructed illustration: a described scan of a person whose liver is firm and shrunken shows a dilated vein running up behind the pancreas, with a smaller channel beside the stomach. Which vein is dilated, and which connection has opened? The answer is the portal vein, with the left gastric and esophageal veins carrying blood to the azygos system. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 3971. Which vein is the continuation of the sigmoid sinus below the jugular foramen? The answer is the internal jugular vein. It begins at the base of the skull in the superior bulb and descends in the carotid sheath. It ends behind the sternal end of the clavicle.

Question 3972. The internal jugular vein lies in which relation to the common carotid artery: lateral to it, medial to it, directly behind it, or directly in front of it? The answer is lateral to it, within the carotid sheath. The vagus nerve lies behind and between the two, and the sheath also contains the deep cervical lymph nodes.

Question 3973. True or false: the internal jugular vein has a valve at its lower end. The answer is true. A pair of valves lies in the inferior bulb, just above the point where the vein joins the subclavian vein. Valves are otherwise few in the veins of the neck.

Question 3974. Which structure lies between the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery as they descend the neck? The answer is the vagus nerve, which lies behind and between them in the carotid sheath. The ansa cervicalis lies on the front of the sheath, and the deep cervical lymph nodes beside the vein.

Question 3975. Which of these veins is a tributary of the internal jugular vein: the facial vein, the external jugular vein, the anterior jugular vein, or the dorsal scapular vein? The answer is the facial vein. The internal jugular vein also receives the lingual, pharyngeal and thyroid veins, while the other three end elsewhere.

Question 3976. Which vein is formed near the angle of the jaw by the union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein with the posterior auricular vein? The answer is the external jugular vein. It descends across the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ends in the subclavian vein, with a pair of valves just above its ending.

Question 3977. A described superficial dissection of the neck shows a vein crossing the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with a plexus of nerves appearing at the middle of the muscle's posterior border. Which structures are shown? The answer is the external jugular vein and the cervical plexus, with the great auricular nerve among its branches.

Question 3978. The external jugular vein ends in which vessel: the internal jugular vein, the subclavian vein, the brachiocephalic vein, or the axillary vein? The answer is the subclavian vein, above the middle of the clavicle. It has a pair of valves just above its ending.

Question 3979. Name the two veins that unite to form the external jugular vein, spoken as a list. The answer is the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein, which meet below and behind the angle of the jaw. The vein then crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Question 3980. A constructed illustration: a small wound in the lower part of the neck lets air enter a vein, and the vein stands out as a cord over the muscle. Which vein is described, and why does air enter this one? The answer is the external jugular vein. It is superficial, and its wall is held open by the deep fascia, so it does not close when cut.

Question 3981. Which vein runs down the front of the neck close to the midline and often opens into the external jugular or subclavian vein? The answer is the anterior jugular vein, which begins below the chin and descends near the midline. The two are joined across the midline by the jugular arch.

Question 3982. Which vein drains the lower part of the thyroid gland and ends in the brachiocephalic vein: the superior thyroid vein, the middle thyroid vein, the inferior thyroid vein, or the facial vein? The answer is the inferior thyroid vein. The superior and middle thyroid veins end in the internal jugular vein, and the pattern varies.

Question 3983. Which of these pairs belongs together: the internal jugular vein with the subclavian vein, the external jugular vein with the internal jugular vein, the anterior jugular vein with the axillary vein, or the facial vein with the subclavian vein? The answer is the internal jugular vein with the subclavian vein. They unite behind the sternal end of the clavicle to form the brachiocephalic vein.

Question 3984. A described venogram of the neck shows a vein running from the base of the skull straight down to the root of the neck, where it joins another vein behind the inner end of the clavicle. Which vein is shown, and which veins does it receive? The answer is the internal jugular vein, receiving the facial and superior thyroid veins before it joins the subclavian vein.

Question 3985. Which structure lies immediately deep to the external jugular vein as the vein crosses the neck? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which the vein crosses on its way down. The investing layer of deep fascia and the platysma lie superficial to it, and the vein runs from the jaw to the subclavian vein.

Question 3986. A constructed illustration: a described radiograph after a thin tube has been passed into a vein below the clavicle shows the tube running medially in front of a muscle in the root of the neck. Which vein holds it, and which muscle lies behind that vein? The answer is the subclavian vein, with the scalenus anterior behind it. The subclavian artery and the brachial plexus lie behind the same muscle.

Question 3987. The subclavian vein is the continuation of which vein, and where does that continuation begin: the axillary vein at the outer border of the first rib, the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen, the brachiocephalic vein at the sternum, or the cephalic vein at the shoulder? The answer is the axillary vein, at the outer border of the first rib. The vein then runs medially in front of the scalenus anterior.

Question 3988. The subclavian vein ends where it joins which vein, and what do the two form: the internal jugular vein, forming the brachiocephalic vein; the external jugular vein, forming the superior vena cava; the cephalic vein, forming the axillary vein; or the basilic vein, forming the brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the internal jugular vein. The two form the brachiocephalic vein behind the sternal end of the clavicle.

Question 3989. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the root of the neck on the left side, lymph leaks from a duct that ends there. Which duct has been injured, and where does it end? The answer is the thoracic duct, which ends at the left venous angle where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. The right lymphatic duct ends on the right.

Question 3990. A described dissection of the root of the neck shows a vein in a groove on the upper surface of the first rib, in front of a small bony ridge, with an artery and a nerve plexus behind a muscle beside it. Which vein is shown? The answer is the subclavian vein, lying in the groove on the first rib in front of the scalene tubercle.

Question 3991. Which vein becomes the subclavian vein as it crosses the outer border of the first rib? The answer is the axillary vein. The subclavian vein then runs medially in front of the scalenus anterior, lying in a groove on the first rib, and joins the internal jugular vein.

Question 3992. Which structure lies immediately in front of the subclavian vein: the scalenus anterior muscle, the clavicle and the subclavius muscle, the brachial plexus, or the cervical pleura? The answer is the clavicle and the subclavius muscle. The vein lies in front of the scalenus anterior, and the artery and brachial plexus behind it.

Question 3993. Which muscle separates the subclavian vein from the subclavian artery at the root of the neck, and what lies behind the vein? The answer is the scalenus anterior muscle, which separates the two vessels. The vein lies in front of the muscle and the artery behind it, with the first rib and cervical pleura below.

Question 3994. Which of these pairs belongs together: the thoracic duct with the left venous angle, the thoracic duct with the right venous angle, the right lymphatic duct with the left venous angle, or the right lymphatic duct with the superior vena cava? The answer is the thoracic duct with the left venous angle. There the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins meet.

Question 3995. A described venogram of the upper limb shows contrast passing from a vein at the outer border of the first rib into a vein running medially in front of a muscle. Which vein has received the contrast: the subclavian vein, the internal jugular vein, the cephalic vein, or the axillary vein? The answer is the subclavian vein, which continues the axillary vein at that border. The scalenus anterior lies behind it.

Question 3996. A transverse section through the root of the neck shows the subclavian vein and the subclavian artery lying one behind the other. Which lies more anteriorly, and what separates them? The answer is that the vein lies in front and the artery behind, separated by the scalenus anterior muscle. The first rib lies below the vein.

Question 3997. Name two veins that join the subclavian vein near its end, spoken as a list. The answer is the external jugular vein and the dorsal scapular vein. The thoracic duct also ends at the left venous angle, close to the same point, and the anterior jugular vein may end there too.

Question 3998. Which statement about the valves of the subclavian vein is correct: it has a pair of valves near its termination, it has valves along its length, it has a single valve at the outer border of the first rib, or it has no valves? The answer is a pair of valves near its termination, close to the venous angle. Those valves keep blood from returning into the vein.

Question 3999. A described section of the root of the neck cuts across the great veins on one side and shows the internal jugular vein above and the subclavian vein below. In which plane does that section lie, and where do the two veins meet? The answer is a coronal plane. They meet at the venous angle, behind the sternal end of the clavicle.

Question 4000. Which two veins unite behind the sternal end of the clavicle to form a brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the internal jugular vein and the subclavian vein, whose meeting point is the venous angle. The left brachiocephalic vein then crosses the midline to join the right one.

To summarize, the superior vena cava is formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins behind the first right costal cartilage, runs to the right of the ascending aorta, receives the azygos vein from behind, and enters the right atrium at the third right costal cartilage. The inferior vena cava begins where the two common iliac veins meet in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra, ascends to the right of the aorta, receives the hepatic veins just below the diaphragm, and passes through the central tendon at the eighth thoracic vertebra, while the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta. The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas, carries blood between two sets of capillaries, and has no valves, so the connections at the esophagus, the anal canal and the umbilicus open when the pressure inside it rises. The internal jugular vein continues the sigmoid sinus from the jugular foramen, lies lateral to the carotid artery, and joins the subclavian vein behind the sternal end of the clavicle, where the thoracic duct ends at the left venous angle, while the subclavian vein itself lies in front of the scalenus anterior in a groove on the first rib. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 41 — Veins, Part Two

This chapter completes the tour of the venous system and then descends to the smallest vessels of all. It follows the veins of the upper limb and the lower limb from the fingers and the toes back to the great veins of the root of the neck and the groin, and it then examines the microcirculation, where arterioles, capillaries and venules exchange fluid, gases and cells with the tissues. It holds one hundred questions, numbered from question four thousand and one, and every one gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind. Superficial and deep veins are described together with the valves that keep blood moving toward the heart, and the capillary bed is described with its sphincters, its exchanges and its lymphatic partner. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4001. Which superficial vein begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous network of the hand and climbs along the lateral border of the arm? The answer is the cephalic vein. Its name comes from the same root as the word head, because it climbs toward the shoulder and the neck. The basilic vein begins at the medial end of that network.

Question 4002. Which of these veins begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous network of the hand: the cephalic vein, the basilic vein, the median cubital vein, or the accessory cephalic vein? The answer is the basilic vein. It runs up the little finger side of the limb, while the cephalic vein runs up the thumb side.

Question 4003. What is the name of the vein that runs obliquely across the front of the elbow and joins the cephalic vein to the basilic vein? The answer is the median cubital vein. It lies in the subcutaneous tissue of the cubital fossa and is the vein most often used when blood is taken. The bicipital aponeurosis lies deep to it.

Question 4004. In the groove between the deltoid muscle and the pectoralis major, which vein ascends toward the shoulder? The answer is the cephalic vein. The deltoid lies lateral to that groove and the pectoralis major lies medial to it. The vein then pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein.

Question 4005. The basilic vein and the paired veins that accompany the brachial artery unite to form which vessel: the subclavian vein, the axillary vein, the cephalic vein, or the brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the axillary vein. The union takes place at the lower border of the teres major muscle. The cephalic vein joins the axillary vein separately, higher up.

Question 4006. A constructed illustration: a cannula placed in a vein on the lateral side of the forearm is left in place for several days, and the vein becomes tender, red and cord-like. Which vein is inflamed? The answer is the cephalic vein. It runs in the subcutaneous tissue, where it is easily cannulated and easily irritated. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 4007. A described venogram of an arm shows one channel running up the lateral border of the limb, another running up the medial border, and a diagonal link between them at the elbow. Which veins are shown? The answer is the cephalic vein laterally and the basilic vein medially, with the median cubital vein as the link.

Question 4008. True or false: the cephalic vein ends in the axillary vein rather than in the basilic vein. The answer is true. The vein crosses the front of the shoulder between the deltoid and the pectoralis major and then pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein.

Question 4009. What name is given to the two veins that accompany the brachial artery through the arm? The answer is the venae comitantes, which means the accompanying veins. Each artery of the arm and the forearm is flanked by two such veins, one on either side. They communicate across the artery at intervals.

Question 4010. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cephalic vein with the lateral side, the basilic vein with the lateral side, the median cubital vein with the back of the wrist, or the dorsal venous network with the palm? The answer is the cephalic vein with the lateral side. The basilic vein belongs to the medial side, and the dorsal venous network lies on the back of the hand.

Question 4011. A small vein sometimes runs beside the cephalic vein on the lateral side of the forearm. Which of these names is given to it: the median cubital vein, the accessory cephalic vein, the median antebrachial vein, or the basilic vein? The answer is the accessory cephalic vein, a normal variant. The median antebrachial vein, when it exists, runs up the middle of the forearm.

Question 4012. The cephalic vein in the lower forearm lies close to which nerve, the one that supplies skin over the lateral side of the forearm? The answer is the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. It is the continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve below the elbow. Because the two run together, a cut down onto the vein can injure the nerve.

Question 4013. Relative to the deep fascia, where do the cephalic vein and the basilic vein lie, and where do the brachial veins lie? The answer is that the cephalic and the basilic veins lie superficial to the deep fascia, and the brachial veins lie deep to it. The basilic vein pierces the fascia in the middle of the arm.

Question 4014. Name the two superficial veins that drain the dorsal venous network of the hand. The answer is the cephalic vein and the basilic vein. The cephalic vein leaves the network at its lateral end and the basilic vein at its medial end. A question of this kind is answered with the two names alone.

Question 4015. At which landmark is the axillary vein formed, and from which vessels? The answer is at the lower border of the teres major, from the union of the basilic vein with the venae comitantes of the brachial artery. It then runs upward and medially, in front of the axillary artery, and ends at the outer border of the first rib.

Question 4016. The deep veins of the upper limb differ from the superficial veins in which way: they are paired beside their artery, they have no valves, they lie outside the deep fascia, or they drain only the skin? The answer is that they are paired beside their artery. They do have valves, and they lie beneath the deep fascia.

Question 4017. A constructed illustration: after unusual effort with the arm held overhead, a person develops a swollen, dusky arm, and the deep veins of the axilla no longer fill on a described venogram. Which vein is obstructed, and why does the arm swell? The answer is the axillary vein. Obstruction raises the pressure behind it, so fluid leaves the capillaries and collects in the tissues.

Question 4018. A described dissection of the front of the elbow shows a vein crossing obliquely over a shining fibrous band, with the brachial artery and the median nerve deep to that band. Which vein has been exposed, and what separates it from the artery? The answer is the median cubital vein, separated from the artery by the bicipital aponeurosis.

Question 4019. A constructed illustration: a person with kidney failure needs repeated access to the bloodstream, and a surgeon connects the cephalic vein to the radial artery at the wrist. Why is the cephalic vein chosen, and why does it enlarge? The answer is that it is superficial, long and easily needled, and it enlarges because arterial pressure now distends it.

Question 4020. Which structure separates the subclavian vein from the subclavian artery at the root of the neck: the first rib, the scalenus anterior muscle, the clavicle, or the sternocleidomastoid muscle? The answer is the scalenus anterior. The vein lies in front of that muscle and the artery behind it, so the vein is the more superficial of the two.

Question 4021. The subclavian vein passes in front of which muscle on its way to join the internal jugular vein? The answer is the scalenus anterior. That muscle separates the vein in front from the subclavian artery and the brachial plexus behind. The two veins unite behind the sternoclavicular joint.

Question 4022. Which two veins unite behind the sternoclavicular joint, and what vessel do they form? The answer is the internal jugular vein and the subclavian vein, which form the brachiocephalic vein. The right brachiocephalic vein is short and nearly vertical, while the left one is longer and crosses the midline. The two unite to form the superior vena cava.

Question 4023. True or false: the basilic vein pierces the deep fascia in the middle of the arm and continues upward as a deep vessel. The answer is true. It leaves the subcutaneous tissue and runs beside the brachial artery, where it joins the venae comitantes of that artery. The cephalic vein stays superficial until it reaches the shoulder.

Question 4024. The cephalic vein is sometimes harvested to bypass a narrowed coronary artery. Which of these features explains why it is suitable: it is long and superficial, it is valveless, it lies between the muscles of the arm, or it drains into the superior vena cava? The answer is that it is long and superficial. Its valves must be dealt with during the operation.

Question 4025. Which of these pairs belongs together: the basilic vein with the medial side of the arm, the cephalic vein with the medial side, the median cubital vein with the back of the hand, or the venae comitantes with the skin? The answer is the basilic vein with the medial side of the arm. The cephalic vein belongs to the lateral side, and the venae comitantes lie deep beside the arteries.

Question 4026. Which superficial vein of the lower limb begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot and ascends in front of the medial malleolus? The answer is the great saphenous vein. It is the longest vein in the body and runs up the medial side of the leg and the thigh to end in the femoral vein.

Question 4027. The small saphenous vein ascends behind the lateral malleolus and ends in which vessel: the femoral vein, the popliteal vein, the great saphenous vein, or the external iliac vein? The answer is the popliteal vein. It enters the popliteal fossa and pierces the deep fascia to join that vein. The great saphenous vein ends in the femoral vein instead.

Question 4028. In which vein does the great saphenous vein end, and through which opening does it pass? The answer is the femoral vein, through the saphenous opening in the deep fascia of the thigh. Just before it ends, the vein receives the superficial epigastric, the superficial circumflex iliac and the superficial external pudendal veins.

Question 4029. Which vein passes behind the lateral malleolus: the great saphenous vein, the small saphenous vein, the popliteal vein, or the femoral vein? The answer is the small saphenous vein. It runs up the back of the calf beside the tendo calcaneus and then between the two heads of the gastrocnemius. The great saphenous vein runs in front of the medial malleolus instead.

Question 4030. A described dissection of the back of the knee shows a vein in the midline of the popliteal fossa joining a deeper vessel between the heads of the gastrocnemius. Which vein is it, and what does it join? The answer is the small saphenous vein joining the popliteal vein. The sural nerve runs beside it.

Question 4031. A constructed illustration: a person who stands for long hours develops swollen, twisted veins on the medial side of the leg, and the skin above the ankle becomes pigmented. Which superficial vein is affected, and why does standing make it worse? The answer is the great saphenous vein. Standing raises the pressure in the superficial veins, and failing valves allow blood to pool downward.

Question 4032. In the popliteal fossa, which of the two great vessels lies nearer the skin: the popliteal artery or the popliteal vein? The answer is the popliteal vein. It lies superficial, or anterior, to the artery, which is the deeper of the two. The tibial nerve lies most superficial of all, just beneath the deep fascia.

Question 4033. True or false: the deep veins of the leg are paired and accompany the arteries of the leg. The answer is true. Each of the anterior tibial, posterior tibial and peroneal arteries is flanked by two companion veins. The popliteal vein is formed where those companions unite.

Question 4034. Which veins unite to form the popliteal vein? The answer is the venae comitantes of the anterior tibial artery and the venae comitantes of the posterior tibial artery, together with the peroneal veins. They unite at the lower border of the popliteus muscle. The popliteal vein then ascends through the popliteal fossa.

Question 4035. Where does the femoral vein lie relative to the femoral artery as the two ascend from the opening in adductor magnus to the groin: posterolateral at the opening and medial in the groin, medial at the opening and posterolateral in the groin, anterior throughout, or lateral throughout? The answer is posterolateral at the opening and medial in the groin. The vein crosses behind the artery as it ascends.

Question 4036. Which of these pairs belongs together: the great saphenous vein with the medial side, the small saphenous vein with the medial side, the popliteal vein with the front of the ankle, or the femoral vein with the back of the calf? The answer is the great saphenous vein with the medial side. The small saphenous vein belongs to the back of the calf and the popliteal vein lies behind the knee.

Question 4037. Name the two superficial veins of the lower limb. The answer is the great saphenous vein and the small saphenous vein. The great saphenous vein runs up the medial side to the femoral vein, and the small saphenous vein runs up the back of the calf to the popliteal vein.

Question 4038. In the femoral triangle the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, the femoral vein and the femoral canal lie in a row from lateral to medial. Which structure lies immediately medial to the femoral vein? The answer is the femoral canal, the small compartment that carries lymph vessels and a lymph node.

Question 4039. Deep vein thrombosis of the leg most often begins in which site: the superficial veins of the thigh, the deep veins and muscular sinuses of the calf, the great saphenous vein at the ankle, or the dorsal veins of the foot? The answer is the deep veins and muscular sinuses of the calf. A clot there can travel to the lungs.

Question 4040. A constructed illustration: a person who has been immobile for a long period develops a swollen, tender calf, and a described ultrasound scan shows that one deep vein does not compress. Which veins of the calf are the usual site? The answer is the posterior tibial and peroneal veins and the muscular sinuses of the soleus. Obstruction raises the pressure behind them, so fluid collects in the ankle.

Question 4041. A described venogram of a leg shows contrast filling two narrow channels on each side of the tibia, a channel beside the fibula, and a single wider vessel behind the knee. Which vessels are shown? The answer is the paired venae comitantes of the tibial arteries, the peroneal veins and the popliteal vein. The deep veins of the leg are doubled until they unite behind the knee.

Question 4042. What is the direction of blood flow through the perforating veins that connect the superficial veins of the leg to the deep veins? The answer is from the superficial veins into the deep veins. Their valves open inward and close against any backward flow into the subcutaneous tissue. When those valves fail, the superficial veins become varicose.

Question 4043. When the great saphenous vein is removed from the leg, which structure is most at risk: the saphenous nerve, the sural nerve, the common peroneal nerve, or the tibial nerve? The answer is the saphenous nerve. It runs beside the vein in the subcutaneous tissue, so numbness follows the medial side of the leg and the foot.

Question 4044. The great saphenous vein passes in front of which bony prominence at the ankle, and which nerve accompanies it there? The answer is the medial malleolus, accompanied by the saphenous nerve. It crosses the lower end of the tibia on the medial side of the limb. The small saphenous vein passes behind the lateral malleolus instead.

Question 4045. A constructed illustration: a person with long-standing varicose veins develops a shallow, slow-healing sore on the skin just above the medial malleolus. Why does this site break down? The answer is that the superficial system is at fault and the skin just above the ankle carries the greatest column of venous pressure. Fluid and pigment collect in the skin, which then fails to heal.

Question 4046. A described section through the calf shows wide venous channels lying within the muscle belly of the soleus and opening into the deep veins beside the tibia. What are these channels? The answer is the muscular sinuses of the soleal veins. They hold a large volume of blood during immobility and are a favored site for a clot to form.

Question 4047. The femoral vein becomes which vessel as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament: the external iliac vein, the internal iliac vein, the great saphenous vein, or the popliteal vein? The answer is the external iliac vein. The change of name takes place beneath the inguinal ligament, where the vein lies medial to the femoral artery.

Question 4048. True or false: the great saphenous vein ends in the popliteal vein. The answer is false. The great saphenous vein ends in the femoral vein at the saphenous opening in the groin. It is the small saphenous vein that ends in the popliteal vein behind the knee.

Question 4049. From which venous structure of the foot do the great saphenous vein and the small saphenous vein arise? The answer is the dorsal venous arch on the back of the foot. The great saphenous vein leaves at the medial end of the arch and the small saphenous vein at the lateral end. The arch itself is fed by the dorsal digital veins of the toes.

Question 4050. Which of these pairs belongs together: the femoral vein with the thigh, the popliteal vein with the ankle, the peroneal vein with the groin, or the dorsal venous arch with the knee? The answer is the femoral vein with the thigh. The popliteal vein lies behind the knee, the peroneal vein beside the fibula, and the dorsal venous arch on the back of the foot.

Question 4051. Which type of capillary has pores in its endothelial cells that are closed by a thin diaphragm and is found in the wall of the intestine? The answer is the fenestrated capillary. The pores let fluid and small molecules cross quickly. Continuous capillaries, by contrast, have no pores.

Question 4052. Which of these is a feature of the wall of a capillary: a single layer of endothelial cells, three coats of muscle, valves along its length, or elastic lamellae? The answer is a single layer of endothelial cells. The capillary wall is the thinnest in the body so that diffusion distances stay short. Smooth muscle, valves and elastic tissue belong to larger vessels.

Question 4053. What is the name of the smallest vessel of the body, a tube of endothelium across whose wall gases and nutrients pass? The answer is the capillary. Its wall is one cell thick and rests on a thin basement membrane. Blood enters it from an arteriole and leaves through a venule.

Question 4054. A described electron micrograph shows a narrow tube whose wall is a single flattened endothelial cell resting on a basement membrane, with dense material sealing the junctions between neighboring cells. Which type of vessel is shown? The answer is a continuous capillary, the kind found in muscle, skin and the nervous system.

Question 4055. Which vessel lies immediately downstream of a capillary bed and is the site where exchange with the tissue fluid continues? The answer is the postcapillary venule. It is wider than the capillary, its wall is thin, and its junctions are looser. White blood cells leave the blood through its wall.

Question 4056. Which vessel carries a ring of smooth muscle at the origin of each capillary and so controls the flow into the capillary bed: the metarteriole, the postcapillary venule, the collecting venule, or the lymphatic capillary? The answer is the metarteriole, which gives off capillaries along its length. The smooth muscle rings are the precapillary sphincters.

Question 4057. A constructed illustration: a person stands without moving for several hours, and by evening the ankles are swollen and the shoes feel tight. Which part of the microcirculation is responsible, and why? The answer is the capillary and the venule, where the column of blood raises the pressure and pushes fluid into the tissues.

Question 4058. True or false: a capillary contains smooth muscle in its wall. The answer is false. The capillary wall is made of endothelial cells and their basement membrane, with no muscle at all. Smooth muscle appears in the arterioles and the metarterioles just before the capillary bed.

Question 4059. What name is given to the short vessel that leaves a terminal arteriole, runs across a capillary bed, gives off capillaries along its course and then becomes a venule? The answer is the metarteriole. It has smooth muscle along its length and is the thoroughfare channel of the bed. Rings of muscle at the capillary origins are the precapillary sphincters.

Question 4060. Which type of capillary is found in the liver, has gaps between its endothelial cells and a discontinuous basement membrane, and allows plasma proteins to leave the blood: the continuous capillary, the fenestrated capillary, the sinusoidal capillary, or the lymphatic capillary? The answer is the sinusoidal capillary. Its gaps are wide enough for proteins and even cells to pass.

Question 4061. A described light micrograph of the kidney shows a tuft of capillaries inside a rounded capsule, with a vessel entering and another leaving at the same pole. Which capillary network is shown? The answer is the glomerulus, whose capillaries are fenestrated and leaky. They are the most permeable capillaries in the body.

Question 4062. Name the three types of capillary found in the body. The answer is the continuous capillary, the fenestrated capillary and the sinusoidal capillary. The continuous type is the commonest and is sealed by tight junctions. The sinusoidal type is the leakiest and lies in the liver, the spleen and the bone marrow.

Question 4063. Which cell lies on the outside of a capillary, shares its basement membrane with the endothelial cell, and can contract to alter the width of the vessel? The answer is the pericyte. It is most numerous on the capillaries of the brain and the retina. Its contraction helps to regulate local flow and permeability.

Question 4064. Which force draws fluid back into a capillary from the tissue fluid: the blood pressure inside the capillary, the osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins, the pressure of the tissue fluid, or the pull of the lymphatic vessels? The answer is the osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins. Albumin holds water in the plasma, and its effect is the colloid osmotic pressure.

Question 4065. Which vessels lie immediately beside a capillary bed and return the small excess of tissue fluid to the bloodstream? The answer is the lymphatic capillaries. They begin blindly in the tissue, and the fluid they collect is called lymph. The lymph then passes through larger vessels and returns to the great veins of the neck.

Question 4066. A constructed illustration: a person with a failing left ventricle develops breathlessness, and a described chest radiograph shows fluid in the air spaces of both lungs. Why does the fluid collect in the lung? The answer is that the failing ventricle raises the pressure in the pulmonary capillaries, so fluid leaves them faster than the lymphatics can return it.

Question 4067. White blood cells leave the bloodstream at which point: the capillary, because its wall has gaps; the postcapillary venule, because its wall is thin and its junctions are loose; the arteriole, because it has smooth muscle; or the metarteriole, because it is wide? The answer is the postcapillary venule. Its junctions are the loosest in the microcirculation, so a white cell can squeeze between the cells.

Question 4068. A described section of the skin of a fingertip shows a coiled vessel with a thick muscular wall connecting a small artery directly to a small vein. What is this structure, and what does it do? The answer is an arteriovenous anastomosis, or glomus body. It opens in the cold to conserve heat and closes when the body must lose heat.
