Beneath the inguinal ligament, in which order do the structures lie from lateral to medial: the nerve, the artery, the vein and the canal; the artery, the nerve, the vein and the canal; the vein, the artery, the nerve and the canal; or the canal, the vein, the artery and the nerve? The answer is the nerve, the artery, the vein and the canal. The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath.

Question 4280. A described view of the groin shows a needle entering below the inguinal ligament, just medial to the point where a pulse is felt. Which vein is being entered, and why must the needle stay below the ligament? The answer is the femoral vein; above the ligament the needle would enter the abdominal cavity.

Question 4281. Which vein is the longest in the body, running from the back of the great toe up the medial side of the limb to the groin? The answer is the great saphenous vein, which passes in front of the medial malleolus and ends in the femoral vein.

Question 4282. Which vein runs up the medial side of the leg and thigh and is the one most often affected by varicose veins: the great saphenous vein, the small saphenous vein, the popliteal vein, or the femoral vein? The answer is the great saphenous vein. It lies just beneath the skin with little support.

Question 4283. What kind of vein connects the superficial veins of the leg to the deep veins through the deep fascia, and in which direction do its valves normally allow blood to flow? The answer is a perforating vein, whose valves direct blood inward from the superficial to the deep system. When they fail, blood is forced outward.

Question 4284. A person has dilated, tortuous veins running down the inner side of the leg from the groin to the ankle. Which vein and which junction are involved: the great saphenous vein and the saphenofemoral junction, the small saphenous vein and the saphenopopliteal junction, the femoral vein and the popliteal junction, or the cephalic vein and the axillary junction? The answer is the great saphenous vein with the saphenofemoral junction.

Question 4285. In the leg, which nerve runs with the great saphenous vein, and where does the vein lie relative to the medial malleolus? The answer is the saphenous nerve, and the vein passes in front of the medial malleolus. A cut beside the vein can divide the nerve.

Question 4286. A constructed illustration: a person has a shallow ulcer just above and behind the medial malleolus, with brown staining of the skin around it. Which system of veins has failed, and why does the ulcer form there? The answer is the superficial system, with failing valves in the perforating veins of the lower leg.

Question 4287. A described photograph of the leg shows veins that are dilated, elongated and twisted, standing out under the skin from the ankle to the groin. Which system is shown, and what has failed? The answer is the superficial venous system, most often the great saphenous vein.

Question 4288. What normally prevents blood from falling back down the veins of the leg: the contraction of the calf muscles with one-way valves, the elasticity of the deep fascia alone, the pressure of the arterial pulse, or the pull of the skin? The answer is the contraction of the calf muscles with one-way valves, which squeeze the deep veins and direct blood toward the heart.

Question 4289. Which superficial vein of the leg ends in the popliteal vein behind the knee? The answer is the small saphenous vein, which begins behind the lateral malleolus and runs up the back of the leg. It may end in the great saphenous vein instead, which is a normal variation.

Question 4290. Through which opening in the deep fascia does the great saphenous vein pass to reach the femoral vein, and what covers that opening? The answer is the saphenous opening, covered by the cribriform fascia. It lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and small superficial veins join the great saphenous vein there.

Question 4291. A varicocele is a dilation of the veins of the pampiniform plexus. Why is it far more common on the left side: the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, the left testicular vein is shorter, the left testis lies lower, or the left vein has more valves? The answer is that the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle and over a longer course.

Question 4292. A described view of the scrotum shows a mass above the testis that feels like a bag of worms and shrinks when the person lies down. Which veins are dilated, and which side is usually affected? The answer is the veins of the pampiniform plexus, usually on the left side.

Question 4293. True or false: the valves in the deep veins of the leg let blood pass outward from the deep system into the superficial veins. The answer is false. The valves of both systems direct blood from the superficial veins into the deep veins and toward the heart.

Question 4294. Which pair belongs together: varicose veins at the lower end of the esophagus with the left gastric vein, dilated veins around the navel with the splenic vein, piles with the middle colic vein, or dilated veins of the buttock with the renal vein? The answer is the first pair. Around the navel the paraumbilical veins join the portal system.

Question 4295. Name the two superficial veins of the lower limb, spoken as a list. The answer is the great saphenous vein and the small saphenous vein. Both lie outside the deep fascia, in the fatty layer under the skin, and the first runs up the medial side of the leg.

Question 4296. Why does a venous ulcer of the leg most often sit just above the medial malleolus: because the perforating veins there carry the highest pressure when the pump fails, because the skin there is thinnest, because the great saphenous vein has no valves there, or because the tibial artery lies nearest the skin? The answer is the first reason.

Question 4297. Which statement about the deep veins of the leg is correct: they lie beneath the deep fascia within the muscle compartments, they lie in the fatty layer under the skin, they have no valves, or they drain only into the small saphenous vein? The answer is that they lie beneath the deep fascia. The perforating veins cross it to join the two systems.

Question 4298. A described venogram shows contrast flowing backward down the great saphenous vein from the groin when the person coughs. Which junction has failed, and what is the normal direction of flow there? The answer is the saphenofemoral junction. Normally a valve there stops blood passing back into the superficial vein.

Question 4299. The popliteal vein ascends through the back of the knee. Which statement is correct: it becomes the femoral vein as it passes through the adductor hiatus, it becomes the great saphenous vein at the ankle, it drains into the small saphenous vein, or it ends in the popliteal fossa? The answer is the first statement. It receives the small saphenous vein.

Question 4300. Varicose veins are more common in the left leg than in the right. Which feature best explains this: the left common iliac vein is crossed by the right common iliac artery, the left common iliac vein is longer, the left leg has fewer valves, or the left great saphenous vein has no perforating veins? The answer is the first feature.

To summarize, the pulse points are the places where an artery can be pressed against bone, among them the radial artery lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis, the brachial artery beside the biceps tendon, the femoral artery at the mid-inguinal point, the popliteal artery deepest in the popliteal fossa, and the posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries at the ankle and the foot. Serious bleeding comes from the dense layer of the scalp, the plexus on the front of the nasal septum, the spleen and the liver beneath the diaphragm, the vessels in the costal groove of the rib above, and the pelvic plexus and internal iliac branches after a fracture of the pelvis. The vessels most at risk are the axillary artery in a shoulder dislocation, the brachial artery above the elbow, the popliteal artery in a dislocated knee, and the profunda femoris artery beside the shaft of the femur. Vascular access uses veins in predictable places: the median cubital vein over the bicipital aponeurosis, the cephalic and basilic veins from the back of the hand, the great saphenous vein in front of the medial malleolus, and the femoral, internal jugular and subclavian veins, each in a known relation to its artery. Varicose veins follow failure of the valves of the superficial veins and their perforators, most often in the great saphenous system, while the deep veins of the leg stay beneath the deep fascia. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 44 — Lymphatic Vessels

This chapter follows the lymph from the tissue spaces back to the blood, and it holds one hundred questions about the vessels that carry it and the nodes that filter it. It begins with the lymphatic capillaries, then follows the collecting vessels and their valves, the lymphatic trunks, the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct, and the way lymph returns to the great veins. The first seventy-five questions deal with the vessels and the last twenty-five with the lymph nodes. Each question is answered immediately, and the reason for the answer follows at once. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4301. Which feature sets a lymphatic capillary apart from a blood capillary of the same region? The answer is that it begins as a blind-ended tube in the tissue spaces. A blood capillary carries blood from an arterial end to a venous end. A lymphatic capillary has no such upstream end, so the fluid it takes up can travel only away from the tissues.

Question 4302. In the wall of a lymphatic capillary, why does tissue fluid enter easily while the lymph inside does not escape? The answer is that the endothelial cells overlap like roof tiles. The flaps swing open when the pressure of the tissue fluid outside them rises. When the pressure inside the vessel is greater, the flaps press shut and hold the lymph in.

Question 4303. True or false: the anchoring filaments pull the endothelial flaps of a lymphatic capillary apart when the tissue around the vessel swells. The answer is true. The filaments run from the endothelial cells to the collagen fibers of the surrounding tissue. As fluid collects and the tissue swells, they pull the flaps open and let more fluid enter.

Question 4304. Which of these is missing from the wall of a lymphatic capillary: an endothelial lining, a complete basement membrane, anchoring filaments, or overlapping cell edges? The answer is a complete basement membrane. The lymphatic capillary rests on a thin and incomplete basal lamina. That loose support helps explain why the vessel is so permeable to fluid and to protein.

Question 4305. A described specimen shows a fine mesh of vessels in the wall of the small intestine, with one vessel running up the middle of each villus. What is that central vessel called? The answer is the central lacteal. It lies in the core of the villus among the blood capillaries. The lacteal takes up the fatty products of digestion and carries them away as chyle.

Question 4306. Which of these is carried back to the blood mainly by the lymphatic vessels: oxygen, digested fat, glucose, or carbon dioxide? The answer is digested fat. Fat enters the lacteals of the small intestine and reaches the bloodstream through the thoracic duct. Oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide travel in the blood itself.

Question 4307. What is the name of the creamy white fluid that fills the intestinal lymphatics after a fatty meal? The answer is chyle. The finely divided fat gives the fluid its milky appearance. Once it leaves the intestine and joins the rest of the lymph, the same fluid is simply called lymph.

Question 4308. Which coat of a collecting lymphatic vessel is lined by endothelium: the tunica intima, the tunica media, the tunica adventitia, or the tunica serosa? The answer is the tunica intima. Around it lies the tunica media, which contains smooth muscle. The outer coat is the tunica adventitia, built largely of collagen, and the three coats are named as they are in a vein.

Question 4309. Which coat of a large collecting lymphatic holds the smooth muscle that drives lymph onward? The answer is the tunica media. Its muscle cells contract in a rhythm and squeeze the column of lymph forward. A vessel with a thicker media can generate a stronger contraction, and the other two coats add little to that pumping.

Question 4310. What is the name of the short segment of a lymphatic vessel that lies between two valves: a lymphangion, a lacteal, a cisterna, or a trabecula? The answer is a lymphangion. Each segment has its own muscular wall and acts as a small pump. The valves at its two ends keep the lymph moving in one direction only.

Question 4311. Why are valves more numerous in lymphatic vessels than in veins of the same size? The answer is that lymph has no central pump behind it. The valves divide the vessel into short pumping segments and stop the lymph from falling back. Blood, by contrast, is driven onward by the heart.

Question 4312. Which of these movements helps push lymph along the thoracic duct: contraction of the diaphragm in breathing, closure of the aortic valve, movement of the eyeball, or chewing? The answer is contraction of the diaphragm in breathing. Its descent lowers the pressure in the chest and draws lymph upward, while the same movement raises the pressure in the abdomen and pushes lymph ahead of it.

Question 4313. Name two pumps, other than the heart, that keep lymph moving in a person who is standing still. The answer is the contraction of skeletal muscle and the movement of the chest in breathing. Muscles squeeze the vessels that run beside them, and the valves make the squeezed lymph move only forward. Both pumps fail when a person is completely still.

Question 4314. A constructed illustration: a person sits without moving for many hours on a long flight, and the ankles swell. Which mechanism of lymph return has failed in that illustration? The answer is the skeletal muscle pump. Without the calf muscles squeezing the deep vessels, both lymph and venous blood pool in the leg. Movement, rather than the heart alone, is what empties the leg.

Question 4315. Which of these gives the correct order of flow through the lymphatic system: lymphatic capillary, collecting vessel, lymph node, trunk; lymph node, lymphatic capillary, collecting vessel, trunk; trunk, lymph node, collecting vessel, lymphatic capillary; or collecting vessel, lymphatic capillary, lymph node, trunk? The answer is lymphatic capillary, collecting vessel, lymph node, trunk. Lymph enters the capillaries first and leaves the body through a trunk.

Question 4316. The superficial collecting lymphatic vessels of the lower limb run in the fatty tissue beside which vein, and where do they end? The answer is the great saphenous vein, and they end in the superficial inguinal nodes. The deep vessels of the limb run instead beside the femoral vessels to the deep inguinal nodes.

Question 4317. A described dissection shows a chain of thin vessels running beside a large artery in the thigh, buried between the muscles. Which set of lymphatic vessels is shown? The answer is a set of deep lymphatic vessels. Deep vessels run with the deep arteries and veins of a limb. Superficial vessels lie instead in the fatty tissue just under the skin.

Question 4318. Which statement about the deep lymphatic vessels of a limb is correct: they run in the subcutaneous fat, they accompany the deep arteries and veins, they drain only the skin, or they open directly into the great veins? The answer is that they accompany the deep arteries and veins. They drain the muscles, the bones and the joints, while the skin drains into superficial vessels.

Question 4319. Which group of lymph nodes receives most of the lymph from the upper limb? The answer is the axillary nodes. The superficial vessels of the limb run beside the basilic vein up the medial side of the arm. The deep vessels follow the brachial vessels to the same group.

Question 4320. A constructed illustration: a small cut on the little finger becomes infected, and a tender lump appears in the armpit. Which group of nodes is reacting in that illustration? The answer is the axillary lymph nodes. Lymph from the little finger travels with the superficial vessels along the medial side of the limb. The nodes enlarge as they filter what the infection has carried to them.

Question 4321. The deep cervical lymph nodes lie along which vessel, and which trunk do they form? The answer is the internal jugular vein, and they form the jugular trunk. They lie beneath the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It ends in the thoracic duct on the left and in the right lymphatic duct on the right.

Question 4322. The lymph nodes of the axilla lie around which vessels, and which trunk do they form? The answer is the axillary vessels, and they form the subclavian trunk. They lie among the fat of the armpit, around the axillary vein and artery. Like the jugular trunk it ends at the venous angle of its own side, where the subclavian vein meets the internal jugular vein.

Question 4323. Which lymphatic trunk drains the chest wall and the thoracic viscera on one side? The answer is the bronchomediastinal trunk. It collects lymph from the nodes of the mediastinum and from the nodes along the trachea and the bronchi. It ends at the venous angle of its own side.

Question 4324. Which unpaired lymphatic trunk lies in the abdomen and drains the small intestine, the colon and part of the liver? The answer is the intestinal trunk. It is formed by the lymph nodes of the mesentery and the nodes in front of the aorta. It joins the cisterna chyli, and its lymph is rich in fat after a meal.

Question 4325. The right and the left lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs and the pelvis. Which two vessels do they lie beside, and what do they join? The answer is the aorta and the inferior vena cava, and they join the cisterna chyli. They are formed by the nodes beside those two vessels. Together with the intestinal trunk they empty into the cisterna chyli.

Question 4326. At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct usually begin in the abdomen? The answer is at the level of the first and second lumbar vertebrae. The sac that forms its lower end is the cisterna chyli. The duct then passes upward through the aortic opening of the diaphragm into the chest.

Question 4327. What is the name of the sac that forms the lower end of the thoracic duct? The answer is the cisterna chyli. It lies on the bodies of the first and second lumbar vertebrae. The intestinal trunk and the two lumbar trunks empty into it. Its shape varies, and in some people it is no more than a small plexus of vessels.

Question 4328. Which part of the skeleton lies immediately behind the thoracic duct as the duct crosses the chest? The answer is the vertebral column, with the thoracic vertebrae forming its wall. The duct lies in the posterior mediastinum, applied to the bodies of those vertebrae. The esophagus and the pericardium lie in front of it.

Question 4329. In the posterior mediastinum, which structure lies on the left side of the thoracic duct and which one lies on its right? The answer is the aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. That pair of neighbors can be used to trace the duct. The vertebral column lies behind it and the esophagus lies in front.

Question 4330. Which structure lies immediately anterior to the thoracic duct in the posterior mediastinum? The answer is the esophagus. The duct lies between the aorta and the azygos vein, against the bodies of the vertebrae. The esophagus lies in front of both the duct and the aorta at that level.

Question 4331. A described lymphangiogram of the chest shows a single thin duct rising through the middle of the back and crossing to one side near the top. Which duct is shown, and to which side does it cross? The answer is the thoracic duct, which crosses to the left. It ends at the left venous angle in the root of the neck.

Question 4332. Where does the thoracic duct end, and into which vein does it open? The answer is at the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular and the left subclavian veins join. In the root of the neck the duct arches laterally and crosses in front of the left subclavian artery. Its terminal part may open as one mouth or as several small ones.

Question 4333. Which regions of the body send their lymph into the thoracic duct? The answer is both lower limbs, the pelvis, the abdomen, the left half of the chest, the left upper limb and the left side of the head and neck. Only the right upper quarter of the body drains elsewhere. The duct therefore carries far more lymph than any other single vessel.

Question 4334. The right lymphatic duct ends at which venous angle, and which two veins form that angle? The answer is the right venous angle, formed by the right internal jugular and the right subclavian veins. The duct drains the right upper limb, the right side of the chest and the right side of the head and neck. In many people it is short or absent.

Question 4335. True or false: the thoracic duct carries lymph from the left side of the head and neck as well as from both lower limbs. The answer is true. The left jugular trunk opens into the duct, while the right jugular trunk opens into the right lymphatic duct. The two sides of the head therefore drain by different routes.

Question 4336. Which of these structures receives lymph from the left half of the thorax: the right lymphatic duct, the thoracic duct, the cisterna chyli only, or the intestinal trunk? The answer is the thoracic duct. The right lymphatic duct takes the right half of the chest. The cisterna chyli lies below the diaphragm and the intestinal trunk drains the gut.

Question 4337. A described dissection of the root of the neck shows a thin-walled duct arching over an artery and turning down into a vein. Which vein is it entering? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein at the left venous angle. The duct crosses in front of the left subclavian artery to reach it. On the right side the same task is done by the right lymphatic duct.

Question 4338. Which statement about the termination of the lymphatic ducts is correct: they open into the inferior vena cava, they open into the superior vena cava, they open at the venous angles, or they open into the pulmonary veins? The answer is that they open at the venous angles. There the subclavian and internal jugular veins join, so lymph returns to the blood just before it reaches the heart.

Question 4339. What happens to the lymph after it enters a venous angle? The answer is that it mixes with the venous blood and is carried to the right side of the heart. From there it passes through the lungs and returns to the arterial circulation. Every drop of tissue fluid that leaves the blood capillaries can therefore find its way back to them.

Question 4340. Which property of lymphatic vessels keeps lymph moving in one direction even when the body is still? The answer is the presence of valves along the vessel. Each valve has two delicate cusps that meet in the middle of the lumen. Lymph pushed past a valve cannot fall back through it, so flow continues in one direction only.

Question 4341. A described section of a collecting lymphatic shows two delicate cusps meeting in the middle of the lumen. What is that structure, and which way does it direct the lymph? The answer is a valve, which directs the lymph in the direction of flow. Fluid coming from the tissue side pushes the cusps apart. Any lymph that tries to return presses them together and closes the vessel.

Question 4342. In the standard anatomical position, in which direction does lymph travel along a superficial lymphatic vessel of the arm: from the armpit toward the fingers, from the fingers toward the armpit, from the skin toward the bone, or in both directions at once? The answer is from the fingers toward the armpit. The vessel begins in the tissue spaces of the hand, and its valves make that the only possible direction.

Question 4343. Which of these tissues has no lymphatic capillaries at all: the dermis, the periosteum, the cornea, or the subcutaneous fat? The answer is the cornea. It is an avascular and transparent tissue that needs no lymph drainage. The dermis, the periosteum and the fatty tissue all contain lymphatic capillaries.

Question 4344. Which of these organs contains no afferent lymphatic vessels: the liver, the spleen, the kidney, or the lung? The answer is the spleen. It has no vessels carrying lymph into it, so lymph leaves it by efferent vessels only. The other three organs have rich lymphatic networks, and lymph from them is filtered by nodes on the way.

Question 4345. A classically taught rule states that one part of the body has no lymphatic vessels in its substance. Which part is it? The answer is the central nervous system, the brain and the spinal cord. Tissue fluid there returns along the spaces around the blood vessels. Lymphatic vessels have since been described in the dura mater beside the venous sinuses.

Question 4346. Which of these tissues is said to lack lymphatic vessels: the skin of the eyelid, the cartilage of the trachea, the lining of the small intestine, or the capsule of the kidney? The answer is the cartilage of the trachea. Cartilage is avascular throughout, so it needs no lymphatics. The other three are vascular tissues with lymphatic capillaries.

Question 4347. In which layer of the skin do lymphatic capillaries begin: the keratin layer, the basal layer of the epidermis, the papillary layer of the dermis, or the subcutaneous fat? The answer is the papillary layer of the dermis. The epidermis itself is avascular and has no lymphatics. The dermal papillae, which carry the capillary loops, are where the lymphatic mesh begins.

Question 4348. Which of these is the main force that drives tissue fluid into a lymphatic capillary: the pumping of the heart, the pressure of the tissue fluid itself, the suction of the veins, or gravity? The answer is the pressure of the tissue fluid itself. Fluid filtered from the blood capillaries raises that pressure and pushes the flaps open.

Question 4349. Which statement about the protein in lymph is correct: it is higher than in blood plasma, equal to blood plasma, lower than blood plasma but higher than freshly filtered tissue fluid, or entirely absent? The answer is that it is lower than plasma but higher than freshly filtered fluid. Protein that leaks into the tissues is collected by the lymphatics and returned to the blood.

Question 4350. What happens to the small amount of protein that constantly leaks from the blood capillaries into the tissues? The answer is that it is collected by the lymphatic capillaries and returned to the blood. A blood capillary cannot take protein back in. Without the lymphatics that protein would accumulate in the tissues and hold water there.

Question 4351. Which of these would follow if the lymphatic vessels of a limb were blocked: tissue fluid would drain faster, protein would accumulate in the tissues and cause swelling, the blood would clot in the capillaries, or the arteries would dilate? The answer is that protein would accumulate and cause swelling. That protein holds water in the tissues, and the swelling is called lymphedema.

Question 4352. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the armpit, a person's arm swells and the skin of the arm feels firm. Which vessels have been interrupted in that illustration? The answer is the lymphatic vessels of the upper limb. Removing the axillary nodes also removes the vessels that ran through them. The swelling is lymphedema, and its management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4353. Which of these agents may block the lymphatic vessels and produce the massive swelling called elephantiasis: a virus, a worm, a fungus, or a crystal? The answer is a worm. The parasite Wuchereria bancrofti lives in the lymphatic vessels and blocks them. The limb then swells with lymph that cannot pass, and the skin thickens over time.

Question 4354. What is the name of the swelling of a limb caused by obstruction of its lymphatic vessels? The answer is lymphedema. The fluid that collects is rich in protein, which is why the swelling is firm rather than soft. It does not pit as readily as the swelling of heart failure or of a low protein state.

Question 4355. A constructed illustration: a newborn has a soft swelling in the side of the neck that lets light through. Which developmental abnormality of lymphatic vessels is illustrated? The answer is a lymphatic malformation, once called a cystic hygroma. Part of the lymphatic network failed to join the veins and dilated into cysts. Such swellings often lie in the posterior triangle of the neck.

Question 4356. Which statement about the origin of the lymphatic system is correct: it grows out from the veins, it grows out from the arteries, it forms from the lymph nodes first, or it forms from the spleen? The answer is that it grows out from the veins. Lymphatic sacs bud from the embryonic veins and spread through the body, and the two largest become the ducts.

Question 4357. Into which veins do the lymphatic vessels of the embryo first open? The answer is the large veins of the neck, near the future venous angles. The lymphatic sacs keep that connection as the body grows. That is why the adult ducts end at the venous angles, where the subclavian and internal jugular veins meet.

Question 4358. Name the largest lymphatic vessel in the body, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the thoracic duct. It begins in the abdomen at the cisterna chyli and ends in the root of the left side of the neck. In an adult it is roughly 38 to 45 centimeters long and about 3 millimeters wide.

Question 4359. Name the three coats of a collecting lymphatic vessel, from the lumen outward, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the tunica intima, the tunica media and the tunica adventitia. The intima is lined by endothelium, the media carries smooth muscle, and the adventitia is the outer coat of collagen. The same three coats are found in veins.

Question 4360. A described lymphangiogram shows a beaded chain of thin vessels climbing the medial side of the thigh toward the groin. What makes the chain look beaded, and where does it end? The answer is the valves along the vessel, and it ends in the inguinal nodes. Each valve marks a short segment, so the column of contrast looks like a string of beads.

Question 4361. What is the effect of breathing on the flow of lymph in the thoracic duct? The answer is that breathing increases the flow. Descent of the diaphragm lowers the pressure in the chest and raises it in the abdomen. Lymph is thus drawn upward from the abdomen and onward toward the neck.

Question 4362. Which statement about the flow of lymph in the body is correct: it depends on a central pump, it depends on the heart alone, it depends on muscle contraction, breathing and the pulsation of arteries, or it stops completely during sleep? The answer is that it depends on muscle contraction, breathing and the pulsation of nearby arteries. There is no central lymphatic pump.

Question 4363. A described transverse section of the abdomen at the level of the second lumbar vertebra shows a small sac lying against the vertebral bodies, with the aorta to its left and the inferior vena cava to its right. What is the sac, and where does it lie? The answer is the cisterna chyli, which lies behind the peritoneum in the posterior part of the abdomen.

Question 4364. Which of these structures does lymph pass through on its way from the small intestine to the thoracic duct: the cisterna chyli, the right lymphatic duct, the axillary nodes, or the deep cervical nodes? The answer is the cisterna chyli. The intestinal trunk opens into it in the abdomen. From there the lymph enters the thoracic duct.

Question 4365. A constructed illustration: a lump in the left side of the neck just above the collarbone presses on the end of the thoracic duct. Which lymph does that lump obstruct? The answer is the lymph from almost the whole body, since the thoracic duct ends there. Such a lump can block the return from the lower limbs, the abdomen and the left upper quarter.

Question 4366. Lymph from the stomach reaches the left supraclavicular lymph nodes by which route? The answer is through the intestinal trunk, the cisterna chyli and the thoracic duct. The duct ends at the left venous angle just below those nodes. Lymph that leaves the duct there can be carried into the left supraclavicular nodes.

Question 4367. Which of these pairs belongs together: the thoracic duct with the right venous angle, the right lymphatic duct with the left venous angle, the thoracic duct with the left venous angle, or the cisterna chyli with the right venous angle? The answer is the thoracic duct with the left venous angle. The right lymphatic duct ends at the right venous angle, and the cisterna chyli lies below the diaphragm.

Question 4368. Which of these pairs belongs together: the intestinal trunk with the lower limbs, the lumbar trunks with the small intestine, the jugular trunk with the head and neck, or the bronchomediastinal trunk with the upper limb? The answer is the jugular trunk with the head and neck. The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs and the pelvis, and the bronchomediastinal trunk drains the chest.

Question 4369. Which of these pairs belongs together: the subclavian trunk with the upper limb, the subclavian trunk with the head, the jugular trunk with the arm, or the intestinal trunk with the neck? The answer is the subclavian trunk with the upper limb. It is formed by the axillary nodes, and each trunk is named for the region it drains.

Question 4370. Which of these pairs belongs together: chyle with the intestine, chyle with the skin, lymph with the blood, or lymph with the stomach only? The answer is chyle with the intestine. Chyle is the milky lymph formed in the small intestine after a fatty meal. All lymph is tissue fluid that has entered the lymphatic vessels.

Question 4371. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anchoring filaments with the lymphatic capillary, the anchoring filaments with the valve, the valve with the tissue spaces, or the lacteal with the skin? The answer is the anchoring filaments with the lymphatic capillary. They tie the endothelial cells of that capillary to the surrounding tissue. A lacteal is a lymphatic capillary of the small intestine.

Question 4372. A described section of the intestinal wall shows a blunt-ended vessel in the center of a finger-like projection, with a network of finer vessels around it. Which vessel is the blunt-ended one? The answer is the lacteal, the central lymphatic of the villus. The fine network around it is the blood capillary bed. Its blind end lets fat enter the villus but not leave it.

Question 4373. A described specimen shows the wall of a large lymphatic vessel cut across, with an inner endothelial lining, a middle layer of smooth muscle and an outer fibrous coat. Which coat is the middle one? The answer is the tunica media. It lies between the intima and the adventitia and carries the muscle that pumps. The outer coat is the tunica adventitia.

Question 4374. Which of these statements about the lymphatic system is correct: it begins and ends in the tissues, it begins in the tissues and ends in the blood, it begins in the blood and ends in the tissues, or it begins and ends in the blood? The answer is that it begins in the tissue spaces and ends in the blood. The capillaries are blind at their tissue end.

Question 4375. What is the name of the fluid in the tissue spaces before it enters a lymphatic capillary? The answer is tissue fluid, also called interstitial fluid. Once it passes between the endothelial flaps it is called lymph. The change of name marks the change of compartment, not a change in the fluid itself.

Question 4376. A described section of a lymph node shows a thin outer coat of connective tissue, with narrow bands passing from it into the substance of the node. What are the outer coat and the bands called? The answer is the capsule and the trabeculae. The trabeculae divide the outer part of the node into compartments. Small blood vessels travel inside them.

Question 4377. A described section of a lymph node shows a narrow channel lying just beneath the capsule and receiving several vessels that pierce the capsule from the surface. What is that channel? The answer is the subcapsular sinus, also called the marginal sinus. The afferent vessels open into it. From it the lymph seeps inward through the cortex toward the medulla.

Question 4378. In which part of a lymph node do the rounded lymphoid follicles lie: the cortex, the medulla, the hilum, or the capsule? The answer is the cortex, the outer part of the node. Each follicle is a mass of lymphocytes, mainly B lymphocytes. The deeper part of the cortex, called the paracortex, holds mainly T lymphocytes.

Question 4379. True or false: a lymph node has more efferent vessels than afferent vessels. The answer is false. Several afferent vessels bring lymph into the node through its convex surface, while only one or two efferent vessels leave it at the hilum. Lymph therefore slows as it passes through the node.

Question 4380. On which part of a lymph node does the efferent vessel leave, and what else passes through that same part? The answer is the hilum, the concave notch on one side of the node, and the artery and vein pass through it too. The hilum is the only place where lymph leaves the node. The convex surface carries the afferent vessels instead.

Question 4381. A described section of a lymph node shows a rounded mass of cells with a pale center and a darker ring around it. What is the pale center called, and what happens there? The answer is the germinal center, where lymphocytes multiply. The cells there have met an antigen carried in by the lymph. The darker ring around it is made of small resting lymphocytes.

Question 4382. Which cells occupy the paracortex of a lymph node in the greatest number: T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, plasma cells, or red blood cells? The answer is T lymphocytes. The paracortex lies deep to the follicles of the cortex. It is also the zone through which lymphocytes enter the node from the blood.

Question 4383. The high endothelial venules of a lymph node lie in which zone relative to the lymphoid follicles, and what enters the node through them? The answer is the paracortex, which lies deep to the follicles, and lymphocytes enter through them. Their tall endothelial cells let those cells leave the blood. The lymphocytes then pass into the substance of the node.

Question 4384. A described section of the central part of a lymph node shows branching cords of cells separated by a network of channels. What are the cords and the channels called? The answer is the medullary cords and the medullary sinuses. Lymph reaches them after seeping through the cortex. The sinuses converge on the hilum, where the efferent vessel begins.

Question 4385. Which cells line the sinuses of a lymph node and remove particles from the lymph: macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, or fibroblasts? The answer is macrophages. They engulf bacteria, dead cells and other particles carried in the lymph. Some of them also present what they have taken up to the lymphocytes of the node.

Question 4386. In which part of a lymph node are plasma cells most numerous: the medullary cords, the germinal centers, the subcapsular sinus, or the capsule? The answer is the medullary cords of the medulla. They are the descendants of activated B lymphocytes. They secrete antibody into the lymph that is passing through the node.

Question 4387. A described cross section of a lymph node shows a dark outer rim, a paler middle zone and a central network of channels. Which zone is the paler middle one? The answer is the paracortex. It lies between the follicles of the outer cortex and the medulla. Lymphocytes enter it from the blood through high endothelial venules.

Question 4388. A constructed illustration: a person has a sore throat and feels tender lumps in the neck below the jaw. Which nodes are involved, and why are they tender? The answer is the deep cervical nodes, and they are tender because the swollen tissue stretches their capsule. They filter the lymph coming from the throat and the tonsils. This illustration is not a particular case.

Question 4389. A constructed illustration: a small lump is found in the upper outer part of the breast, and the first node shown to receive its cells lies in the armpit. What name is given to that first node? The answer is the sentinel node. It is the node that receives lymph from that part of the breast first, as the anatomy predicts.

Question 4390. A constructed illustration: after a long walk a person has a tender swelling in the hollow behind the knee. Which group of nodes is inflamed there? The answer is the popliteal nodes. They lie in the fat of the popliteal fossa. They receive lymph from the deep structures of the leg and from the territory of the small saphenous vein.

Question 4391. Which group of nodes lies in the groin just below the inguinal ligament and drains the skin of the lower limb and the perineum? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes. They lie in the fatty tissue below the ligament. Their efferent vessels pass to the deep inguinal and the external iliac nodes.

Question 4392. A described lymphangiogram of the groin shows a fan of vessels ending in a group of small rounded nodes just below the inguinal ligament. Which group is shown, and where does its lymph go next? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes, and their lymph passes to the deep inguinal and external iliac nodes. The iliac nodes lie inside the pelvis along the external iliac vessels.

Question 4393. Which statement about the size of a normal lymph node is correct: it is about 1 to 2 centimeters long, it is about 10 centimeters long, it is always smaller than 1 millimeter, or it is the size of a walnut? The answer is that a normal node is about 1 to 2 centimeters long. Most are smaller and cannot be felt through the skin.

Question 4394. A constructed illustration: a young man has a swelling of one testis, and the nodes first involved are found in the abdomen rather than in the groin. Which nodes are they, and why? The answer is the para-aortic nodes. The testis carried its vessels and its lymphatics with it as it descended from the abdomen. The skin of the scrotum, by contrast, drains to the inguinal nodes.

Question 4395. A constructed illustration: a person has a firm lump just above the left clavicle, in the angle between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which group of nodes lies there? The answer is the deep cervical nodes, at their lowest point beside the internal jugular vein. The thoracic duct ends just below that point. A lump there can block the return of lymph from much of the body.

Question 4396. A described dissection shows a chain of small rounded nodes running down the neck along the internal jugular vein, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which chain is shown, and which trunk does it form? The answer is the deep cervical chain, which forms the jugular trunk. Its efferent vessels end at the venous angle of their own side.

Question 4397. Which group of nodes lies in the mesentery and drains the small intestine and the colon, and what becomes of their efferent vessels? The answer is the mesenteric nodes, and their efferent vessels form the intestinal trunk. That trunk joins the cisterna chyli in the abdomen. The lymph they carry is rich in fat after a meal.

Question 4398. True or false: the lymph in the medullary sinuses of a lymph node has already passed through the cortex. The answer is true. Lymph enters at the subcapsular sinus, seeps through the cortex and the paracortex, and reaches the medulla. It then leaves by the efferent vessel at the hilum, so the order of flow is from the convex surface inward.

Question 4399. True or false: the capsule and the trabeculae form the framework of a lymph node. The answer is true. The capsule is the outer coat, and the trabeculae are its inward extensions. They divide the cortex into compartments and carry small blood vessels into the node.

Question 4400. Which of these is the direction of lymph flow through a lymph node: from the hilum to the capsule, from the capsule to the hilum, from the medulla to the cortex, or from the efferent vessel to the afferent vessel? The answer is from the capsule to the hilum. Lymph enters the subcapsular sinus and leaves by the efferent vessel at the hilum.

To summarize, the lymphatic system begins in the tissue spaces as blind-ended capillaries whose overlapping endothelial cells and anchoring filaments let fluid in but not out, and it ends where the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct open at the venous angles. Lymph is driven by muscle contraction, breathing, the pulsation of nearby arteries and the valves that divide each vessel into pumping segments, because there is no central lymphatic pump. The intestinal trunk and the two lumbar trunks form the cisterna chyli, and the thoracic duct drains both lower limbs, the abdomen and the whole left upper quarter. A lymph node receives lymph by afferent vessels on its convex surface, filters it through the subcapsular sinus, the cortex and the medulla, and returns it by an efferent vessel at the hilum. The deep cervical, axillary, inguinal, popliteal and para-aortic nodes are the groups a listener meets most often, and each is named for the region whose lymph it filters. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 45 — Lymph Nodes

This chapter examines the lymph nodes and the thoracic duct, the filters and the great collecting vessel of the lymphatic system. It describes what a lymph node is built from, where the named groups of nodes lie, what each group drains, and how lymph travels from the tissues through the nodes and into the thoracic duct. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The clinical items are constructed illustrations rather than real patients, and the measurements are ordinary textbook ranges offered only to describe normal structure. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4401. Which fibrous coat forms the outer covering of a lymph node, and what does it send inward? The answer is the capsule, which sends trabeculae inward. From its inner surface, septa pass into the cortex and carry blood vessels with them. The trabeculae divide the cortex into compartments.

Question 4402. Roughly how many lymph nodes are present in the adult body: 50 to 60, 150 to 200, 500 to 600, or 5,000 to 6,000? The answer is 500 to 600. They lie along the courses of the lymphatic vessels, often in groups where several vessels meet. The largest single collection lies in the mesentery of the small intestine.

Question 4403. A described section through a lymph node shows a dark outer zone of rounded masses and a paler central zone. Which part is the outer zone, and what are the masses? The answer is the cortex, and the masses are the lymphoid follicles. The paler central zone is the medulla, which contains cords and sinuses.

Question 4404. At which surface of a lymph node do the afferent lymphatic vessels enter, and how does their number compare with the vessel that leaves? The answer is the convex surface, while a single efferent vessel leaves at the hilum. Lymph enters widely and leaves by one narrow route, which slows its flow through the node.

Question 4405. Where does the efferent lymphatic vessel leave a lymph node: at the convex surface, at the hilum, through the capsule, or through a trabecula? The answer is at the hilum. The hilum is the concave notch where the capsule is drawn in, and the artery and vein of the node use the same place.

Question 4406. At the hilum of a lymph node, the efferent lymphatic vessel leaves beside which other structures? The answer is the artery and the vein of the node. Blood vessels enter and leave through the hilum, while lymph enters at the convex surface, so the two streams cross the node in opposite directions.

Question 4407. Which space does lymph enter first after crossing the capsule: the medullary sinus, the subcapsular sinus, the cortical sinus, or the trabecular sinus? The answer is the subcapsular sinus, just deep to the capsule. From there lymph seeps through the cortical sinuses toward the medulla and leaves by the efferent vessel at the hilum.

Question 4408. Which zone of a lymph node lies between the follicles of the cortex and the medulla, and which lymphocytes gather there? The answer is the paracortex, or deep cortex, where T lymphocytes gather. The follicles above it are the home of B lymphocytes, so the two zones hold different cells.

Question 4409. Which cells fill the follicles of the cortex: T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, plasma cells, or macrophages? The answer is B lymphocytes. An active follicle shows a pale germinal center where those cells multiply, while plasma cells lie in the medullary cords and T lymphocytes in the paracortex.

Question 4410. True or false: lymph from most tissues passes through at least one lymph node before it returns to the blood. The answer is true. The nodes lie along the lymphatic vessels and act as filters, so particles in the lymph meet the macrophages and lymphocytes of a node. Some lymph passes through two or more nodes in series.

Question 4411. Which group of lymph nodes forms the largest single collection in the body, and where does it lie? The answer is the mesenteric nodes, between the two layers of the mesentery of the small intestine. They lie along the branches of the superior mesenteric artery and receive lymph from the jejunum and the ileum.

Question 4412. About how many nodes lie in the mesentery of the small intestine: 10 to 20, 100 to 150, 300 to 400, or 1,000 to 1,500? The answer is 100 to 150. They are arranged in tiers, with small nodes near the bowel wall and larger ones near the root of the mesentery, where the lymph joins the intestinal trunk.

Question 4413. A described lymphangiogram of the neck shows a chain of nodes along the internal jugular vein, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which group is shown? The answer is the deep cervical nodes. They form a chain from the base of the skull to the root of the neck, while the superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein.

Question 4414. A constructed illustration: a person with a sore throat has a tender node below the angle of the mandible, at the level of the hyoid bone. Which node is enlarged? The answer is the jugulodigastric node, also called the tonsillar node. It lies at the junction of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle with the internal jugular vein and enlarges early in tonsillitis.

Question 4415. What is the name of the large deep cervical node lying at the junction of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle with the internal jugular vein? The answer is the jugulodigastric node. It is also called the tonsillar node because it drains the palatine tonsil, and it enlarges early in a throat infection.

Question 4416. Which muscle lies immediately above the jugulodigastric node, and which large vein lies deep to it? The answer is the posterior belly of the digastric muscle above the node, with the internal jugular vein deep to it. Because the node drains the tonsil, its enlargement points to the throat.

Question 4417. The tip of the tongue drains first to which group of nodes: the submental nodes, the submandibular nodes, the jugulodigastric node, or the occipital nodes? The answer is the submental nodes, which lie under the chin between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles. The posterior third of the tongue drains instead to the deep cervical nodes.

Question 4418. A constructed illustration: an older adult has weight loss and early fullness after meals, and a hard node is found in the left supraclavicular fossa. Which organ should be examined first, and which vessel explains the pattern? The answer is the stomach, by way of the thoracic duct. Lymph from the abdominal organs ascends in the duct to the left venous angle just above that node.

Question 4419. Which left supraclavicular node, named after the physician who described it, may enlarge when a cancer of the stomach spreads along the thoracic duct? The answer is the node of Virchow. It lies in the left supraclavicular fossa behind the sternal head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and its enlargement is a sign of disease that has travelled far from its origin.

Question 4420. Where do the submandibular nodes lie, and toward which group does their lymph pass? The answer is in the submandibular triangle, below the body of the mandible and beside the submandibular gland, and their lymph passes to the deep cervical nodes. They receive lymph from the front of the tongue, the floor of the mouth, and the teeth and gums.

Question 4421. Which group of axillary nodes lies along the axillary vein on the lateral wall of the axilla: the pectoral group, the subscapular group, the lateral group, or the apical group? The answer is the lateral group, also called the humeral group. It lies along the axillary vein and receives most of the lymph from the upper limb.

Question 4422. Which group of axillary nodes lies along the lateral thoracic vessels behind the pectoralis major, and what does it drain? The answer is the pectoral group, also called the anterior group. It receives lymph from the anterior chest wall and from a large part of the breast.

Question 4423. A described dissection of the posterior wall of the axilla shows a row of nodes along the subscapular vessels. Which group is shown, and what does it drain? The answer is the subscapular or posterior group. It drains the back of the chest and the shoulder region, and its efferent vessels pass to the central and apical nodes.

Question 4424. Which group of axillary nodes lies at the apex of the axilla above the upper border of the pectoralis minor, and into which trunk do its vessels drain? The answer is the apical group, whose lymph passes into the subclavian trunk. It forms the highest tier of the axillary nodes, medial to the axillary vein.

Question 4425. A constructed illustration: a tumor of the upper outer quadrant of the breast is found together with nodes in the axilla. About how much of the lymph of the breast reaches the axillary nodes: one quarter, one half, three quarters, or all of it? The answer is about three quarters. The rest passes chiefly to the parasternal nodes beside the internal thoracic vessels.

Question 4426. The lymph of the upper limb drains chiefly into which group of nodes: the cervical nodes, the axillary nodes, the inguinal nodes, or the mediastinal nodes? The answer is the axillary nodes. The superficial vessels of the limb run along its medial and lateral borders and end in that group, and a deep set follows the main vessels to the same nodes.

Question 4427. A described lymphangiogram of the upper limb shows a single small node just above and medial to the elbow, beside the basilic vein. Which node is shown? The answer is the epitrochlear node, also called the cubital node. It receives lymph from the ulnar side of the hand and the medial side of the forearm.

Question 4428. Which node lies 2 to 3 centimeters above the medial epicondyle of the humerus, beside the basilic vein? The answer is the epitrochlear node. It is the only constant node of the upper limb below the axilla, and its enlargement often follows an infection of the hand.

Question 4429. The epitrochlear node lies in the superficial fascia on which side of the arm, and to which group do its efferent vessels pass? The answer is the medial side of the arm, and its efferents pass to the lateral group of axillary nodes. It sits above the medial epicondyle beside the basilic vein.

Question 4430. Which nodes receive lymph from the ulnar side of the hand and the medial side of the forearm: the apical nodes of the axilla, the epitrochlear node, the supraclavicular nodes, or the parasternal nodes? The answer is the epitrochlear node. From it the lymph passes to the lateral group of axillary nodes.

Question 4431. A constructed illustration: a puncture wound on the little finger becomes infected, and a tender node appears above and medial to the elbow. Which node is inflamed, and where does its lymph go next? The answer is the epitrochlear node, whose lymph passes to the lateral axillary nodes. The infection follows the lymphatic vessels that run with the basilic vein.

Question 4432. Which group of nodes lies in the superficial fascia of the groin just below the inguinal ligament? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes. They receive lymph from the lower limb and from the superficial tissues of the lower abdominal wall, the perineum and the external genitalia.

Question 4433. Into which two groups are the superficial inguinal nodes arranged: medial and lateral, horizontal and vertical, deep and superficial, or upper and lower? The answer is a horizontal group and a vertical group. The horizontal group lies below the inguinal ligament and drains the superficial tissues of the abdomen and the perineum, and the vertical group lies along the great saphenous vein.

Question 4434. The deep inguinal nodes lie immediately medial to which vessel, and within which sheath? The answer is the femoral vein, within the femoral sheath. They lie beneath the deep fascia, and their efferents pass through the femoral canal to the external iliac nodes.

Question 4435. Which node is the highest of the deep inguinal group and lies in the femoral canal just below the inguinal ligament? The answer is the node of Cloquet, also called the node of Rosenmuller. It lies medial to the femoral vein at the entrance to the femoral canal.

Question 4436. Where does the node of Cloquet lie: in the popliteal fossa, in the femoral canal medial to the femoral vein, in the adductor canal, or beside the great saphenous vein? The answer is in the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein. It is the highest node of the deep inguinal group.

Question 4437. A described cross section taken just below the inguinal ligament shows the femoral vein within a fibrous sheath, with a small node on the medial side of the vein inside that sheath. Which node is shown? The answer is the node of Cloquet, the highest deep inguinal node. Nodes inside the femoral sheath are deep inguinal nodes, while those outside it in the superficial fascia are superficial inguinal nodes.

Question 4438. Which structures do the popliteal nodes chiefly drain: the deep parts of the leg and the foot, the skin of the thigh, the perineum, or the buttock? The answer is the deep parts of the leg and the foot. They lie in the popliteal fossa around the popliteal vessels and also receive lymph from the knee joint.

Question 4439. Which group of nodes lies in the fat of the popliteal fossa, around the popliteal artery and vein, and receives lymph from the deep parts of the leg? The answer is the popliteal nodes. There are usually 4 to 6 of them, and their efferents ascend to the deep inguinal nodes.

Question 4440. A constructed illustration: a deep infection of the calf muscles is followed by a tender swelling in the popliteal fossa. Which nodes are involved, and where does their lymph go next? The answer is the popliteal nodes, whose lymph passes to the deep inguinal nodes. The deep tissues of the leg drain to them, while the skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Question 4441. True or false: superficial lymph from the foot drains mainly to the superficial inguinal nodes rather than to the popliteal nodes. The answer is true. The superficial tissues of the lower limb drain along the great saphenous vein to the superficial inguinal nodes, except on the lateral side of the foot and leg, which follows the small saphenous vein to the popliteal nodes.

Question 4442. Which nodes receive lymph from the medial half of the breast: the axillary nodes, the parasternal nodes, the popliteal nodes, or the deep cervical nodes? The answer is the parasternal nodes, which lie along the internal thoracic vessels. Lymph from them passes to the bronchomediastinal trunk.

Question 4443. The parasternal nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels. Behind which structures do they lie, and on which side of the sternum? The answer is behind the costal cartilages and lateral to the sternum. They receive lymph from the medial part of the breast and from the anterior chest wall.

Question 4444. Which lymph nodes lie at the root of the mesentery, around the first part of the superior mesenteric artery, and receive the lymph gathered by the mesenteric nodes? The answer is the superior mesenteric nodes. Their efferent vessels join the intestinal trunk, which ends in the cisterna chyli.

Question 4445. A described operation field shows a chain of nodes lying on the front of the abdominal aorta above the origin of the renal arteries, with lymphatic vessels running up from the kidneys and the gonads. Which group is shown? The answer is the para-aortic or lumbar nodes. Their efferents form the lumbar trunks, which end in the cisterna chyli.

Question 4446. Which trunks join to form the cisterna chyli: the right and left lumbar trunks with the intestinal trunk, the right and left jugular trunks, the bronchomediastinal trunks, or the subclavian trunks? The answer is the right and left lumbar trunks together with the intestinal trunk. The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs and the pelvis, and the intestinal trunk drains the gut.

Question 4447. Which of these pairs belongs together: the axillary nodes with the lower limb, the popliteal nodes with the deep calf, the cervical nodes with the foot, or the inguinal nodes with the head? The answer is the popliteal nodes with the deep calf. The axillary nodes drain the upper limb, and the inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and the perineum.

Question 4448. Which of these pairs belongs together: the submental nodes with the tip of the tongue, the submandibular nodes with the tip of the tongue, the occipital nodes with the tip of the tongue, or the supraclavicular nodes with the tip of the tongue? The answer is the submental nodes with the tip of the tongue. The submandibular nodes lie further back and drain the front of the tongue.

Question 4449. Which of these pairs belongs together: the epitrochlear node with the radial forearm, the node of Cloquet with the axilla, the jugulodigastric node with the tonsil, or the popliteal nodes with the buttock? The answer is the jugulodigastric node with the tonsil, which is why it is named the tonsillar node. The epitrochlear node drains the ulnar side of the forearm, and the node of Cloquet lies deep in the groin.

Question 4450. Which of these pairs belongs together: the subscapular nodes with the anterior chest wall, the pectoral nodes with the back of the chest, the lateral nodes with the upper limb, or the central nodes with the lower limb? The answer is the lateral nodes with the upper limb. The pectoral nodes drain the anterior chest wall, and the subscapular nodes drain the back of the chest.

Question 4451. Name two groups of lymph nodes of the neck, spoken as a list. The answer is the submental nodes and the deep cervical nodes. The submental nodes lie under the chin between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles, and the deep cervical nodes form a chain along the internal jugular vein.

Question 4452. Name two structures that enter or leave a lymph node at its hilum, spoken as a list. The answer is the efferent lymphatic vessel and the blood vessels. The artery and vein of the node use the hilum, while the afferent lymphatic vessels enter on the convex surface.

Question 4453. What is the chief work of a lymph node: to pump lymph toward the heart, to filter lymph and give lymphocytes a place to meet foreign material, to make red blood cells, or to store fat? The answer is that it filters lymph and gives lymphocytes a place to meet foreign material. Macrophages in the sinuses remove particles, and lymphocytes respond to what the lymph carries.

Question 4454. What is the name of the milky fluid that fills the lymphatic vessels of the small intestine after a fatty meal? The answer is chyle. The fat absorbed from the gut enters the lymphatic vessels called lacteals and gives the lymph its milky look.

Question 4455. The lymphatic vessels called lacteals are found in which structure: the villi of the small intestine, the crypts of the colon, the alveoli of the lung, or the glomeruli of the kidney? The answer is the villi of the small intestine. Each villus holds a central lacteal that absorbs the products of fat digestion, which is why intestinal lymph is milky after a meal.

Question 4456. A described section of a node taken from a person who died during a bacterial infection shows large pale germinal centers in the follicles and widened sinuses full of cells. Which change is shown? The answer is reactive follicular hyperplasia, the normal response of a node to infection. The germinal centers enlarge as B lymphocytes multiply, and the sinuses fill with macrophages.

Question 4457. A constructed illustration: a child with a sore throat has a small, tender, mobile node in the upper neck, and the node settles when the throat settles. What is the likely nature of the node? The answer is reactive enlargement of a cervical node in response to infection. Tenderness and mobility point to inflammation rather than to a tumor.

Question 4458. Which feature of an enlarged lymph node favors a malignant cause rather than an infection: tenderness on pressure, warmth of the skin over it, a hard and fixed node, or a node that shrinks as the infection resolves? The answer is a hard and fixed node. Infection usually makes a node tender, warm and mobile.

Question 4459. True or false: the right side of the head and the neck drains through the right lymphatic duct into the right venous angle. The answer is true. The right jugular trunk joins that duct, which ends where the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins meet.

Question 4460. Which venous junction receives the lymph of the right upper limb, and by which duct does it arrive? The answer is the right venous angle, by way of the right lymphatic duct. In many people that duct is absent, and its three trunks open separately into the angle.

Question 4461. Which statement about the right lymphatic duct is correct: it is present in every person, it carries lymph from the whole body, it is a short vessel that may be absent, or it is the upper end of the thoracic duct? The answer is that it is a short vessel, about 1 to 2 centimeters long, which may be absent. It drains only the right upper quadrant, and its trunks may open separately.

Question 4462. A described dissection of the small bowel mesentery shows small nodes close to the bowel wall and larger nodes near the root of the mesentery. What are these two sets? The answer is the juxta-intestinal nodes near the bowel and the superior mesenteric nodes near the root. Lymph filters through them in that order and then enters the intestinal trunk.

Question 4463. How does blood reach the tissue of a lymph node: by entering at the hilum and running along the trabeculae, by entering at the convex surface with the afferent lymphatics, by way of the subcapsular sinus, or by capillaries that pierce the capsule? The answer is that the artery enters at the hilum and its branches follow the trabeculae. Lymph enters at the convex surface instead.

Question 4464. A described section of a lymph node shows septa of connective tissue running inward from the capsule and dividing the outer part of the node into compartments. What are these septa called? The answer is the trabeculae, and they divide the cortex into compartments. They carry blood vessels into the substance of the node.

Question 4465. A constructed illustration: a person in a region where a mosquito-borne worm is common develops a leg that is swollen and firm and does not go down with rest. Which structures are blocked? The answer is the lymphatic vessels and nodes of the limb, a condition called lymphedema. Care of such a limb belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4466. In which part of a lymph node do the high endothelial venules lie, the vessels through which lymphocytes re-enter the node from the blood: the follicles, the subcapsular sinus, the paracortex, or the medullary sinuses? The answer is the paracortex, the deep cortex between the follicles and the medulla. Lymphocytes leave the blood through the tall cells that line those venules.

Question 4467. Which cells line the sinuses of a lymph node and remove particulate matter from the lymph as it passes? The answer is the macrophages. They lie in the subcapsular sinus, the cortical sinuses and the medullary sinuses, and they present what they take up to the lymphocytes of the node.

Question 4468. In the medulla of a lymph node, between which spaces do the medullary cords lie, and which cells fill them? The answer is between the medullary sinuses, and the cords are filled with lymphocytes and plasma cells. Lymph flows through the sinuses that surround the cords.

Question 4469. A described cut surface of a lymph node shows a rounded outer border and a single concave notch where the capsule is drawn in. What is that notch called, and which structures use it? The answer is the hilum, through which the efferent lymphatic vessel and the blood vessels pass. The afferent vessels enter on the convex surface.

Question 4470. Which structure of a lymph node lies deepest, nearest the hilum: the lymphoid follicles, the subcapsular sinus, the medullary sinuses, or the outer cortex? The answer is the medullary sinuses. Lymph enters at the convex surface and travels inward, and it reaches the medullary sinuses last before leaving at the hilum.

Question 4471. A constructed illustration: an older adult has a hard, fixed node in the left supraclavicular fossa, and no infection is found in the neck. Which region should be examined first, and which vessel explains the finding? The answer is the abdomen, particularly the stomach, with the thoracic duct explaining it. Investigations belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4472. A described specimen of the floor of the mouth shows two small nodes lying just below the body of the mandible, beside the submandibular gland. Which nodes are shown? The answer is the submandibular nodes. They drain the front of the tongue, the floor of the mouth and the teeth, and their efferent vessels pass to the deep cervical nodes.

Question 4473. Which group of lymph nodes receives lymph from the upper limb and from most of the breast: the cervical nodes, the axillary nodes, the inguinal nodes, or the mediastinal nodes? The answer is the axillary nodes. They lie in the axilla around the axillary vessels, and their lymph passes to the subclavian trunk.

Question 4474. Which lymph nodes lie beside the trachea and at its bifurcation, receiving lymph from the lungs? The answer is the tracheobronchial nodes, which include the paratracheal nodes and those below the bifurcation. On the left their lymph ends in the thoracic duct, and on the right in the right lymphatic duct.

Question 4475. True or false: a normal lymph node is usually too small to be felt through the skin. The answer is true. Most nodes are only a few millimeters across when they are healthy, and they become easy to feel when infection or a tumor enlarges them.

Question 4476. What is the name of the largest lymphatic vessel in the body, which carries lymph from both lower limbs, the abdomen, the left thorax, the left upper limb and the left side of the head and neck? The answer is the thoracic duct. It begins in the abdomen at the cisterna chyli and ends in the root of the neck.

Question 4477. About how long is the thoracic duct in an adult: 5 to 8 centimeters, 12 to 15 centimeters, 38 to 45 centimeters, or 90 to 100 centimeters? The answer is 38 to 45 centimeters. It runs from the upper part of the abdomen, through the chest, to the root of the neck.

Question 4478. What is the name of the dilated lower end of the thoracic duct, which receives the lumbar and intestinal trunks? The answer is the cisterna chyli. It lies at the level of the first and second lumbar vertebrae, and from it the thoracic duct ascends to the left venous angle.

Question 4479. At which level does the cisterna chyli lie: at the twelfth thoracic vertebra, at the first and second lumbar vertebrae, at the third lumbar vertebra, or in the pelvis? The answer is the first and second lumbar vertebrae. It lies in front of the vertebral bodies, behind the aorta and to its right.

Question 4480. The thoracic duct begins behind the right crus of the diaphragm. Between which two vessels does it lie at that point? The answer is the aorta and the azygos vein. It passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm behind the aorta, with the azygos vein to its right.

Question 4481. A described lymphangiogram shows a thin, beaded vessel ascending through the back of the chest from the upper abdomen to the base of the neck. Which vessel is shown? The answer is the thoracic duct. Its beaded look comes from the many valves along its length.

Question 4482. Through which opening of the diaphragm does the thoracic duct pass from the abdomen into the chest: the caval opening, the esophageal opening, the aortic opening, or the opening for the sympathetic trunk? The answer is the aortic opening. The duct passes behind the aorta at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra.

Question 4483. In the lower part of the chest, the thoracic duct lies behind which structure, and which vessels lie on its left and on its right? The answer is that it lies behind the esophagus, with the aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. Near the fourth thoracic vertebra it crosses to the left side of the chest.

Question 4484. A described transverse section of the chest at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra shows a small thin-walled vessel lying between the aorta and the azygos vein, behind the esophagus. Which vessel is it? The answer is the thoracic duct. It lies against the vertebral bodies at that level.

Question 4485. At about which level does the thoracic duct cross from the right side of the chest to the left: the second thoracic vertebra, the fourth or fifth thoracic vertebra, the eighth thoracic vertebra, or the twelfth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the fourth or fifth thoracic vertebra, at the level of the sternal angle. Below that level the duct lies on the right of the midline.

Question 4486. Which lymphatic vessel receives the lymph from the intercostal nodes and from the posterior mediastinal nodes? The answer is the thoracic duct. The intercostal nodes drain the back of the chest wall, and the posterior mediastinal nodes lie beside the esophagus and the aorta.

Question 4487. At which venous junction does the thoracic duct end, and which two veins form that junction? The answer is the left venous angle, formed by the left internal jugular vein and the left subclavian vein. Its lymph therefore enters the blood a short distance above the heart.

Question 4488. Which of these regions sends its lymph through the thoracic duct: the right upper limb, the right side of the head and neck, the left lower limb, or the right side of the chest? The answer is the left lower limb. The thoracic duct drains both lower limbs, the abdomen, the left thorax, the left upper limb and the left side of the head and neck.

Question 4489. Which of these does not send its lymph through the thoracic duct: the left lung, the right side of the head and neck, the small intestine, or the left lower limb? The answer is the right side of the head and neck, whose lymph reaches the right venous angle by the right lymphatic duct. The left lung drains by the left bronchomediastinal trunk.

Question 4490. A described specimen at the root of the neck shows a duct ending in the angle between the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, with three short trunks joining it just before it ends. What are the duct and the trunks? The answer is the thoracic duct, joined by the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks.

Question 4491. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the back of the chest, milky fluid collects in the left pleural cavity over several days. Which structure has been injured, and what is the collection called? The answer is the thoracic duct, and the collection is a chylothorax. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4492. A constructed illustration: a person with obstruction of the lymphatic channels of the abdomen passes urine that looks like milk. Which channel is involved? The answer is the thoracic duct and its abdominal tributaries, and the condition is chyluria. Care belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4493. True or false: the thoracic duct carries the lymph of the left upper limb. The answer is true. The left subclavian trunk gathers the lymph of that limb and joins the thoracic duct at its upper end, while the right upper limb drains by the right subclavian trunk.

Question 4494. Which of these pairs belongs together: the left jugular trunk with the right side of the head and neck, the intestinal trunk with the lower limbs, the lumbar trunks with the gut, or the left bronchomediastinal trunk with the left lung? The answer is the left bronchomediastinal trunk with the left lung. The left jugular trunk drains the left side of the head and neck.

Question 4495. Name the three trunks that join the upper end of the thoracic duct, spoken as a list. The answer is the left jugular trunk, the left subclavian trunk and the left bronchomediastinal trunk. They carry lymph from the left side of the head and neck, from the left upper limb, and from the left side of the chest.

Question 4496. A described sagittal section through the back of the chest shows a thin-walled tube running upward in front of the vertebral column and behind the esophagus. On which side of the midline does it lie below, and on which side above? The answer is the right side below and the left side above. The change takes place near the fourth thoracic vertebra.

Question 4497. Which statement about the valves of the thoracic duct is correct: they are absent, they lie only in the cisterna chyli, they keep lymph moving toward the veins and stop blood from entering the duct, or they close the duct during exercise?
