The answer is that they keep lymph moving toward the veins and stop blood from entering the duct. The valve at its termination guards against backflow.

Question 4498. Which lymphatic vessel lies immediately behind the left subclavian artery as it approaches the left venous angle at the root of the neck? The answer is the thoracic duct. Having crossed to the left in the chest, it ascends behind the left subclavian artery and ends a short distance above that point.

Question 4499. A described section of a vessel wall shows a thin layer of endothelium over elastic fibers and smooth muscle, with valves at intervals, and the vessel carries a milky fluid. Which vessel is it? The answer is the thoracic duct. Its wall is thinner than that of a vein of similar size, and no red blood cells lie within it.

Question 4500. A described dissection of the upper abdomen shows, in place of a single sac, a plexus of small vessels at the level of the first lumbar vertebra, behind the aorta. Which structure is described? The answer is the cisterna chyli, which in many people is a plexus rather than a sac. Its form varies widely.

To summarize, lymph nodes are filters set along the lymphatic vessels, built around a capsule that sends trabeculae inward, with afferent vessels entering the convex surface and a single efferent vessel leaving at the hilum. Lymph enters the subcapsular sinus, passes through the cortical and medullary sinuses and leaves at the hilum, meeting B lymphocytes in the follicles, T lymphocytes in the paracortex and macrophages in the sinuses. The named groups drain their own territories: the deep cervical chain drains the head and the neck, the axillary nodes drain the upper limb and most of the breast, the parasternal nodes drain the medial half of the breast, the mesenteric nodes drain the gut, the inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and the perineum, and the popliteal nodes drain the deep parts of the leg. The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli at the first and second lumbar vertebrae, ascends behind the esophagus between the aorta and the azygos vein, crosses to the left at about the fourth thoracic vertebra and ends at the left venous angle, draining both lower limbs, the abdomen, the left thorax, the left upper limb and the left side of the head and neck, while the right upper quadrant drains by the right lymphatic duct. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 46 — Spleen

This chapter follows the lymph of the body from the abdomen to the great veins and then turns to the organ that filters the blood. It covers the thoracic duct, its origin, its course through the chest and the neck, its relations and its ending, and then the spleen, its position, its coverings, its blood supply, its development and the clinical anatomy that follows from all of them. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4501. Which lymphatic channel is the largest in the body, and where does it end? The answer is the thoracic duct, which ends at the left venous angle. It begins in the abdomen, runs up through the chest, and carries lymph from both legs, the pelvis, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head and chest.

Question 4502. Where does the thoracic duct begin: in the pelvis, in the abdomen behind the diaphragm, in the chest behind the heart, or in the root of the neck? The answer is in the abdomen behind the diaphragm. Its lower end is a dilated sac at the level of the lower border of the twelfth thoracic vertebra. That sac is the cisterna chyli.

Question 4503. What is the name of the dilated sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct, and which trunks empty into it? The answer is the cisterna chyli, which receives the intestinal trunk and the two lumbar trunks. The intestinal trunk carries fat-rich lymph from the small intestine. The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs, the pelvis, and the abdominal wall.

Question 4504. Which vein receives the thoracic duct at the root of the neck, and what is that junction called? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein, at the point where the left internal jugular vein joins the left subclavian vein. That point is the left venous angle. The duct enters it from below and behind.

Question 4505. Which of these regions does the thoracic duct not drain: the left leg, the left arm, the right side of the head, or the left side of the abdomen? The answer is the right side of the head. The right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right half of the chest drain into the right lymphatic duct. Everything else in the body drains into the thoracic duct.

Question 4506. A constructed illustration: during an operation in the upper chest a surgeon divides a thin-walled channel behind the esophagus, and milky fluid collects in the left pleural cavity. Which channel is described? The answer is the thoracic duct. It carries chyle, the fat-rich lymph from the intestine, so a leak into the chest produces a collection of that fluid. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4507. A described section of the chest shows a small thin-walled tube in front of a vertebral body, behind the esophagus, with the aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. Which structure is shown? The answer is the thoracic duct. It ascends through the posterior mediastinum in exactly that plane. A section taken higher, at the level of the sternal angle, would show it crossing to the left.

Question 4508. Which structure forms the lower end of the thoracic duct: the superior vena cava, the cisterna chyli, the portal vein, or the inferior mesenteric vein? The answer is the cisterna chyli. It is a sac-like dilatation behind the right crus of the diaphragm. The other three carry blood rather than lymph.

Question 4509. In the posterior mediastinum, which two structures lie immediately in front of and immediately behind the thoracic duct? The answer is the esophagus in front and the vertebral column behind. The descending aorta lies to its left and the azygos vein to its right. The duct therefore occupies a narrow plane between the gullet and the spine.

Question 4510. True or false: the thoracic duct carries the lymph of the right upper limb. The answer is false. The right upper limb, the right side of the head and neck, and the right half of the chest drain into the right lymphatic duct. The two ducts are unequal partners, the left one serving about three quarters of the body.

Question 4511. Through which opening in the diaphragm does the thoracic duct pass on its way from the abdomen to the chest? The answer is the aortic hiatus. That opening also transmits the aorta and the azygos vein, and it lies behind the diaphragm at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra. The duct runs up behind the aorta through the same gap.

Question 4512. At which level does the thoracic duct cross from the right of the midline to the left: the fourth thoracic vertebra, the eighth thoracic vertebra, the twelfth thoracic vertebra, or the second lumbar vertebra? The answer is the fourth thoracic vertebra. The crossing lies behind the esophagus at the level of the sternal angle. Above that level the duct is a left-sided structure.

Question 4513. A described lymphangiogram shows a channel that begins as a sac in the upper abdomen, runs upward to the right of the midline, and then turns toward the left side of the neck. What explains the turn? The answer is the normal course of the thoracic duct, which crosses the midline in the upper chest at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. The turn is anatomy and not disease.

Question 4514. At the root of the neck the arch of the thoracic duct ends at the left venous angle. Which structure crosses immediately in front of that arch? The answer is the left common carotid artery, together with the left internal jugular vein. Both run in the carotid sheath. The vertebral vessels and the sympathetic trunk lie behind the duct.

Question 4515. A described dissection of the lower chest shows, where one thoracic duct is expected, two parallel thin-walled channels. Which explanation fits best: an enlarged azygos vein, a duplicated thoracic duct, a dilated esophagus, or a replaced right subclavian artery? The answer is a duplicated thoracic duct, a normal variant found in a small minority of people. The two channels usually join above the diaphragm and end together at the left venous angle.

Question 4516. A constructed illustration: a thin-walled channel in the left side of the root of the neck is torn during a procedure on the great veins, and the field fills with milky fluid. Which structure is injured? The answer is the thoracic duct, which ends at the left venous angle. It reaches that point after crossing the midline lower down. The repair belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4517. Which lymphatic trunk joins the thoracic duct from the left lung and the left half of the chest wall? The answer is the left bronchomediastinal trunk. A matching trunk on the right joins the right lymphatic duct instead. Each trunk carries lymph from the lung, the mediastinum, and the chest wall of its own side.

Question 4518. Which statement about the valves of the thoracic duct is correct: it contains no valves, its valves lie only at its lower end, its valves are numerous along its length and direct lymph toward the neck, or its valves allow flow in either direction? The answer is that its valves are numerous along its length and direct lymph toward the neck. Movement and breathing drive the flow, and the valves keep it one way.

Question 4519. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the cisterna chyli with the pelvis, the thoracic duct with the right upper limb, the right lymphatic duct with the right side of the head, or the lumbar trunks with the left arm? The answer is the right lymphatic duct with the right side of the head. The cisterna chyli lies in the upper abdomen, and the lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs.

Question 4520. Between which two structures does the thoracic duct lie as it ascends through the posterior mediastinum, and why does that position matter at operation? The answer is between the esophagus in front and the vertebral column behind, with the aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. Its thin wall makes it easy to overlook.

Question 4521. Which statement about the cisterna chyli is correct: it lies in the chest, it receives the intestinal and lumbar trunks, it drains into the right venous angle, or it is a distinct sac in every person? The answer is that it receives the intestinal and lumbar trunks. It lies in the abdomen behind the right crus of the diaphragm. In many people it is a plexus rather than a distinct sac.

Question 4522. Which channel carries the fat-rich lymph absorbed from a meal in the small intestine, and what is that lymph called? The answer is the thoracic duct, and the lymph is called chyle. Chyle reaches the duct through the intestinal trunk and the cisterna chyli. It looks milky because of the fat it carries.

Question 4523. A described radiograph taken after a lymph vessel has been filled with contrast medium shows a channel ending in a small ampulla behind the medial end of the left clavicle. What is shown? The answer is the terminal part of the thoracic duct, just before it enters the left venous angle. The duct ends in a small dilatation guarded by a pair of valves.

Question 4524. A constructed illustration: an operation high in the left chest leaves a milky collection in the left pleural cavity, while the same operation on the right side does not. Which anatomical fact explains this? The answer is that the thoracic duct crosses to the left at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. Below that level it lies on the right of the midline, and above it lies on the left.

Question 4525. Which statement best explains why the thoracic duct is easily torn during a procedure on the left side of the neck: it is the largest vessel in the neck, it ends at the left venous angle behind the carotid sheath, it is fixed to the prevertebral fascia, or it carries bright red blood? The answer is that it ends at the left venous angle behind the carotid sheath. It is thin walled and easily missed.

Question 4526. Which organ is the largest single mass of lymphoid tissue in the body, and where does it lie? The answer is the spleen, which lies in the left hypochondrium. It sits between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm, deep to the ninth to the eleventh ribs. In the adult it is about 12 centimeters long and about 150 grams in weight.

Question 4527. In which region of the abdomen does the spleen lie: the right hypochondrium, the left hypochondrium, the umbilical region, or the left iliac region? The answer is the left hypochondrium. It lies in the left upper quadrant, behind the lower left ribs. Its long axis runs along the line of the tenth rib.

Question 4528. A described radiograph of the abdomen shows a soft tissue shadow in the left upper quadrant, between the stomach bubble and the left chest wall, with a rounded lower border and a notch on its upper edge. Which organ produces the shadow? The answer is the spleen. The notch on the superior border reflects the lobular way it develops.

Question 4529. Which ligament joins the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach, and which vessels does it carry? The answer is the gastrosplenic ligament, which carries the short gastric vessels. It runs between the hilum of the spleen and the fundus of the stomach. The splenic vessels travel in the separate splenorenal ligament behind it.

Question 4530. Which organ lies immediately in front of and medial to the spleen, in contact with its gastric impression? The answer is the stomach. Its fundus and upper body rest against the visceral surface of the spleen. The spleen therefore lies behind the stomach and to its left.

Question 4531. Which artery supplies the spleen: the left gastric artery, the splenic artery, the superior mesenteric artery, or the left renal artery? The answer is the splenic artery. It arises from the celiac trunk and runs a tortuous course along the upper border of the pancreas. It enters the spleen at its hilum.

Question 4532. Which vein begins at the hilum of the spleen, runs to the right behind the body of the pancreas, and joins the superior mesenteric vein? The answer is the splenic vein. That junction forms the portal vein behind the neck of the pancreas. The splenic vein has no valves along its course.

Question 4533. On the visceral surface of the spleen, which organ lies in the renal impression and which lies in the colic impression? The answer is the left kidney in the renal impression and the left colic flexure in the colic impression. The gastric impression lies above them for the stomach. The splenic hilum occupies the middle of the visceral surface.

Question 4534. A constructed illustration: a person is struck on the left lower chest and later reports pain at the tip of the left shoulder. Which organ is most likely injured, and why is the pain felt there? The answer is the spleen. Blood irritates the diaphragm, and the phrenic nerve carries that sensation to the same spinal segments that supply the skin of the shoulder.

Question 4535. Which structure lies immediately below and medial to the spleen, in contact with its renal impression: the left kidney, the tail of the pancreas, the left suprarenal gland, or the left ureter? The answer is the left kidney. Its upper pole lies in the renal impression on the visceral surface. The tail of the pancreas lies against the hilum.

Question 4536. A constructed illustration: a young person with an enlarged spleen is struck in the left upper abdomen and collapses. Which organ has most likely ruptured, and why does it rupture more easily when enlarged? The answer is the spleen. An enlarged organ has a stretched capsule, and its lower pole extends below the rib cage, where the ribs no longer protect it.

Question 4537. A constructed illustration: a person with longstanding liver disease has an enlarged spleen and dilated veins at the lower esophagus. Which venous arrangement explains both findings? The answer is the splenic vein, which joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. Raised pressure in that system passes back to the spleen and makes it enlarge, and the same pressure reaches the lower esophagus through the left gastric vein.

Question 4538. Which structure lies immediately behind the spleen, separating it from the left lung and the left pleura? The answer is the diaphragm. The convex upper surface of the spleen rests against it. A wound of the left lower chest can therefore injure the spleen and the pleura together.

Question 4539. Which surface of the spleen carries the impressions of the stomach, the left kidney and the left colic flexure? The answer is the visceral surface. It faces downward and medially toward the abdominal cavity. The gastric impression is the largest of the three, and the hilum lies in the middle.

Question 4540. Which statement about the coverings of the spleen is correct: it lies behind the peritoneum, it is covered by peritoneum except at its hilum, it has no peritoneal covering, or it lies within the lesser sac? The answer is that it is covered by peritoneum except at its hilum. It is therefore an intraperitoneal organ. The peritoneum reaches it as the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

Question 4541. A described cross section of the upper abdomen shows an oval organ on the left, behind the stomach and above the left kidney, receiving a tortuous artery at its medial border. Which organ is shown? The answer is the spleen. Its medial border is the hilum, where the splenic vessels enter and leave. The stomach lies in front of it and the kidney below it.

Question 4542. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the gastrosplenic ligament with the short gastric vessels, the splenorenal ligament with the hepatic artery, the falciform ligament with the spleen, or the phrenicocolic ligament with the splenic artery? The answer is the gastrosplenic ligament with the short gastric vessels. The splenorenal ligament carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.

Question 4543. Which statement about the blood held by the spleen is correct: it holds about half of the blood volume of the body, it holds a store of blood that can be shifted into the circulation, it holds blood only in its white pulp, or it receives blood only by way of the portal vein? The answer is that it holds a store of blood that can be shifted into the circulation. It acts as a reservoir that contracts when more circulating blood is needed.

Question 4544. A constructed illustration: a person whose spleen has been removed develops a severe infection with an encapsulated bacterium. Which function of the spleen does this illustrate? The answer is the filtration and immune function of its white pulp. The spleen removes organisms from the blood and mounts a rapid response to those with capsules. Loss of that function raises the risk of such infections.

Question 4545. True or false: the spleen lies in the left hypochondrium with its long axis along the line of the tenth rib. The answer is true. The organ follows the tenth rib from the spine toward the left costal margin. That is why a normal spleen remains hidden beneath the rib cage.

Question 4546. Which part of the spleen removes aged red blood cells from the circulation, and what is the other main part called? The answer is the red pulp, and the other part is the white pulp. Blood seeps through the red pulp, where macrophages take up old and damaged red cells. The white pulp is lymphoid tissue gathered around the central arteries.

Question 4547. A described computed tomography scan of the upper abdomen shows an organ of soft tissue density between the stomach and the left kidney, with the left crus of the diaphragm behind it. What is shown, and what lies in the impression below its hilum? The answer is the spleen, with the left kidney in the renal impression below the hilum. The gastric impression faces the stomach.

Question 4548. Which statement about accessory spleens is correct: they lie inside the main capsule, they are small masses of splenic tissue near the hilum or in the gastrosplenic ligament, they are always malignant, or they are the main organ divided in two? The answer is that they are small masses of splenic tissue near the hilum or in the gastrosplenic ligament. They come from lobules that failed to join the main mass during development.

Question 4549. Name two structures that lie immediately related to the visceral surface of the spleen, spoken as a list. The answer is the stomach and the left kidney. The gastric impression and the renal impression on the visceral surface hold them. The left colic flexure also touches the organ at the colic impression.

Question 4550. On a transverse section of the abdomen at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, in which direction does the spleen lie from the stomach, and in which direction from the left kidney? The answer is behind and to the left of the stomach, and above and lateral to the left kidney. The spleen rests against the diaphragm in the left upper quadrant.

Question 4551. In which part of the embryo does the spleen first appear, and what carries it to its adult position? The answer is the mesoderm of the dorsal mesogastrium, carried to the left by the rotation of the stomach. It forms in the fifth week between the two layers of that mesentery. The same rotation moves the pancreas and helps to create the lesser sac.

Question 4552. What is the normal length of the adult spleen: about 3 centimeters, about 12 centimeters, about 25 centimeters, or about 40 centimeters? The answer is about 12 centimeters. It is about 7 centimeters wide and 3 to 4 centimeters thick, and it weighs about 150 grams. The organ is largest in early adult life and shrinks gradually after middle age.

Question 4553. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan shows a large mass in the left upper quadrant between the stomach and the left kidney, supplied by a branch of the celiac trunk, with the tail of the pancreas against its medial border. Which organ is shown? The answer is the spleen. Its position and its blood supply fit the organ exactly. A pancreatic mass would lie more central.

Question 4554. Which branch of the splenic artery runs in the gastrosplenic ligament to the fundus of the stomach, and which one runs along the greater curvature? The answer is the short gastric arteries and the left gastroepiploic artery. Both arise from the splenic artery. They reach the stomach through the gastrosplenic ligament and the greater omentum.

Question 4555. Which of these structures is not related to the spleen: the diaphragm, the left kidney, the tail of the pancreas, or the right colic flexure? The answer is the right colic flexure. It lies on the right side of the abdomen below the liver. The left colic flexure, and not the right, leaves the colic impression on the spleen.

Question 4556. Which statement about the splenic vein is correct: it lies in front of the pancreas, it runs behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein, it drains into the inferior vena cava, or it carries lymph rather than blood? The answer is that it runs behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein. That junction forms the portal vein behind the neck of the pancreas. Blood from the spleen therefore passes through the liver.

Question 4557. Which artery arises from the celiac trunk, runs a tortuous course to the left, and enters the spleen at its hilum? The answer is the splenic artery. It is the largest branch of the celiac trunk. Its tortuous course lets it stretch as the spleen moves with breathing.

Question 4558. A described section of the abdomen shows an organ wrapped in peritoneum except where vessels enter its medial border, with a fold of peritoneum running from that border to the greater curvature of the stomach. What is that fold called? The answer is the gastrosplenic ligament. It carries the short gastric vessels. The peritoneum leaves the spleen bare only at the hilum.

Question 4559. Which of these functions belongs to the spleen: the production of bile, the storage of bile, the removal of aged red blood cells from the blood, or the absorption of fat from the intestine? The answer is the removal of aged red blood cells from the blood. The red pulp filters the blood and its macrophages take up worn-out cells. Before birth the spleen can also form blood cells.

Question 4560. A constructed illustration: a person has a fracture of the left ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs after a fall, and the left side of the abdomen becomes tender. Which organ lies directly beneath those ribs and is at risk? The answer is the spleen. It lies against the diaphragm under the ninth to the eleventh ribs. A fractured rib on that side can tear its capsule.

Question 4561. Which statement about the development of the spleen is correct: it develops from the endoderm of the gut, it develops in the dorsal mesogastrium and comes to lie on the left, it develops in the ventral mesogastrium, or it develops from the neural crest? The answer is that it develops in the dorsal mesogastrium and comes to lie on the left. Rotation of the stomach carries it to the left side of the abdomen.

Question 4562. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the red pulp with immune responses, the white pulp with filtration of blood, the splenic capsule with smooth muscle, or the splenic hilum with the tail of the liver? The answer is the splenic capsule with smooth muscle. The white pulp is the lymphoid part, and the red pulp filters blood. The hilum transmits the splenic vessels.

Question 4563. The tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum of the spleen inside which ligament, and which organ lies immediately behind that point? The answer is the splenorenal ligament, with the left kidney behind it. The splenic vessels run in the same ligament. Injury to the tail there can release pancreatic enzymes into the surrounding tissue.

Question 4564. What name is given to the notch on the superior border of the spleen, and what does it indicate about the development of the organ? The answer is the splenic notch, which marks a line of incomplete fusion between lobules. Several notches may be present. They are normal, and they help to identify the organ at operation and on imaging.

Question 4565. Which statement about the relations of the spleen is correct: its upper surface touches the left pleura through the diaphragm, its medial border touches the liver, its lower pole rests on the right kidney, or its anterior surface touches the bladder? The answer is that its upper surface touches the left pleura through the diaphragm. That relation explains why an inflamed spleen can irritate the pleura.

Question 4566. A described dissection of the hilum of the spleen shows a tortuous artery lying above a wider thin-walled vein, with a lobulated yellowish mass behind them. Which structures are shown? The answer is the splenic artery above the splenic vein, with the tail of the pancreas behind them. The artery is tortuous and the vein is wider and smooth. The yellowish mass is the tail of the pancreas.

Question 4567. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the gastric impression with the left kidney, the renal impression with the stomach, the colic impression with the left colic flexure, or the splenic hilum with the left ureter? The answer is the colic impression with the left colic flexure. The gastric impression holds the stomach and the renal impression the left kidney. The hilum holds the splenic vessels.

Question 4568. Which statement about the branches of the splenic artery inside the spleen is correct: they join one another freely, they behave as end arteries and each supplies its own segment, they drain straight into the splenic vein without a capillary bed, or they supply the left kidney as well? The answer is that they behave as end arteries and each supplies its own segment. A block of one branch therefore damages only part of the organ.

Question 4569. A constructed illustration: a person with an enlarged spleen has sudden pain in the left upper abdomen after a minor blow, and the blood pressure falls. Which structure has most likely torn? The answer is the capsule of the spleen. When the organ enlarges, the capsule is stretched and the lower pole comes to lie below the rib cage. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4570. True or false: an enlarged spleen descends below the left costal margin and can then be felt on examination. The answer is true. The organ moves downward along its own oblique axis as it enlarges. In health it stays beneath the rib cage and cannot be felt.

Question 4571. Which vessel carries blood from the spleen to the liver? The answer is the splenic vein, which joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. It runs behind the pancreas on its way to the right, and it has no valves.

Question 4572. A described computed tomography scan shows a notched organ against the left chest wall, with the stomach in front of it and the left kidney below and behind it. Which organ is shown? The answer is the spleen, whose long axis follows the tenth rib. The notch lies on its superior border.

Question 4573. Which organ lies immediately in front of the spleen: the left kidney, the stomach, the pancreas, or the left ureter? The answer is the stomach. Its fundus and upper body rest against the gastric impression. The kidney lies below and behind.

Question 4574. Name the two peritoneal ligaments that attach the spleen, spoken as a list. The answer is the gastrosplenic ligament and the splenorenal ligament. The first carries the short gastric vessels, and the second carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.

Question 4575. On a transverse section at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, does the spleen lie in front of or behind the stomach, and in front of or behind the upper pole of the left kidney? The answer is behind the stomach and in front of the upper pole of the left kidney. The kidney lies against the posterior wall.

Question 4576. Which peritoneal ligament carries the splenic vessels from the hilum toward the midline? The answer is the splenorenal ligament, which runs from the hilum to the left kidney. The splenic artery, the splenic vein and the tail of the pancreas all pass through it.

Question 4577. Which statement about the white pulp of the spleen is correct: it filters aged red cells, it is lymphoid tissue around the central arteries, it stores fat, or it produces insulin? The answer is that it is lymphoid tissue around the central arteries. It holds both T lymphocytes and B lymphocytes.

Question 4578. A described specimen shows an organ with a smooth convex surface, and on the other side three shallow impressions around a central hilum. Which organ is this, and which impression is the largest? The answer is the spleen, and the gastric impression is the largest. The renal and the colic impressions lie below it.

Question 4579. Which statement about the spleen and the blood is correct: it makes red blood cells throughout adult life, it stores platelets and can release them when they are needed, it makes plasma proteins, or it destroys white cells only? The answer is that it stores platelets and can release them when they are needed. In disease it can also resume making red cells.

Question 4580. Which structure lies immediately in front of the splenic vein as it runs behind the body of the pancreas, and which vessel lies above it? The answer is the body of the pancreas in front, with the splenic artery above. The left kidney lies behind the vein.

Question 4581. Which statement about the tail of the pancreas is correct: it lies in the gastrosplenic ligament, it lies in the splenorenal ligament close to the splenic hilum, it lies in the lesser omentum, or it lies behind the right kidney? The answer is that it lies in the splenorenal ligament close to the splenic hilum. It is the only part of the pancreas that reaches the spleen.

Question 4582. Which structure forms the upper limit of the spleen, separating it from the left lung? The answer is the diaphragm. The convex upper surface of the spleen lies against it. Above the diaphragm lie the left pleura and the base of the left lung.

Question 4583. A described ultrasound image shows a rounded organ in the left upper abdomen that moves downward as the person breathes in, with a notch on its upper border. Which organ is shown? The answer is the spleen, which moves because it lies against the diaphragm. The notch on its superior border is normal.

Question 4584. In which quadrant of the abdomen does the spleen lie: the right upper quadrant, the left upper quadrant, the right lower quadrant, or the left lower quadrant? The answer is the left upper quadrant. It lies in the left hypochondrium, above the left colic flexure.

Question 4585. A constructed illustration: a person with fever and an enlarged spleen feels pain at the left shoulder when the abdomen is pressed. Which nerve carries that sensation? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which supplies the diaphragm over the spleen. The same spinal segments supply the skin of the shoulder.

Question 4586. Which statement about the position of the spleen in relation to the ribs is correct: it lies deep to the ninth to the eleventh ribs on the left, it lies deep to the fifth to the seventh ribs on the left, it lies below the twelfth rib, or it lies deep to the ribs on the right? The answer is that it lies deep to the ninth to the eleventh ribs on the left. Its long axis follows the tenth rib.

Question 4587. True or false: the splenic vein carries blood from the spleen directly to the inferior vena cava. The answer is false. The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. Blood from the spleen therefore passes through the liver first.

Question 4588. Which vessel runs behind the body of the pancreas while the splenic artery runs above the gland, and where does that vessel end? The answer is the splenic vein, which ends where it joins the superior mesenteric vein. The artery lies along the upper border of the pancreas.

Question 4589. What name is given to a spleen that is displaced from its usual position because its supporting ligaments are lax? The answer is a wandering spleen. The organ can then lie lower in the abdomen or even in the pelvis. The condition may be discovered when the organ twists.

Question 4590. Which statement about the venous drainage of the spleen is correct: the splenic vein runs in front of the pancreas, it receives the inferior mesenteric vein before it joins the superior mesenteric vein, it drains into the left renal vein, or it has many valves? The answer is that it receives the inferior mesenteric vein before it joins the superior mesenteric vein. Together they form the portal vein.

Question 4591. A described specimen of the spleen is cut across, and the cut surface shows small pale nodules scattered through a dark red background. What are the pale nodules? The answer is the white pulp, with the red pulp around it. The white pulp is lymphoid tissue around the central arteries.

Question 4592. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the upper surface of the spleen with the left pleura, the visceral surface with the right lung, the gastric impression with the left ureter, or the renal impression with the colon? The answer is the upper surface of the spleen with the left pleura. The two are separated by the diaphragm.

Question 4593. Which function of the spleen explains the finding of abnormal particles inside red cells in a person whose spleen has been removed: the storage of fat, the removal of particles from red cells in the red pulp, the production of bile, or the secretion of hormones? The answer is the removal of particles from red cells in the red pulp. Without the organ they remain in the circulating red cells.

Question 4594. A described venogram shows the splenic vein blocked near the hilum, with contrast medium flowing backward along veins that run in the gastrosplenic ligament toward the fundus of the stomach. Which veins are shown? The answer is the short gastric veins, which drain the fundus into the splenic vein. When that vein is blocked they dilate.

Question 4595. True or false: accessory spleens near the hilum can enlarge and take over part of the work of the spleen after the main organ is removed. The answer is true. They are small masses of splenic tissue in the gastrosplenic ligament or near the hilum. Their presence is common and is not a disease.

Question 4596. Which border of the spleen carries the notches that help to identify it, and what do they mark? The answer is the superior border, and the notches mark the lines along which its lobules fused. They are a normal feature of the adult organ.

Question 4597. A described arteriogram shows a tortuous artery running to the left along the upper border of the pancreas, breaking into branches that fan out at the medial border of an organ. Which vessel and organ are shown? The answer is the splenic artery and the spleen, whose branches enter at the hilum and supply separate segments.

Question 4598. Which statement about the spleen and the left colic flexure is correct: the flexure leaves an impression on the visceral surface, the flexure lies above the spleen, the flexure is attached to the hilum, or the flexure lies behind the spleen? The answer is that the flexure leaves an impression on the visceral surface. It lies below and in front of the lower pole.

Question 4599. Name the three impressions found on the visceral surface of the spleen, spoken as a list. The answer is the gastric impression, the renal impression and the colic impression. The gastric impression is the largest, and the renal impression holds the left kidney.

Question 4600. Which ligament runs from the left colic flexure to the diaphragm and helps to support the lower pole of the spleen? The answer is the phrenicocolic ligament, which forms a shelf beneath the lower pole. The spleen rests upon it.

To summarize, the thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli in the abdomen behind the diaphragm, passes upward through the aortic hiatus, and crosses to the left at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra before it ends at the left venous angle. It drains both lower limbs, the pelvis, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head and chest, and it carries chyle after a fatty meal. The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium between the stomach and the diaphragm, covered by peritoneum except at its hilum, attached by the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments, supplied by the splenic artery and drained by the splenic vein to the portal vein. Its red pulp filters the blood and its white pulp mounts immune responses, and the ninth to the eleventh ribs protect it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 47 — Thymus

Every account of the body's defenses begins with a small organ that sits in the middle of the chest and with the network of vessels that carries lymph through the whole body. This chapter covers the thymus, its development, its structure and its relations in the mediastinum, and then the great lymphatic territories by which lymph from every region reaches the venous system. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The thymus belongs to the lymphoid organs, and the drainage territories described here are the map a clinician uses to understand where a tumor may travel. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4601. In which part of the mediastinum does the thymus lie: the posterior mediastinum, the anterior part of the superior mediastinum, the middle mediastinum, or the root of the neck? The answer is the anterior part of the superior mediastinum. It occupies the space immediately behind the sternum and in front of the great vessels and the pericardium. In the child it fills that space, and with age it shrinks and is replaced by fat.

Question 4602. Which of these structures lies immediately anterior to the thymus: the sternum, the trachea, the aortic arch, or the pericardium? The answer is the sternum. The gland lies against the back of the manubrium and the upper part of the body of the sternum. The trachea and the aortic arch lie behind it.

Question 4603. A described radiograph of a young child shows a soft-tissue shadow filling the upper part of the anterior mediastinum, with a wavy lower border where the ribs press into it. Which organ is shown? The answer is the thymus. It is relatively large in early life and may widen the upper mediastinal shadow. The wavy border is produced by the ribs indenting the soft gland.

Question 4604. From which pharyngeal pouch does the thymus develop? The answer is the third pharyngeal pouch. Paired buds grow from that pouch on each side and later fuse in the midline. They migrate downward into the anterior mediastinum, which is why thymic tissue sometimes remains in the neck.

Question 4605. Which gland develops from the same pharyngeal pouch as the thymus: the thyroid gland, the superior parathyroid gland, the inferior parathyroid gland, or the ultimobranchial body? The answer is the inferior parathyroid gland. It and the thymus both arise from the third pharyngeal pouch and travel down together. The superior parathyroid gland comes from the fourth pouch.

Question 4606. Which great vessels lie immediately posterior to the thymus? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein and the arch of the aorta. The vein crosses the midline in front of the branches of the arch, and the thymus lies in front of both. The pericardium and the heart lie below its lower pole.

Question 4607. A constructed illustration: a young adult has a mass in the anterior mediastinum and drooping eyelids with weakness that worsens through the day. Which organ is the likely source of the mass? The answer is the thymus. Tumors of the thymus are associated with myasthenia gravis, a disorder of the junction between nerve and muscle. Management of that disorder belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4608. True or false: the thymus reaches its greatest relative size in adult life. The answer is false. The gland is largest in relation to body weight around puberty, and after that it gradually involutes. In the older adult it is a thin fatty remnant in the anterior mediastinum.

Question 4609. Which of these is the whorled structure found in the medulla of the thymus: the lymphoid follicle, the thymic corpuscle, the germinal center, or the medullary cord? The answer is the thymic corpuscle, also called the Hassall corpuscle. It is a coiled mass of flattened epithelial reticular cells. The corpuscles become more numerous with age and are the surest sign that a section comes from the medulla.

Question 4610. Which cells form the thymic corpuscles: the flattened epithelial reticular cells of the medulla, the epithelial reticular cells that seal the cortical capillaries, the lymphocytes of the cortex, or the macrophages of the cortex? The answer is the flattened epithelial reticular cells of the medulla. They pile up into the whorls of the corpuscle. The cells that seal the cortical capillaries stay in the cortex and never form whorls.

Question 4611. Which two zones make up each lobule of the thymus? The answer is the cortex and the medulla. The cortex is the dark outer zone, packed with developing lymphocytes. The medulla is the pale center, where the lymphocytes that survive selection are released.

Question 4612. A described stained section of the thymus shows a deeply stained outer zone crowded with small cells and a pale center containing whorled structures. Which zone is the dark outer one? The answer is the cortex. Its color comes from the dense packing of developing lymphocytes. The pale center with the whorls is the medulla.

Question 4613. A described transverse section of the superior mediastinum is taken at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. Which structure lies between the back of the sternum and the left brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the thymus. The vein crosses the midline behind it, and the trachea lies further back still. This slice therefore shows the gland in its anterior position.

Question 4614. Which membrane lies immediately lateral to the thymus on each side, separating it from the lung? The answer is the mediastinal pleura. The phrenic nerve runs downward on that membrane just lateral to the gland. The lung therefore does not touch the thymus directly.

Question 4615. The arterial supply of the thymus comes mainly from branches of which artery: the internal thoracic artery, the pulmonary trunk, the descending thoracic aorta, or the axillary artery? The answer is the internal thoracic artery. Small branches also reach it from the inferior thyroid artery in the neck. Its veins follow the arteries and drain into neighboring veins.

Question 4616. Into which vein do the veins of the thymus drain: the right brachiocephalic, the left brachiocephalic, the superior vena cava, or the azygos vein? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein, joined by the internal thoracic and inferior thyroid veins. The gland sits directly in front of that large vein. This is why an enlarged thymus can press on it.

Question 4617. Name two secondary lymphoid organs that a mature T lymphocyte leaving the thymus goes on to populate. The answer is a lymph node and the spleen. Lymphocytes that have been selected in the thymus leave by the blood and settle in these organs. There they gather in the regions where they meet the antigens they were selected to recognize.

Question 4618. A constructed illustration: an infant has repeated infections and almost no T lymphocytes in the blood, and imaging shows no thymic shadow. Which part of the embryo failed to develop? The answer is the third pharyngeal pouch. Failure of that pouch leaves the infant without a thymus and without the inferior parathyroid glands. The pattern is a recognized congenital one rather than a disease of the gland itself.

Question 4619. Which cells of the thymus arrive from the bone marrow, and which form its framework? The answer is that the lymphocytes arrive from the bone marrow, while the epithelial framework is endodermal. The epithelial reticular cells come from the third pharyngeal pouch. The two populations meet in the gland and cooperate in the selection of lymphocytes.

Question 4620. In which part of the thymus is the blood-thymus barrier found: the medulla, the cortex, the capsule, or the hilum? The answer is the cortex. The barrier keeps developing lymphocytes in the cortex away from circulating antigens. The medulla is deliberately leaky, so that lymphocytes there can meet antigens.

Question 4621. Which of these forms part of the blood-thymus barrier: fenestrated capillaries, continuous capillaries joined by tight junctions, lymphatic sinuses, or wide venous channels? The answer is continuous capillaries joined by tight junctions. Around them lie a basal lamina, a layer of epithelial reticular cells and macrophages. Together they keep the cortical lymphocytes sealed off from the blood.

Question 4622. True or false: the cortex of each thymic lobule is completely walled off from its neighbors by connective tissue. The answer is false. The septa separate the cortices, but the medulla is continuous from one lobule to the next. A section that seems to show many separate lobules is therefore joined in the middle.

Question 4623. A described section of the thymus shows the lymphoid tissue cut into blocks by bands of connective tissue running inward from the surface, each band carrying small vessels. What are those bands? The answer is the septa, also called trabeculae. They carry blood vessels into the gland. Between them the lymphoid tissue is arranged in lobules, each with its own cortex and a shared medulla.

Question 4624. A described specimen shows a soft, bilobed organ with a finely lobulated surface, taken from the upper chest of a child. Which organ is it? The answer is the thymus. The two lobes are joined by connective tissue across the midline. The lobulated surface reflects the septa that divide the cortex.

Question 4625. Which structure lies immediately below the lower pole of the thymus in the chest? The answer is the fibrous pericardium, over the heart. The gland rests on it and does not usually reach the diaphragm. The pericardium therefore separates the thymus from the heart.

Question 4626. A constructed illustration: a person with a large mass in the anterior mediastinum has swelling of the face and neck. Which vein, lying directly behind the thymus, is being compressed? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein. Blood from the head and the left arm returns through it to the heart. A mass in front of it can narrow it and dam the flow.

Question 4627. Which statement about the thymus in adult life is correct: it grows steadily larger, it is replaced by fat, it becomes a lymph node, or it moves into the abdomen? The answer is that it is replaced by fat. The lymphoid tissue shrinks from puberty onward and the spaces fill with adipose tissue. The remnant stays in the anterior mediastinum.

Question 4628. What name is given to the cortical cells that wrap themselves around clusters of developing lymphocytes? The answer is thymic nurse cells. They are a specialized form of cortical epithelial reticular cell. They enclose the lymphocytes and give them a protected place in which to be tested.

Question 4629. Name two structures that develop from the third pharyngeal pouch. The answer is the thymus and the inferior parathyroid gland. Both begin in the neck and descend to their adult positions. That shared journey explains why parathyroid tissue is sometimes found inside the thymus.

Question 4630. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cortex with positive selection, the medulla with positive selection, the capsule with lymphocyte maturation, or the septa with the thymic corpuscles? The answer is the cortex with positive selection. Lymphocytes that can recognize the body's own marking molecules are kept alive there. Negative selection, which removes the self-reactive ones, happens in the medulla.

Question 4631. The upper poles of the thymus reach into the neck. Deep to which pair of muscles do they lie? The answer is the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles. They lie in the midline of the lower neck, behind those strap muscles. Thymic tissue can therefore present as a neck mass in a child.

Question 4632. Which nerve supplies the thymus with its parasympathetic fibers: the phrenic nerve, the vagus nerve, the sympathetic trunk, or the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the vagus nerve, the tenth cranial nerve. Sympathetic fibers reach it from the sympathetic trunk. These nerves follow the vessels into the gland and have little to do with its immune work.

Question 4633. Which statement about the lymphatic vessels of the thymus is correct: it has both afferent and efferent vessels, it has efferent vessels only, it has afferent vessels only, or it has none? The answer is that it has efferent vessels only. No lymphatic vessel carries lymph into the thymus. The lymphocytes that populate it arrive through the blood.

Question 4634. A described low-power section of the thymus shows several dark lobules whose pale centers join across the septa. Which part of the gland is continuous between the lobules? The answer is the medulla. The septa cut the cortex into separate caps but stop short of the medulla. The lymphocytes that are ready to leave therefore travel through one continuous central channel.

Question 4635. A constructed illustration: a thymic tumor is removed and the pathologist reports that the tumor cells form whorls and carry epithelial markers. From which cells has the tumor arisen? The answer is the thymic epithelial reticular cells. Tumors of the thymus are tumors of its epithelium, not of its lymphocytes. Decisions about treatment belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4636. Down to about which level does the adult thymus reach: the second costal cartilage, the fourth costal cartilage, the eighth thoracic vertebra, or the diaphragm? The answer is the fourth costal cartilage. Below that level the heart and its pericardium fill the anterior mediastinum. In the child the gland often reaches a little lower.

Question 4637. Which structure lies immediately behind the upper part of the thymus in the neck: the trachea, the esophagus, the sternum, or the internal jugular vein? The answer is the trachea. The gland lies in front of the windpipe in the midline. The esophagus lies behind the trachea and is therefore not the immediate posterior relation.

Question 4638. Which of these pairs belongs together: the flattened epithelial reticular cells with the blood-thymus barrier, the thymic nurse cells with the medulla, the thymic corpuscle with the cortex, or the lymphocytes of the medulla with the secretion of antibodies? The answer is the flattened epithelial reticular cells with the blood-thymus barrier. They seal the cortical capillaries and the surface of the lobule. The corpuscles belong to the medulla and the nurse cells to the cortex.

Question 4639. True or false: the thymus is a primary lymphoid organ. The answer is true. A primary lymphoid organ is one in which lymphocytes are produced and selected, and the thymus shares that role with the bone marrow. Lymph nodes, the spleen and the tonsils are secondary organs, in which mature lymphocytes meet antigen.

Question 4640. Which of these is a primary lymphoid organ: a lymph node, the spleen, the thymus, or a tonsil? The answer is the thymus. Lymphocytes are made and selected within it. The other three are secondary lymphoid organs, in which mature lymphocytes respond to antigen.

Question 4641. In the superior mediastinum, which structure lies between the thymus in front and the trachea behind? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein. It crosses from left to right in front of the branches of the aortic arch. The chain from front to back is therefore thymus, vein, trachea.

Question 4642. A constructed illustration: an infant has a soft lump in the lower neck that moves when the infant swallows, and no other abnormality. Which tissue, left behind during its descent, may explain it? The answer is thymic tissue. The gland begins in the neck and travels down to the chest, and fragments may remain along the path. Such a remnant is a normal variation of descent.

Question 4643. A described radiograph of an older adult shows only a thin soft-tissue shadow in the anterior mediastinum where a child has a broad glandular shadow. What has happened to the thymus? The answer is that it has involuted and been replaced by fat. The fatty remnant casts almost no shadow. The change is a normal part of aging and not disease.

Question 4644. Which cells replace the lymphoid tissue of the thymus as the gland involutes? The answer is fat cells. They fill the spaces left as the lymphocytes and epithelial cells decrease in number. The remnant is therefore a fatty body in the anterior mediastinum rather than a lymphoid organ.

Question 4645. Which process removes lymphocytes that would attack the body's own tissues: positive selection in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla, phagocytosis in the blood, or selection in a lymph node? The answer is negative selection in the medulla. Lymphocytes that react strongly against the body's own molecules are made to die there. Positive selection in the cortex does the opposite, keeping those that can recognize the body's marking molecules.

Question 4646. Which feature distinguishes the medulla of the thymus from its cortex: fewer lymphocytes and the presence of thymic corpuscles, a denser packing of lymphocytes, a high rate of cell division, or the blood-thymus barrier? The answer is fewer lymphocytes and the presence of thymic corpuscles. The medulla is paler because its cells are less crowded. The blood-thymus barrier belongs to the cortex.

Question 4647. A described specimen of the thymus from an older adult shows a thin rim of lymphoid tissue around a core of fat. Which two changes does the specimen show? The answer is involution of the lymphoid tissue and its replacement by fat. Both are the ordinary changes of age. The lobular pattern may still be faintly visible in the fatty remnant.

Question 4648. Which statement about the thymus in the newborn is correct: it is very small and hard to see, it is relatively large and may widen the upper mediastinum on a radiograph, it lies in the posterior mediastinum, or it contains no lymphocytes? The answer is that it is relatively large and may widen the upper mediastinum. Its shadow can be mistaken for disease in a child.

Question 4649. A described radiograph of an infant shows a large soft-tissue mass in the upper anterior mediastinum that narrows the air column of the trachea from in front. Which organ is responsible, and from which direction is it pressing? The answer is the thymus, pressing on the trachea from in front. Its size varies widely in infancy, so the finding must be read with the whole picture.

Question 4650. Which statement about positive selection in the thymus is correct: it happens in the cortex and keeps lymphocytes that recognize the body's own molecules, it happens in the medulla and destroys self-reactive cells, it happens in the blood after the cells leave, or it removes lymphocytes that cannot divide? The answer is that it happens in the cortex and keeps lymphocytes able to recognize the body's own molecules. Those that cannot are left to die.

Question 4651. At which structure does the thoracic duct begin? The answer is the cisterna chyli. It is a sac in front of the bodies of the first and second lumbar vertebrae. All the lymph from below the diaphragm reaches it before entering the chest.

Question 4652. Which vessel carries lymph from the left side of the head and neck, the left upper limb, and the whole body below the diaphragm: the right lymphatic duct, the thoracic duct, the left jugular trunk alone, or the azygos vein? The answer is the thoracic duct. The right lymphatic duct takes only the right side of the head, neck and chest and the right upper limb.

Question 4653. A described dissection of the root of the neck shows a thin-walled duct arching upward and laterally to open at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. Which duct is shown? The answer is the thoracic duct. Its arch lies behind the left common carotid artery. It opens into the left venous angle, where the two veins meet.

Question 4654. Which regions of the body are drained by the right lymphatic duct? The answer is the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right side of the chest. It is a short trunk, only about one or two centimeters long. It ends at the right venous angle.

Question 4655. At about which level does the thoracic duct cross from the right side of the mediastinum to the left: the first, the fourth or fifth, the eighth, or the twelfth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the fourth or fifth thoracic vertebra. It begins on the right of the vertebral column and crosses behind the esophagus. Above that level it continues upward on the left.

Question 4656. In the posterior mediastinum, between which two vessels does the thoracic duct ascend? The answer is the descending aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. It lies in front of the vertebral bodies and behind the esophagus. This narrow bed protects the duct but makes it easy to injure.

Question 4657. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the back of the chest, milky fluid collects in the pleural cavity. Which channel has most likely been injured, and what is the fluid? The answer is the thoracic duct, and the fluid is chyle. Chyle is lymph that has taken up fat from the small intestine. Its milky look is the clue to the injury.

Question 4658. True or false: the cisterna chyli receives the intestinal trunk as well as the two lumbar trunks. The answer is true. The intestinal trunk brings the fatty lymph from the gut. The lumbar trunks bring lymph from the lower limbs, the pelvis and the abdominal wall.

Question 4659. What is the name of the milky lymph that drains from the small intestine, and why is it milky? The answer is chyle, and it is milky because it carries absorbed fat. The fat leaves the gut in tiny particles that give the lymph its white color. The lymph vessels of the villi that collect it are called lacteals.

Question 4660. At which venous junction does the thoracic duct end: the right venous angle, the left venous angle, the superior vena cava, or the azygos vein? The answer is the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular and the left subclavian veins meet. The duct sometimes ends in one of those veins instead. From there the lymph joins the blood.

Question 4661. Which group of lymph nodes receives the lymph from the small intestine before it enters the intestinal trunk? The answer is the superior mesenteric nodes. They lie in the mesentery along the superior mesenteric vessels. From them the lymph passes to the cisterna chyli.

Question 4662. A described section of a lymph node shows a fibrous capsule, a dark outer zone with rounded masses of cells, a paler center, and a hilum. In which zone do the rounded masses lie? The answer is the cortex. The rounded masses are the lymphoid follicles, and they enlarge when the node is active. The medulla, nearer the hilum, is the paler center.

Question 4663. A described cross section of the posterior mediastinum shows the esophagus in the midline, the thoracic duct behind it, and two large vessels on either side. Which vessel lies immediately to the left of the duct? The answer is the descending aorta. The azygos vein lies to its right. That pairing gives the duct its standard address in the posterior mediastinum.

Question 4664. Which of these regions does the superficial inguinal group of nodes drain: the skin of the lower limb, the testis, the kidney, or the uterus? The answer is the skin of the lower limb, apart from a strip on the back of the calf and the lateral border of the foot. Those areas drain first to the popliteal nodes.

Question 4665. In the femoral canal, which structure lies immediately medial to the femoral vein? The answer is the deep inguinal lymph node, sometimes called the node of Cloquet. It is the highest of the deep inguinal nodes. Lymph from the deep tissues of the leg reaches it before passing to the external iliac nodes.

Question 4666. To which group of lymph nodes does the testis drain, and why? The answer is the para-aortic, or lumbar, nodes. The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and takes its lymph drainage with it. Lymph from the testis therefore never passes through the inguinal nodes, although the skin of the scrotum does.

Question 4667. A constructed illustration: a young man has a painless swelling of one testis, and imaging shows enlarged nodes deep in the upper abdomen. Which node group is involved? The answer is the para-aortic nodes, beside the abdominal aorta. They lie at the level where the testis began its descent. This pattern of spread follows the embryology of the gland.

Question 4668. Which of these structures drains to the para-aortic nodes rather than to the superficial inguinal nodes: the scrotum, the ovary, the skin of the perineum, or the skin of the lower abdominal wall? The answer is the ovary. Like the testis, it develops high on the posterior abdominal wall. The other three drain to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Question 4669. To which group of lymph nodes does most of the breast drain: the parasternal, the axillary, the deep cervical, or the inguinal nodes? The answer is the axillary group. About three quarters of the lymph from the gland passes there, and the pectoral nodes are often the first to receive it. The remaining lymph leaves by other routes.

Question 4670. Which part of the breast drains to the parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels: the lateral part, the medial part, the lower part, or the skin of the nipple? The answer is the medial part. Its vessels pass through the chest wall beside the internal thoracic artery. Lymph from the lower part of the gland may reach nodes in the abdomen through the sheath of the rectus muscle.

Question 4671. Which of these pairs belongs together: the tip of the tongue with the submental nodes, the tip of the tongue with the occipital nodes, the upper lip with the deep cervical nodes only, or the scalp of the back of the head with the parotid nodes? The answer is the tip of the tongue with the submental nodes. The back of the scalp drains to the occipital nodes instead.

Question 4672. What is the name of the left supraclavicular lymph node that may receive lymph from the abdominal organs? The answer is Virchow's node. It lies just above the left clavicle at the lower end of the thoracic duct. Lymph from the stomach and other abdominal organs can reach it, which is why it is felt for in the neck.

Question 4673. A constructed illustration: a person with a tumor of the stomach has a hard, enlarged node above the left clavicle. Through which channel did the tumor cells reach the neck? The answer is the thoracic duct. Lymph from the gut passes up the duct and can lodge in the node at its termination. The finding is a described illustration of a known pattern and not a diagnosis.

Question 4674. A described lymphangiogram of the leg shows vessels running up the medial side of the calf and the thigh and filling nodes in the groin. Which group is filling? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes. They receive the superficial vessels of the lower limb. The deep vessels of the leg pass first to the popliteal nodes.

Question 4675. Which part of the anal canal drains to the superficial inguinal nodes: the part above the pectinate line, the part below it, the whole canal, or none of it? The answer is the part below the pectinate line. It develops from the outer ectodermal layer, like the skin. The part above the line drains to the internal iliac and para-aortic nodes.

Question 4676. In the root of the neck, which structure lies immediately in front of the arch of the thoracic duct? The answer is the left common carotid artery, with the internal jugular vein beside it. The duct passes behind them before it opens into the venous angle. The carotid sheath and its contents therefore lie in front of the duct at that level.

Question 4677. Which trunks join to form the cisterna chyli? The answer is the two lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. The lumbar trunks drain the lower limbs, the pelvis and the abdominal wall. The intestinal trunk drains the gut and its glands.

Question 4678. Which group of nodes lies at the hilum of each lung and receives the lymph from the lung substance? The answer is the bronchopulmonary, or hilar, nodes. Lymph then passes to the tracheobronchial nodes around the lower trachea. From there it enters the bronchomediastinal trunk on each side.

Question 4679. A described dissection of the upper limb after removal of the axillary nodes shows pitting swelling of the arm. Which channels have been divided? The answer is the lymphatic vessels that carried lymph from the arm to the axillary nodes. With those nodes gone, tissue fluid collects in the limb. The swelling is an illustration of how completely the arm depends on that route.

Question 4680. A constructed illustration: a woman has a hard lump in the upper outer part of the breast and a hard node in the armpit. Which group of axillary nodes is most likely involved? The answer is the pectoral, or anterior, group, which lies along the lower border of the pectoralis minor. About three quarters of the lymph from the breast passes to the axillary nodes. Assessment and treatment belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4681. Which of these pairs belongs together: the popliteal nodes with the lateral border of the foot, the popliteal nodes with the medial side of the thigh, the inguinal nodes with the brain, or the deep cervical nodes with the foot? The answer is the popliteal nodes with the lateral border of the foot. Lymph from that strip travels up the short saphenous route to the popliteal fossa. The medial side of the thigh drains to the inguinal nodes.

Question 4682. Along which vein do the deep cervical lymph nodes lie in the neck? The answer is the internal jugular vein. One of them, the jugulodigastric node, lies below the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. It receives the lymph from the palatine tonsil.

Question 4683. At which venous junction does the right lymphatic duct end? The answer is the right venous angle, where the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins meet. It is a short vessel, about one centimeter long. It may open as several separate small vessels instead of one trunk.

Question 4684. True or false: the thoracic duct carries lymph from both lower limbs. The answer is true. All the lymph from below the diaphragm gathers at the cisterna chyli and passes up the duct. The right lymphatic duct carries no lymph from the limbs below the diaphragm.

Question 4685. Name the three trunks that join the thoracic duct near its termination. The answer is the left jugular trunk, the left subclavian trunk and the left bronchomediastinal trunk. They bring lymph from the left side of the head and neck, the left upper limb and the left side of the chest. The duct ends at the left venous angle just after receiving them.

Question 4686. A described section of the wall of the small intestine shows a blind-ended vessel in the center of each villus. What is that vessel, and what does it carry? The answer is a lacteal, a lymphatic capillary. It carries the fat that has been absorbed by the villus. The fat gives the lymph its milky appearance.

Question 4687. Which structure lies immediately behind the cisterna chyli? The answer is the bodies of the first and second lumbar vertebrae. The sac lies in front of them and behind the aorta. It is the lowest part of the thoracic duct.

Question 4688. What name is given to the lymph nodes that lie around the abdominal aorta and receive lymph from the kidneys and the gonads? The answer is the para-aortic, or lumbar, nodes. They also receive the lymph from the common iliac nodes below. Their efferent vessels form the lumbar trunks.

Question 4689. To which groups of nodes does the cervix of the uterus drain? The answer is the internal and external iliac nodes, with the sacral nodes and the nodes in the parametrium. The upper part of the body of the uterus drains instead to the para-aortic nodes along the ovarian vessels. That difference follows the different origins of the two parts.

Question 4690. A constructed illustration: after a difficult operation in the upper abdomen, a milky fluid collects in both pleural cavities and the person becomes short of breath. Which single channel is the likely source, and which two cavities are involved? The answer is the thoracic duct and the two pleural cavities. Its contents are chyle, the fatty lymph from the gut. Injury high in the chest or neck lets the chyle escape.

Question 4691. A described section of a lymph node shows vessels entering its convex surface and leaving at its hilum. Which vessels enter, and which leave? The answer is that afferent vessels enter the convex surface and one or two efferent vessels leave at the hilum. The flow is one way, from the subcapsular sinus through the cortex to the medulla. A node therefore filters lymph rather than merely storing it.

Question 4692. Which statement about the lymphatics of the diaphragm is correct: the two surfaces are sealed off from one another, the two surfaces communicate through small openings, the diaphragm has no lymphatics, or its lymph drains only to the groin? The answer is that the two surfaces communicate through small openings. Fluid in the abdomen can therefore pass into the pleural lymphatics. That route explains how abdominal fluid can be joined by fluid around the lung.

Question 4693. By which vessels does the thymus drain its lymph, and to which nodes does that lymph pass? The answer is its efferent lymphatic vessels, which pass to the anterior mediastinal, brachiocephalic and tracheobronchial nodes. The thymus has no afferent lymphatics. Its lymphocytes reach it through the blood.

Question 4694. Which groups of nodes receive the lymph from the thyroid gland? The answer is the prelaryngeal, pretracheal and paratracheal nodes, and then the deep cervical nodes. The gland lies against the front and sides of the trachea. This is why a swelling of the gland may be felt to move when the person swallows.

Question 4695. In the superior mediastinum, which structure lies immediately to the left of the thoracic duct? The answer is the left mediastinal pleura. The duct lies against it as it ascends behind the left subclavian artery. Its right side faces the esophagus.

Question 4696. A described lymphangiogram of the arm shows a chain of vessels running up the medial side and a group of nodes in the armpit. Which group of nodes has filled? The answer is the lateral group of axillary nodes, which lies along the axillary vein. The superficial vessels of the arm follow the basilic vein to it. Vessels following the cephalic vein pass instead to the apical nodes.

Question 4697. Which statement about the drainage of the tongue is correct: the tip drains to the submental nodes and the lateral margin to the submandibular nodes, the whole tongue drains to the inguinal nodes, the tip drains to the deep cervical nodes only, or the tongue has no lymphatics? The answer is that the tip drains to the submental nodes and the lateral margin to the submandibular nodes. The midline of the tip drains to both sides.

Question 4698. Which of these pairs belongs together: the kidney with the para-aortic nodes, the kidney with the superficial inguinal nodes, the bladder with the popliteal nodes, or the ovary with the deep cervical nodes? The answer is the kidney with the para-aortic nodes. It lies against the posterior abdominal wall, and its lymph follows its vessels. The bladder drains to the internal and external iliac nodes.

Question 4699. What is the name of the lymph nodes at the hilum of the spleen, and where does their lymph go next? The answer is the splenic, or hilar, nodes, and their lymph passes to the celiac nodes. The spleen lies in the left upper part of the abdomen, behind the stomach. Its lymph joins the intestinal trunk and so reaches the cisterna chyli.

Question 4700. Which of these statements correctly pairs a structure with its draining lymph nodes: the anal margin with the internal iliac nodes, the cervix with the superficial inguinal nodes, the glans of the penis with the deep inguinal nodes, or the kidney with the superficial inguinal nodes? The answer is the glans of the penis with the deep inguinal nodes. The skin of the shaft drains to the superficial inguinal nodes instead.

To summarize, the thymus is a primary lymphoid organ of the anterior superior mediastinum, developed from the third pharyngeal pouch, lying behind the sternum and in front of the left brachiocephalic vein, the aortic arch and the pericardium, and reaching down to about the fourth costal cartilage. Each lobule has a cortex, where lymphocytes are selected positively and sealed off from antigen by the blood-thymus barrier, and a continuous medulla, where negative selection removes self-reactive cells and where the thymic corpuscles lie, and the gland reaches its greatest relative size around puberty before it is replaced by fat. It has efferent lymphatics only, and its lymphocytes arrive by blood. The lymphatic territories then carry lymph to two venous angles: the thoracic duct drains everything below the diaphragm and the left side of the head, neck, chest and upper limb, while the right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right side of the chest. That map explains the familiar patterns, the para-aortic nodes for the testis, the ovary and the kidney, the inguinal nodes for the skin below the umbilicus and the perineum, the axillary nodes for most of the breast, and the node at the end of the duct above the left clavicle. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 48 — General Nervous System Anatomy

This chapter maps the general plan of the nervous system, from the brain and the spinal cord that form the central nervous system to the cranial and spinal nerves that form the peripheral nervous system. It sets out the gray matter that holds the cell bodies, the white matter that carries the tracts, and the neurons and supporting cells from which both are built. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. Every answer names its structure aloud rather than pointing to a picture. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4701. Which two organs make up the central nervous system, and where does each lie? The answer is the brain and the spinal cord. The brain lies in the cranial cavity, wrapped by the meninges and protected by the bones of the skull. The spinal cord runs down inside the vertebral canal. Every other nerve belongs to the peripheral nervous system.

Question 4702. Which three membranes wrap the brain and the spinal cord, spoken in order from the outside inward? The answer is the dura mater, the arachnoid mater and the pia mater. The dura is the tough outer coat, the arachnoid lies against it, and the pia follows every fold of the nervous tissue. All three continue around the spinal cord.

Question 4703. Which of these fluids fills the ventricles of the brain and the space around the spinal cord: blood, cerebrospinal fluid, lymph, or synovial fluid? The answer is cerebrospinal fluid. It is made within the ventricles, and it cushions the brain and the cord. Lymph travels in lymphatic vessels, and synovial fluid lies only inside joint cavities.

Question 4704. Which structure inside the ventricles produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid, using a fringe of small blood vessels covered by ependymal cells? The answer is the choroid plexus.
