It hangs in the lateral ventricles, the third ventricle and the fourth ventricle. The ependymal cells take fluid from the blood and release it into the ventricle.

Question 4705. Through which narrow channel does cerebrospinal fluid pass from the third ventricle into the fourth ventricle? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct, a small tunnel through the midbrain. It is the only route between those two chambers. A block there holds the fluid back in the lateral and the third ventricles and dilates them.

Question 4706. A described section of the brain cut in the midline shows a curved band of white matter whose fibers sweep forward and backward between the two hemispheres. Which structure is shown? The answer is the corpus callosum. Its fibers cross the midline and join matching regions of the hemispheres. It has a rostrum, a genu, a trunk and a splenium.

Question 4707. Which part of the brain lies in the posterior cranial fossa, has two hemispheres joined by a narrow vermis, and is folded into narrow ridges called folia? The answer is the cerebellum. It smooths and coordinates movement that the cortex begins, and it helps to keep balance and posture. It lies below the tentorium cerebelli.

Question 4708. Which of these is not part of the brainstem: the midbrain, the pons, the medulla oblongata, or the thalamus? The answer is the thalamus. The brainstem joins the brain to the spinal cord and is made of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata. The thalamus belongs to the diencephalon, above the brainstem.

Question 4709. Which part of the brainstem holds the centers for the heart, the blood vessels and breathing, so that a small injury there can be fatal? The answer is the medulla oblongata. It lies lowest in the brainstem, just above the foramen magnum. All the long tracts that run between the brain and the spinal cord pass through it.

Question 4710. Which structure lies immediately superior to the midbrain: the pons, the medulla oblongata, the thalamus, or the spinal cord? The answer is the thalamus. The midbrain is the uppermost part of the brainstem, and the thalamus sits above it as part of the diencephalon. The pons lies below the midbrain and the medulla below the pons.

Question 4711. A described horizontal section through the brain shows a large egg-shaped mass of gray matter on each side of a narrow midline cavity, with a band of white matter just lateral to it. Which structure is the gray mass? The answer is the thalamus. Each thalamus relays sensory information to the cerebral cortex. The band beside it is the internal capsule.

Question 4712. Which two arteries climb the front of the brainstem, join to form a single midline vessel, and so help to complete the arterial ring at the base of the brain? The answer is the two vertebral arteries. They unite as the basilar artery, which divides into the posterior cerebral arteries. The internal carotid arteries complete the front of the ring.

Question 4713. Which fold of the dura mater hangs in the midline between the two cerebral hemispheres and carries the superior sagittal sinus in its upper edge? The answer is the falx cerebri. It runs from the vault of the skull down to the corpus callosum. The tentorium cerebelli lies below it and forms a roof over the cerebellum.

Question 4714. Which of these folds of the dura mater forms a roof over the cerebellum and separates it from the occipital lobes: the falx cerebri, the tentorium cerebelli, the falx cerebelli, or the diaphragma sellae? The answer is the tentorium cerebelli. It stretches across the posterior cranial fossa, and its free edge bounds the opening for the brainstem.

Question 4715. Which space lies between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater and normally holds only a thin film of fluid? The answer is the subdural space. It is only a potential space, so it opens when blood or fluid collects there. The subarachnoid space lies deeper and holds the cerebrospinal fluid, and the epidural space lies outside the dura.

Question 4716. A constructed illustration: a person falls and bleeds from the small veins that run from the surface of the brain to a dural venous sinus. Which space fills with blood? The answer is the subdural space. Those bridging veins cross it on their way to the superior sagittal sinus. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4717. A described magnetic resonance image of the head shows a narrow midline cavity filled with fluid, with a larger cavity on each side draining into it. Which part of the ventricular system is the midline cavity? The answer is the third ventricle. The lateral ventricles open into it through the interventricular foramina, and it drains backward through the cerebral aqueduct.

Question 4718. Which statement about the lower end of the spinal cord in the adult is correct: it ends at the twelfth thoracic vertebra, it reaches the sacrum, it ends at the first or second lumbar vertebra, or it fills the whole vertebral canal? The answer is that it ends at the first or second lumbar vertebra. Below that level the canal holds only the roots of the cauda equina.

Question 4719. A constructed illustration: fluid is taken from the lumbar cistern, and the needle is placed low in the back so that the cord is not injured. Why is that level chosen? The answer is that the spinal cord ends above it, so only the roots of the cauda equina lie there. They float in the fluid and move aside.

Question 4720. Which of these openings leads from the third ventricle into the fourth ventricle: the interventricular foramen, the cerebral aqueduct, the central canal, or the median aperture? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct, a narrow channel through the midbrain. The interventricular foramen joins each lateral ventricle to the third, and the median aperture opens the fourth to the subarachnoid space.

Question 4721. Which statement about the arteries of the brain is correct: the middle cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe, the vertebral arteries supply the frontal lobes, the anterior cerebral arteries supply the medial surface, or the internal carotid arteries supply only the cerebellum? The answer is that the anterior cerebral arteries supply the medial surface of each hemisphere. The occipital lobe belongs to the posterior cerebral artery.

Question 4722. A described specimen shows the base of the brain with a ring of vessels around a central structure that has been removed. Which vessel completes the front of that ring on each side after the internal carotid artery divides? The answer is the anterior cerebral artery, joined across the midline by the anterior communicating artery. The ring is the cerebral arterial circle.

Question 4723. A constructed illustration: a person has a sudden severe headache and a stiff neck, and blood is found in the cerebrospinal fluid. A small pouch of the arachnoid mater has ballooned into a vein at the base of the brain. Which space has bled? The answer is the subarachnoid space, which carries the cerebrospinal fluid. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 4724. True or false: the epidural space around the spinal cord lies between the dura mater and the periosteum of the vertebral canal, and it holds fat and a plexus of thin-walled veins. The answer is true. Inside the skull the dura lies against the bone, so no such space exists there.

Question 4725. Which of these pairs belongs together: the falx cerebri with the superior sagittal sinus, the tentorium cerebelli with the inferior sagittal sinus, the falx cerebelli with the straight sinus, or the diaphragma sellae with the cavernous sinus? The answer is the falx cerebri with the superior sagittal sinus, which runs in its upper edge. The diaphragma sellae covers the pituitary gland.

Question 4726. How many pairs of cranial nerves leave the brain, and how many pairs of spinal nerves leave the spinal cord? The answer is 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. The cranial nerves leave through openings in the skull, and the spinal nerves leave through the intervertebral foramina, one on each side at every segment.

Question 4727. Which of these nerves is a cranial nerve: the sciatic nerve, the optic nerve, the median nerve, or the phrenic nerve? The answer is the optic nerve, the second cranial nerve. It carries the fibers of sight from the retina to the brain. The sciatic and median nerves belong to the limbs, and the phrenic nerve comes from the cervical spinal nerves.

Question 4728. Which root of a spinal nerve carries the sensory fibers toward the spinal cord, and where do the cell bodies of those fibers lie? The answer is the posterior root, with its cell bodies in the posterior root ganglion. The anterior root carries the motor fibers outward. The two roots join beyond the ganglion to form the trunk of the nerve.

Question 4729. Which of these nerves is the largest in the body and runs from the pelvis down the back of the thigh: the femoral nerve, the sciatic nerve, the obturator nerve, or the tibial nerve? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It comes from the sacral plexus and leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. The tibial nerve is one of its divisions.

Question 4730. A described dissection of the back shows a nerve emerging from an opening between two vertebrae and at once dividing into a small branch that turns backward and a larger branch that continues forward. What emerges from the opening? The answer is the trunk of a spinal nerve. Its posterior ramus supplies the deep muscles and the skin of the back.

Question 4731. Where does the trunk of a spinal nerve form, and what are the two branches it gives? The answer is that it forms in the intervertebral foramen, where the posterior and the anterior roots join, and it divides into a posterior ramus and an anterior ramus. The posterior ramus turns backward toward the muscles and the skin of the back.

Question 4732. True or false: the anterior rami of the spinal nerves supply the limbs and the front and sides of the trunk. The answer is true. Most anterior rami join one another to form the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses. The posterior rami stay segmental and supply the deep muscles and the skin of the back.

Question 4733. Which plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the four lower cervical spinal nerves and the first thoracic spinal nerve, and gives branches to the upper limb? The answer is the brachial plexus. It lies in the lower part of the neck and behind the clavicle, and its cords surround the axillary artery. The median, ulnar and radial nerves are among its branches.

Question 4734. Which spinal nerves give rise to the phrenic nerve, which supplies the diaphragm: the first and second thoracic, the fifth to the eighth cervical, the first and second lumbar, or the third, fourth and fifth cervical? The answer is the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves. The nerve then descends through the thorax to the diaphragm.

Question 4735. A described dissection of the neck shows a long nerve lying on the front of the scalenus anterior muscle and passing down into the thorax between the subclavian artery and the subclavian vein. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the phrenic nerve. It runs from lateral to medial across that muscle and continues down to the diaphragm.

Question 4736. Which nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it can be struck against the bone, and what does injury there weaken? The answer is the ulnar nerve, and injury weakens the small muscles of the hand. The nerve lies in a shallow groove on the back of the epicondyle, close to the surface.

Question 4737. Which nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the heart, the lungs and most of the abdominal organs: the phrenic nerve, the sciatic nerve, the vagus nerve, or the facial nerve? The answer is the vagus nerve, the tenth cranial nerve. It descends through the neck and thorax into the abdomen. The facial nerve reaches only glands of the head.

Question 4738. A constructed illustration: a person cannot wrinkle the forehead or close one eye, and the corner of the mouth droops on that side. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the facial nerve, the seventh cranial nerve. It supplies the muscles of facial expression on the same side. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 4739. Which nerve is formed in the axilla by two heads that embrace the axillary artery, and later passes through the carpal tunnel to reach the hand? The answer is the median nerve. It runs lateral to the brachial artery in the upper arm and crosses to the medial side lower down. It supplies most muscles that move the thumb.

Question 4740. Which statement about the autonomic nervous system is correct: the parasympathetic fibers arise only from the brainstem, the sympathetic trunk lies on each side of the vertebral column, the sympathetic fibers arise only from the sacral cord, or the parasympathetic fibers reach the limbs? The answer is that the sympathetic trunk lies on each side of the vertebral column from the neck to the sacrum.

Question 4741. A described specimen shows a chain of small swellings joined by a thin cord, lying on the sides of the vertebral bodies behind the pleura. Which structure is shown? The answer is the sympathetic trunk with its chain of ganglia, part of the autonomic nervous system. Each ganglion receives a small branch from a nearby spinal nerve.

Question 4742. A constructed illustration: a person has a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus and cannot lift the arm sideways, with numbness over the outer part of the shoulder. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the axillary nerve. It winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so it is at risk in that fracture.

Question 4743. Which of these pairs belongs together: the phrenic nerve with the diaphragm, the sciatic nerve with the serratus anterior, the femoral nerve with the calf muscles, or the radial nerve with the muscles of the face? The answer is the phrenic nerve with the diaphragm. The sciatic nerve supplies the back of the thigh, the femoral nerve the front of the thigh, and the radial nerve the back of the arm.

Question 4744. Name two things that a spinal nerve supplies through its anterior ramus, spoken as a list. The answer is the muscles of a limb and the skin over the front and sides of the trunk. The anterior ramus is much larger than the posterior ramus, and the anterior rami join to form the plexuses.

Question 4745. Which statement about the dermatomes of the trunk is correct: the bands belong to the autonomic nerves, one band covers the whole chest, each band comes from a cranial nerve, or each spinal nerve supplies a band of skin around the trunk? The answer is that each spinal nerve supplies a band of skin around the trunk. Adjacent bands overlap.

Question 4746. Which part of the nervous tissue is called gray matter, and what does it contain? The answer is the part that holds the cell bodies, the dendrites and the unmyelinated fibers. It forms the cortex of the cerebrum and the cerebellum, and it lies deep in the spinal cord. The white matter around it holds the myelinated fibers.

Question 4747. Which of these structures is made of gray matter: the corpus callosum, the internal capsule, the cerebral cortex, or the pyramidal tract in the medulla oblongata? The answer is the cerebral cortex. It is a folded sheet of gray matter on the surface of each hemisphere. The corpus callosum, the internal capsule and the pyramids are all bundles of white matter.

Question 4748. A described section across the spinal cord shows a butterfly-shaped area of darker tissue in the center with a paler rim around it. Which part is the gray matter, and which horn holds the cell bodies of the motor neurons? The answer is the butterfly-shaped center, with those cell bodies in the anterior horn.

Question 4749. True or false: in the spinal cord the gray matter lies on the outside and the white matter lies in the center. The answer is false. In the spinal cord the gray matter forms a central butterfly shape around the central canal, and the white matter surrounds it. In the cerebrum the arrangement is the opposite.

Question 4750. What name is given to the deep masses of gray matter inside each cerebral hemisphere, which include the caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus? The answer is the basal nuclei, also called the basal ganglia. They help to start and to smooth voluntary movement. The internal capsule separates them from the thalamus.

Question 4751. Which of these horns of the spinal gray matter holds the cell bodies of the motor neurons that leave by the anterior root: the posterior horn, the anterior horn, the lateral horn, or the commissure? The answer is the anterior horn, which is broad and rounded. The lateral horn holds the sympathetic neurons of the thoracic segments.

Question 4752. Which horn of the spinal gray matter lies nearest the posterior root, and what information does it receive? The answer is the posterior horn, which receives the sensory fibers that enter by the posterior root. It lies at the back of the cord, nearest the vertebral spines. Fibers from its cells cross to the opposite side or run up the cord.

Question 4753. Which layers make up the cerebellar cortex, in order from the surface inward: the pyramidal, the granular and the white; the molecular, the granular and the Purkinje; the granular, the Purkinje and the molecular; or the molecular, the Purkinje and the granular? The answer is the molecular layer, then the Purkinje cell layer, then the granular layer. The Purkinje cells alone leave the cerebellar cortex.

Question 4754. A described stained section of the cerebral cortex shows a band of large triangular cells in one layer and a dense layer of small round cells in another. Which are the large triangular cells, and where do their axons go? The answer is the pyramidal cells, and their axons leave the cortex to join the white matter. The small round cells are the granular cells.

Question 4755. Which group of cells in the midbrain contains a dark pigment, sends fibers to the basal nuclei, and is damaged in the disorder that causes tremor and rigidity? The answer is the cells of the substantia nigra. Their fibers release dopamine, which helps to control movement. Loss of those cells is the anatomical basis of Parkinson disease.

Question 4756. Which band of white matter separates the thalamus and the caudate nucleus on its medial side from the lentiform nucleus on its lateral side? The answer is the internal capsule. Its fibers are packed tightly, so a small lesion there can cause a large weakness on the opposite side. The caudate nucleus lies medial to it.

Question 4757. Which statement about the lateral horn of the spinal gray matter is correct: it lies in every segment of the cord, it holds the sensory fibers from the skin, it is present in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, or it lies at the back of the cord? The answer is that it is present in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, and it holds sympathetic motor neurons.

Question 4758. A constructed illustration: a small stroke destroys a patch of gray matter deep in one cerebral hemisphere, and the movements of the opposite hand become slow and jerky. Which gray masses lie there? The answer is the basal nuclei, which include the caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus. They help to smooth movement.

Question 4759. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior horn with the motor neurons, the posterior horn with the motor neurons, the lateral horn with the sensory fibers, or the central canal with the basal nuclei? The answer is the anterior horn with the motor neurons. The posterior horn receives sensory fibers, and the lateral horn holds sympathetic neurons.

Question 4760. Which statement about the gray matter of the brainstem is correct: it lies only on the surface, the columns of cells are broken into separate nuclei by the fibers that cross it, it is absent below the midbrain, or it forms the cerebellar cortex? The answer is that the columns are broken into separate nuclei by the crossing fibers.

Question 4761. Which tissue of the nervous system is called white matter, and why is it pale? The answer is the tissue made mostly of myelinated axons, whose fatty sheaths give it its pale color. It forms the tracts that carry information from one region to another. In the spinal cord it lies on the outside.

Question 4762. Which of these names is given to a bundle of fibers that runs from one part of the central nervous system to another: a nerve, a tract, a ganglion, or a plexus? The answer is a tract. In the peripheral nervous system such a bundle is called a nerve instead, and a ganglion is a collection of cell bodies.

Question 4763. True or false: the corpus callosum is a band of white matter that joins matching areas of the two cerebral hemispheres. The answer is true. Its fibers cross the midline and are called commissural fibers. In a section cut from front to back, its thick body forms a curved roof over the lateral ventricles.

Question 4764. A described horizontal section of the brain shows a broad band of white matter sweeping across the midline and fanning out into the hemisphere on each side. What kind of fibers are shown, and what is this band called? The answer is commissural fibers, and this band is the corpus callosum, which joins the two hemispheres.

Question 4765. Which three groups are used to classify the fibers of the cerebral white matter, according to where they run? The answer is association fibers, which join parts of the same hemisphere; commissural fibers, which cross to the other hemisphere; and projection fibers, which run up to the cortex or down from it. The internal capsule is made of projection fibers.

Question 4766. Which of these fiber groups carries information from the cortex down to the spinal cord: association fibers, commissural fibers, projection fibers, or the fibers of the posterior root? The answer is projection fibers, which include the corticospinal tract. Association fibers link nearby parts of one hemisphere, and commissural fibers cross the midline between the hemispheres.

Question 4767. Which tract lies between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus, and which structures form its medial boundary? The answer is the internal capsule, and the thalamus and the caudate nucleus form its medial boundary. On its lateral side lies the lentiform nucleus. Its fibers run in a tight bundle from the cortex to the cord.

Question 4768. Through which part of the internal capsule do the fibers of the corticospinal tract pass on their way down from the cortex: the anterior limb, the genu, the posterior limb, or the part behind the lentiform nucleus? The answer is the posterior limb. The fibers of the face pass through the genu, and the anterior limb links the frontal lobe with the thalamus.

Question 4769. A described section of the medulla oblongata shows that most of the fibers of the descending tract cross to the opposite side and then continue downward. What is that crossing called, and where does the crossed tract lie? The answer is the pyramidal decussation, and the crossed fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral column of the cord.

Question 4770. Which tract carries the sensations of pain and temperature from the body to the thalamus, and on which side does it cross? The answer is the spinothalamic tract, which crosses within 1 or 2 segments of the level where it enters the spinal cord. Its fibers then ascend in the anterior and lateral columns to the thalamus.

Question 4771. Which tract carries the sense of vibration and of fine touch from the leg, and where do its fibers cross the midline? The answer is the posterior column tract, whose fibers ascend on the same side of the cord and cross in the medulla oblongata. They then run as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus. Fibers from the leg lie nearest the midline.

Question 4772. Which statement about the tracts of the spinal cord is correct: both cross in the spinal cord, both cross in the medulla oblongata, neither crosses, or the spinothalamic fibers cross in the spinal cord and the posterior column fibers cross in the medulla? The answer is that the spinothalamic fibers cross in the cord and the posterior column fibers in the medulla.

Question 4773. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral corticospinal tract with the movement of the limbs, the posterior column with pain and temperature, the spinothalamic tract with vibration, or the medial lemniscus with the sense of smell? The answer is the lateral corticospinal tract with the movement of the limbs. The posterior column carries vibration and fine touch.

Question 4774. A constructed illustration: a person has patchy loss of myelin in the white matter of the brain and the spinal cord, with weakness and numbness that come and go. Which tissue is attacked? The answer is the myelin sheath of the white matter tracts, so signals travel slowly or fail. The gray matter is largely spared.

Question 4775. A constructed illustration: a small hemorrhage destroys the posterior limb of the internal capsule on one side. Which fibers are interrupted, and what follows? The answer is the projection fibers that run between the cortex and the brainstem or the spinal cord. Movement and sensation fail on the opposite side of the body. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 4776. Which three main parts make up a neuron, and which part carries the impulse away from the cell body? The answer is the cell body, the dendrites and the axon, and the axon carries the impulse away. The dendrites bring information toward the cell body. The axon ends in small terminals that pass the message to the next cell.

Question 4777. Which of these names is given to the short branches that carry information toward the cell body of a neuron: the axons, the dendrites, the myelin sheaths, or the nodes of Ranvier? The answer is the dendrites. They form a branching tree around the cell body. The axon is the single long process that carries the message away.

Question 4778. Which type of neuron has a single process that leaves the cell body and then divides into one branch going to the periphery and one going to the spinal cord? The answer is the unipolar neuron, also called the pseudounipolar neuron. The cell bodies of this type lie in the posterior root ganglia of the spinal nerves.

Question 4779. Which of these neurons carries impulses from a sensory receptor toward the central nervous system: a motor neuron, a sensory neuron, an interneuron, or a neuron of the anterior horn? The answer is a sensory neuron, also called an afferent neuron. A motor neuron carries impulses away to a muscle or a gland.

Question 4780. A described specimen of the spinal cord shows a nerve cell whose body lies in a swelling on the posterior root, with one process leaving the cell body and dividing in the shape of the letter T. Which kind of neuron is shown? The answer is a unipolar sensory neuron, with one branch to the skin and one entering the cord.

Question 4781. True or false: in a chemical synapse the impulse crosses from one neuron to the next by the release of a chemical messenger into a narrow gap. The answer is true. The gap is the synaptic cleft, and the messenger is a neurotransmitter. The impulse crosses only from the presynaptic side to the postsynaptic side, so it travels one way.

Question 4782. Which types of supporting cells form the myelin sheath in the central nervous system and in the peripheral nervous system? The answer is the oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and the Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. One oligodendrocyte can wrap several axons, while each Schwann cell wraps only one segment of one axon.

Question 4783. Which of these cells of the central nervous system helps to form the blood-brain barrier and to repair the tissue after injury: the oligodendrocyte, the astrocyte, the microglial cell, or the ependymal cell? The answer is the astrocyte. Its processes touch the capillaries and the neurons, and it forms a scar in the brain. The microglial cell is the phagocyte.

Question 4784. A described section of nervous tissue shows a large star-shaped cell with many processes, some touching a small blood vessel and others touching the surface of neurons. Which cell is shown? The answer is the astrocyte. It supports the neurons, helps to form the blood-brain barrier and takes part in the repair of injury.

Question 4785. Which supporting cells of the peripheral nervous system wrap the cell bodies in a ganglion and form the myelin around a single axon: the satellite cells and the Schwann cells, the astrocytes and the oligodendrocytes, the ependymal cells and the microglial cells, or the Purkinje cells and the granular cells? The answer is the satellite cells and the Schwann cells.

Question 4786. Which of these cells lines the ventricles of the brain and helps to make cerebrospinal fluid: the astrocyte, the ependymal cell, the microglial cell, or the oligodendrocyte? The answer is the ependymal cell. A sheet of these cells covers the choroid plexus, where most of the fluid is made.

Question 4787. Name two chemical messengers of the nervous system and say where each is released, spoken as a list. The answer is acetylcholine, released at the neuromuscular junction and by parasympathetic endings, and norepinephrine, released by most sympathetic endings. Others include dopamine, serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid, which is the main inhibitory messenger of the brain.

Question 4788. Which of these events happens first when an impulse reaches the end of an axon: the neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic cleft, calcium enters the presynaptic terminal, the postsynaptic cell fires, or the vesicles refill? The answer is that calcium enters the presynaptic terminal. It makes the vesicles of neurotransmitter fuse and release their contents into the synaptic cleft.

Question 4789. A described drawing of a synapse shows a small swelling at the end of an axon filled with tiny round sacs, facing a thicker membrane across a narrow gap. What are the sacs, and what is the gap? The answer is that the sacs are the synaptic vesicles, which hold the neurotransmitter, and the gap is the synaptic cleft.

Question 4790. A described section of the spinal cord is cut straight across its long axis. In which direction do the long tracts of the white matter run relative to that cut, and in which column does the lateral corticospinal tract lie? The answer is that the tracts run at right angles to the cut, and that tract lies in the lateral column.

Question 4791. Which part of the neuron is the short region where the axon leaves the cell body, and why is it important in the start of an impulse? The answer is the axon hillock, where the impulse is generated. The cell body and the dendrites add up the messages they receive, and when the sum reaches a threshold the hillock fires.

Question 4792. A constructed illustration: a cut in the forearm divides a nerve, and the part of the axon separated from its cell body swells and then breaks up while its sheath remains. What is that change called? The answer is Wallerian degeneration. Fibers of the peripheral nervous system can regrow along the sheath, but those of the central nervous system cannot.

Question 4793. Which of these statements about the speed of an impulse is correct: all fibers carry it at the same speed, a thin unmyelinated fiber carries it faster, a thick myelinated fiber carries it faster than a thin unmyelinated fiber, or the speed depends only on the length of the axon? The answer is that a thick myelinated fiber is faster. The myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node.

Question 4794. Which of these pairs belongs together: the node of Ranvier with the gap between two myelin segments, the axon hillock with the receiving tip of a dendrite, the synaptic vesicle with the myelin sheath, or the ependymal cell with the movement of a limb? The answer is the node of Ranvier with the gap between two myelin segments, where the impulse is renewed.

Question 4795. A described section through the cerebral hemisphere passes through the midline and shows both lateral ventricles with the corpus callosum above them. In which plane was the brain cut, and does the cut pass through both hemispheres? The answer is a horizontal plane, and it does pass through both hemispheres. A sagittal cut would show only one hemisphere.

Question 4796. A described electron micrograph shows a chain of cells wrapped many times around a single axon, with short bare gaps between the wrappings. Which cells are shown, and what happens at the gaps? The answer is the Schwann cells of a peripheral nerve, and the gaps are the nodes of Ranvier, where the impulse is renewed.

Question 4797. Which of these statements about the regeneration of a divided nerve fiber is correct: a fiber of the central nervous system regrows faster, both regrow equally well, neither regrows at all, or a fiber of the peripheral nervous system can regrow along its sheath? The answer is that a peripheral fiber can regrow along the sheath left by the Schwann cells.

Question 4798. A constructed illustration: a wound divides the median nerve at the wrist, and after it heals the thumb still cannot be opposed. Which cells guide the regrowth of the divided fibers? The answer is the Schwann cells, whose sheath remains as a tube along which the new fiber grows. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 4799. Which statement about the resting membrane potential of a neuron is correct: the inside is positive relative to the outside, the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside, the two sides are equal, or the potential depends only on the size of the cell? The answer is that the inside is negative, largely because the membrane lets potassium leak out.

Question 4800. Name two structures that meet at a synapse, spoken as a list. The answer is the presynaptic terminal of one neuron and the postsynaptic membrane of the next. The impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal, a neurotransmitter crosses the narrow synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic membrane responds. The message passes in one direction only.

To summarize, the central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord, wrapped in the dura mater, the arachnoid mater and the pia mater and cushioned by cerebrospinal fluid made in the choroid plexus. The peripheral nervous system is the 12 pairs of cranial nerves and the 31 pairs of spinal nerves, each spinal nerve formed by a posterior sensory root and an anterior motor root in the intervertebral foramen. Gray matter holds the cell bodies and dendrites, in the cerebral cortex, the basal nuclei, the cerebellar cortex or the horns of the spinal cord, and white matter holds the myelinated axons grouped into association, commissural and projection fibers. The great tracts cross the midline according to their function, the corticospinal tract in the medulla oblongata, the spinothalamic tract in the spinal cord and the posterior column tract in the medulla. Neurons come in sensory, motor and interneuron forms, supported within the central nervous system by astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglial cells and ependymal cells, and outside it by Schwann cells and satellite cells. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 49 — General Nervous System Anatomy, Part Two

This chapter continues the general anatomy of the nervous system by looking at the supporting cells that fill it, the roots by which its nerves leave the spinal cord, and the ganglia in which its nerve cell bodies gather, and it then turns to the cerebrum and its lobes. It covers the glial cells, the dorsal and ventral roots of the spinal nerves, the sensory and autonomic ganglia, and the hemispheres, lobes and deep masses of the brain. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer at once, in the same paragraph, before the reason for that answer. The structures are described as they are in the ordinary body, and where a common variation exists it is noted in the reason. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4801. Which star-shaped supporting cell is the most numerous in the central nervous system, sending many processes out among the nerve cells and the blood vessels? The answer is the astrocyte. Some of its processes end in flat feet on the walls of capillaries. It helps to nourish the nerve cells and to keep the barrier around them tight.

Question 4802. Which of these cells wraps an axon in myelin inside the brain and the spinal cord: the astrocyte, the oligodendrocyte, the ependymal cell, or the microglial cell? The answer is the oligodendrocyte. One oligodendrocyte sends a process to each of several axons and myelinates a segment of every one of them.

Question 4803. Which cells form a single layer that lines the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord and helps to produce the cerebrospinal fluid? The answer is the ependymal cells. Where the lining is folded over a tuft of vessels, in the choroid plexus, they secrete most of it.

Question 4804. Which small cells of the nervous system multiply after an injury, gather at the damaged place and clear away the debris? The answer is the microglial cells. They are phagocytic, and they do not arise from the same embryonic sheet as the nerve cells. They come from mesoderm and enter the nervous system with the blood vessels before birth.

Question 4805. A described peripheral nerve is wrapped by a chain of cells, and each of them forms a single segment of myelin around a single axon. Which cell is described: the astrocyte, the Schwann cell, the oligodendrocyte, or the satellite cell? The answer is the Schwann cell. It serves one segment of one axon outside the central nervous system.

Question 4806. Which flattened cells form a capsule around the nerve cell body inside a ganglion, in the way that astrocytes surround nerve cell bodies in the brain? The answer is the satellite cells. They lie closely around each cell body in the ganglion. Their task matches that of the astrocyte, but it is carried out in the peripheral nervous system.

Question 4807. True or false: the astrocyte helps to build the barrier that keeps many substances in the blood out of the brain tissue. The answer is true. The barrier itself is made by tight junctions between the cells that line the capillary. The foot plates of the astrocytes press against that capillary and signal it to stay tight.

Question 4808. In the developing nervous system, which elongated cells stretch from the inner lining to the outer surface and guide the young nerve cells to their final place? The answer is the radial glial cells. Their long processes form a ladder across the thickness of the wall. Most of them later shorten and become astrocytes.

Question 4809. Three of these cell types arise from the same embryonic sheet as the nerve cells themselves, and one does not: the astrocytes, the oligodendrocytes, the ependymal cells, and the microglial cells. The answer is the microglial cell, which arrives with the blood vessels from mesoderm. The other three are all derived from the wall of the neural tube.

Question 4810. A constructed illustration: a young adult has attacks of numbness, blurred vision and unsteady walking, and the myelin of the brain and spinal cord is under attack. Which cells are the target? The answer is the oligodendrocytes. Loss of their myelin slows conduction along the central pathways, while the peripheral nerves wrapped by Schwann cells are usually spared.

Question 4811. Which glial cell sends foot plates that lie immediately against the outer wall of a capillary in the brain, and what does that position let it do? The answer is the astrocyte. Its end feet cover much of the capillary surface. From there it signals the lining cells to keep their tight junctions and helps to carry nutrients into the tissue.

Question 4812. Which single cell of the central nervous system can myelinate segments of as many as fifty different axons at one time: the astrocyte, the ependymal cell, the microglial cell, or the oligodendrocyte? The answer is the oligodendrocyte. It reaches several neighboring fibers with separate processes, and each process wraps one segment. A Schwann cell serves one axon only.

Question 4813. A described microscopic preparation shows a star-shaped cell with many radiating processes, one of which ends in a broad flat foot on the wall of a small vessel while the others lie among nerve fibers. Which cell is shown? The answer is the astrocyte. The foot on the vessel identifies it. A myelin-forming cell would wrap an axon instead.

Question 4814. After an injury to the brain, which glial cell multiplies and knits its processes together to wall off the damaged area: the ependymal cell, the astrocyte, the Schwann cell, or the satellite cell? The answer is the astrocyte. It forms a scar in the nervous tissue. The scar helps to seal the injury, but it also blocks the regrowth of central axons.

Question 4815. Which statement about the myelin-forming cells is correct: one Schwann cell myelinates several axons, the oligodendrocyte lies only in peripheral nerves, one Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon, or myelin is made by the microglial cells? The answer is that one Schwann cell myelinates a segment of a single axon. The oligodendrocyte of the brain and cord serves several axons instead.

Question 4816. Which of these lies at the meeting point of two Schwann cells along a peripheral axon: the node of Ranvier, the motor end plate, the synaptic cleft, or the dorsal root? The answer is the node of Ranvier, the short bare gap of membrane where the impulse is renewed. The impulse leaps from one node to the next, so conduction is fast.

Question 4817. Name two kinds of supporting cell in the brain and the spinal cord that do not make myelin, spoken as a list. The answer is the astrocytes and the ependymal cells, and the microglial cells belong in the same group. Astrocytes support and scar, and ependymal cells line the cavities. Myelin in the central nervous system comes from the oligodendrocytes alone.

Question 4818. A constructed illustration: an imaging study of an adult shows a rapidly growing tumor in one cerebral hemisphere, and it is described as arising from the supporting cells that nourish nerve cells. Which cell of origin is meant? The answer is the astrocyte. Tumors of astrocytes are the most common malignant tumors of the brain in adults, and they spread by infiltration.

Question 4819. A described electron micrograph shows one cell body with several processes, and each process spirals around a different axon to form a dark ring of myelin. In which part of the nervous system does this cell work, and why can it serve several axons? The answer is the central nervous system, and the cell is an oligodendrocyte.

Question 4820. Which supporting cell would be found wrapped around the nerve cell bodies inside a dorsal root ganglion: the astrocyte, the ependymal cell, the satellite cell, or the oligodendrocyte? The answer is the satellite cell. The other three belong to the central nervous system, and a ganglion lies outside it. The satellite cell is the peripheral counterpart of the astrocyte.

Question 4821. Which root of a spinal nerve carries the fibers that leave the spinal cord to supply the muscles, and in which direction do those fibers run? The answer is the ventral root, also called the anterior root, and its fibers run outward. It is built of motor fibers that begin in the large cells of the anterior horn.

Question 4822. Which of these describes the dorsal root of a spinal nerve: it carries motor fibers away from the cord, it carries sensory fibers toward the cord, it carries both kinds of fiber, or it carries no nerve fibers at all? The answer is that it carries sensory fibers toward the cord. The motor fibers travel outward in the ventral root.

Question 4823. What is the name of the swelling on the dorsal root of a spinal nerve that holds the cell bodies of the sensory fibers? The answer is the dorsal root ganglion. It lies in the intervertebral foramen beside the root. No synapse takes place inside it, because the sensory cell body merely relays the impulse onward to the cord.

Question 4824. How many pairs of spinal nerves leave the spinal cord, and how are they grouped: twenty-one pairs, thirty-one pairs, forty-one pairs, or twelve pairs? The answer is thirty-one pairs, made up of eight cervical, twelve thoracic, five lumbar, five sacral and one coccygeal pair. The first cervical nerve leaves above the first cervical vertebra.

Question 4825. In the cervical region, does a spinal nerve leave the vertebral canal above or below the vertebra of the same number, and where does the first cervical nerve run relative to the vertebral artery? The answer is above the vertebra of the same number, and the first cervical nerve runs behind the vertebral artery. Each cervical nerve takes the number of the vertebra below it.

Question 4826. The nerves of the upper limb are formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerves: the first to the fourth cervical, the fifth cervical to the first thoracic, the first to the twelfth thoracic, or the first to the fifth lumbar? The answer is the fifth cervical to the first thoracic. Those five rami form the brachial plexus.

Question 4827. After a spinal nerve leaves the intervertebral foramen it divides into two branches. Which of them supplies the deep muscles and the skin of the back: the ventral ramus, the dorsal ramus, the gray ramus, or the white ramus? The answer is the dorsal ramus, the smaller posterior branch.

Question 4828. In an adult, the solid spinal cord ends at about which vertebral level, and why is a lumbar puncture made below the third lumbar vertebra? The answer is that the cord ends at the first or second lumbar vertebra, so below the third the canal holds only the loose roots of the cauda equina. A needle placed there can push those roots aside instead of striking the cord.

Question 4829. A described dissection of the lower vertebral canal shows the solid cord ending in a point, with a bundle of nerve roots descending beyond it like the tail of a horse. What is that bundle called, and what does each root in it become? The answer is the cauda equina, and each root runs on to its own intervertebral foramen.

Question 4830. A constructed illustration: a person has pain shooting down the back of the leg after lifting a heavy load, and a disc between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae is described as pressing on one nerve root. Which root is affected? The answer is the fifth lumbar root. A disc herniates backward and outward, where it meets the root leaving at the level below.

Question 4831. True or false: a ganglion that holds sensory nerve cell bodies sits on the ventral root of a spinal nerve. The answer is false. The swelling of nerve cell bodies sits on the dorsal root, which carries fibers toward the cord. The ventral root carries motor fibers outward and bears no such ganglion.

Question 4832. The denticulate ligament anchors the spinal cord to the dura at the side. Does the dorsal root lie in front of that ligament or behind it, and where does the ventral root lie? The answer is that the dorsal root lies behind the ligament and the ventral root in front of it.

Question 4833. A described cross section of the spinal cord shows a butterfly of gray matter with a broad front horn and a slender back horn, and two roots leaving on each side. Which root carries fibers toward the cord, and which carries them away? The answer is that the thinner dorsal root behind carries fibers toward the cord, and the ventral root carries them away.

Question 4834. Which of these pairs belongs together: the dorsal root with the back muscles, the ventral root with the skin of the back, the dorsal ramus with the deep muscles of the back, or the ventral ramus with the joints alone? The answer is the dorsal ramus with the deep muscles of the back. The dorsal root carries sensory fibers, the ventral root carries motor fibers, and the ventral ramus supplies the limbs.

Question 4835. Name the two roots that join to form a spinal nerve, and say what each of them carries. The answer is the ventral root, which carries motor fibers outward, and the dorsal root, which carries sensory fibers inward. The dorsal root bears the ganglion that holds the sensory cell bodies. The two roots meet in the intervertebral foramen.

Question 4836. In a dorsal root ganglion, each nerve cell body gives off a single short process that then divides into two long branches. What name is given to that shape, and where does one branch end? The answer is a pseudounipolar cell. One branch reaches the skin, a muscle or a joint, and the other enters the spinal cord.

Question 4837. In which kind of ganglion does a nerve fiber actually make a synapse with a second nerve cell: the dorsal root ganglion, an autonomic ganglion, a sensory ganglion of a cranial nerve, or the trigeminal ganglion? The answer is an autonomic ganglion. There the fiber that left the central nervous system hands its message to a second cell.

Question 4838. What name is given to the row of ganglia that lies on each side of the vertebral column and is joined into a chain from the neck to the pelvis? The answer is the sympathetic chain, whose ganglia are called paravertebral. A ganglion of the same system in front of the aorta, such as the celiac ganglion, is called prevertebral.

Question 4839. Which of these autonomic ganglia lies in front of the abdominal aorta rather than beside the vertebral column: the superior cervical ganglion, the celiac ganglion, the stellate ganglion, or the otic ganglion? The answer is the celiac ganglion. It lies around the origin of the celiac artery and serves the upper abdominal organs.

Question 4840. Which plexus lies immediately around the origin of the celiac artery from the abdominal aorta, and which two ganglia lie within it? The answer is the celiac plexus, with the celiac ganglia on either side. Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers pass through it to the stomach, the liver, the spleen and the pancreas. Pain from those organs travels back along the same route.

Question 4841. Which large sensory ganglion lies in a pocket of dura on the front of the petrous part of the temporal bone, at the root of the fifth cranial nerve? The answer is the trigeminal ganglion. Its three divisions arise from it to supply the face, the teeth and the muscles of chewing. It is the sensory ganglion of the largest cranial nerve.

Question 4842. Which of these cranial ganglia holds the cell bodies of the parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil: the trigeminal ganglion, the ciliary ganglion, the geniculate ganglion, or the spiral ganglion? The answer is the ciliary ganglion, which lies in the orbit behind the eye. The trigeminal ganglion is sensory, the geniculate serves the facial nerve, and the spiral ganglion serves hearing.

Question 4843. True or false: the deep gray masses called the basal ganglia are true ganglia lying outside the central nervous system. The answer is false. The caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus lie deep inside each cerebral hemisphere. The name is a historical one, and a true ganglion lies outside the central nervous system.

Question 4844. A constructed illustration: a person has a band of painful blisters on one side of the chest that stops at the midline. Which ganglion is meant? The answer is a dorsal root ganglion of a thoracic spinal nerve. The virus travels out along the sensory fibers, and the rash follows one segment.

Question 4845. Which of these pairs belongs together: the dorsal root ganglion with a synapse, an autonomic ganglion with sensory cell bodies, the sympathetic chain with a synapse outside the central nervous system, or a sensory ganglion with motor fibers? The answer is the sympathetic chain with a synapse outside the central nervous system. A dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies and no synapse.

Question 4846. A described dissection shows a chain of small swellings beside the vertebral bodies in the neck, each joined to a spinal nerve by two short connections. What is the chain, and what are the two connections? The answer is the sympathetic chain, joined to each spinal nerve by a gray and a white ramus. The white ramus carries fibers that have just left the cord.

Question 4847. Which small parasympathetic ganglion hangs just below the foramen ovale and sends its fibers to the parotid gland? The answer is the otic ganglion. It is attached to the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, which passes through that opening. Its fibers come from the ninth cranial nerve and join it along the way.

Question 4848. In the neck, does the sympathetic chain lie in front of the carotid sheath or behind it, and what lies immediately behind the chain? The answer is that the chain lies behind the carotid sheath, and the vertebral column lies behind the chain. It rests on the long muscles at the front of the neck, medial to the vagus nerve.

Question 4849. Which statement about the dorsal root ganglion is correct: it contains multipolar cells, it contains no synapse, it lies inside the brain or spinal cord, or it carries motor fibers outward? The answer is that it contains no synapse. Its cells are pseudounipolar sensory cells that relay the impulse straight into the cord.

Question 4850. Name the two great groups into which ganglia are divided by the presence or absence of a synapse, and give one example of each. The answer is the sensory ganglia, such as a dorsal root ganglion, and the autonomic ganglia, such as the celiac ganglion. The sensory ganglion holds cell bodies and no synapse, while the autonomic ganglion holds a synapse.

Question 4851. Which deep groove divides the cerebrum into a left and a right hemisphere, and what sheet of tissue lies within it? The answer is the longitudinal fissure, and the falx cerebri lies in it. The falx is a fold of dura that dips down between the two hemispheres. The two halves are joined below by the corpus callosum.

Question 4852. Which thick band of white matter crosses the midline below the longitudinal fissure and joins the two cerebral hemispheres? The answer is the corpus callosum. Its fibers are commissural, which means that they cross from one side to the other. It is the largest bridge of its kind in the brain.

Question 4853. Which groove runs downward and forward across the upper lateral surface of a hemisphere and separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe? The answer is the central sulcus. It lies between the precentral gyrus in front and the postcentral gyrus behind. Those two gyri carry the motor and the sensory maps of the body.

Question 4854. Which deep cleft on the side of a hemisphere separates the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above? The answer is the lateral sulcus, also called the lateral fissure. Its floor is formed by the insula, a lobe that is hidden from the surface. The cleft runs backward and upward from the front of the temporal region.

Question 4855. Which lobe of the cerebrum lies behind the parietooccipital sulcus at the back of the head: the frontal lobe, the parietal lobe, the occipital lobe, or the temporal lobe? The answer is the occipital lobe. Its chief task is vision, and its primary visual cortex lies on the medial surface. The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus and serves hearing.

Question 4856. Which gyrus lies immediately in front of the central sulcus and holds the large cells that begin the pathway to the skeletal muscles? The answer is the precentral gyrus, which is the primary motor cortex. Its cells are arranged along the gyrus in the order of the body. The body is represented upside down, with the face lowest.

Question 4857. Which gyrus lies immediately behind the central sulcus and receives the signals of touch and position from the opposite side of the body? The answer is the postcentral gyrus, the primary somatosensory cortex. It mirrors the motor map in front of it. The hand and the face take up a very large part of it.

Question 4858. Which area in the lower part of the frontal lobe, usually on the left, plans the movements of speech, so that damage there leaves a person able to understand words but unable to speak them? The answer is the motor speech area of Broca. It lies just in front of the lower end of the precentral gyrus.

Question 4859. Which area at the junction of the temporal and parietal lobes, usually on the left, is needed to understand spoken and written language: the precentral gyrus, the area of Wernicke, the area of Broca, or the calcarine cortex? The answer is the area of Wernicke. Damage there leaves speech fluent but empty of meaning.

Question 4860. On the medial surface of which lobe, and around which sulcus, does the primary visual cortex lie? The answer is the occipital lobe, around the calcarine sulcus. The upper bank of the sulcus receives the upper part of the opposite visual field. The lower bank receives the lower part.

Question 4861. A described preparation shows a gyrus running along the upper surface of the temporal lobe, hidden inside the cleft that separates that lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. Which gyrus is shown, and what does it receive? The answer is the superior temporal gyrus, which carries the primary auditory cortex. Each ear sends fibers to both hemispheres.

Question 4862. Which of these is a lobe of the cerebrum that cannot be seen from the surface until the lips of the lateral sulcus are pulled apart: the occipital lobe, the insula, the parietal lobe, or the cingulate gyrus? The answer is the insula, which lies in the floor of the lateral sulcus and is covered by the opercula. The cingulate gyrus belongs to the limbic lobe.

Question 4863. Which compact band of white matter lies between the thalamus and the caudate nucleus on its inner side and the lentiform nucleus on its outer side, and carries the motor fibers from the cortex? The answer is the internal capsule. Above it those fibers fan out as the corona radiata.

Question 4864. Which large egg-shaped mass of gray matter lies deep in each hemisphere beside the third ventricle and relays almost every sensory pathway to the cortex: the putamen, the thalamus, the amygdala, or the hippocampus? The answer is the thalamus. Every sense except smell passes through it on the way to the cortex. The internal capsule runs along its lateral border.

Question 4865. Which part of the brain lies below and in front of the thalamus, forms the floor of the third ventricle, and controls body temperature, hunger and the hormones of the pituitary gland? The answer is the hypothalamus. A stalk carries its orders down to the pituitary.

Question 4866. Which three deep masses of gray matter are grouped together as the basal ganglia, and what kind of movement do they help to smooth? The answer is the caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus, and they help to smooth voluntary movement. They receive fibers from the whole cortex and send them back through the thalamus.

Question 4867. A constructed illustration: a person suddenly cannot move the right arm or the right leg and cannot speak, though the muscles of the face work on both sides. An artery supplying the lateral surface of the left hemisphere is blocked. Which artery is it? The answer is the middle cerebral artery.

Question 4868. A constructed illustration: after an artery on the medial surface of one hemisphere is blocked, a person loses power and feeling in the opposite leg and foot, while the arm and the face are spared. Which artery is involved? The answer is the anterior cerebral artery, which supplies the medial surface as far back as the parietal lobe.

Question 4869. A constructed illustration: a person reports that one half of the world has vanished from vision in both eyes, and the damage lies at the back of the brain. Which artery supplies the damaged region? The answer is the posterior cerebral artery, which supplies the occipital lobe and its visual cortex. Damage there removes the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes.

Question 4870. Which statement about the motor map on the precentral gyrus is correct: the face lies at the top, the foot lies at the top, the hand lies at the bottom, or the body is represented the right way up? The answer is that the foot lies at the top. The map is upside down, so the face lies lowest.

Question 4871. A described computed tomography section through the brain shows two dark fluid-filled spaces near the midline, and beside each of them a comma-shaped mass of gray matter. Which structures are described? The answer is the lateral ventricles and the heads of the caudate nuclei. The head of the caudate nucleus forms part of the floor of the anterior horn.

Question 4872. A described magnetic resonance imaging section through the brain shows two parallel gyri running down the upper surface with a deep groove between them, and a horizontal cleft entering from the side. Which gyri and which groove are described? The answer is the precentral and postcentral gyri, with the central sulcus between them. The horizontal cleft is the lateral sulcus.

Question 4873. A described section across the brain shows two fluid-filled cavities lying side by side, separated in the midline by a thin partition, with a third cavity between the two thalami below them. Which cavities are described, and what separates the upper pair? The answer is the two lateral ventricles, separated by the septum pellucidum, with the third ventricle below.

Question 4874. Which plane of section cuts across both hemispheres from side to side and shows the corpus callosum above the lateral ventricles, and which plane instead separates the two hemispheres along the midline? The answer is a coronal plane for the first, and a sagittal plane for the second. That is the section used to compare the two sides of the brain.

Question 4875. True or false: the left hemisphere always carries the speech areas. The answer is false, although the left side is the dominant one in most people. In a minority the right hemisphere holds the speech areas, and in others the two sides share the work. Handedness gives only a rough guide.

Question 4876. Which of these pairs belongs together: the occipital lobe with hearing, the temporal lobe with vision, the frontal lobe with the planning of movement, or the parietal lobe with smell? The answer is the frontal lobe with the planning of movement. The occipital lobe serves vision, the temporal lobe serves hearing, and the parietal lobe receives touch and position sense.

Question 4877. Which of these pairs belongs together: the precentral gyrus with touch, the postcentral gyrus with touch, the superior temporal gyrus with vision, or the cortex around the calcarine sulcus with hearing? The answer is the postcentral gyrus with touch. The precentral gyrus holds the motor cortex, the superior temporal gyrus serves hearing, and the calcarine cortex serves vision.

Question 4878. Fibers that link the same region of the two hemispheres, such as the two visual areas, are called which of these: projection fibers, association fibers, commissural fibers, or capsular fibers? The answer is commissural fibers, and the corpus callosum is built of them. Association fibers link one region of a hemisphere with another region on the same side.

Question 4879. A described preparation of a hemisphere with the cortex stripped away shows a broad fan of fibers rising from a narrow band between two deep gray masses and spreading out toward the surface. Which structures are described? The answer is the corona radiata above and the internal capsule below. The fibers run in both directions between the cortex and the lower centers.

Question 4880. A constructed illustration: a person whose behavior has changed, who jokes inappropriately and neglects one side of the body, is found to have a tumor at the front of one hemisphere. Which lobe is involved, and which part of it is disturbed? The answer is the frontal lobe, and the prefrontal cortex is disturbed.

Question 4881. A constructed illustration: a person can see the parts of an object and describe them, yet cannot recognize what the object is, and the damage lies in the occipital lobe. Which cortex is injured, and why is sight itself unaffected? The answer is the visual association cortex around the primary visual area. The picture still arrives, but its meaning cannot be attached to it.

Question 4882. A described lateral view of a hemisphere shows a long cleft running backward from the front, a groove descending toward it from above and behind, and a short groove at the back. Which three grooves are described? The answer is the lateral sulcus, the central sulcus and the parietooccipital sulcus. The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe below from the rest.

Question 4883. Which gyrus lies in the parietal lobe at the end of the superior temporal sulcus, where the pathways for reading and for language meet: the cingulate gyrus, the angular gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus, or the precentral gyrus? The answer is the angular gyrus. Damage on the dominant side can disturb reading.

Question 4884. Which part of the frontal lobe lies in front of the motor and premotor areas and is concerned with planning, judgment and the control of impulses? The answer is the prefrontal cortex. It has no direct part in moving a muscle. Its wide connections with the rest of the brain let it weigh an action before it is taken.

Question 4885. Which area lies just in front of the precentral gyrus and prepares a sequence of movements before the primary motor cortex carries it out: the premotor area, the postcentral gyrus, the angular gyrus, or the calcarine cortex? The answer is the premotor area. It occupies the back of the frontal lobe beside the motor strip. It plans patterns of movement rather than single muscles.

Question 4886. Which small arteries, branches of the middle cerebral artery, pass through the base of the brain to supply the internal capsule and the basal ganglia, and why is their blockage so disabling? The answer is the lenticulostriate arteries. They are fine vessels with little overlap between their territories, so a block in one can cut the motor fibers in the internal capsule.

Question 4887. Which thin partition of nervous tissue separates the two anterior horns of the lateral ventricles in the midline? The answer is the septum pellucidum. It stretches between the corpus callosum above and the fornix below. It forms the medial wall of each lateral ventricle.

Question 4888. Which fringe of vascular tissue lies in the floor of each lateral ventricle and secretes cerebrospinal fluid into it: the falx cerebri, the choroid plexus, the tentorium cerebelli, or the septum pellucidum? The answer is the choroid plexus. It is built of ependymal cells over a core of blood vessels. It continues into the third and the fourth ventricles, where it adds more fluid.

Question 4889. Which statement about the cerebral cortex is correct: it lies deep to the white matter, it is a thin sheet of gray matter on the surface, it contains no nerve cell bodies, or it is present only in the occipital lobe? The answer is that it is a thin sheet of gray matter on the surface. The white matter lies beneath it.

Question 4890. A described photograph of the surface of the brain shows winding ridges separated by narrow grooves that branch over the whole surface. What are the ridges and the grooves called, and why does the surface take this form? The answer is gyri for the ridges and sulci for the grooves. The folding greatly increases the area of the cortex within the skull.

Question 4891. Which lobe of the cerebrum lies immediately above the roof of the orbit and carries the olfactory bulb and tract on its under surface? The answer is the frontal lobe. The olfactory tract runs along the orbital surface below it. Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex without first passing through the thalamus.

Question 4892. True or false: the corpus callosum is the only bridge of fibers joining the two cerebral hemispheres. The answer is false. The anterior commissure and the commissure of the hippocampus also cross the midline, though they are far smaller. The corpus callosum is much the largest of the three.

Question 4893. Which of these pairs belongs together: the motor speech area with the occipital lobe, the sensory speech area with the frontal lobe, the visual cortex with the occipital lobe, or the auditory cortex with the parietal lobe? The answer is the visual cortex with the occipital lobe. The auditory cortex lies in the temporal lobe.

Question 4894. A constructed illustration: after a deep midline operation, a person can pick up an object in the left hand but cannot name it, while an object in the right hand is named at once. Which structure was divided, and why does the difficulty appear on the left? The answer is the corpus callosum. The left hand is served by the right hemisphere, which has lost its link to the speech areas.

Question 4895. A described view of the medial surface of a hemisphere shows a curved band of fibers above a C-shaped gyrus, and a deep sulcus running backward at the lower edge. Which structures are described? The answer is the corpus callosum with the cingulate gyrus above it, and the calcarine sulcus behind. The cingulate gyrus arches over the callosum within the limbic lobe.

Question 4896. In the body of a lateral ventricle, which structure forms the floor and which forms the roof? The answer is that the thalamus and the fornix form the floor, and the corpus callosum forms the roof. The caudate nucleus lies in the lateral wall of the ventricle. The choroid plexus hangs along the floor beside the fornix.

Question 4897. A described view of the medial surface shows a C-shaped gyrus arching immediately above the corpus callosum and continuing backward toward the temporal lobe. Which gyrus is described, and to which lobe is it assigned? The answer is the cingulate gyrus, which belongs to the limbic lobe. Behind it continues as the parahippocampal gyrus.

Question 4898. Three of these structures lie in the temporal lobe: the hippocampus, the primary auditory cortex, and the superior temporal gyrus. Which one does not? The answer is the angular gyrus, which lies in the parietal lobe. The hippocampus lies in the medial part of the temporal lobe. Damage to the angular gyrus on the dominant side disturbs reading.

Question 4899. Which fibers sweep forward into the temporal lobe before turning back to the occipital cortex, and what defect follows damage to them there? The answer is the optic radiation. Its lower fibers loop forward into the temporal lobe before turning backward. Damage to them removes the upper part of the opposite visual field.

Question 4900. A described section through a hemisphere shows the central sulcus running downward and forward, with a thick gyrus in front of it and another behind. Which lobe lies in front of that groove, and which two functions are represented in the two gyri beside it? The answer is the frontal lobe, with the motor cortex in front and the somatosensory cortex behind.

To summarize, the supporting cells each have one clear task: the astrocyte nourishes and scars, the oligodendrocyte myelinates several axons in the brain and cord, the Schwann cell myelinates a single axon outside them, the ependymal cell lines the cavities, and the microglial cell clears debris. A spinal nerve is formed by a ventral root of motor fibers and a dorsal root of sensory fibers, and the dorsal root carries the swelling that holds the sensory cell bodies. Ganglia hold either sensory cell bodies with no synapse, as in a dorsal root ganglion, or the synapse of an autonomic pathway, as in the sympathetic chain. The cerebrum is divided by the longitudinal fissure into two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum, and its surface is marked by the central sulcus between the frontal and parietal lobes, by the lateral sulcus above the temporal lobe, and by the calcarine sulcus behind. The motor and sensory maps lie in the precentral and postcentral gyri, the speech areas lie in the frontal and temporal lobes of the dominant hemisphere, and the deep masses are packed around the internal capsule. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 50 — Brain

This chapter gathers what a listener needs to hold about the surface of the cerebral hemispheres and about the small folded brain that sits beneath the tentorium. It moves through the gyri, the ridges of cortex that carry the named functions, then through the sulci that divide them, and finally through the cerebellum, its lobules, its peduncles and its deep nuclei. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried forward in memory. The landmarks named here are the ones a clinician points to when a scan, a stroke or a seizure has to be explained aloud, and they make the rest of the nervous system easier to learn. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 4901. Which gyrus of the frontal lobe lies immediately anterior to the central sulcus? The answer is the precentral gyrus. It carries the primary motor cortex, whose fibers descend to move the opposite side of the body. The body is represented along it upside down, with the foot highest and the face lowest.

Question 4902. Which of these gyri lies between the superior frontal sulcus and the inferior frontal sulcus: the superior frontal gyrus, the middle frontal gyrus, the inferior frontal gyrus, or the precentral gyrus? The answer is the middle frontal gyrus. The superior frontal gyrus lies above its own sulcus. The inferior frontal gyrus lies below the inferior frontal sulcus, and the precentral gyrus lies behind them all.

Question 4903. Which gyrus of the parietal lobe lies immediately behind the central sulcus, and what does it receive? The answer is the postcentral gyrus, which receives general sensation from the opposite side of the body. It carries the primary somatosensory cortex. Its map of the body mirrors the motor map in front of it, with the foot highest and the face lowest.

Question 4904. Which of these areas lies in the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, usually of the left hemisphere: the visual cortex, the motor speech area, the auditory cortex, or the sensory speech area? The answer is the motor speech area, named for Broca. Damage there leaves speech effortful and sparse while understanding stays relatively preserved. The sensory speech area lies further back in the temporal lobe.

Question 4905. A described view of the left hemisphere shows the lateral sulcus opened to reveal two or three small ridges across the upper surface of the temporal lobe. Which gyri are shown, and what do they serve? The answer is the transverse temporal gyri. They carry the primary auditory cortex and lie hidden inside the lateral sulcus on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus.

Question 4906. Which gyrus of the temporal lobe runs forward from the temporal pole just below the lateral sulcus? The answer is the superior temporal gyrus. Its posterior part holds the sensory speech area named for Wernicke. The middle and inferior temporal gyri lie below it, separated by the superior and inferior temporal sulci.

Question 4907. Which of these gyri arches directly over the corpus callosum: the fusiform gyrus, the parahippocampal gyrus, the cingulate gyrus, or the precentral gyrus? The answer is the cingulate gyrus. It sweeps from front to back above the corpus callosum as part of the limbic lobe. The parahippocampal gyrus lies far below it on the medial surface of the temporal lobe.

Question 4908. The uncus is the hooked medial tip of which gyrus, and where exactly does it lie? The answer is the parahippocampal gyrus, at its anterior and medial end. It lies in the temporal lobe just in front of the hippocampus. Because it sits close to the medial edge of the tentorium, it can be pressed upon when the brain swells.

Question 4909. Which gyrus of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe lies immediately medial to the olfactory sulcus? The answer is the straight gyrus, also called the gyrus rectus. It runs from front to back beside the midline. The olfactory tract lies in the sulcus just lateral to it, and the orbital gyri lie lateral to that.

Question 4910. A described view of the medial surface of the occipital lobe shows a long gyrus lying below a deep sulcus and above the collateral sulcus. Which gyrus is described? The answer is the lingual gyrus. It lies between the calcarine sulcus above and the collateral sulcus below. Its anterior end joins the parahippocampal gyrus.

Question 4911. Which gyrus lies between the collateral sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus on the inferior surface of the hemisphere? The answer is the fusiform gyrus, also called the lateral occipitotemporal gyrus. It lies lateral to the collateral sulcus. The lingual gyrus lies medial to that same sulcus.

Question 4912. Which of these named parts lies between the parieto-occipital sulcus and the calcarine sulcus: the cuneus, the lingual gyrus, the precuneus, or the uncus? The answer is the cuneus. It is a wedge of occipital cortex on the medial surface. The precuneus lies in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus and belongs to the parietal lobe.

Question 4913. A constructed illustration: a patient speaks in short effortful phrases and repeats a single word with great effort, while following simple spoken commands well. Which gyrus of which hemisphere is most likely injured? The answer is the posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere. That region holds the motor speech area. The preserved understanding points away from the sensory speech area behind it.

Question 4914. A constructed illustration: a patient cannot name the fingers of the hand, cannot do simple arithmetic, cannot write, and confuses right and left. Which gyrus of the dominant parietal lobe is involved? The answer is the angular gyrus. The four findings together are described as the syndrome named for Gerstmann. The angular gyrus lies in the inferior parietal lobule around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.

Question 4915. Which folded sheet of cortex lies hidden in the floor of the lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula? The answer is the insula. It is drawn out of sight by the overgrowth of the surrounding opercula during development. A small part of it can still be seen in the depth of the sulcus.

Question 4916. True or false: in the normal brain the cingulate gyrus lies above the corpus callosum and below the cingulate sulcus. The answer is true. It arches over the corpus callosum from the front to the back.
