The sulcus of the corpus callosum separates it from the commissure beneath, and the cingulate sulcus separates it from the medial frontal gyrus above.

Question 4917. Which of these gyri forms the medial wall of the temporal lobe and joins the uncus at its front: the fusiform gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus, the parahippocampal gyrus, or the middle temporal gyrus? The answer is the parahippocampal gyrus. It lies medial to the collateral sulcus and above the hippocampal sulcus. The uncus is its anterior hooked end.

Question 4918. A described view of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe shows an H-shaped groove dividing the cortex into four named strips. Which gyri are those strips? The answer is the orbital gyri. They are named medial, anterior, posterior and lateral. The straight gyrus lies medial to the olfactory sulcus, separate from all four.

Question 4919. Which gyrus curls around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus, and which gyrus curls around the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus beneath it? The answer is the supramarginal gyrus above and the angular gyrus below. Both belong to the inferior parietal lobule. The angular gyrus is the more posterior and inferior of the two.

Question 4920. Which lobule of the medial surface surrounds the medial end of the central sulcus, and which two body regions does it serve? The answer is the paracentral lobule, serving the foot and the leg. It carries the parts of the motor and sensory maps that lie over the top of the hemisphere. It also holds the cortical region concerned with control of the bladder.

Question 4921. Which slender band of cortex lies between the fimbria and the parahippocampal gyrus, its margin cut into small notches? The answer is the dentate gyrus. It belongs to the hippocampal formation. The notches give it the tooth-like appearance that its name describes, and it curls into the hippocampus behind the uncus.

Question 4922. Name two gyri that lie on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, spoken as a list. The answer is the cuneus and the lingual gyrus. The cuneus lies above the calcarine sulcus and the lingual gyrus below it. Both belong to the occipital lobe, and the calcarine sulcus separates them.

Question 4923. Which of these gyri lies in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus on the medial surface: the cuneus, the precuneus, the lingual gyrus, or the fusiform gyrus? The answer is the precuneus. It belongs to the parietal lobe, not the occipital lobe. The cuneus and the lingual gyrus both lie behind that sulcus.

Question 4924. A described view of the insula shows a small central groove dividing it into a larger front part with several short ridges and a smaller back part with one long ridge. Which sulcus and which gyri are described? The answer is the central sulcus of the insula, with the short gyri in front and the long gyrus behind. The island is ringed by the circular sulcus.

Question 4925. A constructed illustration: a patient speaks fluently and at length, but the words are jumbled and meaningless, and the patient does not seem to notice. Which region of which gyrus is most likely injured? The answer is the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the left hemisphere. That region holds the sensory speech area. Fluent but empty speech with poor understanding is its signature.

Question 4926. Which gyrus forms the upper border of the lateral surface of the frontal lobe, running forward above the superior frontal sulcus? The answer is the superior frontal gyrus. Its medial part continues onto the medial surface as the medial frontal gyrus. Its posterior portion on the medial side holds the supplementary motor area.

Question 4927. Which of these pairs is correctly matched: the straight gyrus lateral to the olfactory sulcus, the straight gyrus medial to the olfactory sulcus, the straight gyrus on the lateral surface, or the straight gyrus in the occipital lobe? The answer is the straight gyrus lying medial to the olfactory sulcus. It lies on the orbital surface beside the midline. The olfactory tract runs in that sulcus.

Question 4928. In the medial wall of the hemisphere, which structure lies immediately below the cingulate gyrus, and which lies immediately above it? The answer is the corpus callosum below, with the medial frontal gyrus above. The sulcus of the corpus callosum and the cingulate sulcus mark those two boundaries. The cingulate gyrus therefore sits in a groove of its own.

Question 4929. Which gyrus occupies the lower margin of the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus? The answer is the inferior temporal gyrus. It runs forward to the temporal pole. Behind it the cortex continues into the lateral occipital region, where the boundary between the lobes is only arbitrary.

Question 4930. A described view of the inferior parietal region shows two curved gyri stacked around the ends of two sulci. Which lobule and which two gyri are shown? The answer is the inferior parietal lobule, made of the supramarginal gyrus and the angular gyrus. The supramarginal gyrus arches around the end of the lateral sulcus. The angular gyrus arches around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.

Question 4931. Which of these gyri forms the anterior and medial hook of the temporal lobe that lies beside the amygdala: the fusiform gyrus, the uncus, the cingulate gyrus, or the dentate gyrus? The answer is the uncus. It is the medial, hooked end of the parahippocampal gyrus. The amygdala lies just above and behind it in the temporal lobe.

Question 4932. Which of these pairs belongs together: the precentral gyrus with the primary visual cortex, the postcentral gyrus with the primary motor cortex, the calcarine cortex with the primary auditory cortex, or the transverse temporal gyri with the primary auditory cortex? The answer is the transverse temporal gyri with the primary auditory cortex. The precentral gyrus carries motor cortex and the postcentral gyrus carries somatosensory cortex.

Question 4933. Which gyrus lies between the superior temporal sulcus and the inferior temporal sulcus on the lateral surface? The answer is the middle temporal gyrus. It lies below the superior temporal gyrus. The inferior temporal gyrus lies below it in turn, and the three are stacked like bands along the side of the temporal lobe.

Question 4934. Which band of white matter lies along the ventricular surface of the hippocampus, and into which structure does the dentate gyrus roll behind it? The answer is the alveus, with the dentate gyrus rolling into the hippocampus. The alveus gathers the fibers that leave the hippocampus. They continue as the fimbria and then as the fornix.

Question 4935. A constructed illustration: a patient cannot move the right face or the right arm and has lost speech, while the right leg is barely affected. Which part of the cortex is deprived of blood? The answer is the lower part of the left precentral gyrus. The face and the hand occupy its lowest part, above the lateral sulcus. The leg area lies highest and is spared.

Question 4936. A described view of the lateral surface shows a deep groove running downward and forward toward the lateral sulcus, with a broad gyrus on each side. Which sulcus is described? The answer is the central sulcus. It separates the frontal lobe in front from the parietal lobe behind. It usually stops just short of the lateral sulcus.

Question 4937. Which of these sulci separates the superior parietal lobule from the inferior parietal lobule: the postcentral sulcus, the intraparietal sulcus, the superior temporal sulcus, or the cingulate sulcus? The answer is the intraparietal sulcus. It runs backward through the parietal lobe. The postcentral sulcus lies in front of it and bounds the postcentral gyrus.

Question 4938. Along the medial surface of the occipital lobe, which gyrus lies immediately above the calcarine sulcus, and which lies immediately below it? The answer is the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below. The calcarine sulcus separates them. Both banks of that sulcus carry the primary visual cortex, which is why a lesion there removes the opposite half of the visual field.

Question 4939. Which groove runs across the lateral surface of the hemisphere, separating the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above? The answer is the lateral sulcus, also called the lateral fissure. Its floor is formed by the insula. The middle cerebral artery runs within it.

Question 4940. Which of these structures lies in the floor of the lateral sulcus: the corpus callosum, the insula, the cingulate gyrus, or the dentate gyrus? The answer is the insula. The opercula of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes grow over it and hide it. The middle cerebral artery and its branches course along the surface of the insula.

Question 4941. True or false: the central sulcus separates the precentral gyrus from the postcentral gyrus and marks the boundary between the frontal and parietal lobes. The answer is true. The precentral gyrus lies in front of it and the postcentral gyrus behind it. That single groove therefore separates the motor cortex from the somatosensory cortex.

Question 4942. A described medial view shows a groove that begins below the corpus callosum at the front, arches above it, and ends by turning upward toward the top of the hemisphere. Which sulcus is described? The answer is the cingulate sulcus, whose upturned end is the marginal sulcus. It separates the cingulate gyrus from the medial frontal gyrus. The precuneus lies behind that end.

Question 4943. Which of these sulci marks the boundary between the parietal lobe and the occipital lobe on the medial surface: the collateral sulcus, the parieto-occipital sulcus, the calcarine sulcus, or the olfactory sulcus? The answer is the parieto-occipital sulcus. It runs downward and forward on the medial surface. It separates the precuneus in front from the cuneus behind.

Question 4944. Which sulcus lies on the medial surface of the occipital lobe and separates the cuneus from the lingual gyrus? The answer is the calcarine sulcus. The primary visual cortex lines both of its banks. A lesion that destroys the cortex around it removes vision from the opposite half of the visual field.

Question 4945. A constructed illustration: a patient can write normally but cannot read a word, and the eyes cannot carry what is seen in the right half of the visual field to the reading cortex. Which two structures are injured together? The answer is the left occipital cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum. The combination spares writing while cutting off the reading input. The pattern is called alexia without agraphia.

Question 4946. Which of these grooves separates the cingulate gyrus from the medial frontal gyrus above it: the sulcus of the corpus callosum, the cingulate sulcus, the marginal sulcus, or the collateral sulcus? The answer is the cingulate sulcus. The sulcus of the corpus callosum lies below the cingulate gyrus instead. The marginal sulcus is the ascending end of the cingulate sulcus.

Question 4947. Which landmark on the inferior margin of the hemisphere, taken with a line drawn to the parieto-occipital sulcus, marks the front edge of the occipital lobe? The answer is the preoccipital notch. The line completes the boundary that the sulcus begins. Everything behind that line belongs to the occipital lobe.

Question 4948. A described medial view shows a thin curved groove hugging the upper surface of the great commissure and following it from the rostrum to the splenium. Which sulcus is described, and what does it separate? The answer is the sulcus of the corpus callosum. It separates the corpus callosum below from the cingulate gyrus above. It follows the curve of the commissure for its whole length.

Question 4949. Name two sulci that lie on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, spoken as a list. The answer is the cingulate sulcus and the calcarine sulcus. The cingulate sulcus arches above the corpus callosum, and the calcarine sulcus lies in the occipital lobe. The parieto-occipital sulcus lies on the same surface and is a third.

Question 4950. Which of these sulci lies between the superior temporal gyrus and the middle temporal gyrus: the inferior temporal sulcus, the superior temporal sulcus, the lateral sulcus, or the collateral sulcus? The answer is the superior temporal sulcus. The lateral sulcus lies above the superior temporal gyrus. The inferior temporal sulcus lies one gyrus further down.

Question 4951. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral sulcus with the boundary between the hemispheres, the central sulcus with the boundary between the frontal and parietal lobes, the calcarine sulcus with the boundary between the temporal and parietal lobes, or the parieto-occipital sulcus with the boundary between the temporal gyri? The answer is the central sulcus, which separates the frontal and parietal lobes.

Question 4952. Which sulcus separates the superior temporal gyrus from the middle temporal gyrus? The answer is the superior temporal sulcus. It runs backward along the lateral surface of the temporal lobe. Its posterior end is surrounded by the angular gyrus in the parietal lobe.

Question 4953. Which of these sulci lies between the parahippocampal gyrus and the fusiform gyrus on the inferior surface: the collateral sulcus, the hippocampal sulcus, the olfactory sulcus, or the circular sulcus? The answer is the collateral sulcus. It runs from front to back along the inferior surface. The fusiform gyrus lies lateral to it and the lingual gyrus medial to it.

Question 4954. A described dissection of the temporal lobe shows a groove on its medial surface separating the hippocampus and dentate gyrus from the parahippocampal gyrus beside them. Which sulcus is shown? The answer is the hippocampal sulcus. It lies behind the uncus and follows the curve of the hippocampus. The fimbria lies on the other side of the hippocampus.

Question 4955. A constructed illustration: a patient reports brief episodes of an unpleasant smell that no one else can detect, followed by a few seconds of lip smacking and a dreamy stare. Which medial temporal structure is most likely the origin? The answer is the uncus of the parahippocampal gyrus. Such episodes are described as uncinate fits. The uncus lies in the temporal lobe beside the amygdala.

Question 4956. Which of these sulci contains the olfactory tract and lies lateral to the straight gyrus on the orbital surface: the orbital sulcus, the olfactory sulcus, the cingulate sulcus, or the collateral sulcus? The answer is the olfactory sulcus. It runs from front to back on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe. The straight gyrus lies medial to it.

Question 4957. The precuneus lies immediately in front of which sulcus, and which gyrus lies immediately behind that same sulcus? The answer is the precuneus in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus, with the cuneus behind it. Both lie on the medial surface. The marginal sulcus bounds the precuneus at its front.

Question 4958. Which sulcus of the frontal lobe runs downward and forward just in front of the precentral gyrus? The answer is the precentral sulcus. It forms the anterior boundary of the precentral gyrus. The superior and inferior frontal sulci lie further forward on the lateral surface.

Question 4959. Which of these structures occupies the longitudinal fissure between the two hemispheres: the falx cerebri, the tentorium cerebelli, the corpus callosum, or the insula? The answer is the falx cerebri. It is a fold of dura that descends between the hemispheres. The corpus callosum lies in the depth of the fissure and joins the two halves.

Question 4960. True or false: the lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the frontal lobe and the parietal lobe. The answer is true. The temporal lobe lies below the sulcus, and the frontal and parietal lobes lie above it. The insula forms the floor of the groove between them.

Question 4961. A described view of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe shows a groove shaped like the letter H, with four strips of cortex around it. Which sulcus is shown? The answer is the orbital sulcus. Its crossbar and two limbs divide the orbital gyri into medial, anterior, posterior and lateral parts. The olfactory sulcus lies medial to the whole pattern.

Question 4962. Which sulcus forms the posterior boundary of the postcentral gyrus? The answer is the postcentral sulcus. It lies behind the postcentral gyrus on the lateral surface of the parietal lobe. Beyond it lies the superior parietal lobule, divided further back by the intraparietal sulcus.

Question 4963. Which of these sulci rings the insula and separates it from the opercula: the central sulcus of the insula, the circular sulcus, the hippocampal sulcus, or the calcarine sulcus? The answer is the circular sulcus. The central sulcus of the insula divides the island into a front and a back part. The opercula of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes cover the ring.

Question 4964. A constructed illustration: a blockage of one artery removes the cortex of the lateral surface of the left hemisphere, and the patient loses speech and the use of the right face and arm. Which artery is blocked, and in which groove does it run? The answer is the middle cerebral artery, running in the lateral sulcus. Its branches supply the insula and the opercular cortex.

Question 4965. Which notch on the inferior margin of the hemisphere helps to define the anterior limit of the occipital lobe? The answer is the preoccipital notch. A line drawn from it to the parieto-occipital sulcus completes the boundary. The notch itself lies on the inferior margin of the temporal and occipital junction.

Question 4966. A described view of the medial occipital surface shows a deep sulcus with a thin stripe of cortex along both banks, thicker than the surrounding cortex. Which sulcus is shown, and what does the stripe contain? The answer is the calcarine sulcus, whose banks contain the primary visual cortex. The stripe is the striate cortex. Damage on one side removes the opposite half of the visual field.

Question 4967. Which two structures lie immediately on either side of the sulcus of the corpus callosum? The answer is the corpus callosum below and the cingulate gyrus above. The sulcus follows the curve of the commissure from front to back. The indusium griseum lies on the upper surface of the corpus callosum itself.

Question 4968. Which narrow midline part of the cerebellum joins its two hemispheres and carries the lobules named lingula, culmen and uvula? The answer is the vermis. It lies in the midline between the hemispheres. Each of its lobules corresponds to a named lobule in the hemisphere beside it.

Question 4969. Which of these fissures separates the small anterior lobe of the cerebellum from the large posterior lobe: the horizontal fissure, the primary fissure, the posterolateral fissure, or the calcarine sulcus? The answer is the primary fissure. It runs across the superior surface of the cerebellum. The posterolateral fissure separates the flocculonodular lobe instead.

Question 4970. Name the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles and the part of the brainstem each one joins, spoken as a list. The answer is the inferior peduncles joining the medulla, the middle peduncles joining the pons, and the superior peduncles joining the midbrain. The middle pair is much the largest. The superior pair carries most of the output of the deep nuclei.

Question 4971. A described view of the superior surface of the cerebellum shows a narrow midline strip and, on each side, a large four-sided lobule just behind the primary fissure. Which lobules are shown? The answer is the culmen in the midline with the quadrangular lobule beside it. The quadrangular lobule is the hemispheric part corresponding to the culmen. The declive and the simple lobule lie behind.

Question 4972. Which of these lobes of the cerebellum consists of the nodulus and the two flocculi: the anterior lobe, the posterior lobe, the flocculonodular lobe, or the vermis? The answer is the flocculonodular lobe. It is separated from the rest of the cerebellum by the posterolateral fissure. It is concerned with balance and with the movements of the eyes.

Question 4973. Which rounded lobule of the cerebellum lies on the inferior surface of each hemisphere, close to the foramen magnum? The answer is the tonsil. It lies medial and inferior, beside the brainstem. When the brain swells, the tonsils can be pushed down through the foramen magnum.

Question 4974. True or false: a lesion of one cerebellar hemisphere produces weakness and loss of coordination on the same side of the body. The answer is true. The output of the cerebellum crosses in the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses again in the corticospinal tract. Two crossings leave the signs on the same side as the lesion.

Question 4975. Which of these deep cerebellar nuclei is the largest and lies farthest to the side in each hemisphere: the fastigial nucleus, the globose nucleus, the emboliform nucleus, or the dentate nucleus? The answer is the dentate nucleus. Its folded, tooth-like band of gray matter lies near the roof of the fourth ventricle. The fastigial nucleus lies most medially, in the vermis.

Question 4976. A described section across the cerebellum shows four masses of gray matter on each side, embedded in the white matter a short distance from the midline. Which nuclei are shown? The answer is the fastigial, globose, emboliform and dentate nuclei. The fastigial lies nearest the midline. The globose and emboliform are often grouped together, and the dentate lies farthest out.

Question 4977. Which structure lies immediately above the cerebellar tonsils, and through which opening do the tonsils descend when the pressure inside the skull rises? The answer is the foramen magnum, with the medulla oblongata lying immediately in front of the tonsils. The tonsils are the parts that herniate. They press on the medulla, which can stop breathing.

Question 4978. Which small tufted lobule of the cerebellum hangs from the inferior surface of each middle cerebellar peduncle? The answer is the flocculus. It belongs to the flocculonodular lobe along with the nodulus. It receives input from the vestibular apparatus of the inner ear.

Question 4979. Which of these cerebellar peduncles is the largest and connects the cerebellum to the pons: the inferior peduncle, the middle peduncle, the superior peduncle, or the peduncle of the flocculus? The answer is the middle cerebellar peduncle. It carries the fibers that reach the cerebellum from the cerebral cortex by way of the pons. The inferior peduncle joins the medulla and the superior joins the midbrain.

Question 4980. A constructed illustration: a patient with raised pressure inside the skull becomes drowsy and then stops breathing, and the cerebellar tonsils lie below the foramen magnum. Which structure is compressed, and why is that dangerous? The answer is the medulla oblongata, which lies immediately in front of the tonsils. The medulla holds the centers that drive breathing and control the heart. Its management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4981. A described side view of the cerebellum shows a long fissure running around its margin, separating a superior group of lobules from an inferior group. Which fissure is shown? The answer is the horizontal fissure. It runs along the margin between the superior and inferior surfaces of the posterior lobe. The folium and the superior semilunar lobule lie above it.

Question 4982. Which hemispheric lobule of the cerebellum corresponds to the uvula of the vermis: the tonsil, the biventral lobule, the superior semilunar lobule, or the flocculus? The answer is the tonsil. The biventral lobule corresponds to the pyramis. The flocculus corresponds to the nodulus, and the simple lobule corresponds to the declive.

Question 4983. Which of these pairs belongs together: the nodulus with the flocculus, the culmen with the tonsil, the uvula with the quadrangular lobule, or the declive with the biventral lobule? The answer is the nodulus with the flocculus. The culmen corresponds to the quadrangular lobule, the uvula to the tonsil, and the declive to the simple lobule.

Question 4984. Which lobule of the vermis lies between the uvula above it and the nodulus below it, forming the lowest part of the vermis? The answer is the nodulus. It lies at the bottom of the vermis and joins the two flocculi by the peduncle of the flocculus. Together the nodulus and the flocculi form the flocculonodular lobe.

Question 4985. Which of these deep cerebellar nuclei lies in the midline of the vermis, nearest the roof of the fourth ventricle: the dentate nucleus, the fastigial nucleus, the emboliform nucleus, or the globose nucleus? The answer is the fastigial nucleus. It lies in the vermis, one on each side of the midline. The dentate nucleus lies farthest to the side.

Question 4986. A described section through the cerebellar cortex shows three layers, the outermost sparsely populated, the middle a single row of large flask-shaped cells, and the innermost densely packed. Which layers are shown, and which cells form the middle row? The answer is the molecular layer, the Purkinje cell layer and the granular layer. The Purkinje cells form that row. They are the only cells whose fibers leave the cortex.

Question 4987. Through which part of the brainstem does the superior cerebellar peduncle enter, and where does most of its output end? The answer is the midbrain, ending in the thalamus of the opposite side after crossing. The crossing lies in the midbrain. The thalamus then relays the signal to the motor cortex.

Question 4988. Which lobule of the cerebellar hemisphere lies between the inferior semilunar lobule and the tonsil on the inferior surface? The answer is the biventral lobule, also called the gracile lobule. It corresponds to the pyramis of the vermis. The tonsil lies medial to it and the inferior semilunar lobule above it.

Question 4989. Which of these signs belongs to a lesion of one cerebellar hemisphere: weakness of the opposite arm, loss of coordination of the same arm, loss of pain sensation on the same side, or loss of vision? The answer is loss of coordination of the same arm. Cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion. Weakness and sensory loss from the cortex appear on the opposite side.

Question 4990. True or false: the flocculonodular lobe is concerned with balance and with the control of eye movements. The answer is true. It receives fibers from the vestibular apparatus of the inner ear. Its damage produces unsteadiness and nystagmus. It is the oldest part of the cerebellum in evolutionary terms.

Question 4991. The flocculus of each hemisphere is joined to which midline lobule, and by which band of fibers? The answer is the nodulus, joined by the peduncle of the flocculus. The two flocculi and the nodulus together form the flocculonodular lobe. That lobe sits behind the posterolateral fissure.

Question 4992. Which of these tumors arises at the cerebellopontine angle and damages the nerve of hearing: a tumor of the dentate nucleus, a tumor of the vestibular nerve, a tumor of the optic nerve, or a tumor of the olfactory tract? The answer is a tumor of the vestibular nerve, described as a vestibular schwannoma. It grows where the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves leave the brainstem. Hearing loss in one ear is usually the first sign.

Question 4993. Which of these pairs belongs together: the dentate nucleus with the vermis, the fastigial nucleus with the lateral hemisphere, the dentate nucleus with the lateral hemisphere, or the emboliform nucleus with the flocculus? The answer is the dentate nucleus with the lateral hemisphere. The fastigial nucleus lies in the vermis. The dentate nucleus sits far out among the fibers of the hemisphere.

Question 4994. A constructed illustration: a person has had headache and neck pain for years, and imaging shows the cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum as two pointed pegs. Which developmental arrangement is described? The answer is a Chiari malformation. The tonsils are displaced downward through the opening because the back of the skull is small. Headache made worse by coughing is common, and the decision about treatment belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 4995. A constructed illustration: a patient suddenly has vertigo, unsteady walking and a severe headache, with clumsiness of the left arm and nystagmus but preserved strength. Which part of the brain and which artery are involved? The answer is the left cerebellar hemisphere, supplied by the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery. The cerebellar signs lie on the same side as the lesion. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 4996. Which of these pairs belongs together: the flocculonodular lobe with skilled limb movement, the vermis with balance of the trunk, the lateral hemisphere with eye movements, or the anterior lobe with speech? The answer is the vermis with balance of the trunk. The flocculonodular lobe serves balance and eye movements. The lateral hemispheres serve the coordination of skilled movement of the limbs.

Question 4997. A section is cut in the midline through the whole brain from front to back. Which part of the cerebellum will appear in that section, and what will lie in front of it? The answer is the vermis, with the midbrain, the pons and the medulla in front of it. A midline section passes through no cerebellar hemisphere. The fourth ventricle lies between the brainstem and the cerebellum.

Question 4998. Which of these structures forms the branching white core of each cerebellar hemisphere, visible on a cut surface: the arbor vitae, the corpus callosum, the alveus, or the fimbria? The answer is the arbor vitae. Its branches carry fibers into the many thin leaves of the cerebellar cortex. The gray cortex lies on the surface of every leaf.

Question 4999. Which large cell of the cerebellar cortex is the only source of its outgoing fibers, and what kind of signal does it send? The answer is the Purkinje cell. Its fiber leaves the cortex and ends in the deep cerebellar nuclei. Its signal is inhibitory, so it quiets the cells beneath it rather than exciting them.

Question 5000. A section is cut across the cerebellum in the coronal plane. Which structures will be seen, and how are they arranged? The answer is the vermis in the middle, a hemisphere on each side, and the deep nuclei in the white matter. The dentate nucleus will appear farthest from the midline. The fourth ventricle lies above, between the cerebellum and the brainstem.

To summarize, the lateral surface of the hemisphere is organized by three grooves a listener can place at once: the central sulcus, which separates the precentral motor gyrus from the postcentral sensory gyrus, the lateral sulcus, whose floor holds the insula, and the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, whose banks carry the primary visual cortex. The named gyri follow those grooves: the superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri, with the motor speech area in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere, the superior temporal gyrus holding the auditory cortex and the sensory speech area, the cingulate gyrus arching over the corpus callosum, the parahippocampal gyrus ending in the uncus, and the orbital and medial surfaces carrying the straight gyrus, the orbital gyri and the precuneus. The cerebellum answers to the same method: the vermis in the midline and a hemisphere on each side, the primary fissure dividing anterior from posterior lobe, the posterolateral fissure cutting off the flocculonodular lobe of balance, the horizontal fissure, and the tonsil, biventral lobule, flocculus and central lobule each paired with a named lobule of the vermis. The deep nuclei, the fastigial, globose, emboliform and dentate, sit in the white matter of the arbor vitae, the Purkinje cell is the only output of the cortex, and the middle peduncle is the largest of the three. Because the cerebellar pathway crosses twice, its signs fall on the same side as the lesion, and because the tonsils lie beside the foramen magnum, their herniation compresses the medulla. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 51 — Brain, Part Two

This chapter continues the survey of the brain by looking at its deepest parts: the brainstem, the basal nuclei, the thalamus and the hypothalamus. It passes from the stalk of the brain, with its medulla, pons and midbrain, to the masses of gray matter that shape movement, and then to the thalamus and the small control center beneath it. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The structures named here are the ones a clinician follows when a stroke, a tremor or a disorder of hormone control has to be explained aloud. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 5001. Which paired ridge on the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata carries the fibers that run from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord? The answer is the pyramid. The corticospinal fibers gather into a compact bundle that raises the surface into a ridge. Most of them cross to the opposite side at the lower end of the medulla.

Question 5002. Which of these is the uppermost part of the brainstem: the medulla oblongata, the pons, the midbrain, or the spinal cord? The answer is the midbrain. The brainstem runs upward from the spinal cord as medulla, pons and midbrain in that order. The midbrain therefore lies closest to the thalamus.

Question 5003. What is the name of the broad rounded prominence of the brainstem that lies between the medulla oblongata below and the midbrain above? The answer is the pons. Its name means bridge, because a great band of its fibers crosses to the cerebellum behind it. The basilar artery lies in a groove along its front surface.

Question 5004. Which cranial nerve nucleus lies in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus and supplies the muscle that narrows the pupil: the third, the fourth, the sixth, or the twelfth cranial nerve? The answer is the third cranial nerve. It also supplies most of the other muscles that move the eye and the muscle that raises the upper eyelid. The fourth and sixth nerves supply one muscle each.

Question 5005. A described transverse section of the brainstem shows two thick columns in front, a dark band behind them, a rounded red nucleus on each side, and a narrow channel in the middle. Which part of the brainstem is shown? The answer is the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus. The columns are the cerebral peduncles and the dark band is the substantia nigra.

Question 5006. Which structures lie immediately behind the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain? The answer is the superior and the inferior colliculi. Together they form the tectum, the roof of the midbrain. The superior colliculus lies above the inferior one on each side of the midline.

Question 5007. A constructed illustration: a small blockage of an artery leaves a person weak on the opposite side, with a weak tongue on the side of the lesion and loss of position sense on the other side. Which structure in the medulla is involved? The answer is the pyramid. In the medial medullary syndrome the corticospinal fibers, the twelfth cranial nerve and the medial lemniscus are affected together.

Question 5008. Where do most fibers of the corticospinal tract cross to the opposite side: in the midbrain, in the pons, in the upper medulla, or in the lower medulla? The answer is the lower medulla. The crossing is visible on the surface as the decussation of the pyramids. A small number of fibers stay uncrossed and descend in the anterior corticospinal tract.

Question 5009. True or false: the brainstem is made up of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata. The answer is true. Those three parts join the spinal cord below to the diencephalon above. The cerebellum lies behind the brainstem and is not counted as part of it.

Question 5010. A described section through the back of the head shows a diamond-shaped cavity whose floor is formed by the pons and the medulla and whose roof is formed by the cerebellum. Which cavity is shown? The answer is the fourth ventricle. It is continuous below with the central canal of the spinal cord and above with the cerebral aqueduct. Cerebrospinal fluid fills it.

Question 5011. What is the name of the two thick columns on the front of the midbrain, one on each side of the midline? The answer is the cerebral peduncles. They carry the descending fibers from the cerebral cortex to the brainstem and the spinal cord. The interpeduncular fossa lies in the midline between them.

Question 5012. Which cranial nerve nucleus lies in the pons and supplies the muscles that produce the movements of the face: the third, the fifth, the seventh, or the twelfth cranial nerve? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve. Its fibers loop around the nucleus of the sixth cranial nerve before they leave the brainstem. The fifth cranial nerve supplies the muscles of chewing instead.

Question 5013. Which of these pairs belongs together: the superior colliculus with hearing, the inferior colliculus with sight, the superior colliculus with visual reflexes, or the inferior colliculus with smell? The answer is the superior colliculus with visual reflexes. It receives fibers from the retina and turns the head and the eyes toward a moving object. The inferior colliculus belongs to the pathway for hearing.

Question 5014. Which vessel runs in the midline along the anterior surface of the pons? The answer is the basilar artery. It is formed where the two vertebral arteries join at the lower border of the pons. It lies in a groove on the surface of the pons and gives off branches to the brainstem and the cerebellum.

Question 5015. What is the name of the oval swelling on the lateral side of the upper medulla, just behind the pyramid? The answer is the olive. It is produced by the inferior olivary nucleus, a folded mass of gray matter beneath the surface that sends a large bundle of fibers to the cerebellum.

Question 5016. Which tract in the lateral part of the medulla carries pain and temperature sense from the opposite side of the body: the posterior column, the spinothalamic tract, the corticospinal tract, or the medial lemniscus? The answer is the spinothalamic tract. Its fibers have already crossed in the spinal cord, so those in the medulla come from the opposite side. The posterior column carries fine touch and position sense instead.

Question 5017. A constructed illustration: a blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery leaves a person dizzy, hoarse and unable to swallow, with loss of pain and temperature sense on the face and on the opposite side of the body. Which part of the brainstem is involved? The answer is the lateral part of the medulla, where the vestibular nuclei, the nucleus ambiguus and the spinothalamic tract lie close together.

Question 5018. A described transverse section of the brainstem shows four rounded bumps on the back, two above and two below, with a narrow channel in front of them. At which level was the cut made? The answer is the midbrain, at the level of the colliculi. The four bumps are the superior and inferior colliculi on each side. The channel in front of them is the cerebral aqueduct.

Question 5019. Name two cranial nerves whose fibers leave the brainstem at the junction of the pons and the medulla, spoken as a list. The answer is the sixth cranial nerve and the seventh cranial nerve. The sixth lies nearer the midline and turns the eye outward. The seventh lies farther out and moves the muscles of the face.

Question 5020. Which cranial nerve nucleus lies in the midbrain and supplies the muscle that raises the upper eyelid: the third, the fourth, the sixth, or the seventh cranial nerve? The answer is the third cranial nerve. A lesion of that nerve leaves the eyelid drooping and the pupil wide. The fourth cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle instead.

Question 5021. Which nucleus in the medulla receives the fibers of taste from the back of the tongue and from the throat? The answer is the nucleus of the solitary tract. Taste fibers that travel with the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves all end in it. The same nucleus also receives information from the internal organs.

Question 5022. A described magnetic resonance image of the lower part of the head shows a rounded structure passing through the foramen magnum, with the cerebellum behind it and the vertebral arteries beside it. Which structure is shown? The answer is the medulla oblongata. It is the lowest part of the brainstem and continues below as the spinal cord. The foramen magnum marks the boundary between the two.

Question 5023. The superior cerebellar peduncles carry fibers between the cerebellum and which part of the brainstem? The answer is the midbrain. They leave the cerebellum, run upward and enter the midbrain just below the colliculi. The middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles join the pons and the medulla instead.

Question 5024. A constructed illustration: a person has a drooping eyelid, a wide pupil and an eye that rests turned down and outward. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected? The answer is the third cranial nerve, in a described palsy. The muscles that raise the eyelid and most of the muscles that move the eye lose their supply. The pupil widens because the small fibers that narrow it are lost.

Question 5025. Which of these is the chief function of the reticular formation of the brainstem: fine touch, hearing, wakefulness, or smell? The answer is wakefulness. The reticular formation is a network of cells and short fibers spread through the brainstem. Its ascending fibers keep the cerebral cortex alert, and its descending fibers adjust muscle tone and posture.

Question 5026. True or false: every corticospinal fiber crosses to the opposite side in the medulla oblongata. The answer is false. Most fibers cross at the decussation of the pyramids, but a small group continues uncrossed in the anterior corticospinal tract. Those fibers cross lower down, in the segment of the spinal cord where they end.

Question 5027. Which part of the brainstem continues below into the spinal cord through the foramen magnum? The answer is the medulla oblongata. It is the lowest part of the brainstem and the highest part of the central nervous system within the skull. Its cavity is continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord.

Question 5028. A described transverse section of the lowest part of the brainstem shows a closed central canal, a pair of ridges in front, and a large nucleus on each side behind them. Which part is shown? The answer is the lower medulla oblongata. The ridges are the pyramids, and the nuclei behind them belong to the posterior column pathway.

Question 5029. Which tract lies close to the midline in the medulla and carries fine touch and position sense from the opposite side of the body: the spinothalamic tract, the medial lemniscus, the anterior corticospinal tract, or the inferior cerebellar peduncle? The answer is the medial lemniscus. Its fibers come from the nucleus gracilis and the nucleus cuneatus and cross in the midline as the internal arcuate fibers.

Question 5030. Which depression lies between the two cerebral peduncles on the front of the midbrain, and what emerges from it? The answer is the interpeduncular fossa, from which the third cranial nerve emerges. Small vessels also pass through its floor. The cerebral peduncles form its two sides.

Question 5031. A constructed illustration: a blockage of the basilar artery leaves a person awake but unable to move the limbs or to speak, with only the eyes moving up and down. Which part of the brainstem is destroyed? The answer is the front of the pons, where the descending fibers from the cortex lie close together, while the reticular formation behind them keeps a person awake.

Question 5032. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medulla with the visual cortex, the midbrain with hearing, the medulla with the centers for breathing and for the heart, or the pons with smell? The answer is the medulla with the centers for breathing and for the heart. Those centers lie in the reticular formation of the medulla. The midbrain serves the visual and hearing reflexes instead.

Question 5033. Which dark band of gray matter lies in the midbrain just behind the cerebral peduncle and sends dopamine to the striatum? The answer is the substantia nigra. Its name means black substance, from the pigment in its cells. Its loss is the central change in parkinsonism.

Question 5034. Which brainstem nucleus contains the cells that send parasympathetic fibers to the heart, the lungs and the gut: the nucleus of the third cranial nerve, the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, the nucleus ambiguus, or the facial nucleus? The answer is the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, in the medulla. Its fibers leave with the tenth cranial nerve.

Question 5035. A described specimen shows the front of the whole brainstem, with a pair of ridges beside the midline below, a broad bulge above them, and two thick columns above that. Which three parts are shown, in order from below? The answer is the medulla oblongata, the pons and the midbrain. The ridges below are the pyramids and the columns above are the cerebral peduncles.

Question 5036. Which part of the brainstem lies immediately above the medulla oblongata and immediately below the midbrain? The answer is the pons. It lies in the middle of the three parts of the brainstem. The fourth ventricle lies behind it and the cerebellum lies beyond that.

Question 5037. Which cranial nerve nucleus lies beside the midline in the medulla and supplies the muscles of the tongue: the fifth, the seventh, the twelfth, or the third cranial nerve? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve. It lies close to the midline behind the pyramid, and its fibers leave between the pyramid and the olive. The other three lie higher in the brainstem and farther from the midline.

Question 5038. Which band of fibers crosses the midline in the tegmentum at the junction of the pons and the midbrain and connects the two red nuclei? The answer is the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles. The fibers come from the cerebellum, mainly from the dentate nucleus, and cross on their way to the thalamus. The crossing is a useful landmark at that junction.

Question 5039. Which large gray mass of the basal nuclei is shaped like the letter C and follows the curve of the lateral ventricle? The answer is the caudate nucleus. Its head lies in front of the thalamus, its body runs along the roof of the ventricle, and its tail curves down into the temporal lobe. It belongs to the input side of the basal nuclei.

Question 5040. Which of these structures is part of the lentiform nucleus: the caudate nucleus, the putamen, the amygdala, or the claustrum? The answer is the putamen. The lentiform nucleus is a wedge of gray matter made of the putamen and the globus pallidus. The caudate nucleus lies separately, in the wall of the lateral ventricle.

Question 5041. Which part of the lentiform nucleus is the smaller, paler, medial part that forms the main output of the basal nuclei? The answer is the globus pallidus. It lies medial to the putamen and is divided into an internal and an external segment. Its fibers pass to the thalamus.

Question 5042. True or false: the putamen and the globus pallidus together make up the lentiform nucleus. The answer is true. The two lie side by side and together form a wedge whose point faces the midline. The internal capsule separates the wedge from the caudate nucleus and the thalamus.

Question 5043. Which of these structures is not part of the basal nuclei: the caudate nucleus, the putamen, the globus pallidus, or the thalamus? The answer is the thalamus. The thalamus is the great sensory relay and lies medial to the basal nuclei. The basal nuclei are the caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus, with the amygdala and the claustrum often named beside them.

Question 5044. What is the name of the thin sheet of gray matter that lies between the putamen and the insula, separated from each of them by a narrow band of white matter? The answer is the claustrum. The band between it and the putamen is the external capsule, and the band outside it is the extreme capsule. Its function is still debated.

Question 5045. Which mass of gray matter lies deep in the temporal lobe, in front of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, and belongs to the limbic system: the amygdala, the claustrum, the globus pallidus, or the pulvinar? The answer is the amygdala. It is often grouped with the basal nuclei because of its position. It is concerned with emotion, especially fear, and with the sense of smell.

Question 5046. Which part of the substantia nigra sends dopamine to the striatum, and which part sends fibers to the thalamus and the colliculi? The answer is the pars compacta for dopamine and the pars reticulata for the other fibers. The compact part lies behind and its cells carry pigment. The reticular part lies in front of it and acts as one of the output nuclei of the basal nuclei.

Question 5047. The internal capsule lies between which two groups of structures? The answer is the caudate nucleus and the thalamus on its medial side and the lentiform nucleus on its lateral side. Its fibers run up and down between the cortex and the brainstem. A small lesion there can therefore cause a large paralysis.

Question 5048. A described coronal section through the brain shows a wedge of gray matter whose broad base faces outward and whose narrow point faces the midline, with white matter in front of it and behind it. Which structure is shown? The answer is the lentiform nucleus. The white matter in front of it is the anterior limb of the internal capsule. The white matter behind it is the posterior limb.

Question 5049. Which of these pairs belongs together: the amygdala with the occipital lobe, the caudate nucleus with the cerebellum, the amygdala with the temporal lobe, or the globus pallidus with the frontal pole? The answer is the amygdala with the temporal lobe. It lies in the deep part of that lobe, near the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. The caudate nucleus follows the lateral ventricle instead.

Question 5050. From which of these does the striatum receive its main input: the cerebral cortex, the spinal cord, the cerebellum, or the retina? The answer is the cerebral cortex. Fibers arrive from many areas of the cortex and end in the caudate nucleus and the putamen. The cerebellum sends its fibers to the thalamus instead.

Question 5051. Name the two parts of the substantia nigra, spoken as a list. The answer is the pars compacta and the pars reticulata. The compact part lies behind and holds the pigmented cells that make dopamine. The reticular part lies in front and forms one of the output nuclei of the basal nuclei.

Question 5052. A described transverse section through the diencephalon shows a small round nucleus above the midbrain, medial to the internal capsule, with the substantia nigra behind it. Which nucleus is shown? The answer is the subthalamic nucleus. It lies at the junction of the midbrain and the diencephalon. It belongs to the indirect pathway of the basal nuclei.

Question 5053. A constructed illustration: a small hemorrhage damages a nucleus just above the midbrain, and the person develops sudden violent flinging movements of the arm and the leg on the opposite side. Which nucleus is involved? The answer is the subthalamic nucleus. Its usual activity excites the output nuclei of the basal nuclei, so its loss releases the movement. The illustration is a teaching example and not a real case.

Question 5054. Which of these does an active direct pathway do: excite the internal segment of the globus pallidus, inhibit it and release the thalamus, excite the subthalamic nucleus, or inhibit the cerebral cortex? The answer is that it inhibits the internal segment of the globus pallidus and so releases the thalamus. That nucleus normally holds the thalamus in check. The indirect pathway does the opposite.

Question 5055. Which structure does the indirect pathway use to raise the output of the internal segment of the globus pallidus: the subthalamic nucleus, the amygdala, the claustrum, or the red nucleus? The answer is the subthalamic nucleus. It excites the internal segment, which then holds the thalamus back and makes movement harder. Loss of the subthalamic nucleus therefore releases movement.

Question 5056. The tail of the caudate nucleus lies in the roof of which cavity? The answer is the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. The tail curves downward and forward through the temporal lobe and ends beside the amygdala. The body of the nucleus lies along the roof of the central part of the ventricle instead.

Question 5057. A constructed illustration: an adult develops jerking movements of the limbs, a change of personality and failing memory, and imaging shows that the caudate nucleus has shrunk on both sides. Which nucleus is affected, and why does the movement disorder appear? The answer is the caudate nucleus, whose loss removes part of the indirect pathway that normally restrains movement.

Question 5058. Which of these explains why a small lesion in the internal segment of the globus pallidus reduces rigidity and tremor: because that nucleus is the main output of the basal nuclei, because it is their main input, because it makes dopamine, or because it begins the corticospinal tract? The answer is that it is the main output, and its loss releases the thalamus. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 5059. A described specimen of the insula shows a thin gray sheet with a band of white matter on each side, the inner band separating it from the putamen and the outer band separating it from the cortex. Which structure lies between the two bands? The answer is the claustrum. The inner band is the external capsule and the outer band is the extreme capsule.

Question 5060. Which nucleus lies where the head of the caudate nucleus meets the putamen, below the front of the internal capsule, and is concerned with reward and with addiction? The answer is the nucleus accumbens. It forms part of the ventral striatum. It lies close to the midline in the front part of the base of the brain.

Question 5061. Which structure forms the medial boundary of the putamen: the globus pallidus, the claustrum, the caudate nucleus, or the thalamus? The answer is the globus pallidus. The putamen and the globus pallidus lie side by side within the lentiform nucleus. The claustrum lies lateral to the putamen and the thalamus lies beyond the internal capsule.

Question 5062. In a coronal section through the brain at the level of the interventricular foramen, which of these lists the structures in the correct order from medial to lateral: thalamus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, insula, or insula, thalamus, lentiform nucleus, internal capsule? The answer is thalamus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, insula. The insula lies on the surface of the hemisphere.

Question 5063. Which nucleus of the thalamus receives fine touch and position sense from the opposite side of the body and sends them to the cortex? The answer is the ventral posterior lateral nucleus. It lies in the lateral group of thalamic nuclei. Fibers from the face end in the ventral posterior medial nucleus beside it.

Question 5064. Which of these is the relay for vision on its way to the cortex: the medial geniculate body, the lateral geniculate body, the pulvinar, or the anterior nucleus? The answer is the lateral geniculate body. It lies under the back of the thalamus and receives fibers from the retina. The medial geniculate body serves hearing instead.

Question 5065. What is the name of the small swelling below the pulvinar that receives fibers from the hearing pathway? The answer is the medial geniculate body. It sends its fibers to the hearing area of the temporal lobe. The lateral geniculate body beside it belongs to vision, and the two together are called the metathalamus.

Question 5066. A described horizontal section through the middle of the brain shows a band of gray matter joining the two thalami across the midline, surrounded by the cavity of the third ventricle. Which structure is shown? The answer is the interthalamic adhesion, also called the massa intermedia. It is present in most brains but not in all of them. It carries no large bundle of fibers.

Question 5067. Which thalamic nucleus receives fine touch from the face and sends it to the cortex: the ventral posterior medial nucleus, the ventral posterior lateral nucleus, the ventral anterior nucleus, or the pulvinar? The answer is the ventral posterior medial nucleus. The face is represented there, next to the hand and the body in the nucleus beside it. The ventral posterior lateral nucleus carries the rest of the body instead.

Question 5068. True or false: the thalamus lies on each side of the third ventricle. The answer is true. The two thalami form the greater part of the wall of that cavity. They are joined across the middle in most brains by the interthalamic adhesion.

Question 5069. Which two thalamic nuclei receive fibers from the basal nuclei and the cerebellum and send them to the motor cortex: the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei, the anterior and medial nuclei, the pulvinar and the lateral geniculate body, or the ventral posterior nuclei? The answer is the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei. They lie in the front part of the lateral group. The ventral posterior nuclei carry sensation instead.

Question 5070. Which nucleus of the thalamus lies in the front part of its dorsal surface, receives fibers from the mammillary body, and belongs to the circuit of memory? The answer is the anterior nucleus. It lies just behind the interventricular foramen, inside the internal medullary lamina. Its fibers pass back to the cingulate gyrus.

Question 5071. Which large nucleus forms the back end of the thalamus and is concerned with vision and with the direction of attention? The answer is the pulvinar. It is the largest of the thalamic nuclei and lies above and behind the medial geniculate body. Its connections are mainly with the association areas of the cortex.

Question 5072. Which sheet of white matter divides the thalamus into an anterior part, a medial part and a lateral part: the internal medullary lamina, the external capsule, the corpus callosum, or the cerebral peduncle? The answer is the internal medullary lamina. It is a thin band of fibers that divides the gray matter into the three parts. Small intralaminar nuclei lie within it.

Question 5073. Which cavity lies between the two halves of the thalamus, and what forms its floor? The answer is the third ventricle, whose floor is formed by the hypothalamus. The thalamus forms its two walls. Its roof is a thin sheet of tissue that carries a small knot of vessels.

Question 5074. A described horizontal section through the brain shows a large egg-shaped mass of gray matter beside the midline, with white matter along its outer border and the head of the caudate nucleus in front of it. Which structure is shown? The answer is the thalamus. The white matter along its outer border is the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

Question 5075. Which group of thalamic nuclei lies within the internal medullary lamina and is concerned with awareness and with pain: the intralaminar nuclei, the anterior nucleus, the pulvinar, or the lateral geniculate body? The answer is the intralaminar nuclei, of which the centromedian nucleus is the largest. They project widely to the cerebral cortex and to the striatum. They are not part of the main sensory relay.

Question 5076. A constructed illustration: a small lesion destroys the lateral geniculate body on one side. Which loss of sight follows? The answer is loss of the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes. Fibers from the same half of each retina end in that body. The pupil still reacts to light, because the fibers that serve that reflex leave the pathway before they reach it.

Question 5077. A described magnetic resonance image shows a small lesion in the lateral part of the thalamus on one side, and the person has lost all forms of sensation on the opposite side of the body and the face. Which nucleus is damaged? The answer is the ventral posterior nucleus, whose lateral part serves the body and whose medial part serves the face. Every sensory pathway except smell relays there.

Question 5078. A constructed illustration: months after a small stroke in the thalamus, a person has severe burning pain on the opposite side of the body that is made worse by touch and by cold. Which structure was damaged? The answer is the thalamus, in the thalamic pain syndrome. The pain follows damage to the sensory nuclei and their cortical connections. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 5079. The thalamus is supplied mainly by branches of which artery: the middle cerebral artery, the posterior cerebral artery, the anterior cerebral artery, or the basilar artery? The answer is the posterior cerebral artery. Its small branches enter the back of the thalamus and supply most of it. The front and medial parts receive small branches from the back of the internal carotid artery.

Question 5080. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral geniculate body with hearing, the medial geniculate body with sight, the pulvinar with smell, or the medial geniculate body with hearing? The answer is the medial geniculate body with hearing. It receives fibers from the inferior colliculus and sends them to the temporal lobe. The lateral geniculate body belongs to vision instead.

Question 5081. Name the two nuclei of the metathalamus, spoken as a list. The answer is the lateral geniculate body and the medial geniculate body. They lie beneath the back of the thalamus, one for sight and one for hearing. The pulvinar lies above them.

Question 5082. In a horizontal section through the diencephalon, which of these lists the structures in the correct order from the midline outward: third ventricle, thalamus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, or thalamus, third ventricle, lentiform nucleus, internal capsule? The answer is third ventricle, thalamus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus. The ventricle lies in the midline and the lentiform nucleus lies furthest out. The internal capsule separates the thalamus from the lentiform nucleus.

Question 5083. Which nucleus of the hypothalamus lies above the optic chiasm and makes antidiuretic hormone? The answer is the supraoptic nucleus. Its fibers run down the stalk to the back part of the pituitary gland. The hormone is stored and released there into the blood, where it controls the amount of water lost in the urine.

Question 5084. Where does the hypothalamus lie: above the thalamus, below the thalamus and in front of the midbrain, behind the cerebellum, or inside the temporal lobe? The answer is below the thalamus and in front of the midbrain. It forms the floor of the third ventricle, and the pituitary gland hangs beneath it on a stalk.

Question 5085. What are the names of the two rounded bodies that hang from the back of the floor of the hypothalamus? The answer is the mammillary bodies. They lie behind the infundibulum, one on each side of the midline. They receive fibers from the fornix and belong to the circuit of memory.

Question 5086. Which structure lies in front of the infundibulum and above the pituitary gland: the optic chiasm, the mammillary body, the pineal gland, or the splenium of the corpus callosum? The answer is the optic chiasm, where fibers from the two eyes cross. The infundibulum is the stalk that carries fibers down to the pituitary gland. The mammillary bodies lie behind the stalk.

Question 5087. True or false: the back part of the pituitary gland stores hormones that are made in the hypothalamus. The answer is true. The supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make the hormones, and their fibers carry them down the stalk. The front part of the gland makes its own hormones instead.

Question 5088. Which nucleus of the hypothalamus lies beside the third ventricle above the supraoptic nucleus and makes oxytocin? The answer is the paraventricular nucleus. Its fibers run down the stalk to the back part of the pituitary gland. The same nucleus also sends fibers to the brainstem and the spinal cord.

Question 5089. Which part of the hypothalamus is most concerned with losing heat and with lowering body temperature: the posterior part, the anterior part, the lateral part, or the mammillary bodies? The answer is the anterior part. The posterior part acts in the opposite way and helps to conserve heat. The two together keep the temperature of the body steady.

Question 5090. Which nucleus of the hypothalamus is classically described as the center for the feeling of fullness after a meal: the lateral nucleus, the ventromedial nucleus, the arcuate nucleus, or the suprachiasmatic nucleus? The answer is the ventromedial nucleus. The lateral nucleus is described as the center that drives feeding instead. The two are spoken of as a pair that balances appetite.

Question 5091. Which small nucleus of the hypothalamus lies near the median eminence and sends its fibers into the portal vessels: the arcuate nucleus, the supraoptic nucleus, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or the posterior nucleus? The answer is the arcuate nucleus. It lies in the tuberal region, close to the infundibulum. Its fibers end on the vessels of the median eminence.

Question 5092. A described sagittal section through the middle of the brain shows a small block of tissue below the thalamus, with the optic chiasm in front, a stalk in the middle and two rounded bodies behind. Which region is shown? The answer is the hypothalamus. The stalk is the infundibulum and the rounded bodies are the mammillary bodies.

Question 5093. Which tract carries fibers from the mammillary body to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus? The answer is the mammillothalamic tract. It runs upward and forward through the wall of the third ventricle. The fibers continue from the thalamus to the cingulate gyrus.

Question 5094. A described magnetic resonance image of the head shows a mass above the sella, growing on the stalk of the pituitary gland, with the optic chiasm stretched over it. Which region is compressed, and which structure is usually affected first? The answer is the suprasellar region, with the optic chiasm affected first. Loss of the outer parts of the visual fields follows.

Question 5095. A constructed illustration: after an operation near the base of the brain, a person passes large volumes of dilute urine and is constantly thirsty. Which nuclei have lost their function? The answer is the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. Their fibers carry antidiuretic hormone down the stalk to the back part of the pituitary gland. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 5096. A constructed illustration: a child has attacks of laughter that cannot be controlled, together with a small mass hanging from the region of the tuber cinereum. Which region is involved, and why does the laughing appear? The answer is the hypothalamus, in a described malformation that joins the tuber cinereum. The mass lies within a circuit that normally holds emotional expression in check.

Question 5097. Which nucleus of the hypothalamus lies just above the optic chiasm and sets the daily rhythm of sleeping and waking: the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the supraoptic nucleus, the arcuate nucleus, or the posterior nucleus? The answer is the suprachiasmatic nucleus. It receives fibers directly from the retina by a special pathway. It then adjusts the rhythm of the rest of the body.

Question 5098. A described specimen shows the under surface of the brain with a small gray area behind the infundibulum and in front of the mammillary bodies, dotted with fine vessels. Which part of the hypothalamus is shown? The answer is the tuber cinereum, with the median eminence on its surface. The fine vessels are the portal vessels that carry releasing factors to the pituitary gland.

Question 5099. Which tract descends to end in the mammillary body, and what does it carry? The answer is the fornix, which carries fibers from the hippocampus. It curves downward and forward behind the anterior commissure and ends in the mammillary body. The mammillary body then sends fibers onward to the thalamus.

Question 5100. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraoptic nucleus with oxytocin, the paraventricular nucleus with antidiuretic hormone, the ventromedial nucleus with thirst, or the supraoptic nucleus with antidiuretic hormone? The answer is the supraoptic nucleus with antidiuretic hormone. Both nuclei make both hormones, but the supraoptic nucleus is the classic source. The lateral nucleus is linked with thirst instead.

To summarize, the brainstem is the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata, and it carries the cranial nerve nuclei, the long ascending and descending tracts, and the centers for breathing and for the heart. The basal nuclei, built from the caudate nucleus, the putamen and the globus pallidus, shape movement through the direct and indirect pathways that pass by way of the thalamus, and their damage produces tremor, rigidity, involuntary movement or loss of control. The thalamus relays every sensation except smell, serves sight and hearing through the geniculate bodies and movement through the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei, and wraps around the third ventricle. The hypothalamus, small and placed below the thalamus, governs temperature, thirst, hunger, sleep, the daily rhythm and the hormones released through the pituitary gland. Naming each structure aloud with its neighbor fixes the deep brain in memory, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 52 — Cranial Nerves

Every cranial nerve leaves the skull through a named opening and carries a particular set of fibers, and the first six are the ones a clinician tests at the bedside. This chapter takes them in order: the olfactory nerve, the optic nerve, the oculomotor nerve, the trochlear nerve, the trigeminal nerve and the abducens nerve. Each is described by where its fibers begin, the opening they use and the structures they serve. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately afterwards and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried forward in memory. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 5101. Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell, and where do its receptors lie? The answer is the olfactory nerve, the first cranial nerve. Its receptors are nerve cells in a small patch of specialized lining in the roof of each nasal cavity. Their fibers are unmyelinated and gather into about twenty bundles on each side.

Question 5102. Which opening does the olfactory nerve pass through on its way to the brain: the optic canal, the cribriform plate, the foramen ovale, or the superior orbital fissure? The answer is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. Its many small holes carry the olfactory filaments into the cranial cavity. The other openings carry the optic nerve and the branches of the trigeminal nerve.

Question 5103. Which structure rests on the cribriform plate and receives the olfactory filaments: the olfactory bulb, the trigeminal ganglion, the pituitary gland, or the optic chiasm? The answer is the olfactory bulb. It lies on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe and is the first relay station of the pathway. From it the olfactory tract runs backward along the base of the brain.

Question 5104. A described section through the roof of the nasal cavity shows fine bundles of fibers piercing a perforated plate of bone. Which nerve is shown, and where do those bundles end? The answer is the olfactory nerve, and the bundles end in the olfactory bulb above the plate. The plate is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

Question 5105. True or false: the olfactory pathway reaches the cerebral cortex without passing through the thalamus. The answer is true. Its fibers relay in the olfactory bulb and then run to the piriform cortex and the amygdala. Every other sensory pathway, including the visual pathway, relays in the thalamus first.

Question 5106. Which structure lies immediately above the cribriform plate, and which lies immediately below it? The answer is the olfactory bulb above and the olfactory lining of the nose below. The filaments cross the holes of the plate between the two. A fracture there can tear them and let cerebrospinal fluid escape through the nose.

Question 5107. A constructed illustration: a person struck on the front of the head loses the sense of smell on one side and reports a clear watery discharge from that nostril. Which nerve is injured, and at which bone? The answer is the olfactory nerve, torn as it crosses the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The watery discharge is cerebrospinal fluid.

Question 5108. A described computed tomography study of the anterior cranial fossa shows a fracture line crossing its floor on one side. Which nerve is at risk there? The answer is the olfactory nerve, whose filaments cross that floor through the cribriform plate. Injury removes the sense of smell on the same side.

Question 5109. Which statement about the cells that detect smell is correct: they are nerve cells replaced throughout life, they are supporting cells that never divide, they are endings of the olfactory tract, or they are branches of the trigeminal nerve? The answer is that they are nerve cells replaced throughout life. They are the only sensory nerve cells known to be renewed in an adult.

Question 5110. Which of these runs backward from the olfactory bulb toward the temporal lobe: the olfactory tract, the optic nerve, the oculomotor nerve, or the trigeminal nerve? The answer is the olfactory tract. It divides into a medial and a lateral stria near the anterior perforated substance. The lateral stria carries most of the fibers to the primary olfactory cortex.

Question 5111. Which of these pairs belongs together: the olfactory nerve with the cribriform plate, the optic nerve with the foramen rotundum, the maxillary nerve with the optic canal, or the mandibular nerve with the superior orbital fissure? The answer is the olfactory nerve with the cribriform plate. The maxillary nerve passes through the foramen rotundum and the mandibular nerve through the foramen ovale.

Question 5112. Name two structures of the olfactory pathway that lie inside the cranial cavity, spoken as a list. The answer is the olfactory bulb and the olfactory tract. The bulb rests on the cribriform plate and the tract runs backward from it. Both lie against the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.

Question 5113. Where do most fibers of the olfactory tract end: in the thalamus, in the piriform cortex and the amygdala, in the occipital lobe, or in the cerebellum? The answer is the piriform cortex and the amygdala. Those areas lie in the temporal lobe and form the primary olfactory cortex. No thalamic relay interrupts the pathway on the way.

Question 5114. Which cranial nerve lies immediately above the cribriform plate, and which artery runs beside it in the same region? The answer is the olfactory nerve, with the anterior ethmoidal artery. That artery passes from the orbit into the cranial cavity and then down through the plate beside the filaments. Bleeding from it can follow a fracture of that floor.

Question 5115. Which cranial nerve carries the images formed by the retina to the brain, and where do its fibers begin? The answer is the optic nerve, the second cranial nerve. Its fibers begin in the ganglion cells of the retina and leave the eye at the optic disc. The nerve is really a tract of the brain drawn out into the orbit.

Question 5116. Which opening in the skull does the optic nerve pass through: the superior orbital fissure, the foramen rotundum, the optic canal, or the foramen ovale? The answer is the optic canal. The ophthalmic artery runs through it as well. The superior orbital fissure carries the nerves that move the eye.

Question 5117. What is the name of the pale round area at the back of the retina where the optic nerve fibers leave the eye? The answer is the optic disc. It holds no rods or cones, so it forms the blind spot of the visual field. The central retinal artery and vein enter and leave the eye at the same place.

Question 5118. A described view of the retina shows a small pit packed with cone cells at the center of a yellow patch. Which region is described, and what is special about it? The answer is the fovea centralis, at the center of the macula lutea. It holds the greatest density of cones and gives the sharpest vision.

Question 5119. Which of these lies above the pituitary gland and carries crossing fibers from both eyes: the optic chiasm, the optic disc, the fovea centralis, or the ciliary ganglion? The answer is the optic chiasm. Fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross there. Fibers from the temporal half stay on their own side.

Question 5120. Which fibers cross in the optic chiasm: those from the nasal half of each retina, those from the temporal half of each retina, those from the macula alone, or all the fibers of the left eye? The answer is the fibers from the nasal half of each retina. After the crossing, each optic tract carries the opposite half of the visual field.

Question 5121. In a horizontal section through the base of the brain, two nerves meet in the midline and cross before they continue backward on each side. Which plane is this, and what is that crossing called? The answer is a transverse plane, and the crossing is the optic chiasm. The two optic nerves and the two optic tracts all appear in that section.

Question 5122. A described view of the back of the eye shows a swollen optic disc with blurred margins. What is that appearance called, and what does it reflect? The answer is papilledema, and it reflects raised pressure inside the skull. The pressure travels along the sheath of the optic nerve, which is filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

Question 5123. Which membranes cover the optic nerve and continue as the coverings of the brain, and what fluid lies between them? The answer is the dura mater, the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, with cerebrospinal fluid in the space between. That fluid-filled sheath is why raised pressure inside the skull shows at the optic disc.
