Question 5124. A constructed illustration: a person loses the whole field of vision in one eye while the other eye remains normal. Where does the trouble most likely lie? The answer is in the optic nerve of that eye. Damage to one optic nerve removes the field of that eye alone. Trouble behind the chiasm removes half of each field instead.

Question 5125. A described visual field chart shows loss of the outer half of the field in each eye, with the inner halves normal. Which structure is affected? The answer is the optic chiasm, and the defect is a bitemporal loss. The crossing fibers from the nasal half of each retina are the ones damaged.

Question 5126. Damage to the left optic tract produces which defect: blindness of the left eye, loss of the left half of both fields, loss of the right half of both fields, or loss of the outer halves of both fields? The answer is loss of the right half of both fields, a contralateral homonymous loss. Each tract carries the opposite half of the field from both eyes.

Question 5127. Which structure receives the fibers of the optic tract and sends them on to the occipital lobe? The answer is the lateral geniculate body of the thalamus. From it the fibers run backward as the optic radiation. They end in the visual cortex on either side of the calcarine sulcus.

Question 5128. Which of these pairs belongs together: the optic tract with the lateral geniculate body, the olfactory tract with the ciliary ganglion, the oculomotor nerve with the lateral geniculate body, or the trigeminal nerve with the optic chiasm? The answer is the optic tract with the lateral geniculate body. From there the optic radiation runs to the occipital lobe.

Question 5129. Which vessel supplies the inner part of the retina: the central retinal artery, the ophthalmic vein, the middle meningeal artery, or the posterior communicating artery? The answer is the central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It enters the eye within the optic nerve and divides at the disc. Its branches are the ones seen through an ophthalmoscope.

Question 5130. A described magnetic resonance imaging study of the head shows the optic chiasm in the midline with a rounded structure lying above it and a gland lying below it. Which structures are those? The answer is the hypothalamus above and the pituitary gland below. A swelling of the gland presses upward on the crossing fibers of the chiasm.

Question 5131. A constructed illustration: a person who has had a stroke cannot see the right half of the world from either eye, yet the pupils of both eyes still react to light. Where is the damage? The answer is in the optic radiation or the visual cortex on the left side. The pupils still react because the reflex leaves the pathway before that point.

Question 5132. A bundle of visual fibers sweeps forward into the temporal lobe before it turns back toward the occipital lobe. Which part of the field do those fibers serve? The answer is the upper part of the opposite half of the field. They come from the lower retina, so a lesion in the temporal lobe removes the upper field in both eyes.

Question 5133. Which cranial nerve supplies most of the muscles that move the eyeball, and also lifts the upper eyelid? The answer is the oculomotor nerve, the third cranial nerve. It serves the medial rectus, the superior rectus, the inferior rectus and the inferior oblique. It also serves the levator palpebrae superioris, which raises the lid.

Question 5134. Which of these muscles is not supplied by the oculomotor nerve: the medial rectus, the superior rectus, the lateral rectus, or the inferior oblique? The answer is the lateral rectus, which the abducens nerve supplies. The superior oblique is the other muscle outside its control, and the trochlear nerve supplies it.

Question 5135. Which muscle raises the upper eyelid, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the levator palpebrae superioris, supplied by the oculomotor nerve. Loss of that nerve therefore produces a drooping lid, called ptosis. A small muscle of smooth fibers within the lid assists it.

Question 5136. From which part of the brain stem does the oculomotor nerve emerge: the front of the midbrain, the side of the pons, the back of the midbrain, or the front of the medulla oblongata? The answer is the front of the midbrain, in the hollow between the two cerebral peduncles. From there the nerve runs forward and outward toward the orbit.

Question 5137. A described section through the midbrain shows a nerve leaving from its front surface between the two cerebral peduncles. Which nerve is shown, and which opening will it use to enter the orbit? The answer is the oculomotor nerve, which enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. It passes within the ring of tendon at the apex of the orbit.

Question 5138. Between which two arteries does the oculomotor nerve pass as it leaves the midbrain? The answer is the posterior cerebral artery above and the superior cerebellar artery below. That narrow gap is where the nerve is most often pressed on by a swelling artery. The abducens nerve also runs a long course nearby.

Question 5139. In which small ganglion do the parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve end: the ciliary ganglion, the trigeminal ganglion, the otic ganglion, or the geniculate ganglion? The answer is the ciliary ganglion, which lies behind the eye. The trigeminal ganglion is sensory for the face, and the other two belong to other nerves.

Question 5140. Which opening does the oculomotor nerve pass through to enter the orbit: the optic canal, the foramen rotundum, the superior orbital fissure, or the foramen ovale? The answer is the superior orbital fissure. The trochlear, the abducens and the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve use the same opening. The optic nerve has its own canal.

Question 5141. When the oculomotor nerve is completely paralyzed, in which direction does the eye come to rest: straight ahead, down and out, up and in, or up and out? The answer is down and out. The lateral rectus pulls the eye outward and the superior oblique pulls it downward. Those are the two muscles that the damaged nerve does not serve.

Question 5142. A described photograph of a face shows one upper lid drooping over a wide pupil, with the eye turned down and outward. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the oculomotor nerve on that side. The drooping lid comes from the levator, the wide pupil from the muscle that narrows it, and the eye position from the muscles left unopposed.

Question 5143. Which nerve is compressed when a drooping lid and a widely dilated pupil that does not react to light appear together? The answer is the oculomotor nerve. The fibers that narrow the pupil lie near the surface of the nerve, so compression reaches them first. The levator of the lid fails at the same time, which is why the lid droops.

Question 5144. True or false: when the oculomotor nerve is damaged by loss of its blood supply, the pupil often still narrows when light is shone into the eye. The answer is true. Loss of blood supply strikes the core of the nerve, while the pupil fibers lie on its surface. Compression of the nerve does the opposite and dilates the pupil early.

Question 5145. What is the name of the nucleus in the midbrain that gives rise to the parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve? The answer is the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. Its fibers travel with the nerve to the ciliary ganglion. There they relay, and short ciliary nerves carry them on to the pupil and the lens.

Question 5146. Within the cavernous sinus, where does the oculomotor nerve lie, and which nerve lies immediately below it in the same wall? The answer is that the oculomotor nerve lies in the lateral wall of the sinus, with the trochlear nerve below it. The abducens nerve lies free in the cavity of the sinus beside the internal carotid artery.

Question 5147. Which fibers of the oculomotor nerve lie closest to its surface, so that compression affects them first: the fibers to the medial rectus, the fibers to the inferior oblique, the fibers that narrow the pupil, or the fibers to the levator of the lid? The answer is the fibers that narrow the pupil, which run on the outer part of the nerve.

Question 5148. True or false: the oculomotor nerve supplies both the muscles that move the eyeball and the muscles inside the eye. The answer is true. It serves four muscles that move the eye, the muscle that lifts the lid, the muscle that narrows the pupil and the muscle that focuses the lens.

Question 5149. A described section through the cavernous sinus shows two nerves lying in its lateral wall, one above the other, while a third nerve lies in the middle of the sinus beside an artery. Which nerve lies in the middle? The answer is the abducens nerve, beside the internal carotid artery. It suffers early in disease of that sinus.

Question 5150. Which of these pairs belongs together: the oculomotor nerve and the ciliary ganglion, the optic nerve and the ciliary ganglion, the trigeminal nerve and the ciliary ganglion, or the abducens nerve and the ciliary ganglion? The answer is the oculomotor nerve and the ciliary ganglion. Its fibers relay there on the way to the pupil and the lens.

Question 5151. A constructed illustration: light shone into one eye makes both pupils narrow, but light shone into the other eye makes neither pupil narrow. Which nerve is at fault, and on which side? The answer is the optic nerve of the second eye, for it carries the signal in. Both oculomotor nerves must be working, since both pupils narrow.

Question 5152. Name two muscles supplied by the oculomotor nerve that move the eyeball, spoken as a list. The answer is the medial rectus and the superior rectus. The inferior rectus and the inferior oblique are supplied by it as well. The same nerve lifts the lid and narrows the pupil.

Question 5153. Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle of the eye? The answer is the trochlear nerve, the fourth cranial nerve. It carries motor fibers only and serves a single muscle. Every other nerve that moves the eye serves more than one muscle, and the trochlear is the smallest of the twelve.

Question 5154. Which cranial nerve is the only one to leave the brain stem from its back surface? The answer is the trochlear nerve, which emerges from the back of the midbrain below the lower colliculus. All the other cranial nerves leave from the front or the side. Its fibers then curve around the brain stem to reach the base of the skull.

Question 5155. Which opening does the trochlear nerve pass through to enter the orbit: the optic canal, the foramen ovale, the superior orbital fissure, or the foramen rotundum? The answer is the superior orbital fissure. It enters above the ring of tendon at the orbital apex, so it lies outside that ring. The oculomotor and abducens nerves pass within the ring.

Question 5156. A described dissection of the orbit shows a tendon that bends around a small fibrous pulley on the upper medial wall before it reaches the eye. Which muscle does that tendon belong to, and which nerve serves it? The answer is the superior oblique muscle, served by the trochlear nerve. The pulley itself is the trochlea.

Question 5157. The tendon of the superior oblique muscle passes through its pulley and then runs beneath which muscle before it reaches the eyeball? The answer is the superior rectus. The tendon then inserts on the upper and lateral part of the globe behind its widest point. That insertion explains why the muscle turns the eye inward and depresses it when the eye is turned in.

Question 5158. Which of these is the chief action of the superior oblique muscle when the eye is in the primary position: elevation, intorsion, outward turning, or depression? The answer is intorsion, the rolling of the top of the eye toward the nose. Depression and outward turning are its other actions, and they become stronger when the eye is turned inward.

Question 5159. A constructed illustration: a person sees double when reading or walking down stairs, and one image lies above the other. Which nerve is weak, and which muscle is at fault? The answer is the trochlear nerve, and the weak muscle is the superior oblique. Vertical double vision is worst when the eye is turned in and down.

Question 5160. True or false: the trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle on the same side as the nucleus from which its fibers arise. The answer is false. Its fibers cross completely before they leave the midbrain. The nucleus on one side therefore serves the superior oblique muscle on the other side.

Question 5161. A described photograph shows a person holding the head tilted toward the left shoulder because that position reduces the double vision. Which nerve is weak, and why does the tilt help? The answer is the right trochlear nerve. Tilting the head toward the left takes work away from the weak right superior oblique muscle.

Question 5162. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the head without any fracture, a person has vertical double vision that comes and goes, and both eyes are affected. Which nerve is most likely injured? The answer is the trochlear nerve. It is the thinnest cranial nerve and has the longest course inside the skull, so a head injury often stretches it.

Question 5163. Which cranial nerve is the largest, and what two kinds of fiber does it carry? The answer is the trigeminal nerve, the fifth cranial nerve. It carries general sensation from the face and motor fibers to the muscles of chewing. It has three divisions, which is what its name describes.

Question 5164. From which part of the brain stem does the trigeminal nerve emerge: the side of the pons, the front of the midbrain, the back of the midbrain, or the side of the medulla oblongata? The answer is the side of the pons. It leaves as two roots, a large sensory root and a small motor root. The small root supplies the muscles of chewing.

Question 5165. What is the name of the large sensory ganglion of the trigeminal nerve, and where does it lie? The answer is the trigeminal ganglion, which lies in a small cave on the front surface of the petrous part of the temporal bone. It is the equivalent for the face of a spinal ganglion. From it the three divisions run forward.

Question 5166. Which of the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve carries motor fibers: the ophthalmic division, the maxillary division, the mandibular division, or all three? The answer is the mandibular division. It supplies the muscles that chew and two small muscles of the ear and the soft palate. The other two divisions are purely sensory.

Question 5167. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ophthalmic division with the foramen rotundum, the maxillary division with the foramen ovale, the mandibular division with the foramen ovale, or the ophthalmic division with the foramen ovale? The answer is the mandibular division with the foramen ovale. The ophthalmic division enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.

Question 5168. A described view of the base of the skull shows three openings on one side, one leading to the orbit, one into the upper jaw and one just behind and outside the second. Which nerves pass through them? The answer is the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions of the trigeminal nerve. They leave by the superior orbital fissure, the foramen rotundum and the foramen ovale.

Question 5169. In a described CT section of the skull base, which of these openings lies farthest forward: the foramen ovale, the foramen rotundum, the foramen spinosum, or the jugular foramen? The answer is the foramen rotundum. It lies in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, ahead of the foramen ovale, and both lie ahead of the foramen spinosum and the jugular foramen.

Question 5170. Which of these pairs belongs together: the maxillary division with the upper teeth and the cheek, the mandibular division with the upper teeth and the cheek, the ophthalmic division with the lower lip and the chin, or the maxillary division with the lower teeth and the chin? The answer is the maxillary division with the upper teeth and the cheek. The mandibular division supplies the lower teeth and the chin.

Question 5171. Which division of the trigeminal nerve leaves the skull through the foramen ovale: the ophthalmic division, the maxillary division, the mandibular division, or the abducens nerve? The answer is the mandibular division. It carries sensation from the lower jaw and the tongue and motor fibers to the muscles of chewing. The abducens nerve uses the superior orbital fissure.

Question 5172. Which of these muscles of chewing protrudes the lower jaw forward: the masseter, the temporalis, the lateral pterygoid, or the medial pterygoid? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. The masseter and the temporalis raise the jaw, and the medial pterygoid raises it and helps to protrude it. All four are supplied by the mandibular division.

Question 5173. A constructed illustration: a person cannot feel a light touch on the lower lip and the chin on one side, but the muscles of chewing work normally. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the mental nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from the mandibular division. It leaves the jaw at the mental foramen.

Question 5174. Which two divisions of the trigeminal nerve run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, and which one never enters that sinus? The answer is the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions in the wall, while the mandibular division passes straight out through the foramen ovale. The ophthalmic division continues to the orbit and the maxillary to the upper jaw.

Question 5175. A constructed illustration: when the cornea of one eye is touched lightly, neither eye blinks, and the person cannot feel the touch. Which nerve carries the sensation, and which nerve should have closed the lids? The answer is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve for sensation and the facial nerve for the closing. This is the corneal reflex.

Question 5176. True or false: the cornea receives its general sensation through the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. The answer is true. Its fibers run in the long ciliary nerves, which are branches of the nasociliary nerve. The same division supplies the skin of the forehead, the upper eyelid and the tip of the nose.

Question 5177. Which division of the trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the upper teeth, the palate and the skin over the cheek: the ophthalmic division, the maxillary division, the mandibular division, or the facial nerve? The answer is the maxillary division. The facial nerve is a motor nerve to the muscles of the face and carries no general sensation from the cheek.

Question 5178. Which nerve leaves the skull just below the eye and supplies the upper lip and the side of the nose: the supraorbital nerve, the infraorbital nerve, the mental nerve, or the auriculotemporal nerve? The answer is the infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary division. The mental nerve supplies the chin and the auriculotemporal nerve the side of the head.

Question 5179. Which nerve runs in the canal inside the lower jaw, and through which opening does one of its branches reach the chin? The answer is the inferior alveolar nerve of the mandibular division, and its branch, the mental nerve, leaves by the mental foramen. The same nerve supplies the lower teeth.

Question 5180. Which branch of the mandibular division carries taste fibers from another nerve: the lingual nerve with fibers from the facial nerve, the inferior alveolar nerve with fibers from the optic nerve, the buccal nerve with fibers from the oculomotor nerve, or the auriculotemporal nerve with fibers from the trochlear nerve? The answer is the lingual nerve with fibers from the facial nerve. They carry taste from the front two thirds of the tongue.

Question 5181. Which small muscle of the ear is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, and what does it do? The answer is the tensor tympani, which draws the eardrum inward and dampens loud sound. The division also supplies the tensor of the soft palate. Both are small muscles served alongside the muscles of chewing.

Question 5182. Name two divisions of the trigeminal nerve in which sudden sharp facial pain most often occurs, spoken as a list. The answer is the maxillary division and the mandibular division. That pain comes in short attacks and leaves no numbness between them. Its cause and its treatment belong to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 5183. When the jaw muscles on the left side are weak, which way does the chin move when the mouth is opened: to the left, to the right, straight ahead, or upward? The answer is to the left, toward the weak side. The healthy lateral pterygoid on the right pushes the jaw across. A lesion of the mandibular division on the left produces this.

Question 5184. Which three branches of the trigeminal nerve emerge on the face in a vertical line, and what are they called? The answer is the supraorbital nerve above the eye, the infraorbital nerve below the eye and the mental nerve on the chin. One belongs to each of the three divisions. All three are purely sensory.

Question 5185. A described section of the pons shows a large nerve leaving its side in two parts, one much thicker than the other. Which nerve is shown, and what does each part carry? The answer is the trigeminal nerve, whose thick part carries sensation from the face and whose thin part carries motor fibers. The thin part supplies the muscles of chewing.

Question 5186. Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the dura mater over the tentorium of the cerebellum? The answer is the ophthalmic division. A small recurrent branch runs backward from it to that fold of dura. The other two divisions supply the dura of the middle cranial fossa instead.

Question 5187. Which nerve supplies the masseter, the temporalis and both pterygoid muscles: the ophthalmic division, the maxillary division, the mandibular division, or the facial nerve? The answer is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. It enters the space through the foramen ovale. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of the face, not the muscles of chewing.

Question 5188. Which nucleus of the trigeminal nerve lies in the midbrain and carries the sense of position from the muscles and joints of the jaw? The answer is the mesencephalic nucleus. Its cells are the cell bodies of the sensory fibers themselves, a feature found nowhere else. Their fibers travel with the mandibular division.

Question 5189. Which cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle, the muscle that turns the eyeball outward? The answer is the abducens nerve, the sixth cranial nerve. It carries motor fibers only, and that single muscle is all it serves. A weak lateral rectus leaves the eye turned inward.

Question 5190. From which part of the brain stem does the abducens nerve emerge? The answer is the junction of the pons and the medulla oblongata, near the midline. Its fibers leave from the front surface of the brain stem. The facial nerve emerges just beside it.

Question 5191. Which opening does the abducens nerve pass through to reach the orbit: the optic canal, the foramen rotundum, the foramen ovale, or the superior orbital fissure? The answer is the superior orbital fissure. It enters within the ring of tendon at the orbital apex. The oculomotor and trochlear nerves use the same opening.

Question 5192. A described MRI study shows a nerve running upward along the slope of the clivus and bending over the ridge of the petrous part of the temporal bone. Which nerve is shown, and where does it go next? The answer is the abducens nerve, which bends over that ridge and runs forward in the cavernous sinus. From there it enters the orbit.

Question 5193. Inside the cavernous sinus, which nerve lies closest to the internal carotid artery? The answer is the abducens nerve. It lies free in the cavity of the sinus beside the artery, while the other nerves lie in the wall. That position is why disease of the sinus often affects it first.

Question 5194. A constructed illustration: a person with a large brain tumor and raised pressure inside the skull has double vision when looking to the right, and the right eye cannot turn outward. Which nerve is failing? The answer is the right abducens nerve. Its long course inside the skull makes it the nerve most often stretched by raised pressure, even far from the tumor.

Question 5195. A described photograph of a face shows one eye turned slightly inward while the other looks straight ahead. Which muscle is weak, and which nerve is at fault? The answer is the lateral rectus, supplied by the abducens nerve. The medial rectus is unopposed and pulls the eye inward, and the double image is side by side.

Question 5196. Which muscle is left unopposed when the abducens nerve is paralyzed: the medial rectus, the lateral rectus, the superior oblique, or the levator of the lid? The answer is the medial rectus. With the outward pull lost, the inward pull turns the eye toward the nose. That inward turn is the commonest sign of a weak abducens nerve.

Question 5197. Through which narrow passage does the abducens nerve pass as it leaves the back of the skull and bends over the ridge of the petrous part of the temporal bone? The answer is a small channel beneath the petrosphenoidal ligament, often called Dorello's canal. The nerve is held tightly there, which is one reason it is easily stretched. The trigeminal ganglion lies in a cave at the same ridge.

Question 5198. A constructed illustration: a person with an infection of the middle ear and the tip of the petrous bone has deep pain behind the eye and double vision when looking outward. Which nerves are involved? The answer is the abducens nerve and the trigeminal nerve. Infection near the tip of the petrous bone reaches both, since they pass close by.

Question 5199. Which two nerves enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the ring of tendon at its apex: the oculomotor and the abducens, the trochlear and the abducens, the optic and the oculomotor, or the trochlear and the optic? The answer is the oculomotor and the abducens. The trochlear nerve enters above the ring and the optic nerve uses the optic canal.

Question 5200. What is the name of the rounded ridge on the floor of the fourth ventricle that overlies the nucleus of the abducens nerve? The answer is the facial colliculus. The fibers of the facial nerve loop around the abducens nucleus beneath it. That nucleus sends its fibers out to the lateral rectus muscle of the same side.

To summarize, the olfactory nerve is the only sensory pathway that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay, and its filaments cross the cribriform plate to end in the olfactory bulb. The optic nerve is a tract of the brain wrapped in meninges, and its nasal fibers cross at the chiasm so that each optic tract serves the opposite half of the visual field. The oculomotor nerve supplies four muscles that move the eye, lifts the upper lid and narrows the pupil, and its pupil fibers lie at the surface, which is why compression dilates the pupil early. The trochlear nerve is the thinnest cranial nerve, the only one to leave from the back of the brain stem, and the only one that crosses completely before it supplies the superior oblique. The trigeminal nerve is the largest, with three divisions leaving by the superior orbital fissure, the foramen rotundum and the foramen ovale, and its mandibular division alone carries motor fibers. The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus, runs a long course inside the skull and lies beside the internal carotid artery in the cavernous sinus, so it is the nerve most often stretched by raised pressure.

# Chapter 53 — Cranial Nerves, Part Two

This chapter continues the survey of the twelve cranial nerves and takes up the six that serve the face, the ear, the throat and the tongue: the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, the tenth, the eleventh and the twelfth. It holds one hundred questions, and each one states its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind from one item to the next. The nerves are followed from the brainstem to the openings they use in the skull, through the structures they supply, and on to the way a lesion of each one shows itself. Every full name is spelled out, so the chapter can be listened to on its own. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 5201. Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, the stapedius and the posterior belly of the digastric? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve, the facial nerve. It leaves the brainstem between the pons and the medulla, passes through the internal acoustic meatus, and leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.

Question 5202. Which opening does the facial nerve use to leave the skull: the jugular foramen, the foramen ovale, the stylomastoid foramen, or the hypoglossal canal? The answer is the stylomastoid foramen. It lies at the base of the skull just behind the styloid process. The jugular foramen carries the ninth, tenth and eleventh cranial nerves, and the hypoglossal canal carries the twelfth.

Question 5203. In which swelling along the facial canal do the sensory cell bodies of the facial nerve lie? The answer is the geniculate ganglion. The canal runs sideways, turns sharply backward at that swelling, and then descends to the stylomastoid foramen. The greater petrosal nerve is given off there.

Question 5204. Which nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue: the lingual nerve, the chorda tympani, the hypoglossal nerve, or the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve. It joins the lingual nerve, which belongs to the trigeminal nerve, and travels with it to the tongue.

Question 5205. Which cranial nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that make the submandibular and sublingual glands secrete? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve. The fibers leave the facial nerve as the chorda tympani and end in the submandibular ganglion. From there short fibers pass to the two glands in the floor of the mouth.

Question 5206. Which tiny muscle of the middle ear is supplied by the facial nerve, and what happens when that supply is lost? The answer is the stapedius. It attaches to the stapes and stiffens the chain of ossicles when a sound is loud. A person with a damaged facial nerve may find ordinary sounds uncomfortably loud on that side.

Question 5207. The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve, joins which nerve in the infratemporal region, and what does that nerve carry? The answer is the lingual nerve, which carries general sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue. The taste fibers travel with it but belong to the facial nerve.

Question 5208. The greater petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to which ganglion, and which gland does that ganglion then supply? The answer is the pterygopalatine ganglion, which supplies the lacrimal gland. The same pathway reaches the glands of the nose and the palate. A lesion before the geniculate ganglion therefore dries the eye as well as weakening the face.

Question 5209. Which nerve arises at the geniculate ganglion and runs forward through the skull to reach the pterygopalatine ganglion? The answer is the greater petrosal nerve. It carries the parasympathetic fibers of the facial nerve. The lesser petrosal nerve, which runs close to it, belongs to the ninth cranial nerve instead.

Question 5210. A described dissection shows a nerve leaving the skull behind the ear and dividing into branches inside a gland in front of the ear. Which gland is that, and does the nerve supply it? The answer is the parotid gland, and the facial nerve does not supply it. The nerve only passes through the gland on its way to the face.

Question 5211. A described view of the face shows five branches fanning out from in front of the ear. Which branch runs forward below the angle of the jaw and supplies the muscles of the lower lip? The answer is the marginal mandibular branch. Injury to it leaves the lower lip weak while the rest of the face still moves.

Question 5212. True or false: in a lesion of the fibers that reach the facial nucleus from the motor cortex, the forehead is spared. The answer is true. The motor neurons for the upper face receive fibers from both sides of the cortex, while those for the lower face receive fibers from the opposite side only.

Question 5213. A constructed illustration: during an operation on the parotid gland a branch running along the lower border of the jaw is divided, and later the person cannot pull down the corner of the mouth. Which branch was divided? The answer is the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve. It runs just below the angle of the mandible.

Question 5214. Name two muscles supplied by the facial nerve that are not muscles of facial expression, spoken as a list. The answer is the stapedius and the posterior belly of the digastric. The stylohyoid muscle is a third. All three lie away from the face, which is why they are often forgotten.

Question 5215. Which of these pairs belongs together: the facial nerve with the stylomastoid foramen, the facial nerve with the jugular foramen, the facial nerve with the foramen ovale, or the facial nerve with the hypoglossal canal? The answer is the facial nerve with the stylomastoid foramen. The jugular foramen carries the ninth, tenth and eleventh nerves.

Question 5216. A described series of sections through a temporal bone follows a narrow canal that runs outward, turns sharply backward at a swelling, and then descends to open at the base of the skull. Which nerve runs in that canal, and what is the swelling? The answer is the facial nerve, and the swelling is the geniculate ganglion.

Question 5217. A lesion in the facial canal just before the geniculate ganglion would interrupt which functions: only the movement of the face, only the sense of taste, only the dampening of loud sounds, or the movement of the face together with tearing and taste? The answer is the movement of the face together with tearing and taste. The branches that carry those fibers leave the trunk distal to that point.

Question 5218. Which brainstem nucleus gives the facial nerve its motor fibers, and where does the nerve emerge from the brainstem? The answer is the facial nucleus in the pons, and the nerve emerges at the junction of the pons and the medulla. It appears in the angle between the pons, the medulla and the cerebellum.

Question 5219. A constructed illustration: one side of a face is weak from the forehead down, the eye on that side cannot be closed, and tears no longer form on it. Where does the lesion most likely lie? The answer is the facial canal, proximal to the geniculate ganglion. Weakness of the whole side shows a lower motor neuron lesion, and the loss of tears places the damage before the greater petrosal nerve.

Question 5220. A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen would interrupt which of these: the movement of the lips, the sense of taste in the anterior tongue, the formation of tears, or the dampening action of the stapedius? The answer is the movement of the lips. The chorda tympani, the greater petrosal nerve and the branch to the stapedius all leave the trunk inside the facial canal.

Question 5221. Which arrangement explains why the forehead escapes in a stroke but not in Bell palsy: the upper face receives fibers from both sides of the cortex, it has no cortical supply, the facial nucleus lies below the lesion, or the trigeminal nerve supplies it? The answer is that the upper face receives fibers from both sides of the cortex. Bell palsy damages the nerve itself, so the whole side is weak.

Question 5222. Which cranial nerve carries the sense of hearing from the inner ear to the brainstem? The answer is the eighth cranial nerve, the vestibulocochlear nerve. It is a purely sensory nerve with two divisions. The cochlear division serves hearing and the vestibular division serves balance.

Question 5223. What are the two divisions of the eighth cranial nerve, and what does each serve? The answer is the cochlear division, which serves hearing, and the vestibular division, which serves balance and the sense of the position of the head. The two run together from the inner ear to the brainstem.

Question 5224. In which ganglion do the sensory cell bodies of the cochlear nerve lie? The answer is the spiral ganglion. It lies within the modiolus, the bony core around which the cochlea coils. Its fibers run from the hair cells of the organ of Corti to the cochlear nuclei.

Question 5225. Which structure sits against the oval window at the entrance to the inner ear: the malleus, the incus, the stapes, or the tympanic membrane? The answer is the stapes. Its footplate fits the oval window and passes the vibrations into the fluid of the inner ear. The tympanic membrane lies at the outer end of the chain.

Question 5226. On which membrane do the hair cells for hearing rest, and in which channel of the cochlea do they lie? The answer is the basilar membrane, in the cochlear duct. The cochlear duct is the middle of the three channels and contains endolymph. Above it lies the scala vestibuli and below it the scala tympani, both filled with perilymph.

Question 5227. A described section through the inner ear shows a spiral tube divided into three channels that meet at the apex. Which channels contain perilymph? The answer is the scala vestibuli and the scala tympani. They communicate with each other at the apex through the helicotrema.

Question 5228. The vestibular division carries fibers from which receptors? The answer is the cristae of the three semicircular canals and the maculae of the utricle and the saccule. The cristae respond to rotation, the maculae to tilting and straight-line acceleration. The fibers travel to the vestibular nuclei in the medulla and the pons.

Question 5229. True or false: the eighth cranial nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the inner ear. The answer is false. The eighth nerve is purely sensory and has no motor or secretomotor fibers at all. The nerve beside it in the internal acoustic meatus, the facial nerve, carries the parasympathetic fibers of that region.

Question 5230. A described radiograph of the skull base shows a tumor in the angle between the cerebellum and the pons, and the person has ringing in one ear and poor hearing on that side. Which division of which nerve is involved? The answer is the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve. A tumor there often begins on the vestibular fibers and presses on the cochlear fibers.

Question 5231. A constructed illustration: a person has attacks of a spinning sensation and unsteady walking, while hearing is normal on both sides. Which division of the eighth nerve is most likely affected? The answer is the vestibular division. The cochlear division is spared, which is why hearing remains normal. The receptors involved lie in the semicircular canals, the utricle and the saccule.

Question 5232. Which of these pairs belongs together: the semicircular canals with rotation of the head, the semicircular canals with straight-line acceleration, the cochlea with balance, or the utricle with hearing? The answer is the semicircular canals with rotation of the head. Their cristae respond to turning. The utricle and the saccule respond instead to straight-line acceleration and to gravity.

Question 5233. A described cross section of the internal acoustic meatus shows four bundles of nerve fibers in four quadrants. Which bundle lies in the upper front quadrant? The answer is the facial nerve. The cochlear nerve lies below it in the lower front quadrant. The two divisions of the vestibular nerve occupy the two rear quadrants.

Question 5234. In the internal acoustic meatus, which nerve lies in front of the vestibulocochlear nerve, and what does that position explain? The answer is the facial nerve. Because the facial nerve lies in front and above, a tumor of the eighth nerve often presses on it.

Question 5235. Which two openings of the inner ear are closed by membranes, and which structure closes each? The answer is the oval window, closed by the footplate of the stapes, and the round window, closed by the secondary tympanic membrane. The round window gives the fluid somewhere to move when the stapes pushes inward.

Question 5236. A constructed illustration: a person is struck on the side of the head and afterward hears a continuous ringing sound with reduced hearing, while balance is normal and the eardrum is intact. Which part of the ear most likely holds the injury? The answer is the cochlear division of the eighth nerve or the organ of Corti. The vestibular fibers and the eardrum are spared, since balance and the drum are normal.

Question 5237. Which statement about the fibers of the eighth cranial nerve is correct: the cochlear fibers end in the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem, the cochlear fibers end in the thalamus directly, the vestibular fibers end in the spinal cord, or all of its fibers cross to the opposite side? The answer is that the cochlear fibers end in the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem. The vestibular fibers end mainly in the vestibular nuclei.

Question 5238. A described transverse section of the brainstem at the junction of the pons and the medulla shows a large nerve entering from the side. Which nerve is it, and where do most of its fibers end? The answer is the eighth cranial nerve, and most of its fibers end in the cochlear and vestibular nuclei of that region. The vestibular nuclei lie deeper, beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle.

Question 5239. Which cranial nerve carries the secretomotor fibers that make the parotid gland produce saliva? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve, the glossopharyngeal nerve. Its fibers reach the gland by a long route through the middle ear and the infratemporal fossa. The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland but does not supply it.

Question 5240. Through which opening does the glossopharyngeal nerve leave the skull: the stylomastoid foramen, the jugular foramen, the foramen rotundum, or the hypoglossal canal? The answer is the jugular foramen. The ninth, tenth and eleventh cranial nerves all pass through it, together with the internal jugular vein. The stylomastoid foramen carries the facial nerve.

Question 5241. Which is the only muscle supplied by the ninth cranial nerve? The answer is the stylopharyngeus. It runs from the styloid process down into the wall of the pharynx and helps to lift the pharynx during swallowing. Every other muscle of the pharynx is supplied by the tenth cranial nerve.

Question 5242. From which part of the tongue does the ninth cranial nerve carry taste: the anterior two thirds, the posterior one third, the whole tongue, or the tip only? The answer is the posterior one third. The posterior third is also the part from which the ninth nerve carries general sensation.

Question 5243. Which nerve arises from the inferior ganglion of the ninth cranial nerve, forms a plexus on the promontory of the middle ear, and gives off the lesser petrosal nerve? The answer is the tympanic nerve. It carries the parasympathetic fibers destined for the parotid gland. The lesser petrosal nerve leaves that plexus and ends in the otic ganglion.

Question 5244. Which of these structures does the ninth cranial nerve supply with general sensation: the posterior one third of the tongue, the anterior two thirds of the tongue, the lower lip, or the skin of the forehead? The answer is the posterior one third of the tongue. The anterior two thirds take their general sensation from the lingual nerve.

Question 5245. The carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the ninth cranial nerve, ends beside which two structures in the neck, and what does each do? The answer is the carotid sinus and the carotid body. The sinus is watched for changes in blood pressure and the body for changes in the oxygen content of the blood.

Question 5246. In the gag reflex, which nerve carries the signal in and which nerve carries the movement out? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve inward and the tenth cranial nerve outward. Touching the back of the throat sends sensation along the ninth nerve to the brainstem. The muscles of the pharynx then contract through the tenth nerve.

Question 5247. True or false: the ninth cranial nerve carries both taste and general sensation from the back of the tongue. The answer is true. Its fibers for taste end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius, and its fibers for touch and pain end in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.

Question 5248. A described dissection of the neck shows a nerve lying between the internal and external carotid arteries and giving off a small branch that climbs to the fork of the carotid. Which nerve is shown, and which structure does that branch watch? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve, and the branch is the carotid sinus nerve. It watches the carotid sinus, a small swelling at the fork.

Question 5249. Which of these pairs belongs together: the glossopharyngeal nerve with the parotid gland, the glossopharyngeal nerve with the lacrimal gland, the facial nerve with the parotid gland, or the hypoglossal nerve with the submandibular gland? The answer is the glossopharyngeal nerve with the parotid gland. It passes through the parotid gland without supplying it.

Question 5250. A described section of the brainstem shows a nucleus lying deep in the medulla, close to the fourth ventricle, whose fibers travel to the parotid gland. Which nucleus is it? The answer is the inferior salivatory nucleus. Its fibers join the ninth cranial nerve and leave by the tympanic nerve.

Question 5251. Name the three structures from which the ninth cranial nerve carries sensation, spoken as a list. The answer is the posterior one third of the tongue, the tonsil, and the upper part of the pharynx. The middle ear is a fourth. All of these are places a listener can point to in the mouth and throat.

Question 5252. A described specimen shows a nerve that leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and curves forward to lie on a long slender muscle running from the styloid process to the pharynx. Which nerve is shown, and which movement does that muscle help to perform? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve, and the muscle is the stylopharyngeus, which lifts the pharynx during swallowing.

Question 5253. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the throat the gag reflex is absent on one side and taste is lost at the back of the tongue on that side, while taste at the front is normal. Which nerve was injured? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve. The gag reflex needs it for the incoming signal, and it carries taste from the posterior third.

Question 5254. Which statement about the ninth cranial nerve is correct: it carries parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland, it carries motor fibers to the muscles of the face, it carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue, or it leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen? The answer is that it carries parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland.

Question 5255. Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of the larynx and the greater part of the pharynx? The answer is the tenth cranial nerve, the vagus nerve. It is the longest cranial nerve and reaches from the neck into the abdomen. It also carries parasympathetic fibers to the heart, the lungs and the gut.

Question 5256. Through which opening does the vagus nerve leave the skull, and which other nerves pass through the same opening? The answer is the jugular foramen, through which the ninth and eleventh cranial nerves pass as well. The internal jugular vein leaves the skull through the same opening. The vagus then runs down the neck inside the carotid sheath.

Question 5257. Which muscle of the soft palate is one of the few that the vagus nerve does not supply? The answer is the tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by the trigeminal nerve. All the other muscles of the palate are reached through the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus. In the pharynx the stylopharyngeus is a separate exception.

Question 5258. Which branch of the vagus nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle: the internal laryngeal nerve, the external laryngeal nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, or the pharyngeal branch? The answer is the external laryngeal nerve. It is the smaller of the two branches of the superior laryngeal nerve. The internal laryngeal branch carries sensation from above the vocal folds.

Question 5259. Which nerve hooks around the aortic arch on the left side and around the subclavian artery on the right? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus. On the left it turns beneath the arch close to the ligamentum arteriosum. On the right it turns beneath the subclavian artery before climbing back to the larynx.

Question 5260. Which muscles of the larynx does the recurrent laryngeal nerve supply: all of them, all of them except the cricothyroid, only the cricothyroid, or only the muscles of the epiglottis? The answer is all of them except the cricothyroid. That muscle takes its supply from the external laryngeal nerve. The recurrent nerve also carries sensation from below the vocal folds.

Question 5261. Which two vessels lie immediately in front of the vagus nerve in the carotid sheath? The answer is the common carotid artery medially and the internal jugular vein laterally. The vagus lies behind and between them. All three structures share the sheath, which runs from the base of the skull to the root of the neck.

Question 5262. True or false: the vagus nerve carries taste from the epiglottis. The answer is true. The fibers end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius, the same nucleus that receives taste from the back of the tongue. The vagus also carries sensation from the lining of the larynx.

Question 5263. A described dissection of the neck shows a long nerve running down inside a fibrous sheath together with an artery and a vein. Which nerve is shown, what is the sheath, and how are the three arranged? The answer is the vagus nerve, inside the carotid sheath. The artery lies medial and the vein lateral, with the nerve behind and between them.

Question 5264. Which of these pairs belongs together: the vagus nerve with the jugular foramen, the vagus nerve with the stylomastoid foramen, the facial nerve with the jugular foramen, or the hypoglossal nerve with the foramen ovale? The answer is the vagus nerve with the jugular foramen. The ninth and eleventh cranial nerves leave by the same opening.

Question 5265. Which branch of the vagus nerve lies in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus and is at risk during operations on the thyroid gland? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It climbs upward in that groove to reach the larynx. Damage to it weakens the muscles of the vocal fold on the same side.

Question 5266. Which statement about the two vagus nerves below the lungs is correct: the left forms the anterior vagal trunk and the right the posterior trunk, the right forms the anterior trunk, the two join into a single trunk, or neither of them enters the abdomen? The answer is that the left forms the anterior vagal trunk and the right the posterior trunk.

Question 5267. A described specimen of the thorax shows a nerve on the left side descending in front of the arch of the aorta and then turning upward beneath it. Which nerve is shown, and what does it supply? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. It supplies almost all the muscles of the larynx and carries sensation from below the vocal folds.

Question 5268. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the lower neck a person is hoarse and one vocal fold does not move, while swallowing and taste are normal. Which nerve was most likely injured? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve on that side. The fibers that carry sensation above the vocal folds lie elsewhere, so swallowing is spared. The care of such a person belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 5269. Which statement explains why a tumor at the apex of the right lung may first show as hoarseness: the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the right subclavian artery close to the apex, the right phrenic nerve runs over the apex, the right vagus lies in the neck, or the trachea is pressed? The answer is that the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the right subclavian artery close to the apex.

Question 5270. A constructed illustration: a person has a weak cough and a hoarse voice, and on the same side the soft palate droops and the pharynx does not move when the back of the throat is touched. Which nerve has been injured, and where does the injury most likely lie? The answer is the tenth cranial nerve, most likely where it leaves the skull at the jugular foramen.

Question 5271. A described transverse section of the neck at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra shows a fibrous sheath containing three structures. Which are they, and which of the three lies between the other two? The answer is the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve. The nerve lies behind and between them, inside the sheath.

Question 5272. Which cranial nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve, the accessory nerve. It is a motor nerve with a cranial root and a spinal root. The spinal root arises from the upper part of the spinal cord and climbs into the skull.

Question 5273. The eleventh cranial nerve leaves the skull through which opening: the jugular foramen, the foramen magnum, the hypoglossal canal, or the stylomastoid foramen? The answer is the jugular foramen. Its spinal root, however, enters the skull through the foramen magnum before joining the cranial root. Both openings are part of its course.

Question 5274. From which part of the nervous system does the spinal root of the eleventh cranial nerve arise? The answer is the anterior horn of the upper five or six segments of the spinal cord. Its fibers leave the cord as a series of small rootlets between the front and back roots of the spinal nerves.

Question 5275. Which movement is most weakened when the eleventh cranial nerve is injured on the right side: shrugging the right shoulder, closing the right eye, protruding the tongue, or raising the right eyebrow? The answer is shrugging the right shoulder, because the trapezius on that side is weak. The trapezius also helps to rotate the shoulder blade when the arm is lifted.

Question 5276. Which two muscles form the front and back borders of the posterior triangle of the neck, and which cranial nerve crosses that triangle? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid in front and the trapezius behind, with the eleventh cranial nerve crossing the triangle. The nerve runs down toward the shoulder just beneath the skin, where it is easily injured.

Question 5277. A described dissection of the neck shows a thin nerve crossing a triangle between two large muscles and running downward toward the shoulder. Which nerve is shown, and what does it supply? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve, and it supplies the trapezius. Because it lies just beneath the skin, it is easily injured.

Question 5278. Which of these pairs belongs together: the eleventh cranial nerve with the sternocleidomastoid, the eleventh cranial nerve with the tongue, the twelfth cranial nerve with the trapezius, or the tenth cranial nerve with the shoulder? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve with the sternocleidomastoid. The same nerve supplies the trapezius as well. The twelfth nerve supplies the tongue.

Question 5279. A constructed illustration: after a biopsy of a lymph node in the back of the neck, a person cannot lift the arm above the horizontal on that side and the shoulder droops. Which nerve was injured? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve in the posterior triangle. The trapezius no longer rotates the shoulder blade, so the arm cannot be raised above the horizontal.

Question 5280. Which part of the eleventh cranial nerve joins the vagus nerve and is carried with it to the muscles of the pharynx and the larynx? The answer is the cranial root. It arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla. The spinal root, by contrast, supplies the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius.

Question 5281. Which statement about the eleventh cranial nerve is correct: it carries sensation from the skin of the shoulder, it enters the skull through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen, it supplies the muscles of the tongue, or it carries parasympathetic fibers to the larynx? The answer is that it enters through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen. It carries no parasympathetic fibers.

Question 5282. A described coronal section through the base of the skull shows a small trunk passing upward through a wide opening in the occipital bone and then running sideways to a smaller opening. Which nerve is shown, and which are the two openings? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve. It enters through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen.

Question 5283. In a described section, the spinal root of the eleventh cranial nerve and the vertebral artery both pass through one opening at the base of the skull. Which opening is it, and how do the two lie in relation to each other? The answer is the foramen magnum, with the nerve behind the artery.

Question 5284. After the eleventh cranial nerve is divided on the right side, turning the head to the left becomes weak. Which muscle and which side of the body explain that weakness: the right sternocleidomastoid, the left sternocleidomastoid, the right trapezius, or the left trapezius? The answer is the right sternocleidomastoid. Each sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side.

Question 5285. Name the two muscles supplied by the spinal root of the eleventh cranial nerve, spoken as a list, and say which of them lifts the shoulder. The answer is the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius, and the trapezius lifts the shoulder. The sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side. Both muscles are supplied on the same side as the nerve.

Question 5286. Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, the hypoglossal nerve. It supplies all the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus. That one muscle is supplied by the vagus nerve instead.

Question 5287. Through which opening does the hypoglossal nerve leave the skull: the jugular foramen, the hypoglossal canal, the foramen ovale, or the internal acoustic meatus? The answer is the hypoglossal canal. It lies in the occipital bone just above the occipital condyle. The other three openings carry other nerves and vessels.

Question 5288. Which muscle of the tongue pushes it forward and out of the mouth when it contracts: the styloglossus, the hyoglossus, the genioglossus, or the palatoglossus? The answer is the genioglossus. It runs from the front of the mandible back into the tongue and pulls the tongue forward and down. The styloglossus pulls the tongue up and back instead.

Question 5289. Which of these muscles of the tongue is not supplied by the twelfth cranial nerve: the genioglossus, the hyoglossus, the styloglossus, or the palatoglossus? The answer is the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus nerve. The other three, and all the intrinsic muscles, belong to the twelfth nerve.

Question 5290. Between which two structures does the hypoglossal nerve lie as it descends in the upper part of the neck? The answer is the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein. The nerve passes between them, lying lateral to the artery and medial to the vein. It then turns forward toward the tongue.

Question 5291. When the tongue is protruded, a person with a lesion of the twelfth cranial nerve on the left side shows the tip deviating in which direction: to the left, to the right, upward, or not at all? The answer is to the left, the side of the lesion. The intact right muscle pushes the tongue toward the weak side.

Question 5292. The hypoglossal nerve runs forward deep to which two muscles after it crosses the carotid arteries, and on which muscle does it come to lie? The answer is the posterior belly of the digastric and the stylohyoid, and it then lies on the hyoglossus. It continues forward deep to the mylohyoid. The lingual artery runs deep to the hyoglossus, below the nerve.

Question 5293. True or false: a lesion of the fibers that reach the hypoglossal nucleus from the motor cortex makes the tongue deviate toward the side of the brain lesion. The answer is false. It deviates away from the side of the brain lesion. A lesion of the nerve itself makes the tongue deviate toward the side of the lesion.

Question 5294. A described dissection of the floor of the mouth shows a nerve lying on the surface of a flat muscle that runs from the hyoid bone up into the tongue. Which nerve is shown, and on which muscle is it lying? The answer is the hypoglossal nerve, lying on the hyoglossus.

Question 5295. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the upper part of the neck a person's tongue deviates to the right when it is put out, and the right half of the tongue looks shrunken. Which nerve was injured? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve on the right side. Weakness of the right genioglossus lets the left side push the tongue to the right.

Question 5296. A described series of sections through the base of the skull follows a small canal that runs forward and slightly downward beside the occipital condyle. Which nerve passes through it, and which other structures does it carry? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, together with a small meningeal branch and an emissary vein.

Question 5297. In a described transverse section of the neck just below the base of the skull, one nerve lies between two large vessels. Name the nerve and the two vessels, and state which vessel lies medial to the nerve. The answer is the hypoglossal nerve, between the internal carotid artery medially and the internal jugular vein laterally.

Question 5298. Which statement explains why the tongue may be weak on both sides after a single small lesion in the medulla: the two hypoglossal nuclei lie close together in the midline, the genioglossus crosses the midline, the cortical fibers for the tongue cross twice, or the twelfth nerve supplies both sides of the tongue? The answer is that the two hypoglossal nuclei lie close together in the midline.

Question 5299. A constructed illustration: a person has a shrunken tongue that cannot be moved to either side, with weakness of the arms and the legs. Which nerve is failing, and what does that suggest about the site of the trouble? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, with loss of the motor neurons that supply it. A tongue weak on both sides points to the nerve cells rather than to one cortical pathway.

Question 5300. A described magnetic resonance image of the head and the upper part of the neck shows a nerve leaving the base of the skull beside the occipital condyle and running forward between two vessels. Which nerve is shown, and which group of muscles will it reach? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, which will reach the muscles of the tongue.

To summarize, the seventh cranial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and secretomotor fibers to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands, and it leaves the skull by the stylomastoid foramen. The eighth nerve is purely sensory, with a cochlear division for hearing and a vestibular division for balance, and it runs beside the facial nerve in the internal acoustic meatus. The ninth nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus, carries taste and sensation from the posterior third of the tongue and the pharynx, and sends parasympathetic fibers through the tympanic and lesser petrosal nerves to the parotid gland. The tenth nerve supplies the pharynx and the larynx and carries the recurrent laryngeal nerve around the subclavian artery on the right and the aortic arch on the left. The eleventh nerve has a cranial root that joins the vagus and a spinal root that supplies the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius, while the twelfth nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue, leaves by the hypoglossal canal, and turns the tongue toward the weak side when it fails. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 54 — Spinal Cord

This chapter follows the spinal cord from the cervical enlargement at the top to the dorsal horns that receive the sensory roots. It covers the two enlargements that serve the limbs, the gray matter with its horns, laminae and cell columns, the white matter with its funiculi and long tracts, and the dorsal horn where the sensory fibers arrive. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 5301. Which part of the spinal cord is named the cervical enlargement, and which segments form it? The answer is the widened upper part of the cord, formed by the fifth cervical to the first thoracic segments. The extra tissue there is gray matter for the muscles of the upper limb. Those roots gather into the brachial plexus.

Question 5302. Which of these parts of the cord gives rise to the nerves of the upper limb: the cervical enlargement, the lumbar enlargement, the conus medullaris, or the filum terminale? The answer is the cervical enlargement. Its fifth cervical to first thoracic segments send their roots into the brachial plexus. The lumbar enlargement supplies the lower limb instead.

Question 5303. A described transverse section is oval, wider from side to side than from front to back, with a deep fissure in front and a large ventral horn on each side. At which level was it taken? The answer is the cervical enlargement. That outline and those bulky ventral horns belong to the lower cervical segments. A thoracic section is rounder, with slender horns.

Question 5304. The cervical enlargement lies opposite which part of the vertebral column, and does the cord fill that space? The answer is opposite the lower cervical and first thoracic vertebrae, with the cord nearly filling the canal. Little cerebrospinal fluid surrounds it there. Farther down the canal widens around the cauda equina.

Question 5305. A constructed illustration: after a fall from a motorcycle, one arm hangs limp and numb while the other limbs move normally. The injury is described as a stretch of the roots that enter the cervical enlargement. Which roots are illustrated? The answer is the fifth cervical to the first thoracic roots, which form the brachial plexus. That limb loses its power and its feeling.

Question 5306. How many pairs of cervical spinal nerves leave the cervical part of the spinal cord? The answer is 8 pairs. There are 7 cervical vertebrae but 8 cervical nerves, because the first nerve leaves above the first vertebra. The eighth nerve leaves below the seventh vertebra.

Question 5307. Why is the cervical enlargement wider than the thoracic cord: because it holds more white matter, because its gray matter is enlarged for the muscles of the upper limb, because it carries the meninges, or because the canal is narrower there? The answer is that its gray matter is enlarged for the muscles of the upper limb. More motor neurons are needed there.

Question 5308. What is the name of the deep groove that runs down the front of the spinal cord and carries the anterior spinal artery? The answer is the anterior median fissure. It divides the anterior surface into two halves and reaches almost to the gray matter. The posterior median sulcus behind it is much shallower.

Question 5309. The eighth cervical spinal nerve leaves the vertebral canal at which place: above the seventh cervical vertebra, below the seventh cervical vertebra, above the sixth cervical vertebra, or through the first thoracic vertebra? The answer is below the seventh cervical vertebra. The upper seven cervical nerves pass above their own vertebrae, and the eighth has none of its own.

Question 5310. A described section of the cervical cord shows a ventral horn whose lateral part is much bulkier than its medial part, while a thoracic section shows a slender horn of even width. What does the difference indicate? The answer is that the lateral cell column serves the limb muscles. The medial column serves the deep muscles of the back at every level.

Question 5311. True or false: a transverse section of the cervical cord holds more white matter than a section of the lumbar cord. The answer is true. Every long tract that ascends or descends must pass through the cervical cord, so fibers accumulate above. The lumbar cord has proportionally more gray matter and less white matter.

Question 5312. The denticulate ligament is a fold of which membrane, and where does it attach? The answer is the pia mater, attaching to the dura between the dorsal and the ventral roots. About 21 pairs run down the sides of the cord. They hold the cord in the middle of the canal.

Question 5313. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fifth cervical to the first thoracic segments with the brachial plexus, the cervical enlargement with the lower limb, the lumbar enlargement with the phrenic nerve, or the sacral segments with the upper limb? The answer is the fifth cervical to the first thoracic segments with the brachial plexus. Those segments supply the upper limb.

Question 5314. Ventral rootlets leave the cord along which groove, and dorsal rootlets enter along which other groove? The answer is the anterolateral sulcus for the ventral rootlets and the posterolateral sulcus for the dorsal ones. The two grooves mark the front and the back of each side.

Question 5315. Which dorsal column tract is added to the cord at about the sixth thoracic segment and lies lateral to the other in the neck: the gracile tract, the cuneate tract, the spinocerebellar tract, or the corticospinal tract? The answer is the cuneate tract. It carries fibers from the upper limb, which enter above that level. The gracile tract lies medial to it.

Question 5316. Name the two tracts that lie side by side in the dorsal column of the cervical cord and say what each carries. The answer is the gracile tract, which carries sensation from the lower half of the body, and the cuneate tract, which carries sensation from the upper limb. Both carry fine touch and the sense of position.

Question 5317. In the cervical cord, is the transverse diameter or the anteroposterior diameter the greater, and why is that so? The answer is the transverse diameter. The cervical enlargement widens from side to side as the gray matter for the upper limb grows. In the thoracic cord the two diameters are nearly equal, so the section looks round.

Question 5318. A constructed illustration: an older person has neck pain and clumsy hands, and the described radiograph shows bony spurs narrowing the cervical canal. Which part of the cord is compressed, and what is lost first? The answer is the cervical enlargement, with the hands and the arms affected before the legs. The narrow canal presses on the cord.

Question 5319. A described injury drives the cervical cord backward against a bony spur, and the person loses pain and temperature feeling in both hands while touch is preserved. Which part is damaged: the dorsal columns, the central gray matter and its crossing fibers, the ventral horns alone, or the whole cord? The answer is the central gray matter and its crossing fibers, which lie nearest the center.

Question 5320. A described magnetic resonance image of the neck shows the cord as a gray band with the nerve roots leaving at each level and fluid around it. Which part of the cord is shown? The answer is the cervical cord, where the roots leave at right angles to reach the intervertebral foramina. The fluid there is scanty, so the roots are easy to follow.

Question 5321. Which spinal segments form the lumbar enlargement of the cord, and which limb does it serve? The answer is the second lumbar to the third sacral segments, and it serves the lower limb. The extra gray matter is needed for the muscles of the thigh, the leg and the foot. Its roots gather into the lumbosacral plexus.

Question 5322. Which of these parts of the cord supplies the muscles of the lower limb: the cervical enlargement, the thoracic cord, the lumbar enlargement, or the conus medullaris? The answer is the lumbar enlargement. The second lumbar to the third sacral segments give the lower limb its nerves. The conus medullaris lies below it and serves the pelvic organs.

Question 5323. A described transverse section of the cord is round, with a great deal of gray matter and comparatively little white matter around it. Which level does this describe: the upper cervical cord, the thoracic cord, the lumbar enlargement, or the conus medullaris? The answer is the lumbar enlargement, where much gray matter is needed for the lower limb.

Question 5324. The lumbar enlargement of the cord lies opposite which part of the vertebral column? The answer is the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae, roughly the ninth to the twelfth thoracic. The segments and the vertebrae no longer match one to one there. That is why a needle is placed lower.

Question 5325. A constructed illustration: a person has numbness in the saddle area and difficulty passing urine, with the strength of the legs preserved, after a described injury at the first lumbar vertebra. Which part of the cord is injured? The answer is the conus medullaris. The lowest part of the cord serves the bladder, the bowel and the skin of the saddle area.

Question 5326. At which vertebra does the spinal cord of an adult normally end? The answer is at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra, or the disc just below it. The tapered end there is the conus medullaris. Below it only roots and the filum terminale continue down the canal.

Question 5327. Which of these describes the filum terminale: a bundle of nerve roots, a thin strand of pia mater that anchors the cord, a fold of dura, or a ligament of the vertebral column? The answer is a thin strand of pia mater that anchors the cord. It runs from the tip of the conus medullaris to the coccyx. It carries no nerves.

Question 5328. A described specimen shows the lower end of the cord tapering to a point, with a sheaf of slender strands running down around a central thread. Which structures are shown? The answer is the conus medullaris, the cauda equina and the filum terminale. The strands are the lumbar and sacral roots on their way out.

Question 5329. True or false: in an adult the spinal cord ends above the level of the third lumbar vertebra. The answer is true. The cord ends at about the first lumbar vertebra, well above the third. That is why cerebrospinal fluid is sampled lower down, where the needle meets roots and fluid rather than cord.

Question 5330. The great anterior radicular artery reinforces the blood supply of the lower cord. From which side and at which level does it usually arise? The answer is the left side, at the lower thoracic or upper lumbar levels, most often between the ninth and the twelfth thoracic. It joins the anterior spinal artery and feeds the lumbar enlargement.

Question 5331. Which of these pairs belongs together: the conus medullaris with the tapered end of the cord, the filum terminale with the brachial plexus, the cauda equina with the upper cervical cord, or the lumbar cistern with the fourth ventricle? The answer is the conus medullaris with the tapered end of the cord, which the filum anchors.

Question 5332. Why is a lumbar puncture performed below the second lumbar vertebra in an adult: because the cord ends above that level, because the canal is wider there, because the fluid is cleaner there, or because the roots are absent there? The answer is that the cord ends above that level. The needle enters the lumbar cistern, where the roots float in cerebrospinal fluid.

Question 5333. Name two structures that hold the lower end of the spinal cord in place within the vertebral canal. The answer is the filum terminale and the denticulate ligaments. The filum runs from the tip of the conus medullaris to the coccyx, and the denticulate ligaments fix the sides of the cord to the dura.

Question 5334. Why does the distance between a spinal segment and its matching vertebra grow larger toward the lower end of the column? The answer is that the vertebral column grows faster than the cord. The cord keeps its upper attachments, so its segments are drawn upward. The lower roots must travel far before they leave.

Question 5335. A constructed illustration: after a described injury at the third lumbar vertebra, a person has severe pain down both legs, weakness of both feet and loss of the ankle reflexes, while the saddle area is spared. Which structure is injured? The answer is the cauda equina, the bundle of the lower roots. Each root serves a strip of skin, so both legs are affected.

Question 5336. In the dorsal column of the lumbar cord, which tract is present: the gracile tract alone, the cuneate tract alone, both tracts, or neither tract? The answer is the gracile tract alone. Below the sixth thoracic segment all the entering fibers join the gracile tract, so the cuneate tract has not yet begun.

Question 5337. A described radiograph after a contrast injection shows a column of fluid in the lower canal with fine parallel lines crossing it and no cord visible. Which space has been filled? The answer is the lumbar cistern. The lines are the roots of the cauda equina floating in the fluid. The cord ended above the level that is shown.

Question 5338. What is the name of the widened part of the subarachnoid space below the end of the cord, and what does it contain? The answer is the lumbar cistern, which contains cerebrospinal fluid and the roots of the cauda equina. It extends from the second lumbar vertebra to the second sacral vertebra.

Question 5339. What shape does the gray matter of the spinal cord take in a transverse section? The answer is the shape of a butterfly or a letter H. The two broad ventral horns and the two narrower dorsal horns join across the middle. The white matter surrounds the gray matter on every side.

Question 5340. Which statement about the horns of the gray matter is correct: the dorsal horns are sensory and the ventral horns motor, the dorsal horns are motor and the ventral sensory, both are motor, or both are sensory? The answer is that the dorsal horns are sensory and the ventral horns motor. The dorsal roots carry sensation in, and the ventral horns send axons out.
