The answer is the dorsal root ganglion. Its fiber enters the cord and ascends in the cuneate fasciculus. It ends in the nucleus cuneatus of the medulla.

Question 5761. True or false: the corticospinal tract takes most of its fibers from the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe. The answer is true. The large motor cells of that gyrus give rise to the tract. Its fibers pass through the internal capsule and the brainstem to reach the spinal cord.

Question 5762. Which part of the internal capsule carries the corticospinal fibers on their way from the cortex to the brainstem: the anterior limb, the genu, the posterior limb, or the part behind the lentiform nucleus? The answer is the posterior limb. It is a narrow band of white matter between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus. A small lesion there causes a dense weakness of the opposite side.

Question 5763. Roughly what share of the corticospinal fibers cross in the medulla oblongata, and what is that crossing called? The answer is about nine in ten, at the decussation of the pyramids. The remainder descends uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract. Those fibers cross later, at the segment where they end.

Question 5764. A described section of the spinal cord shows a small bundle of fibers beside the anterior median fissure on each side. Which tract is shown: the anterior corticospinal tract, the lateral corticospinal tract, the dorsal column, or the spinothalamic tract? The answer is the anterior corticospinal tract. It holds the fibers that did not cross in the medulla, and they cross in the cord where they end.

Question 5765. Which pair belongs together: the lateral corticospinal tract with the distal muscles of the limbs, the anterior corticospinal tract with the muscles of the face, the dorsal column with pain, or the spinothalamic tract with vibration? The answer is the lateral corticospinal tract with the distal muscles of the limbs. The anterior tract supplies the axial muscles of the trunk. Fine touch and vibration belong to the dorsal columns.

Question 5766. Which descending tract carries fibers that end on the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves and control the muscles of the face, the tongue and the throat? The answer is the corticobulbar tract. It runs with the corticospinal fibers through the internal capsule. The word bulbar refers to the brainstem.

Question 5767. Which statement about the endings of the corticospinal tract is correct: every fiber ends on a lower motor neuron, most fibers end on interneurons of the spinal gray matter, the tract carries sensation upward, or all of it crosses in the spinal cord? The answer is that most of its fibers end on interneurons. Only a few end directly on the large motor cells of the fingers and the toes.

Question 5768. A constructed illustration: after a small stroke, one arm, one leg and the lower part of the face are weak on the same side of the body. Where is the lesion? The answer is in the internal capsule on the opposite side. Motor fibers run close together there, so one small lesion can weaken a whole side. The illustration is not a record of a real case.

Question 5769. Which large cells of the motor cortex give rise to the thickest fibers of the corticospinal tract? The answer is the large pyramidal cells of Betz. They lie in the precentral gyrus. Their thick axons conduct impulses quickly to the lower motor neurons of the limbs.

Question 5770. A described drawing of the precentral gyrus shows a map in which the foot lies at the top and the face at the bottom, with a huge area for the hand. Which map is shown? The answer is the motor homunculus. The body is represented upside down, and the hand and the face take a share far larger than their size.

Question 5771. Which gyrus lies immediately behind the central sulcus and receives the fibers of the sensory pathways? The answer is the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. It is the primary somatosensory cortex. The precentral gyrus in front of the sulcus is the motor cortex.

Question 5772. Which artery supplies most of the lateral surface of the hemisphere, including the motor and sensory areas for the face and the hand: the anterior cerebral artery, the middle cerebral artery, the posterior cerebral artery, or the basilar artery? The answer is the middle cerebral artery. Its branches run in the lateral sulcus. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface as far back as the foot area.

Question 5773. Which tract carries the sense of position from the leg to the cerebellum without crossing, and through which peduncle does it enter? The answer is the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, which enters through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It carries information from the muscle spindles and tendons of the lower limb. The cerebellum uses it to adjust posture and movement.

Question 5774. Which pair belongs together: the cuneocerebellar tract with the upper limb, the dorsal spinocerebellar tract with the face, the ventral spinocerebellar tract with the eye, or the olivocerebellar fibers with the cerebral cortex? The answer is the cuneocerebellar tract with the upper limb. It carries position sense from the arm and the neck. The dorsal spinocerebellar tract serves the lower limb and the trunk.

Question 5775. Which structure lies between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus and carries both motor and sensory fibers: the corpus callosum, the internal capsule, the fornix, or the cingulum? The answer is the internal capsule. Its fibers run between the two masses of gray matter. A lesion there interrupts a wide range of ascending and descending traffic.

Question 5776. True or false: in an upper motor neuron lesion the muscles become flaccid and wasted and the reflexes are lost. The answer is false. Those are the signs of a lower motor neuron lesion. An upper motor neuron lesion produces spasticity, increased reflexes and an extensor plantar response.

Question 5777. A constructed illustration: one corner of the mouth droops and the arm and the leg on that same side are weak and spastic. Is the lesion above or below the crossing of the corticospinal tract? The answer is above the crossing, in the brain or the brainstem. A single lesion above the medulla weakens the face and the limbs on one side, while a lesion below it would spare the face.

Question 5778. Name two signs of an upper motor neuron lesion and two signs of a lower motor neuron lesion, spoken as a list. The answer is spasticity and increased reflexes for the upper lesion, and flaccidity and wasting for the lower one. The plantar response is extensor in the upper lesion. The tone falls and the reflexes fade in the lower one.

Question 5779. Within the posterior funiculus, which bundle lies medial and which lateral, and what does that arrangement reflect about the body? The answer is that the gracile bundle lies medial and the cuneate bundle lateral. Fibers from the lower limb enter first and are pushed medially as the cord is built upward. Fibers from the upper limb enter higher and stay lateral.

Question 5780. A described section of the midbrain shows a pair of large bundles at the front, each filled with fibers descending from the cortex. Which tracts do those bundles carry? The answer is the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, within the cerebral peduncles. They lie at the front of the midbrain, in the crus cerebri. The substantia nigra lies just behind them.

Question 5781. Which nucleus lies immediately lateral to the cuneate nucleus in the lower medulla, and what sensation does it serve? The answer is the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, which serves pain and temperature from the face. It lies dorsolateral to the cuneate nucleus. The fibers that end there descend in the spinal tract of the same nerve before they cross.

Question 5782. Where do the fibers of the dorsal column pathway cross to the opposite side: in the spinal cord, in the medulla oblongata, in the pons, or in the thalamus? The answer is in the medulla oblongata. They cross as the internal arcuate fibers. The spinothalamic fibers cross in the spinal cord instead.

Question 5783. Which structure is the last relay before the sensory cortex for touch and position sense from the body? The answer is the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus. It lies in the ventral tier of the thalamus. From there the fibers pass through the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus.

Question 5784. A constructed illustration: a person loses pain and temperature sense over the right side of the face and over the left side of the body, with hoarseness and difficulty in swallowing. Where is the lesion? The answer is the lateral medulla on the right side. The spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve are involved before they cross, so the face loses the same sensations on the same side.

Question 5785. A described microscopic section of the spinal cord is stained to show myelin, and a wedge of white matter lies between the posterior gray horn and the posterior median septum. Which funiculus is shown? The answer is the posterior funiculus. It carries the dorsal column fibers upward. Its two bundles are the gracile and the cuneate fasciculi.

Question 5786. Which statement about the spinothalamic tract is correct: it crosses where it enters, it crosses one or two segments above entry, it crosses in the medulla, or it does not cross at all? The answer is that it crosses one or two segments above entry. That crossing lies in the anterior white commissure, so a small cord lesion can spare pain sense at the entering segment.

Question 5787. Which statement is correct: all these sensations travel in one tract, fine touch and vibration travel in the dorsal columns while pain travels in the spinothalamic tract, pain travels in the dorsal columns with vibration, or both pathways cross at the same level? The answer is that fine touch and vibration travel in the dorsal columns while pain travels in the spinothalamic tract. They cross at different levels.

Question 5788. Which pair belongs together: the precentral gyrus with motor control, the postcentral gyrus with the primary visual area, the occipital lobe with hearing, or the temporal lobe with touch? The answer is the precentral gyrus with motor control. The postcentral gyrus is the primary sensory area. Hearing belongs to the temporal lobe and vision to the occipital lobe.

Question 5789. Which long descending tract lies in the anterior funiculus, comes from the vestibular nuclei, and helps to keep posture and muscle tone? The answer is the vestibulospinal tract. It descends uncrossed for the most part. The reticulospinal tract lies beside it and serves similar postural work.

Question 5790. A described brain slice shows a band of white matter running between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus, with a smaller band in front of the thalamus. Which parts of the internal capsule are shown? The answer is the posterior limb and the anterior limb. The genu lies between them and carries the corticobulbar fibers. The posterior limb carries the corticospinal and the sensory fibers.

Question 5791. Which tract lies immediately behind the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord, and which tract lies just lateral to it? The answer is the anterior corticospinal tract, with the anterior spinothalamic tract beside it. Both run in the anterior funiculus. The lateral funiculus behind them holds the lateral corticospinal and the lateral spinothalamic tracts.

Question 5792. Which function belongs to the cerebellum: the conscious perception of touch, the coordination of movement, the secretion of cerebrospinal fluid, or the relay of pain to the cortex? The answer is the coordination of movement. The cerebellum compares the intention of the motor cortex with what the body is actually doing. It acts through the thalamus and the brainstem rather than directly on the lower motor neurons.

Question 5793. A constructed illustration: a person has a tremor that is worst at rest, with rigidity and slow movement, and degeneration is found in the midbrain. Which cells have been lost? The answer is the pigmented cells of the substantia nigra. They send fibers to the striatum and help to smooth the output of the motor cortex, so their loss makes movement slow and stiff.

Question 5794. How does the medial lemniscus run through the brainstem: downward to the spinal cord, upward and laterally through the medulla, the pons and the midbrain to the thalamus, sideways between the hemispheres, or upward through the cerebellum? The answer is upward and laterally through the medulla, the pons and the midbrain to the thalamus. It lies near the midline at first and swings outward as it ascends.

Question 5795. In which part of the nervous system do the cell bodies of the lower motor neurons that supply the muscles of the arm lie? The answer is the anterior horn of the cervical spinal cord. Their axons leave through the ventral roots. They end on the muscle fibers at the motor end plates.

Question 5796. A described cross section of the spinal cord shows a great deal of white matter around a small central mass of gray matter, with a slender posterior horn. Which region of the cord is shown? The answer is the cervical region. White matter is greatest there because many fibers have not yet left the cord. The anterior horn is broad in the regions that supply the limbs.

Question 5797. A constructed illustration: after a penetrating wound of the back, a person has lost position sense in the right leg but retains normal pain and temperature sense. Which tract has been cut: the right dorsal column, the left dorsal column, the right spinothalamic tract, or the left spinothalamic tract? The answer is the right dorsal column, whose fibers have not crossed, so the loss lies on the same side.

Question 5798. Which nucleus of the trigeminal nerve carries the sense of position from the face and the jaw, and where does it lie? The answer is the mesencephalic nucleus, which lies in the midbrain. It is the only sensory nucleus of the brainstem that holds the cell bodies of first order neurons. Its fibers join the pathway that runs to the thalamus.

Question 5799. Which two tracts lie side by side in the anterior funiculus of the spinal cord, one carrying sensation and the other carrying movement? The answer is the anterior spinothalamic tract and the anterior corticospinal tract. The sensory tract lies nearer the surface and the motor tract near the anterior median fissure. Both are small beside the lateral tracts.

Question 5800. Which statement about the crossing of the sensory pathways is correct: all sensory fibers cross where they enter, all cross in the brainstem, some cross in the cord and some in the brainstem, or none of them cross? The answer is that some cross in the cord and some in the brainstem. Pain and temperature cross in the spinal cord, while fine touch and position sense cross in the medulla.

To summarize, the brain and the spinal cord are wrapped in the dura mater, the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, and the cerebrospinal fluid that fills the ventricles and the subarachnoid space is made by the choroid plexus and returned to the blood by the arachnoid granulations. The dural folds divide the cranial cavity, and the venous sinuses they enclose drain the blood of the brain; the middle meningeal artery, the bridging veins and the cavernous sinus are the structures most often named in clinical accounts of the meninges. Pain and temperature cross in the spinal cord while fine touch and position sense cross in the medulla, and the motor pathways descend through the internal capsule and the brainstem. Knowing where each pathway crosses is what turns a lost sensation or a lost strength into a named lesion. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 59 — Major Sensory and Motor Pathways

This chapter follows the great sensory and motor pathways from the receptor to the cortex, and from the cortex back to the muscle. It covers the dorsal column and medial lemniscus pathway, the spinothalamic and trigeminal routes for pain and temperature, the pathways of taste, smell, sight and hearing, and then the descending tracts, the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers, the brainstem motor tracts, the cerebellum and the basal ganglia. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer and its reason at once. Every pathway is described in words rather than shown in a diagram, so that it can be followed by ear. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 5801. Which ascending pathway carries fine touch, vibration and the sense of position from the limbs to the cerebral cortex? The answer is the dorsal column and medial lemniscus pathway. Its fibers run up the back of the cord on the same side, cross in the medulla and end in the thalamus. Pain travels by a different route.

Question 5802. Which region sends its fibers into the fasciculus gracilis: the lower limb, the upper limb, the face, or the abdominal organs? The answer is the lower limb and the lower trunk. That bundle lies on the medial side of the dorsal column. Fibers from the upper limb run beside it in the fasciculus cuneatus.

Question 5803. In which part of the brain do the fibers of the fasciculus gracilis end? The answer is the nucleus gracilis, in the lower medulla. That nucleus lies beside the nucleus cuneatus, which receives the fibers from the upper limb. The cells there are the second neurons of the pathway.

Question 5804. At the back of the medulla, which of the two dorsal column bundles lies lateral to the other? The answer is the fasciculus cuneatus, which lies lateral to the fasciculus gracilis. It carries the fibers from the upper limb and the upper trunk, so it lies beside the cuneate nucleus. The gracile bundle lies nearest the midline.

Question 5805. A described transverse section of the lower medulla shows a stream of fibers arching across the midline just behind the pyramids. Which crossing is shown, and what does it form? The answer is the sensory decussation, formed by the internal arcuate fibers. Those fibers come from the two dorsal column nuclei and gather into the medial lemniscus.

Question 5806. True or false: the fibers of the dorsal column pathway cross the midline in the midbrain. The answer is false. They cross in the lower medulla as the internal arcuate fibers, which form the sensory decussation. By the time they reach the midbrain they have long been on the opposite side.

Question 5807. Which nucleus of the thalamus receives the medial lemniscus? The answer is the ventral posterolateral nucleus. It lies in the lateral part of the thalamus and receives fibers from the opposite side of the body. Its cells send the pathway on to the postcentral gyrus.

Question 5808. Where do the fibers of the dorsal column pathway end in the cortex: the precentral gyrus, the postcentral gyrus, the temporal lobe, or the occipital lobe? The answer is the postcentral gyrus. It is the primary sensory area for the body, and the fibers from the leg end on its medial surface. The precentral gyrus is the motor area instead.

Question 5809. In a coronal section of the hemisphere, where does the sensory area for the foot lie, and which artery supplies it? The answer is on the medial surface in the paracentral lobule, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. The areas for the hand and the face lie out on the convexity, in the territory of the middle cerebral artery.

Question 5810. Which cell gives rise to the first neuron of the pain and temperature pathway? The answer is the cell in the dorsal root ganglion. Its fiber enters the cord and ends in the dorsal horn of the same segment or one nearby. The axon that then crosses the midline belongs to the second neuron.

Question 5811. Where do the fibers of the pain pathway cross to the opposite side: in the anterior white commissure, in the medulla, in the pons, or in the thalamus? The answer is the anterior white commissure. They cross close to the central canal within a segment or two of their entry, and then ascend in the lateral funiculus.

Question 5812. Within the medulla, which structure lies immediately dorsal to the pyramids? The answer is the medial lemniscus. The pyramids carry the corticospinal fibers downward on the front of the medulla, and the lemniscus lies just behind them. Near the midline the two lemnisci lie side by side.

Question 5813. A described transverse section of the cord shows a small cavity at the center of the gray matter, with the crossing fibers just in front of it destroyed while the dorsal columns and the corticospinal tracts look intact. Which fibers are destroyed, and what loss follows? The answer is the crossing spinothalamic fibers, with loss of pain and temperature on both sides.

Question 5814. A constructed illustration: a person loses the sense of pain and temperature over both shoulders and arms, while position sense is preserved, and a cavity is found in the center of the cervical cord. Which fibers have been destroyed? The answer is the crossing spinothalamic fibers near the central canal. Because they cross close to the center, one lesion cuts the fibers from both sides at those segments.

Question 5815. Within the lateral spinothalamic tract, which fibers lie most laterally: those from the sacral segments, the cervical segments, the thoracic segments, or the face? The answer is the fibers from the sacral segments. The tract is laminated, with the sacral fibers outside and the cervical fibers inside. The face is carried elsewhere.

Question 5816. What name is given to the group of tracts that carry pain, temperature and crude touch upward on the front and side of the spinal cord? The answer is the anterolateral system. It includes the spinothalamic, the spinoreticular and the spinomesencephalic tracts. All of them cross the midline close to the segment where they enter.

Question 5817. A described operation divides the anterolateral quadrant of the cord on one side to relieve pain. From which side of the body below the cut is the pain relieved: the same side, the opposite side, both sides, or neither side? The answer is the opposite side. Those fibers have already crossed, so cutting them on one side removes pain from the other. The dorsal column lies behind and is spared.

Question 5818. A constructed illustration: a wound divides the right half of the cord at the sixth thoracic segment. Which sensory loss appears on the right below the wound, and which on the left? The answer is loss of position sense on the right and loss of pain and temperature on the left. The dorsal column fibers cross only in the medulla, while the pain fibers have already crossed in the cord.

Question 5819. In which thalamic nucleus does the second neuron of the pain pathway end: the ventral posterolateral nucleus, the ventral posteromedial nucleus, the lateral geniculate body, or the medial geniculate body? The answer is the ventral posterolateral nucleus. That nucleus receives fibers from the trunk and the limbs. The ventral posteromedial nucleus receives fibers from the face instead.

Question 5820. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fasciculus gracilis with the upper limb, the fasciculus cuneatus with the lower limb, the substantia gelatinosa with the finest pain fibers, or the nucleus gracilis with the face? The answer is the substantia gelatinosa with the finest pain fibers. The gracile bundle carries the lower limb and the cuneate bundle the upper limb.

Question 5821. Which nucleus of the brainstem receives the fibers that carry pain and temperature from the face? The answer is the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. It runs down through the medulla and into the upper cervical cord. Its fibers cross to the opposite side and join the trigeminal lemniscus.

Question 5822. Which nucleus of the head is the only one whose primary cell bodies lie inside the central nervous system: the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, the principal sensory nucleus, the mesencephalic nucleus, or the solitary nucleus? The answer is the mesencephalic nucleus, which carries position sense from the jaw. Every other sensory system keeps its first cell body outside.

Question 5823. Which thalamic nucleus receives the fibers that carry touch from the face? The answer is the ventral posteromedial nucleus. The principal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve sends its crossed fibers there. It lies next to the ventral posterolateral nucleus, which serves the rest of the body.

Question 5824. A described transverse section of the pons shows a large sensory root entering the side of the brainstem and ending in a nucleus beside the motor nucleus of the same nerve. Which nerve is shown, and which nucleus receives the fibers? The answer is the trigeminal nerve, with its principal sensory nucleus. Some of its fibers turn downward into the spinal nucleus.

Question 5825. A constructed illustration: the surface of the eye is touched lightly, and one eye fails to blink. Which nerve carries the sensation, and which carries the command to the muscle? The answer is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and the facial nerve. The first carries the sensation inward, and the second supplies the muscle that closes the lid.

Question 5826. Where do the fibers that carry pain from the face cross the midline: in the midbrain, in the pons, in the medulla and upper cervical cord close to their nucleus, or in the thalamus? The answer is the medulla and upper cervical cord, close to the spinal nucleus. They cross as they leave it and then form the trigeminal lemniscus.

Question 5827. Which nucleus of the brainstem receives the fibers that carry taste from the tongue? The answer is the nucleus of the solitary tract. The fibers arrive with the seventh, the ninth and the tenth cranial nerves. From there the pathway runs to the thalamus and then to the cortex beside the tongue area.

Question 5828. Taste from the front two thirds of the tongue travels by which route: the chorda tympani joining the seventh cranial nerve, the glossopharyngeal nerve alone, the vagus nerve, or the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the chorda tympani joining the seventh cranial nerve. The back third of the tongue is served by the ninth. The hypoglossal nerve carries movement only.

Question 5829. A described section of the medulla shows a lesion at its lateral edge that destroys the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve and the spinothalamic tract on that side. Which losses follow? The answer is loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side of the body and on the same side of the face, because the body fibers have crossed while the facial fibers have not.

Question 5830. Which sensory pathway reaches the cerebral cortex without a relay in the thalamus? The answer is the olfactory pathway. Its fibers run from the olfactory bulb directly to the primary olfactory cortex. Every other sensory pathway is relayed through a thalamic nucleus first.

Question 5831. Which structure is the relay of the visual pathway between the optic tract and the visual cortex: the medial geniculate body, the lateral geniculate body, the pulvinar, or the superior colliculus? The answer is the lateral geniculate body. It lies at the back of the thalamus and sends its fibers along the optic radiation. The medial geniculate body serves hearing.

Question 5832. A described map of the visual pathway marks a lesion at the optic chiasm that divides only the crossing fibers. Which part of the visual field is lost? The answer is the temporal half of each visual field. The crossing fibers come from the nasal half of each retina, which receives light from the temporal field.

Question 5833. Which part of the midbrain is a relay station for hearing on the way to the thalamus? The answer is the inferior colliculus. It lies on the back of the midbrain below the superior colliculus. From it the fibers run to the medial geniculate body and then to the temporal lobe.

Question 5834. Which part of the visual field is lost when the fibers of the optic radiation that sweep forward into the temporal lobe are destroyed: the upper part of the opposite field, the lower part of that field, the same side of the field, or the whole field? The answer is the upper part of the opposite field. That sweep is Meyer's loop, and the parietal fibers carry the lower part instead.

Question 5835. Which tract runs through the brainstem just beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle, close to the midline, and links the nuclei that move the two eyes together? The answer is the medial longitudinal fasciculus. It joins the abducens nucleus on one side to the oculomotor nucleus on the other, and it also carries fibers for the neck reflexes.

Question 5836. A constructed illustration: a person looks to the left, and the right eye fails to turn inward while the left eye turns out normally. Which structure is damaged? The answer is the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the left side, which carries the command from the left abducens nucleus to the right oculomotor nucleus. Convergence is preserved because that pathway lies outside.

Question 5837. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medial geniculate body with vision, the lateral geniculate body with hearing, the ventral posteromedial nucleus with the face, or the ventral posterolateral nucleus with the face? The answer is the ventral posteromedial nucleus with the face. The lateral geniculate body serves vision and the medial geniculate body serves hearing.

Question 5838. Name the two nuclei of the lower medulla that receive the fibers of the dorsal columns, spoken as a list. The answer is the nucleus gracilis and the nucleus cuneatus. The first receives the fibers from the lower limb and the lower trunk. The second receives the fibers from the upper limb and the upper trunk.

Question 5839. Which cells of the cerebral cortex give rise to the large fibers of the corticospinal tract? The answer is the large pyramidal cells of the fifth layer of the motor cortex, named for Betz. They lie chiefly in the precentral gyrus. Their axons form the longest descending pathway in the body.

Question 5840. From which gyrus of the cerebral cortex does the corticospinal tract arise: the postcentral gyrus, the precentral gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus, or the cingulate gyrus? The answer is the precentral gyrus. Cells in its fifth layer send their axons downward, and the area for the leg lies on the medial surface. The postcentral gyrus is the sensory area.

Question 5841. Through which part of the internal capsule do the corticospinal fibers pass on their way to the brainstem? The answer is the posterior limb. They run there in company with the sensory fibers that are traveling upward to the cortex. The fibers for the head lie nearest the bend, in the genu.

Question 5842. A described transverse section of the midbrain shows two large bundles of fibers on the front, one on each side, with a dark band of pigment behind them. Which structure are the bundles, and what lies in the dark band? The answer is the crus cerebri, with the substantia nigra behind it. The fibers for the head lie at the medial edge of each crus.

Question 5843. In the crus cerebri of the midbrain, which fibers lie nearest the midline: those for the head, those for the leg, those for the arm, or those for the trunk? The answer is those for the head. They lie at the medial edge, and the fibers for the leg lie farthest out.

Question 5844. As the corticospinal fibers leave the cortex and gather toward the internal capsule, how do they run: as a fan called the corona radiata, as a compact bundle in the centrum semiovale, as a single tract in the anterior limb, or as a crossing bundle in the corpus callosum? The answer is as a fan called the corona radiata. The fibers converge from a wide area of cortex toward the narrow capsule.

Question 5845. At which level do most of the corticospinal fibers cross the midline, and what is that crossing called? The answer is the lower medulla, at the decussation of the pyramids. About nine tenths of the fibers cross there and descend in the lateral funiculus. The rest continue on the same side in the anterior funiculus.

Question 5846. What proportion of the corticospinal fibers crosses at the decussation of the pyramids: about one tenth, about one half, about nine tenths, or all of them? The answer is about nine tenths. The remainder stays on the same side and forms the anterior corticospinal tract. Those fibers cross later, close to the segments they supply.

Question 5847. A described transverse section of the mid-thoracic cord shows a compact oval bundle in the lateral funiculus, lying among the fibers of the lateral column. Which tract is it, and where do its fibers end? The answer is the lateral corticospinal tract, whose fibers end on the motor neurons of the same side. The fibers for the leg lie farthest out within it.

Question 5848. Within the lateral corticospinal tract, which fibers lie farthest from the gray matter: those for the sacral segments, the cervical segments, the thoracic segments, or the face? The answer is the fibers for the sacral segments. They lie at the outer edge, so a lesion pressing on the surface weakens the legs before the arms.

Question 5849. Which tract descends in the anterior funiculus, crosses in the segment it supplies, and ends on the motor neurons of the trunk muscles: the lateral corticospinal, the anterior corticospinal, the rubrospinal, or the vestibulospinal tract? The answer is the anterior corticospinal tract. It carries the minority of the corticospinal fibers that did not cross in the medulla.

Question 5850. A constructed illustration: a small lesion destroys the posterior limb of the internal capsule on the left side. What pattern of weakness and sensory loss appears? The answer is weakness of the right side of the body with loss of sensation on the same side. Motor and sensory fibers are packed together there, so a small lesion produces a dense deficit.

Question 5851. Which sign of an upper motor neuron lesion is looked for by stroking the sole of the foot? The answer is the Babinski sign. The great toe extends slowly and the other toes spread instead of curling down. The same response occurs in a healthy infant before the tract matures.

Question 5852. Which set of findings belongs to a lower motor neuron lesion: spasticity with exaggerated reflexes, flaccid weakness with wasting and loss of reflexes, a positive Babinski sign with clonus, or weakness without any change in tone? The answer is flaccid weakness with wasting and loss of reflexes. Spasticity with a positive Babinski sign points to a lesion above the decussation.

Question 5853. True or false: most corticospinal fibers end directly on the motor neurons of the spinal cord. The answer is false. Most of them end on small interneurons that then pass the command to the motor neurons. A minority, mainly those serving the hands and the feet, end directly on the motor neurons.

Question 5854. A constructed illustration: one person has a weak, wasted limb with absent reflexes after a nerve injury, and another has a stiff, weak limb with brisk reflexes after a lesion higher up. Which of the two has the upper motor neuron lesion? The answer is the second person, with the stiff limb and the brisk reflexes. Wasting and lost reflexes point to the lower motor neuron.

Question 5855. Name two signs that follow a lesion of the lower motor neuron, spoken as a list. The answer is wasting of the muscle and loss of its reflexes. The muscle also becomes flaccid and may show fine twitching. Sensation is unaffected, because the sensory fibers run by a separate route.

Question 5856. Through which part of the internal capsule do the cortical fibers for the muscles of the head and neck pass? The answer is the genu, the bend between the anterior and the posterior limbs. They lie there in front of the fibers for the limbs. Below, they end on the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves in the brainstem.

Question 5857. A lesion of the left motor cortex weakens the lower half of the face on the right, yet the forehead moves. Why: the upper half is supplied from both sides, the lower half is supplied from both sides, the facial nerve is spared, or the trigeminal nerve takes over? The answer is that the upper half is supplied from both sides. The lower half comes only from the opposite hemisphere.

Question 5858. Which cranial nerve nucleus lies close to the midline of the medulla, beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle, and is reached by cortical fibers from both sides? The answer is the nucleus of the twelfth cranial nerve, which moves the tongue. A lesion of one cortical area therefore does not paralyze the tongue.

Question 5859. A described illustration shows two faces. In the first the whole of one side of the face is weak, forehead included, and in the second only the lower half is weak. Which lesion lies behind the second picture? The answer is a lesion of the motor cortex or of its fibers above the nucleus. The forehead is spared because it receives fibers from both hemispheres.

Question 5860. Which of these pairs belongs together: the twelfth cranial nerve nucleus with the muscles of the tongue, the seventh with the muscles of chewing, the fifth with the muscles of the face, or the tenth with the muscles of the eye? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve nucleus with the muscles of the tongue. The fifth serves chewing and the seventh the face.

Question 5861. A constructed illustration: a deep cut in the neck on one side leaves the tongue pushed toward the weak side when it is put out, with no loss of sensation. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve on that side. The tongue is pushed across by the healthy muscle on the other side.

Question 5862. By which course do the cortical fibers reach the nucleus that moves the tongue: through the genu of the internal capsule, through the posterior limb on the same side only, through the dorsal column, or from the cerebellum? The answer is through the genu of the internal capsule. They cross on the way down and reach the nucleus mainly from the opposite hemisphere.

Question 5863. Which descending tract begins in the red nucleus, crosses in the midbrain and ends in the cervical cord, where it helps to control the muscles of the upper limb? The answer is the rubrospinal tract. It crosses just below the red nucleus, in the ventral tegmental decussation. Its fibers lie in front of the lateral corticospinal tract in the cord.

Question 5864. Which descending tract arises in the vestibular nuclei, runs uncrossed in the anterior funiculus, and increases the tone of the extensor muscles that keep a person upright: the rubrospinal, the vestibulospinal, the tectospinal, or the reticulospinal tract? The answer is the vestibulospinal tract. It carries signals from the inner ear and the cerebellum to the muscles that resist gravity.

Question 5865. Which descending tract begins in the superior colliculus of the midbrain and turns the head toward a sudden sight or sound? The answer is the tectospinal tract. It crosses in the midbrain before descending. Its fibers run in the anterior funiculus of the cervical cord, close to the midline.

Question 5866. A described diagram of the brainstem marks a scattered network of cells running through the pons and the medulla, with fibers passing down on both sides of the cord. Which system is shown, and what does it do? The answer is the reticular formation and its descending tracts, which set the level of activity of the cord and adjust posture and muscle tone.

Question 5867. True or false: the rubrospinal tract crosses the midline in the midbrain and ends mainly on the motor neurons of the upper limb. The answer is true. It crosses in the ventral tegmental decussation below the red nucleus. Its fibers reach the cervical enlargement, where they help to control the flexor muscles of the arm.

Question 5868. Which of these descending tracts arises in the cerebral cortex: the rubrospinal, the vestibulospinal, the reticulospinal, or the corticospinal tract? The answer is the corticospinal tract. It begins in the precentral gyrus and ends on the motor neurons of the cord. The other three begin in the brainstem and belong to the older system for posture.

Question 5869. Which group of cells in the dorsal horn gives rise to the tract that carries unconscious position sense from the lower limb to the cerebellum? The answer is the nucleus thoracicus, also called the dorsal nucleus or the column of Clarke. It lies from the first thoracic to the second lumbar segment, and its fibers ascend on the same side.

Question 5870. Which statement about the ventral spinocerebellar tract is correct: it crosses twice, it never crosses, it crosses only in the medulla, or it ends in the thalamus? The answer is that it crosses twice. Its fibers cross in the cord, run up on the opposite side and cross again in the superior cerebellar peduncle.

Question 5871. A described dissection of the cerebellum shows three pairs of thick stalks joining it to the brainstem, one above, one in the middle and one below. Which stalks are they, and which carries most of the entering fibers from the pons? The answer is the superior, the middle and the inferior cerebellar peduncles, and the middle one carries the pontine fibers.

Question 5872. Which of these fiber groups enters the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle: the pontocerebellar fibers, the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, the fibers from the red nucleus, or the fibers from the globus pallidus? The answer is the dorsal spinocerebellar tract. The inferior peduncle also carries the olivocerebellar and the vestibulocerebellar fibers. The pontocerebellar fibers enter by the middle peduncle.

Question 5873. Over how many segments does the nucleus thoracicus extend: from the first cervical to the first thoracic, from the first thoracic to the second lumbar, from the second lumbar to the fifth sacral, or through the whole cord? The answer is from the first thoracic to the second lumbar segment. It therefore serves the lower limb alone.

Question 5874. A constructed illustration: a lesion destroys one cerebellar hemisphere. Would the disturbance affect the arm and the leg on the same side or on the opposite side? The answer is the same side. The cerebellar hemisphere serves the limbs of its own side, and the person overshoots the target when reaching.

Question 5875. A lesion of the midline part of the cerebellum, the vermis, produces which disturbance: an unsteady trunk with a wide-based gait, weakness of one hand, loss of pain and temperature, or loss of position sense in the toes? The answer is an unsteady trunk with a wide-based gait. The vermis serves posture and the trunk, while the hemispheres control the limbs.

Question 5876. Name the three pairs of cerebellar peduncles, spoken as a list from above downward. The answer is the superior, the middle and the inferior cerebellar peduncles. The superior pair carries most of the fibers leaving the cerebellum. The middle pair carries the pontine fibers, and the inferior pair carries fibers from the medulla and the cord.

Question 5877. Which cells of the cerebellar cortex provide its only output? The answer is the Purkinje cells. They lie in a single row in the middle layer of the cortex. Their axons run to the deep cerebellar nuclei and carry an inhibitory signal.

Question 5878. A described scan of the head shows wide folds on the surface of the cerebellum with wide spaces between them, while the rest of the brain looks normal. Which tissue has been lost, and what does it mean? The answer is cerebellar tissue, lost from the folia of the cortex. A person with such a scan is likely to be unsteady and to overshoot the target.

Question 5879. Which two masses of gray matter together form the striatum? The answer is the caudate nucleus and the putamen. They lie side by side in the wall of the lateral ventricle and in the base of the hemisphere. They share the same kind of cells and the same connections.

Question 5880. In the direct pathway through the basal ganglia, which structure does the striatum inhibit: the internal segment of the globus pallidus, the subthalamic nucleus, the external segment of the globus pallidus, or the thalamus? The answer is the internal segment of the globus pallidus. Inhibiting it releases the thalamus from inhibition, so the cortex is excited and movement is helped.

Question 5881. Which nucleus forms the relay of the indirect pathway between the external segment of the globus pallidus and the internal segment: the caudate nucleus, the subthalamic nucleus, the substantia nigra, or the red nucleus? The answer is the subthalamic nucleus. It excites the internal segment, so the thalamus is held back and movement is restrained. Damage to the nucleus removes that brake.

Question 5882. The output of the basal ganglia leaves the internal segment of the globus pallidus and passes to which part of the thalamus? The answer is the ventral anterior and the ventral lateral nuclei. From there the fibers pass to the motor and premotor areas of the frontal lobe.

Question 5883. A described circuit diagram shows a large mass of gray matter receiving fibers from the whole cortex, sending them by two routes to a pair of deep nuclei, and receiving a return from the thalamus, with no direct connection to the spinal cord. Which system is shown? The answer is the basal ganglia and their loop through the thalamus, which adjust the movement planned by the cortex.

Question 5884. A constructed illustration: a small stroke destroys the subthalamic nucleus on one side, and the opposite arm and leg fling themselves about. Which pathway has lost its brake? The answer is the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia, whose hold on the thalamus is lost. The disturbance shows on the opposite side because the cortical fibers cross.

Question 5885. In the common disorder of slow movement with tremor and rigidity, which cells are lost: the dopamine cells of the substantia nigra, the cells of the caudate nucleus, the cells of the subthalamic nucleus, or the Purkinje cells? The answer is the dopamine cells of the substantia nigra. Losing that signal to the striatum holds the thalamus back, so there is too little movement.

Question 5886. Which of these pairs belongs together: the caudate nucleus with the thalamus, the putamen with the subthalamic nucleus, the internal segment of the globus pallidus with the output of the basal ganglia, or the substantia nigra with the cerebellum? The answer is the internal segment of the globus pallidus with the output. The caudate and the putamen form the striatum, which takes the input.

Question 5887. Which deep nucleus of the cerebellum is the largest and gives rise to most of the fibers that leave it? The answer is the dentate nucleus. It lies in the white matter of each hemisphere, close to the midline of the cerebellum. Its fibers leave by the superior cerebellar peduncle and cross in the midbrain.

Question 5888. A person has weakness of the right arm and leg with a brisk knee reflex, while the face and tongue are spared. Which site fits best: the left internal capsule behind the genu, the left medulla, the right cervical cord, or the left cerebellum? The answer is the left internal capsule behind the genu, which carries the limb fibers and spares the head. A medullary lesion would weaken the tongue too.

Question 5889. A constructed illustration: a person has wasting and twitching of the hand muscles with brisk reflexes and a positive Babinski sign in the same limb. Why do signs of both a lower and an upper motor neuron lesion appear together? The answer is that the disease attacks the motor neurons of the cord and the corticospinal tract at once. The wasted hand reflects the first loss and the brisk reflex the second.

Question 5890. A described magnetic resonance image shows a small bright lesion deep in the left hemisphere, tucked between the lentiform nucleus and the thalamus, and the right side of the body is weak. Which structure is affected, and why is the deficit so complete? The answer is the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Motor and sensory fibers from a wide area of cortex are crowded into that small space.

Question 5891. Which vessels supply the internal capsule: the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery, the anterior cerebral artery, the posterior cerebral artery, or the vertebral artery? The answer is the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery. They run from the base of the brain into the depths of the hemisphere. Their small size makes them a common site of bleeding.

Question 5892. The sensory and motor areas for the leg lie on the medial surface of the hemisphere. Which artery supplies that surface: the anterior cerebral artery, the middle cerebral artery, the posterior cerebral artery, or the basilar artery? The answer is the anterior cerebral artery. The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface, where the face and the hand are represented.

Question 5893. Which of these pairs belongs together: the corticospinal tract with the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the corticobulbar fibers with the posterior limb, the optic radiation with the anterior limb, or the medial lemniscus with the anterior limb? The answer is the corticospinal tract with the posterior limb. The corticobulbar fibers lie at the genu.

Question 5894. True or false: the tracts that carry unconscious position sense to the cerebellum are relayed through the thalamus on the way. The answer is false. The spinocerebellar tracts reach the cerebellum directly, without a relay in the thalamus and without reaching conscious awareness. The dorsal tract stays on the same side of the cord throughout.

Question 5895. Which statement contrasts the two great sensory pathways from the body: the dorsal column crosses in the medulla and the pain pathway in the cord, the dorsal column crosses in the cord and the pain pathway in the medulla, both cross in the midbrain, or neither crosses? The answer is the first. That difference explains the mixed pattern of loss in a half-section of the cord.

Question 5896. A described specimen of the pons shows on each side of the midline a flattened band of fibers lying just behind the basilar part. Which tract is shown, and from where has it come? The answer is the medial lemniscus, which has come up from the medulla and carries the fibers of the dorsal column pathway.

Question 5897. True or false: the corticospinal tract is the only route by which the cerebral cortex influences movement. The answer is false. The cortex also sends fibers to the cranial nerve nuclei, to the basal ganglia, to the cerebellum by way of the pons, and to the centers of the brainstem.

Question 5898. A person cannot feel a pinprick on the right leg but feels the vibration of a tuning fork on that leg normally. Where is the lesion: the left spinothalamic tract, the right dorsal column, the right corticospinal tract, or the left medial lemniscus? The answer is the left spinothalamic tract, since the pain fibers have crossed while the position fibers for that leg still ascend on the right.

Question 5899. Which structure carries the third neuron of the pain pathway from the thalamus to the cerebral cortex? The answer is the posterior limb of the internal capsule. The fibers leave the ventral posterolateral nucleus and run through it in company with the motor fibers. They end in the postcentral gyrus.

Question 5900. A described section of the upper cervical cord shows a band of fibers in the lateral funiculus just behind the dorsal horn, and a second band in the anterior funiculus close to the midline. Which tracts are shown? The answer is the lateral and the anterior corticospinal tracts. The lateral one has already crossed and carries most of the fibers, while the anterior one crosses in the segment it supplies.

To summarize, the dorsal column and medial lemniscus pathway carries fine touch, vibration and position sense, ascends on the same side of the cord, crosses in the lower medulla, relays in the ventral posterolateral nucleus and ends in the postcentral gyrus. Pain and temperature from the body travel by the anterolateral system, whose fibers cross in the anterior white commissure within a segment or two of entry, while pain from the face crosses near the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve and relays in the ventral posteromedial nucleus. The motor pathway begins in the precentral gyrus, passes through the genu and the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the crus cerebri and the pyramids, and crosses in the medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract. The cortex also reaches the cranial nerve nuclei and the cerebellum by way of the pons, and the loops of the basal ganglia through the thalamus set the amount of movement rather than execute it. The cerebellum corrects movement as it happens, with the vermis serving posture and the hemispheres the limbs, and the spinocerebellar tracts bring it the unconscious sense of position without a relay in the thalamus. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 60 — Nose and Nasal Cavity

This chapter works through the nose, the nasal cavity and the paranasal sinuses, and then the pharynx, the muscular tube that carries air and food onward behind them. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind. The nose warms, moistens and filters the air, and the sinuses around it drain into the passages beneath the conchae. The pharynx continues that airway behind the mouth and the larynx, and its muscles make swallowing possible. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 5901. Which two bones meet in the midline to form the bridge of the nose? The answer is the two nasal bones. Each joins its fellow in the middle and the frontal bone above. Below and behind, each meets the frontal process of the maxilla, and together they give the nose its fixed roof.

Question 5902. Which part of the external nose forms the rounded lateral wall of each nostril: the root, the dorsum, the ala, or the columella? The answer is the ala. It is the curved wing on each side of the nostril, supported within by the major alar cartilage. The columella is the strip of skin between the two nostrils.

Question 5903. A described photograph shows the base of the nose, with a median strip of skin between two openings and a groove running from the upper lip to that strip. Which structures are described? The answer is the columella and the philtrum. The columella is the skin-covered lower end of the nasal septum, and the philtrum is the groove of the upper lip.

Question 5904. Which cartilage of the external nose lies immediately deep to the skin at the tip and the ala, and is attached to no bone at all? The answer is the major alar cartilage. Its medial crus forms the lower part of the columella and its lateral crus curls through the ala. It joins the septal cartilage in the midline but reaches no bone.

Question 5905. A constructed illustration: a blow to the front of the nose leaves the organ bent to one side and the airway narrowed. Which structure has most likely been displaced? The answer is the nasal septum, whose front part is the septal cartilage. That cartilage is thin and mobile and is easily pushed off the midline. Blood may also gather under its lining.

Question 5906. True or false: the inferior nasal concha is a part of the ethmoid bone. The answer is false. The superior and middle conchae are projections of the ethmoid, but the inferior concha is a separate bone. It has its own ossification and is the largest of the three.

Question 5907. Which of these forms the roof of the nasal cavity: the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, the horizontal plate of the palatine bone, the body of the maxilla, or the vomer? The answer is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. Its many small holes let the fibers of the olfactory nerve pass upward to the olfactory bulb.

Question 5908. Which two bones form the floor of the nasal cavity, the hard palate that separates the nose from the mouth? The answer is the palatine process of the maxilla and the horizontal plate of the palatine bone. The maxilla forms the front three quarters and the palatine bone the back quarter of that floor.

Question 5909. A described coronal section through the head shows a thin vertical partition in the middle, with a curled shelf of bone on each side above a narrow passage. Which structures are shown? The answer is the nasal septum with the middle concha above the middle meatus on each side. A meatus is the passage beneath a concha.

Question 5910. Which of these opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess, the narrow space above the superior concha: the sphenoid sinus, the frontal sinus, the maxillary sinus, or the nasolacrimal duct? The answer is the sphenoid sinus. It lies in the body of the sphenoid bone and drains forward into that recess. The others open lower down.

Question 5911. Into which passage of the lateral wall of the nose does the nasolacrimal duct open? The answer is the inferior meatus, the space beneath the inferior nasal concha. The duct carries tears from the lacrimal sac down into the nose. That is why weeping makes the nose run.

Question 5912. Which opening lies immediately behind the posterior end of the middle concha, in the lateral wall of the nose? The answer is the sphenopalatine foramen. Through it pass the sphenopalatine artery and the nasopalatine nerve. It opens into the superior meatus and is the gap a surgeon uses when bleeding comes from the back of the nose.

Question 5913. Which of these arteries supplies most of the posterior part of the nasal cavity: the sphenopalatine artery, the facial artery, the ophthalmic artery, or the superior thyroid artery? The answer is the sphenopalatine artery, a branch of the maxillary artery. It enters through the sphenopalatine foramen. The facial and ophthalmic arteries reach only the front.

Question 5914. Name two of the arteries that meet in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, where most nosebleeds begin. The answer is the anterior ethmoidal artery and the sphenopalatine artery, joined there by the greater palatine artery and the septal branch of the superior labial artery. That network is why bleeding there is often brisk.

Question 5915. A constructed illustration: a person blows the nose hard and bright red blood comes from the front of one nostril. From which part of the nasal cavity is the blood most likely coming? The answer is the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, where four arteries meet. The mucosa there is thin and tears easily when the air is dry.

Question 5916. Which of these lies immediately lateral to the posterior ethmoidal air cells, so that a cell extending too far puts it at risk: the optic nerve, the hypoglossal nerve, the maxillary artery, or the mandibular nerve? The answer is the optic nerve. Those cells lie beside the optic canal, and a cell may surround the canal. That variation matters before sinus surgery.

Question 5917. Which nerve carries general sensation from the posterior part of the nasal septum, and through which opening does it reach the nose? The answer is the nasopalatine nerve, which enters through the sphenopalatine foramen. It runs down the septum to the incisive canal. It is a branch of the maxillary nerve.

Question 5918. A described computed tomography scan of the face shows a large air-filled cavity in the body of the maxilla on each side, with a narrow opening high on its medial wall. Which sinus is shown, and why does it drain poorly? The answer is the maxillary sinus, whose opening lies near its roof. Mucus must be pushed upward to leave.

Question 5919. Which of these does not open into the middle meatus: the frontal sinus, the maxillary sinus, the anterior ethmoidal cells, or the posterior ethmoidal cells? The answer is the posterior ethmoidal cells, which open into the superior meatus. The frontal and maxillary sinuses and the anterior ethmoidal cells all drain below the middle concha.

Question 5920. Which of these pairs belongs together: the frontal sinus with the inferior meatus, the sphenoid sinus with the middle meatus, the posterior ethmoidal cells with the superior meatus, or the nasolacrimal duct with the middle meatus? The answer is the posterior ethmoidal cells with the superior meatus. The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

Question 5921. What is the name of the nerve that carries the sense of smell, and through which bone do its fibers pass? The answer is the olfactory nerve, whose fibers pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. It is the first cranial nerve. It is also the only cranial nerve that reaches the brain without relaying in the thalamus.

Question 5922. Which of these describes the epithelium of the olfactory region: ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells, stratified squamous cells with hairs, bipolar nerve cells with supporting cells, or transitional cells? The answer is bipolar nerve cells with supporting cells. The receptor cells of smell are nerve cells themselves. The ciliated columnar epithelium belongs to the respiratory region below.

Question 5923. Which structures lie immediately lateral to the sphenoid sinus, so that a tumor of the sinus may press on them? The answer is the cavernous sinus with the internal carotid artery inside it. The sinus lies in the body of the sphenoid, and only a thin plate of bone separates it from each lateral wall. Above it lies the pituitary fossa.

Question 5924. True or false: the maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus. The answer is true. It opens through the hiatus semilunaris, the curved groove below the ethmoidal bulla. That opening lies high on the medial wall, near the roof of the sinus, which is why the sinus drains so poorly when its lining swells.

Question 5925. A constructed illustration: after a difficult extraction of an upper molar, air and fluid pass between the mouth and the nose on that side. Which structure has been breached? The answer is the floor of the maxillary sinus. The roots of the upper molar teeth lie just below that floor, and in some people the bone between them is paper thin.

Question 5926. Which of these is not a function usually credited to the paranasal sinuses: lightening the skull, adding resonance to the voice, helping to warm and moisten inspired air, or producing cerebrospinal fluid? The answer is producing cerebrospinal fluid, which is made within the ventricles of the brain. The other three are the functions commonly given for these air-filled spaces.

Question 5927. Which paranasal sinus is already present at birth, and which two appear only after birth? The answer is the maxillary sinus, with the frontal and sphenoid sinuses appearing later. The maxillary sinus begins to grow before birth, and the frontal sinus is not visible for some years afterward. The sphenoid sinus keeps enlarging through adolescence.

Question 5928. A described series of computed tomography scans of the same child, taken years apart, shows one air-filled space in the frontal bone that is absent in the first scan and large in the last. Which sinus is shown, and why was it absent? The answer is the frontal sinus, which begins to pneumatize only after birth and enlarges through childhood.

Question 5929. Which of these bones takes part in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity but not in the nasal septum: the vomer, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, the inferior nasal concha, or the septal cartilage? The answer is the inferior nasal concha. The other three all belong to the septum, and the concha is a bone of the lateral wall.

Question 5930. Which part of the nasal cavity is lined by skin rather than mucous membrane, and what does it carry? The answer is the vestibule, the small space just inside each nostril. It carries coarse hairs and glands that trap large particles from the air. A boil in that skin is painful because the skin is bound tightly to the cartilage beneath.

Question 5931. Which of these explains why one nasal passage is often more open than the other at a given moment: the nasal cycle, the position of the septal cartilage, the drainage of the sinuses, or the size of the choanae? The answer is the nasal cycle. The erectile tissue of the conchae engorges and shrinks in turn over some hours.

Question 5932. Which groove lies immediately below the ethmoidal bulla in the middle meatus, and what opens into it? The answer is the hiatus semilunaris, which receives the frontal sinus and the maxillary sinus. The bulla is the rounded elevation above the groove. The uncinate process forms the lower lip of the groove.

Question 5933. A constructed illustration: after a head injury, clear fluid drips from one nostril and the person cannot smell. Which part of the nasal cavity has most likely been fractured? The answer is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. A break there tears the fibers of the olfactory nerve and lets cerebrospinal fluid escape into the nose.

Question 5934. Which of these arteries is most likely torn by a fracture through the roof of the nasal cavity: the anterior ethmoidal artery, the greater palatine artery, the facial artery, or the superior labial artery? The answer is the anterior ethmoidal artery, which runs in the roof beside the cribriform plate. Bleeding from it can be profuse.

Question 5935. A described view through a nasal endoscope shows a rounded swelling above a curved groove, with the openings of two sinuses in the groove beneath. Which region is being viewed? The answer is the middle meatus, with the ethmoidal bulla above the hiatus semilunaris and the uncinate process below it.

Question 5936. Which thin plate of bone forms the medial wall of the orbit and also part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, and why is it easily broken? The answer is the orbital plate of the ethmoid, often called the paper plate. A blow to the eye may drive it inward, so air and infection can pass from the nose into the orbit.

Question 5937. Which of these opens into the inferior meatus of the nose: the nasolacrimal duct, the frontal sinus, the sphenoid sinus, or the posterior ethmoidal cells? The answer is the nasolacrimal duct. It opens beneath the inferior nasal concha, well below the other openings, and it drains tears into the nose.

Question 5938. Which of these pairs belongs together: the frontal sinus with the inferior meatus, the nasolacrimal duct with the superior meatus, the maxillary sinus with the middle meatus, or the sphenoid sinus with the middle meatus? The answer is the maxillary sinus with the middle meatus. The nasolacrimal duct opens below the inferior concha.

Question 5939. Name the three structures that form the nasal septum, spoken as a list. The answer is the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, the vomer and the septal cartilage. The perpendicular plate lies above and behind, the vomer below and behind, and the septal cartilage in front. Narrow crests of the maxilla and the palatine bone run along the floor.

Question 5940. Which of these best explains why the maxillary sinus is the paranasal sinus most often infected: its opening lies high on its medial wall, so that drainage depends on ciliary action; its cavity is the largest of the sinuses; it lies nearest the surface of the face; or it receives no arterial blood? The answer is the high opening. Mucus must be carried upward to leave it.

Question 5941. Which nerve supplies the skin over the upper part of the external nose and the front of the nasal septum? The answer is the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve. Its external nasal branch reaches the skin of the dorsum and the tip. The lower part of the nose is supplied instead by the infraorbital nerve.

Question 5942. Through which opening does the pterygopalatine fossa communicate with the nasal cavity, and what passes through it? The answer is the sphenopalatine foramen, which carries the sphenopalatine artery and the nasopalatine nerve. The fossa lies behind the maxilla and holds the pterygopalatine ganglion. Its opening lies behind the middle concha.

Question 5943. A constructed illustration: a surgeon reaches the pituitary gland through the nose, passing between the conchae and then through the sphenoid sinus. Why does that route give access to the pituitary fossa? The answer is that the sphenoid sinus lies directly below the fossa, and its roof is a thin plate of bone.

Question 5944. Which of these veins offers a route by which infection from the nose may reach the cavernous sinus: the ophthalmic veins, the facial vein, the retromandibular vein, or the external jugular vein? The answer is the ophthalmic veins. They run back through the orbit and the superior orbital fissure, and the channels between them have no valves.

Question 5945. A described radiograph taken with the head tilted back shows two large air-filled triangles below the orbits, their upper borders curved and their lower borders lost against the teeth. Which structures are shown, and where do they drain? The answer is the maxillary sinuses, which drain into the middle meatus and lie just above the molar roots.

Question 5946. True or false: the frontal sinus is present and air filled at birth. The answer is false. The frontal sinus begins to develop only after birth and is not visible on a radiograph for some years. The maxillary sinus is the one already present before birth, and the sphenoid sinus enlarges through adolescence.

Question 5947. Which of these describes the autonomic supply of the glands of the nasal mucosa: secretomotor fibers from the facial nerve with vasoconstrictor fibers from the superior cervical ganglion, fibers from the vagus alone, fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve alone, or no autonomic supply? The answer is the first of these, joined in the nerve of the pterygoid canal.

Question 5948. Which cells of the olfactory epithelium are themselves the receptor cells, and from which cells are they replaced? The answer is the bipolar olfactory neurons, which are replaced throughout adult life from the basal cells. Each neuron sends one process to the surface and a fine fiber upward through the cribriform plate. They are exposed directly to the air.

Question 5949. Which paranasal sinus is the largest, and in which bone does it lie? The answer is the maxillary sinus, which occupies the body of the maxilla. It is shaped like a pyramid with its base against the lateral wall of the nose. Its volume in the adult is about 15 milliliters.

Question 5950. Which of these explains lasting loss of smell after a blow to the back of the head: the brain moves and tears the olfactory fibers at the cribriform plate, the nasal bones break and block the airway, the olfactory bulb is supplied by the facial nerve, or the mucosa swells over the receptors? The answer is that the brain moves within the skull. Those fibers are torn as they pass through that plate.

Question 5951. What name is given to the two openings at the back of the nasal cavity, through which it communicates with the nasopharynx? The answer is the choanae. Each is bounded above by the body of the sphenoid, below by the horizontal plate of the palatine bone, and laterally by the medial pterygoid plate.

Question 5952. A described cross section through the head at the level of the cheek shows the nasal cavity in the middle, each half closed by a thin vertical partition, with curled shelves of bone on the outer walls. What are those shelves called? The answer is the conchae, with a meatus lying beneath each one. The partition is the nasal septum.

Question 5953. Which artery reaches the anterior part of the nasal septum by running up through the incisive canal: the greater palatine artery, the facial artery, the anterior ethmoidal artery, or the posterior ethmoidal artery? The answer is the greater palatine artery, a branch of the maxillary artery. It comes up from the palate and joins the network on the septum.

Question 5954. A constructed illustration: a small child has pushed a bead into one nostril and it cannot be seen at the front. Which part of the nasal cavity should be examined, and why does this matter? The answer is the region beneath the inferior nasal concha, where such an object usually lodges. Removal belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 5955. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterosuperior part of the nasal cavity with the ophthalmic nerve, the posteroinferior part with the ophthalmic nerve, the vestibule with the olfactory nerve, or the olfactory region with the trigeminal nerve? The answer is the anterosuperior part with the ophthalmic nerve, through its anterior ethmoidal branch.

Question 5956. The nasal septum stands vertically in the middle of the face. In which plane of the body does it lie, and what does that plane divide? The answer is the median plane, which divides the body into right and left halves. The septum lies in that plane above the hard palate. A slight deviation to one side is common.

Question 5957. Which of these lies immediately above and behind the superior nasal concha: the sphenoethmoidal recess, the middle meatus, the inferior meatus, or the vestibule? The answer is the sphenoethmoidal recess, into which the sphenoid sinus opens. It is the highest part of the nasal cavity, and the olfactory region lies close to it.

Question 5958. Which structure forms the medial wall of the maxillary sinus, and what opens near the top of that wall? The answer is the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, with the ostium of the sinus near its upper end. The ostium opens into the middle meatus beneath the middle concha. The wall is thin enough for a surgeon to open it.

Question 5959. A described dried skull, viewed from behind with the nasal septum removed, shows three curled shelves of bone on the lateral wall and a passage beneath each one. Which shelf is a separate bone, and what does the lowest passage receive? The answer is the inferior nasal concha, and the inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct.

Question 5960. Which of these best explains why a boil on the upper lip or the side of the nose is treated with concern: venous blood from there can pass by valveless channels to the cavernous sinus, the skin there has no lymphatic drainage, the facial artery there comes from the internal carotid, or the region is supplied by the vagus? The answer is the valveless venous channels.

Question 5961. True or false: the whole of the nasal cavity is lined by mucous membrane. The answer is false. The vestibule just inside each nostril is lined by skin, complete with hairs and glands. Only behind the vestibule does the mucous membrane begin, and only its upper part carries the sense of smell.

Question 5962. A constructed illustration: an older person has repeated heavy nosebleeds that begin at the back of the nose and run down the throat. Which vessel is the likely source, and why is the bleeding not controlled from the front? The answer is the sphenopalatine artery and its branches. They enter behind the middle concha and cannot be seen from the nostril.

Question 5963. Which statement about the middle nasal concha is correct: it is a projection of the ethmoid bone, it is a separate bone of the skull, it lies below the inferior concha, or it has no passage beneath it? The answer is that it is a projection of the ethmoid bone. Beneath it lies the middle meatus.

Question 5964. Which part of the nasal cavity is the narrowest, and why does that matter for the sense of airflow? The answer is the internal nasal valve, the narrow angle where the upper and lower lateral cartilages meet. It offers the greatest resistance in the airway during quiet breathing. A slight narrowing there is felt as a blocked nose.

Question 5965. Which structure forms the roof of the maxillary sinus, and which nerve runs in a canal along that roof? The answer is the floor of the orbit, with the infraorbital nerve in its canal. The nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve and emerges on the face below the eye, supplying the cheek and the upper lip.

Question 5966. A described midline section of the head shows the nasal cavity above the hard palate, opening behind into the nasopharynx, with the soft palate hanging below that opening. Which opening joins the nose to the pharynx, and what closes it during swallowing? The answer is the choana, which the soft palate seals.

Question 5967. A described computed tomography scan of the face shows a horizontal line across one maxillary sinus, with fluid below it and air above. What does that appearance mean, and which wall of the sinus lies closest to the teeth? The answer is a fluid level, which suggests that the sinus holds secretion. Its floor lies above the molar roots.

Question 5968. A described dissection after removal of the middle nasal concha shows a rounded swelling with a curved groove beneath it, and several small openings along the groove. Which structures have been exposed? The answer is the ethmoidal bulla with the hiatus semilunaris below it, which receive the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal drainage.

Question 5969. A constructed illustration: a tube is passed along the floor of the nose into the nasopharynx without touching the conchae. Which structures form that floor, and why is the route chosen? The answer is the palatine process of the maxilla and the horizontal plate of the palatine bone. The floor is straight and wide.

Question 5970. Which of these pairs belongs together: the maxillary sinus with the supraorbital nerve, the frontal sinus with the infraorbital nerve, the maxillary sinus with the infraorbital nerve, or the sphenoid sinus with the olfactory nerve? The answer is the maxillary sinus with the infraorbital nerve and its alveolar branches. The frontal sinus is supplied by the supraorbital nerve.

Question 5971. Which single bone takes part in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, the medial wall of the orbit and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa? The answer is the ethmoid bone. Its cribriform plate forms part of the roof of the nose, and its orbital plate forms the medial wall of the orbit. Its conchae project into the nose.

Question 5972. Which of these best explains why blood collecting between the septal cartilage and its lining can destroy the cartilage: the cartilage has no vessels of its own and is nourished by diffusion from its lining, the blood is under high pressure, the cartilage is really bone, or the collection presses on the ethmoid? The answer is that the cartilage is avascular.

Question 5973. A described computed tomography scan of the skull base shows the sphenoid sinus with one lateral wall so thin that the internal carotid artery seems to lie against the lining. Why does this matter when the sinus is entered? The answer is that the artery may lie within the wall of the sinus in some people.
