Question 5974. Which part of the nasal cavity lies directly below the cribriform plate, and what passes through that plate? The answer is the olfactory region in the roof of the nose, where the receptor cells lie, and the fine fibers of the olfactory nerve pass through the holes of the plate to the olfactory bulb above.

Question 5975. Which of these statements is correct: the maxillary sinus drains upward through an opening near its roof, all sinuses drain downward through openings in their floors, the frontal sinus has no duct, or the sphenoid sinus opens into the inferior meatus? The answer is that the maxillary sinus drains upward. Ciliary action, not gravity, moves the mucus out.

Question 5976. From which level does the pharynx begin, and at which level does it become the esophagus? The answer is that it begins at the base of the skull and ends at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, in front of the sixth cervical vertebra. Below that level it continues downward as the esophagus.

Question 5977. Which of these names the three parts of the pharynx in order from above downward: nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx; oropharynx, nasopharynx and laryngopharynx; nasopharynx, laryngopharynx and oropharynx; or hypopharynx, oropharynx and nasopharynx? The answer is the nasopharynx, the oropharynx and the laryngopharynx. The soft palate and the epiglottis divide them.

Question 5978. A described midline section of the head shows a muscular tube behind the nose, the mouth and the larynx, open in front to all three and closed behind by a median seam. What is that seam, and what is the tube? The answer is the median pharyngeal raphe, and the tube is the pharynx, where the constrictors meet.

Question 5979. Which structures lie immediately in front of the pharynx, from above downward? The answer is the nasal cavity, the mouth and the larynx, each separated from the pharynx by soft tissue only. Behind the pharynx lie the prevertebral fascia and the cervical spine. That is why a collection there pushes the back wall forward.

Question 5980. All the muscles of the pharynx are supplied by the vagus nerve through the pharyngeal plexus, with one exception. Which of these is that exception: the stylopharyngeus, the superior constrictor, the palatopharyngeus, or the cricopharyngeus? The answer is the stylopharyngeus, which the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies. It is the only muscle of the pharynx that nerve moves.

Question 5981. A constructed illustration: some days after an operation on the tonsil, a person complains of pain in one ear although the ear looks normal. Which nerve explains the pain? The answer is the glossopharyngeal nerve, which supplies the region of the tonsil and also sends a branch to the middle ear.

Question 5982. Which muscle forms the floor of the fossa in which the palatine tonsil lies, and which fascia covers that muscle? The answer is the superior constrictor of the pharynx, covered by the pharyngobasilar fascia. Lateral to it runs the carotid sheath. The tonsil is therefore dissected close to the great vessels of the neck.

Question 5983. Which of these is the site at which a pharyngeal pouch pushes backward through the wall of the pharynx: the gap between the thyropharyngeus and the cricopharyngeus, the gap between the superior and middle constrictors, the opening of the auditory tube, or the fossa behind the palatine tonsil? The answer is the first of these, in the midline behind.

Question 5984. A described radiograph taken during a swallow shows a rounded out-pouching from the back of the lower pharynx, in the midline, above the level of the cricoid cartilage. Which structure has herniated, and through which gap? The answer is the mucous membrane of the pharynx, through the gap between the thyropharyngeus and the cricopharyngeus.

Question 5985. Which of these describes the position of the pharyngeal tonsil: in the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx, on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, in the tonsillar fossa between the two arches, or at the base of the tongue? The answer is the roof and the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. When it enlarges it blocks the airway.

Question 5986. Which structure lies in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx behind the opening of the auditory tube, and which large vessel lies close to it? The answer is the pharyngeal recess, with the internal carotid artery beyond its thin wall. That recess is a common site for a tumor to begin, and the artery explains why a biopsy there is taken with care.

Question 5987. Into which part of the pharynx does the auditory tube open, and what is the ridge above that opening called? The answer is the nasopharynx, and the ridge is the torus tubarius. The tube equalizes pressure on the two sides of the eardrum. The salpingopharyngeal fold runs downward from the ridge.

Question 5988. Which of these groups forms the ring of lymphoid tissue around the entrance of the air and food passages: the pharyngeal, tubal, palatine and lingual tonsils; the palatine and lingual tonsils alone; the thymus and the spleen; or the lymph nodes of the neck? The answer is the four sets of tonsils, which surround the upper end of the pharynx.

Question 5989. Which of these pairs belongs together: the nasopharynx with the palatine tonsil, the oropharynx with the pharyngeal tonsil, the laryngopharynx with the piriform fossa, or the nasopharynx with the vallecula? The answer is the laryngopharynx with the piriform fossa. The palatine tonsil lies in the oropharynx, and the pharyngeal tonsil in the nasopharynx.

Question 5990. Name the three constrictor muscles of the pharynx in order from above downward, spoken as a list. The answer is the superior, the middle and the inferior constrictor. The superior arises from the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe and the mandible, the middle from the stylohyoid ligament and the hyoid bone, and the inferior from the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

Question 5991. Which of these passes through the gap between the upper border of the superior constrictor and the base of the skull: the auditory tube with the muscle that lifts the soft palate, the internal carotid artery, the hypoglossal nerve, or the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the auditory tube with the levator veli palatini. The gap is closed in front by fascia.

Question 5992. A constructed illustration: a person with a severe throat infection has a smooth swelling of the back wall of the pharynx and holds the neck stiff. Which space has the collection entered, and why is it dangerous? The answer is the retropharyngeal space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia, which runs down behind the esophagus into the chest.

Question 5993. A described view into an open mouth shows two curved folds on each side with a rounded mass between them, and a midline fold running back to the tongue. Which structures are seen? The answer is the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches with the palatine tonsil between them. The midline fold is the glossoepiglottic fold.

Question 5994. Which fold forms the medial wall of the piriform fossa, and which nerve lies beneath its lining? The answer is the aryepiglottic fold, with the internal laryngeal nerve lying just under the mucosa of the fossa. The fossa lies on each side of the laryngeal inlet. A sharp object such as a fish bone may lodge there.

Question 5995. Which muscle acts as the sphincter at the junction of the pharynx and the esophagus, and what is its state at rest? The answer is the cricopharyngeus, the lower part of the inferior constrictor. It stays contracted at rest and relaxes at the moment of swallowing. Failure of that relaxation is one cause of difficulty in swallowing.

Question 5996. Which of these happens during the pharyngeal stage of swallowing: the soft palate rises to seal the nasopharynx and the constrictors contract in sequence, the soft palate drops to close the mouth, the cricopharyngeus contracts tightly, or the larynx descends? The answer is that the soft palate rises and the constrictors contract in order.

Question 5997. True or false: the muscles of the pharynx are supplied by the vagus nerve alone, with no other nerve taking part. The answer is false. The vagus supplies them through the pharyngeal plexus except for the stylopharyngeus, which the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies. The plexus also receives sympathetic fibers.

Question 5998. Which of these best explains why a tumor in the piriform fossa may first be noticed as pain in the ear: the fossa and the ear are both supplied by branches of the vagus nerve, the fossa lies next to the eardrum, the facial nerve passes through it, or it drains to the ear? The answer is the shared nerve supply through the vagus.

Question 5999. The pharynx is described as ending in front of the sixth cervical vertebra, where the esophagus begins. Which structure lies immediately in front of that junction, and in which direction does the tube continue? The answer is the cricoid cartilage, and the tube continues downward and somewhat to the left toward the chest.

Question 6000. Which part of the pharynx lies above the soft palate and holds the pharyngeal tonsil in its roof, and is a common site for a tumor in the adult? The answer is the nasopharynx. From the front it is entered through the choanae, and a tumor often begins in its lateral recess.

To summarize, the nasal cavity is divided by the septum and opens behind through the choanae into the nasopharynx, and its lateral wall carries three conchae with a passage beneath each one. The sphenoid sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess, the posterior ethmoidal cells into the superior meatus, the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal sinuses into the middle meatus, and the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus. The anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries meet on the anteroinferior part of the septum, where most nosebleeds begin, and the cribriform plate above is both the roof of the nose and the route of the olfactory fibers. The pharynx has three parts, its muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus except for the stylopharyngeus, and the cricopharyngeus holds the lower end closed except during swallowing. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 61 — Larynx

This chapter follows the airway and the food passage from the back of the nose and the mouth down to the entrance of the windpipe. Its first part covers the pharynx, the three regions into which it is divided, the openings that pierce its walls and the spaces that surround it. The larger part then takes the larynx in turn, through its cartilages, its vocal folds and the small muscles that move them. It holds one hundred questions, running from question 6001 to question 6100, and every one of them gives its answer at once and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 6001. Which muscular tube lies behind the nasal cavity, behind the mouth and behind the larynx, and becomes continuous below with the esophagus? The answer is the pharynx. It hangs from the base of the skull as a half-tube that is open in front, where it communicates with each of those three cavities in turn.

Question 6002. Which is the correct order of the parts of the pharynx from above downward: the nasopharynx, the oropharynx and the laryngopharynx; the laryngopharynx, the oropharynx and the nasopharynx; the oropharynx, the nasopharynx and the laryngopharynx; or the laryngopharynx, the nasopharynx and the oropharynx? The answer is the nasopharynx, the oropharynx and the laryngopharynx. Each part is named for the cavity behind it: the nose, the mouth and the larynx.

Question 6003. Which part of the pharynx lies directly behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate? The answer is the nasopharynx. It is continuous in front with the nasal cavity through the two posterior openings called the choanae. The auditory tube opens on its lateral wall.

Question 6004. A described sagittal section through the head shows a mass of soft tissue filling the roof and the back wall of the space behind the nose. Which structure occupies that position? The answer is the pharyngeal tonsil. It is a collection of lymphoid tissue under the mucosa of the roof and the posterior wall. When it enlarges in a child it can block the nasal airway.

Question 6005. Which opening pierces the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, about a finger's breadth behind the back end of the inferior nasal concha: the opening of the maxillary sinus, the opening of the auditory tube, the opening of the frontal sinus, or the opening of the sphenoid sinus? The answer is the opening of the auditory tube. It leads back to the middle ear cavity.

Question 6006. Which fold runs downward from the cartilage of the auditory tube and forms a ridge behind its pharyngeal opening: the salpingopharyngeal fold, the palatopharyngeal arch, the palatoglossal arch, or the median glossoepiglottic fold? The answer is the salpingopharyngeal fold. It covers the salpingopharyngeus muscle, which helps to lift the pharynx during swallowing.

Question 6007. A described sagittal section through the head shows the nasal cavity above, the mouth in front and a wide muscular tube behind them, divided across by the soft palate. Which region is shown, and what does the soft palate separate? The answer is the pharynx, and the soft palate separates the nasopharynx above from the oropharynx below.

Question 6008. A constructed illustration: a child breathes through the mouth at night and snores, and the described tissue in the roof of the nasopharynx is enlarged. Which structure is enlarged, and why does it cause these symptoms? The answer is the pharyngeal tonsil. It sits in the roof and the back wall of the nasopharynx, close to the opening of the auditory tube. The assessment belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6009. True or false: the oropharynx carries both air and food. The answer is true. It lies behind the mouth, between the soft palate above and the upper border of the epiglottis below. Air passes through it in breathing and a bolus passes through it in swallowing, and the two uses share the same space.

Question 6010. Which structure lies in the fossa between the palatoglossal arch in front and the palatopharyngeal arch behind? The answer is the palatine tonsil. The fossa is the interval between the two arches, and the tonsil is a mass of lymphoid tissue that fills it.

Question 6011. Which large artery lies lateral to the palatine tonsil, separated from it only by the wall of the pharynx: the facial artery, the lingual artery, the internal carotid artery, or the ascending pharyngeal artery? The answer is the internal carotid artery. It lies behind the superior constrictor, so it is a feared structure in that region.

Question 6012. Which muscle forms the thickest part of the circular coat of the pharynx and arises from the thyroid and cricoid cartilages: the superior constrictor, the middle constrictor, the inferior constrictor, or the stylopharyngeus? The answer is the inferior constrictor. Its upper fibers are the thyropharyngeal part and its lower fibers the cricopharyngeal part.

Question 6013. Which of these pairs belongs together: the nasopharynx with the pharyngeal tonsil, the oropharynx with the pharyngeal tonsil, the laryngopharynx with the palatine tonsil, or the nasopharynx with the lingual tonsil? The answer is the nasopharynx with the pharyngeal tonsil. The palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx, one on each side.

Question 6014. Which part of the pharynx runs from the upper border of the epiglottis down to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, behind the larynx: the nasopharynx, the oropharynx, the laryngopharynx, or the cervical esophagus? The answer is the laryngopharynx. It opens forward into the larynx through the laryngeal inlet.

Question 6015. Name, spoken as a list, the two arches that bound the fossa of the palatine tonsil. The answer is the palatoglossal arch in front and the palatopharyngeal arch behind. Each arch is a fold of mucosa over a muscle. The palatoglossus runs to the tongue and the palatopharyngeus into the pharyngeal wall.

Question 6016. Which statement describes the piriform fossa: a recess beside the laryngeal inlet, a recess in the roof of the nasopharynx, a pouch between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage, or a space behind the cricoid cartilage? The answer is a recess beside the laryngeal inlet. It lies between the aryepiglottic fold medially and the thyroid cartilage laterally. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve lies under its mucosa.

Question 6017. A constructed illustration: a swallowed fish bone lodges in the recess beside the laryngeal inlet, and the described mucosa there is scratched. Which nerve lies immediately beneath that mucosa and may be injured? The answer is the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It carries sensation from the larynx above the vocal folds, so its injury dulls the protective cough. The removal of the bone belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6018. Which bony process of the skull lies lateral to the pharynx and gives origin to the stylopharyngeus muscle? The answer is the styloid process of the temporal bone. Three muscles arise from it and pass downward into the tongue, the pharynx and the hyoid region.

Question 6019. Which tough fibrous layer lies deep to the pharyngeal muscles and is attached above to the base of the skull? The answer is the pharyngobasilar fascia. It forms the inner coat of the pharyngeal wall and is thickest in the upper part, where the muscle coat is incomplete.

Question 6020. Where is the weak point in the wall of the pharynx: between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor, between the superior and middle constrictors, in the roof of the nasopharynx, or in the posterior wall of the oropharynx? The answer is between the thyropharyngeal and the cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor. The circular fibers are absent in that midline gap behind. A pouch of mucosa can protrude through it.

Question 6021. A constructed illustration: a person reports that food sticks high in the neck and a soft swelling gurgles when pressed. The pouch protrudes backward through a gap in the lower pharyngeal wall. Which gap is described? The answer is the interval between the thyropharyngeal and the cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor. The pouch lies above the cricopharyngeus, the sphincter at the top of the esophagus. The assessment belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6022. True or false: at the level of the fifth cervical vertebra the pharynx lies behind the larynx and in front of the bodies of the cervical vertebrae. The answer is true. The laryngopharynx occupies that interval, and the laryngeal inlet opens forward from it.

Question 6023. True or false: the wall of the pharynx is fixed to the base of the skull and cannot be moved. The answer is false. Only the upper attachment is fixed, while the muscular wall is raised and shortened during swallowing. The constrictors and the stylopharyngeus lift the pharynx over the bolus.

Question 6024. A described sagittal section shows a space filled with loose tissue lying between the back of the pharynx and the front of the vertebral column, running from the base of the skull downward. Which space is shown, and where does it lead? The answer is the retropharyngeal space, and it leads down into the chest behind the esophagus. Because the tissue in it is loose, infection can track along it into the mediastinum.

Question 6025. Which nerve plexus lies on the surface of the middle constrictor and supplies the muscles and the mucosa of the pharynx? The answer is the pharyngeal plexus. It is formed by pharyngeal branches of the vagus nerve and of the glossopharyngeal nerve, together with sympathetic fibers. The vagus supplies the muscles and the glossopharyngeal nerve carries most of the sensation.

Question 6026. Which cartilage of the larynx is the largest and forms the prominence in the front of the neck? The answer is the thyroid cartilage. It is made of two flat plates, called laminae, that meet in the midline at an angle. That angle is sharper in the male, so the prominence is more obvious there.

Question 6027. Which cartilage of the larynx has the shape of a signet ring, narrow in front and broad behind: the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage, the arytenoid cartilage, or the epiglottis? The answer is the cricoid cartilage. It is the only cartilage of the airway that forms a complete ring, and it is narrow in front and tall behind. The arytenoid cartilages sit on its broad posterior part.

Question 6028. Which leaf-shaped cartilage stands in front of the laryngeal inlet and is attached below to the back of the thyroid cartilage? The answer is the epiglottis. Its lower end is narrowed into a stalk, and its broad upper end projects upward behind the tongue.

Question 6029. Which pair of small cartilages sits on the upper border of the cricoid cartilage and moves the vocal folds: the arytenoid cartilages, the corniculate cartilages, the cuneiform cartilages, or the triticeal cartilages? The answer is the arytenoid cartilages. Each is shaped like a three-sided pyramid and carries a vocal process in front and a muscular process at its side.

Question 6030. Which two small cartilages lie within the aryepiglottic fold: the thyroid and the cricoid cartilages, the arytenoid and the triticeal cartilages, the corniculate and the cuneiform cartilages, or the epiglottis and the cricoid cartilage? The answer is the corniculate and the cuneiform cartilages. The corniculate cartilages sit on the tops of the arytenoid cartilages.

Question 6031. Which joint of the larynx lets the thyroid cartilage tilt forward on the cricoid cartilage and so lengthen the vocal fold? The answer is the cricothyroid joint. It lies between the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage and the side of the cricoid cartilage. The movement changes the tension of the fold and therefore the pitch of the voice.

Question 6032. Which ligament joins the lower border of the cricoid cartilage to the first ring of the trachea: the thyrohyoid membrane, the cricotracheal ligament, the cricothyroid membrane, or the lateral thyrohyoid ligament? The answer is the cricotracheal ligament. It is a fibrous ring that continues the wall of the airway downward.

Question 6033. Which membrane lies deep to the laryngeal mucosa and stretches from the vocal ligament down to the upper border of the cricoid cartilage? The answer is the cricothyroid membrane, also called the conus elasticus. Its thickened upper free edge is the vocal ligament, which forms the core of the vocal fold.

Question 6034. Which membrane forms the framework of the aryepiglottic fold and gives its lower free edge to the vestibular ligament: the quadrangular membrane, the cricothyroid membrane, the thyrohyoid membrane, or the cricotracheal ligament? The answer is the quadrangular membrane. It runs from the side of the epiglottis back to the arytenoid cartilage. Its lower edge is free and forms the vestibular ligament above the vocal fold.

Question 6035. A described frontal section through the larynx shows a shield of cartilage in front whose two plates meet at an angle, and below it a narrow ring. Which two cartilages are shown, and which of them is a complete ring? The answer is the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below, and the cricoid is the complete ring.

Question 6036. A described transverse section through the neck shows a gland wrapped around the front and the sides of the airway below the larynx, with its two lobes joined across the midline. Which gland is shown? The answer is the thyroid gland. Its isthmus crosses in front of the second and third rings of the trachea.

Question 6037. Which ridge on the outer surface of the thyroid cartilage runs downward and forward and gives attachment to the sternothyroid and thyrohyoid muscles? The answer is the oblique line. The inferior constrictor of the pharynx also takes origin from the area behind it.

Question 6038. The superior horns of the thyroid cartilage reach which structure, and the inferior horns which: the hyoid bone and the cricoid cartilage, the cricoid and the hyoid, the mandible and the cricoid, or the hyoid and the trachea? The answer is the hyoid bone above and the cricoid cartilage below. The inferior horn forms the cricothyroid joint.

Question 6039. True or false: the epiglottis lies above the level of the vocal folds and is covered by mucous membrane on both of its surfaces. The answer is true. Its anterior surface faces the tongue and forms the valleculae on each side of the midline fold. Its posterior surface faces the laryngeal inlet.

Question 6040. Which of these pairs belongs together: the arytenoid cartilage with the vocal process, the corniculate cartilage with the vocal process, the cuneiform cartilage with the muscular process, or the thyroid cartilage with the muscular process? The answer is the arytenoid cartilage with the vocal process. The vocal ligament attaches to the vocal process at the front of the cartilage.

Question 6041. A described specimen shows a small rounded elevation at the top of each arytenoid cartilage, lying in the back part of the aryepiglottic fold. Which cartilage forms that elevation? The answer is the corniculate cartilage. It caps the apex of the arytenoid cartilage and is covered by the fold.

Question 6042. Which artery enters the larynx through the thyrohyoid membrane, accompanied by the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve: the superior thyroid artery, the superior laryngeal artery, the inferior laryngeal artery, or the ascending pharyngeal artery? The answer is the superior laryngeal artery. It is a branch of the superior thyroid artery and supplies the larynx above the vocal folds.

Question 6043. The laryngeal prominence in the front of the neck is formed by the meeting of which two structures: the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage, the two horns of the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid and the thyroid cartilages, or the epiglottis and the thyroid cartilage? The answer is the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage. They meet in the midline at an angle that projects forward.

Question 6044. A described lateral radiograph of the neck shows a curved soft tissue shadow standing up in front of the airway between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage. Which structure casts that shadow? The answer is the epiglottis. Its broad upper end lies behind the tongue and its stalk is fixed to the back of the thyroid cartilage.

Question 6045. A described transverse section is cut through the larynx at the level of the vocal folds. Where does the airway lie in that section, and what lies on each side of it? The answer is that the airway lies in the middle, between the two vocal folds, with the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid cartilages behind.

Question 6046. Which part of the cricoid cartilage carries the arytenoid cartilages and slopes downward and forward on each side? The answer is the lamina, the tall part behind. It is broad in the midline and carries a facet on each side for the arytenoid cartilage.

Question 6047. A described dissection of the front of the neck shows a broad membrane stretched between the hyoid bone above and the thyroid cartilage below, with a small nodule of cartilage in its thickened lateral edge. Which membrane is shown, and what is the nodule? The answer is the thyrohyoid membrane, and the nodule is the triticeal cartilage. The membrane is pierced by the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Question 6048. Which of these laryngeal cartilages is unpaired: the thyroid cartilage, the arytenoid cartilage, the corniculate cartilage, or the cuneiform cartilage? The answer is the thyroid cartilage. The cricoid cartilage and the epiglottis are also unpaired, so three of the nine cartilages are single.

Question 6049. Name, spoken as a list, the three unpaired cartilages of the larynx. The answer is the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage and the epiglottis. Together they form the front wall and the roof of the laryngeal framework. The paired cartilages, the arytenoids with the corniculate and the cuneiform above them, lie behind.

Question 6050. A constructed illustration: a blow to the front of the neck is followed by noisy breathing, and the described break is in the only cartilage of the airway that forms a complete ring. Which cartilage is broken? The answer is the cricoid cartilage, whose arch in front is the part usually fractured. The folds above it may swell and narrow the airway. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6051. Which U-shaped bone lies above the larynx and is the only bone of the body that does not articulate with another bone? The answer is the hyoid bone. It is held in place by muscles and ligaments, with its body in front and its greater horns projecting backward.

Question 6052. Which statement about the attachment of the epiglottis is correct: its stalk is fixed to the back of the thyroid cartilage, it is fixed to the front of the thyroid cartilage, it is fixed to the cricoid cartilage, or it is attached to no cartilage at all? The answer is that its stalk is fixed to the back of the thyroid cartilage. The thyroepiglottic ligament holds the stalk in place.

Question 6053. A described radiograph of an older adult shows plates of bone laid down within the thyroid cartilage. Which cartilages of the larynx commonly ossify with age? The answer is the thyroid and the cricoid cartilages, and the arytenoid cartilages less often. This change begins in adult life and is a normal part of aging rather than a disease.

Question 6054. A described specimen of the larynx is opened from behind, showing the epiglottis above, then a pair of thick folds, and below them a pair of thinner folds with sharp free edges and a gap between them. Which pair are the vocal folds? The answer is the lower pair, with the sharp free edges. The thicker pair above are the vestibular folds, and the recess between them is the laryngeal ventricle.

Question 6055. Counting both sides, how many cartilages make up the larynx: three, six, nine, or twelve? The answer is nine. Three are unpaired, the thyroid, the cricoid and the epiglottis, and three are paired, the arytenoid, the corniculate and the cuneiform. The cuneiform cartilages are small and may be absent, which is a normal variation.

Question 6056. Which pair of folds stretches from the back of the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid cartilages and produces the voice? The answer is the vocal folds. Each fold contains the vocal ligament, which is its core, and the vocalis muscle beside it. The gap between the two folds is the rima glottidis.

Question 6057. Which two of the folds in the larynx are the true vocal cords: the vocal folds, the vestibular folds, both pairs, or neither pair? The answer is the vocal folds, which are the true cords. The vestibular folds are the false cords and take no part in producing sound. The vocal folds contain the vocal ligament and are covered by stratified squamous epithelium.

Question 6058. What is the name of the narrow gap between the two vocal folds through which air passes? The answer is the rima glottidis. It has a front part between the membranous folds and a back part between the arytenoid cartilages. In the adult it is the narrowest part of the airway above the trachea.

Question 6059. Which fold lies immediately above the vocal fold and forms the upper lip of the laryngeal ventricle? The answer is the vestibular fold. It contains the vestibular ligament, which is the free lower edge of the quadrangular membrane. It takes no part in producing sound.

Question 6060. What is the name of the recess between the vestibular fold above and the vocal fold below, from which a small pouch runs upward? The answer is the laryngeal ventricle, and the pouch is the laryngeal saccule. The saccule lies between the vestibular fold and the thyroid cartilage and is rich in mucous glands.

Question 6061. A described view of the open larynx from above shows two pale folds meeting in front at a sharp point, with a dark gap between them. What is the point called, and what is the gap? The answer is the anterior commissure, and the gap is the rima glottidis.

Question 6062. Which statement about the rima glottidis is correct: it is a narrow wedge during quiet breathing and a narrow slit during speech, it is wide open during speech, it keeps the same shape at all times, or it is closed during quiet breathing? The answer is that it is a narrow wedge during quiet breathing and a narrow slit during speech. In a deep breath it opens into a wide diamond.

Question 6063. Which part of the laryngeal cavity lies below the vocal folds and above the lower border of the cricoid cartilage? The answer is the subglottic space. It is lined by respiratory epithelium and is circular in section. In the infant it is the narrowest part of the whole airway, which is why swelling there is dangerous.

Question 6064. Which artery supplies the larynx below the vocal folds, and with which nerve does it run? The answer is the inferior laryngeal artery, and it runs with the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It is a branch of the inferior thyroid artery. It enters the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint, below the lower border of the inferior constrictor.

Question 6065. Which artery supplies the lining of the larynx below the vocal folds: the superior laryngeal artery, the inferior laryngeal artery, the superior thyroid artery, or the lingual artery? The answer is the inferior laryngeal artery, a branch of the inferior thyroid artery. It ascends with the recurrent laryngeal nerve and enters the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.

Question 6066. Lymph from the part of the larynx above the vocal folds drains to which group of nodes, and why does a growth on the vocal fold itself spread late? The answer is the upper deep cervical nodes, and the vocal folds have almost no lymph vessels. The part below the folds drains to the lower deep cervical nodes and to the nodes in front of the trachea.

Question 6067. A constructed illustration: a person who has been hoarse for several weeks is found to have a growth on the sharp-edged fold inside the larynx. Which fold is described, and which kind of epithelium covers it? The answer is the vocal fold, covered by stratified squamous epithelium. It is the only part of the larynx lined that way. The diagnosis belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6068. True or false: the vestibular folds take part in the production of the voice. The answer is false. They contain the vestibular ligament and many mucous glands, and they help to keep the vocal folds moist. Sound is produced by the vocal folds below them, not by the vestibular folds.

Question 6069. Which of these pairs belongs together: the vocal fold with the vocal ligament, the vestibular fold with the vocal ligament, the vocal fold with the vestibular ligament, or the aryepiglottic fold with the cricoid cartilage? The answer is the vocal fold with the vocal ligament. The vestibular fold contains the vestibular ligament.

Question 6070. What is the name of the small pouch that runs upward from the front of the laryngeal ventricle, between the vestibular fold and the thyroid cartilage? The answer is the laryngeal saccule. Its wall is packed with mucous glands, and their secretion lubricates the vocal folds.

Question 6071. Which muscle lies immediately lateral to the vocal ligament and forms the bulk of the vocal fold? The answer is the vocalis muscle, the medial part of the thyroarytenoid. When it contracts it shortens and thickens the fold and raises the pitch of the voice.

Question 6072. Which statement about the vocal ligament is correct: it is the thickened upper edge of the cricothyroid membrane, the lower edge of the quadrangular membrane, part of the thyrohyoid membrane, or part of the epiglottis? The answer is the thickened upper edge of the cricothyroid membrane, which runs from the thyroid cartilage to the vocal process. The lower edge of the quadrangular membrane is the vestibular ligament.

Question 6073. A described view of the larynx during quiet breathing shows two pale folds separated in front by a dark triangle, and behind them a wider gap between two small cartilages. What are the two parts of the rima glottidis shown? The answer is the intermembranous part in front and the intercartilaginous part behind. The front part lies between the vocal folds and the back part between the arytenoid cartilages.

Question 6074. Which nerve carries sensation from the lining of the larynx above the vocal folds: the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, or the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. The recurrent laryngeal nerve carries sensation from below the folds.

Question 6075. A constructed illustration: after a described operation on one side of the neck, the voice is hoarse and the fold on that side lies motionless near the midline. Which nerve has most likely been injured? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Its fibers supply every intrinsic muscle of the larynx except the cricothyroid, so the adductors act unopposed and the fold comes to rest near the midline.

Question 6076. Name, spoken as a list, the two structures attached to the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage. The answer is the vocal ligament and the vocalis muscle. The process is the small forward-pointing tip of the cartilage. The vocal fold is formed over these two structures.

Question 6077. A described frontal section through the larynx is cut first just above the vocal folds and then just below them. How do the two sections differ? The answer is that above the folds the cavity is wider and leads up into the vestibule, while below them it narrows into the subglottic space.

Question 6078. Which muscle is the only one that can open the rima glottidis and so widen the airway? The answer is the posterior cricoarytenoid. It arises from the back of the lamina of the cricoid cartilage and pulls the muscular process of the arytenoid backward and medially. That movement swings the vocal process outward.

Question 6079. Which muscle pulls the vocal fold inward toward the midline: the posterior cricoarytenoid, the lateral cricoarytenoid, the cricothyroid, or the thyroepiglottic? The answer is the lateral cricoarytenoid. It runs from the upper border of the arch of the cricoid cartilage to the muscular process of the arytenoid. Pulling that process forward rotates the vocal process inward and closes the gap.

Question 6080. Which muscle runs from the front of the cricoid cartilage up to the lower border of the thyroid cartilage and stretches the vocal fold? The answer is the cricothyroid. When it contracts it tilts the thyroid cartilage forward and so lengthens the fold, raising the pitch. It is the only intrinsic muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Question 6081. Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle: the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, or the pharyngeal plexus? The answer is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It runs down on the cricothyroid muscle beside the superior thyroid artery. Injury to it during an operation on the neck weakens the upper range of the voice.

Question 6082. A constructed illustration: a person chokes on a large piece of food, and the described reflex closes the entrance of the larynx. Which muscle closes that entrance? The answer is the aryepiglottic muscle, together with the oblique arytenoid muscles. The fibers run in the aryepiglottic fold from the side of the epiglottis to the arytenoid cartilage and draw the fold inward.

Question 6083. Which muscle lies across the back of the larynx between the two arytenoid cartilages and pulls them together? The answer is the transverse arytenoid. It is a single muscle that spans the gap between the two cartilages. Its action closes the back part of the rima glottidis.

Question 6084. Which muscle shortens and slackens the vocal fold when it acts alone: the cricothyroid, the vocalis, the posterior cricoarytenoid, or the transverse arytenoid? The answer is the vocalis. It pulls the arytenoid cartilage forward toward the thyroid cartilage and so shortens the fold. The cricothyroid does the opposite, lengthening the fold and raising the pitch.

Question 6085. A described dissection of the back of the larynx shows two muscles crossing each other over the back of the cricoid cartilage. Which muscles are they, and what do they do? The answer is the transverse arytenoid and the oblique arytenoid muscles. The transverse fibers run straight across and the oblique fibers cross to the opposite side.

Question 6086. Which structure does the recurrent laryngeal nerve pass beneath as it enters the larynx, and behind which joint does it lie? The answer is the lower border of the inferior constrictor muscle, and it enters behind the cricothyroid joint. It runs up in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus with the inferior laryngeal artery.

Question 6087. A constructed illustration: a person reports that the voice tires and that the upper notes of a song are lost, while the rest of the voice is normal. Which muscle is weak? The answer is the cricothyroid, supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Without it the vocal fold cannot be lengthened and the higher notes cannot be reached. The assessment belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6088. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cricothyroid with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the cricothyroid with the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the posterior cricoarytenoid with the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, or the vocalis with the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the cricothyroid with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All the other intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Question 6089. Which of these muscles is not an intrinsic muscle of the larynx: the cricothyroid, the thyroarytenoid, the sternothyroid, or the aryepiglottic? The answer is the sternothyroid. An intrinsic muscle has both of its attachments on the cartilages of the larynx, while the sternothyroid runs from the sternum to the thyroid cartilage and moves the whole larynx.

Question 6090. Which extrinsic muscle runs from the sternum up to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and steadies the larynx while the cricothyroid tilts it? The answer is the sternothyroid. Without it the pull of the cricothyroid would drag the whole larynx instead of tilting the thyroid cartilage forward.

Question 6091. A constructed illustration: after a described operation on both sides of the neck, breathing becomes noisy and both folds lie close to the midline. Which nerve has been injured, and which muscle has been lost? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and the loss is of the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor. With both folds fixed near the midline the airway is narrow. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6092. Which muscle spans the gap between the two arytenoid cartilages at the back of the larynx? The answer is the transverse arytenoid. It is a single, unpaired muscle that lies behind the mucous membrane of the back wall. Its fibers run from one cartilage across to the other.

Question 6093. Which statement about the thyroarytenoid muscle is correct: it adducts the vocal fold and shortens it, it abducts the fold and lengthens it, it has no effect on the fold, or it acts only on the epiglottis? The answer is that it adducts and shortens the fold. Its lateral part pulls the arytenoid forward and inward, and its medial part is the vocalis.

Question 6094. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, with its medial edge projecting into the laryngeal cavity as a ridge covered by mucosa? The answer is the thyroarytenoid muscle, whose medial edge is the vocalis. That ridge, covered by mucosa, forms the vocal fold. The lateral part of the muscle lies in the wall of the larynx beside the thyroid cartilage.

Question 6095. A described dissection shows muscle fibers running from the back of the cricoid lamina upward and laterally to the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage. Which muscle is shown, and what happens when it contracts? The answer is the posterior cricoarytenoid. Pulling the muscular process backward and medially swings the vocal process outward and opens the rima glottidis.

Question 6096. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cricothyroid with tension of the vocal fold, the posterior cricoarytenoid with tension of the vocal fold, the vocalis with abduction of the vocal fold, or the lateral cricoarytenoid with abduction? The answer is the cricothyroid with tension of the vocal fold. It lengthens and tightens the fold.

Question 6097. Which statement about the aryepiglottic muscle is correct: it narrows the entrance of the larynx during swallowing, it opens the rima glottidis, it lengthens the vocal fold, or it has no action on the larynx? The answer is that it narrows the entrance of the larynx during swallowing. It lies in the aryepiglottic fold and continues the oblique arytenoid muscle forward to the epiglottis.

Question 6098. A constructed illustration: after a described operation high in the neck, a person has lost the sensation that protects the larynx and coughs after drinking. Which nerve is injured, and which part of the lining has lost its sensation? The answer is the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and the lining above the vocal folds has lost its sensation. The protective reflex that closes the inlet is therefore weakened.

Question 6099. A described cross-sectional image taken at the level of the vocal folds shows a small muscle within each fold, just lateral to the sharp edge, and a larger muscle outside it in the wall of the larynx. Which muscles are shown? The answer is the vocalis within the fold and the thyroarytenoid, of which the vocalis is the medial part.

Question 6100. A described larynx is watched from above during quiet breathing and then during speech. Which muscles are chiefly active in each state? The answer is the posterior cricoarytenoid during quiet breathing, which opens the folds, and the lateral cricoarytenoid with the arytenoid muscles during speech, which bring the folds together.

To summarize, the pharynx is a fibromuscular half-tube that hangs from the base of the skull and is divided into the nasopharynx, the oropharynx and the laryngopharynx, each named for the cavity behind it. The auditory tube opens into its lateral wall, the palatine tonsils lie between the two arches, and a weak point between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor is where a pouch of mucosa may protrude. The larynx is built from nine cartilages, three unpaired and three paired, and its cavity is narrowed at the vocal folds, which contain the vocal ligament and the vocalis and are covered by stratified squamous epithelium. The cricothyroid lengthens and tightens the fold and is the only intrinsic muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, while the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor and every other intrinsic muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymph above the folds drains to the upper deep cervical nodes and lymph below them to the lower deep cervical nodes, and the folds themselves have almost no lymph vessels. Naming each structure together with its nerve and its neighbor is what fixes this region in memory, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 62 — Trachea and Bronchi

This chapter follows the airway from the voice box down to the branches inside the lung. It begins with the larynx, where the laryngeal nerves control the voice and guard the entrance to the airway, and then turns to the trachea and the bronchi, their shape, their relations in the neck and the chest, and the way they divide. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately afterwards, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The explanation comes in the same paragraph, and it often says why the tempting wrong answer is wrong as well. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 6101. Which nerve of the neck carries the motor supply to the cricothyroid muscle, the muscle that tenses the vocal cord? The answer is the external laryngeal nerve. It is the smaller of the two branches of the superior laryngeal nerve, which itself arises from the vagus, the tenth cranial nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the other intrinsic muscles of the larynx.

Question 6102. Which of these structures pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to reach the lining of the larynx above the vocal folds: the internal laryngeal nerve, the external laryngeal nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, or the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the internal laryngeal nerve. It carries sensation from the upper part of the laryngeal lining. The external laryngeal nerve stays outside the larynx and supplies the cricothyroid muscle.

Question 6103. A described dissection of the neck follows a small nerve running down beneath the sternothyroid muscle to reach the cricothyroid muscle. Which nerve is described? The answer is the external laryngeal nerve. It is the smaller branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and it carries no sensation from the larynx. The internal laryngeal nerve, by contrast, takes the sensory route through the thyrohyoid membrane.

Question 6104. A described sagittal section of the larynx shows two folds on each side, one above the other, with a pouch between them. Which is the lower fold? The answer is the vocal fold, which contains the vocal ligament. The upper fold is the vestibular fold, and the pouch is the laryngeal ventricle. The vocal folds guard the opening called the rima glottidis.

Question 6105. A constructed illustration: after an operation on the thyroid gland, a person speaks with a hoarse and breathy voice. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It climbs in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus, close to the inferior thyroid artery, and it supplies nearly all the laryngeal muscles. Injury leaves the vocal fold unable to close.

Question 6106. Which cartilage of the larynx is the only one that forms a complete ring, so that the airway cannot be closed by pressing on it? The answer is the cricoid cartilage. It is shaped like a signet ring, narrow in front and tall at the back. The thyroid cartilage and the epiglottis do not form complete rings.

Question 6107. The recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs upward in a groove between two structures of the neck and the upper chest. Which two? The answer is the trachea and the esophagus. That groove is called the tracheoesophageal groove. The nerve runs upward in it to reach the larynx, which is why disease of the esophagus or the trachea can damage the voice.

Question 6108. True or false: the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies every intrinsic muscle of the larynx except one, and the exception is the cricothyroid. The answer is true. The cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve instead. All of the muscles that move the arytenoid cartilages receive their fibers from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Question 6109. Which muscle of the larynx is the only one that pulls the vocal folds apart and so opens the airway? The answer is the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle. It arises from the back of the cricoid cartilage and pulls the muscular process of the arytenoid backward. Its action is the opposite of the lateral cricoarytenoid muscle, which closes the folds.

Question 6110. Which statement about the cricothyroid muscle is correct: it tenses the vocal cords and raises the pitch, it relaxes them and lowers the pitch, it pulls the cords apart, or it closes the laryngeal inlet? The answer is that it tenses the vocal cords and raises the pitch. It tilts the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid. The pitch of the voice depends on that tension.

Question 6111. A described coronal section through the larynx shows a vocal fold on one side turned toward the middle of the airway, while the fold on the other side is held out to the side. What does this suggest? The answer is a paralyzed fold on the side turned inward. The arytenoid cartilage has swung toward the midline, carrying the vocal ligament with it.

Question 6112. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cricothyroid muscle with the internal laryngeal nerve, the posterior cricoarytenoid with the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the thyroarytenoid with the external laryngeal nerve, or the vocal fold with the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the posterior cricoarytenoid with the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Every intrinsic muscle of the larynx is supplied by that nerve except the cricothyroid.

Question 6113. Name the two branches into which the superior laryngeal nerve divides, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the internal laryngeal nerve and the external laryngeal nerve. The internal branch is sensory and pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to supply the lining above the vocal folds. The external branch is motor and supplies the cricothyroid muscle.

Question 6114. A constructed illustration: a person with a large swelling of the aortic arch speaks with a hoarse voice, and no disease can be found in the larynx itself. Which nerve is compressed, and why that side? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. It hooks around the arch of the aorta and lies against it, so a swelling there presses on it.

Question 6115. Which paired cartilage of the larynx carries the vocal process at its front and the muscular process at its side, and so steers the vocal fold? The answer is the arytenoid cartilage. The vocal ligament attaches to the vocal process. Muscles pull on the muscular process to open and to close the airway.

Question 6116. Which nerve carries sensation from the lining of the larynx above the vocal folds: the internal laryngeal nerve, the external laryngeal nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerve, or the glossopharyngeal nerve? The answer is the internal laryngeal nerve. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane beside the superior laryngeal artery. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the lining below the folds instead.

Question 6117. Two structures pass through the thyrohyoid membrane side by side to reach the inside of the larynx. One of them is the internal laryngeal nerve. Which is the other? The answer is the superior laryngeal artery, a branch of the superior thyroid artery. The nerve lies just behind the artery as both pass through the membrane.

Question 6118. A described specimen shows a ring of cartilage shaped like a signet ring, narrow at the front and tall at the back, sitting below the thyroid cartilage. Which cartilage is shown? The answer is the cricoid cartilage. Its tall back part carries the arytenoid cartilages. It is the only complete ring in the airway.

Question 6119. A section cut across the larynx shows the two vocal folds facing each other with a narrow gap between them. In which plane was the section cut, and what is the gap called? The answer is the transverse plane, and the gap is the rima glottidis. A section along the length of the airway would show the folds from the side instead.

Question 6120. Which intrinsic muscle of the larynx runs from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid cartilage and shortens the vocal fold, so relaxing it and lowering the pitch? The answer is the thyroarytenoid muscle. Its inner fibers form the vocalis muscle, which lies beside the vocal ligament. Shortening the fold makes it thicker and lowers the note.

Question 6121. A constructed illustration: an emergency airway must be opened through the front of the neck, and the surgeon must avoid cutting the cricoid cartilage. Which space is used, and why is the cricoid left alone? The answer is the cricothyroid space between the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid. Damage to the cricoid can narrow the airway later.

Question 6122. The nerves of the larynx all arise from one cranial nerve. Which is it: the ninth, the tenth, the eleventh, or the twelfth? The answer is the tenth cranial nerve, the vagus. Its superior laryngeal branch divides into an internal and an external laryngeal nerve. Its recurrent branch climbs back up to the larynx.

Question 6123. The vocal ligament is a thickened band of elastic tissue. Between which two points does it stretch: the vocal process and the thyroid cartilage, the muscular process and the cricoid cartilage, the epiglottis and the arytenoid, or the corniculate and the cuneiform cartilages? The answer is the vocal process and the thyroid cartilage. Its free edge forms the vocal fold.

Question 6124. Which leaf-shaped cartilage of the larynx stands above the opening of the airway and folds down during swallowing? The answer is the epiglottis. Its stem is attached to the thyroid cartilage, and its broad upper part projects into the throat. It helps keep food out of the larynx.

Question 6125. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cricoid cartilage with a complete ring, the thyroid cartilage with the vocal ligament, the arytenoid cartilage with the hyoid bone, or the epiglottis with the cricothyroid joint? The answer is the cricoid cartilage with a complete ring. The arytenoid cartilages sit on the back of the cricoid, and the cricothyroid joint lies between the cricoid and the thyroid.

Question 6126. At which point does the trachea begin in the neck? The answer is at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage. That lies at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra. Above it the airway continues as the larynx, and below it the trachea runs down into the chest.

Question 6127. How many C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage support the human trachea: 6 to 8, 16 to 20, 30 to 34, or more than 40? The answer is 16 to 20 of them. They are incomplete at the back, where the gap is filled by fibrous tissue and the trachealis muscle. The rings keep the airway open while still allowing the neck to bend.

Question 6128. What is the name of the ridge of cartilage that separates the two main bronchi at the lower end of the trachea? The answer is the carina. It is the last tracheal cartilage, drawn up into a keel between the two openings. Its lining is very sensitive, and touching it during a bronchoscopy makes a person cough.

Question 6129. Which structure lies immediately behind the trachea from the neck down to the bifurcation? The answer is the esophagus. The two tubes share a wall of connective tissue, and the trachea lies in front of the esophagus throughout its course. The esophagus is the softer tube and it is flattened from front to back.

Question 6130. At what level does the trachea divide into the two main bronchi: the sternal angle, the jugular notch, the xiphoid process, or the first rib? The answer is the sternal angle, which corresponds to the fourth thoracic vertebra. The ridge at the division is the carina. The bifurcation lies behind the joint where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum.

Question 6131. A described chest radiograph shows a dark vertical band in the middle of the neck and upper chest, with the heart shadow below and slightly to the left. What is that band? The answer is the air-filled trachea. Air absorbs very few radiograph beams, so it appears dark against the soft tissues. The band ends at the bifurcation behind the sternal angle.

Question 6132. Which main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical: the right, the left, both equally, or neither, because the two are the same? The answer is the right main bronchus. It is about 2.5 centimeters long and runs more steeply downward than the left. Because of that shape, an inhaled object is more likely to enter it.

Question 6133. Which muscle forms the back wall of the trachea and fills the gap between the ends of the cartilage rings? The answer is the trachealis muscle. Its fibers run across the gap, and when it contracts it narrows the airway. The lining lies directly against it, without cartilage between them.

Question 6134. A constructed illustration: a small child inhales a peanut and begins to cough and wheeze on the right side. Into which airway has the object most probably passed? The answer is the right main bronchus. It is wider and more vertical than the left, so objects follow the straighter path. The object may then lodge in the right lower lobe.

Question 6135. Which large vein crosses in front of the trachea just above the sternal angle: the left brachiocephalic vein, the right brachiocephalic vein, the superior vena cava, or the azygos vein? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein, formed by the union of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins. It crosses the midline in front of the trachea on its way down.

Question 6136. Which structure arches over the left main bronchus just after the bronchus leaves the trachea: the arch of the aorta, the azygos vein, the pulmonary trunk, or the left subclavian artery? The answer is the arch of the aorta. It hooks over the left bronchus and then descends behind it as the descending aorta. On the right the corresponding structure is the azygos vein.

Question 6137. True or false: the trachea is a complete cartilaginous tube, so that its wall cannot be compressed from behind. The answer is false. The cartilage rings are C-shaped and the back of the tube is completed by muscle and fibrous tissue. That soft back wall allows the esophagus behind it to expand when food is swallowed.

Question 6138. A described computed tomography section of the chest shows a rounded air-filled tube in the middle, with a smaller flattened tube behind it, and two air-filled branches just below. What does the section show? The answer is the trachea dividing at the carina, with the esophagus behind it. The two branches are the right and left main bronchi.

Question 6139. Name three structures that lie in front of the trachea in the lower part of the neck, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the isthmus of the thyroid gland, the inferior thyroid veins, and the sternothyroid muscle. The isthmus lies across the second, third and fourth rings of the trachea. The veins drain downward into the left brachiocephalic vein.

Question 6140. Which kind of cartilage forms the rings of the trachea: hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, fibrocartilage, or calcified bone? The answer is hyaline cartilage. The rings are firm but they can calcify with age, which makes them appear pale on a radiograph. The cartilage of the epiglottis is elastic instead.

Question 6141. What is the name of the pyramidal unit of lung tissue that has its own bronchus and its own artery, and can be removed on its own? The answer is the bronchopulmonary segment. Its apex points toward the hilum, and its base lies at the surface of the lung. The segments are separated by connective tissue septa.

Question 6142. Two tubes descend through the upper chest, one in front of the other, and the softer one is flattened from front to back. Which lies in front, and which lies behind? The answer is the trachea in front and the esophagus behind. The esophagus is the softer of the two and its walls fall together when it is empty. Both are crossed by the arch of the aorta.

Question 6143. A constructed illustration: a tube placed in the trachea through a low opening in the neck has pressed for a long time against the artery that crosses the front of the trachea. Which artery is at risk? The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk. It runs obliquely across the front of the trachea behind the upper part of the sternum. The management of such a problem belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6144. Which structure lies immediately behind the left main bronchus: the esophagus, the azygos vein, the right pulmonary artery, or the thymus? The answer is the esophagus. The left main bronchus runs forward and to the left, passing in front of the esophagus and the descending aorta. On the right the corresponding bronchus passes below the azygos vein.

Question 6145. Which bronchus arises from the right main bronchus above the right pulmonary artery, and so is called eparterial? The answer is the right superior lobar bronchus. It supplies the upper lobe of the right lung. On the left the corresponding artery lies above the bronchus instead.

Question 6146. Which of these pairs belongs together: the right upper lobe with the eparterial bronchus, the right middle lobe with three segments, the left upper lobe with the superior segment, or the right lower lobe with the lingula? The answer is the right upper lobe with the eparterial bronchus. It arises above the right pulmonary artery. The lingula belongs to the left upper lobe.

Question 6147. A described radiograph of a child who choked while eating shows a small dense object lying in the right main bronchus. Why does it lie on that side? The answer is that the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left. It therefore continues the line of the trachea more closely than the left does. The object follows that straighter course.

Question 6148. Within a bronchopulmonary segment, one vessel runs at its center beside the bronchus, and another runs at its edge. Which is which: the artery at the center and the vein at the edge, the vein at the center and the artery at the edge, both at the center, or both at the edge? The answer is the artery at the center with the bronchus, and the vein at the edge.

Question 6149. How many lobes does the right lung have, and what are they called? The answer is three, named the superior lobe, the middle lobe and the inferior lobe. The left lung has only two lobes, because the space that the heart occupies on that side leaves no room for a third. The oblique and horizontal fissures separate the lobes on the right.

Question 6150. Which structure lies in front of the second, third and fourth rings of the trachea: the isthmus of the thyroid gland, the thymus, the left brachiocephalic vein, or the cricoid cartilage? The answer is the isthmus of the thyroid gland. It is the bridge of tissue joining the two lobes of the gland across the front of the airway. Below it the trachea is covered only by veins and strap muscles.

Question 6151. The right main bronchus is called eparterial and the left hyparterial. Which is correct: the right above the right pulmonary artery and the left below the left, both above, both below, or the right below and the left above? The answer is that the right lies above the right pulmonary artery and the left below the left pulmonary artery. The arrangement arises in the embryo.

Question 6152. True or false: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left main bronchus. The answer is true. The left main bronchus is longer, narrower and more horizontal, because it must pass under the arch of the aorta. That difference explains why inhaled objects usually go to the right.

Question 6153. Which part of the airway keeps a fixed opening because cartilage holds it open, so that a narrowing there does not relax with the smooth muscle: the trachea, a bronchiole, an alveolar duct, or a respiratory bronchiole? The answer is the trachea. Its C-shaped rings of cartilage keep the tube open, and the muscle at the back can only narrow it a little. The small airways have no cartilage at all.

Question 6154. A described chest radiograph shows the dark band of the trachea shifted to the right of the midline, with a large white area filling the left side of the chest. What has pushed the trachea? The answer is a collection in the left pleural space, such as fluid, which pushes the middle of the chest toward the opposite side. Lung collapse instead pulls the trachea toward the affected side.

Question 6155. Which structure lies immediately behind the carina, where the trachea divides? The answer is the esophagus. The left main bronchus then runs forward across the front of the esophagus, and the descending aorta lies behind it. The carina is separated from the esophagus only by a thin layer of tissue.

Question 6156. What is the name of the tongue-shaped part of the left lung that hangs below the left upper lobe bronchus and corresponds to the middle lobe on the right? The answer is the lingula. It lies in the left upper lobe and has two segments of its own. It is not a separate lobe, because no fissure separates it.

Question 6157. The bronchi have their own blood supply, separate from the vessels that exchange gas. Where do the bronchial arteries usually arise? The answer is from the descending thoracic aorta. There are usually two on the left and one on the right, and the right one often arises from a posterior intercostal artery.

Question 6158. Which kind of epithelium lines the trachea and the larger bronchi: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, simple squamous epithelium, transitional epithelium, or stratified squamous epithelium? The answer is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. The cilia sweep a film of mucus upward toward the throat. The goblet cells secrete that mucus, which traps dust and organisms.

Question 6159. A constructed illustration: a tumor at the hilum of the left lung presses on a nerve and the voice becomes hoarse, while the vocal fold on that side stops moving. Which nerve is involved, and why is it on that side? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks around the aortic arch and then climbs beside the left bronchus.

Question 6160. A section in one plane shows the trachea cut along its length, with the carina rising as a small ridge between the two main bronchi. Which plane is that? The answer is the coronal plane, which runs from side to side across the chest. A section across the trachea would show its lumen as a circle.

Question 6161. On a chest radiograph, the two main bronchi leave the trachea at a wide angle. What is that angle called and roughly how large is it: the carinal angle at about 60 to 70 degrees, the costal angle at about 90 degrees, the sternal angle at about 30 degrees, or the bronchial angle at about 150 degrees? The answer is the carinal angle, at about 60 to 70 degrees.

Question 6162. In the main bronchi, the C-shaped cartilage rings are replaced by what kind of support? The answer is irregular plates of cartilage, arranged around the tube rather than as rings. Further down, in the bronchioles, the cartilage disappears altogether. The change allows the smaller airways to alter their diameter.

Question 6163. At the hilum of the left lung, which structure lies above the main bronchus: the pulmonary artery, the pulmonary vein, the eparterial bronchus, or the esophagus? The answer is the pulmonary artery. On the right the eparterial bronchus lies above the right pulmonary artery, so the two sides differ. The pulmonary veins lie in front of the bronchus on both sides.

Question 6164. A described bronchogram shows a branching tree within one lobe, filling with contrast material, and the branches end in rounded tips that do not join their neighbors. What is shown? The answer is the bronchial tree within one lobe, with the branches of the individual bronchopulmonary segments. The segments do not communicate with one another, so a segment can be removed alone.

Question 6165. The thoracic duct climbs through the chest behind the trachea. Which structure does it lie behind in the upper part of its course, and where does it cross to the left? The answer is the esophagus, and it crosses at about the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra. Below that level it lies between the aorta and the azygos vein.

Question 6166. How many bronchopulmonary segments are usually present in the right lung: six, eight, ten, or fourteen? The answer is ten. The left lung usually has eight or ten, because some of its segments are fused in the upper lobe. Each segment has its own bronchus and its own artery.

Question 6167. A lung has only two lobes, separated by a single long fissure that runs obliquely. Which lung is it, and what is the fissure called: the left lung with the oblique fissure, the right lung with the oblique fissure, the left lung with the horizontal fissure, or the right lung with the horizontal fissure? The answer is the left lung with the oblique fissure.

Question 6168. A constructed illustration: a person has a chronic infection that has destroyed the support of one bronchus, so that it stays wide and dilated. Which tissue has been lost from the wall? The answer is the cartilage and the elastic tissue of the bronchus. Without that support the airway cannot keep its shape. The dilated airway is described as bronchiectasis when it is seen.

Question 6169. At which level does the trachea end by dividing into the two main bronchi? The answer is at the level of the sternal angle. That point lies at the fourth thoracic vertebra, where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum. Below it the airway continues as two separate bronchi.

Question 6170. Which main bronchus is the longer of the two: the right, the left, neither because they are equal, or the right in some people and the left in others? The answer is the left main bronchus. It is about twice as long as the right and it runs more horizontally to reach the left lung. It passes beneath the arch of the aorta on its way.

Question 6171. A described specimen of the trachea is viewed from behind after the esophagus has been removed. A soft, flat band of tissue spans a gap between the ends of the cartilage rings. What is that band? The answer is the trachealis muscle with its fibrous tissue. The rings are incomplete at the back, and this band completes the tube.

Question 6172. In a young child, which organ lies in front of the lower part of the trachea and the great vessels, and largely disappears with age? The answer is the thymus. It occupies the front of the upper mediastinum in infancy and childhood. In the adult it is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue.

Question 6173. Which statement about the lining of the trachea is correct: the mucus is swept upward toward the throat, the mucus is swept downward into the lungs, the cilia beat in both directions at once, or the lining has no cilia at all? The answer is that the mucus is swept upward toward the throat. The cilia beat in one direction only, carrying trapped dust out of the airway.

Question 6174. Name the two sets of vessels that bring blood to the lungs, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the pulmonary vessels and the bronchial vessels. The pulmonary vessels carry blood for the exchange of gases and they form the greater part of the flow. The bronchial vessels are much smaller and they nourish the walls of the airways themselves.

Question 6175. A constructed illustration: an opening is made into the trachea in the lower part of the neck to secure the airway. Which rings are usually chosen, and which structure in front of them lies across the airway? The answer is the second to fourth rings, with the isthmus of the thyroid gland. The isthmus lies across those rings and covers them.

Question 6176. Which of these pairs belongs together: the right upper lobe with the eparterial bronchus, the left upper lobe with three lobar bronchi, the right middle lobe with the lingula, or the left lower lobe with the horizontal fissure? The answer is the right upper lobe with the eparterial bronchus. The lingula belongs to the left upper lobe, and the horizontal fissure belongs to the right lung.

Question 6177. A small object is inhaled while a person lies on the back. Where is it most likely to come to rest: the lower lobe of the right lung, the left lower lobe, the right upper lobe, or the left upper lobe? The answer is the lower lobe of the right lung. The right main bronchus is more vertical, and gravity carries the object to the lowest part of that lung.

Question 6178. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows a triangular shadow with its apex at the hilum and its base against the front of the chest, below the horizontal fissure. Which lobe is collapsed? The answer is the right middle lobe. The middle lobe is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and behind by the oblique fissure, so it collapses into that wedge shape.

Question 6179. What is the name given to the bronchi that supply the lobes of the lung, one for each lobe? The answer is the lobar bronchi, also called secondary bronchi. They arise from the main bronchi, which are the primary bronchi. The bronchi that supply the bronchopulmonary segments are the segmental or tertiary bronchi.

Question 6180. Which structure lies above the left main bronchus as the bronchus runs toward the left lung? The answer is the arch of the aorta. The bronchus passes beneath the arch, and the aorta then continues downward behind it. On the right side the corresponding structure overhead is the azygos vein.

Question 6181. At which level of the airway does cartilage finally disappear from the wall: the trachea, the main bronchi, the bronchioles, or the alveolar ducts? The answer is at the bronchioles. The bronchi still have plates of cartilage in their walls, but the smallest conducting tubes have none. Smooth muscle alone controls their diameter.

Question 6182. True or false: the pulmonary veins run in the septa between the bronchopulmonary segments, so that each vein drains two neighboring segments. The answer is true. The veins lie at the edges of the segments rather than at their centers. The segmental artery and the bronchus lie together at the center.

Question 6183. A constructed illustration: a child who choked on a small toy now has a lung that is too full of air, with the middle of the chest pushed toward the other side. What has the object done, and why does the right side suffer more often? The answer is that it has acted as a valve, letting air in but not out, and the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.

Question 6184. A described cross section through the hilum of the right lung shows a wide air tube with a large vessel lying below it. Which structure is above, and why is that arrangement named? The answer is the right main bronchus above the right pulmonary artery. Because the bronchus lies above the artery, the airway and that vessel are described as eparterial.

Question 6185.
