Which part of the airway is the most sensitive to touch, so that a bronchoscope touching it sets off a violent cough: the carina, the vocal folds, the trachealis muscle, or the epiglottis? The answer is the carina. Its lining is packed with nerve endings that guard the entrance to the lungs. The same reflex clears the airway when dust reaches that point.

Question 6186. What happens to the lumen of the trachea when the trachealis muscle contracts during a cough? The answer is that the lumen narrows, and the air leaves faster through the smaller opening. The muscle can also narrow the airway when the lining becomes irritated. Its fibers run across the soft back wall of the tube.

Question 6187. Which large vessel lies behind the left main bronchus and to the left of it as it descends through the chest? The answer is the descending thoracic aorta. It begins at the arch, which hooks over the left main bronchus, and then runs down behind and to the left of the bronchus. The esophagus lies between the two on that side.

Question 6188. Which kind of cell in the lining of the airway produces the mucus that traps dust? The answer is the goblet cell. Goblet cells lie among the ciliated cells of the respiratory lining. Their secretion forms a thin film that the cilia carry upward to the throat.

Question 6189. A described barium swallow shows a soft tube descending in front of the vertebral column and behind the trachea, and the swallow stops for a moment as the tube is pressed from the left above. Which two structures are shown in relation? The answer is the esophagus behind and the trachea in front, with the aortic arch pressing from the left above.

Question 6190. A small object is inhaled into a main bronchus. In which part of the lung does it most often come to rest: the lower lobe of the right lung, the lower lobe of the left lung, the middle lobe of the right lung, or the upper lobe of the right lung? The answer is the lower lobe of the right lung, in its posterior basal segment.

Question 6191. Which statement about a bronchopulmonary segment is correct: it has its own bronchus and artery and is separated by a septum, it shares a bronchus with its neighbor, its vein runs at its center, or it cannot be removed without removing the whole lobe? The answer is that it has its own bronchus and artery and is separated by a septum. That is why a single segment can be removed.

Question 6192. Which vein arches over the right main bronchus before it joins the superior vena cava? The answer is the azygos vein. It comes up on the right side of the vertebral column and hooks forward over the bronchus. On the left side the arch above the corresponding bronchus is made by the aorta instead.

Question 6193. Which part of the trachea forms the carina at its lower end? The answer is the last tracheal cartilage. It is drawn up into a ridge that separates the openings of the two main bronchi. Its mucous membrane is very sensitive to touch.

Question 6194. A described computed tomography section across the upper chest shows a rounded air-filled tube in the midline, a flattened soft tube directly behind it, and the vertebral column behind that. What are the two tubes? The answer is the trachea in front and the esophagus behind. The esophagus is flattened because its walls are relaxed and touch each other.

Question 6195. True or false: the left main bronchus runs more horizontally than the right main bronchus. The answer is true. It must pass beneath the arch of the aorta before it reaches the left lung. The right main bronchus descends more steeply, closer to the line of the trachea.

Question 6196. A described chest radiograph of a young child shows one lung larger and more translucent than the other, a flattened diaphragm on that side, and the heart pushed toward the opposite side. What does this pattern show? The answer is air trapped in that lung, which cannot escape. An inhaled object has let air in but not out, and the lung has overinflated.

Question 6197. A constructed illustration: a person who needed a tube in the trachea for a long time later breathes with a whistling sound, and the narrowing lies where the tube pressed against the wall. Why does pressure at that point damage the airway? The answer is that the lining is supplied by small vessels, and pressure stops the flow, so the wall heals with scar tissue.

Question 6198. Where can the trachea be felt through the skin: in the midline of the neck above the sternal notch, at the side of the neck behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle, just below the middle of the clavicle, or in the floor of the mouth? The answer is the midline of the neck above the sternal notch. The rings can be felt there through the skin and the thin strap muscles.

Question 6199. Which of these pairs belongs together: the carina with the fourth thoracic vertebra, the cricoid cartilage with the fourth cervical vertebra, the hilum of the lung with the eighth cervical vertebra, or the thyroid isthmus with the first thoracic vertebra? The answer is the carina with the fourth thoracic vertebra. The cricoid cartilage lies at the sixth cervical vertebra, where the trachea begins.

Question 6200. A described radiograph of the chest shows the dark air column of the trachea ending in a keel, with one branch running steeply downward and the other more horizontally. Which branch is the steeper one, and what follows from that? The answer is the right main bronchus. Its steeper course is why an inhaled object enters the right lung more often than the left.

To summarize, the larynx is supplied by branches of the vagus, the tenth cranial nerve: the internal laryngeal nerve carries sensation from above the vocal folds, the external laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies every other intrinsic muscle and the lining below the folds. The trachea begins below the cricoid cartilage, is held open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, and divides at the carina at the level of the sternal angle and the fourth thoracic vertebra. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, which is why inhaled objects usually enter it, while the left main bronchus is longer and passes beneath the arch of the aorta. Each lung is divided into bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own bronchus and artery and with its veins in the septa between segments. The mucosa of the carina is the most sensitive part of the airway, and the cough it provokes is the reflex that protects the entrance to the lungs. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 63 — Lungs

This chapter examines the lungs as organs: their lobes, the fissures between them, the bronchopulmonary segments within them, the hilum, and the root of the lung. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately and then explains why it is right, so nothing has to be held in mind. The lungs are the paired organs of gas exchange, and their internal geography matters to the radiologist, the physician and the surgeon alike. Every item is written to be answered out loud, so descriptions of films and sections are spoken rather than shown. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 6201. Which of the two lungs is divided into three lobes by its fissures? The answer is the right lung. It carries a superior lobe, a middle lobe and an inferior lobe, separated by an oblique fissure and a horizontal fissure. The left lung is divided into two lobes only, because the heart occupies much of the space on that side.

Question 6202. How many lobes are found in the left lung: two, three, four, or five? The answer is two. The left lung has a superior lobe and an inferior lobe, separated by a single oblique fissure. It has no middle lobe, because the heart lies against that side of the chest and takes the space a middle lobe would need.

Question 6203. What is the name of the tongue-shaped projection of lung tissue that hangs below the cardiac notch of the left lung? The answer is the lingula. It is part of the superior lobe, and it lies just above the oblique fissure. The word means a little tongue, which is what its shape suggests.

Question 6204. The lingula belongs to which lobe of the left lung: the superior lobe, the inferior lobe, the middle lobe, or a lobe of its own? The answer is the superior lobe. The lingula is the lower, forward part of that lobe and lies below the cardiac notch. It is the counterpart of the right middle lobe, but not a separate lobe.

Question 6205. A described chest radiograph shows a deep notch cut into the front of the left lung, with a small tongue of tissue below it. Which lobe carries the notch, and what is the tongue called? The answer is the superior lobe and the lingula. The notch itself is the cardiac notch, produced by the heart pressing against that border.

Question 6206. Does the lingula lie above or below the oblique fissure of the left lung, and in which lobe does that place it? The answer is above the fissure, in the superior lobe. The oblique fissure runs downward and forward across the lung and separates the superior lobe from the inferior lobe. Everything above it on the left, including the lingula, belongs to the superior lobe.

Question 6207. Which surface of a lung lies against the ribs: the mediastinal surface, the diaphragmatic surface, the costal surface, or the interlobar surface? The answer is the costal surface. It is the broad, convex outer surface that follows the curve of the chest wall. The mediastinal surface faces the middle of the chest, and the diaphragmatic surface rests on the diaphragm.

Question 6208. What is the name of the surface of the lung that rests on the dome of the diaphragm? The answer is the diaphragmatic surface. It is concave, because it is molded to the dome of the muscle beneath it. The right diaphragmatic surface is higher than the left, since the liver pushes the right dome upward.

Question 6209. A constructed illustration: a growth at the left hilum narrows the left main bronchus, and airflow to the whole left lung falls. Which lobes of that lung are affected? The answer is both the superior lobe and the inferior lobe. The left main bronchus supplies the entire left lung before it divides.

Question 6210. True or false: the left lung has a middle lobe that is simply smaller than the middle lobe on the right. The answer is false. The left lung has only a superior lobe and an inferior lobe. The lingula occupies the position of that lobe, but it is part of the superior lobe and not a lobe of its own.

Question 6211. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lingula with the left superior lobe, the middle lobe with the left lung, the cardiac notch with the right, or the horizontal fissure with the left? The answer is the lingula with the left superior lobe. It lies below the cardiac notch and above the oblique fissure.

Question 6212. Which lung is shorter and wider than the other, and what accounts for that difference? The answer is the right lung, because the right dome of the diaphragm lies higher than the left. The liver fills the space beneath the right dome and pushes it upward, so the right lung has more room across.

Question 6213. Which statement about the lobes is correct: the right lung has three lobes and the left has two, both lungs have three, the left has three and the right has two, or neither lung has a fissure? The answer is that the right lung has three lobes and the left has two. The middle lobe exists only on the right, where the heart does not intrude.

Question 6214. A described left lung shows a broad groove curving over the mediastinal surface above the hilum, and a notch on the anterior border below it. Name the two features. The answer is an impression of the aortic arch and the cardiac notch. The aorta lies against the mediastinal surface above the root, and the heart presses on the border below.

Question 6215. Which lobe of the right lung is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure: the superior lobe, the middle lobe, the inferior lobe, or the lingula? The answer is the middle lobe, a wedge on the front and outer side of the lung. The lingula lies in the same position on the left, but it is part of the superior lobe.

Question 6216. Which part of the lung rises above the first rib into the neck, and what covers it there? The answer is the apex of the lung, covered by the suprapleural membrane. The apex reaches about 2 to 3 centimeters above the medial third of the clavicle. The tough membrane keeps the apex from expanding upward when the pressure inside the chest falls.

Question 6217. What is the name of the fibrous sheet that stretches over the apex of the lung? The answer is the suprapleural membrane. It is attached to the inner border of the first rib and to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra. Because it is tense, the apex of the lung stays below it even during a deep breath.

Question 6218. A constructed illustration: a sharp instrument enters the base of the neck above the left clavicle. Which part of the lung lies there and is at risk? The answer is the apex of the left lung, which rises into the root of the neck. Such a wound can open the pleural cavity and let air enter.

Question 6219. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows two fissure lines crossing the right lung, one almost horizontal and one running downward and forward, so that three lobes are outlined. Which lobes are shown, and which fissure separates the middle lobe from the inferior lobe? The answer is the superior, the middle and the inferior lobes, separated by the oblique fissure.

Question 6220. Which statement about the cardiac notch is correct: it lies on the anterior border of the left lung, on the posterior border of the right lung, in the groove for the aorta, or in the groove for the azygos vein? The answer is the anterior border of the left lung. The heart presses there and leaves a concave notch, and the lingula lies just below it.

Question 6221. Which fissure separates the superior lobe of the right lung from the middle lobe? The answer is the horizontal fissure. It runs forward from the oblique fissure to the anterior border of the lung. It is found only in the right lung, because only the right lung has a middle lobe.

Question 6222. Which fissure is present in both the right lung and the left lung? The answer is the oblique fissure. It runs downward and forward across each lung and separates the upper part of the lung from the lower part. On the right it separates the superior and middle lobes above from the inferior lobe below.

Question 6223. Which fissure lies between the middle lobe and the inferior lobe of the right lung: the horizontal fissure, the oblique fissure, the azygos fissure, or the inferior accessory fissure? The answer is the oblique fissure. The middle lobe sits above it and the inferior lobe below. The horizontal fissure lies above the middle lobe and separates it from the superior lobe.

Question 6224. On the front of the chest, the horizontal fissure of the right lung lies at the level of which costal cartilage: the second, the fourth, the sixth, or the eighth? The answer is the fourth costal cartilage. From there the fissure runs backward to meet the oblique fissure near the middle of the side of the chest.

Question 6225. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows a single line running downward and forward from the back of the chest to end near the front at the level of the sixth costal cartilage. Which fissure is shown, and which two parts of the lung does it separate? The answer is the oblique fissure, and it separates the upper lobes above from the lower lobe below.

Question 6226. On the chest wall, the oblique fissure follows the course of which rib? The answer is the sixth rib. The fissure begins behind at about the level of the third thoracic spine and runs downward and forward. Its surface marking is a line that curves along the sixth rib to reach the sixth costal cartilage in front.

Question 6227. A described section of the chest is cut in such a way that the whole length of the oblique fissure lies in the plane of the cut. How does that plane run? The answer is obliquely, downward and forward, at an angle to the sagittal, coronal and transverse planes. The fissure therefore cannot be shown in full in any one of the three standard planes.

Question 6228. Which of these pairs belongs together: the horizontal fissure with the right lung, the oblique fissure with the right only, the azygos fissure with the left lung, or the lingula with the inferior lobe? The answer is the horizontal fissure with the right lung. The oblique fissure belongs to both lungs, the azygos fissure is a right-sided variant, and the lingula lies in the superior lobe.

Question 6229. True or false: the horizontal fissure is found in both lungs. The answer is false. Only the right lung has a horizontal fissure, and it separates the superior lobe from the middle lobe. The left lung has a single oblique fissure, because it has no middle lobe.

Question 6230. A constructed illustration: a wound enters the right side of the chest in the midaxillary line at the level of the sixth rib and cuts the lung along the tissue plane that lies there. Which fissure has been opened, and which lobes does it separate? The answer is the oblique fissure, which separates the superior and middle lobes above from the inferior lobe below.

Question 6231. A curved line like a comma crosses the apex of the right lung. Which fissure is described, and what is the wedge of lung behind it called? The answer is the azygos fissure, and the wedge is the azygos lobe. The fold is produced by the arch of the azygos vein and is a normal variant, not a true lobe.

Question 6232. When a small extra fissure separates the medial basal segment from the rest of the right lower lobe, what is it called: the horizontal fissure, the superior accessory fissure, the inferior accessory fissure, or the azygos fissure? The answer is the inferior accessory fissure. It is a normal variant and is absent in most people. The superior accessory fissure separates the superior segment of the lower lobe.

Question 6233. A described chest radiograph shows a fine line crossing the right lung from the hilum toward the front, with a small wedge of lung lying below it and above the oblique fissure. Which fissure is shown, and which lobe does the wedge represent? The answer is the horizontal fissure, and the wedge is the middle lobe.

Question 6234. A described computed tomography section through the chest shows a thin line running forward from the hilum across the right lung, dividing it into an upper part that reaches the front of the chest and a smaller part below. Which fissure is this, and which two lobes does it separate? The answer is the horizontal fissure, separating the superior lobe above from the middle lobe below.

Question 6235. In most people the fissures are not complete, and air can pass from one lobe to another where the pleura is missing. What follows from this: a lobe whose own bronchus is blocked may still be ventilated, the lobes cannot move, the pleural cavities join, or the fissure disappears? The answer is that a lobe with a blocked bronchus may still be ventilated.

Question 6236. What is the name of the wedge-shaped unit of a lobe that is supplied by its own segmental bronchus and its own segmental artery? The answer is the bronchopulmonary segment. It is the largest subdivision of a lobe, and it has its own connective tissue septum. Because each one is separate, a surgeon can remove a single segment.

Question 6237. How many bronchopulmonary segments are usually described in the right lung: eight, nine, ten, or twelve? The answer is ten. The right upper lobe holds three segments, the middle lobe holds two, and the right lower lobe holds five. The segments are named for their position, such as apical, posterior and anterior.

Question 6238. How many bronchopulmonary segments are usually described in the left lung? The answer is eight. The left upper lobe holds four segments and the left lower lobe holds four. The count is smaller than on the right because two pairs of segments are joined.

Question 6239. Which airway supplies one bronchopulmonary segment: the trachea, a main bronchus, a lobar bronchus, or a segmental bronchus? The answer is a segmental bronchus. The trachea divides into the two main bronchi, each main bronchus supplies a whole lung, and each lobar bronchus supplies a lobe. The segmental bronchus is also called the tertiary bronchus.

Question 6240. Which two bronchopulmonary segments make up the middle lobe of the right lung? The answer is the lateral segment and the medial segment. They lie one behind the other in the wedge of the middle lobe. The medial segment rests against the heart, and the lateral segment reaches the side of the chest.

Question 6241. Which segment of a lower lobe lies highest and furthest back, behind all of the other segments of that lobe? The answer is the superior segment. It occupies the top of the lower lobe, immediately behind the oblique fissure. It has its own bronchus, which arises behind the other bronchi of the lower lobe.

Question 6242. Which segment of the right upper lobe occupies the very apex of the lung: the apical segment, the posterior segment, the anterior segment, or the medial segment? The answer is the apical segment. It rises into the root of the neck and lies above the rest of the upper lobe. The posterior segment lies behind it and the anterior segment in front of it.

Question 6243. Within a bronchopulmonary segment the bronchus and the artery run together at the center, while the veins run in the septum at the edge. Which vessels therefore separate one segment from the next? The answer is the pulmonary veins. Because the veins lie between segments rather than inside them, a surgeon removing one segment can follow them as a guide.

Question 6244. A described computed tomography section shows a wedge of lung whose base lies against the pleura and whose apex points toward the hilum, separated from its neighbor by a thin septum in which a vein runs. Which unit is shown, and why does the vein lie in the septum rather than inside the wedge? The answer is a bronchopulmonary segment, and the veins run between segments.

Question 6245. What lies at the center of a bronchopulmonary segment: the segmental bronchus with its artery, the pulmonary vein, the pleural reflection, or the bronchial vein? The answer is the segmental bronchus with its artery. They enter the segment together at its apex, which points toward the hilum. The pulmonary veins lie at the edges of the segment, in the septa between segments.

Question 6246. Which single segment of the left lower lobe takes the place of the anterior basal and medial basal segments of the right lung? The answer is the anteromedial basal segment. On the left these two segments are fused into one. This fusion is one reason the left lung has eight segments rather than ten.

Question 6247. Name the four bronchopulmonary segments of the left upper lobe, spoken as a list. The answer is the apicoposterior segment, the anterior segment, the superior lingular segment and the inferior lingular segment. The apicoposterior segment is formed by the fusion of the apical and posterior segments. The two lingular segments together form the lingula.

Question 6248. True or false: every bronchopulmonary segment has its own segmental bronchus and its own segmental artery. The answer is true. The bronchus and the artery enter the segment together at its apex and branch within it. The pulmonary veins, by contrast, run between segments in the connective tissue septa.

Question 6249. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lingular segments with the left upper lobe, the medial basal segment with the left lower lobe, the apical segment with the middle lobe, or the lateral segment with the right lower lobe? The answer is the lingular segments with the left upper lobe. The left lower lobe has no separate medial basal segment.

Question 6250. A constructed illustration: a child sitting upright inhales a small object, and it lodges in an airway instead of passing further. Which main bronchus is more likely to receive it, and why? The answer is the right main bronchus. It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, and the aortic arch displaces the left main bronchus sideways.

Question 6251. A constructed illustration: a person lying flat on the back inhales vomited material, and it settles in the lowest parts of the lung. Which segments are those? The answer is the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the superior segment of the lower lobe. Flat on the back, those two segments lie furthest back and lowest, so material runs into them.

Question 6252. A described chest radiograph of a person who has been standing shows an opacity in the lowest and most posterior part of the right lower lobe, close to the spine. Which segment is affected? The answer is the posterior basal segment. When a person stands, that segment is the most dependent part of the lung, and material inhaled in that position collects there.

Question 6253. Which segments are removed when a surgeon operates on the lingula: the superior and inferior lingular segments, the lateral and medial segments of the middle lobe, the apical and posterior segments, or the medial basal and lateral basal segments? The answer is the superior and inferior lingular segments of the left superior lobe.

Question 6254. A described specimen shows a wedge of lung with its own bronchus and artery entering at the apex and a thin sheet of connective tissue separating it from the neighboring wedge. What is the wedge, and what runs in the sheet? The answer is a bronchopulmonary segment, with pulmonary veins running in the sheet. The sheet is the intersegmental septum.

Question 6255. On the right side, the bronchus of the superior segment of the lower lobe arises at almost the same level as which other bronchus? The answer is the middle lobe bronchus. Both take origin near the point where the right main bronchus continues into the bronchus of the lower lobe. Surgeons use that level as a landmark when they dissect the hilum.

Question 6256. Which statement about the eparterial bronchus is correct: it is the right upper lobe bronchus and lies above the pulmonary artery, it is the left upper lobe bronchus and lies below the pulmonary artery, it supplies the middle lobe, or it is the first branch of the trachea? The answer is that it is the right upper lobe bronchus, lying above the pulmonary artery.

Question 6257. Which segment of the right lung has no separate counterpart on the left, because it is fused with a neighboring segment there: the medial basal segment, the lateral basal segment, the posterior basal segment, or the superior segment? The answer is the medial basal segment, which is fused with the anterior basal segment to form the anteromedial basal segment of the left lung.

Question 6258. Which segment of the right lower lobe lies against the mediastinal surface of the lung, next to the right atrium? The answer is the medial basal segment. It occupies the inner and lower part of the lobe, close to the heart. It is the segment that has no separate counterpart on the left.

Question 6259. A described axial computed tomography section shows a wedge of dense lung tissue in the posterior part of the right upper lobe, reaching the pleural surface behind the rest of the lobe. Which segment is affected? The answer is the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. It lies behind the apical and anterior segments and reaches the posterior chest wall.

Question 6260. What structure separates one bronchopulmonary segment from the next, and what does it carry? The answer is the intersegmental septum, which carries the pulmonary veins. The septum is a thin sheet of connective tissue continuous with the visceral pleura. Because the veins lie within it, they can be preserved when a single segment is removed.

Question 6261. The left lung is usually described as having eight bronchopulmonary segments rather than ten. Why: two pairs of segments are fused on the left, the left lung has no lower lobe, the lingula replaces four segments, or there are no segmental bronchi? The answer is that two pairs are fused, forming the apicoposterior and anteromedial basal segments.

Question 6262. Into which two segments is the lingula divided? The answer is the superior lingular segment and the inferior lingular segment. They lie one above the other in the tongue of lung below the cardiac notch. Both of them belong to the left superior lobe.

Question 6263. A described specimen shows the trachea dividing into two main bronchi, one wider, shorter and more vertical than the other. Which is the right main bronchus, and why is the left more horizontal? The answer is that the wider, shorter and more vertical tube is the right main bronchus. The left runs more horizontally because the arch of the aorta crosses over it.

Question 6264. Which two segments are supplied by the middle lobe bronchus: the lateral and medial segments, the apical and posterior segments, the anterior and medial basal segments, or the superior and lateral basal segments? The answer is the lateral and medial segments. The middle lobe bronchus arises from the right main bronchus a little below the upper lobe bronchus.

Question 6265. A constructed illustration: a surgeon plans to remove one segment of the right lower lobe that lies against the mediastinum, and must leave the neighboring segments with their venous drainage intact. Which segment is to be removed, and which vessels must be preserved? The answer is the medial basal segment, with the pulmonary veins in the intersegmental septa preserved.

Question 6266. What is the name of the area on the mediastinal surface of the lung where the structures of the root enter and leave? The answer is the hilum of the lung. It lies on the mediastinal surface, roughly in the middle of that surface. The pleura reflects from the mediastinum onto the root at the hilum.

Question 6267. Which structure lies highest in the hilum of the left lung? The answer is the left pulmonary artery. It arches over the left main bronchus before entering the lung. On the right, by contrast, the upper lobe bronchus lies above the pulmonary artery, so the artery is not the highest structure there.

Question 6268. Which structure is the most superior one in the hilum of the right lung? The answer is the eparterial bronchus, which is the bronchus of the upper lobe. It arises from the right main bronchus before that tube enters the lung, and it lies above the pulmonary artery. The lower lobe bronchus lies below the artery.

Question 6269. Which structure lies most anterior in the hilum of each lung: the superior pulmonary vein, the pulmonary artery, the principal bronchus, or the bronchial artery? The answer is the superior pulmonary vein. From front to back the order is the vein, then the pulmonary artery, then the bronchus. The pulmonary veins are the most anterior structures of the root.

Question 6270. How many pulmonary veins leave each hilum: one, two, three, or four? The answer is two, a superior pulmonary vein and an inferior pulmonary vein. Each of them drains part of the lung and carries oxygenated blood. They open into the left atrium, one above the other.

Question 6271. On a normal frontal chest radiograph, how do the two hila usually relate: the left lies higher than the right, the right lies higher than the left, the two lie level, or the hila are formed by the bronchi? The answer is that the left hilum lies higher than the right, usually by about 1 to 2 centimeters. A right hilum that lies higher suggests disease.

Question 6272. A described frontal chest radiograph shows a branching shadow at each hilum, and the left shadow lies slightly higher than the right. Which vessels form most of each hilar shadow, and why do the bronchi contribute little? The answer is the pulmonary arteries. The bronchi are filled with air and cast almost no shadow.

Question 6273. A described axial computed tomography section at the level of the hila shows, on one side, an air-filled tube with the branching vessel above it and in front of it. Which hilum is shown, and what is the relation between the artery and the bronchus there? The answer is the left hilum, where the pulmonary artery lies above the bronchus.

Question 6274. Which nerve lies immediately anterior to the root of the lung on each side, running down in front of the hilum? The answer is the phrenic nerve. It descends between the mediastinal pleura and the pericardium, in front of the root. Because of that position it is at risk during operations on the hilum.

Question 6275. Which nerve lies immediately posterior to the root of the lung, where it gives branches to the pulmonary plexus? The answer is the vagus nerve. It passes behind the root and breaks up into the posterior pulmonary plexus. The phrenic nerve, by contrast, lies in front of the root.

Question 6276. A constructed illustration: a growth at the hilum of the left lung presses on the nerve that lies immediately behind the root there. Which nerve is compressed, and what does it supply in the chest? The answer is the vagus nerve, which supplies parasympathetic fibers to the bronchi and the lungs through the pulmonary plexus.

Question 6277. A constructed illustration: enlarged lymph nodes at the right hilum press on a nerve that runs in front of the root, and the diaphragm on that side stops moving. Which nerve is affected, and where does it lie in relation to the root? The answer is the right phrenic nerve, which lies anterior to the root of the lung.

Question 6278. True or false: the hilum of each lung is surrounded by a reflection of pleura that continues below the root as the pulmonary ligament. The answer is true. The pleura leaves the mediastinum and wraps around the root as a sleeve. Below the hilum the two layers hang down together and form the pulmonary ligament.

Question 6279. Which of these pairs belongs together: the pulmonary ligament with the inferior pulmonary vein, the pulmonary ligament with the main bronchus, the phrenic nerve with the back of the root, or the vagus nerve with the front of the root? The answer is the pulmonary ligament with the inferior pulmonary vein. The ligament hangs below the root and allows the vein to distend.

Question 6280. Name three kinds of structure that pass through the hilum of a lung, spoken as a list. The answer is the principal bronchus, the pulmonary artery and the pulmonary veins, together with the bronchial vessels, the lymphatics and the nerves. The bronchi lie behind and the veins in front. The whole group is wrapped in a sleeve of pleura.

Question 6281. In a described transverse section across the hilum, three structures lie in a row, with a thin-walled vessel in front, a thick-walled vessel in the middle and a cartilage-bearing tube at the back. Name them in order from front to back. The answer is the superior pulmonary vein, the pulmonary artery and the principal bronchus.

Question 6282. Which structure curves over the hilum of the right lung, above the root: the arch of the azygos vein, the arch of the aorta, the left ventricle, or the descending aorta? The answer is the arch of the azygos vein. It crosses above the root and joins the superior vena cava. The arch of the aorta passes over the left root instead.

Question 6283. Which structure arches over the hilum of the left lung, and which two structures pass beneath it to reach that hilum? The answer is the arch of the aorta, and the left pulmonary artery and the left main bronchus pass beneath it. The left main bronchus lies below the arch, which is why it runs more horizontally than the right one.

Question 6284. What is the name of the bundle of structures that suspends the lung from the mediastinum and connects it to the rest of the body? The answer is the root of the lung. It lies at the hilum, where the pleura wraps around it. The root carries the airway, the vessels, the nerves and the lymphatics of the lung.

Question 6285. Which of these structures lies outside the root of the lung: the trachea, the principal bronchus, the pulmonary artery, or the superior pulmonary vein? The answer is the trachea. It ends above the hila by dividing into the two main bronchi. The root of each lung begins with the main bronchus and includes the vessels and the nerves.

Question 6286. Which arteries supply the tissue of the lung itself, as distinct from the pulmonary arteries that carry blood for gas exchange? The answer is the bronchial arteries. They arise from the descending thoracic aorta and from the posterior intercostal arteries. They follow the bronchi and nourish the walls of the airways and the supporting tissue of the lung.

Question 6287. From which vessel do the left bronchial arteries usually arise, and how many of them are there? The answer is the descending thoracic aorta, which gives two left bronchial arteries. The right bronchial artery is usually single and arises from a posterior intercostal artery or from a common trunk with a left one.

Question 6288. What is the main function of the bronchial vessels in the lung: to nourish the tissues of the lung, to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, to drain the pleural cavity, or to supply the pericardium? The answer is to nourish the tissues of the lung. Gas exchange belongs to the pulmonary arteries and veins. The bronchial arteries are much smaller than the pulmonary arteries.

Question 6289. Into which vessel do the bronchial veins of the right lung usually drain: the azygos vein, the superior vena cava, the left atrium, or the internal thoracic vein? The answer is the azygos vein. On the left the bronchial veins drain into the accessory hemiazygos vein. A small amount of bronchial venous blood also returns through the pulmonary veins.

Question 6290. A described dissection of the root of a lung shows the structures wrapped in a tube of pleura, with a double fold hanging down below the hilum like a curtain. What is the fold, and what does it contain? The answer is the pulmonary ligament, which contains the inferior pulmonary vein and some lymphatics.

Question 6291. A described cross section through the root of a lung shows, from front to back, a thin-walled vessel, a thick-walled vessel and a tube with plates of cartilage in its wall. Identify them in order, and say which lies lowest in the left hilum. The answer is the superior pulmonary vein, the pulmonary artery and the principal bronchus, the bronchus lying lowest on the left.

Question 6292. Which large vein arches over the root of the right lung before it enters the superior vena cava? The answer is the azygos vein. Its arch crosses above the hilum and is a useful landmark in the chest. On the left the corresponding structure above the root is the arch of the aorta.

Question 6293. What structure forms a sleeve around the root of the lung and continues below it as the pulmonary ligament? The answer is the pleura. It leaves the mediastinum, covers the root, and follows the lung into the chest. That sleeve allows the root to move as the lung expands without tearing the pleural lining.

Question 6294. A constructed illustration: during an operation a surgeon divides the fold of pleura that hangs below the hilum in order to free the lung. Which structure lying in that fold must be secured before the fold is cut? The answer is the inferior pulmonary vein. It runs in the pulmonary ligament below the root.

Question 6295. A constructed illustration: during removal of the right lung, the surgeon must avoid the structure that arches over the root, because tearing it would cause serious bleeding. Which structure is at risk, and where does it lie relative to the root? The answer is the azygos vein, which arches above and behind the root.

Question 6296. True or false: the pulmonary arteries carry oxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs. The answer is false. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange. The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.

Question 6297. Which of these pairs belongs together: the bronchial arteries with the descending thoracic aorta, the pulmonary arteries with the aorta, the bronchial veins with the left atrium, or the pulmonary veins with the azygos vein? The answer is the bronchial arteries with the descending thoracic aorta. The pulmonary arteries arise from the right ventricle, and the pulmonary veins open into the left atrium.

Question 6298. Name the two sets of arteries that carry blood into the lungs, spoken as a list. The answer is the pulmonary arteries and the bronchial arteries. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange and take the greater part of the flow. The bronchial arteries are small and nourish the tissues of the lung.

Question 6299. Which statement about the pulmonary plexus is correct: it surrounds the root and carries sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers, it lies only inside the hilum, it carries only motor fibers, or it is a branch of the phrenic nerve? The answer is that it surrounds the root and carries both kinds of fiber. The sympathetic fibers widen the bronchi, while the vagal fibers narrow them and increase secretion.

Question 6300. Which structure lies directly in front of the root of the right lung: the superior vena cava, the descending aorta, the esophagus, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the superior vena cava. The esophagus, the descending aorta and the thoracic duct lie behind the root. In front of the left root, by contrast, lies the left ventricle.

To summarize, the right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two, and the lingula below the cardiac notch is the left counterpart of the right middle lobe, though it remains part of the left superior lobe. The oblique fissure is present in both lungs, runs downward and forward to end near the sixth costal cartilage, and the horizontal fissure belongs to the right lung alone at the level of the fourth costal cartilage. Each bronchopulmonary segment has its own segmental bronchus and artery at its center, with the pulmonary veins in the septa between segments, and the right lung holds ten segments against eight on the left. The hilum is the point at which the root enters the mediastinal surface, with the bronchus behind and the superior pulmonary vein in front, the eparterial bronchus highest on the right and the pulmonary artery highest on the left, and the left hilum lying about 1 to 2 centimeters above the right. The root carries the main bronchus, the pulmonary artery, the pulmonary veins, the bronchial vessels, the lymphatics and the nerves, wrapped in pleura that hangs below as the pulmonary ligament. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 64 — Pleura

The pleura is the serous membrane that wraps each lung and lines the inside of the chest, and the diaphragm is the muscular sheet that forms the floor of the chest and the chief muscle of breathing. This chapter takes them in turn, first the two layers of pleura with their recesses, their nerve supply and their surface markings, then the diaphragm with its parts, its three great openings and its action. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 6301. Which serous membrane is wrapped tightly over the surface of each lung and dips into every fissure? The answer is the visceral pleura. It cannot be separated from the lung without tearing the tissue beneath it. The parietal pleura lines the chest wall instead.

Question 6302. What is the name of the narrow, fluid-filled interval between the visceral pleura and the parietal pleura? The answer is the pleural cavity. In health it is only a potential space, because the two layers lie in contact. A film of serous fluid between them lets them slide on each other during breathing.

Question 6303. Which of these is not one of the named parts of the parietal pleura: the costal part, the mediastinal part, the diaphragmatic part, or the pulmonary part? The answer is the pulmonary part. The parietal layer is divided by the surfaces it lines into costal, mediastinal, diaphragmatic and cervical parts. The layer applied to the lung is the visceral pleura.

Question 6304. Which part of the parietal pleura covers the side of the pericardium and the great vessels in the middle of the chest? The answer is the mediastinal pleura. It hangs as a curtain between the lung and the heart. The costal pleura lies farther out, against the ribs.

Question 6305. Which part of the parietal pleura rises above the first rib into the root of the neck: the costal part, the mediastinal part, the cervical part, or the diaphragmatic part? The answer is the cervical part, or cupola. A fibrous sheet, the suprapleural membrane, strengthens it from above. That membrane is attached to the inner border of the first rib and to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra.

Question 6306. Which space of the pleural cavity fills first when fluid collects in an upright person: the costomediastinal recess, the costodiaphragmatic recess, the pulmonary ligament, or the pleural sleeve? The answer is the costodiaphragmatic recess. It is the lowest and most dependent part of the cavity, so fluid gathers there first. On a chest radiograph it appears as a dense shadow that blots out the angle between the diaphragm and the chest wall.

Question 6307. Which of these spaces is a true pleural recess: the costomediastinal recess, the aortic recess, the subphrenic recess, or the coronary recess? The answer is the costomediastinal recess, where the costal and mediastinal pleurae meet behind the sternum. The costodiaphragmatic recess is the other named one. The subphrenic space lies below the diaphragm and outside the chest.

Question 6308. The pleura lining the inner surface of the ribs is supplied by which nerves? The answer is the intercostal nerves. They are the segmental nerves of that wall, and the pleura covering it shares them. The mediastinal pleura and the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura are supplied by the phrenic nerve instead.

Question 6309. Irritation of the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura is felt where, and by which nerve is that sensation carried? The answer is the tip of the shoulder, carried by the phrenic nerve. The phrenic nerve comes from the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments. The skin over the shoulder is supplied by the same segments, so the brain misreads the source.

Question 6310. Is the visceral pleura sensitive to pain? The answer is no. It carries autonomic nerves that follow the bronchi and the vessels, and these do not convey sharp pain. Pleuritic pain comes from the parietal layer, which is richly supplied by somatic nerves.

Question 6311. A constructed illustration: a young adult describes a sharp pain in the side of the chest that worsens on a deep breath and eases when breathing is shallow. Which layer of pleura is inflamed? The answer is the parietal pleura. It is the sensitive layer, and stretching it with each deep breath provokes the pain. The visceral pleura can be diseased without causing pain at all.

Question 6312. A described upright chest radiograph shows a dense shadow at the base of one lung whose upper border curves upward toward the axilla. What does that curve represent? The answer is the upper surface of a pleural effusion. Free fluid settles at the base, and its surface rises higher against the chest wall than near the mediastinum. The lung above recoils away from it.

Question 6313. Which layer lies between the costal parietal pleura and the inner surface of the ribs? The answer is the endothoracic fascia, with the intercostal muscles outside it. This loose fibrous layer allows the pleura to move on the chest wall. Beyond the muscles lie the ribs themselves.

Question 6314. The lower border of the pleura is described in the midaxillary line. At which rib does it lie: the eighth, the tenth, the eleventh, or the twelfth? The answer is the tenth rib. The reflection then runs down and back to reach the twelfth rib beside the vertebral column. At the midclavicular line the pleura reaches only the eighth rib.

Question 6315. True or false: the lower border of the lung lies about two ribs higher than the lower border of the pleura. The answer is true. The pleura turns back below the lung and so forms the costodiaphragmatic recess. That gap of about two ribs is the space into which the lung expands on deep inspiration.

Question 6316. What is the name of the serous membrane that lines the inner surface of the thoracic wall, the mediastinum and the diaphragm? The answer is the parietal pleura. It is continuous with the visceral layer at the root of the lung. The two layers together form a closed sac.

Question 6317. Where does the apex of the lung, covered by pleura, lie in relation to the clavicle? The answer is that it rises about 2 to 3 centimeters above the medial third of the clavicle. The cervical pleura therefore reaches into the root of the neck. A wound above the clavicle can open the pleural cavity.

Question 6318. A described chest radiograph shows one side of the chest uniformly bright with no lung markings, and the lung itself is shrunken toward the middle. What has happened? The answer is a pneumothorax. Air has entered the pleural cavity and the elastic recoil of the lung has collapsed it. The visceral pleura lies against the collapsed lung.

Question 6319. A constructed illustration: fluid is to be drawn from the pleural cavity through the chest wall. Why is the needle passed just above the upper border of the rib below? The answer is that the intercostal nerves and vessels run in a groove on the under surface of each rib. Passing above the lower rib keeps the needle away from them, and the management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6320. Which of these pairs belongs together: the midclavicular line with the tenth rib, the midaxillary line with the eighth rib, the scapular line with the eleventh rib, or the vertebral column with the sixth rib? The answer is the scapular line with the eleventh rib. The pleural reflection reaches the tenth rib in the midaxillary line and the eighth in the midclavicular line.

Question 6321. What is the name of the double fold of pleura that hangs below the root of the lung? The answer is the pulmonary ligament. It is formed where the visceral and parietal layers meet and continue downward. It allows the structures of the root to move a little during breathing.

Question 6322. Which pleura follows the oblique and horizontal fissures of the lung: the costal, the mediastinal, the visceral, or the diaphragmatic? The answer is the visceral pleura. It is applied to the lung surface and therefore dips into every fissure between the lobes. The parietal layer stays on the wall and knows nothing of the fissures.

Question 6323. Why is the costomediastinal recess larger on the left than on the right? The answer is the cardiac notch of the left lung. The heart occupies that notch, so the anterior border of the left lung lies farther from the midline. The left pleura therefore extends further across the front of the pericardium.

Question 6324. A described upright chest radiograph shows a straight horizontal line across the lower chest with a bright zone above it and a dense zone below. What is shown? The answer is a hydropneumothorax, with air above the fluid. Air rises and fluid sinks, so the boundary between them is flat. A collection of fluid alone would show a curved upper border instead.

Question 6325. Name the two named recesses of the pleural cavity, spoken as a list. The answer is the costodiaphragmatic recess and the costomediastinal recess. The first lies at the bottom of the cavity, between the diaphragm and the chest wall. The second lies behind the sternum, where the costal and mediastinal pleurae meet.

Question 6326. Where are the visceral and parietal layers of the pleura continuous with each other? The answer is at the root of the lung. The pleura leaves the mediastinum there and turns onto the lung as a sleeve. Below the root the two layers continue down as the pulmonary ligament.

Question 6327. The visceral pleura takes its blood supply mainly from which vessels: the intercostal arteries, the bronchial arteries, the internal thoracic arteries, or the pulmonary arteries? The answer is the bronchial arteries. They follow the bronchi and supply the tissue around them. The intercostal and internal thoracic arteries supply the parietal layer.

Question 6328. True or false: in a healthy person the pleural cavity contains a small amount of air. The answer is false. It contains only a thin film of serous fluid, and the two pleural layers lie in contact. Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax and separates the layers.

Question 6329. A constructed illustration: a chest wound lets air into the pleural cavity with each breath, and later the heart and the trachea are pushed toward the opposite side. Why does that shift occur? The answer is that pressure in the injured pleural cavity has risen above atmospheric pressure. The trapped air presses the mediastinum across, and the management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 6330. A described dissection of the neck above the clavicle shows a dome of pleura covered by a fibrous sheet and crossed in front by vessels. Which pleura is shown, and what lies immediately in front of it? The answer is the cervical pleura, with the subclavian vessels in front. The fibrous sheet above it is the suprapleural membrane.

Question 6331. Lymph from the costal parietal pleura drains mainly to which nodes: the pulmonary nodes, the intercostal and internal thoracic nodes, the hilar nodes, or the deep cervical nodes? The answer is the intercostal and internal thoracic nodes. They lie with the vessels that supply the same wall. Lymph from the visceral pleura drains instead to the pulmonary nodes along the bronchi.

Question 6332. Where does the phrenic nerve lie in relation to the root of the lung? The answer is in front of it. The nerve descends through the thorax on the side of the pericardium and crosses the front of the root. The vagus nerve passes behind the root instead.

Question 6333. What is the name of the fibrous sheet that covers the dome of the cervical pleura and is attached to the first rib? The answer is the suprapleural membrane. It also gains attachment to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra. It helps to keep the cupola of the pleura in place during breathing.

Question 6334. Which structures lie immediately outside the costal parietal pleura: the ribs and their periosteum only, the endothoracic fascia and the intercostal muscles, the parietal peritoneum, or the pulmonary ligament? The answer is the endothoracic fascia and the intercostal muscles. The fascia is the loose layer against the pleura. Beyond the muscles lie the ribs and their periosteum.

Question 6335. A constructed illustration: after a chest infection, thick pus collects in one pleural cavity and the lung on that side cannot expand. What is that collection called, and which layer lines it? The answer is an empyema of the pleura, lined by the parietal pleura. The pus lies between the two pleural layers. Treatment belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 6336. A described specimen shows a lung encased in a thick gray-white sheet of tumor that follows the surface and fills the fissures, with the lung tissue compressed inside. From which layer did this tumor arise? The answer is the pleura, most often the parietal layer. Such a tumor is called a mesothelioma. The lung is compressed rather than invaded at first.

Question 6337. Which of these pairs belongs together: the costal pleura with the phrenic nerve, the mediastinal pleura with the intercostal nerves, the central diaphragmatic pleura with the phrenic nerve, or the visceral pleura with the intercostal nerves? The answer is the central diaphragmatic pleura with the phrenic nerve. The costal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves and the visceral pleura by autonomic nerves.

Question 6338. Which part of the parietal pleura is applied to the inner surface of the ribs and the intercostal spaces: the costal part, the mediastinal part, the cervical part, or the diaphragmatic part? The answer is the costal part. It is the largest part and forms the outer wall of the pleural cavity. It continues over the diaphragm below as the diaphragmatic pleura.

Question 6339. Which of the two layers of pleura is sensitive: the visceral layer, the parietal layer, both, or neither? The answer is the parietal layer. It is supplied by somatic nerves and is richly sensitive. The visceral layer carries autonomic nerves and cannot feel a cut.

Question 6340. Where does the pleural reflection lie in relation to the twelfth rib near the vertebral column? The answer is that it crosses the twelfth rib. The pleura reaches its lowest point at the back, close to the spine. The lung above it ends about two ribs higher.

Question 6341. Name two arteries that supply the parietal pleura. The answer is the intercostal arteries and the internal thoracic artery. The intercostal arteries reach the costal pleura from behind. The internal thoracic artery and its branches supply the pleura near the front of the chest.

Question 6342. Which statement about the pleura of the right lung is correct: it has a horizontal fissure that the pleura follows, it has a cardiac notch, it has only one fissure, or it lacks a costomediastinal recess? The answer is that it has a horizontal fissure that the pleura follows. The right lung has three lobes and two fissures. The cardiac notch belongs to the left lung.

Question 6343. A described computed tomography scan of the chest shows two thin-walled spaces, one on each side of a central mass, each containing lung tissue. What are these spaces, and what lines them? The answer is the pleural cavities, each lined by parietal pleura and closed by visceral pleura over the lung. The central mass is the mediastinum, holding the heart and the great vessels.

Question 6344. A constructed illustration: after a rib fracture, air escapes from a torn lung into the tissues of the chest wall and the neck, and crackling can be felt under the skin. Which layer has the air entered? The answer is the subcutaneous tissue of the chest wall. The air has also entered the pleural cavity first. The crackling is called subcutaneous emphysema.

Question 6345. True or false: the visceral pleura can be stripped from the lung surface as a complete sheet, leaving the lung intact. The answer is false. It is fused to the lung and sends fine septa into the tissue, so it tears when pulled away. Only the parietal pleura can be separated from the chest wall with ease.

Question 6346. What is the name given to the sleeve of pleura that surrounds the structures entering and leaving the lung? The answer is the pleural sleeve at the root of the lung. It is the point where the parietal pleura becomes the visceral layer. The pulmonary ligament continues downward from it.

Question 6347. Which vessels lie immediately in front of the cervical pleura as it rises into the root of the neck? The answer is the subclavian artery and vein. They cross the cupola in front of it and leave a groove on its surface. The first rib and the suprapleural membrane lie below and above it.

Question 6348. Which part of the parietal pleura lies directly against the fibrous pericardium: the costal part, the mediastinal part, the cervical part, or the diaphragmatic part? The answer is the mediastinal part. On the left it covers most of the side of the pericardium. The phrenic nerve runs down between the pericardium and that pleura.

Question 6349. In a described dissection, a needle passes through the chest wall in the midaxillary line just above the seventh rib. Which structures has it crossed last before entering the pleural cavity? The answer is the intercostal muscle and the endothoracic fascia. The parietal pleura lies immediately inside them. A needle placed much lower risks the costodiaphragmatic recess and the abdomen below.

Question 6350. Disease of the lung itself causes no sharp pain, while disease of the chest wall pleura is painful. Which single difference explains this: the thickness of the two layers, their nerve supply, their distance from the lung, or their blood supply? The answer is their nerve supply. The parietal pleura carries somatic nerves that convey sharp pain. The visceral pleura carries only autonomic nerves, which do not.

Question 6351. Which muscle forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominal cavity? The answer is the diaphragm. It is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle with a central tendon. Its fibers arise from the sternum, the lower ribs and the upper lumbar vertebrae, and all of them insert into that tendon.

Question 6352. Which part of the sternum gives origin to the sternal part of the diaphragm? The answer is the xiphoid process. Two small muscular slips arise from its back and run up to the central tendon. They leave a small gap on each side, the sternocostal triangle.

Question 6353. Which of these is not an origin of the diaphragm: the xiphoid process, the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs, the bodies of the upper lumbar vertebrae, or the medial border of the clavicle? The answer is the medial border of the clavicle. The clavicle gives origin to no part of the diaphragm. The other three are the sternal, costal and lumbar origins.

Question 6354. Which crus of the diaphragm is longer and reaches the higher lumbar vertebrae: the right, the left, both equally, or neither? The answer is the right crus. It arises from the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae and their discs. The left crus arises from the upper two and is shorter.

Question 6355. Which structures pass through the aortic opening of the diaphragm: the aorta and the esophagus, the aorta, the thoracic duct and the azygos vein, the inferior vena cava only, or the esophagus and the vagus nerves? The answer is the aorta, the thoracic duct and the azygos vein. The opening lies at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, between the two crura.

Question 6356. A described chest radiograph shows two curved domes forming the lower border of the lung fields, with the right one lying higher than the left. What are these shadows, and why is the right one higher? The answer is the two halves of the diaphragm, the right raised by the liver beneath it. Both domes move down on inspiration.

Question 6357. A constructed illustration: a person has repeated sudden involuntary contractions of the diaphragm followed by closure of the glottis. What is this, and which nerve carries the irritation? The answer is hiccups, and the irritation travels in the phrenic nerve. It often follows a full stomach or a sudden change of temperature.

Question 6358. Which structures pass through the esophageal opening of the diaphragm: the esophagus alone, the esophagus and the thoracic duct, the esophagus and the two vagal trunks, or the esophagus and the aorta? The answer is the esophagus and the two vagal trunks. Small esophageal branches of the left gastric vessels and lymphatics travel with them. The opening lies at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra.

Question 6359. In which part of the diaphragm does the opening for the inferior vena cava lie? The answer is the central tendon. The opening lies a little to the right of the midline, at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra. The inferior vena cava is bound to its margins.

Question 6360. Spoken from above downward, in what order do the three great openings of the diaphragm lie? The answer is the caval opening first, then the esophageal opening, then the aortic opening. The vena cava passes at the eighth thoracic level, the esophagus at the tenth and the aorta at the twelfth. The caval opening also lies furthest forward.

Question 6361. Which structures pierce the muscular crura of the diaphragm rather than passing through a named opening: the splanchnic nerves, the thoracic duct, the azygos vein, or the inferior vena cava? The answer is the splanchnic nerves. The greater, lesser and least splanchnic nerves pass through the crura on each side. The thoracic duct and the azygos vein pass through the aortic opening instead.

Question 6362. A described sagittal section through the trunk shows three gaps in the diaphragm, one in front within the tendon, one in the middle of the muscle, and one at the back behind the muscle. Which structures pass through the front and the back gaps? The answer is the inferior vena cava in front and the aorta behind. The middle gap carries the esophagus and the vagal trunks.

Question 6363. Which of these pairs belongs together: the caval opening with the tenth thoracic vertebra, the esophageal opening with the eighth, the aortic opening with the twelfth, or the caval opening with the twelfth? The answer is the aortic opening with the twelfth thoracic vertebra. The caval opening lies at the eighth level and the esophageal opening at the tenth.

Question 6364. What is the name of the fibrous arch that joins the two crura of the diaphragm in the midline above the aorta? The answer is the median arcuate ligament. The aorta passes behind it to enter the abdomen. The two crura and this arch together form the aortic opening.

Question 6365. Over which muscle does the medial arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arch? The answer is the psoas major. The ligament is a thickening of the fascia over that muscle. It runs from the body of the first lumbar vertebra to its transverse process.

Question 6366. Over which muscle does the lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arch? The answer is the quadratus lumborum. It runs from the transverse process of the first lumbar vertebra to the twelfth rib. The subcostal nerve and vessels pass behind it on their way to the abdominal wall.

Question 6367. Which nerve supplies the motor power of the diaphragm? The answer is the phrenic nerve. There is one on each side, and together they supply the whole muscular sheet. It reaches the muscle from above, descending through the neck and then through the chest. The intercostal nerves supply only sensation to the outer part of the muscle.

Question 6368. The outer part of the diaphragm receives sensory fibers from which nerves: the phrenic nerve only, the lower intercostal nerves, the vagus nerve, or the sympathetic trunk? The answer is the lower intercostal nerves. They supply the peripheral rim of the muscle. The phrenic nerve supplies sensation to the central part.

Question 6369. True or false: the phrenic nerve is the only nerve that supplies the diaphragm, both for movement and for sensation. The answer is false. The phrenic nerve supplies all of the movement and the sensation of the central part. The outer rim also receives sensory fibers from the lower intercostal nerves.

Question 6370. Name the three parts of the origin of the diaphragm, spoken as a list. The answer is the sternal part, the costal part and the lumbar part. The sternal part arises from the xiphoid process, the costal part from the lower six ribs and their cartilages, and the lumbar part from the crura and the arcuate ligaments.

Question 6371. A described transverse section through the lower chest shows the esophagus in the midline with a nerve trunk on each side of it, and the aorta behind and to the left of the midline. At which level was the section taken? The answer is the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra, where the esophagus passes through the diaphragm. The two nerve trunks are the vagal trunks.

Question 6372. Which vessels pass through the small gap between the sternal and costal parts of the diaphragm: the internal thoracic artery, the superior epigastric artery, the musculophrenic artery, or the inferior epigastric artery? The answer is the superior epigastric artery. It continues the internal thoracic artery downward into the abdominal wall. That gap is the sternocostal triangle.

Question 6373. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the lower neck, one half of the diaphragm no longer descends on inspiration. Which nerve has been injured, and where does it arise? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which arises from the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments. It crosses the neck in front of the scalenus anterior muscle, where it is exposed.

Question 6374. From which spinal segments does the phrenic nerve arise? The answer is the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments. Its fibers leave the neck high up and travel a long way down to the diaphragm. This long course explains why the nerve is at risk in operations on the neck.

Question 6375. Does the left phrenic nerve pass through the same opening as the right one? The answer is no. The right phrenic nerve passes through the opening for the inferior vena cava in the central tendon. The left phrenic nerve pierces the muscular part of the left dome on its own.

Question 6376. Through which opening does the right phrenic nerve reach the abdomen: the caval opening, the esophageal opening, the aortic opening, or the sternocostal triangle? The answer is the caval opening. It travels with the inferior vena cava through the central tendon. The left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome separately.

Question 6377. A described fluoroscopic study shows one dome of the diaphragm moving upward while the other moves downward when the person sniffs sharply. What does this indicate? The answer is paralysis of the dome that rises. A paralyzed hemidiaphragm is pushed up by the pressure in the abdomen when the healthy side contracts. The healthy dome descends as it should.

Question 6378. Which of these pairs belongs together: the posterolateral defect of the diaphragm with the right side, the parasternal defect with the left side, the pleuroperitoneal canal with the posterolateral defect, or the sternocostal triangle with the aortic opening? The answer is the pleuroperitoneal canal with the posterolateral defect. That defect is more common on the left.

Question 6379. What effect does the contraction of the costal part of the diaphragm have on the lower ribs: it raises them, it lowers them, it pulls them inward, or it leaves them unchanged? The answer is that it raises them. With the central tendon fixed, the fibers pull the ribs upward and outward. This widens the chest in its transverse diameter.

Question 6380. A constructed illustration: a newborn baby has difficulty breathing, and a radiograph shows loops of intestine in the left side of the chest, with the heart pushed to the right. Which developmental defect is illustrated? The answer is a posterolateral defect of the diaphragm, through the pleuroperitoneal canal. The abdominal contents have entered the chest.

Question 6381. True or false: the aorta pierces the muscular part of the diaphragm and carries a sleeve of muscle with it. The answer is false. The aorta passes behind the diaphragm, between the two crura, and does not pierce its muscle. The opening lies behind the muscle, at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra.

Question 6382. A described dissection of the diaphragm from the abdominal side shows a broad tendon in the middle, radiating muscle fibers around it, and two muscular legs descending behind. What are the three structures shown? The answer is the central tendon, the muscular part and the crura. The tendon lies in the middle, and the crura descend to the upper lumbar vertebrae.

Question 6383. Which structure passes behind the lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm: the sympathetic trunk, the subcostal nerve, the splanchnic nerves, or the superior epigastric artery? The answer is the subcostal nerve. It runs behind the ligament on its way to the abdominal wall. The sympathetic trunk passes behind the medial arcuate ligament instead.

Question 6384. To which structure above is the central tendon of the diaphragm fused? The answer is the fibrous pericardium. The two are united, so the heart moves with the diaphragm. This is one reason the heart descends a little on deep inspiration. The serous pericardium inside is free, so the heart can still beat within its fibrous sac.

Question 6385. Into which structure do all the muscle fibers of the diaphragm insert? The answer is the central tendon. It is a thin, strong, aponeurotic sheet shaped like a clover leaf. The inferior vena cava passes through it, a little to the right of the midline.

Question 6386. Which muscle is the chief muscle of quiet inspiration: the external intercostal, the diaphragm, the rectus abdominis, or the serratus anterior? The answer is the diaphragm. Its contraction lowers the domes and increases the vertical diameter of the chest. The external intercostals assist by raising the ribs.

Question 6387. A described pair of chest radiographs shows the domes of the diaphragm at a low level, with the ribs sloping steeply upward in the second film. What does the second film show? The answer is the chest at full inspiration. The diaphragm has descended and the ribs have been raised and everted. In the first film the chest was at rest.

Question 6388. A constructed illustration: a collection of pus lies between the right dome of the diaphragm and the liver, and the person has pain at the tip of the right shoulder. Why is the pain felt there? The answer is that the phrenic nerve supplies the central part of the diaphragm. The nerve comes from the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments, the same segments as the skin over the shoulder.

Question 6389. Why does the phrenic nerve arise from the cervical spinal cord: the muscle develops in the neck and drags its nerve down, the nerve branches from the vagus, the muscle grows from the lumbar somites, or the nerve descends from the chest? The answer is that the muscle develops in the neck and carries its nerve supply down as it migrates. This is a developmental explanation for an adult arrangement.

Question 6390. Which of these pairs belongs together: the inferior vena cava with the aortic opening, the esophagus with the caval opening, the aorta with the aortic opening, or the thoracic duct with the caval opening? The answer is the aorta with the aortic opening. The thoracic duct and the azygos vein pass through the same opening in its company.

Question 6391. Which of these structures passes through the diaphragm without using any of its three named openings: the esophagus, the inferior vena cava, the sympathetic trunk, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the sympathetic trunk. It slips behind the medial arcuate ligament. The thoracic duct uses the aortic opening.

Question 6392. What are the two muscular legs called that descend from the diaphragm to the upper lumbar vertebrae? The answer is the crura. The right crus is the longer of the two. Each crus is attached to the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae and to the discs between them, and together they bound the aortic opening behind.

Question 6393. Within the central tendon, on which side of the midline does the opening for the inferior vena cava lie, and where does it lie in relation to the muscular part of the diaphragm? The answer is that it lies to the right of the midline and within the tendon, above the muscle. The vena cava runs almost vertically to reach it. The esophageal opening lies behind and below it.

Question 6394. A constructed illustration: in an older adult, part of the stomach lies beside the esophagus in the chest, having rolled up through the esophageal opening, while the junction of the esophagus and the stomach remains below it. Which kind of hernia is illustrated? The answer is a paraesophageal hernia. In the sliding type the junction itself moves upward instead.

Question 6395. Which statement about the openings of the diaphragm explains why the esophageal opening is the one most likely to widen with age: it lies in the central tendon, it lies between the crura in muscular tissue that can stretch, it lies behind the muscle, or it is bounded by bone? The answer is that it lies between the crura in muscular tissue that can stretch.

Question 6396. A described chest radiograph shows the right dome of the diaphragm much higher than the left, and on screening it rises further on inspiration while the left descends. Which side is paralyzed, and in which direction does it move? The answer is the right dome, moving paradoxically upward. The left dome is working normally.

Question 6397. A described specimen of the diaphragm viewed from below shows a wide central sheet, radiating muscle fibers, and three gaps. Which gap lies furthest to the right, and which openings are bounded by muscle? The answer is that the caval opening lies furthest to the right. The esophageal and aortic openings are bounded by muscle and by the crura between them.

Question 6398. Which organ lies immediately below the right dome of the diaphragm and molds it into a higher curve: the stomach, the liver, the spleen, or the left kidney? The answer is the liver. The right dome is molded over its upper surface and therefore sits higher than the left one. The stomach and the spleen lie below the left dome.

Question 6399. The diaphragm develops from several sources. Which part of it develops from the septum transversum: the crura, the central tendon, the costal part, or the arcuate ligaments? The answer is the central tendon. The pleuroperitoneal membranes form much of the rest of the muscle, and the crura grow from the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus.

Question 6400. Irritation of the outer rim of the diaphragm is felt in the chest wall on the same side, while irritation of the central part is felt at the shoulder. What single fact explains the difference? The answer is that the two regions have different sensory nerves. The outer rim is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves, which supply the chest wall too. The central part is supplied by the phrenic nerve.

To summarize, the pleura is a closed serous sac with a visceral layer fused to the lung and a parietal layer named costal, mediastinal, diaphragmatic and cervical, and the thin film of fluid between the layers lets them slide. Only the parietal layer is sensitive, supplied by the intercostal nerves over the chest wall and by the phrenic nerve over the mediastinum and the center of the diaphragm, which is why irritation there is felt at the shoulder tip. Fluid gathers first in the costodiaphragmatic recess, and the pleural reflection lies about two ribs below the lung.
