The answer is tiers of arterial arcades. The descending colon lies against the abdominal wall behind the peritoneum.

Question 6821. A constructed illustration: a person has lost a long stretch of the distal small intestine at an operation. Which two substances are now poorly absorbed? The answer is vitamin B12 and bile salts, with the terminal ileum removed. The loss of bile salt reabsorption causes watery diarrhea, and the vitamin deficiency follows later. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6822. Which of these statements about the blood supply of the ileum is correct: it comes from the inferior mesenteric artery, from the superior mesenteric artery, from the internal iliac artery, or from the celiac trunk? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery. The ileum belongs to the midgut, and its vessels run with the nerves of the superior mesenteric plexus.

Question 6823. A described dissection shows the terminal ileum lifted forward, uncovering a fold that runs down and to the right behind it. Which fold is shown? The answer is the root of the mesentery, carrying the superior mesenteric vessels and the lymph vessels of the small intestine. It crosses the duodenum, the aorta, and the inferior vena cava.

Question 6824. What is the name of the permanent circular folds of the small intestine that project into the lumen and increase its surface? The answer is the circular folds, also called the valvulae conniventes. They are tallest in the jejunum and small and widely spaced in the lower ileum.

Question 6825. Which of these is the longest part of the small intestine: the duodenum, the jejunum, the ileum, or the cecum? The answer is the ileum. The small intestine is about 6 meters long in an adult, and the ileum makes up rather more than half of that, while the duodenum is the shortest part.

Question 6826. Which part of the large intestine is the widest and lies below the ileocecal junction in the right iliac fossa? The answer is the cecum. It is a blind-ended pouch about 6 centimeters long, and it is the first part of the large intestine. The appendix hangs from its posteromedial wall.

Question 6827. Which of these features is found in the large intestine but not in the small intestine: circular folds, villi, sacculations called haustra, or a mesentery? The answer is haustra. The colon also carries three flat longitudinal bands, the teniae coli, and rows of fatty tags, the appendices epiploicae.

Question 6828. A described specimen shows a short blind pouch with a worm-like tube hanging from its lower part, and three flat bands converging on the base of that tube. Which structure is the pouch? The answer is the cecum, with the three teniae coli. The tube is the appendix, and the bands converging at its base are the surest guide to it.

Question 6829. Which structures lie immediately behind the cecum in the right iliac fossa? The answer is the iliacus and the psoas major muscles, with the femoral nerve and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh lying on them. The posterior surface of the cecum often lacks peritoneum.

Question 6830. A constructed illustration: a loop that includes the cecum and the lower ileum becomes trapped in a swelling of the lower abdominal wall just above the groin. Which named passage has it entered? The answer is the inguinal canal, though such contents may instead pass through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. Which it is belongs to the examining clinician and the local protocol.

Question 6831. True or false: the cecum lies in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. The answer is false. The cecum lies in the right iliac fossa, below the ileocecal junction, at about the level of the anterior superior iliac spine in most people.

Question 6832. Which artery supplies the cecum: the ileocolic artery, the right colic artery, the middle colic artery, or the inferior mesenteric artery? The answer is the ileocolic artery. It gives an anterior cecal branch and a posterior cecal branch. The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon instead.

Question 6833. Which part of the colon is attached to the cecum above the ileocecal junction and runs upward toward the liver? The answer is the ascending colon. It is about 15 centimeters long and lies against the posterior abdominal wall. The peritoneum covers it in front and at the sides only.

Question 6834. Which of these statements about the peritoneum of the cecum is correct: it is completely behind the peritoneum, it is fully covered and often mobile, it has no peritoneal covering at all, or it lies within the lesser sac? The answer is that it is fully covered and often mobile. A cecum with a short mesentery may twist about its own axis.

Question 6835. The cecum lies in front of which nerve as that nerve crosses the iliacus muscle, and what follows from that relation? The answer is the femoral nerve. A distended cecum, or an inflamed appendix behind it, can press on the nerve and cause pain in front of the thigh.

Question 6836. A described section of the lower abdomen on the right shows a wide thin-walled pouch containing gas, with a small tube set in its wall and a flat band running along its surface. Which structure is the pouch? The answer is the cecum, with a tenia coli on its surface. The small tube in the wall is the appendix seen in section.

Question 6837. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cecum with the ileocolic artery, with the middle colic artery, with the inferior mesenteric artery, or with the left colic artery? The answer is the cecum with the ileocolic artery. The cecum belongs to the midgut, so its blood reaches it through the superior mesenteric artery.

Question 6838. A constructed illustration: a person with a mobile cecum arrives with a distended and tender right side of the abdomen, and a described radiograph shows a large gas-filled loop folded over on itself. What has happened? The answer is a twist of the cecum on its mesentery. The cecum is the widest segment of the colon and can rotate about the ileocolic axis. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6839. Which of these statements about the ileocecal junction is correct: the cecum lies above the junction, below it, to its left, or around it on all sides? The answer is that the cecum lies below the ileocecal junction. The ileum enters from above and to the left, and the appendix arises below and behind that opening.

Question 6840. What are the small fatty tags that hang from the outer surface of the colon, and from which part of the large intestine are they absent? The answer is the appendices epiploicae, which are absent from the rectum. They are little pouches of peritoneum filled with fat, and they lie in rows along the colon.

Question 6841. Where is the base of the appendix attached, and how is it recognized at operation? The answer is the posteromedial wall of the cecum, a little below the ileocecal junction, where the three teniae coli converge. Following the bands down to their meeting point leads to the base, which is the surest guide when the appendix is hidden.

Question 6842. Which of these is the most common position of the appendix: retrocecal, pelvic, preileal, or subcecal? The answer is retrocecal, behind the cecum in most people, with the pelvic position next. Because the positions vary so much, the pain of an inflamed appendix may point in different directions.

Question 6843. A described radiograph taken after a barium enema shows a thin blind-ending tube filled with contrast, running upward behind a gas-filled pouch on the right. Which structure is shown? The answer is the appendix in the retrocecal position. It lies behind the cecum and may reach as high as the right kidney.

Question 6844. Which vessel runs in the mesoappendix to reach the appendix, and from which artery does it arise? The answer is the appendicular artery, from the ileocolic artery, running in the free edge of the mesoappendix behind the terminal ileum. It is an end artery, so blockage of it starves the wall of the appendix.

Question 6845. A constructed illustration: an inflamed appendix lies behind the cecum, and the person feels pain when the right hip is straightened against resistance. Which muscle is being stretched? The answer is the psoas major, and the sign is named after it. The appendix rests on that muscle when it lies behind the cecum.

Question 6846. True or false: the appendix carries the same three longitudinal bands as the rest of the colon. The answer is false. The longitudinal muscle of the appendix forms a complete coat around the tube, which is one reason it has no haustra. Its wall also holds abundant lymphoid tissue in the young.

Question 6847. Which of these statements about the referred pain of an inflamed appendix is correct: it is first felt in the right iliac fossa, around the umbilicus, in the left groin, or never in the abdomen? The answer is that it is first felt around the umbilicus. The pain moves to the right iliac fossa only when the outer peritoneum is irritated.

Question 6848. What is the name of the point on the front of the abdomen that lies one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus? The answer is McBurney point, which marks the usual site of the base of the appendix. Tenderness there suggests inflammation of the appendix.

Question 6849. A described appendix is removed, and its tip is black while its base is sound. Which feature of its arterial supply explains this? The answer is that the appendicular artery is an end artery running in the mesoappendix. Blockage of the main trunk starves the tip first, while the base still receives branches from the cecum.

Question 6850. A described dissection shows a small tube whose mesentery contains a vessel and whose wall is thickened by many pale nodules in a young person. Which structure is shown? The answer is the appendix with its lymphoid follicles. The nodules are most numerous between the ages of ten and twenty and shrink with age.

Question 6851. A retrocecal appendix lies against which structures, and why may the pain then be felt in the back or the thigh? The answer is the right kidney, the right ureter, and the psoas major muscle. Irritation of the psoas makes the person hold the hip flexed and causes pain when it is straightened.

Question 6852. A constructed illustration: a person in late pregnancy has pain felt higher than usual on the right side of the abdomen. Where has the appendix moved? The answer is upward, because the enlarging uterus lifts the cecum and the appendix out of the pelvis. This is why the usual site of tenderness changes in pregnancy.

Question 6853. Which of these structures lies closest to the appendix when it lies behind the cecum: the right ureter, the spleen, the left kidney, or the pancreas? The answer is the right ureter. It runs down on the psoas muscle behind the cecum, so an inflamed appendix lying against it may cause pain on passing urine.

Question 6854. Name, as a list of three, the guides a surgeon uses to find the base of the appendix when it lies hidden behind the cecum. The answer is the three teniae coli, the ileocecal junction, and the terminal ileum. The bands are followed down to the point where all three meet.

Question 6855. Which of these pairs belongs together: a pelvic appendix with the rectum, a retrocecal appendix with the stomach, a preileal appendix with the spleen, or a subcecal appendix with the left kidney? The answer is a pelvic appendix with the rectum. It hangs over the brim of the pelvis and rests near the bladder and the rectum.

Question 6856. Which of these statements about the appendix is correct: it has no muscle in its wall, it holds abundant lymphoid tissue in the young, it always measures 2 centimeters, or it opens into the ascending colon? The answer is that it holds abundant lymphoid tissue in the young. The appendix opens into the cecum below the ileocecal orifice.

Question 6857. Which small tube hangs from the cecum and is the commonest site of sudden inflammation in the right lower abdomen? The answer is the vermiform appendix. It is a blind-ended tube that opens into the cecum and carries its own small mesentery, the mesoappendix.

Question 6858. A described frontal radiograph taken after a barium enema shows a pouch on the right filled with contrast, and no contrast entering the thin tube that hangs below it. Which structures are shown? The answer is the cecum and the appendix. The appendix fills only when the contrast runs back into its narrow lumen.

Question 6859. Which of these statements explains why an inflamed appendix in the pelvic position may cause diarrhea and a frequent need to pass urine: it lies against the rectum and the bladder, against the stomach, against the left kidney, or within the lesser sac? The answer is that it lies against the rectum and the bladder. Tenderness may then be found only on examination through the rectum.

Question 6860. Which layer of the wall of the appendix runs all the way around the tube, in contrast to the colon where it gathers into three bands? The answer is the longitudinal muscle coat. Because it is complete, the appendix is a smooth tube without haustra. Its circular muscle lies within it.

Question 6861. Which part of the colon runs upward from the cecum to the right colic flexure, lying against the posterior abdominal wall? The answer is the ascending colon. It is about 15 centimeters long and is covered by peritoneum in front and at the sides. The right kidney and the right ureter lie behind it.

Question 6862. Which of these parts of the colon lies between the right colic flexure and the left colic flexure: the ascending colon, the transverse colon, the descending colon, or the sigmoid colon? The answer is the transverse colon. It crosses the abdomen and hangs on its own mesentery, the transverse mesocolon, and it is the most mobile part of the colon.

Question 6863. A described barium enema shows a tube crossing the middle of the abdomen with a scalloped outline of rounded pouches, hanging lower in the middle than at either end. Which part of the colon is shown? The answer is the transverse colon, and the pouches are haustra. They appear because the three longitudinal bands are shorter than the bowel itself.

Question 6864. Which flexure of the colon lies higher and further back than the other, and is attached to the diaphragm by a fold of peritoneum? The answer is the left colic flexure, also called the splenic flexure. The phrenicocolic ligament holds it up beneath the spleen.

Question 6865. Which of these statements about the right colic flexure is correct: it lies higher than the left colic flexure, lower than it, in the pelvis, or behind the spleen? The answer is that it lies lower than the left colic flexure. It sits under the right lobe of the liver and in front of the right kidney.

Question 6866. Which part of the colon descends on the left side of the abdomen from the left colic flexure to the brim of the pelvis? The answer is the descending colon. It is about 25 centimeters long and lies behind the peritoneum, in front of the left kidney and the left psoas muscle.

Question 6867. True or false: the descending colon has a mesentery like the transverse colon. The answer is false. The descending colon lies behind the peritoneum against the posterior abdominal wall, and only the transverse and sigmoid parts of the colon carry a mesocolon. The ascending colon is fixed in the same way.

Question 6868. Which of these sites in the colon is a watershed where the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries meet: the cecum, the right colic flexure, the left colic flexure, or the appendix? The answer is the left colic flexure. The middle colic artery meets the left colic artery there, and the channel between them is weak.

Question 6869. A described radiograph taken after a barium enema shows a colon of normal length with smooth haustra, and a narrow segment low in the pelvis where the column of contrast ends. Which junction is it? The answer is the rectosigmoid junction. It is a second watershed, between the inferior mesenteric artery and the vessels of the pelvis.

Question 6870. The transverse mesocolon is attached to the posterior abdominal wall along which structure, and what lies behind that attachment? The answer is the lower border of the pancreas, with the duodenum and the pancreas behind it. The middle colic artery runs between the two layers of the mesocolon.

Question 6871. Which part of the colon begins at the brim of the pelvis on the left, forms an S-shaped loop, and ends at the third sacral vertebra? The answer is the sigmoid colon. It hangs on the sigmoid mesocolon and is the narrowest part of the colon.

Question 6872. Which of these structures lies immediately behind the sigmoid colon: the left ureter, the right kidney, the spleen, or the gallbladder? The answer is the left ureter. It crosses the brim of the pelvis behind the sigmoid colon and its mesocolon, and the left gonadal vessels lie behind it as well.

Question 6873. A constructed illustration: an older person has long-standing pain in the left lower abdomen, and a described radiograph shows small out-pouchings along the wall of the sigmoid colon. Where do these pouches push through? The answer is at the points where the small arteries pierce the muscle wall. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 6874. A described radiograph shows a large gas-filled loop that rises out of the pelvis and crosses to the right upper abdomen, with the haustra gathered around a central line. Which part of the colon is described? The answer is the sigmoid colon. It hangs on a long mesocolon, so it can rotate about its own axis.

Question 6875. Which of these pairs belongs together: the transverse colon with the greater omentum, the transverse colon with the spleen, the descending colon with the liver, or the sigmoid colon with the right kidney? The answer is the transverse colon with the greater omentum. The greater omentum hangs from the stomach and folds down over the transverse colon.

Question 6876. What are the three flat longitudinal bands on the surface of the colon called, and how many are there? The answer is the teniae coli, and there are three. They are shorter than the bowel, so the wall gathers into haustra between them. One lies where the mesocolon is attached, one where the omentum hangs, and one is free.

Question 6877. A described person has brisk painless bleeding from the large intestine. Which of these statements fits best: it comes from the right colon, from the rectum, from the appendix, or from the small intestine? The answer is that it comes from the right colon. The pouches there lie beside the small arteries, so the bleeding is often brisk and painless.

Question 6878. The left colic flexure is attached to which structure above it, and which organ lies immediately above and lateral to it? The answer is the diaphragm, by the phrenicocolic ligament, with the spleen above and lateral to it. The tail of the pancreas lies close behind the flexure.

Question 6879. Which of these statements explains why a growth in the right colon may cause anemia while one in the left causes obstruction: the right colon is wider and its contents are liquid, it is narrower, the left colon is wider, or the left colon lacks a blood supply? The answer is that the right colon is wider and its contents are liquid. The left colon is narrower and carries solid stool.

Question 6880. A constructed illustration: a young child has bouts of pain, a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen, and stool mixed with blood and mucus. Which part of the gut has telescoped into which? The answer is that the terminal ileum has slipped into the cecum. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 6881. Which artery runs along the inner border of the colon and joins the branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries? The answer is the marginal artery. It lies in the mesocolon close to the wall of the bowel and keeps the colon alive when a main branch narrows.

Question 6882. A described specimen of the colon shows a segment from the left side, with rows of fatty tags on its surface and peritoneum only at the front. Which part of the colon was removed? The answer is the descending colon, and the tags are appendices epiploicae. That part of the colon lies behind the peritoneum.

Question 6883. Which of these statements explains why the sigmoid colon is the commonest site of a twist in older people: it has a long mesentery and a narrow lumen, it is fixed to the posterior wall, it lies behind the peritoneum, or it has no blood supply? The answer is that it has a long mesentery and a narrow lumen, so a loaded loop can rotate on its axis.

Question 6884. In a described transverse section of the abdomen at the level of the third lumbar vertebra, which of these structures lies most anterior: the body of the vertebra, the inferior vena cava, the transverse colon, or the aorta? The answer is the transverse colon. It crosses the abdomen in front of the duodenum and the pancreas.

Question 6885. Which artery supplies the left colic flexure: the middle colic artery, the left colic artery, the right colic artery, or the ileocolic artery? The answer is the left colic artery, a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery. The middle colic artery approaches the same flexure from the superior mesenteric side, and the two meet there.

Question 6886. Which part of the large intestine runs from the third sacral vertebra to the anorectal junction, and has no haustra and no teniae coli? The answer is the rectum. It is about 12 centimeters long, and its lower dilated part is the rectal ampulla.

Question 6887. Which of these features is absent from the rectum: a muscular wall, a mucosal lining, haustra, or a blood supply? The answer is haustra. The rectum has no sacculations and no separate longitudinal bands, and its longitudinal muscle forms a complete coat around the tube.

Question 6888. A described section through the pelvis shows a tube lying in front of the sacrum, with a muscular sling passing behind its lower end. Which structure is the tube? The answer is the rectum, and the sling is the puborectalis part of the levator ani. It pulls the junction of the rectum and the anal canal forward and keeps the anorectal angle.

Question 6889. In the male, which structures lie immediately in front of the rectum, and which pouch lies between them and the rectum? The answer is the urinary bladder, the seminal vesicles, and the prostate, with the rectovesical pouch between. That pouch is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the male.

Question 6890. A constructed illustration: a growth low in the rectum has spread to the lymph nodes of the groin. Which part of the rectum is involved? The answer is the lowest part of the rectum and the anal canal below the pectinate line. That region drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, unlike the upper rectum.

Question 6891. True or false: the peritoneum covers the whole of the rectum. The answer is false. The upper third is covered on its front and sides, the middle third only in front, and the lower third not at all, which is why the lower rectum lies outside the peritoneal cavity.

Question 6892. Which artery supplies the upper part of the rectum: the superior rectal artery, the middle rectal artery, the inferior rectal artery, or the internal pudendal artery? The answer is the superior rectal artery. It is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery below the brim of the pelvis.

Question 6893. Which line in the anal canal marks the meeting of the hindgut and the proctodeum? The answer is the pectinate line, also called the dentate line. Above it the lining is columnar and the veins drain to the portal system, and below it the veins drain to the systemic system.

Question 6894. Which of these statements explains why internal hemorrhoids are painless while external hemorrhoids are painful: the internal ones lie above the pectinate line, the internal ones lie below the line, the external ones lie above the line, or neither kind has a nerve supply? The answer is that the internal ones lie above the pectinate line, where the nerve supply is visceral. External hemorrhoids lie below the line, in skin.

Question 6895. A described radiograph taken after a barium enema shows a column of contrast that stops low in the pelvis, and the outline of a smooth tube curving forward behind the bladder. Which part of the gut is shown? The answer is the rectum. It has no haustra and no longitudinal bands, so its outline is smooth.

Question 6896. A constructed illustration: on examination through the back passage, a rounded firm structure is felt in front of the rectum in a man. Which organ is being felt? The answer is the prostate gland. In a woman the cervix is felt in the same position through the front wall of the rectum.

Question 6897. Which of these pairs belongs together: the upper rectum with the superior rectal artery, the upper rectum with the internal pudendal artery, the anal canal with the portal vein, or the lower rectum with the middle colic artery? The answer is the upper rectum with the superior rectal artery, the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery.

Question 6898. Name, as a list of three, the arteries that supply the rectum and the anal canal. The answer is the superior rectal artery, the middle rectal arteries, and the inferior rectal arteries. The superior one comes from the inferior mesenteric artery, the middle ones from the internal iliac arteries, and the inferior ones from the internal pudendal arteries. They join one another, so the rectum has a rich supply.

Question 6899. Which of these statements about the veins of the rectum is correct: the superior rectal vein drains to the systemic system, all three drain to the portal system, all three drain to the systemic system, or the rectum has no veins? The answer is that the superior rectal vein drains to the portal system and the other two to the systemic system. The two systems meet in the wall of the rectum.

Question 6900. In a described sagittal section of the pelvis, the structures lie in the order pubic symphysis, bladder, prostate, rectum. Which of these statements is correct: the rectum lies in front of the bladder, the prostate lies in front of the bladder, the rectum lies behind all the others, or the pubic symphysis lies most posterior? The answer is that the rectum lies behind all the others, in front of the sacrum.

To summarize, the ileum is the longest and most distal part of the small intestine, it carries aggregated lymphoid nodules on its antimesenteric border, and its terminal segment absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts before opening into the cecum through the ileocecal valve. The large intestine begins at the cecum, its widest part, in the right iliac fossa, and the appendix rises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the three teniae coli converge. The colon carries haustra, three longitudinal bands, and rows of fatty appendices epiploicae, and only its transverse and sigmoid parts have a mesentery. The midgut colon is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery and the hindgut colon and upper rectum by the inferior mesenteric artery, with watersheds at the left colic flexure and the rectosigmoid junction. The rectum has no haustra and no teniae, its peritoneal covering decreases from above downward, and the pectinate line divides the anal canal into a visceral upper part and a somatic lower part. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 70 — Liver

This chapter follows the large intestine from the cecum to the anal canal and then turns to the liver, the largest gland in the body. It describes the parts of the colon and their features, the anal canal with its two sphincters and its pectinate line, and then the lobes, ligaments, segments, blood supply and relations of the liver. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. The questions are written to be answered aloud, so no figure, table or diagram is needed anywhere. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 6901. Which part of the large intestine lies below the opening of the small intestine, is the widest part of the colon, and carries the appendix on its lower end? The answer is the cecum. It lies in the right iliac fossa, below the ileocecal junction. Because it is wide and thinly walled, it distends most when the colon is blocked.

Question 6902. Which of these features marks the base of the appendix on the cecum: the confluence of the three taeniae coli, the pectinate line, the right colic flexure, or the ileocecal valve? The answer is the confluence of the three taeniae coli. The flat bands of longitudinal muscle run along the colon and meet at the appendix, so following them down leads to it.

Question 6903. Which small blind tube opens into the cecum, contains lymphoid tissue, and has no known digestive function in the adult? The answer is the appendix, also called the vermiform appendix. It arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum, and its position varies, the retrocecal position being the most common.

Question 6904. The ascending colon is described as a retroperitoneal structure. Which structure lies immediately behind its upper part, and which organ lies above it? The answer is the right kidney behind it, with the liver above it. The ascending colon is covered by peritoneum on its front and sides only, which keeps the gut fixed.

Question 6905. A constructed illustration: a young adult has vague pain around the navel that later settles in the right lower abdomen. Which structure lies at a surface point one third of the way from the front of the hip bone to the umbilicus? The answer is the appendix. The early pain is felt near the navel because the appendix carries visceral nerve fibers.

Question 6906. A described specimen of the colon shows three flat bands of muscle, a row of fatty tags along each band, and sacculations between them. Which three features are described? The answer is the taeniae coli, the appendices epiploicae, and the haustra. The bands are shorter than the gut itself, which is why the wall puckers into haustra.

Question 6907. Name two features of the large intestine that are not found on the small intestine, spoken as a list. The answer is the taeniae coli and the haustra, with the appendices epiploicae as a third. The small intestine has a smooth continuous muscle coat and no sacculations.

Question 6908. Which flexure of the colon lies immediately below the liver and turns the ascending colon into the transverse colon: the splenic flexure, the right colic flexure, the sigmoid flexure, or the anorectal flexure? The answer is the right colic flexure, also called the hepatic flexure. It lies in the right upper abdomen, against the lower surface of the liver.

Question 6909. Which part of the large intestine has a mesentery of its own and is therefore the most mobile part of the colon? The answer is the transverse colon. Its mesocolon suspends it from the back wall, and it hangs down across the abdomen below the stomach.

Question 6910. At the splenic flexure, which organ lies immediately above the flexure, and which structure tethers the flexure to the diaphragm? The answer is the spleen above it, with the phrenicocolic ligament tethering it. The flexure lies higher than the right colic flexure and is the most fixed part of the colon.

Question 6911. True or false: the three taeniae coli of the colon continue unchanged onto the rectum. The answer is false. The bands fan out at the lower end of the sigmoid colon, and the rectum has a complete longitudinal coat instead. The fatty tags also stop there.

Question 6912. A constructed illustration: a loop of bowel twists on its own mesentery in the left lower abdomen of an older adult, and the loop is greatly distended. Which part of the colon is described, and what makes it prone to twisting? The answer is the sigmoid colon, whose long mesocolon and narrow base allow it to rotate.

Question 6913. A described computed tomography section of the lower abdomen shows a widely dilated, gas filled loop whose two limbs converge toward the left iliac fossa. Which part of the colon is shown? The answer is the sigmoid colon, twisted on its mesentery. The two limbs meeting near the left iliac fossa are the described appearance of that twist.

Question 6914. Which artery supplies the cecum, the ascending colon, and the right half of the transverse colon: the inferior mesenteric artery, the superior mesenteric artery, the internal iliac artery, or the left colic artery? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery. The boundary between its territory and that of the inferior mesenteric artery lies near the splenic flexure.

Question 6915. Which artery runs along the inner border of the colon and joins the branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries into one continuous channel? The answer is the marginal artery. It lies in the mesocolon close to the bowel wall, and it lets a long segment of colon survive on one feeding vessel.

Question 6916. In the left lower abdomen, which structure lies immediately behind the sigmoid colon and is at risk when the sigmoid is diseased? The answer is the left ureter, with the left iliac vessels and the piriformis muscle behind it as well. The sigmoid colon lies in front of those structures.

Question 6917. A constructed illustration: a person has bright red bleeding from above the pectinate line and feels no pain at all. Which kind of dilated vein is described? The answer is an internal hemorrhoid. The lining above the pectinate line carries visceral nerve fibers, so it is not sensitive to pain, and its veins drain into the portal system.

Question 6918. Which statement about the pectinate line is correct: above it the lining is mucosa draining to the portal vein, above it the lining is skin draining to the inferior vena cava, below it the lining is mucosa draining to the portal vein, or below it the lining is skin draining to the portal vein? The answer is mucosa above the line draining to the portal vein.

Question 6919. What is the name of the jagged line in the anal canal that marks the change from mucosa above to skin below, and which folds hang above it? The answer is the pectinate line, with the anal columns above it. The line also marks the level of the small anal valves.

Question 6920. Which muscle of the anal canal is smooth and involuntary, and which one is skeletal and under voluntary control? The answer is the internal anal sphincter, which is smooth, and the external anal sphincter, which is skeletal. The internal sphincter is a thickening of the circular muscle coat of the gut.

Question 6921. A constructed illustration: a person reports a very tender, hard, bluish swelling at the very edge of the anus after straining, and sitting is painful. Which structure is involved, and why is this lesion so tender? The answer is an external hemorrhoid, below the pectinate line, where somatic nerves make it exquisitely sensitive.

Question 6922. About how long is the anal canal, and which way does it run: about 3 to 4 centimeters, running downward and backward, about 12 centimeters, running downward and forward, about 3 to 4 centimeters, running downward and forward, or about 8 centimeters, running straight down? The answer is about 3 to 4 centimeters, running downward and backward, from the anorectal junction to the anal margin.

Question 6923. The anal canal is described as running downward and backward from the rectum. Which muscle pulls its upper part forward and so creates the anorectal angle? The answer is the puborectalis muscle. It slings around the junction from the pubis and holds the junction forward. Losing that forward pull flattens the angle.

Question 6924. Which of these pairs belongs together: the transverse colon with a mesentery of its own, the ascending colon with a mesentery of its own, the descending colon with a mesentery of its own, or the rectum with a mesentery of its own? The answer is the transverse colon. The ascending and descending colon are retroperitoneal, and the rectum lies against the sacrum.

Question 6925. Which structures lie immediately in front of the lower rectum in the male, and which lie in front of it in the female? The answer is the seminal vesicles and the prostate in the male, and the vagina and the cervix in the female. Behind the rectum lie the sacrum and the coccyx.

Question 6926. Which statement about the liver is correct: it is the largest gland in the body and lies in the right upper abdomen, it lies mainly in the left upper abdomen, it is the smallest organ of the abdomen, or it lies behind the peritoneum on the left? The answer is that it is the largest gland in the body and lies in the right upper abdomen, weighing about 1.5 kilograms.

Question 6927. Which peritoneal fold lies on the front of the liver, runs from the diaphragm and the front abdominal wall to the liver, and separates its right and left lobes? The answer is the falciform ligament. Its free lower edge carries the round ligament of the liver, and it is the fold seen running up from the umbilicus.

Question 6928. A described section of the upper abdomen shows the liver filling the right side, with a thin band running from the front abdominal wall to its upper surface and a small rounded cord below it. Which two structures are described? The answer is the falciform ligament with the round ligament in its free edge. That cord is the closed umbilical vein.

Question 6929. The round ligament of the liver lies in the free edge of which fold, and what was it before birth? The answer is the falciform ligament, and before birth it was the umbilical vein. After birth the vessel closes and becomes a fibrous cord. Inside the liver that cord joins the left branch of the portal vein.

Question 6930. Which part of the liver is not covered by peritoneum and lies directly against the diaphragm: the bare area on the posterior surface, the whole of the left lobe, the quadrate lobe, or the gallbladder bed? The answer is the bare area on the posterior surface. The coronary ligament runs around its edge, and the triangular ligaments close it off.

Question 6931. A constructed illustration: a person is struck on the lower right ribs, and blood collects in the peritoneal cavity while one part of the liver stays fixed against the diaphragm. Which ligament marks the boundary of the part of the liver that lies outside the peritoneum? The answer is the coronary ligament. The bare area between its two layers touches the diaphragm.

Question 6932. On the visceral surface of the liver, which two smaller lobes lie between the fissure for the round ligament and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum? The answer is the quadrate lobe in front and the caudate lobe behind. Both belong to the functional left lobe, and the gallbladder lies beside the quadrate lobe.

Question 6933. A described specimen shows the liver from the front, with a large lobe on the right and a smaller one on the left, divided by a pale fold. Which lobe is the larger, and which fold divides them? The answer is the right lobe, divided from the left by the falciform ligament.

Question 6934. Which statement about the caudate lobe is correct: it lies between the inferior vena cava and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum, it lies in front of the quadrate lobe, it is part of the right lobe in every scheme, or it has no blood supply of its own? The answer is that it lies between the inferior vena cava and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum. It is segment one.

Question 6935. True or false: the whole surface of the liver is covered by peritoneum. The answer is false. The bare area on the posterior surface lies directly against the diaphragm with no peritoneal covering at all. The rest of the liver is almost entirely covered by peritoneum.

Question 6936. In the porta hepatis, which structure lies most anteriorly, which lies most posteriorly, and which lies between the two? The answer is that the hepatic ducts lie most anteriorly, the portal vein most posteriorly, and the hepatic artery proper between them. The porta is the gateway through which vessels enter and leave.

Question 6937. Which veins drain the liver into the inferior vena cava and run between the segments: the portal veins, the hepatic veins, the cystic veins, or the phrenic veins? The answer is the hepatic veins. There are usually three of them, named right, middle and left, and they leave the liver on its posterior surface.

Question 6938. A described magnetic resonance image of the liver shows a vertical plane marked by a large vein running from the upper surface down toward the inferior vena cava. Which vein is shown, and what plane does it mark? The answer is the middle hepatic vein, marking the plane between the right and left halves of the liver.

Question 6939. Which large vein lies in a groove on the posterior surface of the liver, and which part of the liver is left uncovered beside it? The answer is the inferior vena cava in the groove, with the bare area beside it. The hepatic veins open into the cava along that groove.

Question 6940. Which of these describes the fundus of the gallbladder: the rounded end that projects below the liver edge at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, the narrow end joining the cystic duct, the part fixed to the liver, or the part in the porta hepatis? The answer is the rounded end that projects below the liver edge at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.

Question 6941. Which structure inside the cystic duct carries a series of crescent-shaped folds that keep the duct open and help to hold bile? The answer is the spiral valves of the cystic duct. They run along its inner surface, and they are a normal feature of the duct rather than true valves.

Question 6942. A constructed illustration: a person has severe pain in the right upper abdomen after a fatty meal, and the gallbladder is described as distended with a stone lodged at its neck. Which duct leaves the gallbladder at that point, and where does it run? The answer is the cystic duct, which runs backward and downward to join the common hepatic duct.

Question 6943. Which artery usually supplies the gallbladder, and from which vessel does it arise: the cystic artery from the right hepatic artery, the cystic artery from the left hepatic artery, the left gastric artery, or the superior mesenteric artery? The answer is the cystic artery from the right hepatic artery. It runs in the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the liver.

Question 6944. A described series of images of the biliary tree shows a narrow duct leaving the gallbladder, joining another duct that comes down from the liver, and the two forming one wider channel that runs down behind the first part of the duodenum. Which three ducts are shown? The answer is the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the common bile duct.

Question 6945. Which of these pairs belongs together: the hepatic portal vein with blood from the gut, the hepatic vein with blood from the gut, the hepatic artery with blood from the gut, or the cystic vein with blood from the gut? The answer is the hepatic portal vein, which carries blood from the gut to the liver. The hepatic veins carry it away.

Question 6946. Which fold of peritoneum is the only one attached to the front of the liver, and what does it contain in its free edge? The answer is the falciform ligament, which contains the round ligament of the liver in its free edge. It runs from the umbilicus and the diaphragm to the liver and separates its two lobes.

Question 6947. Which two veins unite to form the portal vein, and where: the splenic and the superior mesenteric veins behind the neck of the pancreas, the splenic and the inferior mesenteric veins in front of the pancreas, the hepatic veins at the liver, or the gastric and cystic veins at the porta? The answer is the splenic and the superior mesenteric veins behind the neck of the pancreas.

Question 6948. A described section through the upper abdomen shows the liver on the right, with a pear-shaped sac lying against its lower surface and a thick vein running up behind the liver. Which structures are shown? The answer is the gallbladder against the liver and the inferior vena cava behind it. The gallbladder lies in a fossa on the visceral surface.

Question 6949. What is the ligamentum venosum of the liver, and between which two parts of the liver does it lie? The answer is the closed ductus venosus, and it lies in the fissure between the caudate lobe and the left lobe. Before birth that channel carried blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava.

Question 6950. In the segmental scheme of the liver, how many segments are described, and which segment is the caudate lobe: eight segments, with the caudate lobe as segment one, four segments, with the caudate lobe as segment four, eight segments, with the caudate lobe as segment eight, or six segments? The answer is eight segments, with the caudate lobe as segment one.

Question 6951. Which lobe of the liver lies on its visceral surface between the gallbladder and the fissure for the round ligament? The answer is the quadrate lobe. It lies in front of the porta hepatis. It belongs to the functional left lobe, although it lies to the right of the falciform ligament.

Question 6952. A constructed illustration: a person with long-standing liver disease has dilated veins running away from the umbilicus in the falciform ligament, and fluid in the abdomen. Which veins have opened up, and why do they meet at that point? The answer is the paraumbilical veins, which link the portal vein to the veins of the abdominal wall.

Question 6953. Which of these organs lies in contact with the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver: the right kidney, the spleen, the pancreas, or the left lung? The answer is the right kidney. The right colic flexure and the duodenum also lie against the right lobe. The spleen lies to the left of the liver and touches the stomach.

Question 6954. A described cast of the portal system shows a trunk dividing into two branches, each of which breaks into a tree of smaller branches that do not join across the boundary. What does this casting show about the segments of the liver? The answer is that each segment has its own portal branch, and the branches do not meet across the boundaries.

Question 6955. True or false: the falciform ligament marks the boundary between the right and the left halves of the liver in the functional sense. The answer is false. It separates the anatomical right and left lobes, but the functional division runs from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava. The left half of the liver includes the quadrate lobe.

Question 6956. Which fold of peritoneum runs from the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and to the first part of the duodenum? The answer is the lesser omentum. Its free right edge contains the portal triad and forms the front wall of the epiploic foramen, so it joins the liver to the stomach.

Question 6957. Where do the superficial lymph vessels of the liver drain: to the celiac lymph nodes, to the inguinal lymph nodes, to the axillary lymph nodes, or to the sacral lymph nodes? The answer is the celiac lymph nodes. Deep lymph vessels follow the portal tract and the hepatic veins, and some of them end in the posterior mediastinal nodes.

Question 6958. Name two peritoneal folds that attach the liver to the diaphragm and to the front abdominal wall, spoken as a list. The answer is the falciform ligament and the coronary ligament. The right and left triangular ligaments also attach the liver to the diaphragm, and the lesser omentum joins it to the stomach.

Question 6959. A described view at operation shows a pale fold running from the umbilicus up to the liver, with a firm cord in its lower free edge that disappears into the liver substance. Which two structures are shown, and what does that cord represent? The answer is the falciform ligament and the round ligament, the closed umbilical vein.

Question 6960. Which statement is correct: the left triangular ligament is formed where the layers of the coronary ligament meet on the left, the left triangular ligament contains the portal vein, the bare area lies on the front of the liver, or the bare area is covered by the lesser omentum? The answer is that the left triangular ligament is formed where the layers of the coronary ligament meet on the left.

Question 6961. What is the name of the common variant in which a tongue-like process of the right lobe of the liver extends downward below the costal margin, and whom does it usually affect? The answer is the Riedel lobe, and it is more common in women. It is a normal variant rather than a sign of disease.

Question 6962. A constructed illustration: after an infection in the upper abdomen, pus collects between the right lobe of the liver and the diaphragm, and the person feels pain at the tip of the right shoulder. Which nerve carries that pain, and where does it arise? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which arises from the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments.

Question 6963. Which nerves supply the liver: sympathetic fibers from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve, only sympathetic fibers, only parasympathetic fibers, or somatic fibers from the lower intercostal nerves? The answer is sympathetic fibers from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve, running with the vessels of the portal tract.

Question 6964. A described radiograph of the abdomen shows a large soft tissue shadow filling the upper right side, with the lower ribs crossing it and the diaphragm above it. Which organ forms that shadow, and where does its upper border lie? The answer is the liver, whose upper border reaches the fifth rib, with its lower border along the costal margin.

Question 6965. Which pouch of the peritoneal cavity lies between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney, and why does it matter in a person lying face upward? The answer is the hepatorenal pouch, which is then the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity. Fluid therefore collects there first, above the right colic flexure.

Question 6966. Which of these best describes the hepatorenal pouch: the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when a person lies face upward, the space behind the peritoneum around the kidney, the space inside the lesser omentum, or the groove beside the inferior vena cava? The answer is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when a person lies face upward.

Question 6967. Which vessel carries the greater part of the blood flow to the liver, and which carries the greater part of its oxygen: the portal vein and the hepatic artery proper, the hepatic artery proper and the portal vein, the hepatic veins and the portal vein, or the inferior vena cava and the hepatic artery? The answer is the portal vein for flow and the hepatic artery proper for oxygen.

Question 6968. Which of these pairs belongs together: the right lobe with the right colic flexure, the left lobe with the right kidney, the caudate lobe with the gallbladder, or the quadrate lobe with the spleen? The answer is the right lobe with the right colic flexure. The right kidney also lies against the right lobe, while the left lobe lies against the stomach.

Question 6969. Which lobe of the liver is the largest: the right lobe, the left lobe, the caudate lobe, or the quadrate lobe? The answer is the right lobe. It forms most of the upper surface and the whole of the right side of the organ, while the left lobe crosses the midline into the epigastrium.

Question 6970. A described view of the liver from below shows the left lobe lying across the midline, with the stomach and the esophagus behind it and the lesser omentum running from its edge. Which lobe is shown, and which two organs lie against it? The answer is the left lobe, with the stomach and the esophagus against it, reaching the esophageal opening.

Question 6971. True or false: the liver is the largest gland in the body and receives blood from two sources. The answer is true. It receives blood through the portal vein and through the hepatic artery proper, and the portal vein carries the greater part of the flow while the artery carries the greater part of the oxygen.

Question 6972. Which statement about the hepatic veins is correct: they run between the segments and open into the inferior vena cava, they run inside each segment beside the portal branch, they open into the portal vein, or they drain into the stomach? The answer is that they run between the segments and open into the inferior vena cava. There are usually three of them.

Question 6973. Which segment of the liver lies between the inferior vena cava behind and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum in front, and why is it treated separately at operation? The answer is the caudate lobe, which is segment one. It receives branches from both the right and the left portal veins, and its own small veins drain straight into the inferior vena cava.

Question 6974. A constructed illustration: a fall breaks the ninth and tenth ribs on the right, and the person becomes pale with pain in the right upper abdomen. Which organ lies immediately behind those ribs and is the one most likely to be torn? The answer is the liver, whose right lobe lies under the right dome of the diaphragm behind the lower ribs.

Question 6975. Which fold carries the closed umbilical vein to the liver, and into which vessel does it run there: the falciform ligament into the left portal branch, the lesser omentum into the right portal branch, the coronary ligament into the hepatic vein, or the round ligament into the inferior vena cava? The answer is the falciform ligament, with the remnant running into the left portal branch.

Question 6976. A described magnetic resonance image of the liver shows eight territories, each outlined by the planes of the hepatic veins and supplied at its center by a branch of the portal vein. Which scheme is being shown, and what does each territory have of its own? The answer is the segmental scheme, in which each segment has its own portal branch.

Question 6977. During a deep breath in, the diaphragm descends. Which way does the liver move, and by about how much? The answer is downward, by a few centimeters. The liver is held against the diaphragm by the coronary ligament and by the pressure within the abdomen. A liver that does not move with breathing is abnormal.

Question 6978. Which space lies immediately above the right dome of the diaphragm and above the part of the liver that reaches highest, and why can a wound of the lower chest reach the liver through it? The answer is the right pleural recess, separated from the liver by the diaphragm alone. The pleura therefore rises higher than the liver does.

Question 6979. Which pear-shaped sac lies on the visceral surface of the liver, between the quadrate lobe and the right lobe, and stores bile? The answer is the gallbladder. It lies in a fossa on the visceral surface and is covered by peritoneum on its lower surface. Its fundus projects below the liver edge.

Question 6980. Which of these pairs belongs together: the bare area with the diaphragm, the bare area with the stomach, the bare area with the portal vein, or the bare area with the gallbladder? The answer is the bare area with the diaphragm. It is the part of the liver not covered by peritoneum, lying directly against the diaphragm within the coronary ligament.

Question 6981. Where does the liver lie for the most part, and where is its lower border in the midclavicular line: the right hypochondrium, with the lower border at the costal margin, the epigastrium, with the lower border at the umbilicus, the left hypochondrium, or the right lumbar region? The answer is the right hypochondrium, with the lower border at the costal margin.

Question 6982. A described computed tomography section of the upper abdomen shows a large organ on the right, with the lower ribs and the diaphragm around it and a small round sac against its inner surface. Which organ and which sac are shown? The answer is the liver and the gallbladder, the liver lying under the right dome of the diaphragm.

Question 6983. The fundus of the gallbladder is described as projecting below the lower border of the liver. At which surface point does it appear, and what lies beside it? The answer is the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the right linea semilunaris meets the costal margin. The fundus touches the front abdominal wall there.

Question 6984. Which of these describes the cystic duct: it runs from the neck of the gallbladder to join the common hepatic duct and contains spiral folds, it drains the liver directly, it carries bile into the duodenum on its own, or it joins the portal vein? The answer is that it runs from the neck of the gallbladder to join the common hepatic duct and contains spiral folds.

Question 6985. In which fold of peritoneum does the common bile duct run on its way to the duodenum, and against which organ does it lie? The answer is the free edge of the lesser omentum, and it lies against the back of the first part of the duodenum and then in a groove on the pancreas. It ends at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

Question 6986. Name the three structures that make up the portal triad, spoken as a list. The answer is the portal vein, the hepatic artery proper and the bile duct. They run together in the free edge of the lesser omentum and enter the liver at the porta hepatis. The portal vein lies behind the other two.

Question 6987. Which statement about the position of the liver is correct: its upper border reaches the fifth rib in the midclavicular line and it moves with breathing, it is fixed and does not move with breathing, its upper border lies at the umbilicus, or it lies below the costal margin? The answer is that its upper border reaches the fifth rib in the midclavicular line and it moves with breathing.

Question 6988. A described section of the upper abdomen shows the liver and the gallbladder in front, a thick vein immediately behind the liver, and the right kidney below and behind. Which vein is shown, and what groove does it occupy? The answer is the inferior vena cava, in the groove on the posterior surface of the liver.

Question 6989. True or false: the gallbladder lies behind the peritoneum and is fixed to the back wall of the abdomen. The answer is false. It lies in a fossa on the visceral surface of the liver and is covered by peritoneum on its lower surface. It moves with the liver and not with the abdominal wall.

Question 6990. Which of these carries oxygen-rich blood to the liver: the hepatic artery proper, the portal vein, the hepatic vein, or the inferior vena cava? The answer is the hepatic artery proper. The portal vein carries blood that is rich in nutrients but lower in oxygen, and the hepatic veins carry blood away from the liver.

Question 6991. Which lobe of the liver lies behind the porta hepatis, between the fissure for the ligamentum venosum and the groove for the inferior vena cava, and drains into the inferior vena cava by its own small veins? The answer is the caudate lobe. It is the only lobe with that independent drainage, and it is segment one.

Question 6992. Which of these pairs belongs together: the round ligament with the closed umbilical vein, the round ligament with the closed ductus venosus, the ligamentum venosum with the closed umbilical vein, or the falciform ligament with the portal vein? The answer is the round ligament with the closed umbilical vein. The ligamentum venosum is the closed ductus venosus.

Question 6993. From which germ layer does the liver develop, and in which fold does it grow: the endoderm of the foregut in the ventral mesentery, the ectoderm of the surface in the dorsal mesentery, the mesoderm of the somites, or the endoderm of the hindgut? The answer is the endoderm of the foregut, growing in the ventral mesentery, which becomes the falciform ligament and the lesser omentum.

Question 6994. A described specimen of a liver shows a firm organ with a finely nodular surface and a shrunken right lobe. Which organ is shown, and what does the nodular surface indicate about the normal smooth architecture? The answer is the liver, and the nodules replace the normal smooth lobules. This is the described appearance of long-standing liver disease.

Question 6995. Which structures lie immediately above and immediately behind the right lobe of the liver? The answer is the diaphragm above and the right kidney behind and below it. The right colic flexure and the duodenum also lie against its visceral surface. The right lung lies above the diaphragm.

Question 6996. Which parts of the liver receive blood from the left branch of the portal vein: the left lobe along with the quadrate lobe, the whole right lobe, the gallbladder bed alone, or the bare area only? The answer is the left lobe along with the quadrate lobe. The functional left half of the liver therefore does not match the anatomical left lobe.

Question 6997. A constructed illustration: a person becomes yellow, and imaging shows a dilated duct running down from the liver and stopping in a groove on the back of the pancreas. Which duct is obstructed, and which two ducts formed it? The answer is the common bile duct, formed by the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 6998. Which artery supplies the gallbladder, and in which triangle does it run? The answer is the cystic artery, running in the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the lower surface of the liver. It usually arises from the right hepatic artery.

Question 6999. Which plane separates the right half of the liver from the left half in the functional sense: the plane running from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava, the plane of the falciform ligament, the plane of the lesser omentum, or the plane of the coronary ligament? The answer is the plane running from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava.

Question 7000. Which veins open into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm after running between the segments of the liver: the right, middle and left hepatic veins, the portal veins, the cystic veins, or the phrenic veins? The answer is the right, middle and left hepatic veins, whose openings lie on the posterior surface. The portal vein enters at the porta hepatis instead.

To summarize, the colon is marked by the taeniae coli, the haustra and the appendices epiploicae, and the transverse colon alone carries a mesentery of its own. The ascending colon lies against the right kidney and below the liver, the splenic flexure is tethered by the phrenicocolic ligament, and the marginal artery joins the territories of the two mesenteric arteries. Above the pectinate line the lining is mucosa draining to the portal vein and the internal anal sphincter is smooth, while below the line the lining is skin and the external sphincter is skeletal. The liver is the largest gland, the right lobe is by far the largest, the falciform ligament carries the round ligament, the bare area against the diaphragm is bounded by the coronary ligament, and the portal triad runs with ducts in front, artery between and portal vein behind. Its functional halves are divided by the plane from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava, its eight segments are separated by the hepatic veins and centered on portal branches, and the caudate lobe is segment one. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 71 — Gallbladder and Biliary System

This chapter covers the gallbladder and the biliary tree first, and then the pancreas, moving from the surface of each organ to its ducts, its blood supply and its neighborhood. It holds one hundred questions, opening with the gallbladder and its drainage and closing with the development of the pancreas. Each question states its answer immediately, before the next question begins, so nothing has to be carried in mind. The two organs are neighbors in the upper abdomen, and the reason to hear them together is that their ducts share one opening into the bowel. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7001. The gallbladder is a pear-shaped sac that lies on the under surface of the liver and stores bile. Which of its parts projects below the sharp lower border of the liver? The answer is the fundus. The fundus is the wide blind end, turning downward and forward to touch the anterior abdominal wall, while the body and the neck lie further back against the liver.

Question 7002. Which part of the gallbladder is the narrow funnel that turns downward and backward to continue as the cystic duct? The answer is the neck. The neck lies in the gallbladder fossa and curves in a gentle S shape before it becomes the duct. A small bulge on its right side is Hartmann's pouch.

Question 7003. Which of these lists gives the parts of the gallbladder in order from the closed end to the duct: body, fundus, neck; fundus, body, neck; neck, fundus, body; or fundus, neck, body? The answer is fundus, body, neck. Bile leaves the organ by the neck, so the fundus is the closed end.

Question 7004. Which duct drains the gallbladder and joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct? The answer is the cystic duct. It is about 3 to 4 centimeters long and runs backward, downward and to the left from the neck. Its lining carries a spiral fold that helps to keep the duct open.

Question 7005. On the visceral surface of the liver, between which two lobes does the gallbladder fossa lie, and what sits within it? The answer is the right lobe and the quadrate lobe, with the gallbladder lying in the fossa. The fossa is a shallow depression on the under surface, in front of the porta hepatis.

Question 7006. Which of these statements about the common hepatic duct is correct: it is formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts, it is formed by the cystic duct and the left hepatic duct, it drains only the right lobe of the liver, or it opens directly into the stomach? The answer is that it is formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts at the porta hepatis.

Question 7007. What is the name of the duct formed where the cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct, and roughly how long is it? The answer is the common bile duct, about 8 centimeters long. It runs down in the free edge of the lesser omentum and then passes behind the first part of the duodenum.

Question 7008. A described magnetic resonance image of the biliary tree shows a long duct running down behind the duodenum and ending in a swelling that joins a second duct before both enter the bowel wall. What is that swelling? The answer is the hepatopancreatic ampulla. It lies within the wall of the second part of the duodenum.

Question 7009. A constructed illustration: a person has severe pain in the right upper abdomen after a fatty meal, and the pain also reaches the right shoulder. Which organ is the source, and which nerve carries the shoulder pain? The answer is the gallbladder, with the phrenic nerve carrying the pain from the diaphragm.

Question 7010. What is the name of the small pouch on the right side of the neck of the gallbladder in which a stone may become stuck? The answer is Hartmann's pouch. It is a dilatation of the neck, and a stone lodged there presses on the cystic duct. The gallbladder then distends behind the block.

Question 7011. Which of these sets bounds the triangle in which the cystic artery is found: the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the under surface of the liver; the common bile duct, the duodenum and the pancreas; the portal vein, the aorta and the stomach; or the hepatic ducts, the spleen and the diaphragm? The answer is the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the under surface of the liver.

Question 7012. Which artery usually supplies the gallbladder, and from which artery does it arise? The answer is the cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery. The right hepatic artery comes from the proper hepatic artery. The cystic artery runs through the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the liver.

Question 7013. True or false: the wall of the gallbladder contains a muscularis mucosae and a true submucosa. The answer is false. The wall has a mucosa resting on a lamina propria, a muscle coat arranged in no fixed layers, and a perimuscular coat, but it has no submucosa and no muscularis mucosae.

Question 7014. Into which part of the small intestine does the common bile duct open, and on which wall of it? The answer is the second part of the duodenum, on its posteromedial wall. The opening is the major duodenal papilla, about 8 to 10 centimeters below the pylorus. The descending duodenum wraps around the head of the pancreas.

Question 7015. Name, as a short answer, the two ducts that unite to form the common bile duct. The answer is the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct. The common hepatic duct brings bile down from the liver, the cystic duct brings bile from the gallbladder, and their union marks the beginning of the common bile duct.

Question 7016. Which of these structures guards the entry of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum: the pyloric sphincter, the sphincter of Oddi, the ileocecal valve, or the internal anal sphincter? The answer is the sphincter of Oddi. It surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla and keeps the contents of the bowel out of the ducts between meals.

Question 7017. A described computed tomography scan of the upper abdomen shows a rounded fluid-filled sac lying between the right lobe of the liver and the duodenum, with dilated ducts beside it. Which organ is distended, and what does the picture suggest? The answer is the gallbladder, with an obstruction lower in the biliary tree.

Question 7018. In the free edge of the lesser omentum, which of the bile duct, the hepatic artery and the portal vein lies most posterior, and which lies furthest to the right? The answer is the portal vein posteriorly and the bile duct furthest to the right. The hepatic artery lies in front and to the left of the vein.

Question 7019. Which fold of mucosa winds along the inside of the cystic duct and helps to keep its lumen open? The answer is the spiral valve. It runs along the duct rather than closing it, so it does not act as a true valve. It also makes the duct easy for a surgeon to recognize.

Question 7020. A constructed illustration: a stone leaves the gallbladder, travels down the cystic duct, and becomes stuck where the duct is narrowest. Where has it most likely stopped? The answer is the lower end of the common bile duct, as it passes through the duodenal wall. The duct dilates above the block.

Question 7021. Which of these organs makes bile: the gallbladder, the liver, the pancreas, or the spleen? The answer is the liver. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile but does not make it. The liver produces about 600 to 1000 milliliters of bile each day, and bile salts within that fluid help to digest fat.

Question 7022. What is the name of the small outpouchings of gallbladder mucosa that push into the muscle layer and become prominent in adenomyomatosis? The answer is the Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. They are normal diverticula of the mucosal surface. When the wall thickens, they are seen as tiny pockets within it.

Question 7023. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fundus with the blind lower end, the neck with the spiral valve, the common bile duct with the cystic artery, or the cystic duct with the hepatopancreatic ampulla? The answer is the fundus with the blind lower end. The spiral valve lies in the cystic duct, and the ampulla ends the common bile duct.

Question 7024. A described cholangiogram shows dye filling two ducts that join at the hilum of the liver, and a third duct joining them from below and to the right. Which three ducts are described? The answer is the right hepatic duct, the left hepatic duct and the cystic duct. A stone would appear as a gap in that column of dye.

Question 7025. Which parts of the bowel lie against the body and the neck of the gallbladder? The answer is the transverse colon and the first and second parts of the duodenum. The body rests upon the transverse colon, and the duodenum lies against the neck. The fundus faces the abdominal wall instead.

Question 7026. What happens to bile while it is stored in the gallbladder: is it diluted, is it concentrated, is it mixed with pancreatic juice, or is it absorbed completely? The answer is that it is concentrated. Water and salts are absorbed across the wall, while bile salts, pigments, cholesterol and phospholipids stay behind. It may become five to ten times stronger.

Question 7027. A described transverse section of the upper abdomen shows a rounded structure on the visceral surface of the liver, to the right of the quadrate lobe. In which plane is the section taken, and in which direction does the lower end of the structure point? The answer is a transverse plane, with the lower end pointing downward and forward.

Question 7028. What is the name of the small opening on the inner wall of the duodenum through which bile enters the bowel? The answer is the major duodenal papilla. It lies on the posteromedial wall of the second part of the duodenum, and the pancreatic duct usually shares the same opening.

Question 7029. A constructed illustration: during an operation in the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the liver, an artery is divided close to the liver. Which artery has probably been injured, and what does it supply? The answer is the right hepatic artery, which supplies the right lobe and gives off the cystic artery.

Question 7030. Which of these statements about the blood supply of the gallbladder is correct: the cystic artery usually comes from the right hepatic artery, it usually comes from the left hepatic artery, it comes from the gastroduodenal artery, or the gallbladder has no named artery? The answer is that the cystic artery usually comes from the right hepatic artery, though it may arise elsewhere.

Question 7031. True or false: the gallbladder stores bile and empties it into the duodenum after a meal. The answer is true. Between meals the sphincter at the lower end of the bile duct stays closed, so bile backs up the cystic duct into the gallbladder. After a meal the gallbladder contracts and the sphincter relaxes.

Question 7032. A described ultrasound image of the upper abdomen shows an elongated sac with a bright wall lying beneath the liver, dark fluid inside it, and a bright band at its lower end. What is the structure, and what does the bright band most likely represent? The answer is the gallbladder, with a stone at its neck.

Question 7033. Which lymph node lies beside the cystic duct and receives lymph from the gallbladder? The answer is the cystic node. Lymph then passes to the nodes around the portal vein and onward to the coeliac nodes. Some lymph from the fundus drains directly into the liver instead.

Question 7034. Name, as a short answer, the three structures that make up the portal triad in the free edge of the lesser omentum. The answer is the bile duct, the hepatic artery and the portal vein. They run together from the porta hepatis down to the duodenum, with the vein lying behind the other two.

Question 7035. Which structure lies immediately behind the common bile duct in the free edge of the lesser omentum, and which lies to its left? The answer is the portal vein behind and the hepatic artery to the left. The duct is therefore the most anterior and the most rightward of the three, which makes it easy to reach from the front.

Question 7036. Which hormone makes the gallbladder contract and relaxes the sphincter at the end of the bile duct: secretin, cholecystokinin, gastrin, or insulin? The answer is cholecystokinin. It is released by cells in the duodenal wall when fat and protein enter the bowel. Its companion, secretin, makes the pancreas pour out a watery alkaline juice.

Question 7037. A constructed illustration: a person with inflammation around the gallbladder reports pain at the tip of the right shoulder as well as in the upper abdomen. Which nerve explains the shoulder pain, and by which segments does it reach the skin? The answer is the phrenic nerve, carrying fibers from the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments, which also supply the skin over the shoulder.

Question 7038. From which embryonic structure does the gallbladder develop, and at about which week does it appear? The answer is the hepatic diverticulum of the foregut, in the fourth week. That diverticulum grows into the septum transversum and divides, its cranial part forming the liver and its ducts and its caudal part forming the gallbladder and the cystic duct.

Question 7039. Which of these pairs belongs together: the cystic duct with the gallbladder, the common bile duct with the liver, the pancreatic duct with the spleen, or the hepatic duct with the duodenum? The answer is the cystic duct with the gallbladder. The common hepatic duct comes from the liver, and the pancreatic duct comes from the pancreas.

Question 7040. A described operative photograph shows a small artery crossing the triangle formed by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the liver, with a lymph node beside it. Which artery and which node are shown? The answer is the cystic artery and the cystic node. Because a variant artery in this triangle may be the only supply of the right lobe, the anatomy is defined before anything is divided.

Question 7041. Which feature of the gallbladder wall allows the organ to distend: a thick submucosa, muscle bundles arranged in no fixed layers, a complete ring of cartilage, or a lining of stratified squamous cells? The answer is muscle bundles arranged in no fixed layers. The muscle coat has no orderly inner circular and outer longitudinal arrangement, so the wall can stretch.

Question 7042. At which level does the fundus of the gallbladder lie, and where can it be felt on the abdominal wall? The answer is the transpyloric plane, at the tip of the ninth right costal cartilage. That point lies where the lateral edge of the rectus sheath meets the costal margin. The same plane passes through the pylorus and the neck of the pancreas.

Question 7043. Which part of the gallbladder is the widest, and which part is the closed end? The answer is the body, which is the widest part, and the fundus, which is the closed end. The neck is the narrow part that opens into the cystic duct, and the body lies between the fundus and the neck.
