Question 7044. A constructed illustration: a person has pale stools, dark urine and yellow skin, and imaging shows dilated ducts within the liver but a gallbladder of normal size. Where is the obstruction, and why is the gallbladder not enlarged? The answer is the common hepatic duct above the cystic duct, so bile never reaches the gallbladder.

Question 7045. Which of these statements about the lining of the gallbladder is correct: it is a single layer of columnar cells with microvilli, it is stratified squamous epithelium, it is ciliated throughout, or it is transitional epithelium? The answer is a single layer of columnar cells with microvilli. These cells absorb water and salts from the stored bile, and they rest on a lamina propria.

Question 7046. A described radiograph taken after dye is injected into the bile ducts shows a normal duct system with a small sac hanging from it below and to the right. Which structure is the sac, and which duct connects it to the system? The answer is the gallbladder and the cystic duct. A stone would appear as a gap in the dye.

Question 7047. What is the name of the muscle that surrounds the lower end of the common bile duct alone, above the ampulla: the sphincter of the bile duct, the pyloric sphincter, the sphincter of the pancreatic duct, or the internal anal sphincter? The answer is the sphincter of the bile duct. It lies within the duodenal wall and, with its neighbors, forms the sphincter of Oddi.

Question 7048. A described specimen shows a gallbladder whose fundus is folded back on itself like a cap. What is this variation called, and is it important? The answer is a Phrygian cap. It is a harmless fold of the fundus found in a small minority of people, and on a radiograph it may mimic a stone or a fold of the wall.

Question 7049. Which statement best explains why the gallbladder fills with bile between meals: the liver pumps bile at high pressure, the sphincter at the duodenal end of the duct is closed, the cystic duct has a valve that pulls bile in, or the gallbladder draws bile inward? The answer is that the sphincter at the duodenal end of the duct is closed, so bile takes the path of least resistance up the cystic duct.

Question 7050. A constructed illustration: after a long illness in which a person took nothing by mouth, stones are found in a gallbladder that never emptied. Which property of the gallbladder best explains this? The answer is that it keeps concentrating the bile that the liver continues to make. Water is absorbed while the bile sits, so its cholesterol and salts may crystallize.

Question 7051. The pancreas lies against the posterior abdominal wall, and peritoneum covers only its front. Which word describes this position? The answer is retroperitoneal. The gland cannot be lifted forward, because its posterior surface is attached to the tissues behind it. Only the tail, lying in a fold of peritoneum, has any freedom.

Question 7052. Which part of the pancreas lies within the curve of the duodenum? The answer is the head. It is the broad right-hand part of the gland, and the second part of the duodenum wraps around its right border. The uncinate process hangs from its lower and left side.

Question 7053. Which of these statements about the position of the pancreas is correct: it lies across the first and second lumbar vertebrae, it lies in the pelvis, it lies in front of the stomach, or it lies within the lesser sac? The answer is that it lies across the first and second lumbar vertebrae. Its head is lower than its tail.

Question 7054. Which part of the pancreas hooks backward and to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels? The answer is the uncinate process. It arises from the lower part of the head and passes behind the superior mesenteric vein and artery, so those vessels lie in front of it.

Question 7055. The portal vein is formed behind which part of the pancreas, and which two veins unite there? The answer is the neck of the pancreas, where the splenic vein meets the superior mesenteric vein. The new vein then runs upward in the free edge of the lesser omentum toward the liver.

Question 7056. Which part of the pancreas lies directly in front of the portal vein: the head, the neck, the body, or the tail? The answer is the neck. The vein is formed behind it, and the neck is the narrow part of the gland between the head and the body. The superior mesenteric vessels pass in the groove beneath it.

Question 7057. Into which organ does the tail of the pancreas project, and along which vessels does it run? The answer is the spleen, along the splenic vessels. The tail reaches the hilum of the spleen. It is the only part of the gland that lies free within a peritoneal fold, the splenorenal ligament.

Question 7058. Into which part of the bowel does the main pancreatic duct usually open, and with which duct does it share that opening? The answer is the second part of the duodenum, sharing the major duodenal papilla with the common bile duct. The two ducts join first in the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

Question 7059. A described computed tomography scan of the upper abdomen shows a long glandular organ lying across the midline behind the stomach, its head wrapped by the duodenum and its tail reaching the spleen. Which organ is described, and which large vein lies behind its neck? The answer is the pancreas, with the portal vein behind its neck.

Question 7060. A described transverse section of the upper abdomen shows the stomach in front and a long gland behind it, with a narrow space between the two. What is that space, and what is the gland? The answer is the lesser sac, with the pancreas behind it. The spleen lies to the left in the same section.

Question 7061. Which fault in development produces a ring of pancreatic tissue around the second part of the duodenum: failure of the dorsal bud to appear, division of the ventral bud with migration in two directions, failure of the two ducts to fuse, or absence of the uncinate process? The answer is division of the ventral bud with migration in two directions, so that it encircles the bowel.

Question 7062. True or false: the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ, and peritoneum covers only its anterior surface. The answer is true, with one small exception. The head, neck and body lie against the posterior wall, while the tail runs into the splenorenal ligament and is covered on both sides.

Question 7063. What is the name of the smaller pancreatic duct that usually opens above the main duct at a separate small papilla? The answer is the accessory pancreatic duct. It drains the upper part of the head of the gland. It usually joins the main duct, but in some people it remains separate.

Question 7064. Which of these does the pancreas secrete: only digestive enzymes, only hormones, both digestive enzymes and hormones, or neither? The answer is both. The acinar cells make enzymes and a watery alkaline fluid, and the islets of Langerhans make insulin, glucagon and other hormones. The endocrine part is only a small fraction of the gland.

Question 7065. A constructed illustration: a person has deep pain in the upper abdomen that bores through to the back and eases when sitting forward. Which organ lies against the structures that produce that back pain? The answer is the pancreas. It lies against the aorta and the coeliac plexus, so its pain is felt deeply and centrally.

Question 7066. Which pair of arteries supplies the head of the pancreas: the superior pancreaticoduodenal and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, the splenic and the left gastric arteries, the cystic and the right hepatic arteries, or the left and right gastroepiploic arteries? The answer is the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries. The superior one comes from the gastroduodenal artery.

Question 7067. Which structures lie immediately behind the body of the pancreas? The answer is the aorta, the superior mesenteric artery, the left kidney and the splenic vein. The splenic vein runs along the back of the gland. The left crus of the diaphragm and the left renal vessels also lie behind it.

Question 7068. Which groove on the neck of the pancreas carries the superior mesenteric vessels, and what lies behind those vessels? The answer is the groove on the neck, with the uncinate process behind them. The vein and the artery pass in front of the uncinate process, so the gland partly encircles the vessels.

Question 7069. Which of these statements about the control of pancreatic secretion is correct: secretin makes the gland pour a watery alkaline juice, secretin makes the gland pour enzymes, cholecystokinin makes the gland pour bicarbonate, or both hormones come from the stomach? The answer is that secretin makes the gland pour a watery alkaline juice. Cholecystokinin makes the acinar cells pour enzymes.

Question 7070. Which of these pairs belongs together: the head of the pancreas with the duodenum, the tail of the pancreas with the liver, the neck of the pancreas with the spleen, or the body of the pancreas with the rectum? The answer is the head of the pancreas with the duodenum. The tail lies against the spleen, and the body lies behind the stomach.

Question 7071. Which of these best describes pancreatic juice: about 1500 milliliters a day and rich in bicarbonate, about 150 milliliters a day and rich in acid, about 1500 milliliters a day and free of enzymes, or about 5 liters a day and rich in bile salts? The answer is about 1500 milliliters a day and rich in bicarbonate. Its enzymes work best in that alkaline setting.

Question 7072. A described magnetic resonance image of the pancreatic ducts shows a short duct joining the bile duct and a longer duct running the length of the gland and opening separately above it. What pattern is described? The answer is that the dorsal and the ventral ducts have failed to fuse, a pattern called pancreas divisum, in which the long duct carries most of the juice.

Question 7073. A described ultrasound image shows a long narrow gland lying across the midline behind the stomach, with a bright line running along its middle. What is the gland, and what is the bright line? The answer is the pancreas, with the main pancreatic duct. Gas in the bowel in front often hides the gland.

Question 7074. A described transverse section shows a gland whose head lies to the right of the midline and whose tail lies to the left, with a duct running through its middle. Which gland is shown, and in which direction does the duct run? The answer is the pancreas, with its duct running from the tail on the left toward the head on the right.

Question 7075. Name, as a short answer, the two ducts of the pancreas, and say where each usually opens. The answer is the main pancreatic duct, which opens at the major duodenal papilla, and the accessory pancreatic duct, which opens at the minor papilla above it. The main duct joins the common bile duct first.

Question 7076. What is the name of the swelling where the pancreatic duct and the common bile duct join before they enter the duodenum: the pyloric canal, the hepatopancreatic ampulla, the cystic duct, or the pancreatic notch? The answer is the hepatopancreatic ampulla. It lies within the wall of the second part of the duodenum.

Question 7077. A constructed illustration: a growth in the head of the pancreas presses on the structures running through it. Which two ducts are most likely to be blocked, and which vein behind the head may also be compressed? The answer is the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct, with the portal vein behind the head. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7078. True or false: the tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament and moves with the spleen. The answer is true. The tail is the only part of the gland that is not fixed to the posterior abdominal wall, and it reaches the hilum of the spleen along with the splenic vessels.

Question 7079. Which statement best explains why pancreas divisum leaves most of the pancreatic juice draining through a small opening: the ventral duct never forms, the dorsal and the ventral ducts fail to fuse, the sphincter of Oddi closes the main duct, or the bile duct drains the whole gland? The answer is that the two ducts fail to fuse, so the dorsal duct carries most of the juice to the smaller minor papilla.

Question 7080. Which kidney lies immediately behind the body and the tail of the pancreas, and which vessels run between them? The answer is the left kidney, with the left renal vessels. The splenic vein also runs along the back of the gland. The right kidney lies further away, behind the head and the duodenum.

Question 7081. Which cells of the pancreas make insulin, and in which part of the gland are they found? The answer is the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, scattered through the gland and most numerous in the body and the tail. The acinar cells around them make the digestive enzymes.

Question 7082. Which of these statements about the veins of the pancreas is correct: the head drains into the portal vein and the body and tail into the splenic vein, all pancreatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava, the gland has no veins of its own, or all its veins drain into the left renal vein? The answer is the first of these. The splenic vein then carries that blood to the portal vein.

Question 7083. A described computed tomography scan of a person with long-standing pancreatic disease shows a widened duct running the length of the gland with several bright deposits along it. What do the bright deposits represent, and what do they suggest? The answer is calcium within the duct, suggesting chronic inflammation of the gland. The duct is widened behind them.

Question 7084. The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses which of these organs: the pancreas, the spleen, the right kidney, or the gallbladder? The answer is the pancreas, along its anterior border. From that line the two layers of the mesocolon pass down onto the transverse colon. The attachment marks the lower limit of the lesser sac.

Question 7085. Which of these pairs belongs together: the beta cell with insulin, the acinar cell with bile, the alpha cell with bicarbonate, or the duct cell with glucagon? The answer is the beta cell with insulin. The alpha cells make glucagon, the delta cells make somatostatin, and the acinar cells make the digestive enzymes.

Question 7086. Which statement best explains why pancreatic pain is felt deeply in the upper abdomen and the back, while gallbladder pain is felt in the right upper abdomen: the pancreas lies closer to the skin, the two organs send pain fibers to different spinal segments, the gallbladder has no pain fibers, or the pancreas is supplied by the phrenic nerve? The answer is that the two organs send pain fibers to different spinal segments.

Question 7087. A constructed illustration: a newborn vomits after every feed, and imaging shows a dilated first part of the duodenum with a ring of tissue around the second part. Which fault in development is present? The answer is an annular pancreas, formed when the ventral bud migrates in two directions and encircles the duodenum. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7088. Which parts of the pancreas develop from the ventral bud, and which from the dorsal bud? The answer is that the ventral bud forms the lower part of the head and the uncinate process, while the dorsal bud forms the upper head, the body and the tail. The ventral bud rotates around the duodenum before the two fuse.

Question 7089. Which artery supplies the body and the tail of the pancreas, and from which vessel does it arise? The answer is the great pancreatic artery and the other pancreatic branches of the splenic artery. That artery runs along the upper border of the gland and gives off these branches on its way to the spleen.

Question 7090. A described specimen shows a pale lobulated gland lying on a tray, with a narrow end on the left and a broad end on the right. Which end lies nearest the duodenum, and which end lies nearest the spleen? The answer is that the broad head lies nearest the duodenum and the narrow tail nearest the spleen.

Question 7091. A described scan shows a long duct running through the whole gland and a shorter duct above it, the two opening into the duodenum at separate points. Which duct carries most of the juice, and why does the arrangement matter? The answer is the long main duct. The accessory duct drains only the upper head, so its opening is smaller.

Question 7092. True or false: small patches of pancreatic tissue are sometimes found in the wall of the stomach or the small intestine, and they are normal variations. The answer is true. Such patches may contain islets and usually cause no trouble. They are found most often in the stomach and the upper small intestine.

Question 7093. A constructed illustration: a person develops painless yellow skin and a gallbladder that can be felt below the liver, and imaging shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which duct is blocked, and why is the gallbladder enlarged? The answer is the common bile duct, blocked below the cystic duct, so bile still reaches and fills the gallbladder. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7094. Which of these pairs belongs together: the splenic artery with the body and tail of the pancreas, the gastroduodenal artery with the tail, the superior mesenteric artery with the tail, or the left gastric artery with the head? The answer is the splenic artery with the body and the tail. The head is supplied by the pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

Question 7095. Which structures lie between the tail of the pancreas and the spleen at the hilum: the splenic vessels and the splenorenal ligament, the bile duct and the portal vein, the aorta and the left crus, or the transverse mesocolon and the left colic flexure? The answer is the splenic vessels and the splenorenal ligament. The tail runs with the splenic artery and vein into the hilum.

Question 7096. The uncinate process lies between which two large vessels, and what lies immediately behind it? The answer is the superior mesenteric vessels in front and the aorta behind. The portal vein forms above and to its right. Because of these relations the process is often hidden behind the mesenteric vessels.

Question 7097. A described transverse section of the upper abdomen at the level of the first lumbar vertebra shows the pancreas in the midline, the aorta behind it, the superior mesenteric artery arising in front of it, and the left kidney behind and to the left. Which structure lies immediately in front of the pancreas in that section? The answer is the stomach.

Question 7098. A constructed illustration: a deep wound in the upper abdomen divides the neck of the pancreas and the vessels passing behind it. Which large vein is most likely to be injured, and what does it drain? The answer is the portal vein, which drains blood from the gut, the spleen and the pancreas to the liver. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7099. A described computed tomography scan shows a rounded collection of fluid lying behind the stomach with the pancreas thickened beside it. Which structure does the fluid lie against, and what does the collection suggest? The answer is the pancreas, suggesting a collection that formed after inflammation of the gland. The lesser sac lies in front of the pancreas.

Question 7100. Which statement best explains why the head and the tail of the pancreas have different blood supplies: the two parts develop from different buds, the head shares the supply of the duodenum and the tail that of the spleen, the head lies in front and the tail behind, or the tail has no artery? The answer is that the head shares the supply of the duodenum and the tail that of the spleen.

To summarize, the gallbladder lies in the gallbladder fossa between the right lobe and the quadrate lobe of the liver, stores and concentrates bile, and empties through the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. That duct runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, where the portal vein lies behind it and the hepatic artery to its left, and it ends with the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla in the second part of the duodenum. The pancreas is a retroperitoneal gland lying across the first and second lumbar vertebrae, with its head in the curve of the duodenum, its neck over the portal vein, and its tail reaching the hilum of the spleen. The uncinate process lies behind the superior mesenteric vessels, while the aorta, the left kidney and the splenic vein lie behind the body of the gland. The ventral pancreatic bud forms the lower part of the head and the uncinate process, and the dorsal bud forms the rest, and their ducts usually fuse into one main channel. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 72 — Kidneys

This chapter examines the kidneys, the paired organs that filter the blood and make urine, and it works inward through the cortex, the medulla, the renal pyramids and the calyces. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately, followed by the reason the answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. The questions begin with the position and coverings of the kidney, then follow the tissue inward to the calyces that collect what the pyramids deliver. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7101. Which paired organs lie behind the peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall, one on each side of the vertebral column, between the twelfth thoracic and the third lumbar levels? The answer is the kidneys. Each lies against the posterior wall of the abdomen. In the adult each one is about 11 to 12 centimeters long.

Question 7102. Which covering lies directly against the surface of the kidney and can be peeled away from it: the fibrous capsule, the perirenal fat, the renal fascia, or the peritoneum? The answer is the fibrous capsule. It is a smooth sheath wrapped tightly around the organ. The perirenal fat and the renal fascia lie outside it.

Question 7103. Which large organ rests against the upper part of the anterior surface of the right kidney, and how does it affect the position of that kidney? The answer is the liver, which presses on the upper pole and holds the right kidney lower than the left. The right suprarenal gland caps the same pole.

Question 7104. Which structure lies immediately anterior to the lower part of the right kidney: the descending colon, the ascending colon, the spleen, or the stomach? The answer is the ascending colon. It runs up the right side of the abdomen in front of that kidney. The descending colon and the spleen lie on the left.

Question 7105. Which muscle lies immediately behind the kidney, along the medial part of its posterior surface? The answer is the psoas major. The kidney rests on the psoas major and the quadratus lumborum, with the diaphragm above the upper pole. The twelfth rib crosses the same posterior surface. Behind the kidney therefore lies muscle, not peritoneum.

Question 7106. Which statement about the left kidney is correct: it lies against the spleen and the pancreas, it lies in front of the peritoneum, it is related to the duodenum, or it lies lower than the right kidney? The answer is that it lies against the spleen and the pancreas. The stomach lies above and in front of it.

Question 7107. A described coronal section shows a kidney with a smooth outer rim and a central cavity filled with fat, vessels and a funnel-shaped tube. Name the cavity and the tube. The answer is the renal sinus and the renal pelvis. The sinus opens at the hilum, and the pelvis funnels downward to become the ureter.

Question 7108. Which structure lies most anterior in the hilum of the kidney, in front of the artery and the pelvis? The answer is the renal vein. From front to back the hilum holds the vein, then the artery, then the pelvis. The ureter leaves behind those vessels.

Question 7109. Name the outer layer of the kidney that lies immediately deep to the fibrous capsule and contains the renal corpuscles. The answer is the renal cortex. It forms a shell about 1 centimeter thick and dips between the pyramids as the renal columns. The corpuscles and the convoluted tubules lie within it.

Question 7110. Which structure in the renal cortex consists of a cluster of capillaries inside a double-walled cup? The answer is the renal corpuscle. The cup is the glomerular capsule and the tuft inside it is the glomerulus. Blood enters and leaves the tuft through the afferent and the efferent arterioles. The corpuscle is the beginning of the nephron.

Question 7111. Which statement about the renal cortex is correct: it lies deep to the medulla, it contains the loops of Henle, it receives blood from the interlobular arteries, or it is drained by the minor calyces? The answer is that it receives blood from the interlobular arteries. Those vessels run outward from the arcuate arteries toward the capsule.

Question 7112. The band of cortex that lies between two adjacent renal pyramids has a name. What is it called, and which vessels run through it? The answer is a renal column, and it carries the interlobar arteries and veins. The column bridges the outer shell of the kidney and the tissue near the sinus.

Question 7113. Which of these lies at the boundary between the cortex and the medulla: the interlobular artery, the arcuate artery, the segmental artery, or the afferent arteriole? The answer is the arcuate artery. It arches over the base of each pyramid and marks that boundary. The interlobular arteries arise from it. The arcuate artery is the continuation of the interlobar artery.

Question 7114. A described microscopic section of the cortex shows round tufts of capillaries surrounded by coiled tubules, with straight tubules running in bundles toward the surface. What are those bundles called? The answer is the medullary rays, straight tubules extending from the base of a pyramid into the cortex. They carry collecting ducts and loops of Henle.

Question 7115. True or false: the renal cortex is the region of the kidney that contains the renal pyramids. The answer is false. The pyramids belong to the medulla, and each points its apex toward the renal sinus. The cortex is the outer shell that arches over their bases. The columns of cortex also belong to that outer shell.

Question 7116. A described ultrasound image of a normal kidney shows an outer band of medium gray, inner triangular areas that are darker, and a bright central region. Which zone is bright? The answer is the renal sinus, whose fat reflects the sound waves. The dark triangles are the medullary pyramids. Each dark triangle sends its tip toward the bright center.

Question 7117. Which of these pairs belongs together: the renal cortex with the glomeruli, the renal medulla with the glomeruli, the renal cortex with the loops of Henle, or the renal medulla with the convoluted tubules? The answer is the renal cortex with the glomeruli. The corpuscles lie in the cortex and the loops of Henle descend into the medulla.

Question 7118. A described computed tomography scan taken after contrast shows a bright outer rim of kidney tissue and a darker inner zone. Which zone is the bright rim, and why is the inner zone darker? The answer is the renal cortex, and the inner zone is the medulla. Contrast reaches the cortex first because most of the blood flow goes there.

Question 7119. Which structures arch over the base of a renal pyramid, between it and the cortex above? The answer is the arcuate artery and the arcuate vein. They follow the line of the base and give off the interlobular vessels. A renal column runs down on each side of the pyramid. They mark the boundary between the cortex and the medulla.

Question 7120. A constructed illustration: a needle biopsy is taken from the outer part of a kidney. Which layer does the sample come from, and which structures should it contain? The answer is the renal cortex, with renal corpuscles, convoluted tubules and medullary rays. A sample from deeper would contain the straight tubules of the medulla.

Question 7121. Name two structures that lie within the renal cortex, spoken as a list. The answer is the renal corpuscle and the convoluted tubule. Both lie among the coils of the cortical labyrinth between the medullary rays. The collecting ducts pass through on their way inward. The glomerulus sits inside the corpuscle, and the tubule coils around it.

Question 7122. Which structure forms the outer shell of the kidney, lies immediately under the fibrous capsule, and gives the organ a granular surface in the newborn? The answer is the renal cortex. In the fetus and the infant it is divided into visible lobules, and the surface stays bumpy until childhood. In most adults the lobules fuse.

Question 7123. Which statement about the renal columns is correct: they are part of the medulla, they separate the pyramids and carry vessels, they contain the renal papillae, or they drain into the minor calyces? The answer is that they separate the pyramids and carry vessels. The interlobar arteries and veins run through a column toward the arcuate vessels.

Question 7124. A described specimen shows a kidney cut in half, with a band of tissue arching over darker triangular areas and dipping inward between them. What is the dipping part called, and which vessels run in it? The answer is a renal column, carrying the interlobar vessels. The darker triangles are the medullary pyramids.

Question 7125. In the cortex, which vessel gives rise directly to the afferent arterioles of the glomeruli: the arcuate artery, the interlobular artery, the interlobar artery, or the segmental artery? The answer is the interlobular artery. It runs outward through the cortex between the medullary rays. The efferent arteriole leaves the glomerulus behind. The peritubular capillaries then surround the tubules.

Question 7126. Name the structure at the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle where the afferent arteriole meets the distal tubule. The answer is the juxtaglomerular apparatus. It holds the granular cells of the arteriole and the macula densa of the tubule, and it lies close to the glomerulus it serves. The apparatus lies in the cortex, beside its glomerulus.

Question 7127. Which of these zones contains the longest loops of Henle: the outer medulla, the inner medulla, the cortex, or the renal sinus? The answer is the inner medulla, close to the papilla. The juxtamedullary nephrons have these long loops, while the nephrons near the surface have short ones. The longest of them come close to the tip of the papilla.

Question 7128. Which statement about the renal lobule is correct: it is a pyramid with its cortex, it is a medullary ray with the cortex around it, it is bounded by the calyces, or it is another name for a lobe? The answer is that it is a medullary ray with the cortex around it. The renal lobe is the larger unit, a pyramid with its cortex. Several lobules lie within one lobe.

Question 7129. A constructed illustration: a tumor arises from the tubular epithelium of the kidney and grows along the renal vein. From which zone did it arise, and which structure is it invading? The answer is the renal cortex, and it is invading the renal vein. The tubular epithelium lies in the cortex, and the veins of the cortex drain toward the hilum.

Question 7130. Immediately outside the fibrous capsule of the kidney lie two coverings. Name them, in the order in which they are met. The answer is the perirenal fat and then the renal fascia. The fat lies against the capsule, and the fascia wraps the kidney and the fat together. Outside it lies more fat, the pararenal fat.

Question 7131. In a coronal section the cortex is described as arching over the base of each pyramid. Toward which surface of the kidney does the base of a pyramid face? The answer is the outer surface. The base lies against the cortex near the capsule, and the apex points inward to the renal sinus.

Question 7132. Which statement about the blood flow of the renal cortex is correct: it receives less blood than the medulla, it receives most of the renal blood flow, it is supplied only by the renal vein, or it has no capillary network? The answer is that it receives most of the renal blood flow. The medulla receives a much smaller share.

Question 7133. Which vessels mark the boundary between the cortex and the medulla on a cut surface of the kidney? The answer is the arcuate arteries and veins, whose arching line follows the base of every pyramid. The interlobular arteries continue outward from them into the cortex. Each renal column carries vessels up to that line.

Question 7134. Which zone of the kidney lies immediately deep to the fibrous capsule and immediately outside the medulla? The answer is the renal cortex. It is the outer shell of the organ, and the medulla lies within it. The cortex sends columns inward between the pyramids. The columns of cortex are continuous with it.

Question 7135. Which of these pairs belongs together: the renal cortex with the medullary rays, the renal medulla with the glomeruli, the renal cortex with the renal papillae, or the renal medulla with the convoluted tubules? The answer is the renal cortex with the medullary rays, bundles of straight tubules that project into the cortex from the base of a pyramid.

Question 7136. The arcuate arteries arch over the bases of the renal pyramids. At which boundary do they lie? The answer is the boundary between the cortex and the medulla. They mark the corticomedullary junction and give off the interlobular arteries. The interlobar arteries reach them from the columns below.

Question 7137. Name the inner region of the kidney, which contains the triangular structures whose apices point toward the renal sinus. The answer is the renal medulla. It lies deep to the cortex and is divided into pyramids by the renal columns. Its outer and inner parts hold tubules of different length. Each pyramid ends at a papilla, which a calyx receives.

Question 7138. Which statement about the two kinds of nephron is correct: cortical nephrons have the longest loops, juxtamedullary nephrons lie close to the medulla, every nephron reaches the papilla, or all loops lie in the cortex? The answer is that juxtamedullary nephrons lie close to the medulla. Their loops descend far into the medulla beside the vasa recta.

Question 7139. True or false: in a horseshoe kidney the band joining the two kidneys lies below the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery. The answer is true. That band, the isthmus, joins the lower poles in front of the great vessels. It catches beneath the artery as the kidney ascends and holds the organ low.

Question 7140. A constructed illustration: an image of both kidneys shows small streaks of calcium and tiny cysts inside the medullary pyramids, while the cortex looks normal. Which structures are affected? The answer is the collecting ducts within the pyramids. The ducts are dilated and hold urine, and calcium is deposited in the same region.

Question 7141. A described microscopic section shows parallel straight tubules running toward a rounded tip that opens into a cavity. Which region of the kidney is shown? The answer is the medulla, at the tip of a renal pyramid. That tip is the papilla, where the collecting ducts open. The cavity beyond the tip is the beginning of a calyx.

Question 7142. Which structure carries the urine from the tip of a renal pyramid into the next part of the collecting system? The answer is the collecting duct, which opens at the papilla. Several ducts open close together on the surface of each papilla, and beyond them the urine enters a minor calyx. Urine leaves the papilla only through these openings.

Question 7143. Which statement about the loops of Henle is correct: they lie entirely in the cortex, they descend into the medulla and return to the cortex, they open into a minor calyx, or they surround the glomerulus? The answer is that they descend into the medulla and return to the cortex. Their length decides how deep they reach.

Question 7144. Which structure lies between two medullary pyramids, enhances exactly as the cortex does, and can be mistaken for a tumor: a renal column, a renal papilla, a minor calyx, or the renal capsule? The answer is a renal column. It is normal cortical tissue, so it enhances in step with the cortex. The other three structures do not enhance in that pattern.

Question 7145. A described vertical section of the kidney shows a series of cones whose bases meet the cortex and whose tips open into small cups. What are the tips called? The answer is the renal papillae. Each is the apex of a medullary pyramid and is perforated by the openings of the collecting ducts.

Question 7146. Which two regions of the kidney lie on either side of the arcuate vessels? The answer is the cortex above and the medulla below. The arcuate line follows the boundary between them, arching over the base of every pyramid. Renal columns carry the vessels up to that line. The papillae of the pyramids point away from that line.

Question 7147. Which statement about the medulla of a child's kidney is correct: the pyramids are absent, the pyramids are prominent and the surface is lobulated, the medulla has not yet formed, or the calyces lie outside the kidney? The answer is that the pyramids are prominent and the surface is lobulated. The fetal kidney is divided into visible lobules.

Question 7148. Name the anomaly in which the lower poles of the two kidneys are joined across the midline by a band of tissue in front of the great vessels. The answer is a horseshoe kidney. Its isthmus is trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery as the organ ascends, so the joined kidney stays low in the abdomen. The collecting systems of the two halves often face forward.

Question 7149. A constructed illustration: a person with long-standing diabetes loses the blood supply to the innermost part of the kidney, and fragments of papillae break away. Which zone has been damaged? The answer is the renal medulla, at the papillae, which receive the least blood flow and suffer first when it falls.

Question 7150. Which structure opens onto the surface of a renal papilla: the proximal convoluted tubule, the collecting duct, the loop of Henle, or the afferent arteriole? The answer is the collecting duct. Between 10 and 25 ducts open on each papilla, forming a small perforated area on its tip. The ducts deliver urine from the nephrons above them.

Question 7151. What name is given to the striped bands of straight tubules that run from the base of a pyramid into the cortex? The answer is the medullary rays. They mark out the lobules within the cortex and carry collecting ducts and loops of Henle. In section they run at right angles to the capsule.

Question 7152. Which statement about the medullary rays is correct: they are part of the medulla, they contain collecting ducts and loops of Henle, they contain the glomeruli, or they lie in the renal sinus? The answer is that they contain collecting ducts and loops of Henle. They project into the cortex from the base of a pyramid.

Question 7153. A described microscopic preparation shows the medulla with two bands: a striped outer band and a paler inner band around the papilla. What are those bands? The answer is the outer zone and the inner zone of the renal medulla. The outer zone carries straight vessels and tubules in bundles. The inner zone consists of thin limbs and collecting ducts.

Question 7154. Which statement about the blood supply of the medulla is correct: it is richer than that of the cortex, it comes only from the renal vein, it comes from the straight vessels and is small, or it is supplied by the interlobular arteries? The answer is that it comes from the straight vessels and is small. The vasa recta descend from the efferent arterioles of the juxtamedullary nephrons.

Question 7155. Name two structures of the renal medulla that run as straight tubes, spoken as a list. The answer is the loop of Henle and the collecting duct. The loop descends from the cortex and returns to it, and the collecting duct runs on to the papilla. Both lie among the straight vessels that serve the medulla.

Question 7156. Which straight vessels run down among the loops of Henle and return blood from the region of the papilla toward the cortex? The answer is the vasa recta. They share the hairpin shape of the loops they accompany, and their thin walls let water move in and out. They carry blood back toward the cortex.

Question 7157. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan shows the cortex as a bright outer band and the medulla as a darker inner zone, while the center of the organ returns a strong signal. What fills that center? The answer is the fat of the renal sinus, with the pelvis and the calyces lying within it.

Question 7158. Which of these pairs belongs together: the renal medulla with the vasa recta, the renal cortex with the vasa recta, the renal medulla with the peritubular capillaries, or the renal cortex with the papilla? The answer is the renal medulla with the vasa recta. Those straight vessels run down among the loops of Henle.

Question 7159. A constructed illustration: in sickle cell disease a period of poor blood flow damages the papillae first. Why do the papillae suffer before the cortex? The answer is that the medulla has a marginal blood supply, carried by straight vessels that take only a small share of the flow. The cortex, with its richer flow, withstands the same period.

Question 7160. Which large vein crosses in front of the aorta, and between which two vessels can it be compressed? The answer is the left renal vein, compressed between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. It is longer than the right because it must cross the midline. The right renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava.

Question 7161. Which of these explains a single kidney that is larger than usual but shows a normal cortex, medulla and calyces: congenital absence of the other kidney, a horseshoe kidney, a duplex collecting system, or an ectopic pelvic kidney? The answer is congenital absence of the other kidney. The remaining organ carries the whole function and grows larger, but its internal structure stays normal.

Question 7162. A described section through the renal sinus shows rounded profiles of tissue surrounded by fat, with no cortex around them. What are those profiles? The answer is the renal papillae, the apices of the medullary pyramids. They project into the sinus and each is capped by a minor calyx. The cortex lies far away, at the outer border of the organ.

Question 7163. Name the cone-shaped structures of the renal medulla whose bases lie against the cortex and whose apices point toward the renal sinus. The answer is the renal pyramids. A kidney usually holds 8 to 18 of them, and each with its cortex forms a renal lobe. The number of pyramids differs from one kidney to the next.

Question 7164. Which structures separate one renal pyramid from the next: the renal columns, the minor calyces, the medullary rays, or the arcuate arteries? The answer is the renal columns. Each column is a band of cortical tissue that runs from the outer shell to the sinus. The interlobar vessels pass through it between the pyramids.

Question 7165. A described image of the kidney taken after contrast is given shows triangular areas of dense material within the medulla. What are those triangles? The answer is the renal pyramids. The contrast is concentrated within the tubules that run through them. They stand out against the cortex.

Question 7166. What is formed by the union of two or more minor calyces, and into which structure does it open? The answer is a major calyx, which opens into the renal pelvis. A major calyx is a broad channel that carries urine onward from the cups around the papillae. It lies within the renal sinus, behind the renal vessels.

Question 7167. Why are the arteries that climb between the renal pyramids called interlobar arteries: because they pass between the lobes, because they supply both kidneys, because they cross the calyces, or because they lie inside one lobe? The answer is that they pass between the lobes. A lobe is a pyramid with the cortex over its base, and the artery climbs through a renal column between two lobes.

Question 7168. Which statement about the renal pyramids is correct: a normal kidney has about 3 of them, a normal kidney has 8 to 18 of them, they lie within the cortex, or each one drains into the renal vein? The answer is that a normal kidney has 8 to 18 of them. The number varies from person to person.

Question 7169. In a coronal section a pyramid lies with its base at the outer border of the medulla and its apex directed inward. Toward which part of the kidney does the apex point? The answer is toward the renal sinus and the hilum. The base faces the cortex on the outer side. The apex is the papilla, which the calyx receives.

Question 7170. True or false: every renal pyramid is drained by its own separate minor calyx. The answer is false. Two or more pyramids may fuse at their apices to form a compound papilla, and one minor calyx then receives them together. This is common at the upper pole of the kidney. A compound papilla is a normal variation.

Question 7171. Which of these is a pyramid together with the cortex that covers its base: a renal lobule, a renal lobe, a renal column, or a renal papilla? The answer is a renal lobe, the larger unit of the kidney. A lobule is a medullary ray with the cortex around it. A column is cortical tissue, and a papilla belongs to the medulla.

Question 7172. A constructed illustration: an image of a child's kidney shows the pyramids outlined by bands of tissue on every side, so that the surface looks bumpy. What is the most likely explanation? The answer is persistent fetal lobation, a normal variant. The grooves between the lobules usually smooth out in childhood. Those grooves lie over the renal columns.

Question 7173. A constructed illustration: a plane through the lateral border of the kidney is chosen because it crosses few vessels. Which two groups of arteries lie on either side? The answer is the anterior and the posterior branches of the renal artery. They supply the front and the back and do not join one another.

Question 7174. An ectopic kidney lies in the lesser pelvis in front of the sacrum. Which structure lies immediately in front of it, and why is its renal artery unusually short? The answer is the peritoneum, and the artery is short because the kidney never ascended. It kept the blood supply it received at its original level, from a nearby pelvic vessel.

Question 7175. A described dissection shows the medulla divided into cones, each with a striated base and a rounded tip, and bands of paler tissue between the cones. Which two structures are described? The answer is the renal pyramids and the renal columns. The paler bands are the columns of cortical tissue. The base of each cone lies against the cortex above it.

Question 7176. Which of these pairs belongs together: a renal pyramid with the medulla, a renal pyramid with the cortex, a renal column with the medulla, or a medullary ray with the sinus? The answer is a renal pyramid with the medulla. The pyramids are the visible units of the medulla. The columns and rays are cortical.

Question 7177. Which structure forms the apex of a renal pyramid and projects into a minor calyx: the renal papilla, the renal column, the medullary ray, or the arcuate vein? The answer is the renal papilla. Each pyramid ends in a papilla, though the apices of neighboring pyramids may fuse. A fused apex is called a compound papilla.

Question 7178. Which structure of the kidney lies deepest, projecting into the renal sinus at the center of the organ? The answer is the renal papilla, the apex of a medullary pyramid. The base of that pyramid and the capsule lie near the outer surface.

Question 7179. A described computed tomography scan shows a wedge of kidney tissue from the capsule to the sinus that does not enhance, while the rest of the kidney does. Which vessels supply it? The answer is the segmental arteries. Because they do not join one another, one blocked artery leaves a whole wedge without blood.

Question 7180. Which statement about the segmental arteries of the kidney is correct: they join one another freely, they are end arteries supplying separate wedges, they supply only the cortex, or they arise from the renal vein? The answer is that they are end arteries supplying separate wedges. Each serves a defined part with no useful overlap.

Question 7181. Name the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the tip of a renal pyramid and collects the urine leaving it. The answer is the minor calyx. Several minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and a short neck joins the cup to the rest of the system. The cup is lined by the same epithelium as the ureter.

Question 7182. Which of these comes immediately after the minor calyx as urine leaves the kidney: the major calyx, the ureter, the renal pelvis, or the collecting duct? The answer is the major calyx. Several minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and the major calyces then unite to form the renal pelvis. The pelvis narrows below and continues as the ureter.

Question 7183. How many minor calyces does a normal kidney usually contain, and how many major calyces does it have? The answer is 7 to 13 minor calyces and usually 3 major calyces. The major calyces are named the upper, the middle and the lower. The pelvis forms where they join. A kidney with a different number of calyces is still normal.

Question 7184. True or false: the collecting ducts, the calyces, the renal pelvis and the ureter all develop from the same outgrowth. The answer is true. That outgrowth is the ureteric bud, which grows into the tissue that becomes the kidney. Its branches form the collecting ducts and its stem forms the pelvis and the ureter.

Question 7185. Which statement about the minor calyces is correct: each one surrounds a renal papilla, each one surrounds a renal column, they drain into the other kidney, or they lie within the cortex? The answer is that each one surrounds a renal papilla. The cup catches the urine that the collecting ducts deliver.

Question 7186. A described image of the kidney shows a central branching structure filled with contrast, with rounded cups at its outer ends. What is that whole structure? The answer is the collecting system within the sinus, the pelvis and the calyces. The cups at the ends are the minor calyces. The channels that join the cups are the major calyces and the pelvis.

Question 7187. Within which cavity of the kidney does the renal pelvis lie, and what else does that cavity hold? The answer is the renal sinus, which also holds the calyces, the renal vessels and a quantity of fat. The sinus is the cavity that opens at the hilum of the kidney.

Question 7188. A constructed illustration: in a child with a duplex system, the ureter from the upper part of the kidney is obstructed, while the ureter from the lower part lets urine flow backward. Which part shows dilated calyces? The answer is the upper part. Its obstructed ureter makes its calyces dilate. The lower part is the one that allows backward flow.

Question 7189. True or false: the renal fascia encloses the kidney, the perirenal fat and the suprarenal gland in one compartment. The answer is true. The fascia passes around the kidney and the fat and also encloses the suprarenal gland above. Because they share that envelope, the two organs move together. The fascia also separates the kidney from the pararenal fat.

Question 7190. Which of these pairs belongs together: the minor calyx with a renal papilla, the minor calyx with the renal cortex, the major calyx with a single papilla, or the pelvis with the perirenal fat? The answer is the minor calyx with a renal papilla. Its cup receives the apex of a pyramid.

Question 7191. A constructed illustration: a stone forms in the collecting system and grows until it fills the pelvis and the major calyces, taking the shape of the cavity. Which structures does it occupy? The answer is the renal pelvis, the major calyces and the minor calyces. A stone of that shape lies within the renal sinus.

Question 7192. Which structure lies between the apex of a renal pyramid and the renal pelvis? The answer is the minor calyx, with the major calyx beyond it. The cup receives the papilla, and its neck leads to the major calyx. It then funnels the urine onward into the ureter.

Question 7193. Which statement about the calyces is correct: the minor calyces are always 3 in number, the major calyces are usually 3 in number, the major calyx surrounds the papilla, or the calyces lie in the cortex? The answer is that the major calyces are usually 3 in number. The minor calyces number 7 to 13.

Question 7194. A described section through the renal sinus shows a funnel-shaped space that divides into three broad channels, each of which divides into several small cups. Name the funnel and the channels. The answer is the renal pelvis and the major calyces. The small cups are the minor calyces. Each small cup embraces the apex of a pyramid.

Question 7195. Name the narrowing at which the renal pelvis becomes the ureter, and state where it lies. The answer is the ureteropelvic junction, at the lower part of the hilum. The pelvis tapers into the ureter there, about level with the second lumbar vertebra. The junction is a common place for a stone to lodge.

Question 7196. When the ureteropelvic junction is blocked, which part of the collecting system dilates first: the minor calyces, the major calyces, the renal pelvis, or the ureter? The answer is the minor calyces. The cups around the papillae lie nearest the obstruction and change first. If the pressure continues, the pelvis and the major calyces dilate as well.

Question 7197. A constructed illustration: urine is forced back into the tissue at the margin of a minor calyx. Which structure normally seals that margin? The answer is the attachment of the minor calyx to the base of the papilla. Where it gives way, urine enters the medulla. The seal keeps the urine inside the cup.

Question 7198. Name two structures that lie within the renal sinus, spoken as a list. The answer is the renal pelvis and the calyces. The sinus also holds the renal vessels and a quantity of fat, and it opens at the hilum of the kidney. They lie behind the vessels. The fat around them fills the rest of the cavity.

Question 7199. Which of these explains why the number of minor calyces need not equal the number of renal pyramids: two papillae may fuse into one compound papilla, one pyramid may have two calyces, the calyces may drain into the cortex, or the pelvis may receive a papilla? The answer is that two papillae fuse into one compound papilla, which a single calyx receives. The major calyx unites several minor calyces.

Question 7200. Which of these structures opens into a minor calyx: the collecting duct, the loop of Henle, the proximal convoluted tubule, or the arcuate artery? The answer is the collecting duct, which ends at the papilla that the calyx cups. The other structures never open into the collecting system. The duct is the last part of the uriniferous tubule.

To summarize, the kidneys are paired retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall, each wrapped in a fibrous capsule with perirenal fat and renal fascia outside it, and each divided into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex contains the renal corpuscles, the convoluted tubules and the medullary rays, and it sends columns of cortical tissue between the pyramids, while the medulla is built of 8 to 18 renal pyramids whose apices form the papillae, where the collecting ducts open. The arcuate vessels mark the boundary between the two zones, the interlobular arteries supply the cortex, and the vasa recta serve the medulla, which has the poorer blood supply. The collecting system begins at the papilla with a minor calyx, minor calyces unite into a major calyx, the major calyces form the renal pelvis, and the pelvis leaves the hilum as the ureter. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 73 — Kidneys, Part Two

This chapter continues the study of the kidney and then follows the stream of urine out of it. It begins with the renal pelvis, the calyces and the hilum, the door through which the vessels and the collecting system leave the organ, and then follows each ureter from the kidney down to the bladder. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. Nothing has to be held in mind until an answer key, because the answer arrives in the same paragraph. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7201. Which structure collects urine from the major calyces and funnels it downward into the ureter: a renal pyramid, the renal pelvis, a renal column, or the renal capsule? The answer is the renal pelvis. It is the expanded upper end of the collecting system, and it lies inside the renal sinus. At its lower end it narrows and continues without a break as the ureter.

Question 7202. What is the name of the cavity inside the kidney that contains the pelvis, the calyces, the blood vessels and a pad of fat? The answer is the renal sinus. It opens onto the medial border of the kidney through the hilum, so the collecting system can leave the organ there. Its fat surrounds the other contents and separates them from one another.

Question 7203. What name is given to the vertical slit on the medial border of the kidney through which the vessels, the nerves and the pelvis pass? The answer is the renal hilum. It is the doorway into the renal sinus rather than a simple hole, and it transmits the renal vein, the renal artery and the renal pelvis in that order from front to back.

Question 7204. Within the hilum, which of the three main structures lies most anterior and which lies most posterior? The answer is the renal vein in front and the renal pelvis behind, with the renal artery between them. That order is worth memorizing, because a surgeon who approaches the pedicle from the front meets the vein first and the pelvis last.

Question 7205. A described coronal section of a kidney shows several cup-shaped chambers, each one wrapped around the tip of a medullary pyramid. What are those chambers, and what do they receive? The answer is the minor calyces, and each one receives urine from the papilla it cups. Several minor calyces then join to form a major calyx.

Question 7206. What is the name of the pointed tip of a renal pyramid, the part that projects into a minor calyx? The answer is the renal papilla. Its surface is pierced by many small openings, the area cribrosa, through which the collecting ducts deliver urine. From the calyx the urine has no way back into the medulla.

Question 7207. How many major calyces does one kidney usually have: one, two or three, five, or eight? The answer is usually two or three. A superior and an inferior major calyx are the rule, and a middle one is often present between them. They unite at the medial part of the sinus to form the renal pelvis.

Question 7208. A constructed illustration: a young person has intermittent aching pain in one loin, and a study shows a dilated renal pelvis with a normal ureter below it. Which structure is most likely crossing and obstructing the pelviureteric junction? The answer is an accessory renal artery running to the lower pole. Such an artery is a common variant, and it crosses the junction exactly where the pelvis narrows into the ureter.

Question 7209. True or false: at the hilum the renal vein lies in front of the renal artery. The answer is true. The vein is the most anterior of the three main structures, the artery lies in the middle, and the pelvis lies at the back. That is also the order in which a surgeon meets them.

Question 7210. Which structure leaves the kidney at the lower part of the hilum: the renal vein, the renal artery, the renal pelvis, or the renal capsule? The answer is the renal pelvis. It tapers at the lower end of the hilum and then continues as the ureter. The vein and the artery enter and leave higher up in the hilum.

Question 7211. What is the funnel-shaped part of the collecting system that lies inside the renal sinus and receives the major calyces? The answer is the renal pelvis. It is the last chamber within the kidney, and below it the tube continues as the ureter. Its shape varies, and both a broad and a narrow pelvis are normal.

Question 7212. Which division of the renal artery passes behind the renal pelvis, and why does that relation matter? The answer is the posterior division, which gives the posterior segmental artery. It curves behind the pelvis on its way to the posterior surface of the kidney. The pelvis therefore has to be moved aside before that artery can be seen.

Question 7213. A described specimen shows one calyx cupped over two separate papillae instead of one. What is that calyx called, and where is it usually found? The answer is a compound calyx, and it is most often found at the upper and the lower pole. There the pyramids fuse, so two or three papillae open into a single chamber.

Question 7214. What is the name of the band of cortical tissue that runs between two renal pyramids and carries vessels inward? The answer is a renal column. It is cortex that has been pushed between the pyramids, and it is continuous with the cortex at the surface. The vessels within it supply the neighboring medulla.

Question 7215. Which large vessel does the left renal vein cross on its way to the inferior vena cava: the aorta, the portal vein, the left gonadal vein, or the inferior mesenteric vein? The answer is the aorta. The left renal vein is longer than the right one because it has to cross the midline. The right renal vein is short and crosses nothing.

Question 7216. Which vein from the left side of the body joins the left renal vein instead of draining directly into the inferior vena cava? The answer is the left gonadal vein. The left suprarenal vein usually joins the left renal vein as well. On the right side both of those veins drain into the inferior vena cava on their own.

Question 7217. Name, as a list of two, the veins that most often join the left renal vein. The answer is the left suprarenal vein and the left gonadal vein. The left inferior phrenic vein often joins it too. One consequence is that the left renal vein carries blood not only from the kidney but also from the adrenal gland and the gonad.

Question 7218. Which statement about the two renal arteries is correct: the right artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava, the left artery is longer and passes behind the cava, the two are always the same length, or the right artery arises from the cava? The answer is that the right artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava.

Question 7219. A described contrast study of a kidney shows a branching tree of chambers filling from the papillae outward. Through which parts of that tree does the contrast pass, in order? The answer is the minor calyces, then the major calyces, then the renal pelvis. From the pelvis it runs on into the ureter. The whole tree lies inside the renal sinus.

Question 7220. A constructed illustration: a person has blood in the urine after a minor knock, and a study suggests that the left renal vein is compressed between the aorta and the artery to the small intestine. Which vein is involved, and what is its normal course? The answer is the left renal vein, which normally crosses in front of the aorta below that artery.

Question 7221. Which of these pairs belongs together: a minor calyx with a renal papilla, a major calyx with the ureter, the renal pelvis with the renal capsule, or a renal column with the bladder? The answer is a minor calyx with a renal papilla. The papilla projects into the calyx, and it is the pelvis, not the major calyx, that is continuous with the ureter.

Question 7222. Where may a normal renal pelvis lie: always inside the renal sinus, always outside the kidney, either inside the sinus or partly outside the hilum, or inside the peritoneal cavity? The answer is that it may lie either inside the sinus or partly outside the hilum. Both appearances are normal variants. A pelvis that projects outside the kidney is not in itself a disease.

Question 7223. What is the name of the opening on the medial border of the kidney that leads into the space holding the calyces? The answer is the hilum. It is a vertical slit rather than a round hole, and its edges are formed by the medial border of the organ. Behind it lies the renal sinus.

Question 7224. Inside the renal sinus, does the pelvis lie in front of or behind the branches of the renal vessels? The answer is behind them. The artery and its branches lie in front of the pelvis, and the veins lie in front of the artery. The pelvis therefore occupies the back of the sinus.

Question 7225. True or false: the substance of the kidney can be cut without pain, while stretching its fibrous coat is painful. The answer is true. The parenchyma itself carries no pain fibers, but the capsule and the pelvis do. That is why obstruction and swelling cause pain while a needle passed into the kidney does not.

Question 7226. A constructed illustration: a person has a dull, constant ache in one flank that never comes in waves, and a study shows a swollen kidney with a normal collecting system. Which covering of the kidney is being stretched? The answer is the fibrous capsule. It is richly supplied with pain fibers, and slow swelling stretches it, so the pain is steady rather than colicky.

Question 7227. A described frontal section of a kidney shows a fan of triangular stripes whose bases face the surface and whose tips point inward. What are those stripes, and where do their tips end? The answer is the renal pyramids, and their tips are the papillae, which open into the minor calyces. Cortex fills the spaces between the pyramids.

Question 7228. Into which structure does the renal pelvis empty: the bladder, the renal vein, the ureter, or the renal capsule? The answer is the ureter. The point at which the two meet is the pelviureteric junction, and it lies at the lower end of the hilum. From there the tube runs downward on the posterior abdominal wall.

Question 7229. At which vertebra does each renal artery arise from the abdominal aorta? The answer is the second lumbar vertebra. The two arteries leave the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery, and the right one then passes behind the inferior vena cava. Their level is a useful landmark for the whole kidney.

Question 7230. Which way does the renal hilum face in a person standing upright, and how does the upper pole compare with the lower pole? The answer is that the hilum faces anteromedially and the upper pole lies more medial than the lower pole. The long axis of the kidney therefore slopes downward and laterally. That tilt follows the lateral border of the psoas major.

Question 7231. Why does blocking one segmental artery of a kidney damage a wedge of tissue rather than the whole organ: because the segments share one artery, because the segmental arteries are end arteries, because the artery supplies both kidneys, or because the capsule takes over the supply? The answer is that the segmental arteries are end arteries, so only the segment they supply is lost.

Question 7232. Which artery, when it is present as an accessory vessel, commonly crosses the pelviureteric junction on its way to the lower pole of the kidney? The answer is an accessory lower polar renal artery. It arises from the aorta and reaches the lower pole below the hilum. It is one recognized cause of intermittent obstruction at the junction.

Question 7233. Name, in order from front to back, the three main structures that pass through the renal hilum. The answer is the renal vein, the renal artery and the renal pelvis. Lymphatic vessels and autonomic nerves travel with them, and the fat of the sinus fills the spaces between them. The same order holds inside the sinus.

Question 7234. A constructed illustration: a person has recurrent pain in one flank after drinking a large volume of fluid, and a study shows a normal ureter with a dilated pelvis and calyces above it. Which junction is failing, and what is the ordinary anatomy of that junction? The answer is the pelviureteric junction, where the funnel-shaped pelvis narrows into the ureter at the lower end of the hilum.

Question 7235. A described study shows a kidney whose calyces and pelvis are wider than usual and whose medulla is thinned outward. What has happened to the collecting system, and where does the cause lie? The answer is that the system is dilated, and the cause lies below it, at the pelviureteric junction or in the ureter. The parenchyma thins because the pressure behind the obstruction is passed back to it.

Question 7236. Which part of a renal pyramid projects into a minor calyx: the base, the apex, the column, or the capsule? The answer is the apex, which is also called the papilla. The base of the pyramid faces outward toward the cortex, and the cortex wraps around it. The apex points inward toward the sinus.

Question 7237. What fills the renal sinus around the pelvis, the calyces and the vessels, and becomes more abundant with age? The answer is fat. It cushions the collecting system and the vessels, and in older people it is plentiful enough to widen the apparent outline of the sinus on a scan. Fat is one of the normal contents of that space.

Question 7238. Which organ rests against the hilum of the left kidney, and which vessels run near it there? The answer is the tail of the pancreas, with the splenic vessels. The hilum of the left kidney therefore faces the pancreas, whereas the hilum of the right kidney faces the descending part of the duodenum. Both of those organs lie in front of the kidney.

Question 7239. To which group of lymph nodes does lymph from a kidney drain first: the inguinal nodes, the para-aortic nodes near the origin of the renal artery, the iliac nodes, or the nodes at the hilum of the lung? The answer is the para-aortic nodes, at about the level of the second lumbar vertebra. Lymph from the capsule drains to the same group.

Question 7240. True or false: the left kidney usually lies a little higher than the right. The answer is true. The right kidney is pushed downward by the large right lobe of the liver, which occupies the space above it. The difference is small, and it is a normal finding rather than a sign of disease.

Question 7241. A described cross section of the abdomen at the second lumbar vertebra shows the two kidneys, and in front of the left one a vein running across the midline. Which vein is it, and what does it cross? The answer is the left renal vein, which crosses in front of the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava. The right renal vein is short and crosses nothing.

Question 7242. How many minor calyces does one kidney usually contain: about 3, about 7 to 13, about 20, or exactly 30? The answer is about 7 to 13. Each minor calyx is cupped over one or more papillae, and they join in groups to form two or three major calyces.

Question 7243. What is the name of the collecting chamber formed where the major calyces unite, before the ureter begins? The answer is the renal pelvis. It lies within the renal sinus, and it leaves the kidney at the lower end of the hilum. Its wall is thin and can be seen clearly when it is filled with contrast.

Question 7244. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior division of the renal artery with the apical, upper, middle and lower segmental arteries, the posterior division with all four of those arteries, the renal vein with the segmental arteries, or the renal pelvis with the segmental arteries? The answer is the anterior division with those four segmental arteries. The posterior division gives the single posterior segmental artery.

Question 7245. A constructed illustration: a stone has lodged where the renal pelvis becomes the ureter, and the person has severe waves of pain in one flank. Which junction holds the stone, and where is that junction? The answer is the pelviureteric junction, at the lower end of the renal hilum, where the funnel of the pelvis narrows into the ureter. It is the first narrow point of the tube.

Question 7246. Why can a surgeon remove one segment of a kidney without destroying the rest of the organ: because all the segments share one artery, because each segment has its own end artery, because the capsule supplies the cortex, or because the pelvis feeds the medulla? The answer is that each segment has its own end artery. The plane between the anterior and the posterior territories has very few vessels.

Question 7247. A described dissection of the kidney shows the medial border opened, with a vein lying in front, an artery behind it, and a funnel-shaped tube behind both. Which structures are these, in that order? The answer is the renal vein, the renal artery and the renal pelvis, in the hilum from front to back.

Question 7248. Which muscle lies immediately behind the renal pelvis and the upper ureter as they leave the kidney? The answer is the psoas major. Both the pelvis and the ureter rest against its anterior surface, and the medial edge of that muscle marks their line of descent through the abdomen.

Question 7249. Which statement about the renal pelvis is correct: it is formed by the union of the major calyces, it is formed by the union of the minor calyces, it lies outside the renal fascia, or it drains into the renal vein? The answer is that it is formed by the union of the major calyces. It carries urine away, and it never carries blood.

Question 7250. A described coronal section of the abdomen passes through both kidneys and shows the pelvis of each one lying below and behind the vessels. In which plane was the kidney cut, and why does the pelvis appear behind the vessels? The answer is a coronal plane along the long axis of the kidney. The pelvis lies behind the vessels because it occupies the back of the renal sinus.

Question 7251. What name is given to each of the two muscular tubes that carry urine from a kidney to the bladder? The answer is the ureter. Each one begins at the pelviureteric junction and ends at the wall of the bladder, and each is about 25 to 30 centimeters long.

Question 7252. Which of these describes the course of a ureter: from the bladder up to the kidney, from the renal pelvis downward to the bladder, from the kidney to the urethra, or from the kidney to the colon? The answer is from the renal pelvis downward to the bladder. Urine travels in that direction only, helped by waves of contraction in the wall of the tube.

Question 7253. A described contrast study outlines a thin tube running down the posterior abdominal wall and crossing a muscle on each side. Which muscle does it cross, and on which surface does the tube lie? The answer is the psoas major, and the ureter lies against its anterior surface, behind the peritoneum. The tube follows the line of that muscle all the way to the pelvis.

Question 7254. In front of which vessel does each ureter cross the pelvic brim: the abdominal aorta, the common iliac artery at its bifurcation, the external iliac vein, or the inferior vena cava? The answer is the common iliac artery at its bifurcation. That crossing lies close to the sacroiliac joint, and it is one of the points at which the ureter is narrow.

Question 7255. Which vessels cross in front of the abdominal ureter on their way to the gonad? The answer is the gonadal vessels, the testicular artery and vein or the ovarian artery and vein. They cross the ureter obliquely, so the ureter lies behind them. That crossing is a useful landmark when the tube is being traced downward.

Question 7256. A described study shows both ureters outlined, each one lying against a triangular muscle behind the peritoneum and then turning into the pelvis. Where does each tube change direction, and what does it cross at that point? The answer is at the pelvic brim, where it crosses the common iliac artery at its bifurcation.

Question 7257. A constructed illustration: a person has severe waves of pain that begin in one loin and travel down to the groin, and a study shows a small stone at the pelvic brim. Which structure holds the stone, and why does the pain travel downward? The answer is the ureter, whose pain is referred along the segments that supply it, from the upper lumbar region toward the groin.

Question 7258. Apart from the gonadal vessels, which vessels cross the right ureter in front? The answer is the right colic and ileocolic vessels. On the left side the corresponding crossing is made by the left colic vessels. The ureter itself passes behind all of them, and it also passes behind the descending part of the duodenum on the right.

Question 7259. In the female pelvis, which artery crosses the ureter and lies above it: the internal pudendal artery, the uterine artery, the obturator artery, or the superior gluteal artery? The answer is the uterine artery. It runs medially toward the uterus and crosses over the ureter, which passes beneath it on its way to the bladder.

Question 7260. True or false: the ureter lies behind the peritoneum along its whole abdominal course. The answer is true. It is a retroperitoneal structure, so it stays outside the peritoneal cavity as it runs down to the pelvic brim. It keeps that position in the pelvis as well.

Question 7261. At which point is the lumen of the ureter narrowest: at the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, where it passes through the wall of the bladder, or halfway down the abdomen? The answer is where it passes through the wall of the bladder. Stones lodge most often there, and also at the two narrow points above it.

Question 7262. What is the name of the short part of the ureter that runs obliquely through the wall of the bladder? The answer is the intramural part. It is about 2 centimeters long, and its oblique course is what keeps urine from running back up the tube. It is the narrowest part of the whole ureter.

Question 7263. Inside the pelvis, does the ureter lie in front of or behind the internal iliac artery, and where does it turn toward the bladder? The answer is that it lies in front of the internal iliac artery. It runs down the lateral wall of the pelvis and turns forward and medially near the ischial spine to reach the bladder.

Question 7264. A constructed illustration: during an operation to remove the uterus, the surgeon must identify a tube running close to the cervix.
