Which structure is it, and what is its relation to the uterine artery there? The answer is the ureter, which passes beneath the uterine artery close to the lateral part of the cervix.

Question 7265. A described dissection of the female pelvis shows an artery running medially toward the uterus and a tube passing below it on its way to the bladder. Which two structures are shown, and which one lies higher? The answer is the uterine artery and the ureter, with the artery lying higher. The tube passes beneath the artery and then runs forward to the bladder.

Question 7266. In the male pelvis, which structure crosses the ureter from its lateral to its medial side: the ductus deferens, the obturator nerve, the middle rectal artery, or the inferior epigastric artery? The answer is the ductus deferens. It crosses above the ureter, and the ureter then passes beneath it before it enters the bladder.

Question 7267. What is the name of the outermost coat of the ureter, the layer that carries its blood vessels and allows the tube to be freed at operation? The answer is the adventitia. Inside it lie the muscular coat and the mucous membrane, and the vessels run along the tube within the adventitia.

Question 7268. Which of these pairs belongs together: the abdominal ureter with the psoas major, the pelvic ureter with the diaphragm, the pelviureteric junction with the bladder, or the intramural ureter with the kidney? The answer is the abdominal ureter with the psoas major. The pelvic ureter runs against the lateral wall of the pelvis instead.

Question 7269. Name, in order from above downward, the three points at which the ureter is narrow. The answer is the pelviureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim, and the point at which the tube enters the wall of the bladder. These are the places where a stone is most likely to stop.

Question 7270. By what means is urine carried along the ureter: by gravity alone, by waves of contraction of its muscular wall, by suction from the bladder, or by the movement of the diaphragm? The answer is waves of contraction of its muscular wall. Gravity helps, but the tube itself propels the urine, and it does so whether the person is standing or lying down.

Question 7271. True or false: the wave of contraction that carries urine down the ureter continues even after every nerve to the tube has been cut. The answer is true. The muscle of the ureter starts its own contraction, so the tube can still propel urine after it has been separated from its nerve supply.

Question 7272. What is the name of the ridge raised inside the bladder by the oblique course of the ureter through its wall? The answer is the ureteric fold. It runs from the ureteric orifice toward the internal urethral orifice at the neck of the bladder. It is one of the landmarks of the inside of the bladder.

Question 7273. Which nerves carry the pain of a stone in the ureter: fibers from the upper abdomen, sympathetic fibers from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments, the vagus nerve, or the phrenic nerve? The answer is the sympathetic fibers from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments, with the sacral parasympathetic fibers. Pain is therefore felt in the loin and the groin rather than deep in the chest.

Question 7274. Which part of the gut lies in front of the right ureter near the hilum of the kidney? The answer is the descending part of the duodenum. The ureter passes behind it on the right side. Further down, the right ureter also lies behind the root of the mesentery and the cecum.

Question 7275. A described plain radiograph of the abdomen shows two long soft-tissue shadows running from the region of the kidneys downward and medially toward the pelvis. Which structures are they, and what line do they follow? The answer is the ureters, and their line follows the lateral edge of the psoas major on each side.

Question 7276. A constructed illustration: a person has pain in one flank that comes in waves and spreads to the groin, and the urine contains blood. Which structure is most likely partly blocked, and how does its pain behave? The answer is the ureter. The pain is colicky rather than steady, and it does not settle with rest or with a change of position.

Question 7277. Which statement about the blood supply of the ureter is correct: it comes from a single artery, it comes from several arteries that join along its length, it comes only from the renal artery, or it has no supply of its own? The answer is that it comes from several arteries that join along its length. Branches of the renal, gonadal, aortic, iliac and vesical arteries all reach it.

Question 7278. Which artery of the pelvis sends a branch that climbs the ureter and helps to keep its lower part alive after the vessels above have been divided? The answer is the uterine artery in the female, with the corresponding vesical branches in the male. Those branches run upward in the adventitia and join the ones from above.

Question 7279. A described section through the base of the bladder shows a tube running obliquely through the muscular wall for about 2 centimeters before it opens inside. What does that arrangement achieve? The answer is that it makes a valve. When the bladder contracts and the pressure inside it rises, the oblique passage is squeezed shut, so urine cannot run back up the tube.

Question 7280. A constructed illustration: a child has an infection of the urinary tract, and a study shows urine running back from the bladder into one ureter. Which part of the ureter is failing to close, and what is its usual length? The answer is the intramural part, whose oblique course is normally about 2 centimeters long. A short intramural segment is a recognized cause of such backflow.

Question 7281. Which statement about the opening of the ureter is correct: it lies in the trigone of the bladder, it lies in the urethra, it lies at the apex of the bladder, or it lies in the rectum? The answer is that it lies in the trigone. The two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice mark the corners of that smooth triangular area.

Question 7282. A described view of the inside of the bladder shows a smooth triangular area with two slit-like openings above and a third opening below. What is that area, and what forms its upper corners? The answer is the trigone, and its upper corners are the two ureteric orifices. The lower corner is the internal urethral orifice.

Question 7283. Which of these pairs belongs together: the three narrow points of the ureter with the sites where stones lodge, the three narrow points with the sites of urine formation, the trigone with the kidney, or the renal pelvis with the urethra? The answer is the three narrow points with the sites where stones lodge. They are the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the bladder wall.

Question 7284. In the male pelvis, which structures lie close to the lower ureter as it approaches the bladder? The answer is the ductus deferens, which crosses above it, and the seminal vesicle, which lies near it. The ureter then runs forward and pierces the wall of the bladder.

Question 7285. Where does each ureter open: into the renal pelvis, into the bladder, into the urethra, or into the colon? The answer is into the bladder. It opens at the ureteric orifice on the trigone, having passed obliquely through the muscular wall of the bladder. Nothing but urine passes through it.

Question 7286. What is the name of the junction at which the renal pelvis becomes the ureter? The answer is the pelviureteric junction. It lies at the lower end of the renal hilum, and it is the first of the three narrow points of the ureter. Its narrowing is part of normal anatomy.

Question 7287. A described contrast study shows a column of urine that stops abruptly in the lower part of one ureter, with a small rounded defect at the point where it stops. What does the defect represent, and why did it stop there? The answer is a stone lodged at one of the narrow points. The narrowest point of the tube is where it passes through the wall of the bladder.

Question 7288. What happens to the intramural part of the ureter when the bladder fills and contracts: it opens wider, it is compressed and closes, it is pulled out of the bladder wall, or it grows longer? The answer is that it is compressed and closes. The pressure of the full bladder squeezes the oblique passage shut, and that is what stops urine from running back up the tube.

Question 7289. A constructed illustration: a person has pain in one loin that comes in waves, and a study shows a stone at the pelviureteric junction. Which structure is obstructed, and what lies immediately above the stone? The answer is the ureter at its first narrow point, with the renal pelvis immediately above it.

Question 7290. How long is the part of the ureter that runs through the wall of the bladder: about half a centimeter, about 2 centimeters, about 6 centimeters, or about 12 centimeters? The answer is about 2 centimeters. That oblique passage acts as a valve, and it is the narrowest part of the whole tube.

Question 7291. In the female pelvis, which structure lies immediately in front of the lower ureter as the ureter approaches the bladder? The answer is the lateral part of the vagina, with the cervix above and medial to the tube. The ureter passes above the lateral vaginal fornix, and that relation is why it is at risk during operations on the pelvis.

Question 7292. To which region is pain from the lower end of the ureter usually referred: the back of the neck, the groin and the external genitalia on the same side, the sole of the foot, or the top of the shoulder? The answer is the groin and the external genitalia on the same side. Pain from the upper ureter is felt in the loin instead.

Question 7293. What name is given to the opening of the ureter into the bladder? The answer is the ureteric orifice. There are two of them, one on each side of the trigone, and each is a slit rather than a round hole. Urine enters the bladder through them.

Question 7294. Why is the pain of a stone in the ureter described as colic rather than as a steady ache: because the stone cuts the wall, because the muscular wall contracts in waves against the obstruction, because the peritoneum becomes inflamed, or because the kidney itself is painless? The answer is that the muscular wall contracts in waves against the obstruction. Each wave brings a fresh surge of pain.

Question 7295. A described study of a doubled collecting system on one side shows two ureters, one opening low and medially and dilated above, the other opening higher and laterally and showing backflow. Which ureter drains the upper part of the kidney? The answer is the one that opens low and medially. In a complete duplication the upper part drains through the lower opening.

Question 7296. Which of these pairs belongs together: a ureter that opens low and medially with the upper part of a duplicated kidney, one that opens low and medially with the lower part, one that opens high and laterally with the upper part, or both with the same part? The answer is the low and medial opening with the upper part of the kidney. The two buds cross as they descend.

Question 7297. Why does one kidney have two ureters in a complete duplication: because the metanephric tissue divides late, because the ureteric bud divides before it reaches the metanephric tissue, because the wall of the bladder grows too far upward, or because the renal pelvis lies outside the hilum? The answer is that the ureteric bud divides before it reaches the metanephric tissue, so two buds grow into it.

Question 7298. During an operation on the back of the abdomen, how is the ureter usually identified: by its pulsation, by its adhesion to the peritoneum, by its yellow color, or by the fact that it lies inside the peritoneal cavity? The answer is by its adhesion to the peritoneum. As the peritoneum is peeled back, the ureter comes with it, and its fine network of vessels marks it out.

Question 7299. Why is the ureter supplied by branches of many different arteries: because it has no anastomoses in its wall, because it develops from the mesonephric duct and takes branches from the vessels it passes, because it develops from the peritoneum, or because no other artery reaches it? The answer is that it develops from the mesonephric duct and takes branches from the vessels it passes. Those branches join along its length.

Question 7300. What is the name of the tube that continues the renal pelvis downward and opens into the bladder? The answer is the ureter. It is about 25 to 30 centimeters long, it lies behind the peritoneum, and it is narrowest where it passes through the wall of the bladder.

To summarize, the renal pelvis is formed by the union of two or three major calyces, fed by minor calyces cupped over the renal papillae, and the whole collecting system lies within the fat-filled renal sinus that opens at the hilum. At the hilum the renal vein lies most anterior, the renal artery in the middle and the renal pelvis most posterior, and the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta and usually receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins. Each ureter runs from the pelviureteric junction down the posterior abdominal wall on the psoas major, behind the peritoneum, crosses the pelvic brim in front of the common iliac artery at its bifurcation, and enters the bladder obliquely for about 2 centimeters. The three narrow points are the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the bladder wall, and they are the places where stones lodge. The intramural part acts as a valve, the uterine artery crosses the tube in the female and the ductus deferens in the male, and the muscle of the tube drives urine onward by its own waves. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 74 — Urinary Bladder

This chapter follows the urine from the kidney to the bladder. It begins with the ureter, the narrow tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder, and then turns to the urinary bladder itself: its shape when empty and when full, the surfaces and relations of each part, the trigone, the detrusor, the two sphincters, the nerve supply, the blood supply and the way the organ develops. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately in the words The answer is, and then explains why that answer is right. Nothing has to be held in mind, and no answer key has to be waited for. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7301. Which muscular tube carries urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder? The answer is the ureter. Each kidney sends one ureter down to the bladder, where it opens at the upper corner of the trigone. The tube lies behind the peritoneum along its whole abdominal course.

Question 7302. About how long is the adult ureter: 5 to 8 centimeters, 12 to 15 centimeters, 25 to 30 centimeters, or 40 to 45 centimeters? The answer is 25 to 30 centimeters. It begins at the renal pelvis in the upper abdomen and ends at the bladder in the pelvis. The right ureter is a little shorter than the left because the right kidney sits lower.

Question 7303. In the abdomen, the ureter descends immediately anterior to which muscle, which forms the bed on which it lies? The answer is the psoas major. The tube runs down the front of that muscle with the peritoneum in front of it. Because the muscle slopes forward as it descends, the ureter also passes forward on its way to the pelvis.

Question 7304. Which is the narrowest point of the ureter, where a stone may stick and cause colic? The answer is the ureterovesical junction, where the tube passes through the wall of the bladder. The other two narrow points are the ureteropelvic junction and the crossing of the pelvic brim. A stone may lodge at any of the three.

Question 7305. A described radiograph taken after contrast shows two thin curved tubes running from the kidneys to the pelvis. Which structures are shown, and what is the examination called? The answer is the ureters, shown on an excretory urogram. The contrast outlines the collecting system of each kidney and the tube below it. The tubes taper as they approach the bladder.

Question 7306. A constructed illustration: a person has waves of severe pain in the loin that later move toward the groin. Where is the stone most likely lodged at the start? The answer is the ureteropelvic junction. It is the first of the three narrow points of the ureter. As the stone travels down, the pain travels with it.

Question 7307. At the pelvic brim, the ureter crosses in front of which large artery? The answer is the common iliac artery, where it divides. The tube passes over the bifurcation and then continues downward in front of the external iliac artery. This crossing is one of the three narrow points of the ureter.

Question 7308. In the female pelvis, which artery crosses above and in front of the ureter on its way to the uterus? The answer is the uterine artery. The ureter passes below the artery and then runs forward to the bladder, about 2 centimeters lateral to the cervix. Surgeons describe the arrangement as water running under a bridge.

Question 7309. In the male pelvis, which structure crosses from lateral to medial above the ureter before the ureter reaches the bladder: the ductus deferens, the obturator nerve, the middle rectal artery, or the internal pudendal artery? The answer is the ductus deferens. It crosses above and medial to the ureter as it runs to the prostate. The ureter continues below it into the bladder.

Question 7310. True or false: the ureter lies behind the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. The answer is true. It descends on the psoas major with peritoneum covering only its front. For that reason a surgeon reaches the tube from the front by pushing the peritoneum aside.

Question 7311. Name three arteries that supply the ureter, spoken as a list. The answer is the renal artery, the gonadal artery and the superior vesical artery. The abdominal aorta and the iliac arteries also send small branches to it. The supply is segmental, so each branch feeds only part of the tube.

Question 7312. From which embryonic structure does the ureter develop, and from what does that structure itself arise? The answer is the ureteric bud, which grows out of the mesonephric duct. The bud pushes into the metanephric tissue and induces the kidney to form. Its upper end widens into the renal pelvis and its stalk becomes the ureter.

Question 7313. Which part of the bladder develops from the mesonephric duct, so that its lining differs from the rest: the apex, the trigone, the superior surface, or the urachus? The answer is the trigone. The remaining lining of the bladder comes from the endoderm of the urogenital sinus. The trigone therefore has a mesodermal origin, which is one reason its mucosa is smooth and fixed.

Question 7314. On the right side, which part of the bowel crosses in front of the ureter in the upper abdomen? The answer is the descending part of the duodenum. The right ureter also passes behind the root of the mesentery and is crossed by the right colic vessels. On the left side the sigmoid colon and its mesentery cross the ureter lower down.

Question 7315. A constructed illustration: a person with a stone in the ureter feels pain that begins in the loin and travels to the groin. Why does it travel in that direction? The answer is that the pain follows the nerve supply of the ureter. Its sensory fibers reach the spinal cord between the eleventh thoracic and the second lumbar segments.

Question 7316. A described section of the ureter wall shows a stretchy lining of several cell layers, a middle coat of smooth muscle and an outer fibrous coat. Which lining is described, and how is the muscle arranged? The answer is transitional epithelium over an inner longitudinal and an outer circular layer. In the lower third a third, outermost longitudinal layer appears.

Question 7317. Why does the lower end of the ureter pass obliquely through the wall of the bladder instead of opening straight into it? The answer is that the oblique tunnel is compressed when the bladder contracts. The tube runs about 2 centimeters within the muscle before it opens. Rising pressure in the bladder therefore closes the tunnel and urine cannot pass back up.

Question 7318. In an empty bladder the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice mark the corners of a triangle. How is that triangle placed, and which corner is lowest? The answer is that it lies on the base of the bladder, with the internal urethral orifice at the lowest corner. The two ureteric orifices lie above and behind the internal opening.

Question 7319. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ureteropelvic junction with the renal pelvis, the ureterovesical junction with the pelvic brim, or the intramural part with the psoas major? The answer is the ureteropelvic junction with the renal pelvis. The intramural part lies within the wall of the bladder and the pelvic part runs from the brim to the bladder.

Question 7320. What name is given to the short segment of the ureter that lies inside the wall of the bladder, and about how long is it? The answer is the intramural part, about 2 centimeters long. It runs obliquely through the muscle of the bladder wall. Its slit-like opening at the inner end is the ureteric orifice.

Question 7321. A constructed illustration: during a pelvic operation in a woman the ureter is injured about 2 centimeters from the cervix. Which named vessel marks that dangerous point? The answer is the uterine artery where it crosses the ureter. The ureter passes below the artery as it runs to the uterus.

Question 7322. Which statement about the blood supply of the ureter is correct: one artery supplies the whole tube, the supply is segmental, only the renal artery supplies it, or the supply comes only from below? The answer is that the supply is segmental. Branches arrive from the renal artery above and from the iliac and vesical arteries below.

Question 7323. A described computed tomography scan shows a small rounded dot on the psoas major in front of a lumbar vertebra. Which structure is shown, and what crosses in front of it? The answer is the ureter, with the gonadal vessels in front. The tube appears as a dot because the section is transverse.

Question 7324. In both sexes, which vessels cross the front of the ureter about halfway down its course on the psoas major? The answer is the gonadal vessels, the testicular vessels in the male and the ovarian vessels in the female. They cross the ureter obliquely as they run down toward the pelvis. Below that crossing the ureter continues to the pelvic brim.

Question 7325. A child has a kidney drained by two collecting systems. Which statement explains the double ureter: the ureteric bud divided early, the mesonephric duct failed to form, or the urogenital sinus grew too far? The answer is that the ureteric bud divided early. One bud drains the upper part of the kidney and the other the lower part.

Question 7326. When the urinary bladder is empty, in which part of the body does it lie? The answer is the pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis. It rests on the pelvic floor and lies below the peritoneum. In that state it cannot be felt through the abdominal wall.

Question 7327. About how much urine does a normal adult bladder hold when it is comfortably full: 100 to 150 milliliters, 300 to 500 milliliters, 1,000 to 1,200 milliliters, or 1,500 to 2,000 milliliters? The answer is 300 to 500 milliliters. The first desire to void comes much earlier, at about 150 to 250 milliliters. These figures describe ordinary anatomy.

Question 7328. In the male, which structures lie between the base of the bladder and the rectum? The answer is the seminal vesicles and the ampullae of the ductus deferens. They lie against the lower part of the base. Above them the peritoneum dips down between the bladder and the rectum to form the rectovesical pouch.

Question 7329. A described ultrasound scan shows a rounded black space behind the pubic symphysis with bright echoes below it. What is the black space, and why does it look black? The answer is a full bladder, which looks black because urine does not reflect sound. The bright echoes come from the pelvic floor. A full bladder is a window for the organs behind it.

Question 7330. A constructed illustration: a person cannot pass urine and has a tender swelling rising above the pubic symphysis. Which organ is distended, and why does it rise? The answer is the urinary bladder, which rises into the abdomen as it fills. The peritoneum is pushed upward in front of it. The swelling is dull to percussion because it holds fluid.

Question 7331. The apex of the bladder is joined to the umbilicus by which fibrous remnant? The answer is the median umbilical ligament. It is the remains of the urachus, the channel that once joined the bladder to the allantois. It runs upward in the midline behind the front wall of the abdomen.

Question 7332. Which of these describes the trigone of the bladder: a raised fold at the apex, a smooth triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice, the fold of peritoneum over the fundus, or the ring of muscle at the bladder neck? The answer is the smooth triangle between the openings. Its mucosa is bound to the muscle and stays smooth.

Question 7333. In the female, which structure lies immediately behind the base of the bladder? The answer is the vagina, with the cervix above it. The peritoneum passes from the uterus onto the bladder and forms the vesicouterine pouch between the two organs. The bladder lies in front of the vagina and below the uterus.

Question 7334. True or false: when it is empty, the bladder lies entirely within the pelvis. The answer is true. The empty bladder sits behind the pubic symphysis and below the pelvic peritoneum. It rises into the abdomen only when it fills, and the peritoneum is carried up with it.

Question 7335. Which of these pairs belongs together: the apex with the pubic symphysis, the base with the abdominal wall, the superior surface with the pelvic floor, or the inferolateral surface with the umbilicus? The answer is the apex with the pubic symphysis. The apex points forward and upward toward that bone. The inferolateral surfaces rest on the pelvic floor.

Question 7336. Which muscle forms the main wall of the bladder and expels urine from it? The answer is the detrusor muscle. Its fibers are smooth and run in interlacing bundles in several directions. When it contracts the bladder empties and the internal urethral orifice opens.

Question 7337. In the male, which structure prevents semen from passing backward into the bladder during ejaculation: the external urethral sphincter, the internal urethral sphincter, the bulbospongiosus muscle, or the levator ani? The answer is the internal urethral sphincter, a thickening of smooth muscle at the bladder neck. It closes while the bladder wall relaxes.

Question 7338. A constructed illustration: a person leaks a little urine when coughing. Which muscle group has most likely become weak, and where does it lie? The answer is the pelvic floor, especially the levator ani. Those muscles support the bladder and the urethra from below. The external urethral sphincter is part of the same supporting mechanism.

Question 7339. A described midline magnetic resonance image of a male pelvis shows the bladder in front, the rectum behind and a rounded gland below the bladder neck. Which section is this, and what is the gland? The answer is a sagittal section, and the gland is the prostate. The base of the bladder rests on the prostate and the urethra leaves through it.

Question 7340. What is the name of the peritoneal pouch between the bladder and the rectum in the male, and why does it matter? The answer is the rectovesical pouch. When a person lies on the back it is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity. Fluid that escapes into the abdomen therefore collects there and can be felt through the front wall of the rectum.

Question 7341. Which artery is the main supply of the upper part of the bladder? The answer is the superior vesical artery. It arises from the umbilical artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery. The inferior vesical artery supplies the lower part and the base in the male.

Question 7342. Where does blood from the bladder drain: into the portal vein, into the internal iliac veins through the vesical plexus, or into the femoral veins? The answer is into the internal iliac veins through the vesical plexus. The plexus lies in the loose tissue beside the bladder and the prostate. It connects with the prostatic and rectal veins.

Question 7343. Name the three coats of the wall of the bladder, spoken as a list from within outward. The answer is the mucosa, the muscular coat and the adventitia. The mucosa carries transitional epithelium and the muscular coat is the detrusor. The adventitia is the loose fibrous coat that binds the bladder to the structures around it.

Question 7344. A constructed illustration: a person has painless blood in the urine and a growth is found on the inner surface of the bladder. From which tissue does such a growth most often arise? The answer is the transitional epithelium of the mucosa. Growths of this lining are the most common tumors of the urinary tract. The treatment belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7345. A described transverse section is taken through the pelvis at the level of the hip joints. In what order do the pelvic organs lie from front to back in the male? The answer is the bladder, then the seminal vesicles, then the rectum. The bladder lies behind the pubic bones in the midline. The rectum lies against the sacrum and the coccyx behind.

Question 7346. Which nerves carry the parasympathetic fibers that empty the bladder: the hypogastric nerves, the pelvic splanchnic nerves, the pudendal nerve, or the obturator nerve? The answer is the pelvic splanchnic nerves, which come from the second to the fourth sacral segments. They make the detrusor contract and relax the internal urethral sphincter. The hypogastric nerves do the opposite.

Question 7347. Which nerve supplies the external urethral sphincter, the voluntary muscle that holds urine back? The answer is the pudendal nerve. Its branches run to the muscles of the deep perineal pouch, where the sphincter lies. Because that muscle is skeletal, it can be tightened at will.

Question 7348. True or false: the internal urethral sphincter is under voluntary control. The answer is false. It is made of smooth muscle and is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. The voluntary muscle at the outlet is the external urethral sphincter, which lies further down in the deep perineal pouch.

Question 7349. Which of these pairs belongs together: the pelvic splanchnic nerves with contraction of the detrusor, the hypogastric nerves with contraction of the detrusor, the pudendal nerve with relaxation of the detrusor, or the sympathetic fibers with opening of the internal sphincter? The answer is the pelvic splanchnic nerves with contraction of the detrusor. The hypogastric nerves relax the detrusor and close the internal sphincter.

Question 7350. A constructed illustration: a person with an injury of the spinal cord above the sacral segments has no voluntary control of the bladder, yet it still empties reflexly. Which part of the reflex arc remains intact? The answer is the sacral spinal cord with the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Only the path from the brain to that center is interrupted.

Question 7351. A described scan after contrast shows two thin tubes entering the back of a rounded organ in the pelvis at its upper corners. Which organ is shown, and where do the tubes open? The answer is the bladder, with the ureters opening at the upper corners of the trigone. Those corners are the two ureteric orifices.

Question 7352. Which two openings mark the upper corners of the trigone of the bladder, and which opening marks its lowest corner? The answer is the two ureteric orifices above and the internal urethral orifice below. The triangle between the three is smooth and keeps the same size whatever the bladder is doing. Each ureteric orifice is a slit rather than a round hole.

Question 7353. From which embryonic tube does the median umbilical ligament, the remnant that runs from the bladder to the umbilicus, derive? The answer is the urachus, the lower end of the allantois. In the fetus it drains the bladder into the umbilical cord. After birth it closes and becomes a solid fibrous cord.

Question 7354. Why does the trigone of the bladder have a different origin from the rest of the organ: its lining comes from the mesonephric ducts, from the allantois, from the rectum, or from the peritoneum? The answer is that its lining comes from the mesonephric ducts. The lower ends of the ducts are drawn into the growing bladder and form the trigone.

Question 7355. A constructed illustration: an older man cannot pass urine and the bladder is distended. Which gland has enlarged: the prostate, the seminal vesicle, the bulbourethral gland, or the levator ani? The answer is the prostate, which surrounds the first part of the urethra below the bladder. As it enlarges it narrows that channel. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7356. Name two structures that help to hold the bladder in position, spoken as a list. The answer is the pubovesical ligaments and the pelvic floor formed by the levator ani. The ligaments run from the pubic bones to the neck of the bladder. The pelvic floor carries the organ from below and resists its descent.

Question 7357. At about what volume of urine does a person first feel the desire to empty the bladder: 50 milliliters, 150 to 250 milliliters, 400 to 500 milliliters, or 900 milliliters? The answer is 150 to 250 milliliters. At that point the bladder holds far less than its full capacity. The sensation comes from stretch receptors in the wall of the bladder.

Question 7358. In the male bladder, what is the name of the small elevation seen just behind the internal urethral orifice, and what produces it? The answer is the uvula vesicae, produced by the median lobe of the prostate. It lies below the trigone at the bladder neck. It can lift the lower edge of the trigone and interfere with complete emptying.

Question 7359. A described view through a cystoscope shows a smooth pale triangle with an opening at each corner. Which region is viewed, and what are the openings? The answer is the trigone, with the two ureteric orifices above and the internal urethral orifice below. Its mucosa is smooth because it is fixed to the muscle.

Question 7360. Which muscles form the floor and the lateral wall on which the bladder rests? The answer is the levator ani and the obturator internus. The levator ani forms the pelvic floor under the bladder. The obturator internus lies against the lateral wall of the pelvis, separated from the organ by fascia and veins.

Question 7361. A constructed illustration: a blow to the lower abdomen ruptures a full bladder and urine appears in the peritoneal cavity. Where was the tear, and why did urine reach that space? The answer is the superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum. A full bladder rises into the abdomen and that part of its wall is stretched thin. The urine therefore escapes into the peritoneal cavity.

Question 7362. To which groups of lymph nodes does lymph from the bladder drain: the superficial inguinal nodes, the internal and external iliac nodes, the lateral aortic nodes only, or the deep inguinal nodes? The answer is the internal and external iliac nodes. Some vessels also reach the lateral aortic nodes. Lymph from the upper part of the bladder may follow the ureter upward to those nodes.

Question 7363. Which of these statements is correct: the detrusor expels urine, the trigone stores urine, the urachus forms the pelvic floor, or the uvula vesicae lies at the apex? The answer is that the detrusor expels urine. The trigone is a fixed smooth area and not a store. The urachus is the fibrous remnant that runs from the bladder to the umbilicus.

Question 7364. True or false: the bladder receives no sympathetic nerve fibers. The answer is false. Sympathetic fibers reach it through the hypogastric plexus from the upper lumbar segments. They relax the detrusor and close the internal urethral sphincter. The parasympathetic fibers from the sacral segments do the opposite.

Question 7365. In the female, the peritoneum runs from the uterus onto the bladder and forms which pouch between the two organs? The answer is the vesicouterine pouch. It is a shallow pouch that lies above the bladder and in front of the uterus. The corresponding pouch in the male is the deeper rectovesical pouch behind the bladder.

Question 7366. Which statement about the position of the bladder is correct: it never changes position, it lies in the abdomen when empty, or it rises into the abdomen as it fills? The answer is that it rises into the abdomen as it fills. The peritoneum is pushed upward ahead of it. When full its upper part can be reached above the pubic symphysis.

Question 7367. A constructed illustration: a person has burning on passing urine, goes often and has tenderness above the pubic symphysis. Which organ is inflamed, and which of its surfaces lies against the front of the abdomen when it is full? The answer is the bladder, and its superior surface. Inflammation makes the wall irritable, so even a little urine provokes the desire to void.

Question 7368. A described transverse ultrasound scan shows a rounded black area in the midline of a full bladder, with two thin tubes entering at the back corners. What shape is the bladder here, and why is this view useful? The answer is an ovoid shape, and the full bladder acts as a window for scanning the organs behind it. The tubes are the ureters approaching the trigone.

Question 7369. What lies immediately in front of the empty bladder, and what occupies the space between? The answer is the pubic symphysis, with the retropubic space between the two. That space holds loose fat and the vesical venous plexus. It is the plane through which the bladder is reached from the front, above the pubic bone.

Question 7370. What is the name of the space between the pubic symphysis and the bladder, and what does it contain? The answer is the retropubic space. It contains loose fatty tissue and the veins of the vesical plexus. Because the tissue there is loose, the space can hold a large collection of blood after a fracture of the pelvis.

Question 7371. When the bladder is full, why can a needle be passed into it just above the pubic symphysis: the peritoneum is pushed up out of the way, the pelvis has no peritoneum, or the rectum lies in front? The answer is that the peritoneum is pushed up out of the way. In the empty bladder that fold lies close above the symphysis.

Question 7372. A constructed illustration: after a long labor a woman cannot hold her urine, and a passage is found between the bladder and the vagina. Which two walls were pressed together? The answer is the base of the bladder and the front wall of the vagina. They lay between the pubis in front and the head of the baby behind.

Question 7373. Which of these pairs belongs together: the trigone with a smooth fixed mucosa, the detrusor with a transitional lining, or the urachus with the bladder neck? The answer is the trigone with a smooth fixed mucosa. The detrusor is muscle and not a lining. The urachus is the fibrous remnant that runs from the bladder to the umbilicus.

Question 7374. Which surface of the bladder is covered by peritoneum? The answer is the superior surface. The peritoneum passes over it and then continues onto the anterior abdominal wall or, in the female, onto the uterus. The base and the inferolateral surfaces lie below the peritoneum and are covered only by fascia.

Question 7375. Why is the mucosa of the trigone always smooth while the rest is folded when the bladder is empty: it has no submucosa, it has no epithelium, it is covered by peritoneum, or it has no blood supply? The answer is that it has no submucosa and is fixed to the muscle. The rest of the mucosa has a loose submucosa and gathers into folds.

Question 7376. A described magnetic resonance image of a male pelvis shows the base of the bladder resting on a rounded gland, with a tube passing through the gland from the bladder. Which gland and which tube are shown? The answer is the prostate and the urethra. The ejaculatory ducts pass through the gland behind that tube.

Question 7377. In the male, which two ducts pass through the prostate and open into the urethra just below the neck of the bladder? The answer is the two ejaculatory ducts. Each is formed by the union of the ductus deferens with the duct of the seminal vesicle. They open on a small elevation in the urethra called the seminal colliculus.

Question 7378. True or false: the bladder lies below the peritoneum and outside the peritoneal cavity. The answer is true. Only its superior surface is covered by peritoneum, and that covering is reflected off onto the wall of the abdomen. The organ is therefore described as extraperitoneal rather than intraperitoneal.

Question 7379. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the lower abdomen a person has blood in the urine and cannot pass urine, and the bladder is full. Which structure has most likely been torn: the bladder wall, the ureter, the rectum, or the psoas major? The answer is the bladder wall. A full, tense bladder is torn more easily than an empty one, and the blood then appears in the urine.

Question 7380. Which point of the bladder is lowest when a person stands, and which opening lies there? The answer is the neck of the bladder, where the internal urethral orifice opens. It is the lowest corner of the trigone. Urine therefore collects at the neck and the last of it leaves the bladder there.

Question 7381. In the female, which additional artery commonly supplies the lower part of the bladder: the ovarian artery, the vaginal artery, the superior gluteal artery, or the internal pudendal artery? The answer is the vaginal artery. It is a branch of the internal iliac artery and lies beside the vagina. The superior and inferior vesical arteries still supply most of the organ.

Question 7382. A described sagittal section of a male pelvis shows the bladder as a triangle behind the pubis, with one surface facing the rectum and another facing the abdominal wall above. Which surfaces are these? The answer is the base, which faces backward and downward toward the rectum, and the superior surface, which faces upward and forward. The apex points forward toward the pubic symphysis.

Question 7383. A described radiograph after contrast has been put into the bladder shows a smooth rounded shadow with a flat lower border. Which organ is outlined, and what does an irregular outline suggest? The answer is the bladder, and an irregular outline suggests a growth or a stone. Contrast outlines the inner surface, so anything projecting into the cavity shows as a filling defect.

Question 7384. A constructed illustration: a child born with a defect of the lower spine cannot empty the bladder completely, and the sphincter tightens while the detrusor contracts. Which two sets of nerves are failing to work together? The answer is the pelvic splanchnic nerves and the pudendal nerve. The detrusor and the external sphincter normally act in turn rather than together.

Question 7385. Which of these pairs belongs together: the apex with the umbilicus, the base with the pelvic floor, or the superior surface with the rectum? The answer is the apex with the umbilicus, joined by the median umbilical ligament. The base faces the rectum and the seminal vesicles in the male. The trigone lies on the base near the neck.

Question 7386. What is the name of the venous network that surrounds the bladder? The answer is the vesical venous plexus. It lies in the loose tissue beside the bladder and the prostate and drains into the internal iliac veins. It communicates with the prostatic plexus and with the rectal veins.

Question 7387. From which segments of the spinal cord do the pelvic splanchnic nerves arise: the first to the third lumbar, the eleventh thoracic to the second lumbar, the second to the fourth sacral, or the fourth to the fifth lumbar? The answer is the second to the fourth sacral segments. They pass through the sacral foramina to the pelvic plexus, and their fibers empty the bladder.

Question 7388. Toward which two structures does the apex of the bladder point? The answer is the pubic symphysis and the umbilicus. The apex lies behind the upper part of the symphysis. It is joined to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament and is the highest point of the empty bladder.

Question 7389. A constructed illustration: a newborn has an open lower abdominal wall and the back wall of the bladder is exposed. Which statement about this fault is correct: the front of the bladder is open, the trigone is absent, the posterior wall is missing, or the urachus is duplicated? The answer is that the front of the bladder is open, while the posterior wall and the trigone are present.

Question 7390. A described section through the bladder outlet shows a ring of smooth muscle in the bladder wall and a ring of striped muscle around the urethra below it. Which two sphincters are shown? The answer is the internal urethral sphincter and the external urethral sphincter. The inner one is involuntary and the outer one is voluntary.

Question 7391. Which muscle of the bladder contracts to expel urine, and what kind of muscle is it? The answer is the detrusor, which is smooth muscle. Its bundles run in several directions and interlace with one another. It receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, which have opposite effects on it.

Question 7392. Which structures form the upper corners of the trigone of the bladder: the two internal urethral orifices, the two ureteric orifices, the median umbilical ligament and the uvula, or the two ejaculatory ducts? The answer is the two ureteric orifices. The lowest corner is the internal urethral orifice. The triangle between these three points never changes its shape.

Question 7393. A described cross section of the bladder wall shows a lining that is folded in one region and smooth in another. Which two regions are described, and what lies beneath the smooth one? The answer is the folded mucosa of the body and the smooth mucosa of the trigone, where there is no submucosa. The folds disappear as the bladder fills.

Question 7394. In the male, which structures lie behind the base of the bladder: the prostate and the pubic symphysis, the rectum with the seminal vesicles and the ampullae of the ductus deferens, or the urethra with the vagina and the cervix? The answer is the rectum, the seminal vesicles and the ampullae of the ductus deferens. The peritoneum dips between them as the rectovesical pouch.

Question 7395. A constructed illustration: a tube is passed into the bladder of a man whose prostate is enlarged, and the tube meets an obstacle below the bladder. Which part of the urethra has narrowed: the prostatic part, the membranous part, the spongy part, or the intramural part? The answer is the prostatic part, which the gland surrounds just below the neck of the bladder.

Question 7396. Why does urine not pass back up the ureter when the bladder contracts: the orifice has a flap of mucosa, the intramural part is compressed by bladder muscle, the peritoneum holds it shut, or the kidney draws it back? The answer is that the intramural part is compressed by the muscle of the bladder. The oblique course turns the rising pressure into a closing force.

Question 7397. Which statement about the emptying of the bladder is correct: the detrusor relaxes while the sphincters contract, the detrusor contracts while the internal sphincter relaxes, the detrusor contracts while the external sphincter contracts, or the detrusor does not change at all? The answer is that the detrusor contracts while the internal sphincter relaxes. The external sphincter is then relaxed at will.

Question 7398. A described coronal section of the pelvis shows a rounded organ in the midline with two tubes entering its upper and outer corners and a single channel leaving its lowest point. Which organ and which three openings are shown? The answer is the bladder, with the two ureteric orifices above and the internal urethral orifice below. The three openings mark the corners of the trigone.

Question 7399. A described sagittal section through a male pelvis shows the bladder in front and a smaller rounded organ directly below its neck, wrapped around a tube. Which organ is shown, and how does it relate to the bladder? The answer is the prostate, which lies below the neck of the bladder and surrounds the first part of the urethra.

Question 7400. Which statement about the ureters and the bladder is correct: the ureters open at the apex, they open at the lateral angles of the trigone, or the organs lie above the peritoneum? The answer is that they open at the lateral angles of the trigone and the bladder empties through its neck. The oblique passage of each ureter prevents urine from flowing back.

To summarize, each ureter is a muscular tube about 25 to 30 centimeters long that runs behind the peritoneum from the renal pelvis to the bladder, descending on the psoas major and crossing the pelvic brim in front of the common iliac artery. Its three narrow points are the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim and the ureterovesical junction, and its lower end passes obliquely through the bladder wall so that rising pressure closes it. In the female the uterine artery crosses above the ureter near the cervix, and in the male the ductus deferens crosses above it. The bladder lies in the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis when empty and rises into the abdomen as it fills, and it is extraperitoneal, with peritoneum only on its superior surface. Its base faces the rectum and the seminal vesicles in the male and the vagina in the female, and its smooth fixed trigone is marked by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. The detrusor is emptied by parasympathetic fibers from the second to the fourth sacral segments, and the pudendal nerve carries the voluntary control of the external sphincter. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 75 — Urethra

Every drop of urine that leaves the body passes through the urethra, and this chapter follows that tube from the urinary bladder to the exterior. The first twenty-five questions deal with the bladder, its parts, its muscle, its sphincters and its relations, and the remaining seventy-five deal with the urethra itself, the four named parts of the male urethra and the much shorter female urethra. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The urethra is the only part of the urinary tract that differs markedly between the sexes, and that difference runs through the questions that follow. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7401. Which narrow tube carries urine from the urinary bladder to the exterior of the body? The answer is the urethra. In the male it passes through the prostate gland, the perineal membrane and the penis, while in the female it is a short straight tube that opens into the vestibule. It is the final part of the urinary tract.

Question 7402. The urinary bladder is described in four named parts. Which one is the rounded part that points forward and upward behind the pubic symphysis: the fundus, the apex, the neck, or the trigone? The answer is the apex. The fundus is the base behind, the neck is the lowest part, and the trigone is a smooth area inside the base.

Question 7403. Which fibrous cord runs from the apex of the bladder up the front of the abdominal wall to the umbilicus? The answer is the median umbilical ligament. It is the remains of the urachus, the fetal tube that drained the bladder into the umbilical cord. After birth the tube closes and becomes this cord.

Question 7404. The smooth triangular area inside the bladder has three corners. Which openings form its two upper corners and its lower corner? The answer is the two ureteric orifices above and the internal urethral orifice below. The two orifices above are joined by a raised ridge, the interureteric crest.

Question 7405. Which muscle forms the main wall of the urinary bladder: the detrusor, the sphincter urethrae, the levator ani, or the rectus abdominis? The answer is the detrusor. Its fibers run in several directions and contract as a whole to expel urine. The other three muscles belong to the pelvic floor or the abdominal wall.

Question 7406. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fundus with the median umbilical ligament, the apex with the ureteric orifices, the neck with the internal urethral orifice, or the trigone with the prostate gland? The answer is the neck with the internal urethral orifice. The neck is the lowest and most fixed part of the bladder, and the urethra leaves the organ from it.

Question 7407. Which part of the inside of the bladder is a smooth triangle whose mucosa is firmly fixed to the muscle and never thrown into folds? The answer is the trigone. Its corners are the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. Because the mucosa is adherent, the area stays smooth when the bladder empties.

Question 7408. A described view through a cystoscope shows a pale smooth triangle with a raised ridge running between two small openings. Which structure is the ridge? The answer is the interureteric crest. It joins the two ureteric orifices across the base of the bladder and is a useful guide when the base is examined from inside.

Question 7409. Which statement about the capacity of the adult urinary bladder is correct: it holds about 300 to 500 milliliters, it holds about 50 milliliters, it holds about 2 liters, or its capacity never changes? The answer is that it holds about 300 to 500 milliliters. When it fills, it rises out of the pelvis into the abdomen.

Question 7410. In the male, which structure lies immediately behind the urinary bladder and which lies immediately in front of it? The answer is the rectum behind and the pubic symphysis in front. Above, the bladder is covered by peritoneum, and below it rests upon the prostate gland.

Question 7411. True or false: the peritoneum covers only the superior surface of the urinary bladder, while the rest of the organ lies outside the peritoneal cavity. The answer is true. The peritoneum is reflected from the bladder onto the abdominal wall and onto the rectum, so the organ is described as extraperitoneal.

Question 7412. A constructed illustration: a person cannot pass urine and a rounded swelling is felt above the pubic symphysis. Which organ is distended, and how does it displace the peritoneum? The answer is the urinary bladder, which rises into the abdomen and pushes the peritoneum upward ahead of it. The swelling lies in the midline and is dull to percussion.

Question 7413. Which ring of muscle lies at the neck of the bladder, surrounds the beginning of the urethra, and is made of smooth muscle? The answer is the internal urethral sphincter. It is well developed in the male and poorly developed in the female. Being smooth muscle, it works without voluntary control.

Question 7414. Which nerves carry the parasympathetic fibers that empty the bladder: the pelvic splanchnic nerves, the pudendal nerves, the obturator nerves, or the genitofemoral nerves? The answer is the pelvic splanchnic nerves. They arise from the second to the fourth sacral segments, and their fibers make the detrusor contract.

Question 7415. Which part of the autonomic nervous system reaches the bladder through the hypogastric plexus, and what does it do there? The answer is the sympathetic part, from the eleventh thoracic to the second lumbar segments. It relaxes the detrusor and, in the male, tightens the internal urethral sphincter.

Question 7416. A described computed tomography scan of the pelvis shows the bladder filled with contrast, with a ureter entering its base on each side. Which structure joins the two entry points across the base? The answer is the interureteric crest. It marks the upper border of the trigone and shows where the two ureters open.

Question 7417. Which structure lies immediately in front of the empty urinary bladder in the male: the pubic symphysis, the rectum, the seminal vesicle, or the prostate gland? The answer is the pubic symphysis. The prostate lies below the bladder, and the rectum and the seminal vesicles lie behind it, so only the symphysis is truly anterior.

Question 7418. Name, as a list in one sentence, the two structures that open into the urinary bladder and the single tube that leaves it. The answer is the two ureters and the urethra. The ureters open at the two upper corners of the trigone, and the urethra leaves from its lower corner.

Question 7419. Which small rounded elevation lies just behind the internal urethral orifice in the male bladder, formed by the middle lobe of the prostate gland? The answer is the uvula vesicae. It projects into the bladder at the lower end of the trigone. Enlargement of that lobe raises the uvula and can hinder the outflow of urine.

Question 7420. Which artery is the main supply of the base of the bladder and of the prostate gland: the superior vesical, the inferior vesical, the obturator, or the internal pudendal? The answer is the inferior vesical artery. The superior vesical artery supplies the upper part and the fundus, and the other two reach the bladder only by small branches.

Question 7421. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the lower abdomen with the bladder full, free fluid is found inside the peritoneal cavity. Which part of the bladder is likely torn, and why there? The answer is the superior surface, which is the only part covered by peritoneum. A rupture there spills urine into the peritoneal cavity.

Question 7422. A described specimen of the bladder is cut open to show its inner surface. Over most of the surface the mucosa is thrown into folds, but one small area is smooth. Which area is it, and why is it smooth? The answer is the trigone, because its mucosa is firmly bound to the muscle beneath.

Question 7423. Which statement explains why the mucosa over the trigone stays smooth when the bladder empties: it is firmly attached to the muscular wall, it has no epithelium, it is covered by peritoneum, or it lies outside the bladder? The answer is that it is firmly attached to the muscular wall, so it cannot be thrown into folds.

Question 7424. In a standing person the empty bladder lies wholly inside the pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis. In which direction does the full bladder expand, and what does it push ahead of it? The answer is upward into the abdomen, pushing the peritoneum ahead of it. The bladder becomes an abdominal organ as it fills.

Question 7425. Which statement about the position of the bladder in a newborn infant is correct: it lies mostly in the abdomen, it lies wholly within the pelvis, its neck lies at the pubic symphysis, or it lies behind the rectum? The answer is that it lies mostly in the abdomen. The pelvis is small at birth, and the bladder descends as the pelvis grows during childhood.

Question 7426. In the female, which tube is about 4 centimeters long, runs downward and forward, and opens into the vestibule? The answer is the urethra. It lies in front of the vagina and behind the pubic symphysis, and it is much shorter and straighter than the male urethra.

Question 7427. Which of these lists the parts of the male urethra in order from the bladder outward: prostatic, membranous, spongy; spongy, prostatic, membranous; membranous, spongy, prostatic; or prostatic, spongy, membranous? The answer is prostatic, membranous, spongy. A short preprostatic segment lies within the bladder wall before the prostatic part begins, and the whole tube is about 18 to 20 centimeters long.

Question 7428. In the male, the membranous part of the urethra lies below and behind the inferior border of the pubic symphysis. Which vein lies in front of it, between it and the arcuate pubic ligament? The answer is the deep dorsal vein of the penis. That vein passes beneath the symphysis to reach the prostatic plexus, and the urethra lies behind it.

Question 7429. A described radiograph is made by injecting contrast into the external urethral opening so that the whole male urethra is outlined. Which part appears as a short narrow segment between the prostate gland and the bulb of the penis? The answer is the membranous urethra. It is the shortest part of the tube and the least distensible.

Question 7430. Which part of the male urethra lies within the prostate gland, is the widest and most dilatable part of the tube, and receives the ejaculatory ducts and the prostatic ducts? The answer is the prostatic urethra. It is about 3 to 4 centimeters long and runs obliquely through the gland from above downward and forward.

Question 7431. Which part of the male urethra is the longest, beginning at the bulb of the penis and ending at the external urethral opening: the prostatic part, the membranous part, the spongy part, or the preprostatic part? The answer is the spongy part, which is about 15 centimeters long and lies within the corpus spongiosum.

Question 7432. Which short segment of the male urethra is about 1 to 1.5 centimeters long and passes obliquely through the wall of the bladder before the prostate gland is reached? The answer is the preprostatic part, also called the intramural part. Its oblique course helps to close the tube as the bladder fills.

Question 7433. Which of these pairs belongs together: the prostatic urethra with the corpus spongiosum, the membranous urethra with the external urethral sphincter, the spongy urethra with the prostate gland, or the preprostatic urethra with the perineal membrane? The answer is the membranous urethra with the external urethral sphincter. That sphincter surrounds the membranous part in the deep perineal pouch.

Question 7434. A described midsagittal magnetic resonance image of the male pelvis shows a single tube passing through the prostate gland above and piercing a firm membrane below on its way to the bulb. Which tube and which parts are shown? The answer is the urethra, shown in its prostatic, membranous and bulbar parts.

Question 7435. In the male, which part of the urethra is the widest and most dilatable, and which part is the least distensible? The answer is that the prostatic part is the widest and the membranous part the least distensible. The external urethral orifice is the narrowest point of the whole tube.

Question 7436. The prostatic urethra carries a midline ridge on its posterior wall. What is the name of the rounded elevation on that ridge, and what lies on either side of it? The answer is the seminal colliculus, flanked by the prostatic sinuses. Into those sinuses the ducts of the prostate gland open.

Question 7437. Which rounded elevation on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra is the landmark that surgeons and endoscopists call the verumontanum? The answer is the seminal colliculus. It lies in the middle of the prostatic urethra. The two ejaculatory ducts and the prostatic utricle open upon it.

Question 7438. Name, spoken as a list, the two kinds of opening that are found on the seminal colliculus of the prostatic urethra. The answer is the two ejaculatory ducts and the prostatic utricle. The utricle is a small blind pouch in the midline, and the ducts open one on each side of it.

Question 7439. Two small slit-like openings lie on the seminal colliculus, one on each side of a small blind pouch. Which ducts end at those openings? The answer is the two ejaculatory ducts. Each is formed by the union of the ductus deferens with the duct of the seminal vesicle behind the bladder.

Question 7440. Into which part of the prostatic urethra do the many small ducts of the prostate gland open: the urethral crest, the prostatic sinuses, the seminal colliculus, or the prostatic utricle? The answer is the prostatic sinuses. These are the grooves on either side of the urethral crest, and about twenty prostatic ducts open into them.

Question 7441. A described endoscopic view of the prostatic urethra shows a midline ridge with a rounded elevation upon it and small openings in the grooves on either side. Which structure is the ridge, and which are the grooves? The answer is the urethral crest with the seminal colliculus upon it, and the prostatic sinuses on either side.

Question 7442. True or false: the prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra. The answer is true. It is also the part that receives the ejaculatory ducts and the prostatic ducts, and it is about 3 to 4 centimeters long.

Question 7443. A constructed illustration: an older man reports difficulty in starting the flow of urine and a weak stream. Which part of the urethra is compressed, and by what? The answer is the prostatic urethra, compressed by the enlarging prostate gland. The gland surrounds that part of the tube. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7444. Which gland lies immediately below the urinary bladder, surrounds the first part of the urethra, and is pierced by the two ejaculatory ducts? The answer is the prostate gland. It is described in lobes and is separated from the rectum behind it by a fascial septum. The urethra leaves the bladder through its substance.

Question 7445. Which part of the male urethra is about 1 to 2 centimeters long, pierces the perineal membrane, and is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter: the prostatic, the membranous, the spongy, or the preprostatic part? The answer is the membranous part. It is the shortest part of the tube and the least distensible.

Question 7446. Which part of the male urethra is the shortest and the least able to be stretched, and how long is it? The answer is the membranous part, which is about 1 to 2 centimeters long. It lies in the deep perineal pouch between the prostate gland above and the bulb of the penis below.

Question 7447. Which muscle surrounds the membranous part of the urethra, lies in the deep perineal pouch, and provides voluntary control of the flow of urine? The answer is the external urethral sphincter, also called the sphincter urethrae. It is made of striated muscle and is supplied by the pudendal nerve.

Question 7448. A constructed illustration: a person has a fracture of the pelvis, and blood appears at the external urethral opening. Which part of the urethra is torn, and why is that part at risk? The answer is the membranous part, because it is short, it is fixed to the perineal membrane and it lies just below the prostate gland.

Question 7449. A described magnetic resonance image of the male pelvis follows the urethra from the bladder to the tip of the penis. Which two segments are surrounded by muscle, and which segment lies within erectile tissue? The answer is that the preprostatic and prostatic segments are surrounded by the internal sphincter and the prostate, the membranous segment by the external sphincter, and the spongy segment lies within the corpus spongiosum.

Question 7450. Into which part of the urethra do the ducts of the bulbourethral glands open: the prostatic part, the membranous part, the bulbar part of the spongy urethra, or the navicular fossa? The answer is the bulbar part of the spongy urethra. The ducts are long and open about 2.5 centimeters below the perineal membrane.

Question 7451. In which direction does the membranous part of the urethra run as it passes from the prostate gland to the bulb of the penis? The answer is downward and forward. It pierces the perineal membrane on that oblique course, and the change of direction at the bulb forms one of the two curves of the male urethra.

Question 7452. Which of these pairs belongs together: the internal urethral sphincter with striated voluntary muscle, the external urethral sphincter with smooth involuntary muscle, the internal urethral sphincter with a ring of smooth muscle at the bladder neck, or the detrusor with the pelvic diaphragm? The answer is the internal urethral sphincter with a ring of smooth muscle at the bladder neck.

Question 7453. Which sphincter of the urethra is under voluntary control and can be tightened at will: the internal urethral sphincter, the external urethral sphincter, the detrusor, or the uvula vesicae? The answer is the external urethral sphincter. It is made of striated muscle and is supplied by the pudendal nerve.

Question 7454. True or false: the external urethral sphincter is made of striated muscle and is under voluntary control. The answer is true. It surrounds the membranous part of the urethra in the deep perineal pouch, and the internal sphincter, which is smooth muscle, lies at the bladder neck.

Question 7455. A constructed illustration: a woman leaks urine when she coughs, and the support of her urethra is being assessed. Which muscles close the female urethra, and in which part of the perineum does the middle of the urethra lie? The answer is the sphincter urethrae and the compressor urethrae, with the urethra in the deep perineal pouch.

Question 7456. Which of these structures lies within the deep perineal pouch of the male: the prostate gland, the bulb of the penis, the bulbourethral glands, or the seminal vesicles? The answer is the bulbourethral glands. They lie one on each side of the membranous urethra, within the sphincter urethrae, and their ducts pass downward to the bulb.

Question 7457. Which part of the male urethra lies within the corpus spongiosum and is surrounded along its length by erectile tissue? The answer is the spongy part, also called the penile part. It begins at the bulb, runs forward within the penis and ends at the external urethral opening. It is the longest part of the tube.

Question 7458. Which part of the male urethra begins in the bulb of the penis, runs forward within the corpus spongiosum, and is about 15 centimeters long? The answer is the spongy part. It is the longest part of the urethra, and it ends at the external urethral opening on the glans.

Question 7459. Which dilatation of the spongy urethra lies within the glans penis and is named for its boat-like shape? The answer is the navicular fossa. It lies just behind the external urethral opening. The mucosa of the fossa is stratified squamous, unlike the rest of the spongy urethra.

Question 7460. Which statement about the narrow points of the male urethra is correct: the external urethral orifice is the narrowest point, the prostatic urethra is the narrowest, the spongy urethra is the narrowest, or all parts are equally wide? The answer is that the external urethral orifice is the narrowest point. The internal urethral orifice and the membranous part are the other narrow points.

Question 7461. A described radiograph made with contrast injected into the urethra shows a short narrowed segment in the region just below the perineal membrane. Which part of the urethra is narrowed, and what is the common cause of narrowing there? The answer is the bulbar part of the spongy urethra. It is a common site of narrowing after inflammation because of its shape and its mucous glands.

Question 7462. Which small mucous glands open along the spongy urethra, and which of them is the largest, lying on the roof of the navicular fossa? The answer is the urethral glands of Littre, and the largest is the lacuna magna. Their openings face backward, so an instrument passed forward may catch in them.

Question 7463. Which statement about the lining of the male urethra is correct: the prostatic part is lined by transitional epithelium, the spongy part by transitional epithelium, the membranous part by stratified squamous epithelium, or the navicular fossa by columnar epithelium? The answer is that the prostatic part is lined by transitional epithelium, as the bladder is.

Question 7464. A described coronal section through the penis shows three columns of erectile tissue, and the urethra lies within the one on the ventral side. Which column contains the urethra? The answer is the corpus spongiosum. It lies below the two corpora cavernosa, and it alone carries the urethra.

Question 7465. A constructed illustration: a cyclist falls astride the crossbar and has bruising of the perineum with blood at the external urethral opening. Which part of the urethra is most likely torn? The answer is the bulbar part of the spongy urethra. It is fixed below the perineal membrane and is crushed against the pubic arch.

Question 7466. A constructed illustration: after an injury to the urethra, urine tracks into the scrotum, the penis and the lower abdominal wall but not into the thighs. Which layer limits it, and why does it spare the thigh? The answer is the membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia, which is attached behind to the perineal membrane and on each side to the deep fascia of the thigh.

Question 7467. A described computed tomography image of the perineum after an injury shows a collection of fluid in the superficial perineal pouch. Which layer forms the deep boundary of that pouch, and where is it attached? The answer is the membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia, and it is attached behind to the perineal membrane.

Question 7468. Which statement about the external urethral opening of the male urethra is correct: it is a vertical slit at the tip of the glans, it lies within the prostate gland, it is the widest part of the tube, or it lies below the perineal membrane? The answer is that it is a vertical slit at the tip of the glans. It is the narrowest point of the whole urethra.

Question 7469. True or false: the male urethra has two curvatures, one fixed around the lower border of the pubic symphysis and one mobile in front of it. The answer is true. The fixed curve lies below the symphysis, and the mobile part is created by the penis itself and can be straightened.

Question 7470. A catheter is passed along the male urethra while the penis is lifted upward. Which of the two curvatures does that lift straighten, and which one remains? The answer is that the mobile curve in front of the pubic symphysis is straightened, and the fixed curve below the symphysis remains. The tip must therefore be directed upward at that point.

Question 7471. How long is the female urethra, and what is its usual width: about 4 centimeters long and 6 millimeters wide, about 15 centimeters long and 6 millimeters wide, about 4 centimeters long and 2 centimeters wide, or about 20 centimeters long and 1 centimeter wide? The answer is about 4 centimeters long and 6 millimeters wide.

Question 7472. Which tube in the female is embedded in the anterior wall of the vagina, opens into the vestibule, and lies behind the pubic symphysis? The answer is the urethra. It is about 4 centimeters long, and its wall is fused with that of the vagina along most of its length.

Question 7473. In the female, the external urethral opening lies in the vestibule. Which structure lies immediately in front of that opening, and which opening lies immediately behind it? The answer is the glans of the clitoris in front and the opening of the vagina behind. The urethral opening lies about 2.5 centimeters behind the glans.

Question 7474. Which small glands lie beside the female urethra and open by short ducts on either side of the external urethral opening? The answer is the paraurethral glands, also called the glands of Skene. They are the female counterpart of the prostate gland and lie in the wall of the urethra.

Question 7475. Which statement about the sphincters of the female urethra is correct: the internal urethral sphincter is a thick ring of smooth muscle, the external urethral sphincter is the main voluntary sphincter in the deep perineal pouch, the urethra has no sphincter at all, or the internal sphincter is striated? The answer is that the external urethral sphincter is the main voluntary sphincter.

Question 7476. A described midsagittal magnetic resonance image of the female pelvis shows a short tube lying between the bladder above, the vagina behind and the pubic symphysis in front. Which structure is shown, and which part of the pelvic floor does it pierce? The answer is the urethra, which pierces the pelvic diaphragm and then the perineal membrane.

Question 7477. A constructed illustration: a woman has recurrent urinary infection, and an image shows a small pocket lying beside the urethra within the anterior wall of the vagina. Which structure is the pocket? The answer is a urethral diverticulum. It lies beside the urethra and may be felt through the anterior vaginal wall. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7478. Name, spoken as a list of two, the muscles that compress the female urethra as it passes through the deep perineal pouch. The answer is the sphincter urethrae and the compressor urethrae. Both are striated muscles of the deep perineal pouch, and they help to keep the urethra closed.

Question 7479. The whole of the female urethra and the lower part of the male urethra develop from which structure: the mesonephric duct, the urogenital sinus, the paramesonephric duct, or the metanephric blastema? The answer is the urogenital sinus. The upper part of the male urethra forms from the vesicourethral canal, which is the upper part of the same sinus.

Question 7480. A described transverse section through the female perineum shows the urethra in the midline, the vagina behind it and erectile tissue on either side. Which structure lies immediately behind the urethra, and with which structure is its wall fused? The answer is the vagina, whose anterior wall is fused with the urethra.

Question 7481. A constructed illustration: a woman has a fracture of the pelvis, and blood appears at the external urethral opening. Where along the urethra is the injury most likely, and why? The answer is where the urethra passes through the pelvic floor near the neck of the bladder, because the short tube is fixed there against the bone.

Question 7482. Which artery is the main supply of the spongy part of the urethra: the internal pudendal artery, the superior vesical artery, the obturator artery, or the inferior epigastric artery? The answer is the internal pudendal artery. Its bulbar and dorsal branches reach the bulb and the penile urethra, and its branches also supply the perineal muscles.

Question 7483.
