Which statement about the lymphatic drainage of the urethra is correct: the whole tube drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, the distal part to the superficial inguinal nodes and the proximal part to the internal iliac nodes, it drains to the para-aortic nodes, or not at all? The answer is that the distal part drains to the superficial inguinal nodes and the proximal part to the internal iliac nodes.

Question 7484. Which nerve carries sensation from the spongy part of the urethra, and from which main nerve does it arise? The answer is the dorsal nerve of the penis, which arises from the pudendal nerve. It runs along the dorsum of the penis beside the deep dorsal vein and the dorsal artery.

Question 7485. Which nerve plexus supplies the prostatic part of the urethra: the pudendal nerve, the prostatic nerve plexus, the obturator nerve, or the sciatic nerve? The answer is the prostatic nerve plexus. It is formed mainly by branches of the inferior hypogastric plexus, which carry both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers.

Question 7486. A described image shows a small rounded gland lying beside the membranous urethra, above the bulb and below the perineal membrane, with a long duct running down to open into the bulb. Which gland is shown? The answer is the bulbourethral gland. It lies in the deep perineal pouch, and its duct opens about 2.5 centimeters below the membrane.

Question 7487. A described image made while an infant boy passes urine shows a dilated posterior urethra with a thin oblique line below it. Which part of the urethra is dilated, and what forms the line? The answer is the prostatic urethra, dilated behind a posterior urethral valve that arises from the urethral crest.

Question 7488. Which statement explains why the urethral opening lies on the dorsal surface of the penis in epispadias: the urethral folds failed to fuse, the genital tubercle developed abnormally so that the urethral groove formed on the dorsal surface, the prostate gland is enlarged, or the bulbourethral glands are absent? The answer is that the genital tubercle developed abnormally, placing the groove on the dorsal surface.

Question 7489. A constructed illustration: an infant boy has a urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis, some distance behind the glans. Which structures failed to fuse during development? The answer is the urethral folds. They normally meet in the midline to form the spongy urethra, and the opening may lie anywhere along the ventral surface.

Question 7490. Which statement about the urethra in the two sexes is correct: the male urethra serves both urine and semen, the female urethra carries semen, the two are of the same length, or the male urethra opens into the vestibule? The answer is that the male urethra serves both urine and semen. The female urethra carries urine only.

Question 7491. Which kind of epithelium lines the prostatic urethra, and which kind lines the navicular fossa at the far end of the tube? The answer is transitional epithelium in the prostatic part and stratified squamous epithelium in the navicular fossa. The membranous and spongy parts are lined mainly by stratified columnar epithelium.

Question 7492. Which of these pairs belongs together: the navicular fossa with transitional epithelium, the prostatic urethra with stratified squamous epithelium, the spongy urethra with stratified columnar epithelium, or the membranous urethra with transitional epithelium? The answer is the spongy urethra with stratified columnar epithelium, which also lines the membranous part.

Question 7493. In the male, the spongy urethra lies in the corpus spongiosum. Which two structures lie immediately above it within the penis, and which fascia wraps all three columns together? The answer is the two corpora cavernosa above it, with the deep fascia of the penis around all three.

Question 7494. True or false: the female urethra is longer than the male urethra. The answer is false. The female urethra is about 4 centimeters long, while the male urethra is about 18 to 20 centimeters long. The female tube is also straighter, and it runs almost directly from the neck of the bladder to the vestibule.

Question 7495. On which wall of the female urethra does the urethral crest lie: the anterior wall, the posterior wall, the lateral wall, or the floor of the vestibule? The answer is the posterior wall. It is a low longitudinal ridge, and it is the female counterpart of the urethral crest of the prostatic urethra.

Question 7496. A described coronal section of the male perineum shows the urethra in the midline, surrounded by a ring of striated muscle, with two small glands beside it and the bulb of the penis below. Which part of the urethra is shown? The answer is the membranous part, lying in the deep perineal pouch between the membrane and the bulb.

Question 7497. Which of these pairs belongs together: the dorsal nerve of the penis with the prostatic urethra, the pudendal nerve with the spongy urethra, the pelvic splanchnic nerves with the external urethral sphincter, or the obturator nerve with the bladder? The answer is the pudendal nerve with the spongy urethra, from which its dorsal branch carries sensation.

Question 7498. Which structure forms the immediate posterior relation of the female urethra along its length, and through which opening in the pelvic floor does the urethra pass? The answer is the anterior wall of the vagina, and the urethra passes through the urogenital hiatus of the pelvic diaphragm before piercing the perineal membrane.

Question 7499. A catheter is passed along the male urethra with the penis held upward. From the bulb, in which direction does the tube run to the perineal membrane, and in which direction does it then continue through the prostate into the bladder? The answer is upward and backward in both segments, with the change of direction at the bulb.

Question 7500. Which of these structures does not open directly into the urethra: the ejaculatory ducts, the prostatic ducts, the duct of the bulbourethral gland, or the duct of the seminal vesicle? The answer is the duct of the seminal vesicle. It joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, and only that duct opens into the urethra.

To summarize, the urinary bladder has an apex joined to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament, a fundus, a neck and a smooth trigone whose corners are the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. Its wall is the detrusor, it is emptied by the pelvic splanchnic nerves and it is held closed by the internal and external urethral sphincters, and only its superior surface carries peritoneum. The male urethra is about 18 to 20 centimeters long and is described in four parts, the preprostatic, prostatic, membranous and spongy parts, of which the prostatic part is the widest and most dilatable and the membranous part the shortest and least distensible, while the external urethral orifice is the narrowest point of the tube. The membranous part pierces the perineal membrane within the deep perineal pouch, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter and flanked by the bulbourethral glands, and the spongy part runs through the corpus spongiosum to dilate as the navicular fossa within the glans. The female urethra is about 4 centimeters long, lies in front of the vagina and behind the pubic symphysis, and is closed by the sphincter urethrae and the compressor urethrae. Rupture of the urethra lets urine into the superficial perineal pouch or the pelvis, and the distal urethra drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes while the proximal urethra drains to the internal iliac nodes. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 76 — Male Reproductive Anatomy

This chapter examines the male reproductive organs, both those that lie outside the pelvis and those within it: the testis and its coverings, the epididymis, the vas deferens, and the seminal vesicle. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The material runs from the descent of the gonad to the duct system that carries sperm and the gland that adds to the seminal fluid. It is educational material and supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7501. Deep to the serous sac around the testis lies a tough white fibrous coat that sends septa into the gland. What is it called? The answer is the tunica albuginea. Its posterior thickening forms the mediastinum testis, and its septa divide the gland into lobules. The serous sac outside it is the tunica vaginalis.

Question 7502. At the posterior border of the testis the fibrous coat thickens into a partition that carries the rete testis. What is it called? The answer is the mediastinum testis. The septa of the gland radiate from it, and vessels and the duct system enter and leave at this border.

Question 7503. Which cells of the testis lie in the tissue between the seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone? The answer is the interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells. They lie close to the capillaries between the tubules and respond to luteinizing hormone. The cells inside the tubules do not make testosterone.

Question 7504. Which cells of the seminiferous tubule form the blood-testis barrier and secrete inhibin? The answer is the sustentacular cells, also called Sertoli cells. They reach from the base of the tubule to its lumen and nurse the developing sperm. Their tight junctions shield the maturing germ cells from the immune system.

Question 7505. About twelve to twenty coiled tubes carry sperm from the rete testis into the head of the epididymis. What are they called? The answer is the efferent ductules. Their convolutions form the lobules of the head of the epididymis. Each is lined by ciliated and absorptive cells that move and concentrate the sperm.

Question 7506. A small remnant attached to the upper pole of the testis is derived from the duct that becomes the uterine tube in the female. What is it? The answer is the appendix testis. It is a remnant of the paramesonephric duct and lies at the upper pole under the tunica vaginalis. It can twist and cause acute scrotal pain in a child.

Question 7507. A small stalked appendage hangs from the head of the epididymis and comes from the duct that forms the epididymis itself. What is it? The answer is the appendix epididymis. It is a remnant of the mesonephric duct, from which the epididymis, the vas deferens and the seminal vesicle all develop.

Question 7508. Which network of veins wraps around the testicular artery in the spermatic cord and cools the blood before it reaches the testis? The answer is the pampiniform plexus. Its veins surround the artery and exchange heat with it in a countercurrent arrangement. Higher in the cord the plexus condenses into the testicular vein.

Question 7509. Which thin muscular covering of the spermatic cord comes from the internal oblique muscle and lifts the testis? The answer is the cremaster muscle. It forms loops over the cord and the testis and contracts in cold and when the skin of the upper thigh is stroked. The dartos muscle in the scrotal wall also wrinkles the skin.

Question 7510. Which vessel gives rise to the testicular artery: the internal iliac artery, the abdominal aorta, the external iliac artery, or the femoral artery? The answer is the abdominal aorta. The testicular artery arises from the aorta in the upper abdomen, below the renal artery, and descends to the deep inguinal ring. It can be injured high in the abdomen.

Question 7511. Lymph from the testis itself drains to which group of nodes: the superficial inguinal nodes, the para-aortic nodes, the internal iliac nodes, or the deep inguinal nodes? The answer is the para-aortic nodes. The testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall and drags its lymphatics with it as it descends. The skin of the scrotum drains to the groin instead.

Question 7512. The right testicular vein ends in the inferior vena cava. Into which vessel does the left testicular vein usually drain? The answer is the left renal vein. The left vein is longer and joins the renal vein at a right angle, while the right joins the vena cava obliquely. That helps explain why a varicocele is far more common on the left.

Question 7513. Which covering of the testis is a remnant of the peritoneal outpouching that followed the gonad into the scrotum: the tunica albuginea, the tunica vaginalis, the internal spermatic fascia, or the dartos layer? The answer is the tunica vaginalis. It is the lower part of the processus vaginalis, which normally closes above the testis. Its visceral layer covers the gland.

Question 7514. Which part of the testis is not covered by the visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis: the anterior surface, the lateral surface, the posterior border, or the lower pole? The answer is the posterior border. There the serous layer is reflected onto the epididymis, leaving a bare strip for vessels, nerves and the duct system. The sinus of the epididymis is the recess beside it.

Question 7515. A young man has a soft swelling above the left testis that feels like a bag of worms and empties when he lies down. Which anatomical feature best explains why the left side is affected far more often? The answer is the drainage of the left testicular vein. It is longer than the right and joins the left renal vein at a right angle. That length and that angle make the left side far more vulnerable.

Question 7516. Pain from a testis is often felt first where: in the scrotum, in the periumbilical region, in the groin, or in the perineum? The answer is the periumbilical region. The testis carries its sympathetic supply from the tenth thoracic segment of the spinal cord, so visceral pain is referred to the matching dermatome around the navel. The skin of the scrotum feels pain where it lies.

Question 7517. Which of these structures is found within the spermatic cord: the femoral artery, the vas deferens, the inferior epigastric artery, or the ilioinguinal nerve? The answer is the vas deferens. The cord also holds the testicular artery, the artery to the vas deferens, the cremasteric artery, the pampiniform plexus, lymph vessels and sympathetic nerves. The inferior epigastric artery lies outside the cord.

Question 7518. The septa of the testis divide the gland into about how many lobules: about twenty to thirty, about one hundred, about two hundred to three hundred, or about one thousand? The answer is about two hundred to three hundred. Each lobule holds one to four highly coiled seminiferous tubules. Their combined uncoiled length is measured in hundreds of meters.

Question 7519. During descent of the testis, which structure guides the gland from the posterior abdominal wall to the scrotum: the processus vaginalis, the gubernaculum, the inguinal ligament, or the round ligament? The answer is the gubernaculum. It is a cord of mesenchyme that runs from the lower pole of the gonad to the future scrotum and holds the gland on its path. Androgens drive the descent.

Question 7520. When the skin of the upper medial thigh is stroked, the testis on that side rises. Which nerves carry this reflex: the femoral and obturator nerves, the ilioinguinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, the pudendal nerve alone, or the sciatic nerve? The answer is the ilioinguinal nerve as the afferent limb and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve as the efferent limb.

Question 7521. A boy has sudden severe pain in the scrotum, the testis lies high and horizontal, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on that side. Which anatomical arrangement is the usual cause? The answer is the bell-clapper deformity, in which the tunica vaginalis extends high onto the cord. The testis then hangs freely in the serous sac and can twist on its cord. The horizontal lie and the absent reflex separate this from inflammation.

Question 7522. A testis that has not descended into the scrotum carries an increased risk of which two problems: torsion and hernia, malignancy and impaired sperm production, hydrocele and varicocele, or infection and stones? The answer is malignancy and impaired sperm production. The undescended gland is exposed to a higher temperature, which damages the germinal epithelium. The scrotum keeps the testis cooler than the abdomen.

Question 7523. A described ultrasound of the scrotum shows two oval organs of even texture, each about four centimeters long, with a smaller structure hugging the back of each one. What is the smaller structure? The answer is the epididymis. It lies along the posterior and posterolateral border of the testis, head above and tail below. A thin dark line of fluid around the gland is the tunica vaginalis.

Question 7524. A described specimen has been cut across the testis, showing a fan of fine septa running from a thick white coat at the back of the gland to the surface. What does that show? The answer is the lobular structure of the testis. The septa pass from the mediastinum testis to the tunica albuginea and enclose the lobules. Each lobule holds one to four coiled seminiferous tubules.

Question 7525. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the groin shows a rounded cord of tissue passing through the inguinal canal, with a thick-walled tube at its posterior part. What is the tube? The answer is the vas deferens. It is the firmest and most posterior structure in the spermatic cord and feels like a whipcord through the scrotal skin. The vessels and nerves lie in front of it.

Question 7526. A described transverse section through the scrotum shows, from outside inward, thin pigmented skin, a layer of smooth muscle, a fibrous sac, and two oval glands separated by a midline partition. Which layer lies immediately outside the fibrous sac? The answer is the dartos muscle with its fascia. It replaces the fatty layer of the superficial fascia, so the scrotum holds no fat.

Question 7527. A described venogram of the spermatic cord shows a tangled mass of veins beside the left testis, with a single vein ascending from it to join a larger horizontal vein. Which vessel does that vein join? The answer is the left renal vein. The tangled mass is a varicocele of the pampiniform plexus. On the right the corresponding vein would end in the inferior vena cava.

Question 7528. A described section of a seminiferous tubule shows a wall several cells thick, with small cells near the base and tall columnar cells reaching from base to lumen. What are those tall cells? The answer is the sustentacular cells. They support and nourish the developing germ cells and form the blood-testis barrier with their tight junctions. The cells between them are germ cells.

Question 7529. Which structure lies immediately posterior and posterolateral to the testis, hugging it from the upper pole to the lower? The answer is the epididymis. Its head caps the upper pole, its body lies along the posterior border, and its tail turns upward at the lower pole. The tail then continues as the vas deferens.

Question 7530. The testis hangs at the lower end of the spermatic cord in the scrotum. Which structure lies immediately above and behind the testis at its junction with the cord? The answer is the tail of the epididymis. The tail is fixed to the lower pole and is the point at which the duct of the epididymis becomes the vas deferens.

Question 7531. Within the spermatic cord, which structure lies at the posterior part, behind the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus? The answer is the vas deferens. It lies at the back of the cord and can be rolled between the fingers as a firm cord. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve runs with the vessels in front of it.

Question 7532. In the standing body, the testis lies in the scrotum below and in front of which bony landmark, close to the root of the penis? The answer is the pubic tubercle. The cord leaves the superficial inguinal ring just above and lateral to the tubercle and passes down to the testis. The scrotum hangs below the root of the penis.

Question 7533. The visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis covers the testis and then turns onto the wall of the scrotum. Where does it leave the gland uncovered, and what is the recess beside the epididymis called? The answer is the posterior border, and the recess is the sinus of the epididymis. Vessels and the duct enter the gland through that bare strip.

Question 7534. A constructed illustration: a painless swelling of one side of the scrotum in a newborn glows when a light is held against it. Between which two layers has the fluid collected? The answer is between the visceral and the parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis. That collection is a hydrocele. A swelling that does not glow is more likely to be a hernia.

Question 7535. A constructed illustration: a young boy has sudden scrotal pain, and a small tender blue nodule is seen at the upper pole of the testis, with the gland itself lying normally. Which structure has twisted? The answer is the appendix testis. It is a remnant of the paramesonephric duct and hangs from the upper pole, where it can twist on its pedicle.

Question 7536. A constructed illustration: a small ulcerated growth on the skin of the scrotum is found, and nodes in the groin are enlarged. Which nodes are involved, and why are they not the nodes that a testicular tumor would reach? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes. The skin of the scrotum drains there as the skin of the perineum does.

Question 7537. A constructed illustration: a described computed tomography scan of the abdomen in a young man with a painless testicular lump shows enlarged nodes beside the aorta at the level of the second lumbar vertebra. Why are these nodes involved? The answer is that the testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and carries its lymphatics with it as it descends. The para-aortic nodes are its first nodes.

Question 7538. True or false: in most men the right testis lies lower in the scrotum than the left. The answer is false. The left testis usually lies a little lower than the right, and the left cord is the longer of the two. That difference in height is a normal finding and not a sign of disease.

Question 7539. True or false: the scrotum has no layer of fat under its skin. The answer is true. The fatty layer of the superficial fascia is replaced in the scrotum by the dartos muscle and its fascia, which wrinkle the skin. The skin itself is thin and pigmented and carries sweat glands.

Question 7540. Which of these pairs belongs together: the interstitial cells with inhibin, the sustentacular cells with testosterone, the interstitial cells with testosterone, or the sustentacular cells with the pampiniform plexus? The answer is the interstitial cells with testosterone. These cells lie between the tubules and respond to luteinizing hormone. The sustentacular cells secrete inhibin and androgen-binding protein.

Question 7541. Which of these pairs belongs together: the rete testis with the mediastinum, the efferent ductules with the tail of the epididymis, the seminiferous tubules with the vas deferens, or the duct of the epididymis with the rete testis? The answer is the rete testis with the mediastinum. The straight tubules open into the rete, which lies in the fibrous mediastinum. The efferent ductules leave it to form the head of the epididymis.

Question 7542. Name, in order, the three parts of the duct system that carry sperm from the seminiferous tubules to the head of the epididymis, spoken as a list. The answer is the straight tubules, the rete testis and the efferent ductules. The straight tubules leave the lobules and open into the rete testis. From there the ductules carry the sperm into the head.

Question 7543. Which part of the epididymis is the largest, sits on the upper pole of the testis, and receives the efferent ductules? The answer is the head. The efferent ductules enter it and form its lobules, which are also called the coni vasculosi. The head is the only part that receives new sperm.

Question 7544. Which part of the epididymis lies at the lower pole of the testis and continues upward as the vas deferens? The answer is the tail. It is the lowest and smallest part of the epididymis and serves as the main store of mature sperm. From the tail the duct turns upward into the spermatic cord.

Question 7545. The duct of the epididymis is a single tube packed into the organ in tight coils. Roughly how long would it be if it were uncoiled: about six centimeters, about sixty centimeters, about six meters, or about sixty meters? The answer is about six meters. The coils are bound together by connective tissue, which gives the organ its firm texture. The vas deferens continues from it as a straighter tube.

Question 7546. What is the name of the narrow groove that separates the body of the epididymis from the side of the testis? The answer is the sinus of the epididymis. It is the recess between the gland and the serous covering that lies between them. Fluid can collect there and may look like a cyst on an ultrasound study.

Question 7547. What name is given to the lobules of the head of the epididymis, each formed by the coils of one efferent ductule? The answer is the coni vasculosi. Each efferent ductule coils on itself to form a cone-shaped lobule, and the lobules together make up the head. The ductules then join the single duct of the epididymis.

Question 7548. Which statement about the epididymis is correct: it lies along the anterior surface of the testis, it lies along the posterior border with its head above and its tail below, its head lies at the lower pole, or it lies free in the scrotum? The answer is that it lies along the posterior border with its head above and its tail below.

Question 7549. The epididymis is described as a comma-shaped organ. Which part of it lies at the upper pole of the testis: the head, the body, the tail, or the ampulla? The answer is the head. The head is the broad upper end and receives the efferent ductules. The body runs down the posterior border and the tail ends at the lower pole.

Question 7550. Which of these is the main function of the epididymis: production of sperm, storage and maturation of sperm, production of seminal fluid, or production of testosterone? The answer is storage and maturation of sperm. Sperm leave the testis immature and acquire progressive motility as they pass along the duct. The tail is the main reservoir until ejaculation.

Question 7551. Where do sperm acquire the ability to swim forward: in the seminiferous tubules, in the rete testis, in the duct of the epididymis, or in the seminal vesicle? The answer is in the duct of the epididymis. The cells lining the duct absorb fluid and add proteins to the surface of the sperm. Sperm that reach the tail are mature but held in an inactive state.

Question 7552. Which arteries supply the epididymis: the testicular artery and the artery to the vas deferens, the internal pudendal artery alone, the inferior epigastric artery alone, or the obturator artery? The answer is the testicular artery and the artery to the vas deferens. The two anastomose along the duct system, so the epididymis survives when one is tied. The cremasteric artery supplies the coverings.

Question 7553. Lymph from the epididymis drains to which nodes: the superficial inguinal nodes, the para-aortic nodes, the internal iliac nodes, or the deep inguinal nodes? The answer is the para-aortic nodes. The epididymis is a derivative of the mesonephric duct and keeps the drainage of the posterior abdominal wall. Only the skin of the scrotum drains to the groin.

Question 7554. A man has no sperm in his semen, but a biopsy of the testis shows normal spermatogenesis. Which part of the duct system is most likely blocked if the glands are normal: the seminiferous tubules, the efferent ductules, the ureter, or the renal pelvis? The answer is the efferent ductules, the only route out of the testis.

Question 7555. A described specimen shows a small comma-shaped organ lying in the groove along the back of a testis, firm to the touch, with a broad upper end and a pointed lower end. Which organ is shown? The answer is the epididymis. The broad upper end is the head and the pointed lower end is the tail. The coiled duct inside gives the organ its firmness.

Question 7556. A described ultrasound of the scrotum shows a small dark oval swelling at the upper pole of the epididymis, separate from the testis, with no flow inside it. Which structure is it, and why does it move with the gland? The answer is a cyst of the epididymis. It arises from the coils of the duct. The epididymis is fixed to the testis, so the two move together.

Question 7557. A described MRI of the scrotum shows a comma-shaped structure of intermediate signal hugging the back of each testis, broader above than below. Which part of it lies highest? The answer is the head of the epididymis. It caps the upper pole and is broader than the body and the tail. The tail lies at the lower pole and becomes the vas deferens.

Question 7558. A described section through the back of a testis shows a serous space between the gland and the wall of the scrotum, and a recess where the serous layer dips between the gland and a comma-shaped organ. What is that recess? The answer is the sinus of the epididymis. The serous layer is the tunica vaginalis, reflected off the posterior border.

Question 7559. Which part of the epididymis lies immediately above the upper pole of the testis, capping it? The answer is the head. It is the broad upper end and receives the efferent ductules from the rete testis. Below it the body runs down the posterior border of the gland.

Question 7560. The epididymis lies along one border of the testis. Is that border anterior, posterior, medial or lateral? The answer is posterior, though its body and tail also lie somewhat posterolateral. That position is why the epididymis cannot be felt from the front of the scrotum as easily as the gland. Vessels and the duct enter at that border.

Question 7561. Two small appendages may be seen in the scrotum. One hangs from the upper pole of the testis and the other from the head of the epididymis. Which is which? The answer is that the appendix testis lies on the upper pole of the gland and the appendix epididymis lies on the head of the epididymis. They come from different ducts.

Question 7562. A constructed illustration: a man has tenderness in the scrotum that is greatest behind and above the testis, and the gland itself feels normal. Which structure is inflamed? The answer is the epididymis. Inflammation usually begins in the tail and spreads along the body to the head. The testis may become tender later if the inflammation spreads.

Question 7563. A constructed illustration: an infection of the bladder and the prostate spreads down the duct system to the scrotum. Which structure carries it to the epididymis? The answer is the vas deferens. It joins the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct and the urethra. Infection travels along its lumen and the tissue around it.

Question 7564. A constructed illustration: a young man is found to have no vas deferens on either side, and his epididymis is small and poorly formed. Which developmental duct has failed? The answer is the mesonephric duct. The epididymis, the vas deferens, the seminal vesicle and the ejaculatory duct all arise from it. This combination is associated with cystic fibrosis.

Question 7565. True or false: the duct of the epididymis is formed from the same embryonic duct that forms the vas deferens. The answer is true. Both are derivatives of the mesonephric duct, which also gives rise to the seminal vesicle. The efferent ductules, by contrast, come from the mesonephric tubules.

Question 7566. Which of these pairs belongs together: the efferent ductules with the tail of the epididymis, the efferent ductules with the head of the epididymis, the duct of the epididymis with the rete testis, or the appendix testis with the mesonephric duct? The answer is the efferent ductules with the head. They enter the head and form its lobules.

Question 7567. Which thick-walled muscular tube begins at the tail of the epididymis, ascends in the spermatic cord and carries sperm toward the urethra? The answer is the vas deferens. Its wall is made of three coats of smooth muscle, which give it a cord-like feel. Its narrow lumen is lined by a columnar epithelium.

Question 7568. Just before it joins the duct of the seminal vesicle, the vas deferens widens into a dilated terminal part. What is that part called? The answer is the ampulla. It lies behind the base of the bladder, medial to the seminal vesicle. There the ampulla joins the duct of the seminal vesicle.

Question 7569. The duct of the seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the vas deferens to form which structure, and where does it open? The answer is the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra. It is a short tube that passes through the prostate. It ends on the seminal colliculus beside the opening of the prostatic utricle.

Question 7570. Near the base of the bladder the vas deferens crosses another tube that carries urine, and the ureter is said to pass beneath it like water under a bridge. Which tube lies deep to the vas at that point? The answer is the ureter. The vas deferens crosses it from lateral to medial on its way to the ampulla.

Question 7571. The vas deferens is a long tube that runs from the scrotum to the prostate. About how long is it: about five centimeters, about fifteen centimeters, about forty-five centimeters, or about ninety centimeters? The answer is about forty-five centimeters. Most of that length lies in the pelvis. Its thick muscular wall propels sperm during ejaculation.

Question 7572. Which of these structures lies within the spermatic cord: the appendix testis, the vas deferens, the head of the epididymis, or the tail of the epididymis? The answer is the vas deferens. It joins the cord at the lower end, where the tail of the epididymis turns upward. The appendix testis hangs from the upper pole and lies outside the cord.

Question 7573. Which covering of the spermatic cord is derived from the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle: the internal spermatic fascia, the cremasteric fascia, the external spermatic fascia, or the tunica vaginalis? The answer is the external spermatic fascia. The internal spermatic fascia comes from the transversalis fascia and the cremasteric fascia from the internal oblique.

Question 7574. As the vas deferens enters the abdomen it hooks around a vessel on the deep surface of the anterior abdominal wall. Which vessel: the inferior epigastric artery, the external iliac artery, the obturator artery, or the superior vesical artery? The answer is the inferior epigastric artery. That hook marks the deep inguinal ring, where the vas turns downward.

Question 7575. Which artery supplies the vas deferens: the internal pudendal artery, the superior vesical artery, the obturator artery, or the middle rectal artery? The answer is the superior vesical artery, through a small artery to the vas deferens. That artery runs a long course in the cord and anastomoses with the testicular artery, so the vas can be divided safely.

Question 7576. After a vasectomy, in which the vas deferens is divided on each side, which statement is correct: the testes stop making sperm, the semen no longer contains sperm but still contains fluid from the glands, ejaculation stops, or the testes shrink? The answer is that the semen no longer contains sperm but still contains fluid from the glands. The testes continue to make sperm, which are absorbed above the block.

Question 7577. A described dissection of the scrotum shows a whitish cord that can be rolled between the fingers above the testis, firmer than the veins beside it. Which structure is it? The answer is the vas deferens. Its muscular wall makes it feel like a whipcord, which is how it is identified at operation. The veins of the pampiniform plexus are softer and lie in front of it.

Question 7578. A described MRI of the pelvis in cross section shows two thin-walled ducts running medially between the base of the bladder and the rectum, close to the midline, just above the prostate. What are they? The answer is the two ejaculatory ducts. Each is formed by the union of a vas deferens and a seminal vesicle duct. They pass forward through the prostate.

Question 7579. A described specimen shows a thick-walled tube that widens near its end and is joined from the side by the duct of a lobulated gland, the two forming a single narrower channel. Which two structures have joined? The answer is the ampulla of the vas deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle. Their union forms the ejaculatory duct.

Question 7580. Within the spermatic cord, which structure lies directly posterior to the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus? The answer is the vas deferens. It runs at the back of the cord, where it is protected by the other structures. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve runs with the vessels in front of it.

Question 7581. A constructed illustration: during the repair of an indirect inguinal hernia in a man, the surgeon identifies a firm white cord at the posterior part of the sac and takes care to preserve it. Which structure is it, and why is it preserved? The answer is the vas deferens. Dividing it would block the passage of sperm while leaving the testis to make them.

Question 7582. A constructed illustration: during an operation on the pelvis, a tube running downward on the lateral wall is traced toward the bladder, and the surgeon notes a second tube crossing it from above and lateral. Which structure crosses in front of the ureter? The answer is the vas deferens, which crosses the ureter just above the seminal vesicle.

Question 7583. True or false: the vas deferens and the appendix testis arise from the same embryonic duct. The answer is false. The vas deferens arises from the mesonephric duct, which also forms the epididymis, the seminal vesicle and the ejaculatory duct. The appendix testis is a remnant of the paramesonephric duct, which becomes the uterine tube.

Question 7584. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ejaculatory duct with the prostatic urethra, the ejaculatory duct with the membranous urethra, the ampulla of the vas deferens with the scrotum, or the vas deferens with the tunica vaginalis? The answer is the ejaculatory duct with the prostatic urethra. The duct passes through the prostate and opens on the seminal colliculus.

Question 7585. Name the two structures whose ducts join to form the ejaculatory duct, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the ampulla of the vas deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle. Each side has one ejaculatory duct, and the two run through the prostate. They open into the prostatic urethra beside the prostatic utricle.

Question 7586. In a described transverse section of the male pelvis, the vas deferens lies lateral to the bladder and the seminal vesicle lies behind it. On which side of the seminal vesicle does the ampulla lie, and where does the ureter pass? The answer is that the ampulla lies medial to the seminal vesicle, and the ureter passes above and medial to it.

Question 7587. Which paired lobulated gland lies behind the base of the urinary bladder, above the prostate and in front of the rectum? The answer is the seminal vesicle. It is a coiled tube about five centimeters long, surrounded by a fibrous coat. Its lower end joins the ampulla of the vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct.

Question 7588. Which sugar is found in high concentration in the fluid of the seminal vesicle and serves as a source of energy for sperm? The answer is fructose. Its presence in the semen marks seminal vesicle function, and its absence suggests blocked ejaculatory ducts or absent vesicles. The secretion is alkaline and makes up about sixty per cent of the seminal fluid.

Question 7589. Which statement about the position of the seminal vesicle is correct: it lies in front of the bladder, it lies in front of the rectum and behind the bladder, it lies below the prostate, or it lies above the bladder? The answer is that it lies in front of the rectum and behind the bladder. A thin fibrous septum separates it from the rectum. The prostate lies below it.

Question 7590. The seminal vesicle is a coiled tube that is about how long: about five millimeters, about five centimeters, about fifteen centimeters, or about forty-five centimeters? The answer is about five centimeters. It is much shorter than the vas deferens, which is about forty-five centimeters. Its coiled structure gives it a lobulated surface.

Question 7591. Lymph from the seminal vesicle drains mainly to which nodes: the superficial inguinal nodes, the para-aortic nodes, the internal iliac nodes, or the deep cervical nodes? The answer is the internal iliac nodes. The seminal vesicle is a pelvic organ and follows the pelvic pattern of drainage. The testis drains to the para-aortic nodes instead.

Question 7592. A man has a very small volume of semen, and the fluid contains no fructose. Which structure is most likely blocked on both sides: the vas deferens, the ejaculatory duct, the urethra, or the epididymis? The answer is the ejaculatory duct. Fructose comes from the seminal vesicle, whose duct joins the vas deferens to form that duct. A block there keeps the fluid of both glands out of the semen.

Question 7593. A described transrectal ultrasound shows two lobulated structures above the prostate, one on each side of the midline, each with a coiled and cystic texture. Which structures are shown? The answer is the seminal vesicles. They lie behind the base of the bladder and above the prostate. Their lobulated pattern reflects the coiled tube inside.

Question 7594. A described MRI of the pelvis shows a cyst replacing the seminal vesicle on one side, and the kidney on that same side is absent. Which developmental duct links the two findings? The answer is the mesonephric duct. The seminal vesicle arises from it, and the ureteric bud that forms the kidney also sprouts from it. A fault there can affect both.

Question 7595. The ampulla of the vas deferens and the seminal vesicle lie close together behind the bladder. Which lies medial to the other, and which structure passes just above the seminal vesicle? The answer is that the ampulla lies medial to the seminal vesicle, and the ureter passes above and medial to it.

Question 7596. A constructed illustration: during removal of the rectum, the surgeon must separate it from the bladder and the seminal vesicles, and a thin fibrous layer between them is divided. Which structures lie in front of that layer? The answer is the seminal vesicles, the ampullae of the vas deferens and the prostate. The layer is the rectovesical septum, which keeps the two surfaces apart.

Question 7597. True or false: the seminal vesicles store sperm until ejaculation. The answer is false. Sperm are stored mainly in the tail of the epididymis, where they are held in an inactive state. The seminal vesicles add a fructose-rich, alkaline fluid to the semen, but they are not a reservoir for sperm.

Question 7598. Which of these pairs belongs together: the seminal vesicle with the para-aortic nodes, the seminal vesicle with the internal iliac nodes, the testis with the internal iliac nodes, or the scrotal skin with the para-aortic nodes? The answer is the seminal vesicle with the internal iliac nodes. It is a pelvic organ. The testis drains to the para-aortic nodes.

Question 7599. Name two structures that lie immediately above the prostate and behind the base of the bladder, spoken as a list. The answer is the seminal vesicles and the ampullae of the vas deferens. Each ampulla joins the duct of the seminal vesicle on its own side to form the ejaculatory duct. Those ducts then pass downward through the prostate.

Question 7600. In a described sagittal section of the male pelvis, one structure lies just behind the base of the bladder and just in front of the rectum, with the prostate below it and the rectovesical pouch above it. Which structure is it, and where does it lie? The answer is the seminal vesicle, and it lies below the peritoneum, outside the peritoneal cavity.

To summarize, the testis is covered by the tunica vaginalis, a remnant of the processus vaginalis, and by the tunica albuginea, whose posterior thickening forms the mediastinum testis and holds the rete testis within it. The seminiferous tubules are lined by germ cells and sustentacular cells, the interstitial cells between them make testosterone, and sperm leave by the straight tubules, the rete testis and the efferent ductules into the head of the epididymis. The epididymis lies on the posterior border of the gland, matures and stores sperm, and continues at its tail as the vas deferens, which ascends in the spermatic cord, crosses the ureter above the seminal vesicle and joins the duct of that gland to form the ejaculatory duct. The testis and the epididymis drain to the para-aortic nodes, the scrotal skin to the superficial inguinal nodes, and the seminal vesicles to the internal iliac nodes. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 77 — Male Reproductive Anatomy, Part Two

This chapter continues the male reproductive system and takes up three parts in turn: the prostate gland, the penis and the scrotum. It begins deep in the pelvis with the prostate, its lobes and zones, its capsule and its relations to the bladder and the rectum, and then follows the ejaculatory ducts and the prostatic urethra through it. From there it moves to the penis, its erectile bodies, its coverings and the vessels and nerves of its dorsal bundle, and it ends with the scrotum, its layers, the spermatic cord and the descent of the testis. It holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The structures described here lie close together in a small space, and their relations are what the questions test. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 7601. Which gland of the male pelvis lies immediately below the neck of the urinary bladder and surrounds the first part of the urethra? The answer is the prostate gland. Its base faces upward against the bladder and its apex points downward onto the pelvic floor. It lies behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the rectum.

Question 7602. Which of these structures lies immediately in front of the rectum in the male: the prostate gland, the urinary bladder, the seminal vesicle, or the ductus deferens? The answer is the prostate gland. The bladder sits above it, and the seminal vesicles lie above and behind its base. A thin fascial layer separates the gland from the rectum behind.

Question 7603. Which pad of fat and which venous plexus lie between the prostate gland and the pubic symphysis? The answer is a pad of retropubic fat and the prostatic venous plexus. The fat fills the small space behind the pubic bone. The plexus lies against the front and the sides of the gland.

Question 7604. What are the two ends of the prostate gland called, and which way does each one face? The answer is the base above and the apex below. The base is broad and lies against the neck of the urinary bladder. The apex is narrow and rests on the perineal membrane, where the urethra leaves the gland.

Question 7605. Which lobe of the prostate gland lies behind the urethra and between the two ejaculatory ducts, and can project upward into the bladder? The answer is the median lobe. It is the part most often blamed for a rounded filling defect at the base of the bladder. The right and the left lobes lie on either side of the urethra.

Question 7606. A described transverse section through the base of the bladder shows a smooth rounded elevation pushing up from below, with the urethra in front of it. Which part of the prostate gland is shown? The answer is the median lobe, enlarged upward into the bladder. The urethra lies in front of it and the ejaculatory ducts pass behind and below it.

Question 7607. Which zone of the prostate gland surrounds the first part of the urethra and is the usual site of benign prostatic hyperplasia? The answer is the transition zone. It is a small zone, making up about one tenth of the glandular tissue. Because it encircles the urethra, its enlargement narrows the stream of urine.

Question 7608. Which zone of the prostate gland occupies the posterior and lateral parts of the gland and is the usual site of carcinoma: the central zone, the transition zone, the peripheral zone, or the anterior fibromuscular stroma? The answer is the peripheral zone. It holds about seventy per cent of the glandular tissue. It is the part felt through the front wall of the rectum.

Question 7609. Which paired glands lie above and behind the base of the prostate gland, one on each side of the ampulla of the ductus deferens? The answer is the seminal vesicles. Each is a coiled tube about 5 centimeters long. Its duct joins the ampulla of the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct.

Question 7610. A constructed illustration: an older man reports that his stream of urine has become weak and that he must rise at night. Which zone of the prostate gland is enlarging to narrow the urethra? The answer is the transition zone, in benign prostatic hyperplasia. The enlarged tissue squeezes the prostatic urethra from all sides. The management of the condition belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7611. Which zone of the prostate gland forms a cone around the ejaculatory ducts: the anterior fibromuscular stroma, the central zone, the posterior lobe, or the median lobe? The answer is the central zone. It surrounds the ejaculatory ducts as they pass through the gland. Its ducts open beside the seminal colliculus.

Question 7612. Which part of the prostate gland is a sheet of fibromuscular tissue lying in front of the urethra, with almost no glandular tissue in it? The answer is the anterior fibromuscular stroma. It forms the front surface of the gland and blends with the capsule. Because it is not glandular, it takes little part in either hyperplasia or carcinoma.

Question 7613. True or false: the prostate gland lies behind the pubic symphysis and below the urinary bladder. The answer is true. The gland occupies the floor of the pelvis in the midline. The pubic bone lies in front of it and the bladder above it, and the rectum lies behind it.

Question 7614. Which of these pairs belongs together: the transition zone with the region around the proximal urethra, the peripheral zone with the region around the ejaculatory ducts, the central zone with the front of the gland, or the anterior fibromuscular stroma with the region behind the rectum? The answer is the transition zone with the region around the proximal urethra. The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts.

Question 7615. Which fibrous coat wraps the prostate gland and sends septa into its substance? The answer is the prostatic capsule. It is a firm fibrous sheath that encloses the gland and blends with the surrounding pelvic fascia. The septa carry vessels and ducts into the glandular tissue.

Question 7616. Which nerves run in the posterolateral corner of the prostate gland, beside the capsule, and what function do they serve? The answer is the cavernous nerves, which carry the fibers for erection. They lie in the neurovascular bundles on each side. Their position is the reason surgeons try to spare that corner of the gland.

Question 7617. A constructed illustration: after an operation on the prostate gland, a man can no longer achieve an erection, though his sensation and his urine stream are normal. Which structures lying against the posterolateral surface of the gland were most likely injured? The answer is the cavernous nerves in the neurovascular bundles. They run beside the capsule toward the penis.

Question 7618. A described midline section through the prostate gland shows two slender tubes passing downward and forward through its posterior part to open beside a small midline pouch. Which tubes are shown and where do they end? The answer is the ejaculatory ducts, opening at the seminal colliculus. Each is formed by the union of the ductus deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle.

Question 7619. What is the name of the rounded elevation on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra, at which the ejaculatory ducts open? The answer is the seminal colliculus. It sits on a raised ridge called the urethral crest. The prostatic sinuses lie on each side of it, and the prostatic ducts open into them.

Question 7620. Which of these structures is a small blind pouch on the seminal colliculus, taken to be a remnant of the paramesonephric duct: the prostatic utricle, the prostatic sinus, the urethral crest, or the ampulla of the ductus deferens? The answer is the prostatic utricle. It opens between the two ejaculatory duct openings. In the female the same duct system forms the uterus.

Question 7621. Name two features seen on the lining of the prostatic part of the urethra, spoken as a list. The answer is the urethral crest with the seminal colliculus, and the prostatic sinuses on each side. The crest is a midline ridge on the posterior wall, and the colliculus is the rounded swelling on it.

Question 7622. Where do the ducts of the prostate gland open: on the seminal colliculus, into the prostatic sinuses, into the urinary bladder, or into the ejaculatory ducts? The answer is into the prostatic sinuses. Those are the grooves on each side of the urethral crest. About twenty small ducts open there, and none of them opens into the bladder.

Question 7623. In a described sagittal section, the ejaculatory duct enters the prostate gland at its posterior surface and ends at the seminal colliculus. In which direction does it run through the gland, and what does it pass behind? The answer is downward and forward, passing behind the median lobe. The two ducts converge as they approach the colliculus.

Question 7624. Which thin fascial layer lies between the posterior surface of the prostate gland and the front of the rectum? The answer is the rectovesical fascia. It separates the gland from the rectum and keeps the two planes distinct. In front of it runs the prostate, and behind it the rectal wall.

Question 7625. A constructed illustration: a firm nodule is felt through the front wall of the rectum on the posterior surface of an enlarged prostate gland, and the median sulcus is lost on that side. Which zone of the gland and which surface does the nodule most likely occupy? The answer is the peripheral zone of the posterior surface, where carcinoma usually begins.

Question 7626. Which artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery, is the main supply to the prostate gland? The answer is the inferior vesical artery. It reaches the gland along its posterolateral surface. The artery varies: it may arise instead from the internal pudendal artery or from the middle rectal artery.

Question 7627. The prostatic venous plexus drains into which veins: the internal iliac veins, the external iliac veins, the inferior mesenteric vein, or the superficial inguinal veins? The answer is the internal iliac veins. The plexus lies around the sides and the base of the gland. It also communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus inside the spinal canal.

Question 7628. A described cast of the pelvic veins shows a rich network wrapped around the base and the sides of the prostate gland, receiving a midline vein from the dorsum of the penis. Which two sets of vessels are shown? The answer is the prostatic venous plexus and the deep dorsal vein of the penis.

Question 7629. Why may carcinoma of the prostate gland spread early to the bones of the vertebral column: because the prostatic veins join the internal vertebral venous plexus, because the prostate lies against the spine, because its lymphatics follow the aorta, or because the gland has no capsule? The answer is that the prostatic veins join the internal vertebral venous plexus. That valveless network lets cells reach the vertebrae directly.

Question 7630. To which groups of lymph nodes does the prostate gland drain? The answer is the internal iliac nodes and the sacral nodes. A few vessels also reach the obturator nodes along the pelvic wall. The drainage follows the internal iliac vessels rather than the inguinal nodes.

Question 7631. True or false: lymph from the prostate gland drains to the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin. The answer is false. The gland drains to the internal iliac and sacral nodes deep in the pelvis. Only the skin of the scrotum and the skin of the penis drain to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Question 7632. Which of these pairs belongs together: the inferior vesical artery with the prostate gland, the internal pudendal artery with the prostate gland, the external iliac vein with the prostate gland, or the superficial inguinal nodes with the prostate gland? The answer is the inferior vesical artery with the prostate gland, which it supplies. The internal pudendal artery supplies the penis, and the gland drains to the internal iliac nodes.

Question 7633. From which plexus do the nerves to the prostate gland reach it: the inferior hypogastric plexus, the lumbar plexus, the sacral plexus, or the celiac plexus? The answer is the inferior hypogastric plexus. It lies beside the rectum and the bladder. Its sympathetic fibers tighten the smooth muscle, and its parasympathetic fibers drive secretion.

Question 7634. Sympathetic fibers to the prostate gland arise from which segments of the spinal cord, and along which nerves do they travel? The answer is the first and second lumbar segments, travelling by way of the hypogastric nerves. They reach the inferior hypogastric plexus beside the rectum. The parasympathetic fibers come instead from the second to the fourth sacral segments.

Question 7635. A described specimen of the prostate gland is sliced across, and a firm pale nodule sits in the posterior part of the gland, well away from the urethra. Which zone is involved, and why is the urethra undistorted? The answer is the peripheral zone, which lies behind and to the sides. Carcinoma there grows away from the urethra, so it may cause no urinary symptoms until it is large.

Question 7636. Why does benign prostatic hyperplasia narrow the urine stream while an early carcinoma in the same gland often does not: the hyperplasia surrounds the urethra, the hyperplasia always blocks the bladder neck, the carcinoma never grows, or the carcinoma lies in the capsule? The answer is that the hyperplasia surrounds the urethra. It arises in the transition zone, which encircles the tube. Carcinoma begins in the peripheral zone, far away.

Question 7637. Against which structure does the base of the prostate gland rest, and on which does its apex sit: the base on the bladder and the apex on the perineal membrane, the base on the perineal membrane and the apex on the bladder, both on the bladder, or both on the rectum? The answer is the base on the bladder and the apex on the perineal membrane. The urethra leaves at the apex.

Question 7638. A constructed illustration: a man cannot pass urine, and a tender swelling is felt above the pubic symphysis. Which part of the prostate gland is most likely pressing on the urethra? The answer is the transition zone and the median lobe, enlarged in benign prostatic hyperplasia. Relief of the obstruction belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7639. A described specimen of an adult prostate gland measures about 3 centimeters long, 4 centimeters wide and 2 centimeters thick. Which organ of the male pelvis is this, and how does an enlarged gland differ from it? The answer is the prostate gland, about the size of a walnut. In hyperplasia it may grow to several times that size, mainly through the transition zone.

Question 7640. A described section shows the prostatic urethra as a wide slit running through the gland, with a ridge on its posterior wall and two slender ducts opening beside a small pouch. Which part of the male urethra is shown, and why is it the widest? The answer is the prostatic part, the widest and most dilatable part of the tube. It is about 3 centimeters long.

Question 7641. Which three masses of erectile tissue make up the body of the penis? The answer is the two corpora cavernosa and the single corpus spongiosum. The two corpora cavernosa lie side by side on the dorsal side. The corpus spongiosum lies in the midline on the ventral side and carries the urethra.

Question 7642. Which of the erectile bodies of the penis contains the spongy part of the urethra: the right corpus cavernosum, the left corpus cavernosum, the corpus spongiosum, or the glans? The answer is the corpus spongiosum. It lies below the two corpora cavernosa and widens at both ends. The urethra runs through its whole length.

Question 7643. A described transverse section of the penis shows two large rounded bodies side by side above a smaller rounded body, each wrapped in a tough white coat. Which structures are shown? The answer is the two corpora cavernosa above and the corpus spongiosum below. The tough white coat around each is the tunica albuginea.

Question 7644. Which erectile body of the penis lies in the midline, and which side of the penis does it occupy? The answer is the corpus spongiosum, and it occupies the ventral side. The two corpora cavernosa lie above it on the dorsal side. The urethra runs inside the corpus spongiosum.

Question 7645. What is the expanded lower end of the corpus spongiosum called, and what is its expanded upper end called? The answer is the bulb below and the glans above. The bulb lies in the root of the penis and receives the urethra. The glans forms the tip of the penis and covers the ends of the corpora cavernosa.

Question 7646. Which part of the penis forms the root and is fixed to the ischiopubic rami on each side: the glans, the bulb, the crura of the corpora cavernosa, or the prepuce? The answer is the crura of the corpora cavernosa, one on each side. The bulb of the corpus spongiosum lies between them in the midline. The glans and the prepuce belong to the free part.

Question 7647. A constructed illustration: a man falls astride a bar and blood collects in the penis and the perineum, while the urethra is intact. Which erectile bodies lie against the bone and were most likely injured? The answer is the crura of the corpora cavernosa, fixed to the ischiopubic rami. The bulb of the corpus spongiosum lies between them and may be spared.

Question 7648. What is the name of the fold of skin that covers the glans of the penis, and what is the small fold beneath it called? The answer is the prepuce, with the frenulum beneath the glans. The prepuce is a double layer of skin that can be drawn back over the glans. The frenulum is the midline fold that tethers it.

Question 7649. Which fascia wraps the two corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum together and carries the dorsal vessels and nerves: the superficial fascia, the deep fascia of the penis, the tunica albuginea, or the dartos? The answer is the deep fascia of the penis. The tunica albuginea lies deeper still, around each erectile body separately.

Question 7650. A described cross section shows a tough fibrous envelope around each erectile body, a common envelope around all three, and a bundle of vessels and nerves lying in the groove between the two upper bodies. Which envelopes and which bundle are shown? The answer is the tunica albuginea around each body, the deep fascia around all three, and the dorsal neurovascular bundle.

Question 7651. Which vein lies in the midline of the dorsum of the penis, deep to the deep fascia and above the two dorsal arteries? The answer is the deep dorsal vein of the penis. It lies in the groove between the two corpora cavernosa. Behind the penis it passes under the pubic symphysis and drains into the prostatic venous plexus.

Question 7652. Which artery runs inside the corpus cavernosum and supplies the erectile tissue: the dorsal artery of the penis, the deep artery of the penis, the artery of the bulb, or the external pudendal artery? The answer is the deep artery of the penis, one in each corpus cavernosum. Its coiled helicine branches open into the spaces of the erectile tissue. The dorsal artery supplies the skin and the glans.

Question 7653. Which nerve carries sensation from the skin of the penis, and from which nerve does it arise? The answer is the dorsal nerve of the penis, from the pudendal nerve. It runs in the dorsal neurovascular bundle, deep to the deep fascia and lateral to the deep dorsal vein. It gives branches to the glans and the prepuce.

Question 7654. True or false: the skin of the shaft of the penis drains its lymph to the superficial inguinal nodes. The answer is true. The skin and the prepuce drain to the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin. The erectile tissue and the glans drain deeper, to the deep inguinal nodes and the internal iliac nodes.

Question 7655. Which of these pairs belongs together: the glans with the corpus spongiosum, the glans with the corpus cavernosum, the bulb with the corpus cavernosum, or the crus with the corpus spongiosum? The answer is the glans with the corpus spongiosum, whose upper end it forms. The bulb is the lower end of the same body, and each crus belongs to a corpus cavernosum.

Question 7656. Which statement about the tunica albuginea of the penis is correct: it surrounds each erectile body separately, it surrounds all three bodies together, it lies outside the deep fascia, or it contains the dorsal nerve? The answer is that it surrounds each erectile body separately. It is a tough fibrous coat that keeps the erectile tissue in shape. The deep fascia wraps all three bodies together.

Question 7657. Which suspensory structure runs from the front of the pubic symphysis to the deep fascia of the penis and holds the organ against the front of the pelvis? The answer is the suspensory ligament of the penis. It is a triangular band of fibrous tissue. A looser fold, the fundiform ligament, comes from the front of the sheath of the rectus muscle.

Question 7658. A described dissection of the free part of the penis shows the skin and the superficial fascia removed, leaving a tough sleeve that must be opened to reach a vein, two arteries and two nerves. What is that sleeve, and what lies inside it? The answer is the deep fascia of the penis, containing the deep dorsal vein, the two dorsal arteries and the two dorsal nerves.

Question 7659. Which structure lies immediately deep to the pubic symphysis as the penis passes forward and drains the blood from the erectile tissue into the prostatic venous plexus? The answer is the deep dorsal vein of the penis. It passes below the symphysis and behind the suspensory ligament. There it joins the prostatic venous plexus.

Question 7660. A constructed illustration: during erection a sudden pain is felt in the shaft, the penis swells into a dark bruise on one side, and it curves away from that side. Which structure has most likely torn? The answer is the tunica albuginea of one corpus cavernosum. Blood then escapes into the tissue around it. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7661. Which statement about the external urethral orifice is correct: it lies at the tip of the glans and is the narrowest point, it lies at the base of the glans and is the widest, it lies in the bulb, or it lies at the neck of the bladder? The answer is that it lies at the tip of the glans and is the narrowest point. The spongy part behind it is wider.

Question 7662. Which two muscles of the root of the penis cover the crura and the bulb? The answer is the ischiocavernosus over each crus and the bulbospongiosus over the bulb. They lie in the superficial perineal pouch. They help to empty the urethra and to maintain erection.

Question 7663. Name the three parts into which the penis is divided, spoken as a list. The answer is the root, the body and the glans. The root is fixed to the pelvis and holds the crura and the bulb. The body is the free shaft, and the glans is the expanded tip covered by the prepuce.

Question 7664. Which of these structures does not lie in the dorsal neurovascular bundle of the penis: the deep dorsal vein, the dorsal artery, the dorsal nerve, or the deep artery of the penis? The answer is the deep artery of the penis. It runs inside each corpus cavernosum, not on the dorsum. The other three lie in the groove between the two corpora cavernosa.

Question 7665. In a described transverse section of the penis, how do the two corpora cavernosa lie relative to the corpus spongiosum, and where does the urethra lie? The answer is that the two corpora cavernosa lie dorsally, side by side, and the corpus spongiosum lies ventrally in the midline. The urethra lies inside the corpus spongiosum. The deep dorsal vein lies in the groove between the two dorsal bodies.

Question 7666. Which ligament of the penis is the deeper of the two, and from which structure does it arise? The answer is the suspensory ligament, arising from the front of the pubic symphysis. It runs to the deep fascia of the penis. The more superficial fold is the fundiform ligament, which comes from the sheath of the rectus abdominis muscle.

Question 7667. Which nerve provides the parasympathetic fibers that produce erection of the penis, and from which plexus does it come? The answer is the cavernous nerve, from the inferior hypogastric plexus. It travels beside the prostate gland and the seminal vesicles. Its fibers relax the smooth muscle of the helicine arteries.

Question 7668. Which statement about the venous drainage of the penis is correct: the deep dorsal vein drains to the prostatic plexus, both sets of veins drain to the inferior vena cava, both drain to the internal iliac veins, or every vein lies deep to the deep fascia? The answer is that the deep dorsal vein drains to the prostatic plexus. The superficial veins drain to the external pudendal veins.

Question 7669. A described specimen shows a penis in which the urethra opens on the underside of the shaft, well behind the glans, and the prepuce hangs over the tip as a hood. Which developmental defect is shown, and which folds failed to close? The answer is hypospadias, from failure of the urogenital folds to fuse along the ventral surface.

Question 7670. Which glands open into the spongy part of the urethra within the bulb of the penis: the bulbourethral glands, the prostate gland, the seminal vesicles, or the glands of the prepuce? The answer is the bulbourethral glands, one on each side. Their long ducts open into the first part of the spongy urethra. The prostate gland opens instead into the prostatic urethra.

Question 7671. True or false: the lymphatic drainage of the glans of the penis follows the same path as that of the skin of the shaft. The answer is false. The skin and the prepuce drain to the superficial inguinal nodes. The glans and the erectile tissue drain to the deep inguinal nodes and onward to the internal iliac nodes.

Question 7672. Which of these pairs belongs together: the dorsal nerve with sensation from the glans, the cavernous nerve with sensation from the glans, the deep dorsal vein with erection, or the deep artery with the drainage of the glans? The answer is the dorsal nerve with sensation from the glans. The cavernous nerve controls erection, the deep dorsal vein drains the erectile tissue, and the deep artery supplies it.

Question 7673. A constructed illustration: a man has no sensation over the glans of the penis after a perineal injury, though he can still achieve an erection. Which nerve has been injured, and why does erection remain? The answer is the dorsal nerve, a somatic sensory branch of the pudendal nerve. The cavernous nerves that produce erection arise from the pelvic plexus and may be spared.

Question 7674. A constructed illustration: urine leaks from the underside of the penis after a straddle injury, and the perineum is swollen with dark blood above the deep fascia. Which part of the urethra is most likely torn? The answer is the spongy urethra within the corpus spongiosum. The blood and urine then follow the space deep to the deep fascia.

Question 7675. A described radiograph after a study with a contrast agent shows the urethra narrowing at the tip of the glans and widening just behind it and again within the prostate gland. Which three points of the male urethra are illustrated? The answer is the external urethral orifice, which is narrowest, the navicular fossa, which is wide, and the prostatic part, which is widest.

Question 7676. What is the name of the pouch of skin that hangs below the root of the penis and holds the two testes? The answer is the scrotum. Its skin is pigmented and wrinkled and carries a midline ridge. Each testis lies in its own compartment inside it.

Question 7677. Which structure divides the scrotum into two compartments, one for each testis: the scrotal septum, the dartos muscle, the tunica vaginalis, or the raphe? The answer is the scrotal septum. It runs in the midline between the two testes. The raphe is the ridge seen on the outside of the skin.

Question 7678. A described section across the scrotum shows two oval bodies side by side, each wrapped in a serous sac and separated by a midline wall of tissue. What is the wall, and what are the sacs? The answer is the scrotal septum and the two tunica vaginalis sacs. Each sac is a closed serous space around one testis, left behind by the peritoneum.

Question 7679. Which thin serous sac covers the front and the sides of the testis, and from which membrane is it derived? The answer is the tunica vaginalis, derived from the peritoneum. Its visceral layer covers the testis and its parietal layer lines the scrotum. Between them lies a small space holding a film of fluid.

Question 7680. Which layer of the scrotum is a network of smooth muscle in the superficial fascia, with no fat in it: the dartos muscle, the cremaster muscle, the external spermatic fascia, or the internal spermatic fascia? The answer is the dartos muscle. Its contraction wrinkles the skin and raises the testes. The absence of fat helps the scrotum lose heat.

Question 7681. Which muscle of the spermatic cord is derived from the internal oblique muscle of the abdomen and raises the testis? The answer is the cremaster muscle. Its fibers form a series of loops around the cord and the testis. The external spermatic fascia, in contrast, comes from the external oblique muscle.

Question 7682. A constructed illustration: a young man is struck on the scrotum during sport and the whole pouch fills with dark blood. Which layer, continuous with the superficial fascia of the abdomen, allows the blood to spread widely? The answer is the dartos layer of the scrotum. Its loose tissue and its lack of fat let fluid track freely.

Question 7683. Which duct leaves the back of the testis and carries sperm upward through the inguinal canal toward the prostate gland? The answer is the ductus deferens. It begins at the tail of the epididymis and runs up in the spermatic cord. Behind the bladder it widens as the ampulla and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle.

Question 7684. Which of these arteries supplies the testis: the testicular artery from the abdominal aorta, the cremasteric artery from the inferior epigastric artery, the artery to the ductus deferens, or the external pudendal artery? The answer is the testicular artery, arising from the abdominal aorta at the level of the second lumbar vertebra. The other three supply the coverings and the duct.

Question 7685. A described cast of the vessels of the spermatic cord shows a long artery from above, a coil of veins around it, and a small artery joining the duct behind. Which three sets of vessels are shown? The answer is the testicular artery, the pampiniform plexus of veins, and the artery to the ductus deferens. The vein coil lies in front of the duct.

Question 7686. Which nerve supplies the skin of the front of the scrotum: the ilioinguinal nerve, the pudendal nerve, the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, or the obturator nerve? The answer is the ilioinguinal nerve. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the skin next to it. The back of the scrotum is supplied by branches of the pudendal nerve.

Question 7687. To which group of lymph nodes does the skin of the scrotum drain? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin. They lie just below the inguinal ligament. The testis inside the scrotum drains to a different set of nodes, high in the abdomen.

Question 7688. A constructed illustration: pain from a diseased testis is felt in the skin around the navel rather than in the groin. Which segment of the spinal cord carries the sensory fibers, and why does the pain appear there? The answer is the tenth thoracic segment, because the testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall and takes its nerve supply with it.

Question 7689. Which vein does the right testicular vein usually join: the right renal vein, the inferior vena cava, the left renal vein, or the internal iliac vein? The answer is the inferior vena cava. The left testicular vein joins the left renal vein instead. That difference is why a varicocele is far more common on the left side.

Question 7690. True or false: the testis itself drains its lymph to the superficial inguinal nodes in the groin. The answer is false. The testis follows its artery back to the para-aortic nodes beside the abdominal aorta. It is the skin of the scrotum that drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Question 7691. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ilioinguinal nerve with the front of the scrotum, the pudendal nerve with the front of the scrotum, the genitofemoral nerve with the back of the scrotum, or the obturator nerve with the scrotum? The answer is the ilioinguinal nerve with the front of the scrotum. The pudendal nerve supplies the back, and the genitofemoral nerve the adjoining skin.

Question 7692. Which coil of veins lies in the spermatic cord above the testis and acts as a countercurrent heat exchanger? The answer is the pampiniform plexus. The cool venous blood in the coil takes heat from the warm arterial blood on its way down. In this way the testis is kept 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below body temperature.

Question 7693. Which statement about the descent of the testis is correct: it passes through the inguinal canal and drags a fold of peritoneum with it, it passes behind the peritoneum, it crosses the front of the pubic symphysis, or it remains inside the abdomen? The answer is that it passes through the inguinal canal and drags a fold of peritoneum with it. That fold becomes the tunica vaginalis.
