The answer is the uterus. Its fundus lies above the openings of the tubes and its cervix projects into the vagina. The ovary lies lateral to it against the pelvic wall.

Question 7903. Which part of the uterus is the narrow lower portion that projects into the vagina and carries the external opening? The answer is the cervix. Its supravaginal part lies above the attachment of the vagina and its vaginal part lies within the canal. The internal opening lies at its junction with the body.

Question 7904. The uterine tube has four parts. Which of these is the widest and is the usual site of fertilization: the intramural part, the isthmus, the ampulla, or the infundibulum? The answer is the ampulla. It lies between the narrow isthmus and the funnel-shaped infundibulum, whose fimbriae reach toward the ovary.

Question 7905. A described radiograph of the female pelvis is taken after contrast medium fills the cavity of the uterus; the cavity appears as a narrow triangle with two fine curved lines running outward from its upper corners. Which structures do those lines represent? The answer is the uterine tubes, which carry the contrast outward toward the ovary.

Question 7906. Which almond-shaped organ lies on the lateral wall of the female pelvis, is not covered by peritoneum, and releases an oocyte in each cycle? The answer is the ovary. It sits in the ovarian fossa and is held by the mesovarium, the ovarian ligament and the suspensory ligament. Its surface is covered by germinal epithelium.

Question 7907. On the lateral wall of the female pelvis the ovary rests in a shallow depression. Which structure forms the anterior boundary of that depression, and which structures form the posterior boundary? The answer is the obliterated umbilical artery in front, with the ureter and the internal iliac artery behind. Knowing those limits keeps the ovary from being confused with the pelvic wall.

Question 7908. Which peritoneal fold drapes over the uterus, the uterine tubes and the ovaries, and is divided into the mesometrium, the mesosalpinx and the mesovarium? The answer is the broad ligament. It stretches from the sides of the uterus to the lateral pelvic wall, and the uterine artery and the ureter run in its base.

Question 7909. True or false: the round ligament of the uterus runs from the fundus through the inguinal canal and ends in the labium majus. The answer is true. It is the female remnant of the gubernaculum and helps to hold the uterus in its forward-leaning position. Unlike the ovarian ligament, it does not attach the ovary to the uterus.

Question 7910. Name the two ligaments that attach the ovary to its neighbors, one joining it to the uterus and one joining it to the pelvic wall. The answer is the ovarian ligament and the suspensory ligament of the ovary. The ovarian ligament runs from the lower pole of the ovary to the uterus, and the suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels to the pelvic wall.

Question 7911. Which expanded, funnel-shaped end of the uterine tube carries the finger-like processes that sweep over the ovary? The answer is the infundibulum. Its fimbriae open into the peritoneal cavity, so an ovum released at ovulation is already outside the closed lumen of the tube. The tube then narrows into the ampulla.

Question 7912. Which of these parts of the broad ligament is the mesentery of the uterine tube: the mesometrium, the mesosalpinx, the mesovarium, or the parametrium? The answer is the mesosalpinx. The mesometrium supports the uterus and the mesovarium suspends the ovary. The parametrium is the fibrous tissue beside the cervix, at the base of the ligament.

Question 7913. A described transverse section of the female pelvis is cut at the level of the cervix. The bladder lies in front, the rectum behind, and a firm mass of tissue sits on each side beside the cervix with a thin tube running through it. Which structures lie in that tissue? The answer is the ureters and the uterine arteries. The ureter passes below the artery.

Question 7914. In the base of the broad ligament the ureter and the uterine artery cross each other. Which of the two lies nearer the cervix, and which one passes above the other? The answer is that the ureter lies nearer the cervix and the uterine artery passes above it. That crossing is remembered as water running under a bridge.

Question 7915. A constructed illustration: during a pelvic operation a surgeon works close to the side of the cervix and later reports a watery discharge from the vagina. Which structure was most likely injured? The answer is the ureter, which passes about 2 centimeters lateral to the cervix below the uterine artery. This is an illustration only, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7916. Which vessel supplies the uterus and arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery: the ovarian artery, the uterine artery, the middle rectal artery, or the internal pudendal artery? The answer is the uterine artery. It reaches the uterus in the base of the broad ligament and joins the ovarian artery along its side. The ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta.

Question 7917. Which artery arises from the internal iliac artery, runs in the base of the broad ligament, and crosses above the ureter to reach the side of the uterus? The answer is the uterine artery. Its branches supply the uterus, the upper part of the vagina and part of the uterine tube. It meets the ovarian artery near the horn of the uterus.

Question 7918. Into which vessel does the left ovarian vein usually drain: the left renal vein, the inferior vena cava, the left internal iliac vein, or the splenic vein? The answer is the left renal vein. The right ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava. The same pattern holds for the testicular veins in the male.

Question 7919. Which of these pairs belongs together: the uterine artery with the internal iliac artery, the ovarian artery with the internal iliac artery, the internal pudendal artery with the abdominal aorta, or the middle rectal artery with the external iliac artery? The answer is the uterine artery with the internal iliac artery. The ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta.

Question 7920. Which group of lymph nodes receives the lymph from the ovary and from the testis: the superficial inguinal nodes, the deep inguinal nodes, the internal iliac nodes, or the para-aortic nodes? The answer is the para-aortic nodes. Both gonads develop high on the posterior abdominal wall and carry their lymphatics with their vessels. The scrotum drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

Question 7921. A described lymphangiogram fills a chain of nodes beside the abdominal aorta, on both sides of the great vessels just below the renal vessels. Which organs are most likely to have contributed that lymph? The answer is the ovaries or the testes, whose lymphatics follow the gonadal vessels upward to the para-aortic nodes.

Question 7922. Which erectile structure of the female lies beneath the pubic arch, is formed of two crura and a glans, and is the homologue of the penis? The answer is the clitoris. Its crura are attached to the ischiopubic rami and its glans lies at the anterior end of the vestibule. It is supplied by the dorsal nerve of the clitoris.

Question 7923. Which of these female external structures is the homologue of the scrotum: the labium minus, the labium majus, the clitoris, or the hymen? The answer is the labium majus. It is a rounded fold of skin and fat that contains the termination of the round ligament. The labium minus is a thinner fold with no scrotal counterpart.

Question 7924. Where does the greater vestibular gland lie in relation to the vaginal opening and the bulb of the vestibule? The answer is that it lies posterolateral to the vaginal opening, in the superficial perineal pouch, behind the bulb of the vestibule. Its duct opens between the hymen and the labium minus. It is also called the Bartholin gland.

Question 7925. A constructed illustration: a woman is described with a tender, rounded swelling at the posterior part of one side of the vestibule, and the duct of a small gland is thought to be blocked. Which gland is involved? The answer is the greater vestibular gland, posterolateral to the vaginal opening. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7926. Which structure is the fibromuscular mass at the center of the perineum, between the vaginal opening in front and the anus behind, into which several muscles converge: the perineal membrane, the perineal body, the urogenital diaphragm, or the ischial spine? The answer is the perineal body. The bulbospongiosus, the external anal sphincter and the transverse perineal muscles all meet there.

Question 7927. Which midline structure lies between the posterior wall of the vaginal opening and the anterior wall of the anal canal, and gives attachment to the perineal muscles? The answer is the perineal body. It is a pyramidal fibromuscular mass in the female, and the corresponding mass in the male lies between the bulb of the penis and the anal canal.

Question 7928. The perineum is described as a diamond, and a line between the two ischial tuberosities divides it into two triangles. Which triangle lies in front of that line, and which lies behind it? The answer is the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind. The urogenital triangle contains the external genitalia.

Question 7929. Which of these structures lies in the superficial perineal pouch of the female: the urethra, the greater vestibular gland, the deep transverse perineal muscle, or the internal pudendal artery? The answer is the greater vestibular gland. The pouch also holds the crura of the clitoris, the bulb of the vestibule and the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles. The urethra lies in the deep pouch.

Question 7930. A described sagittal section of the male perineum shows a thick triangular mass of tissue behind the bulb of the penis and in front of the anal canal. Which structure is it, and which muscles attach to it? The answer is the perineal body, to which the bulbospongiosus, the external anal sphincter and the transverse perineal muscles are attached. The membranous urethra passes above it.

Question 7931. Which gland lies immediately below the urinary bladder, surrounds the first part of the urethra, and is described as having a base, an apex and lobes? The answer is the prostate. Its base lies against the neck of the bladder and its apex rests on the perineal membrane. The ejaculatory ducts pass through its posterior part.

Question 7932. Which of these structures lies immediately anterior to the rectum in the male and can be felt through its wall: the urinary bladder, the prostate, the seminal vesicle, or the testis? The answer is the prostate. Its posterior surface lies against the anterior wall of the rectum, separated from it by a thin layer of fascia.

Question 7933. The ejaculatory ducts and the seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder. In which direction do the ejaculatory ducts run to reach the urethra, and which gland do they pass through? The answer is that they run forward and downward through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra. They open on the seminal colliculus, beside the prostatic utricle.

Question 7934. Which two structures join to form the ejaculatory duct: the ductus deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle, the ductus deferens and the epididymis, the seminal vesicle and the prostate, or the epididymis and the testis? The answer is the ductus deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle. The union takes place just behind the base of the bladder.

Question 7935. A constructed illustration: an older man is described with difficulty in starting the flow of urine, and the part of the gland that surrounds the urethra is enlarged. Which zone of the prostate is described? The answer is the transition zone, which narrows the prostatic urethra. The peripheral zone is the usual site of carcinoma. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7936. Which of these is the paired gland that lies behind the bladder, above the prostate and lateral to the ampulla of the ductus deferens: the bulbourethral gland, the seminal vesicle, the prostate, or the epididymis? The answer is the seminal vesicle. It secretes a fructose-rich fluid that forms part of the semen, and its duct joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct.

Question 7937. Which paired sac lies between the fundus of the urinary bladder and the rectum, above the prostate, and joins its duct to the ductus deferens? The answer is the seminal vesicle. It is about 5 centimeters long and its lower end lies close to the base of the prostate. It is separated from the rectum by the rectovesical pouch and by fascia.

Question 7938. A described magnetic resonance image of the male pelvis in the sagittal plane shows the bladder above, the rectum behind, and a small rounded gland below the bladder with a tube running through it. Which structure is the gland, and what is the tube? The answer is the prostate, with the prostatic urethra running through it.

Question 7939. Which group of lymph nodes first receives lymph from the prostate: the superficial inguinal nodes, the internal iliac and sacral nodes, the para-aortic nodes, or the deep cervical nodes? The answer is the internal iliac and sacral nodes, together with the external iliac nodes. The prostate lies deep in the pelvis, unlike the testis.

Question 7940. True or false: the prostate lies within a fibrous capsule and is separated from the rectum by a layer of fascia. The answer is true. The capsule is surrounded by a venous plexus, and the fascia behind the gland separates it from the rectum. The prostate is also supported below by the perineal membrane.

Question 7941. Which firm muscular tube carries sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct, and can be felt as a cord behind the testis? The answer is the ductus deferens. It ascends behind the testis into the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal and crosses above the ureter in the pelvis. Its wall is thick and its lumen is narrow.

Question 7942. Which of these describes the course of the ductus deferens after it leaves the scrotum: through the inguinal canal and then above the ureter, through the inguinal canal and then below the ureter, behind the rectum to the seminal vesicle, or through the obturator canal? The answer is through the inguinal canal and then above the ureter. It then forms the ampulla beside the seminal vesicle.

Question 7943. In the pelvis the ductus deferens and the ureter cross each other. Which of the two lies more laterally, and which one passes in front of the other? The answer is that the ureter lies more laterally and the ductus deferens crosses in front of it, running from lateral to medial. That places the ductus deferens above the ureter.

Question 7944. Which part of the ductus deferens lies immediately medial to the seminal vesicle and joins its duct to form the ejaculatory duct: the ampulla, the isthmus, the tail, or the infundibulum? The answer is the ampulla. It is the dilated terminal part of the ductus deferens. The isthmus belongs to the uterine tube.

Question 7945. A described radiograph is taken after contrast is injected into the ductus deferens. A thin line rises from the scrotum, loops over the brim of the pelvis, and ends in a small dilated sac beside the base of the bladder. Which structure is that sac, and which does it join? The answer is the ampulla, which joins the duct of the seminal vesicle.

Question 7946. A constructed illustration: a clinician describes palpating a firm, cord-like structure behind the testis in the upper part of the scrotum, separate from the softer vessels beside it. Which structure is it, and which canal does it enter? The answer is the ductus deferens, which enters the inguinal canal. Any procedure belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7947. Which of these is the coiled tube that lies on the posterior surface of the testis, where sperm complete their maturation: the ductus deferens, the epididymis, the seminal vesicle, or the rete testis? The answer is the epididymis. Its head, body and tail lie against the testis, and its tail continues as the ductus deferens. The rete testis lies inside the testis.

Question 7948. Which structure caps the upper pole of the testis and is formed by the coiled efferent ductules? The answer is the head of the epididymis. Its body and tail continue downward along the posterior border of the testis. The tail turns upward and becomes the ductus deferens.

Question 7949. Which serous sac surrounds the front and the sides of the testis and is derived from the peritoneum: the tunica albuginea, the tunica vaginalis, the tunica vasculosa, or the dartos? The answer is the tunica vaginalis. Its visceral layer covers the testis and its parietal layer lines the scrotum. Fluid collecting between the two layers is a hydrocele.

Question 7950. Which of these pairs belongs together: the head of the epididymis with the efferent ductules, the tail of the epididymis with the rete testis, the tunica albuginea with the peritoneum, or the dartos with the cremaster muscle? The answer is the head of the epididymis with the efferent ductules. The dartos is smooth muscle in the scrotal wall.

Question 7951. A described ultrasound image of the scrotum shows a rounded oval organ with a uniform gray texture and a small curved structure hugging its back. Which structures are shown? The answer is the testis with the epididymis behind it. A thin dark line around the front of the testis is the fluid in the tunica vaginalis. The spermatic cord is seen above them.

Question 7952. From which vessel does the testicular artery arise: the internal iliac artery, the external iliac artery, the abdominal aorta, or the inferior epigastric artery? The answer is the abdominal aorta. It arises at about the level of the second lumbar vertebra, below the renal arteries. It descends through the abdomen and the inguinal canal to reach the testis.

Question 7953. Which network of veins wraps around the testicular artery in the spermatic cord and cools the blood before it reaches the testis? The answer is the pampiniform plexus. It lies above and behind the testis and drains upward into the testicular vein. Its arrangement keeps the temperature of the testis below that of the body.

Question 7954. The right and the left testicular veins end differently. Into which vein does each drain, and why does the difference matter? The answer is that the right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava and the left into the left renal vein, which is one reason a varicocele is more common on the left.

Question 7955. A constructed illustration: a young man is described with a bag of worms felt above the left testis, worse on standing, and the veins of the cord are dilated. Which veins are described, and into which vein do they drain? The answer is the pampiniform plexus, draining into the left testicular vein. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7956. Which group receives lymph from the testis, and which from the scrotum: superficial inguinal for the testis and para-aortic for the scrotum, para-aortic for the testis and superficial inguinal for the scrotum, internal iliac for both, or para-aortic for both? The answer is para-aortic for the testis and superficial inguinal for the scrotum. The testis keeps the high lymphatics of its abdominal origin.

Question 7957. Which group of lymph nodes receives the lymph from the skin of the scrotum and the skin of the vulva? The answer is the superficial inguinal nodes. The skin of the perineum drains to the same group. The testis and the ovary, by contrast, drain to the para-aortic nodes because they began their development on the posterior abdominal wall.

Question 7958. A described cross-section of the spermatic cord shows a thick-walled tube with a tiny lumen, a plexus of thin-walled vessels around a small artery, and a thin fibrous remnant at the front. Which structures are described? The answer is the ductus deferens, the pampiniform plexus and the vestige of the processus vaginalis.

Question 7959. Which of these structures does not lie within the spermatic cord: the ductus deferens, the testicular artery, the pampiniform plexus, or the femoral nerve? The answer is the femoral nerve. It lies in the femoral triangle, well outside the cord. The cord also carries lymphatics, the artery to the ductus deferens and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.

Question 7960. True or false: the cremaster muscle is derived from the internal oblique muscle of the abdominal wall and raises the testis. The answer is true. Its fibers form the cremasteric fascia around the cord and the testis. The external spermatic fascia comes instead from the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle.

Question 7961. Which opening of the inguinal canal lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle, within the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle? The answer is the superficial inguinal ring. The deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery in the transversalis fascia. The spermatic cord passes through both openings.

Question 7962. Which of these structures is derived from the paramesonephric duct: the ductus deferens, the uterine tube, the seminal vesicle, or the epididymis? The answer is the uterine tube. The paramesonephric ducts also form the uterus, the cervix and the upper part of the vagina. The other three structures come from the mesonephric duct.

Question 7963. The gubernaculum guides the descent of the gonad. Into which two adult structures does it persist in the female, and where does each attach? The answer is the ovarian ligament and the round ligament of the uterus. The ovarian ligament joins the ovary to the uterus, and the round ligament runs through the inguinal canal to the labium majus.

Question 7964. A constructed illustration: a girl is described with a small swelling in the groin, found to be a cyst of a remnant of the peritoneal process that accompanied the round ligament. Which structure is described: a cyst of the canal of Nuck, a hydrocele, a varicocele, or a cyst of the ductus deferens? The answer is a cyst of the canal of Nuck, the homologue of the persistent processus vaginalis in the male.

Question 7965. A described section of the ovary shows a surface layer of small cells, a dense fibrous coat beneath it, and, deeper, follicles at different stages of growth, one of them large and fluid-filled. Which structures are described? The answer is the germinal epithelium, the tunica albuginea and the ovarian follicles. The large follicle is a mature vesicle, which will rupture at ovulation.

Question 7966. A constructed illustration: a woman is described with sudden lower abdominal pain, and at operation a swelling is found in the widest part of one uterine tube. Which part is described? The answer is the ampulla, the widest and longest part of the tube and the usual site of fertilization. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7967. Which of these ligaments contains the ovarian vessels and must be identified before the ovary is moved: the ovarian ligament, the round ligament, the suspensory ligament of the ovary, or the cardinal ligament? The answer is the suspensory ligament of the ovary, which runs to the lateral pelvic wall and carries the ovarian artery and vein.

Question 7968. Which fold of peritoneum runs from the lateral end of the ovary to the wall of the pelvis and carries the ovarian vessels? The answer is the suspensory ligament of the ovary, also called the infundibulopelvic ligament. It lies above the ovarian fossa. The mesovarium, by contrast, attaches the ovary to the back of the broad ligament.

Question 7969. Which two arteries anastomose along the side of the uterus and the uterine tube: the uterine and the ovarian, the ovarian and the internal pudendal, the vaginal and the middle rectal, or the uterine and the obturator? The answer is the uterine and the ovarian arteries. Their anastomosis means the uterus can receive blood from either source. The ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta.

Question 7970. Which of these pairs belongs together: the mesosalpinx with the uterine tube, the mesovarium with the uterus, the mesometrium with the ovary, or the parametrium with the rectum? The answer is the mesosalpinx with the uterine tube. The mesovarium suspends the ovary, the mesometrium supports the uterus, and the parametrium is the tissue beside the cervix.

Question 7971. A constructed illustration: a rectal examination detects a small rounded structure in front of the rectum, below the base of the bladder, with a groove across its middle. Which structure is being described, and which structure lies immediately above it? The answer is the cervix, with the body of the uterus above it. The groove is the external opening of the cervix.

Question 7972. Which two terms describe the usual position of the uterus, one for the angle between the cervix and the vagina and one for the angle between the body and the cervix: anteversion and anteflexion, retroversion and retroflexion, anteversion and retroflexion, or retroversion and anteflexion? The answer is anteversion and anteflexion. A retroverted uterus is a common variant.

Question 7973. Name the deepest recess of the vaginal fornix and say which structure lies above it. The answer is the posterior fornix, with the rectouterine pouch above it. The anterior fornix lies in front of the cervix and is related to the base of the bladder. Two lateral fornices lie beside the uterine arteries.

Question 7974. Which structure lies immediately above the posterior fornix of the vagina and is related to it: the bladder, the rectouterine pouch, the ovary, or the ureter? The answer is the rectouterine pouch. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when the body is upright. The bladder lies above the anterior fornix instead.

Question 7975. Which peritoneal pouch lies between the uterus and the rectum in the female, and which pouch lies between the bladder and the rectum in the male? The answer is the rectouterine pouch in the female and the rectovesical pouch in the male. In the female the vesicouterine pouch lies between the bladder and the uterus.

Question 7976. A constructed illustration: fluid is described collecting in the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity of a woman, and a needle is said to have reached it through the posterior wall of the vagina. Which pouch is described, and which two organs bound it? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, bounded by the uterus and the rectum. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7977. Which peritoneal pouch lies between the uterus in front and the rectum behind, and is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, also called the pouch of Douglas. It lies behind the posterior fornix of the vagina. In the male the corresponding pouch lies between the bladder and the rectum.

Question 7978. A described sagittal section of the female pelvis shows the bladder in front, the uterus tipped forward over it, and the rectum behind, with two peritoneal recesses, one shallow in front of the uterus and one deep behind it. Which recesses are they? The answer is the vesicouterine pouch in front and the rectouterine pouch behind. The rectouterine pouch is the deeper.

Question 7979. A constructed illustration: a woman is described with a collection in the pelvis that has tracked to the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity and now lies behind the cervix. Which pouch is described, and which structure forms its floor? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, whose floor is the posterior fornix of the vagina. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 7980. True or false: the ovary is covered by peritoneum in the same way as the uterus. The answer is false. The ovary is suspended within the peritoneal cavity, but its surface is covered by germinal epithelium and not by peritoneum. That is why an ovum released at ovulation passes into the peritoneal cavity before it enters the uterine tube.

Question 7981. Which ligament runs from the upper part of the uterus, through the inguinal canal, and ends in the labium majus? The answer is the round ligament of the uterus. It is the female remnant of the gubernaculum and helps to keep the uterus leaning forward. Within the canal it is accompanied by the ilioinguinal nerve and by a small artery.

Question 7982. Which structure passes through the inguinal canal in the female, and into which part of the external genitalia does it end? The answer is the round ligament, which ends in the labium majus. It leaves the pelvis at the deep ring and emerges at the superficial ring.

Question 7983. Which structure lies immediately anterior to the rectum in the female pelvis, and which lies immediately anterior to that structure? The answer is the vagina and the cervix, with the urinary bladder in front of them. The rectouterine pouch lies above, between the uterus and the rectum.

Question 7984. A described coronal magnetic resonance image of the female pelvis shows a pear-shaped organ in the midline with a narrow lower part, and two thin tubes running outward from its upper corners, each ending near a small oval structure. Which structures are shown? The answer is the uterus, the uterine tubes and the ovaries. The narrow lower part is the cervix.

Question 7985. A described specimen shows a uterus turned to one side, with a thick artery crossing a thin tube on the side of the cervix. Which two structures are shown, and which of them lies nearer the cervix? The answer is the uterine artery crossing the ureter, with the ureter nearer the cervix. The artery passes above the ureter and then turns upward along the uterus.

Question 7986. A constructed illustration: after a difficult delivery a woman is described with loss of sensation over the perineum, and the nerve that supplies it is thought to have been stretched. Which nerve is described, and where does it run? The answer is the pudendal nerve, which runs in the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7987. Which nerve supplies the muscles of the perineum and the skin of the external genitalia: the obturator nerve, the pudendal nerve, the femoral nerve, or the sciatic nerve? The answer is the pudendal nerve. It arises from the second, third and fourth sacral spinal nerves. Its branches include the inferior rectal nerve, the perineal nerve and the dorsal nerve of the penis or the clitoris.

Question 7988. A described vertical plane runs through the body from side to side and divides it into a front part and a back part. Which plane is it, and which two triangles of the perineum does it pass between? The answer is the coronal plane, between the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.

Question 7989. Which sheet of muscle forms the pelvic diaphragm and is pierced by the urethra and the anal canal? The answer is the levator ani. With the coccygeus muscle it forms the pelvic diaphragm. Its parts are named pubococcygeus, puborectalis and iliococcygeus, and it forms the floor of the pelvic cavity.

Question 7990. A described view of the pelvic floor from above shows a funnel of muscle with a slit in front and a larger opening behind, and a small muscle behind the funnel running back to the coccyx. Which structures are shown? The answer is the levator ani, with the urogenital hiatus in front and the rectal hiatus behind, and the coccygeus muscle behind it.

Question 7991. A described coronal section of the pelvis shows a thick muscle sling passing from the pubis backward around a tube in the midline, with fat-filled spaces on each side. Which muscle is shown, and what are those spaces? The answer is the levator ani, with the ischioanal fossae on each side.

Question 7992. Which of these pairs belongs together: the bulbospongiosus with the bulb of the vestibule, the ischiocavernosus with the anal canal, the external anal sphincter with the clitoris, or the levator ani with the thigh? The answer is the bulbospongiosus with the bulb of the vestibule. The ischiocavernosus covers the crus of the clitoris, and the external anal sphincter surrounds the anal canal.

Question 7993. Which muscle forms a sling behind the anal canal, is part of the levator ani, and keeps the anorectal junction in front of the tip of the coccyx? The answer is the puborectalis. It arises from the pubis on each side and passes behind the rectum. Its tone produces the anorectal angle.

Question 7994. Which of these pairs belongs together: the pudendal nerve with the external anal sphincter, the inferior rectal nerve with the bladder, the dorsal nerve of the clitoris with the uterus, or the genitofemoral nerve with the ovary? The answer is the pudendal nerve with the external anal sphincter, whose inferior rectal branch supplies the sphincter.

Question 7995. A constructed illustration: after a delivery a woman is described with a tear that extends backward through the tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus, and the muscles that meet there are separated. Which structure is torn? The answer is the perineal body, joined by the bulbospongiosus, the external anal sphincter and the transverse perineal muscles. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 7996. Which structures bound the ischioanal fossa on its medial and lateral sides: the levator ani medially and the obturator internus laterally, the obturator internus medially and the levator ani laterally, the pelvic diaphragm medially and the rectum laterally, or the perineal membrane medially and the gluteus maximus laterally? The answer is the levator ani medially and the obturator internus laterally.

Question 7997. Name the two glands of the male reproductive tract that lie behind the bladder and above the perineal membrane, and say which of them surrounds the urethra. The answer is the seminal vesicle, which lies behind the bladder, and the prostate, which surrounds the first part of the urethra. The bulbourethral glands lie in the deep perineal pouch.

Question 7998. Which small paired gland lies in the deep perineal pouch of the male and sends a duct into the bulb of the urethra? The answer is the bulbourethral gland, also called the Cowper gland. It lies beside the membranous part of the urethra and below the prostate. It is the homologue of the greater vestibular gland in the female.

Question 7999. Which zone of the prostate surrounds the urethra and is the usual site of the benign enlargement that narrows it: the peripheral zone, the central zone, the transition zone, or the anterior fibromuscular stroma? The answer is the transition zone. It surrounds the prostatic urethra above the openings of the ejaculatory ducts. The peripheral zone is the usual site of carcinoma.

Question 8000. True or false: the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein while the left ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava. The answer is false. Both the left testicular vein and the left ovarian vein drain into the left renal vein, which is one reason a varicocele is more common on the left.

To summarize, the female reproductive organs are the uterus and the vagina, with the uterine tubes, the ovaries and the broad ligament around them, while the male organs are the prostate, the seminal vesicles, the ductus deferens and the testis. The ureter passes below the uterine artery about 2 centimeters lateral to the cervix. The ovary and the testis drain to the para-aortic nodes, while the vulva and the scrotum drain to the superficial inguinal nodes, and the right gonadal vein ends in the inferior vena cava while the left ends in the left renal vein. The perineal body, the perineal membrane and the two perineal pouches give the perineum its structure, and the pudendal nerve supplies its muscles and its skin. The vaginal fornices and the two peritoneal pouches fix the relations of the uterus to the bladder and the rectum. This is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 81 — Pituitary Gland

The two small glands that govern the pace and the chemistry of the whole body sit in the neck and at the base of the brain, and this chapter examines both of them. It begins with the pituitary gland, its seat in the sella turcica, its two lobes of different origin, the hormones it releases, the portal vessels that feed it, and the crowded space that surrounds it, and it then turns to the thyroid gland, its place in the front of the neck, its blood supply, the nerves that run beside it, its development, and its follicles. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The questions are gathered in the order in which the structures meet the listener, first the pituitary gland and then the thyroid gland. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 8001. In which hollow of the skull does the pituitary gland lie, and in which bone is that hollow carved? The answer is the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone. The fossa is the deepest part of the sella turcica, the saddle-shaped depression on the upper surface of the body of the sphenoid. The gland rests in it like a pea in a cup.

Question 8002. What is the name of the small circular fold of dura mater that forms the roof of the pituitary fossa? The answer is the diaphragma sellae. It is pierced in the middle by a small opening, through which the stalk of the gland passes upward to the brain. It separates the gland below from the subarachnoid space above.

Question 8003. What is the stalk that joins the pituitary gland to the floor of the brain called: the infundibulum, the habenula, the mamillary body, or the pineal stalk? The answer is the infundibulum. It carries the nerve fibers of the hypothalamus downward and the small portal blood vessels that reach the anterior lobe.

Question 8004. Which structure lies immediately above the pituitary gland and is the first to be pressed by a tumor that grows upward out of the sella? The answer is the optic chiasm. It lies in the midline just above the diaphragma sellae. The crossing fibers from the nasal half of each retina lie lowest, so they are compressed first.

Question 8005. A constructed illustration: a person describes losing the outer half of the field of vision in each eye, while the inner halves remain clear. Which structure is being compressed, and what is that pattern called? The answer is the optic chiasm, and the pattern is bitemporal hemianopia. Growth of the gland presses on the crossing fibers drawn from the nasal half of each retina.

Question 8006. Which cranial nerve runs through the interior of the cavernous sinus rather than in its lateral wall: the third, the fourth, the sixth, or the first division of the fifth? The answer is the sixth cranial nerve. It lies free in the sinus beside the internal carotid artery. The oculomotor, the trochlear and the ophthalmic nerves lie in the wall.

Question 8007. Within the cavernous sinus, on each side of the gland, which large vessel runs forward and gives small branches to the pituitary? The answer is the internal carotid artery. It grooves the side of the body of the sphenoid and lies against the medial wall of the sinus. The gland lies medial to it.

Question 8008. Which part of the pituitary gland develops from an upward pouch of the roof of the primitive mouth? The answer is the anterior lobe, also called the adenohypophysis. The pouch, named after Rathke, is a diverticulum of surface ectoderm. It loses its connection with the mouth and becomes the glandular lobe.

Question 8009. Which part of the pituitary gland develops as a downward extension of the diencephalon? The answer is the posterior lobe, also called the neurohypophysis. It is formed from the floor of the third ventricle and remains joined to the brain by the infundibulum. This is why it is nervous tissue rather than glandular tissue.

Question 8010. Which of these hormones is stored in the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland: growth hormone, oxytocin, prolactin, or thyroid stimulating hormone? The answer is oxytocin. It is made in the hypothalamus and carried down the axons of the infundibulum for storage. The other three are made and released by the anterior lobe.

Question 8011. Which two nuclei of the hypothalamus send their axons down the infundibulum to end in the posterior lobe? The answer is the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. Their cell bodies lie in the wall of the third ventricle above the optic chiasm. Their axons form the hypothalamohypophyseal tract.

Question 8012. True or false: the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland manufactures the two hormones that it releases. The answer is false. The hormones are made in the cell bodies of the hypothalamic neurons. They travel down the axons and are stored in the posterior lobe until a nerve impulse releases them into the blood.

Question 8013. Which hormone of the anterior lobe acts on the cortex of the adrenal gland: growth hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, prolactin, or follicle stimulating hormone? The answer is adrenocorticotropic hormone. It drives the secretion of cortisol and of the adrenal androgens. Its release rises and falls with the demands of the day.

Question 8014. Which hormone of the anterior lobe tells the thyroid gland to make and release its own hormones? The answer is thyroid stimulating hormone. It is made by the thyrotroph cells of the anterior lobe. Its level in the blood falls when the thyroid hormones rise, a feedback loop the listener can picture.

Question 8015. Name two hormones of the anterior lobe that act on the gonads, spoken as a list. The answer is follicle stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone. Together they are called the gonadotropins. They drive the growth of the ovarian follicle and the production of sperm.

Question 8016. Which cell of the anterior lobe secretes prolactin: the somatotroph, the lactotroph, the thyrotroph, or the corticotroph? The answer is the lactotroph. Prolactin starts and maintains the secretion of milk after birth. Dopamine from the hypothalamus holds its release in check. The name of the cell comes from the hormone that it makes.

Question 8017. A described microscopic section of the gland shows cords and clusters of cells lying between wide blood-filled sinusoids, with no follicles and no colloid anywhere. Which part of the gland is shown? The answer is the anterior lobe. Its cells are arranged in cords and nests rather than in rounded follicles. Follicles filled with colloid belong to the thyroid gland.

Question 8018. A described radiograph of the skull in profile shows a sella turcica that is deepened and ballooned, with its floor sunk into the sphenoid sinus. Which structure has enlarged to produce that appearance? The answer is the pituitary gland, usually because of a tumor within it. The gland enlarges inside the bony cup and erodes its floor. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8019. A constructed illustration: a person has a drooping eyelid, an eye that cannot look inward, and a wide pupil on one side. Which cranial nerve is compressed as the gland enlarges sideways? The answer is the oculomotor nerve, the third cranial nerve. It lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus beside the gland.

Question 8020. Which of these pairs belongs together: thyrotropin releasing hormone with the thyrotroph, corticotropin releasing hormone with the lactotroph, growth hormone releasing hormone with the gonadotroph, or gonadotropin releasing hormone with the somatotroph? The answer is thyrotropin releasing hormone with the thyrotroph. Each releasing factor from the hypothalamus has its own target cell in the anterior lobe.

Question 8021. Immediately below the floor of the sella turcica lies which air-filled space, and why does that relation matter? The answer is the sphenoid sinus. The sinus lies between the pituitary fossa above and the nasopharynx below. Its position is what allows the gland to be reached through the nose.

Question 8022. A constructed illustration: a person with a known pituitary tumor suddenly has a severe headache, loses vision in both eyes, and becomes drowsy. What has most likely happened within the gland? The answer is bleeding into the tumor, a state called pituitary apoplexy. The swelling presses on the optic chiasm and the cavernous sinus at once. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8023. A described section through the head passes from front to back exactly in the midline and shows the pituitary gland in its fossa, with the sphenoid sinus below it and the third ventricle above it. In which plane is the section cut, and where does the gland lie? The answer is the median plane, with the gland above the sphenoid sinus and below the third ventricle.

Question 8024. A described magnetic resonance image of the head shows a small bean-shaped structure in the sella with a bright spot at its posterior end, next to the stalk. Which part of the gland is the bright spot, and what does it hold? The answer is the posterior lobe, which stores antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin. The stored hormones are bound to carrier proteins, and that is what gives the bright signal.

Question 8025. Which of these structures lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus: the optic nerve, the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, the facial nerve, or the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve. The optic nerve lies above and medial in the optic canal. The facial and hypoglossal nerves never enter the sinus at all.

Question 8026. What lies immediately above the diaphragma sellae, in the space that a pituitary tumor enters when it grows upward? The answer is the suprasellar cistern, with the optic chiasm in front of the infundibulum. The circle of Willis surrounds the region. Once a tumor breaks through the roof of the fossa it can press on these structures.

Question 8027. Which part of the adenohypophysis forms a thin collar that wraps around the infundibulum? The answer is the pars tuberalis. It is the upward extension of the anterior lobe along the stalk. The pars distalis is the main body of the lobe and the pars intermedia lies against the posterior lobe.

Question 8028. The secretory cells of the anterior lobe have no direct arterial supply of their own. By which arrangement are they fed: a portal venous system from the median eminence, a direct arterial plexus, lymphatic channels, or the cerebrospinal fluid? The answer is a portal venous system. Small arteries supply the median eminence, and the capillary bed there drains into veins that carry the hypothalamic factors down to the lobe.

Question 8029. Which artery supplies the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland: the inferior hypophyseal artery, the superior hypophyseal artery, the middle meningeal artery, or the ophthalmic artery? The answer is the inferior hypophyseal artery. It reaches the gland below the diaphragma sellae. The superior hypophyseal arteries supply the median eminence and the stalk instead.

Question 8030. True or false: the pituitary gland lies within the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone. The answer is true. The sella turcica is the saddle-shaped depression on the upper surface of the body of the sphenoid. Its deepest part, the hypophyseal fossa, holds the gland, and only the stalk leaves the fossa above.

Question 8031. A described dissection lays open the cavernous sinus on one side of the gland so that its contents can be seen. Which structure lies lowest in the lateral wall of the sinus? The answer is the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve. Above it lie the ophthalmic nerve, the trochlear nerve and the oculomotor nerve, in that order from below upward.

Question 8032. A pituitary tumor erodes downward through the floor of the sella. Which air-filled cavity does it enter first, and which fluid may then leak from the nose? The answer is the sphenoid sinus, with leakage of cerebrospinal fluid. The floor of the fossa is only a thin plate of bone above the sinus. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8033. A constructed illustration: after a difficult delivery with heavy bleeding, a woman cannot breastfeed, feels cold and tired, and loses her body hair. Which part of the gland has failed? The answer is the anterior lobe, a state called Sheehan syndrome. The gland, enlarged in pregnancy, is compressed when the blood pressure falls at delivery. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8034. Name the two hormones stored and released by the posterior lobe, spoken as a list. The answer is oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone. Oxytocin acts on the uterus and on the muscle of the breast. Antidiuretic hormone acts on the kidney to conserve water.

Question 8035. Which hormone, released from the posterior lobe, makes the collecting ducts of the kidney reabsorb water? The answer is antidiuretic hormone. Without it the kidney passes large volumes of dilute urine, a state called diabetes insipidus. The hormone is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus.

Question 8036. Which anterior lobe hormone acts on the liver and on the growth plates of the long bones: prolactin, growth hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone, or adrenocorticotropic hormone? The answer is growth hormone. It promotes growth of the skeleton in childhood and helps to regulate metabolism in adults. Its release is greatest during deep sleep.

Question 8037. A described section of the gland shows glandular tissue of one origin in front and nervous tissue of another origin behind, with a narrow cleft and scattered small cysts lying between them. Which developmental remnant is the cleft? The answer is the remnant of Rathke pouch. The pouch gives rise to the anterior lobe and normally closes off. Its remains can form a cyst.

Question 8038. Which of these pairs belongs together: the somatotroph with growth hormone, the lactotroph with thyroid stimulating hormone, the thyrotroph with prolactin, or the corticotroph with oxytocin? The answer is the somatotroph with growth hormone. Each cell type of the anterior lobe makes its own product, and the names of the cells follow the names of the hormones they make.

Question 8039. Which structure, filled with venous blood, lies on each side of the pituitary gland and receives the ophthalmic veins? The answer is the cavernous sinus. The two sinuses lie against the sides of the body of the sphenoid and connect with each other. The gland lies between them.

Question 8040. A constructed illustration: after an injury that tears the infundibulum, a person passes large volumes of dilute urine and is constantly thirsty. Which hormone has been lost, and from which part of the gland? The answer is antidiuretic hormone, from the posterior lobe. The axons that carry it are cut, so the lobe cannot release it. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8041. Which hormone causes the muscle of the breast to contract and eject milk: prolactin, oxytocin, growth hormone, or luteinizing hormone? The answer is oxytocin. Prolactin builds and maintains the secretion of milk, while oxytocin ejects it. The two hormones work together, and a listener should keep them apart.

Question 8042. What is the name of the small raised area of the hypothalamus from which the infundibulum descends and into which the superior hypophyseal arteries send their blood? The answer is the median eminence. It lies on the floor of the third ventricle behind the optic chiasm. Its capillaries are the first limb of the hypophyseal portal system.

Question 8043. A described magnetic resonance image in the midline shows a sella that is not filled by gland tissue, with the infundibulum descending into it and the gland flattened against the floor. What is this appearance called, and what does it usually mean? The answer is an empty sella. It usually means that the diaphragma sellae is incomplete and cerebrospinal fluid has pushed the gland aside.

Question 8044. A described specimen of the base of the brain shows a rounded body hanging from a stalk behind the optic chiasm and between the two halves of the circle of Willis. Which structure is shown? The answer is the pituitary gland, hanging on the infundibulum. The stalk carries the fibers and the portal vessels that connect it with the hypothalamus.

Question 8045. Which tumor of this region arises from remnants of the pouch that forms the anterior lobe and often shows flecks of calcium above the sella in a child: a craniopharyngioma, a meningioma, an acoustic neuroma, or a chordoma? The answer is a craniopharyngioma. It grows above the diaphragma sellae and presses on the optic chiasm. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8046. What general name is given to the pituitary gland together with its stalk, the name used for the whole structure at the base of the brain? The answer is the hypophysis. The glandular front part is the adenohypophysis and the nervous back part is the neurohypophysis. The name itself means the outgrowth that lies below.

Question 8047. A described cross section of the head at the level of the sella shows a small gland in the midline, a venous channel on each side of it, and a thin layer of bone below it. Which structure lies immediately on each side of the gland? The answer is the cavernous sinus. Each sinus carries the internal carotid artery and several cranial nerves in its wall and interior.

Question 8048. Which of these statements about the position of the gland is correct: it lies between the two cavernous sinuses, it lies behind the sphenoid sinus, it lies in front of the frontal sinus, or it lies within the temporal bone? The answer is that it lies between the two cavernous sinuses. The gland occupies the midline of the sella, with a sinus on either side.

Question 8049. Which thin strip of tissue lies against the back of the anterior lobe and is a remnant of the wall of the pouch that formed the gland: the pars intermedia, the pars tuberalis, the pars distalis, or the median eminence? The answer is the pars intermedia. It lies between the two lobes and is poorly developed in the adult human gland.

Question 8050. Which statement about the blood supply of the pituitary gland is correct: the anterior lobe is fed mainly by portal veins, the posterior lobe is fed mainly by portal veins, neither lobe receives blood, or both lobes are supplied only by the middle meningeal artery? The answer is that the anterior lobe is fed mainly by portal veins from the median eminence. The posterior lobe receives arterial blood directly.

Question 8051. In the front of the neck, the thyroid gland wraps around which air passage, and just below which structure does it lie? The answer is the trachea, just below the larynx. The gland sits against the front and the sides of the upper windpipe. Its two lobes lie on either side, joined across the midline.

Question 8052. What is the name of the narrow band of thyroid tissue that joins the two lobes across the midline? The answer is the isthmus. It crosses in front of the upper part of the trachea. In some glands it is absent, and in others a third lobe rises from it.

Question 8053. The isthmus of the thyroid gland usually crosses in front of which tracheal cartilages: the first and second, the second to the fourth, the fifth and sixth, or the cricoid cartilage alone? The answer is the second to the fourth. The gland is fixed at that level, which is why it rises with the larynx when a person swallows.

Question 8054. Which pair of flat muscles lies immediately in front of each lobe of the thyroid gland, covering it before the skin is reached? The answer is the sternothyroid and the sternohyoid muscles. They form the strap muscles of the neck. They must be parted to reach the gland at operation.

Question 8055. Which artery reaches the upper pole of the thyroid gland as the first branch of the external carotid artery: the superior thyroid artery, the inferior thyroid artery, the thyroidea ima artery, or the lingual artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery. It runs downward to the upper pole beside the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Question 8056. Which artery reaches the lower pole of the thyroid gland, arising from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery. It approaches the gland from below and behind, and it is closely related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve along the way.

Question 8057. In the groove between the trachea and the esophagus, which nerve runs upward toward the larynx, and how does it relate to the inferior thyroid artery? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which passes among the branches of the artery. The nerve may run in front of, behind, or between those branches, and the variation is normal.

Question 8058. A constructed illustration: after an operation on the thyroid gland, a person's voice becomes hoarse and one vocal cord does not move. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It supplies all the muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8059. A described dissection of the lower pole of the thyroid gland shows a pale nerve crossing beneath the gland and dividing into small branches beside the artery. Which structures are shown? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior thyroid artery. The two lie in the same small space and are easily confused with each other.

Question 8060. Which of these pairs belongs together: the superior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery, the inferior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery, the superior thyroid artery with the subclavian artery, or the thyroidea ima artery with the facial artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery. It is its first branch.

Question 8061. What is the name of the small third lobe of thyroid tissue that rises from the isthmus in about half of all glands? The answer is the pyramidal lobe. It is the remains of the lower end of the thyroglossal duct. It usually lies just to the left of the midline.

Question 8062. Which veins of the thyroid gland drain directly into the internal jugular vein: the superior and middle thyroid veins, the inferior thyroid veins, the thyroidea ima vein, or the vertebral veins? The answer is the superior and middle thyroid veins. The inferior thyroid veins drain into the brachiocephalic veins instead.

Question 8063. Into which veins do the inferior thyroid veins empty: the internal jugular veins, the brachiocephalic veins, the superior vena cava, or the external jugular veins? The answer is the brachiocephalic veins. They leave the lower part of the gland and run downward in front of the trachea. The left one is usually the longer of the two.

Question 8064. Which sheath lies posterolateral to each lobe of the thyroid gland, carrying the common carotid artery and the internal jugular vein? The answer is the carotid sheath. The gland lies medial to it in the front of the neck. This is why an enlarging gland can press upon the vessels within it.

Question 8065. A described microscopic section of the gland shows rounded sacs lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells and filled with pink material. What are the sacs, and what is the pink material? The answer is thyroid follicles filled with colloid. The colloid holds thyroglobulin, the store from which the thyroid hormones are built.

Question 8066. What kind of epithelium lines a thyroid follicle: simple squamous, simple cuboidal, stratified squamous, or pseudostratified columnar? The answer is simple cuboidal epithelium. The cells take iodide from the blood and build the thyroid hormones. The follicle is the unit in which the gland stores them.

Question 8067. Name the two hormones that the follicles of the thyroid gland produce. The answer is thyroxine and triiodothyronine. Both contain iodine, and triiodothyronine is the more active of the two at the cell. They raise the rate at which the body uses oxygen.

Question 8068. Name two effects of thyroid hormone on the body, spoken as a list. The answer is a raised rate of metabolism and a normal growth of the brain and skeleton. Every cell responds by using more oxygen and giving off more heat. In a child the hormone is needed for normal mental development.

Question 8069. True or false: the thyroid gland is the largest endocrine gland in the body. The answer is true. It weighs about 25 grams in a normal adult. The pituitary gland weighs only about half a gram, and the adrenal glands together weigh less than the thyroid.

Question 8070. Which cells of the thyroid gland secrete calcitonin, a hormone that lowers the level of calcium in the blood: the follicular cells, the parafollicular cells, the parathyroid cells, or the cells of the parotid gland? The answer is the parafollicular cells. They lie between the follicles and are also called the clear cells of the gland.

Question 8071. From which embryonic structure do the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland arise? The answer is the ultimobranchial body, an outgrowth of the lower pharyngeal pouches. The cells migrate into the gland from the neural crest. They are the only part of the thyroid that does not come from the thyroglossal duct.

Question 8072. On which surface of the thyroid gland do the parathyroid glands usually lie, and how many are usually present? The answer is the posterior surface, with four glands in all, two on each side. The upper pair lies near the middle of the lobe. The lower pair lies near the lower pole.

Question 8073. The inferior parathyroid gland and the thymus share which origin: the third pharyngeal pouch, the fourth pharyngeal pouch, the second pharyngeal pouch, or the thyroglossal duct? The answer is the third pharyngeal pouch. The superior parathyroid glands come from the fourth pouch. This is why the lower glands travel farther down the neck.

Question 8074. A described specimen shows the back of a thyroid lobe, where four small flattened bodies lie in the fat, two above and two below. Which structures are they, and what do they secrete? The answer is the parathyroid glands, which secrete parathyroid hormone. That hormone raises the level of calcium in the blood.

Question 8075. A constructed illustration: a person has a swelling in the front of the neck that moves up and down when swallowing and now presses on the windpipe, so that breathing is hard when lying flat. What is the swelling, and why does it move? The answer is an enlarged thyroid gland, called a goiter, which moves because the pretracheal fascia binds it to the larynx. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8076. Why does the thyroid gland rise and fall with every swallow: it is attached to the larynx by the pretracheal fascia, it lies within the carotid sheath, it is fixed to the vertebral column, or it is bound to the esophagus? The answer is that it is attached to the larynx by the pretracheal fascia.

Question 8077. Which layer of deep cervical fascia forms the false capsule that binds the thyroid gland to the larynx? The answer is the pretracheal fascia. It wraps the gland and the trachea and is attached to the thyroid cartilage. The gland's own fibrous capsule lies inside it.

Question 8078. True or false: a midline swelling of the neck that moves upward when the tongue is put out is usually a cyst of the thyroglossal duct. The answer is true. The duct once ran from the foramen cecum of the tongue down to the gland. The cyst follows the path of the duct and is pulled by the tongue.

Question 8079. A described photograph of the front of the neck shows the larynx above and, just below it, a reddish gland shaped like a butterfly whose wings curve around the sides of the windpipe. Which gland is shown? The answer is the thyroid gland. Its two lobes lie on either side of the trachea and its isthmus crosses in front.

Question 8080. Which hormone raises the rate at which the cells of the body use oxygen: insulin, thyroxine, calcitonin, or parathyroid hormone? The answer is thyroxine. It acts on almost every cell and helps to set the rate of metabolism. Calcitonin and parathyroid hormone act on calcium instead.

Question 8081. Which hormone of the thyroid gland lowers the level of calcium in the blood? The answer is calcitonin. It is made by the parafollicular cells and works against parathyroid hormone. Its effect is small in the adult but clear during the growth of a child.

Question 8082. Behind the thyroid gland lie two tubes, one directly in front of the other. Which are they, and in what order? The answer is the trachea in front and the esophagus behind it. The gland wraps the front and the sides of the airway. The tracheoesophageal groove separates the two tubes and carries the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Question 8083. A constructed illustration: a person has a swelling of the whole thyroid gland, a rapid heart rate, weight loss, and eyes that appear to bulge. What is the usual cause of this picture? The answer is Graves disease, in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid gland. The gland makes too much hormone. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8084. Which statement about papillary carcinoma of the thyroid gland is correct: it spreads mainly through lymph vessels, it spreads mainly through the blood to the bones, it arises from the parafollicular cells, or it never involves lymph nodes? The answer is that it spreads mainly through lymph vessels. Follicular carcinoma spreads through the blood instead.

Question 8085. A described microscopic section of a thyroid tumor shows branching papillae, crowded cells with clear empty-looking nuclei, and small round calcified bodies scattered through the tissue. Which tumor is described? The answer is papillary carcinoma. The calcified bodies are called psammoma bodies. It is the commonest thyroid cancer and it spreads to lymph nodes.

Question 8086. Which of these pairs belongs together: the parafollicular cell with calcitonin, the follicular cell with calcitonin, the parathyroid cell with thyroxine, or the thyrotroph with parathyroid hormone? The answer is the parafollicular cell with calcitonin. The follicular cells make thyroxine and triiodothyronine, and the parathyroid cells make parathyroid hormone.

Question 8087. A described transverse section of the neck at the level of the thyroid shows a gland wrapping the front and the sides of a cartilaginous tube, with a muscular tube behind it and a sheath holding large vessels on either side. Which structures are the two tubes? The answer is the trachea in front and the esophagus behind. The carotid sheath lies laterally on each side.

Question 8088. Which of these arteries may reach the isthmus of the thyroid gland in the midline from below: the thyroidea ima artery, the superior thyroid artery, the lingual artery, or the occipital artery? The answer is the thyroidea ima artery. It is present in only some people and may arise from the brachiocephalic trunk or from the arch of the aorta.

Question 8089. A constructed illustration: an older person has a large thyroid swelling that extends behind the sternum and now cannot lie flat because of noisy, difficult breathing. Which structure is compressed, and why does the position matter? The answer is the trachea, which is pressed by the part of the gland lying behind the sternum. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8090. Injury to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery weakens which function: the ability to shout loudly, the ability to make high-pitched sounds, the ability to swallow solid food, or the ability to feel the skin of the neck? The answer is the ability to make high-pitched sounds, because the nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle.

Question 8091. A described view of the operative field at the lower pole of the thyroid shows a red artery dividing into branches that embrace the gland, with a nerve running up in the groove behind the trachea. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery and the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Their closeness is the reason for careful dissection there.

Question 8092. In the front of the neck, between which two layers does the thyroid gland lie: between the skin and the strap muscles, between the strap muscles and the trachea, between the trachea and the esophagus, or between the esophagus and the vertebral column? The answer is between the strap muscles and the trachea, wrapped in the pretracheal fascia.

Question 8093. Which nerve lies in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus as it runs up toward the larynx? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. On the right it hooks around the subclavian artery and on the left around the arch of the aorta. It supplies almost all the muscles of the larynx.

Question 8094. A thyroglossal duct cyst is usually found where: in the midline of the neck just below the hyoid bone, at the angle of the jaw, in the floor of the mouth, or in the upper part of the chest? The answer is the midline just below the hyoid bone. It may lie anywhere along the path the duct once followed.

Question 8095. A described photograph shows a child with a smooth round swelling in the middle of the front of the neck, and the swelling rises when the child puts out the tongue. Which structure is the swelling, and from what does it come? The answer is a thyroglossal duct cyst, from a remnant of the duct by which the gland descended.

Question 8096. A constructed illustration: a young person has a lump at the base of the tongue that bleeds easily, and no thyroid tissue can be felt in the neck. What is the likely explanation? The answer is a lingual thyroid, an ectopic gland that failed to descend. The base of the tongue is the commonest ectopic site. The treating clinician decides what is done.

Question 8097. If the thyroid gland fails to descend from the floor of the pharynx during development, where does the glandular tissue remain? The answer is at the base of the tongue, which is called a lingual thyroid. The gland begins as a diverticulum at the foramen cecum. It normally travels down the front of the pharynx to the neck.

Question 8098. Which of these pairs belongs together: the thyroid gland with the pretracheal fascia, the thyroid gland with the carotid sheath, the thyroid gland with the prevertebral fascia, or the thyroid gland with the investing fascia of the neck? The answer is the thyroid gland with the pretracheal fascia, which binds it to the larynx.

Question 8099. True or false: the inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the external carotid artery. The answer is false. It arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery and runs upward to the lower pole. The superior thyroid artery is the one that comes from the external carotid artery.

Question 8100. Which statement about the blood supply of the thyroid gland is correct: the gland receives the superior and inferior thyroid arteries on each side, it receives only the inferior thyroid artery, it has no arteries and is fed by diffusion, or it is supplied by the facial artery? The answer is that it receives the superior and inferior thyroid arteries on each side, and sometimes a midline thyroidea ima artery as well.

To summarize, the pituitary gland lies in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone, roofed by the diaphragma sellae and flanked by the cavernous sinuses with the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves in their walls. Its anterior lobe comes from Rathke pouch and is fed by the hypophyseal portal veins from the median eminence, while its posterior lobe comes from the diencephalon and stores oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. The optic chiasm lies just above the gland and is the first structure compressed by a growing tumor, which is why a loss of the outer half of each visual field is such a telling sign. The thyroid gland wraps the front and sides of the trachea below the larynx, bound to the larynx by the pretracheal fascia so that it moves on swallowing, and it is supplied by the superior and inferior thyroid arteries with the recurrent laryngeal nerve running in the groove behind. Its follicles store colloid and make thyroxine and triiodothyronine, its parafollicular cells make calcitonin, and the parathyroid glands lie on its posterior surface. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 82 — Parathyroid Glands

This chapter turns to three sets of endocrine glands that are read together because they lie close to one another and work as partners. It begins with the thyroid gland, its capsule, its blood supply, its development and its relations in the front of the neck, then takes the four small parathyroid glands that sit on the posterior surface of the thyroid and control the calcium of the body fluids, and it closes with the paired adrenal glands that cap the kidneys. It holds one hundred questions, and every question states its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind from one item to the next. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 8101. Which gland lies in the front of the neck, wrapped around the upper trachea and joined across the midline by a narrow bridge of tissue? The answer is the thyroid gland. Its two lobes lie on either side of the airway and the isthmus crosses in front of it. The gland rises when the person swallows, because the pretracheal fascia binds it to the larynx.

Question 8102. Which artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery and runs down to the upper pole of the thyroid gland: the superior thyroid artery, the inferior thyroid artery, the lingual artery, or the facial artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery. It leaves the external carotid just above the carotid bifurcation and reaches the upper pole. The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

Question 8103. Which nerve lies in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus, immediately posterior to the lateral lobe of the thyroid gland? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It climbs in that groove to reach the larynx, where it supplies every laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid. The lateral lobe of the gland lies directly in front of it.

Question 8104. Which layer lies immediately deep to the strap muscles and forms a false capsule around the thyroid gland: the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, the pretracheal fascia, the prevertebral fascia, or the carotid sheath? The answer is the pretracheal fascia. It encloses the gland and binds it to the larynx, which is why the gland moves with swallowing. The strap muscles lie superficial to it.

Question 8105. What is the name of the narrow band of thyroid tissue that crosses the midline in front of the second, third and fourth tracheal rings? The answer is the isthmus. It joins the two lobes across the front of the airway and lies within the pretracheal fascia. A small pyramidal lobe may rise from it as a remnant of the thyroglossal duct.

Question 8106. A constructed illustration: after an operation on the front of the neck the voice is hoarse and one vocal cord does not move. Which nerve has most likely been injured? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It runs in the tracheoesophageal groove behind the thyroid lobe, where it is easily caught or stretched. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve lies higher and weakens the cricothyroid instead.

Question 8107. Which nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery toward the upper pole and is at risk when that artery is tied very high: the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, or the ansa cervicalis? The answer is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It supplies the cricothyroid muscle, so its injury lowers the pitch of the voice.

Question 8108. A described transverse section of the neck shows a gland wrapped across the front of the airway, with a shield-shaped cartilage above it and the trachea behind. Which gland is shown, and which cartilage lies above it? The answer is the thyroid gland, with the thyroid cartilage above it. The cricoid cartilage lies just below the thyroid cartilage.

Question 8109. True or false: the thyroid gland has a true fibrous capsule that sends septa into its substance, and a looser false capsule formed by the pretracheal fascia. The answer is true. The thin true capsule adheres closely to the gland. The pretracheal fascia lies outside it, separated from it by a small amount of loose tissue.

Question 8110. Which artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk and supplies the lower pole of the thyroid gland: the inferior thyroid artery, the superior thyroid artery, the thyroidea ima artery, or the ascending pharyngeal artery? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery. It passes behind the carotid sheath and then turns medially to reach the gland. It also supplies the parathyroid glands.

Question 8111. Which veins drain the lower part of the thyroid gland directly into the brachiocephalic vein, without joining the internal jugular vein? The answer is the inferior thyroid veins. They descend in front of the trachea in the midline. The superior and middle thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular vein instead.

Question 8112. The inferior thyroid artery passes behind the carotid sheath and then turns medially toward the gland. Which nerve does it meet on that course, and why does the crossing matter? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which may pass in front of the artery or behind it. That variable crossing makes the nerve easy to injure when the artery is tied.

Question 8113. A constructed illustration: a child has a smooth swelling in the midline of the neck that moves upward both when swallowing and when the tongue is pushed forward. From which structure does the swelling arise? The answer is a remnant of the thyroglossal duct. The duct descends from the foramen cecum of the tongue to the thyroid gland, and a cyst may form anywhere along that path.

Question 8114. Which hormone is secreted by the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland: calcitonin, thyroxine, triiodothyronine, or parathyroid hormone? The answer is calcitonin. These cells, also called C cells, lie between the follicles and lower the level of calcium in the blood. Thyroxine and triiodothyronine come from the follicular cells.
