Question 8115. A described microscopic section of an endocrine gland shows many rounded sacs lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells and filled with a pink, glassy material. Which gland is shown, and what is the material inside the sacs? The answer is the thyroid gland, with colloid inside its follicles. The colloid stores the precursor of the thyroid hormones.

Question 8116. Which pair belongs together: the superior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery, the superior thyroid artery with the subclavian artery, the inferior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery, or the inferior thyroid artery with the facial artery? The answer is the superior thyroid artery with the external carotid artery. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

Question 8117. Which small artery, present in only a minority of people, may ascend in the midline in front of the trachea to reach the isthmus of the thyroid gland: the thyroidea ima artery, the ascending cervical artery, the transverse cervical artery, or the suprascapular artery? The answer is the thyroidea ima artery. It usually arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and is a hazard in midline surgery of the neck.

Question 8118. Which ring of cartilage lies immediately above the first tracheal ring, is the only complete ring of the airway, and sits just above the isthmus of the thyroid gland? The answer is the cricoid cartilage. It is narrow at the front and broad at the back, where the arytenoid cartilages sit. The thyroid cartilage lies above it.

Question 8119. Name two arteries that supply the thyroid gland, spoken as a list. The answer is the superior thyroid artery and the inferior thyroid artery. The superior artery supplies the upper pole and comes from the external carotid. The inferior artery supplies the lower pole and the parathyroid glands as well.

Question 8120. Which vein drains the middle of the thyroid gland and opens into the internal jugular vein: the superior thyroid vein, the middle thyroid vein, the inferior thyroid vein, or the anterior jugular vein? The answer is the middle thyroid vein. It is short and runs from the lateral surface of the lobe to the internal jugular vein. The inferior thyroid veins drain into the brachiocephalic vein.

Question 8121. A constructed illustration: a person has a bleeding mass at the base of the tongue, and no thyroid tissue can be found in the usual place in the neck. What is the mass, and why is it in the tongue? The answer is a lingual thyroid, formed when the thyroglossal duct fails to descend. The gland begins at the foramen cecum and travels downward, so arrest leaves it high.

Question 8122. A described sagittal section of the neck shows a narrow tract running from the back of the tongue downward, passing in front of the hyoid bone and the laryngeal cartilages. What is this tract, and what does it become in the adult? The answer is the thyroglossal duct, which normally disappears. Its only remnant in the adult is the foramen cecum at the back of the tongue.

Question 8123. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the thyroid gland and contains the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve? The answer is the carotid sheath. It lies posterolateral to the lobe, separated from it by the pretracheal fascia. The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies between the gland and the trachea instead.

Question 8124. Which posterolateral projection of the thyroid lobe is a condensation of connective tissue that acts as a landmark for the recurrent laryngeal nerve at operation: the pyramidal lobe, the tubercle of Zuckerkandl, the isthmus, or the ligament of Berry? The answer is the tubercle of Zuckerkandl. When it is present, the nerve usually lies just medial to it.

Question 8125. In a transverse section of the neck, where does the isthmus of the thyroid gland lie relative to the trachea, and which way do the lobes extend from it? The answer is that the isthmus lies in front of the trachea, and the lobes extend backward and laterally on each side. The gland therefore wraps around the front and the sides of the airway.

Question 8126. Which small glands, usually four in number, sit on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland and produce parathyroid hormone? The answer is the parathyroid glands. There are normally two superior and two inferior glands, each about the size of a small pea. They are brownish yellow and lie within the capsule of the thyroid gland.

Question 8127. The superior parathyroid glands develop from which pharyngeal pouch: the third, the fourth, the second, or the first? The answer is the fourth pharyngeal pouch. The third pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and to the thymus, which is why an inferior gland may be found in the chest.

Question 8128. A described posterior view of the thyroid gland shows four small brownish bodies, two near the upper poles and two near the lower poles, each lying within the capsule. Which glands are shown? The answer is the parathyroid glands. Their position on the posterior border keeps them close to the inferior thyroid artery and its branches.

Question 8129. Which structure must be identified and preserved when an inferior parathyroid gland is removed, because it runs in the tracheoesophageal groove immediately medial to the gland? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It lies in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus, behind the lobe of the thyroid gland. Injury to it paralyses the muscles of the larynx.

Question 8130. Which parathyroid gland is more constant in position, and where does it usually lie? The answer is the superior gland, which usually lies near the middle of the posterior border of the thyroid lobe. It sits about one centimeter above the point where the inferior thyroid artery enters the gland.

Question 8131. Which artery provides the main blood supply to the parathyroid glands: the superior thyroid artery, the inferior thyroid artery, the thyroidea ima artery, or the ascending pharyngeal artery? The answer is the inferior thyroid artery. It supplies both pairs of glands in most people and also supplies the lower pole of the thyroid gland.

Question 8132. A constructed illustration: some days after an operation on the front of the neck, a person reports tingling around the mouth and in the hands. Which glands were most likely disturbed? The answer is the parathyroid glands, with a fall in the level of calcium in the blood. They lie within the thyroid capsule and depend on the inferior thyroid artery.

Question 8133. Which cells of the parathyroid gland are the most numerous and secrete parathyroid hormone? The answer is the chief cells, also called principal cells. They are small and pale with dark nuclei, and they lie in cords among the capillaries. The larger oxyphil cells are fewer and appear only after childhood.

Question 8134. Parathyroid hormone raises the level of which substance in the blood: calcium, phosphate, potassium, or sodium? The answer is calcium. The hormone also lowers the level of phosphate and acts on bone, on the kidney and on the gut. Its release is controlled by the calcium level in the blood itself.

Question 8135. True or false: every person has exactly four parathyroid glands. The answer is false. Four is the usual number, but five or more glands occur, and fewer than four is also possible. The glands are small, so an extra one is easily missed at operation.

Question 8136. Which pair belongs together: the superior parathyroid glands with the fourth pharyngeal pouch, the inferior parathyroid glands with the fourth pharyngeal pouch, the superior parathyroid glands with the third pharyngeal pouch, or the inferior parathyroid glands with the second pharyngeal pouch? The answer is the superior glands with the fourth pouch. The third pouch gives the inferior glands and the thymus.

Question 8137. A described microscopic section of a small gland shows cords of pale cells with dark nuclei and a rich network of capillaries, with no rounded follicles and no colloid. Which gland is shown? The answer is a parathyroid gland. Its solid cords and its store of fat cells distinguish it from the thyroid gland.

Question 8138. The inferior parathyroid gland lies near the lower pole of the thyroid gland. Which two structures are its closest important neighbors, and why does its position vary so much? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior thyroid artery. The gland develops from the third pouch with the thymus and descends far, so it may be carried into the chest.

Question 8139. Why are the inferior parathyroid glands more variable in position than the superior glands: they descend further with the thymus, they develop from the fourth pouch, they lack a blood supply, or they lie inside the thyroid substance? The answer is that they descend further with the thymus. The superior glands come from the fourth pouch and move a shorter distance.

Question 8140. Which cells of the parathyroid gland are larger, stain more deeply, and appear only after childhood? The answer is the oxyphil cells. They are thought to be inactive or degenerating chief cells and have no known separate secretion. They increase in number as a person grows older.

Question 8141. A constructed illustration: while a parathyroid gland is being removed from the tracheoesophageal groove, the surgeon works close to a nerve that supplies the larynx. Which nerve is it, and what would injury cause? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Injury causes hoarseness and weakness of the vocal cord on that side.

Question 8142. Parathyroid hormone acts on which organ to increase the reabsorption of calcium: the kidney, the liver, the spleen, or the pancreas? The answer is the kidney. There it also increases the excretion of phosphate and helps to produce the active form of vitamin D, which raises the absorption of calcium from the gut.

Question 8143. A described computed tomography section of the neck shows a rounded soft tissue mass below the lower pole of the left thyroid lobe, separate from the gland, with the esophagus medial to it. Which gland is the most likely source of the mass? The answer is an inferior parathyroid gland, which may lie below the lower pole. Its long descent with the thymus explains this position.

Question 8144. Name the two arteries that may supply a parathyroid gland, spoken as a list. The answer is the inferior thyroid artery and the superior thyroid artery. The inferior artery is the main supply in most people, and the two vessels anastomose with one another along the posterior border of the thyroid lobe.

Question 8145. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the parathyroid glands when they occupy their usual place on the posterior border of the thyroid lobe? The answer is the carotid sheath, containing the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve. The tracheoesophageal groove lies on the medial side of the gland.

Question 8146. About how large is a normal parathyroid gland, and what color is it when it is seen at operation? The answer is about 5 millimeters long, the size of a grain of rice, and brownish yellow. Its small size and its color make it easy to confuse with a lobule of fat.

Question 8147. Which statement about the blood supply of the parathyroid glands is correct: the inferior thyroid artery supplies both pairs in most people, the superior thyroid artery is the only supply, the glands are supplied by the thyroid veins, or each gland has a single end artery? The answer is that the inferior thyroid artery supplies both pairs. Fine branches also come from the superior thyroid artery, and together they form a plexus.

Question 8148. A constructed illustration: a person has a high calcium level that persists after one enlarged parathyroid gland has been removed, and no second gland can be found in the neck. Where might that gland lie? The answer is in the mediastinum, within or beside the thymus. An inferior gland develops from the third pouch with the thymus and may descend into the chest.

Question 8149. A described microscopic section of an enlarged parathyroid gland shows sheets of chief cells with almost no fat, while a normal gland has fat cells throughout its stroma. What does the loss of fat indicate? The answer is an overactive gland. Normal parathyroid tissue contains much fat, which is replaced when the gland becomes hyperplastic or adenomatous.

Question 8150. Into which vessels do the parathyroid veins drain: the thyroid veins, the internal jugular vein directly, the azygos vein, or the vertebral veins? The answer is the thyroid veins. The parathyroid glands lie within the capsule of the thyroid gland, so their small veins join the venous plexus of the thyroid gland and follow the thyroid veins.

Question 8151. From which pharyngeal pouch do the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus arise together? The answer is the third pharyngeal pouch. The two structures travel downward together, and the thymus drags the parathyroid gland with it. That shared journey explains why an inferior gland may be found in the chest.

Question 8152. True or false: the parathyroid glands lie outside the fibrous capsule of the thyroid gland and can be lifted away without opening that capsule. The answer is false. They usually lie within the capsule on the posterior surface, although they may lie outside it in some people. The capsule must be opened to reach them.

Question 8153. Which pair belongs together: parathyroid hormone with a raised calcium level, parathyroid hormone with a lowered calcium level, calcitonin with a raised calcium level, or calcitonin with a raised phosphate level? The answer is parathyroid hormone with a raised calcium level. Calcitonin does the opposite and lowers the level of calcium in the blood.

Question 8154. A described posterior view of the neck shows a small gland behind the upper pole of the thyroid lobe near the cricothyroid junction, and another gland below the lower pole near the thymus. Which glands are shown, and which one is more likely to lie in the chest? The answer is the parathyroid glands, and the lower one is the more likely.

Question 8155. Which chain of ganglia lies behind the carotid sheath, posterior to the thyroid and parathyroid glands, and may be injured in a deep dissection of the posterior border? The answer is the sympathetic trunk. Injury to it on one side causes a drooping eyelid and a constricted pupil. It lies against the prevertebral muscles.

Question 8156. Which feature distinguishes a parathyroid gland from a thyroid gland in a section: the parathyroid has follicles filled with colloid, the parathyroid has cords of cells and much fat, the parathyroid is lined by ciliated cells, or the parathyroid contains thyroid follicles? The answer is cords of cells and much fat. The thyroid gland has follicles filled with colloid.

Question 8157. Which statement about parathyroid hormone is correct: it raises the calcium level by acting on bone and kidney, it lowers the calcium level by acting on bone, it is secreted by the thyroid follicles, or it is stored in colloid? The answer is that it raises the calcium level by acting on bone and kidney. It is not stored, so it is released as it is made.

Question 8158. What is the name of the hormone secreted by the chief cells of the parathyroid gland? The answer is parathyroid hormone. It is the main regulator of the level of calcium in the blood and of the balance of calcium in bone. Its secretion rises when the calcium level in the blood falls.

Question 8159. In a transverse section of the neck at the level of the thyroid isthmus, place these structures from front to back: the parathyroid gland, the trachea, the prevertebral fascia, and the esophagus. The answer is the trachea in front, with the parathyroid gland behind and lateral to it, the esophagus behind the trachea, and the prevertebral fascia behind them all.

Question 8160. Which change in the blood does parathyroid hormone produce: it raises calcium and lowers phosphate, it raises both calcium and phosphate, it lowers calcium and raises phosphate, or it lowers both? The answer is that it raises calcium and lowers phosphate. Those two movements together keep the product of the two from rising.

Question 8161. A described section of an enlarged parathyroid gland shows two cell types, one small and pale and one large and deeply staining, with a rim of compressed normal tissue at the edge. What does that rim most likely represent? The answer is normal gland compressed by an adenoma. A rim of normal tissue favors an adenoma rather than hyperplasia.

Question 8162. Which gland lies deep to the pretracheal fascia on the posterior border of the thyroid lobe, in the space bounded by the carotid sheath on the lateral side and the tracheoesophageal groove on the medial side? The answer is a parathyroid gland. It lies within the thyroid capsule, which is why it moves with the thyroid gland when the person swallows.

Question 8163. Which two pairs of small glands lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland? The answer is the superior parathyroid glands and the inferior parathyroid glands. There are usually four in all, and each pair sits within the capsule on the posterior border of a lobe.

Question 8164. Which statement about the position of the superior parathyroid gland is correct: it lies near the cricothyroid junction, it lies below the inferior thyroid artery, it lies within the thymus, or it lies in the carotid sheath? The answer is that it lies near the cricothyroid junction, about a centimeter above the point where the inferior thyroid artery enters the gland.

Question 8165. A constructed illustration: a person has muscle spasm and tingling after an operation on the thyroid gland, and the level of calcium in the blood is low. Which structures were injured or deprived of their blood supply? The answer is the parathyroid glands. They lie within the thyroid capsule and depend on the inferior thyroid artery, so they are at risk in that operation.

Question 8166. A described operative view of the posterior surface of the thyroid lobe shows a small brown gland with a vessel entering its hilum from below and the recurrent laryngeal nerve crossing deep to it. Which gland is shown? The answer is a parathyroid gland. Its main supply is the inferior thyroid artery, which enters from below.

Question 8167. Why does removal of the thyroid gland put the parathyroid glands at risk even when the surgeon stays outside the thyroid capsule: the glands may lie outside the capsule, the glands lie in the carotid sheath, the glands are supplied by the thyroid veins, or the glands lie in the mediastinum in most people? The answer is that the glands may lie outside the capsule, and their artery is at risk as well.

Question 8168. Which pair belongs together: calcitonin with a lowered calcium level, calcitonin with a raised calcium level, parathyroid hormone with a lowered calcium level, or parathyroid hormone with a lowered phosphate level? The answer is calcitonin with a lowered calcium level. Calcitonin comes from the thyroid gland, while parathyroid hormone raises calcium and lowers phosphate.

Question 8169. Which parathyroid glands lie at the lower poles of the thyroid gland and are supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid artery? The answer is the inferior parathyroid glands. They are the more variable pair, because they develop from the third pharyngeal pouch and descend with the thymus into the upper chest.

Question 8170. Which statement about the parathyroid glands is correct: they are usually four in number and lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland, they lie in front of the thyroid gland, they are part of the thyroid gland, or they lie within the thymus in every adult? The answer is that they are usually four and lie on the posterior surface.

Question 8171. A described computed tomography section of the upper chest shows a small rounded soft tissue mass beside the arch of the aorta, below the lower pole of the thyroid gland. Which gland might this be, and why is it there? The answer is an inferior parathyroid gland that descended with the thymus into the mediastinum during development.

Question 8172. Which cell does parathyroid hormone act on first in bone, and how does that raise the level of calcium: it stimulates the osteoblast, which then activates the osteoclast, it stimulates the osteoclast directly, it inhibits the osteoblast only, or it acts on cartilage cells? The answer is that it stimulates the osteoblast, which then activates the osteoclast.

Question 8173. Which description of the actions of parathyroid hormone is correct: it raises blood calcium, lowers blood phosphate and increases the active form of vitamin D, it lowers blood calcium and raises phosphate, it acts only on bone, or it acts only on the gut? The answer is the first description. The hormone works on bone, on the kidney and on the gut together.

Question 8174. True or false: each parathyroid gland is supplied by a single end artery, so that tying one small vessel always destroys the gland. The answer is false. The glands are supplied by a fine plexus fed by the inferior and superior thyroid arteries, so flow may continue through another branch.

Question 8175. Which hormone lowers the level of calcium in the blood and comes from the thyroid gland rather than from the parathyroid glands? The answer is calcitonin, from the parafollicular cells. It inhibits the osteoclasts and so reduces the release of calcium from bone. Parathyroid hormone has the opposite effect.

Question 8176. Which paired glands sit on the upper poles of the kidneys, one on each side, in the fatty tissue behind the peritoneum? The answer is the adrenal glands, also called the suprarenal glands. Each is enclosed in the same fatty capsule and renal fascia as the kidney, so it moves with the kidney when that organ descends.

Question 8177. Which vein drains the right adrenal gland: the right renal vein, the inferior vena cava, the right hepatic vein, or the azygos vein? The answer is the inferior vena cava. The right adrenal vein is very short and enters the vena cava directly, which makes it easy to tear. The left vein drains into the left renal vein.

Question 8178. Which large vein lies immediately in front of and medial to the right adrenal gland? The answer is the inferior vena cava. The right gland is squeezed between the liver above and the vena cava on its medial side, and that pressure gives it its triangular shape. The left gland lies beside the aorta instead.

Question 8179. A described transverse section of the abdomen shows a triangular gland against the back wall, with the liver in front of it and a large vein at its medial edge. Which gland is shown, and on which side of the body does it lie? The answer is the right adrenal gland, which lies on the right side.

Question 8180. Which three zones make up the cortex of the adrenal gland, from the outside inward? The answer is the zona glomerulosa, the zona fasciculata and the zona reticularis. The outer zone makes mineralocorticoids, the middle zone makes glucocorticoids, and the inner zone makes androgens.

Question 8181. A constructed illustration: a person loses weight, has low blood pressure and notices darkening of the skin, and both adrenal glands are found to be destroyed. Which part of the gland is failing, and which hormones are lacking? The answer is the cortex of the gland, with cortisol and aldosterone lacking. The management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8182. The superior suprarenal artery is a branch of which vessel: the inferior phrenic artery, the aorta, the renal artery, or the celiac trunk? The answer is the inferior phrenic artery. The middle suprarenal artery comes from the aorta, and the inferior suprarenal artery comes from the renal artery.

Question 8183. Which cells of the adrenal medulla secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine? The answer is the chromaffin cells. They lie in clusters around the medullary veins and release their hormones into the blood when the sympathetic nerves fire. The cortex around them makes steroid hormones instead.

Question 8184. True or false: the adrenal medulla develops from the same tissue as the sympathetic ganglia. The answer is true. Both come from neural crest cells, which is why the medulla behaves like a modified sympathetic ganglion. The cortex develops from a different layer altogether.

Question 8185. The cortex of the adrenal gland develops from which tissue: intermediate mesoderm, neural crest, endoderm of the gut, or ectoderm of the skin? The answer is intermediate mesoderm. The medulla comes from neural crest cells instead, so the two parts of the gland have separate origins and separate functions.

Question 8186. A described microscopic section of an adrenal gland shows an outer layer of rounded clusters, a wide middle layer of straight cords, and an inner layer of branching cords around a central mass of pale cells. Which layers are shown? The answer is the three zones of the cortex, surrounding the medulla.

Question 8187. Which structures lie immediately in front of the left adrenal gland, and what separates the gland from the peritoneal cavity? The answer is the pancreas and the spleen, with the stomach above them. The peritoneum covers the front of the gland, and the pancreas lies directly against it.

Question 8188. A constructed illustration: a person has episodes of high blood pressure and palpitations, and a tumor of the adrenal medulla is found. Which cells are involved, and where do they lie? The answer is the chromaffin cells of the medulla, in the center of the gland. They release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood.

Question 8189. The left adrenal vein drains into which vessel: the inferior vena cava, the left renal vein, the left gonadal vein, or the splenic vein? The answer is the left renal vein. The left vein is longer than the right one and joins the renal vein before that vessel crosses in front of the aorta.

Question 8190. Which pair belongs together: the zona glomerulosa with mineralocorticoids, the zona fasciculata with mineralocorticoids, the zona reticularis with glucocorticoids, or the medulla with androgens? The answer is the zona glomerulosa with mineralocorticoids. The fasciculata makes glucocorticoids, the reticularis makes androgens, and the medulla makes catecholamines.

Question 8191. A described computed tomography section of the upper abdomen shows a small triangular gland on the right, between the liver and the inferior vena cava, and a larger crescent-shaped gland on the left, medial to the spleen. Which glands are shown? The answer is the right and left adrenal glands.

Question 8192. Name two arteries that supply the adrenal gland apart from the superior suprarenal artery, spoken as a list. The answer is the middle suprarenal artery from the aorta and the inferior suprarenal artery from the renal artery. The three arteries anastomose, so the gland has no end arteries.

Question 8193. Which zone of the adrenal cortex lies immediately deep to the capsule and secretes aldosterone? The answer is the zona glomerulosa. It is the outermost and narrowest zone, arranged in rounded clusters. It is the only source of aldosterone, which controls the balance of sodium and potassium.

Question 8194. Why does the right adrenal gland have a pyramidal shape while the left is crescent-shaped: the right gland is compressed between the liver and the inferior vena cava, the left gland contains more medulla, the right gland develops from different tissue, or the left gland is covered by peritoneum? The answer is that the right gland is compressed between the liver and the vena cava.

Question 8195. A constructed illustration: during an operation on the left kidney, bleeding comes from a short vein that joins the renal vein near the hilum. Which vessel is it likely to be, and where does it drain? The answer is the left suprarenal vein. It joins the left renal vein, which then crosses in front of the aorta.

Question 8196. Which layer of fat surrounds the adrenal gland and the kidney, and which fascia encloses both of them? The answer is the perirenal fat, enclosed by the renal fascia. The adrenal gland lies within that fascia and moves with the kidney when the kidney descends toward the pelvis.

Question 8197. A described magnetic resonance imaging section shows a gland sitting on the upper pole of the left kidney, behind the pancreas and medial to the spleen. Which gland is shown, and which vein will drain it? The answer is the left adrenal gland, drained by the left suprarenal vein into the left renal vein.

Question 8198. Which zone of the adrenal cortex lies deepest, next to the medulla, and produces androgens? The answer is the zona reticularis. It is the innermost zone, arranged in branching cords around the medulla. Its androgens are weak compared with those produced by the testis.

Question 8199. Which statement about the arterial supply of the adrenal gland is correct: it is supplied by three arteries on each side, it has a single end artery, it is supplied only by the middle suprarenal artery, or it is supplied by the renal vein? The answer is that it is supplied by three arteries on each side. They anastomose freely, so tying one does not usually cause infarction.

Question 8200. A small mass of adrenal tissue is found at operation along the course of the gonadal vessels in the pelvis, separate from the gland. Which of these is it most likely to be: an adrenal rest, a parathyroid rest, a thyroid rest, or a thymic rest? The answer is an adrenal rest, which is cortical tissue carried along with the descending gonad.

To summarize, the thyroid gland lies in front of and beside the upper trachea, joined by an isthmus that crosses in front of the second to fourth tracheal rings, and it is held to the larynx by the pretracheal fascia, so it rises with swallowing. Its blood comes from the superior thyroid artery of the external carotid and the inferior thyroid artery of the thyrocervical trunk, and its veins drain to the internal jugular and brachiocephalic veins, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove immediately behind each lobe. The four parathyroid glands lie within the capsule on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, the superior pair from the fourth pharyngeal pouch and the inferior pair from the third pouch with the thymus, which is why an inferior gland may be found in the mediastinum. They are supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid artery, their chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone, and that hormone raises the level of calcium and lowers the level of phosphate by acting on bone, kidney and gut. The adrenal glands cap the upper poles of the kidneys behind the peritoneum, each with a cortex of three zones and a medulla of chromaffin cells that arises from neural crest, and while three arteries supply each gland, the right vein drains to the inferior vena cava and the left vein drains to the left renal vein. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 83 — Adrenal Glands

This chapter takes up four small endocrine structures that lie deep in the body and speak to it in chemical signals: the paired adrenal glands that cap the kidneys, the endocrine tissue in the pancreas, the pineal gland in the roof of the third ventricle, and the hypothalamus at the base of the brain. It covers the position, the relations, the blood supply and the nerve supply of each, and the hormones they make. It holds one hundred questions, and every question states its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be carried in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 8201. Which paired glands sit on the upper poles of the kidneys, one on each side, inside the same fatty envelope as the kidney? The answer is the adrenal glands, also called the suprarenal glands. They lie behind the peritoneum and are enclosed with the kidney by the renal fascia. The right gland is shaped like a pyramid and the left like a crescent.

Question 8202. Which statement about the arterial supply of the adrenal gland is correct: branches of three different arteries reach it, only the renal artery supplies it, only the aorta supplies it, or one artery divides inside it? The answer is that three different arteries reach it. The superior suprarenal arteries come from the inferior phrenic artery, the middle suprarenal artery from the aorta, and the inferior suprarenal artery from the renal artery.

Question 8203. Which zone of the adrenal cortex lies immediately beneath the fibrous capsule, and which group of hormones does it make? The answer is the zona glomerulosa, which makes the mineralocorticoid aldosterone. Its cells lie in rounded clusters just under the capsule, and the enzyme needed to make aldosterone is confined to this zone.

Question 8204. Which zone of the adrenal cortex is the widest and lies between the zona glomerulosa and the zona reticularis: the zona fasciculata, the zona reticularis, the medulla, or the capsule? The answer is the zona fasciculata. Its cells are arranged in long straight cords that run inward from the capsule, and it makes the glucocorticoid cortisol.

Question 8205. Which large vein lies immediately medial to the right adrenal gland, so that the two are separated by only a thin layer of tissue? The answer is the inferior vena cava. The right adrenal gland lies behind the liver and against the right side of that vessel, and its short vein drains straight into it.

Question 8206. A described transverse section of the upper abdomen, taken through the upper pole of the right kidney, shows a triangular gland lying behind the liver and against the side of a large vein. Which gland is described, and which vein lies against it? The answer is the right adrenal gland, with the inferior vena cava against it. It lies behind the peritoneum, inside the renal fascia.

Question 8207. Which part of the adrenal gland is described as a modified sympathetic ganglion, and what does it secrete? The answer is the adrenal medulla, which secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine. Its cells are called chromaffin cells and lie in the center of the gland, where nerve fibers end directly on them.

Question 8208. Which fibers end on the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla: preganglionic sympathetic fibers, postganglionic sympathetic fibers, preganglionic parasympathetic fibers, or postganglionic parasympathetic fibers? The answer is preganglionic sympathetic fibers. They arrive through the greater splanchnic nerve from the lower thoracic segments and the first lumbar segment. A postganglionic fiber would mean a relay outside the gland.

Question 8209. A constructed illustration: a person has attacks of pounding headache, sweating and a racing heart, and imaging shows a small mass in the center of one adrenal gland. Which cells are giving rise to the attacks? The answer is the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, which release epinephrine and norepinephrine in bursts. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8210. Which organ lies immediately in front of the left adrenal gland, so that the two are separated only by peritoneum? The answer is the pancreas. Its body and tail cross in front of the left adrenal gland, and the spleen and the stomach lie in front of it as well.

Question 8211. A described dissection of the posterior abdominal wall shows a crescent-shaped gland lying above the left kidney, with the spleen against its outer border and the tail of the pancreas crossing its front. Which gland is described, and on which side? The answer is the left adrenal gland, on the left side. Its crescent shape and its relations distinguish it from the triangular right gland.

Question 8212. Which of these pairs belongs together: the zona glomerulosa with aldosterone, the zona fasciculata with androgens, the zona reticularis with cortisol, or the medulla with insulin? The answer is the zona glomerulosa with aldosterone. That outer zone is the only place where aldosterone is made. The zona fasciculata makes cortisol, the zona reticularis makes weak androgens, and insulin comes from the pancreas.

Question 8213. Into which vein does the right suprarenal vein drain: the right renal vein, the inferior vena cava, the right hepatic vein, or the portal vein? The answer is the inferior vena cava. The right suprarenal vein is very short and passes straight into that vessel, because the gland lies against it.

Question 8214. Into which vein does the left suprarenal vein drain: the inferior vena cava, the left renal vein, the splenic vein, or the left hepatic vein? The answer is the left renal vein. The left vein is longer than the right one and joins the left renal vein before that vessel crosses the aorta.

Question 8215. True or false: the cortex of the adrenal gland is formed from neural crest cells that migrate into the gland. The answer is false. The cortex is formed from the intermediate mesoderm of the urogenital ridge, the same tissue that gives rise to the kidney. The neural crest cells form the medulla instead.

Question 8216. Which embryonic tissue gives rise to the medulla of the adrenal gland, and what does that origin explain? The answer is the neural crest. Those cells migrate into the cortical primordium and settle in its center, where they become chromaffin cells. Their origin explains why the medulla behaves like a sympathetic ganglion and releases catecholamines.

Question 8217. Which large artery lies immediately behind the left renal vein, so that the vein crosses in front of it on its way to the inferior vena cava? The answer is the abdominal aorta. The left renal vein is longer than the right for that reason, and it receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins.

Question 8218. A described computed tomography scan of the upper abdomen shows two organs lying behind the peritoneum on either side of the spine, each with a smaller gland sitting on its upper pole. What are the two organs, and what caps them? The answer is the kidneys, each capped by an adrenal gland. The smaller gland is easily mistaken for part of the kidney.

Question 8219. A constructed illustration: a person with a long illness has low blood pressure, tiredness and darkening of the skin, and both adrenal cortices are destroyed. Which hormones are missing? The answer is the glucocorticoids and the mineralocorticoids, made by the zona fasciculata and the zona glomerulosa. The darkening follows the rise in the pituitary hormone that drives the cortex.

Question 8220. Which hormone is made by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex: cortisol, aldosterone, epinephrine, or testosterone? The answer is aldosterone. It acts on the kidney to hold sodium and to lose potassium, and it is the main mineralocorticoid of the body. Cortisol comes from the zona fasciculata and epinephrine from the medulla.

Question 8221. Which zone of the adrenal cortex lies deepest, right against the medulla? The answer is the zona reticularis. Its cells form an irregular network rather than straight cords, and they make weak androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone. The medulla lies immediately inside it, and the zona fasciculata lies outside it.

Question 8222. The inferior suprarenal artery arises from which vessel: the renal artery, the aorta, the inferior phrenic artery, or the superior mesenteric artery? The answer is the renal artery. It reaches the gland from below and also sends small branches to the upper part of the ureter. The middle suprarenal artery comes from the aorta.

Question 8223. Which statement about the nerve supply of the adrenal medulla is correct: the fibers end directly on the secretory cells, the fibers relay in a ganglion beside the gland, the fibers are parasympathetic, or the gland has no nerve supply? The answer is that the fibers end directly on the secretory cells. They are preganglionic sympathetic fibers arriving along the splanchnic nerves, and with no relay the medulla can act very quickly.

Question 8224. A described dissection of the posterior abdominal wall shows a gland lifted away from the upper pole of the kidney, with a thick layer of fat beneath it and a thin fibrous envelope around both organs. Which coverings are described? The answer is the perirenal fat and the renal fascia. The adrenal gland lies within the same envelope as the kidney.

Question 8225. What name is given to the small extra masses of adrenal cortical tissue that are sometimes found in the fat around the gland or lower down along the path of the gonad? The answer is accessory adrenal cortical tissue, sometimes called adrenal rests. They are a common variation rather than a disease, and they contain cortical tissue only.

Question 8226. Which part of the pancreas lies within the curve of the duodenum, so that the gut wraps around its right border? The answer is the head of the pancreas. The descending and horizontal parts of the duodenum curve around it. The uncinate process hangs down from the head behind the superior mesenteric vessels.

Question 8227. Which part of the pancreas reaches the spleen, lying inside a fold of peritoneum: the head, the neck, the body, or the tail? The answer is the tail. It is the only part of the pancreas that is not behind the peritoneum, because it runs in the splenorenal ligament with the splenic vessels. The head lies against the duodenum instead.

Question 8228. Which vein lies immediately behind the neck of the pancreas, formed there by the union of two other veins? The answer is the portal vein. The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck, and the new vessel then runs upward to the liver. The neck of the pancreas therefore lies directly in front of it.

Question 8229. What name is given to the round clusters of endocrine cells scattered through the pancreas, and which cells lie at the center of each cluster? The answer is the islets of Langerhans, with the beta cells at the center. The beta cells make insulin and are surrounded by the other cell types. The islets form only a small part of the organ.

Question 8230. Which cells of the pancreatic islet make insulin: the beta cells, the alpha cells, the delta cells, or the cells that make pancreatic polypeptide? The answer is the beta cells. They lie in the center of the islet and are the most numerous of its cells. The alpha cells at the edge make glucagon.

Question 8231. A described transverse section of the upper abdomen shows a long gland lying behind the stomach, with a large vein running in a groove along its back and the spleen at its left end. Which organ is described, and which vein lies in the groove? The answer is the pancreas, with the splenic vein in the groove, behind the stomach.

Question 8232. A constructed illustration: a person slowly turns yellow, and imaging shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which duct is being compressed as it passes behind that part of the gland? The answer is the common bile duct. It runs down behind the head of the pancreas and joins the pancreatic duct before opening into the duodenum. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8233. Which of these pairs belongs together: the beta cells with insulin, the alpha cells with somatostatin, the delta cells with glucagon, or the islet cells with pancreatic juice? The answer is the beta cells with insulin. The alpha cells make glucagon and the delta cells make somatostatin, while the digestive enzymes of pancreatic juice come from the acinar cells.

Question 8234. The head of the pancreas is supplied by two pancreaticoduodenal arteries. Where do they arise: one from the gastroduodenal artery and one from the superior mesenteric artery, both from the splenic artery, both from the aorta, or one from each gastric artery? The answer is that one arises from the gastroduodenal artery and one from the superior mesenteric artery. Their branches meet between the duodenum and the head.

Question 8235. Which part of the pancreas hooks backward and downward behind the superior mesenteric vessels, and where does it lie relative to them? The answer is the uncinate process. It springs from the lower part of the head and passes behind the superior mesenteric artery and vein. Its position explains why a mass there can press on those vessels.

Question 8236. A described computed tomography scan shows a ring of pancreatic tissue completely encircling the descending part of the duodenum. What is this arrangement called, and from which developmental event does it arise? The answer is an annular pancreas, which arises when the ventral pancreatic bud divides and one part encircles the gut. The ring may narrow the duodenum. It is a variation present from birth.

Question 8237. Which vessels lie immediately to the left of the head of the pancreas, so that the head is said to lie to their right? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery and the superior mesenteric vein. The head and the uncinate process wrap around them. The portal vein is formed behind the neck just above them.

Question 8238. A constructed illustration: a blow to the upper abdomen drives a handlebar into the belly, and the injury lies in the midline just below the sternum. Which organ lies against the vertebral column there and is easily crushed against it? The answer is the pancreas. Its body crosses in front of the aorta and the vertebral column at the level of the first lumbar vertebra.

Question 8239. Into which part of the gut does the main pancreatic duct open: the stomach, the first part of the duodenum, the descending part of the duodenum, or the jejunum? The answer is the descending part of the duodenum. There it joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla and opens on the major duodenal papilla. The accessory pancreatic duct opens above it.

Question 8240. A described specimen of the duodenum shows a small raised opening on its inner surface, with a duct entering it from behind. Which opening is described, and which two ducts meet before it? The answer is the major duodenal papilla, where the main pancreatic duct and the common bile duct meet. They join in the wall of the duodenum to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

Question 8241. Which part of the pancreas lies inside a fold of peritoneum and is therefore the only part that is not retroperitoneal? The answer is the tail. It runs in the splenorenal ligament together with the splenic vessels. The head, the neck and the body all lie behind the peritoneum.

Question 8242. True or false: the islets of Langerhans are most numerous in the tail of the pancreas. The answer is true. The tail holds a greater density of islets than the rest of the gland, even though it is the smallest part. That is one reason why a mass of the islet cells is often found there.

Question 8243. Which cells of the pancreatic islet make somatostatin: the delta cells, the beta cells, the alpha cells, or the acinar cells? The answer is the delta cells. They lie among the other cells of the islet, and their hormone damps the release of its neighbors. The acinar cells are not endocrine and pour enzymes into the ducts.

Question 8244. Which artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas, giving branches to the body and the tail, and is itself a branch of the celiac trunk? The answer is the splenic artery. It is remarkable for its tortuous course, and it lies in a groove along the upper border of the gland. The gastroduodenal artery supplies the head instead.

Question 8245. Name the two ducts of the pancreas, spoken as a list. The answer is the main pancreatic duct and the accessory pancreatic duct. The main duct runs the length of the gland and opens together with the common bile duct. The accessory duct, when it is present, opens a little above it at the minor papilla.

Question 8246. The pancreas develops from two buds of the embryonic gut. Which parts does the ventral bud form: the body and the tail, the lower head and the uncinate process, the whole gland, or only the tail? The answer is the lower part of the head and the uncinate process. The ventral bud rotates backward beneath the dorsal bud and fuses with it.

Question 8247. Within a pancreatic islet the cells are supplied in a particular order. Which statement is correct: the beta cells receive blood first, the alpha cells receive blood first, all the cells are supplied equally, or the islet has no blood supply? The answer is that the beta cells receive blood first, so insulin washes over the other cells before it leaves. That lets insulin damp the release of glucagon.

Question 8248. A constructed illustration: a person has repeated spells of shakiness and confusion that settle after food, and a small mass is found in the tail of the pancreas. Which cells are overactive? The answer is the beta cells of the islets, which are making too much insulin. The tail holds the greatest density of islets. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8249. A described section of the pancreas, viewed through a lens, shows many small round clusters of pale cells with capillaries running between them, set among larger darker lobules. What are the round clusters, and what do they form? The answer is the islets of Langerhans, the endocrine part of the gland. The darker lobules around them are the acini, which make the digestive enzymes.

Question 8250. Which cells lie at the edge of a pancreatic islet and make glucagon? The answer is the alpha cells. They form a rim around the beta cells in the center of the islet. Glucagon raises the level of sugar in the blood and so opposes insulin.

Question 8251. Which small cone-shaped gland lies in the roof of the third ventricle, behind the thalamus and above the midbrain? The answer is the pineal gland, also called the pineal body or the epiphysis. Its name comes from its shape, which resembles a pine cone. It is attached to the roof of the third ventricle by a short stalk.

Question 8252. Which structure lies immediately above and behind the pineal gland, forming the back of the corpus callosum? The answer is the splenium of the corpus callosum. The pineal gland sits in the small space between the splenium above and the superior colliculi below. The great cerebral vein curves over the gland in the same region.

Question 8253. Which arteries supply the pineal gland: the posterior choroidal arteries, the anterior cerebral arteries, the middle meningeal arteries, or the ophthalmic arteries? The answer is the posterior choroidal arteries, which are branches of the posterior cerebral artery. They also supply the choroid plexus of the third ventricle. The gland has a rich blood supply for its small size.

Question 8254. A described radiograph of the skull, taken from the front, shows a small dense fleck lying in the midline above and behind the sella. What is the fleck, and why is it useful on such a film? The answer is calcification in the pineal gland. Because the gland lies in the midline, the fleck shows whether the brain has been pushed to one side.

Question 8255. Which cells of the pineal gland make melatonin, and from which part of the nervous system do they come? The answer is the pinealocytes, which are modified nerve cells derived from the roof of the diencephalon. They convert serotonin into melatonin and release it into the blood and the cerebrospinal fluid. Supporting cells lie between them.

Question 8256. True or false: the pineal gland lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so substances in the blood can reach its cells directly. The answer is true. Its capillaries are fenestrated rather than tight, which places it among the small group of organs around the third and fourth ventricles that lack the barrier. That arrangement lets the gland sample the blood.

Question 8257. Which of these pairs belongs together: the pineal gland with melatonin, the adrenal cortex with epinephrine, the pancreatic islets with bile, or the posterior pituitary with insulin? The answer is the pineal gland with melatonin. Epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla and not the cortex, insulin comes from the pancreatic islets, and bile comes from the liver.

Question 8258. A described section of the brain passes from front to back through the pineal gland and the third ventricle, dividing the brain into a right and a left part. In which plane does that section lie? The answer is a sagittal plane, and it shows the gland in the midline of the roof of the third ventricle. A section placed to one side would miss the gland.

Question 8259. Which nerve fibers reach the pineal gland: postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion, preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the spinal cord, fibers from the vagus nerve, or fibers from the optic nerve? The answer is postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion. They travel along the blood vessels to the gland, and the optic nerve does not reach it, though light influences it by a longer route.

Question 8260. A constructed illustration: a growing mass in the pineal region blocks the narrow channel between the third and the fourth ventricle, and the ventricles above it swell. Which channel is blocked? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct of the midbrain. The pineal gland lies just above and behind the tectal plate, so a mass there presses on the aqueduct. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8261. What name is given to the gritty concretions of calcium salts that are commonly found in the pineal gland of an adult? The answer is corpora arenacea, also called brain sand. They lie among the cells of the gland and grow more numerous with age. They are why the gland often appears as a dense fleck on a plain radiograph.

Question 8262. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain in the midline shows a small cyst in the pineal region, with a vein curving over its upper surface. Which vein is described? The answer is the great cerebral vein, which receives the two internal cerebral veins behind the gland. It runs above the pineal gland and below the splenium of the corpus callosum.

Question 8263. A constructed illustration: a person cannot look upward, and the pupils do not narrow when a light is shone into the eye, though the eyes still focus on a near object. A mass lies in the pineal region. Which structure is pressed on? The answer is the tectal plate, especially the superior colliculi and the pretectal area above them, which lie below the gland.

Question 8264. Name the two small bands of fibers that form the upper and lower laminae of the pineal stalk, spoken as a list. The answer is the habenular commissure and the posterior commissure. They lie one above the other in the roof of the third ventricle, and the pineal stalk is attached between them. The upper one belongs to the habenular nuclei.

Question 8265. How does light reaching the eye change the output of the pineal gland: it increases the release of melatonin, it reduces the release of melatonin, it has no effect, or it makes the gland secrete insulin? The answer is that light reduces the release of melatonin. The signal travels from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus and then by a long route to the gland.

Question 8266. True or false: the pineal gland lies in front of the thalamus. The answer is false. It lies behind the thalamus, in the roof of the third ventricle, and it belongs to the epithalamus. The structures in front of the thalamus include the interventricular foramen and the front part of the third ventricle.

Question 8267. In the pathway that carries the light signal to the pineal gland, which structure lies immediately after the suprachiasmatic nucleus: the superior cervical ganglion, the paraventricular nucleus, the pineal gland itself, or the retina? The answer is the paraventricular nucleus. From there the signal descends the spinal cord and leaves in the upper thoracic segments, and the fibers of the superior cervical ganglion then reach the gland.

Question 8268. Which structure lies immediately below the pineal gland and forms the roof of the midbrain? The answer is the tectal plate, formed by the superior and the inferior colliculi. The pineal gland rests just above the superior colliculi. A mass in the gland therefore presses on them before it presses on anything else.

Question 8269. A described specimen shows a small lobulated body attached by a short stalk to the roof of the third ventricle, lying behind the two thalami. Which organ is shown? The answer is the pineal gland. Its stalk carries the two commissures, and the gland hangs down behind the third ventricle. It is one of the smallest organs of the body.

Question 8270. From the roof of which part of the brain does the pineal gland develop as a small outpouching: the diencephalon, the telencephalon, the midbrain, or the cerebellum? The answer is the diencephalon. The gland grows out from the roof of the third ventricle, which is part of the diencephalon, and that origin explains why its cells are nerve cells.

Question 8271. Which cells form the endocrine part of the pineal gland, and from which germ layer are they derived? The answer is the pinealocytes, which come from the neuroectoderm of the diencephalon. They are modified nerve cells that make melatonin. They are not derived from the neural crest, which separates them from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

Question 8272. Into which veins does the pineal gland drain: the internal cerebral veins, the superior sagittal sinus, the transverse sinus, or the cavernous sinus? The answer is the internal cerebral veins. They pass backward above the gland and unite to form the great cerebral vein. From there the blood reaches the straight sinus.

Question 8273. At which synapse do the nerve fibers that control the pineal gland relay: the superior cervical ganglion, the ciliary ganglion, the pterygopalatine ganglion, or the otic ganglion? The answer is the superior cervical ganglion. Its postganglionic fibers follow the blood vessels into the gland. The other three ganglia supply the eye, the nasal lining and the salivary glands.

Question 8274. A described computed tomography scan of the head shows a small dense dot in the midline between the two halves of the brain. Which structure has calcified, and why is its position helpful? The answer is the pineal gland. Because it lies in the midline, a shift of the dot to one side suggests that the brain has been pushed across.

Question 8275. A described section is cut from side to side through the head, dividing the brain into a front and a back part, and it passes through the pineal gland. In which plane does it lie? The answer is a coronal plane, also called a frontal plane. It shows the gland in the midline between the two thalami.

Question 8276. Which part of the brain forms the floor and the lower walls of the third ventricle, lying below the hypothalamic sulcus? The answer is the hypothalamus. It lies at the base of the brain, below the thalamus, and it stretches from the region in front of the optic chiasm to the mammillary bodies behind.

Question 8277. Which structure lies immediately in front of the hypothalamus and carries fibers from the retina toward the brain? The answer is the optic chiasm. It lies at the front of the floor of the third ventricle, just above the pituitary gland. Behind it lies the infundibulum, and behind that the mammillary bodies.

Question 8278. Which of these structures marks the front of the hypothalamus: the lamina terminalis, the mammillary bodies, the splenium of the corpus callosum, or the pineal gland? The answer is the lamina terminalis, a thin sheet that closes the front of the third ventricle. The mammillary bodies mark the back of the hypothalamus.

Question 8279. Which two nuclei of the hypothalamus make antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin, and where do their axons end? The answer is the supraoptic nucleus and the paraventricular nucleus, whose axons run down the stalk to the posterior pituitary. The hormones are stored in the nerve endings there and released into the blood. The supraoptic nucleus lies above the optic tract.

Question 8280. Which small nucleus lies just above the optic chiasm and acts as the clock that sets the daily rhythm of the body: the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the arcuate nucleus, the ventromedial nucleus, or the mammillary body? The answer is the suprachiasmatic nucleus. It receives fibers straight from the retina and keeps the rhythms of the body in step with daylight.

Question 8281. A described coronal section through the front of the brain shows a small paired nucleus sitting just above the optic chiasm on each side of the third ventricle, with dark fibers entering it from the optic pathway. Which nucleus is shown? The answer is the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Fibers of the retinohypothalamic tract reach it directly from the retina.

Question 8282. A constructed illustration: after an operation in the region above the pituitary gland, a person passes large volumes of dilute urine day and night. Which tract has been damaged? The answer is the supraopticohypophyseal tract, which carries axons from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei to the posterior pituitary. Cutting the stalk above the gland leaves those nerve endings unable to release their hormone.

Question 8283. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supraoptic nucleus with antidiuretic hormone, the arcuate nucleus with oxytocin, the suprachiasmatic nucleus with growth hormone, or the mammillary body with insulin? The answer is the supraoptic nucleus with antidiuretic hormone. The paraventricular nucleus makes oxytocin as well as antidiuretic hormone, and the arcuate nucleus makes the releasing hormones.

Question 8284. Which pathway carries the releasing hormones from the hypothalamus to the front of the pituitary gland: the supraopticohypophyseal tract, the tuberoinfundibular tract with the portal veins, the mammillothalamic tract, or the fornix? The answer is the tuberoinfundibular tract together with the hypophyseal portal veins. Its fibers come from the arcuate nucleus and end on the capillaries of the median eminence.

Question 8285. Which structure lies immediately below the hypothalamus and is joined to it by a hollow stalk? The answer is the pituitary gland, also called the hypophysis. The stalk, called the infundibulum, carries the axons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei down to the back of the gland. The front of the gland is controlled through the portal veins.

Question 8286. Which two rounded bodies lie at the back of the floor of the hypothalamus, one on each side of the midline? The answer is the mammillary bodies. They receive fibers from the hippocampus through the fornix and send fibers on to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. They belong to the circuit that is concerned with memory.

Question 8287. True or false: the median eminence lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so substances in the blood can reach its cells. The answer is true. Its capillaries are fenestrated, and the releasing hormones pass from the nerve endings there into the hypophyseal portal veins. This is what allows the hypothalamus to read the chemical state of the blood.

Question 8288. A described sagittal section of the brain shows, from front to back in the midline, a flat crossing of fibers, then a hollow stalk, then a rounded swelling, and finally two small rounded bodies. Which region is displayed by that row of structures? The answer is the floor of the hypothalamus, with the optic chiasm, the infundibulum and the mammillary bodies in order.

Question 8289. A constructed illustration: a person never feels thirsty, drinks very little, and passes large amounts of dilute urine, and a small lesion is found in the front of the hypothalamus. Which nucleus is most likely involved? The answer is the supraoptic nucleus, whose cells sense the concentration of the blood and release antidiuretic hormone. Damage to it removes both the thirst and the hormone signal.

Question 8290. Name the two nuclei whose axons form the supraopticohypophyseal tract, spoken as a list. The answer is the supraoptic nucleus and the paraventricular nucleus. Their axons run through the infundibulum into the posterior pituitary. The hormones they carry are released into the blood from the nerve endings there.

Question 8291. Which part of the hypothalamus drives the responses that lose heat, such as flushing and sweating, and which part drives the responses that save heat? The answer is the anterior part for losing heat and the posterior part for saving it. The anterior region lies above the optic chiasm and the posterior region near the mammillary bodies.

Question 8292. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the hypothalamus and separates it from the lentiform nucleus? The answer is the internal capsule. Its fibers run between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus, and the hypothalamus lies medial to them. The optic tract also lies along the lateral surface of the hypothalamus.

Question 8293. Which region of the hypothalamus is called the feeding center, and which nucleus is called the satiety center? The answer is the lateral hypothalamic area for feeding and the ventromedial nucleus for satiety. Damage to the ventromedial nucleus removes the brake on eating, and damage to the lateral area removes the drive to eat.

Question 8294. Which nucleus of the hypothalamus makes the releasing hormones that control the front of the pituitary gland, and what is its other name? The answer is the arcuate nucleus, also called the infundibular nucleus. It lies in the middle part of the hypothalamus, close to the median eminence, and its cells are the source of the tuberoinfundibular tract.

Question 8295. Which statement about the hypophyseal portal system is correct: it carries releasing hormones from the median eminence to the front of the pituitary gland, it carries antidiuretic hormone to the kidney, it drains the posterior pituitary into the neck, or it carries oxytocin to the breast? The answer is that it carries releasing hormones from the median eminence to the front of the pituitary gland.

Question 8296. Which structure forms the back of the floor of the hypothalamus, at the point where the hypothalamus meets the midbrain? The answer is the mammillary bodies, behind which lies the tegmentum of the midbrain. Together with the posterior nucleus they make up the posterior part of the hypothalamus.

Question 8297. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan in the sagittal plane shows a rounded mass in the space above the pituitary gland, pushing the optic chiasm upward and flattening the floor of the third ventricle. Which two structures are being compressed? The answer is the optic chiasm and the hypothalamus, with the pituitary stalk stretched over the mass. Such a mass can disturb both vision and hormone control.

Question 8298. A constructed illustration: a person who has recovered from a blow to the base of the brain no longer feels hungry and has lost much weight, and the damage lies in one part of the hypothalamus. Which part is it? The answer is the lateral hypothalamic area, the feeding center. Damage there removes the drive to eat, while damage to the ventromedial nucleus has the opposite effect.

Question 8299. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ventromedial nucleus with the sensation of fullness after a meal, the lateral hypothalamic area with the clock of the body, the suprachiasmatic nucleus with the drive to eat, or the paraventricular nucleus with vision? The answer is the ventromedial nucleus with the sensation of fullness after a meal. The lateral area drives eating, and the suprachiasmatic nucleus keeps daily time.

Question 8300. Which bundle carries fibers from the hippocampus to the mammillary body: the fornix, the mammillothalamic tract, the stria terminalis, or the medial forebrain bundle? The answer is the fornix, which arches forward beneath the corpus callosum and ends in the mammillary body. From there the mammillothalamic tract carries the signal to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

To summarize, the adrenal glands cap the upper poles of the kidneys inside the renal fascia, with a cortex of three zones making aldosterone, cortisol and weak androgens, and a medulla of chromaffin cells that behaves as a modified sympathetic ganglion under the control of preganglionic fibers. The cortex comes from intermediate mesoderm and the medulla from neural crest, three arteries supply each gland, and the right vein drains into the inferior vena cava while the left drains into the left renal vein. The endocrine pancreas lies in the islets of Langerhans, most numerous in the tail, where beta cells make insulin, alpha cells make glucagon and delta cells make somatostatin. The pineal gland sits in the midline behind the thalamus and above the superior colliculi, is supplied by the posterior choroidal arteries, and is controlled by sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion. The hypothalamus forms the floor of the third ventricle, sends axons to the posterior pituitary and releasing hormones to the portal veins, and holds the nuclei for temperature, feeding, thirst and the daily rhythm. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 84 — Eye

This chapter walks around the eye itself, the globe that turns light into a signal the brain can read, and it takes the listener through the coats of that globe and the contents they enclose. It begins with the eyeball as a whole, then covers the cornea, the sclera, the choroid, the retina and finally the lens. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The eye is the one part of the body where living nerve tissue and blood vessels can be seen directly, and every structure named here supports that view. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 8301. The wall of the eyeball is built of three concentric coats. What is the name of the outermost coat, and which two parts does it have? The answer is the fibrous coat, made of the sclera and the cornea. The sclera is the opaque white part that covers most of the surface. The cornea is the transparent part at the front, and this tough coat holds the shape of the eye.

Question 8302. Which of these fills the large space behind the lens and in front of the retina: the aqueous humor, the vitreous body, the cerebrospinal fluid, or the tears? The answer is the vitreous body. It is a clear gel that fills the posterior segment of the eyeball and presses the retina against the wall.

Question 8303. The lens divides the interior of the eye into an anterior segment and a posterior segment. Which structures lie in the anterior segment, and what fills the posterior segment? The answer is that the aqueous humor and the iris lie in the anterior segment, and the vitreous body fills the posterior segment.

Question 8304. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the orbits shows a rounded structure with three concentric bands of different brightness and a clear oval body near its front. Which organ is shown, and which coat lies between the other two? The answer is the eyeball, with the vascular coat between the fibrous coat and the retina. The clear oval body is the lens.

Question 8305. The eyeball lies in the bony orbit. What is the name of the fatty tissue that cushions it there and allows it to move freely? The answer is the orbital fat. It fills the space around the globe inside the cone of muscles. The eyeball itself is not fixed to the bone.

Question 8306. A constructed illustration: a blunt blow to the eye causes blood to layer in the space between the cornea and the iris. Which space has filled, and which structures are the likely source of the blood? The answer is the anterior chamber, with blood coming from the iris and the ciliary body. That space normally holds clear aqueous humor.

Question 8307. At which places are the coats of the eye firmly attached to one another: at the fovea, at the optic disc and the ora serrata, at the cornea, or at the equator? The answer is at the optic disc and the ora serrata. The choroid is fixed to the sclera at those two places, while the retina is fixed to the pigment epithelium more widely.

Question 8308. The optic axis passes through the centers of the cornea and the posterior pole, while the visual axis runs from the point being looked at to the fovea. How do the two lines differ? The answer is that they are not the same line. The visual axis lies a little to the nasal side of the optic axis, and the two cross at the nodal point.

Question 8309. Which coat of the eye carries the iris, the ciliary body and the choroid, and by what name is that whole coat known? The answer is the vascular coat, also called the uvea. It lies between the fibrous coat outside and the retina inside. The iris is its most anterior part and the choroid its most posterior part.

Question 8310. The vitreous body lies immediately behind which structure, and immediately in front of which coat of the eye? The answer is behind the lens and in front of the retina. It fills the posterior segment, which is the larger of the two segments of the eyeball. The retina is pressed against the wall by it.

Question 8311. Which of these best describes the shape of the normal adult eyeball: a perfect sphere, a sphere a little longer from front to back than across, a flattened disc, or a cone? The answer is a sphere a little longer from front to back than across. Its diameter is about 24 millimeters in each direction. The cornea bulges slightly in front of that rounded shape.

Question 8312. True or false: the three coats of the eye are the same length, so all three reach the front of the eye together. The answer is false. The sclera becomes the cornea at the front, the choroid continues forward as the ciliary body, and the retina ends at the ora serrata. Each coat therefore ends at a different line.

Question 8313. A described section of the front of the eye shows one space between the cornea and the iris and a narrow slit between the iris and the lens, both filled with the same clear fluid. Which two chambers are described, and why is one a slit? The answer is the anterior chamber and the posterior chamber. The posterior chamber is narrow because the iris lies close to the lens.

Question 8314. Which clear fluid fills the chambers in front of the lens, and which two structures does it nourish? The answer is the aqueous humor, which nourishes the cornea and the lens. Neither of those structures has blood vessels of its own, so both depend on this fluid. It is made by the ciliary body and leaves the eye at the angle between the cornea and the iris.

Question 8315. Which structure secretes the fluid that fills the chambers in front of the lens: the corneal endothelium, the ciliary epithelium, the iris stroma, or the lens capsule? The answer is the ciliary epithelium. It covers the ciliary processes, and the fluid it makes nourishes the cornea and the lens. The corneal endothelium removes fluid from the eye rather than making it.

Question 8316. Name the three coats of the eyeball in order from outside inward, and say which of them reaches the very front of the eye. The answer is the fibrous coat, the vascular coat and the neural coat. Only the fibrous coat reaches the front, where it becomes the transparent cornea.

Question 8317. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sclera with the transparent front of the eye, the choroid with the pigmented vascular layer behind the retina, the retina with the white outer coat, or the iris with the gel behind the lens? The answer is the choroid with the pigmented vascular layer behind the retina. The sclera is the white outer coat and the retina the neural coat.

Question 8318. Which transparent structure forms the window at the front of the eye, and what lies immediately behind it? The answer is the cornea, with the aqueous humor of the anterior chamber behind it. It is the front part of the fibrous coat and is continuous with the sclera at its edge. It has no blood vessels, so it stays clear.

Question 8319. How many layers does the cornea have: two, three, five, or eight? The answer is five. They are the epithelium, the anterior limiting membrane, the stroma, the posterior limiting membrane and the endothelium. The epithelium is the outermost of the five and the endothelium the innermost, and the stroma forms most of the thickness.

Question 8320. A described section through the front of the eye shows a transparent layer that is thicker in the middle than at its edge, with a single layer of flat cells on its inner surface. Which structure is described, and what is that inner layer? The answer is the cornea, and the inner layer is the endothelium. The endothelium pumps fluid out of the cornea and keeps it clear.

Question 8321. A constructed illustration: a contact lens is worn for far too long, and the cornea becomes swollen and cloudy over its whole surface. Which layer has failed in its work? The answer is the endothelium. It normally pumps fluid out of the stroma, and when it cannot, the cornea takes up water and loses its transparency.

Question 8322. What is the name of the ring-shaped junction where the cornea meets the sclera, and what lies in its depth? The answer is the limbus, with the trabecular meshwork in its depth. Aqueous humor leaves the eye through that meshwork. The stem cells that renew the corneal surface also lie at the limbus.

Question 8323. Which of these statements about the cornea is correct: it is the most sensitive part of the eye, it is richly supplied with blood vessels, it is opaque, or it contains the rods and cones? The answer is that it is the most sensitive part of the eye. It is packed with nerve endings from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

Question 8324. Immediately deep to the corneal epithelium lies which layer, and immediately deep to the corneal endothelium lies which space? The answer is the anterior limiting membrane deep to the epithelium, and the anterior chamber deep to the endothelium. The stroma lies between the two limiting membranes. The endothelium therefore has aqueous humor on its inner face.

Question 8325. True or false: the cornea is the main refracting surface of the eye. The answer is true. It provides about two thirds of the total refractive power of the eye. The lens provides the rest and can change its power, but the cornea cannot.

Question 8326. Which of these statements about the corneal endothelium is correct: it is a single layer of cells, it is several cells thick, it lies beneath the epithelium, or it plays no part in keeping the cornea clear? The answer is that it is a single layer of cells. It lines the inner surface of the cornea, next to the aqueous humor.
