Question 8327. A described view of an eye shows a cornea that is cloudy over its whole surface, with fine new vessels growing in from the limbus. What has happened to the cornea, and why has it lost its clarity? The answer is that it has been scarred and has grown new vessels. Scar tissue and vessels scatter light instead of letting it pass straight through.

Question 8328. Which layer of the cornea lies between the two limiting membranes and forms most of its thickness? The answer is the stroma. It is made of many thin layers of collagen fibers lying in regular sheets. That regular arrangement is what lets the cornea stay clear.

Question 8329. A constructed illustration: the corneal reflex is absent on one side while it is normal on the other. Which nerve carries the sensory limb of that reflex? The answer is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, with the surface of the cornea touched. The motor limb is carried by the facial nerve to the muscle that closes the lids.

Question 8330. Which of these pairs belongs together: the corneal epithelium with the tear film, the corneal stroma with the endothelium, the corneal endothelium with the iris, or the limbus with the fovea? The answer is the corneal epithelium with the tear film. The epithelium is kept moist and supplied with oxygen by the tears.

Question 8331. Which of these explains why the cornea refracts more light than the lens, although the two have a similar curve: it is denser, it meets air while the lens is bathed in fluid, it is thicker, or it has more cells? The answer is that it meets air while the lens is bathed in fluid. The change in refractive index there is greater than at the lens.

Question 8332. Which structure forms the white outer coat of the eye, and what is its main job? The answer is the sclera. It is a tough fibrous layer that keeps the shape of the eyeball and protects what lies inside. The muscles that move the eye are attached to it.

Question 8333. The sclera is thinnest at which of these places: around the optic nerve, just behind the insertions of the rectus muscles, at the equator, or at the limbus? The answer is just behind the insertions of the rectus muscles. The tendons of those muscles blend with the sclera there, over its thinnest part. The sclera is thickest at the back, around the optic nerve.

Question 8334. Which coat lies immediately deep to the sclera at the back of the eye, and which coat lies immediately inside that one? The answer is the choroid deep to the sclera, with the retina inside the choroid. The coats are stacked from outside inward as the sclera, the choroid and the retina. At the front the sclera continues as the cornea.

Question 8335. A described section through the wall of the eye at the back shows a thick white fibrous layer pierced by a bundle of nerve fibers and by several small vessels around it. Which coat is pierced, and which opening does the nerve use? The answer is the sclera, pierced by the optic nerve through the scleral canal.

Question 8336. Where does the optic nerve leave the eyeball, and what is the opening through the sclera called? The answer is at the optic disc, through the scleral canal. The disc lies about 3 millimeters to the nasal side of the posterior pole. The fibers of the retina converge there to form the nerve.

Question 8337. A constructed illustration: an eye is painful and inflamed, and the white coat looks thin and bluish. Which coat is affected, and why does the blue color appear? The answer is the sclera, and the bluish tinge appears because it has become thin enough to let the dark choroid show through. The illustration is described only.

Question 8338. Which of these structures passes through the sclera at the back of the eye: the optic nerve, the trochlea, the levator palpebrae superioris, or the lacrimal gland? The answer is the optic nerve. It leaves the eye through the sclera and carries the fibers of the retina toward the brain. The other structures lie in the orbit or in the eyelid.

Question 8339. Name two kinds of vessel that pierce the sclera around the optic nerve. The answer is the short posterior ciliary arteries and the long posterior ciliary arteries. The short ones supply the choroid, and the long ones run forward to the front of the eye. Small veins also leave the eye through the sclera.

Question 8340. A described dissection of the front of the eye shows a narrow channel running around the eye in the deepest part of the junction between the cornea and the sclera. What is that channel, and what flows along it? The answer is the venous channel called the canal of Schlemm, which carries aqueous humor away from the eye.

Question 8341. Which of these statements about the fibers of the sclera is correct: they are arranged irregularly in all directions, they lie in regular parallel sheets, they are evenly spaced, or they form no bundles? The answer is that they are arranged irregularly in all directions. That irregular arrangement scatters light and makes the sclera white.

Question 8342. Which coat lies immediately between the sclera and the retina, and which retinal layer rests against it? The answer is the choroid, with the pigment epithelium of the retina against it. That epithelium is the outermost layer of the retina. The choroid supplies the outer part of the retina with blood.

Question 8343. A described view of the back of the eye shows a pale round disc with vessels radiating from it, and beside the disc a dark crescent. What is that crescent, and what does it show about the sclera? The answer is a crescent of choroid and retinal pigment, seen where the scleral ring around the disc is incomplete.

Question 8344. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sclera with the opaque outer coat, the cornea with the vascular coat, the choroid with the fibrous coat, or the retina with the middle coat? The answer is the sclera with the opaque outer coat. The cornea is the transparent front of that same fibrous coat.

Question 8345. Which layer of the eye lies between the sclera and the retina, and what kind of tissue is it? The answer is the choroid, a dark and vascular layer. It is the posterior part of the vascular coat. It nourishes the outer part of the retina and is firmly joined to the pigment epithelium inside.

Question 8346. Which of these describes the blood supply of the choroid: a single artery, a rich network of vessels arranged in layers, a capillary bed supplied by branches of the central retinal artery, or no supply of its own? The answer is a rich network of vessels arranged in layers. The innermost layer is a dense bed of capillaries, fed by the short posterior ciliary arteries.

Question 8347. Immediately outside the choroid lies which coat, and immediately inside it lies which layer of the retina? The answer is the sclera outside and the pigment epithelium inside. The choroid is firmly joined to that epithelium. This is why the retina lifts away from the wall as a sheet when it detaches.

Question 8348. A described section of the back of the eye shows a dark layer packed with vessels, thicker at the back than at the front, ending at a scalloped line. What is that line, and what lies just beyond it? The answer is the ora serrata, and beyond it the ciliary body continues forward. The retina ends at the same scalloped line.

Question 8349. What is the name of the dark pigment in the choroid that absorbs stray light inside the eye? The answer is melanin. It lies in the pigment cells of the choroid. By absorbing light it stops reflections that would blur the picture formed on the retina.

Question 8350. A constructed illustration: a patient notices a sudden curtain across the vision, and a sheet of retina is found lifted from the wall of the eye. Which two layers have come apart, and which layer stays where it is? The answer is the neural retina and the pigment epithelium, which have separated. The pigment epithelium stays with the choroid, and fluid collects in the space between.

Question 8351. Which layer of the choroid lies closest to the retina: the layer of large vessels, the layer of medium vessels, the layer of capillaries, or the suprachoroidal space? The answer is the layer of capillaries. It lies immediately outside the pigment epithelium and is fed by the short posterior ciliary arteries. The suprachoroidal space lies on the outer side of the choroid, beside the sclera.

Question 8352. A described dissection shows a thin brown layer peeled from the inner surface of the sclera, loosely joined to it except at two fixed points. Which layer is it, and where is it fixed? The answer is the choroid, fixed at the optic nerve behind and at the ora serrata in front. The space between it and the sclera is the suprachoroidal space.

Question 8353. Which arteries supply the choroid, and which supply the iris and the ciliary body? The answer is that the posterior ciliary arteries supply the choroid, and the anterior ciliary arteries supply the iris and the ciliary body. The short posterior ciliary arteries pierce the sclera around the optic nerve.

Question 8354. Which of these structures lies between the retina and the sclera: the cornea, the choroid, the lens, or the vitreous body? The answer is the choroid. It lies between the retina inside and the sclera outside. The lens and the vitreous body lie in the middle of the eye, in front of the retina.

Question 8355. A described study of the vessels of the eye shows one set of arteries fanning out behind the eye and another running forward toward the front. Which two systems are shown, and which parts of the vascular coat do they supply? The answer is the posterior ciliary arteries for the choroid and the anterior ciliary arteries for the iris and the ciliary body.

Question 8356. True or false: the choroid is loosely joined to the sclera but firmly joined to the retina. The answer is true. Only the suprachoroidal space and a few vessels and nerves join the choroid to the sclera, whereas its attachment to the pigment epithelium is much firmer. The choroid is also firmly fixed to the sclera at the optic nerve and at the ora serrata.

Question 8357. Name the three parts of the vascular coat of the eye, spoken from front to back. The answer is the iris, the ciliary body and the choroid. All three are continuous with one another. Together they form the uvea, the middle coat of the eye.

Question 8358. Which of these functions belongs to the choroid: it changes the shape of the lens, it absorbs stray light and nourishes the outer retina, it moves the eye, or it makes the aqueous humor? The answer is that it absorbs stray light and nourishes the outer retina. Its pigment stops light from scattering inside the eye.

Question 8359. Which coat of the eye contains the light-sensitive cells, and what are those cells called? The answer is the retina, and its light-sensitive cells are the rods and the cones. The rods work in dim light and the cones in bright light and in color. The retina is the innermost of the three coats.

Question 8360. Where in the retina are the cones packed most densely: at the optic disc, at the fovea, at the ora serrata, or at the equator? The answer is at the fovea. The fovea lies at the center of the macula and gives the sharpest vision. The optic disc has no light-sensitive cells at all.

Question 8361. A described section of the retina shows a layer of rods and cones on its outer side and a layer of nerve fibers on its inner side, next to the vitreous body. Which layer is outermost, and which way does light travel through them? The answer is that the rods and cones lie outermost, against the pigment epithelium, and light must cross the nerve fiber layer first.

Question 8362. Which part of the retina has no light-sensitive cells and is therefore called the blind spot? The answer is the optic disc. It is the place where the fibers of the optic nerve leave the eye. The retinal vessels also enter and leave there.

Question 8363. Which of these structures lies at the center of the macula: the optic disc, the fovea, the ora serrata, or the ciliary body? The answer is the fovea. The macula is the small area of the retina that gives the sharpest vision, and the fovea is its center. The optic disc lies about 3 millimeters to its nasal side.

Question 8364. Which retinal layer rests directly against the pigment epithelium, and which retinal layer faces the vitreous body? The answer is that the rods and cones rest against the pigment epithelium, while the layer of nerve fibers faces the vitreous body. Light therefore crosses the whole thickness of the retina before it reaches the receptors.

Question 8365. A constructed illustration: pressure inside the skull is raised, and the disc at the back of the eye is swollen with blurred margins. Why does that pressure reach the eye? The answer is that the sheath around the optic nerve carries cerebrospinal fluid from the skull to the back of the eye, so the disc swells.

Question 8366. What is the name of the small central area of the retina that gives the sharpest vision, and what is its center called? The answer is the macula, and its center is the fovea. The fovea contains cones only. Around the macula the retina holds a mixture of rods and cones.

Question 8367. Which cells of the retina work in dim light: the cones, the rods, the ganglion cells, or the pigment cells? The answer is the rods. They are far more numerous than the cones and respond to very little light. They do not separate colors, so a dim scene looks gray.

Question 8368. A described section through the retina at the fovea shows the layers pushed to the side so that the receptors lie near the surface, with a thick rim of cells around them. Why is vision sharpest at that point? The answer is that the cones there are packed tightly and light reaches them with little scattering.

Question 8369. Which vessels supply the inner part of the retina: the choriocapillaris, branches of the central retinal artery, the anterior ciliary arteries, or the suprachoroidal vessels? The answer is branches of the central retinal artery. That artery enters the eye at the optic disc and divides into branches that run in the nerve fiber layer.

Question 8370. A described view of the retina shows a delicate pattern of vessels radiating from a pale round area and crossing the inner surface of the retina. Which vessels are these, and from where do they come? The answer is the branches of the central retinal artery and its veins, radiating from the optic disc.

Question 8371. Which of these orders of the retinal layers runs from outside inward: pigment epithelium, rods and cones, then nerve fibers; rods and cones, pigment epithelium, then nerve fibers; nerve fibers, rods and cones, then pigment epithelium; or pigment epithelium, nerve fibers, then rods and cones? The answer is the pigment epithelium, then the rods and cones, then the nerve fibers. That order is why light crosses the nerve fibers first.

Question 8372. True or false: the retina has two separate blood supplies, one for its outer part and one for its inner part. The answer is true. The outer part, including the receptors, is nourished by the choriocapillaris of the choroid, and the inner part by branches of the central retinal artery. Those two systems meet but do not overlap.

Question 8373. A constructed illustration: an older patient has lost central vision in one eye while the outer parts of the field are still seen. Which part of the retina is affected, and which cells are most affected there? The answer is the macula, and the cones at the fovea are affected first.

Question 8374. Which part of the retina has no blood vessels crossing its center, and why does that help vision? The answer is the fovea, whose center is free of vessels. If vessels crossed it, they would scatter light before it reached the cones. Its supply comes from the choriocapillaris behind it.

Question 8375. Which of these statements about the rods and cones is correct: the rods are more numerous and work in dim light, the cones are more numerous, the rods give color vision, or the cones work only in dim light? The answer is that the rods are more numerous and work in dim light. Cones are concentrated at the fovea and give sharp colored vision.

Question 8376. A described view shows pale bundles of fibers arching above and below a darker central area and running toward a pale round disc. What are those bundles, and why do they curve? The answer is the nerve fiber layer of the retina, whose fibers run to the optic disc. They curve around the macula because they cannot pass through the fovea.

Question 8377. A line is drawn from the center of the cornea straight back through the pupil to the retina. Which structures does that line cross, in order from front to back? The answer is the cornea, the aqueous humor of the anterior chamber, the pupil, the lens, the vitreous body and finally the retina. That line is the optic axis.

Question 8378. Which cells of the retina send their fibers out of the eye to form the optic nerve? The answer is the ganglion cells, whose axons form the nerve fiber layer. The fibers gather at the optic disc and leave the eye there. Their cell bodies lie in the ganglion cell layer.

Question 8379. Which of these statements about the fovea is correct: it contains cones only, it contains rods only, it is the place where the optic nerve leaves the eye, or it is the thickest part of the retina? The answer is that it contains cones only. Each cone there is joined to a single bipolar cell, which gives fine detail.

Question 8380. Which retinal layer lies immediately inside the pigment epithelium, and which cells are found in it? The answer is the layer of rods and cones, which holds the outer parts of the receptor cells. The pigment epithelium wraps around the tips of those receptors. That close contact is what is lost when the retina detaches.

Question 8381. A constructed illustration: a patient with long-standing raised blood pressure has a swollen disc and small hemorrhages that follow the bundles of nerve fibers in the retina. Why do those hemorrhages take that shape? The answer is that the fibers of the nerve fiber layer run in bundles toward the optic disc, and blood tracks along them.

Question 8382. Which part of the retina lies farthest forward, ending at a scalloped edge near the equator of the eye? The answer is the front edge of the retina, which ends at the ora serrata. Beyond that line the ciliary body continues forward. The retina does not reach the front of the eye.

Question 8383. Which of these explains why the optic disc is a blind spot: it holds no receptors, it has no blood supply, it lies too far forward, or it is covered by the choroid? The answer is that the disc holds no receptors, only the axons of the ganglion cells on their way out of the eye. The brain fills in the missing part of the picture, so the gap is not noticed.

Question 8384. Which of these pairs belongs together: the macula with the sharpest vision, the optic disc with the sharpest vision, the ora serrata with color vision, or the fovea with the blind spot? The answer is the macula with the sharpest vision. The fovea lies at its center and holds the greatest density of cones.

Question 8385. Which of these structures separates the neural retina from the choroid: the sclera, the pigment epithelium, the vitreous body, or the ciliary body? The answer is the pigment epithelium. It is the outermost layer of the retina and lies against the choroid. The neural retina can separate from it, and that separation is a retinal detachment.

Question 8386. Which structure of the eye changes its shape to focus on objects at different distances, and what is that change called? The answer is the lens, and the change is accommodation. The ciliary muscle controls it. When that muscle contracts, the lens becomes rounder and the eye focuses on something near.

Question 8387. Which of these holds the lens in place: the suspensory ligament, the optic nerve, the canal of Schlemm, or the ora serrata? The answer is the suspensory ligament. Its fibers run from the ciliary body to the equator of the lens. They keep the lens centered behind the pupil.

Question 8388. A described section through the front of the eye shows a flattened oval body with a dense center, hung by fine strands from a ring of tissue. Which structure is described, and what is the ring? The answer is the lens, suspended from the ciliary body. The fine strands form the suspensory ligament, and the dense center is the nucleus.

Question 8389. Which part of the lens lies in the center, and which part surrounds it? The answer is that the nucleus lies in the center and the cortex surrounds it. The lens grows through life by adding new fibers to the outside. That is why the nucleus is its oldest part.

Question 8390. Which of these statements about the lens is correct: it supplies about one third of the power of the eye and can be changed, it supplies most of the power, it has no refractive power, or it refracts more than the cornea? The answer is that it supplies about one third of the power of the eye and can be changed. The lens adjusts its power to focus on near objects.

Question 8391. A constructed illustration: the pupil of one eye looks white instead of black, and that eye does not see well. Which structure lies directly behind the pupil, and how does the loss of its clarity explain the appearance? The answer is the lens. A clear lens lets light pass, so the pupil looks black, while a cloudy lens scatters light back and looks white.

Question 8392. Immediately behind the iris and the pupil lies which structure, and which clear gel lies immediately behind that? The answer is the lens behind the iris and the vitreous body behind the lens. The posterior chamber, filled with aqueous humor, lies between the iris and the lens. The vitreous body fills the rest of the eye behind the lens.

Question 8393. Which muscle changes the shape of the lens, and what happens to the lens when that muscle contracts? The answer is the ciliary muscle, and the lens becomes rounder and thicker. That change increases its power for near vision. When the muscle relaxes, the lens flattens again for distance.

Question 8394. Which of these is the transparent structure that lies immediately behind the pupil: the cornea, the lens, the retina, or the choroid? The answer is the lens. It lies behind the iris and the pupil and in front of the vitreous body. The cornea lies in front of the pupil.

Question 8395. True or false: the lens goes on adding new fibers throughout life, so its center is its oldest part. The answer is true. New fibers are laid down at the edge of the lens, so it grows larger and less elastic with age.

Question 8396. A constructed illustration: a person cannot see distant objects clearly, and the eye is longer than usual from front to back. Where does the image form, and which structure inside the eye could change the focus? The answer is that the image forms in front of the retina, and the only structure that can change the focus is the lens.

Question 8397. Which of these describes the fibers of the lens correctly: they lose their nuclei as they mature and fill the lens, they are replaced every year, they contain blood vessels, or they are the same cells as the corneal epithelium? The answer is that they lose their nuclei as they mature and fill the lens. They are never replaced.

Question 8398. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ciliary muscle with the shape of the lens, the suspensory ligament with the size of the pupil, the iris with the shape of the lens, or the cornea with the shape of the lens? The answer is the ciliary muscle with the shape of the lens. The iris controls the size of the pupil instead.

Question 8399. Which of these structures is found between the iris and the vitreous body: the cornea, the lens, the retina, or the sclera? The answer is the lens. It lies behind the iris, and the vitreous body lies behind it. The cornea lies in front of the iris.

Question 8400. Which of these explains why the lens must change shape to focus on a near object: the distance from the lens to the retina changes, the refractive power of the eye must increase, the pupil must widen, or the cornea must flatten? The answer is that the refractive power of the eye must increase. The lens does that by becoming rounder.

To summarize, the eyeball is built of three concentric coats: the fibrous coat of sclera and cornea outside, the vascular coat of choroid, ciliary body and iris in the middle, and the neural coat of retina inside. The cornea is the transparent front window, without blood vessels but richly supplied with nerves, and its endothelium pumps fluid out to keep it clear. The sclera is the tough white outer coat, thinnest behind the insertions of the rectus muscles and pierced at the back by the optic nerve. The choroid is the dark vascular layer between the sclera and the retina, and the retina carries the rods and cones, with the fovea at the center of the macula for sharp vision and the optic disc for the blind spot. The lens lies behind the pupil and the iris, held by the suspensory ligament, and the ciliary muscle changes its shape to add power for near vision. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 85 — Eye, Part Two

This chapter continues the study of the eye by moving through the iris, the ciliary body, the vitreous body, the optic nerve, and the muscles that turn the globe. It holds one hundred questions, and each one states its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The structures described here work together as one optical and mechanical system, and the questions follow them in that order. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 8401. Which part of the eye is the colored diaphragm that hangs in front of the lens and has a hole at its center? The answer is the iris. The hole is the pupil, through which light passes to reach the lens. The iris forms the most anterior part of the uveal tract.

Question 8402. Which two spaces does the iris separate: the anterior and posterior chambers, the posterior chamber and the vitreous body, the anterior chamber and the vitreous body, or the vitreous body and the subretinal space? The answer is the anterior and posterior chambers. The anterior chamber lies between the cornea and the iris, and the posterior chamber is the ring behind the iris.

Question 8403. Which muscle of the iris is a ring of circular fibers that narrows the pupil when it contracts? The answer is the sphincter pupillae. Its fibers encircle the pupillary margin, so shortening them draws the margin inward like a purse string. It is also called the pupillary constrictor.

Question 8404. Which sheet of the iris is arranged in radial fibers that run from the root toward the pupillary margin and widen the pupil when it contracts? The answer is the dilator pupillae. Its fibers run outward like the spokes of a wheel, so shortening them pulls the margin open. It lies deep to the stroma.

Question 8405. Which fibers make the pupil narrow when light falls on the eye: sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion, parasympathetic fibers carried by the third cranial nerve, fibers of the fourth cranial nerve, or fibers of the sixth cranial nerve? The answer is parasympathetic fibers carried by the third cranial nerve. They reach the sphincter through the short ciliary nerves.

Question 8406. Which fibers widen the pupil in dim light: parasympathetic fibers of the third cranial nerve, sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion, fibers of the optic nerve, or fibers of the fourth cranial nerve? The answer is sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion. They run with the internal carotid artery and reach the iris through the long ciliary nerves.

Question 8407. True or false: the pupil looks black because the iris contains no pigment at all. The answer is false. Every iris has a pigmented posterior epithelium, and the black appearance comes from light being absorbed inside the eye. The pigment in the front of the iris is what makes the eye brown, hazel, green, or blue.

Question 8408. Which vessels form the major arterial circle at the root of the iris: the long posterior ciliary arteries and the anterior ciliary arteries, the short posterior ciliary arteries alone, the central retinal artery and its branches, or the ophthalmic artery and the angular artery? The answer is the long posterior ciliary arteries and the anterior ciliary arteries. The circle lies in the ciliary body near the iris root.

Question 8409. Which structure lies immediately behind the pupillary margin of the iris, so that the margin rests lightly against it? The answer is the lens. The posterior chamber is only a narrow ring between the iris and the lens, and the pupillary margin glides over the front of the lens as the pupil changes size. The cornea lies in front of the iris.

Question 8410. The outer edge of the iris joins the ciliary body at the thinnest part of the iris. What is that junction called, and why does it matter? The answer is the iris root, which tears more easily than the rest of the iris. A blunt blow to the eye can detach the iris there, an injury described as iridodialysis.

Question 8411. A described optical section through the front of the eye shows a thin pigmented sheet hanging from the side wall, with a clear space in front and a clear round body behind. What does the sheet represent? The answer is the iris. The clear space is the anterior chamber, and the round body behind is the lens.

Question 8412. A described close-up of a normal iris shows a raised circular ridge partway between the root and the pupil, with pits and radiating ridges on its outer side. What is that ridge? The answer is the collarette, which marks the junction of the pupillary zone and the ciliary zone. The pits are the crypts, and the outer zone carries the contraction furrows.

Question 8413. A constructed illustration: a person has a drooping upper lid, an eye that turns outward and downward, and a pupil on that side that is wide and does not narrow in light. Which muscle of the iris has lost its nerve supply? The answer is the sphincter pupillae. The third cranial nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers to it.

Question 8414. A constructed illustration: one pupil is smaller than the other, the upper lid on that side droops slightly, and the skin of that side of the face does not sweat. Which muscle of the iris has failed, and under whose control does it normally lie? The answer is the dilator pupillae, which is supplied by sympathetic fibers. Losing that supply leaves the sphincter unopposed.

Question 8415. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sphincter pupillae with widening the pupil, the dilator pupillae with narrowing the pupil, the collarette with the junction of the two zones of the iris, or the iris root with the center of the pupil? The answer is the collarette with the junction of the two zones. The sphincter narrows the pupil and the dilator widens it.

Question 8416. Name the two muscles of the iris and say in which direction each one moves the pupil. The answer is the sphincter pupillae, which narrows the pupil, and the dilator pupillae, which widens it. The sphincter is a ring of circular fibers and the dilator is a sheet of radial fibers.

Question 8417. A described transverse section through the front of an eye shows a thin pigmented sheet whose peripheral edge is continuous with a triangular mass of tissue behind it, with a narrow gap between the two at the angle. Which two structures are continuous there? The answer is the iris and the ciliary body, joined at the iris root. The gap is the iridocorneal angle.

Question 8418. A described illustration: a person has small irregular pupils that do not narrow when a light is shone into either eye, yet they do narrow when the person looks at a near object. Which part of the reflex pathway is at fault: the optic nerve, the sphincter pupillae, the midbrain region that links them, or the ciliary muscle? The answer is the midbrain region that links them. The near response reaches the sphincter by a separate route.

Question 8419. Why does an eye with very little pigment in the front of the iris still look blue: because the iris epithelium is blue, because the blood within the iris is blue, because short wavelengths of light are scattered back by the fine texture of the stroma, or because the lens is blue? The answer is that short wavelengths are scattered back by the fine texture of the stroma. Brown eyes simply carry more melanin there.

Question 8420. Which layer of the iris continues backward as the pigmented epithelium of the ciliary body and the retina, and where does it lie? The answer is the posterior pigmented epithelium of the iris, the deepest of the iris layers. It faces the posterior chamber and rests against the lens at the pupillary margin.

Question 8421. Which part of the eye is the ring of tissue between the root of the iris and the retina, containing both muscle and secretory epithelium? The answer is the ciliary body. In section it is triangular, with its base against the sclera and its apex toward the lens. It belongs to the uveal tract.

Question 8422. What happens to the lens when the ciliary muscle contracts: it becomes flatter for distant vision, it becomes more convex for near vision, it moves into the anterior chamber, or it does not change? The answer is that it becomes more convex for near vision. Contraction slackens the suspensory fibers, and the elastic lens rounds up.

Question 8423. What are the many small ridges on the inner surface of the ciliary body that produce the fluid filling the front of the eye? The answer is the ciliary processes. They are covered by a double layer of epithelium whose inner layer secretes aqueous humor. They lie in the pars plicata.

Question 8424. What is the name of the ring of fine fibers running from the ciliary body to the capsule of the lens and holding the lens in place? The answer is the zonule of Zinn, also called the suspensory ligament. Tension in these fibers keeps the lens flattened until the ciliary muscle contracts.

Question 8425. Which nerve supply makes the ciliary muscle contract for near vision: sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion, parasympathetic fibers carried by the third cranial nerve, fibers of the fourth cranial nerve, or fibers of the optic nerve? The answer is parasympathetic fibers carried by the third cranial nerve. They relay in the ciliary ganglion and reach the muscle by the short ciliary nerves.

Question 8426. Where does aqueous humor go as it leaves the anterior chamber: through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm, into the vitreous body, into the optic nerve, or into the choroid? The answer is through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm. From there it passes to the aqueous veins.

Question 8427. True or false: aqueous humor is produced in the anterior chamber and then flows backward through the pupil. The answer is false. It is produced by the epithelium of the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber, and it flows forward through the pupil into the anterior chamber before leaving at the angle.

Question 8428. Which two structures does the zonule of Zinn connect, and what does the connection allow? The answer is the ciliary body and the capsule of the lens. When the ciliary muscle contracts, the ring narrows and the fibers slacken, so the lens becomes more convex.

Question 8429. In which tissue does the canal of Schlemm lie, and at which part of the globe is it found? The answer is the sclera at the corneoscleral limbus, at the iridocorneal angle. Aqueous humor reaches it after passing through the trabecular meshwork, and from the canal it drains into the aqueous veins.

Question 8430. A described section through the wall of the eye shows a triangular mass of tissue with its base against the sclera and its apex toward the lens, its inner surface thrown into many small ridges. What is this tissue, and what covers its inner surface? The answer is the ciliary body, with the ciliary processes on its inner surface.

Question 8431. A described section of the iridocorneal angle shows fluid passing between beams of connective tissue into a thin-walled channel buried in the sclera. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the trabecular meshwork and the canal of Schlemm. This is the main route by which aqueous humor leaves the eye.

Question 8432. A described section of the inner wall of the eye shows the retina ending in a wavy line, with a smooth dark zone beyond it and ridges beginning further forward. What is the wavy line called, and what lies beyond it? The answer is the ora serrata, beyond which lie the pars plana and then the ciliary processes.

Question 8433. A constructed illustration: a medication that blocks the parasympathetic supply to the eye leaves the pupil wide and makes reading blurred for a few hours. Which muscle has been paralyzed, and why does reading suffer? The answer is the ciliary muscle, which can no longer change the shape of the lens. The pupil is wide for the same reason.

Question 8434. A constructed illustration: a middle-aged person must hold reading material farther away, although the pupils react normally and the eye is otherwise healthy. Which structure has lost its elasticity, and what is the effect? The answer is the lens, which can no longer become convex enough for near vision. The ciliary muscle still contracts normally.

Question 8435. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ciliary muscle with the production of aqueous humor, the ciliary epithelium with accommodation, the zonule of Zinn with suspension of the lens, or the canal of Schlemm with the secretion of aqueous humor? The answer is the zonule of Zinn with suspension of the lens. The ciliary muscle acts in accommodation.

Question 8436. Name the two routes by which aqueous humor leaves the eye, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the trabecular route and the uveoscleral route. Most of the fluid passes through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm, while a smaller amount seeps through the ciliary muscle and the sclera.

Question 8437. Which group of fibers in the ciliary muscle pulls on the scleral spur and helps keep the trabecular meshwork open: the circular fibers, the radial fibers, the longitudinal fibers, or the fibers of the dilator pupillae? The answer is the longitudinal fibers, which run forward from the choroid to the scleral spur.

Question 8438. Which three structures make up the uveal tract: the iris, the ciliary body and the choroid, the cornea, the iris and the lens, the retina, the choroid and the sclera, or the iris, the lens and the vitreous body? The answer is the iris, the ciliary body and the choroid. These three are continuous with one another.

Question 8439. A constructed illustration: in one eye the outflow of aqueous humor is blocked at the angle, the globe becomes hard, and the optic nerve head becomes cupped. Which structures are involved, and why does sight fail? The answer is the trabecular meshwork and the optic nerve, whose fibers are damaged by the raised pressure. The ciliary epithelium continues to secrete fluid.

Question 8440. Why does the epithelium covering the ciliary body consist of two layers, one pigmented and one not? The answer is that the two layers are the two walls of the optic cup. The outer wall becomes the pigmented layer, and the inner wall becomes the non-pigmented layer that secretes aqueous humor.

Question 8441. Which structure is the transparent gel that fills the large chamber behind the lens and in front of the retina? The answer is the vitreous body. It occupies about four fifths of the volume of the globe and gives the eye its shape. It is also called the vitreous humor.

Question 8442. Of what is the vitreous body mainly made: water with fine collagen fibers and hyaluronic acid, blood plasma with red cells, a meshwork of elastic fibers, or a thin film of aqueous humor? The answer is water with fine collagen fibers and hyaluronic acid. The gel is about ninety-nine per cent water, and its few cells lie in the cortex.

Question 8443. Which two things does the vitreous body lack, unlike almost every other tissue of the eye? The answer is blood vessels and nerves. It is nourished by diffusion from the tissues around it, mainly the ciliary body and the retina. Its avascular nature helps it stay clear.

Question 8444. What is the name of the narrow channel that runs through the vitreous body from the optic disc to the back of the lens? The answer is the hyaloid canal, also called the canal of Cloquet. It is the remains of the path taken by the hyaloid artery in the fetus.

Question 8445. Where is the vitreous body attached most firmly to the wall of the eye: at the optic disc, at the macula, at the vitreous base over the ora serrata, or at the posterior pole? The answer is at the vitreous base over the ora serrata. There the gel is fused with the retina and the pars plana, and the attachment lasts for life.

Question 8446. Which statement describes a main function of the vitreous body: it refracts light more than the cornea does, it holds the retina against the wall of the eye, it produces aqueous humor, or it changes shape for near vision? The answer is that it holds the retina against the wall of the eye. It also transmits light and cushions the globe.

Question 8447. True or false: the vitreous body is renewed continuously, in the same way as the aqueous humor. The answer is false. The vitreous body is formed before birth and is never replaced. Its gel slowly liquefies with age, which is one reason floaters become common later in life.

Question 8448. Which structure lies immediately in front of the vitreous body, separated from it by the thin hyaloid membrane? The answer is the lens, together with the ring of fibers of the zonule. The vitreous body fills the space behind the lens and in front of the retina.

Question 8449. The vitreous base straddles which two structures, and why does that matter? The answer is the ora serrata, where the retina behind it meets the pars plana of the ciliary body in front. Because the gel is fused to both, traction there can tear the retina.

Question 8450. A described section of an eye shows a clear gel filling the space behind the lens, with a narrow channel running through it from the lens to the optic disc. What is the channel, and what ran through it before birth? The answer is the hyaloid canal, which carried the hyaloid artery.

Question 8451. A described specimen of an aging eye shows the gel collapsed away from the back wall, with a small ring-shaped opacity that had lain around the optic disc before it detached. What has happened? The answer is a posterior vitreous detachment, the ring being the part of the gel that had been attached around the disc.

Question 8452. A described microscopic section of the outer part of the vitreous body shows fine collagen fibers and a few scattered cells but no blood vessels. What region is shown, and what are the cells? The answer is the cortex of the vitreous body, and the cells are the hyalocytes that lie near its surface.

Question 8453. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the eye, a person sees many dark specks drifting across the vision, and a red haze lies behind the lens. Which structure contains the blood? The answer is the vitreous body. Because it is a gel, blood within it clears slowly, and the specks are shadows of the drifting clot.

Question 8454. A constructed illustration: a person suddenly sees flashes of light and a shower of floaters, and a shadow begins to rise across the side of the vision. Which sequence of events in the vitreous is described? The answer is separation of the gel from the retina with a tear, which lets fluid lift the retina from the wall. The treating clinician decides what follows.

Question 8455. Which of these pairs belongs together: the vitreous base with the optic disc, the hyaloid canal with the remnant of the hyaloid artery, the cortex of the vitreous with the retinal pigment epithelium, or the vitreous body with the production of aqueous humor? The answer is the hyaloid canal with the remnant of the hyaloid artery.

Question 8456. Name two places, other than the vitreous base, where the vitreous body is attached to the retina. The answer is the margin of the optic disc and the region of the macula. Attachments are also found along the larger retinal vessels, and all of them weaken with age.

Question 8457. Which change in the vitreous body explains why floaters become more common with age: the gel becomes firmer and shrinks away from the lens, the gel liquefies and forms pockets while its fibers clump, the gel fills with blood vessels, or the gel is replaced by aqueous humor? The answer is that the gel liquefies and forms pockets while its fibers clump.

Question 8458. Why does the vitreous body bend light far less than the cornea does: because it lies behind the lens, because its refractive index is close to that of water and of the tissues around it, because it contains no collagen, or because light does not pass through it? The answer is that its refractive index is close to that of water. Light is bent mainly at the cornea.

Question 8459. In the embryo a vessel runs through the developing vitreous body from the optic disc to the lens and then disappears. What is that vessel, and what does it leave behind? The answer is the hyaloid artery, which leaves behind the hyaloid canal. If part of it persists, a fine strand may remain behind the lens.

Question 8460. When the retina detaches, fluid from the vitreous collects in a space that does not exist in the healthy eye. What is that space called, and which two layers does it separate? The answer is the subretinal space, which separates the retina from the retinal pigment epithelium. The fluid reaches it through a tear.

Question 8461. Which cranial nerve carries the fibers that leave the retina and run to the brain, and what kind of fibers are they? The answer is the second cranial nerve, the optic nerve, which carries special sensory fibers for sight. Its fibers arise from the ganglion cells of the retina and pass backward to the optic chiasm.

Question 8462. From which cells of the retina do the fibers of the optic nerve arise: the rods, the cones, the bipolar cells, or the ganglion cells? The answer is the ganglion cells. Their axons run along the inner surface of the retina, converge at the optic disc, and leave the eye as the optic nerve.

Question 8463. At which point in the retina do the fibers of the optic nerve leave the eye, and why is that point blind? The answer is the optic disc, where the fibers converge and turn backward. It contains no rods or cones, so it forms the blind spot.

Question 8464. Which vessels enter and leave the eye at the optic disc and supply the inner layers of the retina? The answer is the central retinal artery and the central retinal vein. They run inside the optic nerve for part of their course and branch on the surface of the disc.

Question 8465. The optic nerve is wrapped in which coverings, and what fills the space between them: a single fibrous sheath with lymph, the three meninges with cerebrospinal fluid, a layer of fat, or the capsule of the orbit? The answer is the three meninges, with cerebrospinal fluid between the arachnoid and the pia. That space is continuous with the space around the brain.

Question 8466. Which two structures pass through the optic canal: the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery, the optic nerve and the oculomotor nerve, the optic nerve and the trochlear nerve, or the optic nerve and the abducens nerve? The answer is the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery. The artery lies inferolateral to the nerve.

Question 8467. True or false: the optic nerve is a peripheral nerve, built like the nerves that supply the limbs. The answer is false. It is a tract of the central nervous system, and its fibers are myelinated by the same cells that myelinate the brain. That is why it is wrapped in meninges.

Question 8468. Which small collection of nerve cells lies immediately lateral to the optic nerve in the orbit, between the nerve and the lateral rectus muscle? The answer is the ciliary ganglion. The parasympathetic fibers for the pupil relay there before reaching the eye through the short ciliary nerves.

Question 8469. At the optic chiasm, which fibers cross to the opposite side, and which stay on the same side? The answer is that fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross, while fibers from the temporal half stay on the same side. This is why a lesion of the chiasm removes the outer halves of both visual fields.

Question 8470. A described axial section through the orbit shows a band of tissue running from the back of the globe to the apex of the orbit, lying in the middle of the cone of muscles. Which structure is shown? The answer is the optic nerve. It is surrounded by orbital fat and lies free within the muscle cone.

Question 8471. A described scan shows a mass growing upward from the region of the sella turcica and pressing on the structure above it. Which structure is compressed, which fibers are lost first, and what does the person notice? The answer is the optic chiasm, whose crossing fibers are lost first, removing the outer half of each visual field.

Question 8472. A described view of the back of the eye shows a disc whose margins are blurred and raised, with the vessels riding over the swelling and no cupping. What does this appearance indicate? The answer is swelling of the optic disc from raised pressure within the skull, because the sheath of the nerve communicates with the space around the brain.

Question 8473. A constructed illustration: a person loses the sight of one eye suddenly and without pain, and the retina looks pale except for a cherry-red spot at the macula. Which vessel is blocked? The answer is the central retinal artery. The macula stays red because the choroid beneath it still shows through the thin retina there.

Question 8474. A constructed illustration: a young person has blurred vision in one eye and pain when the eye is moved. Which structure is inflamed, and why does movement hurt? The answer is the optic nerve. Its sheath is supplied by sensory nerves and is tethered within the orbit, so moving the eye pulls on the inflamed nerve.

Question 8475. Which of these pairs belongs together: the optic disc with the crossing of fibers, the optic chiasm with the blind spot, the lateral geniculate body with the relay of visual fibers, or the optic radiation with the retina? The answer is the lateral geniculate body with the relay of visual fibers. From it the fibers pass to the occipital cortex.

Question 8476. A described examination: when a light is swung from one eye to the other, the pupil narrows on the first side and widens on the second, and the second eye also sees less well. Which structure is at fault? The answer is the optic nerve of the second eye. Its signal is weaker, so the pupil dilates when the light reaches it.

Question 8477. Why does the optic disc swell when pressure inside the skull rises: because the nerve carries no sheath, because the space within its sheath communicates with the space around the brain, because the nerve produces cerebrospinal fluid, or because the retina secretes fluid? The answer is that the space within its sheath communicates with the space around the brain.

Question 8478. Which fibers of the right optic nerve remain on the right side at the chiasm, and where do they end? The answer is the fibers from the temporal half of the right retina, which end in the right lateral geniculate body. Fibers from the nasal half cross to the left side.

Question 8479. In an axial section through the orbit, in which direction does the optic nerve run from the back of the globe, and through which opening does it leave the orbit? The answer is backward and medially, through the optic canal. Because the two canals converge, the nerves form a shape like an X as they approach the chiasm.

Question 8480. The retina and the optic nerve develop from an outgrowth of the embryonic brain. Which adult features of the optic nerve follow from that origin: its covering of meninges and its myelin, its supply from the facial artery, its bony canal, or its union with the ciliary body? The answer is its covering of meninges and its myelin. A structure derived from the brain keeps its coverings.

Question 8481. Which muscle turns the eye directly outward, away from the nose? The answer is the lateral rectus. It arises from the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit and inserts on the lateral side of the globe. Its opponent, the medial rectus, turns the eye inward.

Question 8482. Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle: the third cranial nerve, the fourth cranial nerve, the sixth cranial nerve, or the optic nerve? The answer is the sixth cranial nerve, the abducens nerve. It has the longest intracranial course of the nerves that move the eye, so it is often affected by raised pressure within the skull.

Question 8483. Which muscle of the eye sends its tendon through a fibrous pulley attached to the frontal bone on the medial wall of the orbit? The answer is the superior oblique. The pulley is the trochlea. After passing through it, the tendon turns backward and outward to reach the globe.

Question 8484. Which muscle arises from the floor of the orbit just lateral to the lacrimal groove and turns the eye upward when the eye is turned inward? The answer is the inferior oblique. It runs backward and outward below the globe, and it is the only muscle of the orbit that does not arise from the apex.

Question 8485. Which set of actions belongs to the superior rectus when the eye is in the primary position: elevation, intorsion and adduction; depression, extorsion and abduction; pure elevation; or pure abduction? The answer is elevation, intorsion and adduction. Because the muscle approaches the globe at an angle, its pull is not purely upward.

Question 8486. Which muscles arise from the common tendinous ring at the apex of the orbit: the four rectus muscles, the four rectus muscles and the superior oblique, all six muscles that move the eye, or the two oblique muscles alone? The answer is the four rectus muscles. The superior oblique arises above and medial to the ring, and the inferior oblique from the floor.

Question 8487. True or false: the medial rectus muscle is supplied by the sixth cranial nerve. The answer is false. It is supplied by the third cranial nerve, like the superior and inferior rectus muscles and the inferior oblique. The sixth cranial nerve supplies only the lateral rectus.

Question 8488. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the levator palpebrae superioris, so that the two are often described together as a single sheet? The answer is the superior rectus. The levator lies above it, arising from the roof of the orbit, and both run forward to the globe and the lid.

Question 8489. Which muscle lies immediately above the floor of the orbit and is at risk when the floor is fractured and the contents of the orbit are displaced downward? The answer is the inferior rectus. It runs forward just above the bone, so it may be caught in the break, and the eye then cannot look upward.

Question 8490. A described axial section through both orbits shows a muscle running forward along the medial wall of each orbit, separated from the nasal cavity by a thin plate of bone. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the medial rectus. It lies against the ethmoid air cells, which is why surgery there can injure it.

Question 8491. A described coronal section through the orbits shows, around the optic nerve on each side, a ring of four muscles set at the four points of the compass. Which muscles form the ring? The answer is the four rectus muscles, superior, inferior, medial and lateral. The oblique muscles lie outside this cone.

Question 8492. A described specimen of the orbit viewed from above shows a rounded tendon passing through a small fibrous ring on the medial wall and then turning sharply backward. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the superior oblique, and the ring is the trochlea. No other muscle of the orbit changes direction in this way.

Question 8493. A constructed illustration: a person cannot turn one eye outward, and objects appear as two images side by side. Which muscle is weak, and which nerve is at fault? The answer is the lateral rectus, supplied by the sixth cranial nerve. The images are separated horizontally because the eyes no longer point together.

Question 8494. A constructed illustration: a person sees two images, one above the other, and the separation is worst when going down stairs or when the head is tilted to one side. Which muscle is weak? The answer is the superior oblique, the main depressor when the eye is turned inward, so its weakness shows most in that position.

Question 8495. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral rectus with the third cranial nerve, the superior oblique with the fourth cranial nerve, the medial rectus with the sixth cranial nerve, or the inferior oblique with the optic nerve? The answer is the superior oblique with the fourth cranial nerve. The lateral rectus is supplied by the sixth and the medial rectus by the third.

Question 8496. Which muscle of the orbit arises from the roof of the orbit above the common tendinous ring and lies immediately beneath the bone: the superior rectus, the levator palpebrae superioris, the superior oblique, or the medial rectus? The answer is the levator palpebrae superioris, which raises the upper lid. The superior rectus lies immediately below it.

Question 8497. Which set of actions belongs to the inferior oblique: elevation, extorsion and abduction; depression, intorsion and adduction; pure depression; or pure intorsion? The answer is elevation, extorsion and abduction. Like the superior oblique, it approaches the globe from behind, so its action depends on the position of the eye.

Question 8498. A constructed illustration: a person tilts the head to one side and the eye on that side rises while the other eye stays level, producing a vertical double image. Which muscle is weak on the side that rises? The answer is the superior oblique. In the tilting test the weak muscle fails to hold the eye steady.

Question 8499. In an axial section through an orbit, which muscles lie on either side of the optic nerve, and how do they relate to the walls of the orbit? The answer is the medial rectus against the medial wall and the lateral rectus against the lateral wall. The nerve lies in the middle of the cone between them.

Question 8500. Which muscle of the orbit arises from the orbital surface of the maxilla, passes below the globe and inserts on its upper and outer surface behind the equator? The answer is the inferior oblique. It is the only muscle of the eye that arises from the front of the orbit.

To summarize, the iris is the pigmented diaphragm in front of the lens, and its two muscles set the size of the pupil: the sphincter pupillae narrows it under parasympathetic fibers of the third cranial nerve, and the dilator pupillae widens it under sympathetic fibers. The ciliary body lies between the iris root and the ora serrata, and its muscle changes the shape of the lens for near vision while its epithelium secretes aqueous humor, which leaves the eye at the iridocorneal angle through the trabecular meshwork and the canal of Schlemm. The vitreous body is an avascular gel formed before birth that holds the retina against the wall and is never replaced, and its strongest attachment is the vitreous base over the ora serrata. The optic nerve is a tract of the brain wrapped in meninges, and it runs backward and medially through the optic canal, so raised pressure within the skull can swell its disc. The six muscles that move the eye arise from the apex or the floor of the orbit, and the fourth and sixth cranial nerves supply the superior oblique and the lateral rectus while the third supplies the rest. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 86 — Ear

The ear is two organs in one small space: a mechanical receiver that gathers sound, and a fluid-filled analyzer that turns it into nerve signals. This chapter follows the path of sound from the auricle, through the external acoustic meatus, across the tympanic membrane, along the three ossicles of the middle ear, and into the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus of the inner ear. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately after it, with the reason, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The items follow the route the sound travels, beginning with the external ear, then the middle ear, the ossicles, the tympanic membrane and the inner ear. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 8501. Which part of the ear is the visible elastic cartilage flap on the side of the head, and what tissue forms its lowest part? The answer is the auricle, also called the pinna, whose lobule is fat and fibrous tissue rather than cartilage. The auricle collects sound and funnels it into the ear canal.

Question 8502. How long is the external acoustic meatus in an adult: about 10 millimeters, about 25 millimeters, about 50 millimeters, or about 80 millimeters? The answer is about 25 millimeters. Most of that length lies within the temporal bone, and only the outer part is cartilaginous. In an infant the canal is shorter, which is one reason the small ear needs care.

Question 8503. A described otoscopic view shows the outer part of the ear canal lined by skin with fine hairs and yellow wax, and the deeper part lined by thin pale skin with no hairs. Which parts of the canal are shown? The answer is the cartilaginous part outside and the bony part deeper. The cartilaginous part carries the hairs and the wax glands, while the bony part has neither.

Question 8504. Which nerve supplies the skin of the anterior wall and the roof of the external acoustic meatus? The answer is the auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. It also supplies the skin in front of the ear and over the temple. Pain from a boil in that part of the canal is therefore felt in front of the ear.

Question 8505. Which glands in the ear canal produce the wax that protects it, and in which part of the canal do they lie? The answer is the ceruminous glands, which are modified sweat glands lying in the cartilaginous part. Their secretion mixes with the oil of the sebaceous glands to form cerumen.

Question 8506. In which part of the ear canal are hairs, sebaceous glands and ceruminous glands found together: the bony part, the cartilaginous part, both parts equally, or neither part? The answer is the cartilaginous part. It is the outer third and is continuous with the skin of the auricle. The bony part is lined by skin so thin that it lies on the periosteum.

Question 8507. A constructed illustration: a swimmer has an itchy, painful ear canal that is tender when the auricle is pulled, and the canal is swollen and wet. Which condition does this describe, and which layer is inflamed? The answer is inflammation of the external ear, with the skin of the canal involved. Such illustrations show why the canal is a common site of trouble after water exposure. The care of it belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 8508. True or false: the external acoustic meatus is a straight tube that runs directly from the auricle to the tympanic membrane. The answer is false. The canal is shaped like a gentle S, curving first forward and then backward. That is why the auricle is pulled upward and backward during examination in an adult.

Question 8509. What name is given to the curved rim that forms the outer border of the auricle? The answer is the helix. It runs from the front of the ear around the top and down to the lobule. The ridge inside it, dividing the concha from the rest of the auricle, is the antihelix.

Question 8510. Which nerve supplies the skin of the back of the auricle and the lower part of the concha: the auriculotemporal nerve, the great auricular nerve, the lesser occipital nerve, or the facial nerve? The answer is the great auricular nerve, which comes from the cervical plexus. The lesser occipital nerve supplies the upper part of the back of the auricle. The auriculotemporal nerve serves the front.

Question 8511. Which nerve explains a cough when the skin of the deep canal is touched with a speculum: the facial nerve, the glossopharyngeal nerve, the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, or the mandibular division of the trigeminal? The answer is the auricular branch of the vagus nerve. It supplies the posterior wall of the canal and the concha. Because the vagus also supplies the throat, stimulating its auricular branch can provoke a cough.

Question 8512. A described illustration shows an infant whose ear canal runs almost horizontally and is shorter than an adult canal, with the tympanic membrane nearly flat. How should the auricle be drawn during examination, and why? The answer is that it is pulled downward and backward. The infant canal is short and nearly straight, so the membrane is easier to see from below.

Question 8513. In a standing person the external acoustic meatus is not directed straight sideways. In which two directions does it run as it leaves the auricle? The answer is forward and slightly downward. That direction protects the canal and helps it drain.

Question 8514. Which part of the auricle is composed of fat and fibrous tissue and contains no cartilage? The answer is the lobule, the soft lowest part of the ear. All the rest of the auricle is supported by a single piece of elastic cartilage.

Question 8515. Which nerve supplies the skin of the anterior wall of the external acoustic meatus and the temple in front of the ear? The answer is the auriculotemporal nerve. The great auricular nerve, the lesser occipital nerve and the auricular branch of the vagus supply the back of the auricle. The pattern explains why ear pain can be felt in the jaw or the temple.

Question 8516. Which of these pairs belongs together: the helix with the prominent flap in front of the canal, the tragus with the curved outer rim, the concha with the deep bowl beside the canal, or the lobule with the firm cartilage of the ear? The answer is the concha with the deep bowl beside the canal. The tragus is the flap in front of the canal, and the lobule has no cartilage.

Question 8517. Into which lymph nodes does the auricle drain: only the deep cervical nodes, the parotid nodes in front with the mastoid and superficial cervical nodes behind, the nodes below the jaw, or the nodes in the armpit? The answer is the parotid nodes in front with the mastoid and superficial cervical nodes behind. The pattern follows the nerve and blood supply of the region.

Question 8518. A described study compares the ear canal to a tube closed at one end by the tympanic membrane, which boosts sounds of particular frequencies. Why does the canal behave this way, and which range does it favor? The answer is that the canal acts as a resonator, and being about 25 millimeters long it amplifies sounds of roughly 2 to 4 kilohertz. That range carries much of the information in speech.

Question 8519. A described dissection exposes the bowl-shaped hollow of the auricle that lies just outside the opening of the ear canal. What is that hollow called? The answer is the concha. The canal begins at the depth of the concha, and the tragus partly covers its opening. The concha helps gather sound into the canal.

Question 8520. A described specimen shows the auricle forming from small swellings around the first pharyngeal groove. From which arches do these swellings arise, and what does that origin explain? The answer is the first and second pharyngeal arches, which give six small hillocks. Because the middle ear and the ossicles arise from the same arches, a child born with a malformed auricle may also have a malformed middle ear.

Question 8521. Which nerve supplies the skin of the posterior wall of the ear canal and the skin over the back of the auricle? The answer is the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, with a small contribution from the great auricular nerve. The vagus branch also supplies the concha. The facial nerve sends a small branch to the same region.

Question 8522. A constructed illustration: a newborn has a small, poorly formed auricle and no visible ear canal on one side. Which structures may share the developmental fault, and why? The answer is the middle ear and the ossicles, which form from the same first and second pharyngeal arches as the auricle. The inner ear usually escapes, because it develops from a separate patch of ectoderm.

Question 8523. In which part of which bone does the tympanic cavity lie? The answer is the petrous part of the temporal bone. It is a narrow air-filled space between the tympanic membrane outside and the inner ear inside. Its roof is a thin plate of bone beneath the middle cranial fossa.

Question 8524. Which of these names the part of the tympanic cavity that lies above the level of the tympanic membrane: the hypotympanum, the mesotympanum, the epitympanum, or the mastoid antrum? The answer is the epitympanum, also called the attic. The mesotympanum lies at the level of the membrane and the hypotympanum below it.

Question 8525. A described view of the medial wall of the middle ear shows a rounded bulge of bone, an opening above it closed by the footplate of a small bone, and a second opening below it closed by a membrane. What are these three features? The answer is the promontory, the oval window and the round window. The promontory covers the first turn of the cochlea.

Question 8526. Which structure forms the roof of the tympanic cavity and separates it from the middle cranial fossa: the tegmen tympani, the mastoid antrum, the pyramid, or the promontory? The answer is the tegmen tympani. It is a thin plate of bone, in places only a fraction of a millimeter thick. Infection can spread upward through it in rare cases.

Question 8527. Which tube connects the tympanic cavity with the nasopharynx, and what is its main function? The answer is the pharyngotympanic tube, also called the auditory tube. It equalizes the pressure on the two sides of the tympanic membrane.

Question 8528. How many walls has the tympanic cavity, and which one carries the oval and round windows: four walls with the windows on the roof, five with the windows on the floor, six with the windows on the medial wall, or three with the windows on the lateral wall? The answer is six walls, with the windows on the medial wall. That medial wall faces the inner ear.

Question 8529. Why is infection of the middle ear more common in infants than in adults? The answer is that the pharyngotympanic tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal in the infant. Secretions from the throat therefore reach the middle ear more easily.

Question 8530. Which large vein lies immediately below the floor of the tympanic cavity, and which nerve runs across that floor? The answer is the internal jugular vein below, with the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve crossing the floor. The floor is a thin plate of bone over the vein. That nerve is one of the roots of the tympanic plexus.

Question 8531. Which is the smallest skeletal muscle in the body, which nerve supplies it, and what does it do? The answer is the stapedius, supplied by the facial nerve, and it pulls the stapes to damp the vibration of the ossicular chain. It lies in a small bony pyramid on the posterior wall of the middle ear.

Question 8532. Which nerve supplies the tensor tympani muscle: the facial nerve, the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, the glossopharyngeal nerve, or the vagus nerve? The answer is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. The tensor tympani pulls the handle of the malleus inward and tenses the tympanic membrane. The stapedius, its partner, is supplied by the facial nerve.

Question 8533. A described dissection follows a fine nerve that leaves the facial nerve in its canal, crosses the medial surface of the malleus, passes between the malleus and the incus, and leaves the middle ear by a small fissure. Which nerve is it, and what does it carry? The answer is the chorda tympani, which carries taste from the front two thirds of the tongue. After leaving the middle ear it joins the lingual nerve.

Question 8534. Which opening in the posterior wall of the tympanic cavity leads backward and upward into the mastoid antrum? The answer is the aditus to the mastoid antrum. Through it the mucous membrane of the middle ear is continuous with the air cells of the mastoid process.

Question 8535. A constructed illustration: a child has a red bulging tympanic membrane, fever and tenderness over the bone behind the ear. Which two cavities are involved, and how do they connect? The answer is the tympanic cavity and the mastoid air cells, joined by the aditus to the mastoid antrum. The illustration shows how infection passes from the middle ear into the mastoid.

Question 8536. Which of these pairs belongs together: the roof of the middle ear with the jugular bulb, the floor with the tegmen tympani, the medial wall with the oval window, or the anterior wall with the mastoid air cells? The answer is the medial wall with the oval window. The roof lies under the tegmen tympani and the floor over the jugular bulb.

Question 8537. Which structure runs in the medial wall of the middle ear just above the oval window: the chorda tympani, the facial nerve in its bony canal, the internal carotid artery, or the pharyngotympanic tube? The answer is the facial nerve in its bony canal. It runs horizontally above the oval window and then turns downward in the posterior wall. The chorda tympani branches from it lower down.

Question 8538. Into which space does the pharyngotympanic tube open, and at what level does that opening lie? The answer is the nasopharynx, at the level of the back of the nasal cavity behind the soft palate. The opening lies just above the floor of the nasopharynx. Its cartilage and muscle help it open during swallowing.

Question 8539. True or false: the tympanic cavity is filled with air and is lined by mucous membrane that is continuous with the lining of the pharyngotympanic tube. The answer is true. The cavity is an air space, and its lining is a thin mucous membrane. That continuity is why infection can travel from the throat to the middle ear.

Question 8540. What is the small bony projection on the posterior wall of the tympanic cavity, and which muscle tendon emerges from its summit? The answer is the pyramidal eminence, and the tendon of the stapedius emerges from it. Its tendon runs forward to the neck of the stapes.

Question 8541. Name the two muscles of the middle ear and the nerve that supplies each one. The answer is the tensor tympani, supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, and the stapedius, supplied by the facial nerve. Both act as dampers when loud sound reaches the ear.

Question 8542. A constructed illustration: a person has a discharging ear for months and then develops weakness of the face on the same side. Which nerve is involved, and why does middle ear disease threaten it? The answer is the facial nerve, which runs in a bony canal in the medial and posterior walls of the middle ear. A thin bony roof over the canal lets disease reach the nerve.

Question 8543. A described surgical view shows a nerve running horizontally above the oval window and then turning sharply downward in the posterior wall. What is the name and the course of that nerve? The answer is the facial nerve. It enters the temporal bone by the internal acoustic meatus, runs in the medial wall above the oval window, and turns down to leave by the stylomastoid foramen.

Question 8544. Which wall of the tympanic cavity separates it from the internal carotid artery, and what opening does that wall carry: the roof, the anterior wall with the pharyngotympanic tube, the floor with the jugular bulb, or the posterior wall with the aditus? The answer is the anterior wall, which carries the opening of the pharyngotympanic tube. The carotid canal lies just in front of that thin wall.

Question 8545. Which special sense is carried by the chorda tympani, and from which part of the tongue does it come? The answer is taste, from the front two thirds of the tongue. The nerve crosses the middle ear and leaves to join the lingual nerve. It also carries secretomotor fibers to the salivary glands below the jaw.

Question 8546. Which ossicle of the middle ear is attached to the tympanic membrane, and by which of its parts? The answer is the malleus, attached by its handle, also called the manubrium. The handle is fixed to the fibrous layer of the membrane along its upper part.

Question 8547. Which ossicle lies between the malleus and the stapes in the chain? The answer is the incus. Its body lies in the attic and articulates with the head of the malleus. Its long process runs downward and ends in a small knob that meets the head of the stapes.

Question 8548. Which is the smallest bone in the human body, and where does its base sit? The answer is the stapes, whose base, or footplate, sits in the oval window. It is shaped like a stirrup, with a head, a neck and two crura. Its base is held in the window by a ring of ligament.

Question 8549. Which of these lists the parts of the malleus: head, neck, lateral process and handle; body, long crus and short crus; head, neck and two crura; or base, apex and spiral lamina? The answer is head, neck, lateral process and handle. The second list describes the incus and the third describes the stapes.

Question 8550. A described specimen shows three small bones in a chain from a membrane to a small window, joined end to end and suspended in an air space by fine ligaments. Which bones are shown, and what is their function? The answer is the malleus, the incus and the stapes. They conduct vibration from the tympanic membrane to the oval window and match the impedance of air to that of fluid.

Question 8551. Which part of the incus articulates with the head of the stapes: the body, the short crus, the long crus with its lenticular process, or the lateral process? The answer is the long crus with its lenticular process. The long process runs downward behind the posterior part of the membrane. Its tip becomes the lenticular process, which forms the incudostapedial joint.

Question 8552. From which pharyngeal arches do the ossicles develop: the malleus and the incus from the first arch with the stapes from the second, all three from the first arch, all three from the second, or the malleus from the second with the others from the first?
