Which part of the bowel is shown? The answer is the sigmoid colon, with diverticula. It has a mesentery and lies in the left iliac fossa.

Question 8986. A constructed illustration: discomfort begins around the navel and later settles in the right iliac fossa, where pressing the wall is most tender at a point on the line between the umbilicus and the right anterior superior iliac spine. Which structure is inflamed? The answer is the vermiform appendix, and the tender point is McBurney point. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8987. Which of these structures lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum, within the hepatoduodenal ligament: the portal vein, the splenic artery, the left gastric artery, or the inferior vena cava? The answer is the portal vein, with the proper hepatic artery and the bile duct beside it. The splenic and left gastric arteries run along the pancreas.

Question 8988. Name two organs that lie behind the peritoneum and are therefore described as retroperitoneal. The answer is the kidneys and the pancreas, and the duodenum and the great vessels are also retroperitoneal. Such organs lie against the posterior abdominal wall and are covered by peritoneum only on their front.

Question 8989. Which muscle of the posterior abdominal wall lies immediately lateral to the psoas major, medial to the twelfth rib, and behind the kidney? The answer is the quadratus lumborum, which extends and laterally flexes the trunk. The psoas major lies in front of it and flexes the hip.

Question 8990. Which nerve of the lumbar plexus emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major and supplies the skin and muscles of the front of the thigh: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the genitofemoral nerve, or the ilioinguinal nerve? The answer is the femoral nerve. The obturator nerve emerges from the medial border instead.

Question 8991. Which structures cross immediately in front of the abdominal inferior vena cava as it ascends to the liver? The answer is the head of the pancreas and the third part of the duodenum above, with the root of the mesentery below. The inferior vena cava lies to the right of the aorta and in front of the vertebral column.

Question 8992. A described transverse section of the abdomen at the level of the third lumbar vertebra shows a vertebral body in the middle, two kidneys behind, and two large vessels in front of it. Which of those vessels lies to the left of the midline? The answer is the abdominal aorta. The inferior vena cava lies to its right.

Question 8993. At which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta end by dividing into the two common iliac arteries: the third lumbar, the fourth lumbar, the fifth lumbar, or the twelfth thoracic? The answer is the fourth lumbar vertebra, a little to the left of the midline. The common iliac arteries divide at the pelvic brim.

Question 8994. Which structure crosses the midline in front of the aorta and the inferior vena cava: the third part of the duodenum, the second part of the duodenum, the head of the pancreas, or the ascending colon? The answer is the third part of the duodenum. The second part descends on the right of the midline.

Question 8995. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a person has bruising over the left lower ribs and blood in the urine, and the described scan shows a collection behind the peritoneum on that side. Which organ is most likely injured? The answer is the left kidney, which lies behind the peritoneum under the eleventh and twelfth ribs. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 8996. True or false: the spleen lies entirely behind the peritoneum and is held in place by the renal fascia. The answer is false. The spleen is covered by peritoneum except at its hilum and is held by the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments. It lies against the left kidney but is not fixed by the renal fascia.

Question 8997. Which ligament contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas, and connects the spleen to the left kidney: the gastrosplenic ligament, the splenorenal ligament, the falciform ligament, or the phrenicocolic ligament? The answer is the splenorenal ligament. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the spleen to the stomach and carries the short gastric arteries.

Question 8998. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the upper abdomen shows a rounded organ on the left, behind the stomach and in front of the left kidney, with vessels entering its hilum. Which organ is shown? The answer is the spleen, and the vessels enter at its hilum. It lies below the left dome of the diaphragm.

Question 8999. The left renal vein crosses the midline in front of which structure: the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the left kidney, or the superior mesenteric artery? The answer is the abdominal aorta. It then passes behind the superior mesenteric artery to reach the inferior vena cava, and that crossing explains why it can be compressed.

Question 9000. A constructed illustration: a person has fractures of the left ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs and becomes pale and faint, and the described scan shows blood around the spleen and in the peritoneal cavity. Which organ has been injured, and why does the blood enter the peritoneal cavity? The answer is the spleen, which is covered by peritoneum and lies under those ribs. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

To summarize, the mediastinum is divided by the transverse thoracic plane into a superior and an inferior part, and the inferior part into anterior, middle and posterior divisions, with the heart in the middle. The transverse pericardial sinus lies between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk in front and the superior vena cava behind, and the trachea divides at the carina, where the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical. Each lung is divided by fissures into lobes and by bronchi into segments, the pleura forms the costodiaphragmatic recess and the cupola, and the intercostal vein, artery and nerve lie in the costal groove from above downward. The diaphragm has three main openings, the caval opening at the eighth thoracic vertebra, the esophageal opening at the tenth and the aortic hiatus at the twelfth, and the phrenic nerve runs in front of the root of the lung. In the abdomen the peritoneum forms the greater and lesser sacs, the mesentery and the omenta, the foregut is supplied by the celiac trunk, the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery and the hindgut by the inferior mesenteric artery, and blood from the gut, the spleen and the pancreas reaches the liver by the portal vein. The kidneys, the ureters, the pancreas, the duodenum and the great vessels lie behind the peritoneum, the inguinal canal and the femoral canal are the two passages through which a hernia may descend, and this chapter is educational material that does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 91 — Abdomen, Part Two

This chapter works through the abdomen below the diaphragm, taking its walls, its organs and its peritoneal spaces one at a time. It covers the anterior abdominal wall and the inguinal canal, the peritoneum and the spaces it creates, the stomach and the intestines, the liver with its biliary passages, the spleen, the pancreas, the kidneys and the posterior abdominal wall with its great vessels. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be kept in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 9001. Which flat muscle of the anterior abdominal wall is the most superficial, with fibers running downward and forward from the lower ribs to the iliac crest and the pubic bone? The answer is the external oblique muscle. Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament along its lower edge, and the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis lie deep to it.

Question 9002. The inguinal ligament is the folded lower edge of which structure: the aponeurosis of the external oblique, the internal oblique muscle, the transversus abdominis, or the fascia transversalis? The answer is the aponeurosis of the external oblique. It stretches from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle and forms the floor of the inguinal canal.

Question 9003. A described dissection of the groin shows a strong band running from the front of the hip bone to the pubic bone, with a canal above it. What is this band, and what does it form? The answer is the inguinal ligament, which forms the floor of the inguinal canal, and below its medial end lies the femoral canal.

Question 9004. Which area lies immediately medial to the inferior epigastric artery, bounded below by the inguinal ligament and medially by the rectus sheath, and is the site of a direct inguinal hernia? The answer is the weak area of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, known as Hesselbach's triangle. A direct hernia pushes through it, while an indirect hernia enters the canal lateral to the same artery.

Question 9005. A constructed illustration: a man lifts a heavy load and feels sudden pain in the groin, and the swelling that follows passes through the deep inguinal ring. Which structure has the swelling entered, and where does it lie relative to the inferior epigastric artery? The answer is the inguinal canal, lateral to that artery. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 9006. True or false: in the female the inguinal canal contains the round ligament of the uterus. The answer is true. The canal carries the round ligament in the female and the spermatic cord in the male, and the ilioinguinal nerve runs in it and leaves through the superficial ring.

Question 9007. Which of these pairs belongs together: the superficial inguinal ring with the fascia transversalis, the deep inguinal ring with the fascia transversalis, the deep inguinal ring with the external oblique aponeurosis, or the inguinal ligament with the internal oblique? The answer is the deep ring with the fascia transversalis, which it pierces lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. The superficial ring is a gap in the external oblique aponeurosis.

Question 9008. Which structure forms the roof of the inguinal canal: the external oblique aponeurosis, the arching fibers of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis, the inguinal ligament, or the fascia transversalis? The answer is the arching fibers of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. They pass above the cord from the abdominal wall to the pubis, while the inguinal ligament forms the floor.

Question 9009. Which midline band of connective tissue separates the two rectus abdominis muscles and is formed by the interwoven aponeuroses of the three flat muscles? The answer is the linea alba. It runs from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, narrow below the navel and broad above it, and it carries few vessels.

Question 9010. A described transverse section of the anterior abdominal wall, cut above the navel, shows the rectus abdominis enclosed in a sheath. Which aponeuroses lie in front of the muscle, and which behind it? The answer is the external oblique and the anterior layer of the internal oblique in front, and the posterior layer of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis behind.

Question 9011. Which nerve runs within the inguinal canal in front of the spermatic cord and supplies the skin of the upper medial thigh? The answer is the ilioinguinal nerve. It is a branch of the first lumbar nerve and enters the canal lateral to the deep ring, then leaves with the cord through the superficial ring.

Question 9012. Which of these organs lies behind the peritoneum: the stomach, the ascending colon, the transverse colon, or the jejunum? The answer is the ascending colon. It lies against the posterior abdominal wall and is covered by peritoneum only on its front and sides, while the transverse colon and the jejunum hang on mesenteries.

Question 9013. A described dissection of the upper abdomen shows a double sheet of peritoneum hanging from the greater curvature of the stomach down over the intestines. What is this sheet, and which two layers form it? The answer is the greater omentum, formed by the two layers of the dorsal mesogastrium, which fuse below the stomach and enclose a fatty apron.

Question 9014. Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen, and what lies in front of it? The answer is the inferior vena cava, covered by parietal peritoneum. In front lies the free edge of the lesser omentum, containing the portal vein, the bile duct and the hepatic artery, and the foramen joins the greater sac to the lesser sac.

Question 9015. A constructed illustration: a person with long-standing liver disease has dilated veins radiating from the navel. Which anastomosis has opened, and between which two venous systems? The answer is the portocaval anastomosis around the navel, joining the portal vein by way of the paraumbilical veins to the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall. The radiating pattern is called caput medusae.

Question 9016. True or false: in the male the peritoneal cavity is a closed sac that does not communicate with the exterior. The answer is true. The peritoneum forms a closed serous sac in the male, while in the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, the uterus and the vagina.

Question 9017. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lesser sac with the space behind the stomach, the greater sac with the bursa behind the stomach, the lesser omentum with the spleen, or the greater omentum with the liver? The answer is the lesser sac with the space behind the stomach. The lesser sac, also called the omental bursa, lies behind the stomach and the lesser omentum.

Question 9018. Through which opening does the lesser sac communicate with the greater sac: the epiploic foramen, the root of the mesentery, the gastrosplenic ligament, or the pyloric orifice? The answer is the epiploic foramen, also called the omental foramen. It is a small opening behind the free edge of the lesser omentum, and the other three are folds of peritoneum or a muscular opening of the stomach.

Question 9019. Which part of the stomach lies above the level of the opening of the esophagus and rises with the left dome of the diaphragm? The answer is the fundus. It is the highest part of the stomach and usually holds a bubble of swallowed air, while the body lies below it and the pyloric part to the right.

Question 9020. Which organ lies immediately behind the stomach, forms the floor of the lesser sac and carries the splenic artery along its upper border? The answer is the pancreas. Its body and tail lie against the posterior wall of the lesser sac, so the stomach lies in front of it, separated by the cavity of the lesser sac.

Question 9021. Which part of the stomach is the narrow funnel that leads into the duodenum, and which ring of muscle surrounds its opening? The answer is the pyloric part, with the pyloric sphincter around the pyloric canal. The canal is about 2 centimeters long in the adult, and the sphincter controls the emptying of the stomach.

Question 9022. Which artery supplies the greater curvature of the stomach from the left: the left gastric artery, the left gastro-omental artery, the right gastric artery, or the short gastric arteries? The answer is the left gastro-omental artery. It arises from the splenic artery and runs along the greater curvature, while the short gastric arteries supply the fundus.

Question 9023. A described contrast study shows the stomach as a curved shadow with a rounded upper part holding gas and a narrow lower end. Which parts are shown, and what does the narrowing mark? The answer is the fundus above, the body in the middle and the pyloric part below, with the narrowing at the pyloric canal. The pyloric sphincter there guards the exit into the duodenum.

Question 9024. Which two arteries run along the lesser curvature of the stomach, one from the left and one from the right? The answer is the left gastric artery and the right gastric artery. The left arises from the celiac trunk and the right from the hepatic artery, and they meet along the lesser curvature and supply both surfaces of the stomach.

Question 9025. A constructed illustration: a person vomits blood and a study shows bleeding from a vessel high on the lesser curvature of the stomach. Which artery is the likely source, and where does it arise? The answer is the left gastric artery, a direct branch of the celiac trunk. It runs down the lesser curvature, and management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 9026. Which of these pairs belongs together: the fundus with the pyloric canal, the body with the cardia, the pyloric antrum with the pyloric canal, or the cardia with the greater curvature? The answer is the pyloric antrum with the pyloric canal. The antrum is the wider part of the pyloric region and narrows into the canal, while the cardia surrounds the opening of the esophagus.

Question 9027. Which part of the duodenum is the only mobile part, with a mesentery of its own: the first part, the second part, the third part, or the fourth part? The answer is the first part, also called the duodenal cap. It runs upward and backward from the pylorus, and the other three parts lie behind the peritoneum and are fixed.

Question 9028. Which structure marks the junction of the duodenum and the jejunum, and by which muscle is it suspended? The answer is the duodenojejunal flexure, suspended by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum. That muscle runs from the right crus of the diaphragm to the flexure, which lies to the left of the aorta behind the peritoneum.

Question 9029. A constructed illustration: a person with an ulcer in the second part of the duodenum has pain that bores into the back. Which structure lying behind that part explains the pain? The answer is the head of the pancreas, which lies behind the second part of the duodenum, and the ulcer may penetrate into it.

Question 9030. A described specimen of the small intestine shows an upper segment with thick walls and few vascular arcades, and a lower segment with thin walls and many arcades. Which segment lies above, and which below? The answer is the jejunum above and the ileum below. The jejunum is thicker walled and more vascular, while the ileum has more arcades and larger lymphoid nodules.

Question 9031. Which part of the small intestine is the widest, thickest and most vascular, and occupies the upper left part of the abdomen? The answer is the jejunum. It begins at the duodenojejunal flexure and forms the upper two fifths of the coiled small intestine, and its walls are heavy and crowded with vessels.

Question 9032. Which statement about the ileum is correct: its walls are thicker than those of the jejunum, its vessels form few arcades, it carries large lymphoid nodules, or its loops lie mainly in the upper left abdomen? The answer is that it carries large lymphoid nodules. The ileum lies mainly in the lower right abdomen and has thinner walls than the jejunum.

Question 9033. A described specimen shows one segment of bowel with long straight vessels running from the last arcade to the wall, and another with short vessels and many arcades. Which segment is which? The answer is the jejunum with the long straight vessels and the ileum with the many arcades. The jejunum is thicker walled and lies higher, and the ileum carries larger lymphoid nodules.

Question 9034. Which vessel crosses immediately in front of the third part of the duodenum, and which vessel lies behind that same part? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery in front and the aorta behind. The third part of the duodenum can therefore be narrowed between the two, squeezed in the narrow angle where they cross.

Question 9035. A constructed illustration: a thin young person vomits bile-stained fluid, and a study shows the duodenum compressed between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. Which part is compressed? The answer is the third part, which crosses the aorta behind that artery, and the narrow angle between them pinches it.

Question 9036. True or false: the fourth part of the duodenum ascends on the right side of the aorta to reach the duodenojejunal flexure. The answer is false. The fourth part ascends on the left side of the aorta, crosses the left psoas muscle and lies behind the peritoneum before it turns forward at the flexure.

Question 9037. Which of these features distinguishes the large intestine from the small intestine: taeniae coli, a complete longitudinal muscle coat, villi on the mucosa, or a mesentery along its whole length? The answer is taeniae coli, the three flat bands of longitudinal muscle. The large intestine also shows haustra and fatty appendices, while the small intestine bears villi.

Question 9038. Which three flat bands of longitudinal muscle run along the colon and spread out at the rectum to form a complete coat? The answer is the taeniae coli. They are named the mesocolic, the omental and the free taeniae. They are shorter than the colon, so the wall between them is thrown into sacculations called haustra.

Question 9039. Which part of the colon runs upward on the right side against the posterior abdominal wall and is covered by peritoneum only in front and at the sides: the transverse colon, the ascending colon, the sigmoid colon, or the cecum? The answer is the ascending colon. It lies behind the peritoneum from the cecum to the right colic flexure.

Question 9040. A described transverse section of the posterior abdominal wall shows a kidney on each side, capped at the upper pole. Which kidney lies lower in the body, and what caps its upper pole? The answer is the right kidney, which lies lower because the liver occupies the space above it, and the right suprarenal gland caps its upper pole.

Question 9041. Which part of the large intestine is the widest and lies lowest in the right iliac fossa, below the junction with the small intestine? The answer is the cecum. It receives the ileum at the ileocecal junction, where the ileocecal valve guards the opening, and the appendix hangs from its posteromedial wall.

Question 9042. Which line has, one third of the way along it, the surface point that marks the base of the appendix: the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, the umbilicus to the pubic symphysis, the iliac crest to the umbilicus, or the xiphoid process to the umbilicus? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, at the point named after McBurney, and the tip may lie elsewhere.

Question 9043. A described contrast enema shows a wide tube with sacculations along its wall, three flat bands running lengthwise and small fatty tags. Which part of the bowel is shown, and what are the sacculations called? The answer is the colon, and the sacculations are the haustra. The bands are the taeniae coli and the tags are the appendices epiploicae.

Question 9044. Which muscle lies immediately behind the appendix when its tip hangs downward into the pelvis, and which part of the bowel lies in front of it? The answer is the psoas major behind and the terminal ileum in front. An inflamed appendix lying on the psoas may cause pain on extending the hip, and it may also lie behind the cecum.

Question 9045. A constructed illustration: pain begins around the navel and later settles in the right lower quadrant, where pressing the abdominal wall hurts most. Which structure is inflamed, and why did the pain move? The answer is the appendix. The early pain is referred to the umbilical region and the later pain to the peritoneum of the right iliac fossa.

Question 9046. Which of these pairs belongs together: haustra with the small intestine, taeniae coli with the colon, villi with the colon, or appendices epiploicae with the jejunum? The answer is taeniae coli with the colon. The colon carries three flat bands of longitudinal muscle, while the small intestine bears villi and has no taeniae or haustra.

Question 9047. Which artery supplies the ascending colon and the right half of the transverse colon, and which supplies the rest of the colon? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery for the right side and the inferior mesenteric artery for the left side. The two territories meet near the splenic flexure, and that meeting point is a weak place in the blood supply.

Question 9048. Which named vessel runs along the inner border of the colon and joins the branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries? The answer is the marginal artery of the colon. It lies along the mesenteric border and links the two arterial territories, and the junction near the splenic flexure is the weakest point of that chain.

Question 9049. Name two organs of the abdomen that lie behind the peritoneum, spoken as a pair. The answer is the kidneys and the pancreas. The ascending and descending parts of the colon, the duodenum except its first part, and the suprarenal glands are also behind the peritoneum, and such organs are covered by peritoneum on one surface only.

Question 9050. Which two veins unite to form the portal vein: the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein, the splenic vein and the inferior mesenteric vein, the hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava, or the gastric veins and the esophageal veins? The answer is the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein, which join behind the neck of the pancreas.

Question 9051. Which large vein carries the blood of the digestive organs to the liver, lies behind the first part of the duodenum and runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum? The answer is the portal vein. It is formed behind the neck of the pancreas and ends in the liver, and because it has no valves the blood can flow back when the liver is obstructed.

Question 9052. Which structure separates the right lobe of the liver from the left lobe on the front of the organ: the falciform ligament, the ligamentum venosum, the inferior vena cava, or the gallbladder? The answer is the falciform ligament. It runs from the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and carries the ligamentum teres in its free edge.

Question 9053. A described dissection of the upper abdomen shows a large organ under the right dome of the diaphragm, with a fold running from its front to the abdominal wall and a fibrous cord in the free edge of that fold. What are the fold and the cord? The answer is the falciform ligament and the ligamentum teres, and the cord is the remains of the umbilical vein.

Question 9054. Which structure lies between the liver and the stomach, and what does its free edge contain? The answer is the lesser omentum, whose free edge contains the portal vein, the bile duct and the hepatic artery. It runs from the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach, and behind its free edge lies the epiploic foramen.

Question 9055. A constructed illustration: after a fatty meal a person has severe pain in the right upper abdomen that radiates to the right shoulder. Which structure lies beneath the diaphragm on that side and can irritate it? The answer is the liver, with the gallbladder against its visceral surface. Irritation of the diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder, and management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 9056. Which artery usually supplies the gallbladder: the right hepatic artery by way of the cystic artery, the left hepatic artery, the gastroduodenal artery, or the left gastric artery? The answer is the right hepatic artery by way of the cystic artery, which passes through the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the liver.

Question 9057. Which veins drain the liver into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm: the hepatic veins, the portal vein, the splenic vein, or the superior mesenteric vein? The answer is the hepatic veins. There are usually three of them, and they open into the inferior vena cava within the bare area of the liver.

Question 9058. Which part of the liver lies against the diaphragm without a covering of peritoneum, between the layers of the coronary ligament? The answer is the bare area. It lies on the posterior surface of the right lobe, and the coronary ligament surrounds it, its two layers meeting at the right and left triangular ligaments.

Question 9059. At which of these places does blood pass from the portal system to the systemic veins: the esophagus, the stomach wall, the small intestine, or the spleen? The answer is the lower end of the esophagus, where the left gastric vein meets the esophageal veins. Other such places are the navel, the rectum and the back of the colon.

Question 9060. A described computed tomography scan of the upper abdomen, known as a CT scan, shows a large organ on the right under the diaphragm, a flat gland crossing the midline in front of the spine, and a rounded organ behind the stomach on the left. Which three structures are described? The answer is the liver, the pancreas and the spleen.

Question 9061. Which organ lies in the left hypochondrium behind the stomach and in contact with the ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs? The answer is the spleen. It lies within the peritoneum and is held by the gastrosplenic and lienorenal ligaments, and its smooth surface faces the diaphragm while its hilum faces the stomach.

Question 9062. Which artery supplies the spleen: the splenic artery from the celiac trunk, the left gastric artery, the superior mesenteric artery, or the left gastro-omental artery? The answer is the splenic artery from the celiac trunk. It runs a tortuous course along the upper border of the pancreas, while the splenic vein runs behind the pancreas.

Question 9063. A described specimen of the spleen cut across shows a dark red interior with small pale spots and a hilum on one side. What enters and leaves at the hilum, and what are the pale spots? The answer is the splenic artery and vein at the hilum, and the pale spots are the white pulp. The red pulp surrounds them.

Question 9064. Which organ lies immediately anterior to the medial surface of the spleen and is joined to it by the gastrosplenic ligament? The answer is the stomach. The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric arteries and the left gastro-omental artery between the two organs, and the lienorenal ligament joins the spleen to the left kidney behind.

Question 9065. A constructed illustration: a blow to the left lower chest is followed by pain in the left upper abdomen and signs of internal bleeding. Which organ has most likely been injured? The answer is the spleen, which lies under the ninth to eleventh ribs, so a fracture of those ribs may tear it. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 9066. True or false: the spleen lies behind the peritoneum, fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. The answer is false. The spleen is covered by peritoneum except at its hilum and lies within the peritoneal cavity, held by the gastrosplenic and lienorenal ligaments and by the pressure of the surrounding organs.

Question 9067. Which two ligaments hold the spleen: the gastrosplenic and lienorenal ligaments, the falciform and coronary ligaments, the gastrocolic and phrenicocolic ligaments, or the gastrohepatic and hepatoduodenal ligaments? The answer is the gastrosplenic and lienorenal ligaments. The first joins the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach and the second to the left kidney.

Question 9068. Which gland lies across the posterior abdominal wall behind the stomach and has a head, a neck, a body and a tail? The answer is the pancreas. Its head lies in the curve of the duodenum and its tail reaches the spleen, and it lies behind the peritoneum with its duct joining the bile duct.

Question 9069. Which duct carries the pancreatic juice to the duodenum, and with which duct does it join: the main pancreatic duct with the bile duct, the accessory pancreatic duct with the cystic duct, the main pancreatic duct with the cystic duct, or the accessory duct with the bile duct? The answer is the main pancreatic duct with the bile duct, which open together at the major duodenal papilla.

Question 9070. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the upper abdomen, known as an MRI scan, shows a flat gland lying across the spine with a duct running through it. Which gland is shown, and where does its duct end? The answer is the pancreas, whose main duct runs the length of the gland and opens into the duodenum with the bile duct.

Question 9071. Which paired organs lie behind the peritoneum on either side of the great vessels, with the right one placed a little lower than the left? The answer is the kidneys. They lie between the twelfth thoracic and the third lumbar levels, and the right kidney is pushed down by the liver above it.

Question 9072. From front to back, which is the order of the structures at the hilum of the kidney: vein, artery, pelvis; artery, vein, pelvis; pelvis, artery, vein; or vein, pelvis, artery? The answer is vein, artery, pelvis. The renal vein lies in front, then the renal artery, and the renal pelvis lies behind them within the renal sinus.

Question 9073. A described computed tomography scan after contrast shows the two kidneys and a tube running down from each hilum toward the pelvis. What is the tube, and how is the urine collected before it? The answer is the ureter, the continuation of the renal pelvis. Urine is collected in the minor calyces, then the major calyces, then the pelvis.

Question 9074. Which gland caps the upper pole of each kidney, and which parts of the bowel lie in front of the right kidney? The answer is the suprarenal gland on each side, with the duodenum and the ascending colon in front of the right kidney. In front of the left kidney lie the stomach, the spleen, the pancreas and the jejunum.

Question 9075. A constructed illustration: a person has severe colicky pain from the loin to the groin, and a study shows a stone in the upper urinary passage. At which three places does that passage normally narrow? The answer is the renal pelvis, the brim of the pelvis and the entry into the bladder. The stone lodges where the tube is narrowest.

Question 9076. Which of these pairs belongs together: the kidney with the peritoneum, the kidney with the renal fascia, the ureter with the peritoneum, or the suprarenal gland with the spleen? The answer is the kidney with the renal fascia. That fascia surrounds the kidney and its fat, while the kidney and the ureter lie behind the peritoneum and are not covered by it.

Question 9077. Which statement about the arteries of the kidney is correct: each kidney usually receives one artery that divides into segmental branches, the segmental branches join freely with one another, the kidney receives two arteries in every person, or the arteries enter at the lower pole? The answer is that each kidney usually receives one artery that divides into segmental branches, and those branches behave as end arteries.

Question 9078. Which gland sits on the upper pole of each kidney, triangular on the right and crescent shaped on the left, and produces hormones? The answer is the suprarenal gland. The right gland lies against the liver and the inferior vena cava, and the left lies against the spleen, the stomach and the pancreas.

Question 9079. Name two structures that pass through the diaphragm at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra, spoken as a pair. The answer is the aorta and the thoracic duct. The azygos vein also passes through the same opening behind the diaphragm, which lies behind the muscle and in front of the vertebral column.

Question 9080. Which statement about the coverings of the kidney is correct: the renal fascia lies outside the perinephric fat, the perinephric fat lies outside the renal fascia, the fibrous capsule lies outside the perinephric fat, or the renal fascia is the same as the capsule? The answer is that the renal fascia lies outside the perinephric fat. The capsule lies on the kidney and the fat surrounds it.

Question 9081. Which muscle of the posterior abdominal wall arises from the bodies of the lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae and inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur? The answer is the psoas major. It lies beside the lumbar spine and forms a rounded swelling in the lower abdomen, and the lumbar plexus is buried within its substance.

Question 9082. Which nerve of the lumbar plexus emerges from the medial border of the psoas major and supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the genitofemoral nerve, or the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve? The answer is the obturator nerve. It leaves the medial border and passes through the obturator canal, while the femoral nerve leaves the lateral border.

Question 9083. A described dissection of the posterior abdominal wall shows a large muscle beside the spine with a network of nerves emerging through it, and a large vessel on its medial side. Which structures are shown? The answer is the psoas major with the lumbar plexus and the aorta. The plexus lies within the muscle, and the inferior vena cava lies to the right of the spine.

Question 9084. Which structure lies immediately in front of the right crus of the diaphragm at the level of the esophageal opening, and which nerves run with it? The answer is the esophagus, with the two vagal trunks. The esophagus passes through the opening at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra, and the vagal trunks lie on its front and back.

Question 9085. A constructed illustration: after a stab wound in the flank, a person cannot extend the hip and has numbness over the front of the thigh. Which plexus has been injured? The answer is the lumbar plexus, which lies within the psoas major. Its branches supply the muscles of the thigh and the skin over them, and management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 9086. True or false: the opening for the inferior vena cava lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra. The answer is true. The esophageal opening lies at the tenth thoracic vertebra and the aortic opening at the twelfth, and the phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm from above.

Question 9087. Which three arteries arise from the celiac trunk: the left gastric, the splenic and the common hepatic; the right gastric, the splenic and the superior mesenteric; the left gastric, the inferior mesenteric and the common hepatic; or the splenic, the renal and the common hepatic? The answer is the left gastric, the splenic and the common hepatic arteries, which arise at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra.

Question 9088. Which short artery arises from the front of the aorta just below the diaphragm and supplies the stomach, the spleen, the liver and the upper duodenum? The answer is the celiac trunk. It divides into the left gastric, the splenic and the common hepatic arteries, while the superior mesenteric artery arises a little lower and supplies the midgut.

Question 9089. Which of these arteries is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery: the ileocolic artery, the left colic artery, the middle rectal artery, or the splenic artery? The answer is the ileocolic artery. It supplies the end of the ileum, the cecum and the appendix, while the left colic artery arises from the inferior mesenteric artery.

Question 9090. A described computed tomography angiogram of the abdomen shows three arteries arising close together from the front of the aorta, the lowest of them running downward and to the left. Which arteries are shown? The answer is the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery. The lowest one supplies the descending colon, the sigmoid colon and the upper rectum.

Question 9091. Name the lymph sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct and name one group of vessels that empties into it. The answer is the cisterna chyli, which receives the intestinal lymph trunk and the two lumbar trunks. It lies in front of the first two lumbar vertebrae, and the thoracic duct begins at it.

Question 9092. Which parts of the bowel are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery: the descending colon, the sigmoid colon and the upper rectum; the cecum, the ascending colon and the appendix; the jejunum and the ileum; or the stomach and the spleen? The answer is the descending colon, the sigmoid colon and the upper rectum, supplied by an artery arising at the level of the third lumbar vertebra.

Question 9093. A described specimen of the lower abdomen shows a wide tube with sacculations descending on the left side toward the pelvis, with fatty tags along it. Which part of the bowel is shown, and what supplies it? The answer is the descending colon and its continuation, the sigmoid colon, supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery. The tags are the appendices epiploicae.

Question 9094. Pain from the midgut is referred to which region of the body surface: the epigastric region, the umbilical region, the suprapubic region, or the left iliac region? The answer is the umbilical region. The midgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery and its pain is felt around the navel, while foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium.

Question 9095. Which nerve forms the posterior vagal trunk as it enters the abdomen: the right vagus nerve, the left vagus nerve, the greater splanchnic nerve, or the phrenic nerve? The answer is the right vagus nerve. The left vagus forms the anterior trunk in front of the esophagus, and the posterior trunk is the larger of the two.

Question 9096. Which chain of ganglia lies in front of the lumbar vertebrae and sends the splanchnic nerves to the abdominal organs? The answer is the sympathetic trunk. The greater splanchnic nerve comes from the fifth to the ninth thoracic ganglia, and the lesser and least splanchnic nerves follow below and end in the celiac and related ganglia.

Question 9097. A tumor of the body of the pancreas often causes deep pain in the back because the organ lies against which structure: the celiac plexus, the inferior vena cava, the left ureter, or the transverse colon? The answer is the celiac plexus, which lies behind the pancreas around the celiac trunk and carries the pain fibers of the upper abdominal organs.

Question 9098. Which line on the posterior wall of the rectus sheath marks the level below which the sheath has no posterior wall and the rectus muscle lies against the fascia transversalis? The answer is the arcuate line. It lies about halfway between the navel and the pubic symphysis, and below it all three aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus muscle.

Question 9099. Which space in the lower back can allow a lumbar hernia, bounded above by the twelfth rib, behind by the erector spinae and in front by the internal oblique: the superior lumbar triangle, the inferior lumbar triangle, the femoral ring, or the obturator canal? The answer is the superior lumbar triangle. The inferior lumbar triangle lies between the latissimus dorsi and the external oblique.

Question 9100. A described cross section through the abdomen shows a cavity lined by a thin membrane, with a large organ on the right, a rounded organ behind the stomach on the left, and two bean-shaped organs against the back wall. Which four structures are described? The answer is the liver, the spleen and the two kidneys, the last lying behind the peritoneum.

To summarize, the anterior abdominal wall is built of three flat muscles whose aponeuroses form the rectus sheath, and the inguinal canal runs above the inguinal ligament between the deep ring in the fascia transversalis and the superficial ring in the external oblique aponeurosis. The peritoneum forms the greater sac and the lesser sac, which communicate through the epiploic foramen behind the free edge of the lesser omentum. The stomach lies in front of the pancreas, the colon carries taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae, and the jejunum differs from the ileum in wall thickness, arcades and lymphoid nodules. The liver receives the portal vein and drains by the hepatic veins, the spleen lies within the peritoneum against the ninth to eleventh ribs, and the kidneys lie behind the peritoneum with the suprarenal glands capping their upper poles. The posterior wall carries the psoas major with the lumbar plexus and the celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries, and the diaphragm opens for the inferior vena cava at the eighth thoracic vertebra, the esophagus at the tenth and the aorta at the twelfth. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 92 — Pelvis and Perineum

The pelvis is the bony ring that carries the weight of the trunk to the lower limbs, and the perineum is the shallow diamond of soft tissue that closes it below. This chapter covers the bones and joints of the pelvic ring, the inlet, the midplane and the outlet, the muscles of the pelvic wall and the pelvic floor, the bladder, the rectum, the internal reproductive organs and the fascia that holds them, the vessels and nerves that cross the pelvic brim, and the two triangles of the perineum with the perineal body between them. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The relations described here are the ones a clinician uses at the bedside, in the operating room and at delivery. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 9101. Which three bones fuse during childhood to form each hip bone, and where do they meet? The answer is the ilium, the ischium and the pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. A Y-shaped plate of cartilage joins them there until the middle teens. The ilium forms the upper part, the ischium the lower and posterior part, and the pubis the front.

Question 9102. Which of these landmarks is the front upper corner of the hip bone: the ischial spine, the anterior superior iliac spine, the pubic tubercle, or the sacral promontory? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine. It is the front end of the iliac crest and the point where the inguinal ligament begins. The pubic tubercle lies much lower and nearer the midline.

Question 9103. Which small pointed projection of the hip bone separates the greater sciatic notch above from the lesser sciatic notch below? The answer is the ischial spine. It gives attachment to the sacrospinous ligament and lies at the level of the pelvic floor.

Question 9104. A described radiograph of an adult pelvis shows a smooth ridge running forward and downward across the inner surface of the hip bone from the sacroiliac joint to the pubis. Which ridge is shown? The answer is the arcuate line of the ilium. It continues forward as the pectineal line and forms the lateral part of the pelvic brim.

Question 9105. Which part of the hip bone bears the weight of the body when a person sits: the iliac crest, the ischial tuberosity, the acetabular rim, or the superior pubic ramus? The answer is the ischial tuberosity. It is the rough lower end of the ischium and lies just under the skin of the buttock. The iliac crest and the pubis lie too high to take that weight.

Question 9106. Which of these lies on the upper border of the body of the pubis, a little to the side of the midline, and gives attachment to the medial end of the inguinal ligament: the pubic tubercle, the ischial spine, the iliopubic eminence, or the lesser trochanter? The answer is the pubic tubercle. The inguinal ligament stretches from it to the anterior superior iliac spine.

Question 9107. Which of these is the iliac fossa: the socket of the hip joint, the smooth concave surface on the inner side of the ilium, the groove for the obturator nerve, or the rough area between the two gluteal lines? The answer is the smooth concave surface on the inner side of the ilium. It forms part of the false pelvis and gives origin to the iliacus muscle.

Question 9108. A described dried hip bone shows a deep notch on its posterior border, bounded below by a sharp spine, with a smooth surface above where a muscle leaves the pelvis. Which notch is shown? The answer is the greater sciatic notch. The piriformis muscle passes through it.

Question 9109. Which of these marks the middle of the pelvic brim at the back and is the point from which the obstetric conjugate is measured: the sacral promontory, the ischial spine, the pubic tubercle, or the arcuate line? The answer is the sacral promontory. It is the upper front edge of the first sacral vertebra, at the junction with the fifth lumbar vertebra.

Question 9110. Which of these is true of the sacrum: it is formed by five fused vertebrae, it has three pairs of sacral foramina, it articulates with the femur, or it forms the whole of the pelvic floor? The answer is that it is formed by five fused vertebrae. Four pairs of sacral foramina carry the branches of the sacral spinal nerves.

Question 9111. Which bone forms the lowest part of the vertebral column and the posterior point of the diamond of the perineum? The answer is the coccyx. It is made of three to five small vertebrae fused into a curved triangle.

Question 9112. The obturator foramen lies below and in front of the acetabulum. Which structures pass through the small canal at its upper part? The answer is the obturator nerve with the obturator artery above it and the obturator vein below it. The canal is the gap between the obturator membrane and the superior border of the foramen.

Question 9113. Which structures together form the boundary of the pelvic inlet? The answer is the sacral promontory, the alae of the sacrum, the arcuate lines of the ilia, the pectineal lines, the pubic crests and the upper border of the pubic symphysis. Together they form the pelvic brim.

Question 9114. Which of these is the shortest front to back diameter of the pelvic inlet: the obstetric conjugate, the diagonal conjugate, the transverse diameter, or an oblique diameter? The answer is the obstetric conjugate. It runs from the sacral promontory to the upper posterior margin of the pubic symphysis and measures about 11 centimeters in the average pelvis.

Question 9115. Which plane of the pelvic cavity is the narrowest, and which two landmarks define its width? The answer is the midplane, defined by the two ischial spines, about 10 to 10.5 centimeters apart. It is the narrowest fixed plane that a fetal head must pass.

Question 9116. True or false: the ischial spines form part of the bony boundary of the pelvic outlet. The answer is false. The outlet is bounded by the pubic symphysis, the ischiopubic rami, the ischial tuberosities, the sacrotuberous ligaments and the coccyx. The spines lie above and within that ring and mark the midplane instead.

Question 9117. Which of these statements about the false pelvis is correct: it lies below the pelvic brim, it contains the urinary bladder, it lies above the pelvic brim and holds coils of small intestine, or it is closed below by the pelvic diaphragm? The answer is that it lies above the pelvic brim and holds coils of small intestine. It is part of the abdominal cavity.

Question 9118. The plane of the pelvic inlet is described in a standing person. In which kind of plane does it lie, and how is it tilted? The answer is an oblique plane, tilted so that its posterior border at the sacral promontory lies higher than the pubic symphysis. The inlet therefore faces upward and forward.

Question 9119. Which of these best describes the sacroiliac joint: a fibrous suture, a primary cartilaginous joint, a synovial joint reinforced by very strong posterior ligaments, or a freely mobile ball and socket joint? The answer is a synovial joint reinforced by very strong posterior ligaments. Its stability comes from those ligaments and from the wedge shape of the sacrum.

Question 9120. Which ligament runs from the ischial spine to the side of the sacrum and coccyx, and which opening does it help to close? The answer is the sacrospinous ligament, which helps to close the lesser sciatic foramen. It lies in front of the sacrotuberous ligament.

Question 9121. True or false: the sacrotuberous ligament runs from the ischial tuberosity to the sacrum and helps to form the lesser sciatic foramen. The answer is true. It is a strong band felt as the lower edge of the buttock. With the sacrospinous ligament it closes the lesser sciatic foramen.

Question 9122. Which of these pairs belongs together: the inguinal ligament with the pubic symphysis, the sacrospinous ligament with the ischial tuberosity, the sacrotuberous ligament with the ischial tuberosity, or the lacunar ligament with the iliac crest? The answer is the sacrotuberous ligament with the ischial tuberosity. The sacrospinous ligament runs to the ischial spine instead.

Question 9123. The inguinal ligament is a thickening of which structure, and between which two bony points does it stretch? The answer is the lower border of the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle, stretching from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It forms the floor of the inguinal canal. The femoral vessels pass beneath its middle.

Question 9124. Which structure lies immediately deep to the inguinal ligament at the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle? The answer is the femoral nerve, which lies lateral to the femoral artery. The artery lies next, and the femoral vein lies medial to the artery.

Question 9125. Which of these boundaries belongs to the femoral ring: the inguinal ligament in front, the femoral vein behind, the ischial tuberosity medially, or the sciatic nerve laterally? The answer is the inguinal ligament in front. The ring is bounded behind by the pectineal ligament, medially by the lacunar ligament and laterally by the femoral vein. A femoral hernia passes through it into the femoral canal.

Question 9126. A described dissection of the lateral wall of the pelvis shows a flat muscle arising from the inner surface of the obturator membrane and converging toward the lesser sciatic foramen below the spine. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the obturator internus. Its tendon leaves through that foramen to reach the greater trochanter. Its fascia thickens into the tendinous arch of the pelvic floor.

Question 9127. A described specimen of the posterior pelvic wall shows a pear-shaped muscle arising from the front of the sacrum and passing out of the greater sciatic foramen above a large nerve. Which muscle is shown? The answer is the piriformis. It inserts on the upper border of the greater trochanter. It turns the extended thigh outward and steadies the head of the femur.

Question 9128. Which of these muscles belong to the levator ani: the obturator internus, the pubococcygeus, the coccygeus, or the piriformis? The answer is the pubococcygeus. The levator ani is made of the pubococcygeus, the puborectalis and the iliococcygeus. The coccygeus lies behind it and is a separate muscle.

Question 9129. Which part of the levator ani forms a sling behind the anorectal junction and maintains the anorectal angle? The answer is the puborectalis. Its fibers run from the back of the pubis on each side, around the bowel, and pull it forward. Loss of its tone contributes to fecal incontinence.

Question 9130. Which of these muscles lies immediately behind the levator ani, running from the ischial spine to the side of the coccyx: the coccygeus, the obturator internus, the piriformis, or the puborectalis? The answer is the coccygeus. It helps to support the pelvic viscera and to steady the coccyx. It forms the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm.

Question 9131. Which of these nerves supplies the levator ani: the obturator nerve, the nerve to levator ani from the sacral plexus, the femoral nerve, or the ilioinguinal nerve? The answer is the nerve to levator ani from the sacral plexus. It arises from the third and fourth sacral spinal nerves and runs on the upper surface of the muscle. The pudendal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter instead, though small branches pass between the two.

Question 9132. A described cross section through the pelvis at the level of the hip joints shows a muscular sheet sloping down and back from the pubis to the coccyx, with fat-filled spaces below it on each side of the anal canal. Which sheet is shown? The answer is the pelvic diaphragm. It separates the pelvic cavity above from the perineum below.

Question 9133. Name the two muscles that form the pelvic diaphragm, spoken as a list. The answer is the levator ani and the coccygeus. The levator ani is the larger and forms a sling around the urethra, the vagina and the anorectal junction. The coccygeus lies behind it, running from the ischial spine to the coccyx.

Question 9134. What is the tendinous arch of the pelvic floor, and which muscle arises from it? The answer is a thickened line of fascia on the obturator internus, from which the levator ani arises. It runs from the back of the pubis to the ischial spine.

Question 9135. What is the name of the smooth triangular area on the inner surface of the bladder, marked by two ureteric openings above and the internal urethral opening below? The answer is the trigone. Its mucosa is smooth and firmly attached to the muscle, so it does not wrinkle when the bladder empties.

Question 9136. Which of these structures is the remnant of the urachus and runs from the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus: the median umbilical ligament, the medial umbilical ligament, the round ligament, or the urogenital mesentery? The answer is the median umbilical ligament. It is a single midline fold in the adult. The medial umbilical ligaments are paired and are the remnants of the umbilical arteries.

Question 9137. Which muscle of the bladder wall contracts to empty the bladder during urination? The answer is the detrusor muscle. It is a mesh of smooth muscle in the wall of the bladder that squeezes urine into the urethra.

Question 9138. Which structure lies immediately in front of the bifurcation of the common iliac artery as it crosses the pelvic brim? The answer is the ureter. It crosses the brim just in front of the division of the artery into its external and internal iliac branches. This is one of the three places where a urinary stone may lodge.

Question 9139. Which of these sets names the three places where the ureter is normally narrowed: the renal pelvis, the pelvic brim and the bladder wall; the aorta, the rectum and the urethra; the diaphragm, the sacrum and the anal canal; or the kidney, the colon and the prostate? The answer is the renal pelvis, the pelvic brim and the bladder wall. Stones lodge at these three points.

Question 9140. A constructed illustration: during an operation to remove the uterus, the surgeon ties the uterine artery close to the cervix and the ureter is injured. Why does the ureter lie at risk at that point? The answer is that the ureter passes below and behind the uterine artery about 2 centimeters from the cervix. The vessel crosses above it, which is why the relation is remembered as water under the bridge. This is an illustration and not a real case.

Question 9141. Which of these statements about the urethral sphincters is correct: the internal urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle and voluntary, the external urethral sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary, the external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle and voluntary, or neither sphincter lies in the perineum? The answer is that the external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle and voluntary. It surrounds the membranous urethra in the deep perineal pouch. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle at the neck of the bladder.

Question 9142. A described contrast study of the bladder shows a smooth rounded outline with a small notch at its lowest point. Which part of the bladder is the notch, and what does it mark? The answer is the neck of the bladder, marking the internal urethral opening. The trigone lies just above it.

Question 9143. What is the name of the dilated lower part of the rectum that rests on the pelvic floor and stores feces? The answer is the rectal ampulla. It lies above the anorectal junction and below the sacral flexure of the rectum. It has no sacculations and no taeniae coli.

Question 9144. Which of these is the arrangement of the transverse folds of the rectum: three folds with the largest near the middle, two folds one on each side, four folds in a spiral, or no folds at all? The answer is three folds with the largest and most constant near the middle. They are also called the rectal valves.

Question 9145. True or false: the internal anal sphincter is a voluntary muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve. The answer is false. The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle, a thickening of the circular muscle of the rectum, and it is involuntary. The external anal sphincter is the voluntary one and is supplied by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve.

Question 9146. A described sagittal section through the rectum and anal canal shows the bowel curving back over the coccyx, then turning forward and down to open at the anus, with a thickening of the circular muscle around the upper part of the canal. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the anorectal flexure and the internal anal sphincter. The flexure is produced by the puborectalis sling.

Question 9147. Which structure lies immediately in front of the rectum in the female, and which bony structures lie behind it? The answer is the uterus and the vagina in front, and the sacrum with the coccyx behind. In the male the prostate and the seminal vesicles lie in front instead.

Question 9148. What is the name of the wavy line in the anal canal that marks the junction of the visceral part above and the somatic part below? The answer is the pectinate line, also called the dentate line. Above it the lining is columnar and the vessels follow the rectal supply. Below it the lining is stratified squamous and drains with the perineum.

Question 9149. A described dissection of the male pelvis shows a firm gland wrapped around the first part of the urethra, lying below the neck of the bladder and in front of the rectal ampulla. Which gland is shown? The answer is the prostate. Its base is against the bladder and its apex rests on the pelvic floor. The seminal vesicles lie above its base.

Question 9150. On which part of the male urethra does the seminal colliculus lie: the prostatic part, the membranous part, the spongy part, or the navicular fossa? The answer is the prostatic part. The two ejaculatory ducts open on the colliculus, one on each side.

Question 9151. A described midline image of a male pelvis shows the bladder above, a rounded gland below it, the rectum behind, and a thin dark line marking the perineal membrane under the gland. Which gland is shown? The answer is the prostate. The seminal vesicles lie above its base and against the bladder.

Question 9152. What is the name of the lobe of the prostate that lies between the ejaculatory ducts and the urethra, and what does its enlargement obstruct? The answer is the median lobe, and it obstructs the prostatic urethra. It lies behind the urethra and projects upward into the base of the bladder. Its enlargement lifts the trigone and produces the uvula of the bladder.

Question 9153. Which of these veins drains the prostatic venous plexus: the inferior vena cava directly, the internal iliac veins, the portal vein, or the superficial external pudendal vein? The answer is the internal iliac veins. The plexus also communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus, which has no valves. That connection is one route by which tumor cells from the prostate reach the bones of the spine.

Question 9154. A constructed illustration: an older man cannot pass urine, and a firm, enlarged gland is felt through the front wall of the rectum. Which part of the gland is most likely compressing the urethra? The answer is the median lobe of the prostate. The clinician is feeling the posterior surface of the gland through the rectal wall. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 9155. Which of these parts of the uterus lies above the openings of the uterine tubes and forms its domed upper end: the fundus, the cervix, the isthmus, or the posterior fornix? The answer is the fundus. It is the part of the uterus above the level at which the tubes enter.

Question 9156. Which of these describes the usual position of the uterus: anteverted and anteflexed, retroverted and retroflexed, anteverted and retroflexed, or held backward against the sacrum? The answer is anteverted and anteflexed. Anteversion means that the cervix tilts forward on the vagina, and anteflexion means that the body bends forward on the cervix. A retroverted uterus is a common normal variant.

Question 9157. Which structure lies immediately below and behind the uterine artery about 2 centimeters from the cervix? The answer is the ureter. The artery crosses above the ureter and then runs along the side of the uterus. This crossing is the reason the ureter is at risk during pelvic operations.

Question 9158. What is the name of the band of fascia that runs from the cervix and the upper vagina to the lateral wall of the pelvis and helps to hold the cervix in place? The answer is the cardinal ligament, also called the transverse cervical ligament. It is a thickening of the pelvic fascia at the base of the broad ligament. The uterosacral ligaments run backward from the cervix to the sacrum instead.

Question 9159. Which of these is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in a woman, lying between the uterus and the rectum: the vesicouterine pouch, the rectouterine pouch, the paravesical fossa, or the rectovesical pouch? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, also called the pouch of Douglas. It lies behind the uterus and above the posterior vaginal fornix. Fluid in the abdomen collects there and can be reached through that fornix.

Question 9160. A constructed illustration: a woman with a missed period has pain and bleeding, and a pregnancy is found in the widest part of a uterine tube. Which part is involved, and why is it the usual site? The answer is the ampulla, which is the widest and longest part of the tube. It is where fertilization normally occurs.

Question 9161. A constructed illustration: a person with a full bladder takes a blow to the lower abdomen and the bladder ruptures at its weakest point. Which part of the bladder has torn, and where does the urine collect? The answer is the superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum, and the urine collects in the peritoneal cavity. A tear below the peritoneum instead fills the retropubic space. This is an illustration and not a real case.

Question 9162. Into which two divisions does the internal iliac artery branch, and how are they named? The answer is the anterior and posterior divisions. The posterior division gives the iliolumbar, the lateral sacral and the superior gluteal arteries. The anterior division gives the visceral branches together with the obturator, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal arteries.

Question 9163. Which of these nerves leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the sciatic nerve, or the pudendal nerve? The answer is the obturator nerve. It arises from the second, third and fourth lumbar spinal nerves and supplies the medial muscles of the thigh.

Question 9164. What is the perineum, and where does it lie? The answer is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic diaphragm. It is bounded in front by the pubic symphysis, on each side by the ischiopubic rami and the ischial tuberosities, and behind by the sacrotuberous ligaments and the coccyx.

Question 9165. Which of these structures forms the front point of the diamond of the perineum: the coccyx, the pubic symphysis, the ischial tuberosity, or the sacral promontory? The answer is the pubic symphysis. The two ischial tuberosities form the lateral corners of the diamond. The coccyx forms the posterior point.

Question 9166. A described dissection of the perineum shows a diamond of skin and fat divided into two triangles by an imaginary line joining the two ischial tuberosities. Which structures lie in front of that line and which behind it? The answer is the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind. The anterior triangle contains the external genitalia and the openings of the urinary tract.

Question 9167. Which triangle of the perineum lies immediately in front of the line between the ischial tuberosities, and which muscle sheet lies above it? The answer is the urogenital triangle, with the pelvic diaphragm above it. The perineal membrane stretches across the triangle below that diaphragm. The anal triangle lies behind the same line.

Question 9168. Which of these structures lies in the anal triangle: the bulb of the penis, the greater vestibular gland, the anal canal, or the clitoris? The answer is the anal canal. The triangle also contains the ischioanal fossae and the external anal sphincter.

Question 9169. What is the ischioanal fossa, and where is it found? The answer is a wedge-shaped space filled with fat on each side of the anal canal. It lies below the pelvic diaphragm and medial to the obturator internus and the ischial tuberosity.

Question 9170. Which structures lie immediately medial to the ischioanal fossa, and which lie lateral to it? The answer is the levator ani and the external anal sphincter medially, and the obturator internus with the ischial tuberosity laterally. The fossa narrows to an apex where those two walls meet. Its anterior wall is the posterior border of the perineal membrane.

Question 9171. A described transverse section through the anal canal shows a fat-filled space on each side, a tunnel in the lateral wall of each space carrying a nerve and vessels, and a muscle sheet sloping down toward the midline. Which structures are shown? The answer is the ischioanal fossae, the pudendal canals and the levator ani. The canals lie in the lateral wall beside the obturator internus.

Question 9172. A constructed illustration: an infection in the fat of the perineum on one side of the anal canal later appears on the other side. Through which route has it spread? The answer is the communication between the two ischioanal fossae behind the anal canal, deep to the anococcygeal ligament. Infection can also track forward into the urogenital triangle. This is an illustration and not a real case.

Question 9173. What is the pudendal canal, and what does it contain? The answer is a tunnel in the fascia on the medial side of the obturator internus, carrying the pudendal nerve and the internal pudendal vessels. It lies in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.

Question 9174. Which spinal nerve roots give rise to the pudendal nerve, and what territory does it supply? The answer is the second, third and fourth sacral spinal nerves, and it supplies the muscles and skin of the perineum. Its branches include the inferior rectal nerve and the dorsal nerve of the penis or the clitoris.

Question 9175. A constructed illustration: a cyclist has burning pain in the perineum and numbness of the skin of the scrotum after long rides. Which nerve is compressed, and where? The answer is the pudendal nerve, compressed in the pudendal canal against the obturator internus. Pressure from the saddle is transmitted to the canal.

Question 9176. A described dissection shows a nerve and an artery winding around the sacrospinous ligament just medial to the ischial spine, then turning forward into a canal in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the pudendal nerve and the internal pudendal artery. They leave the pelvis below the piriformis and return through the lesser sciatic foramen. Both then run forward in the pudendal canal.

Question 9177. What is the perineal membrane, and between which structures does it stretch? The answer is a tough triangular sheet of fascia stretched between the two ischiopubic rami. It forms the floor of the deep perineal pouch and the roof of the superficial perineal pouch. The urethra passes through it in the male, and the urethra and the vagina pass through it in the female.

Question 9178. Which pouch lies immediately above the perineal membrane, and which lies immediately below it? The answer is the deep perineal pouch above and the superficial perineal pouch below. The membrane is the partition between them.

Question 9179. Which of these structures lies in the deep perineal pouch: the bulb of the penis, the external urethral sphincter, the greater vestibular gland, or the crura of the penis? The answer is the external urethral sphincter. The pouch also contains the deep transverse perineal muscle and, in the male, the bulbourethral glands. The bulb and the crura lie below the perineal membrane.

Question 9180. A constructed illustration: a clinician plans a pudendal nerve block for a procedure on the perineum and must find the nerve where it is most accessible. Which bony landmark guides the needle, and which structure does the nerve lie against there? The answer is the ischial spine, against which the nerve lies as it crosses the sacrospinous ligament. The block is placed just medial and posterior to the spine. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 9181. Which of these structures lies in the superficial perineal pouch of the male: the bulb of the penis, the prostate, the seminal vesicle, or the membranous urethra? The answer is the bulb of the penis. The pouch also holds the crura of the penis, the ischiocavernosus, the bulbospongiosus and the superficial transverse perineal muscles.

Question 9182. What is the fascia that encloses the superficial perineal pouch and is continuous with the dartos of the scrotum and the membranous layer of the abdominal wall? The answer is the superficial perineal fascia, also called the fascia of Colles. It attaches to the ischiopubic rami on each side and to the posterior border of the perineal membrane. That attachment keeps fluid in the pouch from reaching the thigh.

Question 9183. A constructed illustration: urine leaks from a torn urethra below the perineal membrane and collects in the scrotum, the penis and the lower abdominal wall, but not in the thighs. Why does it spare the thighs? The answer is that the superficial perineal fascia is attached to the ischiopubic rami and to the posterior border of the perineal membrane. Fluid therefore follows the loose tissue upward into the abdominal wall instead.

Question 9184. A described dissection of the superficial perineal pouch in the male shows three pairs of muscles, a midline bulb pierced by the urethra, and two crura fixed to the ischiopubic rami. Which structures are shown? The answer is the bulbospongiosus over the bulb, the ischiocavernosus over each crus, and the superficial transverse perineal muscles. The bulb is the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum.

Question 9185. Which of these muscles covers the bulb of the penis: the ischiocavernosus, the bulbospongiosus, the superficial transverse perineal, or the external anal sphincter? The answer is the bulbospongiosus. It compresses the bulb and the spongy urethra and helps to expel the last drops of urine. The ischiocavernosus covers each crus of the penis instead.

Question 9186. Which structure lies immediately below the perineal membrane in the male: the membranous urethra, the bulb of the penis, the prostate, or the bladder? The answer is the bulb of the penis. It lies in the superficial perineal pouch and contains the first part of the spongy urethra. The membranous urethra lies above the membrane, in the deep pouch.

Question 9187. A described dissection of the female perineum shows two small glands at the posterior end of the bulbs of the vestibule, each with a duct opening beside the vaginal opening. Which glands are shown? The answer is the greater vestibular glands. They lie in the superficial perineal pouch and their ducts are easily blocked.

Question 9188. Which of these structures belongs to the superficial perineal pouch of the female: the bulbs of the vestibule, the external urethral sphincter, the deep transverse perineal muscle, or the membranous urethra? The answer is the bulbs of the vestibule. The pouch also holds the crura of the clitoris, the greater vestibular glands and the superficial transverse perineal muscles. The other structures lie in the deep perineal pouch.

Question 9189. A described view of the female external genitalia shows a midline cleft between two folds of skin, a small erectile organ in front of it, and two openings within the cleft. Which structures are shown? The answer is the labia majora, the glans of the clitoris, and the external urethral and vaginal openings. The labia minora lie between the two larger folds.

Question 9190. The perineum is described as the floor of the pelvis. In which plane does it lie relative to the pelvic diaphragm, and what separates the two? The answer is that the perineum lies below the pelvic diaphragm and is separated from the pelvic cavity by it. The perineal membrane lies in the urogenital triangle below the diaphragm.

Question 9191. Which of these pairs belongs together: the bulbospongiosus with the crus of the penis, the ischiocavernosus with the bulb of the penis, the bulbospongiosus with the bulb of the penis, or the external anal sphincter with the clitoris? The answer is the bulbospongiosus with the bulb of the penis. The ischiocavernosus covers the crus. The external anal sphincter encircles the anal canal.

Question 9192. What is the perineal body? The answer is a fibromuscular node in the midline between the anal canal behind and the vagina or the bulb of the penis in front. It lies at the center of the perineum, just below the perineal membrane.

Question 9193. Which muscles are attached to the perineal body? The answer is the bulbospongiosus, the superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, the external anal sphincter and part of the levator ani. The posterior wall of the vagina is attached there in the female.

Question 9194. A constructed illustration: a woman tears the tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus during a difficult delivery. Which structure has been injured, and which attachments have been lost? The answer is the perineal body, with loss of the attachments of the bulbospongiosus, the transverse perineal muscles and the external anal sphincter. The result is a weakened pelvic floor. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 9195. True or false: in the female the perineal body lies between the vagina and the anal canal. The answer is true. It lies in the midline of the perineum below the perineal membrane. In the male the same body lies between the bulb of the penis and the anal canal.

Question 9196.
