Question 9410. Which structure sits at the fork of the common carotid artery and is supplied by a branch of the ninth cranial nerve? The answer is the carotid sinus, a small dilatation at the beginning of the internal carotid artery. The sinus nerve of the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies it. The carotid body lies close by and receives branches from the same nerve.

Question 9411. Which spinous process is the most prominent one at the base of the neck when the head is bent forward? The answer is the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra, the vertebra prominens. The cervical spines above it are short and often split. The first thoracic spine may be equally prominent in some people.

Question 9412. A finger pressed upward behind the angle of the mandible meets a hard transverse bar. Which structure is it? The answer is the transverse process of the atlas, the first cervical vertebra. The atlas has no body and no spinous process, so this process is the part reached. The transverse process of the axis lies below it.

Question 9413. True or false: the spinous process felt at the base of the neck is always the first thoracic vertebra. The answer is false. The most prominent spine there is usually the seventh cervical vertebra, because its spine is long and unpaired. In some people the first thoracic spine is equally prominent, so the level is settled by counting.

Question 9414. Which bony angle can be felt at the lower back corner of the jaw, below the ear? The answer is the angle of the mandible. The masseter muscle covers its outer surface, and the parotid gland wraps around its posterior border. It is the point where the body of the mandible meets its vertical ramus.

Question 9415. Which structure lies immediately in front of the external acoustic opening and glides forward when the mouth opens? The answer is the head of the mandible, which forms the temporomandibular joint. It sits in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. A finger placed there feels it move as the jaw opens.

Question 9416. A described photograph of the side of the head shows a slender bony bridge from the cheek to the front of the ear, with a hollow above and below. Which structure is it? The answer is the zygomatic arch, formed by the zygomatic bone in front and the temporal bone behind. The masseter muscle passes down from it and the temporalis muscle deep to it.

Question 9417. Which pair of small bones forms the bridge of the nose? The answer is the two nasal bones. They meet in the midline between the two maxillae and are covered only by skin and a little muscle. A finger run down the bridge feels them end where the nasal cartilages begin.

Question 9418. Which midline projection can be felt under the chin at the front of the jaw? The answer is the mental protuberance, the front of the body of the mandible. It is the triangular prominence that forms the chin, covered by the mentalis muscle. Just above it on each side lies the opening for the mental nerve.

Question 9419. Which notch can be felt at the upper margin of the orbit, and which nerve passes through it? The answer is the supraorbital notch, with the supraorbital nerve. It lies at the junction of the medial and middle thirds of the upper orbital margin. In some people it is closed into a foramen instead, which is a normal variation.

Question 9420. Which pair belongs together: the inion with the external occipital protuberance, the glabella with the angle of the mandible, the nasion with the mastoid process, or the gonion with the bridge of the nose? The answer is the inion with that protuberance. The glabella lies between the eyebrows, the nasion at the root of the nose, and the gonion at the angle of the mandible.

Question 9421. A described view of the side of the skull shows a small thin area where four bones meet, bounded by a curved line. Which region is it, and what lies beneath it? The answer is the pterion, with the middle meningeal artery beneath it. The frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet there. A blow to that point can tear the artery.

Question 9422. Which opening is felt as a small depression on the front of the cheek, a finger width below the middle of the lower orbital margin? The answer is the infraorbital foramen. The infraorbital nerve and vessels pass through it to the cheek, the upper lip and the side of the nose. It lies roughly in line with the supraorbital notch.

Question 9423. Which pair belongs together: the hyoid bone with the third cervical vertebra, the cricoid cartilage with the second cervical vertebra, the thyroid cartilage with the seventh cervical vertebra, or the sternal angle with the second cervical vertebra? The answer is the hyoid bone with the third cervical vertebra. The cricoid lies at the sixth and the thyroid cartilage at the fourth and fifth.

Question 9424. Which structure lies at the level of the suprasternal notch: the first thoracic vertebra, the second thoracic vertebra, the fourth thoracic vertebra, or the ninth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the second thoracic vertebra. The notch is the hollow at the top of the sternum between the clavicles. The sternal angle lies lower, at the fourth thoracic vertebra.

Question 9425. True or false: the sternal angle lies at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. The answer is true. The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. It marks the second costal cartilage on each side and the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae.

Question 9426. Which landmark on the front of the chest gives the level of the second costal cartilage, and why does that help when the ribs are counted? The answer is the sternal angle. The second costal cartilage joins the sternum at that ridge, so a finger placed there finds the second rib. The ribs are then counted downward.

Question 9427. Which small pointed bone is felt in the midline at the lower end of the sternum, and at the level of which vertebra does it lie? The answer is the xiphoid process, at the ninth thoracic vertebra. It is the lowest part of the sternum and may be forked as a normal variation. The costal margin meets on each side above it.

Question 9428. A described view of the front of the trunk shows the lower border of the chest as two curved lines meeting below in a shallow V. Which structure forms the apex of the V? The answer is the xiphoid process, with the costal margin formed by the cartilages of the seventh to the tenth ribs. The eleventh and twelfth ribs end free below it.

Question 9429. Which ribs contribute their cartilages to the costal margin, and which two end free? The answer is that the seventh to the tenth ribs join the costal margin, while the eleventh and twelfth end free. The free ribs are called floating ribs and carry no cartilage to the sternum. Their ends lie in muscle.

Question 9430. Which two ribs have no attachment to the sternum or to the costal margin? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth ribs, the floating ribs. They arise from the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae and end in the muscles of the abdominal wall. Being short and mobile, they can be broken by a blow from behind.

Question 9431. Which part of the scapula can be felt at the level of the seventh rib and the seventh thoracic vertebra? The answer is the inferior angle of the scapula, the lowest point of the triangular bone. It lies against the chest wall. When the arm is raised above the head it moves upward and outward, so the level shifts.

Question 9432. A described view of the back shows a flat triangular bone beside the spine, with a ridge across its upper part. Which ridge is it, and at which vertebra does its root lie? The answer is the spine of the scapula, whose root lies at the third thoracic vertebra. It divides the back of the scapula into parts above and below. Its outer end is the acromion.

Question 9433. Which bony hook can be felt by pressing deeply into the front of the shoulder, just below the outer third of the clavicle? The answer is the coracoid process of the scapula. The coracobrachialis, the short head of the biceps and the pectoralis minor arise from it. The front fibers of the deltoid cover it, so deep pressure is needed.

Question 9434. A constructed illustration: a person falls onto the point of the shoulder, and afterward a hard ridge is felt under the skin across the upper chest. Which bone is broken? The answer is the clavicle. It lies just under the skin along its whole length, without a cushion of muscle. It usually breaks at the junction of its middle and outer thirds.

Question 9435. Which structure lies immediately behind the medial end of the clavicle? The answer is the first rib, with the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus passing over it. The first rib is deep to the clavicle and cannot be felt through the skin. The lower trunk of the brachial plexus crosses it.

Question 9436. Which bony point forms the tip of the shoulder and gives the level from which the arm hangs? The answer is the acromion of the scapula. It is the outer end of the spine of the scapula and lies just under the skin. The deltoid muscle arises from it and from the spine. It meets the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.

Question 9437. A described photograph of a bent elbow from behind shows three bony points that form a triangle when the elbow bends and a straight line when it straightens. Which points are they? The answer is the olecranon and the two epicondyles of the humerus. The medial epicondyle lies on the inner side and the lateral one on the outer side.

Question 9438. Which bony projection forms the point of the elbow and is covered only by a bursa and loose skin? The answer is the olecranon, the upper end of the ulna. It fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus when the elbow straightens. The tendon of the triceps muscle inserts on its upper surface.

Question 9439. A constructed illustration: a blow lands on the inner side of the elbow, and afterward the little finger feels numb and the grip is weak. Which nerve is exposed there? The answer is the ulnar nerve, which runs in a groove behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Only skin and a thin layer of fascia cover it.

Question 9440. Which bone of the forearm turns when the palm is rotated, and where is its head felt at the elbow? The answer is the radius, whose head lies in the depression just below the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. It turns against the capitulum of the humerus. The ulna stays fixed while the radius swings around it.

Question 9441. Which of the two bony points at the wrist lies farther from the elbow: the radial styloid process or the ulnar styloid process? The answer is the radial styloid process, about one centimeter farther down. It is the lower end of the radius. The ulnar styloid lies higher and projects a little farther backward.

Question 9442. Which tendon lies immediately medial to the radial artery at the wrist? The answer is the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis. It stands out when the wrist is bent against resistance. The radial artery lies just lateral to it, resting on the lower end of the radius. The two are felt together at the pulse point.

Question 9443. Which small bone can be felt as a hard nodule at the base of the fleshy pad on the little finger side of the wrist? The answer is the pisiform bone, a pea-shaped carpal bone lying in the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris. The ulnar nerve passes just lateral to it. It is the most easily felt carpal bone.

Question 9444. A described view of the back of the hand shows a triangular hollow at the base of the thumb, bounded by tendons, with a pulse running through it. Which hollow is it, and which bones form its floor? The answer is the anatomical snuffbox, floored by the scaphoid and the trapezium. The abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis bound one side, and the extensor pollicis longus the other.

Question 9445. Which bony hook lies deep in the fleshy pad on the little finger side of the hand, just beyond the pisiform? The answer is the hook of the hamate. It projects forward from the hamate bone and is felt through the muscles of the pad. The ulnar nerve and artery pass beside it through a short tunnel on their way to the palm.

Question 9446. A constructed illustration: a person falls on the outstretched hand, and later there is tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb. Which bone is most likely injured, and why is the injury easily missed? The answer is the scaphoid. Its blood supply enters at the far end, so a break near the wrist can starve the bone.

Question 9447. Which tendon lies just under the skin in the middle of the front of the wrist and leads the examiner to the median nerve? The answer is the tendon of the palmaris longus. It crosses the wrist in the midline and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum. The median nerve lies deep to it, within the carpal tunnel.

Question 9448. True or false: the tendon of the palmaris longus can be felt in every forearm. The answer is false. The muscle is absent in about one in seven people, which is a normal variation. When it is present it stands out as a fine cord if the wrist is bent while the thumb and the little finger are pressed together.

Question 9449. Name two tendons that can be felt at the front of the wrist, one on the thumb side and one in the midline. The answer is the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis and the tendon of the palmaris longus. The first lies near the thumb side, just medial to the radial pulse. The second runs down the middle of the wrist when present.

Question 9450. Which bony ridge can be felt along the top of the hip, and at the level of which vertebra does its highest point lie? The answer is the iliac crest, whose highest point lies at the fourth lumbar vertebra. The crest runs from the front to the back of the pelvis. It is the usual guide to the fourth lumbar spine.

Question 9451. Which cord-like band can be felt from the bony point at the front of the hip to the pubic region, and what lies below its midpoint? The answer is the inguinal ligament, with the femoral vessels just below its midpoint. It stretches from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It forms the fold of the groin.

Question 9452. A described photograph of the lower back shows two dimples, one on each side, at the top of the buttocks. Which bony points lie beneath them? The answer is the two posterior superior iliac spines, at the level of the second sacral segment. The dimples are made by the skin being tethered to the spines beneath. They are the best guide to the sacroiliac joints.

Question 9453. A constructed illustration: a pulse is felt in the groin, halfway between the bony point at the front of the hip and the middle of the pubis. Which vessel is it? The answer is the femoral artery. It enters the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament at that midpoint. The femoral vein lies just medial to it, and the femoral nerve lateral to it.

Question 9454. Which midline joint of the pelvis can be felt at the front, below the hair line? The answer is the pubic symphysis, where the two pubic bones meet. Its disc softens and widens in pregnancy as a normal change. In front of it lies the pubic crest, with the pubic tubercle at its outer end.

Question 9455. A horizontal plane is imagined through the highest points of the two iliac crests. Which plane is it, and at which vertebra does it cross the spine? The answer is the supracristal plane, at the fourth lumbar vertebra. It is used to identify the fourth lumbar spine. The umbilicus lies higher, at the disc between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae.

Question 9456. Which pair belongs together: the anterior superior iliac spine with the outer end of the inguinal ligament, the pubic tubercle with the ischial spine, the greater trochanter with the sacral promontory, or the ischial tuberosity with the iliac crest? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine with the outer end of the inguinal ligament. The pubic tubercle is the inner end of the same ligament.

Question 9457. Which bony point is the most lateral part of the hip, felt on the outer side of the upper thigh? The answer is the greater trochanter of the femur, a square projection at the junction of the neck and the shaft. The gluteal muscles insert on it. It lies at the level of the hip joint.

Question 9458. Which bony point is felt below the fold of the buttock when the hip is straight, but disappears when the hip is bent? The answer is the ischial tuberosity, the lower end of the ischium and the bone on which the body rests when sitting. When the hip is flexed the gluteus maximus slides over it.

Question 9459. A described view of the front of the knee shows a flat triangular bone, a thick band from it, and a bony bump where the band ends. Which structures are they? The answer is the patella, the patellar tendon and the tibial tuberosity. The patella is the largest sesamoid bone of the body and lies in the tendon of the quadriceps.

Question 9460. Which bone is felt as a round head on the outer side of the knee, below the outer condyle of the tibia? The answer is the head of the fibula. The tendon of the biceps femoris and the lateral collateral ligament of the knee attach to it. The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just below.

Question 9461. A constructed illustration: a blow falls on the outer side of the knee, and afterward the foot cannot be lifted at the ankle, though the knee still straightens. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the common fibular nerve, which winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin. Its branches supply the muscles that lift the foot.

Question 9462. Which bony point forms the inner bump of the ankle and gives attachment to the deltoid ligament? The answer is the medial malleolus of the tibia. It lies about one centimeter higher than the outer bump. The tendon of the tibialis posterior passes behind it, and the posterior tibial pulse is felt just behind it.

Question 9463. Which of the two ankle bumps lies lower and farther back: the medial malleolus or the lateral malleolus? The answer is the lateral malleolus, the lower end of the fibula. It forms the outer wall of the ankle joint and gives attachment to the lateral ligaments. The medial malleolus lies higher and farther forward.

Question 9464. A described view of the back of the heel shows a thick cord from the calf and a broad bony mass beneath it. Which structures are they? The answer is the calcaneal tendon and the calcaneus. The tendon, also called the Achilles tendon, is formed by the soleus and the two heads of the gastrocnemius. It inserts on the back of the calcaneus.

Question 9465. Which bony tuberosity is felt on the inner border of the foot, just below and in front of the medial malleolus? The answer is the tuberosity of the navicular bone, where the tendon of the tibialis posterior inserts. It is the highest point of the medial longitudinal arch.

Question 9466. Which bony point lies on the outer side of the foot, halfway along its border, and gives insertion to a muscle of the little toe? The answer is the base of the fifth metatarsal bone, where the tendon of the peroneus brevis inserts. It projects as a small knob that is easily bruised. A stumble that rolls the foot inward pulls on it.

Question 9467. A pulse is felt on the top of the foot, lateral to the tendon that stands out when the great toe is lifted. Which artery is it? The answer is the dorsalis pedis artery. It runs forward from the ankle between the tendons of the extensor muscles. The tendon beside it belongs to the extensor hallucis longus.

Question 9468. Where is the posterior tibial pulse felt, and which structures lie beside it? The answer is behind the medial malleolus, between that bone and the calcaneal tendon. The artery runs there with the tibial nerve and the deep tendons of the calf. The pulse is felt about a finger width behind the bony point.

Question 9469. Which pair belongs together: the dorsalis pedis pulse with the top of the foot, the popliteal pulse with the front of the ankle, the posterior tibial pulse with the groin, or the carotid pulse with the back of the knee? The answer is the dorsalis pedis pulse with the top of the foot. The popliteal pulse is felt behind the knee and the posterior tibial pulse behind the medial malleolus.

Question 9470. Name the two pulse points that are felt in the foot, spoken as a list. The answer is the dorsalis pedis artery and the posterior tibial artery. The first lies on the top of the foot, lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The second lies behind the medial malleolus.

Question 9471. Which pulse is felt in the hollow behind the knee when the knee is slightly bent? The answer is the popliteal pulse. The popliteal artery lies deepest in the hollow, against the back of the knee joint. Fascia and fat cover it, so the knee is bent to relax them. The popliteal vein lies superficial to it.

Question 9472. Which two small bones lie beneath the head of the first metatarsal bone, within the tendons that pass under the ball of the great toe? The answer is the two sesamoid bones of the flexor hallucis brevis. They lie in the tendon and glide over the metatarsal head. They take part in carrying the weight of the body.

Question 9473. A described view of the inner border of the foot shows a curved arch lifting the middle of the sole from the ground. Which arch is it, and which bones form it? The answer is the medial longitudinal arch. It is supported behind by the calcaneus and in front by the head of the first metatarsal, The tibialis posterior tendon holds it up.

Question 9474. A constructed illustration: a person lands heavily on the foot, and later the body of the ankle bone loses its blood supply although the break is thin. Which bone is involved? The answer is the talus. Vessels enter it from below and behind and run backward into the body of the bone. A break through the narrow neck can cut that supply.

Question 9475. True or false: the calcaneal tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon of the body, and it inserts on the calcaneus. The answer is true. It is formed by the gastrocnemius and the soleus and receives the plantaris tendon on its inner side. It raises the heel and lifts the body onto the toes.

Question 9476. Which point on the front of the chest gives the position of the apex of the heart, and where is it? The answer is the apex beat, felt in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. The apex of the heart lies there, directed downward, forward and to the left. It is the lowest and most lateral point of the heart.

Question 9477. In the examination of the heart, where is the sound of each valve best heard? The answer is that the mitral valve is heard at the apex, the tricuspid at the lower left border of the sternum, the aortic at the right second intercostal space and the pulmonary at the left second space. The sounds travel along the blood flow, not to the valve itself.

Question 9478. Which dome of the diaphragm lies higher in the chest, and why? The answer is the right dome, because the liver lies beneath it. The right dome reaches about the fourth intercostal space at rest and the left the fifth. Both descend with a deep breath. This is why the right lung is shorter than the left.

Question 9479. A described percussion map of the front of the chest shows dullness below the right costal margin, dullness beside the left border of the sternum, and a clear note elsewhere. Which organs cause the dullness? The answer is the liver on the right and the heart behind the left border of the sternum. Air-filled lung gives a clear note and solid organ dullness.

Question 9480. A constructed illustration: a hand lies flat on the right side of the abdomen, and an organ edge slips beneath it as the person breathes in. Which organ is being examined? The answer is the liver. Its lower border lies just below the right costal margin in health and moves down with the breath. It fills the right upper part of the abdomen.

Question 9481. Which ribs protect the spleen, and where does its tip lie in the healthy adult? The answer is the ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs, with the tip of the spleen just behind the left costal margin. The spleen is not felt in health. When it enlarges it moves downward and forward, and its notch can then be felt.

Question 9482. Which organ lies behind the left costal margin, extends from the ninth to the eleventh rib, and is not normally palpable? The answer is the spleen. It lies in the left upper part of the abdomen, behind the stomach and below the diaphragm. Its long axis follows the line of the tenth rib. It is the largest mass of lymphoid tissue.

Question 9483. A constructed illustration: one hand lies behind the right flank and the other below the costal margin, and they are pressed together during a deep breath. Which organ is caught between them? The answer is the right kidney. It lies lower than the left because the liver occupies the space above it. Its lower pole descends with a deep breath.

Question 9484. In the examination of the breast, into which parts is the surface divided, and what is the tail that reaches toward the armpit? The answer is the four quadrants, upper and lower, inner and outer, with the axillary tail reaching into the armpit. The tail passes through an opening in the deep fascia. The upper outer quadrant holds the largest share of the gland.

Question 9485. A described view of the groin shows a triangular opening above and medial to the pubic tubercle, with a cord passing through it. Which opening is it? The answer is the superficial inguinal ring, which transmits the spermatic cord. In the female it carries the round ligament of the uterus. The ring is a slit in the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle.

Question 9486. Which cord-like structure can be felt within the inguinal canal in the male, and which three structures pass inside it? The answer is the spermatic cord, containing the ductus deferens, the testicular artery and the plexus of veins around it. It also carries the cremaster muscle and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. It leaves the canal at the superficial ring.

Question 9487. Which artery is felt in the hollow at the front of the elbow, and on which side of the tendon of the biceps does it lie? The answer is the brachial artery, medial to the tendon of the biceps. The tendon forms the lateral boundary of the hollow and can be rolled between the fingers. The median nerve lies just medial to the artery.

Question 9488. Which muscle contracts at the knee jerk and which at the ankle jerk, and which nerve carries each? The answer is the quadriceps at the knee jerk, through the femoral nerve, and the muscles of the calf at the ankle jerk, through the tibial nerve. The knee jerk tests the third and fourth lumbar segments. The ankle jerk tests the first and second sacral segments.

Question 9489. Which of these structures lies most medial at the front of the elbow: the tendon of the biceps, the brachial artery, the median nerve, or the radial nerve? The answer is the median nerve, which lies medial to the brachial artery. From the medial side the order is the median nerve, the brachial artery, then the tendon of the biceps. The radial nerve lies farther out.

Question 9490. Which muscle is tested when a person stands on one leg and the pelvis on the opposite side drops? The answer is the gluteus medius of the standing leg. It arises from the outer surface of the ilium and inserts on the greater trochanter. It holds the body level over the hip. The gluteus minimus assists it, and the superior gluteal nerve supplies both.

Question 9491. A described photograph shows a tape measure from the bony point at the front of the hip to the bony point on the inner side of the ankle. Which measurement is being taken? The answer is the true length of the lower limb, from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus. The tape follows the limb without its curves. The apparent length uses the umbilicus instead.

Question 9492. When a lower limb is measured, which two points give its true length: the anterior superior iliac spine and the medial malleolus, the umbilicus and the medial malleolus, the iliac crest and the calcaneus, or the pubic symphysis and the lateral malleolus? The answer is the anterior superior iliac spine and the medial malleolus. The umbilicus and the same ankle point give the apparent length.

Question 9493. True or false: in the examination of the abdomen, palpation is always performed before auscultation. The answer is false. Auscultation comes first, because pressing on the abdomen can change the sounds made by the bowel. Palpation and percussion follow, and any tender area is examined last.

Question 9494. Which pair belongs together: the otoscope with the tympanic membrane, the tendon hammer with the tympanic membrane, the tape measure with the reflexes, or the tuning fork with the length of a limb? The answer is the otoscope with the tympanic membrane. The tendon hammer tests the deep tendon reflexes, the tape measure the length of a limb, and the tuning fork the hearing.

Question 9495. Name two pulse points that are used when a lower limb is examined, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the femoral artery in the groin and the popliteal artery behind the knee. Two more lie below them, the posterior tibial artery behind the medial malleolus and the dorsalis pedis artery on the top of the foot.

Question 9496. Two vertical lines are imagined on the left side of the chest, one from the middle of the clavicle and one from the middle of the armpit. Which line passes through the apex beat? The answer is the midclavicular line, which passes through the apex beat in the fifth intercostal space. The midaxillary line runs through the armpit and marks the base of the lung.

Question 9497. A constructed illustration: a firm organ lies below the left costal margin, and the examiner must decide whether it is the spleen or the kidney. Which features of the spleen decide the question? The answer is that the spleen moves down and forward with the breath and lies close under the costal margin, with a notch on its upper border. The kidney lies deeper and is held between two hands.

Question 9498. Which structure lies in the transpyloric plane, at the first lumbar vertebra: the pylorus of the stomach, the umbilicus, the bifurcation of the aorta, or the pubic symphysis? The answer is the pylorus of the stomach. The same plane cuts the tips of the ninth costal cartilages and the neck of the pancreas. The umbilicus lies lower, at the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae.

Question 9499. A described computed tomography section across the upper part of the abdomen shows the liver on one side, the spleen on the other, and two kidneys behind the other organs. Which plane is it? The answer is a transverse plane at the level of the twelfth thoracic or first lumbar vertebra. At that level the kidneys lie behind the peritoneum.

Question 9500. Which surface point marks the base of the appendix: a point one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, the transpyloric plane, or the tip of the ninth costal cartilage? The answer is the point one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The position of the appendix varies, so this is only a guide.

To summarize, the surface of the body is a map of the bones beneath it, and the points that can be felt through the skin are the fixed marks on that map. The inion, the mastoid process, the hyoid bone, the laryngeal prominence and the cricoid cartilage give the levels of the neck, while the jugular notch, the sternal angle, the xiphoid process and the costal margin give the levels of the chest. The iliac crest, the anterior superior iliac spine, the pubic symphysis, the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter give the levels of the pelvis and the hip, and in the limbs the acromion, the epicondyles, the olecranon, the styloid processes, the head of the fibula and the two malleoli are the guides, with the pulses lying beside them. An examination is built on these marks, because the apex beat, the liver, the spleen, the kidney, the inguinal canal and the joints are all found by first finding the bone or the cartilage that lies next to them. Saying each landmark aloud, together with the structure beside it, is what fixes the map in memory. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 96 — Anatomical Examination

This chapter turns to the living body as it is examined at the bedside, the anatomy that is used with the eyes, the hands and a stethoscope. It covers the surface landmarks that lead the examiner to deeper structures, the four classical methods of examination and the order in which they are applied, and the tests that reveal the position, the size and the movement of the organs beneath. It holds one hundred questions, and every one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. The last part follows the nerves and the vessels that can be examined without cutting. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 9501. Which of the four classical methods of examination uses the hands to feel the size, the texture and the tenderness of a structure? The answer is palpation. Inspection uses the eyes, percussion a light tap, and auscultation a stethoscope. Palpation brings the examining hand into contact with the tissues beneath the skin.

Question 9502. During an examination of the abdomen, which method is carried out before palpation: auscultation, percussion, deep palpation, or measurement of the girth? The answer is auscultation. Pressing on the abdomen can change the faint bowel sounds and make them harder to hear. Percussion and palpation therefore follow the stethoscope.

Question 9503. Which method of examination produces a note by tapping one finger against another finger laid flat on the body wall? The answer is percussion. The finger on the body acts as a plate and the striking finger as a hammer. A resonant note comes from air in the lung and a dull note from solid tissue such as the liver.

Question 9504. True or false: inspection is the first method applied in the examination of any region of the body. The answer is true. The examiner looks before touching, because the surface shows swelling, wasting, discoloration and asymmetry before the hands disturb anything. Palpation and percussion come afterwards.

Question 9505. As the examiner counts the ribs from above, which rib lies at the level of the sternal angle? The answer is the second rib. The sternal angle is the ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum, and the second costal cartilage joins the sternum at that ridge.

Question 9506. Which statement about counting the ribs is correct: the first rib can be felt in front, the second rib lies at the sternal angle, the twelfth rib is the easiest to feel, or the ribs are counted from below? The answer is that the second rib lies at the sternal angle. The first rib hides behind the clavicle and the lower ribs are covered by muscle.

Question 9507. What is the name of the notch felt at the top of the sternum, between the two clavicles? The answer is the jugular notch, also called the suprasternal notch. It lies at the level of the second thoracic vertebra, with the trachea in the midline just above it.

Question 9508. A described chest radiograph shows a dark vertical band running down the middle of the upper chest and dividing into two branches behind the heart. Which structure is that band? The answer is the trachea. Air absorbs little of the beam, so the air-filled tube appears dark, and the two branches are the main bronchi.

Question 9509. A constructed illustration: a patient takes a deep breath, and the examiner sees that the right side of the chest moves less than the left. Which side is abnormal, and why does the difference matter? The answer is that the right side is abnormal. The two sides are compared at the same level, so a difference points to the side that moves less.

Question 9510. In a healthy adult, where is the apex beat usually felt: in the second intercostal space at the left sternal edge, in the fourth intercostal space, in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, or below the xiphoid process? The answer is the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, over the apex of the heart.

Question 9511. Which surface line is drawn vertically downward from the midpoint of the clavicle, and why is it useful on the chest? The answer is the midclavicular line. It runs parallel to the midline and crosses the fifth intercostal space, where the apex beat is felt, and it marks the upper border of the liver below the diaphragm.

Question 9512. What is the name of the small pointed process at the lower end of the sternum? The answer is the xiphoid process. It lies at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra in the adult and is cartilaginous in youth, so it may be felt as a nodule in the midline.

Question 9513. Which of these pairs belongs together: the jugular notch with the top of the sternum, the xiphoid process with the upper end of the sternum, the sternal angle with the lower end of the sternum, or the costal margin with the clavicle? The answer is the jugular notch with the top of the sternum. The costal margin is the lower edge of the rib cage.

Question 9514. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows a flat vertical bone in front, with the heart shadow behind it and the vertebral bodies at the back. Which bone is the flat one in front? The answer is the sternum. In a lateral view the beam travels from side to side, so the front and the back of the chest lie at opposite edges.

Question 9515. The lower edge of the rib cage, felt as a curved border on each side of the abdomen, is formed by which costal cartilages: the fifth to the seventh, the seventh to the tenth, the ninth to the twelfth, or the fourth to the sixth? The answer is the seventh to the tenth. They join one another in the midline to form the costal margin.

Question 9516. A constructed illustration: a needle is passed into the chest wall just below the lower border of a rib. Which structure of the costal groove is at greatest risk, and how do the three structures lie from above downward? The answer is the intercostal nerve. The vein lies highest in the groove, the artery in the middle and the nerve lowest.

Question 9517. At which vertebral level does the crest of the ilium lie, felt as the highest point of the hip bone? The answer is the fourth lumbar vertebra. The level is used to count the lumbar spines, because the crests are easy to feel on both sides.

Question 9518. The umbilicus lies at the level of which vertebra in a healthy adult? The answer is the third lumbar vertebra. The navel is a fixed landmark on the front of the abdomen, and the disc between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae lies just above it.

Question 9519. Name two structures that lie in the midline of the anterior abdominal wall, spoken as a list. The answer is the linea alba and the umbilicus. The linea alba is the band of fibrous tissue between the two rectus sheaths, running from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis.

Question 9520. Which structure separates the right rectus abdominis muscle from the left one: the linea alba, the inguinal ligament, the arcuate line, or the pectineal line? The answer is the linea alba, the fibrous band in the midline of the abdominal wall. The arcuate line marks the lower end of the posterior wall of the rectus sheath.

Question 9521. A described photograph of an athlete's abdomen shows a vertical groove in the middle and three or four horizontal grooves crossing the muscle on each side. Which muscle is shown, and what are those bands? The answer is the rectus abdominis, with its tendinous intersections, which divide it into segments and are attached to the front of its sheath.

Question 9522. A constructed illustration: tenderness is greatest at a point one third of the way from the front of the right hip bone to the umbilicus. Which structure lies beneath that described point? The answer is the appendix, at the base of its attachment to the cecum. The point is named after McBurney. The appendix may lie elsewhere, so tenderness there is a guide rather than a proof.

Question 9523. In percussion of the abdomen, where does the dullness of the liver begin in the midclavicular line? The answer is at the fifth intercostal space. The upper border of the liver lies under the dome of the diaphragm, and the dullness extends down to the costal margin. Above it the note is resonant, because the lung lies beneath the tapping finger.

Question 9524. Percussion over the stomach gives a low-pitched, drum-like note, while percussion over the liver gives a dull note. Which statement explains the difference: the stomach contains air and the liver is solid, the stomach is larger, the liver lies behind the peritoneum, or the stomach lies against the spine? The answer is that the stomach contains air and the liver is solid. Air resonates, and a solid organ does not.

Question 9525. In a healthy adult, can the spleen be felt below the left costal margin, and if not, why not? The answer is that it cannot, because it lies deep to the ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs in the left midaxillary line. It must enlarge to about three times its normal size before its tip reaches the costal margin.

Question 9526. A described transverse section of the abdomen shows a thick-walled tube just in front of a vertebral body, slightly left of the midline, with a thinner vessel to its right. Which two vessels are described? The answer is the aorta on the left and the inferior vena cava on the right, both in front of the vertebra and behind the pancreas.

Question 9527. A constructed illustration: a patient cannot pass urine and a rounded swelling is felt in the lower abdomen, rising out of the pelvis. Which structure is distended, and why is it not felt when it is empty? The answer is the urinary bladder. When full it rises above the pubic symphysis, and when empty it lies behind that bone, out of reach of the hand.

Question 9528. Which of these pairs belongs together: the iliac crest with the fourth lumbar vertebra, the umbilicus with the first lumbar vertebra, the sternal angle with the third thoracic vertebra, or the jugular notch with the fifth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the iliac crest with the fourth lumbar vertebra, while the umbilicus lies at the third lumbar vertebra.

Question 9529. A described section across the abdomen shows the right kidney and the left kidney on the two sides of the vertebral column, with the inferior vena cava in front of the spine. In which plane was this section cut? The answer is a transverse plane. The section passes across the body, so both sides appear at once.

Question 9530. A described section of the trunk shows the bodies of the vertebrae cut through the middle and the aorta in front of them. Which plane produced that section, and why is only one kidney seen on its face? The answer is the median plane. A cut through the middle divides the body into right and left halves, so each face carries one kidney.

Question 9531. Which bone lies in front of the knee joint, within the tendon of the quadriceps muscle? The answer is the patella. It is the largest sesamoid bone in the body, and its posterior surface glides on the femur. It increases the power of the quadriceps by holding the tendon away from the joint.

Question 9532. A prominence is felt on the front of the upper end of the tibia, just below the knee, where the tendon of the quadriceps attaches. Which of these is it: the tibial tuberosity, the head of the fibula, the medial malleolus, or the adductor tubercle? The answer is the tibial tuberosity. The head of the fibula lies at the back and outer side of the knee.

Question 9533. Which structures bound the diamond-shaped hollow behind the knee, and what lies within it from the surface inward? The answer is the popliteal fossa, bounded above by the hamstring tendons and below by the two heads of the gastrocnemius. Within it the tibial nerve lies most superficial, with the popliteal vein and then the popliteal artery deeper.

Question 9534. A constructed illustration: a patient cannot straighten the knee against resistance after a fall, and the patella is no longer felt as a separate bone. Which structure has been torn? The answer is the tendon of the quadriceps above the patella or the patellar ligament below it. Either tear removes the pull of the quadriceps from the tibia.

Question 9535. A described drawing of the knee shows fluid bulging on both sides of the patella when the joint is full. Which space explains the bulging, and with which cavity does it communicate? The answer is the suprapatellar pouch, which communicates freely with the knee joint. Because it extends above the patella, fluid can be pressed from one side of the joint to the other.

Question 9536. Which muscle forms the rounded contour of the shoulder and is tested by asking the patient to lift the arm against resistance? The answer is the deltoid. It rises from the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula and ends on the humerus, and it abducts the arm from about fifteen degrees onward.

Question 9537. Which muscle initiates abduction of the shoulder in the first fifteen degrees: the deltoid, the supraspinatus, the teres major, or the pectoralis major? The answer is the supraspinatus. Its tendon passes under the acromion from the fossa above the spine of the scapula, and the deltoid then continues the movement.

Question 9538. Which vein runs in the groove between the deltoid and the pectoralis major, and what is that groove used for in examination? The answer is the cephalic vein, and the groove is the deltopectoral groove. The vein is a guide to that interval, where the examiner places a finger to find the coracoid process.

Question 9539. A constructed illustration: a patient reports pain in the shoulder when the arm is raised sideways between about sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees, while the movement is painless below and above that arc. Which structure is involved, and why does the pain occupy only part of the arc? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, which is pressed against the acromion during that arc.

Question 9540. Which bony point is felt at the outer side of the wrist, just above the base of the thumb? The answer is the styloid process of the radius, which lies about one centimeter distal to the styloid process of the ulna. The radial artery passes close to it before entering the hand.

Question 9541. The hollow at the base of the thumb, seen when the thumb is extended, is bounded by two tendons. Which structures form its floor: the scaphoid and the trapezium, the lunate and the triquetrum, the hamate and the pisiform, or the capitate and the trapezoid? The answer is the scaphoid and the trapezium, crossed by the radial artery before it passes into the palm.

Question 9542. A described photograph of the palm shows a fleshy mound at the base of the thumb, raised above the level of the palm. Which group of muscles forms that mound, and which nerve supplies them? The answer is the thenar muscles, supplied by the median nerve. They move the thumb away from the palm and across it, and wasting of the mound is an early sign of injury.

Question 9543. Which bone forms the heel and can be felt as the point of the heel after the skin and the fat are passed? The answer is the calcaneus. It is the largest bone of the foot, the Achilles tendon attaches to its back, and its body rests on the ground behind the arch.

Question 9544. Which bony prominence is felt on the inner side of the ankle, and which bone does it belong to? The answer is the medial malleolus of the tibia. The lateral malleolus on the outer side belongs to the fibula and lies lower and further back.

Question 9545. A described examination of a standing patient shows a flattened arch of the foot and a heel tilted outward. Which of these ligaments supports the arch that has given way: the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, the long plantar ligament, the deltoid ligament, or the anterior talofibular ligament? The answer is the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, also called the spring ligament, which runs from the calcaneus to the navicular.

Question 9546. True or false: the inguinal ligament is the thickened lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis and stretches from the front of the hip bone to the pubic tubercle. The answer is true. It is felt as a firm band when the examiner presses along the groin, and the femoral vessels pass beneath it into the thigh.

Question 9547. Which of these sets of boundaries belongs to the femoral triangle: the inguinal ligament above with the sartorius laterally and the adductor longus medially, the inguinal ligament below with the sartorius medially, the gluteus maximus with the gracilis, or the inguinal ligament with the iliopsoas and the rectus femoris? The answer is the inguinal ligament above, with the sartorius laterally and the adductor longus medially.

Question 9548. A described photograph of the palm shows three creases crossing it, one near the wrist, one curving around the base of the thumb, and one running across the hand below the fingers. Which crease is the distal one, and what does it mark? The answer is the crease below the fingers, which marks the line of the metacarpophalangeal joints.

Question 9549. Which small mound of muscle lies on the inner side of the palm, opposite the mound at the base of the thumb? The answer is the hypothenar eminence, formed by the muscles that move the little finger and supplied by the ulnar nerve. The hollow between the two mounds is the hollow of the palm.

Question 9550. Within the femoral triangle, in what order do the femoral nerve, artery and vein lie from the outer side inward? Which of these is correct: nerve, artery and vein, vein, artery and nerve, artery, nerve and vein, or nerve, vein and artery? The answer is nerve, artery and vein from lateral to medial. The vein, the most medial, lies next to the opening into the abdomen.

Question 9551. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a patient lies with the right leg shorter than the left and turned outward, and the greater trochanter lies higher than on the other side. Which part of which bone is most likely broken, and why is the limb shortened? The answer is the neck of the femur. The muscles pull the shaft upward and rotate it outward.

Question 9552. In a standing person, the tip of the greater trochanter lies at the level of which structure: the pubic tubercle, the anterior superior iliac spine, the ischial tuberosity, or the fifth lumbar vertebra? The answer is the pubic tubercle. A line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the ischial tuberosity passes through the trochanter when the hip is normal.

Question 9553. A described radiograph of a normal hip shows a continuous curved line running from the lower border of the neck of the femur into the upper border of the opening in the pelvis. Which of these is correct: it is unbroken in a normal hip, it is broken in every adult, it crosses the joint in the middle, or it marks the greater trochanter? The answer is that it is unbroken.

Question 9554. Where is the femoral pulse best felt: above the inguinal ligament, at its midpoint with the artery just below it, at the pubic symphysis, or at the outer end of the ligament? The answer is at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, with the artery just below it. There the vessel lies in the groove between the iliopsoas and the adductor longus.

Question 9555. Which cartilage forms the prominence in the front of the neck that moves when the voice changes pitch? The answer is the thyroid cartilage. Its upper part forms the laryngeal prominence, and the vocal folds lie within the larynx behind it. It lies at the level of the fourth and fifth cervical vertebrae.

Question 9556. The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. At which vertebral level does it lie: the fourth cervical, the sixth cervical, the second thoracic, or the seventh cervical? The answer is the sixth cervical vertebra. It is the narrowest part of the adult airway, and the trachea begins below it.

Question 9557. The isthmus of the thyroid gland lies in front of which tracheal rings, and which nerve lies behind it? Which of these is correct: the second and third rings with the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the first ring with the facial nerve, the fifth and sixth rings with the phrenic nerve, or the fourth ring with the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the second and third rings, with the recurrent laryngeal nerve behind the gland.

Question 9558. A midline swelling in the neck rises when the patient swallows and again when the patient puts out the tongue. Which of these does that indicate: a thyroglossal cyst attached to the tongue, a swelling of the thyroid gland, an enlarged lymph node, or a branchial cyst? The answer is a thyroglossal cyst. It lies on the path the thyroid took down from the tongue, so the tongue pulls it.

Question 9559. A described photograph of the neck shows a long muscle running from behind the ear down to the upper chest, dividing each side into a smaller front part and a larger back part. Which muscle is shown, and what are the two parts called? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid, dividing the neck into the anterior triangle and the posterior triangle.

Question 9560. Name the two triangles into which each side of the neck is divided by the sternocleidomastoid muscle, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior triangle and the posterior triangle. The anterior triangle contains the carotid sheath, and the posterior triangle contains the accessory nerve and the brachial plexus.

Question 9561. Which bony prominence can be felt just behind the ear, and which muscle attaches to it? The answer is the mastoid process of the temporal bone, to which the sternocleidomastoid attaches. It is filled with air cells that communicate with the middle ear, and the facial nerve leaves the skull just in front of it.

Question 9562. Which muscle pulls the head of the mandible and the articular disc forward when the mouth is opened? Which of these is correct: the lateral pterygoid muscle, the medial pterygoid muscle, the masseter, or the temporalis? The answer is the lateral pterygoid. The disc divides the joint into two compartments, so the upper one glides while the lower one hinges.

Question 9563. Which of these pairs belongs together: the zygomatic arch with the temporal bone and the zygomatic bone, the mastoid process with the maxilla, the mental protuberance with the occipital bone, or the angle of the mandible with the frontal bone? The answer is the zygomatic arch with the temporal bone and the zygomatic bone, felt as a bridge in front of the ear.

Question 9564. A described lateral radiograph of the skull shows a hollow in the middle of the base, shaped like a saddle, with a rounded shadow sitting inside it. Which structure is the hollow, and what normally lies in it? The answer is the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, which holds the pituitary gland above the air-filled sphenoid sinus.

Question 9565. The duct of the parotid gland crosses the face to open inside the mouth. Which of these statements is correct: it opens opposite the upper second molar tooth, it opens under the tongue, it opens opposite the lower first molar, or it opens behind the last molar? The answer is that it opens opposite the upper second molar tooth. It crosses the masseter muscle and turns inward to pierce the cheek.

Question 9566. True or false: the duct of the parotid gland can be felt as a firm ridge running across the surface of the masseter muscle when the cheek is pressed against the teeth. The answer is true. The duct lies on the muscle and is crossed by the branches of the facial nerve.

Question 9567. Which arch of bone is felt in the face just in front of the ear and below the outer corner of the eye? The answer is the zygomatic arch, formed by the zygomatic process of the temporal bone and the temporal process of the zygomatic bone. The masseter muscle rises from its lower border.

Question 9568. When the spine is examined from behind, which of these is seen in a healthy person: a midline furrow with the spines in a straight line, a lateral curve toward the right, a prominent angle at the eighth thoracic vertebra, or a gap between the fourth and fifth lumbar spines? The answer is a midline furrow with the spines in a straight line.

Question 9569. A described photograph of the back shows two flat triangular bones whose inner edges lie parallel to the spine, with their lower angles at the level of the seventh rib. Which bones are shown, and how many ribs lie above each lower angle? The answer is the scapulae, with the seventh rib at the lower angle. The spine of each scapula lies at the level of the third thoracic vertebra.

Question 9570. The lower border of the pectoralis major forms which fold of the chest wall, and which fold behind it is formed by the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the anterior axillary fold in front and the posterior axillary fold behind. Between them lies the axilla, through which the vessels and nerves pass to the arm.

Question 9571. A described examination of an older patient shows a rounded swelling in the groin, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and beside the femoral vein. Which of these is it: a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia, an enlarged lymph node, or a saphenous varix? The answer is a femoral hernia, which passes below the inguinal ligament, while an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle.

Question 9572. Which angle is formed at the lower end of the sternum between the converging costal margins, and what is it called? The answer is the infrasternal angle, also called the costal angle. It is wide in a broad chest and narrow in a long one, giving the examiner an idea of the shape of the rib cage.

Question 9573. Tactile fremitus is tested with the flat of the hand while the patient speaks. Which of these is correct: it is increased over consolidated lung and reduced over fluid, it is increased over fluid, it is absent over normal lung, or it is felt only at the apex? The answer is that it is increased over consolidated lung and reduced over fluid. Sound travels better through solid tissue than through fluid.

Question 9574. A described photograph of a young person's chest shows a deep funnel-shaped hollow in the lower part of the sternum, drawing the ribs inward on both sides. Which deformity is shown, and in which direction is the sternum displaced? The answer is pectus excavatum, in which the sternum is pushed backward. The heart lies behind the sternum and may be displaced.

Question 9575. True or false: in a healthy adult the spleen can usually be felt as a soft tip below the left costal margin on deep inspiration. The answer is false. The spleen lies deep to the ribs and is not palpable unless it is enlarged, when it grows downward and forward and its notch may be felt.

Question 9576. Which artery is felt as a pulse on the outer side of the front of the wrist, above the base of the thumb? The answer is the radial artery. It lies just lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis, where it can be pressed against the radius before it curves into the palm.

Question 9577. Which artery is felt in the hollow at the base of the thumb when the wrist is extended: the ulnar artery, the radial artery, the median artery, or the anterior interosseous artery? The answer is the radial artery. It crosses the floor of that hollow, formed by the scaphoid and the trapezium.

Question 9578. Which artery is felt on the top of the foot, just lateral to the tendon that raises the big toe? The answer is the dorsalis pedis artery, which lies between the tendons of the extensor hallucis longus and the extensor digitorum longus. Its pulse may be absent in a healthy person when the artery is small.

Question 9579. Which nerve lies in the carpal tunnel, and which tendon forms a guide to the tunnel at the wrist? The answer is the median nerve, with the tendon of the palmaris longus as the guide. The nerve passes deep to that tendon and to the transverse carpal ligament, with the flexor tendons.

Question 9580. A described photograph of a hand shows a flattened mound at the base of the thumb, and the thumb cannot be drawn across the palm. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the median nerve. Its branch to the thenar muscles is lost, and sensation is lost over the outer three and a half fingers.

Question 9581. A pinprick is felt over the pad of the thumb. Which spinal segment supplies that area: the fifth cervical, the sixth cervical, the seventh cervical, or the eighth cervical? The answer is the sixth cervical segment. The fifth covers the outer side of the arm and the seventh the middle finger.

Question 9582. A constructed illustration: a cut across the front of the wrist leaves the little finger numb and the fingers unable to spread apart. Which nerve has been cut, and where does it lie at the wrist? The answer is the ulnar nerve, on the inner side of the wrist beside the ulnar artery. It supplies the muscles between the fingers and the muscles of the little finger.

Question 9583. A blow to the inner side of the elbow causes numbness of the little finger. Which of these explains the injury: the ulnar nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle, the median nerve crosses the front of the elbow, the radial nerve lies behind the lateral epicondyle, or the ulnar nerve passes through the cubital fossa? The answer is that the ulnar nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle, covered only by skin and fascia.

Question 9584. Which of these pairs belongs together: the facial nerve with the muscles of facial expression, the trigeminal nerve with the muscles of the tongue, the hypoglossal nerve with the muscles of chewing, or the accessory nerve with the muscles of the eye? The answer is the facial nerve with the muscles of facial expression, while the trigeminal nerve carries sensation from the face and supplies the muscles of chewing.

Question 9585. True or false: the knee jerk is tested by tapping the patellar ligament while the leg hangs relaxed, and it depends on the third and fourth lumbar segments. The answer is true. The tap stretches the quadriceps, and the muscle contracts in reply, so the reflex tests the segments that supply it.

Question 9586. Behind the medial malleolus, in what order do the structures pass from the inner side outward on their way to the sole? The answer is the tendon of tibialis posterior, the tendon of flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery, the tendon of flexor hallucis longus and the tibial nerve. The nerve lies most lateral of the five, under the flexor retinaculum.

Question 9587. Which tendon is tapped to test the biceps reflex, and which spinal segments does that reflex test? The answer is the tendon of the biceps brachii, and the reflex tests the fifth and sixth cervical segments. The examiner places a thumb on the tendon in the cubital fossa and strikes the thumb.

Question 9588. Tapping the Achilles tendon while the foot hangs relaxed makes the foot point downward. Which of these is correct: the reflex tests the first and second sacral segments, it tests the fifth lumbar segment, it tests the fourth lumbar segment, or it tests the first thoracic segment? The answer is the first and second sacral segments. The tibial nerve carries the reflex, and its loss points to those roots.

Question 9589. A described map of the skin shows bands running around the trunk, one at the level of the nipples, one at the level of the umbilicus and one at the level of the groin. Which spinal segments supply those three bands? The answer is the fourth thoracic at the nipples, the tenth thoracic at the umbilicus and the first lumbar at the groin.

Question 9590. A constructed illustration: a patient cannot lift the front of the foot and drags the toes, and sensation is lost over the front of the shin and the top of the foot. Which nerve is involved, and where is it most exposed to injury? The answer is the common fibular nerve, at the neck of the fibula, where it lies against bone under the skin.

Question 9591. A patient cannot extend the wrist and the fingers, and the back of the hand is numb between the thumb and the index finger. Which nerve is injured, and in which groove of the humerus does it lie? The answer is the radial nerve, in the spiral groove on the back of the humerus, where a fracture of the shaft may injure it.

Question 9592. Name two places where the ulnar nerve can be felt against bone, spoken as a list. The answer is behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus and at the inner side of the wrist. At the elbow it lies in a groove covered only by skin and fascia.

Question 9593. Which of these pairs belongs together: injury of the radial nerve with wrist drop, injury of the median nerve with clawing of the ring and little fingers, injury of the ulnar nerve with loss of the biceps reflex, or injury of the axillary nerve with loss of the ankle jerk? The answer is injury of the radial nerve with wrist drop, while the ulnar nerve produces clawing.

Question 9594. A described photograph of the side of the neck shows a thin nerve crossing the large posterior triangle from above downward, just under the skin, on its way to the shoulder. Which nerve is shown, and which muscles does it supply? The answer is the accessory nerve, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius and lies near the surface as it crosses.

Question 9595. Through which opening does the facial nerve leave the skull, and which movement is lost when it is injured? Which of these is correct: the stylomastoid foramen, with loss of the muscles of facial expression, the foramen ovale, with loss of chewing, the jugular foramen, with loss of the gag reflex, or the optic canal, with loss of sight? The answer is the stylomastoid foramen, with loss of the muscles of facial expression.

Question 9596. The corneal reflex is tested by touching the clear front of the eye with a wisp of cotton. Which of these describes it correctly: the eye closes, with the trigeminal nerve carrying the sensation and the facial nerve the movement, the pupil narrows, the jaw closes, or the eye waters? The answer is that the eye closes, with the trigeminal nerve carrying the sensation and the facial nerve the movement.

Question 9597. A constructed illustration: a patient opens the mouth, and the jaw deviates to the left, the side on which chewing is weak. Which muscle has lost its pull: the left lateral pterygoid, the right lateral pterygoid, the left masseter, or both pterygoids equally? The answer is the left lateral pterygoid, so the healthy muscle on the right pulls the jaw across and the chin turns toward the weak side.

Question 9598. Touching the back of the throat makes the soft palate rise and the throat tighten. Which two cranial nerves carry that reflex? The answer is the ninth and the tenth cranial nerves. The ninth carries the sensation from the back of the throat, and the tenth supplies the muscles that lift the palate.

Question 9599. Which of these statements about the arteries felt in the head is correct: the facial artery is felt where it crosses the lower border of the jaw, the temporal artery is felt behind the ear, the facial artery is felt behind the angle of the jaw, or the temporal artery is felt over the mastoid process? The answer is the facial artery, felt where it crosses the lower border of the jaw in front of the masseter.

Question 9600. A described angiogram of the hand shows two arches, one deep in the palm and one nearer the surface, joined by small vessels, with the radial artery entering the palm between the first two metacarpals. Which arch lies nearer the skin, and which artery completes it from the inner side? The answer is the superficial palmar arch, completed by the ulnar artery.

To summarize, the examination of the body rests on inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, applied in that order except in the abdomen, where auscultation precedes palpation so that the bowel sounds are not disturbed. The surface landmarks carry the deeper anatomy: the sternal angle marks the second rib, the iliac crest the fourth lumbar vertebra, the umbilicus the third, and the midclavicular line the apex beat in the fifth intercostal space. Percussion separates the dull note of the liver and the spleen from the tympanitic note of the stomach. The neurovascular examination adds the pulses at the wrist, the foot and the groin, and the nerves that lie against bone, together with the reflex arcs and the dermatomes. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 97 — Neurovascular Examination

This chapter joins two subjects that meet at the bedside: the examination that maps nerves and vessels onto the living body, and the bony injuries that so often damage them. The first half covers the pulses, the named nerves, the reflexes and the areas of skin a clinician tests by hand, and the second half covers the fractures and dislocations of the limbs, the girdles and the spine. It holds one hundred questions, and every one answers immediately, then gives the reason. This is educational material, and it does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 9601. Which artery is felt on the thumb side of the front of the wrist, where the pulse is usually taken? The answer is the radial artery. It lies just lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis, covered only by skin and fascia. The ulnar artery lies on the little finger side and is harder to feel.

Question 9602. Which vessel is pressed against the shaft of the humerus to control bleeding from a wound of the upper limb: the axillary artery, the brachial artery, the radial artery, or the ulnar artery? The answer is the brachial artery, which runs down the medial side of the arm close to the bone. The radial and the ulnar arteries lie below the elbow.

Question 9603. A described recording shows a strong pulse behind the medial malleolus and a weaker one on the top of the foot. Which vessels are these? The answer is the posterior tibial artery behind the malleolus and the dorsalis pedis artery on the top of the foot, which lies beside the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The dorsalis pedis pulse is absent in some healthy people.

Question 9604. Which nerve lies in a shallow groove behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where a knock sends tingling into the little finger? The answer is the ulnar nerve. Only skin and fascia cover it there, which is why the spot is called the funny bone. The tingling is felt in the little finger and half of the ring finger.

Question 9605. Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum, and which muscles of the thumb does it supply? The answer is the median nerve, which supplies the thenar muscles that move the thumb away from the palm and oppose it. It also supplies the first two lumbricals. The ulnar nerve enters the hand outside the tunnel.

Question 9606. Which nerve supplies the deltoid muscle and the skin over the lower shoulder: the axillary nerve, the radial nerve, the suprascapular nerve, or the musculocutaneous nerve? The answer is the axillary nerve, which winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and also supplies the teres minor. The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and the infraspinatus.

Question 9607. A constructed illustration: after a described fracture of the middle of the humerus, the wrist hangs, the fingers cannot be straightened, and the back of the hand is numb. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the radial nerve, which lies in the spiral groove against the bone and supplies the muscles that straighten the wrist and the fingers.

Question 9608. True or false: the ankle reflex tests the first sacral segment of the spinal cord. The answer is true. Tapping the tendon behind the ankle makes the calf muscles contract, and the impulse travels through the tibial nerve and the first sacral root. Loss of that reflex is an early sign of pressure on the root.

Question 9609. Which nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it can be felt as a firm cord just under the skin? The answer is the common fibular nerve. It divides into superficial and deep branches that supply the outer side and the front of the leg. Injury there causes a foot drop.

Question 9610. A described dissection of the back of the knee shows a nerve on the medial side, another nerve on the lateral side, and a large vessel deepest of all. Which three structures are shown in that order? The answer is the tibial nerve medially, the common fibular nerve laterally and the popliteal artery deepest, with the popliteal vein between the artery and the nerves.

Question 9611. Which of these structures lies deepest in the back of the knee: the tibial nerve, the popliteal artery, the small saphenous vein, or the common fibular nerve? The answer is the popliteal artery, which lies against the bone and the back of the joint. The two nerves lie nearer the surface, and the small saphenous vein runs in the fat under the skin.

Question 9612. Which structure lies immediately behind the medial malleolus, in company with the tibial nerve and the tendons of the deep muscles of the leg? The answer is the posterior tibial artery. It lies between the tendon of the flexor digitorum longus and the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus. The order from the medial side is tendon, tendon, artery, nerve, tendon.

Question 9613. A constructed illustration: a person describes tingling in the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger that wakes them at night, while the little finger is spared. Which nerve is compressed, and where? The answer is the median nerve, at the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. The little finger is spared because the ulnar nerve supplies it.

Question 9614. Which nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle and supplies the quadriceps muscle? The answer is the femoral nerve, which enters the thigh behind the inguinal ligament and also carries feeling from the front of the thigh. One of its branches, the saphenous nerve, runs down the medial side of the leg.

Question 9615. Which nerve carries the knee reflex: the femoral nerve, the sciatic nerve, the obturator nerve, or the tibial nerve? The answer is the femoral nerve, which carries the impulse through the third and fourth lumbar segments. Tapping the tendon below the kneecap makes the quadriceps contract. The ankle reflex travels through the tibial nerve instead.

Question 9616. Name the two nerves that supply the small muscles of the hand, and say which fingers each one serves. The answer is the median nerve and the ulnar nerve. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and the first two lumbricals and carries feeling from the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger and half of the ring finger, while the ulnar nerve supplies the rest.

Question 9617. A described dissection of the front of the forearm shows one nerve running down the middle between the two groups of muscles and another running down the medial side beside an artery. Which nerves are shown? The answer is the median nerve in the middle and the ulnar nerve medially, with the ulnar artery beside it. The median nerve lies deep to the flexor carpi radialis.

Question 9618. A constructed illustration: a deep wound over the front of the elbow divides one nerve, and the person can no longer bring the tips of the thumb and the index finger together. Which nerve is divided? The answer is the median nerve, through its anterior interosseous branch, which supplies the flexor pollicis longus and part of the flexor digitorum profundus.

Question 9619. Which nerve leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and runs down the back of the thigh? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It is the largest nerve in the body, and it divides into the tibial and the common fibular nerves. It supplies the muscles of the back of the thigh before that division.

Question 9620. Which of these pairs belongs together: the biceps reflex with the radial nerve, the triceps reflex with the musculocutaneous nerve, the knee reflex with the femoral nerve, or the ankle reflex with the obturator nerve? The answer is the knee reflex with the femoral nerve. The biceps reflex runs through the musculocutaneous nerve and the triceps reflex through the radial nerve.

Question 9621. Which nerve supplies the diaphragm: the phrenic nerve, the vagus nerve, an intercostal nerve, or the sympathetic trunk? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which arises from the third, fourth and fifth cervical segments and runs down through the neck and the chest. The intercostal nerves supply the muscles between the ribs.

Question 9622. In a described cross section of the middle of the arm, the humerus lies at the center with a nerve in a groove on its back and the main artery on its medial side. Which nerve and which artery are those? The answer is the radial nerve in the spiral groove and the brachial artery medial to the bone. The nerve passes between the two heads of the triceps.

Question 9623. Which nerve lies immediately medial to the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, after crossing in front of the artery higher in the arm? The answer is the median nerve, which enters the forearm between the two heads of the pronator teres. The brachial artery divides into the radial and the ulnar arteries just below that point.

Question 9624. Which nerve supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the sciatic nerve, or the inferior gluteal nerve? The answer is the obturator nerve, which comes from the second, third and fourth lumbar segments and leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal. It also carries feeling from the inner side of the thigh.

Question 9625. Which of these muscles is supplied by the ulnar nerve: the abductor pollicis brevis, the opponens pollicis, the first dorsal interosseous, or the superficial head of the flexor pollicis brevis? The answer is the first dorsal interosseous. The ulnar nerve supplies most of the small muscles of the hand, while the thenar muscles are supplied mainly by the median nerve.

Question 9626. A described study of the back of the leg shows a nerve lying against the tibia deep to the soleus muscle, alongside the posterior tibial vessels. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the tibial nerve, which supplies the muscles of the back of the leg. It passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

Question 9627. A constructed illustration: a wound on the little finger side of the wrist divides one nerve, and the person can no longer grip a sheet of paper between the fingers.
