Question 10053. Which small gland is seen as a thin triangular or Y-shaped structure sitting on the upper pole of each kidney? The answer is the adrenal gland. The right one lies between the liver and the upper pole of the right kidney, and the left one lies medial to the upper pole of the left kidney. Both lie within the renal fascia.

Question 10054. A constructed illustration: a scan shows a small bright stone in the line of the ureter just below the kidney, with the tract above it wider than on the other side. Which structure is obstructed, and what does the appearance above it show? The answer is the ureter, and the widening shows that urine is being held back. The collecting system of that kidney is fuller than normal.

Question 10055. Which statement about the space behind the peritoneum is correct: the kidneys, the adrenal glands, the aorta and the inferior vena cava lie behind it, the stomach and the spleen lie behind it, the small bowel lies behind it, or the bladder lies behind it? The answer is that the kidneys, the adrenal glands and the great vessels lie behind the peritoneum, as do the pancreas, the duodenum and the ascending and descending colon.

Question 10056. Which structure lies immediately in front of the right kidney at the level of the second lumbar vertebra: the duodenum, the spleen, the pancreas, or the sigmoid colon? The answer is the duodenum. It lies against the medial part of the right kidney, and the right colic flexure lies in front of the lower lateral part.

Question 10057. A described section of the upper abdomen shows a pear-shaped sac of fluid with nearly the density of water, tucked under the right lobe of the liver. Which organ is described? The answer is the gallbladder. It lies against the under-surface of the liver and holds bile, which is close to water in density. Concentrated bile looks denser and more like soft tissue.

Question 10058. True or false: without contrast, the wall of the aorta and the blood inside it cannot be told apart, because both have the density of soft tissue. The answer is true. Blood and the wall of the vessel have almost the same density, so they appear as one gray ring. After contrast the column of blood becomes bright.

Question 10059. Which structure lies most anteriorly in the female pelvis: the urinary bladder, the uterus, the rectum, or the sacrum? The answer is the urinary bladder. It lies behind the pubic symphysis, with the uterus and the vagina behind it and the rectum behind those. The sacrum forms the back wall of the pelvis.

Question 10060. Which bone forms the roof of the socket of the hip joint, seen as a thick arch of bone over the head of the femur? The answer is the ilium. All three bones join in the socket, but the ilium forms its roof and the ischium its back. The pubis forms the front and the lower part.

Question 10061. A constructed illustration: a scan shows the aorta and the inferior vena cava lying together in front of the spine with a large collection of blood around them, and the organs in front are pushed forward. Which space is described, and what else lies in it? The answer is the space behind the peritoneum. It also holds the kidneys, the adrenal glands, the pancreas, the duodenum and the ascending and descending colon.

Question 10062. Which statement about the psoas major muscle is correct: it runs from the sides of the lumbar vertebrae downward and outward to the lesser trochanter, it lies behind the vertebral bodies, it lies medial to the aorta at every level, or it lies inside the peritoneal cavity? The answer is that it runs to the lesser trochanter. It is a flexor of the hip, and it lies lateral to the great vessels.

Question 10063. Which two veins join behind the neck of the pancreas, and which vessel do they form? The answer is the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein, which form the portal vein. The portal vein then runs upward and to the right behind the first part of the duodenum to reach the liver.

Question 10064. A described image shows a part of the bowel crossing in front of the great vessels from the left side toward the right, with sacculations along its wall and a wider caliber than the rest of the bowel. Which part is described? The answer is the transverse colon. Its haustral folds give it a segmented outline. The small bowel has more numerous and thinner folds.

Question 10065. Which pair of muscles is seen on a section of the abdomen as two flat bands on either side of the midline just beneath the skin, divided by a dark line? The answer is the rectus abdominis muscles, separated by the linea alba. They lie within the rectus sheath, in front of the peritoneum, with fat of the abdominal wall in front of them.

Question 10066. Which of these pairs belongs together: the liver with the right upper quadrant, the spleen with the right upper quadrant, the appendix with the left upper quadrant, or the stomach with the right iliac fossa? The answer is the liver with the right upper quadrant. The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant, and the appendix lies in the right iliac fossa.

Question 10067. In the midline of the abdomen, which order of structures runs from the front to the back: skin, rectus abdominis, small bowel, aorta, vertebral body; skin, aorta, small bowel, vertebral body, rectus abdominis; skin, small bowel, rectus abdominis, aorta, vertebral body; or skin, vertebral body, aorta, small bowel, rectus abdominis? The answer is skin, rectus abdominis, small bowel, aorta, vertebral body. The muscles lie in front and the great vessels against the spine.

Question 10068. A described image shows a long vein crossing in front of the aorta from left to right to reach the inferior vena cava, with an artery passing in front of that vein. Which vein and which artery are described? The answer is the left renal vein and the superior mesenteric artery. The vein drains the left kidney across the midline, and the artery crosses in front of it.

Question 10069. A constructed illustration: after a fall, a scan shows a break through the neck of the femur with the head held in the socket. Which structure within the bone is at risk, and what does its loss threaten? The answer is the blood supply running along the neck in the fold of the capsule. If it is torn, the head may lose its blood supply and die.

Question 10070. Below the inguinal ligament, which structure lies immediately lateral to the femoral vein: the femoral artery, the femoral nerve, the pubic tubercle, or the great saphenous vein? The answer is the femoral artery. From lateral to medial the order is the nerve, the artery, the vein, and the lymph nodes. The nerve lies outside the sheath.

Question 10071. Which tendon lies closest to the bone behind the medial malleolus of the ankle, with the artery and the nerve behind it? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior. From the bone outward the order is the tibialis posterior, the flexor digitorum longus, the artery, the nerve, and the flexor hallucis longus. The tendon supports the arch of the foot.

Question 10072. A section of the thigh shows the skin in front, the femur in the middle, and a large mass of muscle behind it. In which direction must the listener move to pass from the skin to the femur, and which plane lies at right angles to that direction? The answer is backward, that is posteriorly, and the coronal plane lies at right angles to it.

Question 10073. Why are the bones of the skull base hard to examine on a plain radiograph but easy to see on a computed tomography scan? The answer is that the scan shows a section in which the structures above and below it do not overlap. On a radiograph all the layers lie one over another, so the base is hidden by everything in front of it.

Question 10074. A described image of the hand shows a row of five long bones between the small bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Which bones are described? The answer is the metacarpal bones. They form the framework of the palm, and each one carries a finger. The thumb has two phalanges and the other fingers have three.

Question 10075. Which statement about the appearance of normal fat is correct: it is darker than muscle and brighter than air, it is brighter than bone, it has the same density as water, or it has the same density as muscle? The answer is that it is darker than muscle and brighter than air. Fat lies just below water on the scale, which is why it outlines organs so clearly.

Question 10076. Which part of a vertebra is the bony arch behind the body that encloses the spinal canal? The answer is the vertebral arch, whose pedicles and laminae form it.

Question 10077. Which structure is a cushion between two vertebral bodies, with a darker center and an outer ring of fibers? The answer is the intervertebral disc, whose center is the nucleus pulposus.

Question 10078. In a growing child, which structure is a dark band across the end of a long bone, between the shaft and the bony cap? The answer is the growth plate, which is cartilage and closes with age.

Question 10079. Which structure in the lower neck is a complete ring of cartilage, with a narrow front and a broad back, below the thyroid cartilage? The answer is the cricoid cartilage.

Question 10080. Which muscle forms a sling from the pubis to the coccyx and separates the pelvic cavity from the perineum: the levator ani, the obturator internus, the piriformis, or the gluteus maximus? The answer is the levator ani.

Question 10081. About a minute after contrast is given into a vein, which structures are brightest: the aorta, the portal vein and the liver, the ureters and the bladder, or the bones? The answer is the portal vein and the liver.

Question 10082. Which substance is the zero point of the density scale of a computed tomography image: air, fat, water, or cortical bone? The answer is water. Air lies far below it, fat just below.

Question 10083. Which of these lies in the posterior mediastinum, in front of the vertebral column: the thymus, the esophagus, the ascending aorta, or the pulmonary trunk? The answer is the esophagus. The others lie in the middle mediastinum.

Question 10084. A small nodule is seen on one section but not above or below it. Which effect explains this: partial volume averaging, contrast, beam hardening, or motion? The answer is partial volume averaging, because the nodule fills only part of that section.

Question 10085. A scan of a restless person shows a doubled outline of the diaphragm and the aorta. Which artifact is this: motion, beam hardening, partial volume averaging, or metal streak? The answer is motion, because the structure moved during the scan.

Question 10086. Which structure is a small joint between the articular processes of two adjacent vertebrae, behind the spinal canal? The answer is the facet joint, whose enlargement can narrow the canal.

Question 10087. On a computed tomography image, which statement about muscle and tendon is correct: both look the same, muscle is much brighter, tendon is as dense as bone, or both are darker than fat? The answer is that both look the same.

Question 10088. On a section through the larynx, which structures lie on either side of the airway: the vocal cords, the tonsils, the parotid glands, or the longus colli muscles? The answer is the vocal cords, with the muscles that move them.

Question 10089. Which structure is a fan of fat and vessels that suspends the small bowel from the posterior abdominal wall? The answer is the mesentery, which carries the vessels of the small bowel.

Question 10090. Why do the bones of a newborn look less bright than those of an adult: they hold less mineral, they hold more air, thicker muscle covers them, or they lie nearer the scanner? The answer is that they hold less mineral.

Question 10091. A described image of a young child shows a soft tissue mass in the upper chest, with the trachea and the great vessels behind it. Which structure is described? The answer is the thymus, which shrinks and is replaced by fat with age.

Question 10092. A described section through the neck shows a ring of bone around a dark canal, a gray cord within it, and small joints behind. Which structures are described? The answer is a cervical vertebra, the spinal cord, and the facet joints.

Question 10093. A described image shows curved lines crossing the abdomen that follow no organ boundary and change position from one section to the next. What do they represent? The answer is a reconstruction artifact.

Question 10094. True or false: the bright and dark streaks that radiate from a metal implant are an artifact of the scan rather than a structure of the body. The answer is true, because dense metal absorbs the beam unevenly.

Question 10095. True or false: the open sutures of a young child's skull appear as dark lines on a computed tomography scan. The answer is true, because they are fibrous and not yet ossified.

Question 10096. Which of these pairs belongs together: the arterial phase with the aorta, the portal venous phase with the gallbladder, the delayed phase with the lung, or the unenhanced phase with the great vessels? The answer is the arterial phase with the aorta.

Question 10097. Which of these pairs belongs together: beam hardening with dark bands between two dense bones, motion with a doubled edge of a still organ, partial volume with a sharp edge, or metal with a smooth density? The answer is beam hardening with dark bands between two dense bones.

Question 10098. Which canal lies on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa, medial to the obturator internus muscle, and carries the internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve? The answer is the pudendal canal.

Question 10099. A constructed illustration: a child swallows a coin, and on the frontal image it lies flat, high in the chest. In which passage does it lie? The answer is the esophagus. A coin in the trachea stands on edge.

Question 10100. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the left lower ribs, a scan shows free fluid around the spleen and a broken tenth rib. Which organ is the source of the fluid? The answer is the spleen, with blood in the peritoneal cavity.

To summarize, a computed tomography image is a map of density, running from air at the black end, through fat and water, to muscle and bone at the white end. Window settings decide which tissues spread across the gray shades, and the plane of the section decides which structures appear together. Each region has its landmarks: the liver above the lower right kidney, the pancreas in front of the great vessels, the aorta to the left of the midline with the inferior vena cava to its right, and the bladder in front of the rectum. Contrast brightens the vessels, then the liver and the portal vein, and last the collecting systems, while artifacts from metal, motion, beam hardening, and partial volume can imitate disease. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 102 — MRI Anatomy

This chapter reads the magnetic resonance image as a map of the body, beginning with the signal that fat, fluid, muscle and bone each give, and then following that contrast through the brain, the head and neck, the spine, the joints, the chest, the abdomen and the pelvis. Magnetic resonance imaging, known as MRI, is described here as anatomy only, because nothing can be shown and every sequence and every section is spoken in words. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10101. On a T2-weighted image, which tissue gives the brightest signal: subcutaneous fat, cerebrospinal fluid, cortical bone, or skeletal muscle? The answer is cerebrospinal fluid. Free water has a long relaxation time, so the fluid in the ventricles and around the cord shines. Fat is at its brightest on a T1-weighted image.

Question 10102. On a T1-weighted image, which tissue is brighter than every other soft tissue and also fills the marrow of the long bones? The answer is fat. It shortens the T1 relaxation time, so it returns the strongest signal of all. Subcutaneous fat and yellow marrow are the brightest things on the image.

Question 10103. A described image of the head shows the fluid in the lateral ventricles as dark spaces while the fat beneath the scalp is bright. Which sequence produced it? The answer is a T1-weighted sequence. On it fat is bright and water is dark, the reverse of a T2-weighted image. Gray and white matter lie between the two extremes.

Question 10104. Which tissue appears black on both a T1-weighted and a T2-weighted image and forms the hard outer shell of a long bone? The answer is cortical bone. Dense bone holds very little free water, so it returns almost no signal on either sequence. The marrow inside the bone is bright, which is why the outline of a bone is drawn by its marrow.

Question 10105. On a T1-weighted image of the chest, which structure appears as a dark circle beside the vertebral column: the aorta, the thymus, a lymph node, or the esophagus? The answer is the aorta. In a spin echo sequence the flowing blood leaves the slice before it can be imaged, so the lumen gives no signal. The wall of the vessel and the fat around it are seen instead.

Question 10106. True or false: on a T2-weighted image the edema that collects in injured tissue is brighter than the normal muscle around it. The answer is true. Edema is free water with a long relaxation time, so it shines against the darker muscle. Suppressing the fat signal makes that brightness even easier to see.

Question 10107. After a gadolinium-containing contrast agent is given, which normal structure improves in signal because it has no blood-brain barrier: the pituitary gland, the cortical bone, the subcutaneous fat, or the vitreous humor? The answer is the pituitary gland. Its capillaries are fenestrated, so contrast leaks into the gland and into the infundibulum above it. Fat is bright even without contrast.

Question 10108. On a T1-weighted image through the upper abdomen, which structure forms a bright band around the kidney: the perirenal fat, the renal cortex, the psoas muscle, or the pancreas? The answer is the perirenal fat. Fat is the brightest tissue on a T1-weighted image. The cortex is slightly brighter than the medulla inside it, and the psoas and the pancreas are intermediate gray.

Question 10109. Which of these four pairs belongs together: T1-weighted with bright fat, T1-weighted with bright cerebrospinal fluid, T2-weighted with dark fluid, or fat-suppressed T2 with bright fat? The answer is T1-weighted with bright fat. Cerebrospinal fluid is dark on a T1-weighted image, it is bright rather than dark on T2, and suppressing the fat removes the fat signal.

Question 10110. Name two materials that appear black on both a T1-weighted and a T2-weighted image because they hold almost no water. The answer is cortical bone and air. Both contain very few mobile protons, so neither returns a signal. Tendons and ligaments look much the same, though they may show a faint signal.

Question 10111. On a T2-weighted image of the brain, which tissue is brighter, the gray matter of the cortex or the white matter beneath it? The answer is the gray matter. It holds more free water than the myelin-rich white matter, so it shines more brightly on this sequence. On a T1-weighted image the two reverse.

Question 10112. On a T1-weighted image of the brain, which tissue is brightest: the white matter, the gray matter, the cerebrospinal fluid, or the cortical bone of the skull? The answer is the white matter. Its myelin and its lipids shorten T1, so it outshines the gray matter. The fluid and the cortical bone are both dark.

Question 10113. A described midsagittal image shows a thick curved band of white matter arching above the lateral ventricle, thin in the middle and swelling at both ends. Which structure is shown? The answer is the corpus callosum. Its front end is the genu and its back end the splenium, and it joins the two hemispheres across the midline.

Question 10114. Which paired tract of white matter lies beneath the corpus callosum, above the thalamus, and ends in the mammillary body behind the infundibulum? The answer is the fornix. It carries fibers from the hippocampus toward the hypothalamus. On a midline image it is the thinner band below the corpus callosum.

Question 10115. On an axial image through the frontal horns, which thin structure lies between the two lateral ventricles: the septum pellucidum, the fornix, the corpus callosum, or the third ventricle? The answer is the septum pellucidum. It is a double membrane stretched between the corpus callosum above and the fornix below.

Question 10116. On an axial image at the level of the thalamus, which band of white matter separates the thalamus from the lentiform nucleus: the internal capsule, the external capsule, the corpus callosum, or the cingulum? The answer is the internal capsule. Its posterior limb lies between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus and carries the corticospinal fibers.

Question 10117. A constructed illustration: a person suddenly cannot move the right arm or the right side of the face, and the described image shows a small bright area in the left internal capsule on a diffusion-weighted study. Which tract is interrupted? The answer is the corticospinal tract. Its fibers cross in the medulla, so a lesion on the left weakens the right side.

Question 10118. True or false: on a T2-weighted image the gray matter of the cortex is brighter than the white matter beneath it. The answer is true. Gray matter holds more free water and so has a longer T2 relaxation time. On a T1-weighted image the white matter is the brighter of the two.

Question 10119. On an axial image, which structure lies in the depth of the sylvian fissure, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula: the insula, the amygdala, the hippocampus, or the caudate nucleus? The answer is the insula. It is hidden beneath the opercula, and the middle cerebral artery runs along its surface.

Question 10120. A described sagittal image shows a deep sulcus running downward and forward across the convexity, with a thicker gyrus in front of it and a thinner gyrus behind. Which sulcus is shown, and which gyri border it? The answer is the central sulcus, with the precentral gyrus in front and the postcentral gyrus behind. The precentral gyrus is the motor strip.

Question 10121. A described axial image shows a rounded mass of gray matter bulging into the lateral wall of the frontal horn of a lateral ventricle. Which structure is it? The answer is the head of the caudate nucleus. It lies beside the ventricle and above the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

Question 10122. On a T2-weighted image of the basal ganglia, which part is darker than the putamen beside it: the globus pallidus, the caudate nucleus, the thalamus, or the claustrum? The answer is the globus pallidus. It collects iron, which shortens the T2 relaxation time and darkens the tissue. The putamen also darkens with age.

Question 10123. A described coronal image shows two egg-shaped masses of gray matter on either side of a narrow midline slit, with a rounded mass below each one at the base of the brain. Which structures are shown? The answer is the two thalami beside the third ventricle, with the cerebral peduncles below them. The slit between the thalami is the third ventricle.

Question 10124. On an axial image at the level of the pons, which space lies immediately behind the pons and in front of the cerebellum: the fourth ventricle, the third ventricle, the interpeduncular cistern, or a lateral ventricle? The answer is the fourth ventricle. It is a diamond-shaped space behind the brainstem and below the cerebellum.

Question 10125. A described T2-weighted image at the level of the midbrain shows two thick pillars of white matter in front of a small central channel, with a dark band behind each pillar. What are the pillars, and what is the channel? The answer is the cerebral peduncles in front and the cerebral aqueduct behind. The dark band is the substantia nigra, darkened by iron.

Question 10126. A described axial image shows a broad belly of tissue in the midline of the brainstem with a small channel behind it, flanked by two wing-like masses of the cerebellum. Which level is shown? The answer is the pons. Its basis bulges forward, and the middle cerebellar peduncles run from its sides into the cerebellar hemispheres.

Question 10127. A single described section shows the corpus callosum from the rostrum in front to the splenium behind, the third ventricle below it, and the brainstem cut lengthwise. In which plane was the section taken? The answer is the midsagittal plane. Only a section in the midline shows the whole callosum from end to end and the brainstem in profile.

Question 10128. A constructed illustration: a small mass at the pineal region compresses the narrow channel between the midbrain and the cerebellum, and the described images show enlarged lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth. Which channel is obstructed? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct. It connects the third ventricle above to the fourth below, so the fluid backs up above it.

Question 10129. On a coronal T2-weighted image, which elongated structure of gray matter lies in the medial part of the temporal lobe, below the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle? The answer is the hippocampus. It lies medial to the temporal horn and behind the amygdala, and it is best seen in a plane along its length.

Question 10130. Which of these connects the pons to the cerebellar hemisphere, is the largest of the cerebellar peduncles, and forms part of the lateral wall of the fourth ventricle: the superior, the middle, the inferior, or the cerebral peduncle? The answer is the middle cerebellar peduncle. It carries fibers from the pontine nuclei across to the opposite hemisphere.

Question 10131. On an axial image of the orbit, which structure runs in the middle of the cone of eye muscles, from the back of the eye to the apex of the orbit? The answer is the optic nerve. The medial and the lateral rectus muscles lie on either side of it, and it passes through the optic canal to reach the chiasm.

Question 10132. On a T2-weighted image of the eye, which of these gives the brightest signal: the vitreous humor, the lens, the sclera, or the eye muscle? The answer is the vitreous humor. It is almost all water, so it shines on a T2-weighted image. The lens and the sclera are fibrous and dark, and the muscles are intermediate gray.

Question 10133. A described sagittal image shows a small rounded gland sitting in a bony cup behind a sinus, joined to the brain above by a thin stalk. Which structure is shown? The answer is the pituitary gland in the sella turcica. Its posterior lobe is bright on T1-weighted images, and the stalk above it is the infundibulum.

Question 10134. On an axial image through the sella, which venous channel lies immediately lateral to the pituitary gland and beside the internal carotid artery: the cavernous sinus, the superior sagittal sinus, the straight sinus, or the transverse sinus? The answer is the cavernous sinus. The carotid artery and the sixth cranial nerve pass through it.

Question 10135. A constructed illustration: a described image shows a rounded mass rising out of the sella and pressing on the structure that crosses above it, and the person has lost the outer half of each visual field. Which structure is compressed? The answer is the optic chiasm. Its crossing fibers come from the nasal retina of each eye.

Question 10136. In the internal acoustic meatus, which nerve occupies the anterior superior quadrant: the facial nerve, the cochlear nerve, the superior vestibular nerve, or the inferior vestibular nerve? The answer is the facial nerve. The cochlear nerve lies below it in front, and the two vestibular nerves lie behind them both.

Question 10137. In a described image, the parotid gland is divided into a superficial and a deep part by a plane that contains the facial nerve. Which vein runs in that same plane and marks the division? The answer is the retromandibular vein. It lies just behind the ramus of the mandible and deep to the gland.

Question 10138. On an axial image of the neck, the internal jugular vein lies lateral to which structure: the internal carotid artery, the trachea, the thyroid gland, or the esophagus? The answer is the internal carotid artery. The vein is the more lateral of the two, and the vagus nerve lies behind and between them.

Question 10139. A described sagittal image through the side of the head shows a small fibrous disc between the head of the mandible and the articular surface above it, dividing the joint into two compartments. Which joint is shown? The answer is the temporomandibular joint. Its disc moves forward with the condyle when the mouth opens.

Question 10140. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the pituitary gland with the sella turcica, the pineal gland with the sella turcica, the pituitary gland with the posterior cranial fossa, or the pineal gland with the orbit? The answer is the pituitary gland with the sella turcica. The pineal gland lies above the midbrain, behind the third ventricle.

Question 10141. On a T2-weighted sagittal image of the spine, which part of the intervertebral disc is bright: the nucleus pulposus, the annulus fibrosus, the vertebral endplate, or the ligamentum flavum? The answer is the nucleus pulposus. It is rich in water and shines on a T2-weighted image, while the fibrous ring around it stays dark.

Question 10142. On an axial image through the first cervical vertebra, which dark band lies immediately behind the dens and holds it against the front of the bony ring? The answer is the transverse ligament of the atlas. It is the strongest part of the cruciform ligament, and it keeps the dens from pressing on the spinal cord.

Question 10143. A described sagittal image shows the lower part of the cerebellum with two rounded tonsils above a bony ring, through which the spinal cord and its coverings pass downward. Which level is shown? The answer is the foramen magnum. The tonsils lie just above it, and the medulla becomes the spinal cord as it passes through.

Question 10144. The vertebral artery ascends through a series of small bony rings beside the cervical vertebral bodies. From which vertebra upward do those rings carry the artery: the first cervical, the third cervical, the fourth cervical, or the sixth cervical? The answer is the sixth cervical vertebra. The artery enters the transverse foramen there and climbs to the atlas.

Question 10145. A constructed illustration: a described sagittal image shows disc material bulging backward and to the left at the lowest lumbar level, and the person has pain shooting down the left leg. Which structure is compressed? The answer is the traversing nerve root in the lateral recess, which the disc presses as the root travels past that level toward its foramen.

Question 10146. True or false: on a T2-weighted image the cerebrospinal fluid around the spinal cord is bright and the cord itself is darker. The answer is true. Fluid is bright on T2, while the cord is intermediate gray, so the fluid outlines it. The nerve roots cross that bright space on their way out.

Question 10147. In an adult, at which vertebral level does the tapered lower end of the spinal cord usually lie: the first or second lumbar vertebra, the fifth lumbar vertebra, the twelfth thoracic vertebra, or the first sacral vertebra? The answer is the first or second lumbar vertebra. Below it the canal holds the cauda equina, a bundle of roots.

Question 10148. On an axial T2-weighted image of the spine, which structure forms a dark band joining the laminae behind the spinal canal: the ligamentum flavum, the posterior longitudinal ligament, the anterior longitudinal ligament, or the interspinous ligament? The answer is the ligamentum flavum. It is elastic fibrous tissue, dark on every sequence, and it lies behind the canal.

Question 10149. Which statement about the intervertebral disc on a T2-weighted image is correct: the nucleus pulposus loses its bright signal with age, the nucleus pulposus becomes brighter with age, the annulus fibrosus becomes bright with age, or the disc gives no signal at any age? The answer is that the nucleus loses its bright signal with age. It dries out, and the darkening comes before any bulge appears.

Question 10150. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the nucleus pulposus with a bright signal on T2, the annulus fibrosus with a bright signal on T2, cortical bone with a bright signal on T1, or cerebrospinal fluid with a bright signal on T1? The answer is the nucleus pulposus with a bright signal on T2. The other three are dark on the sequence named.

Question 10151. On a T1-weighted sagittal image of the lumbar spine, which tissue fills the space between the thecal sac and the bony canal and appears bright? The answer is the epidural fat. Fat is bright on a T1-weighted image, so it outlines the dark thecal sac from behind. Inside the sac the cerebrospinal fluid is dark on this sequence.

Question 10152. Which structure lies within the thecal sac below the lower end of the spinal cord: the cauda equina, the conus medullaris, the ligamentum flavum, or the filum terminale alone? The answer is the cauda equina. It is a bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots descending to their openings, and it floats in the cerebrospinal fluid.

Question 10153. A described T2-weighted image shows a bright column of fluid in the lower canal, within which a bundle of dark rounded strands hangs downward like a horse's tail. Which level is this, and what are the strands? The answer is the lower lumbar canal, and the strands are the cauda equina, descending from the end of the cord.

Question 10154. At the level of a lumbar disc, which part of the canal does the traversing nerve root occupy before it enters its foramen: the lateral recess, the central canal, the anterior epidural space, or the posterior epidural space? The answer is the lateral recess. It lies between the disc in front and the facet joint behind.

Question 10155. A constructed illustration: a described image shows a large central disc bulge at a thoracic level pressing the cord against the bone behind it, and the person has stiffness in both legs with difficulty walking. Which structure is compressed? The answer is the spinal cord within the vertebral canal. In the thoracic region the canal is narrow, so a central bulge reaches the cord quickly.

Question 10156. True or false: the ligamentum flavum lies in front of the spinal cord and separates it from the vertebral bodies. The answer is false. The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae behind the canal, so it lies behind the cord. The posterior longitudinal ligament is the one in front of the cord.

Question 10157. Which structure lies in the canal immediately in front of the thecal sac, separating it from the back of the vertebral bodies: the posterior longitudinal ligament, the ligamentum flavum, the interspinous ligament, or the supraspinous ligament? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It runs down the back of the vertebral bodies inside the canal, and a disc meets it as it bulges backward.

Question 10158. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the conus medullaris with the tapered end of the cord, the conus medullaris with the roots below it, the filum terminale with the upper end of the cord, or the cauda equina with the tapered end of the cord? The answer is the conus medullaris with the tapered end of the cord. The roots below it are the cauda equina.

Question 10159. In a described image of the lower back, a thin strand continues downward through the fused sacral segments after the thecal sac has ended. Which structure is it? The answer is the filum terminale, a strand of pia mater that anchors the cord to the coccyx. It lies in the sacral canal and returns almost no signal.

Question 10160. Name the two spaces that surround the spinal cord within the vertebral canal, one outside the dura and one inside the arachnoid. The answer is the epidural space and the subarachnoid space. The epidural space holds fat and veins, and the subarachnoid space holds cerebrospinal fluid. The dura and the arachnoid lie between them.

Question 10161. A described coronal image of the shoulder shows a dark band running from the top of the scapula across the top of the humeral head to end on the greater tubercle. Which structure is it? The answer is the tendon of supraspinatus. It passes beneath the acromion, where the tendon is most often torn.

Question 10162. Which of these muscles forms part of the rotator cuff of the shoulder: the teres major, the supraspinatus, the deltoid, or the latissimus dorsi? The answer is the supraspinatus. The supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor and the subscapularis blend with the capsule, while the others do not.

Question 10163. A described axial image of the shoulder shows a dark triangular rim attached to the edge of the shallow socket of the scapula, deepening it around the head of the humerus. Which structure is shown? The answer is the glenoid labrum. It is fibrous and dark on every sequence, and a tear shows as a bright line within it.

Question 10164. On an axial image of the upper end of the humerus, which structure lies in the groove between the greater and the lesser tubercle: the tendon of the long head of the biceps, the tendon of the short head of the biceps, the axillary nerve, or the coracohumeral ligament? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps, held in the groove by the transverse humeral ligament.

Question 10165. A constructed illustration: a person cannot begin to lift the arm sideways, and the described T2-weighted image shows a bright line running through the dark tendon above the humeral head. Which tendon is torn? The answer is the tendon of supraspinatus. It begins abduction and passes beneath the acromion, where it is most often injured.

Question 10166. True or false: tendons and ligaments appear dark on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images because they contain very little free water. The answer is true. Their collagen holds few mobile protons, so they return almost no signal. A tear brings water into the tissue and turns part of it bright.

Question 10167. At the elbow, which nerve lies in the groove behind the medial epicondyle: the median nerve, the ulnar nerve, the radial nerve, or the musculocutaneous nerve? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It passes through the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, where it can be felt as a rounded cord.

Question 10168. On an axial image of the wrist, which structure lies in the tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum, in the middle of the tendons that surround it? The answer is the median nerve. It lies just beneath the retinaculum, with the flexor tendons around it, while the ulnar nerve and artery lie outside the tunnel.

Question 10169. A described coronal image of the wrist shows a dark triangular plate stretched between the lower end of the ulna and the carpal bones beside it. Which structure is shown? The answer is the triangular fibrocartilage complex. It cushions the ulnar side of the wrist and stays dark on every sequence.

Question 10170. On an axial image through the wrist, which structure connects the scaphoid to the lunate and appears as a dark band between them: the scapholunate ligament, the triangular fibrocartilage, the flexor retinaculum, or the ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist? The answer is the scapholunate ligament. A tear widens the gap and changes the alignment of the carpal bones.

Question 10171. On an image of the knee, which structure lies between the femur and the tibia, is shaped like a C on the medial side, and stays dark on every sequence? The answer is the medial meniscus. The menisci are fibrocartilage, so they return almost no signal unless a tear brings fluid into them.

Question 10172. On a T2-weighted image of the knee, what does a bright line reaching the surface of the dark meniscus indicate: a tear, a normal variant, a blood vessel, or calcification? The answer is a tear. Fluid has entered the substance of the meniscus through the break. Normal meniscal signal does not reach the surface.

Question 10173. A described sagittal image of the knee shows a dark band running from the front of the tibia upward and backward to the inner surface of the lateral condyle of the femur, within the joint. Which ligament is shown? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur.

Question 10174. A fluid-filled swelling appears behind the knee, between the tendon of the medial head of the gastrocnemius and the tendon of the semimembranosus. Which space does it occupy? The answer is the popliteal fossa, and the swelling is a popliteal cyst. It communicates with the joint between those two tendons.

Question 10175. A constructed illustration: a described T1-weighted image shows a curved dark line running through the bright marrow of the femoral head, with a second bright line beside it on the T2-weighted image. What does this pattern indicate? The answer is avascular necrosis of the femoral head. The double line marks the boundary between dead bone and living bone.

Question 10176. Which of these tendons inserts on the back of the calcaneus and is the thickest tendon in the body: the Achilles tendon, the tibialis posterior tendon, the peroneus longus tendon, or the flexor hallucis longus tendon? The answer is the Achilles tendon, formed by the gastrocnemius and the soleus. It stays dark on every sequence.

Question 10177. In a described axial image of the ankle, which dark band runs from the front of the lateral malleolus to the neck of the talus? The answer is the anterior talofibular ligament. It is the most often injured ligament of the ankle, and it is seen best with the foot turned slightly inward.

Question 10178. A described axial image behind the medial malleolus shows a flattened nerve lying between the flexor tendons and the bone, deep to a fibrous band. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the tibial nerve. It passes through the tarsal tunnel with the tendons of tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus.

Question 10179. On a T1-weighted image, a child's vertebral marrow is less bright than an adult's. Which explanation is correct: red marrow holds more water and less fat than yellow marrow, it holds more fat, it contains more iron, or the two marrows look the same on T1? The answer is that red marrow holds more water and less fat, so it is darker. It is replaced by yellow marrow with age.

Question 10180. Which of these four pairs belongs together: the medial meniscus with a C shape, the lateral meniscus with a C shape, the anterior cruciate ligament with the back of the tibia, or the Achilles tendon with the tibia? The answer is the medial meniscus with a C shape. The lateral meniscus is more circular, and the Achilles tendon ends on the calcaneus.

Question 10181. On a magnetic resonance image of the chest, why do the lungs appear almost black: they contain very little water, they contain too much fat, they are filled with flowing blood, or they hold iron? The answer is that they contain very little water, and the many boundaries between air and tissue disturb the field. Only the vessels stand out.

Question 10182. A described axial image of the heart shows a thin dark line running around the myocardium, just outside the bright fat that fills the grooves of the heart. Which structure is that dark line? The answer is the pericardium. It is fibrous and returns almost no signal, so it stands out against the fat on both sides of it.

Question 10183. A described axial image through the heart shows four dark blood-filled chambers, two with thick muscular walls and two with thin walls behind them. Which chambers are shown? The answer is the two ventricles in front, with their thick walls, and the two atria behind them. The chambers look dark because the blood is flowing.

Question 10184. On an axial image at the level of the aortic arch, which structure lies to the right of the trachea and in front of the right main bronchus: the superior vena cava, the descending aorta, the esophagus, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the superior vena cava. The arch of the aorta lies to the left and crosses in front of the trachea.

Question 10185. Which structure ascends through the posterior mediastinum from the abdomen to the root of the neck, lying behind the esophagus and in front of the vertebral column: the thoracic duct, the azygos vein, the phrenic nerve, or the vagus nerve? The answer is the thoracic duct. It carries lymph upward and empties into the left venous angle.

Question 10186. On an axial image of the chest wall, which muscle lies immediately deep to the breast and forms the front wall of the axilla: the pectoralis major, the serratus anterior, the latissimus dorsi, or the trapezius? The answer is the pectoralis major. Its fibers run from the clavicle, the sternum and the ribs to the humerus.

Question 10187. A constructed illustration: a described image shows a small mass in the upper outer part of the breast, close to the fold of the armpit. Toward which group of lymph nodes does lymph from that quadrant normally drain? The answer is the axillary nodes. The upper outer quadrant is the most common site, and its lymph follows the axillary tail.

Question 10188. On an axial image at the level of the left atrium, which structure lies immediately behind the heart: the esophagus, the trachea, the thymus, or the sternum? The answer is the esophagus. It descends behind the left atrium and in front of the descending aorta, while the trachea has already divided above this level.

Question 10189. A described T1-weighted image shows the walls of the heart as intermediate gray while the blood inside the chambers is black. What accounts for the black chambers? The answer is the flow of blood, which carries it out of the slice before it can be imaged. The myocardium itself gives an intermediate signal.

Question 10190. Name the two great veins that enter the right atrium, one from above and one from below. The answer is the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava. The superior vena cava enters from above, and the inferior vena cava enters from below, close to the interatrial septum.

Question 10191. On a T1-weighted image of the upper abdomen, which organ lies under the right dome of the diaphragm and gives a signal slightly brighter than the spleen beside it? The answer is the liver. On a T2-weighted image the relation reverses, and the spleen becomes the brighter of the two.

Question 10192. On an axial image at the level of the pancreas, which vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas and lies in front of the inferior vena cava: the portal vein, the splenic vein, the left renal vein, or the inferior mesenteric vein? The answer is the portal vein. It is formed where the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein.

Question 10193. A described T1-weighted image through a kidney shows an outer rim brighter than the inner columns of tissue, which run toward the fatty center of the organ. Which parts are shown? The answer is the renal cortex, brighter than the medulla, with the fat of the renal sinus in the middle. The cortex wraps around the pyramids.

Question 10194. On an axial image of the upper abdomen, which vessel crosses in front of the aorta and behind the superior mesenteric artery on its way to the inferior vena cava: the left renal vein, the right renal vein, the splenic vein, or the left gonadal vein? The answer is the left renal vein. It drains the left kidney, the left adrenal gland and the left gonadal vein.

Question 10195. A constructed illustration: a described image shows a small rounded mass in an adrenal gland, bright on one T1-weighted image and much darker on a second image taken at a different echo time. Which tissue does the mass contain? The answer is fat, the behavior of a benign adenoma of the adrenal cortex. Water and fat lose signal when their protons are out of phase.

Question 10196. On a T2-weighted image of the prostate, which zone lies at the back of the gland and is the brightest part: the peripheral zone, the central zone, the transition zone, or the anterior fibromuscular stroma? The answer is the peripheral zone. It wraps the gland behind, and most cancers of the prostate begin in it.

Question 10197. On a T2-weighted sagittal image of the pelvis, which organ shows three layers, a bright inner stripe, a thin dark band around it, and a thicker intermediate layer outside? The answer is the uterus. The bright stripe is the endometrium, the dark band is the junctional zone, and the outer layer is the myometrium.

Question 10198. A constructed illustration: a described axial image of the pelvis shows a pear-shaped muscle passing out of the greater sciatic foramen, with a thick nerve lying below it. Which muscle and nerve are shown? The answer is the piriformis muscle and the sciatic nerve, which leaves the pelvis below the muscle and may be pressed against it.

Question 10199. Which muscle forms the greater part of the pelvic diaphragm and separates the pelvic cavity above from the perineum below: the levator ani, the obturator internus, the piriformis, or the coccygeus? The answer is the levator ani. It slopes downward and forward from the side wall of the pelvis, and the urethra, the vagina and the rectum pass through it.

Question 10200. A single described section through the pelvis shows the bladder in front, the uterus in the middle and the rectum behind, all in one midline slice. In which plane was the section taken, and where does the bladder lie relative to the uterus? The answer is the midsagittal plane, with the bladder in front of the uterus and the rectum behind it.

To summarize, every structure on a magnetic resonance image is placed by the signal it gives and by the sequence that produced it. Fat is bright on T1-weighted images, free water is bright on T2-weighted images, and cortical bone, air and flowing blood are dark on both, while tendons, ligaments, menisci and the labrum stay dark on every sequence, so that a tear shows as a bright line. In the brain the white matter is brighter than the gray on T1 and darker than it on T2, and the corpus callosum, the fornix, the thalami, the basal ganglia, the internal capsule, the midbrain, the pons and the fourth ventricle are each recognized by shape and by their neighbors, while the pituitary gland enhances because it has no blood-brain barrier. In the spine the nucleus pulposus is bright on T2, the annulus and the ligaments are dark, the epidural fat is bright on T1, and the cord ends as the conus medullaris with the cauda equina below it. In the chest and the abdomen the dark lung, the pericardium, the flow void of the heart chambers, the bright perirenal fat and the three layers of the uterus are the landmarks. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 103 — Ultrasound Anatomy

This chapter reads two imaging methods as maps of the body: twenty-five questions on magnetic resonance imaging, followed by seventy-five questions on ultrasound. Magnetic resonance imaging comes first, because its contrast between fat, fluid, muscle and bone shows the deep structures clearly, and ultrasound follows, because it places a probe on the skin and pictures the organs beneath it. Both are spoken in words, since nothing can be shown, so the listener hears what a section or a scan would display. The chapter holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is right. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10201. A described magnetic resonance image of the head taken in the midline from the side shows a broad curved band of white matter arching above the thalamus and joining the two hemispheres. Which structure is it? The answer is the corpus callosum. Its fibers cross the midline and connect matching areas of the two hemispheres, and the band is seen in full only in that midline section.

Question 10202. On a magnetic resonance image weighted to show fluid brightly, which structure is the brightest: the cerebrospinal fluid, the spinal cord, the cortical bone, or the outer ring of an intervertebral disc? The answer is the cerebrospinal fluid. It fills the spinal canal as a bright column around the darker cord.

Question 10203. A described magnetic resonance image of the knee from the side shows two dark triangular wedges between the rounded end of the femur and the flat top of the tibia. Which structures are the wedges? The answer is the menisci. Fibrocartilage gives little signal, so each appears as a dark triangle in section, deepening the socket of the joint.

Question 10204. On a described cross-sectional magnetic resonance image of the abdomen at the third lumbar vertebra, a round vessel lies immediately in front of the vertebral body and a little to the left of the midline. Which vessel is it? The answer is the abdominal aorta. It descends in front of the spine and slightly to the left, with the inferior vena cava to its right.

Question 10205. In a described midline magnetic resonance image of the head, a small rounded structure sits in the hollow of the sphenoid bone, below the crossing of the optic nerves. Which structure is it? The answer is the pituitary gland. It rests in the sella turcica and is joined to the brain above by a thin stalk.

Question 10206. On a magnetic resonance image weighted to show fat brightly, which tissue returns the strongest signal: fat, cortical bone, skeletal muscle, or cerebrospinal fluid? The answer is fat. It outlines the marrow, the subcutaneous layer and the spaces between muscles, while cortical bone and flowing blood return little signal.

Question 10207. A constructed illustration: a person with pain shooting down the back of the leg has a magnetic resonance image showing a disc bulging backward and to one side between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. Which nerve root is most likely compressed? The answer is the fifth lumbar nerve root. A disc at that level presses the root that runs on past it toward the foot.

Question 10208. True or false: on most magnetic resonance images, cortical bone and ligaments return little signal and appear dark. The answer is true. Dense collagen and mineralized bone hold few mobile protons, so they give almost no signal, while fat and fluid stand out as bright.

Question 10209. Within an intervertebral disc on a described magnetic resonance image, which part is bright on a sequence that emphasizes fluid: the central nucleus pulposus, the outer annulus fibrosus, the vertebral end plate, or the posterior longitudinal ligament? The answer is the central nucleus pulposus. It holds water and gives a bright center, while the fibrous ring around it stays dark.

Question 10210. A described cross-sectional magnetic resonance image of the brain shows a band of white matter shaped like a bent V, between a deep gray mass on its inner side and a lens-shaped gray mass on its outer side. Which structure is the band? The answer is the internal capsule. Its fibers carry messages between the cerebral cortex and the structures below it.

Question 10211. In a described cross-sectional magnetic resonance image of the pelvis, a large nerve leaves the pelvis below a muscle that runs out through the greater sciatic foramen. Which nerve lies immediately inferior to that muscle? The answer is the sciatic nerve. The muscle is the piriformis, and in a small minority of people the nerve passes through it instead.

Question 10212. A described magnetic resonance image of the ankle shows a thick dark tendon curving behind the medial malleolus and running on to the bones of the midfoot. Which tendon is it? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior muscle. A fibrous band holds it down behind the malleolus, and its main insertion is on the navicular bone.

Question 10213. In a described four-chamber magnetic resonance image of the heart, which chamber forms the front wall and lies closest to the chest wall: the right ventricle, the left ventricle, the left atrium, or the right atrium? The answer is the right ventricle. It wraps around the front of the heart, while the left ventricle forms the apex and the back.

Question 10214. A described magnetic resonance image of the leg shows a nerve winding around the neck of the fibula, where a small mass presses on it. Loss of which movement would follow: turning the sole outward and lifting the toes, turning the sole inward, bending the knee, or straightening the hip? The answer is turning the sole outward and lifting the toes. That is the work of the common fibular nerve.

Question 10215. Which of these pairs belongs together: a T2-weighted image with bright fat, a T1-weighted image with bright cerebrospinal fluid, a T2-weighted image with bright cerebrospinal fluid, or a T1-weighted image with dark fat? The answer is a T2-weighted image with bright cerebrospinal fluid. Fluid is bright on that sequence, and fat is bright on the T1-weighted one.

Question 10216. Name two tissues that return little signal on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted magnetic resonance images, spoken as a list. The answer is cortical bone and tendons. Neither holds much free water, so each stays dark on both sequences, while fat and fluid change brightness most between them.

Question 10217. A described magnetic resonance image of the abdomen taken across the body shows a kidney split into an outer rim and a set of darker triangular wedges that point toward the center. Which parts are the rim and the wedges? The answer is the cortex outside and the medullary pyramids inside, and the cortex also dips between the pyramids.

Question 10218. In a described magnetic resonance image of the liver, which vessel separates the right lobe from the left lobe: the middle hepatic vein, the right hepatic vein, the portal vein, or the inferior vena cava? The answer is the middle hepatic vein. It runs in the plane between the two halves, and the right hepatic vein divides the right half further.

Question 10219. In a described cross-sectional magnetic resonance image of the upper abdomen, a long vessel crosses in front of the aorta on its way to the left kidney. Which vessel is it? The answer is the left renal vein. It is longer than the right renal vein because the inferior vena cava lies on the right.

Question 10220. In a described cross-sectional magnetic resonance image of the neck, two oval lobes lie on either side of the trachea and in front of the great vessels. Which gland forms them? The answer is the thyroid gland. The lobes are joined across the front of the airway by the isthmus, and the gland moves when the person swallows.

Question 10221. A described magnetic resonance image of the female pelvis from the side shows a pear-shaped organ behind the bladder with a bright central band and a darker ring around it. Which layer is the bright band? The answer is the endometrium, the lining of the uterus. The darker ring is the myometrium, the muscle of the uterine wall.

Question 10222. In an adult, the lower end of the spinal cord lies at the first or second lumbar vertebra. Which explanation fits: the vertebral column grows faster than the cord, a fibrous thread pulls the cord down, the sacrum forms only after birth, or the cord stops growing at birth? The answer is that the vertebral column grows faster. The two are level in the fetus, and the canal then outgrows the cord.

Question 10223. A described magnetic resonance image of the shoulder shows a tendon passing beneath the arch of the acromion and above the head of the humerus. Which tendon is it: the supraspinatus, the subscapularis, the teres major, or the long head of the biceps? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon. It runs through the narrow space under the acromion, where it is the tendon most often torn.

Question 10224. A constructed illustration: a person has ringing in one ear and unsteady balance, and a magnetic resonance image shows a small mass in the angle between the cerebellum and the pons. Which cranial nerve is involved? The answer is the eighth cranial nerve, the vestibulocochlear nerve. It runs through that angle carrying fibers for hearing and for balance.

Question 10225. A described image of the head shows a section running across the body at right angles to its long axis, displaying the two lateral ventricles side by side, the third ventricle in the midline, and a deep groove on each side. Which plane produced it, and what does it divide? The answer is the transverse plane, which divides the body into an upper and a lower part.

Question 10226. On a described ultrasound image of the right upper abdomen, a pear-shaped sac lies against the under surface of the liver with a black interior and a bright thin wall. Which structure is it? The answer is the gallbladder. Bile is fluid, so it returns no echoes and appears black.

Question 10227. On an ultrasound image, which of these structures appears black because it contains fluid: the lumen of the gallbladder, the pancreas, the spleen, or the wall of the stomach? The answer is the lumen of the gallbladder. Fluid lets sound pass through without reflecting it, so it looks black, while solid organs have an even gray texture.

Question 10228. A described ultrasound image shows a bright curved line inside the gallbladder, and behind it the picture is dark, with the deep tissues hidden. What does that bright line represent? The answer is a gallstone. The stone reflects sound strongly, and the dark band behind it is the acoustic shadow it casts.

Question 10229. On a described ultrasound image of the liver, the gallbladder lies in a shallow bed between the right part of the liver and a small square lobe. Which lobe lies immediately to the left of that bed? The answer is the quadrate lobe. It lies on the under surface of the liver, beside the groove for the round ligament.

Question 10230. A described ultrasound image of a kidney shows an outer layer that is slightly darker than the bright middle of the organ and sends small columns inward between darker triangles. Which part is that outer layer? The answer is the renal cortex. The triangles are the medullary pyramids, and the cortex arches over their bases.

Question 10231. In the normal kidney on ultrasound, which part is the brightest: the renal sinus, the renal cortex, the medullary pyramid, or the blood in the renal vein? The answer is the renal sinus. It holds fat around the collecting system, and fat reflects sound strongly. The pyramids are the darkest part.

Question 10232. A described ultrasound image of a kidney shows a black branching structure in the center of the organ, with rounded black spaces spreading into it and the cortex stretched thin around them. What does the image show? The answer is a kidney swollen by trapped urine, with the collecting system widened by fluid that cannot drain.

Question 10233. A constructed illustration: a person has severe cramping pain in the flank that comes in waves, and ultrasound of the kidney shows a bright stone with a dark shadow behind it, lodged where the collecting system leaves the organ. Which structure holds the stone? The answer is the ureter, where it begins at the renal pelvis. A stone there blocks the flow of urine.

Question 10234. On a described cross-sectional ultrasound image of the neck, a thin-walled vessel that can be pressed flat lies immediately lateral to the common carotid artery. Which vessel is it: the internal jugular vein, the external carotid artery, the vertebral artery, or the inferior thyroid artery? The answer is the internal jugular vein, which lies beside the artery in the carotid sheath.

Question 10235. Which of these vessels is easily pressed flat by the ultrasound probe because its wall is thin and its pressure is low: the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, the femoral artery, or the abdominal aorta? The answer is the internal jugular vein. Veins collapse when the probe presses on them, while arteries keep their round shape.

Question 10236. A described ultrasound image of the front of the neck shows a gland shaped like a butterfly, with two lobes lying on either side of the windpipe and joined across the front. Which gland is it? The answer is the thyroid gland. It moves with the larynx when the person swallows.

Question 10237. A described ultrasound image of the neck taken across the body shows a butterfly-shaped structure in front of the trachea, with a very even gray texture, and two round dark vessels beside it. Which structure is in the middle? The answer is the thyroid gland, whose lobes lie on either side of the airway. The dark vessels are the common carotid artery and the internal jugular vein.

Question 10238. True or false: on ultrasound, a stone casts a dark shadow behind it, while a simple cyst makes the tissues behind it look brighter than their neighbors. The answer is true. A stone reflects sound back and leaves a shadow, and fluid transmits it well, so the tissue behind a cyst is brightened.

Question 10239. On a described ultrasound image across the abdomen, two large vessels lie in front of the spine. One pulsates, and the vessel beside it is thinner walled and changes width with breathing. Which vessel is the second one: the inferior vena cava, the aorta, the superior mesenteric artery, or the left renal vein? The answer is the inferior vena cava, which lies to the right of the aorta.

Question 10240. Which of these pairs belongs together: the head of the pancreas lying against the inferior vena cava, the tail of the pancreas against the gallbladder, the body of the pancreas against the spleen, or the neck of the pancreas against the left kidney? The answer is the head of the pancreas with the inferior vena cava, which lies behind it.

Question 10241. A constructed illustration: an older person has a pulsing feeling in the middle of the abdomen, and ultrasound shows a segment of a vessel wider than the part above it that expands with every beat. Which vessel is involved? The answer is the abdominal aorta. The widening is described as an illustration, and its cause belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 10242. Which of these pairs belongs together: the spleen with the left upper abdomen behind the stomach, the gallbladder with the left upper abdomen, the right kidney with the left upper abdomen, or the tail of the pancreas with the right iliac fossa? The answer is the spleen with the left upper abdomen behind the stomach. The gallbladder and the right kidney lie on the right.

Question 10243. Name two organs of the right upper abdomen that lie against the diaphragm, spoken as a list. The answer is the liver and the gallbladder. The dome of the liver lies against the diaphragm, and the gallbladder rests on the under surface of the liver. Both move with the diaphragm during breathing.

Question 10244. A described ultrasound image of the liver shows a branching tube whose walls are bright and whose lumen is black, unlike the hepatic veins nearby, whose walls are barely seen. Which vessel is it? The answer is the portal vein. Its fibrous sheath reflects sound and shows as a bright wall.

Question 10245. A described ultrasound image taken along the free edge of the lesser omentum shows three tubes running together toward the liver: one with a bright wall and a black lumen, one with a thick wall that pulsates, and one with a thin wall. Which structures form that bundle? The answer is the portal vein, the proper hepatic artery and the common bile duct, which run together as the portal triad.

Question 10246. In a described ultrasound image taken along the free edge of the lesser omentum, which of these structures lies in that fold together with the proper hepatic artery and the common bile duct: the portal vein, the inferior vena cava, the splenic vein, or the left gastric artery? The answer is the portal vein. The three structures form the portal triad.

Question 10247. Within the portal triad, one tube lies behind the other two. The proper hepatic artery lies to the left and in front, and the common bile duct lies in front and to the right. Which structure lies most posteriorly? The answer is the portal vein, which forms the back of the triad and is the largest of the three.

Question 10248. A constructed illustration: a person has yellow skin and eyes, and ultrasound shows black branching tubes throughout the liver, with the main duct below the liver wider than the vessel beside it. Which structure is most likely blocked? The answer is the common bile duct. Bile is dammed up behind the block, so the ducts widen.

Question 10249. Which organ on ultrasound has a smooth bright capsule around an even texture, and is crossed by bright lines that follow the branches of the portal vein: the liver, the spleen, the pancreas, or the kidney? The answer is the liver. The kidney, by contrast, is clearly divided into cortex and medulla.

Question 10250. A described ultrasound image of the left upper abdomen shows a crescent-shaped organ with an even texture, lying behind the stomach and above the left kidney. Which organ is it? The answer is the spleen. It lies against the diaphragm and is tucked behind the stomach and the tail of the pancreas.

Question 10251. A described ultrasound image across the left upper abdomen shows a crescent of even gray tissue behind a hollow organ with a bright folded lining, and above a bean-shaped organ with a bright center. Which structure is the crescent? The answer is the spleen. The hollow organ in front of it is the stomach, and the bean-shaped one below is the left kidney.

Question 10252. Which part of the pancreas lies closest to the spleen and reaches farthest to the left: the head, the neck, the body, or the tail? The answer is the tail. It runs toward the spleen along the splenic vessels, while the head lies on the right against the duodenum.

Question 10253. Which part of the pancreas lies directly in front of the place where the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein: the head, the neck, the body, or the tail? The answer is the neck. The portal vein is formed behind the neck, so the gland lies in front of the vein at that point.

Question 10254. A described ultrasound image of the stomach shows its wall as five layers lying one over another, from a bright inner line to a bright outer line, with dark bands between them. What does that pattern represent? The answer is the coats of the stomach wall together with the surfaces between them. Mucosa, submucosa, muscle and serosa each reflect sound differently.

Question 10255. True or false: the pancreas lies behind the stomach and in front of the splenic vein. The answer is true. It is a retroperitoneal organ, so the peritoneum covers only its front, and the stomach lies in front of it. The splenic vein runs along its back.

Question 10256. A described ultrasound image of the female pelvis taken in the midline shows a pear-shaped organ lying behind the bladder with a bright line down its center. Which organ is it? The answer is the uterus. It is tipped forward over the bladder, and the bright line is its lining. Behind it lies the rectum.

Question 10257. A described ultrasound image of the female pelvis shows a pear-shaped organ behind the bladder, and within it a bright band that thickens and thins with the phase of the monthly cycle. Which structure is the band? The answer is the endometrium, the lining of the uterus. The muscle around it, the myometrium, is darker.

Question 10258. A described ultrasound image of the female pelvis shows an oval organ beside the uterus, and inside it several small black circles arranged around the edge. Which organ is it, and what are the circles: the ovary with follicles, the uterus with glands, the bladder with pouches, or the rectum with gas? The answer is the ovary with follicles, which are filled with fluid and so appear black.

Question 10259. A described ultrasound image of the female pelvis shows the ovary hanging beside the uterus. Which vessel of the pelvic wall lies immediately lateral to and behind the ovary? The answer is the internal iliac artery. The ovary lies in a shallow hollow on the lateral wall of the pelvis.

Question 10260. Name two structures that lie in front of the uterus in the female pelvis and are seen together in a midline scan, spoken as a list. The answer is the urinary bladder and the pubic symphysis. Behind the uterus lie the rectum and the sacrum.

Question 10261. A constructed illustration: a person in the first weeks of pregnancy has an ultrasound scan of the pelvis, which shows a small black sac inside the uterus and, within the sac, a small round ring. Which structure is the ring? The answer is the yolk sac. It shows that the sac is a true pregnancy sac within the uterus.

Question 10262. In a described ultrasound image of a pregnant uterus, a dark fluid surrounds a small curled shape and lies between that shape and the wall of the uterus. What is the dark fluid? The answer is amniotic fluid, which fills the amniotic cavity and lets the fetus move and grow. Being fluid, it returns no echoes.

Question 10263. A described ultrasound image of the pelvis shows a thin-walled black rounded structure lying just behind the pubic bone and rising into the lower abdomen. Which structure is it? The answer is the urinary bladder. When it is full its wall is thin and its interior is black.

Question 10264. Which structure lies immediately behind the pubic symphysis when it is full, and is used on ultrasound as a window to the organs behind it: the urinary bladder, the rectum, the uterus, or the prostate gland? The answer is the urinary bladder. Filled with urine, it lets the deeper organs be seen.

Question 10265. A described ultrasound image of the shoulder shows a structure running to the bone with bright parallel lines inside it, and its surface is wrapped in a thin dark rim. Which structure and which covering are shown? The answer is a tendon with its sheath. The bright parallel lines are the fibers of the tendon.

Question 10266. On ultrasound, which tissue produces a bright line at its surface with a dark band beneath it, hiding everything under the surface: fat, muscle, the cortex of a bone, or a tendon? The answer is the cortex of a bone. Sound cannot pass through bone, so it is reflected at the surface and casts a shadow.

Question 10267. In a described ultrasound image of the shoulder, one tendon passes beneath the acromion and above the head of the humerus. Which tendon is it, and where does it lie? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon, which lies above the head of the humerus and below the acromion. It is one of the four tendons of the rotator cuff.

Question 10268. A constructed illustration: a person has pain when lifting the arm sideways, and ultrasound shows a small black collection between the acromion and the tendon beneath it. Which space holds that fluid? The answer is the subacromial bursa, which lies between the acromion and the supraspinatus tendon and lets it glide.

Question 10269. A described ultrasound image of the back of the knee shows a black collection lying between a tendon on the inner side and a muscle beside it, just below the joint line. Between which two structures does it lie? The answer is the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of the gastrocnemius, where a popliteal cyst forms.

Question 10270. Which recess of the knee joint lies above the kneecap, between the femur and the quadriceps tendon, and is where fluid is most easily seen on ultrasound: the suprapatellar recess, the subpopliteal recess, the posterior recess, or the cruciate recess? The answer is the suprapatellar recess, the upper part of the joint cavity.

Question 10271. A described ultrasound image of the abdomen shows the abdominal aorta as a long tube running from the top of the picture to the bottom, with the bodies of the vertebrae as a bright line behind it and the inferior vena cava beside it. Along which axis was this section taken? The answer is the long axis of the body, in a sagittal plane.

Question 10272. A described ultrasound image taken across the upper abdomen shows two black circles side by side in front of the spine. Which one lies on the right side of the person being examined, and what is its relation to the other? The answer is the inferior vena cava, and it lies immediately to the right of the aorta. The side of the picture is not the side of the person.

Question 10273. In a described ultrasound image of the groin, three structures lie in a row within the femoral triangle; from lateral to medial they are a nerve, an artery and a vein. Which structure is in the middle? The answer is the femoral artery. It lies between the femoral nerve, which is lateral to it, and the femoral vein, which is medial.

Question 10274. True or false: in the femoral triangle, the femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery. The answer is true. The order from lateral to medial is nerve, artery, vein, and the narrow space beside the vein lies most medially. The nerve leaves the triangle above the vessels.

Question 10275. Which vein lies just under the skin of the inner thigh and joins the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament: the great saphenous vein, the small saphenous vein, the popliteal vein, or the external iliac vein? The answer is the great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body. The small saphenous vein ends behind the knee.

Question 10276. In the femoral triangle, the femoral vein lies immediately medial to the femoral artery. Which structure lies immediately medial to the femoral vein, forming the most medial compartment of the triangle? The answer is the femoral canal, a short passage that carries lymph vessels and a lymph node.

Question 10277. A described ultrasound image of a leg vein shows that the vein does not close when the probe presses on it, and that its lumen holds bright material instead of being black. Which interpretation fits: the vein contains a clot, the vein is normal, the structure is an artery, or the structure is a nerve? The answer is that the vein contains a clot. A normal vein closes under gentle pressure.

Question 10278. True or false: a normal vein is easily pressed flat by the ultrasound probe, while a normal artery keeps its round shape under the same pressure. The answer is true. The wall of a vein is thin and its pressure is low, so the probe closes it, while an artery stays open.

Question 10279. A described ultrasound image of the upper abdomen shows a bright curved line above the liver, and above that line a second picture of the liver itself, with its vessels running the wrong way.
