Which of these pairs belongs together: the paramesonephric duct with the uterus and the uterine tube, the mesonephric duct with the uterus, the urogenital sinus with the ovary, or the gonadal ridge with the prostate? The answer is the paramesonephric duct with the uterus and the uterine tube.

Question 10496. The ovary descends from the posterior abdominal wall into the pelvis along the gubernaculum. Which two ligaments does the gubernaculum become in the female? The answer is the ovarian ligament and the round ligament of the uterus, which lie in line with each other on either side of the uterine tube.

Question 10497. Which pair of swellings on either side of the urogenital opening gives rise to the scrotum in the male and to the labia majora in the female? The answer is the labioscrotal swellings, also called the genital swellings. In the male they fuse in the midline, and the seam between them remains as the raphe of the scrotum.

Question 10498. A described dissection of the scrotum of an infant shows a narrow channel running from the abdomen into the scrotum beside the spermatic cord, with a little fluid inside it. What is the channel? The answer is a patent processus vaginalis, a pocket of peritoneum that normally closes before birth.

Question 10499. Name two tissues that develop from the somites, spoken as a list. The answer is the vertebrae with the ribs, from the sclerotome, and the skeletal muscles, from the myotome. The dermis of the back also comes from the somite. The somites lie in pairs along the back, and they give the body its segmented plan.

Question 10500. A constructed illustration: a newborn is described with loops of bowel lying outside the body to the right of the umbilicus, with no sac covering them. Which defect is illustrated, and how does it differ from a defect in which the bowel lies inside a sac? The answer is gastroschisis, in which the body wall itself failed to close, so no sac formed; when the bowel returns inside a sac the defect is an omphalocele. The care of the infant belongs to the treating clinician.

To summarize, the three germ layers divide the work of building the body, with the ectoderm forming the skin and the nervous system, the endoderm lining the gut and the airway, and the mesoderm building the skeleton, the muscles, the blood and the kidneys. The notochord induces the neural plate, the neural crest migrates widely to form the sensory ganglia, the melanocytes, the adrenal medulla and much of the face, and programmed cell death carves out the digits and the spaces around the organs. Each pharyngeal arch carries its own nerve, artery and cartilage, so the muscles of mastication, of facial expression and of the larynx can be traced to the arches they came from. The heart is the first organ to work, the gut rotates counterclockwise about the superior mesenteric artery while the liver and the pancreas bud from the foregut, and the kidney passes through three sets of organs before the metanephros takes over. The urinary and genital tracts share a common origin, which explains the course of the ureter, the trigone of the bladder and the descent of the gonad. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 106 — Cardiovascular Development

This chapter follows the embryo from the first beating of the heart tube to the finished organs, and it holds one hundred questions on how the body is built. It begins with the heart and the great vessels, moves to the nervous system, then to the bones and the muscles, and closes with the abnormalities that appear when a step goes wrong. Each question is answered immediately after it is asked, and the reason follows the answer. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10501. Which chamber of the heart is formed mainly by the cells of the first heart field? The answer is the left ventricle. The first heart field lies in the splanchnic mesoderm and folds into the primary heart tube. The second heart field adds the right ventricle and much of the outflow tract.

Question 10502. Which segment of the heart tube lies between the primitive atrium and the bulbus cordis: the sinus venosus, the primitive ventricle, the truncus arteriosus, or the aortic sac? The answer is the primitive ventricle. It follows the primitive atrium in the series, and the bulbus cordis follows it and becomes most of the right ventricle.

Question 10503. The single heart tube is formed when two vessels in the pericardial cavity fuse in the midline. What are they called? The answer is the endocardial tubes. They arise from the cardiogenic mesoderm on each side and are brought together as the embryo folds. Their fusion begins at the cranial end.

Question 10504. Which of these provides the muscular wall of the heart tube: the endocardium, the cardiac jelly, the splanchnic mesoderm around the tube, or the proepicardial organ? The answer is the splanchnic mesoderm, whose cells become the myocardium. The endocardium lines the lumen and the cardiac jelly lies between the two.

Question 10505. The dilated venous end of the heart tube, later absorbed into the wall of the right atrium, is called what? The answer is the sinus venosus. Its right horn is taken into the right atrium and its left horn becomes the coronary sinus. Blood from the yolk sac, the placenta and the body wall reaches the heart through it.

Question 10506. In which direction does the heart tube normally bend, and what is that bending called? The answer is that it bends to the right, a movement called dextral looping. That bend places the future right ventricle on the right and the future left ventricle on the left. A bend to the left is a rare reversal.

Question 10507. A described section of an early embryo shows a straight tube in the pericardial cavity, wide at one end and narrow at the other, with the narrow end opening into arched vessels. Which segment lies at the narrow end? The answer is the truncus arteriosus, which continues into the aortic sac and the aortic arches. The wide venous end begins with the sinus venosus.

Question 10508. The bulbus cordis lies between which two segments of the heart tube, and which chamber does most of it become? The answer is that it lies between the primitive ventricle and the truncus arteriosus, and most of it becomes the right ventricle. Its proximal part joins the right ventricle.

Question 10509. Which structure divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and the pulmonary trunk: the septum primum, the aorticopulmonary septum, the endocardial cushions, or the muscular ventricular septum? The answer is the aorticopulmonary septum, which grows through the truncus in a spiral. Cells from the neural crest take part in it, and its spiral course makes the two great vessels cross.

Question 10510. True or false: the heart is the first organ to begin working in the embryo. The answer is true. It begins to beat during the fourth week, while most other organs are still faint outlines. Blood moves through the embryo before the kidneys, the lungs or the gut take shape.

Question 10511. The opening in the atrial septum that lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left before birth is called what? The answer is the foramen ovale, bounded by the free edge of the septum secundum. The flap of the septum primum lies over it on the left and closes it after birth, leaving the fossa ovalis.

Question 10512. Which part of the interventricular septum forms from the fusion of the endocardial cushions with the aorticopulmonary septum: the muscular part, the membranous part, the inlet part, or the trabecular part? The answer is the membranous part. The muscular part grows upward from the floor of the ventricle, and a defect is left below the aortic valve when the membranous part fails to close.

Question 10513. A described cast of the great vessels shows one wide trunk leaving the ventricles, with a spiral ridge inside dividing it into two channels. Which structure is described? The answer is the aorticopulmonary septum, whose two channels become the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Its spiral course turns the pulmonary trunk in front of the aorta.

Question 10514. Which aortic arch artery lies immediately caudal to the fourth arch on each side, and what do its branches become? The answer is the sixth aortic arch, whose branches become the pulmonary arteries. On the left the sixth arch also forms the ductus arteriosus. The fifth arch is rudimentary and usually disappears.

Question 10515. A constructed illustration: a newborn has a continuous murmur and bounding pulses, and the short vessel joining the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta has stayed open. Which structure is involved? The answer is the ductus arteriosus, which before birth carries blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta. It normally closes after birth and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

Question 10516. Which pair belongs together: the right horn of the sinus venosus with the smooth wall of the right atrium, the left horn with the ligamentum teres, the left umbilical vein with the ligamentum venosum, or the ductus venosus with the coronary sinus? The answer is the right horn with the smooth wall of the right atrium. The left horn becomes the coronary sinus, while the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.

Question 10517. Which of these is formed from the right anterior cardinal vein together with the right common cardinal vein: the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, the azygos vein, or the left brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the superior vena cava. The left brachiocephalic vein comes from an anastomosis between the two anterior cardinal veins, and the azygos vein from the right posterior cardinal vein.

Question 10518. Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetal liver? The answer is the umbilical vein, in particular the left umbilical vein. It runs inside the umbilical cord and enters the liver, where most of its blood passes into the ductus venosus. The right umbilical vein disappears early.

Question 10519. A described dissection of a fetal heart shows a flap of thin tissue on the left side of the atrial septum that can be pushed aside with a probe. Which structure is shown? The answer is the valve of the foramen ovale, formed by the septum primum. It lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left, and after birth it seals the opening.

Question 10520. Which of these carries the most oxygenated blood in the fetus: the umbilical vein, an umbilical artery, the ductus arteriosus, or the superior vena cava? The answer is the umbilical vein, which returns from the placenta where the fetal blood has taken up oxygen. The umbilical arteries carry the least oxygenated blood back to the placenta.

Question 10521. The remnant of the ductus arteriosus lies immediately distal to which structure, and what is that remnant called? The answer is that it lies immediately distal to the left subclavian artery, at the end of the aortic arch, and the remnant is the ligamentum arteriosum. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it.

Question 10522. A constructed illustration: a deeply cyanosed newborn is found to have the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk arising from the left. Which developmental error explains this? The answer is a failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral. The septum still divides the truncus into two vessels, but it does not twist, so they stay parallel.

Question 10523. In tetralogy of Fallot the aorticopulmonary septum deviates in which direction: anteriorly, posteriorly, to the left, or to the right? The answer is anteriorly, which narrows the pulmonary outflow and leaves the aorta overriding the ventricular septal defect. The other two features are the septal defect itself and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Question 10524. Name the fetal vessel that carries oxygenated blood to the fetus and the vessels that carry it away. The answer is the umbilical vein, which brings oxygenated blood to the fetus, and the two umbilical arteries, which take it away. All three run in the umbilical cord, and the arteries arise from the internal iliac arteries.

Question 10525. A described cross section of a newborn heart shows a probe passing from the right atrium into the left atrium through an opening in the septum. Which opening is shown, and what closes it? The answer is the foramen ovale, closed by the flap of the septum primum. The rise in pressure in the left atrium presses that flap against the septum secundum, leaving the fossa ovalis.

Question 10526. Which of the three germ layers gives rise to the entire nervous system? The answer is the ectoderm. A thickened strip of it, the neural plate, lies above the notochord and folds into a groove and then a tube. The skin that covers the back comes from the same layer.

Question 10527. Which of these lists the three primary brain vesicles: the prosencephalon, the mesencephalon and the rhombencephalon; the telencephalon, the diencephalon and the myelencephalon; the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the brainstem; or the thalamus, the pons and the medulla? The answer is the prosencephalon, the mesencephalon and the rhombencephalon. The other names belong to the secondary vesicles or to adult structures.

Question 10528. Which cells arise at the crest of the neural folds, leave the nervous system and migrate widely through the embryo? The answer is the neural crest cells. They form the sensory and autonomic ganglia, the Schwann cells and the adrenal medulla, among other structures, and are sometimes called the fourth germ layer.

Question 10529. Which secondary brain vesicle gives rise to the medulla oblongata: the myelencephalon, the metencephalon, the diencephalon, or the telencephalon? The answer is the myelencephalon, the lowest part of the hindbrain. The metencephalon gives the pons and the cerebellum, and the diencephalon gives the thalamus and the hypothalamus.

Question 10530. A described transverse section of an early embryo shows a closed tube just beneath the surface ectoderm, with a solid rod of cells immediately below it. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the neural tube above and the notochord below. The tube will form the brain and the spinal cord, and the notochord later becomes part of the intervertebral disc.

Question 10531. The groove on the inner wall of the neural tube that separates the motor columns from the sensory columns is called what? The answer is the sulcus limitans. It runs along the length of the tube on each side. The basal plate lies below it and becomes motor, while the alar plate above it becomes sensory.

Question 10532. Which structure produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid: the ependymal lining of the central canal, the arachnoid granulations, the choroid plexus, or the pia mater? The answer is the choroid plexus, a fringe of vascular tissue covered by ependymal cells that hangs in each ventricle. The arachnoid granulations absorb the fluid back into the venous blood.

Question 10533. The pouch of oral ectoderm that grows upward toward the base of the brain and forms the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland is called what? The answer is Rathke pouch. It loses its connection with the roof of the mouth and comes to lie in the sella turcica, while the posterior lobe comes from the diencephalon.

Question 10534. In which region does the neural tube first close: the cervical region, the head, the lower back, or the tail? The answer is the cervical region. Closure begins there and runs in both directions, so the tube is briefly open at each end. The cranial opening closes a little before the caudal one.

Question 10535. A described section of the spinal cord of a fetus shows a narrow central canal lined by cells, with a rounded mass of gray matter on each side. Which plate forms the dorsal part of that gray matter? The answer is the alar plate, which lies above the sulcus limitans and receives the sensory fibers. The basal plate below gives the motor cells of the ventral horn.

Question 10536. Which structure lies immediately ventral to the neural tube, and what does it become in the adult? The answer is the notochord, which becomes the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs. It runs beneath the tube and induces the overlying ectoderm to form the nervous system, and the vertebral bodies later form around it.

Question 10537. Which of these is a derivative of the neural crest: the Schwann cell, the oligodendrocyte, the astrocyte, or the ependymal cell? The answer is the Schwann cell, which wraps the axons of the peripheral nerves and forms their myelin sheath. The other three are support cells of the central nervous system and come from the neural tube.

Question 10538. True or false: the microglia of the brain are derived from the neural crest. The answer is false. The microglia come from mesodermal precursors that migrate into the nervous system from the yolk sac. They are the resident scavenger cells of the brain.

Question 10539. Which cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord in the adult? The answer is the ependymal cells, a single layer that keeps the cerebrospinal fluid in contact with the nervous tissue. The choroid plexus is built from the same cells together with blood vessels.

Question 10540. The channel that connects the third ventricle with the fourth in the adult brain is derived from the cavity of which vesicle: the telencephalon, the diencephalon, the mesencephalon, or the myelencephalon? The answer is the mesencephalon, whose cavity narrows into the cerebral aqueduct as the walls thicken. The cavity of the telencephalon becomes the lateral ventricles.

Question 10541. A described section of a fetal brain shows a thin roof over a large cavity, with a fringe of vascular tissue hanging into it and thick walls of gray matter around it. Which cavity and which structure are shown? The answer is a lateral ventricle with its choroid plexus. The thin roof and the large cavity belong to the telencephalon, which forms the cerebral hemisphere.

Question 10542. The fourth ventricle lies between which two structures, and through which openings does it communicate with the space around the brain? The answer is that it lies between the cerebellum behind and the pons and medulla in front, and it communicates through the lateral apertures and the median aperture. The fluid leaves through them into the subarachnoid space.

Question 10543. Which of these is not derived from the neural crest: the adrenal medulla, the melanocytes of the skin, the pia mater and the arachnoid mater, or the cortex of the adrenal gland? The answer is the cortex of the adrenal gland, which comes from the intermediate mesoderm. The medulla of the same gland comes from the neural crest and behaves like a sympathetic ganglion.

Question 10544. A constructed illustration: a newborn has a thin sac over the lower back, and the sac contains nerve tissue. Which defect is this, and which opening failed to close? The answer is a myelomeningocele, from failure of the caudal neuropore. The vertebral arches are missing, so the sac and its nerves lie outside the canal.

Question 10545. Failure of the cranial neuropore to close leaves which defect: anencephaly, spina bifida, hydrocephalus, or a cleft palate? The answer is anencephaly. Without a closed tube the cranial vault fails to form and the exposed brain tissue degenerates. Spina bifida follows failure at the caudal end.

Question 10546. Which pair belongs together: the mesencephalon with the cerebral aqueduct, the myelencephalon with the cerebellum, the diencephalon with the medulla, or the telencephalon with the third ventricle? The answer is the mesencephalon with the cerebral aqueduct. The metencephalon gives the cerebellum, while the diencephalon encloses the third ventricle.

Question 10547. Name the two layers of the meninges that are derived from the neural crest. The answer is the pia mater and the arachnoid mater. Together they form the leptomeninges, the delicate coverings that lie against the brain and the spinal cord. The thick outer dura mater comes from the mesoderm.

Question 10548. Within the wall of the neural tube, does the alar plate lie above or below the sulcus limitans, and is it sensory or motor? The answer is that the alar plate lies above the sulcus limitans and is sensory, while the basal plate below it is motor. That dorsal sensory and ventral motor arrangement persists in the adult spinal cord.

Question 10549. A constructed illustration: an infant's head enlarges steadily, and the lateral ventricles are dilated while the channel between the third and the fourth ventricle is narrow. Which structure is narrowed? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct, part of the midbrain. Its narrowing blocks the flow of cerebrospinal fluid and dilates the ventricles above it.

Question 10550. A described section of a fetal brain shows an outpouching of the wall of the diencephalon that reaches the surface ectoderm and will form the retina and the optic nerve. Which structure is described? The answer is the optic vesicle, from the diencephalon. The surface ectoderm thickens into the lens and the stalk narrows into the optic nerve.

Question 10551. Which blocks of mesoderm lie on each side of the neural tube and give rise to the vertebrae and the skeletal muscles? The answer is the somites, which form in pairs from the paraxial mesoderm beginning near the head. About forty-four pairs are formed, and each one splits into three parts.

Question 10552. Which part of a somite gives rise to the vertebral column: the sclerotome, the myotome, the dermatome, or the somatopleure? The answer is the sclerotome, whose cells migrate around the notochord and the neural tube to enclose them. The myotome forms muscle and the dermatome forms the dermis of the back.

Question 10553. The thickened strip of ectoderm at the tip of a developing limb bud that directs its growth is called what? The answer is the apical ectodermal ridge. It lies at the outer margin of the bud and signals the mesoderm beneath it to keep growing. Removing it stops the limb from lengthening.

Question 10554. Which of these bones develops by intramembranous ossification, without a cartilage model: the parietal bone, the femur, the humerus, or a vertebra? The answer is the parietal bone, which forms directly in a sheet of mesenchyme. The other three all pass through a cartilage model first.

Question 10555. A described section through a limb bud shows a solid core of mesenchyme covered by ectoderm, with a thickened ridge of ectoderm along the outer edge. What is the ridge, and what does it do? The answer is the apical ectodermal ridge, which drives growth from the shoulder toward the fingers and keeps a zone of dividing cells alive beneath it.

Question 10556. True or false: the upper limb buds appear before the lower limb buds. The answer is true. The arms begin as small swellings on the body wall a few days before the legs do. Later the legs catch up in length, while the arms stay ahead in the finer movements of the fingers.

Question 10557. Which part of the somite gives the deep muscles of the back, and which nerves supply them? The answer is the epaxial part of the myotome, supplied by the dorsal rami of the spinal nerves. The hypaxial part forms the muscles of the body wall and the limbs and is supplied by the ventral rami.

Question 10558. Which part of a somite forms the dermis of the back: the sclerotome, the myotome, the dermatome, or the notochord? The answer is the dermatome, whose cells spread beneath the ectoderm and form the deep layer of the skin of the back. The notochord is not part of a somite and becomes the nucleus pulposus.

Question 10559. Which structure lies in the center of the intervertebral disc, and from which tissue does the ring around it develop? The answer is the nucleus pulposus, the remnant of the notochord, with the annulus fibrosus around it developing from the sclerotome. Together they allow movement between two vertebral bodies.

Question 10560. A described section of a developing long bone shows a cartilage shaft with a collar of bone around its middle and a cavity forming inside. What is the collar? The answer is the bony collar around the diaphysis, the first bone to appear. It forms beneath the perichondrium without a cartilage model, and the shaft inside is hollowed into the marrow cavity.

Question 10561. Where does the primary ossification center of a long bone appear: in the shaft, in the upper epiphysis, in the lower epiphysis, or in the epiphyseal plate? The answer is in the shaft, that is, in the diaphysis. Secondary centers appear later in the epiphyses at each end, and growth in length continues at the epiphyseal plate.

Question 10562. The band of cartilage that separates the shaft of a growing long bone from its end and allows the bone to lengthen is called what? The answer is the epiphyseal plate, which lies between the diaphysis and the epiphysis. Cartilage is replaced by bone on the shaft side, and when the plate closes, growth in length stops.

Question 10563. A constructed illustration: a newborn's foot is turned inward and downward, and the sole faces the other foot. Which deformity is this? The answer is clubfoot, also called talipes equinovarus. The heel is drawn up and the forefoot turns inward. The bones themselves are normal at first, and the deformity lies in the soft tissues around the ankle.

Question 10564. Which of these describes the rotation of the upper limb bud: it rotates laterally so the extensor muscles lie posterior, it rotates medially so the extensors lie anterior, it does not rotate, or it rotates so the thumb lies medial? The answer is that it rotates laterally, so the extensor muscles come to lie on the back of the arm. The lower limb rotates the other way.

Question 10565. Why is the diaphragm supplied by nerves from the upper cervical segments, although the muscle lies far below the neck? The answer is that the muscle develops in the neck from the septum transversum and then descends, carrying its nerve supply with it. That is why the phrenic nerve runs so long a course.

Question 10566. A described radiograph of the hand of a young child shows a gap of dark cartilage between the shaft of each bone and a separate rounded center at its end. What are those centers, and what will happen to them? The answer is the secondary ossification centers of the epiphyses. Each will grow until it fills the epiphysis and then fuses with the shaft, and the dark gap is the epiphyseal plate.

Question 10567. Which pair belongs together: the sclerotome with the vertebral body, the myotome with the dermis, the dermatome with the skeletal muscle, or the somite with the notochord? The answer is the sclerotome with the vertebral body. The myotome gives skeletal muscle and the dermatome the dermis of the back, while the notochord is a separate midline rod.

Question 10568. True or false: the sternum develops from two bars of mesoderm that fuse in the midline, and they join from above downward. The answer is true. The two sternal bars form in the front of the chest wall and meet first at the top, which is why a split in the sternum is found at the lower end.

Question 10569. How are the separate fingers and toes formed from the solid plate of the limb bud: by growth of new tissue between them, by cell death between them, by fusion of separate rays, or by a second wave of somite cells? The answer is by cell death in the tissue between them, a programmed breakdown of the mesenchyme between the digital rays. When that fails, the digits stay joined.

Question 10570. Name the three parts of a somite and say what each becomes. The answer is the sclerotome, which becomes the vertebral column and the ribs, the myotome, which becomes skeletal muscle, and the dermatome, which becomes the dermis of the back. All three come from the same block of paraxial mesoderm beside the neural tube.

Question 10571. A constructed illustration: a child has a short neck, a low hairline at the back and very limited turning of the head, and the cervical vertebrae are fused. Which anomaly is this? The answer is the Klippel-Feil anomaly, in which the cervical somites fail to separate so two or more vertebrae are joined. The number of fused segments varies.

Question 10572. The upward peg of bone on which the head turns, formed from the sclerotome of the first cervical segment, is called what? The answer is the dens of the axis, also called the odontoid process. It belongs developmentally to the first cervical vertebra but fuses with the second, and the first loses its own body and becomes a ring.

Question 10573. A described sagittal section of the vertebral column of a fetus shows a rod of tissue running through the middle of each vertebral body and swelling inside each disc. What is that rod, and what will remain of it? The answer is the notochord, whose remnant inside each disc is the nucleus pulposus. The vertebral bodies form around it and replace it almost completely.

Question 10574. A constructed illustration: a newborn girl has a hip that can be pushed out of its socket, and the socket itself is shallow. Which developmental problem is this, and which structure is too shallow? The answer is developmental dysplasia of the hip, with a shallow acetabulum. The socket forms from the ilium, the ischium and the pubis and deepens late in development.

Question 10575. An extra rib that arises from the seventh cervical vertebra and may press on the lower part of the brachial plexus develops from which structure: the costal process of a cervical sclerotome, the sternal bar, the dermatome, or the notochord? The answer is the costal process of a cervical sclerotome. Every vertebra has costal elements, and in the thorax they grow into ribs.

Question 10576. Which congenital heart defect is the most common of all, a hole in the septum between the two ventricles? The answer is the ventricular septal defect. It usually lies in the membranous part of the septum, just below the aortic valve. Many small defects close on their own.

Question 10577. Which of these is the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect: the ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot, coarctation of the aorta, or an atrial septal defect? The answer is tetralogy of Fallot, whose four features are pulmonary stenosis, a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. The other three are acyanotic.

Question 10578. A described radiograph of a child's chest shows a small boot-shaped heart with a lifted apex and dark, underfilled lungs. Which congenital defect does this suggest? The answer is tetralogy of Fallot. The narrow pulmonary outflow leaves the lungs underfilled, and the enlarged right ventricle lifts the apex.

Question 10579. A newborn has a continuous murmur and bounding pulses, and the vessel that joined the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta before birth has failed to close. Which vessel is it, and what should it have become? The answer is the ductus arteriosus, which should have become the ligamentum arteriosum. While open, it lets blood flow from the aorta into the pulmonary circulation.

Question 10580. A child has a defect in the upper part of the atrial septum near the fossa ovalis, and blood passes from the left atrium to the right. Which defect is this: an ostium secundum atrial septal defect, a ventricular septal defect, a patent ductus arteriosus, or tricuspid atresia? The answer is an ostium secundum atrial septal defect. The shunt runs from left to right because the left atrial pressure is higher after birth.

Question 10581. Which pair belongs together: a patent ductus arteriosus with the vessel joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, an atrial septal defect with the ventricular septum, a ventricular septal defect with the atrial septum, or coarctation with the pulmonary valve? The answer is a patent ductus arteriosus with the vessel joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. The two septal defects are named for the septum they lie in.

Question 10582. The fossa ovalis, the remnant of the fetal opening between the atria, lies in which part of the interatrial septum, and on which side does its flap lie? The answer is that it lies in the lower part of the septum, with the flap of the septum primum on its left side. The firmer septum secundum lies on the right.

Question 10583. In the adult form of coarctation of the aorta, where does the narrowing lie: just proximal to the ductus arteriosus, just distal to the ductus arteriosus, at the aortic root, or in the ascending aorta? The answer is just distal to the ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the ductus. The infantile form lies proximal to it, and the adult form produces collateral circulation and notching of the ribs.

Question 10584. The ductus arteriosus joins which two vessels, and where does its aortic end lie relative to the left subclavian artery? The answer is that it joins the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch, and its aortic end lies just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it there.

Question 10585. The congenital defect in which the two shelves of tissue that should meet in the midline of the roof of the mouth fail to fuse is called what? The answer is a cleft palate. The shelves grow from the maxillary processes and meet from front to back, and when they fail to meet the mouth and the nose stay connected.

Question 10586. In which anomaly is the tricuspid valve displaced downward into the right ventricle, so that part of the ventricle lies above the valve? The answer is the Ebstein anomaly. The displaced valve leaves the upper part of the right ventricle as part of the atrium, so the right atrium is large and the working right ventricle is small.

Question 10587. In transposition of the great arteries, what is the essential error: the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left, both vessels arise from the right ventricle, the septum fails to close, or the pulmonary trunk is narrowed? The answer is that the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left. The two circulations then run in parallel.

Question 10588. A described section of the heart of a newborn shows a very small left ventricle with a thick wall, a tiny aortic valve and a large right ventricle. Which anomaly is shown? The answer is a hypoplastic left heart. The left side cannot pump blood to the body, so the right ventricle must do it through the ductus arteriosus.

Question 10589. In a heart with tetralogy of Fallot, the aorta lies immediately above which defect, and what is that position called? The answer is that it lies immediately above the ventricular septal defect, a position called overriding. The aorticopulmonary septum has deviated, so the aorta sits over the hole and blood from both ventricles can enter it.

Question 10590. True or false: a cleft lip results from failure of the maxillary process to fuse with the medial nasal process. The answer is true. The two processes meet on each side of the upper lip and normally merge. When they do not, a gap is left, which may reach into the nose and the palate.

Question 10591. Which pair belongs together: anencephaly with failure of the cranial neuropore to close, spina bifida with failure of the cranial neuropore, a cleft palate with failure of the neural tube, or a patent ductus arteriosus with failure of the neural crest to migrate? The answer is anencephaly with failure of the cranial neuropore. Spina bifida belongs to the caudal opening and a cleft palate to the facial processes.

Question 10592. In which anomaly is the lower part of the cerebellum and the brainstem displaced downward through the foramen magnum? The answer is the Chiari malformation. The common form is associated with a myelomeningocele and with hydrocephalus, and the displaced tissue can block the flow of cerebrospinal fluid.

Question 10593. A child has a patch of hair and a dimple over the lower spine, with no sac, and a vertebral arch is missing beneath the skin. Which defect is this: spina bifida occulta, a myelomeningocele, an encephalocele, or a meningocele? The answer is spina bifida occulta. The arch is missing, but the cord and its coverings stay inside the canal.

Question 10594. A constructed illustration: a newborn has no cranial vault above the orbits, and the tissue at the top of the head is degenerated. Which defect has occurred, and at which end of the neural tube? The answer is anencephaly, from failure of the cranial neuropore to close during the fourth week. Without a closed tube the vault cannot form over the brain.

Question 10595. On a described chest radiograph of a child with coarctation of the aorta, small notches are seen along which border of which ribs? The answer is along the inferior border of the third to the eighth ribs. The enlarged intercostal arteries press on the bone from below and hollow it out.

Question 10596. A constructed illustration: a newborn with a large ventricular septal defect is breathless and feeds poorly, and a loud murmur is heard over the left side of the chest. Which structure carries the extra blood flow? The answer is the pulmonary trunk, since blood is shunted from the left ventricle into the lungs. The murmur comes from the turbulent flow rather than from the hole itself.

Question 10597. A double aortic arch forms a complete ring around which pair of structures: the trachea and the esophagus, the aorta and the pulmonary trunk, the two bronchi, or the two recurrent laryngeal nerves? The answer is the trachea and the esophagus. The two arches pass on either side of them and compress both, so the infant wheezes and feeds poorly.

Question 10598. A constructed illustration: a premature infant has a machinery murmur, and the vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta has stayed open. Which structure is involved, and why does blood flow from the aorta into the lungs? The answer is the ductus arteriosus. After birth the aortic pressure is higher, so blood runs the other way and the lungs receive too much.

Question 10599. A described section of a heart shows a single large atrioventricular opening with a common valve, a defect in the lower part of the atrial septum and a defect in the upper part of the ventricular septum. Which anomaly is shown? The answer is a common atrioventricular canal. The endocardial cushions have failed to fuse, so the septa above and below stay incomplete.

Question 10600. A newborn is in respiratory distress, and loops of bowel are found in the left side of the chest. Which structure failed to close the opening through which they entered: the pleuroperitoneal membrane, the septum transversum, the dorsal mesentery, or the pleuropericardial membrane? The answer is the pleuroperitoneal membrane, which closes the pleuroperitoneal canal. When it fails, the abdominal contents herniate into the chest.

To summarize, the heart begins as two endocardial tubes that fuse into a single tube, which loops to the right and is then divided by the aorticopulmonary septum, the endocardial cushions and the parts of the interventricular septum. The aortic arches, the cardinal veins and the umbilical and vitelline veins leave behind the great vessels and their adult remnants, among them the ligamentum arteriosum, the ligamentum teres, the ligamentum venosum and the fossa ovalis. The nervous system comes from the neural plate, closes first in the cervical region and divides into five secondary vesicles, while the neural crest supplies the sensory and autonomic ganglia, the Schwann cells, the adrenal medulla, and the pia mater and arachnoid mater. The skeleton and the muscles come from the somites, whose sclerotome, myotome and dermatome become the vertebrae, the muscles and the skin of the back, while the limb bud grows under the apical ectodermal ridge. Congenital defects are the visible record of a step that did not finish, from the septal defects and tetralogy of Fallot to the neural tube defects, the cleft lip and palate, and the anomalies of the hip and the cervical spine. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 107 — Neighboring Structures

This chapter explores the structures that lie next to one another throughout the body, from the front of the neck to the ankle, and asks which neighbor is which. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately and then explains why it is right. Neighboring relations are what a listener needs at the bedside, where a structure is found by the landmarks around it. This is educational material and supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10601. Which structure lies immediately posterior to the isthmus of the thyroid gland in the front of the neck? The answer is the trachea. The isthmus crosses the front of the airway, usually over the second, third, and fourth tracheal rings. The two lobes wrap around the sides of the larynx and the trachea.

Question 10602. Which of these structures lies within the carotid sheath in the neck: the phrenic nerve, the internal jugular vein, the sympathetic trunk, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the internal jugular vein. The sheath also holds the common carotid artery and the vagus nerve. The phrenic nerve lies on the front of the scalenus anterior, and the sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath.

Question 10603. Within the carotid sheath, where does the vagus nerve lie in relation to the common carotid artery and the internal jugular vein? The answer is behind both and between them. The vein lies lateral to the artery, and the nerve runs in the groove behind them. That is why the nerve is reached last when the sheath is opened.

Question 10604. A described transverse section of the neck passes through the middle of the thyroid gland, with a ring of gland around the airway. Which structure lies immediately posterolateral to each lobe? The answer is the carotid sheath. It holds the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies nearer the midline.

Question 10605. A constructed illustration: a surgeon frees the lower pole of the thyroid gland, near the inferior thyroid artery, and the voice becomes hoarse afterwards. Which nerve lies at risk there? The answer is the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It ascends in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus, behind the gland. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10606. True or false: the parathyroid glands usually lie against the posterior surface of the thyroid gland. The answer is true. There are usually four of them, two on each side, tucked against the back of the lobes. The upper pair sits near the middle of the lobe and the lower pair near its lower pole.

Question 10607. Which salivary gland curves around the posterior border of the mylohyoid muscle, so that part of it lies above that muscle in the floor of the mouth? The answer is the submandibular gland. Its superficial part lies below the muscle and its deep part above it. The sublingual gland lies entirely above the muscle.

Question 10608. Which of these structures passes through the parotid gland: the facial nerve, the hypoglossal nerve, the lingual nerve, or the maxillary artery? The answer is the facial nerve. Its trunk divides inside the gland into branches that fan out across the face. The maxillary artery lies deep to the gland, and the hypoglossal and lingual nerves lie lower.

Question 10609. After leaving the front of the parotid gland, which muscle does the parotid duct cross before it pierces the cheek? The answer is the masseter. The duct runs forward across the surface of that muscle, turns inward at its front border, and pierces the buccinator opposite the upper second molar tooth. The facial nerve crosses the same muscle, but higher up.

Question 10610. Name the two muscles that form the floor of the submandibular triangle. The answer is the mylohyoid and the hyoglossus. The mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the mouth, and the hyoglossus lies deep to it. The submandibular gland rests on both, and the hypoglossal and lingual nerves pass between them.

Question 10611. A described specimen of the side of the neck shows a vein running obliquely across a broad strap muscle spanning from the mastoid region to the sternum and the clavicle. Which vein is shown? The answer is the external jugular vein. It lies superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein.

Question 10612. Which of these cranial nerves runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus: the sixth, the fourth, the optic, or the twelfth? The answer is the fourth cranial nerve. The third and the first and second divisions of the fifth lie in the same wall. The sixth nerve passes through the cavity of the sinus itself.

Question 10613. Within the cavernous sinus, which cranial nerve lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery as the artery runs forward? The answer is the sixth cranial nerve. It crosses the cavity of the sinus rather than lying in its wall, and it is the only cranial nerve that does so. That relation explains why it is often affected early by disease there.

Question 10614. A constructed illustration: a patient has a drooping upper eyelid, a fixed and dilated pupil, and double vision, with the eye turned outward. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the third cranial nerve. It supplies the muscle that lifts the upper lid and most of the muscles that move the eye. The sixth nerve could weaken one muscle but could not drop the lid.

Question 10615. Which of these passes through the superior orbital fissure: the optic nerve, the ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve, the ophthalmic artery, or the maxillary nerve? The answer is the ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve. The third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves pass through the same fissure. The optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery use the optic canal instead.

Question 10616. Which cavity of the skull lies immediately above the roof of the orbit, separated from it by a thin plate of bone? The answer is the anterior cranial fossa. The roof of the orbit is formed by the orbital plate of the frontal bone, and the frontal lobe rests on its upper surface. The floor of the orbit lies above the maxillary sinus.

Question 10617. True or false: the medial wall of the orbit is thinner than its roof and its floor. The answer is true. The medial wall is formed largely by the paper-thin orbital plate of the ethmoid bone. The roof is the orbital plate of the frontal bone, and the floor is the orbital surface of the maxilla, and both are stouter.

Question 10618. A described coronal section through the orbits shows the eyeballs on each side of the nasal cavity, with a thin plate of bone between the orbit and the ethmoid air cells. Which wall of the orbit is being cut? The answer is the medial wall. It separates the orbit from the ethmoid air cells and the nasal cavity.

Question 10619. Into which of the nasal meatuses does the nasolacrimal duct open? The answer is the inferior meatus. The duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac down the side of the nose and opens beneath the inferior nasal concha. The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus instead.

Question 10620. Which pair belongs together: the maxillary sinus with the inferior meatus, the frontal sinus with the middle meatus, the posterior ethmoid cells with the inferior meatus, or the sphenoid sinus with the middle meatus? The answer is the frontal sinus with the middle meatus. The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus too. The posterior ethmoid cells open into the superior meatus and the sphenoid sinus above it.

Question 10621. The floor of the maxillary sinus lies immediately above which structures: the roots of the upper molar teeth, the hard palate, the zygomatic arch, or the temporalis muscle? The answer is the roots of the upper molar teeth. The floor is formed by the alveolar process, and its thin bone may be pierced by the roots. A dental infection can spread into the sinus.

Question 10622. A constructed illustration: a person has bleeding from one nostril after a blow to the front of the nose. Which region of the nasal cavity, rich in anastomosing vessels, is the usual source? The answer is the anterior part of the nasal septum. Several arteries meet there in a plexus on the mucosa. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10623. A transverse section is taken through the middle of the orbit, cutting the eyeball and the optic nerve. Does the lacrimal gland lie medial or lateral to the eyeball at that level? The answer is lateral. The gland sits in a fossa in the frontal bone at the upper outer corner of the orbit. The medial side of the section holds the ethmoid air cells.

Question 10624. Which muscle lies immediately deep to the zygomatic arch: the temporalis, the masseter, the medial pterygoid, or the lateral pterygoid? The answer is the temporalis. It fills the temporal fossa, and its tendon passes deep to the arch to reach the coronoid process of the mandible. The masseter lies superficial to the arch and to the ramus of the mandible.

Question 10625. A described specimen of the infratemporal fossa shows a fan-shaped muscle filling the temporal fossa, a muscle running downward and backward to the angle of the mandible, and a nerve lying between them. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve. It enters through the foramen ovale and supplies the muscles of mastication.

Question 10626. Through which opening does the mental nerve leave the mandible? The answer is the mental foramen. It lies on the outer surface of the body of the mandible, below the second premolar tooth. The nerve is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and supplies the skin of the chin and the lower lip.

Question 10627. Which of these structures lies in the submental triangle: the submandibular gland, the submental lymph nodes, the hypoglossal nerve, or the external carotid artery? The answer is the submental lymph nodes. The triangle is bounded by the two anterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the hyoid bone, with the mylohyoid as its floor. The submandibular gland lies in the triangle beside it.

Question 10628. In the posterior triangle of the neck, on which muscle does the accessory nerve run before it disappears beneath the trapezius? The answer is the levator scapulae. The nerve crosses the floor of the triangle just above the middle of that muscle. It is superficial there, which is why it is easily injured.

Question 10629. Between which two muscles does the brachial plexus emerge in the neck: the anterior and middle scalene, the middle and posterior scalene, the sternocleidomastoid and the anterior scalene, or the trapezius and the levator scapulae? The answer is the anterior and middle scalene. The subclavian artery also passes between them. The posterior scalene lies behind the middle scalene.

Question 10630. Which nerve lies on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle as it descends through the neck? The answer is the phrenic nerve. It runs almost vertically down the front of that muscle and then passes in front of the subclavian artery into the thorax. It is the motor nerve of the diaphragm.

Question 10631. A described radiograph of the cervical spine shows a vertical canal running through the side of each vertebra from the sixth upward. Which vessel passes through that canal? The answer is the vertebral artery. It enters the canal at the sixth cervical vertebra and ascends to the skull. Its first part lies between the anterior scalene muscle and the longus colli.

Question 10632. Which of these statements about the cervical sympathetic trunk is correct: it lies within the carotid sheath, it lies immediately behind the carotid sheath, it lies within the pretracheal fascia, or it lies in front of the trachea? The answer is that it lies behind the carotid sheath. It runs on the prevertebral muscles, separated from the sheath by the prevertebral fascia. The vagus nerve lies inside the sheath.

Question 10633. True or false: in the thorax the thoracic duct lies on the right of the midline for the whole of its course. The answer is false. It ascends first on the right and then crosses to the left at about the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra. It continues upward behind the esophagus and the arch of the aorta.

Question 10634. The recurrent laryngeal nerve on the right side loops around which structure: the arch of the aorta, the right subclavian artery, the right common carotid artery, or the first rib? The answer is the right subclavian artery. On the left, the nerve loops under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum. Both then ascend between the trachea and the esophagus.

Question 10635. In the thorax, how do the phrenic nerve and the vagus nerve lie in relation to the root of the lung? The answer is that the phrenic nerve lies in front of the root and the vagus nerve behind it. Both descend through the mediastinum on opposite sides of the root. The phrenic nerve continues to the diaphragm.

Question 10636. At which bony landmark does the trachea divide into its two main bronchi? The answer is the sternal angle. Behind it the trachea bifurcates, at the lower border of the fourth thoracic vertebra. The arch of the aorta also begins and ends at that level, and the second costal cartilage joins the sternum there.

Question 10637. Which structure lies immediately behind the left atrium of the heart: the esophagus, the trachea, the thymus, or the sternum? The answer is the esophagus. The left atrium forms much of the posterior surface of the heart, and the esophagus runs behind it in the posterior mediastinum. The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum.

Question 10638. A described lateral radiograph of the chest shows a narrow vertical channel passing down behind the heart shadow and in front of the vertebral bodies. Which structure is shown? The answer is the esophagus. It descends first behind the trachea and then behind the left atrium. The descending aorta lies behind it and slightly to the left.

Question 10639. A constructed illustration: a person has difficulty swallowing, and imaging shows a very large left atrium. Given its position, which structure is most likely compressed? The answer is the esophagus. The left atrium forms the posterior surface of the heart, and the esophagus lies directly behind it. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10640. Which statement about the two main bronchi is correct: the right is narrower and longer, the right is wider and more vertical, the two are equal in width, or the left is wider? The answer is that the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical. That is why an inhaled foreign body more often enters the right side. The left main bronchus runs more horizontally.

Question 10641. Which vein arches over the root of the right lung before it joins the superior vena cava? The answer is the azygos vein. It drains the posterior wall of the abdomen and the thorax and ascends on the right of the vertebral column. On the left the corresponding vein is the hemiazygos, which does not arch over the lung root.

Question 10642. In the costal groove, which of these lists the intercostal structures in the correct order from above downward: artery, vein, nerve; vein, artery, nerve; nerve, vein, artery; or vein, nerve, artery? The answer is vein, then artery, then nerve. They run between the internal and the innermost intercostal muscles, sheltered by the lower border of the rib. The nerve lies lowest and is the most exposed.

Question 10643. The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra, and which two structures pass through it? The answer is the twelfth thoracic vertebra, with the aorta and the thoracic duct. The esophageal hiatus lies at the tenth thoracic vertebra and the opening for the inferior vena cava at the eighth. Each opening carries its own contents.

Question 10644. A described computed tomography section of the thorax at the level of the aortic arch shows a curved vessel passing backward on the left of the trachea, and a smaller vessel crossing in front of the vertebral column on the right. Which two structures are shown? The answer is the aortic arch and the azygos vein. The arch passes over the left main bronchus.

Question 10645. Which structure occupies the anterior mediastinum in a child, lying in front of the aortic arch and the brachiocephalic veins: the thymus, the trachea, the esophagus, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the thymus. It is largest in childhood and shrinks with age, but remains as fatty tissue in the adult. The thoracic duct lies in the posterior mediastinum.

Question 10646. Under which structure does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loop before it ascends to the larynx? The answer is the arch of the aorta. The nerve hooks beneath the arch, just behind the ligamentum arteriosum, and then climbs between the trachea and the esophagus. On the right it loops under the right subclavian artery.

Question 10647. Which structure lies immediately behind the root of the left lung: the descending aorta, the superior vena cava, the right atrium, or the thymus? The answer is the descending aorta. It runs down the posterior mediastinum and forms a groove on the medial surface of the left lung. The superior vena cava lies on the right side.

Question 10648. A constructed illustration: a person has a fracture of a lower rib, and the fragment turns inward into the costal groove. Which structure in the groove is most exposed to injury? The answer is the intercostal nerve, which lies lowest. The intercostal artery lies above it and the intercostal vein above that. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10649. Which pair belongs together: the aortic hiatus with the twelfth thoracic vertebra, the esophageal hiatus with the twelfth, the caval opening with the tenth, or the esophageal hiatus with the eighth? The answer is the aortic hiatus with the twelfth thoracic vertebra. The esophageal hiatus lies at the tenth and the caval opening at the eighth.

Question 10650. A described cross-section of the thorax at the level where the trachea has just divided shows two bronchi, two large vessels, and a muscular tube lying behind the left bronchus. Which structure is that tube? The answer is the esophagus. It lies behind the left main bronchus and in front of the descending aorta.

Question 10651. Which structure lies immediately medial to the second part of the duodenum: the head of the pancreas, the right kidney, the gallbladder, or the transverse colon? The answer is the head of the pancreas. The second part descends in front of the right kidney, and the head of the pancreas lies in its curve. The gallbladder lies above the first part.

Question 10652. Against which ribs does the spleen lie in the left upper abdomen? The answer is the ninth, tenth, and eleventh ribs. The spleen sits in the left hypochondrium, behind the stomach and above the left kidney. Its long axis follows the line of the tenth rib, and the diaphragm separates it from the left pleural cavity.

Question 10653. Which two vessels lie immediately behind the neck of the pancreas: the superior mesenteric artery and vein, the aorta and the inferior vena cava, the splenic vessels, or the left renal vessels? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery and vein. The neck passes in front of them and the uncinate process hooks behind. The splenic vessels run along the upper border of the body.

Question 10654. Which large vein crosses in front of the abdominal aorta, between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery, on its way to the inferior vena cava? The answer is the left renal vein. It is longer than the right renal vein, which runs a short course to the inferior vena cava. The left gonadal and suprarenal veins drain into it.

Question 10655. A described computed tomography section of the upper abdomen shows a long gland across the midline in front of two large vessels. Which gland is shown, and which vessels lie behind its neck? The answer is the pancreas, with the superior mesenteric artery and vein behind its neck. The body lies in front of the aorta, and the splenic vein runs along its back.

Question 10656. Where is the portal vein formed: behind the neck of the pancreas, in front of the liver, at the hilum of the spleen, or within the lesser omentum? The answer is behind the neck of the pancreas. There the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein. It then ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum.

Question 10657. Why does the right kidney lie lower than the left kidney in the normal body? The answer is the size of the liver. The right lobe of the liver occupies the space above the right kidney and presses it downward. The left kidney lies higher, with the spleen and the stomach above it, and the right kidney lies against the duodenum.

Question 10658. Which structure crosses in front of the third part of the duodenum: the superior mesenteric artery, the inferior mesenteric artery, the common bile duct, or the portal vein? The answer is the superior mesenteric artery. The third part runs across the aorta and is crossed by the artery and its vein. The common bile duct lies behind the first part.

Question 10659. Name two large vessels that lie immediately posterior to the body of the pancreas. The answer is the aorta and the splenic vein. The body of the pancreas lies in front of the aorta and the superior mesenteric vessels, and the splenic vein runs in a groove on its posterior surface. The inferior vena cava lies further to the right.

Question 10660. A described radiograph of the abdomen shows the outlines of two bean-shaped organs on either side of the spine, the right one lower than the left. Which organs are shown, and what caps each above? The answer is the kidneys, each capped by an adrenal gland. The right kidney lies lower because of the liver above it.

Question 10661. Which statement about the appendix is correct: its base lies one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, it arises from the sigmoid colon, it lies within the lesser sac, or it always hangs over the pelvic brim? The answer is that its base lies there. The appendix arises from the cecum, and its position varies.

Question 10662. Where does the fundus of the gallbladder lie in relation to the anterior abdominal wall? The answer is at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage. The fundus projects below the inferior border of the liver and touches the anterior abdominal wall. The body rests against the duodenum and the transverse colon.

Question 10663. The ureter crosses the pelvic brim immediately in front of which structure: the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, the sacroiliac joint, the fifth lumbar vertebra, or the rectum? The answer is the bifurcation of the common iliac artery. The ureter then runs down the lateral wall of the pelvis in front of the internal iliac artery.

Question 10664. In the female pelvis, how does the ureter lie in relation to the uterine artery and the cervix? The answer is that it passes behind the uterine artery and lateral to the cervix. The artery crosses above it, which is why they are said to cross like a bridge over water. The ureter then enters the bladder.

Question 10665. A constructed illustration: during an operation in the female pelvis, a structure running behind the uterine artery and beside the cervix is divided, and urine later leaks from the vagina. Which structure was injured? The answer is the ureter. It passes close to the cervix before it enters the bladder. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10666. A described sagittal section of the male pelvis shows the bladder in front, a muscular tube behind it, and a gland below the bladder. Which structure lies directly between the bladder and the rectum? The answer is the seminal vesicle with the ampulla of the ductus deferens. The prostate lies below the bladder and is pierced by the urethra. The rectum lies behind them.

Question 10667. Which structure lies immediately in front of the rectum in the male: the prostate and the seminal vesicles, the sacrum, the coccyx, or the pubic symphysis? The answer is the prostate and the seminal vesicles. The prostate lies below the bladder and behind the pubic symphysis. The bladder lies above both.

Question 10668. What is the name of the peritoneal pouch that lies behind the cervix and in front of the rectum in the female? The answer is the rectouterine pouch. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when a person is standing. The corresponding pouch in the male lies between the bladder and the rectum.

Question 10669. Which statement about the inferior vena cava is correct: it lies to the left of the aorta, it lies to the right of the aorta behind the liver, it passes through the aortic hiatus, or it lies in front of the liver? The answer is that it lies to the right of the aorta and behind the liver. In the bare area it touches the liver directly.

Question 10670. Which pair belongs together: the left kidney with the spleen above it, the right kidney with the stomach above it, the left kidney with the liver above it, or the right kidney with the spleen above it? The answer is the left kidney with the spleen above it. The right kidney has the liver above it and the stomach in front.

Question 10671. A described magnetic resonance image of the female pelvis shows a pear-shaped organ in the midline, with a fold of peritoneum over it and a tube curving laterally. Which organ is shown, and what lies behind its lower part? The answer is the uterus, with the rectum behind the cervix. The bladder lies in front, and the ureters pass close to the cervix.

Question 10672. A lumbar puncture is performed at the third and fourth lumbar interspace. At which level does the spinal cord normally end: the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra, the fifth lumbar vertebra, the twelfth thoracic vertebra, or the second sacral vertebra? The answer is the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra. Below it lies the cauda equina. The dural sac ends lower still.

Question 10673. A constructed illustration: the gallbladder of a person becomes inflamed, and the inflammation spreads to the parts of the bowel that touch it. Which two parts would most likely be involved? The answer is the first part of the duodenum and the transverse colon. Its body rests against both. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10674. Which four organs form the bed on which the stomach rests when a person lies on the back? The answer is the spleen, the pancreas, the left kidney, and the left adrenal gland. The transverse colon and its mesocolon also lie against the back of the stomach. All of these lie behind the stomach in the left upper abdomen.

Question 10675. Which structures lie immediately posterior to the ascending colon: the right kidney and the duodenum, the spleen and the pancreas, the left kidney and the left ureter, or the stomach and the liver? The answer is the right kidney and the duodenum. The ascending colon lies on the posterior abdominal wall. On the left, the descending colon lies against the left kidney.

Question 10676. Where does the sciatic nerve lie in the gluteal region in relation to the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter? The answer is about midway between the two, deep to the gluteus maximus. It emerges from the pelvis below the piriformis muscle. It is the largest nerve in the body and passes down the back of the thigh.

Question 10677. A described transverse section through the gluteal region shows the sciatic nerve lying on the posterior surface of a muscle that fills the buttock, with a smaller muscle above it. Which two muscles are these? The answer is the gluteus maximus over the nerve and the piriformis above it. The gluteus medius lies higher and more lateral.

Question 10678. Which structures leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle: the superior gluteal nerve and vessels, the sciatic nerve, the pudendal nerve, or the inferior gluteal nerve? The answer is the superior gluteal nerve and vessels. The sciatic, inferior gluteal, and pudendal nerves all leave below the piriformis.

Question 10679. Which nerve hooks around the ischial spine and the sacrospinous ligament before it re-enters the pelvis? The answer is the pudendal nerve. It leaves the pelvis below the piriformis, winds around the spine, and passes through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal. From there it supplies the perineum.

Question 10680. True or false: in the femoral triangle the femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery. The answer is true. The nerve lies outside the femoral sheath, while the artery and the vein lie inside it. From lateral to medial the order is nerve, artery, vein, and then the femoral canal.

Question 10681. Within the femoral sheath, which of these describes the arrangement from lateral to medial: vein, artery, canal; artery, vein, canal; canal, vein, artery; or artery, canal, vein? The answer is artery, then vein, then canal. The femoral canal occupies the most medial compartment and contains lymph nodes. The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath.

Question 10682. Which pair belongs together: the axillary nerve with the quadrangular space, the radial nerve with the carpal tunnel, the median nerve with the spiral groove, or the ulnar nerve with the cubital fossa? The answer is the axillary nerve with the quadrangular space. The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove and the median nerve through the carpal tunnel.

Question 10683. Which vein lies immediately in front of the medial malleolus at the ankle? The answer is the great saphenous vein. It ascends in front of the medial malleolus and then along the medial side of the leg and the thigh. It ends by joining the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament.

Question 10684. Behind the medial malleolus, which structure lies immediately behind the tendon of the tibialis posterior: the flexor digitorum longus, the Achilles tendon, the sural nerve, or the small saphenous vein? The answer is the flexor digitorum longus. From front to back the order is tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery, the tibial nerve, and the flexor hallucis longus.

Question 10685. A described coronal magnetic resonance image of the ankle shows a rounded bony prominence on the inner side, with several tendons and a nerve passing behind it in a tunnel. Which nerve lies within that tunnel? The answer is the tibial nerve. It runs behind the medial malleolus with the posterior tibial artery. The tunnel is roofed by the flexor retinaculum.

Question 10686. A constructed illustration: a person fractures the neck of the fibula and afterwards cannot lift the foot, so the toes drag when walking. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the common fibular nerve. It winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is superficial and easily damaged. The tibial nerve lies behind the medial malleolus.

Question 10687. In the popliteal fossa, which structure lies most deeply, against the capsule of the knee joint: the popliteal artery, the popliteal vein, the tibial nerve, or the common fibular nerve? The answer is the popliteal artery. The popliteal vein lies superficial to it and the tibial nerve more superficial still. The common fibular nerve runs along the lateral wall.

Question 10688. In the cubital fossa, on which side of the brachial artery does the median nerve lie? The answer is the medial side. Within the fossa the structures lie in a line from lateral to medial: the radial nerve, the tendon of the biceps, the brachial artery, and the median nerve. The artery ends by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries.

Question 10689. In the wrist, how does the median nerve lie in relation to the flexor retinaculum and to the tendons that share the carpal tunnel with it? The answer is that the nerve lies deep to the retinaculum, within the tunnel, and superficial to the tendons. It is the most superficial structure in the carpal tunnel. The ulnar nerve passes outside the tunnel.

Question 10690. Which nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist, alongside the ulnar artery: the ulnar nerve, the median nerve, the radial nerve, or the anterior interosseous nerve? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It passes through a small canal on the medial side of the wrist, outside the carpal tunnel. The median nerve passes deep to the retinaculum.

Question 10691. A described transverse section through the wrist shows a fibrous band over a row of tendons, with a single nerve just beneath the band and a small nerve and artery outside it. Which nerve lies beneath the band? The answer is the median nerve. The ulnar nerve and artery lie outside, on the little finger side.

Question 10692. True or false: the axillary vein lies in front of and medial to the axillary artery. The answer is true. The vein lies closest to the front of the axilla and partly overlaps the artery. The cords of the brachial plexus lie lateral, medial, and posterior to the artery.

Question 10693. Which cord of the brachial plexus lies immediately behind the axillary artery? The answer is the posterior cord. It gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves. The lateral and medial cords lie in front of the artery, one on each side of it.

Question 10694. Beneath which ligament does the suprascapular nerve pass as it enters the back of the shoulder region? The answer is the transverse scapular ligament. The nerve runs through the suprascapular foramen, while the suprascapular artery passes above the ligament. The nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles.

Question 10695. A constructed illustration: a person fractures the middle of the humerus and afterwards cannot extend the wrist or the fingers. Which nerve has been injured, and where does it run? The answer is the radial nerve, in the spiral groove on the back of the humerus. It lies between the medial and lateral heads of the triceps. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10696. Which of these pairs belongs together: the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal nerve, the cricothyroid membrane with the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the trapezius with the median nerve, or the diaphragm with the ulnar nerve? The answer is the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal nerve. Its internal branch pierces the membrane to supply the larynx above the vocal folds.

Question 10697. A sagittal section is taken through the chest just to the left of the midline. Which chamber of the heart lies directly behind the sternum in that section? The answer is the right ventricle. It is the most anterior chamber and lies behind the sternum and the left costal cartilages. The left ventricle lies behind it and to the left.

Question 10698. Name two structures that lie in the popliteal fossa behind the knee. The answer is the popliteal artery and the tibial nerve. The popliteal vein and the common fibular nerve also pass through the fossa. The artery lies deepest, against the joint capsule, and the tibial nerve is the most superficial.

Question 10699. A constructed illustration: a person dislocates the shoulder, and afterwards the shoulder is flattened and a patch of skin over the deltoid is numb. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the axillary nerve. It winds through the quadrangular space close to the surgical neck of the humerus. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10700. Which nerve lies in the groove behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, beside the superior ulnar collateral artery? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It is the nerve that produces tingling in the little finger when the elbow is struck. It then passes between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris into the forearm.

To summarize, a structure is remembered by the neighbors it keeps: the thyroid isthmus lies in front of the trachea, the carotid sheath holds the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs behind the gland between the trachea and the esophagus. The parotid duct crosses the masseter, the submandibular gland hooks around the mylohyoid, and the fourth cranial nerve runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus while the sixth passes through its cavity. The phrenic nerve lies in front of the root of the lung and the vagus behind it, and the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve lie in that order from above downward. The pancreas lies in front of the aorta and the superior mesenteric vessels, the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta, and the spleen, the pancreas, the left kidney, and the left adrenal gland form the bed of the stomach. The ureter passes behind the uterine artery, the sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis below the piriformis, the femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery, and the median nerve lies deep to the flexor retinaculum while the ulnar nerve passes outside it. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 108 — Anatomical Spaces

Anatomical spaces are the rooms of the body: the fossae of the skull, the compartments of the mediastinum, the recesses of the peritoneal cavity, and the fossae and canals of the limbs. This chapter describes the walls, the contents, and the openings of those spaces, together with the fascial compartments whose septa divide the limbs into groups of muscles. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question and then explains why that answer is right. Most of these items therefore ask for a boundary or a relation rather than for a name alone. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10701. Which cone-shaped bony space of the skull holds the eyeball, its muscles, and the optic nerve, and is bounded above by the frontal bone and below by the maxilla? The answer is the orbit. Its roof separates it from the anterior cranial fossa, and its floor separates it from the maxillary sinus. The medial wall is the thinnest wall and the lateral wall the thickest.

Question 10702. Which of these openings lies between the lateral wall and the floor of the orbit: the optic canal, the superior orbital fissure, the inferior orbital fissure, or the infraorbital foramen? The answer is the inferior orbital fissure. It carries the maxillary nerve and the infraorbital vessels, which run forward in the floor of the orbit and leave by the infraorbital foramen below the eye.

Question 10703.
