The superior orbital fissure lies between which two parts of the sphenoid bone: the body and the lesser wing, the lesser wing and the greater wing, the greater wing and the frontal bone, or the maxilla and the zygomatic bone? The answer is between the lesser wing and the greater wing. The oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, and abducens nerves pass through it.

Question 10704. A described coronal section through the face shows a narrow cavity divided in the middle by a vertical plate of bone and cartilage, with three curled bony shelves on each side wall and an opening below each shelf. Which cavity is described? The answer is the nasal cavity. The vertical plate is the nasal septum, and the curled shelves are the superior, middle, and inferior nasal conchae, which overhang the meatuses beneath them.

Question 10705. Which structure forms the midline partition of the nasal cavity, built from the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and the vomer below? The answer is the nasal septum. The septal cartilage fills the front of the partition between those two bones. A deviated septum is a common variant and narrows one nasal passage without disturbing the other.

Question 10706. Which of these air-filled cavities opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha: the frontal sinus, the maxillary sinus, the sphenoidal sinus, or the anterior ethmoidal air cells? The answer is the sphenoidal sinus. The posterior ethmoidal air cells open into the superior meatus just below it. The frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal cells all open into the middle meatus.

Question 10707. A described radiograph of the face after a blow to the eye shows the floor of the orbit sagging downward into the maxillary sinus, with a soft tissue shadow hanging from the broken edge. Which structure is most likely trapped there, and which nerve is at risk? The answer is the inferior rectus muscle, with the infraorbital nerve at risk. The thin floor gives way before the bony rim does.

Question 10708. The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit, the nasal cavity, the infratemporal fossa, and the middle cranial fossa. Which of these openings carries the maxillary nerve into the back of the fossa: the inferior orbital fissure, the sphenopalatine foramen, the foramen rotundum, or the pterygoid canal? The answer is the foramen rotundum.

Question 10709. Which small pyramid-shaped space lies behind the maxilla, in front of the pterygoid plates, and below the apex of the orbit, and contains the maxillary nerve and the pterygopalatine ganglion? The answer is the pterygopalatine fossa. Every wall of it is pierced by an opening, which is why a lesion there can cause pain in the face, the nose, and the palate at the same time.

Question 10710. Which of these structures lies in the infratemporal fossa, below and behind the maxilla: the maxillary artery, the internal carotid artery, the ophthalmic artery, or the facial artery? The answer is the maxillary artery. It crosses the fossa and gives off the middle meningeal and inferior alveolar branches there. The facial artery crosses the lower border of the mandible at the front.

Question 10711. A described lateral view of the skull shows a broad shallow depression on the side of the head, bounded above by a curved line and below by an arch of bone that runs forward to the cheek. Which space is shown, and which muscle fills it? The answer is the temporal fossa, filled by the temporalis muscle, which passes deep to the zygomatic arch to reach the jaw.

Question 10712. A constructed illustration: a deep cut in front of the ear divides branches of a nerve that fan out across the side of the face, and the forehead on that side cannot be wrinkled. Which space has been entered, and which nerve is injured? The answer is the parotid space and the facial nerve. The nerve divides inside the parotid gland, so a wound there can split it into separate branches.

Question 10713. Which of these pairs belongs together: the temporal fossa with the temporalis muscle, the pterygopalatine fossa with the masseter muscle, the infratemporal fossa with the orbicularis oculi, or the orbit with the medial pterygoid muscle? The answer is the temporal fossa with the temporalis muscle. The masseter lies outside the ramus of the mandible, and the pterygoid muscles lie in the infratemporal fossa.

Question 10714. Which space lies in the floor of the mouth above the mylohyoid muscle, between the tongue and the mandible, and holds the sublingual gland and the deep part of the submandibular gland? The answer is the sublingual space. It wraps around the back of the mylohyoid to reach the submandibular space, so infection can pass between the two.

Question 10715. Which muscle forms the floor of the submandibular space: the geniohyoid, the mylohyoid, the hyoglossus, or the digastric? The answer is the mylohyoid. It runs from the mandible to the hyoid bone and separates the sublingual space above from the submandibular space below. The digastric lies below it and does not form the floor.

Question 10716. True or false: the retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia in front and the alar fascia behind, and the danger space lies behind the alar fascia. The answer is true. The alar fascia is the thin sheet that divides the two. Because both spaces reach the upper chest, infection in the neck can travel down into the mediastinum.

Question 10717. Which space of the neck lies immediately behind the alar fascia and in front of the prevertebral fascia, and runs from the base of the skull down to the diaphragm? The answer is the danger space. It communicates freely with the posterior mediastinum, which is why infection in it travels so far before it is noticed.

Question 10718. Name the three main structures that lie together inside the carotid sheath of the neck. The answer is the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve. The artery lies medially, the vein laterally, and the nerve between and behind them.

Question 10719. A described cross section of the neck shows a wedge of fat lying between the muscles of the pharynx medially and the muscles of the jaw laterally, with the carotid sheath behind it. Which space is described, and why is it called the crossroads of the neck? The answer is the parapharyngeal space, which touches the parotid, the masticator, and the visceral spaces.

Question 10720. A constructed illustration: a collection of pus forms beside a tonsil and pushes the soft palate and the uvula toward the opposite side of the throat. Which space is involved, and which large vessel lies just outside its wall? The answer is the peritonsillar space, with the internal carotid artery nearby. That artery lies only a short distance lateral to the tonsil.

Question 10721. Which space lies in the middle of the chest between the two pleural sacs, behind the sternum and in front of the vertebral column? The answer is the mediastinum. It is divided into a superior part above the sternal angle and an inferior part below.

Question 10722. Which of these structures lies in the middle mediastinum: the heart and the pericardium, the thymus, the esophagus, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the heart and the pericardium. The middle mediastinum also holds the ascending aorta, the pulmonary trunk, and the phrenic nerves. The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum, and the esophagus and thoracic duct lie behind the pericardium.

Question 10723. A described sagittal section of the chest shows a muscular tube running down behind the heart, with a large vessel to its left, a smaller tube behind it, and a chain of nodes beside it. Which part of the mediastinum is shown, and which structures lie in it? The answer is the posterior mediastinum, with the esophagus, the descending aorta, the thoracic duct, and the azygos vein.

Question 10724. A horizontal plane is drawn through the sternal angle and the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. Which important levels does that plane mark? The answer is the plane between the superior mediastinum and the inferior mediastinum, and the level of the bifurcation of the trachea and of the second costal cartilage. It is also where the arch of the aorta begins and ends.

Question 10725. A described frontal radiograph of the chest shows a dark space at each side of the heart that reaches down into the angle between the diaphragm and the chest wall. Which space is shown, and what is the lowest part of it called? The answer is the pleural cavity, and its lowest part is the costodiaphragmatic recess, which the lung does not fill during quiet breathing.

Question 10726. During quiet breathing, which space remains unoccupied by lung at the lower border of the chest: the costomediastinal recess, the costodiaphragmatic recess, the oblique sinus, or the transverse sinus? The answer is the costodiaphragmatic recess. The lower border of the lung never reaches the lowest point of the pleural cavity.

Question 10727. When fluid collects in the pleural cavity, which of these places is the lowest point of the space in a person sitting upright: the costodiaphragmatic recess, the costomediastinal recess, the root of the lung, or the oblique sinus? The answer is the costodiaphragmatic recess. It is the most dependent part of the pleural cavity when the body is vertical.

Question 10728. Which passage of the pericardial cavity lies behind the aorta and the pulmonary trunk and in front of the superior vena cava, and joins the two sides of the cavity? The answer is the transverse sinus of the pericardium, through which a tube can be passed behind the great vessels. The oblique sinus lies behind the left atrium instead.

Question 10729. Which of these boundaries defines the oblique sinus: the reflection of serous pericardium around the four pulmonary veins and the inferior vena cava, the gap between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk, the fold over the superior vena cava, or the space between the two layers of fibrous pericardium? The answer is the reflection around the pulmonary veins and the inferior vena cava. The sinus lies behind the left atrium.

Question 10730. Which recess of the mediastinum lies to the right of the midline behind the esophagus, bounded above by the azygos vein and in front by the right atrium, and appears as a soft tissue line on a frontal chest radiograph? The answer is the azygoesophageal recess. It is a pleural reflection rather than part of the esophagus, and enlarged nodes can obliterate it.

Question 10731. True or false: the mediastinum is a single closed cavity with its own lining, separate from the two pleural cavities. The answer is false. The mediastinum is a region between the pleural sacs, not a cavity with a lining of its own, and its structures lie in loose connective tissue.

Question 10732. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior mediastinum with the thymus, the middle mediastinum with the esophagus, the posterior mediastinum with the heart, or the superior mediastinum with the rectum? The answer is the anterior mediastinum with the thymus. The heart lies in the middle mediastinum and the esophagus in the posterior part.

Question 10733. Which of these structures lies in the superior mediastinum: the arch of the aorta, the left ventricle, the right atrium, or the pericardium? The answer is the arch of the aorta. The superior mediastinum also holds the thymus, the trachea, the esophagus, and the thoracic duct.

Question 10734. A described transverse section at the top of the chest shows a kidney-shaped opening bounded behind by a vertebra, on each side by a first rib, and in front by the top of the sternum. Which opening is shown, and what passes through it? The answer is the superior thoracic aperture, through which pass the trachea, the esophagus, the great vessels, and the nerves to the upper limb.

Question 10735. Which part of the peritoneal cavity lies below the diaphragm and in front of the stomach and the transverse colon, and reaches the space behind the stomach through the epiploic foramen? The answer is the greater sac, which forms most of the peritoneal cavity. The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and the lesser omentum and is much smaller.

Question 10736. Which of these structures forms the anterior wall of the lesser sac: the stomach and the lesser omentum, the pancreas, the diaphragm, or the left kidney? The answer is the stomach and the lesser omentum. The posterior wall is formed by the pancreas and the posterior abdominal wall.

Question 10737. Which structures bound the epiploic foramen: in front the free edge of the lesser omentum with the portal vein, behind the peritoneum over the inferior vena cava, above the caudate lobe of the liver, and below which part of the gut? The answer is below the first part of the duodenum. Those four boundaries make the foramen the only natural way into the lesser sac.

Question 10738. A constructed illustration: a loop of bowel slips through the opening behind the free edge of the lesser omentum and becomes trapped in the space behind the stomach. Which opening is involved, and which structure in its front wall is at risk of compression? The answer is the epiploic foramen, with the portal vein at risk.

Question 10739. Which space lies between the diaphragm above and the liver below on the right side of the abdomen, and is divided by the falciform ligament into a right and a left part? The answer is the subphrenic space. The right part is divided again by the coronary ligament into an anterior and a posterior part.

Question 10740. A described frontal view of the abdominal cavity shows a channel running down the outer side of the ascending colon on the right and another down the outer side of the descending colon on the left. Which channels are shown, and where does fluid in them collect? The answer is the paracolic gutters. Fluid in the right gutter runs down toward the pelvic cavity.

Question 10741. Which of these recesses of the peritoneal cavity lies between the right kidney and the right lobe of the liver: the hepatorenal pouch, the splenorenal recess, the rectouterine pouch, or the vesicouterine pouch? The answer is the hepatorenal pouch. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in a person lying face upward, so fluid gathers there first.

Question 10742. Which of these pairs belongs together: the supracolic compartment with the stomach and the liver, the infracolic compartment with the rectum, the lesser sac with the spleen alone, or the greater sac with the kidneys? The answer is the supracolic compartment with the stomach and the liver. It lies above the transverse colon, and the infracolic compartment below it holds the coils of the small intestine.

Question 10743. A constructed illustration: after an infection within the abdomen, fluid gathers in the lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity, behind the uterus and in front of the rectum. Which space is involved, and which two organs lie immediately in front of it and behind it? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, with the uterus in front and the rectum behind.

Question 10744. Which pouch of the peritoneal cavity lies between the rectum behind and the uterus in front in the female, and is the lowest point of the cavity when she lies face upward? The answer is the rectouterine pouch, also called the pouch of Douglas. In the male the corresponding lowest point is the rectovesical pouch.

Question 10745. Which of these peritoneal pouches lies between the urinary bladder and the uterus: the rectouterine pouch, the vesicouterine pouch, the hepatorenal pouch, or the omental bursa? The answer is the vesicouterine pouch. It is shallower than the rectouterine pouch, which lies behind the uterus instead.

Question 10746. True or false: the kidneys, the ureters, and the ascending and descending parts of the colon lie behind the peritoneum and are therefore called retroperitoneal. The answer is true. They rest against the posterior abdominal wall and are covered by peritoneum only on the front. The stomach and the spleen lie within the peritoneal cavity instead.

Question 10747. Which space surrounds the kidney and its capsule, holds the perinephric fat, is bounded by the renal fascia, and encloses the adrenal gland as well? The answer is the perirenal space. It is closed above and open below toward the pelvis. The fat lying outside the renal fascia occupies the pararenal space.

Question 10748. A described transverse section through the abdomen shows a large vessel resting on the bodies of the vertebrae, a gland crossing in front of it, and two bean-shaped organs on either side behind a thin membrane. Which region is shown, and which great vessels lie in it at that level? The answer is the retroperitoneum, with the aorta and the inferior vena cava.

Question 10749. Which wedge-shaped space of fat lies on each side of the anal canal between the skin below and the levator ani above, and allows the canal to expand as the bowel opens? The answer is the ischioanal fossa. Its medial wall is the anal canal and the levator ani, and its lateral wall carries the pudendal canal.

Question 10750. Which of these structures runs in the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa: the internal pudendal artery and the pudendal nerve, the sciatic nerve, the obturator nerve, or the femoral artery? The answer is the internal pudendal artery and the pudendal nerve.

Question 10751. Which space lies immediately behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the urinary bladder, is filled with loose fat and veins, and can be entered without opening the peritoneal cavity? The answer is the retropubic space, also called the space of Retzius. It lies below and outside the peritoneum, which is why the bladder can be reached there.

Question 10752. Which of these spaces lies immediately outside the renal fascia and contains only fat: the perirenal space, the pararenal space, the lesser sac, or the rectovesical pouch? The answer is the pararenal space. The perirenal space, by contrast, lies inside the renal fascia and holds the kidney, the adrenal gland, and the perinephric fat.

Question 10753. Which of these spaces of the pelvis lies between the urinary bladder and the pubic bones: the rectovesical pouch, the retropubic space, the rectouterine pouch, or the ischioanal fossa? The answer is the retropubic space. It lies outside the peritoneal cavity and below the peritoneum, while the rectovesical pouch lies behind the bladder in the male.

Question 10754. Which pyramid-shaped space lies between the upper part of the arm and the side of the chest, with its apex pointing up toward the root of the neck and its base formed by the skin of the armpit? The answer is the axilla. It holds the axillary vessels and lymph nodes and the cords and branches of the brachial plexus.

Question 10755. Which of these structures lies in the axilla: the axillary artery and the brachial plexus, the femoral nerve, the sciatic nerve, or the median cubital vein? The answer is the axillary artery and the brachial plexus. The cords of the plexus surround the second part of the artery.

Question 10756. Which space of the shoulder region is bounded above by the teres minor, below by the teres major, medially by the long head of the triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus? The answer is the quadrangular space. The axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through it.

Question 10757. A constructed illustration: a fall on the shoulder drives the head of the humerus downward and the person cannot lift the arm away from the side, with numbness over the outer part of the shoulder. Which nerve is injured, and through which space does it run? The answer is the axillary nerve, which passes through the quadrangular space.

Question 10758. A described dissection of the back of the shoulder shows two gaps, one bounded above by the teres minor and below by the teres major, and a second beside the humerus with the teres major above it. Which two spaces are shown, and what passes through each? The answer is the triangular space, with the circumflex scapular artery, and the triangular interval, with the radial nerve.

Question 10759. Which of these pairs belongs together: the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve, the triangular space with the radial nerve, the cubital fossa with the sciatic nerve, or the carpal tunnel with the ulnar nerve? The answer is the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve. The radial nerve passes through the triangular interval, and the ulnar nerve passes outside the carpal tunnel.

Question 10760. Which triangular hollow lies on the front of the elbow, bounded above by a line between the two epicondyles and on each side by the muscles of the forearm? The answer is the cubital fossa. The biceps tendon lies in the middle of it, with the brachial artery medial to the tendon and the median nerve medial to the artery.

Question 10761. Which of these structures lies in the cubital fossa: the brachial artery, the axillary artery, the radial artery at the wrist, or the ulnar nerve at the elbow? The answer is the brachial artery. It divides into the radial and the ulnar arteries at the lower border of the fossa.

Question 10762. Which structures pass through the carpal tunnel, and which nerve lies outside it? The answer is the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis, the flexor digitorum profundus, and the flexor pollicis longus, together with the median nerve, while the ulnar nerve passes outside. The tunnel is bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum.

Question 10763. A constructed illustration: a person wakes with numbness in the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger, and half of the ring finger, and the muscles at the base of the thumb are wasted. Which nerve is compressed, and through which space does it pass? The answer is the median nerve, which passes through the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum.

Question 10764. A described dissection of the front of the wrist shows a small channel on the little finger side of the flexor retinaculum, between it and a small hook of bone, with a nerve and an artery running through it. Which channel is shown, and what does it carry? The answer is the ulnar canal, carrying the ulnar nerve and the ulnar artery.

Question 10765. Which triangular hollow lies on the back of the hand at the base of the thumb, is bounded by the tendons of two muscles, and becomes deepest when the thumb is pulled away from the palm? The answer is the anatomical snuffbox. The radial artery crosses its floor. The scaphoid and the trapezium are the bones beneath that floor.

Question 10766. Which tendon forms the medial boundary of the anatomical snuffbox: the extensor pollicis longus, the abductor pollicis longus, the extensor pollicis brevis, or the extensor indicis? The answer is the extensor pollicis longus. The abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis form the lateral boundary.

Question 10767. True or false: the radial artery and the scaphoid bone both lie in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, so a fracture of the scaphoid can cause tenderness there. The answer is true. The hollow is felt between the thumb tendons, and the artery crosses the bone. Tenderness in the hollow after a fall is a reason to look for a fracture.

Question 10768. Which triangular space lies in the upper part of the front of the thigh, bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the sartorius, and medially by the adductor longus? The answer is the femoral triangle. From lateral to medial its contents are the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, and the femoral vein, with lymph nodes beside the vein.

Question 10769. Which structure lies most laterally within the femoral triangle: the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, the femoral vein, or the femoral canal? The answer is the femoral nerve. It lies outside the femoral sheath and lateral to the artery. The femoral canal is the smallest and most medial compartment of the sheath.

Question 10770. Which compartment of the femoral sheath lies most medially, contains lymph nodes and fat, and is the route by which a femoral hernia descends? The answer is the femoral canal. Its upper opening is the femoral ring, bounded in front by the inguinal ligament and medially by the lacunar ligament. The femoral vein lies just lateral to it.

Question 10771. A constructed illustration: a soft swelling appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in the groin crease and enlarges on coughing. Through which opening has it passed, and which structure lies immediately medial to that opening? The answer is the femoral ring, with the lacunar ligament immediately medial to it.

Question 10772. A described dissection of the medial side of the thigh shows a narrow tunnel running from the apex of the femoral triangle to an opening in a broad tendon above the knee, carrying an artery, a vein, and a nerve. Which tunnel is shown, and what forms its roof? The answer is the adductor canal, roofed by the sartorius and the vasto adductor membrane.

Question 10773. Which diamond-shaped hollow lies behind the knee, bounded above by the tendons of the hamstring muscles and below by the two heads of the gastrocnemius? The answer is the popliteal fossa. It contains the popliteal artery and vein, the tibial and common fibular nerves, and fat, and its floor is the back of the femur and the knee joint.

Question 10774. Which of these structures lies deepest in the popliteal fossa: the popliteal artery, the popliteal vein, the tibial nerve, or the small saphenous vein? The answer is the popliteal artery, which lies against the capsule of the knee joint. The popliteal vein lies nearer the skin than the artery, and the tibial nerve lies nearest the skin of the three.

Question 10775. Name the two nerves and the main artery that lie in the popliteal fossa. The answer is the tibial nerve, the common fibular nerve, and the popliteal artery. The tibial nerve runs straight down through the fossa and into the back of the leg. The common fibular nerve follows the tendon of the biceps femoris toward the neck of the fibula.

Question 10776. Which fascial compartment of the arm lies in front of the humerus and between the medial and lateral intermuscular septa, and holds the biceps brachii, the brachialis, and the coracobrachialis? The answer is the anterior compartment of the arm. All three muscles are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.

Question 10777. Which nerve supplies the muscles of the posterior compartment of the arm: the musculocutaneous nerve, the radial nerve, the median nerve, or the ulnar nerve? The answer is the radial nerve. It runs in the spiral groove against the back of the humerus between the heads of the triceps, so a fracture of the middle of the shaft can injure it.

Question 10778. Which structure separates the anterior and the posterior compartments of the arm on the medial side, and which nerve crosses it from behind to reach the front? The answer is the medial intermuscular septum, with the ulnar nerve. The nerve passes from the posterior compartment through the septum just above the elbow.

Question 10779. A described transverse section of the forearm shows a thick sleeve of fascia, two bones joined by a membrane, and a group of muscles in front of the membrane whose tendons point toward the wrist. Which compartment is described, and which nerve supplies most of it? The answer is the anterior compartment, supplied mainly by the median nerve.

Question 10780. Which compartment of the hand lies between the metacarpal bones, is closed by deep fascia in front and behind, and holds the muscles that spread the fingers apart and draw them together? The answer is the interosseous compartment. The dorsal interossei abduct the fingers and the palmar interossei adduct them, and the ulnar nerve supplies both groups.

Question 10781. Which of these structures lies in the posterior compartment of the forearm: the extensor digitorum, the flexor digitorum profundus, the pronator teres, or the palmaris longus? The answer is the extensor digitorum. The compartment is supplied by the radial nerve through its deep branch, the posterior interosseous nerve. The other three muscles lie in the anterior compartment.

Question 10782. A constructed illustration: after a fracture of the upper forearm the limb becomes tense and painful when the fingers are stretched, and the radial pulse is still present. Which compartment is under pressure, and which nerves are threatened? The answer is the anterior compartment of the forearm, where the median and ulnar nerves and the flexor muscles are at risk.

Question 10783. True or false: the deep fascia of the thigh, the fascia lata, is thickened on the lateral side as the iliotibial tract, which receives the insertion of the gluteus maximus and the tensor fasciae latae. The answer is true. The tract runs down to the lateral condyle of the tibia, and the fascia sends septa inward to form the thigh compartments.

Question 10784. Which compartment of the thigh lies in front of the femur and between the lateral and medial intermuscular septa, holds the quadriceps femoris and the sartorius, and is supplied by the femoral nerve? The answer is the anterior compartment of the thigh. Its muscles extend the knee, and the femoral vessels run in its upper part.

Question 10785. Which nerve supplies the muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the sciatic nerve, or the tibial nerve? The answer is the obturator nerve. It enters the thigh through the obturator canal and supplies the adductor group. The femoral nerve supplies the anterior compartment instead.

Question 10786. Which opening in the tendon of the adductor magnus carries the femoral artery and vein out of the adductor canal into the popliteal fossa, where the artery takes the name popliteal? The answer is the adductor hiatus. It lies just above the knee, and the vessels change their name as they pass through it.

Question 10787. A described transverse section through the middle of the thigh shows a large group of muscles behind a single bone, separated from the front and the medial groups by septa, with a long nerve running down among them. Which compartment is shown, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the posterior compartment, supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.

Question 10788. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the front of the leg the limb becomes tense and shiny, and the person cannot lift the foot or the toes and cannot feel the skin between the first two toes. Which compartment is under pressure, and which nerve is failing? The answer is the anterior compartment of the leg, with the deep fibular nerve.

Question 10789. Which compartment of the leg holds the fibularis longus and the fibularis brevis, lies against the lateral surface of the fibula, and is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve? The answer is the lateral compartment. Its tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus, and the tendon of the longus crosses the sole of the foot.

Question 10790. Which of these nerves supplies the deep posterior compartment of the leg: the tibial nerve, the superficial fibular nerve, the deep fibular nerve, or the saphenous nerve? The answer is the tibial nerve. It runs down with the posterior tibial vessels and supplies the flexor muscles of the ankle and the toes. The deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior compartment instead.

Question 10791. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior compartment of the leg with the deep fibular nerve, the lateral compartment with the tibial nerve, the posterior compartment with the superficial fibular nerve, or the anterior compartment of the forearm with the radial nerve? The answer is the anterior compartment of the leg with the deep fibular nerve. The lateral compartment is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

Question 10792. Name three structures that pass through the carpal tunnel. The answer is the median nerve and the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis and the flexor digitorum profundus. The tendon of the flexor pollicis longus passes through it as well. The ulnar nerve and the ulnar artery pass outside it in the ulnar canal.

Question 10793. Which of these muscles lies in the deep part of the posterior compartment of the leg: the flexor hallucis longus, the gastrocnemius, the soleus, or the plantaris? The answer is the flexor hallucis longus. It lies against the back of the fibula and the interosseous membrane with the tibialis posterior and the flexor digitorum longus. The other three lie in the superficial part.

Question 10794. A described dissection behind the medial malleolus shows a tunnel roofed by a thick band of fascia, with a nerve, an artery, and several long tendons passing through it into the sole. Which tunnel is shown, and why is it a site of nerve compression? The answer is the tarsal tunnel, the narrow gateway between the leg and the sole, where the tibial nerve divides.

Question 10795. Which statement about the interosseous membrane of the leg is correct: it separates the anterior compartment from the posterior compartment and lets the anterior tibial vessels through an opening above, it separates the lateral compartment from the anterior compartment, it is pierced by nerves only, or it is absent below the ankle? The answer is the first statement.

Question 10796. Which compartment of the foot lies in the middle of the sole between the medial and the lateral compartments, holds the flexor digitorum brevis and the tendons of the long flexors, and is roofed by a septum? The answer is the central compartment of the sole. The interosseous compartment lies above it, and the medial compartment holds the muscles of the great toe.

Question 10797. Which of these structures lies in the lateral compartment of the sole: the abductor digiti minimi, the abductor hallucis, the flexor digitorum brevis, or the dorsal interossei? The answer is the abductor digiti minimi, which lies along the outer border of the foot with the flexor digiti minimi brevis and the opponens digiti minimi. The abductor hallucis lies in the medial compartment.

Question 10798. A constructed illustration: a person reports burning pain and tingling along the sole and the outer side of the heel, worse after standing, with weakness of the small muscles of the foot. Which nerve is compressed, and where does it lie? The answer is the tibial nerve, in the tarsal tunnel behind and below the medial malleolus.

Question 10799. In a transverse section through the middle of the leg, which compartment lies immediately behind the interosseous membrane, and which compartment lies between the anterior compartment and the skin on the outer side of the limb? The answer is the deep posterior compartment behind the membrane, and the lateral compartment on the outer side.

Question 10800. Which compartment of the hand holds the muscles of the thumb and lies on the outer side of the palm beneath the thenar fascia: the thenar compartment, the hypothenar compartment, the adductor compartment, or the midpalmar space? The answer is the thenar compartment. The hypothenar compartment lies on the little finger side, and the adductor compartment lies deeper against the palm.

To summarize, an anatomical space is defined by its walls, its contents, and the openings that connect it to its neighbors, and that triad is what every question in this chapter tested. The orbit, the nasal cavity, the fossae of the head and neck, the divisions of the mediastinum, the greater and lesser sacs with the epiploic foramen, the peritoneal and pelvic recesses, and the fossae and canals of the limbs each have a short list of boundaries worth saying aloud. The fascial compartments of the limbs are closed rooms bounded by deep fascia, intermuscular septa, bones, and interosseous membranes, and each contains a named group of muscles with one dominant nerve: the musculocutaneous nerve in the front of the arm, the radial nerve behind it, the obturator nerve in the medial thigh, and the deep fibular nerve in the front of the leg with the tibial nerve behind it. Pressure inside a compartment threatens its muscles and its nerve, while disease in a space threatens whatever passes through it, so the boundaries and the contents are the facts to keep. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 109 — Fascial Compartments

This chapter maps the sheets of connective tissue that wrap the muscles, gather them into working groups, and carry the vessels and nerves between those groups. It covers the deep fascia of the limbs and the trunk, the intermuscular septa and interosseous membranes that divide one compartment from another, the retinacula that roof the tunnels at the wrist and the ankle, and the fascial layers of the neck and the abdominal wall. It holds one hundred questions, and every one gives its answer straight after the question and then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind. Each compartment is defined by its walls, so the questions are answered with boundaries and contents rather than with labels. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10801. Which sheet of dense connective tissue lies deep to the superficial fascia, wraps the muscles of a limb and sends septa inward to the bone? The answer is the deep fascia. It is tough and almost free of fat, and it binds the muscles of a region together. It also forms the retinacula at the wrist and the ankle.

Question 10802. Which of these muscles lies in the anterior compartment of the arm: the triceps brachii, the brachialis, the anconeus, or the brachioradialis? The answer is the brachialis. The compartment also holds the biceps brachii and the coracobrachialis, and the musculocutaneous nerve supplies all three. The triceps lies behind and the brachioradialis belongs to the forearm.

Question 10803. A described transverse section of the arm shows a single bone, two thick fascial walls running from the bone to the deep fascia, and muscle on either side of each wall. Which structures are those walls? The answer is the medial and the lateral intermuscular septa. They divide the limb into an anterior and a posterior compartment.

Question 10804. Which intermuscular septum of the arm separates the triceps brachii behind from the brachialis in front? The answer is the medial intermuscular septum. The ulnar nerve descends along it from the front of the arm to the back. The lateral septum separates the triceps from the brachioradialis.

Question 10805. What is the name of the deep fascia of the thigh, which encloses its muscles and is attached above to the inguinal ligament? The answer is the fascia lata. It is strongest on the lateral side, where it forms the iliotibial tract. It sends septa inward to the femur.

Question 10806. Which of these muscles belongs to the anterior compartment of the leg: the peroneus longus, the tibialis anterior, the gastrocnemius, or the flexor hallucis longus? The answer is the tibialis anterior. The compartment also holds the long extensors of the toes and the peroneus tertius. The peroneus longus lies laterally and the other two lie behind.

Question 10807. A constructed illustration: after a fracture of the tibia a person has severe pain in the front of the leg, worse when the toes are stretched. Which compartment is affected, and why is the pressure dangerous? The answer is the anterior compartment of the leg. Its fascial walls scarcely stretch, so swelling raises the pressure and can cut off the blood supply. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10808. True or false: in a limb the deep fascia lies between the superficial fascia and the muscles. The answer is true. The superficial fascia is the fatty layer just beneath the skin. The deep fascia lies deep to it and superficial to the muscle.

Question 10809. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral compartment of the leg with the superficial peroneal nerve, the anterior compartment with the tibial nerve, the posterior compartment with the deep peroneal nerve, or the anterior thigh with the obturator nerve? The answer is the lateral compartment with the superficial peroneal nerve. The anterior compartment takes the deep peroneal nerve and the posterior the tibial nerve.

Question 10810. Which strong sheet joins the shafts of the radius and the ulna, and in which direction do its fibers run? The answer is the interosseous membrane, whose fibers run downward and medially from the radius to the ulna. Force applied to the hand crosses it to the radius and then to the elbow.

Question 10811. Which muscle forms the roof of the adductor canal: the adductor magnus, the sartorius, the vastus medialis, or the adductor longus? The answer is the sartorius, with its fascia. The adductor magnus forms the posterior wall and the vastus medialis the lateral wall. The femoral vessels and the saphenous nerve pass through the canal.

Question 10812. A described transverse section of the leg shows three muscles in front of the interosseous membrane, two against the fibula, and a large mass behind. How many compartments does the section show? The answer is four. A transverse septum divides the posterior mass into a superficial and a deep part.

Question 10813. Which of these septa separates the lateral compartment of the leg from the anterior compartment: the anterior intermuscular septum, the posterior intermuscular septum, the transverse intermuscular septum, or a medial one? The answer is the anterior intermuscular septum, attached to the anterior border of the fibula. The posterior septum separates the lateral compartment from the posterior one.

Question 10814. A constructed illustration: a runner has a tight, aching outer side of the leg after a set distance, and the pressure in one compartment is raised after exercise. Which compartment and which nerve are most often involved? The answer is the lateral compartment of the leg and the superficial peroneal nerve. It is the least distensible of the four compartments. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10815. Name the two intermuscular septa of the leg that run from the fibula to the deep fascia, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior intermuscular septum and the posterior intermuscular septum. Together with the interosseous membrane they help divide the leg into four compartments.

Question 10816. Which fascial sheath encloses the rectus abdominis muscle, and what forms it? The answer is the rectus sheath, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall. It is complete above the arcuate line and deficient behind the muscle below it.

Question 10817. Which of these layers of the abdominal wall is the deepest of the flat muscles: the external oblique, the internal oblique, the transversus abdominis, or the rectus abdominis? The answer is the transversus abdominis, whose fibers run across the abdomen. Behind it lie the extraperitoneal fat and then the peritoneum.

Question 10818. A described dissection of the front of the abdomen strips the skin and then a layer of fat, and the next sheet is thin, membranous and attached below to the fascia lata. Which layer has been reached? The answer is the membranous layer of the superficial fascia. Its attachment below the inguinal ligament keeps fluid from tracking into the thigh.

Question 10819. The linea alba is a midline band on the front of the abdomen; which structures fuse to form it? The answer is the aponeuroses of the external oblique, the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis. The band runs from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis.

Question 10820. Which large fascial sheet covers the deep muscles of the back, extends from the sacrum to the thoracic region and encloses the erector spinae? The answer is the thoracolumbar fascia. In the lumbar region it has a posterior, a middle and an anterior layer. The latissimus dorsi attaches to it.

Question 10821. Which of these relations at the thoracolumbar fascia is correct: the erector spinae lies between its posterior and middle layers, the quadratus lumborum lies behind the posterior layer, the latissimus dorsi lies deep to the anterior layer, or the fascia stops at the chest? The answer is the first. The quadratus lumborum lies between the middle and the anterior layers.

Question 10822. Which of these pairs belongs together: the clavipectoral fascia with the axilla, the crural fascia with the arm, the renal fascia with the lung, or the thoracolumbar fascia with the neck? The answer is the clavipectoral fascia with the axilla. It fills the space below the clavicle and behind the pectoralis minor, and the cephalic vein pierces it.

Question 10823. A constructed illustration: a deep infection of the perineum spreads along a fascial plane but is held below the pelvic diaphragm. Which fascia forms that floor? The answer is the pelvic diaphragm, formed by the levator ani and the coccygeus with their fasciae. It separates the perineum from the pelvic cavity above. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10824. What is the name of the deep fascia of the leg, which encloses its muscles and forms the retinacula at the ankle? The answer is the crural fascia. Above it is continuous with the fascia lata and below with the fascia of the foot. Its septa divide the leg into four compartments.

Question 10825. A described transverse section of the thigh shows three muscle groups, one in front, one medially and one behind, separated by thick fascial walls running from the outer sleeve to the femur. What are those walls? The answer is the intermuscular septa of the thigh, which run from the deep fascia to the linea aspera.

Question 10826. Which intermuscular septum of the thigh separates the anterior compartment from the posterior compartment? The answer is the lateral intermuscular septum. It is attached to the lateral lip of the linea aspera and is the strongest of the three. The medial septum separates the anterior from the medial compartment.

Question 10827. Which of these muscles lies in the posterior compartment of the thigh: the adductor magnus, the semitendinosus, the vastus medialis, or the pectineus? The answer is the semitendinosus. It is joined by the semimembranosus and the biceps femoris, and the group is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, except for the short head of the biceps femoris. Their action is to extend the hip and flex the knee.

Question 10828. Which band of deep fascia forms the roof of the carpal tunnel and holds the flexor tendons against the wrist? The answer is the flexor retinaculum, also called the transverse carpal ligament. It is attached to the scaphoid and the trapezium laterally and to the pisiform and the hamate medially.

Question 10829. True or false: the carpal tunnel is bounded behind by the carpal bones and in front by the flexor retinaculum. The answer is true. The bones form an arch with a concave front, and the retinaculum bridges it as a roof. The tunnel therefore has almost no room to expand.

Question 10830. A described transverse section through the wrist shows a fibrous band bridging a bony arch, and inside the arch a nerve lying just under the band with tendons around it. Which nerve is described? The answer is the median nerve, within the carpal tunnel. It lies most superficially in the tunnel, immediately beneath the retinaculum.

Question 10831. Which space of the hand lies between the metacarpal bones and holds the muscles that pull the fingers together: the thenar compartment, the adductor compartment, the interosseous compartment, or the hypothenar compartment? The answer is the interosseous compartment. It contains the dorsal and the palmar interossei, supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Question 10832. A constructed illustration: a person wakes with tingling in the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger, worse at night. Which compartment is implicated, and which structure in it is compressed? The answer is the carpal tunnel, and the structure compressed is the median nerve. The tunnel is a closed compartment roofed by the flexor retinaculum. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10833. Which of these structures does not lie in the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus: the tendon of the tibialis posterior, the posterior tibial artery, the tibial nerve, or the tendon of the peroneus longus? The answer is the tendon of the peroneus longus. It runs behind the lateral malleolus instead. The other three lie under the flexor retinaculum with the long flexors of the toes.

Question 10834. Which compartment of the sole lies between the medial and the lateral compartments and contains the flexor digitorum brevis? The answer is the central compartment of the sole. It lies between two septa that run from the deep fascia down to the bones. The medial compartment holds the muscles of the great toe.

Question 10835. Which layer of the deep cervical fascia encloses the thyroid gland and the trachea: the investing layer, the pretracheal layer, the prevertebral layer, or the carotid sheath? The answer is the pretracheal layer. It lies in front of the trachea and the esophagus. The investing layer encircles the neck instead.

Question 10836. A described transverse section through the neck at the level of the thyroid gland shows a midline tube wrapped by a fascial layer, a sheath around the great vessels on each side, and a strong layer in front of the spine. Which layers are shown? The answer is the pretracheal layer, the carotid sheath and the prevertebral layer. All three are parts of the deep cervical fascia.

Question 10837. Which fascial tube of the neck contains the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve? The answer is the carotid sheath. It is formed by all three layers of the deep cervical fascia. Within it the vein lies lateral to the artery and the nerve lies between them.

Question 10838. A constructed illustration: an infection behind the pharynx tracks down between two fascial layers to the diaphragm. Which space is described, and which layers bound it? The answer is the danger space, between the alar fascia in front and the prevertebral fascia behind. It lies behind the retropharyngeal space, which stops higher in the chest. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10839. Which of these pairs belongs together: the investing layer with the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid, the pretracheal layer with the scalene muscles, the prevertebral layer with the thyroid gland, or the carotid sheath with the pharynx? The answer is the investing layer with the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid. The pretracheal layer encloses the thyroid gland and the prevertebral layer covers the scalenes.

Question 10840. Which part of the deep cervical fascia encloses the thyroid gland and lies in front of the trachea? The answer is the pretracheal layer. It is also called the visceral layer. Below, it blends with the fibrous pericardium, and behind it lies the esophagus.

Question 10841. A described dissection opens the sheath of the rectus abdominis above the navel and finds the aponeuroses in front of the muscle, then opens it below the navel and finds them behind it. What is the name of the line at which this changes? The answer is the arcuate line. Below it only the transversalis fascia lies behind the muscle.

Question 10842. Which fascial layer of the neck lies immediately in front of the prevertebral fascia and forms the back wall of the retropharyngeal space: the buccopharyngeal fascia, the alar fascia, the investing layer, or the carotid sheath? The answer is the alar fascia. The space between it and the prevertebral fascia is the danger space.

Question 10843. Which of these statements about the parotid fascia is correct: it is part of the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia, it lies deep to the parotid duct, it encloses the submandibular gland, or it blends with the pleura? The answer is the first. It forms a strong capsule around the gland and is attached above to the zygomatic arch.

Question 10844. Which fascia extends from the clavicle into the axilla, encloses the subclavius and the pectoralis minor, and is pierced by the cephalic vein? The answer is the clavipectoral fascia. It fills the gap between the clavicle and the upper border of that muscle. Below the pectoralis minor it continues as the suspensory ligament of the axilla.

Question 10845. A described dissection of the chest wall shows a strong fascial sheet pierced by a vein running up toward the shoulder, with a small muscle above the sheet and a larger muscle below it. Which fascia is shown? The answer is the clavipectoral fascia, pierced by the cephalic vein. The thoracoacromial vessels pierce it as well.

Question 10846. Which of these is the most likely explanation when a hand becomes tense and painful after a crush injury and the fingers are held flexed: torn thenar muscles, an interosseous compartment under pressure, a divided carpal tunnel, or a cut retinaculum? The answer is an interosseous compartment under pressure. The fascia and the metacarpals leave no room for swelling, so the muscles within are compressed.

Question 10847. Which intermuscular septum does the radial nerve pierce as it passes from the back of the arm into the front, and which does the ulnar nerve pierce going the other way? The answer is that the radial nerve pierces the lateral septum and the ulnar nerve the medial septum. The radial nerve has already run in the spiral groove.

Question 10848. In a described transverse section of the leg the interosseous membrane appears as a band between two bones. Which way does the anterior compartment lie relative to the membrane? The answer is in front of it. The deep posterior compartment lies behind the membrane, which therefore separates the two.

Question 10849. Which of these statements about the compartments of the thigh is correct: the medial compartment holds the adductor group, the anterior compartment holds the hamstrings, the posterior compartment is supplied by the femoral nerve, or the lateral septum separates the anterior from the medial compartment? The answer is the first. The anterior compartment holds the quadriceps and the hamstrings lie behind.

Question 10850. Which of these statements about the femoral sheath is correct: it is formed by the transversalis fascia and the iliac fascia, it encloses the femoral nerve, it is a thickening of the deep fascia, or it wraps the hip joint? The answer is the first. It encloses the femoral artery and vein and the femoral canal, but not the nerve, which lies lateral to it.

Question 10851. Which nerve and which artery pass through the quadrangular space together and wind around the surgical neck of the humerus? The answer is the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery. The space lies between the teres minor above, the teres major below and the long head of the triceps medially. The nerve supplies the deltoid.

Question 10852. In the cubital fossa, which of these structures lies most laterally: the median nerve, the brachial artery, the tendon of the biceps brachii, or the radial nerve? The answer is the tendon of the biceps brachii. From lateral to medial the order is the tendon, the artery and the median nerve. The radial nerve lies in the floor.

Question 10853. A described radiograph shows a fracture line through the middle of the shaft of the humerus, with a spike of bone pointing upward. Which nerve is most at risk in the groove against the back of the bone? The answer is the radial nerve. It runs in the spiral groove between the origins of the triceps.

Question 10854. In the upper arm the median nerve lies lateral to the brachial artery; where do the two cross, and on which side does the nerve lie below? The answer is that they cross in the middle of the arm, and the nerve lies medial to the artery below. It then passes through the cubital fossa medial to the artery.

Question 10855. A constructed illustration: a deep cut across the front of the wrist leaves the thumb and the index finger numb, and the thumb can no longer be opposed. Which nerve has been divided? The answer is the median nerve. It lies just under the skin and the retinaculum in the middle of the wrist. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10856. Which nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it can be felt as a cord and is easily injured? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It lies in the groove between the epicondyle and the olecranon, in the cubital tunnel. It then enters the forearm between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris.

Question 10857. Which of these is the order of the main structures in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial: vein, artery, nerve; nerve, artery, vein; artery, nerve, vein; or vein, nerve, artery? The answer is nerve, artery, vein. The nerve lies outside the femoral sheath and the vein lies most medially. Medial to the vein lies the empty femoral canal.

Question 10858. True or false: the femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath and lateral to the femoral artery. The answer is true. The sheath holds the artery, the vein and the femoral canal. The nerve lies lateral to the artery and outside the sheath.

Question 10859. Which of these pairs belongs together: the deep peroneal nerve with the anterior compartment of the leg, the tibial nerve with the lateral compartment, the superficial peroneal nerve with the posterior compartment, or the femoral nerve with the back of the thigh? The answer is the deep peroneal nerve with the anterior compartment. The superficial peroneal nerve supplies the lateral compartment.

Question 10860. Which nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it lies just beneath the skin and is easily injured by a blow or by prolonged pressure? The answer is the common peroneal nerve. It divides there into the deep and the superficial peroneal nerves. Injury weakens the muscles that lift the foot.

Question 10861. Behind the medial malleolus, which of these lies most anteriorly: the tendon of the tibialis posterior, the posterior tibial artery, the tibial nerve, or the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior. From front to back the order is the tibialis posterior, the flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery, the tibial nerve and the flexor hallucis longus.

Question 10862. A described transverse section through the knee shows a diamond-shaped space behind the joint, filled with fat, with a large nerve nearest the skin, a vein beneath it and an artery deepest against the bone. Which space and which artery are shown? The answer is the popliteal fossa, with the popliteal artery deepest.

Question 10863. Which of these relations of the pudendal nerve is correct: it leaves the pelvis below the piriformis and crosses the sacrospinous ligament, it leaves above the piriformis, it passes through the obturator canal, or it lies in front of the sacrum? The answer is the first. It hooks around the ischial spine, medial to the internal pudendal artery, and enters the pudendal canal.

Question 10864. A constructed illustration: some weeks after a hip operation a person cannot abduct the hip and leans over that side when walking. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the superior gluteal nerve, which supplies the gluteus medius, the gluteus minimus and the tensor fasciae latae. It leaves the pelvis above the piriformis. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10865. Which of these structures lies most superficially in the popliteal fossa: the popliteal artery, the popliteal vein, the tibial nerve, or the common peroneal nerve? The answer is the tibial nerve. It lies nearest the skin, with the vein beneath it and the artery deepest against the bone.

Question 10866. Which artery can be felt in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, between the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis? The answer is the radial artery. It crosses the lateral side of the wrist and turns into the palm between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous.

Question 10867. Which of these structures passes through the carpal tunnel: the ulnar nerve, the radial artery, the median nerve, or the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris? The answer is the median nerve. It passes with the tendons of the long flexors of the fingers and the thumb. The ulnar nerve and artery pass outside the tunnel.

Question 10868. A described dissection of the palm lifts a triangular sheet of deep fascia and finds septa running from it to the third and the fifth metacarpals. Which sheet is described? The answer is the palmar aponeurosis, whose septa separate the thenar, the hypothenar and the central compartments of the palm. The interosseous compartment lies deeper.

Question 10869. At the wrist, which structure lies immediately medial to the ulnar artery as both pass into the palm? The answer is the ulnar nerve. They travel together through a canal at the medial side of the wrist. The artery then curls across the palm as the superficial palmar arch.

Question 10870. Which large nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and descends in the back of the thigh? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It is the largest nerve in the body and lies deep to the gluteus maximus at first. It divides into the tibial and the common peroneal nerves.

Question 10871. Which of these structures leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis: the sciatic nerve, the superior gluteal nerve, the inferior gluteal nerve, or the pudendal nerve? The answer is the superior gluteal nerve. It runs between the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus. The other three leave below the muscle.

Question 10872. A constructed illustration: after a shoulder is dislocated downward the deltoid cannot be lifted and the skin over it is numb. Which nerve has been injured, and where does it wind around the neck of the humerus? The answer is the axillary nerve, in the quadrangular space. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10873. True or false: the great saphenous vein ascends in front of the medial malleolus accompanied by the saphenous nerve. The answer is true. The nerve lies immediately beside the vein and supplies the skin of the medial side of the leg and the foot. The small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus.

Question 10874. A described dissection of the front of the thigh shows a triangle bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the sartorius and medially by the adductor longus, with a nerve lateral to an artery and a vein medial to it. Which triangle is shown? The answer is the femoral triangle. Its floor is formed by the iliacus, the psoas and the pectineus.

Question 10875. Through which opening does the obturator nerve leave the pelvis, and which compartment of the thigh does it enter? The answer is the obturator canal, and it enters the medial compartment. There it supplies the adductor group, except the hamstring part of the adductor magnus. The obturator artery and vein run with it.

Question 10876. Name two structures that pass through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis, spoken as a list. The answer is the sciatic nerve and the inferior gluteal nerve. The pudendal nerve passes below the muscle as well. Only the superior gluteal nerve passes above it.

Question 10877. Which fascial sheath of the neck contains the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve, and how do the three lie within it? The answer is the carotid sheath, with the vein lateral, the artery medial and the nerve between and behind them. It is formed by all three layers of the deep cervical fascia.

Question 10878. At the root of the neck, which relation is correct: the subclavian vein lies in front of the scalenus anterior and the subclavian artery behind it, the artery lies in front of the vein, both lie behind the muscle, or both lie in front of it? The answer is that the vein lies in front and the artery behind. The brachial plexus also passes behind the muscle.

Question 10879. A described transverse section at the level of the cricoid cartilage shows a midline tube wrapped by a gland, two thick tubes beside it, and a strong layer covering the muscles in front of the spine. Which structures are shown? The answer is the trachea with the thyroid gland, the common carotid arteries and the prevertebral layer.

Question 10880. A constructed illustration: a person has numbness and tingling down the inner side of the arm and into the little finger when the arm is held overhead. Which passage is implicated? The answer is the thoracic outlet, between the first rib, the clavicle and the scalenus anterior. The lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass through it. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10881. Which of these relations within the carotid sheath is correct: the vagus nerve lies between the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery, the vein lies medial to the artery, the nerve lies in front of both, or the sheath contains the sympathetic trunk? The answer is the first. The vein lies lateral to the artery and the sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath.

Question 10882. In an intercostal space, in what order do the vein, the artery and the nerve lie below a rib, and where do they run? The answer is the vein highest, then the artery, then the nerve, all in the costal groove along the lower border of the rib. The rib above them shields the bundle.

Question 10883. In the free edge of the lesser omentum, which of these structures lies most posteriorly: the common bile duct, the proper hepatic artery, the portal vein, or the cystic duct? The answer is the portal vein. It lies behind the other two, with the bile duct in front and to the right and the hepatic artery in front and to the left.

Question 10884. A described dissection of the left side of the root of the neck shows a thin-walled duct ascending behind the carotid sheath and opening at the junction of two veins. Which duct is shown? The answer is the thoracic duct, which ends at the junction of the left internal jugular and the left subclavian veins. On the right a much shorter duct ends there.

Question 10885. Which of these structures crosses the ureter in the female pelvis, a relation that matters when the ureter is found at operation: the uterine artery, the internal iliac vein, the obturator nerve, or the round ligament of the uterus? The answer is the uterine artery. It crosses above and in front of the ureter beside the cervix.

Question 10886. Which structure crosses above and medial to the ureter in the male pelvis as it descends to the prostate? The answer is the ductus deferens. The two lie close together beside the seminal vesicle, and the ureter passes beneath the duct. In the female the uterine artery takes that relation.

Question 10887. Which of these relations of the left renal vein is correct: it passes in front of the aorta and behind the superior mesenteric artery, it passes behind the aorta, it drains into the inferior vena cava without crossing, or it lies behind the left kidney? The answer is the first. It receives the left suprarenal and gonadal veins.

Question 10888. The median nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of which muscle, and which branch does it give off there? The answer is the pronator teres, and the branch is the anterior interosseous nerve. That branch then runs down the front of the interosseous membrane.

Question 10889. In a described transverse section through the middle of the forearm, which nerve lies in the midline between the superficial and the deep flexor muscles? The answer is the median nerve. It descends behind the flexor digitorum superficialis and in front of the flexor digitorum profundus. The ulnar nerve lies on the medial side.

Question 10890. A constructed illustration: a person cannot bend the tip of the thumb or of the index finger, and no feeling is lost in the hand. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the anterior interosseous nerve, which arises from the median nerve between the two heads of the pronator teres. It has no cutaneous branches, so sensation is spared. The management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 10891. Which branch of the radial nerve winds through the supinator muscle to reach the back of the forearm, and what does it supply there? The answer is the deep branch of the radial nerve, which becomes the posterior interosseous nerve. It supplies the extensor muscles of the wrist and the fingers. Its injury causes weakness without numbness.

Question 10892. Which of these structures lies within the cavernous sinus: the internal carotid artery, the optic nerve, the facial nerve, or the hypoglossal nerve? The answer is the internal carotid artery, which runs through the sinus beside the sixth cranial nerve. The third and fourth cranial nerves lie in its lateral wall.

Question 10893. True or false: the hypoglossal nerve crosses the internal and the external carotid arteries on its way to the tongue. The answer is true. It descends between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein, then crosses both arteries lateral to them. It finally passes deep to the posterior belly of the digastric.

Question 10894. Which of these pairs belongs together: the axillary nerve with the quadrangular space, the radial nerve with the carpal tunnel, the median nerve with the cubital tunnel, or the ulnar nerve with the spiral groove? The answer is the axillary nerve with the quadrangular space. The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove and the median nerve through the carpal tunnel.

Question 10895. Which of these relations of the facial nerve within the parotid gland is correct: it lies superficial to the retromandibular vein, it lies deep to that vein, it lies deep to the external carotid artery, or it lies medial to the styloid process? The answer is the first. The vein separates the nerve from the external carotid artery, which lies deep to it.

Question 10896. Name two structures found within the suboccipital triangle, spoken as a list. The answer is the vertebral artery and the dorsal ramus of the first cervical nerve, also called the suboccipital nerve. The triangle is bounded by the rectus capitis posterior major and the two obliquus muscles.

Question 10897. A described transverse section of the arm shows a large nerve lying on the medial side of the brachial artery. Was the section taken above or below the point where the two cross, and which nerve is it? The answer is below the crossing, and the nerve is the median nerve. Above that point the nerve lies lateral to the artery.

Question 10898. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around which structure, and why is it longer than the nerve on the right? The answer is the arch of the aorta, just beyond the ligamentum arteriosum. The left fourth and sixth aortic arches persist as the arch and the ductus, so the nerve is dragged down below them. On the right the nerve hooks the right subclavian artery.

Question 10899. Which of these statements about the vertebral artery is correct: it ascends through the transverse foramina and turns backward around the atlas, it enters the skull through the jugular foramen, it lies in front of the scalenus anterior, or it is a branch of the external carotid artery? The answer is the first. It joins its fellow to form the basilar artery.

Question 10900. Which vein runs down the side of the neck, superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and becomes prominent when a person strains? The answer is the external jugular vein. It begins near the angle of the jaw and ends in the subclavian vein. It is covered only by skin and the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia.

To summarize, the deep fascia is the tough sleeve that wraps the muscles of a limb and sends intermuscular septa inward to the bone, and those septa, with the interosseous membranes and the bones, define the compartments. Each compartment has its own muscles, its own nerve and its own vessels, so the anterior compartment of the leg lifts the foot with the deep peroneal nerve, the lateral compartment turns it outward with the superficial peroneal nerve, and the posterior compartment pushes it down with the tibial nerve. The retinacula turn bony arches into closed tunnels at the wrist and the ankle, and the median nerve suffers first in the carpal tunnel while the ulnar nerve travels outside it. In the neck the deep cervical fascia divides into an investing layer, a pretracheal layer, a prevertebral layer and the carotid sheath, and the space between the alar fascia and the prevertebral fascia carries infection down into the chest. The neurovascular relationships follow the same logic: the femoral nerve lies lateral to the artery and outside the femoral sheath, the structures of the popliteal fossa run from the skin inward as nerve, vein and artery, and those behind the medial malleolus run from the tibialis posterior in front to the flexor hallucis longus behind. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 110 — Orthopedic Anatomy

Orthopedic anatomy is the anatomy that decides how a limb carries weight, where a joint gives way, and what lies in the path of an operation. This chapter works through the bones, the joints, the ligaments, the tendons and the muscles of the limbs and the spine as the orthopedic clinician meets them: the structure of bone and the way it heals, the named fracture patterns, the compartments of the limbs, the stabilizers of the shoulder, the elbow, the hip, the knee and the ankle, and the surface landmarks that guide an examination. It holds one hundred questions, and every question is answered immediately after it is asked and then explained, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 10901. Which tendon of the rotator cuff passes beneath the acromion and the coracoacromial arch and is the one most often torn? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon. It runs from the fossa above the spine of the scapula to the top of the greater tubercle, and the arch presses on it whenever the arm is raised.

Question 10902. Which word describes a break in which the bone is shattered into several separate pieces: transverse, comminuted, spiral, or greenstick? The answer is comminuted. A comminuted break has more than two fragments, while a transverse break runs straight across the shaft and a spiral break twists along it.

Question 10903. A described radiograph of the wrist shows a break at the far end of the radius, with the hand and the small distal fragment carried backward so that the forearm takes on a dinner fork outline. Which fracture is described? The answer is a Colles fracture. The break lies in the last part of the radius, and the backward tilt of the fragment gives the shape.

Question 10904. A break of the surgical neck of the humerus endangers a nerve that lies immediately behind the bone at that level. Which nerve lies in that position? The answer is the axillary nerve. It passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels and supplies the deltoid and the skin over it.

Question 10905. A constructed illustration: a young person falls onto an outstretched hand and afterwards has tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb. Which carpal bone is likely injured, and why is the injury easily missed? The answer is the scaphoid. A break across its waist may not be seen at once, and the part beyond can lose its blood supply.

Question 10906. True or false: the periosteum covers the whole surface of a long bone, including the parts that lie inside a joint. The answer is false. The periosteum stops at the edge of the articular cartilage, and that bare cartilage is what lets the joint surfaces glide on one another.

Question 10907. Which of these muscles is not part of the rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, or teres major? The answer is teres major. The cuff is formed by supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, whose tendons blend into the capsule, while teres major passes below the shoulder and does not join it.

Question 10908. Which tendon is the thickest and strongest in the body, and where does it attach? The answer is the Achilles tendon, which attaches to the back of the calcaneus. It is formed where the gastrocnemius and the soleus come together above the heel, and it lifts the heel at every step.

Question 10909. The anterior talofibular ligament runs forward from the front edge of the lateral malleolus to the neck of the talus. On which side of the ankle joint does it lie, and in which direction does it run? The answer is the lateral side, running forward and slightly downward. It is the weakest of the lateral ligaments and the first to give way when the foot rolls inward.

Question 10910. A described radiograph of the hip shows a break across the neck of the femur, with the shaft riding upward while the head stays in the socket. Why is the blood supply of the head at risk? The answer is that the vessels run along the neck inside the capsule. A break there tears them, and the head beyond may lose its supply.

Question 10911. Which of these pairs belongs together: the patella with the quadriceps tendon, the patella with the Achilles tendon, the fabella with the triceps tendon, or the sesamoid of the great toe with the plantar fascia? The answer is the patella with the quadriceps tendon. The patella is a sesamoid bone inside that tendon, and the fabella lies in the tendon of the gastrocnemius instead.

Question 10912. Name two of the structures that pass through the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum, spoken as a list. The answer is the median nerve and the tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis, along with those of the flexor digitorum profundus and the flexor pollicis longus. The ulnar nerve crosses the wrist outside the tunnel, on the medial side.

Question 10913. Which of these structures is torn from the front rim of the glenoid when the shoulder dislocates forward: the acromion, the labrum, the coracoacromial ligament, or the coracoid process? The answer is the labrum, and such a tear is called a Bankart lesion. The head may also dent the back of its own head, which is a Hill-Sachs lesion.

Question 10914. Which meniscus of the knee is held more firmly to the deep surface of the joint capsule, and which ligament shares that attachment?
