The answer is the medial meniscus, which is attached to the deep part of the tibial collateral ligament. Because of that attachment it moves less than the lateral one and is torn more often.

Question 10915. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the front of the leg the skin is intact but the front of the shin is tightly swollen, and the person cannot lift the foot. Which compartment is involved, and which nerve is affected? The answer is the anterior compartment, with the deep peroneal nerve. That nerve runs down against the interosseous membrane and supplies the muscles that lift the foot.

Question 10916. Which ligament connects the laminae of neighboring vertebrae, contains a high proportion of elastic fibers, and lies immediately in front of the spinal cord? The answer is the ligamentum flavum. Its elastic tissue lets it stretch when the neck bends back without pinching the canal.

Question 10917. A described radiograph of a knee after a twisting injury shows a small oval fragment torn from the outer edge of the tibial plateau below the joint line. Which structure has been avulsed: the tibial collateral ligament, the anterolateral ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, or the patellar tendon? The answer is the anterolateral ligament with part of the lateral capsule. That small avulsion is strongly associated with a tear of the anterior cruciate ligament.

Question 10918. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the knee shows the joint filled with fluid and a dark band in the middle that no longer runs in a straight line. Which ligament is torn? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It normally runs upward and backward from the front of the tibia to the back of the femur.

Question 10919. True or false: the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus in a groove where it can be felt as a cord. The answer is true. That groove is the cubital tunnel, and because the nerve lies just under the skin a knock there sends tingling into the little finger.

Question 10920. Which of these carpal bones bridges the two rows of the wrist and is the one most often broken: the lunate, the scaphoid, the capitate, or the pisiform? The answer is the scaphoid. Blood enters it near the thumb and flows backward toward the forearm, so a break across its waist leaves the proximal part poorly supplied.

Question 10921. Which ligament wraps around the head of the radius and holds it against the radial notch of the ulna? The answer is the annular ligament of the radius. It forms about four fifths of a ring, and the notch completes it, so the head of the radius can turn inside it when the palm is turned over.

Question 10922. Which nerve lies against the back of the shaft of the humerus in the spiral groove, between the origins of the two heads of the triceps? The answer is the radial nerve, with the profunda brachii artery beside it. A break of the shaft can injure it, and the muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers then fail.

Question 10923. Which ligament is the first to be torn when the foot rolls inward under the ankle: the deltoid ligament, the anterior talofibular ligament, the calcaneofibular ligament, or the posterior talofibular ligament? The answer is the anterior talofibular ligament. It is the weakest of the lateral ligaments, while the deltoid ligament lies on the medial side.

Question 10924. Which carpal bone lies at the outer end of the proximal row of the wrist, between the radius above and the trapezium below? The answer is the scaphoid. It is the largest bone of the proximal row and the one that bridges the two rows, and a fall on the outstretched hand drives the radius against it.

Question 10925. A constructed illustration: after a break in the middle of the shaft of the humerus, the person cannot straighten the wrist or the fingers and the back of the hand feels numb. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the radial nerve. It lies in the spiral groove against the bone at that level.

Question 10926. In the classification of injuries to the growth plate, which type runs along the plate and then out through a corner of the metaphysis: the first, the second, the third, or the fourth type? The answer is the second type, which is the commonest of the group. The third and fourth types cross the joint surface or the plate itself.

Question 10927. Which vessels, running in the reflected fold of the capsule, provide most of the blood to the adult head of the femur? The answer is the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery. They creep along the neck beneath the capsule, and a displaced break of the neck tears them and leaves the head with only the small vessel in the ligament of the head.

Question 10928. A described computed tomography scan of the pelvis shows a gap at the front between the two pubic bones and a step at the back where the sacrum meets the ilium. What has happened to the ring of the pelvis? The answer is that the ring is broken in two places and is unstable. A ring of bone cannot break at one point alone without giving way somewhere else.

Question 10929. Which nerve is most often injured when the head of the femur leaves the socket through the back of the hip joint: the femoral nerve, the obturator nerve, the sciatic nerve, or the superior gluteal nerve? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and passes immediately behind the joint.

Question 10930. Which nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin, where it can be rolled against the bone? The answer is the common peroneal nerve. It lies at the lateral side of the knee, and because it is so superficial a blow there or a tight bandage can injure it.

Question 10931. Which tendon carries the pull of the quadriceps from the lower pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity? The answer is the patellar tendon. It is the continuation of the quadriceps tendon below the kneecap, and a sudden pull can tear it in an older person.

Question 10932. A constructed illustration: after a fall the elbow is dislocated backward, the pulse at the wrist is lost, and the hand is pale. Which vessel is in danger, and why does its position explain the injury? The answer is the brachial artery. It lies in front of the joint, so a backward dislocation stretches it across the front of the elbow.

Question 10933. Which of these bones forms the medial malleolus at the ankle: the fibula, the tibia, the talus, or the calcaneus? The answer is the tibia. Its lower end is broad, and its medial corner hangs down as the medial malleolus, while the fibula forms the lateral malleolus on the outer side.

Question 10934. A described computed tomography scan of the lower spine shows a vertebral body broken in several directions, with a piece of its back wall pushed into the canal. Which pattern of injury is this? The answer is a burst fracture. The whole body is broken rather than just its front, and the fragment carried backward can press on the cord.

Question 10935. Which muscle forms the rounded contour of the shoulder, is supplied by the same nerve as the skin over it, and is the chief abductor of the arm once the movement has begun? The answer is the deltoid. It arises from the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, and the axillary nerve supplies both it and the shoulder skin.

Question 10936. Which tendon forms the border of the hollow at the base of the thumb on the little finger side: the abductor pollicis longus, the extensor pollicis brevis, the extensor pollicis longus, or the extensor carpi radialis longus? The answer is the extensor pollicis longus. It hooks around the lower end of the radius to reach the thumb.

Question 10937. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior compartment of the leg with the tibial nerve, the posterior compartment with the tibial nerve, the anterior compartment with the sural nerve, or the lateral compartment with the femoral nerve? The answer is the posterior compartment with the tibial nerve. It runs down the back of the leg, and the anterior compartment takes the deep peroneal nerve.

Question 10938. Which muscle arises just below the lateral condyle of the femur, inside the capsule of the knee, and passes backward and downward to the tibia? The answer is the popliteus. Its tendon lies between the lateral meniscus and the capsule, and it unlocks the knee by turning the tibia inward at the start of bending.

Question 10939. Which structure is the chief restraint against a blow that drives the knee inward and opens the joint on the outer side: the anterior cruciate ligament, the tibial collateral ligament, the fibular collateral ligament, or the patellar tendon? The answer is the tibial collateral ligament on the inner side, which is often torn together with the medial meniscus.

Question 10940. Which muscle arises from the outer surface of the ilium between the two gluteal lines and keeps the pelvis level when the opposite foot is lifted? The answer is the gluteus medius. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, and when it is weak the pelvis drops on the unsupported side.

Question 10941. A described radiograph of the ankle shows the space between the tibia and the fibula widened, with a break high in the fibula near the knee and no break of either malleolus. Which injury is this? The answer is a Maisonneuve fracture. The force tears the syndesmosis and then breaks the fibula far above the ankle.

Question 10942. A constructed illustration: a young person twists a straight leg, and the kneecap slips outward over the ridge of the femur before returning. Which soft tissue structure on the inner side of the knee is torn? The answer is the medial patellofemoral ligament, the chief check against sideways displacement of the kneecap.

Question 10943. Which structures lie immediately behind the sternoclavicular joint and are therefore at risk when the inner end of the clavicle is driven backward: the trachea alone, the great veins and the arch of the aorta, the phrenic nerve alone, or the esophagus alone? The answer is the great veins and the arch of the aorta, with the trachea and the esophagus behind them. That is why a backward dislocation at this joint is taken seriously.

Question 10944. Which thick band of fibrous tissue stretches from the front of the calcaneus to the bases of the toes and holds up the arch of the foot? The answer is the plantar fascia. It runs forward beneath the sole in several slips, and pain at its attachment under the heel is common after long standing.

Question 10945. A described radiograph of the foot shows a small fragment pulled away from the outer side of the base of the fifth metatarsal bone. Which tendon has pulled it off? The answer is the tendon of the peroneus brevis, which attaches there. A twisted foot can produce a similar appearance.

Question 10946. Which nerve leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and then runs down the back of the thigh? The answer is the sciatic nerve. It is the largest nerve in the body, and below the hip it divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves.

Question 10947. Which of these muscles does not join the group whose tendons attach to the inner surface of the upper tibia as the pes anserinus: the sartorius, the gracilis, the semitendinosus, or the semimembranosus? The answer is the semimembranosus, which attaches behind the inner condyle instead. The three tendons of the pes anserinus spread out like a goose foot.

Question 10948. Name the two ligaments that cross one another in the middle of the knee joint, and say what each one checks. The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament and the posterior cruciate ligament. The anterior one stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur and the posterior one stops it from sliding backward.

Question 10949. Which bony prominence on the front of the upper tibia receives the patellar tendon and can be felt just below the kneecap? The answer is the tibial tuberosity. In a growing child it has its own center of ossification, and a sudden pull can separate it from the bone.

Question 10950. True or false: the fibula carries the weight of the body from the knee down to the ankle. The answer is false. The tibia carries the weight, while the fibula serves mainly for muscle attachment and as the outer wall of the ankle.

Question 10951. A described view inside the knee shows a C-shaped rim of fibrocartilage lying on the flat upper surface of the tibia, thicker at its outer edge and fixed at both ends. Which structure is shown? The answer is the medial meniscus. It is attached to the deep surface of the capsule, which is why it is torn more often than the lateral one.

Question 10952. Which nerve is at risk during an approach to the hip from the outer side, where the gluteus medius is split above the greater trochanter: the femoral nerve, the sciatic nerve, the superior gluteal nerve, or the obturator nerve? The answer is the superior gluteal nerve. It enters the buttock above the piriformis and runs between the gluteus medius and minimus.

Question 10953. A constructed illustration: after a twisting injury the knee swells and then locks so that it cannot be straightened, and a click is felt when it finally moves. Which structure is most likely caught between the bones? The answer is a torn meniscus. A displaced part of the cartilage slips between the femur and the tibia and blocks the movement.

Question 10954. Which large quadrilateral prominence can be felt on the outer side of the upper thigh and gives attachment to the gluteus medius and minimus? The answer is the greater trochanter of the femur. It lies at the junction of the neck and the shaft on the outer side, and in the adult its tip is level with the pubic tubercle.

Question 10955. Which structures lie immediately behind the posterior cruciate ligament, between it and the skin at the back of the knee? The answer is the posterior part of the capsule, with the oblique popliteal ligament behind it, and then the popliteal vessels. The artery is the deepest structure in the hollow of the knee.

Question 10956. A described radiograph of a child's elbow taken from the side shows a thin dark shadow in front of the lower humerus and another behind it, with no visible break. What does the posterior shadow mean? The answer is that fluid in the joint has pushed a fat pad backward, which points to an undisplaced fracture above the condyles.

Question 10957. Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel with the flexor tendons and is compressed in the condition that causes tingling in the first three fingers: the ulnar nerve, the median nerve, the radial nerve, or the musculocutaneous nerve? The answer is the median nerve. It lies just beneath the flexor retinaculum, and the ulnar nerve crosses the wrist outside the tunnel.

Question 10958. Which structure holds the dens of the axis against the back of the front arch of the atlas and so keeps the spinal cord from being pressed when the head turns? The answer is the transverse ligament of the atlas. It stretches between the two lateral masses, and if it gives way the dens can move backward against the cord.

Question 10959. Which ligament resists a force that turns the sole of the foot outward: the anterior talofibular ligament, the calcaneofibular ligament, the deltoid ligament, or the plantar fascia? The answer is the deltoid ligament on the medial side of the ankle. It is a strong triangular band, and the lateral ligaments resist the opposite movement.

Question 10960. Which of these bones forms the heel and takes the weight of the body first as the foot meets the ground: the talus, the calcaneus, the navicular, or the cuboid? The answer is the calcaneus, the largest bone of the foot. It lies below and behind the talus, which passes the weight on to it.

Question 10961. Which of these pairs belongs together: a break of the surgical neck of the humerus with the axillary nerve, a break of the shaft with the axillary nerve, a break of the shaft with the radial nerve, or a break of the medial epicondyle with the radial nerve? The answer is the surgical neck with the axillary nerve. The shaft break endangers the radial nerve, and the medial epicondyle break the ulnar nerve.

Question 10962. Which structure forms the shallow socket into which the head of the humerus fits: the acromion, the glenoid cavity, the coracoid process, or the greater tubercle? The answer is the glenoid cavity on the lateral border of the scapula. It is deepened only a little by the ring of fibrocartilage at its edge, and that shallowness allows the wide movement of the shoulder.

Question 10963. Which tendon runs in the groove on the front of the upper end of the humerus, held there by the transverse humeral ligament? The answer is the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii. It leaves the shoulder joint through the groove and runs down inside the sheath of the muscle.

Question 10964. A constructed illustration: a child injures the inner side of the lower humerus, and years later the elbow tilts outward at an increased angle and the little finger side of the hand is weak. Which part of the bone was damaged, and which nerve suffers late? The answer is the medial part of the growth plate, with a late palsy of the ulnar nerve. The inner side stops growing while the outer side continues, so the elbow tilts outward.

Question 10965. Within the femoral triangle, which of these lies most lateral: the femoral vein, the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, or the lymph nodes? The answer is the femoral nerve. From lateral to medial the order is nerve, artery, vein and then the lymph nodes, and the nerve lies outside the sheath of the vessels.

Question 10966. A described radiograph of the hand shows a break across the neck of the fifth metacarpal bone with the head tilted forward toward the palm. Which injury is this? The answer is a boxer's fracture. The neck gives way when the closed fist strikes a hard surface, and the pull of the muscles makes the finger droop.

Question 10967. True or false: the anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur. The answer is true. It runs upward and backward from the front of the tibia to the back of the femur, and it also resists twisting and hyperextension of the knee.

Question 10968. Which sheet of fibrous tissue joins the shafts of the radius and the ulna and carries the force of the hand up to the arm? The answer is the interosseous membrane of the forearm. Its fibers run downward and medially from the radius to the ulna, and it also gives attachment to muscles.

Question 10969. Which structure is the chief restraint against the tibia being driven backward on the femur: the anterior cruciate ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, the tibial collateral ligament, or the iliotibial band? The answer is the posterior cruciate ligament. It is the stronger of the cruciate pair and is injured when a bent knee is struck from the front.

Question 10970. At the wrist, which structure lies immediately medial to the ulnar artery, between the artery and the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris? The answer is the ulnar nerve. It crosses the front of the wrist just outside the carpal tunnel, so a cut there endangers both the nerve and the artery.

Question 10971. A described radiograph of the neck shows a break through the narrow bridge of bone between the upper and lower articular surfaces of the second cervical vertebra, with its body slipped forward on the vertebra below. Which injury is this? The answer is a break through the pars interarticularis of the axis. Both sides give way, and the body of the vertebra moves forward.

Question 10972. Which nerve leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen and supplies the muscles that pull the thigh inward: the femoral nerve, the sciatic nerve, the obturator nerve, or the pudendal nerve? The answer is the obturator nerve. It comes from the lumbar plexus and passes through the upper part of the foramen with the obturator vessels.

Question 10973. Which long flat band of fibrous tissue runs down the outer side of the thigh from the iliac crest to the outer condyle of the tibia? The answer is the iliotibial band. It is the thickened part of the fascia lata, it receives the insertion of the gluteus maximus, and it helps steady the knee.

Question 10974. To which bony point does the Achilles tendon attach: the navicular bone, the calcaneal tuberosity, the lateral malleolus, or the head of the talus? The answer is the calcaneal tuberosity on the back of the heel. The tendon is the thickest in the body and lies just under the skin.

Question 10975. A described radiograph of the forearm shows a break of the ulna just below the elbow with the head of the radius displaced forward out of its ring. Which injury is this? The answer is a Monteggia fracture. The radial head must be looked for in every radiograph of a broken forearm.

Question 10976. Which of these pairs belongs together: the lateral compartment of the leg with the superficial peroneal nerve, the lateral compartment with the deep peroneal nerve, the anterior compartment with the superficial peroneal nerve, or the posterior compartment with a peroneal nerve? The answer is the lateral compartment with the superficial peroneal nerve. That compartment holds the peroneus longus and brevis, and the deep peroneal nerve belongs to the front of the leg.

Question 10977. Name two structures, one nerve and one artery, that pass into the sole of the foot behind the medial malleolus. The answer is the tibial nerve and the posterior tibial artery. Both run down the back of the leg and turn forward under the flexor retinaculum beside the tendons of the deep muscles.

Question 10978. Which roughened area on the upper radius receives the tendon of the biceps brachii? The answer is the radial tuberosity. It lies on the medial side of the bone just below the neck, and the tendon turns as it reaches it so that the muscle can both bend the elbow and turn the palm upward.

Question 10979. Which bones form the floor of the hollow at the base of the thumb: the lunate and the triquetrum, the scaphoid and the trapezium, the capitate and the hamate, or the pisiform and the hamate? The answer is the scaphoid and the trapezium. The hollow is bounded by the tendons of the thumb, and tenderness in its floor after a fall points to the scaphoid.

Question 10980. The neck of the femur runs upward and inward from the shaft to the head. In which of the three reference planes does that line lie, and what is the angle between the neck and the shaft called? The answer is the frontal plane, and the angle is the angle of inclination. In the adult it is a little over one hundred and twenty degrees.

Question 10981. A described magnetic resonance imaging scan of the wrist, taken months after a fall, shows the part of the scaphoid nearest the forearm as dark and without signal while the part near the thumb looks normal. What has happened? The answer is that the proximal part has lost its blood supply and has died. Blood enters the bone near the thumb and flows backward toward the forearm.

Question 10982. Which artery gives the branches that creep up the back of the neck of the femur inside the capsule, and where do those branches lie? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery, whose branches run in the reflected fold of the capsule along the neck. The ligament of the head carries only a small vessel of its own.

Question 10983. A constructed illustration: after the head of the humerus has left its socket downward, the shoulder looks squared and the skin over its outer side is numb. Which nerve is injured, and what movement will be weak? The answer is the axillary nerve, and abduction of the arm will be weak. The nerve winds around the surgical neck, close to the lower part of the capsule.

Question 10984. Which of these structures is not found behind the medial malleolus: the tibial nerve, the posterior tibial artery, the tendon of the flexor hallucis longus, or the sural nerve? The answer is the sural nerve, which runs down the back of the leg and along the outer border of the foot. The others pass under the flexor retinaculum into the sole.

Question 10985. Which ligament of the hip joint arises from the ischium, spirals upward and outward over the back of the neck of the femur, and becomes tight when the hip is fully flexed? The answer is the ischiofemoral ligament. It checks the last part of flexion and inward rotation and helps to hold the head in its socket.

Question 10986. True or false: the medial meniscus is more firmly fixed to the capsule of the knee than the lateral meniscus. The answer is true. The medial meniscus is attached along its outer edge to the deep part of the tibial collateral ligament, while the lateral one is more mobile.

Question 10987. A described specimen of the hip shows a ring of fibrocartilage around the rim of the socket, with a tear in its front and upper part. What is the ring? The answer is the acetabular labrum. It deepens the socket and helps to seal the joint, and its front and upper part is the part most often torn.

Question 10988. Which of these structures forms the roof over the head of the humerus and the tendon of the supraspinatus: the acromion alone, the coracoacromial arch, the coracoid process alone, or the spine of the scapula? The answer is the coracoacromial arch, formed by the acromion, the coracoid process and the ligament between them. The subacromial bursa lies beneath it.

Question 10989. Which rough elevation on the outer surface of the middle of the humerus marks the insertion of the muscle that forms the contour of the shoulder? The answer is the deltoid tuberosity. It lies about halfway down the shaft on the outer side, and the deltoid pulls on it to lift the arm away from the body.

Question 10990. A constructed illustration: a middle-aged person develops a painful, flat foot, and the tendon felt just behind the medial malleolus is no longer strong. Which tendon has failed, and what does it normally do? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior. It attaches mainly to the navicular bone and holds up the arch of the foot.

Question 10991. Which of these pairs belongs together: the gluteus medius with the inferior gluteal nerve, the gluteus medius with the superior gluteal nerve, the gluteus maximus with the superior gluteal nerve, or the tensor of the fascia lata with the sciatic nerve? The answer is the gluteus medius with the superior gluteal nerve. The gluteus maximus takes the inferior gluteal nerve.

Question 10992. Which structure passes out of the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen: the tendon of the obturator internus, the sciatic nerve, the tendon of the piriformis, or the obturator externus? The answer is the tendon of the obturator internus. It turns around the spine of the ischium, while the sciatic nerve and the piriformis pass through the greater sciatic foramen.

Question 10993. A described radiograph of the foot shows that the base of the second metatarsal bone has moved away from the bone beside it and the front of the foot is shifted outward. Which joint has given way? The answer is the tarsometatarsal joint, and the injury is a Lisfranc disruption. The second metatarsal is the keystone of that line of joints.

Question 10994. Which structure lies immediately deep to the flexor retinaculum in the middle of the wrist, superficial to the tendons of the flexor digitorum? The answer is the median nerve. It runs down the middle of the front of the wrist, and the long flexor tendons lie behind it and to either side.

Question 10995. Which structure lies immediately behind the dens of the axis and is at risk when the dens is broken at its base: the vertebral artery, the spinal cord, the esophagus, or the recurrent laryngeal nerve? The answer is the spinal cord. It lies in the canal just behind the dens, separated from it only by the transverse ligament.

Question 10996. Which of these is the largest sesamoid bone in the body: the pisiform, the patella, the fabella, or the sesamoid of the great toe? The answer is the patella. It develops inside the tendon of the quadriceps and lies in front of the knee joint, and a sesamoid bone is one that lies within a tendon.

Question 10997. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the elbow, the little finger and the ring finger are bent and cannot be straightened, the spaces between the fingers are hollowed, and the inner side of the hand is numb. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the ulnar nerve, which lies behind the medial epicondyle and supplies most of the small muscles of the hand.

Question 10998. Which structure is the chief check against hyperextension of the knee: the anterior cruciate ligament, the patellar tendon, the iliotibial band, or the oblique popliteal ligament? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It is taut when the knee is straight, and it also limits inward rotation of the tibia.

Question 10999. Which structure forms the flat upper surface of the lower end of the tibia that carries the weight of the body onto the talus? The answer is the tibial plafond. It is the roof of the ankle joint, and because it carries the whole weight a break through it disturbs the joint surface.

Question 11000. Which part of which bone forms the knuckle of a finger: the base of the proximal phalanx, the head of the metacarpal, the neck of the metacarpal, or the base of the metacarpal? The answer is the head of the metacarpal. It is the rounded far end of the bone and joins the first bone of the finger.

To summarize, bone carries load along its length, its periosteum stops at the articular cartilage, and the growth plate is the weak point of a child's skeleton. The named breaks each fix a bone, a level and a direction, from the Colles fracture of the radius and the scaphoid waist to the boxer's fracture of the fifth metacarpal, the Monteggia and Galeazzi pairs, the Segond avulsion and the Maisonneuve break high in the fibula. Blood enters several bones from one end, so the head of the femur, the proximal part of the scaphoid and the talus are at risk after a break near the neck. The ligaments hold each joint in a fixed order, with the cruciate ligaments inside the knee, the tibial and fibular collateral ligaments at its sides, the deltoid ligament against eversion at the ankle and the anterior talofibular ligament against inversion, while the nerves lie where the bone is thinnest, the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the radial nerve in the spiral groove, the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle and the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 111 — Neurological Anatomy

Neurological anatomy is the map a clinician needs before any examination of the nervous system can mean anything, and this chapter walks that map from the spinal cord upward. It covers the membranes around the brain and the cord, their blood supply, the plexuses of the limbs, the twelve cranial nerves, the tracts and nuclei of the brainstem, and the injuries that bring each of them to the bedside. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately and then explains why, so nothing has to be held in mind. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 11001. Which membrane of the meninges lies directly against the brain, following it into every sulcus? The answer is the pia mater. It is the innermost of the three and is too thin to be peeled from the cortex. The dura and the arachnoid lie outside it, with cerebrospinal fluid between the arachnoid and the pia.

Question 11002. The space between the arachnoid and the pia is filled with cerebrospinal fluid. Which of these names it: the epidural space, the subdural space, the subarachnoid space, or the extradural space? The answer is the subarachnoid space. It surrounds the whole brain and cord and carries the arteries into the sulci. The subdural space is only potential, and the epidural lies outside the dura.

Question 11003. A described magnetic resonance image of the lower spine shows the tapered end of the cord with a thin strand continuing down toward the sacrum. Which strand is shown? The answer is the filum terminale, a thread of pia mater that anchors the cord to the coccyx. The cord itself ends at the conus medullaris.

Question 11004. How many pairs of spinal nerves leave the cord: twenty-eight, thirty-one, thirty-three, or thirty-six? The answer is thirty-one. There are eight cervical pairs, twelve thoracic, five lumbar, five sacral and one coccygeal. Each pair leaves the vertebral canal through its own intervertebral foramen, just above or below its own vertebra.

Question 11005. Within the vertebral canal, which structure lies immediately anterior to the dura of the cord: the ligamentum flavum, the posterior longitudinal ligament, the lamina, or the pedicle? The answer is the posterior longitudinal ligament. It runs down the back of the vertebral bodies and discs, and the dura rests against it. The ligamentum flavum lies behind the cord.

Question 11006. A constructed illustration: a needle enters the lower back at the third lumbar spine to obtain cerebrospinal fluid. Which space does it enter, and why is that level chosen? The answer is the subarachnoid space. The cord ends about the first or second lumbar vertebra, so below that only descending roots can be touched. The needle passes between the laminae.

Question 11007. Which single artery runs down the anterior midline of the cord and supplies its anterior two thirds? The answer is the anterior spinal artery, formed from branches of the two vertebral arteries. It lies in the anterior median fissure. The posterior columns and horns are supplied by the two posterior spinal arteries.

Question 11008. The upper cervical cord gains an extra supply from which artery, which ascends through the foramen magnum beside the cord: the vertebral, the basilar, the occipital, or the posterior cerebral? The answer is the vertebral artery. It gives the anterior spinal artery and small branches along the nerve roots. Lower down the cord depends on those radicular arteries.

Question 11009. True or false: in the adult the lower end of the cord lies at the first or second lumbar vertebra. The answer is true. The cord and the vertebral column grow at different rates, so the cord ends well above the bottom of the dural sac. Below it only the roots of the cauda equina descend.

Question 11010. A described specimen of the lower dural sac shows a spray of nerve roots descending around a thin central strand, like a horse's tail. What is that collection called, and why does it descend? The answer is the cauda equina. Those roots travel down to reach the foramina below the end of the cord. The thin central strand is the filum terminale.

Question 11011. The phrenic nerve, the motor nerve of the diaphragm, arises chiefly from which roots: the second, third and fourth cervical, the fourth and fifth cervical, the first and second thoracic, or the fifth and sixth cervical? The answer is the second, third and fourth cervical. They form the cervical plexus and give the phrenic nerve. Irritation of the diaphragm can be felt at the shoulder.

Question 11012. Which large vein lies immediately anterior to the anterior scalene muscle, while the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass behind it? The answer is the subclavian vein. It crosses the first rib in front of the muscle and joins the internal jugular vein behind the clavicle. In the lower neck the vein lies in front of the artery.

Question 11013. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the shoulder, an arm hangs with the elbow straight and the palm turned backward. Which roots of the brachial plexus are injured? The answer is the fifth and sixth cervical roots, which form the upper trunk. The shoulder muscles and the flexors of the elbow are paralyzed, and the forearm stays pronated.

Question 11014. In the axilla the brachial plexus is rearranged into cords named for their relation to which artery: the axillary, the subclavian, the brachial, or the profunda brachii? The answer is the axillary artery. The lateral, posterior and medial cords surround it before dividing into the terminal nerves. They travel with it in the axillary sheath.

Question 11015. Which nerve of the upper limb arises from the posterior cord and winds through the spiral groove on the back of the humerus? The answer is the radial nerve. That groove lies against the shaft, so a fracture of the middle of the humerus can injure it. It supplies the extensors of the arm and forearm and the skin over the back of the hand.

Question 11016. A described magnetic resonance image of the neck base shows nerve roots emerging between two muscles and joining into three trunks. Which structures are shown? The answer is the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, between the anterior and middle scalene muscles. The fifth and sixth cervical roots form the upper trunk, the seventh runs alone, and the eighth cervical with the first thoracic forms the lower trunk.

Question 11017. Which of these muscles is supplied by the median nerve: the flexor carpi ulnaris, the abductor pollicis brevis, the first dorsal interosseous, or the extensor digitorum? The answer is the abductor pollicis brevis, a thenar muscle. The median nerve reaches it by a recurrent branch that turns back around the flexor retinaculum. The flexor carpi ulnaris and the interossei are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Question 11018. Which of these pairs belongs together: the ulnar nerve with the groove behind the medial epicondyle, the radial nerve with the medial epicondyle, the median nerve with the spiral groove, or the axillary nerve with the cubital tunnel? The answer is the ulnar nerve with the groove behind the medial epicondyle. Striking it sends a shock down the little finger. The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel.

Question 11019. Name two nerves of the upper limb that arise from the medial cord of the brachial plexus, spoken as a list. The answer is the ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The medial cord also gives the medial pectoral nerve and a root to the median nerve. The ulnar nerve is the largest of its branches.

Question 11020. Which nerve supplies the deltoid and the skin over the lower part of the shoulder, and is stretched when the shoulder dislocates? The answer is the axillary nerve. It arises from the posterior cord and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. It also supplies the teres minor.

Question 11021. Which nerve is most often injured when a fracture crosses the middle of the shaft of the humerus: the axillary, the radial, the median, or the ulnar nerve? The answer is the radial nerve. It lies in the spiral groove against the bone, so the fracture and the callus that follows can trap it. The wrist drops because the extensors are paralyzed.

Question 11022. Which nerve arises from the lumbar plexus, descends beside the psoas muscle, and supplies the front of the thigh? The answer is the femoral nerve. It leaves the abdomen under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery. It supplies the quadriceps and the skin of the front of the thigh and the medial side of the leg.

Question 11023. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the outer side of the knee, a person cannot lift the foot and the toes drag. Which nerve is injured in its described position? The answer is the common fibular nerve, also called the peroneal nerve. It winds around the neck of the fibula under the skin, where it is easily compressed. It supplies the muscles that lift the foot.

Question 11024. A described magnetic resonance image of the pelvis shows a thick nerve leaving the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle. Which nerve is shown, and what does it supply? The answer is the sciatic nerve, the largest nerve in the body. It runs down the back of the thigh, supplies the hamstrings and then divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

Question 11025. Within the femoral triangle, which structure lies immediately lateral to the femoral artery: the femoral vein, the femoral nerve, the great saphenous vein, or the adductor longus? The answer is the femoral nerve. From medial to lateral the order is vein, artery, nerve, so the pulse is felt just medial to the nerve. The vein lies medial to the artery.

Question 11026. Which nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg, which lift the foot: the tibial, the deep fibular, the superficial fibular, or the sural nerve? The answer is the deep fibular nerve. It also supplies the small muscles on the top of the foot and the skin between the first two toes. The superficial fibular nerve turns the foot outward.

Question 11027. True or false: the obturator nerve supplies the muscles of the medial compartment of the thigh. The answer is true. It arises from the second, third and fourth lumbar roots and leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen. It supplies the adductors and a small area of skin on the inner thigh.

Question 11028. Which nerve runs down the medial side of the leg beside the great saphenous vein and supplies the skin there? The answer is the saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve. It accompanies the vein below the knee. It carries sensation from the medial side of the leg and the instep.

Question 11029. In the popliteal fossa, which of these lies most superficial, nearest the skin: the popliteal artery, the popliteal vein, the tibial nerve, or the common fibular nerve? The answer is the tibial nerve. From the surface inward the order is nerve, vein, then artery, which lies deepest against the bone. That order matters when a swelling presses on them.

Question 11030. A described magnetic resonance image of the ankle shows a nerve passing behind the medial malleolus in a tunnel with tendons and vessels. Which nerve is shown, and what does pressure there cause? The answer is the tibial nerve, in the tarsal tunnel roofed by the flexor retinaculum. Pressure causes numbness and burning of the sole and weakness of the small muscles of the foot.

Question 11031. A constructed illustration: after a deep cut behind the knee, a person cannot rise on tiptoe. Which nerve and which muscle group are involved? The answer is the tibial nerve and the calf muscles, the gastrocnemius and the soleus. They plantar flex the ankle and are the chief muscles of standing on tiptoe. The ankle jerk also depends on that nerve.

Question 11032. The ankle reflex depends chiefly on which root: the fourth lumbar, the fifth lumbar, the first sacral, or the second sacral? The answer is the first sacral root. Tapping the Achilles tendon stretches the calf muscles, and the reflex arc runs through that root. The knee jerk depends chiefly on the third and fourth lumbar roots.

Question 11033. Within the carotid sheath in the neck, which structure lies immediately posterior to the internal carotid artery? The answer is the vagus nerve, the tenth cranial nerve. The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the artery, and the vagus lies behind, between the two. The sheath holds the artery medially, the vein laterally and the nerve behind.

Question 11034. Which cranial nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the heart, the lungs and the gut, and by which ordinal is it named? The answer is the tenth cranial nerve, the vagus. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and descends in the carotid sheath. Its branches reach the chest and the abdomen, where they slow the heart and drive the gut.

Question 11035. Which of these cranial nerves carries no motor fibers at all: the optic, the oculomotor, the trigeminal, or the hypoglossal? The answer is the optic nerve, the second cranial nerve, which is purely sensory. The oculomotor and hypoglossal are almost purely motor, and the trigeminal carries both sensation and the motor supply to the muscles of chewing.

Question 11036. Which of these pairs belongs together: the third cranial nerve with the superior oblique, the fourth cranial nerve with the superior oblique, the sixth with the medial rectus, or the twelfth with the soft palate? The answer is the fourth cranial nerve with the superior oblique. That muscle turns the eye down and in, so its palsy tilts the head. The sixth nerve supplies the lateral rectus.

Question 11037. A described cross section of the midbrain shows a nucleus in the floor of the cerebral aqueduct and a nerve emerging between the two cerebral peduncles. Which cranial nerve is shown? The answer is the third cranial nerve, the oculomotor. Its nucleus lies in the midbrain in front of the aqueduct. Its fibers pass through the red nucleus and leave between the peduncles.

Question 11038. Which nerve leaves the brainstem between the pons and the medulla, medial to the facial nerve: the fifth, the sixth, the eighth, or the twelfth? The answer is the sixth cranial nerve, the abducens. It runs forward through the subarachnoid space and the cavernous sinus to the lateral rectus. That long course makes it the first nerve to suffer when pressure rises inside the skull.

Question 11039. Name two of the cranial nerves that carry parasympathetic fibers to the head, spoken as a list. The answer is the third cranial nerve, the oculomotor, and the seventh, the facial. The oculomotor fibers constrict the pupil, and the facial fibers reach the tear glands and the salivary glands below the jaw. The ninth and tenth nerves carry the same kind of fibers further down.

Question 11040. Which cranial nerve is tested by asking a person to push out the tongue, and by which ordinal is it named? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, the hypoglossal, which leaves the skull through its own canal beside the foramen magnum. A palsy of one side makes the tongue deviate toward the weak side.

Question 11041. Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression: the fifth, the seventh, the ninth, or the twelfth? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve, the facial. It leaves the skull through the internal acoustic meatus and then the stylomastoid foramen. Its palsy drops the corner of the mouth and prevents the eye from closing.

Question 11042. A described section of the internal acoustic meatus shows two nerves side by side, one toward the cochlea and one toward the vestibule. Which cranial nerve is shown, and what are its two parts? The answer is the eighth cranial nerve, with a cochlear part for hearing and a vestibular part for balance. The facial nerve travels with them into the same canal.

Question 11043. Which cranial nerve is the great sensory nerve of the face, and how many divisions does it have? The answer is the fifth cranial nerve, the trigeminal, which has three. The ophthalmic division supplies the forehead and the eye, the maxillary the cheek and the upper teeth, and the mandibular the lower jaw and the tongue.

Question 11044. Which division of the trigeminal nerve supplies the skin of the lower lip and the chin: the ophthalmic, the maxillary, the mandibular, or the facial? The answer is the mandibular division. It leaves the skull through the foramen ovale and also supplies the muscles of chewing. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of expression, not the skin.

Question 11045. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the cheek, the skin over the upper jaw and the upper lip is numb while the face still moves. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the maxillary division of the fifth cranial nerve. It leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum and crosses the back of the cheekbone. Because the facial nerve is intact, the face still moves.

Question 11046. Which vessel lies immediately anterior to the pons, separating it from the clivus? The answer is the basilar artery, formed where the two vertebral arteries join at the lower border of the pons. It runs upward in the midline and divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

Question 11047. A nucleus in the medulla sends its fibers out to the muscles of the tongue. Which cranial nerve does it belong to: the ninth, the tenth, the eleventh, or the twelfth? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, the hypoglossal. Its nucleus lies near the midline in the lower medulla, and its fibers leave between the pyramid and the olive.

Question 11048. Which cranial nerve runs up through the foramen magnum and supplies the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve, the accessory. Its fibers arise in the upper cervical cord and ascend into the skull before turning back out. That ascent explains why it leaves the skull again through the jugular foramen.

Question 11049. True or false: the seventh cranial nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue. The answer is true. Those fibers travel with the lingual nerve and then join the facial nerve through the chorda tympani. The posterior third sends its taste fibers with the ninth cranial nerve instead.

Question 11050. A described magnetic resonance image of the base of the skull shows a large opening through which the medulla and its membranes pass, with a nerve beside the cord. Which opening and which nerve are shown? The answer is the foramen magnum, with the eleventh cranial nerve beside the cord. The vertebral arteries pass through it as well.

Question 11051. A constructed illustration: a small infarct in the medial medulla leaves the tongue weak on one side and the limbs weak on the other, with loss of position sense there too. Which pattern is illustrated: lateral medullary syndrome, medial medullary syndrome, a half section of the cord, or a central cord cavity? The answer is medial medullary syndrome. The twelfth nerve, the pyramid and the medial lemniscus are damaged together.

Question 11052. Which vessel runs in the midline in front of the pons, formed where the two vertebral arteries join? The answer is the basilar artery. It lies in the groove on the front of the pons and gives the pontine branches, the labyrinthine artery and the superior cerebellar arteries. At the upper border of the pons it divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

Question 11053. A constructed illustration: a slowly growing mass between the cerebellum and the pons causes deafness and ringing in one ear, and later numbness of the face on that side. Which nerve is pressed first? The answer is the eighth cranial nerve, at the cerebellopontine angle near the internal acoustic meatus. The facial nerve lies beside it and is pressed later.

Question 11054. Which of these forms the medial wall of the lateral ventricle: the septum pellucidum, the corpus callosum, the thalamus, or the head of the caudate nucleus? The answer is the septum pellucidum, a thin double membrane between the two lateral ventricles. The corpus callosum forms the roof, the thalamus part of the floor, and the caudate nucleus the lateral wall.

Question 11055. What is the name of the great band of white matter that joins the two cerebral hemispheres beneath the longitudinal fissure? The answer is the corpus callosum. Its fibers cross the midline and connect matching areas of the two hemispheres. Its middle part is the body, its front end the genu, and its back end the splenium.

Question 11056. A described coronal section of the brain shows a fan of white matter converging between the basal ganglia and the thalamus. Which structure is shown, and what happens when it is destroyed? The answer is the internal capsule. Its fibers carry movement and sensation between the cortex and the lower centers, and because they are packed so tightly a small lesion can paralyze the opposite side.

Question 11057. A constructed illustration: a small bleed in the posterior limb of the internal capsule weakens the face, the arm and the leg on the opposite side. Which of these tracts has been interrupted: the spinothalamic tract, the corticospinal tract, the posterior column, or the spinocerebellar tract? The answer is the corticospinal tract. A lesion the size of a pea can cause a dense paralysis.

Question 11058. Which of these pairs belongs together: the precentral gyrus with the motor cortex, the postcentral gyrus with the motor cortex, the superior temporal gyrus with vision, or the occipital lobe with hearing? The answer is the precentral gyrus with the motor cortex. It lies in front of the central sulcus and sends out the corticospinal fibers. The occipital lobe serves vision.

Question 11059. Name two structures that lie within the posterior cranial fossa, spoken as a list. The answer is the cerebellum and the brainstem, meaning the pons and the medulla. The fossa is the lowest and largest of the three, roofed by the tentorium cerebelli. The internal acoustic meatus and the jugular foramen open into it.

Question 11060. Which part of the brainstem lies between the pons above and the spinal cord below and holds the centers for the heart and for breathing? The answer is the medulla oblongata. It contains the nuclei of several cranial nerves and the crossing of the corticospinal fibers. The fourth ventricle lies behind it.

Question 11061. The gag reflex is tested by touching the back of the throat. Which cranial nerve carries its sensory limb: the seventh, the ninth, the eleventh, or the twelfth? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve, the glossopharyngeal. It carries sensation from the back of the throat and the posterior third of the tongue. The tenth nerve lifts the palate.

Question 11062. Which cranial nerve supplies the parotid gland with its secretomotor fibers, and through which ganglion do they pass? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve, the glossopharyngeal, through the otic ganglion. The fibers leave the skull through the jugular foramen and reach the ganglion below the foramen ovale. From there they travel with a branch of the fifth nerve.

Question 11063. A constructed illustration: a person has a hoarse voice, the soft palate droops on one side, and the gag reflex is lost there. Which nerve is damaged, and through which opening does it leave the skull? The answer is the tenth cranial nerve, the vagus, through the jugular foramen. It supplies the muscles of the palate, the pharynx and the larynx.

Question 11064. A described magnetic resonance image of the brain shows a narrow slit of fluid in the midline between the two thalami, roofed by a thin membrane with a fringe of vessels. Which space is shown? The answer is the third ventricle. It opens in front into the lateral ventricles and narrows behind into the cerebral aqueduct.

Question 11065. Which structure lies immediately behind the brainstem and below the occipital lobes, separated from the cerebrum by the tentorium cerebelli? The answer is the cerebellum, which fills the posterior cranial fossa behind the pons and the medulla. Its two hemispheres are joined in the midline by the vermis.

Question 11066. Which of these forms the roof of the fourth ventricle: the cerebellum, the pons, the medulla, or the thalamus? The answer is the cerebellum. The floor is formed by the pons and the medulla, and the roof by the cerebellar vermis and thin sheets of tissue. The ventricle narrows above into the cerebral aqueduct and opens below into the subarachnoid space.

Question 11067. True or false: most fibers of the corticospinal tract cross to the opposite side in the lower medulla. The answer is true. The crossing is visible as the decussation of the pyramids on the front of the medulla. After crossing, the fibers descend in the lateral column of the cord to the lower motor neurons.

Question 11068. Which ascending tract lies in the posterior column of the cord and carries vibration and position sense from the leg? The answer is the fasciculus gracilis, which ends in the nucleus gracilis of the medulla. It lies on the medial side of the posterior column, next to the midline. The fibers from the arm lie lateral to it in the fasciculus cuneatus.

Question 11069. A lesion divides one half of the spinal cord. Pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side and position sense on the same side. What is that pattern called: Brown-Sequard syndrome, syringomyelia, tabes dorsalis, or a central cord lesion? The answer is Brown-Sequard syndrome, the result of a half section of the cord. The spinothalamic fibers have already crossed, while the posterior column fibers have not.

Question 11070. A described transverse section of the spinal cord shows a cavity in the center of the gray matter, with loss of pain and temperature in both arms and preserved position sense. Which condition is illustrated? The answer is syringomyelia. The cavity begins near the center of the cord and destroys the crossing spinothalamic fibers as they pass. The sensory loss therefore appears on both sides.

Question 11071. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the front of the head, a person can no longer smell. Which nerve and which part of the skull are involved? The answer is the first cranial nerve, the olfactory, and the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. Its fine fibers pass through the holes of that thin plate. Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose may follow.

Question 11072. Which cranial nerve passes through the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery: the second, the third, the fourth, or the sixth? The answer is the second cranial nerve, the optic nerve, which carries sight from the retina to the optic chiasm. The third, fourth and sixth nerves reach the eye muscles through the superior orbital fissure instead.

Question 11073. Within the cavernous sinus, which cranial nerve lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery? The answer is the sixth cranial nerve, the abducens, running forward in the sinus beside the artery. The third and fourth nerves and the first two divisions of the fifth lie in the wall of the sinus.

Question 11074. Which cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward? The answer is the sixth cranial nerve, the abducens, which has the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve. Because it turns the eye outward, a palsy leaves the eye turned inward by the unopposed medial rectus.

Question 11075. Which cranial nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure and supplies the superior oblique: the third, the fourth, the sixth, or the first division of the fifth? The answer is the fourth cranial nerve, the trochlear, the only one to leave the back of the brainstem. Its muscle turns the eye down and in, so its palsy makes the person tilt the head.

Question 11076. Which of these pairs belongs together: the jugular foramen with the ninth, tenth and eleventh nerves, the foramen rotundum with the mandibular division, the internal acoustic meatus with the twelfth nerve, or the hypoglossal canal with the eighth? The answer is the jugular foramen with the ninth, tenth and eleventh nerves. The mandibular division leaves through the foramen ovale.

Question 11077. A described magnetic resonance image of the base of the skull shows a nerve passing through a small canal of its own in the occipital bone beside the foramen magnum. Which nerve is shown? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, the hypoglossal, in the hypoglossal canal. It supplies the muscles of the tongue, and its course is short and direct.

Question 11078. Which cranial nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue: the seventh, the ninth, the tenth, or the twelfth? The answer is the ninth cranial nerve, the glossopharyngeal, whose fibers reach the tongue by way of the lingual branch. The seventh nerve carries taste from the anterior two thirds instead.

Question 11079. A described section of the brain is cut from front to back exactly through the midline and shows the corpus callosum along its whole length. In which plane is it cut, and how much of the brain does it show? The answer is the median plane, a sagittal section through the middle. It shows the medial surface of both hemispheres, with the corpus callosum between them.

Question 11080. Which plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves, and which nerve descends from it to the diaphragm? The answer is the cervical plexus, from which the phrenic nerve descends. The plexus also gives the small nerves that supply the skin of the neck and the back of the head.

Question 11081. Which plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the lower four cervical nerves and the first thoracic: the cervical, the brachial, the lumbar, or the sacral? The answer is the brachial plexus, which passes between the scalene muscles and then through the axilla. Its five roots join into three trunks, six divisions, three cords and five terminal nerves.

Question 11082. A described dissection of the neck shows a nerve lying on the front of the scalene muscle and descending to enter the chest between the subclavian vein and the subclavian artery. Which nerve is shown, and which muscle does it supply? The answer is the phrenic nerve, which supplies the diaphragm. It carries fibers from the third, fourth and fifth cervical roots.

Question 11083. Which nerve emerges from the medial border of the psoas muscle and leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen? The answer is the obturator nerve, from the second, third and fourth lumbar roots. It supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh and the skin over the inner side of the thigh.

Question 11084. Which roots form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus: the fifth and sixth cervical, the eighth cervical and first thoracic, the seventh cervical alone, or the fourth cervical? The answer is the fifth and sixth cervical roots, which join between the scalene muscles and divide into two. The eighth cervical and first thoracic roots form the lower trunk.

Question 11085. A constructed illustration: a person wakes with a face that droops on one side, cannot close the eye and cannot wrinkle the forehead, while the arms and legs move normally. Which nerve is affected? The answer is the seventh cranial nerve, the facial. The whole side is weak, including the forehead, which shows that the nerve itself is at fault.

Question 11086. Which structure lies immediately deep to the parotid gland and divides it into a superficial and a deep part? The answer is the facial nerve, the seventh cranial nerve, which enters the gland from behind and breaks into its branches within it. The parotid duct crosses the masseter and opens beside the upper molar teeth.

Question 11087. A constructed illustration: a person cannot lift the shoulder and cannot turn the head against resistance, while the arms and legs are strong. Which of these nerves is damaged: the ninth cranial nerve, the tenth, the eleventh, or the twelfth? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve, the accessory, at the jugular foramen. Its fibers supply the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius.

Question 11088. Which cranial nerve supplies the muscle that lifts the upper eyelid, and where is its nucleus? The answer is the third cranial nerve, the oculomotor, whose nucleus lies in the midbrain in front of the cerebral aqueduct. A palsy of the nerve drops the eyelid and turns the eye outward and down.

Question 11089. True or false: the nerve to the stapedius muscle and the chorda tympani are branches of the fifth cranial nerve. The answer is false. Both belong to the seventh cranial nerve, the facial, given off inside the bony canal as it runs to the stylomastoid foramen. The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.

Question 11090. A described cross section of the spinal cord through the cervical enlargement shows a broad anterior horn. Which cells does that horn hold, and what do their fibers supply? The answer is the lower motor neurons, whose fibers supply the muscles of the arm. The horn is wide here because so many muscles of the hand and forearm are represented.

Question 11091. Which of these tracts carries the impulses that produce voluntary movement: the spinothalamic, the corticospinal, the posterior column, or the spinocerebellar? The answer is the corticospinal tract, which begins in the motor cortex and ends on the lower motor neurons of the cord. The posterior column carries vibration and position sense.

Question 11092. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the internal capsule: the thalamus, the lentiform nucleus, the caudate nucleus, or the corpus callosum? The answer is the lentiform nucleus, made of the putamen and the globus pallidus. The thalamus lies on the medial side, and the capsule is the narrow gate for nearly all fibers to and from the cortex.

Question 11093. A constructed illustration: blood from a burst swelling at the base of the brain spreads through the fluid around the brain and the cord. Which space holds it, and where does that fluid normally return to the blood? The answer is the subarachnoid space, with absorption into the dural venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations. Blood there irritates the meninges and stiffens the neck.

Question 11094. Which artery supplies most of the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere: the anterior cerebral, the middle cerebral, the posterior cerebral, or the basilar? The answer is the middle cerebral artery, which runs in the lateral sulcus and sends branches over the insula and the convexity. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface.

Question 11095. Which artery arises from the vertebral artery and supplies the lateral part of the medulla and the lower surface of the cerebellum? The answer is the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, which winds around the upper medulla. Blockage of it produces a lateral medullary syndrome with loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side of the body.

Question 11096. A described computed tomography scan of the head shows a small patch of low density in the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Which tract has been damaged, and what will the person be unable to do? The answer is the corticospinal tract, and the opposite side of the body cannot be moved. The fibers are packed so closely that a tiny lesion causes a large weakness.

Question 11097. Which of these connects the third ventricle to the fourth: the cerebral aqueduct, the interventricular foramen, the central canal, or the median aperture? The answer is the cerebral aqueduct, a narrow channel through the midbrain. The interventricular foramen joins each lateral ventricle to the third, and the central canal lies in the cord.

Question 11098. Which of these pairs belongs together: the middle cerebral artery with the lateral surface, the anterior cerebral artery with the occipital lobe, the posterior cerebral artery with the frontal lobe, or the basilar artery with the medial surface? The answer is the middle cerebral artery with the lateral surface. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface, and the posterior cerebral artery the occipital lobe.

Question 11099. A described section of the brainstem is cut at right angles to its long axis and shows the cerebral aqueduct surrounded by a thick cap of gray matter, with two large peduncles in front. Which part is shown, and in which plane? The answer is the midbrain, cut in a transverse plane. The two peduncles carry the corticospinal fibers down toward the pons.

Question 11100. Which swelling on the posterior root of a spinal nerve holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that enter the cord? The answer is the posterior root ganglion, also called the dorsal root ganglion. Each spinal nerve has one, lying in the intervertebral foramen. The anterior root beside it carries the fibers that leave the cord.

To summarize, the brain and the cord are wrapped in the dura mater, the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, and the cerebrospinal fluid that cushions them lies in the subarachnoid space and returns to the blood through the arachnoid granulations. The spinal cord ends near the first or second lumbar vertebra, so the roots below it form the cauda equina, and its blood comes from the anterior spinal artery in front and the two posterior spinal arteries behind. The plexuses of the limbs are built from named roots, and each nerve has a place where it is most exposed, from the spiral groove of the humerus for the radial nerve to the neck of the fibula for the common fibular nerve. The twelve cranial nerves are named by ordinal, and each carries its own mixture of fibers and leaves through its own opening in the skull. Knowing where each tract crosses, where each nerve lies, and which artery supplies which surface is what lets an examination finding be read back to a structure.

# Chapter 112 — Cardiovascular Anatomy

This chapter works through the clinical anatomy of the heart, the great vessels and the thoracic cavity, taking the listener from the chambers and valves to the arteries and veins of the trunk and limbs, and then through the chest wall, the pleura, the lungs, the mediastinum and the diaphragm. It holds one hundred questions, and every question gives its answer immediately and then explains why that answer is correct, so nothing has to be held in mind until the end. The items are written to be answered out loud. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 11101. Which chamber of the heart receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs? The answer is the left atrium. The four pulmonary veins open into it, two from each lung. Blood then passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta and around the body.

Question 11102. Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs: the aorta, the pulmonary trunk, a pulmonary vein, or the superior vena cava? The answer is the pulmonary trunk. It divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries, one for each lung. The pulmonary veins are the exception, carrying oxygenated blood back to the heart.

Question 11103. Which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall? The answer is the left ventricle. It drives blood through the whole body, so it works against a much higher pressure than the right ventricle does. Its wall is about three times as thick as the wall of the right ventricle, which pumps only to the lungs.

Question 11104. The tricuspid valve guards the opening between which two chambers: the right atrium and the right ventricle, the left atrium and the left ventricle, the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, or the left ventricle and the aorta? The answer is the right atrium and the right ventricle. Its three cusps are anchored by chordae tendineae to the papillary muscles.

Question 11105. Which chamber of the heart lies immediately behind the body of the sternum and the costal cartilages of the third to fifth ribs? The answer is the right ventricle. It forms most of the anterior surface of the heart, so a needle crossing the lower sternum reaches it first. The left ventricle lies behind it.

Question 11106. Which heart valve has only two cusps and guards the left atrioventricular opening? The answer is the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve. Its two cusps are named anterior and posterior, and they are tethered by chordae tendineae. It opens when the left atrium contracts and closes when the left ventricle contracts.

Question 11107. A described chest radiograph shows the heart as a shadow about one third to one half of the width of the chest, with its long axis pointing downward and to the left. Which chamber forms the lower left border of that shadow? The answer is the left ventricle. The right border of the shadow is formed by the right atrium.

Question 11108. A constructed illustration: a person has sudden central chest pain and injury of the front of the left ventricle. Which artery, running between the ventricles, is blocked? The answer is the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery. It supplies the front of both ventricles and the front of the septum. Management belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol.

Question 11109. In most people, which artery supplies the posterior part of the interventricular septum and the back of the left ventricle? The answer is the right coronary artery, through its posterior interventricular branch. It also supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, the sinoatrial node and the atrioventricular node. A left dominant circulation is a normal variant.

Question 11110. Which small group of specialized muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium sets the resting rhythm of the heart? The answer is the sinoatrial node. It lies at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium. It fires faster than any other part of the conduction system, so it acts as the pacemaker.

Question 11111. True or false: the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood toward the heart. The answer is true. They return blood that has been oxygenated in the lungs to the left atrium. They are the only veins in the body that carry oxygenated blood, just as the pulmonary arteries are the only arteries that carry deoxygenated blood.

Question 11112. Which structure lies immediately behind the left atrium and can be pressed on when that chamber enlarges: the esophagus, the trachea, the thymus, or the right main bronchus? The answer is the esophagus. It descends in the posterior mediastinum in contact with the back of the left atrium. An enlarged left atrium can press on it and make swallowing difficult.

Question 11113. Which artery supplies the sinoatrial node in about three fifths of people? The answer is the right coronary artery. It reaches the node through a small branch that circles the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium. In the remaining people the node is supplied by the left coronary artery, which is a normal variation.

Question 11114. Between which two structures does the atrioventricular node lie? The answer is the interatrial septum and the opening of the coronary sinus. It sits in the lower part of the interatrial septum, just above the attachment of the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve. The atrioventricular bundle leaves it and runs into the interventricular septum.

Question 11115. A described dissection shows a fibrous ring around each valve, the four rings fused into a single plate. What is that plate called, and what does it separate? The answer is the fibrous skeleton, which separates the atria from the ventricles. It anchors the valve cusps and insulates the atrial muscle from the ventricular muscle, so the two contract in sequence.

Question 11116. Where on the chest wall is the sound of the mitral valve best heard? The answer is the apex of the heart, in the fifth intercostal space just medial to the midclavicular line. The valve lies behind the sternum, but its sound is carried to the apex. The aortic valve is heard at the right edge of the sternum instead.

Question 11117. Which great vessel lies behind the pulmonary trunk and slightly to its right as both leave the heart? The answer is the ascending aorta. The pulmonary trunk arises in front of it and to its left. The aorta then arches backward over the left lung.

Question 11118. What is the name of the double-layered sac that encloses the heart and the roots of its great vessels? The answer is the pericardium. Its outer fibrous layer is tough and its inner serous layer is smooth. Between the two serous layers lies a thin film of fluid that lets the heart beat without friction.

Question 11119. A constructed illustration: fluid collects in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart, and a needle is passed below the xiphisternum. Which chamber, lying behind the lower sternum, is most at risk? The answer is the right ventricle, the most anterior chamber. The needle is angled toward the left shoulder. The procedure belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 11120. In a described transverse section through the chest, the right ventricle lies in front and the left ventricle behind. Which surface of the heart faces the diaphragm? The answer is the inferior surface, formed mainly by the two ventricles. It rests on the central tendon of the diaphragm, and the long axis runs downward, forward and to the left.

Question 11121. Which branch of the aortic arch arises first, on the right: the left common carotid artery, the brachiocephalic trunk, the left subclavian artery, or the left vertebral artery? The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk. It is the first and largest branch of the arch. The arch then gives off the left common carotid and the left subclavian arteries in turn.

Question 11122. Which is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch? The answer is the brachiocephalic trunk. It arises from the highest point of the arch and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint. Its two branches are the right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery, and the left side has no such trunk.

Question 11123. A described computed tomography section of the upper chest shows a vessel that arches backward over the left main bronchus and then descends beside the vertebral column. Which vessel is shown? The answer is the aortic arch, which continues as the descending thoracic aorta. The arch passes over the root of the left lung, and the descending part lies to the left of the vertebral bodies.

Question 11124. A described narrowing of the aorta lies just distal to the left subclavian artery. Which structure marks that site: the azygos vein, the left main bronchus, the ligamentum arteriosum, or the phrenic nerve? The answer is the ligamentum arteriosum. It is the fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus, which joined the pulmonary trunk to the aorta there. The narrowing lies opposite it.

Question 11125. Which fibrous band connects the left pulmonary artery to the underside of the aortic arch? The answer is the ligamentum arteriosum. In the fetus it was the ductus arteriosus, which carried blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta and so past the lungs. After birth it closes and becomes a fibrous cord.

Question 11126. Which fetal vessel becomes the ligamentum arteriosum after birth? The answer is the ductus arteriosus. It shunted blood away from the fetal lungs, which were not yet working. Its closure in the first days of life is one of the changes that separate the pulmonary circulation from the systemic one.

Question 11127. True or false: the coronary arteries arise from the pulmonary trunk. The answer is false. They arise from the left and right aortic sinuses at the root of the aorta, just above the aortic valve. Blood enters them during diastole, when the aortic valve is closed and the sinuses fill.

Question 11128. Into which chamber of the heart does the coronary sinus empty? The answer is the right atrium. It opens just above and medial to the opening of the inferior vena cava, beside the valve of the inferior vena cava. It collects most of the venous blood returning from the wall of the heart.

Question 11129. A constructed illustration: a catheter is passed into a large vein at the root of the neck, where two veins join to form a single trunk. Which two veins join there?
