The answer is the internal jugular vein and the subclavian vein, which form the brachiocephalic vein. The right one is short and vertical, while the left crosses the midline behind the manubrium.

Question 11130. Which two veins unite to form the superior vena cava? The answer is the right and left brachiocephalic veins. They join behind the lower border of the first right costal cartilage. The superior vena cava then descends to empty into the right atrium, and the azygos vein joins it just above the heart.

Question 11131. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior interventricular branch with the front of the ventricles, the circumflex branch with the right ventricle, the right coronary artery with the left atrium, or the posterior interventricular branch with the left ventricle? The answer is the anterior interventricular branch with the front of the ventricles. It runs between the ventricles and supplies both of them.

Question 11132. Which coronary artery runs in the groove between the right and left ventricles on the front of the heart? The answer is the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery. It descends toward the apex and turns around it to meet the posterior interventricular branch. The circumflex branch runs in the coronary sulcus on the left side instead.

Question 11133. A described angiogram of the lower limb shows a vessel that passes through an opening in the adductor magnus muscle to reach the back of the knee. Which artery is shown? The answer is the femoral artery, which becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus. Before that it lies in the adductor canal, deep to the sartorius muscle.

Question 11134. On the left side of the neck, which structure lies immediately lateral to the trachea and medial to the internal jugular vein? The answer is the left common carotid artery. It ascends in the carotid sheath alongside the vagus nerve, which lies between it and the internal jugular vein. The thyroid gland overlaps all three from the front.

Question 11135. Name the two arteries that arise from the left coronary artery, spoken as a list. The answer is the anterior interventricular branch and the circumflex branch. The anterior interventricular branch runs down the front of the heart between the ventricles, and the circumflex branch follows the coronary sulcus around the left side.

Question 11136. Which artery is felt as a pulse on the lateral side of the front of the wrist, just above the base of the thumb? The answer is the radial artery. It lies against the lower end of the radius, covered only by skin and fascia. The ulnar artery lies on the other side of the wrist and is deeper.

Question 11137. The femoral artery is the continuation of which vessel below the inguinal ligament? The answer is the external iliac artery. It enters the thigh at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, where its pulse can be felt. The internal iliac artery stays in the pelvis and supplies its walls and organs.

Question 11138. A constructed illustration: a knee is dislocated backward, the pulse at the ankle is lost, and the foot is pale. Which artery, lying deepest in the popliteal fossa, is most likely injured? The answer is the popliteal artery. The popliteal vein and the tibial nerve lie superficial to it. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 11139. A described dissection of the thigh shows a triangle bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the sartorius and medially by the adductor longus. Which structure lies in the middle of that triangle? The answer is the femoral artery. The femoral vein lies medial to it and the femoral nerve lateral to it.

Question 11140. Which two arteries form the anastomosis around the scapula that can keep the arm supplied when the subclavian artery is blocked? The answer is the suprascapular artery and the circumflex scapular artery. The suprascapular artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk and the circumflex scapular artery from the subscapular artery. They meet on the back of the scapula.

Question 11141. True or false: an arterial anastomosis around a joint can keep blood flowing to the distal limb when the main artery is blocked. The answer is true, because the branches that meet around the joint provide an alternative route. The anastomoses around the scapula and the elbow are the classic examples, though the flow may be enough only for survival.

Question 11142. Within the femoral triangle, how does the femoral vein lie relative to the femoral artery? The answer is immediately medial to it. The artery lies lateral and the vein medial, with the femoral nerve further lateral still. This order is remembered as nerve, artery and vein from lateral to medial.

Question 11143. Which vein of the lower limb is the longest in the body and runs up the medial side of the leg and thigh? The answer is the great saphenous vein. It begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot and ends in the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament, joined by many tributaries along the way.

Question 11144. Which two veins unite behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein? The answer is the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein. The portal vein carries blood from the gut to the liver. The inferior mesenteric vein usually joins the splenic vein rather than the portal vein itself.

Question 11145. A described transverse section through the chest shows three structures in front of the vertebral bodies: a vessel on the right, a vessel on the left, and a thin-walled duct between them. Which duct is it, and where does it end? The answer is the thoracic duct, which ends at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.

Question 11146. A constructed illustration: a young athlete collapses during exertion, and a coronary artery arises from the wrong aortic sinus and passes between the great vessels. Which artery is most often involved? The answer is the left coronary artery arising from the right aortic sinus. Its course between them lets it be squeezed when the aorta expands. The right coronary artery can do the same, but less often.

Question 11147. Which of these pairs belongs together: the subclavian artery with the arm, the common carotid artery with the leg, the renal artery with the lung, or the coronary artery with the diaphragm? The answer is the subclavian artery with the arm. It continues as the axillary artery after crossing the first rib and then as the brachial artery.

Question 11148. Name the three veins that empty into the right atrium, spoken as a list. The answer is the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava and the coronary sinus. The first two return blood from above and below the diaphragm. The coronary sinus returns most of the blood that has passed through the wall of the heart.

Question 11149. A described transverse section through the upper chest shows the trachea dividing into two tubes, with a large vessel lying above the division. Which structure is dividing, and what are the two tubes? The answer is the trachea, dividing into the right and left main bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, and the arch of the aorta lies above it.

Question 11150. In a left dominant coronary circulation, which artery gives off the posterior interventricular branch? The answer is the left coronary artery, through its circumflex branch. It then supplies the back of both ventricles and the posterior part of the interventricular septum. In most people the right coronary artery is dominant instead, and the pattern is a normal variation.

Question 11151. Which bone forms the front of the thoracic cage, between the clavicles above and the xiphoid process below? The answer is the sternum. Its upper part is the manubrium, its middle part is the body, and its pointed lower end is the xiphoid process. The manubrium joins the body at the sternal angle.

Question 11152. Which statement about the ribs is correct: 7 pairs reach the sternum directly, 12 pairs reach it directly, 5 pairs reach it directly, or 3 pairs are floating? The answer is that 7 pairs reach the sternum directly. The eighth, ninth and tenth pairs join the costal cartilages above them. The eleventh and twelfth pairs are free at the front.

Question 11153. Which ribs are described as floating, and where do their front ends lie? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth ribs, whose front ends lie free in the muscles of the abdominal wall. No costal cartilage joins them to the sternum. They lie over the upper part of the kidney behind them.

Question 11154. Which structure lies at the level of the sternal angle: the first costal cartilage, the second costal cartilage, the xiphoid process, or the twelfth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the second costal cartilage. The same level marks the fourth thoracic vertebra, the bifurcation of the trachea, and the upper border of the arch of the aorta.

Question 11155. Which structure lies immediately below the intercostal artery in the costal groove of a rib? The answer is the intercostal nerve. From above downward the groove holds the intercostal vein, then the artery, then the nerve. The three run between the internal and the innermost layers of the intercostal muscles.

Question 11156. What is the name of the dome-shaped muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen? The answer is the diaphragm. It has a right dome and a left dome, joined in the middle by a central tendon. Three openings pierce it, one for the inferior vena cava, one for the esophagus and one for the aorta.

Question 11157. A described radiograph of the chest shows a dome-shaped shadow on each side, higher on the right, with a sharp angle where it meets the chest wall. Which structures are shown? The answer is the two halves of the diaphragm. The right dome is higher because the liver lies beneath it, and the sharp angle is the costophrenic angle.

Question 11158. A constructed illustration: a tube is placed into the chest through the fifth intercostal space behind the midaxillary line, passing over the upper border of the sixth rib. Which structures is that route avoiding? The answer is the intercostal nerve, artery and vein of the fifth rib, which run along its lower border. The needle passes above the rib below to stay clear of them.

Question 11159. Which of these structures lies within the mediastinum: the left lung, the thoracic duct, the first rib, or the pectoralis major muscle? The answer is the thoracic duct. It ascends through the posterior mediastinum in front of the vertebral bodies. The lungs lie in the pleural cavities on either side, and the first rib and the pectoralis major lie outside the mediastinum.

Question 11160. What is the name of the membrane that lines the inside of the thoracic cavity and folds over the surface of the lung? The answer is the pleura. Its parietal layer lines the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum, and its visceral layer covers the lung. A thin film of fluid between them lets the lung slide as it expands.

Question 11161. True or false: the right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two. The answer is true. The right lung is divided by an oblique fissure and a horizontal fissure into upper, middle and lower lobes. The left lung is divided by the oblique fissure alone and has a cardiac notch.

Question 11162. Which large vein crosses the midline behind the manubrium, in front of the great vessels? The answer is the left brachiocephalic vein. It runs from the left side of the root of the neck across to join the right brachiocephalic vein. In a child the thymus lies in front of it. The two veins unite to form the superior vena cava.

Question 11163. The descending thoracic aorta comes to lie beside which structure, and on which side? The answer is the vertebral column, on its left side. It begins at the fourth thoracic vertebra and descends to the diaphragm. The esophagus lies in front of it and crosses to its right as it descends.

Question 11164. Which main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so that an inhaled object is more likely to enter it? The answer is the right main bronchus. It gives off its upper lobe branch above the pulmonary artery. The left main bronchus is longer and more horizontal, and it passes below the aortic arch.

Question 11165. A described radiograph of the chest shows a curved shadow filling the lowest part of one side of the chest, with the lung edge above it and a blunt costophrenic angle. Which space has filled with fluid? The answer is the pleural cavity, at its lowest point, the costodiaphragmatic recess. That recess dips below the lung, and fluid collects there first.

Question 11166. Which of these structures lies in the posterior mediastinum: the thymus, the thoracic duct, the phrenic nerve, or the left brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the thoracic duct. The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum, the phrenic nerve runs in the middle mediastinum in front of the root of the lung, and the left brachiocephalic vein lies in the superior mediastinum.

Question 11167. Which structure lies behind the manubrium of the sternum in a young child, in front of the great vessels? The answer is the thymus. It lies in the anterior mediastinum and is largest in childhood. It shrinks with age and is replaced by fat, so in an adult it is barely visible.

Question 11168. Which nerve runs in front of the root of the lung and supplies the diaphragm? The answer is the phrenic nerve. It arises from the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves. It descends through the mediastinum, crosses in front of the root of the lung, and reaches the diaphragm from above.

Question 11169. A constructed illustration: a growth at the top of a lung presses on the chain of ganglia against the upper ribs, and the person has a drooping eyelid and a small pupil on that side. Which chain is compressed? The answer is the sympathetic trunk, which lies behind the parietal pleura and carries fibers to the head and the upper limb.

Question 11170. Which structure passes through the diaphragm at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra: the aorta, the esophagus, the inferior vena cava, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the esophagus. The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon at the eighth thoracic vertebra, and the aorta passes behind the diaphragm at the twelfth. The vagus nerves accompany the esophagus.

Question 11171. A described computed tomography section at the level of the carina shows the two main bronchi separated by a ridge of tissue, with a tube lying immediately behind them. Which ridge is described? The answer is the carina, with the esophagus immediately behind it. The carina is the ridge at the last ring of the trachea.

Question 11172. Which structures lie between the internal and the innermost layers of the intercostal muscles? The answer is the intercostal nerve, artery and vein. They run in the costal groove along the lower border of the rib above. Their order from above downward is vein, artery and nerve. The innermost layer separates them from the pleura.

Question 11173. Which of these pairs belongs together: the thoracic duct with the left venous angle, the thoracic duct with the right venous angle, the right lymphatic duct with the left venous angle, or the azygos vein with the left atrium? The answer is the thoracic duct with the left venous angle, at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. The right lymphatic duct ends at the right venous angle.

Question 11174. Which vein runs up the right side of the posterior mediastinum and arches over the root of the right lung? The answer is the azygos vein. It drains the posterior intercostal veins of the right side and the hemiazygos vein from the left. It ends in the superior vena cava.

Question 11175. Which structure lies highest in the root of the right lung: the pulmonary artery, the upper lobe bronchus, the pulmonary veins, or the bronchial arteries? The answer is the upper lobe bronchus, also called the eparterial bronchus because it lies above the pulmonary artery. Below the artery runs the bronchus to the middle and lower lobes, and the pulmonary veins lie lowest and in front.

Question 11176. A constructed illustration: a growth in the upper mediastinum causes a swollen face and distended veins over the chest wall, worst when the person lies flat. Which large vein, lying to the right of the midline behind the sternum, is compressed? The answer is the superior vena cava. It carries blood from the head, neck and upper limbs to the right atrium.

Question 11177. A described radiograph is taken with the beam passing from the front to the back, and the heart shadow looks wider than usual. Why does the heart look enlarged in that view? The answer is that the heart lies farther from the film, so its shadow is magnified. In the standard view the heart lies close to the film.

Question 11178. In the lower part of the posterior mediastinum, which structure lies in front of the descending thoracic aorta and slightly to its right? The answer is the esophagus. It descends in front of the aorta and then passes through the diaphragm with the vagus nerves. The thoracic duct lies behind the esophagus, between the aorta and the azygos vein.

Question 11179. Which of these structures is not found in the middle mediastinum: the heart, the phrenic nerve, the thoracic duct, or the ascending aorta? The answer is the thoracic duct, which lies in the posterior mediastinum. The middle mediastinum holds the pericardium, the heart, the ascending aorta, the pulmonary trunk, the phrenic nerves and the roots of the lungs.

Question 11180. Which muscle forms the front wall of the axilla and the anterior fold of the armpit? The answer is the pectoralis major. It arises from the clavicle, the sternum and the upper costal cartilages and inserts on the humerus. It adducts and medially rotates the arm, and its lower border forms the front fold of the armpit.

Question 11181. Which of these pairs belongs together: the phrenic nerve with the diaphragm, the vagus nerve with the diaphragm, the sympathetic trunk with the larynx, or the intercostal nerve with the pelvis? The answer is the phrenic nerve with the diaphragm. It carries fibers from the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves, while the vagus nerve supplies the heart, the lungs and the gut.

Question 11182. Name the three openings of the diaphragm, spoken as a list. The answer is the opening for the inferior vena cava, the opening for the esophagus and the opening for the aorta. The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon at the eighth thoracic vertebra, the esophagus at the tenth, and the aorta behind the diaphragm at the twelfth.

Question 11183. Which statement about the opening for the inferior vena cava is correct: it lies in the central tendon, it lies between the crura, it lies behind the diaphragm, or it lies in the left muscular part? The answer is that it lies in the central tendon. It is the only opening in the central tendon, at the eighth thoracic vertebra. The aorta passes between the crura instead.

Question 11184. Which bone forms the upper part of the sternum, above the sternal angle? The answer is the manubrium. It joins the body of the sternum at the sternal angle. Its upper border carries the jugular notch, which can be felt at the base of the neck, and its sides join the clavicles and the first costal cartilages.

Question 11185. A described section of the chest shows the pleural cavity on each side separated from the mediastinum by a membrane that reflects over the root of the lung. Which membrane is described? The answer is the parietal pleura, which becomes continuous with the visceral pleura at the root of the lung. Below the root the two layers hang down as the pulmonary ligament.

Question 11186. Which nerve hooks around the aortic arch just behind the ligamentum arteriosum? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. It arises from the left vagus nerve beside the arch and turns upward beneath it. It ascends in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus to reach the larynx. The right one hooks around the right subclavian artery.

Question 11187. Which statement about the pleura is correct: the parietal pleura is sensitive and the visceral pleura is not, both layers are equally sensitive, the visceral pleura alone is sensitive, or neither layer is sensitive? The answer is that the parietal pleura is sensitive and the visceral pleura is not. It is supplied by the intercostal and phrenic nerves, and the visceral layer has no pain fibers.

Question 11188. A constructed illustration: fluid in the chest is drained through the seventh intercostal space, with the needle passed just above the eighth rib. Why is it passed above that rib? The answer is that the intercostal nerve, artery and vein run along the lower border of the rib above the space. Passing above the rib below keeps the needle clear of them.

Question 11189. True or false: the parietal pleura covers the surface of the lung. The answer is false. The visceral pleura covers the surface of the lung and dips into the fissures. The parietal pleura lines the inside of the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum. The two layers are continuous at the root of the lung.

Question 11190. Which structures bound the superior thoracic aperture, the opening at the top of the chest? The answer is the first thoracic vertebra, the first ribs and the upper border of the manubrium. The opening is smaller than the lower opening of the chest. The trachea, the esophagus, the great vessels and the nerves of the upper limb all pass through it.

Question 11191. A described section through the lower chest shows two muscular pillars descending from the vertebral bodies and arching over the aorta. Which structures are shown? The answer is the right and left crura of the diaphragm, which bound the aortic opening behind the diaphragm. The right crus is the larger, and the aorta passes between them at the twelfth thoracic vertebra.

Question 11192. A described dissection shows an artery descending just lateral to the sternum, deep to the costal cartilages, with a nerve lateral to it. Which artery and which nerve are shown? The answer is the internal thoracic artery and the phrenic nerve. The artery arises from the subclavian artery, and the nerve crosses in front of the root of the lung.

Question 11193. Which bone of the thoracic cage carries a groove on its upper surface for the subclavian artery? The answer is the first rib. It is the shortest and most curved of the ribs, and it lies almost horizontally. The subclavian vessels and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross over it.

Question 11194. Which structure separates the first part of the subclavian artery from its third part: the clavicle, the anterior scalene muscle, the first rib, or the sternocleidomastoid? The answer is the anterior scalene muscle. The first part of the artery lies medial to it and the third part lateral to it. The trunks of the brachial plexus lie behind the artery.

Question 11195. Which of these pairs belongs together: the internal thoracic artery with the chest wall, the thoracic duct with the right atrium, the phrenic nerve with the abdominal wall, or the intercostal artery with the pleural cavity? The answer is the internal thoracic artery with the chest wall. It descends behind the costal cartilages and ends as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

Question 11196. Which of these structures lies most posterior in the superior mediastinum: the trachea, the esophagus, the arch of the aorta, or the left brachiocephalic vein? The answer is the esophagus, which lies against the vertebral column. In front of it lie the trachea and the great vessels, and the thoracic duct ascends behind it.

Question 11197. A described computed tomography section through the lower chest shows one large vessel piercing the central tendon of the diaphragm and another passing behind it between the two crura. Which two vessels are shown? The answer is the inferior vena cava and the aorta. The esophagus passes through the muscular part at a level between them, so each opening lies at a different vertebral level.

Question 11198. A constructed illustration: sudden chest pain begins in the front of the chest and moves to the back between the shoulder blades. Which part of the aorta lies behind the heart and corresponds to the second site of pain? The answer is the descending thoracic aorta, which begins at the fourth thoracic vertebra and runs down to the diaphragm. Management belongs to the treating clinician.

Question 11199. Which statement about the azygos vein is correct: it arches over the right lung root and ends in the superior vena cava, it arches over the left lung root, it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein, or it lies in the anterior mediastinum? The answer is that it arches over the right lung root and ends in the superior vena cava. It drains the posterior intercostal veins of the right side.

Question 11200. Below the fourth thoracic vertebra the thoracic duct lies on the right of the midline, and above it lies on the left. Which structure does it cross behind as it changes sides? The answer is the esophagus. It crosses behind it at about the fourth thoracic vertebra, then ascends on the left, so its position depends on the level of the section.

To summarize, the right atrium receives the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava and the coronary sinus, while the left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins, and the left ventricle carries the thickest wall because it drives blood through the whole body. The coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses, the right coronary artery usually supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, and the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery supplies the front of the ventricles and the front of the septum. The great vessels hold fixed relations, with the pulmonary trunk in front of the ascending aorta, the brachiocephalic trunk as the first branch of the arch, and the ligamentum arteriosum joining the left pulmonary artery to the arch. In the chest, the second costal cartilage marks the sternal angle, the intercostal bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above the space, and the diaphragm opens for the inferior vena cava, the esophagus and the aorta. The parietal pleura is sensitive to pain while the visceral pleura is not, the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left, and the thoracic duct crosses behind the esophagus before ending at the left venous angle. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 113 — Abdominal Anatomy

The abdomen holds the organs of digestion, the urinary passages and the great vessels that serve them, and it is the region where an injury can hide behind an intact wall. This chapter covers the peritoneum and its folds, the liver and the biliary tree, the stomach and the intestines, the pancreas and the spleen, the kidneys and the ureters, and the vessels and nerves of the back wall; its second half turns to the structures that are torn, compressed or obstructed when a person arrives acutely unwell. It holds one hundred questions, and each one gives its answer immediately after the question, then explains why that answer is right, so nothing has to be held in mind to the end. Every clinical item here is a constructed illustration rather than a real case, and where management is mentioned it belongs to the treating clinician and the local protocol. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 11201. A described dissection shows a double fold of peritoneum hanging from the greater curvature of the stomach and draping over the coils of the small intestine. Which structure is described? The answer is the greater omentum. It is the largest fold of peritoneum, and its fatty apron lies between the abdominal wall and the viscera.

Question 11202. Which layer of the peritoneum is sensitive to pain: the visceral layer, the parietal layer, the greater omentum, or the mesentery? The answer is the parietal layer. The visceral peritoneum is supplied by autonomic nerves and feels only stretch, while the parietal layer carries somatic nerves and localizes pain sharply.

Question 11203. Which fold of peritoneum runs from the left side of the stomach to the spleen and carries the short gastric vessels and the left gastroepiploic vessels? The answer is the gastrosplenic ligament. It is part of the greater omentum, and the spleen lies behind its lateral end.

Question 11204. The celiac trunk supplies the derivatives of which part of the embryonic gut: the foregut, the midgut, the hindgut, or the whole gut? The answer is the foregut. It feeds the stomach, the duodenum as far as the major papilla, the liver, the gallbladder, the pancreas and the spleen.

Question 11205. Which part of the liver rests directly against the diaphragm with no covering of visceral peritoneum, and is therefore named the bare area? The answer is the posterior part of the right lobe. The coronary ligament marks its margins, and the inferior vena cava grooves the liver close beside it.

Question 11206. Deep to the neck of the pancreas, the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form which vessel? The answer is the portal vein. The gland lies in front of the junction, so the vein is created behind the pancreas and then runs upward to the liver.

Question 11207. A described section of the upper abdomen shows a long lobulated gland whose head is clasped by the curve of the duodenum and whose tail reaches the spleen. Which organ is shown, and which duct runs along it? The answer is the pancreas, with the pancreatic duct. That duct joins the common bile duct at the major duodenal papilla.

Question 11208. Which fold of peritoneum runs from the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach, and what is its free right edge called? The answer is the lesser omentum, whose free edge is the hepatoduodenal ligament. The bile duct and the hepatic artery lie in it in front of the portal vein.

Question 11209. Within the free edge of the lesser omentum, which structure lies most posterior: the common bile duct, the proper hepatic artery, the portal vein, or the lymph nodes? The answer is the portal vein. The bile duct lies anterior and to its right, and the hepatic artery anterior and to its left.

Question 11210. A constructed illustration: several hours after a fatty meal, a person has severe pain in the right upper abdomen that is also felt beneath the right shoulder. Which organ is inflamed, and which nerve carries the pain? The answer is the gallbladder, with the right phrenic nerve. The gallbladder touches the diaphragm, and irritation of that surface is felt at the shoulder.

Question 11211. Which part of the stomach lies highest in the standing body: the pylorus, the fundus, the body, or the pyloric canal? The answer is the fundus. It rises above the level of the opening of the esophagus, and swallowed gas collects there, which is why it may be seen on a chest radiograph.

Question 11212. Which ring of thickened circular muscle guards the outlet of the stomach and controls the passage of food into the duodenum? The answer is the pyloric sphincter. The pylorus lies to the right of the midline at the level of the first lumbar vertebra.

Question 11213. A described contrast study of the upper gut shows a loop of bowel that curves around the head of the pancreas and ends where a duct opens on its medial wall. Which part of the gut is shown, and what is that opening called? The answer is the duodenum, opening at the major duodenal papilla.

Question 11214. Which part of the duodenum passes across the front of the aorta and is itself crossed in front by the superior mesenteric artery? The answer is the third, or horizontal, part. It lies between the aorta behind and the superior mesenteric artery in front, and it is a place where the bowel can be compressed.

Question 11215. Which part of the small intestine has a thick wall, tall folds and a mesentery clear enough to show its vessels: the jejunum or the ileum? The answer is the jejunum. It occupies the upper part of the peritoneal cavity, while the ileum lies below it and is thinner walled.

Question 11216. Which feature marks the ileum rather than the jejunum: tall circular folds, aggregated lymphoid nodules, a thick wall, or few arterial arcades? The answer is aggregated lymphoid nodules. They lie in the wall on the side opposite the mesentery and grow more numerous toward the large intestine.

Question 11217. True or false: the appendix opens into the cecum a little below the point where the ileum joins it. The answer is true. The opening lies on the posteromedial wall of the cecum, below the ileocecal junction, and the appendix hangs free from that point in a variable direction.

Question 11218. Which surface point for the appendix lies one third of the way along a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus? The answer is McBurney point. It marks the base of the appendix, and tenderness there is one of the signs of appendicitis.

Question 11219. A constructed illustration: a young person has pain that begins around the navel and settles in the right lower abdomen, where the abdominal wall is guarded. Which organ lies beneath that point? The answer is the appendix. Its visceral afferents follow the sympathetic nerves to the tenth thoracic segment, which is why the early pain is felt near the navel.

Question 11220. Which of these parts of the large intestine has no mesentery and lies behind the peritoneum: the appendix, the transverse colon, the sigmoid colon, or the ascending colon? The answer is the ascending colon. It is covered by peritoneum only in front, and the descending colon has the same arrangement.

Question 11221. At what level does the left kidney lie, and which kidney sits a little lower? The answer is the level of the twelfth thoracic to the third lumbar vertebra, with the right kidney lower. The liver occupies the space above the right kidney and pushes it downward.

Question 11222. A described scan of the upper abdomen shows a small golden gland sitting like a cap on the upper pole of each kidney, enclosed with the kidney in the same fat and fascia. Which glands are shown? The answer is the suprarenal glands. The right one is triangular and the left one is crescent shaped.

Question 11223. Which structure lies in front of the upper part of the left kidney and shares the same bed behind the peritoneum: the cecum, the liver, the pancreas, or the appendix? The answer is the pancreas. Its body and tail lie across the left kidney, and the spleen rests against the upper lateral border of that kidney.

Question 11224. Which artery supplies the middle part of the suprarenal gland and arises directly from the abdominal aorta? The answer is the middle suprarenal artery. The gland also receives superior branches from the inferior phrenic artery and inferior branches from the renal artery. Those three sources overlap, which is why the gland survives when one of them is tied.

Question 11225. Which kidney lies lower in the body: the right, the left, both at the same level, or the left in men and the right in women? The answer is the right. The liver above it takes the space that the left kidney uses, so the right kidney lies about 2 centimeters lower.

Question 11226. Which of these pairs belongs together: the left renal vein with the inferior vena cava, the left gonadal vein with the inferior vena cava, the right gonadal vein with the left renal vein, or the sigmoid vein with the portal vein? The answer is the left renal vein with the inferior vena cava. The left gonadal and left suprarenal veins join it, while the right gonadal vein joins the inferior vena cava.

Question 11227. Which vein crosses in front of the aorta and behind the superior mesenteric artery, and what may happen to it there? The answer is the left renal vein. It is longer than the right one because it must cross the midline, and the artery above it can narrow it. The narrowing is a described variation rather than a disease in most people.

Question 11228. A described operation shows a tube crossing the brim of the pelvis in front of the common iliac bifurcation. Which structure is it: the ureter, the femoral nerve, the inferior epigastric artery, or the round ligament of the uterus? The answer is the ureter. It is the structure most easily caught at that crossing.

Question 11229. A described scan of the back wall of the abdomen shows the aorta dividing into two vessels in front of the fourth lumbar vertebra, and each of those vessels dividing again at the brim of the pelvis. Which vessels are shown? The answer is the two common iliac arteries. Each one divides into an external and an internal iliac artery at the brim.

Question 11230. Which is the lowest of the unpaired branches of the abdominal aorta: the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery, the inferior mesenteric artery, or the middle suprarenal artery? The answer is the inferior mesenteric artery. The middle suprarenal artery is a paired branch, and it arises above the inferior mesenteric artery.

Question 11231. Up to which point does the inferior mesenteric artery supply the gut: the first part of the duodenum, the middle of the transverse colon, the cecum, or the upper rectum? The answer is the upper rectum. Its territory begins at the splenic flexure and runs to the upper part of the rectum.

Question 11232. At which point along the colon is the blood supply least secure, where the territory of the superior mesenteric artery meets that of the inferior mesenteric artery? The answer is the splenic flexure. The marginal artery is often thin there, so that segment is the most vulnerable when flow falls. This is a normal arrangement and not a disease.

Question 11233. A described contrast study of the colon shows a segment that crosses the abdomen from right to left, bears pouches along its length and carries small fatty tags. Which part of the colon is shown? The answer is the transverse colon. It hangs from a mesentery that allows it to move, and its right end lies below the liver.

Question 11234. Which midline band of fibrous tissue runs from the pubic symphysis to the xiphoid process and is formed by the interlocking aponeuroses of the abdominal muscles? The answer is the linea alba. It is narrow below the umbilicus and broad above it, and it marks the midline of the abdominal wall.

Question 11235. Which structure passes through the inguinal canal in the male: the round ligament of the uterus, the spermatic cord, the femoral nerve, or the saphenous vein? The answer is the spermatic cord. In the female the canal carries the round ligament of the uterus, and the femoral nerve passes below the inguinal ligament instead.

Question 11236. In the inguinal region, does the inferior epigastric artery lie medial or lateral to the deep inguinal ring? The answer is that the artery lies medial to the ring. The ring is a defect above the middle of the inguinal ligament, and it lies lateral to the artery. A hernia that enters it therefore passes lateral to the artery.

Question 11237. A constructed illustration: a person lifts a heavy load and feels a dragging pain in the groin, and a swelling appears above and medial to the pubic tubercle and passes into the scrotum. Which kind of hernia is described? The answer is an indirect inguinal hernia. It enters the deep inguinal ring, lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, and follows the spermatic cord.

Question 11238. In the femoral triangle, which of the three main structures lies most lateral: the femoral nerve, the femoral artery, or the femoral vein? The answer is the femoral nerve. From lateral to medial they are the nerve, the artery and the vein, and the lymph nodes lie in the canal medial to the vein.

Question 11239. A described dissection of the front of the thigh shows three structures arranged from lateral to medial below the inguinal ligament. Which order is correct: vein, artery, nerve; nerve, vein, artery; nerve, artery, vein; or artery, nerve, vein? The answer is nerve, artery, vein. The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath, while the artery and the vein lie within it.

Question 11240. A described cross section of the front of the abdomen, below the umbilicus, shows the rectus muscle in a sheath whose front wall is made of two aponeuroses while its back wall is thin. Which layer forms that back wall? The answer is the transversalis fascia. Below the arcuate line all the aponeuroses pass in front of the muscle, so the fascia lies directly behind it.

Question 11241. True or false: the inguinal ligament is formed by the folded lower border of the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. The answer is true. It runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle, and the deep fascia of the thigh hangs from its lower edge.

Question 11242. Which opening in the diaphragm lies at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra and carries the aorta and the thoracic duct? The answer is the aortic hiatus. It lies behind the diaphragm between its two crura, so the aorta passes behind the muscle rather than through it.

Question 11243. Which structures pass through the esophageal opening of the diaphragm, and at which vertebral level does that opening lie? The answer is the esophagus and the two vagus nerves, at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra. The opening lies in the muscular part of the diaphragm, in front of the aorta.

Question 11244. Which structures pass through the opening in the central tendon of the diaphragm: the aorta and the thoracic duct, the esophagus and the vagus nerves, the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve, or the sympathetic trunk and the splanchnic nerves? The answer is the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve. That opening lies at the eighth thoracic vertebra, highest of the three.

Question 11245. Which of these pairs belongs together: the caval opening with the tenth thoracic vertebra, the esophageal opening with the eighth thoracic vertebra, the aortic opening with the twelfth thoracic vertebra, or the aortic opening with the eighth thoracic vertebra? The answer is the aortic opening with the twelfth thoracic vertebra. The caval opening lies at the eighth and the esophageal opening at the tenth.

Question 11246. A described dissection behind the aorta at the level of the first lumbar vertebra shows a sac into which several lymph trunks from the lower limbs and the gut drain. Which structure is shown, and into what does it continue upward? The answer is the cisterna chyli, which continues as the thoracic duct. It lies behind the aorta and in front of the vertebral column.

Question 11247. A constructed illustration: a person with long-standing liver disease has dilated veins running outward from the umbilicus, and the superficial veins of the abdominal wall are engorged. Which veins have opened up? The answer is the paraumbilical veins, which join the superficial veins of the abdominal wall. Blood that cannot pass through the liver is carried to the body wall instead.

Question 11248. Name three places where the veins of the portal system join the veins of the body wall, spoken as a list. The answer is the lower esophagus, the umbilicus and the rectum. There the left gastric veins meet the esophageal veins, the paraumbilical veins meet the veins of the wall, and the superior rectal vein meets the middle and inferior rectal veins.

Question 11249. True or false: the psoas major muscle arises from the sides of the lumbar vertebral bodies and from the discs between them. The answer is true. It also takes origin from the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, and it passes under the inguinal ligament to reach the lesser trochanter of the femur.

Question 11250. Which vessel is formed at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra by the union of the two common iliac veins, and lies to the right of the aorta: the portal vein, the inferior vena cava, the left renal vein, or the thoracic duct? The answer is the inferior vena cava. It ascends in front of the vertebral column and passes through the diaphragm to reach the heart.

Question 11251. A described specimen of the airway shows that one main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the other. Which side is a swallowed object more likely to enter? The answer is the right side. The right main bronchus continues the line of the trachea more directly, so a foreign body follows it into the right lung.

Question 11252. Within an intercostal space, where does the bundle of nerve and vessels lie: deep to the under surface of the rib above, deep to the upper surface of the rib below, in the middle of the space, or outside the rib cage? The answer is deep to the under surface of the rib above. The bundle rests in the groove there, and the inner intercostal muscle separates it from the pleura.

Question 11253. A described chest radiograph shows one side of the chest more translucent than the other, with the lung collapsed toward the midline and the heart and trachea pushed to the opposite side. Which condition is shown? The answer is a tension pneumothorax, with air under pressure in the pleural cavity. The pressure pushes the mediastinum across, and that is what makes the injury dangerous.

Question 11254. Which chamber of the heart lies immediately behind the body of the sternum and the costal cartilages beside it, and is therefore the chamber most exposed to a wound of the front of the chest? The answer is the right ventricle. It forms most of the anterior surface of the heart, with the right atrium to its right.

Question 11255. In cardiac tamponade, which chambers of the heart are compressed first: the left atrium and left ventricle, the right atrium and right ventricle, the aorta and the pulmonary trunk, or the coronary veins? The answer is the right atrium and the right ventricle. They are the thinnest walled and the lowest pressured chambers, so they fill last when the sac is tight.

Question 11256. A constructed illustration: a narrow wound enters the left side of the chest beside the sternum in the fourth intercostal space and reaches the heart. Which chamber is most likely to be wounded? The answer is the right ventricle. It lies immediately behind the sternum and the left fourth costal cartilage, so a wound beside the sternum reaches it first.

Question 11257. A described scan of the chest after a sudden stop in a road collision shows a widened upper mediastinum, with blood around the aorta just beyond the point where the left subclavian artery leaves it. Which part of the aorta is injured? The answer is the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery. There the aorta is fixed against the vertebral column by the ligamentum arteriosum.

Question 11258. Which organ lies beneath the left ninth to the eleventh ribs and is the organ most often injured in a blunt blow to the upper abdomen? The answer is the spleen. It is a soft organ with a thin capsule, and it lies in the left upper quadrant behind the stomach and the ribs.

Question 11259. Which structure lies immediately beneath the left lower ribs in the midaxillary line, so that a fracture of those ribs may tear it: the liver, the spleen, the right kidney, or the gallbladder? The answer is the spleen. It is protected by the ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs, and its long axis follows the line of the tenth rib.

Question 11260. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the left lower chest, a person has pain in the left upper abdomen and also complains of pain at the tip of the left shoulder, worse on breathing in. Which organ is likely injured, and which nerve explains the shoulder pain? The answer is the spleen, with the left phrenic nerve. Blood under the diaphragm irritates that nerve, and the pain is felt over the shoulder.

Question 11261. Which part of the pancreas lies against the spleen, so that the two are often injured together in a blow to the left upper abdomen? The answer is the tail of the pancreas. It reaches the spleen along the splenic vessels, and the spleen lies behind its lateral end. Both rest at the level of the eleventh thoracic vertebra.

Question 11262. In a road collision a lap belt crosses the abdomen and presses a structure against the vertebral column. Which structure lies in that position and is injured: the stomach, the gallbladder, the third part of the duodenum, or the appendix? The answer is the third part of the duodenum. It crosses in front of the spine, and the pancreas lies behind it in the same line of compression.

Question 11263. The abdomen is divided by two planes crossing at the umbilicus into four quadrants. In which quadrant does the spleen lie? The answer is the left upper quadrant. It sits behind the stomach and the left lower ribs, above and to the left of the umbilicus.

Question 11264. A described wound track enters the left side of the chest at the level of the eighth rib and passes downward and medially. Which two cavities could lie in that path, and which structure separates them? The answer is the pleural cavity and the peritoneal cavity, separated by the diaphragm. The left dome of the diaphragm rises to about the level of the eighth rib in the midclavicular line.

Question 11265. A fracture of the pelvis tears vessels on its inner surface and causes heavy bleeding. Which vessels are the usual source: the femoral artery and vein, the presacral venous plexus and the superior gluteal artery, the obturator and sciatic nerves, or the inferior epigastric vessels? The answer is the presacral venous plexus and the superior gluteal artery. Both lie against the bone inside the pelvis.

Question 11266. Which part of the urethra is torn when the pelvis is fractured, at the point where the urethra passes through the perineal membrane? The answer is the membranous part, the short segment between the prostate and the bulb of the penis. It is the fixed point of the urethra, so it tears when the ring of the pelvis gives way.

Question 11267. In the female pelvis, which structure lies immediately lateral to the cervix of the uterus and passes over the ureter, close to it? The answer is the uterine artery. The ureter passes beneath the artery about 2 centimeters lateral to the cervix, which is why the two are described as water running under a bridge.

Question 11268. A constructed illustration: a person falls astride a hard edge and cannot pass urine, with blood at the urinary opening and bruising of the perineum and scrotum. Which part of the urethra is torn? The answer is the bulbar part in the perineum. It is the fixed part of the anterior urethra, and blood and urine spread into the perineum and the scrotum.

Question 11269. A described radiograph of the pelvis shows breaks through both the superior and the inferior pubic rami on each side, with the fragments undisturbed. Which kind of injury is shown, and which structure is at risk? The answer is a straddle fracture, with the bulbar urethra at risk. The bony ring gives way at its weakest points, which are the pubic rami.

Question 11270. When a full bladder ruptures after a blow to the lower abdomen, why does urine usually enter the peritoneal cavity: because the peritoneum covers the dome of the bladder, because the bladder lies behind the peritoneum, because the urethra is torn, or because the rectum is perforated? The answer is that the peritoneum covers its dome. A full bladder rises above the pubic symphysis, and the peritoneum over its dome tears with it.

Question 11271. True or false: the right kidney lies a little lower than the left because the liver occupies the space above it. The answer is true. The right kidney is pressed downward by the liver, so its upper pole lies about 2 centimeters lower than the upper pole of the left kidney.

Question 11272. Which structure of the abdomen lies behind the peritoneum and may be injured in a blunt blow to the front of the abdomen, with signs that appear only hours later: the stomach, the transverse colon, the duodenum, or the jejunum? The answer is the duodenum. It lies against the vertebral column behind the peritoneum, so blood and gut contents collect in the tissue there.

Question 11273. In an emergency, which artery can be pressed against the superior ramus of the pubis at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament? The answer is the femoral artery. It lies at that point between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, with the femoral vein medial to it.

Question 11274. Which of these pairs belongs together: a blow to the left lower ribs with the spleen, a blow to the right lower ribs with the spleen, a fractured pelvis with the appendix, or a stab below the left costal margin with the gallbladder? The answer is a blow to the left lower ribs with the spleen. The spleen lies beneath the ninth to the eleventh ribs on the left.

Question 11275. Name three structures that lie behind the peritoneum in the abdomen, spoken as a list. The answer is the kidneys, the pancreas and the duodenum. The ureters, the suprarenal glands, the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava and the ascending and descending parts of the colon lie there too.

Question 11276. After a severe injury, pressure rises inside the abdomen and the diaphragm is pushed upward. Which structure reflects that pressure because it lies in the pelvis with a soft wall: the stomach, the bladder, the rectum, or the gallbladder? The answer is the bladder. It lies in the pelvis, and the pressure within it follows the pressure in the abdomen around it.

Question 11277. Which artery supplies the appendix, and from which vessel does it arise? The answer is the appendicular artery, from the ileocolic artery. It runs in the mesentery of the appendix, along the free edge of that fold, and it belongs to the superior mesenteric territory.

Question 11278. A described dissection of the right lower abdomen shows the appendix hanging over the muscle that runs down the back wall of the abdomen, with its tip pointing toward the brim of the pelvis. On which muscle does it rest? The answer is the psoas major. It flexes the hip joint and steadies the lumbar spine, and it passes beneath the inguinal ligament.

Question 11279. A described upright radiograph of the chest shows a crescent of gas under both domes of the diaphragm, with no gas in the stomach below the left dome. What does that gas indicate, and where has it come from? The answer is free gas in the peritoneal cavity, from a perforated hollow organ. Gas rises to the highest part of the abdomen, which is under the diaphragm.

Question 11280. Which part of the duodenum is the usual site of perforation: the anterior wall of the first part, the posterior wall of the first part, the anterior wall of the third part, or the medial wall of the second part? The answer is the anterior wall of the first part. That part is mobile and lies in front of the pancreas, so its contents spill into the abdominal cavity.

Question 11281. A constructed illustration: a person has sudden severe pain in the upper middle of the abdomen, the abdominal wall becomes rigid, and the radiograph shows gas under the diaphragm. Which part of the gut has perforated? The answer is the first part of the duodenum, on its anterior wall. That segment is the most mobile part of the duodenum, and it lies in front of the pancreas.

Question 11282. A described contrast study of the upper gut shows a small crater in the wall of the first part of the duodenum, with the fold pattern drawn toward it. Which structure is shown, and on which wall does it lie? The answer is an ulcer of the duodenum on the anterior wall. That wall faces the peritoneal cavity, which is why it is the site that perforates.

Question 11283. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the gut from which point to which point: from the stomach to the cecum, from the second part of the duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, from the cecum to the rectum, or from the rectum to the anal canal? The answer is from the second part of the duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.

Question 11284. Which kind of hernia passes through the narrow channel bounded in front by the inguinal ligament and behind by the pectineal ligament, and is the most likely to strangulate? The answer is a femoral hernia. Its neck is the femoral ring, a narrow opening that admits only a finger, and the firm lacunar ligament lies at its medial edge.

Question 11285. Which ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, and what is the effect of that boundary on a hernia passing there? The answer is the lacunar ligament, the reflected part of the inguinal ligament. That sharp edge narrows the ring and can cut into the bowel within it. The femoral vein lies lateral to the ring and the pectineal ligament behind it.

Question 11286. A constructed illustration: a person has a firm, tender lump in the groin that lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and does not descend into the scrotum. Which kind of hernia is described? The answer is a femoral hernia. It passes below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, while an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle.

Question 11287. True or false: a direct inguinal hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring. The answer is false. A direct hernia pushes through the medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, medial to the inferior epigastric artery, while an indirect hernia is the one that enters the deep ring.

Question 11288. A described dissection of the inguinal region shows a peritoneal sac entering the abdominal wall lateral to the inferior epigastric artery and then running down the canal. Which kind of hernia does the sac represent? The answer is an indirect inguinal hernia. It enters the deep inguinal ring, which lies lateral to the artery, and it travels within the coverings of the spermatic cord.

Question 11289. The weak triangle in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is bounded by the inferior epigastric artery, the inguinal ligament and the rectus sheath. In which position does each lie: artery laterally, ligament below and sheath medially; artery medially, ligament above and sheath laterally; artery below, ligament laterally and sheath above; or artery above, ligament medially and sheath below? The answer is artery laterally, ligament below and sheath medially.

Question 11290. On which ribs does the spleen rest, and at which line is its surface marking drawn? The answer is the ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs on the left, in the midaxillary line. Its long axis follows the tenth rib, and the organ descends when a person breathes in.

Question 11291. Name three structures that may be injured when a lap belt compresses the abdomen against the vertebral column, spoken as a list. The answer is the duodenum, the pancreas and the mesentery of the small intestine. The duodenum and the pancreas lie directly in front of the spine, and the mesentery can be torn by the sudden change in speed.

Question 11292. Which solid organ is most often injured in a blunt injury to the abdomen: the liver, the spleen, the kidney, or the pancreas? The answer is the spleen. It lies in the left upper quadrant behind the ribs and the stomach, and it is a soft organ with a thin capsule that tears easily. The liver is injured second most often.

Question 11293. A described ultrasound examination of the abdomen shows dark fluid lying between the liver and the right kidney, in the space where the peritoneum reflects from one to the other. Which space is shown, and why does fluid collect there? The answer is the hepatorenal pouch. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when a person lies on the back, so free fluid gathers there first.

Question 11294. Which of these pairs belongs together: the hepatorenal pouch with a person lying on the back, the rectouterine pouch with a person lying face down, a ruptured spleen with right shoulder pain, or a ruptured bladder with pain under the left ribs? The answer is the hepatorenal pouch with a person lying on the back, because that pouch is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity.

Question 11295. In which quadrant of the abdomen does the spleen lie: the right upper, the left upper, the right lower, or the left lower? The answer is the left upper quadrant. It lies behind the stomach and beneath the left dome of the diaphragm, above the level of the umbilicus.

Question 11296. A constructed illustration: a person has sudden lower abdominal pain and faints, and the abdomen is tender with signs of bleeding inside. Which structure has ruptured, and in which pouch does the blood collect first? The answer is a pregnancy in a uterine tube, with blood collecting in the rectouterine pouch. That pouch is the lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity.

Question 11297. Which of these pairs belongs together: a fractured pelvis with the membranous urethra, a straddle injury with the membranous urethra, a fractured pelvis with the bulbar urethra, or a stab wound of the loin with the appendix? The answer is a fractured pelvis with the membranous urethra. That part is fixed at the pelvic floor and tears when the ring of the pelvis breaks.

Question 11298. Which organ rises out of the pelvis and can be felt above the pubic symphysis when it is full, and lies behind that joint? The answer is the urinary bladder. When empty it lies entirely within the pelvis, and as it fills it rises into the abdomen and pushes the peritoneum off the front of the abdominal wall.

Question 11299. When the abdominal aorta ruptures below the kidneys, where does the blood usually collect: in the peritoneal cavity, in the retroperitoneal tissue, in the pleural cavity, or in the pelvis only? The answer is in the retroperitoneal tissue. The aorta lies behind the peritoneum against the vertebral column, so blood spreads through the loose tissue there and may present as back pain.

Question 11300. A described wound enters the left side of the chest in the eighth intercostal space in the midaxillary line and passes downward through the diaphragm. Which organ lies beneath that point: the stomach, the spleen, the left lobe of the liver, or the left kidney? The answer is the spleen. The left dome of the diaphragm rises to that level, and the spleen lies below it against the ninth to eleventh ribs.

To summarize, the peritoneum has a parietal layer that localizes pain sharply and a visceral layer that feels only stretch, and its folds, the greater omentum, the lesser omentum, the gastrosplenic ligament and the mesenteries, carry the vessels of the gut. The foregut is supplied by the celiac trunk, the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery down to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, and the hindgut by the inferior mesenteric artery, with the watershed at the splenic flexure. The bare area of the liver, the portal vein formed behind the neck of the pancreas, the third part of the duodenum that crosses the aorta, and the ascending colon that lies behind the peritoneum are relations worth hearing again. The right kidney lies lower than the left, the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta, and the ureter crosses the pelvic brim in front of the common iliac bifurcation. In emergency anatomy the spleen is the organ most often injured by a blunt blow to the left upper abdomen, the right ventricle lies behind the sternum in the path of a wound beside it, the third part of the duodenum and the pancreas are compressed against the spine by a lap belt, and the membranous urethra is torn by a fractured pelvis while the bulbar urethra is torn in a straddle injury. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 114 — Structure and Function

This chapter treats shape as the explanation of what a structure does and of how it fails. It moves through bone, cartilage, joints, muscle, tendon, skin, vessels, heart, lymphatics, airway, gut, urinary tract and glands, asking what each form is for. It holds one hundred questions, and every answer follows its question immediately with the reason it is right. The last twenty-five items turn that reasoning toward injury, asking which structure a described mechanism puts at risk. This is educational material, and it does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 11301. Which kind of bone tissue forms the hard outer shell of a long bone, and which fills the interior? The answer is that cortical bone forms the shell and cancellous bone fills the interior. Cortical bone is dense and resists bending. Cancellous bone is a network of thin plates that resists compression where load enters at a joint.

Question 11302. What is the advantage of a long bone shaft built as a hollow tube: it is lighter for the same strength, it is heavier but stiffer, it stores more marrow, or it grows faster? The answer is that it is lighter for the same strength. Material far from the center resists bending better than material at the axis, and the marrow cavity costs almost nothing.

Question 11303. A described section of a long bone shows a dense outer layer, a spongy interior at both ends, and a central cavity of fatty tissue. Which parts are shown? The answer is the cortex, the cancellous bone of the ends, and the marrow cavity. The fat is yellow marrow, which replaces red marrow in the shaft.

Question 11304. A described specimen shows thin plates of bone arranged in arches that cross one another near a joint. What is this arrangement, and what decides the direction of the plates? The answer is cancellous bone, whose plates follow the lines of stress. When loading changes, the plates slowly remodel along the new lines.

Question 11305. Why do the plates in the neck of the femur cross in two opposing arcs: to resist tension above and compression below, to fill space, to carry marrow, or to speed healing? The answer is to resist tension above and compression below. The upper arc carries the pull of the pelvis, and the lower arc carries the body weight into the shaft.

Question 11306. By what path does the weight of the body leave the pelvis and enter the shaft of the femur? The answer is through the head and the neck, by way of the arches of cancellous bone, into the shaft. The load then joins the thick inner cortex of the shaft.

Question 11307. Which of these pairs belongs together: hyaline cartilage with the knee joint surface, fibrocartilage with the outer ear, elastic cartilage with the intervertebral disc, or hyaline cartilage with the pubic symphysis? The answer is hyaline cartilage with the knee joint surface. The outer ear is elastic, and the disc and the pubic symphysis are fibrocartilage.

Question 11308. What is the name of the smooth, glassy cartilage that covers the ends of bones inside a joint? The answer is hyaline cartilage. It has no blood vessels and no nerves, so it cannot feel pain and heals poorly. Synovial fluid keeps it slippery, which is why a joint moves almost without friction.

Question 11309. A described radiograph shows the neck of the femur running upward and inward from the shaft to the head. In which plane must the limb lie for that angle to appear true? The answer is the frontal plane. That plane divides the body into front and back parts, and any other view foreshortens the neck.

Question 11310. Which of these is a ball and socket joint: the shoulder, the elbow, the ankle, or the joint between the atlas and the axis? The answer is the shoulder. Its rounded head sits in a shallow socket and moves in every direction, including rotation. The elbow and the ankle are hinges.

Question 11311. What are the two parts of an intervertebral disc, and which lies in the center? The answer is the annulus fibrosus around the outside and the nucleus pulposus in the center. The annulus is built of rings of fibrocartilage. The nucleus is a soft core that spreads compression onto those rings.

Question 11312. A described midline section of the lower spine shows a disc whose soft center has been pushed backward. What has happened, and what lies in that space? The answer is a disc herniation, and the space holds a spinal nerve root. The soft center escapes through a tear in the outer rings and presses on the root.

Question 11313. Where does the nucleus pulposus lie within a disc, and which way does it move when the spine bends? The answer is that it lies slightly behind the center and moves backward. Bending forward squeezes the front of the disc and pushes the core backward, which is why a disc usually bulges backward.

Question 11314. How does a sesamoid bone such as the patella change the action of the muscle that runs through it: it lengthens the lever arm, it shortens the muscle, it adds a joint, or it has no effect? The answer is that it lengthens the lever arm by holding the tendon away from the joint. The tendon then pulls at a better angle, so the same force turns the joint more.

Question 11315. Which of these is a sesamoid bone, a small bone embedded in a tendon where it crosses a joint: the patella, the talus, the clavicle, or the calcaneus? The answer is the patella, the largest sesamoid bone. It lies in the tendon of the quadriceps at the front of the knee.

Question 11316. A described specimen from the knee shows two C-shaped pads of fibrocartilage resting on the flat upper surface of the tibia. What are they, and what do they do? The answer is the menisci. They deepen the flat tibial surface, spread the load of the femur, and help absorb shock.

Question 11317. In which of these places does fibrocartilage form the main tissue: the articular surface of the hip, the intervertebral disc, the epiglottis, or the trachea? The answer is the intervertebral disc. Fibrocartilage resists compression and tearing at once, which is what a disc must do. The hip surface is hyaline cartilage.

Question 11318. A described section through the knee shows a wedge of tissue between the femur and the tibia, with fibers in two directions. What is it, and why does its shape matter? The answer is a meniscus, whose wedge turns the flat tibial surface into a shallow socket. The two fiber directions resist tearing and squeezing.

Question 11319. Where does the medial meniscus sit in relation to the medial collateral ligament of the knee? The answer is that the meniscus lies deep to the ligament and is attached to it. The deep fibers of the ligament blend with the outer edge of the meniscus, so a tear of one often tears the other.

Question 11320. Which of these pairs belongs together: a hinge joint with movement in one plane, a saddle joint with movement in no plane, a pivot joint with gliding only, or a ball and socket joint with no movement? The answer is a hinge joint with movement in one plane. A pivot joint turns about one axis, and a saddle joint moves in two planes.

Question 11321. What is the name of the ring of fibrocartilage attached to the rim of the shoulder socket? The answer is the glenoid labrum. It deepens the shallow socket and gives the head of the humerus a better fit. It also gives attachment to the capsule.

Question 11322. Why does the shoulder dislocate more often than the hip: the socket is shallower, the ligaments are absent, the capsule is thicker, or the bone is smaller? The answer is the shallower socket. The glenoid is a small, flat dish that allows wide movement at the cost of stability, while the acetabulum is a deep cup.

Question 11323. True or false: the labrum of the shoulder is a rim of hyaline cartilage that deepens the socket. The answer is false. The labrum is a rim of fibrocartilage attached to the bony edge of the glenoid. It widens the contact area and adds stability.

Question 11324. A described membrane lines the inside of a joint capsule but stops at the edge of the cartilage. What is it, and what does it produce? The answer is the synovial membrane. It secretes the fluid that lubricates the joint and feeds the cartilage, which has no blood vessels.

Question 11325. Which statement about a pivot joint is correct: it allows rotation about one axis, it allows gliding in two planes, it permits no movement, or it allows movement in three planes? The answer is rotation about one axis. The joint between the atlas and the axis lets the head turn, and the joints of the forearm turn the palm.

Question 11326. A described section through the hip joint shows a ring of fibrocartilage around the rim of the socket. What is the ring, and how does it work? The answer is the acetabular labrum. It deepens the cup, grips the head, and helps seal the fluid inside, whose film resists the head being pulled out.

Question 11327. What kind of joint is formed where two bones are united by a pad of fibrocartilage that allows only slight movement: a hinge joint, a cartilaginous joint, a pivot joint, or a saddle joint? The answer is a cartilaginous joint. The joints between the vertebral bodies and between the pubic bones are of this kind.

Question 11328. A described section through a joint in front of the ear shows a disc of fibrocartilage dividing the cavity into two spaces. Which joint is shown, and what does the disc allow? The answer is the temporomandibular joint. The disc lets the jaw both hinge and slide forward.

Question 11329. Which joint lies between the first cervical vertebra and the second, and what movement does it allow: the head to nod, the head to turn, the shoulder to circle, or the jaw to open? The answer is the joint between the atlas and the axis, which turns the head. Nodding happens higher up.

Question 11330. Name two joints that allow rotation only, spoken as a list. The answer is the joint between the atlas and the axis, and the joint between the radius and the ulna near the elbow. Both are pivot joints, turning about a single long axis. Together they turn the head and the palm.

Question 11331. A described spindle-shaped structure lies within a skeletal muscle, wrapped in a capsule and supplied by a nerve. What is it, and what does it report? The answer is a muscle spindle. It lies parallel to the ordinary fibers and senses how far and how fast the muscle stretches, which adjusts its tension.

Question 11332. Which part of a sarcomere shortens when a muscle contracts: the thick filaments, the thin filaments, the distance between the two sets of filaments, or the Z lines themselves? The answer is the distance between the two sets of filaments. The filaments keep their own length and slide past one another.

Question 11333. A described microscopic section of muscle shows long parallel fibers with fine cross bands and many nuclei at the edge. Which kind of muscle is shown? The answer is skeletal muscle. The cross bands are the regular overlap of thick and thin filaments, and the many nuclei show fused cells.

Question 11334. At the place where a tendon joins a bone, which tissue lies between the two, and why does it matter? The answer is fibrocartilage that gradually changes from tendon into bone. That gradual change spreads the pull over a wider area and removes a sharp corner where a tendon would tear away.

Question 11335. A described cord of dense regular connective tissue joins the end of a muscle to a bone. What is this structure? The answer is a tendon. Its fibers are packed in parallel in the direction of pull, which makes it very strong and almost inextensible.

Question 11336. Which of these pairs belongs together: epimysium with the whole muscle, perimysium with a single fiber, endomysium with a bundle of fibers, or epimysium with a single fiber? The answer is epimysium with the whole muscle. The perimysium wraps a bundle, and the endomysium wraps each fiber.

Question 11337. How does a pennate muscle differ from a parallel muscle of the same size: it develops more force but shortens less, it develops less force but shortens more, it moves the joint further, or it has no tendon? The answer is more force and less shortening. More fibers fit into the same volume because they attach at an angle to the tendon.

Question 11338. Name two muscles whose fibers run at an angle to their tendon, spoken as a list. The answer is the rectus femoris of the thigh and the deltoid of the shoulder. A muscle of this kind is called pennate, and it trades distance for force.

Question 11339. Which of these pairs belongs together: a multipennate muscle with the deltoid, a parallel muscle with the gastrocnemius, a bipennate muscle with the biceps brachii, or a circular muscle with the rectus abdominis? The answer is a multipennate muscle with the deltoid. The gastrocnemius is bipennate and the biceps brachii is parallel.

Question 11340. In most limb muscles the effort is applied between the joint and the load, which makes them what kind of lever: first class, second class, third class, or fourth class? The answer is third class. The muscle pulls between the fulcrum of the joint and the weight. This favors speed and range over force, which is why limbs move quickly.

Question 11341. Why does the middle part of the deltoid raise the arm with the greatest effect? The answer is that its fibers lie farthest from the axis of the joint, so its lever arm is longest. A longer lever arm gives more turning effect for the same force, and the other parts lie nearer the axis.

Question 11342. A described section of a muscle shows fibers converging from one side onto a tendon on the other side. What arrangement is shown, and what does it do to the force? The answer is a unipennate arrangement. The fibers join the tendon at an angle, so more of them fit and it pulls harder.

Question 11343. A described specimen shows a broad flat sheet of tendon that spreads over the side of the abdomen and joins the muscle to the midline. What is this sheet? The answer is an aponeurosis. It gives a wide area for fibers to attach and spreads their pull over a broad surface, as in the palm.

Question 11344. Why can the calf muscles lift the whole body weight at the ankle: the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort, the fulcrum lies between the load and the effort, the effort lies between the load and the fulcrum, or no lever is involved? The answer is that the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort. The toes are the fulcrum, and the calf pulls on the heel behind the ankle.

Question 11345. True or false: a pennate muscle can shorten further than a parallel muscle with the same length of fiber. The answer is false. A pennate muscle develops more force but shortens less, because its fibers pull at an angle to the tendon. The parallel muscle gives up force for a longer range.

Question 11346. Which of these pairs belongs together: intercalated discs with cardiac muscle, many nuclei at the edge of the fiber with smooth muscle, spindle-shaped cells with skeletal muscle, or voluntary control with cardiac muscle? The answer is intercalated discs with cardiac muscle. Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with one central nucleus.

Question 11347.
