Why does the impulse travel faster through the conducting fibers of the heart than through the ordinary muscle: the fibers are larger, the fibers are wrapped in fat, they release more calcium, or they are shorter? The answer is that the fibers are larger. A wider fiber carries current more easily along its inside, and its junctions pass the impulse on quickly.

Question 11348. A described chest radiograph shows a dense white shadow behind the sternum, with dark lungs on either side and the ribs crossing in front. What does the shadow represent, and why is it white? The answer is the heart and the mediastinum. Dense tissue absorbs more of the beam than air does.

Question 11349. A described organ is bean-shaped, has a capsule, an outer zone crowded with round nodules, and a center with cords of cells. What organ is it, and what does it do? The answer is a lymph node. It filters the lymph passing through it and gives lymphocytes a place to meet what they must answer.

Question 11350. Where in a lymph node do B lymphocytes gather, and where do T lymphocytes gather? The answer is that B lymphocytes gather in the outer cortex and T lymphocytes in the deep cortex just inside it. The medulla at the center holds macrophages and plasma cells.

Question 11351. What are the two tissues of the spleen, and what does each do: red pulp filters blood and white pulp fights infection, red pulp stores iron and white pulp makes antibodies, red pulp filters lymph and white pulp stores iron, or red pulp makes antibodies and white pulp filters blood? The answer is that red pulp filters blood and white pulp fights infection. White pulp surrounds small arteries and holds lymphocytes.

Question 11352. True or false: the thymus is largest in adult life, when the immune system is most active. The answer is false. The thymus is largest in childhood and then slowly shrinks as its tissue is replaced by fat. It is where T lymphocytes are trained, and most of that work is done early.

Question 11353. A described collection of lymphoid tissue sits in the wall of the throat, with folds of tissue and deep crypts on its surface. What is it, and where is it placed? The answer is a tonsil. It sits at the entrance to the throat, where it samples what is breathed and swallowed. Its crypts give a large surface for that contact.

Question 11354. A described section of a small organ shows a fibrous capsule sending bands inward, a dark outer zone of round nodules, and a pale center with cords of cells. What organ is shown? The answer is a lymph node, and the nodules of its outer zone are lymphatic nodules. The bands from the capsule are trabeculae.

Question 11355. Where in the lung does the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide take place: the trachea, the bronchi, the bronchioles, or the alveoli? The answer is the alveoli. Their walls are one cell thick and lie against the capillaries, so gas crosses a very short distance. The airways above them only carry air.

Question 11356. Why does the lung of a premature infant tend to collapse: the alveoli are too few, the surfactant that lowers surface tension is not yet made, the airways are too wide, or the diaphragm is weak? The answer is that the surfactant is not yet made. Surface tension in the film lining each alveolus pulls its walls together, and surfactant reduces that tension.

Question 11357. A described section of an airway shows a wall held open by C-shaped plates of cartilage, with a band of smooth muscle behind them. Which part of the airway is shown? The answer is a bronchus. The plates keep the airway from collapsing during a forced breath, and the muscle can narrow the tube.

Question 11358. Why does the dome of the diaphragm flatten when it contracts, and what does that do to the chest? The answer is that its fibers run from the central tendon to the lower ribs and the vertebral column, so shortening pulls the center down and the ribs up. That enlarges the chest from top to bottom.

Question 11359. In which direction do the fibers of the external intercostal muscles run, and what does that do: downward and forward, so they raise the ribs, downward and backward, so they lower the ribs, straight down, or around the chest? The answer is downward and forward, so they raise the ribs. The internal intercostal fibers run the other way.

Question 11360. A described section through the side wall of the nose shows three curled shelves of bone covered by moist membrane, with air spaces between them. What are these shelves, and what are they for? The answer is the conchae. They increase the surface over which air passes, so it is warmed, moistened, and cleaned.

Question 11361. A described flap of elastic cartilage stands at the root of the tongue and folds over the opening of the voice box during swallowing. What is it? The answer is the epiglottis. Its elastic cartilage springs upright again when swallowing ends, and it keeps food out of the airway.

Question 11362. True or false: the wall of the small intestine is built of four coats, one of which is a muscle layer that moves the contents along. The answer is true. From the outside inward the coats are the serous coat, the muscle coat, the submucous coat, and the mucous membrane. The muscle coat has two layers.

Question 11363. What are the finger-like projections of the lining of the small intestine for: to increase the surface for absorbing food, to move the contents along, to make enzymes, or to store fat? The answer is to increase the surface for absorbing food. Each projection is covered with cells whose free edge carries even finer folds.

Question 11364. A described ring of thickened circular muscle guards the outlet of the stomach and opens only at intervals. What is it, and what does it do? The answer is the pyloric sphincter. It holds food in the stomach long enough to be mixed, then releases it in small amounts.

Question 11365. A described transverse section through the upper abdomen shows a large organ on the right and a smaller one on the left. Which plane was used, and where do the two organs lie? The answer is a transverse plane, and the section shows the liver on the right and the spleen on the left. It divides the body into upper and lower parts.

Question 11366. A described microscopic section of the liver shows six-sided units, each with a vessel at its center and plates of cells running outward like the spokes of a wheel. What are these units, and what runs between the plates? The answer is the liver lobules. Between the plates run the channels that carry bile outward and the spaces where blood is processed.

Question 11367. Why can the pancreas be described as two glands in one: it makes enzymes and also makes hormones, it stores bile and releases it, it filters blood and makes lymph, or it absorbs food and makes acid? The answer is that it makes enzymes and also makes hormones. Most of the gland pours enzymes into a duct, while small clusters release hormones into the blood.

Question 11368. A described section of the kidney shows a round tuft of capillaries pushed into a cup-shaped capsule. What is the tuft called, and where is it found? The answer is the glomerulus, and it lies in the cortex of the kidney. Blood is filtered through its walls into the capsule, and the fluid becomes urine.

Question 11369. Why does the loop of Henle let the kidney make urine more concentrated than the blood: its two limbs carry fluid in opposite directions and build a salt gradient, it stores water, it makes red cells, or it reabsorbs protein? The answer is the opposite directions of flow. Salt is pumped out of the ascending limb, which water cannot leave.

Question 11370. A described section of the kidney shows an outer zone of round bodies and a deeper zone of triangular areas with stripes running toward the center. Which parts are shown, and what do the stripes mean? The answer is the cortex outside and the medulla inside, with the renal pyramids within the medulla. The stripes are parallel tubules and vessels.

Question 11371. True or false: the ureter moves urine to the bladder by gravity alone. The answer is false. Its wall carries smooth muscle in two layers, and waves of contraction push the urine along whatever the position of the body. The same waves are felt as colic when the tube is blocked.

Question 11372. What is the name of the smooth muscle of the wall of the urinary bladder? The answer is the detrusor muscle. Its fibers run in several directions and contract as one to empty the bladder. As the bladder fills, the fold of membrane at its base flattens out.

Question 11373. What is the structural unit of the thyroid gland: a follicle lined by cells and filled with stored secretion, a cluster of nerve cells, a duct opening onto the skin, or a knot of capillaries? The answer is a follicle lined by cells and filled with stored secretion. The cells take iodine from the blood and build the hormones.

Question 11374. Why does a tumor of the adrenal medulla raise the blood pressure in sudden attacks, while a tumor of the cortex does not? The answer is that the medulla releases its hormones straight into the blood, while the cortex releases steroids that act more slowly. The medulla is part of the sympathetic nervous system.

Question 11375. Name two features of the small intestine that increase its surface area, spoken as a list. The answer is the villi of its lining and the circular folds of its wall. Each villus is covered with cells whose free border carries fine projections, and together they multiply the surface many times.

Question 11376. A constructed illustration: a player plants a foot and turns sharply, and the knee gives way with a sudden pop and fast swelling. Which ligament inside the knee is most likely torn? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. It stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur, and a twist with the foot fixed loads it most.

Question 11377. Which ligament is most often torn when the ankle turns inward: the anterior talofibular ligament, the deltoid ligament, the calcaneofibular ligament, or the spring ligament? The answer is the anterior talofibular ligament. It is the weakest part of the outer complex and lies first in the path of the turning foot.

Question 11378. A described specimen shows a strong triangular ligament running from the medial malleolus down to the bones of the foot on the inner side. Which structure is it, and what movement does it resist? The answer is the deltoid ligament, which resists turning the sole outward. It is stronger than the ligaments on the outer side.

Question 11379. A described radiograph of the wrist shows a crack across the lower end of the radius, with the fragment tilted backward. What injury is shown? The answer is a break of the lower end of the radius with backward displacement, the break of a fall on the outstretched hand. The hand is driven back, and the fragment follows.

Question 11380. A constructed illustration: an older person has pain when raising the arm sideways through the middle of the arc, and the pain eases once the arm is high. Which structure is inflamed? The answer is the supraspinatus tendon, which passes beneath the arch over the shoulder. There the tendon is pressed hardest against the arch.

Question 11381. Why is the ulnar nerve so easily injured behind the inner side of the elbow: it lies in a shallow groove with little covering, it lies deep under muscle, it passes through a bony tunnel, or it runs beside the artery? The answer is that it lies in a shallow groove. A knock on the medial epicondyle tingles in the little finger.

Question 11382. A constructed illustration: a deep cut across the front of the wrist leaves the thumb unable to oppose and the palm numb on its outer half. Which nerve is most likely cut? The answer is the median nerve. It lies just under the skin in the middle of the wrist, where the branch to the thumb muscles leaves it.

Question 11383. How does the radial nerve relate to the shaft of the humerus, and why does that matter after a break? The answer is that the nerve lies in a spiral groove on the back of the shaft, close against the bone. A break across the middle can press on or tear it, and the wrist then cannot be lifted.

Question 11384. A constructed illustration: a blow strikes the outer side of a fixed knee, and the joint opens on the inner side, with pain along the inner joint line. Which two structures are injured together, and why? The answer is the medial collateral ligament and the medial meniscus. The deep fibers of the ligament are attached to the meniscus.

Question 11385. Why does bleeding into a joint after a ligament tear make the whole joint swell so quickly: the synovial membrane is rich in blood vessels, the cartilage bleeds, the bone bleeds, or the fluid is secreted? The answer is that the synovial membrane is rich in blood vessels. Blood irritates the membrane, which then secretes more fluid.

Question 11386. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the outstretched hand, a person has tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb and pain when the wrist is loaded. Which bone is most likely broken? The answer is the scaphoid. It lies in the floor of that hollow and bridges the two rows of carpal bones.

Question 11387. A described radiograph taken a week after a fall shows a fine crack across a small bone at the base of the thumb, with no displacement. Which bone is shown, and why is the injury followed closely? The answer is the scaphoid. Its blood enters near the far end, so a break across the middle can starve the piece nearest the thumb.

Question 11388. Which carpal bone is broken most often, and why does the fragment nearest the thumb heal so poorly? The answer is the scaphoid, because its blood enters near the far end and travels backward along the bone. A break across its waist cuts off the supply to the piece nearest the thumb, and that piece may die.

Question 11389. A constructed illustration: an older person breaks the neck of the femur, and months later the head of the bone crumbles. Why did the head lose its blood supply? The answer is that the vessels to the head run along the neck, and a break there tears them. The head keeps only the small artery in the ligament to its pit.

Question 11390. After a break of the surgical neck of the humerus, which nerve is most at risk: the axillary nerve, the radial nerve, the median nerve, or the ulnar nerve? The answer is the axillary nerve, which winds around the back of the surgical neck against the bone. It supplies the deltoid, so the shoulder becomes flat.

Question 11391. A constructed illustration: a small child is lifted by one hand, and the arm then hangs with the palm turned down. Which structure has slipped, and why does it slip so easily at this age? The answer is the head of the radius, pulled partly out of the ring of ligament that holds it. In a small child that ring is loose.

Question 11392. How does the common fibular nerve relate to the neck of the fibula, and why does that relation matter? The answer is that the nerve wraps around the lateral side of the fibular neck just beneath the skin. A blow there or a tight cast can injure it, and the foot then drops.

Question 11393. A constructed illustration: a middle-aged person feels a sudden snap at the back of the ankle while pushing off and cannot rise on the toes. Which structure has ruptured? The answer is the Achilles tendon. Squeezing the calf no longer moves the foot, and the gap can often be felt above the heel.

Question 11394. Why does the Achilles tendon rupture most often in the zone a few centimeters above its insertion: the tendon is thinnest and least supplied with blood there, the tendon is widest there, the bone is weakest there, or the skin is thinnest there? The answer is that the tendon is thinnest and least supplied there.

Question 11395. A described radiograph of the hand shows a break across the neck of the fifth metacarpal, with the head of the bone tilted toward the palm. Which injury is shown, and why does the head tilt? The answer is a boxer's fracture. The pull of the small muscles of the hand tilts the head forward, and the knuckle is lost.

Question 11396. A constructed illustration: after a seizure, a person holds the arm against the chest and cannot lift it, with numbness over the outer side of the shoulder. Which joint has dislocated, and which nerve is injured? The answer is the shoulder joint, dislocated backward, with injury to the axillary nerve. Backward dislocation follows a strong muscular pull.

Question 11397. A described specimen shows a small ligament running from the pit in the head of the femur to the floor of the socket, carrying an artery with it. What is this ligament called? The answer is the ligament of the head of the femur. It is weak, and its artery supplies only a small part of the head.

Question 11398. A constructed illustration: a rider is thrown and the knee is forced into a bent position, and the knee can no longer be straightened. What has happened inside the joint? The answer is a torn meniscus whose flap has turned into the joint. The piece is caught between the femur and the tibia, blocking extension.

Question 11399. Why does a break of the shaft of the tibia often injure the vessel that passes between the two bones of the leg: the bones are bound by a membrane and the vessel lies against it, the vessel runs inside the bone, the muscles press on it, or the skin is tight? The answer is that the bones are bound by a membrane and the vessel lies against it.

Question 11400. Which statement explains why the medial meniscus is torn more often than the lateral one: it is attached to the medial collateral ligament and moves less, it is larger, it has a better blood supply, or it lies deeper in the joint? The answer is that it is attached to the medial collateral ligament and moves less, so it cannot slide away.

To summarize, structure and function answer one another throughout this chapter: a hollow shaft is light for its strength, cancellous plates follow the lines of stress, hyaline cartilage gives a nearly frictionless surface, and fibrocartilage takes compression where a pad must also resist tearing. The shape of a joint sets its range of movement, from the shallow glenoid that trades stability for mobility to the deep acetabulum that does the opposite, while the labrum and the menisci deepen a socket that would otherwise be too flat. The arrangement of muscle fibers decides whether a muscle is built for force or for distance, so a pennate muscle pulls harder and a parallel muscle shortens further, and the levers of a limb favor speed over force. The same reasoning explains injury, because the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial meniscus, the supraspinatus tendon, the scaphoid, the fibular neck and the watershed of the Achilles tendon are each weak for a reason that can be named. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

# Chapter 115 — Structure and Injury

This chapter closes the bank by joining structure to the two things a listener meets first in practice, the injury that damages a structure and the symptom that points to it. It covers bone, joint, ligament, muscle, vessel, and nerve, first as the target of a particular force and then as the source of a particular complaint. It holds one hundred questions, and every one of them gives its answer straight after the question and then explains why that answer is right. Each scenario is a constructed illustration rather than a real patient, and nothing here replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 11401. Which bone of the forearm gives way when a person falls onto the outstretched hand, breaking just above the wrist with the lower fragment tilted backward? The answer is the radius. It carries the hand and takes the force of the fall, so its lower end bends and breaks first. The wrist joint holds the lower end of the ulna in place.

Question 11402. A described radiograph shows a break across a small bone in the hollow bounded by two tendons at the base of the thumb. Which bone is broken: the scaphoid, the lunate, the triquetrum, or the pisiform? The answer is the scaphoid. It bridges the two rows of carpal bones and takes the impact, and its blood supply enters at the far end, so a break near the thumb end heals badly.

Question 11403. Which bone of the shoulder girdle is the one most often broken in the body, and at which part does it give way? The answer is the clavicle, which usually breaks through its middle third. It acts as a strut between the sternum and the shoulder blade and takes force carried up from the arm.

Question 11404. A break through the surgical neck of the humerus most threatens which nerve: the axillary nerve, the radial nerve, the median nerve, or the musculocutaneous nerve? The answer is the axillary nerve. It passes close to the surgical neck on its way to the deltoid, so injury weakens the lifting of the arm.

Question 11405. A constructed illustration: a cyclist falls on the arm, and a described radiograph shows a break across the middle of the shaft of the humerus. The wrist droops and the fingers cannot be straightened. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the radial nerve, which lies against the bone in the spiral groove, where a midshaft break presses on it.

Question 11406. A constructed illustration: a child falls and the elbow swells, with a described radiograph showing a break just above the condyles of the humerus. Which nerve is most at risk: the median nerve, the ulnar nerve, the radial nerve, or the musculocutaneous nerve? The answer is the median nerve, which crosses the front of the elbow close to the bone beside the brachial artery.

Question 11407. Which muscle is attached to the bony point at the back of the elbow and pulls the broken fragment upward when that point is fractured? The answer is the triceps. Its tendon inserts on the olecranon process of the ulna, so the fragment is drawn away from the shaft.

Question 11408. A constructed illustration: a described radiograph shows breaks through the pubic rami on both sides with widening of the joint between the pubic bones, and blood appears at the urinary opening. Which structure is torn? The answer is the membranous part of the urethra, which is fixed where it passes through the pelvic floor and tears there.

Question 11409. A described radiograph shows a break across the neck of the femur with the shaft riding upward. Which vessel is most likely torn, so that the head loses its supply: the obturator artery, the medial circumflex femoral artery, the lateral circumflex femoral artery, or the artery of the ligamentum teres? The answer is the medial circumflex femoral artery, whose branches climb the neck and enter the head.

Question 11410. Which nerve lies immediately posterior to the shaft of the femur and is at risk when the shaft is broken and the fragments displace backward? The answer is the sciatic nerve, which runs down the back of the thigh behind the bone. Such a break can also release a large volume of blood into the thigh.

Question 11411. A constructed illustration: a person in a vehicle collision drives the knee against the dashboard and the hip is dislocated backward. The limb is shortened, turned inward, and held against the other leg. Which nerve is most likely stretched? The answer is the sciatic nerve, which lies directly behind the hip joint.

Question 11412. Which bone lies in front of the knee within the tendon of the quadriceps and may be broken by a direct blow or by a violent contraction of that muscle? The answer is the patella. The quadriceps pulls on it from above and the patellar ligament holds it from below.

Question 11413. A described radiograph shows the tibia displaced forward on the femur after a severe twisting injury with no bone broken. Which structure is most likely torn: the popliteal artery, the great saphenous vein, the common fibular nerve, or the saphenous nerve? The answer is the popliteal artery, which lies against the back of the joint and is fixed above and below.

Question 11414. A described cross section of the leg shows the tibia and the fibula joined by a membrane, with a group of muscles in front of it. Which nerve runs in that front compartment, and what happens when the compartment swells? The answer is the deep fibular nerve, which fails first, weakening the lifting of the foot.

Question 11415. When the foot is forced into inversion, tearing the ligaments on the outer side of the ankle, which ligament is injured most often? The answer is the anterior talofibular ligament. It is the weakest of the three lateral ligaments and the first to give way as the foot rolls inward.

Question 11416. A described radiograph shows a break through the upper part of the fibula with widening of the space between the tibia and the fibula at the ankle. What has happened? The answer is that the force broke the fibula high instead of at the lateral malleolus, and the membrane joining the two bones is torn.

Question 11417. A described radiograph taken after a fall from a height shows the heel bone crushed, with the angle between its upper surface and the joint above it flattened. Which bone is injured, and which part of the spine should also be examined? The answer is the calcaneus, since the same force travels up the leg to a lumbar vertebral body.

Question 11418. A described radiograph shows a break across the base of the fifth bone of the foot, where its shaft meets its base, without any twisting of the ankle. Which fracture is this? The answer is a break at the base of the fifth metatarsal, which heals slowly because the blood supply to that part is poor.

Question 11419. Which bone of the foot most often develops a crack from repeated marching and running, felt as pain in the front of the foot that worsens with each step? The answer is the second metatarsal or the third. These bones are long and thin and take the greatest load as the foot rolls forward.

Question 11420. A described section of the side of the skull shows a thin area where four bones meet above and in front of the ear. A blow there tears an artery running in a groove on the inner surface. Which artery is it? The answer is the middle meningeal artery, and blood collects between the skull and the dura.

Question 11421. A described person who has struck the head shows bruising behind the ear and around both eyes, and clear fluid runs from the nose. Which part of the skull is fractured? The answer is the base of the skull, since blood tracks along the deep planes and cerebrospinal fluid escapes through a torn covering of the brain.

Question 11422. True or false: a described vertebral body crushed by a fall from a height can drive bone backward into the canal and injure the spinal cord. The answer is true. The body gives way and its back wall is pushed into the space that holds the cord, so that wall must be assessed.

Question 11423. A described radiograph of the neck after a fall shows a break through the peg of bone rising from the second cervical vertebra. Which joint is involved? The answer is the joint between the first and second cervical vertebrae, where that peg is the pivot for turning the head and displacement may press on the cord.

Question 11424. Which of these pairs belongs together: the scaphoid with tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb, the clavicle with tenderness at the elbow, the calcaneus with tenderness over the knee, or the patella with tenderness behind the heel? The answer is the scaphoid with tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb.

Question 11425. In the chest wall, the nerve and vessels that run below each rib lie in which position relative to that rib, and why does a break endanger them? The answer is that they lie in a groove along the lower border of the rib itself, so a break tears the bundle running in its own groove.

Question 11426. True or false: when several ribs are broken in two places on the same side, the segment between the breaks moves inward as the person breathes in. The answer is true, and that is called a flail segment. The isolated piece is drawn inward while the rest of the cage expands.

Question 11427. Which bone lies in the middle of the front of the chest and may be broken across its body by a direct blow, with the heart lying immediately behind it? The answer is the sternum. Its body is joined to the ribs by costal cartilages, and its upper end is the manubrium.

Question 11428. A constructed illustration: a person is struck on the left side over the lower ribs, and the described radiograph shows breaks of the ninth, tenth, and eleventh ribs. Which organ behind them is most exposed? The answer is the spleen, which lies under the left dome of the diaphragm and holds a rich blood supply.

Question 11429. A constructed illustration: a blow lands on the right side over the lowest ribs, and the described radiograph shows a break of the tenth rib there. Which large organ lies in that zone? The answer is the liver, whose right lobe rises high beneath the right dome of the diaphragm.

Question 11430. Which of these pairs belongs together: the eleventh and twelfth ribs with the kidney, the first rib with the stomach, the fifth rib with the bladder, or the seventh rib with the rectum? The answer is the eleventh and twelfth ribs with the kidney, for their lower ends lie over the upper pole of the kidney behind.

Question 11431. A described chest radiograph shows a lung separated from the chest wall by a band of air, with no lung markings beyond the edge of the lung. Which space is filled with air? The answer is the pleural cavity, which opened when the pleura and the chest wall were torn.

Question 11432. A described radiograph after a sudden stop in a collision shows the shadow of the aorta widened at one point. Where does that vessel tear? The answer is where the arch becomes the descending aorta, just beyond the short band joining it to the pulmonary artery.

Question 11433. A constructed illustration: a dislocated shoulder has been reduced, and afterward the person cannot lift the arm and reports numbness over the outer deltoid. Which structure was injured? The answer is the axillary nerve, which is stretched as it wraps around the neck of the humerus.

Question 11434. A person twists the knee while running and afterwards the joint fills with blood and gives way when turning. Which ligament is most likely torn: the anterior cruciate ligament, the posterior cruciate ligament, the medial collateral ligament, or the lateral collateral ligament? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament, which stops the tibia from sliding forward and rotating too far.

Question 11435. A blow lands on the outer side of the knee and forces the joint inward, opening its inner side. Which ligament is torn, and which structure of the same side is injured next? The answer is the medial collateral ligament, followed by the medial meniscus, since the three structures at that corner are linked.

Question 11436. Which structure lies between the femur and the tibia at the edges of the joint, is shaped like a letter C on one side, and tears when the knee is twisted while bearing weight? The answer is the meniscus. Its torn fragment may block straightening of the knee.

Question 11437. Which structure is torn when a sudden push-off is followed by a snap at the back of the heel, a gap that can be felt, and inability to stand on tiptoe? The answer is the Achilles tendon. It carries the force of the calf muscles to the heel bone, and squeezing the calf no longer pulls the foot down.

Question 11438. Which muscle of the rotator cuff is torn most often, and what movement does it begin? The answer is the supraspinatus, which begins abduction of the shoulder and passes beneath the arch formed by the acromion and the coracoacromial ligament. Pain in the middle of the arc of lifting the arm is the usual complaint.

Question 11439. A constructed illustration: a skier falls holding a pole, and the thumb is forced away from the hand at the joint between the thumb and the palm. Which ligament is torn? The answer is the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb, which lies on the inner side of that joint and may fold back as it tears.

Question 11440. Which ligament runs beneath the head of the talus, from the heel bone to the boat-shaped bone, and holds up the arch of the foot? The answer is the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, also called the spring ligament. When it gives way, the head of the talus drops and the arch flattens.

Question 11441. A described radiograph shows a break across the neck of the fibula, and the person cannot lift the foot and cannot feel a light touch over the outer side of the leg. Which nerve is injured? The answer is the common fibular nerve, which winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin.

Question 11442. A constructed illustration: a child falls onto the elbow and a described radiograph shows the small bony prominence on the inner side broken away and displaced downward. Which nerve may be injured? The answer is the ulnar nerve, which passes in a groove behind that prominence.

Question 11443. Which nerve lies on the outer surface of the serratus anterior muscle and may be injured during removal of the breast, so that the shoulder blade stands out from the chest wall? The answer is the long thoracic nerve. When the muscle it supplies is weak, the blade wings away from the chest.

Question 11444. Which of these pairs belongs together: the eleventh cranial nerve with the trapezius muscle, the fifth cranial nerve with the diaphragm, the tenth cranial nerve with the deltoid, or the seventh cranial nerve with the tongue? The answer is the eleventh cranial nerve with the trapezius, which it supplies alongside the sternocleidomastoid.

Question 11445. A described drawing of a newborn shows the arm held against the side and turned inward, with the forearm straight and the palm facing backward. Which part of the brachial plexus was damaged? The answer is the upper trunk, formed by the fifth and sixth cervical nerves, which supply the muscles lifting the arm and bending the elbow.

Question 11446. Which of these pairs belongs together: numbness of the space between the first two toes with the deep fibular nerve, numbness of the little finger with the median nerve, numbness of the thumb with the ulnar nerve, or numbness of the sole with the radial nerve? The answer is numbness between the first two toes with the deep fibular nerve.

Question 11447. Which nerve runs with the long saphenous vein in front of the inner ankle bone and supplies the skin of the inner border of the foot? The answer is the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve that is purely sensory below the knee. It may be injured where the vein is cut for access.

Question 11448. A constructed illustration: a cut crosses the cheek in front of the ear, and the person can no longer close the eye on that side or hold food in the corner of the mouth. Which nerve has been divided? The answer is the facial nerve, which emerges from the skull behind the ear and enters the parotid gland before dividing.

Question 11449. Which structure is avulsed when the tip of a finger is struck and the straightening of the joint nearest the nail is lost, so that the tip droops? The answer is the tendon of the extensor muscle at the last joint of the finger, torn from the base of the last bone.

Question 11450. Which of these pairs belongs together: the medial collateral ligament with a blow from outside, the posterior cruciate ligament with a blow to the front of the bent knee, the anterior cruciate ligament with a blow from behind, or the lateral collateral ligament with a blow from inside? The answer is the medial collateral ligament with a blow from outside, which opens the inner side of the knee.

Question 11451. Name two places in the knee where blood collects after a tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, spoken as a list. The answer is the joint cavity and the space beneath the quadriceps muscle. The torn ligament bleeds into the joint, and the fluid spreads upward under the muscle above the knee.

Question 11452. Which structure is injured when the back of the knee is cut and the foot cannot be pushed down or turned inward, while feeling is lost over the sole? The answer is the tibial nerve, which lies in the middle of the popliteal fossa, deep to the popliteal vein and artery.

Question 11453. True or false: a break of the medial malleolus of the tibia may occur with the fibula intact when the foot is forced outward strongly. The answer is true. The deltoid ligament on the inner side either tears or pulls the medial malleolus away with it.

Question 11454. A described radiograph shows a break of the lower end of the radius with the lower fragment displaced forward rather than backward. What force caused it? The answer is a fall onto the back of the bent wrist, and the displaced fragment may press on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

Question 11455. Which of these structures lies immediately behind the medial malleolus, in a tunnel that also carries the tibial artery: the tibial nerve, the saphenous nerve, the deep fibular nerve, or the sural nerve? The answer is the tibial nerve, which passes beneath the fibrous band holding the ankle tendons in place.

Question 11456. Which membrane suspends the spleen, the stomach, and the transverse colon from the structures lying behind the abdomen, and which two of them hang freely? The answer is the peritoneum, which forms their mesenteries. The stomach and the transverse colon are the mobile two.

Question 11457. A described specimen shows a long bone with a break that spirals around the shaft after a twisting force. Why does it spiral? The answer is that the crack follows the direction of the force, and the fibers of the bone run in a spiral around the shaft.

Question 11458. A described radiograph shows the head of the humerus lying below and in front of the socket of the shoulder blade after a fall. Which structure on the front of the head is at risk? The answer is the axillary artery and the nerves of the axillary region, which lie against it.

Question 11459. A described section shows a break of the shaft of the radius and the ulna at the same level, with the two bones bowed toward each other. Why do the fragments come together? The answer is that the membrane joining the bones pulls them together, and the muscles of the forearm shorten the gap.

Question 11460. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior dislocation of the hip with the limb held turned outward, the posterior dislocation of the hip with the limb held turned outward, the anterior dislocation of the shoulder with the arm held against the chest, or the posterior dislocation of the elbow with the forearm straight? The answer is the anterior dislocation of the hip with the limb turned outward.

Question 11461. A constructed illustration: a worker lifts heavy loads for years and reports pain over the front of the elbow that worsens with gripping. Which structure is strained? The answer is the common tendon of the flexor muscles, which attaches to the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

Question 11462. Which statement about a torn meniscus is correct: the torn fragment may block the knee so that it cannot straighten, the knee gives way only when standing still, the swelling appears only after several weeks, or the joint line is tender on the outer side only? The answer is that the fragment may block the knee so that it cannot straighten.

Question 11463. A described radiograph shows a break across the neck of the femur with the head staying in its socket. Which two features of the limb are seen, and why? The answer is shortening and turning outward. The muscles around the hip pull the shaft upward while the head stays in place.

Question 11464. Which statement about a sprained ankle is correct: the swelling is greatest below and in front of the outer ankle bone, the swelling is greatest above the inner ankle bone, the foot cannot be turned outward, or the heel cannot bear weight at all? The answer is that the swelling is greatest below and in front of the outer ankle bone.

Question 11465. A described cross section of the lower leg shows four compartments separated by sheets of deep fascia. Which statement is correct: the front compartment holds the muscle that lifts the foot, the outer compartment holds the calf muscles, or the back compartment holds the muscle that turns the foot outward? The answer is that the front compartment holds the muscle that lifts the foot.

Question 11466. Which structure is torn when a direct blow to the front of the thigh causes the muscle to tear within its sheath, and a firm swelling appears that does not cross the knee? The answer is the quadriceps muscle, since the sheath holds the blood inside and the knee can still be straightened.

Question 11467. Which statement about the knee is correct: the posterior cruciate ligament prevents the tibia from sliding backward, the anterior cruciate ligament prevents backward sliding, the medial collateral ligament prevents the knee from bending, or the lateral collateral ligament attaches to the medial meniscus? The answer is that the posterior cruciate ligament prevents the tibia from sliding backward.

Question 11468. What is the name given to the condition in which the pressure inside a closed compartment of the limb rises until the tissues within it are starved of blood? The answer is compartment syndrome. The fascia around the compartment cannot stretch, so the swelling raises the pressure, and pain on stretching the muscles comes first.

Question 11469. Which structure passes down the back of the thigh from the pelvis and can be pressed against the bone by a broken shaft of the femur? The answer is the sciatic nerve, which leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and runs down beneath the hamstrings.

Question 11470. A described radiograph shows a break through the odontoid process. Which movement of the head becomes unsafe, and why? The answer is turning, because that peg is the pivot around which the first cervical vertebra and the head rotate on the second. Losing that pivot lets the first vertebra slide forward on the second.

Question 11471. A described radiograph shows a break of the dens with the fragment still attached to the body of the second cervical vertebra. Which statement is correct: the break lies at the base of the dens, the break lies in the arch of the first vertebra, the break lies through the third vertebra, or the break lies through the spinous process? The answer is that the break lies at the base of the dens.

Question 11472. Which statement about the ligaments of the vertebral column is correct: the ligaments joining the bodies run both in front of and behind them, the ligament joining the spines is the strongest, the ligament joining the arches is elastic, or the discs lie between the spines? The answer is that the ligaments joining the vertebral bodies run both in front of and behind them.

Question 11473. Which tissue forms the outer covering of a bone and carries the vessels that nourish its surface, and which tissue lines the marrow cavity? The answer is the periosteum outside and the endosteum within. The periosteum is stripped from the bone in a severe injury, which is why a bare piece may die.

Question 11474. Which of these bones is most often broken by a fall onto the outstretched hand in a young adult: the scaphoid, the calcaneus, the patella, or the clavicle? The answer is the scaphoid, which lies directly in the line of force from the palm and takes the weight through its narrow waist.

Question 11475. Which of these pairs belongs together: the clavicle with the middle third, the patella with the upper third of the thigh, the calcaneus with the middle of the leg, or the olecranon with the middle of the forearm? The answer is the clavicle with the middle third, while the olecranon belongs to the elbow.

Question 11476. A described section of a bone shows a dense outer layer and a spongy inner layer arranged along the lines of force. Which tissue is which, and why does the arrangement matter? The answer is compact bone outside and cancellous bone within, whose spicules lie along the directions in which the bone carries load.

Question 11477. Which statement about a break of a long bone in a child is correct: the bone may bend or crack on one side only because it is more flexible, it always breaks cleanly across, it never disrupts growth, or it never heals? The answer is that the bone may bend or crack on one side only, which is a greenstick injury.

Question 11478. A described radiograph shows a break across the shaft of the tibia that has opened through the skin. Why is that break more serious than a closed one? The answer is that the wound lets organisms reach the bone, and the bone loses the covering that carries its blood.

Question 11479. Which structure lies between the two rows of carpal bones and cushions the wrist, and may be dislocated in a fall onto the palm? The answer is the lunate, which lies in the middle of the wrist and bears the force passing from the hand to the radius.

Question 11480. A described specimen shows a joint whose surfaces are covered by smooth gristle, with a cavity between them and a capsule with a lining around the whole. Which kind of joint is described, and what does the lining secrete? The answer is a synovial joint, whose lining secretes synovial fluid to nourish and lubricate the surfaces.

Question 11481. Which of these structures is the weakest link in the shoulder and gives way most often when the arm is forced upward: the tendon of the supraspinatus, the head of the humerus, the acromion, or the clavicle? The answer is the tendon of the supraspinatus, which passes beneath the acromion through a narrow space.

Question 11482. True or false: a break of the first rib is dangerous mainly because the structures crossing it lie close by. The answer is true. The nerves and vessels of the arm pass over the first rib, and the dome of the pleura rises above it into the base of the neck.

Question 11483. Which structure forms the socket of the hip joint, and which three bones join to make it? The answer is the acetabulum, formed by the ilium, the ischium, and the pubis. The three parts fuse during the teenage years into a deep cup.

Question 11484. Which structure gives way first when the ankle is forced into eversion, so that the inner side of the joint opens: the deltoid ligament, the anterior talofibular ligament, the calcaneofibular ligament, or the posterior talofibular ligament? The answer is the deltoid ligament, which either tears or pulls the medial malleolus away.

Question 11485. Which structure joins the patella below and attaches to the tibia, completing the pull of the quadriceps? The answer is the patellar ligament. It is a continuation of the quadriceps tendon across the knee, and the patella increases the leverage of the muscle.

Question 11486. Which statement about the hip joint is correct: it is a ball and socket joint with the deepest socket in the body, it is a hinge joint, it is a saddle joint, or it is a plane joint? The answer is that it is a ball and socket joint, and its socket is deepened by a ring of fibrocartilage around the rim.

Question 11487. A blow to the upper arm just below the shoulder causes pain and swelling in the middle of the arm. Which structure does the force press onto the bone, causing numbness over the back of the hand? The answer is the radial nerve, which lies in the spiral groove against the shaft.

Question 11488. Which statement about a torn calf muscle is correct: the pain and swelling lie in the calf and worsen when the ankle is stretched upward, the pain lies behind the knee only, the swelling crosses the knee, or the foot cannot be lifted? The answer is that the pain and swelling lie in the calf and worsen when the ankle is stretched upward.

Question 11489. Name three structures that pass through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle, spoken as a sentence. The answer is the sciatic nerve, the inferior gluteal artery, and the pudendal nerve. The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis here and then re-enters through the lesser foramen.

Question 11490. Which structure lies in the floor of the front of the elbow, between the tendon of the biceps above and the muscles of the forearm below, and contains the end of the brachial artery? The answer is the cubital fossa, whose roof is the skin and fascia and whose floor is the brachialis.

Question 11491. Which statement about the elbow is correct: the joint allows bending and straightening only, it allows turning of the palm, it is a ball and socket joint, or it has no capsule? The answer is that it allows bending and straightening only, for it is a hinge between the humerus and the ulna.

Question 11492. A described cross section of the upper arm shows a bone surrounded by muscles, with a neurovascular bundle lying on its inner side. Which structures lie in that bundle? The answer is the brachial artery, the median nerve, and the veins accompanying the artery.

Question 11493. Which statement about the knee is correct: the joint depends on ligaments and muscles rather than on the shape of its surfaces for stability, it is as stable as the hip, it is held by a single ligament, or it moves only in one plane? The answer is that it depends on ligaments and muscles rather than on the shape of its surfaces.

Question 11494. True or false: a fall onto the point of the shoulder can break the clavicle even though the blow did not touch that bone. The answer is true. The force travels along the arm and the shoulder blade to the strut of the clavicle, which gives way at its thinnest part.

Question 11495. Which structure becomes inflamed where it attaches to the outer prominence of the elbow when a sport involves repeated throwing, causing pain when the wrist is lifted? The answer is the common tendon of the extensor muscles, whose pain is felt on gripping and on lifting the back of the hand.

Question 11496. Which of these pairs belongs together: a break of the femoral neck with the medial circumflex femoral artery, a break of the clavicle with the popliteal artery, a break of the tibia with the axillary nerve, or a break of the fibula with the median nerve? The answer is a break of the femoral neck with the medial circumflex femoral artery.

Question 11497. Which statement about a dislocated shoulder is correct: the head of the humerus usually leaves its socket downward and forward, it usually leaves backward, it never damages a nerve, or it always damages the radial nerve? The answer is that the head usually leaves downward and forward, where the capsule is thinnest.

Question 11498. Which statement about fractures in older people is correct: the bone loses mass with age and breaks with less force, the bones become harder, only the joints become stiffer, or the number of bone cells increases? The answer is that the bone loses mass with age, since the fine struts inside are lost first.

Question 11499. Which structure is most often injured when a heavy weight is lifted with the back bent rather than straight: the fibrous ring of the disk between two lumbar vertebrae, the vertebral body, the spinous process, or the ligament of the arches? The answer is the fibrous ring of the disk, against which the soft center is forced backward.

Question 11500. A described radiograph of a healed bone shows a thickened ridge along the line where a crack once ran. What does this thickening represent? The answer is callus, which is new bone laid down at the site of the break and later reworked until the bone regains its shape.

To summarize, the structures of the body fail in patterns that their own anatomy makes predictable. The scaphoid and the femoral head lose their blood supply because it enters at one end, while the radial nerve fails at the spiral groove, the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle, and the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck. The diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve, the appendix begins with pain around the navel through the tenth thoracic segment, and the ureter sends pain from the loin to the groin. Visceral pain is dull and poorly localized, while the parietal pleura, the peritoneum, and the joint capsule give sharp pain at the site of injury. The hip refers pain to the knee through the obturator nerve. This chapter is educational material and does not replace an anatomy course, a dissection, or clinical training.

# Chapter 116 — Structure and Clinical Examination

The last chapter of this bank brings structure and the bedside together, because the anatomy a clinician can name is the anatomy a clinician can find. It covers the links between structure and symptoms, and then the examination itself, from inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation to the special tests that put a named structure under strain. It holds one hundred questions, and every one gives its answer immediately and then explains why it is right, so nothing has to be held in mind. The questions are written to be answered aloud, in the order in which a listener would work through a patient. This is educational material, and it supports rather than replaces an anatomy course, a dissection, a clinical training program, or the judgment of a teacher.

Question 11501. A constructed illustration: blood or infection under the diaphragm irritates its underside, and the person feels an ache at the tip of the shoulder. Which nerve carries that pain, and why is it felt there? The answer is the phrenic nerve, from the third, fourth and fifth cervical spinal nerves. Those segments also supply the skin over the shoulder, so the brain refers the signal there.

Question 11502. A person describes pain in the upper right abdomen that spreads to the right shoulder blade after a meal. Which of these structures lies beneath that pain: the gallbladder, the stomach, the appendix, or the left kidney? The answer is the gallbladder. It rests on the undersurface of the liver against the diaphragm, whose irritation refers pain to the shoulder.

Question 11503. A person reports a cramping pain in the calf that comes on after walking a certain distance and eases with rest. Narrowing of which artery most often explains it? The answer is the superficial femoral artery. It passes through the adductor canal, where the muscles around it compress the artery, so the calf is starved of blood only while it works.

Question 11504. A constructed illustration: a disk between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae presses on a nerve root, and pain shoots down the outer side of the thigh and leg to the top of the foot. Which nerve root is compressed? The answer is the fifth lumbar root, which leaves the spine at that level and joins the sciatic nerve.

Question 11505. Early in appendicitis the pain is a dull ache around the navel rather than in the right lower abdomen. The fibers that carry it travel with which nerve, and where do they enter the spinal cord? The answer is the tenth thoracic spinal nerve. The appendix belongs to the midgut, whose pain is referred to the tenth thoracic dermatome, the band of skin around the navel.

Question 11506. A person has a sharp pain in the lower chest that worsens on a deep breath and on coughing. Irritation of which structure explains it: the lung tissue, the visceral pleura, the parietal pleura, or the diaphragm? The answer is the parietal pleura. It carries somatic pain fibers, while the visceral pleura covering the lung has none of its own.

Question 11507. A stone blocks the duct that carries bile from the liver and the gallbladder to the duodenum, and the person turns yellow. Which structure is obstructed? The answer is the common bile duct. It is formed where the common hepatic duct joins the cystic duct and opens into the duodenum beside the pancreatic duct.

Question 11508. A constructed illustration: after a blow to the outer side of the knee, the person cannot lift the front of the foot and the top of the foot is numb. Which nerve has been injured? The answer is the common fibular nerve, winding around the neck of the fibula. It lies just beneath the skin there, against bone, with no muscle to shield it.

Question 11509. True or false: pain arising in the wall of the gut is poorly localized and is usually felt in the midline of the abdomen. The answer is true. The gut is supplied by autonomic nerves that carry little information about position, so the pain is referred to the midline. Pain from the peritoneum lining the wall is sharp and localizes well instead.

Question 11510. A described radiograph of the hip shows a break across the neck of the femur, and the limb lies short and turned outward. Which structure has been divided, and why does the limb shorten? The answer is the neck of the femur. The break lies inside the capsule, and the muscles around the hip draw the shaft upward while the foot rotates outward.

Question 11511. A constructed illustration: an older person becomes hoarse, and a growth is found at the top of the left lung. Which nerve is pressed, and why is the left side more often affected? The answer is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. It hooks under the arch of the aorta before climbing to the larynx, so a growth at the left apex traps it against the aorta.

Question 11512. An enlarged left atrium can press on a muscular tube that runs down behind the heart, and the person reports that food sticks on swallowing. Which structure is compressed? The answer is the esophagus. It descends through the posterior mediastinum behind the left atrium, and its upper part lies behind the trachea.

Question 11513. After a blow to the front of the head, a person can no longer smell, although the nose is clear. Injury to which structure explains the loss? The answer is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, which carries the fibers of the olfactory nerve from the nose to the brain. Those fine fibers tear when the plate fractures.

Question 11514. Which of these pairs belongs together: flank pain with a stone in the ureter, flank pain with a stone in the gallbladder, shoulder pain with a stone in the ureter, or navel pain with a stone in the gallbladder? The answer is flank pain with a stone in the ureter. A stone in the ureter blocks the urine and stretches the renal pelvis, and the pain is felt in the loin.

Question 11515. Name two structures that a growth in the head of the pancreas commonly presses on, spoken as a list. The answer is the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. Both run through the head of the gland and join at the ampulla before opening into the duodenum, so one is usually obstructed with the other.

Question 11516. A stone descending from the kidney lodges where the ureter is narrowed by a vessel it crosses. Which of these is that point: where it crosses the common iliac artery, where it lies against the psoas muscle, where the gonadal vein joins it, or where it passes behind the ductus deferens? The answer is where it crosses the common iliac artery at the brim of the pelvis.

Question 11517. In one illustration, blood collects above the tentorium of the cerebellum and stretches the dura there, and the person feels the pain across the forehead. Which nerve carries the pain from that part of the dura? The answer is the trigeminal nerve. Its branches supply that dura, and the pain is referred to the forehead and the eye.

Question 11518. A described photograph shows the muscles at the base of the thumb wasted, the outer three and a half fingers numb, with the little finger spared. Which nerve is compressed, and where does it lie? The answer is the median nerve in the carpal tunnel at the wrist. It lies beneath the retinaculum with the flexor tendons, while the ulnar nerve passes outside the tunnel.

Question 11519. True or false: cramping pain in the calf that appears with walking and disappears with rest points to disease of the deep veins of the leg. The answer is false. That pain comes from narrowing of the arteries, most often the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal. Venous disease gives a heavy ache, worse at the end of the day and eased by raising the leg.

Question 11520. In one illustration, an older person describes a deep boring pain in the middle of the back for some weeks. Which of these structures can produce it when its wall stretches: the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the portal vein, or the stomach? The answer is the abdominal aorta. It lies against the vertebral column, and the stretching of its wall is felt in the back.

Question 11521. A constructed illustration: a person under strain feels a heavy pain behind the breastbone that spreads to the inner side of the left arm. The fibers of the heart enter the spinal cord at which segments, and why is the pain felt in the arm? The answer is the upper thoracic spinal nerves. Those segments also receive the skin of the inner arm, so the signal is referred there.

Question 11522. A person with a stone in the ureter feels an intense ache in the loin that moves down and forward into the groin. Which spinal segments carry that pain? The answer is the tenth thoracic to the first lumbar segments. The kidney and the ureter are supplied by the least and lumbar splanchnic nerves, whose fibers enter at those levels, so the pain follows their dermatomes.

Question 11523. A burning pain rises behind the breastbone after meals and is worse when lying flat. Which structure is being irritated? The answer is the esophagus. It runs down through the posterior mediastinum, pierces the diaphragm in front of the aorta, and its lowest part lies within the abdomen.

Question 11524. A person has pain in the right loin that travels down and forward toward the groin. Describe the direction of that spread using the words superior, inferior, lateral and anterior. The answer is that it spreads inferiorly and anteriorly, from the loin above and behind to the groin below and in front.

Question 11525. A constructed illustration: during removal of lymph nodes from the armpit a nerve on the side of the chest wall is divided, and afterwards the shoulder blade stands out from the back when the arm is pushed forward. Which nerve was divided? The answer is the long thoracic nerve, which supplies the serratus anterior. Without that muscle the medial border of the scapula lifts from the chest wall.

Question 11526. Which ridge is felt across the front of the chest at the level of the second costal cartilage, and which vertebra lies at the same level behind? The answer is the sternal angle, with the disk between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. It marks where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum, and where the second rib is counted.

Question 11527. When the radial pulse is felt at the wrist, which of these lies immediately medial to the artery: the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis, the tendon of the palmaris longus, the ulnar artery, or the median nerve? The answer is the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis. The artery lies lateral to it, against the lower end of the radius, where it can be pressed against bone.

Question 11528. The iliac crest is used as a surface landmark for the level of which vertebra, and what is the name of the line that joins the two crests? The answer is the fourth lumbar vertebra, and the line is the supracristal plane. It is the level at which the spinal cord has ended and only the roots of the cauda equina remain.

Question 11529. Where exactly is the apex beat of the heart felt, and which chamber produces it? The answer is the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, about 9 centimeters from the midline, produced by the left ventricle. It is the lowest and most lateral point at which the heart meets the chest wall.

Question 11530. Which of these lies at the level of the second thoracic vertebra: the suprasternal notch, the sternal angle, the xiphisternal joint, or the apex of the heart? The answer is the suprasternal notch. It is the hollow at the top of the sternum between the clavicles, and the trachea is felt just above it.

Question 11531. The xiphisternal joint, felt at the lower end of the sternum, lies at the level of which vertebra, and which two structures lie just below it? The answer is the ninth thoracic vertebra, with the central tendon of the diaphragm and the upper border of the liver below.

Question 11532. True or false: the cricoid cartilage lies at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra, where the pharynx becomes the esophagus. The answer is true. The cricoid is the only complete ring of the airway and the landmark for that level. The thyroid cartilage above it lies at the fourth and fifth cervical vertebrae.

Question 11533. Which of these pairs belongs together: the sternal angle with the second costal cartilage, the suprasternal notch with the third costal cartilage, the xiphisternal joint with the seventh cervical vertebra, or the iliac crest with the second lumbar vertebra? The answer is the sternal angle with the second costal cartilage. Counting ribs from that ridge is reliable, because the first rib lies hidden behind the clavicle.

Question 11534. Which of these points marks the surface position of the gallbladder: where the lateral border of the rectus sheath meets the costal margin, where the midline meets the costal margin, 5 centimeters below the xiphisternal joint, or halfway from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine? The answer is where the lateral border of the rectus sheath meets the costal margin, at the ninth costal cartilage.

Question 11535. A point is marked one third of the way along the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Which structure lies deep to that point, and how constant is its position? The answer is the base of the appendix, at McBurney point. The base is fairly constant there, though the tip may hang into the pelvis or lie behind the cecum.

Question 11536. In the popliteal fossa behind the knee, which structure lies deepest against the back of the joint, and which lies most superficial? The answer is the popliteal artery deepest and the tibial nerve most superficial, with the popliteal vein between them. The small saphenous vein runs on the surface above the deep fascia.

Question 11537. Which heart valve is heard best at the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line: the aortic, the pulmonary, the tricuspid, or the mitral? The answer is the mitral valve. Its sound is conducted to the apex, which points downward and to the left.

Question 11538. A described chest radiograph taken from behind shows the right border of the heart formed by one chamber and most of the left border formed by another. Which chambers are they? The answer is the right atrium on the right border and the left ventricle on the left. The left atrium contributes only a small part of the left border below the pulmonary artery.

Question 11539. A constructed illustration: the examiner presses deeply into the left lower abdomen and then lifts the hand away quickly, and the person winces. Which structure is being stretched, and what is the sign called? The answer is the parietal peritoneum, and the sign is rebound tenderness. The parietal peritoneum is supplied by somatic nerves, so it is acutely sensitive to stretch.

Question 11540. Percussion over normal lung gives a resonant note and over the liver a dull one. Which of these gives a stony dull note: normal lung, the liver, the stomach filled with gas, or fluid in the pleural cavity? The answer is fluid in the pleural cavity. Fluid transmits sound poorly, so it damps the note far more than solid liver does.

Question 11541. At the suprasternal notch the trachea is felt in the midline. Which structure lies immediately behind the trachea at that level? The answer is the esophagus. It begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage and descends behind the trachea in the visceral compartment of the neck. The thyroid gland wraps around the front and sides of the airway above.

Question 11542. Which pulse is felt on the top of the foot, lateral to the tendon that runs to the big toe? The answer is the dorsalis pedis artery. It lies against the bones of the foot and is often the easiest pulse to find when the ankle pulses are faint.

Question 11543. Behind the medial malleolus, which structure lies immediately against the bone, first in the line that passes beneath the flexor retinaculum? The answer is the tendon of the tibialis posterior muscle. The tendons of the flexor digitorum longus and the flexor hallucis longus, the posterior tibial artery and the tibial nerve follow behind.

Question 11544. Name the two borders of the femoral triangle that meet at its apex, spoken as a list. The answer is the medial border, the adductor longus, and the lateral border, the sartorius. The inguinal ligament forms the base above, and the iliopsoas and the pectineus form the floor.

Question 11545. A described ultrasound image of the neck shows a gland shaped like a butterfly, wrapped around the front and the sides of the airway just below the larynx. Which gland is it, and which structure does it lie directly in front of? The answer is the thyroid gland, lying in front of the trachea and the lower larynx. Its isthmus crosses the midline over the second and third tracheal rings.

Question 11546. Which muscle is tested when a person turns the head to one side against the examiner's hand, and which cranial nerve supplies it? The answer is the sternocleidomastoid, supplied by the eleventh cranial nerve. The same nerve supplies the trapezius, tested by shrugging the shoulders against resistance.

Question 11547. Which of these muscles is tested when the examiner asks the person to screw up the eyes tightly: the orbicularis oculi, the orbicularis oris, the levator palpebrae superioris, or the frontalis? The answer is the orbicularis oculi, supplied by the seventh cranial nerve. That nerve supplies every muscle of facial expression, and its weakness leaves the eye open.

Question 11548. Which structure is tested by the anterior drawer test at the knee? The answer is the anterior cruciate ligament. The examiner pulls the upper end of the tibia forward with the knee bent, and movement beyond that of the other knee means it has torn.

Question 11549. Which of these muscles is weak when the pelvis drops on the side opposite the standing leg: the gluteus medius, the gluteus maximus, the iliopsoas, or the adductor longus? The answer is the gluteus medius of the standing side, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. It holds the pelvis level while the opposite foot is off the ground.

Question 11550. Where is the common carotid pulse felt in the neck, and which muscle forms the guide to it? The answer is at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. It lies in the carotid sheath there, with the internal jugular vein lateral and the vagus nerve behind.

Question 11551. Which cranial nerve is tested by asking the person to push the tongue against the inside of the cheek while the examiner presses on the outside? The answer is the twelfth cranial nerve, which supplies the muscles of the tongue. It is also tested by asking the person to protrude the tongue and move it from side to side.

Question 11552. Which muscle is tested by asking the person to press the index finger outward against the examiner's hand, and which nerve supplies it? The answer is the first dorsal interosseous, supplied by the ulnar nerve. That nerve also supplies the other small muscles of the hand, so wasting between the thumb and the index finger follows its injury.

Question 11553. A described lateral radiograph of the neck shows the first cervical vertebra with no body and no spine, and a tooth-shaped process rising from the second into it. Name the two vertebrae and the process. The answer is the atlas, the axis, and the odontoid process, or dens, of the axis. The atlas is a ring, and the dens is the pivot on which the head turns.

Question 11554. Which of these muscles begins abduction of the arm at the shoulder, carrying it through the first 15 degrees: the supraspinatus, the deltoid, the teres minor, or the infraspinatus? The answer is the supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve. It runs above the joint beneath the acromion, where its tendon wears easily.

Question 11555. A constructed illustration: after a fall on the outstretched hand there is tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb. Which bone is fractured, and why is the break easily missed? The answer is the scaphoid. It lies in that hollow, and its blood supply enters at the far end, so a break near the wrist can starve the fragment nearest the forearm.

Question 11556. A person is asked to stand on tiptoe on one foot. Which muscles produce the movement, and which nerve root is being tested? The answer is the gastrocnemius and the soleus, with the first sacral nerve root. They share the calcaneal tendon, and the same root carries the ankle jerk.

Question 11557. Which structure is put under strain by the McMurray test, in which the examiner rotates the bent knee while straightening it: the meniscus of the knee, the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial collateral ligament, or the patellar tendon? The answer is the meniscus of the knee. A torn meniscus clicks or traps between the bones as the joint rotates.

Question 11558. True or false: when the abdomen is examined, auscultation is performed before palpation and percussion. The answer is true. Palpation and percussion stir the bowel and change the sounds the examiner is trying to hear, and they may cause discomfort that makes the rest harder.

Question 11559. A described transverse section through the middle of the arm shows the humerus with a nerve lying in a groove on its back. Which nerve is it, and what does injury at that level cause? The answer is the radial nerve in the spiral groove. It supplies the muscles that extend the wrist and fingers, so a break of the humeral shaft there causes wrist drop.

Question 11560. Which of these pairs belongs together: the anterior drawer test with the anterior cruciate ligament, the McMurray test with the medial collateral ligament, the Trendelenburg sign with the gluteus maximus, or the straight leg raise with the hip flexors? The answer is the anterior drawer test with the anterior cruciate ligament. The examiner pulls the tibia forward and compares the knees.

Question 11561. A described photograph of the back shows two dimples over the lower part of the spine, one on each side. Which bony points do they mark, and at which vertebral level do they lie? The answer is the posterior superior iliac spines, at the level of the second sacral segment.

Question 11562. Which structure lies immediately in front of the right kidney, and which three lie in front of the left kidney? The answer is the liver in front of the right kidney, with the duodenum and ascending colon beside it, and the stomach, spleen and pancreas in front of the left. Both are retroperitoneal, so their anterior surfaces face the peritoneal cavity.

Question 11563. Percussion over the spleen is dull. Between which ribs does the organ lie in the midaxillary line: the fifth and seventh, the seventh and ninth, the ninth and eleventh, or the eleventh and twelfth? The answer is between the ninth and eleventh ribs. The spleen lies behind the stomach and below the diaphragm.

Question 11564. A constructed illustration: a swelling appears in the groin below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Through which opening has it passed, and which vessel lies immediately lateral to that opening? The answer is the femoral canal, with the femoral vein lateral to it. The canal is the most medial part of the femoral sheath and the narrowest passage into the thigh.

Question 11565. Which of these glands moves upward when a person swallows and can be seen to do so: the thyroid gland, the parotid gland, the submandibular gland, or the tonsil? The answer is the thyroid gland. It is bound to the larynx by fascia and rises with it during swallowing. The other three do not move in that way.

Question 11566. Which structure is felt as a rounded cord running from the pubic tubercle toward the scrotum, and which structures does it contain? The answer is the spermatic cord, containing the ductus deferens, the testicular artery, the pampiniform plexus of veins and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. It carries the coverings of the abdominal wall down with it.

Question 11567. Which part of the breast extends into the armpit and must be examined as part of the breast: the axillary tail, the areola, the lobules, or the lactiferous ducts? The answer is the axillary tail. It passes through an opening in the deep fascia at the lower border of the pectoralis major, and it can be mistaken for a lump in the armpit.

Question 11568. Which of these structures lies at the level of the third cervical vertebra: the hyoid bone, the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage, or the sternal angle? The answer is the hyoid bone. It can be felt between the chin and the thyroid cartilage, and moves upward when a person swallows.

Question 11569. A described dissection of the sole of the foot shows a thick band of tough tissue running from the heel to the bases of the toes, with the short muscles lying deep to it. Which structure is it, and what does it do? The answer is the plantar aponeurosis. It holds up the arch of the foot and protects the vessels and nerves beneath it.

Question 11570. A described radiograph of the pelvis shows a large oval opening on each side, below and in front of the hip socket. Name the opening, and say which structures pass through it. The answer is the obturator foramen, closed by a membrane, through which the obturator nerve and vessels leave the pelvis. It is the largest opening in the skeleton.

Question 11571. Which reflex is tested by tapping the tendon just below the kneecap, and which two nerve roots carry it? The answer is the knee jerk, carried by the third and fourth lumbar nerve roots. The tap stretches the quadriceps muscle, and the muscle contracts in reply.

Question 11572. Which of these reflexes is lost when the first sacral nerve root is compressed: the knee jerk, the ankle jerk, the biceps jerk, or the abdominal reflex? The answer is the ankle jerk. The first sacral root supplies the calf muscles through the tibial nerve, which the calcaneal tendon tap tests.

Question 11573. In the normal plantar reflex the toes curl downward when the sole is stroked. Which of these tracts carries that response: the corticospinal tract, the spinothalamic tract, the dorsal columns, or the spinocerebellar tract? The answer is the corticospinal tract, whose fibers run from the motor cortex to the spinal cord.

Question 11574. Which muscles are tested when the examiner asks the person to spread the fingers apart against resistance, and which nerve supplies them? The answer is the dorsal interossei, supplied by the ulnar nerve. Between the metacarpal bones they pull the fingers away from the midline of the hand.
